_childDocuments_.review: All three of the GameBoy Advance CastleVania games are a good time, albeit with each game having their annoyances. Circle of the Moon has aged a bit, and some of the drop rates to even get the cards in which to activate your various abilities can be a little bit of a stress test. Harmony of Dissonance suffers from somewhat bad pacing, and it being somewhat difficult to tell what the game wants you to do at certain times. Additionally the way they structured teleportation makes the game REALLY bad about needless backtracking at times.Aria of Sorrow, which is easily the best title of the set also has some issues with exceptionally low drop rates for specific souls, and even a little bit of vagueness on where you're meant to be going at any given time. However all three remain worth playing, and this collection is a fair way of doing so. A lot of the difficulty in drop rates can be somewhat mitigated with the games built in rewind feature which allows you to farm enemies that are more difficult to farm much more easily.The new display feature lets you know your progress on important items such as if an enemy's card drop has been acquired yet, a monster's soul has been absorbed, or if a relic or piece of furniture can be found in that area. Sadly this doesn't tell you how many of each soul you've gathered, but it can be a good "at a glance" way of telling if you're finished with an area.The collection also included Dracula X, which is sort of a dumbed down version of CastleVania Rondo of Blood. This is a weird inclusion for a few reasons. One, it's a traditional style CastleVania rather than a Metroidvania. Symphony of the Night, or Dawn of Sorrow are far more logical inclusions considering both feature characters that appear in Aria of Sorrow. Still, hard to complain about a bonus game.The price point is a bit much, as there aren't really many features here to encourage you to get this over simply acquiring the original releases in some capacity. But if you like this style of game you'll probably be happy with the collection.
_childDocuments_.name: Castlevania Advance Collection

_childDocuments_.review: I can only speak for Aria of Sorrow right now, but that game alone is worth the $20 asking price. Throwing in the other two GBA Igavanias *and* Dracula X on the side? 100% worth it.If you haven't played a Castlevania before, and you're coming into this from the perspective of a Metroidvania fan—perhaps you played Hollow Knight or Bloodstained and want something of similar quality—I'd recommend starting with Aria of Sorrow.Aria is definitely the most polished of the three games, and is the most 'classic Metroidvania' out of all of them.Regarding the other three games, I've haven't seen Drac X yet, but from what I've seen on-stream of HoD and CotM, they're excellent games as well, albeit with a bit steeper of a learning curve and more dated graphics.I only have two complaints about the Advance collection: it would be a dream come true if there were rebindable keyboard controls, to allow people to use the WASD we've all probably gotten used to; and to disable to pause menu so it doesn't interrupt your sessions on accident because you were trying to backdash.Anyways, with that said, please, *please*, pick up the Advance Collection and give it a go. Castlevania is a genre-definer for a reason, and there is arguably no better way to experience it than through Aria of Sorrow.
_childDocuments_.name: Castlevania Advance Collection

_childDocuments_.review: circle of the moon:underrated.  sotn was a hard act to follow and circle is very stripped down by comparison, but it's good.  on a computer monitor the infamous visuals really shine, it's got a dark, muted scheme that looks great.  music is fine, it's got a good rendition of my jam from bloodlines but it plays through like half the map which starts to get old.  pretty hard compared to sotn, a couple ballbusters among the bosses, and dracula is probably the hardest dracula of all the games i've played.  overall very good.harmony of dissonance:this one's kind of a cluster♥♥♥♥.  the dual-castle setup is very confusing and makes for a ton of backtracking, they went too far in the opposite direction after the visuals backlash on circle, on a computer screen the graphics are downright garish, and the music's nothing subpar.  it's fine though in general. nothing horrible, 2.5 out of 5 or so.aria of sorrow:this one's good too.  good music, good balanced visuals, reasonably challenging in some parts.  the soul thing is fun, more fun than the cards or spellbooks of the other games.  sucks that dracula's dead though.dracula x:well, the game's worth it for the three above, right?

_childDocuments_.review: This collection is worth it for Aria of Sorrow by itself. It's an absolutely incredible game (just like Symphony). I've spent 15 hours alone in Aria and I'm not even close to doing everything that I want to do. Circle of the Moon is fantastic. It's definitely a bit of a nostalgia game, but it is so much fun. Although Rondo of Blood is my favorite classic style Castlevania, Dracula X is close enough until I can get the Requiem Collection on Steam. The sound chip isn't the same, but it's more than good. The final battle sucks.
_childDocuments_.name: Castlevania Advance Collection

_childDocuments_.review: Circle of the Moon is probably the hardest of the metroidvania games in this collection. If you experienced this after Symphony of the Night it might have betrayed your expectations and explain why this game didn't receive a warm welcome during its initial release. Years later, I think it stands on its own and adds unique takes to the genre. Nathan walks rather slowly and he has limited control over his jumps. He can however, jump pretty high, Double jump and dash function are also unlocked early. Unfortunately, dashing is enabled by double tapping and that usually hurts your thumb in the long run.Nathan main weapon is the Vampire Killer whip, but this game has many weapon options which he can utilize using the DSS card system.  Accessing DSS requires you to collect magic cards from enemies, and that can require grinding.All of these magic cards are unlocked at the start, during 2nd play-through in MAGICIAN MODE, but unfortunately your attack power is also considerably lower. Because of this boss fights often becoming a constant barrage of using magic spells and special moves that feels more like a chore instead of enjoyment.Harmony of DissonanceUnlike Circle of the Moon, this was developed by Symphony of the Night's team. Unfortunately, this shows too much. It feels too familiar at times. Juste controls a lot like Alucard. He feels weightless. His jumps are floaty. And for some reason he has both a dash and backdash at the start of the game with almost zero cooldown time. That means you can dash forever.As Juste, you only have a vampire killer whip, and few special move spells depending on your sub weapon and spell book combination. It's similar to Circle of the Moon in a way, but with less variety. Sadly, I must also point out that the sound fonts or synth the used  in this game are well, a dissonance.  And that really hurts the music experienceAria of SorrowThis game had several good ideas, many of which, made it to Bloodstained. This can be a considered a modern sequel to Symphony of the Night and it has aged well. But it has a similar problem like Harmony of Dissonance, but to a lesser degree. If you have played Bloodstained, some of these gameplay themes might feel too familiar.Soma is quite mobile, but he doesn't have Juste's unlimited dashes. You shouldn't feel uncomfortable playing as Soma. This is also the only game in this collection where you are not  limited to using a whip as his main weapon. This game introduces the soul equip system similar to the one seen in Bloodstained. Soma has 3 soul slots: one for a projectile, one for a toggled ability, and one for a passive ability.  Some souls are clearly better than the others, but you will need to switch souls as needed to progress through the game. I am also glad to report that the music in this game doesn't suffer any noticeable bad music synth issues like Dissonance.Dracula X / Vampire's KissThis is the oldest game chronologically, and it is not a metroidvania. This is a linear action platformer, and it is challenging. When I first cleared this years ago, I had to use save stats to beat the game. Years later, I can do a bit better. Now I only need to reload my save stats before boss battles, and not during them. As this iteration of Richter Belmont, your moves will feel restrained and vulnerable compared to his Symphony of the Night's iteration. This will force you to play carefully and perhaps, overly suspicious when advancing through your first play through.The game's art style has aged really well. It actually looks more detailed than the Game Boy Advance ports. The music is phenomenal.  But as said, this game is challenging. And don't expect to get the good ending without looking up a guide.Still, it's a blast from the past, even if it's not for everyone.
_childDocuments_.name: Castlevania Advance Collection

_childDocuments_.review: The games are mixed, however Aria of Sorrow by itself is worth the price tbh.As a collection is great! It comes with QoL features like a WHOLE compendium of items and enemies so you don't have to look up guides to see what does what. It also has the gadget feature which helps with exploration and collecting, In Harmony of Dissonance it tells you if there are key items in a section when you are exploring it, in circle of the moon it tells you when an enemy can drop a card, and in Aria it tells you if you've collected an enemy's soul... However because every enemy has a soul save few, you'll get annoyed quickly by the notifications, so turn this feature off for Aria.
_childDocuments_.name: Castlevania Advance Collection

_childDocuments_.review: After Symphony Of The Night, the games in this collection define what Castlevania is, excluding Dracula X. Each of these games finds a way to make Dracula's castle new again; the different areas of the castle, the enemies, the music, it all comes together to create some of the best, most memorable experiences in gaming ever created. So in addition to just having the convenience of not having to set up an emulator and locate the ROMs, there are some other benefits. In Aria and CoTM, there's a handy indicator that pops up to let you know the enemy you're attacking has a card / soul that can be collected. Christ, that's helpful. And then you have the option to save and load through a secondary menu, which saves you a bit of time when you're on you're wait to get killed by Camilla for the third time. And then there's the rewind feature, which is excellent for farming, or accidental deaths (no way that monster could kill me if I was trying, I just got distracted, you know?)There's some other junk, too, like a gallery with concept and box art, which really lays on the nostalgia. There's a setting to play it in full screen, and you can change up the key binds.This bundle comes highly recommended if you like one of the items in this bundle (excluding Dracula X) and never played any of the others. Or, if you're a fan of Metroidvanias, like Bloodstained. Or if you just like good games at all. Buy it, gift it, and make new Steam accounts to buy it again, so Konami finally works up the motivation to make a follow up to this masterpiece of a series.
_childDocuments_.name: Castlevania Advance Collection

The addition of Dracula X was nice too.  The ports are flawless and with the ability to save anywhere and 3 different screen size plus different filters make it great.

_childDocuments_.review: These games are the same ones that you might’ve played originally back in the day. The collection contains several regional versions of the games, which is a nice touch, as it was originally absent from the previous Castlevania collection Konami has released (but added with an update later on). It also has some artwork, the ability to listen to all of the game soundtracks and some little quality of life things. For example, each GBA title has a special widget that you can enable, that will help you track progress with the collectible elements in the game (for example, if you’ve gotten the soul of the enemy in Aria of Sorrow). There’s also a rewind button combination, which is nice and welcome and you can rebind some keys on the gamepad (though, not on the keyboard for some reason), per each game. Again – sadly, these games are exactly as they were, with no fixes to known issues or oddities, which is a shame as some of these titles are among the best metroidvanias of all time. But it’s a really well-made collection, though I personally found it more comfortable with a DualSense (or any DualShock), as controlling the games with the D-pad is the way they were originally designed. Though, perhaps, you may find the D-pad position on your controller comfortable to use as the main control input anyway.Castlevania: Dracula XUnlike the rest of the games, this isn’t originally a GBA game and is instead a SNES version of the PC Engine classic Rondo of Blood. It follows the same premise and works very similarly to the more advanced original, but it is a less complex game overall. There’s only one level variation, instead of two different routes, just two optional people to save for the best ending and even the levels that are similar to the ones used in the original are much simpler in layout. That said, it’s still a solid game if you’re a fan of the classic action platforming Castlevania games. As I was never a fan of those, I was glad this collection has the rewind, so I still managed to enjoy the game. As surprising as its inclusion in this collection is.Castlevania: Circle of the MoonThe only GBA game in the collection I’ve not completed before. And replaying it now I remember why. While it has a fantastic soundtrack, does look very good emulated in higher resolution and while it does have some cool gameplay ideas, I found the game mostly frustrating. In many ways, it feels like an attempt to combine ideas from the classic Castlevania games in terms of action and controls with the more flexible and level/equipment-dependent design of Symphony of the Night. Your character has some of the more crazy movement abilities from SotN, for example, and you do gain experience and level up, along with finding items that upgrade your stats. But your weapon is always the Vampire Killer whip, the controls are rather stiff and have a delay for some actions and the action is pretty hard. Actually, no. It starts somewhat challenging and interesting, but ends up with fury inducing boss fights.Its main “gimmick” is the collection of cards that may drop from some enemies. You can equip a pair of cards (divided into 2 rows) to get a special effect, from extending your range or increasing damage, to something akin to the “freeze beam” from Metroid series and other curious combinations. While a cool concept, the game seems to assume you’re going to always grind these as some of the boss fights feel almost impossible without some of the card combinations, despite the fact that card drop chance is completely random. Plus, the world of this game is not particularly fun to explore and I’m almost sure many people will get utterly confused about where to go next every time they’ll get a major ability unlock. I enjoyed it at the start, and I like quite a few elements from the game, but overall Circle of the Moon isn’t a very enjoyable experience. And the final boss fight design is just terrible.Castlevania: Harmony of DissonanceNow this one is really fun. You’re still using a Vampire Killer whip with no way to switch weapons (though you can upgrade it a bit), but the movement is so much more fluid and unlike classic Castlevania. In fact, I can’t think of any other title in the series, where you have dedicated buttons to dashing both right and left, meaning that you can use this ability all of the time, as defense and offense, and as a fun way of movement. There are no crazy collection requirements in this one too, apart from the optional “decorate the room” quest, so no need to grind for unlockables.Though, that said, the game gets super easy rather quickly if you find a good magic combination. Personally, I don’t find it problematic, as the exploration is extremely fun, but some people might find it disappointing. What is definitely disappointing is that the look of the game was seriously simplified and as a result the game often looks older than the previous entry. It’s not super distracting, but it’s hard to ignore. That said, the soundtrack is mostly fantastic, as expected. If you like the exploration part of metroidvania games, Harmony of Dissonance might be one of the best Castlevania entries for you. I loved replaying it a lot.Castlevania: Aria of SorrowI’ve always considered this one to be among not just my favorite Castlevania titles, but also one of the best metroidvania games of all time. I know, people tend to love Symphony of the Night the most, and for a good reason. That title was incredibly ambitious and has a ton of cool little details. Yet, personally, I’ve always liked Aria more. It’s a really well-made game, with fantastic soundtrack, cool locations and fun mechanics, having a lot of what made Symphony great, but in a more controlled and manageable amount. Plus, while the story is, as always for most 2D Castlevania games, primitive, the main idea behind it is really fun and it pays off really wonderfully in the end.Its main feature is the idea of collecting souls of the killed enemies, each soul giving you one of three types of abilities (well, four, but the fourth one is almost never dropped from an enemy). One “bullet” soul, working similarly to the typical Castlevania items or one-off spells. One “guardian” soul, that works more like a summon or change form from previous games. And one “enchanted” soul, that gives you a passive ability, from stat boosting to some very unique things. And it’s really cool, as in this game some movement abilities remain equipable souls without ever becoming a permanent background unlock, making sure that some movement possibilities mean limitations to some other things you could do.Yet, if you want to start going for the 100% of all souls, then I hope you have enough patience. Because this game gets super grindy with this and there’s nothing you can do about it. Some souls just have an incredibly low chance of dropping, even when the resulting soul is barely useful, if at all, and even with all possible boosts, you can spend hours grinding to get it. If you don’t plan to do it, though, and just wish to explore everything and get the most out of the game, it’s totally fine and is probably a more enjoyable experience anyway. I went for 100%, but still loved my time replaying Aria of Sorrow.Overall, while I do wish this could be a complete engine port of the games with some of the benefits that you can expect from a thing like that, I’m still glad that Castlevania Advance Collection exists as it does. It’s a really good collection, with 2 good, if not ideal, and 2 fantastic titles that you should definitely check. As even for Harmony and Aria alone, this collection is worth it. I’ve had a great time playing these games and if you’re a fan of metroidvanias and didn’t have a chance to experience these games before, definitely give it a go.

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:+CASTLE-FREAKING-VANIA+Some of the best games in the series in one collection!+Fantastic soundtrack (minus Harmony of Dissonance).+Smooth emulation and clearer audio.+New DSS card/Collectible/Soul tracking.Cons:-Music is Harmony of Dissonance kills my soul.-Why doesn't the game full-screen on start-up?Anyone who knows me knows that Castlevania is my life. It is my all-time favorite video game series and I even own physical copies of every game in existence (even Judgment). I had followed rumors of the Advance Collection for a while and then suddenly it pops up on Steam! The three Gameboy Advance titles are among the best games in the series, and even though it's not everyone's favorite, the SNES Dracula X was a welcome surprise addition!All four games are emulated flawlessly with cleaned up audio to remove the crunchy compression of the original GBA. Even blown up to the big screen they all still look fantastic. Circle of the Moon is an underrated masterpiece with an amazing soundtrack, cool card ability system, and unforgiving difficulty! Harmony of Dissonance is better graphically, but my least favorite of the trilogy due to it being incredibly easy and pain on the ears in the audio department. Aria of Sorrow took the best of both previous titles and combined them into an unforgettable and unique entry in the series with a great story, stellar visuals, awesome music, and it's deep soul-collecting mechanics. Dracula X SNES isn't Rondo of Blood, but still graphically impressive with a great soundtrack and boasts that classic Castlevania challenge!Added to the collection are some new quality of life changes. In Circle of the Moon the game notifies you if an enemy is capable of dropping a DSS card which is VERY useful when trying to collect them all! In Harmony there are indicators on the side of the screen that notify you if an area has a collectible or important upgrade you haven't found. Aria of Sorrow keeps track of what souls you have and have not collected with indicators on the side of the screen. Also included is a save anywhere feature and the ability to rewind gameplay. This is a big help when farming for hard to get drops from enemies, but I feel it destroys some of the challenge the series is known to give. At least these are optional so true, die-hard fans can play the games as intended.The only other gripe aside from Harmony's god-awful music I have is that the game does not auto full-screen when you boot it up. There isn't even an option to do so and forcing it through steam launch options doesn't seem to work. It's easily circumvented by pressing alt+enter, but it's just odd to default to a windowed mode every time.Hopefully Konami stays on the right track with these collections and we eventually get the DS, 64, and PS2 games in the future! Castlevania Advance Collection is a wonderful treat to Castlevania fans everywhere and for only $20 for four phenomenal games it's worth it a million times over!
_childDocuments_.name: Castlevania Advance Collection

_childDocuments_.review: This is the best way to play 3 classic castlevania games. Save-states, an in-game encyclopedia for each game, higher quality versions of songs, and a special "gadget" that does useful stuff like advise you which monsters have DSS cards or souls. There's absolutely no complaint about the 3 metroidvania GBA titles.My only complaint is that they got the atrocious "localization" of Rondo of blood, Dracula X. To give context, the original rondo of blood was an amazing CV game released on the turbografx, with alternate stage paths leading to whole other stages, a second character to play as, and even two different endings. In terms of raw stage design and game structure, it's completely unmatched among Castlevania games.For some godforsaken reason, Konami thought something was wrong with it, and stripped everything that made the game good and released it on SNES. They removed or changed entire stages (generally making them much much worse) and went more for a "let's shove 50 enemies and only 2 small platforms on screen" approach of difficulty instead of Rondo's more thought out difficulty. Dracgula X is a terrible game, and made Richter look absolutely pathetic in NA till the amazing full-on remake of Rondo of blood (Dracula X chronicles) came out worldwide and corrected his previous faults in dracula X. Play Aria, Circle and harmony from this collection and find yourself a way to play Dracula X chronicles or the original rondo of blood.

_childDocuments_.review: If your a veteran or new to the metroidvania style games... It's time to play the series that brought that genre into existence. Rather then rating the whole 4 games as one package... i'll break it down into it's parts.Castlevania: Circle of the Moon...This was the first Castlevania game I remember playing on the Gameboy Advance... and it was beautiful. It took the classic game with it's whip and sub-weapons... and added an awesome Duel Set-up System (DSS system for short). It transformed the game into something that was memorable. Were the cards hard to grind for? yes. Was it worth it? Oh my yes. The DSS system allowed you to choose two cards (one card each from two sets) to create magical abilities... everything from how sub-weapons worked, to encasing you in rock armor, to making your whip electrified if you spun it. Add to that multiple endings and alternate versions of the main characters (your playing the same characters but with different 'advantage'. Example: the magician starts with all DSS cards but his stats are more aimed at use of them vs use of whips or sub-weapons) and it feels like a classic design made better. Castlevania: Harmony of Dissonance...This might be harsh because I got the pleasure of playing Circle of the Moon first...but this game felt like a step back for the Castlevania series. When I gave the Bon Appetit kiss to Circle of the Moon... I have to take it back and face palm after playing this game. It did something I liked, but in turn butchered other things. The DSS system was scraped in favor of a 'fusion system'. This system required you to combine sub-weapons with magical books, which while some deliver some spectacular visuals... feel very situational. second you can't switch between the various sub-weapons (you never could) so if you needed to use a ice ability but had the wrong sub-weapon... you were basically out of luck. What it did right though was finally give a forward and rear dash... unfortunately even this was meh at best. Using two buttons to dash left or right, but instead of one doing forward and one back... the left always shifted left and the right always right. This means if you hit the left dash button... you will go forward if you're looking left and backwards if your facing right. This is reversed if your looking the other way. The whip spin is just sad and forces you to stick to primary attacks and sub-weapons. Still, despite not being not as good as at least two other games on this bundle... it still is a decent game once you understand and adapt to it's nuances.Castlevania: Aria of Sorrow... (or as I call it Castlevania: Return of the Great)Wow... what Harmony of Dissonance did to make me believe it had killed the series, Aria of Sorrow did to restore (and it did so in a BIG way). In this game you play as Soma, who is about to learn a whole lot about himself and you get to play the bloody path to fighting/overcoming destiny. Right off the bat you are introduced to the Dominance system. In short, you have the potential to claim souls of those you defeat to grant you special powers that you can use in a variety of ways. While similar to DSS from Circle of the Moon, it's key difference lies in it's simplicity. The souls you claim fall under 4 different classes: Bullet, Guardian, Enchanted, and Ability. Bullet and Guardian souls use MP. Enchanted and Ability souls do not (Ability souls can be turned on and off in a start menu, but why would you want to?). Bullets do as they sound... they are projectiles or are like sub-weapons. Guardian stay activated as long as you hold the button down (or until you deactivate it with a second button press). Enchanted souls provide a passive ability such as an increase in luck or gaining MP when you take damage. Ability souls are needed to progress in the story and get around to different parts of the castle. You get to choose one of each of the three main types (Bullet, Guardian, and Enchanted) to use in combination and can change them at any time. Some souls are key to acquiring others or can only be acquired though special way. But souls aren't the only trick in Soma's trenchcoat... Weapons, Armors and Accessories compliment these already wonderful soul abilities. Gone is the whip (and for good reason as you will find out) and in are various sharp and stabby type things. You start with simple pocket knife, but trust me you won't be using it for long. You will often find multiple copies of some weapons/armor (which can be sold off for cash) and will quickly find a certain weapon type to your liking. Don't be quick to dispose of a weapon just because a new one does 'more damage'. Some do elemental damage which can quickly make that weaker weapon on paper... be god tier and save your life. Just like the souls though, they aren't all created equally. Some are situational and some are just plain bad (or for those looking for a much bigger challenge). One thing I haven't touched on in previous games... is the difficulty. Castlevania games have been regularly judged by a single boss's difficulty.... Death. Yes that grim reaping, thick-skulled, pain in the you know what that shows up in almost every Castlevania game is here and boy is he a handful this time. This games Death is one of the most difficult versions of the bone head in the series. You have been warned. Anyways... the big thing that makes this game so amazing is that unlike other games in this series where your goal is to reach the next boss... Aria of Sorrow makes the journey to that point just as important. Every enemy has the potential to drop a new weapon, soul, etc... to you collection. That one enemy that you can easily avoid (or in some cases don't even know that the enemy is there) could give you something that will drastically impact your playing. A good example if the Kyoma Demon... You probably will only ever encounter it at two places in the game. Even then... you probably will overlook it because you'll be too busy fighting other enemies or pass by it and not even notice it. It's soul though grants a powerful tool to your belt. Some will require RNG to be on your side to even engage it. Some will require a lot of patience and quick reflexes. In any case, this game fully restored my love of the series... unfortunately the sequel to this game was not included in this bundle and it is a real shame. It would have been perfect.Castlevania: Dracula X...Um what? This is suppose to be a rework of the game Castlevania: Rondo of Blood. I never heard anything good about this or the game it was a rework of and at the time of this review... I have yet to play it.Things other then the games...Ok aside from the games, there are some things that I found were beneficial in this collection. First there are ease of use features like remapping button configurations. This made playing the games much more enjoyable and since I played 3 of the games on Gameboy advance as well... I can say they have kept it true to the original, but remap allows me to do things more fluidly and easily. Second is the ability to toggle on and off certain features that weren't in the original games but are very helpful. One in particular was when I was playing Aria of Sorrow... when I killed an enemy, it would tell me if I was missing a soul that I could acquire from it. While this can be found in game... it takes going through a series of menus. Having it right there the minute It was defeated... was immensely helpful. This was also very true for Circle of the Moon's DSS cards too. Since they are much rarer and there isn't anything I know off the top of my head that tells you who has what card or if you can even acquire one from defeating it.All in all I found most of the games in this collections great. I wished they had included Aria of Sorrow's sequel (Castlevania: Dawn of Sorrow) but It was released on the Nintendo DS vs the Gameboy Advance. If your into Metroidvania games... This is a must have.
_childDocuments_.name: Castlevania Advance Collection

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a few years since legendary porting team M2 chose to bless us with the first Castlevania Collection, which focused on the early linear Classicvania titles. Now, much like Dracula himself, M2 has risen once again to deliver the follow-up, which covers the Game Boy Advance era's open-ended Metroidvania titles (plus the SNES' Dracula X).The original collection stood out as being of somewhat lesser quality in comparison to M2's other efforts. The aspect ratio options did not function correctly, there were no other graphical options and the UI had a habit of crashing when brought up after toggling full screen on and off. Moreover, while the emulation was mostly sound, Super Castlevania IV suffered from some mild popping in its audio emulation. Finally, there was no way to enter and exit full-screen or to even simply quit the game without utilizing keyboard shortcuts. So how does this follow-up stack up in comparison? Luckily, the more egregious issues have been dealt with, though some annoyances remain. Like before, there are no graphical filters to choose from, though you do get a nice bevy of features to compensate. Firstly, you can now manually alter the sampling rate of the audio emulation in the GBA games, which is almost unheard of in official emulations. Save States make a return, though they've also added the option to rewind gameplay as well on top of a built-in recording feature. You even get the ability to toggle on and off a feature that adds on-screen guidance during gameplay to help the player with keeping track of potential item-drops from enemies, which is quite nifty. Finally, there's a gallery and music player built in as well, which even features complete scans of each game's manuals for your viewing pleasure.With all of these features, there's no denying that this second installment completely trumps the first in just about every way. Unfortunately, some wrinkles from that first release have been retained, chief among them them being that you're still incapable of toggling between windowed and full-screen without utilizing keyboard shortcuts, making a gamepad-only experience rather tricky since the game will default to a windowed view on start-up. There is also the aforementioned lack of graphical options, such as graphical filters or an in-game V-sync toggle. Luckily, the aspect ratio settings do work as intended this time around.In summary, this collection is a herculean improvement over the first in just about every aspect, though some odd shortcomings still remain. All the same, these issues do not outnumber the staggering amount of nice features and spotless emulation quality. So long as you can overlook the lack of graphical options and required keyboard utilization for toggling between full screen and windowed mode, then this is a must-own compilation that features the definitive versions of some of the GBA's finest titles, and, despite what some may say, Dracula X is far from a bad time as well. Considering the prices that these titles demand on the aftermarket, this makes for an excellent way to experience these classics with some extra quality of life features.

name: Twin Mirror
detailed_description: Sam Higgs left his hometown, and everyone he knows, behind two years ago. But the death of his best friend Nick calls the former investigative journalist back to confront the town’s troubled past—and his own. He soon becomes drawn into a dangerous web of intrigue as all is not as it seems in the small town of Basswood, West Virginia. Forced to face himself and the townsfolk, Sam struggles to balance the scales of reconciliation and his life-changing investigation. He must decide how much he’s willing to risk to uncover the mysteries of his hometown. REMEMBER, REFLECT, REVEAL Explore Sam’s unique and analytical ways in his expansive Mind Palace, where you can revisit his past, relive old memories, and reconstruct events. There, you can go through possible scenarios, envision how things could’ve gone, and follow the clues to your next lead. Be careful, though—the Mind Palace is a reflection of Sam’s state of mind, for better or worse.  THE TWIN MIRROR You can also speak with your Double, who is the more social and empathic side of yourself that nobody else can see. You must navigate the dangers of Sam’s conflicted thoughts and feelings together: will your Double become a trusted confidante or an unwelcome guest?  CHOOSE YOUR PATH In Twin Mirror, every decision you make alters the course of your investigation, as well as your relationships in Basswood. Trust others or rely only on yourself in your hunt for the truth. But no matter your choices, your story is yours. Take a look in the mirror—what will you see?

_childDocuments_.review: With   achieved something. Something great on the field of adventure games. Then came  (a slight deviation from their narrative-driven approach) and later a sequel to  was released. One could clearly see the folks at  were making longer and better games. So far so good.Now, with  and  they took a step back. They are both shorter games - they appear to be smaller projects (the former was not released on the PS being complete X exclusive). With  the episodic format was completely ditched and, as many of us have experienced it in the last couple of years with other titles, it was Epic exclusive but only for a year. So far this has been their sole game where  was doing self-publishing.The story of  revolves around Sam, a journalist, who returns to his hometown called Basswood after several years of absence. We learn that Sam wrote an article that resulted in the closing of the local coal mine. As hundreds became unemployed Sam resorted to leaving and not looking back at his fellow (and very angry) townsfolk. But now he's back. He's back because his friend, Nick, passed away.As we progress we get to know more and more inhabitants of Basswood (who either welcome Sam or would like to see him leave once again) and start an investigation as Sam does not want to believe his best friend died in a car accident. Something sinister is afoot. He knows that as following a night of heavy drinking his shirt in the hotel is completely blood-stained. No, Sam didn't kill anybody! I was afraid at first they'd play that card. No, he just doesn't remember at first where the blood comes from. He later on meets Anna (his and Nick's ex) and they look into these matters together.Now, certain sections require us to collect clues. As Sam finds all clues in a specific location he tries to visualise what happened in the past at that particular place. Forget Max's time rewind ability or Sean's telekinetic solution to this anger - after  what  employs is something a bit more down-to-earth this time. This is also the place where Sam escapes to when panic starts setting in. These running / timed sequences I did not particularly like.Sam has a Double, a kind of twin that inhabits his mind palace. He often pops-up at key conversations and provides Sam with guidance. As this is once again a narrative-driven adventure game  did not forget to give us several endings. But the key approach now is found in our relationship with the Double: Sam either listens to him and follows a more social approach or follows the process he got to learn as a journalist and employs a more analytical route. When a very important decision is to be made the game pauses and different wording indicates the two options we can choose from. However, each option has a specific colour in line with Sam's above-mentioned approach. As we make progress throughout the game Sam keeps his journal updated. We will notice here and there that some of the updates have the same coloration (blue or yellow) which means the system is present when making smaller decisions, too. The ultimate question. It is shorter than either of the  titles and it almost lacks any supernatural elements (Sam's mind palace can be considered as such but this is definitely not on par with Max's and Daniel's abilities). Even Tyler and Alison had telepathic abilities in . Again, this appears to be a smaller project with fewer locations and fewer characters. Everything else is great - they are the usual high quality we have gotten used to from this studio. But 5-6 hours is enough to see Sam's story through and the revelation at the end is not something you could not have expected. It is still a title I recommend but nowhere near as good as any predecessor Dontnod made. Are you a fan? It should be in your library already. First time looking for something new, something more narrative-driven? Pick  instead.

_childDocuments_.review: The general opinion about  is that it doesn’t manage to reach the same high bar that other games developed / published by  already set, and after I played the game several times already, I can understand where this statement is coming from. If you expect a moving narrative or a story similar in greatness as for example the one that  offers, then you won’t find it here. But by all means don’t take that as “ is a bad game” - it isn’t, it just lacks the depth, the spark, and the impact that their other games have on you when you play them.Still,  is an immersive game. If I were to describe it, I’d say it’s more of a movie rather than a game considering that the player interactions are kept to a minimum. One playthrough takes around 7 hours and it’s extremely linear, consisting mostly in watching the scripted cutscenes and dialogues based on the choices you make. In that regard,  does some things very well, but it also has its faults. It’s mainly advertised as a “Choose Your Own Adventure” game, albeit most of the choices don’t matter for how the story unravels up to the ending sequences - regardless of what you choose, the outcome is identical and you have pretty much the same idea, but expressed through different words no matter what you pick. The choices that do count though are color-coded and frankly, I was relieved that the game shows me that I am about to make a meaningful decision which is bound to affect the rest of the game. Even the earlier choices from this category can have repercussions in the late parts of the game. Unfortunately, there are only 6-7 choices like this, and they are split into two categories: analytical and social, leading you to slightly different playthroughs and quite different endings.You take the role of Sam Higgs - a journalist who comes back to his small hometown of Basswood to attend the funeral of his best friend Nick only to find out that he was actually murdered. Sam can’t stop his investigative nature and together with his ex-girlfriend Anna, sets on a quest to find the culprit and expose his deeds to the whole town. Since it’s a detective-themed story, one would expect some plot twists, unfortunately  fails to deliver them. Surely, there are some unexpected things happening, but the game is mostly  predictable (apart from maybe who the big bad is) and also doesn’t manage to give you that feeling of thrill, of keeping you on your toes until you find the identity of the killer.The name of the game comes from the fact that Sam has a split personality, with his alter ego accompanying him at every step. The duality of his brain is the one that gives the two distinctive paths in the game - while Sam is rather cold and cynical (and also ), his twin ego tries to encourage Sam to be more social, more caring towards others. At least, that is the whole idea of the game - but for me, these two personalities were so similar that I had real trouble grasping the distinctive aspects between them. The alter ego is neither a devil on Sam’s shoulder, nor an angel with a mission to protect Sam, but indeed more of a twin, an  meant to dispute Sam’s actions or bicker at him. Still, choosing to listen to him would lead Sam on a social path, while ignoring his advice will result in him remaining an analytical person.There are plenty of characters to encounter, but most of them have only a couple of dialogue lines. Apart from Sam, Nick and Anna (and marginally Nick’s daughter) the characters are not at all developed, and the collectible items that you can find lying around and which reveal a piece of their background story are not enough to grant them distinctive personalities. Perhaps the original plan was to give them a more substantial role into the plot, yet as the game is now, it feels that these characters are mostly treated as fillers - they don’t add anything meaningful to the story, aside from them forming together the small and intertwined community of Basswood. Since they remain undeveloped, they won’t make you empathize with them or connect to them in any way.Possibly the nicest part of the game is Sam’s mind palace - a place where he can revisit old memories triggered by various collectibles that you can gather, but also where he can reconstruct a key sequence of actions related to the murder. These detective sequences involve first scanning the scene for clues, then answering correctly to three questions based on the info you gathered from your surroundings. This will trigger a live simulation of the actions expressed by your choices. If they are incorrect, the game won’t penalize you in any way but you won’t progress further until you get all of them right (which shouldn’t be that difficult since there are only 9 possibilities and the correct choices are usually pretty obvious).Perhaps the biggest issue is the inability to skip cutscenes. With a game as linear as  is and as heavy in cinematic sequences as it is, plus having two separate routes of which most of the content is the same, rewatching several hours of cutscenes in a second playthrough without a way to skip already seen scenes is utterly annoying. Outside the main choices, most of the players would probably want to see alternative options in dialogues with all the characters, however there’s no indication about what you selected in the previous playthroughs, in order to avoid selecting it again.For the asking price of $30, I feel that the game fails short to deliver a memorable experience, plus it doesn’t justify the high price considering that you can finish it in 7 hours (unless you want to see all endings / do a second playthrough for the main alternative choices). The plot is rather slow-paced and it lacks those factors that stimulate your brain, that tingly sensation that a murder mystery should give you. It’s still enjoyable to play if you like heavy narrative games, in which you sit back and relax and don’t mind repetition in subsequent playthroughs. It's undoubtedly a beautiful game, with high-quality 3D graphics, fully voiced lines, great soundtrack and Dontnod’s classic formula focusing on internal conflicts, yet it feels somewhat mediocre compared to their other works.

_childDocuments_.review: By the time Twin Mirror made it's way to Steam, I had all but forgotten about it. I'm a huge fan of DONTNOD's (DON'T NOD? Hate the name change) games in general, especially the  series. So when I had heard very little about Twin Mirror after its launch, I was suspicious to say the least. It pains me to say that this game drops the ball in almost every area that counts.In fact, in a lot of ways it reminds me of another DONTNOD game that I hated, : Little to no justification for the superpower, no small, quiet moments, no real characters outside of the main two. Everything here feels rushed and fumbled. What sucks most is I honestly enjoyed the first hour or two; it felt like it was setting itself up to be a darker, more mature story than other DONTNOD affairs. But in the end, it gets caught up in trying to separate  from  and just feels totally out of step with itself.It has some of the stiffest dialogue I've heard from a DONTNOD game, almost as though it was written in another language and then translated. The facial animations and lip syncing are just terrible, which I can usually see passed, but this whole game is basically serious dialogue. It's distracting and compounds the stiff, stilted deliveries.The game suffers most from the way you engage with clues or interactables. Not quite looking from the right direction prevents you from seeing the "Look/Examine" options. But sometimes items simply , so you spend time walking back and forth/changing your angle of approach repeatedly because you think maybe you've just missed it.On top of that, the fact that you have to discover the clues in the right order during the handful of investigations is really frustrating. An early investigation in a bar felt awful, especially as the first time engaging with the system. I kept walking up to an item on the ground that I could very clearly tell was a clue, but couldn't interact with it until I had engaged with a series of events leading up to it. At least the game tells you  you've found all the clues, but going to an item you can CLEARLY see is a clue, and it not being marked as one, is really confusing and frustrating.Once you've found the clues, you spend time in your "Mind Palace", setting the events in the right order, but it's really a matter of trial and error. There are no consequences for getting things wrong, other than being forced to watch the same unskippable cut scene play out over and over until you get them right. This would have been an opportunity to have some branching narrative, with different investigation outcomes etc. You can almost feel the episodic,  length game wishing to exist here; This whole game could have been Chapter 1 of a much larger story (although I'm glad I didn't have to wait months in between chapters), with more attention paid to the characters and town.For a game that takes itself so seriously, there's a surprising lack of depth. I just wish we could stop being so obsessed with super powers and these alternate states of consciousness that give the protagonists some kind of ethereal advantage in life. Slowly meandering through shattered pieces of a character's past within their own mind to deal with internal struggles is rarely interesting or necessary, and here it feels completely at odds with itself. At least we can hope that Deck Nine continues to develop the  series, as they seem to have a much firmer grasp on interesting, narrative-driven games.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this another masterpiece from Dontnod, the makers of Life is Strange, Vampyr or Remember Me? Well, the production values are high. You get a gorgeous cinematic adventure, fully voiced, with a rather good story. The gameplay consists of examining your sourroundings, talking to everyone, making choices. This is interrupted by little action sequences, like running through your subconsciousness, trying to escape... something evil. The story is good, if you like slower-paced games with an evolving story. What starts with you returning to your hometown for a funeral soon gets far more complicated. You are a reporter, who a few years ago wrote an article that lead to problems for many of the towns inhabitants - so most people now don't really like you. You left the town (and your now deceased best friend and his little daughter) after your girlfriend dumped you a few years ago. Or was it because of the article you wrote? Now you return - guilt-ridden, depressive, and with a split personality. You talk with your other self all the time, or the other self talks to you. And your friend's death... was it really just a horrible car accident?A high-quality and well-written thriller with mature topics, many conversations and a few action minigames. Find out the truth behind your friend's death - and don't become crazy or killed on the way.

_childDocuments_.review: 12.6h (100% achievement, finished the game twice) 7h No. Yes (~15 achievements). No. is a story-rich game, telling the story of Sam, who is visiting his hometown to attend his best friend's funeral. Sam has two personalities that conflict with each other. On one side, he has an imaginary friend with a lot of empathy. On the other side, he has great analytical thinking that always seeks the truth even if it hurts those around him. It's a story about choosing a side while trying to figure out what actually happened.- Multiple endings based on your choices- Lack of replayability options- Sometimes input won't work when you are interacting with objects or peopleIntel Core i5-9300H 2.40GHz, 8GB RAM, NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1650The models look realistic, but the human skin doesn't look as realistic at up close. Moreover, I found the character's head to constantly shake while talking. I know that they are trying to mimic people who like to nod whenever they are talking, but the movement just feels unnatural to me. Other than that, the visuals are fine. I like how the mind realm inside Sam's head was constructed from glass pieces. It looks cool and distinct at the same time.As a story-rich game, I found it to be okay. The story can feel boring at first though, especially since you usually just chitchat with people about the town. The plot will pick itself up as you play - it's not that intense, but it's good enough to keep you going.What I found interesting is the situation our main character, Sam, is in. He has two distinctive personalities. There is his imaginative friend who always tells him about how to mingle with people and learn to tone down his attitude; have more sympathy for people and think of what they feel before taking. And then there is his analytical side who always seeks the truth and tells people what they need to hear, even if they are not in the state to hear them. The latter personality is his default one, making him sound like a jerk since he tends to talk without any regard for the current situation. The choices present in the game will mostly refer to these 2 sides, about which side are you willing to choose.However, despite the great concept, I don't like how the ending was. You are forced to choose between the two sides. There is no option where both sides can mingle even though they both have their strength; his social side always knows how to comfort people while his analytical side is always good at seeking the truth. The thing is, choosing a side means that you have to sacrifice some things in the game, meaning that you can't have an ending where everything is truly solved and you are content with your life. Well, I guess that's life.Replaying the game can be a hassle, though. I found that there isn't much variation to the story despite the numerous choices that you can make. Those choices usually only change a minor part of the story in that chapter, making most of the story redundant. Moreover, sometimes the game will also reuse some dialogues for both choices. The dialogue might flow smoothly, but I just find it weird when the voice shifts tones.The gameplay in this game is mostly just walking around and interacting with either people or objects. I hated that you can't run most of the time. Your walking speed is slow, and you need to cover a lot of ground. Moreover, there is no way to highlight interactable objects to make finding objects easier.Your analytical side also has a realm that can be used to reconstruct scenes. I liked this gameplay the most - it helps to kill the boredom from the story. You need to find clues and choose from some options as to what happened. It's pretty easy to find the right answer, and failing usually poses no risk. It also has other, varying minigames. It's mostly about finding something, whether it's a set of patterns that you must follow or your imaginary friend. They might require some tries since they can be vague, but the game gives you hints for that and it won't be too hard to solve - it only took me a few tries, with most of them being solved on the first try.I finished the game for the first time at 7h. The game has 4 endings with 1+ minor variation. Two endings look too similar to each other, though. However, the game lacks replayability options. There are collectibles that you can find, but you can't play through the chapter select just for collecting the collectibles that you missed - you need to collect those and other collectibles from that point of the story to collect them all. There is also no way to speed up the dialogues and the checkpoints are spread quite far. Lastly, your save will be overwritten if you load from chapter select, making you unable to do another chapter select for earlier chapters unless you finish the game again.There wasn't anything special to the story, but it wasn't that bad either. I liked the concept of clashing personalities that the main character has, and his abilities are also showcased strongly in the game to show their strength. However, that's where it ends. The story can feel boring at times, and there isn't much that you can get from it. I enjoyed some of the gameplay, though, particularly the one that is related to his analytical side. I can recommend the game, but get it on a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: (TWM) is a third-person narrative adventure set in present-time West Virginia, USA. Protagonist Sam Higgs, an investigative journalist, has to go back to Basswood - a remote town where he used to live and work at - to attend his best friend's funeral after a tragic car accident. Soon enough, despite the conflicts sparked by his comeback, Sam hears about suspicions on Nick's accident: his death may hide more than meets the eye, after all.TWM takes place in your typical small town, where all citizens know each other and anything new becomes the talk of town quickly. In Sam's case, his return is not seen as a positive event by most, due to the nature of his job. Years before he exposed facts that influenced the town as a whole - not everyone took this well. Nick's passing weighs heavily both on him and his now-reunited acquaintances, each in their own way. Whether Sam tries to reconcile and avoid conflict, or keeps being a stoic misanthrope focused only on getting things done, will entirely be up to you. Most characters react plausibly in dialogues, or to the protagonist's actions, their personalities / archetypes feel consistent throughout the story.Sam manifests a rare mental condition, both blessing and curse, that allows extremely detailed analysis of facts and information. This helped him become a successful investigative reporter, but also comes with a heavy price to pay as far as social relations are concerned. Sam will often talk to "Him", an imaginary friend only he can see and perceive, that will try to help out and act as a "conscience" of sorts - especially when the protagonist becomes overwhelmed or is being too emotionally-detached. Of course, you may decide to ignore Him completely and act solely on your decisions - especially given that his suggestions may not always be the best course of action.The "Mind Palace" is where Sam's skills truly shine, allowing him not only to collect and relive his own memories based on personally-linked items found in the world, but also formulate hypotheses about facts by choosing between several options at hand. Only one of them will be correct, though, so don't expect branching investigations based on right or wrong choices, not that deeply anyway. Some variants of the Palace will see Sam struggling against fears, sudden events or panic attacks, which manifest as literal waking nightmares that play out as chase sequences, puzzles and more. This visual manifestation of a mind's troubles is spot-on, and really manages to convey the dread, panic, fear or whatever other negative sentiment Sam may experience.As in any narrative adventure worth its salt, TWM presents a range of major choices in each chapter, that will affect Sam's relation with characters in significant ways, or even determine a character's fate as a whole sometimes. Mainly, these take the shape of dialogue branches where you can withhold or reveal critical information, take a decision, or choose a course of action. These major choices are complemented by a wider range of lesser dialogue options, mostly related to Sam's general attitude towards people - they won't influence the story drastically, but may change the way some characters see Sam as a person, and this will actually show in they way they act later on, in subtle or more prominent ways. While this title nails the psychological and interpersonal relations compartments, it results weaker in those sections that have action-oriented themes or anyway entail actual life-threatening choices. Without spoilers, I'll just say that DONTNOD's guys should really double check the actual damage a firearm can do to a human body, how law enforcement training works, and several other things they just didn't put much attention about. Not mere technicalities, as these factors make certain situations evolve in less plausible ways, in relation to Sam's choices. Particularly near the end, I was dumbfounded at seeing how stupidly a certain part plays out.Despite having the potential to make more significant choices / diverging paths along the way, as a way to promote replayability, TWR in the end opts for a mostly streamlined main story that no matter the choices, will end up in the same situations at the end of the day. This is a common issue of Narrative Adventures, that only few of them managed to overcome, thus being truly "branching" in their choices. In any case, replaying the game to see the reactions of characters and possible alternate endings could be worth for those that really want to see all the "shades of grey" it has to offer, so it's not for nil.
