_childDocuments_.review: Recent game from my beloved developers DontNod and i'm really sad after playing Twin Mirror. It's probably the worst game they have ever made.The game retains the same formula DonNod uses for their games (except Remember Me and Vampyr). It's a narrative game with choices, high emphasis on story and decisions which affects you. But it fails at basically everything. Don't get me wrong, I still enjoyed the game for the story but it doesn't feel anything special, it's nothing to remember, don't expect Life is Strange here, don't even expect Tell Me Why.If you thought that Tell Me Why is slow then you haven't played this one. Although the game is extremely short it feels like it drags forever and nothing is happening.This time the story revolves around a mysterious death of Nick -  friend of the main character. As a journalist he decides to investigate his death and starts his detective journey. Yes it's like a detective game, you investigate stuff. But of course it's all linear, there's nothing to miss. There are only few locations to explore. You look at objects, talk with other characters and that's it.Sometimes you need to investigate and reconstruct the event which happened earlier. You enter some kind of detective mode and try to glue everything together. It's a tedious task, you basically try different things until you get it right. You can't fail, it's slow and tedious.Sometimes you get to mind place. It's inside your head, you enter that place when you remember something and watch a cut-scene of the memory or enter that place to talk to Him. He is your invisible friend. Like he's living inside your head and tries to tell you what to do and what decisions to make. Which brings us to choices. You choose either His advice or you trust yourself.Sounds pretty cool? It's isn't. Choices do not matter, they change absolutely nothing. There are different endings but despite the ending you get same dialogues with maybe two new lines. It basically two endings, well maybe 3 but watching them feels like a drag because you're rewatching same scenes. And which ending you will get is decided at the very end of the game. Character development is non existent. There's not enough time to get to know any character, you talk to them a little and that's it, you move on. Choices make no difference at all. Worst part is that you need to replay the game making “different choices” to get all the achievements. It's just boring. And you know what's the worst part? You can't skip the cut-scenes so replaying this is a pain.Now the story itself is interesting. It's a mystery story and it's fun to learn new things, to uncover all the secrets. But there's not enough content. The game is unfinished. And you can clearly see that little effort has been put into making this game. Like you listen to two women chatting and after couple of sentences the voices stop but you can see they're still talking, this is common. Surroundings are dead, the world is dead. It's pretty but it's dead.Graphics. Looks good in screenshot, looks bad playing the game. Emotionless wooden faces and non-existent facial animations. But the models look very realistic. Low on budget? Go artistic style like in Life is Strange or Walking Dead. This is not as bad as police simulator but I definitely see some similarities, not a lot of work has been put into it.The main character is so generic that it feels like someone opened up the character creation tool and left everything on default.Environments look good but they're dead. You won't see cars driving past, people walking around, vegetation moving, nothing. And if you look somewhere farther away you see low-res texture there.Performance is terrible. Game constantly switches to 60fps. If you go to the menu and back the framerate unlocks for some time, until next cut-scene. At times it feels like the game is running on 30fps. It's a mess.It's a cinematic experience so obviously no ultrawide support because ♥♥♥♥ cinematic experience. Fortunately smart people know how to make ultrawide fixes so it works. Do developers care about that? Nope.Sound is the only area where developers didn't mess up. While the music isn't as good as in their previous games it's still pretty good.Voice acting is good too and it compensates in some way for non-existent animations.This is an unfinished game with good concept and story, it deserves a neutral rating. If you're a hardcore fan of narrative games it might be worth playing this if you get it on sale, a real sale, 75% off or a bundle. It's slow, it's boring, it's ugly, it's too short. Better save your money for Life is Strange remasters, those games are masterpieces.
_childDocuments_.name: Twin Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: Twin Mirror is a story-driven interactive game. Your choices matter. I won't get into details but the story is rather mediocre at best. There are two different strands: The main story and the characters' inner conflict. The inner conflict will have a decision for you to make in the last quarter of the game and honestly: I couldn't care more. They definitely weren't able to make the characters likable and important enough for me to care.The story is also pretty predictable and since it feels like only 10 people live in this small town, you couldn't be surprised of what the "twists" (if you even call any of that a twist). There are no QTE events through the game that offers a mechanic to plan what could happen in some situations. For that, you will be in a mind palace. It sounds more intelligent than it actually is. Samuel isn't a Sherlock Holmes and most "predictions" or rather, possibilities to plan/reconstruct what happened are a joke to anyone having more than two brain cells. Add to that, that at some point the mind palace changes completely and you can't plan ahead anymore. You will just think about what to do and decide on one thing. Before, you could see all scenarios and need to choose the right one. There isn't a logic behind that. It seems unlogical just like many other things in this game.Aside from that, the game is a walk and talk-fest just like many other games in the genre. Nothing bad with that. Well, there are many decisions to make but the outcome is rather small most of the time. Aside from a few different endings, there isn't anything significant happening based on your decisions. In fact, many things you can't decide. Most mind palaces you need to solve just like the game wants it to play out. Even if you want to try something different - you just can't - which is lame and lazy. The atmosphere is good. The graphics and the voice-over are nice enough and the music is okayish, nothing special. The game takes place in a very small town and all of the atmospheres tell you that. Instead of listing the good and bad things, like I usually do, I will just tell you my opinion on this one. After being an Epic Exclusive I totally forgot about the game (before that, I really wanted it, since it was from the creators of LiS). When the game came to steam, I was happy about it. Got it pretty cheap (around 13€) and played it a couple of months later. I'm just happy I did not pay full price for this joke of a game. You can play through the game in 4 to 5 hours, there aren't meaningful decisions to make except for 2 or 3, resulting in different endings (all of them pretty close to the end of the game), the story is mediocre and predictable, illogical and can't suck you in. Characters aren't strong enough especially compared to LiS.I guess they outsourced this game and not one person from the original LiS Team worked on this one though LiS2 wasn't that good either and I start to believe it was a lucky one-hit-wonder. This game is a time- and money-waster. Don't go for it. I certainly can't recommend it. Rather play Alfred Hitchcock's Vertigo, Life is Strange, Heavy Rain, or any of the TellTale Games (except for Batman maybe).
_childDocuments_.name: Twin Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: This has to the most underrated game I have ever played. I don't know how it has only 7/10 approval rating on the website. The story was well done & the amount of choices given to the character made it even better. The game isn't very long, but then again, I really appreciated how the developers didn't try to stretch out of the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Twin Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: I am a big fan of DONTNOD so I was excited to see a new title to play. Twin Mirror has a solid story, good voice acting, and some interesting mechanics related to the inner workings of the mind. You play as Sam - a journalist who has returned to his home town for a funeral and stumbles upon a murder and a conspiracy which beg to be solved. It is a worthy 'choices matter' adventure but not nearly as engaging as Life is Strange or Tell Me Why.The characters lack the depth developed in previous games and I never felt any emotional connection with them. The 'mind' segments are artfully done but often confusing to navigate with very fuzzy objectives. You end up in a 'try this and try that' until you figure out what actions are needed to complete and exit these segments.Completionists will need to play the majority of the game through twice and then repeat the last couple of chapters (on both runs) to view all unique endings. My second play through felt like a chore because there was no way to skip scenes or speed conversations that I had already experienced.The game is best played with a controller. The keyboard and mouse implementation are a bit counter-intuitive because the WASD keys are used for movement AND for context menus that are activated with the mouse. I started out with the keyboard but soon found I was often moving when I meant to select from a menu.  This is further complicated by the fact that the character often blocks your view of the object you are attempting to interact with.The game is divided into chapters/scenes with an autosave that occurs regularly as you proceed. When you have finished the game, there is an option to restart from any scene (to pick up missed collectibles or make different choices).  Be advised that, when you return to a chapter/scene, you are starting the game over (from that point). This means that collectibles must be rediscovered in all subsequent chapters in order to earn related achievements.Overall, I enjoyed Twin Mirror and would recommend it to those who favor'choices matter' adventures and who are fans of previous DONTNOD titles. You might consider waiting for it to go on sale, as it is a bit shorter and less complicated than their previous titles.
_childDocuments_.name: Twin Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: I would only recommend this game on a big sale. I 100% the game. There is an illusion of choice, and your actions don't matter, there is a predetermined path that you will follow regardless of the options you choose during gameplay. The voice acting and performance of the characters is really bad a lot of the time, sometimes the lip sync is bad or non existent. I Finnish the game on Steamdeck and didn't encounter any bugs or glitches.
_childDocuments_.name: Twin Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine "Deadly Premonition", with the same kind of small town archetypes and a very similar hero. And now take out all of the goofiness, the jokes, the comedy, the collectibles and the wonky car. And replace it with the boring dystopia that it would be in reality, and what Francis York and Zack would look like if they grew up in that reality, starting with the medication they would have to take. Yeah, this won't be for everyone, and you will have to be in the mood. A lot of people will just be plain bored or disappointed because they expected a murder mystery you solve with superpowers, but that's really just the cover of this book. Don't expect a technical marvel, but it's polished, well-designed and with only few exceptions has exactly the right pacing and playtime. But I don't think that the motivations, symbolism and themes are as relatable and accessible to everyone like in Dontnod's other games. Which is one underlying theme of the game, right along with the conclusion that you shouldn't take it personal.
_childDocuments_.name: Twin Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: Potentially my GOTY.I can feel the sorrow in this game, that slight bitter smell lingers, from the first scene at the lookout point to the end of the game. A bittersweet journey.The CG of Sam driving is a fab way to bring an introduction. Giving just the right amount of info, it tells the story of the town as well as gives the good status of Sam, and why he is here.Upon arriving at the Lookout Point, I immediately feel a strong connection to the real world - just reading the brief on the board and seeing the outlines that are marked on the map is interesting. This lookout feels real. Going farther to the info board/hunting hours, the closed trail, the carved tree, the telescope etc., this place feels real. Phone buzzed with messages, you can even see the "..." goes on indicating typing and the signal cut out logo. Details made this game stand out.Just as soon as it links to the real world, the Mind Palace appears as a surreal place full of memories. With a good amount of fact and mystery, companions only Sam can see and hear, it is very interesting to make me beg for more. Twin Mirror triumphs in both story and presentation, making it a beautiful emotional game, offers players freedom to choose their own path and lead to different conversations and multi endings. Before entering the pub for Nick's wake, Sam meets his daughter and she asks for investigation on her old man's death. I wasn't expecting this. Like later gameplay, the game offers 2 choices: accept or refuse. They may only differ in conversations, but as Sam is told, poke around risks being poked back, or let down the poor girl while you know something is not right, but if you go deeper you may hurt them worse. Dude this is so good. Given a general idea to the player what might happen but not going too much, let them find out step by step and be happy or regret in their initial actions, the Interactive Fiction tag shines, kudos to the devs.What I also find amazing is, living in another culture though I have never heard let alone anticipate in any "wake", I understand it. The talks at the pub are well written, full audio is top-notch, and the actions as well as movements are smooth. More than a time I feel the pleasure of a triple A game quality, as well as the wonderful thyme of a Hollywood blockbuster movie - a highlight of every 15 mins of gameplay. Twin Mirror is good at keeping me interested, all the places has quite a few objects to interact with and articles are for the right amount of words - not a wall of texts yet not too simple, and I love the decorations on the wall - just look at the photos at the pub, those are not random but well selected ones, well set the atmosphere for the local pub, and the memorial made for memorize Nick. I must congrats the art design, time and time again I find it is amazing how this game is able to catch all the beauty - be the human or the landscape or a interior design, the camera does not always fixed when a conversation happens, rather, the camera is smart and rotates, goes closer or farther to let player see the same things from different angle, making the scene clever and interesting.Mind Palace is such a great setting. In normal time it reflects memories, when Sam faces severe events, this place becomes a phobia and he needs to escape. Most are intense, but far less than any horror games, which made me love the creativity - I am unsure if any of them are inspired by real symptoms from claustrophobia patients, but that scene chased by a man with mirrors written "guilty" is incredible. So are the room with many locked doors, the pick of real "You" at the end. After I finished the game I immediately came back and played again.The characters feel real and loveable, the game gives important leads to characters/relationships but I managed to dig deeper to see a bigger map, very pleased to do so and though there are no collectibles, the game has a detailed memento. At the end Sam is able to both make a choice for himself and for the people in this town, there are a total of 5 but 3 main endings, 2 are more like alternatives. I finished the first run in 6.5 hours, devoted another 1.5 hours to experience it all. Whoever wrote this game is really good, my solute to this person I hope to play more games from him. It has a happy ending where Sam stays with a clear name, able to embrace the life he used to dodge with family and friends around. It also has sorrow ending where a loved one is gone leading to more unbearable misery but people being stronger. Lose or gain, through my 8 hours of gameplay I understand life is always about ups and downs, it can be hard to expect what is coming next, and it can happen fast. No one is perfect but together people stand stronger. I especially love the idea that Sheriff shares at the end: When we are born God puts an angel and a demon in us, and through life we see they fight over, mostly the angel wins and occasionally the demon takes control. So true, aren't we all humans? I find many words in this game very meaningful. Also, interesting to see the true ending, the real mastermind behind the crime.Fab game, worth replay. The detective part is interesting, Twin Mirror is very balanced, I recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Twin Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: ORIGINAL POST & REVIEW - 01-05-2024:Picked-up recently Twin Mirror (for Steam) from January 2024 Humble Choice by Dontnod...and also just finished my 1st playthrough of it. After 8.2 hours or so, this one's in the books and delivers a really good murder-mystery cinematic-adventure game here in the Choose Your Own Adventure style, which is no surprise given Dontnod's pedigree (i.e. see the original Life Is Strange).You play as Sam, who is an investigative reporter, who returns to this small-town of Basswood, in which many in the town aren't happy with him for something he did way in the past. Also, the small-town is financially hitting hard times, given what's been going on there, without heading too far into Spoiler Turf.Sam's brother recently died, which leads to him investigating that, as a lot of pieces here don't even add up. Not only that, his ex-girlfriend lives here and Sam often has conversations with another more Social and out-going version of himself - and I'll leave a lot of the story there at that & even gameplay stuff about that out, so I don't head into Spoiler Turf, since the story and chooses should be experienced for yourself; it's a good one.Sam often has this place called The Mind Palace, where he can take care of interesting matters. He can relive old memories, plan out strategies on how to manipulate situations and events ahead of time like it's a game of chess, and even re-create scenes from piecing evidence together. Besides the decisions-making, these are mostly the puzzles & real interesting stuff in the game, which are always real cool, interesting, and/or trippy.While I do wish there was more of these Mind Palace memories, puzzles and/or decisions, but what's there is always great and interesting - it's one of the best aspects of this game, to go along with the story & CYOA stuff (Choose Your Own Adventure) stuff. I should note that none of these puzzles are difficult, so...if you're looking for something like Myst or Riven type of hard, this isn't that type of adventure game.The story, character development, voice-acting, and anything pertaining to that stuff is definitely on point & really good. While the graphics technically isn't going to win awards here, everything is absolutely fine in that regard and executed solidly. I also even on my 3060m-based laptop (with also R5 5600H, 16GB RAM, 1TB SSD, W11) did not have any performance issues here, easily at a stable locked-45fps on my side. This isn't an action 60fps type of game and didn't need it, IMHO - so I was lazy and didn't change any of those framerate-locking stuff over in MSI Afterburner. Didn't have any stutters, performance issues, or anything here at 1080p at 45fps - and yes, this was maxed-out in its settings; this was butter smooth here.It's possible I'll give this another run-through, as I didn't really get probably the "best" sort of ending with how everything turned out in the end, even though this game probably has multiple endings, especially given how there feels like a few key decisions can be made very close to the end and at the end - but all of the pieces fit well & were executed very well with lots of impact and emotion, by the end of my playthrough.Regardless, after 8.2 hours on my 1st playthrough - yes, this is another really good murder-mystery/cinematic-adventure game with decision-making here from Dontnod. If a murder-mystery & cinematic=style CYO adventure sounds up your alley, you'll like this; I know I did. This is an easy recommendation, especially since it's in the $12 bundle and/or if you can catch this on sale. It was pretty good, to say the least - and I really enjoyed this one.

_childDocuments_.review: Yes, you can play this game in VR using the completely FREE Unreal Engine VR mod by Praydog. You do have to use synchronized sequential though to get it to look its best. Performance was actually pretty good on my RTX 3080. I used an Xbox one controller, although I imagine you could use motion controllers as a gamepad as well.There were some minor issues though. The biggest one is that sometimes the camera pans to areas that block your view. That happens more than you'd think, but only during the cinematics. The other big issue is that the searched items are kind of small in VR and can be difficult to spot. You're really pixel hunting in VR although since I haven't played this game in pancake, I can't say that this problem is only in VR.Other than that, I would say this game is an underrated gem. I can't figure why it doesn't have a positive review overall score on Steam. It may be a bit pricey considering it can be beat in less than 7 hours. However, you can probably find on a deep discount nowadays on Steam. So as long as you buy it on sale, there really isn't any reason to complain about content versus price.It's a good detective story. The story doesn't meander. It is well focused. I would say the characters are pretty realistic overall. It's a slice of small town life mixed with a murder mystery / thriller. I think it's underrated.

_childDocuments_.review: Twin Mirror is an example of a Studio having a good track record but still somehow managing to drop the ball. Even if you overlook the surface level negativities such as the poor voice acting and short playtime (about 5 hours) you run into much more deep-rooted issues.I do not know anything about the development of this game so I will not speculate on what could have happened but it just feels hollow, voiceless and muddled about what it is trying to achieve.
_childDocuments_.name: Twin Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: You play as Samuel, a journalist who have some mental challenges and an imaginary friend that is the best wingman one could ever wish for. The story is centered around a small town where a mining industry had to shut down following an article you published about the lack of security and protection for the workers. Not only did you have to receive hate from a lot of people who lost their jobs, but your girlfriend declined to marry you, so you decided to leave town. But, you return after two years for your best friends funeral, Without spoiling the story, you find the need to investigate your friend’s death, and that leads you to a much bigger discovery. Together with your imaginary friend, and your mental powers, you start your investigation, and the choices you make (actions and dialogues) matter towards the ending of the game. So the gameplay is similar to games like Heavy Rain and Quantum Break (I highly recommend them if you haven’t played them yet). You scan the environment for clues and solve minor puzzles, and depending on how well you do, you get one of several endings.
_childDocuments_.name: Twin Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: In their first self-published title, DON’T NOD decided to take their proven formula of choice-based games in a more mature and dark way, improving on various fronts while leaving some persistent problems hanging.Although it started as initially gripping, the game falls into a terrible mistake: it utilizes too many ideas and mechanics, only to never fully adhere to even one. What begins as an intriguing murder mystery ends with one of the most lackluster endings I've ever seen, brimming with unfulfilled potential but also some highly valuable elements.In Twin Mirror, we walk in the shoes of the formal investigative reporter Samuel Higgs, who - after two years of absence - returns to his birthplace, Basswood. However, the reason behind his visit is far from idyllic - his best friend, Nick, whom he has known since his youth, tragically passed away recently in a car crash. To make his visit even more perplexing, Sam isn’t exactly a welcomed member in the town: two years ago, an article he penned made the local mine shut down, making many people jobless. After this and a failed marriage proposal, Sam decided to leave the town for good - and originally never planned to return.Naturally, Sam only wanted this visit to last for a day - however, he quickly finds himself to be the center of many people’s attention, including both his ex-girlfriend and his late friend’s daughter, who all want one thing: to learn the truth about Nick’s accident.If this alone wasn’t enough reason to stay, a series of events tailored with a drunken night would make Sam a potential murder suspect… And thus, the investigation begins, which, at the start of the game, is a real treat for every aspiring sleuth. While the opening scenario isn’t anything novel, the story manages to go in some quite interesting directions with multiple twists and intriguing turns. The initial and highly idyllic image of the beautiful riverside town soon starts to fade into something more dark and wicked.But not just Basswood - people Sam has known for ages all seem to have secrets buried deep within them, especially our late friend, Nick.In my eyes, each form of media that mainly revolves around investigation heavily depends on the climax of the story. If the revelation itself isn’t executed well, even an overall good story can leave an underwhelming experience - and this is exactly what happened with Twin Mirrors.The story kept me well-entertained until the very end: while some occasional hiccups and a few smaller flaws bugged me, I was truly curious how the story would end. Simply saying that the final confrontation was underwhelming would be an understatement: it was one of the worst scenes I’ve ever witnessed in a video game, and definitely by far the most disappointing end for me to finish a story. Allowing more time for the story to unfold would’ve definitely helped the game overall, but to fix an ending like this, it wouldn’t have been enough. As with most other DON’TNOD games, the gameplay mostly revolves around exploration, interacting with different objects and people, and making - sometimes smaller, sometimes more major - decisions. But that’s not all - mechanics include the heavily underutilized mind palace and the completely redundant ‘chasing’ sequences, among others.The developers definitely learned the lessons from their previous games, because investigating Basswood and its surroundings proved to be an amazing experience. Each level is richly detailed - whether we are in a forest or in the center of the town, every location feels believable and alive. The signature stylized graphics look as nice as ever, minus the notorious lip-syncing issues. Often, you can find various documents or props scattered through the levels that won’t progress the story further but will give you some insights about the past or the other characters. Secrets can also be found, including memories and personal objects that will all enrich the narrative.One tool that Sam utilizes in his investigations is a place called the mind palace. This is a complex and ever-changing structure that lives in his head, and it exists as a way to determine how an event unfolded in time and to connect the accompanying evidence. While this could’ve been easily the main part of the game, it sadly turned out to be quite modest feature-wise, since it gives you zero freedom and essentially holds your hand throughout the investigation, making you miss the eureka moments that are so important in a game like this.Making decisions isn’t as relevant as in their previous games - many of them only change some minor things in the chemistry between the characters. Decisions directly influencing the four possible endings of the game mostly occur at the very end of the narrative, making them feel a bit weightless and unnecessary. Making this title a fully linear experience would’ve been a totally reasonable choice as well.Sometimes another perspective can help in a decision-making situation. In moments like this, Sam’s twin comes to help and offers some options you can explore (but don’t think of him as like in a Dr. Jerkyll and Mr. Hyde way). His presence is a mystery in itself - which will get explored to some extent, but his existence is utterly useless in my eyes. As with a number of other things in this game - it has the potential to change the game for the better, but it isn’t put to full use.
_childDocuments_.name: Twin Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: By far the weakest Dontnod game I've played in every respect: plot, characters, settings, and game play. The visuals are nice but they feel really generic compared to the detailed world-building in their other games. The characters are dull. The plot is basic. There is the vague implication of neurodivergence in two of the characters but it doesn't really make sense. The game mechanisms (the Mind Palace and a sort of imaginary doppelganger called Him) don't really connect to the plot or add anything to the game play. Often the Mind Palace is just an annoying repeat of what you already know. And for a detective story, there's very little detection or deduction to be done. The options are illogical and your choices largely don't matter. There's no challenge to it - you can't really get the sleuthing wrong. Anyway, it was an adequate diversion for a few hours but I wouldn't recommend it. The other Dontnod games (Life Is Strange 1, 2 and True Colors; Tell Me Why) are a lot more sophisticated and if you're looking for a small-town detective mystery, The Painscreek Killings is much more satisfying.
_childDocuments_.name: Twin Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: "Twin Mirror" is a cinematic adventure game in a third-person 3D perspective. Story and gameplay are considerably weaker than in DontNod's other games, but still (just) decent enough to eke out a positive rating from me.You play Samuel Higgs, a reporter who tried to help improve the dangerous working conditions of coal miners in a contemporary US small-town, but ended up causing the shutdown of the mine and a subsequent economical crisis. You fled the town, but (at the start of the game) return after 2 years to attend the funeral of your former best friend. You talk to the town citizens, many of whom are either angry because you destroyed their livelihood, or disappointed and hurt because you left without saying a word. Pretty soon, you also get involved in a murder case, investigate further, and discover deeper entanglements. The two goals of a) patching things up with people you've hurt and b) exposing the criminals don't always align, you'll have to decide what's more important to you.Helping you (but sometimes also annoying you) is an imaginary twin that keeps making suggestions on how to handle certain situations. How you handle this twin, is the third main story arc of the game.Taken together, all this creates a mature, serious story that I found interesting to play through, but it's also a pretty hard sell in several regards. The guilt-ridden, self-doubting, socially handicapped main character isn't particularly likable or interesting, and he rarely shows emotions, which makes it harder to relate to him. I did not _dis_like him, but I felt more like a distant friend trying to help someone with personal issues, rather than "being" the character.  Additionally, the game's often drab atmosphere creates an uninviting world that many players simply won't enjoy immersing themselves in. There aren't many attempts to lighten things up with humor either.While I found the crime plot interesting enough, it is pretty straightforward, down-to-earth, and at least partially predictable. It starts very slowly, but then gets resolved in a sequence of scenes that feels rushed (due to the lack of detail), even though it rarely conveys a sense of urgency. There's also a surprising amount of carelessness in the storytelling - for example, the protagonist is worried about the police associating him with the murder, but leaves fingerprints all over the place.Most of the characters are believable, well-written, and as interesting as the "generic US small-town" setting permits, but you only interact with them once or twice and you cannot influence their paths much (if at all). You successively reveal background information about them, but this feels a bit like reading the developers' character concepts - the degree to which this information is actually implemented in the dialogs, is rather mediocre. Several side plots screamed for further development, but just fizzled out.The game has multiple endings, but while I enjoyed my playthrough and was satisfied with the ending, I did not feel compelled to explore other venues, which is rather unusual for me.In short - this game's story isn't bad, but it is surprisingly weak compared to the studio's other products, and on top of that, it doesn't even fully realize its own limited potential, because it seems to have been rushed to the finish line.Gameplay consists mostly of exploring small areas, finding clues. solving puzzles, and talking to NPCs. In the conversations, you sometimes have to choose between up to 4 options.The puzzles are very easy. They keep the player engaged, but don't detract from the story, and you can't really get stuck. With the exception of a confrontation toward the end, choosing incorrect solutions does not have any repercussions, the game simply lets you try again until you get it right.Unfortunately, the integration of some puzzles into the game world is oddly lackluster. One puzzle clumsily breaks the player's immersion by referring to the game's control scheme on an in-game document, the clue makes zero sense in the context of the game world itself. In another scene, the game forces you to callously destroy a beautiful sculpture while the artist is present - it keeps telling you that "there is no other option to create a distraction", but this is rubbish, the developers just didn't care to implement alternative solutions that would have been glaringly obvious in the presented situation.Some of the puzzles involve reconstructing an event in your imagination, which is very nicely implemented. You explore the area (in your mind), examine clues, decide on hypotheses of what they mean, and the game will then simulate the event based on your hypotheses. This will either explain the event correctly, or cause a contradiction (in which case you can change hypotheses and try again)."Twin Mirror" has fairly high production values, which is part of the reason why it still gets a recommendation from me. The graphics are fairly detailed, the art direction successfully recreated a realistic US small-town setting, the sound effects are fitting and enhance the atmosphere. Some animations look a bit unnatural, and the lip-syncing is a bit off (especially with regard to bilabials on some characters), but those are nitpicks that didn't affect my experience much. The music does an excellent job of supporting the atmosphere, creating drama where appropriate, but never pushing into the foreground.The voice-acting is believable and generally very good, conversations flow naturally, but some characters still feel lackluster due to weaknesses of the script. The kid (Joan) in particular sounds much too mature for her age, but that's how she was written. The protagonist often sounds very distant, but again, that's his personality.The game offers 4-step quality settings for textures, shadows, AA, effects, and post-processing. Separate volume sliders for SFX, music, and voice let you finetune your audio experience. Subtitles can be adjusted in size and contrast. Four save slots exist, and there's an in-game function for copy/pasting save states between them, which is a brilliant idea that I would like to see other games pick up.While the above gives the impression of a polished product, the controls are unfortunately terrible. To interact with an object, you need to approach it until a mouse prompt appears, press and hold the left mouse button, and then press a directional key to select the desired action. If you're too far away, get too close, or aren't quite coming from the angle that the game wants, the mouse prompt won't appear. Since there are also purely cosmetic elements that never have a mouse prompt, I often kept wondering if a given object was non-interactive or if I just wasn't approaching it the "right" way. Additionally, when you try to press directional keys to select an action, the game sometimes interprets this as a movement command, and you can't actually interact with the object even though the prompts are right on the screen. Finally, leaving an investigation screen sometimes left my camera perspective stuck until I entered and left the main menu. You can rebind keys, but when I did that, the directional dialog controls stopped working, so I played with default controls.The clunkiness of this interface is a shame for a product with otherwise high production values. This feels like an unnecessarily convoluted control scheme that was developed first and foremost for gamepads, and then ported half-heartedly to PC without much effort or testing.Even though it falls disappointingly short in several regards, I think the game's story and high production values still warrant a careful recommendation. I'd wait for at least a 50% off sale though - and if you played other DontNod games before, rein in your expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for January 2024, and this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before February 6th, 2024, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.Another unique story from DONTNOD.DONTNOD is a company best known for Life Is Strange and Life is Strange 2, but also Remember Me, Vampyr, and Tell Me Why.  Twin Mirror fits in with Life is Strange, and Tell Me Why introduces players to Sam, an investigative journalist who returns to town due to his best friend dying though there is a clear estrangement. But Twin Mirrors is like most DONTNOD Games where it sets up a compelling story and interesting characters early on, as well as hinting at larger and deeper truths.  In the first hour, all I can think about is how I want to know more and unravel some of the larger stories here, and also I will say around an hour in there’s a huge moment, which opens up a ton of new questions. On the other hand, this is a narrative adventure… AKA “Choices matters game” as Telltale makes, and I’ve seen enough of these to tell you, that your choices won’t truly matter, it might change the path but there’s almost always going to be one or two possible endings in the final chapter, which isn’t a bad thing, considering when choices do matter and are spread out over the entire game, that means a 6-hour replay to see a slightly different scene.   Also, some of the targeting on this game was a little frustrating, hopefully, those were only issues early on.  Finally, the mind palace idea sounds great, but then there was a rather weak running down a corridor challenge that was quite bad.Pick this up if you like DONTNOD’s previous work. As I said, their character development and how they build mysteries is a big selling point here, and I’m curious how it pays off, but I also get why some people aren’t huge fans of this genre, and that’s ok too.  If you enjoyed this review or want to know what I think of other games in the bundle, check out the full review on or subscribe to my Youtube channel:

_childDocuments_.review: How far are you willing to go in your search for the truth? What can you do once you find it? Will the reality also result in closure, no matter how inconvenient and damaging it can be? The answers left a bittersweet taste for me but I admit that I wouldn’t have wanted anything less from a detective story that’s truly bordering the neo-noir subgenre without any of its inherent  clichés. DONTИOD Entertainment makes a triumphant return to game development with this self-published title which earned its spurs on Epic Games in 2020, before unifying its episodic format for the definitive edition of Twin Mirror on Steam in late 2021.The protagonist isn’t plagued by any crippling vices or influenced by any damsels in distress. There are also no obvious elements of absurdity or fever dreams like you’d find in Deadly Premonition, for example. Twin Mirror is more akin to Alan Wake in certain narrative aspects, yet the horror elements are more subtle since we’re talking about murders involving people instead of shadow monsters. Subtlety is the keyword here. No caricature characters or shower scenes either, so we can dismiss any David Cage influences. Twin Mirror is no Twin Peaks, in spite of the title similaties. And for an entirely fictional small town, Basswood manages to recreate the feeling of a place that has long since passed its glory days. The setting is as important as the game’s diversified cast. A Virginian former mining town is in search of a new identity. With a “gentle push”, it could escape uncertainty and depopulation.Sam Higgs fled Basswood as it was a dead end to both his career and personal life. Returning for a funeral, the freelance journalist which still treasures the hard-hitting truth that previously landed him in hot water, also realizes that the death of a former colleague is shrouded in mystery and a hastily concluded investigation. Getting to the bottom of this story shall reveal just how convoluted certain events can become depending on one’s outlook and approach. You see, our hero faces an internal struggle with his alter ego in regards to being less analytical and more empathetic with those around him. Players will have the final say, as they shape this private investigation and the protagonist’s interactions with former friends and local authorities. Choices bear far-reaching consequences. And few things are as clearly cut as they’re initially presented. Asking the right questions may not lead towards the answers you were looking for. As with DONTИOD’s previous projects, Twin Mirror is also skillfully powered by the Unreal Engine 4 without any technical issues to report by yours truly. The visual style is more similar to “Tell Me Why” than “Life is Strange”s comic book influences. Disabling the subititles (or never using them at all), can allow plenty of opportunities for beautiful screenshots. It’s a cinematic experience, after all. I managed to capture over 100 images in my single playthrough taken to completion. As I shall detail below, the story branches to such an extent as requiring a replay at a later date, if you want to experience everything Twin Mirror has to offer.  No glitches, bugs or crashes shall deter you. A photo mode would have been welcome, but you can always return to previously completed chapters in order to take in the sights.The voice acting is on par with the visuals. Professional voice actors sound convincing, while the soundtrack also maintains the gloomy atmosphere that marks the majority of Twin Mirror’s unfolding events. I couldn’t find an instance in which I might have been annoyed by the game’s sound department. There’s no lack of enthusiasm in the line delivery either. That’s certainly not the rule of thumb when working with child actors, but the dev team’s experience is clearly shown in their casting choices.Circumstantial evidence, conflicting testimonies and the generally suspicious behavior in some of Basswood’s residents, all paint a complex conspiracy which our hero has a chance to unravel or even bury further into obscurity, if the players choose to. To say that the ending can change a lot considering the plethora of options and interactions, would be an understatement. Twin Mirror’s Steam Achievements hint at this, yet you must be aware that it will take two full playthroughs in order to complete this title 100%. You cannot “cheese it” by simply restarting a few key chapters to alter the endings. The commitment is worth it and I do consider that veritable replay value. Be thorough in your investigation.Interviewing / interrogating NPCs is half the fun, since afterwards you must also piece together the puzzles formed from clues and statements. I wish there would have been more room for mistakes here. The term “lying by omission” was perfectly exemplified in LA Noire. Being a superficial investigator still solved the cases, even if in a rather unsatisfactory manner. It would have presented another facet of reality as journalists and detectives alike have to deal with setbacks in their perpetual search for the unapologetic truth.Returning to Sam’s inner conflict, you will have to interact with both his sharply dressed alter ego and Higgs’ own “Mind Palace” which sounds and looks exactly what you’d expect if you’ve seen the Sherlock reboots featuring Benedict Cumberbatch. You will have to eventually make a hard decision in regards to the investigative approach, but early on you can experiment and settle for whichever method suits you better. You can definitely roleplay as a cold-hearted private eye or a concerned citizen trying to lend a hand without offending anyone. Turning a blind eye and skipping town is also a valid option. Freedom of choice which confirms the age old adage attributed to Edmund Burke: In case you’re wondering if there’s a romantic silver lining even for this murder mystery, yes, there is a subplot you can freely explore and that will certainly shape the protagonist’s final choices. I’m glad that the story isn’t ending in a cliffhanger, though sequels should never be ruled out in this day and age of remasters and reboots. Twin Mirror sticks to its proverbial guns with an original tale still tailored by player decisions. If you’re a fan of plot twists, all the better. Save some for a future playthrough. I sure will. It’s been an eye-opening journey.+ Steam Achievements.+ Beautiful graphics & sounds.+ Compelling storyline and characters.+ Replay value through freedom of choice.- Not enough room for investigative error.- No Steam Trading Cards.

_childDocuments_.review: Imagine you're walking through your apartment and your roommate is watching the hot new Netflix original series that is totally impossible to find via a simple Google search of its title. It's called something like "Before" or "Between" or "The Time". Some generic title like that. They don't want the show to be found because they know it's bad. Now imagine you sit down with your roommate and start watching the show 3 episodes in.That's Twin Mirror. This game is so unremarkable in every way, shape, and form that it's actually impressive - especially coming from Don't Nod, who have a knack for creating stories that are genuinely special, even if just in little ways. The character dynamics feel wrong, the dialogue being things people don't say (again, something Don't Nod definitely improved on after the first Life is Strange), and the characters are mostly forgettable and pointless. There are a dozen characters that just add nothing to the narrative.And then there's Sam. Sam is the biggest piece of ♥♥♥♥ protagonist and I found myself actively HOPING for him to die. Characters look to him for guidance and protection despite his entire character arc *before* and *during* this game's narrative demonstrating that he is not worthy of those things. There's a notable section of the game about going to a commune of homeless recovering addicts and Sam looks at one of these people and decides he should destroy her artistic outlet entirely and possibly burn down the shelter she has while endangering everyone else... So he can talk to a guy that he could talk to if he just walked in another direction.The biggest choice in the game, at the end of course, is also poorly telegraphed. The entire concept of "Him" (Sam's imaginary friend, who is very excitingly just some boring white twink version of himself) feels like a poor demonstration of masking. And in the final choice, you're given a cloudy description of whether you want this ♥♥♥♥♥♥ unlikable (in a bad way) protagonist to unhealthily integrate into society in one way or another way. Either way, the entire choice is about deciding how a neurodivergent man should fit into society.This game is bad. Stick with Don't Nod's other games (maybe skip Life is Strange 2, as well) if you want a meaningful narrative with good characters. They all have shortcomings, but the heart of each shines through and makes those flaws acceptable. This game just sucks. And damn they were so proud of getting a license for Pac-Man for this slop.

_childDocuments_.review: Twin Mirror is a short story-driven game that shifts and manipulates time. You play as Sam, who returns to the town of Basswood for the funeral of his friend, Nick. Sam keeps questioning how Nick could have died until he eventually uncovers that his friend was murdered. Throughout the game, you get guidance from your imaginary friend to help with decisions, though it’s up to you whether to listen to him or not. Every decision you make affects the storyline that you actively shape. I didn't expect such a well-crafted story game in around 9 hours. The story is excellent, and interacting with it is also great, I rate the story very highly. On the downside, I’d say the graphics could use some improvement, they’re not bad, but something feels lacking. Overall, I would rate Twin Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: A game from DON'T NOD that fell completely under the radar. I just accidentally stumbled upon it and for an accidental stumble, it's pretty good! Starts out with a kind of Twin Peaks/Alan Wake vibe, if a small town mystery is your thing,. However, ends up somewhere sort of predictable and unexciting. This game lets your mind run wild with possibilities and then reels you back into normality as you realize there's not as much cool stuff going on as you thought there would be. Less... magic, or whatever. Well, none, really, just a guy that sometimes gets lost in his own imagination. That said, it does some visually interesting things (reminded me heavily of Control) and I did enjoy the process of collecting clues and putting crime scenes back together. Even though the game fell short of what I hoped it would be, I really enjoyed it. Played with a friend, took us a little under 7 hours to complete. Would recommend only buying the game on sale - both for the length, and because it's not exactly the most memorable or moving game experience you've ever had.

_childDocuments_.review: So, I did like this game, but it is a little rough around the edges.First of all, it does not feel as polished as the 'Life is Strange' games and it is pretty short.But gameplay-wise, it is a little more interesting than at least the first LiS-game. I liked the adventure-ness of it all, but then again, I grew up a Point & Click Adventure nerd, so maybe it's just me. The riddles were a little superficial and rather easy to solve, but at least there are some other things to do here than just to walk around.The decisions in this feel a little meh. They rarely have actual consequences (apart from a few towards the ending) and feel pretty flat.My biggest issue with this game is that is has no real premise. It isn't sure what it wants to say and that leaves a void. It doesn't take a clear stand on where it stands on mental health or happiness vs. truth seeking or doing the right thing vs. doing the easy thing. Pretty much everything is up for interpretation and that's what makes the story fall short.The first 2/3 of the game, I really enjoyed myself. It was like watching a rather decent detective show in an overall interesting setting with some average characters. The last third felt a little random to me and the 'whodunit' of it all was too obvious.Visually, this is pretty, but nothing close to 'LiS True Colors'.All in all: This was a nice playthrough. I enjoyed myself. Some things bugged me.If you want a short little playtrough of something while you're lying around sick (like me when I played this), it's some solid light entertainment that won't worsen your headache. If you're willing to look past the weird mixed messaging on mental health. SPOILER:Because honestly: Choosing hapiness and choosing being 'different' aren't opposites.

_childDocuments_.review: Another 'Life Is Strange'-esque game from Don't Nod.The twist here is that the protagonist has a manifest part of his conscience that he can commune with. Throughout the game the player will have to choose between expressing between two social paths for the protagonist.On one hand you can be analytical with a Sherlock Holmes style 'mind palace' but at the cost of becoming less empathetic, while on the other hand you can listen to your ulterior conscience and become more sociable and happy but at the cost of greater analytical skills.The first play-through (and its definitely Don't Nod's shortest offering) is great, with a satisfying story and interesting characters. Additionally the permutations of the ending are great and fun to experiment with however the main flaw comes with the poor execution of replay-ability.As per usual with these games the choices don't  make the biggest of changes other than certain decisions near the end and due to the inability to skip cut-scenes or fast forward to certain points, getting through the subsequent play-throughs can be a bit of a slog.Overall I would say there is definitely wasted potential when it comes to the lack of permutations/changes through different play-throughs (other than the ending) but would recommend when its on a sale as a short, fun narrative thriller.
_childDocuments_.name: Twin Mirror

_childDocuments_.review: Another pretty decent Choice-based "detective" game from DontNod. Not too harsh on system specs either.Visually appealing and strikingly beautiful as usual along with nice BGMs wherever possible.Overall, somewhat decent story-line, not too long or short (6-7 hrs, as long as you don't waste wayyy too much time on making certain important "situation" decisions). Focuses and bulks massively on internal monolgue and so-called "mental mazes". Probably a game that focused wayyy too much on just "directly important/objective" stuff than actually letting the story unfold in its own flow. Quite a shallow (almost anti-climatic) ending with not much you can really do except for listen to the ending narration and LET IT END. Probably a bit more work into the story would've brought out the potential for a "detective" game.Another main issue I have always had with such Choice-based games is not having a way to skip repeated dialogues or scenes. (Tests my patience every time, ughh!). But at least they had a way of "running" (AKA brisk jogging if you may).Quite enjoyable game and can definitely be tried more than once if you wanna get multiple/ALL endings. (I haven't yet, but "might" go back to it once I've forgotten the story enough to not get boring along with the unskippable unwanted interactions, lol). Might take some grind and research to get ALL mementos and memories. So, replayability depends on you being a perfectionist achiever.Will recommend trying out once for striking visuals if nothing else matters (especially if you get it on sale like me!)

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I only finished this game once and haven't seen more than one of the endings.Twin Mirror is a short CYOA game, clocking about 5-6 hours long. Despite the length, I think it turned out alright. The theme remains consistent and doesn't feel like any scene is a filler. It's a small package that does what DONTNOD does well. The landscape, the lighting, the soundtracks and ambient sounds, the aesthetics, the vibes, and the supernatural scenes, all of these would already justify the game's purchase already.However, there are still some issues that can't escape the curse of being a DONTNOD game. First, the facial animations still look unnatural. This problem persisted and still does since Life is Strange 1. It's not as noticeable in this game, but if you're not always looking at the subtitles, you'll know what I mean. It's mostly because of how static a character's face and muscles on it are, even for a casual conversation. It's a running issue for DONTNOD's games ever since they started making CYOA games, I wish they can figure it out soon. Second, some dialogues are poorly written or mistranslated. It's not as bad in this game, most of the lines feel natural, even some emotional lines were delivered beautifully, but the bad are definitely jarring when you hear it. Even for a non-native like me can point one out right away.Don't get this wrong, I think this game is a good game. It's a story driven game, no more than 6 hours long, with a very relatable concept and good visuals. It's a solid buy on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I can only recommend this game at historic low price to gamers who think an occasional novel concept in a game matters more than being able to feel for the characters, like I feel. This is the most mediocre third person story game I've completed. Also, if you expect this to be an AAA branching story game like Life Is Strange (by the same devs) or Detroit, functionally or visually, you will be disappointed, because it is more like an indie effort (it is self published). Twin Mirror's novelties are not elaborate, because the game can be completed in as little as 5 hours unless you get stuck finding something thats required to progress. There are very few things I found to be great, though there isn't much that I found to be really bad about it. The game plays out somewhat like a movie, and not an open world or adventure, in how it is a bit more on-rails in terms of being locked to a certain location until you do/find something or not being able to talk to someone until something else happens.Here is what you need to know, spoiler free:?The protagonist, Sam, is bland which can make it tough to connect or relate to him, but that's his personality since he talks with his own social and empathic side, and it becomes obvious quick that he's not normally either quality. So that weirdness is important when he returns to his hometown.+The other characters are a bit more hit than miss for me in terms of caring about them, but their acting was always well done for small town characters.?Use of Unreal Engine 4 was a mixed bag. Mouth animations were somewhat weak, but visuals were otherwise decent. FPS is randomly locked for scenes at 60 FPS, and toggling VSYNC will unlock it, but in a different scene it will lock again. I couldn't tell much of a difference between 60 and more FPS since the game is mostly dialog and there isn't much "action" in terms of on lots of screen movement.-There are only automatic save points, which will result in a loading animation in the lower right, the game wont tell you when you last saved if you try to exit the game, and the saves should be more often. I talked with characters for 5-10 minutes in one of the scenes near the beginning, and when I quit I had to either go through the dialog again or skip it and hope that wasn't a choice in & of itself.+Investigation occasionally has a neat mechanic called Mind Palace where after finding clues, you reconstruct a scene where something happened. It was used a good number of times for how long the game is, but I would've enjoyed playing the game longer if there were more mind palaces.+I like and its unique how the game focuses almost as much on the protagonist's inner self, emotions, and struggles as the game does on the investigation plot. It manifests this in different parts of the game in a couple of different ways.?You have as much time as you want to make choices, with the exception of choices where someone is talking on and on, and you have the choice to interrupt them or not. Not choosing an option is the same as listening to whoever the camera is focused on.?After each major scene/chapter, the menu has a journal option which shows info you have learned about every character, documents the prior choices you made for each individual completed chapter, and gives the % of global or friends players that made the same choice.?After playing through the whole game once, any chapter can be revisited, and different choices can be made.-Mouse controls are not intuitive, controller was better, because with mouse either I had to click at the same time I press a keyboard button or the camera position I would need to get the prompt to view or interact with something was often awkward. Camera positioning was slightly less awkward with controller.?Most dialog options as well as choices seem to affect relationships more than they affect actual events, but the status of some relationships will absolutely affect at least a few key events, because there are a few pieces of inner dialog that reflect on this.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought Twin Mirror on sale for a little over £5, and for that price, I'll recommend it.It's an evocative choice-based game by DontNod, and features a similar mechanic to the memory concept in Remember Me, Life Is Strange, and Tell Me Why, this time in the form of a Mind Palace that allows players to access memories and explore potential consequences of their actions.It also introduces a 'split personality/invisible friend' plot device, which provides a context for certain choices. From the promotional videos this looks like a strong, ambitious concept, but it falls short in its execution, with a predictable plot and limited impact of player choices. It feels far less refined than LiS, so it's surprising that this title is the more recent release.Despite its flaws, Twin Mirror offers an acceptable one-time, casual gaming experience for a discounted price, and it's a good introduction to this genre. At full price, or if you've played any of the other titles, there's a good chance you'll be disappointed. If you're looking for a more engaging and thought-provoking choice-based detective game with a dark flavour, Disco Elysium is one better option.

That last one may be an intentional character choice but it's not really enjoyable to watch.I got what I think is a good ending, though it's honestly hard to tell.First chapter is the most boring and it takes a long time to get sucked in, but I was at least curious enough to finish the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I started up Dontnod's "Twin Mirror". It's no traditional point 'n click  but other than moving the main character around with the arrow keys, I'm still pointing and clicking stuff 😃I'm really pulled into this story. It's like I don't have any hard time at all identifying with the main character.I'm Sam Higgs, former journalist of a local newspaper, who left town after my girlfriend broke up with me and the residents blamed me for the local mine, the biggest employer in the region, going out of business after writing a devastating article about its bad condition. It was either expose what was wrong with it and forcing it to shut down, or keeping silent and waiting for disaster to strike, killing lots of people probably which would force a shutdown anyway.My best friend Nick has been killed in a car crash, and I return to the town to pay my respects. Once back, I'm reunited with my best friend's daughter, who thinks he was murdered instead, and my ex girlfriend, who apparently started a relationship with Nick after I left, and some other familiar local faces.I've got a constant companion, origins yet unknown, but he's like a Clark Kent version of myself, a twin if you will, residing in my mind. He's always giving me advice and commenting on my actions and decisions. I have to talk to people, look for clues, then go into a "mind palace" where I relive my memories.This world with its characters is very real. It all plays out as a movie with great cinematography, actors, music. I don't feel like I'm playing a game, but I'm living as Sam simply making the best choices I can, pretty much acting as I would myself in his situation.The controls can get a bit wonky, since you're moving the camera instead of a cursor over the hotspots, and Sam has to be close enough to activate them. Then you can choose your verb action, but not all hotspots have them; some only show a description. Luckily a mouse icon appears when there are more possibilities, but I find myself often moving around hotspots trying to trigger that mouse icon, not really sure whether there is supposed to be one or not. This might be better if you're playing with a controller, though...3,5 hours into "Twin Mirror" the plot thickens. I'm enjoying almost everything about this game. Only annoying part is the strange arcade-like sequences Sam has to face in his mind palace. First one involved dodging doors, which was really hard without a controller. The second one was very much a QTE: locate one different form amongst a multitude, then quickly hit the right key before it disappears. In both sequences you have to do this a couple of times in a row, and if you miss one, you have to start from scratch.I always have a penchant for games taking place in a "real" world instead of a fantasy or futuristic one, so as far as the setting's concerned this game is right up my alley. I really like the story, but the controls using keyboard and mouse remain clunky. The entire setup doesn't so much follow other Dontnod games like "Life is Strange" and "Tell Me Why" but rather those of Quantic Dreams like "Fahrenheit/Indigo Prophecy" and "Heavy Rain".At first it feels there's a lot of freedom in this game, but if you prioritise wrongly, its linearity will prevent you to do the things you saved for later. Finished "Twin Mirror" in 8 hours! Had to make some difficult choices in the end. Not really satisfied with how things ended up, wondering if you can get a "perfect" ending in this game...It wasn't always obvious which consequences a particular choice would have. Other than your typical fork in the roads, you also have to choose how to respond to people in conversations.The investigation part of the game isn't that hard. You can only move forward once you found everything you need. Then in the mind palace where you reconstruct (or in some case PRE-construct) things, I don't know if it's possible to do something wrong there. As far as I can tell I always got it right. So I think the game always forces you to make the right decision; the puzzle is basically finding the right combination of parameters, a little bit like in Frogware's Sherlock Holmes games.I really liked the characters in this game and I feel like I've only scratched their surface. Don't Nod's got some great writers on board if they can pull in their players like this. I like these cinematic games with very human stories. They're like novels to me.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: This is simply a cross between "Detroit: Becoming Human", MINUS the photo-realistic graphics and the latest "Sherlock Holmes" title, MINUS the open world. It's mechanics are VERY clunky and its tech "oh hum" for 2022, but overall, it delivers a fairly compelling story at its own level.The game's premise here lifted straight from "Holmes". A detective with a uncanny ability to see every detail about every object and 'read people' suffers from deep-seated character flaws and has... a twin brother in his head. Sounds familiar? It should be. At times I had to double check I wasn't playing "Holmes".The game has no branching to speak of - there are 5 endings yes, but all are decided at the very end of the game. In the last 5 minutes of it in fact. You will likely not get the one you expected or went for. Since these are the only branches, youtube is your friend. This is unlike "Detroit: becoming human" which had such as complex branching storyline that no amount of youtube would have been enough to recreate the experience of it. In other words, it's not innovative on that front either.Some worry that the game is 'woke'. It honestly isn't. There are references to a character who might be woke but that character never behaves in a way that's offensive to those that would be on the more 'traditional' side of things.The game loop is an absolute copy of "Holmes" - you arrive at a scene, collect evidence, then reconstruct the crime based on a series of hypotheses. It's click for click the SAME game, until it returns to the 'linear' storyline in 3rd person view akin to "Detroit".A big flaw of its game is its VERY awkward control scheme, something that earned it a lot of negative reviews. Sometimes, you can observe an object in detail, sometimes not! They build this awkward menu that appears only when you're at the EXACT distance needed and comes and goes, frequently annoyingly so, leading you to miss on important facts for no reason. Example: - so much so that if your character (always in 3rd person) faces the element in question, the menu will not be visible!SUW is NOT supported at all. Sure you can run the game in SUW, but the game will become unplayable. At times, menus won't be available at all - you're likely to miss half the clues if running this in SUW, and sometimes you'll be totally blocked. Finally there's the performance impact of a game not designed/optimized for SUW - we're talking a drop to 10fps average from a 160fps average at 'standard' resolutions. Shame, because SUW is on to good effect, you get this Tarantino-esque anamorphic feel you don't get in any other type games (Panini projection perhaps).They need to patch this - but likely will never do so.RT is totally absent, and therefore there is no need for any type of DLSS tech. Video optiosn are seemingly all but missing outside of the very basics. In-game mirrors do but look ... pixelated and do not track your head movement. The game has this weird "uncanny valley" feel throughout. Texture varies between 'oh hum' and 'bad for 2022'. Geometry is equivalently disapointing, and so are characters meshes.Clocking at 7h if you're taking your time, and 6h if you go just for the basics (my 11 is from messing with graphic setting for this review), It's evident you should buy instead the two titles it's directly lifted from. Graphic fans will be very disapointed and the lack of SUW, HDR and RT is disheartening in a world were some walking simulators such as "Observer: System Redux" have best-in-class graphics.As for this game, it's a VERY timid thumb up - as long as you can get it on discount and expect a basic story within a basic game engine.

_childDocuments_.review: Twin Mirror~~~~~~~~~~Twin Mirror is a brand-new Choices-Matter, Crime-Drama that revolves around our protagonist, an ex-investigative journalist, Sam Higgs.Returning to his hometown of Basswood after his friend’s death, Sam Higgs finds himself tangled in the mystery behind the death as well as his own anxious, ill mind. Plot: As a story-driven, choices matter gameplay which revolves around the protagonist and the people around him.You start off in a car with Sam, trying not to be late for his friend’s funeral, yet still managing to be late after Sam decides to take a detour down memory lane. While stopping by a cliff overlooking his old town of Basswood, Sam Higgs’ mind takes over, and he is thrown right into a nostalgic lane full of the memories that he has been trying to avoid for so long.Here the game will hint as to how the gameplay is going to progress, but you won’t really get it until further along into the story.As an old friend keeps messaging to ask if Sam is going to make it or not, you will encounter your first choices regarding what to reply. Sam finally decides to visit his town, where is not welcome due to his work as an investigative journalist, exposing the lack of mining regulations, the major source of income for the town. Sam made a lot of people upset, and he will have to encounter these people further along with the story. The major plot starts as Sam is told that his friend’s death was no ordinary accident! Nothing adds up, and Sam is forced into extending his stay at Basswood. Now he must confront the people of Basswood and his mind at the same time, all the while trying to decipher the murder mystery. Gameplay: Twin Mirror is basically a walking simulator turned into an investigative crime drama. The game has two sides to it - 1. Where you’ll have to confront the reality around you and navigate through it all the while tolerating his twin unnamed imaginary friend. 2. Confronting your mind palace where you see both old memories and current surroundings, reconstruct scenes and replay them.Twin Mirror’s investigation scheme is as simple as it gets; you visit each and every corner of an area and talk to each person to uncover clues. During this process, it does take up a good amount of time per scene; the good thing is that the story is pretty good, and the bad thing is that every important character gets poor on-screen time.It’s enough to convey the scenes but not enough time to get to know the characters or relate to them. I believe the story writers could’ve done a better job at exploring some of the important characters further without taking up so much time. Controls: Twin Mirror’s control scheme is very straightforward and easygoing. Basic WASD movement and mouse controls with key combinations while doing investigation work. This is all fun and good, but I do wish the investigation controls here could be a bit smoother and with quicker response. You need to walk up to each character and clues, which, combined with the slow investigation, interaction and inspection does take a good amount of time. The nameless ghost: While Sam Higgs is roaming around the city in the present, an estranged nameless character keeps popping up from nowhere and confronting, confusing, and contradicting Sam’s thoughts and judgments. For the most part, this nameless character does its job quite well, but same as with every other character, the storytellers botched it.  This could’ve been one of the best characters of 2021, but missed the mark. Voice over and body language: The actors who played the characters did a phenomenal job at portraying each character and conveying the scenes. Each line of dialogue, no matter how impactful, dull, or misplaced, the voice-over work was on point. I wish I could say the same for the body language and movement of the characters, but sadly this was a big letdown.  The movements were slow and felt sluggish; even when performing simple turns it felt very wrong and out of place. Maybe this is something to consider for future updates! World Design: Twin Mirror is set in a quiet little town called Basswood. It’s a stunning town that feels both well lived-in and empty at the same time.Basswood’s weather is mostly dull and cloudy with the brief warmth of sunshine, which I loved, and I felt like this affected my immersion a lot. Music and sound effects: Twin Mirror offers a fine assortment of good music and tunes which definitely impacts the immersion and re-playability of the game, as the game comes with multiple endings.The same goes for all the sound effects. Rich and well done.Positives: +	Good story+	Strong character profile even though conflicted +	Simple yet effective gameplay+	Great voice-over work+	Good music +	Predictable, but a good drama to go through Negatives: -	Movement and interaction controls could be improved-	Body language could be improved -	Characters are not well explained or explored Conflicted on multiple fronts, help Sam Higgs during his investigations, conflicts, and self-evaluation. 8/10Key provided by the developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

_childDocuments_.review: Returning to a chapter in your life you’ve closed is never easy. Returning to it due to the death of your best friend Nick here in your hometown of Basswood, especially after burning the bridge is simply audacious. You play Sam Higgs, a former investigative journalist for the Basswood Jungle who left for 2 years after writing a piece that resulted in the closure of the town’s mine which made you plenty of enemies. A short stop to pay your respects turns into what could be the next big story to grace the small town after Nick’s daughter, Joan (Bug) pleaded with you to look into the death of her father with the help or deterrence of He, your emphatic Double that only exists for you.Twin Mirrors is a narrative adventure game that brings anything new to the table but has the fundamental parts and gameplay to the genre and does it very well. Relying heavily on it’s narrative strength Twin Mirrors manages to capture it’s visual storytelling with the environments and pieces in Basswood. You learn about characters by interacting with them, finding snippets of a note they leave behind, or items/momentos they lost or leave behind at locations, items they hid in locked drawers. Every information you interact with and find are then written in your journal that help fill out the bigger picture to the characters you meet.In every section of the game you’re able to explore the locations you’re in and learn about the story of what happened there and how it links to the overarching goal by interacting with objects and characters. Some items will have a special meaning to you and will bring you to your Mind Palace, where you recall and relive memories. The Mind Palace is also where you enter to deduce, understand and envision the outcome of the clues you find in order to solve mysteries and unanswered questions along the way.The characters you meet or live with makes Basswood more than a small isolated town. Your dialogue choice could help or hinder your goal in learning about important information. The interaction with He helps bring emotion to the otherwise logical but empty side of Sam. Anna is an epitome of dealing with the past to make good of the future even if it is uncomfortable. What makes Twin Mirrors an enjoyable game is the fact that DONTNOD knows the right amount to give the player in every moment of the game. No dialogue felt too long, no location inspection felt too big and aimless, no recreation of a scenario will swarm you with too many possibilities, nothing is stretched too far. When a game delivers you the right amount of everything, that’s when you initially feel content but soon after you’re hoping for more. And that’s how you keep fans coming back.

_childDocuments_.review: Very highly recommended. Just because a company designs a game a certain way doesn't mean all of their games have to exactly the same.
