_childDocuments_.review: A pretty (as expected with a Chinese Room game) with good music (as expected with a Chinese Room game) but it's also a very simple puzzle platformer with barely any puzzles just walking (also as expected with a Chinese Room game) and narration that tells a story (as expected with... I think you get the point by now). Make no mistake, this is a walking simulator disguised as a puzzle platformer, and while that's not automaticaly a bad thing it is in this case. While it looks pretty good, and the enviorments are nice and varied for the most part (but for the love of Gaben, cut down on the bloom effects next time...) the gameplay is mediocre at best, I could easily mention dozen games that does the same thing better. Each level have the exact same structure, you walk to the right have a few levers and cranks to interact with to open up the path ahead, a few QTE and then ends in a chase scene that works as a bridge to how you end up in the next area. The plot and framing device is alright I guess, it tries a bit too much to be funny but most of the jokes doesn't land. The controls are passable, but stiff and the animations are nothing to write home about. But it's not just mediocre gameplay that stands in the way, there are also a few very anoying marks against it. Many of the achievements are locked behind needlessly having to replay the levels since the collectables are only available on the second time you play it, for literaly no reason other than to pad the length of the gamne. They are also not hidden and you can't relly miss them (unless they get obscured by the insane amount of bloom...) so there are no exploration involved searching for branching paths or hidden nocks.  There are also a few times where the game broke and i respawned just to instantly die again, creating a loop. Had to restart the level (Happend once in level 4 and several times in 8, and I could recreate it so it wasn't a isolated incident)It's a mobile port, and as a mobile game it might be decent game, but I can't recomend this with so many other games that does the same thing as Little Orpheus, but better.
_childDocuments_.name: Little Orpheus

_childDocuments_.review: Everything I l o v e about video games: QTEs, mediocre and unchallenging platforming, unskippable cutscenes, unskippable long animations, actions that take 3 button presses to execute or the game has no idea if you actually wanted to do the thing and collectables that are there to force you to replay levels without the ability to skip custcenes.The jumping area is a nightmare. You need at least 5 meters of platform in front of you which mean you can't make tight turns and jumps. If you want to jump off a vine first you have to tap to have your character face a certain way (even if he already is) and they you are granted the ability to jump off. I've gotten bored of the cutscenes the moment I had to sit through the whole level 3 times. Maybe you enjoy cutscenes that consist of 2 people sitting at a table - I do not. At about level two you realise you can doomscroll on your phone while also playing the game. The soviet theme is about as deep as the puddle you get from slicing a tomato. Can't comment on the russian pronunciation of the interjected words, because I don't speak it nor on the referenced, possibly made up, russian writers. The only saving grace of this game is that it's fairly pretty. There is some really nice sets, some neat assets.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll keep this brief.The only positive thing I can say is that the game has nice looking locations with enough variety. _childDocuments_.review: A light-hearted, narrative focused, 2D/3D Platformer.From the same studio behind Dear Esther, Amnesia: A Machine For Pigs, and Everybody's Gone To The Rapture, a focus on narrative over much else is to be expected.The difficulty for this game ranges from Very Low to at most Medium. Automatic save spots are placed quite liberally, meaning that if you do experience a death or failure, you will have very little to replay to get back to that spot.The plot is out of this world, literally, and the script, characters, and sense of humour are perfect for this Pulp Sci-Fi tale inspired by books, comics, and films from anywhere between the 40s to the 60s.The soundtrack is perfect, Jessica Curry once again nailing it.The full game can be completed in around 4 hours, though if you're wanting to grab all achievements you will need to double this (I am at just under 8 hours for play time at time of writing), with each episode of the game (9 in total) taking anywhere from 15 to 25 minutes to complete.More linear games that are relatively quick & easy to complete, with a focus on narrative, and for a good price, are needed at the moment, and I'm happy to see The Chinese Room doing this.Definitely worth your time if you're looking for something light, simple, and narrative focused.

_childDocuments_.review: WARNING! Unplayable due to soft lock bug in later episodes!In the second to last episode, the game breaks at a certain point and instantly kills you with no regard for your hitbox.A bit later if you do everything correctly, the game decides that it is a failure state and counts you as dead and forces a restart, even if you are still alive and moving! Worst of all, is when you respawn on that broken part or in the air and continuously fall and respawn only to die again. Restarting the level does not fix it.The developers have abandoned this game.There is no fix ! ! !What a pity, because the game ain't that bad.It is quite short and easy, a relaxing experience with a lot of narration. Each level is unique and beautiful.Reminds me of much better games in the same genre like: "Planet Alpha" and "Black The Fall".If it had more puzzles and challenging gameplay like "Limbo" or "Inside" it would have been appreciated.The "Trine" series has combat, puzzles and very beautiful levels while also making you platform your way to the Right like all the mentioned games do.The Soviet storyline is the stereotypical parody but has authentic elements like the pop culture talk of that time.Those who know, will instantly realize the references. Guess it will fly over the heads of most Westerners.The whole game is ramblings of a madman, the most unreliable of narrators, so everything we see most probably did not happen. We basically are riding his dreams, that's the kind of game this is.Taking all these points into consideration:It would have been a passable run-of-the-mill little game but the game breaking bugs killed it for me.Skip this one until they fix.   (which will be never)

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a very good game. It's charming but it's not something I'd recommend. The Chinese Room's walking sims all have the same sort of problem and that's that they've never managed to fuse narrative into gameplay in interesting ways. They're overly reliant on audio logs and voice-over in general, and that's just not a terribly interesting way to get information or be told a story when you're playing a game. They've been awarded for their storytelling chops, which will always baffle me, but I digress. I don't have a problem with Walking Sims. But really, the way The Chinese Room approaches telling stories in their games has never felt compelling or fused in any sort of meaningful way. Little Orpheus looks like a platformer with some puzzles. It almost seems like Inside or Limbo but it's far less intricate or as masterful as those games. It's a walking sim wearing the skin of a puzzle platformer. Basically, there's the game you're playing and the conversation you're listening to and neither really complement or inform each other that well. The protagonist is being interrogated some time after the game's events and it functions as a way to tell you what to do next (which is kind of dumb, the game is chokingly linear) or give context to what's going on. But what's going on isn't all that terribly complicated so I just feel like I'm being described what I'm playing and I already know what I see because I'm playing it. Some of the sights and sounds are cool and the art team should be commended for putting in a lot of effort, keeping in mind this was originally a mobile game. However, the designers and the writers maybe should have worked on an alternate solution to merge the story they wanted to tell through gameplay. They're running parallel together, not as one.

_childDocuments_.review: I know the reviews are mixed and I agree with a bit of both sides, however I still recommend the game BUT want to let y'all know the details.The game has beautiful designs and a quirky/funny story to go along with it. The controls are very simple and a super easy game to complete. You are going to take about 30-ish minutes per episode and is a great game to play when you don't know what you wanna play.The game DOES crash A LOT during the 8th episode which really sucks, however I got around it by restarting the game every time it did crash until I got to the end. The story does get a bit repetitive or starts to lack luster after a bit. Also, if you are an Achievement Hunter, you HAVE to play through the game twice to receive all the achievements for the game and yes that includes the dreaded episode 8. The puzzles are not hard, which can turn people away, however like another reviewer stated it is basically a game to shut your brain down and just play. If you don't like that kinda game then I wouldn't recommend it to you.Finally, I did receive this game through a bundle, which if possible I would recommend. However, if not possible I would wait for a sale of some kind if you aren't too sure about the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Ivan Ivanovich is sent down below the Earth's crust in his capsule the "Little Orpheus" in an attempt to see if there really is land that humans can potentially habitat. 3 years later Little Orpheus is gone, the bomb powering the LO is gone, and now Ivan is being interrogated by General Yurkovoi and now we'll hear about where Ivan really was within these last 3 years and what really happened to Little Orpheus.Let's talk about the gameplay right off the back and uh well it's pretty much a walking simulator with very light puzzles and platforming. Nothing bad, but that's kinda all it is, the good thing with this though is that no matter how old or young you are you can jump right into the title without any real issue, heck you could play the entirety of the game with one hand if needed.Gameplay isn't the reason why you should be playing 'Little Orpheus,' you should be playing for the story and obviously the atmosphere. You go into these levels finding giant dinosaurs, navigating the stomach of a whale, finding a lost civilization, etc, etc, it's a really fun game to go through in this regard.The music is so good, just watch the trailer above, but it really does feel like something out of an Indiana Jones or even sometimes a Star Wars movie, like it is so good and one of the strongest things in Little Orpheus. The story again is good and I'm not gonna spoil it, but I also really love the old cartoon gimmick they do, at the end of each episode a narrator will say things like "Will our intrepid yet doomed hero survive the jaws of the ferocious dinosaur? Will he meet his end, miles underground as an aperitif for a ravenous raptor?" etc, but anyways it is just so fun for them to have done it this way, really does make you feel like a kid watching cartoons.  The dialogue between Ivan and Yurkovoi is also really funny at times, Ivan telling these extravagant yet unbelievable scenarios as Yurkovoi isn't buying s**t.I did experience a couple bugs here, not a lot, but it still wasn't a flawless playthrough. Episode 8 the last episode in the main game was where most of the issues happen. You reach a point where the game will spawn an additional Ivan, he doesn't do anything, but you'll continue through all fine and you will start to die, over and over until you eventually fall through the level where you need to quit and restart. After this is didn't happen again, but I can confirm this will happen as it did the exact same thing when I was playing through "The Lost Recordings' mode.Oh replayability, well, there is some. After beating each level you will be able to play these in "The Lost Recordings," you just play through each level collecting orbs, these orbs will grant you some costumes and some concept art of the game with Ivan giving commentary on these. You will not be needing a guide since the game is entirely linear and these orbs will be spawned right in front of you. The mode itself is kinda lame as it's just regoing through the game, but I really did enjoy unlocking the concept art and hearing the commentary from Ivan about different scenarios or "parts of the story he didn't get time to tell," would love to see more of this sorta thing in more games.The TL;DR: Little Orpheus is something I would indeed recommend...... ON A SALE. Yes the story is really good, gives you really great atmospheres, and funny banter between our hero Ivan and Yurkovoi. The gameplay however is a point where I see people just not wanting to grab it and it is understandable, there are people who simply don't like walking simulators no matter how good the story is. The game also takes under 5 hours to complete and even with The Lost Recordings it really is a hard sell at full price. It is however an extremely easy game for people who want another game for achievement hunting.OH it also works flawlessly on Linux for the penguin gang and Deckers.
_childDocuments_.name: Little Orpheus

_childDocuments_.review: I'm honestly shocked at how much praise this game has. It's not bad but it's just sooo slow and boring. It's practically a side-scrolling walking sim. The levels are massive compared to your little character and his run speed is achingly slow.I realise it's meant to be narrative driven, but that doesn't mean it has to be devoid of any real challenge. Also for being narrative driven, because of the slow character speed you often get long gaps between the narration, so it pops in at random times and feels very disjointed. They could've increased the speed/shortened the levels and still told the same story in half the time.The respawn points are frequent fortunately but even still, there are some frustrating design choices that led to a handful of deaths in a row, and the slow run speed made any degree of backtracking all the more frustrating. Couple of examples, when a scripted cinematic event happens and you lose control during the in-game cinematic, widescreen bars appear. However they don't disappear when the cinematic ends, so there is literally zero indication that you have control again, and often you need to hit the ground "running" after these to not die within a few seconds. Eventually I learned to just never release the stick. Another example is one scene when a giant worm is chasing you, and you need to duck or jump under giant veins. But the camera angle is a weird perspective and there is no shadow under the veins, so I died 5 or 6 times trying to figure out the right timing for the first duck, which was just...maddening.To rub salt in the wound, the option to find collectibles appears halfway through the game, but only on repeat playthroughs of the levels, and you can't even skip the cutscenes! Basically my nightmare in this game at this point.I'm going to finish it because I'm curious enough about the story but I really can't recommend this game. You're better off just watching a youtube playthrough if you're interested in the style/story.

_childDocuments_.review: Hands down the weakest and most confusing title from  studio thus far. “Confusing” might initially seem like an inappropriate choice of word here, since  was never known for the approachability of their artistic vision. However, in the case of , the confusion arises not from the audience’s receiving end, where one tries to see through the fog of obscurity, to analyze its artistic motivation, to deduce the message it conveys, etc. No, this time, the confusion stems from figuring out how this game came to be in the first place, and how it ended up like this –  was first released in 2020 as an Apple Arcade exclusive, then two years later did this re-release on other big screen platforms. Judging from this business decision, it is apparently a side hustle project aimed at reaching a broader audience. Which is also the first time on record that they stepped out of their comfort zone - the First Person “Walking Simulator” - a once niche now ubiquitous genre in which they pioneered over a decade ago. Just don’t get me wrong, by no means  is a market-oriented cash grab, it is nevertheless a genuine product. They managed to carry this cinematic platformer out without compromising too much of their artistic integrity: albeit cloaked in a thick layer of seemingly goofy slapstick, you can still discern their signature nihilistic undertone underneath, somehow (if you squint hard enough).Unfortunately, all of these were buried under another overarching layer of faeces mountain: the mind-numbingly monotonous level design. Neither the platforming nor the puzzle sequences ever went beyond the difficulty level of those shape sorter toys for toddlers. The overall experience is plainly hypnotic, and this is not just a figure of speech, I literally fell asleep multiple times during my play sessions. For such a well-explored genre, the design philosophy they adopted this time is unbelievably obsolete, even by ‘90s standards. Most of my playtime I was in a half-awake autopilot mode, driven by the delusion that they may still got one last twist up their sleeve to redeem all these disappointments. After all, I just can’t persuade myself to believe that a pioneering and experienced studio like  would take such a conservative approach to their new business venture.

_childDocuments_.review: + The story is funny. It's light and constantly evolving and intriguing. A little dramatic at the end which I like and find logical. Also very surprised by all the references to russian history and geo. Omsk/Tomsk mixing up was especially heartwarming for me as I live around these two.Unfortunately this is the only positive moment in the game.- The game is boring as hell. My biggest complain is that playthrough is very primitive. There is only 3 actions (jump, slide/crouch, interact) and levels are very poor for unique situations. You just run, jump and sometimes activate somethign to go through. No single puzzle that require to think. It's just "you see the lever - you pull the lever to go".- No challenge at all*. It's more like audiobook in the sense that you play just to hear the next dialog and watch next cutscene.- Though the cutscenes are not skippable. In 2024, really? Can't imagine that it was unintentional.- Unexpected challenge at the end. Imagine how you playing the game with the difficulty 1/10 and the final sequence is 15/10. Who the hell thought this is a good design?- Critical bugs even 2 years after release. The 'death bug' in chapter 8 was reported 1,5 years ago and seems like very simple mistake in level design. Still not fixed. Obviously the game is fully abandoned.I'd love to give it a positive review despite all the cons. At the end it was pretty entertaining and short enough to bear with boring gameplay. But the bugs were the last drop. Very disappointed by 'The chinese room'.
_childDocuments_.name: Little Orpheus

_childDocuments_.review: Is Little Orpheus a game made by The Chinese Room, the developers of Dear Esther, Amnesia: A Machine for Pigs, Everybody's Gone to the Rapture. Little Orpheus (I know I mentioned it twice) and Still Wakes The Deep (didn't play it). The short answer is  a resounding YES, the long answer will be in the review below and it might shock you. That is a great cliffhanger! I could use more of them in my reviews ;)I started with the facts because  I think it is important to establish what type of games these developers create. On the surface they are walking sims and most of the reviews complain about the game play part. Well good morning ladies and gents ! If you are playing  The Chinese Room's games for the game play I think you are in the wrong universe,When they developed A Machine For Pigs people went mad because they didn't get more of playing hide and seek like in the first Amnesia game. Now over the years YouTube was slowly flooded with video essays praising the great story,music and atmosphere.Everybody's Gone to the Rapture flew under most people's radar and (surprise surprise) the game was again a YT hit during and after the COVID pandemic.I think the pattern is clear. They make great stories. Everybody's Gone to the Rapture has one of the best stories told in video game format. What you 100% can expect from  The Chinese Room's games is great story telling and atmosphere, smart writing, great voice acting, solid audio design and very good music. All of that in a walking sim format (more or less). If you don't like the things they do than their game's are not for you,Little Orpheus is a short game,it is a very funny game but it will not be everyone's cup of tea. I liked it but I think this type of humor is really an unfamiliar territory to the majority of people who played this game. I will not lecture people on this type of humor. I am happy that the developers take risks with every new project because this game is similar to one of my favorite TV Shows (Yugoslavian) made in the 70's.  I wanted to write a review for this game but this is just a big THANK YOU message to the whole team.

_childDocuments_.review: “Tovarish Privalov…IVAN IVANOVICH!” Little Orpheus is a an example of a linear story-heavy platformer done right: juicy and rich visuals, great themed music (although a bit cliché), that conveys the atmosphere and bizarre but captivating plot.   We are playing as Ivan Ivanovich Privalov – a Soviet interiornaut (an upside down astronaut) in alternative universe who was given a mission to reach the Earth core in a special machine, called Little Orpheus. The game leads us through his memories (but are they memories?) while he is being interrogated by the General.  At first I was a bit unpleasantly surprised by the relatively low ratings on Steam, however looking through screenshots, I decided to give this game a try. And wasn’t disappointed!It took me a little less than 4,5 hours to beat the game, and a total of 9 hours to collect 100% of achievements. This is the only thing that remotely looks like a problem in Little Orpheus.  You see, I prefer to get all 100% of achievements in game via the first playthrough, but the developers have decided that the player should play the game at least twice (and if he/she is inattentive, than 2,5 times), before he is able to beat it completely. To me, this game shines when you play it the very first time, but to replay it right after you have beaten it feels kinda repetitive, since you are going through all the same scenes and twists.  Overall, it’s a smart parody of Soviet Union, full of irony and humour, which emerges the player in various bright worlds.7,75/10, Recommend. This game is certainly worthy of much more attention and recognition than it got so far.
_childDocuments_.name: Little Orpheus

_childDocuments_.review: If this game came out back when I was a young kid in the early-mid 90s, I'd have had a field day. I'd have played this 100 times, shown all my friends, and would have never stopped talking about it. It is incredibly charming and whimsical. The humor is somewhat dry and childish, but never in a way that feels forced or contrived. The environments in each level are absolutely stunning, vibrant, and rich in color. The voice acting is simplistic in nature and mainly serves as a narrative purpose. It's in no way, shape, or form forgettable or bland. It's full of life and character, in a way that I rarely see video games (of any genre) be. It's a nostalgic trip that reminds me of watching cartoons back when I was a kid, except this time, you're inside the cartoon. There's dinosaurs, giant worms, and so much more. The best part? Every single frame looks absolutely gorgeous. I know that I've already stated this, but I simply cannot state it enough, because I'm still reeling over how pretty this game is! However, a pretty game doesn't mean anything if it doesn't have personality, charm, and memorable characters or environments. This game has plenty of all of the above. I highly recommend this to all the kids at heart who want a slice of nostalgia.

_childDocuments_.review: If I had to describe Little Orpheus in the simplest terms possible, I would say:"Little Nightmares if you took out the puzzles and replaced all the horror with whimsy."Little Orpheus is a walking simulator with ever so slight platforming elements. The story revolves around a Russian cosmonaut drilling to the center of the earth to see if it can be colonized, but he loses the rocket drill, and Little Orpheus which is powered by an atomic bomb. The whole game revolves around Ivan telling a Russian general the story of how he lost Little Orpheus and the bomb, coming up with the most outrageous story anybody has ever heard. Filled with danger and suspense.Gameplay is as bare bones as it can get. Hold the D key and do some jumping every now and then. No puzzles, no precise movement, nothing. The story and visuals are clearly what the devs want you to focus on.  The game does look downright gorgeous, and the story is... alright. Nothing spectacular but it is far from boring. My only problems with Little Orpheus can be classified as nitpicks. I love a Russian accent as much as the next guy, but these accents are so thick that I could barely understand Ivan or the General sometimes. And the subtitles... WHO thought it was a good idea to put the subtitles at the TOP of the screen? It irks me to my soul.If you're interested in hearing a mentally unwell cosmonaut blab his gob off to a disgruntled general for 4 hours, you will like this just fine.

_childDocuments_.review: Loved it! It's a small vignette of a game, four hours in total, and it has a very cool premise of the story: you have a definitely unreliable narrator spinning a fairy tale during an interrogation. You never learn what actually happened, but you play the fantasy as it unfolds. I've never seen this point of view in games, and here, I think, it's done very well, the story indeed touches on the tropes you would expect this guy to bring up. The graphics are obviously inexpensive but the artistic style is a perfect match for the game. Unfortunately, I have to kick off a couple of points for clunky platforming (at one point, I spent about ten attempts to press a lever in time, not because it was hard to reach but because the guy had to be positioned just right for the lever pushing button to register, and you didn't have time to try several times) and bugs (one of the levels just completely broke for me, automatically killing me right after respawn, but fortunately restarting the game fixed it). But I still enjoyed this little story very much, and this is exactly the kind of game I'd love to see more of!

_childDocuments_.review: Soviet Journey to the Center of the EarthThis is a great story driven cinematic platformer, with lots of funny moments. as a Russian speaker It was quite funny to hear a bunch of Russian words being used every once in a while during the narration.I liked the way chapters are structured as if you watch an episode of a TV show, and each chapter is taking place in a completely different environment.Gameplay itself is that of a very simple platformer, with a bunch of easy puzzles, light stealth and chase sequences, none of which are difficult. At times it even feels as if you are playing a walking simulator disguised as a platformer.The game also plays great on Deck, but I wish there was steam cloud support. I wanted to replay the game sometime in the future to try and find the collectibles but now I'm forced to use the original device I played on. (Unless ofc I move my saves manually..)Overall I'd recommend this game to fans fans of story driven titles that enjoy exploring some cool locations with nice graphics and like chill gameplay without much of a challenge.

_childDocuments_.review: I originally played this on an iPhone with Apple Arcade, though I didn't get to finish the game.  I decided to buy it here the moment it released because the graphics and story are really well put together.  It's a lightly paced platformer with some fairly simple puzzles, so don't go into the game expecting Portal-style mind-boggling.  The gameplay lasts about 5-6 hours and for me it was worth the price.  The visuals have some inspiration from the American McGee Alice in Wonderland games, and it's more of an interactive exploration game than a challenging puzzler.  There's no inventory, powerups or anything like that.Don't let that put you off though.  It's a fantastic beautiful game and is worth the £8.99 just to experience it.  There're no trading cards but the achievements are pretty fun. _childDocuments_.review: Incredibly underwhelming, story drags on and on with no actual progress to a plot, it's just to show different looking levels. they also made like 3 layers to this story structure, with the most outer layer being this whole story part of some comedy TV show, and it goes literally nowhere and feels so out of place, I have no idea why they chose this direction. the gameplay also is unappealing, it's the most basic side scroller you can possibly imagine with barely any variety in mechanics, you can barely fail since everything poses little to no difficulty. most of deaths I've experienced in this game happened because of glitches and me daydreaming due to this game's boringness. and they expect people to play through this game twice for a platinum trophy, because the collectibles in this game don't appear on the first playthrough. don't let The Chinese Room name fool you too, people who made Dear Esther and Everybody's Gone to the Rapture are all long gone, all it remains is their name.Now I was aware of all of this, and still gave this game a chance because I like to lick commie jackboots daily and got this game from a bundle but am still disappointed. only buy at a huge discount if you're interested or better yet, find a better game.

_childDocuments_.review: Little Orpheus is a little more than a platformer; it's an experience, at least to me personally, it struck not one chord, but many at a time. I'll make this one brief as it's quite the perfect definition of an "underrated gem"; as in it's an amazing game that didn't sell well, for one reason or another... Maybe gamers nowadays do tend to value repetitive shooters over amazing platformers, but I digress! You're taking on the role of Ivan, a fugitive... that appeared out of nowhere after three years of vanishing. The thing is, Ivan was a cosmonaut, tasked with the most epic mission to take Little Orpheus to find the center of the Earth; Little Orpheus being the most valuable piece of machinery ever made by the Soviets. Faced with charges of desertion, lying to an officer and tampering with valuable government property, he is now being interrogated by a General... who discovers that most of what he is saying is ABSOLUTE RUBBISH.That's right, the adventure you're playing all played out inside Ivan's head... who's got quite the vivid imagination, I might add. This graphical game art is designed to give you a glimpse into the mind of a raving madman; a very colorful, diverse world awaits you. However, do not mistake this game for a "puzzle-platformer"; it is JUST a platformer, there are absolutly no puzzles and even the platforming side of things is not that great.. It's very linear and requires zero dexterity to go through the levels.What's likeable about the game is how these two very charismatic individuals are making observations in the background while you're playing; one making up more and more lies as he rambles on, and the other trying his best to maintain his cool and not shoot him dead and be done with it. There are also a number of collectibles, but you're required to play through a level twice to be able to find them... Worse still, in my opinion, is the fact that collecting them is directly tied with bonus content.All in all, Little Orpheus is a very lovely little game that I enjoyed quite a bit... I wouldn't have gone through the trouble of collecting those pesky orbs if I hadn't. It's a  platformer with what might seem at first like a very superficial story, but trust me when I say, the deeper you look at Ivan's state of mind and his own interactions with the general, the more you feel bad for the guy.ENOUGH, PRIVIET!! ENOUGH!

_childDocuments_.review: 3.2 hours. 2/10. Bad. Dumb. Great. 2D story-driven casual platformer. Alright. - Movement felt clunky throughout the entire game.- Chapter 8 has a bug that occurred to me as well as to multiple other people according to steam community. Once you reach a certain point, it restarts to the checkpoint by itself and sometimes creates your clone that you can go through. Then, once you progress a little it kills you, teleports you a little lower, then keeps on killing you over and over again. You can't do anything except watch. If you manage to get past this, activating a platform that takes you to the next area also triggers this effect but instead of killing you it keeps doing the death animation and you cannot progress. Restarting the entire chapter doesn't fix it. Broken ass game.If you have this bug, I managed to get through it by doing this: .ᶠʳᵒᵐ ᵐʸ ᶠᶦʳˢᵗ ᵖˡᵃʸᵗʰʳᵒᵘᵍʰLittle Orpheus is a game about Ivan Ivanov and his . It has great graphics, beautiful environments with even better looking landscapes. It has interesting locations, different mechanics in the chapters and the dialogue is fun to listen to but it all falls short in the end. The story is bad. Well, it starts fun and it continues to be fun with every chapter even though you get hints here and there on what the story is based upon until it completely plummets at the culmination. You see, this game is a really casual platformer, and the only thing that pushes you forward is the story, so if the story is not worth the time then there is really no point in playing it at all. For me, the views alone don't sell it. You go along this entire adventure waiting to see how it ends and it just doesn't deliver. It doesn't deliver anything. Not only does it not deliver anything it also breaks the entire immersion of the time period and destroys the personality of one of the characters to at least somehow fit their weird ending.If you forget the story's end, everything leading up to that point was enjoyable. The views and scenery were honestly fantastic. The gameplay was simple but fun. It did have a bug so gamebreaking in chapter 8 even restarting the chapter altogether didn't fix it. It's almost as if it was ignored during production, not to mention ignored until almost a year after release.TLDR;Beautiful scenery, simple story-driven platformer with an awful culmination. I'd pass on it.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a huge Chinese Room fan; Everybody's Gone to the Rapture is one of my favorite games. EGTtR is beautiful, intriguing, has a big cast of well-written characters, and has some devastating emotional moments. This game...well it is pretty, I guess. The writing isn't BAD, but it's incredibly repetitive and the characters hardly change or develop. The whole thing is a shaggy dog story, where each episode feels pointless and is dropped as soon as the next starts. Drawing attention to a story being pointless nonsense doesn't make it not pointless or nonsense! It all just feels like filler.I don't need gameplay to be fantastic, but when it's the only thing to lean on, the barebones platforming just can't hold my attention. The soundtrack is good but doesn't get to really shine until the last chapter.This game (appropriately enough) just feels so hollow. This concept could work for two episodes, but stretching it over eight just exposes how there's nothing there. Incredibly disappointing.

_childDocuments_.review: So here's what's good, what's bad and what's ugly about this little game.Visual style is amazing. It's Chinese Room - they know what they're doing when it comes to artistic side of their projects. It's a game about a journey into the center of the Earth and adventure that awaits in the strange fantastic places that are down below. You will visit few different locations, each with very distinctive idea behind, each with it's own colors and themes. They all look really amazing and it's pure joy to traverse those areas and watch those colorful views in the backgrounds.Unfortunately this is where good things end, and bad things start.There is a little to no gameplay here. Comparing to thier other games (was Dear Esther even a game?) it's a step into right direction, but this game was similar to their take on Amnesia years ago - you as a player have not much to do. This is a game where you often just run in one direction for long periods of time, with a bit of jumping here and there and puzzles so simple and easy, that they are almost insulting. Chinese Room managed to create first platformer-walking sim. Indeed, quite an achievement.So what did I found ugly? The narration. You see, the game takes a form of a story told by the protagonist during an interrogation. And he's constantly talking - perhaps to fill the void created by the boring gameplay. It's supposed to be funny - and perhaps to some degree it is, but it was mostly annoying and because of that I have actually lost interest in the story and was praying for this guy to finally shut up. Not to mention soviet Russia vibe that doesn't help the game too much - especially now.I'm going to give it positive review, but I can only recommend this to people who are not familiar with platformers and want to start with something easy before they'll dive into more complex games.ps: I have left the game running for hours in the background at least 3 times - please do not expect this game to be as long as my game time suggests. You should probably complete the game in less than 5 hrs.

_childDocuments_.review: One thing I didn't know before buying this: it's a "remaster" of a mobile game. I'm sure it's great on a phone, but we're talking about a PC game here.It delivers nothing on the gameplay side of things. You just run, jump here and there, move an object from time to time, have a QTE that is not quick (like 5s to react), and that's it. You're supposed to avoid being seen by enemies but the patterns are not difficult to see.The story is meh. It tries to be funny but is not. Some jokes are older than me.Graphics are what is saving this game from being a complete disaster, and probably what made it good on mobile. It got launched in 2020 on iOS, and for an indie game it's good, not great. The T-rex made me think of a plastic toy I had when I was little, that's cool.There are collectibles, but they only appear after you've beaten a level, so you have to finish this game twice if you want everything (you can't skip cutscenes). Not my cup of tea.It's also presented as episodic. I don't know if that's a remnant of the mobile game, but it doesn't really work as a complete package, especially when it's so short.Also, several bugs, some preventing you from finishing a chapter.TLDR: Boring and unfulfilling.

Explain me the logic chain, how on Earth you, guys, from interesting T-rex hide'n'wait'run sequences, came to boring sluggish cogs climbing?! Pfff!That "battle" in a flying fish. Where you actually have to do some basic dodges and shoot down projectiles. So you ARE able to make interesting moments, but did so only right at the end of the game? Where were you all these 9 chapters? :(

_childDocuments_.review: This was great! The classic side-scrolling platforming isn't overly unusual or challenging (or to be nicer about it, it's "intuitive") but it serves its purpose perfectly well for a game of this length. It reminded me a little of a classic PS1 era gem, Heart of Darkness (although HoD was far harder). Meanwhile, the whole thing is beautiful to look at, the story is hilarious, and the unlikely hero is one of the most likeable characters in any game I've played recently.I've seen other reviews complaining about bugs. I ran into one or two where poor platforming failed to properly trigger a re-spawn. This was far from game-breaking, though. A quick restart got me going again, and the autosave function acts regularly enough that I rarely lost more than about 30 seconds of gameplay.The game is short (probably ~4 or 5 hours if you don't replay to get the collectables) but it's well worth the time. There's probably little risk of DLC, but I'd play it if they ever released any.

_childDocuments_.review: A word of advice before you purchase.This is NOT a sidescrolling action platformer. The only real action you may find will only wait for you at the end of episode 9. If you want to purchase the game with the intention of playing something like Rayman or Ori - this game will not be the right choice for you.What it IS instead, is a walking simulator put in a side scroller platmormer shell. The game is very story-oriented and expects you to pay more attention to the dialogue and imagery than the gameplay. To be fair, the game's visuals, soundtrack, and story are its main strong points and I think that the developers did a great job when it comes to that. The game is also bug-free for the most part. The only bug I ever encountered was during ep. 8 when you reach the weights that move up and down. The main character could respawn in the wrong place after death or sometimes even die randomly when approaching them from a safe spot, but it was easily fixed with me just restarting the game (the checkpoint was set right before that area so I didn't even lose progress).Overall I think this was a pretty good game and it is definitely a novelty when it comes to the casual walking simulator genre. And as long as you treat the game like that and don't expect it to be something that it is not, I think you will also have a good time playing it over a couple of evenings.

_childDocuments_.review: I got this in a bundle, be mindful that it is a mobile game ported to computer.Little Orpheus is an episodic platformer game consisting of 9 episodes. The story goes on blabbering a bit too much cause our character Ivan is trying hard to stall an interrogation. We were supposed to find out whether the center of the earth could be inhabitable or not, but on our way to do that we lost an atomic bomb that was powering our rocket drill code named Little Orpheus. Our general is not happy about that. Despite the blabbering, the voice acting is well done. The sound track is really good. The game itself looks amazing but it is a borderline walking simulator with a bit of jumping and moving objects around here and there. Why I give it a negative review is because in episode 8 my checkpoints get all sorts of messed up, I instantly respawn falling through the textures or dead. I tried restarting the episode a couple of times, restarting from checkpoint, restarting the whole game a couple of times, nothing fixed it for me, sooner or later episode 8 will get messed up. For the sake of not leaving unfinished business, I went on YouTube to see how the game ends.. Reality is that even without any game breaking bugs I would have given this a mediocre rating if I could because obviously there are better, more engaging platformers out there gameplay & story wise. If you're purposefully looking for something that doesn't consume a lot of brainpower then by all means go ahead, keeping in mind that you risk your game getting soft locked by the end.

_childDocuments_.review: Little Orpheus is a beautiful side-scroller with an exciting and gripping story. The visual beauty of the game in the colourful and breathtaking worlds is accompanied by enchanting music. The gameplay is simple: you run through the story, jump and duck. There is nothing more. But the levels and world design are really well done and because the story is told so beautifully, you don't get bored.The two Russian main characters are unforgettable and entertaining. A simple but great game. Definitely worth a recommendation.

_childDocuments_.review: So, a bit of an advance warning: This is less of a game, and more of an interactive series of "episodes." Now, don't get me wrong - there's still solid game elements. You have to successfully jump from platform to platform, you have to avoid the enemies, you have to pull the switches, etc... But when compared with others in the genre like Inside or Stela or others like that, this particular one really has a feel of a little movie translated into game form.That being said, it is FANTASTIC. I usually get a little bored with the "mostly story, partly game" type games, but this is one of the few that really did an amazing job of it. There is just so much to love about Little Orpheus.I don't want to give away the story(ies), so you play as Ivan, a cosmonaut who was... well, sent on a rocket-drill powered by an atomic bomb to drill to the center of the earth to prove it's hollow. I mean... yep, that's where we're at here. A few years later, you find yourself being interrogated by the general, demanding to know why your mission has failed. What do you tell him?And so...... Ivan tells his story about what happened, and his epic chase after Little Orpheus, the powerhouse of his drill.You then embark on a series of quests (episodes) into fantastic, bizarre worlds, filled with dinosaurs, enslaved Avatar-like creatures, giant worms, evil undersea monsters.. even pollution incarnate. Needless to say, it's all very bizarre and highly fantastical.Everything about this game screams attention to detail. The world is remarkably animated, the music keeps it exciting (and sometimes the music is tied directly to what you're doing!), and the atmosphere created in these worlds gives a feel of really being involved. It is so bizarre and so much fun to play.I only got about 4 hours of playtime before getting through all the episodes, but let me tell you, I wasn't let down at all. The amazing humor, the driven plot, the way the game keeps you involved in the story, makes the time just FLY by. By the time I was starting the "bonus" episode, I found myself getting that same feeling I get when I'm 20 pages from the end of a really good book - I just HAVE to know how it ends, but I don't want it to at the same time.The drawbacks are not sufficient to cause me any grief. Like I said, it's less of an involved game - playing something like Inside, you might die a billion times trying to get a certain task just right. In Little Orpheus, you might get a little lazy/sloppy with your jumping and miss a platform, or you might get caught by an unexpected enemy, but overall there's really not too great of a challenge. There's not much in the way of puzzles, either, but that's fine - there's enough interactivity with the environment that you still get that feel of being part of the world you're in. There are also a couple bugs... Two or three times during the play-through, I accidentally worked myself into spots where I was "caught" and had to exit the game and restart, but the length of level between checkpoints is usually small enough that it wasn't too much of a hassle to just re-do a small part to get back to where I was. I could also have used a few more "episodes," but again, it's fine :-)As for my usual "is it worth full price?" Well, seeing as how I bought it as part of a bundle, the 50-cents-something I paid was WAY more than worth it. $12.99? If I had to go back and pay $12.99 for the experience I just made it through, I probably would. It really was that great. If it's on sale, go for it - any kind of a sale will make it a steal. (I see it's on sale right now for just under 8 bucks... That's a GREAT point that I don't think ANYONE would be dissatisfied with.)So yes, heavy heavy recommend. This game will draw you in, keep you playing, and leave you shaking your head and laughing. This Ivan guy is SUCH a dork. Very worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: A charming and simple puzzle platformer, heavy on the story and graphics and light on gameplay mechanics.Coming from the acknowledged masters of the Walking Simulator(tm), it is probably not surprising that this run-to-the-right puzzle platformer emphasises the atmosphere, environments and story at the expense of challenging gameplay. Having said that, the story, imagination and soundtrack is top-notch and in my opinion more than enough to keep you playing to the end.For comparison, the closest games I've played to this would be Limbo or Inside, but the tone is completely different. Inside, but it's a comedy about a soviet cosmonaut pretty much sums it up.So, my advice would be to accept this for the game it is trying to be. It's not a challenging platformer a la Cuphead. It's an entertaining tale built around simple platform mechanics.

_childDocuments_.review:
The year is 1962 and NASA are trying to put a man on the moon. In a remote corner of Siberia, a Soviet cosmonaut is heading in the other direction. Comrade Ivan Ivanovich is dropped into an extinct volcano in his exploration capsule, Little Orpheus, to explore the center of the earth. He promptly vanishes. Three years later he emerges claiming to have saved the world. He has also lost the atomic bomb powering the Little Orpheus. He is taken to a top secret bunker deep below the Ural mountains to be debriefed by the fearsome General Yurkovoi, a man so frightening even Stalin won’t buy him a drink. The General rolls up his sleeves, fixes Ivan with a steely glare and say “So... where have you been comrade? And where is my bomb?”

And Ivan looks him right back in the eye and says “Well General, you might not believe what happened to me, but I’ll do my best. Because it happened like this...”

Join our bold yet hapless hero as he explores lost civilizations, undersea kingdoms, prehistoric jungles and lands beyond imagination. Gasp as he battles the subhuman tribe of the Menkv and escapes the clutches of dreadful monsters! Cheer as he triumphs over impossible odds and brings socialism to the subterranean worlds!

Little Orpheus is a technicolor side-scrolling adventure game inspired by classic movies like Flash Gordon, Sinbad and The Land that Time Forgot. Delivered in eight bite-size, commute-friendly episodes, Little Orpheus is simple enough for casual players but rich enough for seasoned adventure fans.

If you’re a fan of old school family blockbusters, want a rollercoaster story that’ll take you to the Earth’s core and beyond, or are just in some need of ideologically correct entertainment, join the most unlikely hero to hit Apple Arcade on an adventure beyond belief. With stunning visuals, brilliant acting and a world-class score, Little Orpheus is a pocket-epic you’ll never forget.

Comrades, to the center!

name: Berserk Boy
detailed_description: In the distant future, a mad scientist and his army of darkness seek to enslave the people of Earth. Hope for all humanity rests with The Resistance, but are they enough? Enter Kei, a rookie hero who is transformed by mysterious Orb energy into BERSERK BOY! With high-speed action and the power to defeat evil, BERSERK BOY must face off against the diabolical Dr. Genos and his army of Dark Energy minions. Can he save the world before it's too late? It's time to GO BERSERK! Features Unleash your ultimate form: with the power of the Berserk Orbs - Lightning, Fire, Earth, Air, and Ice - and become a force to be reckoned with! Go Berserk! Become a master of speed and skill as you chain together combos to fill your Berserk Meter and unleash devastating special attacks! Upgrade your abilities and become an unstoppable force! Explore the sprawling world of New Hope City! and beyond, unlock hidden missions along the way. Jump, dash, slam, and slide through multiple stages with Metroidvania elements as you discover alternate paths and hidden collectibles! BERSERK BOY brings retro gaming: into the modern age with slick and stylish platforming action. Inspired by the genre greats, you'll be able to play for big scores and fast times in this modern adventure with a retro feel.

_childDocuments_.review: Picked this one up due to the excellent pixel art on display and because it's nice to see indie devs filling niches that major publishers no longer seem interested in serving. Unfortunately, this one really doesn't live up to its predecessors.Pros:1) Excellent visuals, the pixel art here is fantastic and I didn't notice any awkward hitboxes or platforms. There's a decent variety across levels and enemies and overall it's just an excellent throwback visually to megaman days of yore.2) Music is also great, it does a good job of getting you excited and is a great addition to the genre. No complaints here.Cons:1) Level design falls short in a lot of ways, particularly once you get flight. Bizarrely the devs persist in putting platforming segments beyond that acquisition, even though the player can just fly over them at their leisure.2) Similarly to above, the home base is needlessly huge. There a tons of empty rooms and halls that eventually can host a number of useless NPCs who have nothing of importance to say, but you will waste an annoying amount of time dashing through them. Also aggravating is the base is periodically attacked by random mooks, and there's no map, so if one straggler is somewhere you just have to comb over the place until you locate it, which leads to yet more wasted time.3) Balance of the orbs (classes) is comically bad. The first form is incredible, with an I-frame-heavy dash that deals damage and a seeking projectile, with subsequent forms being no improvement. The final one is particularly bad, as it has the megaman-style gun arm with less range than the dash, limited ammo count, AND the ammo doesn't regenerate when you're in another class. I have no idea how the devs playtested their own game and didn't see how wildly off balance this is.4) Devs couldn't make up their mind regarding insta-kills so you get both, applied randomly. What I mean by this is that some pits are marked with skulls to show they'll instantly kill you if you fall in, but then there are other unmarked pits that do the same. There are spikes that just deal health damage, and there are spikes that also instantly kill you. This leads to an annoying amount of confusion, particularly if you're trying to hunt for collectibles.5) The story is pure incoherent garbage. There's some silly lore video you can watch in your room to give a tiny amount of context to the story, but it's still bad and it's clear no serious thought went into it. You can barely even accuse the characters or villains of having genuine motivation or even character at all, they are as bland as can be.6) There is a bizarre fixation of speedrunning, which is infuriating. Speed is one of the primary things they grade you on, and from what I experienced all secret levels are time trials. I've played my share of classic megaman games, and speedrunning was not a focus of them, so it's getting really irritating to see devs continue to push the genre in that direction.7) This is the most heinous one, which is why I saved it for last. The game has two collectibles to find in levels, resistance members to teleport to safety, and medals. Medals serve zero purpose whatsoever until you get to the end of the game and find out the last level is gated behind finding 50 of them, and resistance members serve no purpose aside from unlocking tiresome time trial levels, which ALSO give nothing for beating them. In the Megaman series, in Metroid, in Castlevania, exploring and finding secrets is exciting and rewarding because it unlocks new capabilities, new weapons, or even just extra lives. In Berserk Boy, you get NOTHING. ZIP. NADA. I just stopped exploring at all because there's legitimately no point, and I am blown away that the devs could take so much inspiration from the old greats and somehow not parse the value of meaningful secrets.Overall the game greatly disappointed me, and I saw no reason to slog through finding the remaining medals to go fight the last boss. Even if I had done so, I would guess that the game's runtime would still be quite low, and given the large list of annoyances and missed opportunities above it still wouldn't be worth the price. If you're looking for a much better Megaman throwback, just go pick up Gravity Circuit.
_childDocuments_.name: Berserk Boy

_childDocuments_.review: If you were a tween boy at some point in your life you probably consumed Berserk Boy’s influences in your media diet. It’s a multimedia stew of spiky hair Dragonball characters and Megaman form changes unlocked via boss kills. You even get a tone setting and gloriously corny 2000’s anime intro. I love the dramatic villain pan.Berserk Boy is great stuff, and maybe the most inspired choice is how it weaves those form changes into its platforming. Part of being a Berserker means that most of your early forms are melee and being melee necessitates closing gaps. Multiple speeds, angles and variations of something like a 3D sonic homing attack are the bread and butter of how you get from A to Z, which also means that your enemies aren’t just obstacles but valuable, hurdle-able platforms in their own right.That Sonic comparison grows in prominence the more you play, too. You’ve got grind rails, you’ve got robot commanding antagonists and you’ve these really pronounced and colorful trails as you sprint that really reminded me of Sonic Advanced 2, all set to the tune of a bubbly retro soundtrack by Sonic Mania Composer Tee Lopes.But any game isn’t defined by what it takes from but, how it takes, what it omits, and what it remixes. If you’re here for a recommendation I can confidently say that Berserk Boy is a totally good totally playable adventure with a campy tone, great movement, and killer aesthetic; but it’s also naggingly undermined by one particular inspiration that just does not fit as well as the others do.Because the thing that’s keeping me from being in love with Berserk Boy and holding me at ‘in like’, is that ‘Berserk Boy’ the four hour action platformer is so much better than ‘Berserk Boy’ the eight hour metroidvania. A fake out final boss that pushes you into a return trip through all the same levels with a keener eye for those collectables before you get to the actual ending is not only a deflating momentum killer, but one that’s kind of incongruent with the frantic rollercoaster platforming that these levels are designed around.Let’s not start there, though. Berserk Boy begins with Kei’s techy friend, Dizzie, picking up spiked power readings on her computer. Could it be a ‘Berserk Orb’, they wonder? We set off to validate the game’s name and find that first Berserk Orb; one of five acquired from each of the game's main bosses which each give Kei a new super duper form.You’ll also quickly notice the biggest deviation from Mega Man: you can’t pick which order you wanna fight these “Berserk Masters” in; level progression is as plain as it gets with a linear unlock of worlds. In the context of Berserk Boy, that’s actually a good thing. You do lose that Mega Man ordering strategy that comes from prioritizing bosses based on what they give and who their upgrades counter, but you gain levels that are specifically designed to take advantage of forms the game knows you have.Each gets their own attack and their own mobility spell which runs the gamut from dashes to double jumps to literal flight. Most of those mobility spells have some interaction with enemies; sometimes it's a reset and sometimes it's a directional pivot, but that’s what changes the way you look at these levels.Getting from beginning to end is a process of doing the usual platformer schtick of running and jumping but also identifying enemy daisy chains you can use to propel yourself forward. That makes it less of a game with combat and platforming and more of a game with combat-platforming, where the plan is to get on a movement rollercoaster and stick to it. It has an undeniable flow state to it, where you can zone out and just feel the rhythm of its movement. Levels are long, checkpoints are frequent, and you can play them all with or without a lives system depending on your preference.Back at home base you have a hub world you access each of the levels from that occasionally sports some objectives of its own and also is where you buy permanent upgrades; and it’s here where you first notice the game has some ambitions beyond just conventional action platforming. Those upgrades are prohibitively expensive, a playthrough of all the levels once over will barely get you like a quarter of them.I knew this thing had ‘with Metroidvania elements’ written in its store description: you could clearly see inaccessible doors requiring forms you don’t have yet, but the specifics are manifest after you kill the ‘final boss’. He escapes, you don’t roll credits, everyone kind of depressingly wanders around the hub in fear of him still being out there, and you find out that your next course of action is to talk to this robot guy who will power you up for a rematch if you collect 50 berserk boy tokens!You’ll have some by this point just natively, there’s five in each level tucked away in secret spots, but many are hard to find or outright inaccessible on a first playthrough. For me it basically demanded an entire replay of the whole game to get what I needed, and importantly that second play was not as fun.Not just because of the diminishing returns of having just played the game but also because this more scavenger-hunty second pass just does not fit with the way our Berserk Boy moves through the world. Those fluid enemy railroads that you ride and bounce off of are all the sudden a whole lot less fluid: where you’re constantly needing to interrupt your flow state to check out some corner in hopes of a secret token.There’s lots of dead leads too because half of the time you find a secret it’s just a ‘resistance fighter’ to be saved, which increments a meter you need to unlock that levels’ time trial. It was clearly going for that satisfaction that comes with going back to the beginning parts of a Metroid or Vania with all of your new powers, but it doesn’t work in Berserk Boy both because even these beginning levels are fast paced action packed platforming levels, and because there’s no mystery about what lives behind those doors.There are no secrets to find, only Berserk Boy tokens and the resistance fighters. Without that sense of discovery and mystery, you have an experience that tries to emulate the mechanics of a metroidvania but none of the incentives. It ends up feeling really tedious, and I was constantly thinking to myself of how much better it would be if that lame upgrade shop had its rewards hidden in the levels instead.I do like Berserk Boy. That whole first half experience of platforming and fighting your way through levels is enjoyable. You get this escalation of power and options with the new forms, you get tightly balanced retro difficulty without being sadistic, and you worm your way ever closer to killing the final bad guy in a satisfying progression. It’s fun if not groundbreaking, I’ve just got its lamest elements most fresh in my head.It got me thinking a lot about framing. If this same exact retread was an optional post game for enthusiasts rather than a mandatory requirement for credits, it would have been way cooler. But if you’re here to ‘beat the game’, you will not get a satisfying story or gameplay conclusion until you’ve eaten your vegetables and gotten all those tokens. Berserk Boy is still a charming and action packed nostalgic package that is worth a play, I just pause on whether or not it's worth that second play. It’s a great platformer and a bad metroidvania and, as much as I don’t want to judge a fish by its ability to climb trees, what am I supposed to do if it insists on climbing?

_childDocuments_.review: This game is receiving heaps of praise. I wish I felt the same.Pros:-Moving and attacking feels good-The Art Stills look incredible-Some really good looking backgroundsCons:-A lottl;dr It's obvious a lot of love went into getting Berserk Boy's game feel right. I wish the same amount of love went anywhere else. The first time pickup Berserk Boy you think: "Hey, moving and attacking feels pretty good." After an hour, you realize that the way it feels hasn't changed. Five hours in and three bosses (+six minibosses) down, you have the same realization. After clearing nine levels, defeating multiple bosses, and getting three new forms you're doing the exact same things you did in the first five minutes of gameplay. Berserk Boy peaked the moment you picked it up, and it didn't have to be that way. Forms should have been the game's primary draw, giving the player various options to overcome challenges. Instead every form ends up worse than the first. You can easily beat the entire game using Lightning Justice, and only change forms for the segments where the game demands using a form's gimmick to get through. Even then, Lightning can usually clear it with a double dash. The enemy variety should have challenged the player and got them approaching situations differently, but you get maybe six enemies overall the whole game and you deal with all of them in the same way: dash straight into them. The level design doesn't support the lack either, and doesn't challenge you to approach enemies in different ways like the older platformers Berserk Boy leans on.Boss patterns suffer too, with the repetition of fighting the same miniboss twice and then a boss that uses a similar if not identical attack pattern. This is where the game's difficulty and creativity should have shined, instead it leans more into spectacle than good game design. This is where the tires start to come off: As you play what is effectively the same level with different backgrounds, you'll notice other things, like how crunchy, stiff and uneven the sprite work is, how lackluster the level layouts are, how the backgrounds are so much better than anything else in the game, how the CG's in the cutscenes are too good for this game, and how there is a dire lack of anything outside of the levels themselves. A lot of this could have been excusable if there was any intrigue to speak of, a story to tell, or even interesting dialogue. Instead, all they could muster for that gets squeezed into the cutscene. Everything else is a walking trope or a meme of some kind (I really didn't need Flame Hyenard II). Antagonists never get elaborated on, how they do anything they do or even their plan isn't explained, they just are. They're the bad guys, you must fight them, that's it.Made worse when the game keeps threatening to be interesting and hinting there's more going on. But it never delivers, the big moment at the end falls flat (the bird isn't a character until this moment), and the lackluster power-up you get feels pointless, all in service of a Sonic 3 homage. None of it feels earned, especially after the cliffhanger of an ending that just resets the status quo.This game is carried entirely on it's initial impression, and if the game could have elevated a couple of other aspects to match that, maybe I'd see it the way others did. Bonus Round: Only a couple of levels have parallaxing and those are the best looking ones in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Berserk Boy is a  platformer that is so  with forcing its numerous ideas onto the player, that it forgets what made the games that inspired it good, namely: being a fun ride. That being said, this is also one of the few games that actually  like a worthy MegaMan successor, which is why I'm inclined to advise you to get it (so long as you think that it looks fun).  While this title suffers from a lot of first-gen woes, if the developers listen to feedback, in time we can all have an amazing sequel on our hands. I'm just going to say it how it is: Berserk Boy is mediocre. And I'm willing to bet that most of the 9/10s that the game got are given out by people who didn’t play this platformer through. That being said, I still think that you should support Berserk Boy Games, because there is great potential for a sequel here. I'm going to be honest about my opinion too: a lot of what I'm about to describe can be labelled as "first-gen woes". Playing this title often made me want to replay MegaMan X5 and MegaMan Zero 4. Obviously, Berserk Boy wears its inspiration from those series on its sleeve. To me, the central issues with this game are a striking lack of QA and bad game design. More specifically: mechanics that have a great deal of momentum clashing with levels that seemingly have one sole purpose: to diminish that momentum. A great example of this are the different berserk modes that you can switch through. They take way too long to change from and to. This, in turn, ruins the game’s general flow. Not only that, but every form has its own mechanic associated with it, sometimes numerous even, which wouldn’t be an issue if they were fun to deal with.But they are not, because the level design uses them as a form of gatekeeping. In a way, the game wants to put you in a certain frame of mind. It repeatedly throws the same obstacles your way, but in different sequences, only to give you excuses to use the different berserk modes.That would’ve been fine if at least one of them was more or equally as fun as the first one you get. Not only that, but all of them have different abilities, right? Well, some of those transfer over to all the forms, but others: not. And that’s for the same reason too: so that the devs can force you to use their ideas. And here’s where it gets confusing: at times, you can ignore these signals and successfully pass through such segments through other means. That’s great, right? Well, it would’ve been, if it were a feature. But it is not, which is proven by how the game doesn’t always let you do that, by penalty of immediate death. This naturally leads to rapid difficulty spikes, which aren’t earned. Playing Berserk Boy feels like the game is using its ideas to challenge the player, instead of presenting the player with a series of challenges, which they can use experience and skill ro solve. This is exactly why Berserk Boy feels inspired by, but very far from equal to Megaman X, Zero or even the ZX series. Those games are great, because they have a solid base, which was further expanded on. And Berserk Boy already had such a base: the first berserk mode (lightning). I am certain that if all the other modes simply granted extra abilities to that central gameplay style, the entire adventure would offer a much better experience. Oh, and on the topic of comparing the series: I urge the devs to go back and check the time it takes to complete the levels in those games, because most take about five minutes to best. Berserk Boy’s stages, in turn, require about ten minutes and the game certainly overstays its welcome. Not only that, but this decision makes it very hard to want to replay it. In contrast, I can replay X5 daily, because it’s fast and fun. On the story: as someone who actually thinks that the continuous plot across the MMX, MMZ and MMZX series was awesome, I must say that I got nothing from Berserk Boy’s plot. It was difficult to follow. It often felt like the game story’s elements were there to fulfil some sort of requirement; to fit the mould of the game’s progenitors, instead of those elements and tropes being present, because they bring actual value to the game itself. I don’t see myself replaying Berserk Boy anytime soon. If I have to be honest: I probably won't play it ever again. But I’m hopeful for the sequel, because the good in here is really good. And I think that you should get this game if it looks like a fun time to you. How can I possibly say that after all of the negatives that I just mentioned?Well, easy: these aren’t negatives. This is feedback for the developers. And they should use it when making their next game. Because Berserk Boy is the first game to successfully bring me true MegaMan vibes. And that means something.

_childDocuments_.review: GO BERSERK!!Berserk Boy has this amazing ability to successfully pull together things I love like the high-speed allure of Sonic, the boss battles, progression and style of the Mega Man Z/X series, and even precision platforming reminiscent of Celeste. The best part of this fusion of inspirations is that goes beyond just homages to make some that feels totally new and different. Keeping true to a retro aesthetics but with welcome modern sensibilities. The journey is filled with gorgeous pixel art and matched with a RIPPING soundtrack. There's a lot to love here and you can just feel the passion throughout. Just when I thought I'd had my fill with the main campaign things like the EX Missions started to really give me a test and flex the design. There's enough here to be worth it but it stays tight at the core because it cuts bloat. I know I'll be revisiting this one over again when I've got a classic itch! Big Recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: If you love Mega Man, specifically the Zero and ZX games, this is an absolute treat. The platforming controls are tight, all of the powers you obtain are utilized in fun manners as you play. The music is incredible and the game overall feels great to play.Mastering the platforming in this is so much fun. Same with finding all the collectibles, some of them are hidden extremely well, and overall it gives a nice level of challenge to newcomers while not being boring for veterans of games similar to this.Even after I've finished it, I keep coming back to it to play stages over and over so I can demolish my time and get through it faster. That right there is what makes Berserk Boy really cement itself as one of the greats. PICK THIS UP and you will have a hard time putting it down.Update: The dev works hard fixing the bugs and listening to player feedback. Super helpful!

_childDocuments_.review: It's fine enough. It feels really good to move. It aped Copen's thing from Gunvolt pretty hard and I don't begrudge that one bit. Fighting stuff rules. But the level design is getting me down. Rather than surveying obstacles in front of me and deciding how I want to utilize my kit as one does in Mega Man, I'm switching weapons every three seconds to utilize some bespoke interaction that requires a specific weapon. This platform only moves with the fire ability, this wire is only grabbable with the ice ability. Better switch switch switch to navigate the premade line the level designer intended. That probably still sounds like a good time to someone reading this, and to you, I say this game deserves your support. There's something to be said about the flow state of reading the cues the stage is giving you and responding immediately. It's like speedrunning the stage before you've even properly played it. It's definitely a high quality product and deserves a positive rating. I just don't think it's for me.

Fun game but the levels get extremely repetitive and I have no interest in replaying them to find obscurely hidden secrets with no map or radar. If the game would have just ended I probably would have left a positive review, but man what a lame way to arbitrarily double the playtime of a game that wears out its welcome by the end.
