_childDocuments_.review: I love story based games like this, especially multiplayer ones, but I can't in good conscience leave a good review.Please beware, I will have spoilers below and just complaints I wrote down while playing this game. We had to restart a lot and it was so very buggy the entire time that the last hour my wife and I just didn't explore too much, or atleast I didn't because my character's head was backwards and I couldn't point my light anywhere.Not to mention, exploration is a joke in multiplayer because you get interupted by another players' action and it skipping ahead, or being in some action scene so the other player only has enough time to do anything until the sequence is over.In short, it feels like there was no quality assurance for this game at all, especially for multiplayer.SPOILERT ALERT BELOW;Please beware this all happened in multiplayer.GLITCHES- There are so, so many visual glitches. There are clipping items and people, floating characters and more, giving a wrong button prompt on the keyboard.- Camera glitches where you can't look around or where if you examine an object, you get stuck in that object's view until your partner goes to the next area and makes you recover. I had to look at my wives screen to move my character cause my screen was stuck in an examination for atleast ten minutes early in the game.- Cutscenes don't work properly in multiplayer when hiding, whoever 'triggers' the event or hides first, sees it all, the rest seems people shifting around/teleporting with no explanation. This shifting around also happens during the camera scenes where you are watching the other player. - At one point, it said Charlie for me, my wife saw a cutscene of Charlie, then it said she was Jamie and I was Erin, even if I was Charlie. - I got my DLC from buying the Collector's edition, yet I was never able to access it ingame.- At one point, at the saw with Monica and Ryan, Marc decided to on his own just run back on all the way where we came, without my wife touching her keyboard. He just kept running, as funny as it was to see him 'nope I'm out' it was a big issue that forced us to restart. - It keeps saying with the breathing stuff that the other player failed, even if they didn't or weren't even part of it (I did breathing as Charlie, it said my wife failed, she had no such thing). Luckily it was visual only, it did not affect anything.- Erin (dead) appeared in two or three cutscenes, once in the cameraroom, once past the maze.GAMEPLAY- The game keeps switching out characters between players instead of letting the same player use the same character(s) over and over. This meant they then ggt dialogue prompts they have NO idea about. Maybe they should keep one character to a specific player as much as they can.- Make it a setting or way that players don't push to the next area until BOTH players are done exploring thoroughly, or give a better hint at what'll skip to the next area. House of Ashes introduced the >>>>>> on some  objects, but they're rarely used. It's infuriating if your gameplay is cut off due to the other playing accidentally moving on.- In other games, you could look over another players' shoulder to examine things alongside them, you can't do that anymore. Why?- Coins and some other collectibles don't share, which is very discouraging for players that like to really make the most out of their experience together.- Important events not being able to be triggered (like finding important information or turning on the lights) because other player went ahead without knowing what would happen if they did, ties in to above issues. That main things are locked behind this especially is pretty bad.- No tutorial for useable items when another player already had it; i.e. I didn't get information on businesscards for Charlie cuz my wife played him when that happened the first time.- Lights aren't consecutive to both players. If you interact with an item, it goes off for yourself or the other player or something, meaning afterwards it's on for one player but not the other, then using the item will switch it off for the one who had it on and vice versa.- While I played as Charlie, he walked into incinerator due to other player solving a puzzle, despite no proper hints to show what would happen. I had NO choice in the matter, Charlie went from locked door to not being anywhere suddenly; like what the hell? Give players a choice.- Taking the pictures as Marc is a nice idea, but they are stressful. Give some kind of prompt of what you can take pictures of so you don't have to open the camera non-stop, especially with how awkward it moves around. Also, why can you take pictures? They didn't mention evidence at - Keyboard controls seem not as polished as controller and are quite frankly awful.- Can't shimmy/crouch into areas together, just like you can't do most actions together anymore. Another feeling multiplayer wasn't ready.- Dialogue in Multiplayer does NOT line up. It depends on people's secrets who have been found I think. Sometimes people have extra dialogue, others don't. This means things just don't like up at all and it's very strange; even asking hints from the narrator is different. My wife and I heard two different hints.- Codes were very hard to find according to my wife (I wasn't there for that part in the game), meaning it takes too long in multiplayer to find them on time before it skips ahead.- The camera room was badly designed, with player 2 just watching a glitchy thing and unable to act or do anything at all. Even if we ended up being succesful, it didn't matter at all. It was so, so glitchy.- Jamie is killed in the barn if you go up as Kate (Erin is dead at this point), I go up as I feel that was a smarter option, and so Jamie just stands there and dies, without me being able to intervene. You can do everything right and still be punished, why?- There was a section of having to smash a button, then it suddenly switches to another one- naturally I'm still smashing it, so it registered the second button as wrong and a character died over it. (I loaded) It makes no sense.- Segment of chasing (Jamie/Erin(?)/Kate) and the Pool as Marc doesn't let Marc explore, cause the others are forced to be in a chase/can't slow down.If you want to have some SAW like mechanics in a game, make a SAW game. There was several ideas mixed together that in this that didn't work out at all.- Black screen during final confrontation for one player. Had to restart and then restart the entire last part, so much for immersion and tension. Also, minimal helping each other in a fight... Why? That makes it more fun.This is all written past 9/12/2022, by the way, when they had plenty of time to patch things. The devs don't seem to care. I waited over a week for updates and nothing.It feels like a lot was missing and that the game was incomplete. I love these kind of games but it didn't feel finished and made for two players at all. I'm sorry for the negative review, but this was disapointing after knowing you guys have done this kind of game before,  for years and should be improving more.There are so many missing interactions that could've been fun. Too many plotholes(eg): Why did he survive a massive fall, why did he survive so much trauma? He bleeds like a human. We see 'robot' puppets throughout the game, but the story doesn't continue as to why or what that means. What happened to the construction workers? What was the WHOLE story with the man and his daughter?Some pro's;- Interesting plot at first, tense and scary at some parts, but it just became.. Ugh. Typical, no brain horror that doesn't make sense.- We got to play together more as characters, instead of seperate chapters, which was fun.- The unique inventory things added in this game were nice, but underused.TLDR this game was NOT ready for release at all.

_childDocuments_.review: Well. As quite a big fan as these games I was wholeheartedly disappointed with this game. I'll list you a few pros and cons and then give an overview:Pros:- The premise is very good. Being based around a real serial killer and being more focused around SAW/Slasher flicks kind of concept made the game much more enjoyable to me as it was somewhat based on real to life things that could happen as apposed to paranormal/Alien Vampires.- The atmosphere for the most part was again very good they seemed to put more focus on the action. There wasn't a lot of time wasting they established what was happening and boom it was a go. Exploring the house felt genuinely creepy at times. Cons:- The game is ridiculously buggy. Textures and characters not loading properly, freezes, crashes, frame stutters, the game looks good in parts but has been really poorly optimised. I played it with a friend and we spent easily 2+hrs of our play time reloading the game and replaying segments because the game had bugged out in some way or crashed, and when you're doing this it completely ruins any suspense or tension which is not ideal for a horror game.- The characters just don't fit together at all. I wouldn't say that in any of the Dark Anthology games that there has been great chemistry between the characters but this was by far the worst. All of the love/hate relationships between them felt extremely forced and massively underwritten. I only wanted the characters to live out of my own pride rather than the fact that I didn't want to miss out on a interesting character. - The new inventory system felt massively underwhelming it was something that initial had some promise but as you progressed through the game it just felt completely pointless as you couldn't really utilise anything in your inventory until the game needed you to do so. Maybe have it where Jaime could only have a screwdriver or a flashlight and allow the players to have to think and try and plan for future events as the game is built around thinking ahead and making decisions. To me it just seemed a feature that was added without a great deal of contextualisation or game play in mind.- For me these games don't have to have complex game play mechanics, maybe have something that requires a bit of thought from the players (*cough* *cough* my previous point) but you had these segments that required you to move a box 10 feet in order to get over a wall. I mean why? What is the point apart from it being an artificial game lengthener it didn't add anything apart from me getting frustrated at the awkward controls of moving said boxes.Overall for what it is the game is okay. Its defiantly the worst of the Dark Anthology season 1 but it does have a couple of redeeming qualities which is the premise and the atmosphere. I would say wait. Wait until they have patched and fixed all the broken stuff and then play it as otherwise you're just going to have a massively underwhelming and frustrating experience. A last little note as well all of this is based off of my experience of a shared story, playing it with a friend. However, there are still several bugs in the solo mode so be wary of that as well. Wait for them to fix the game then play. 2/5 (at time of review)

I would not recommend buying this to play online with a friend in its current state.Major issues (mostly caused by syncing problems):- Client player is not be able to aim their flashlight.- QTEs sometimes bug out and don't give you enough time to react, had 2 characters die because of this.- Some of the "aim and fire" QTEs are too short and it's not clear where you have to aim.- Models appearing and disappearing.- Characters that died appearing in some later cutscenes for a brief period of time.- Entire scenes getting skipped because the other player did something without an indication that it would advance the game.- Some extremely low detail models, specially on outside scenes.Most of these games have been visually impressive but this one leaves much to be desired, I saw low res textures frequently and the quality of reflections in many scenes wasn't great either, with or without raytracing.If you're gonna play it in singleplayer it might be worth it, but it was the worst experience I've had in multiplayer and I've been playing these games with the same friend on release since Man of Medan.

_childDocuments_.review: Out of all the Dark Pictures Anthology games so far, this one is the most gruesome and creepy. It has issues, but it is much better than the reviews make it out to be.The good: The story is a bit slow to get started but once it gets going the game is a genuinely creepy/scary experience. I worry for the game devs who came up with all the ways the characters can meet a grisly end, there are so many disturbing endings in this game, much more so than the other Dark Pictures Anthology games. If you're looking for a 'so bad it's good' B-movie slasher multiplayer game experience--this is it.The bad: Multiplayer is quite buggy (visual glitches, disconnects & crashes). The devs really dropped the ball here. By now, they've had plenty of time to fix the problems, and remember--this is a mature engine they are using, and it's the 4th game in a series. The bugs are inexcusable. The last update came out Dec 2022... considering the hefty price, at the very minimum they could have released further patches rather than abandon the game. Baffling decision making when presumably they are trying to grow the franchise and create another season. The saving grace is at least the game autosaves, so if it crashes you can still go back to the last autosave which usually isn't too far away.The ugly: The actors that play the main characters perform inconsistently, and sometimes their acting is incredibly stilted.tl;dr If you liked the other Dark Pictures Anthology games, buy this one on sale and you'll be pleasantly surprised.House of Ashes > The Devil in Me > Man of Medan > Little Hope

_childDocuments_.review: Prefacing my review with saying I play with my partner, and I like to play with a Dualshock controller, not with mouse/keyboard (I struggled with previous Dark Pictures Anthology games with mouse/keyboard controls). My partner and I have played every game in the series at least once.The Devil in Me brings in a couple of new game mechanics that I found interesting. This game relied a little less on the Keep Calm skill checks and added in a few items that could be pulled out in scenes to aid your story. I thoroughly enjoyed the first game in The Dark Pictures Anthology series, and this game reminds me a lot of it. Especially with the fact that this game was actually quite scary, and had a real sense of danger that the first game had, but the following games weren't up to par with. This game checks the need for decent horror. THE GAME GETS BETTER AFTER THE BEGINNING. In the beginning story line, the voice actors were very bizarre and the faces of the characters didn't quite align. It put me off to the game at first and I genuinely almost stopped playing because of it. I'm glad that I pushed through the beginning part and got to the real story. I can understand the poor reviews from the beginning, but TRUST, it gets so much better. Overall the game is a 7/10 in my opinion. Of course there is your typical camera angle struggles but that just comes with the game series.

_childDocuments_.review: A friend and I love the Dark Pictures games generally and have a ritual of playing through each of them in online co-op shortly after launch. Generally they're great games and I recommend them if you enjoy horror and interactive storytelling. There's so much to recommend in their storytelling, environments, and tech.BUT:This one was ruined by bugs and inconsistencies. One of our character deaths was either triggered by a glitch or an illogical sequence and felt totally unfair. As with lots of other players reviews, we had characters stuck in walls, t-posing, animation glitches, teleportation, even dead characters briefly reappearing in later scenes!It's such a shame because with a narrative game like this you only get one chance to experience it for the first time.Once (or if) the bugs are fixed, I would recommend it, but not until then.

_childDocuments_.review: The plot is much more primitive than it was in the House of Ashes. Protagonists and their interaction are also pretty one-dimensional, especially after complex conflicts between characters in the House of Ashes. Also one of the things that could give more suspense, complexity, or at least pure interest -  were barely used as such at all.Interesting gameplay feature developers brought in this part - minor unique abilities for each protagonist. Such as ability to pick stash locks or use a flashlight. But since the route within the locations is pretty linear - this is not the game changer.Basically - The game is totally playable, sometimes scary, sometimes interesting. It could be but at one level with the first parts of Dark Pictures Antology - but totally not with the previous one, which is upsetting.

_childDocuments_.review: You know those bad horror movies where all the characters do stupid things and you're left there screaming at the TV wishing you could control them? You know how The Dark Pictures Anthology is awesome because you CAN control them? Well, ya cant. I have a lot of problems with this installment, not including the bugs, so let's get started.1) Choice-making & Butterfly effect  This is the element to these games that make The Dark Anthology stick out as a game series. It's what they're all about. Does this game have much of it? No. During the prologue you make one optional choice, and have very few other dialogue options. The beginning to the actual game is worse. You sit there for maybe 15 minutes of screentime just watching the characters talk- watching. Your opinion doesn't matter. All of the butterfly effect pages will fill in. "Bearing updated" From choices that weren't even your own. Just updates on how the show is going. 2) Movement The actual animation and movement is some of the best that I've seen from them.. but how much of it? Way too much. You have more parkour time in the game than making discoveries or building relationships with characters (or having the option to). No, you run around pressing a single button. "Space". In order to jump, climb, crawl, shimmy, etc. Get ready to be holding "W" and spamming space. 3) Bad Characters Look, these series have always had those "annoying" characters that no-body likes. They also usually do a great job of character arcs throughout (depending on how they are played. but that's the point, YOU get to play them) Off the bat, none of the characters are likable (with the exception of the camera guy and the director), and seemingly just get worse. The forced hatred and discord, as well as the injected "love" plotlines. There are good ways to do them!! Having the character option for the girls to kiss during their first interaction seemed forced and like we were supposed to clap for dancing monkeys. A poor attempt at representation that comes across as fetishization. All in all, I didn't finish this game. Returned it after 2 hours. Finished watching the gameplay on YouTube.Not worth $40.Not worth $10. I just hope this series can go back to making their good games! Little Hope was AMAZING. Man of Medan was genuinely SCARY and Until Dawn is still iconic. They're going down hill and I just wish they could get back on track.

_childDocuments_.review: The story here isn't terrible, although it's a bit longer than the previous games. Not particularly original, but the atmosphere and setting are definitely the eeriest of season one. While the first 3 games of season one relied heavily on cheap jump scares, The Devil in Me only has a handful of jump scares, and there's a couple good one's that are cleverly done.The atmosphere in this game is blood chilling at times. You know exactly whats going on, which creates a feeling of dread and annoyance at the same time. The annoyance comes from The Devil in Me is not as technically polished as the previous 3 games in season one. I ran into a bug that forced me to reload my last checkpoint, and there were a couple other small bugs like Jamie's flashlight not working near the end of the game when she clearly has it on her, and Charlie getting stuck and rubberbanding around when squeezing through a tight spot, but otherwise the game was stable throughout.The Devil in Me feels very different from the first 3 games. There's less mystery and the plot twists don't hit the same. As the player, it feels as though the game is targeting you personally, rather than letting you be the observer who makes decisions. You're at the whim of supernatural forces, yet those forces are entirely contrived and lazy. I can understand why this game has mixed reviews. It's as though the developers were overworked and angry, and took that anger out on the player. I still recommend playing if you can get the game on sale, but don't expect the same level of quality as in prior Dark Pictures games.

_childDocuments_.review: The Good:+ Fairly well done atmosphere + H.H. Holmes is an interesting topic that doesn’t get much exposure + A bit more “interactive” than previous Supermassive gamesThe Bad:- Terrible camera placement/control- Technical issues with textures, lighting, delayed prompts, and character facial design- Story and character development felt rather undercookedThe Bottom Line: The Devil in Me follows the crew of an independent television series when they’re invited to a remote island in Lake Michigan to visit a meticulously recreated World’s Fair Hotel. As H.H. Holmes - America’s first and possibly most prolific serial killer - is the subject of their current project, the chance to walk the rebuilt halls of his infamous “murder castle” is too great of an opportunity for the crew to pass up. Dreams of finally achieving notoriety and success quickly turn into a nightmare for them though as they discover too late that they may be the newest victims of the killer from beyond the grave…As with all of Supermassive’s titles, The Devil in Me isn’t so much of a traditional game as it is a kind of “interactive horror movie”. The player controls the various characters as they explore a series of environments and attempt to survive the ordeal - picking up clues along the way to unravel the mystery and having to make both dialogue and situational choices that decide not only the different directions the narrative can go, but also the fates of the characters. Any/all characters can die at various points throughout the game and their survival (or lack thereof) can alter how events unfold and what experiences the player has.  Unfortunately, not much has been innovated or expanded on from previous installments in the series; however, it did feel like there was a small increase in interactivity. There are more opportunities for the player to engage with the environments as well as a VERY basic inventory system that allows the free use of light sources when exploring, tools to help investigate or obtain clues, and the utilization of items in situations that could potentially save characters or present alternative choices and actions. This is a good improvement for the series, but if Supermassive is hoping to appeal to a wider audience by evolving the gameplay - they still have quite a ways to go. While I enjoyed these minor improvements and the return to a less hair-brained narrative than House of Ashes’ Operation Iraqi Freedom vs Mesopotamian vampire aliens, The Devil in Me really failed to appeal to me largely due to what felt like a lack of polish and uptick in technical issues. For starters, the camera placement and controls have never been great in Supermassive’s games but this time around it felt especially horrendous. In most environments, the camera is way too close to your character which makes navigation clunky and the search for clues/interaction points more difficult than usual - forcing you to swing the camera around like a lunatic in every room just to find things or proceed through the environment. True technical issues also seemed to be more present in this game than in previous ones. Inconsistent texture quality, inexplicable dips in frame rate, delayed interaction prompts, and issues with the lighting and brightness hampered my experience throughout. On top of this, various other issues were present such as the player’s light source automatically switching off every time you interacted with something (forcing you to turn it back on), various janky and stiff animations, more than a few instances of voice acting that just did not sound convincing or appropriate, and the uncanny valley feeling cropping up often as character’s eyes just didn’t behave like normal human eyes at all. As a fan of Supermassive and these style of games, it honestly kills me to say it, but The Devil in Me is their most disappointing installment yet.It’s not frightening or anxiety inducing at all, it’s narrative - despite having an interesting basis - is more jumbled than usual and lacks any kind of satisfying conclusion, and it’s lack of polish was just too consistently noticeable to overlook. A lackluster finale for The Dark Pictures Season One for certain, but hopefully not a sign of things to come with the forthcoming Directive 8020…Final Verdict = 6 out of 10 Mustachioed Masks

_childDocuments_.review: The game so ass i`m bouta write a whole essayThe Dark Pictures Anthology: Devil in Me is the fourth game in series by Supermassive Games Bandai Namco. After playing the game, I was left disappointed with a feeling of being shаt on.  It has many flaws and shortcomings, and even though It is not the first game by them, they somehow made it worse than the previous ones. The game is full of with bugs, glitches,  that ruin the immersion and enjoyment of the game. The graphics are mediocre at best, with poor lighting, and awkward animations. The sound design is also bad with terrible facial animations and voice acting that ruin the immersion and the atmosphere. The characters look like plastic dolls and their expressions do not match their emotions. Half of the lines are also cringy, Developers tried to make the characters talk like a teenager does, but made it mad corny,  It also suffers from frequent frame drops, while ran on RTX 30 series gpu. The game's story is also disappointing and poorly written. The game tries to create a sense of mystery, but the plot is predictable and boring. It also fails to develop its characters, who are stereotypical, and annoying.  The game advertises a friend pass feature that allows you to play with a friend online for free, but it does not work at all. I tried to invite my friend several times, but we could not connect or join each other's sessions. Only after visiting the community hub of the game I read that Friend passes were discontinued, That begs the question "Do i need to constantly check Bandai Namco`s website to know that it was discontinued? Why even include the friend pass code with the game, in the first place?". Reading the reviews of those who got to play it in co-op game often disconnects, desynchronizes, or freezes when playing with others, making the experience frustrating and unenjoyable.I do not recommend to anyone. It is a waste of time and money. To summorize, the game is a technical mess, a gameplay bore, and a narrative disaster. The game has nothing to offer, except  regret. It should be avoided at all costs.

_childDocuments_.review: This has to be the worst Dark Picture game I've ever played. The characters are so buggy and glitchy, multiplayer is even more glitchy, everything is just glitchy and buggy. Playing with my partner our games bugged out to where we had to actually restart them about 4 times in just one session. Running and walking was the worst, if my character wasn't constantly looking behind them or their body wasn't glitched out, the character would get stuck on nothing or would randomly spin around 180 degrees, or the camera would just not follow the character. so you'd be staring into a wall, and no matter what you do, you cant fix the camera unless you quit to the menu. And don't get me started on the story. I would have LOVED to be invested in these characters and I would have loved to ACTUALLY explore, but any time my partner would move slightly towards the next "scene", my character would be forced to move to the next cut scene even though I was no where near that area and no where near done exploring my area. Not only that but the story felt so rushed and half of it didn't make sense probably because we missed something because we weren't able to explore BECAUSE it kept jumping us forward and forcing us to move ahead. It felt like it was a split linear story as well since I wasn't with my partner for a good majority of the game, unlike the other Dark Picture games where you were with your partner 90% of the game which made those feel a lot more fun and coherent story wise. I loved playing House of Ashes because it had the perfect amount of quick time events along with a great story and the multiplayer actually felt like a multiplayer game, not a game where I play one half of the story and my partner plays a different half and we rarely actually play together. I have never been more disappointed in a game than this one.

_childDocuments_.review: The Devil in Me is the latest entry in Supermassive's Dark Picture Anthology, and it does not disappoint.  As the final chapter in season One, I fully enjoyed it and now I can't wait for Season Two to start.     The characters where probably the most well written of the series so far, with believable dialog, and believable interactions/conflicts.  These characters had a history together, and it showed.  Some games like this it feels like the characters only existed when the game is started, so for the depth and history to be made apparent really helps make these guys more interesting.     The setting was terrifying.  The ominous situations in which you arrive, the secretive manner in which you are instructed to behave until you get into the hotel, and then the initial view/entering of the hotel.  And then once things really start to pick up, the Hotel and the surrounding grounds becomes even more terrifying.  The hotel felt like an actual character in the game.  It had an oppressive atmosphere, and at times navigating it was just as terrifying as dealing with the actual killer.       The sound was phenomenal.  The music was used to perfection, and the ambient background noise, like things falling over, tree limbs rubbing overhead, just added to the already oppressive atmosphere of the game.     I felt the voice acting and mocap was great, and they are getting better with facial features.  I feel like they where more than just wooden mannequins whose lips moved with the voice actor's words.  The fear was visible in their faces at times.     The new mechanics added to this entry worked.  Characters having an inventory and a tool that allowed them to do certain things, like open drawers and lock boxes, fix fuse boxes, or even using a pencil to see what was written on the preceding page that was torn off.  The addition of some basic platform style elements added verticality and other challenges for navigating, adding another puzzle aspect to the game.     All in all, a near perfect conclusion to Season One.  I can't wait for Season Two, or whatever game they do next.  Supermassive knows what they are doing, and they do it very well!10 out of 10

This game does have some of the best deaths of the series so far in my opinion, but when it comes to the ending there is not too much variety. I believe there are like two mayor varieties, each with their own differences depending on the choices you make. In my first playthrough, only Kate, Charlie and the dog survived. _childDocuments_.review: I'm enjoying the story so far, and the new gameplay elements are neat. However, during my 5 hour session with a friend (we are playing together in 'Share a Story' mode) it is one of the buggiest, most broken experiences I've had in a long while.Animations/cutscenes cutting short or not playing at all, interactables totally breaking the character camera and requiring restarts. Controlling your light source being impossible (if you have to explore a dark room half the time your source will face directly at the ground, nullifying it), puzzles clearly not being built for KB/M and showing with horrible controls (took us over 5 minutes to do a puzzle that should've taken 1, due to bugged controls), and the overall netcode being so laughably bad that, on multiple occasions, we have had completely different results/cutscenes play out from within the SAME EXPERIENCE. We literally had completely different story results playing at the same time!This is all ontop of the fact that it took us nearly a full hour to debug the problems with the game on launch. Incorrect resolution, HDR on by default, mouse not registered on the screen properly, etc. Imagine trying to sort through settings, that keep resetting, while not being able to correctly click the buttons nor see half of them due to the screen res being bugged, and the time taking to apply being over 10s every time due to HDR/fullscreen.Now, outside of the bugs, the game really isn't that bad! Fun, campy story, good characters and the new gameplay is a really nice touch to the game. Hell, even the solo mode might be okay. My only complaint here is that, in similar fashion, it does seem a little undercooked. (Some scenes skip sporadically, animations don't seem complete at times and there's clear moments where facial animations are just completely gone (thought that just may be another bug!)). Although, these issues are way easier to overlook and really don't impact the experience as much.Just wait until they update the game or until it's on sale, especially don't buy it if you were planning to play the 'shared' mode with a friend, unless you have a high tolerance for insane bugs it just won't be enjoyable.EDIT: Just for further clarity on tastes/expectations, I really liked the previous dark pictures games, even found Little Hope not that bad, and this game really aint an exception if you like that style of campy fun-horror. It's purely just the bugs/lack of polish that bring this one down.

_childDocuments_.review: After "The Quarry", The Devil In Me is a return to form, with added mechanics that don’t break the consistency of the series gameplay and which also allowed me breathe a sigh of relief because yes - you will have characters dropping like flies if you don’t pay full attention once more. The Devil In Me plays magnificently, without a single bug yet, and besides some issues with certain tight spaces they’ve really managed to master their camera work and perspective. Although I still long for a first person perspective button (quick glances around the room can really save time) I found myself able to scan a room more effectively than any of the previous entries in the series allowed.  The load times are tight, the graphics are flawless, the facial animations are still top tier, transitions are smooth, just all in all in all a real pleasure to play.  This entry into the series introduces several new mechanics including a small inventory based system  (integrated into gameplay perfectly), a hiding mechanic (similar, but easier, than the heartbeat), and fancy new coins which may or may not prove invaluable to you as you stumble through the darkness of the murder hotel deluxe.After an absolutely slammer of an opening scene, lending from the true story of a prolific serial killer, the team continues to build an amazing horror saga throughout - enjoyable to both gamer and viewer alike. The pacing is fantastic, and the balance between Control/Story/QTE is the best to come out of the series yet. There are a few moments you may disagree but ultimately I think it’s easily going to claim the favourite of the series for many Dark Pictures fans.And selling at the lower price point once again (WTF was that with The Quarry?! GTFOutta here) this game is an absolute must buy for any Suppermassive fans.  If you catch it on sale - great, but this entry is unequivocally worth the full price point - no question. 5/5 - Absolute banger of a horror night

_childDocuments_.review: Seeing the other comments, I thought they were over exaggerating about how broken this game was, but boy was I wrong. I played the game through online and it was the most broken game from steam that I've played. It felt more like I was beta...Nay! Alpha testing this game.- Character models would disappear at random.- In several places I clipped through walls and floors.- Desync on whether the flashlights were toggled on/off.- Desync on cutscenes with mine running longer than my friends, this was caused by some of the cutscenes showing different character dialog than my friends side.- Controls randomly stopped working at several points during the game on both controller (What I played on), and keyboard/mouse (What my friend played on)-  The game could not keep track of our decisions and would show both sides of cutscenes one after another.- Held objects would be stuck on the character models at some point causing them to glitch out the models during cutscenes- The other player would get "stuck" at during co-op moments. On their end, they would be exploring the room, but on mine they would be standing still as if the other player was AFK.- When the other player wasn't "stuck" they would be teleporting around the rooms like older games with bad internet connections.- If one player finished their section too fast, the other player would just get a montage of where they were supposed to go, completely skipping any content that could have been found. And during those moments, it's not like the other player can wait as they would be in a chase sequence and have to finish one way or die.- The facial animations (which looked amazing in the last game) barely worked with eyebrows being stuck in place or eyes not looking where they're supposed to.- Unlike the last game where one player was assigned a group of characters and the other player assigned the rest, in this game players are given control at random, making it so that you have to pause the game and explain what you did last with that character to give some semblance of coherency.- Actions such as shimmying, crawling, crouching, jumping and balancing are SO FREAKING SLOW and can only be done by one character at a time AND held a majority of the disappearing acts with the models.At first, the broken-ness of the game seemed kind of quirky and easy to make fun of, but after the first 3 hours (AKA before the SAW-like games started) it quickly lost it's charm and just became frustrating. To all who think that they can "Look past some of the bugs" like I did, DO NOT BUY THIS GAME, IT IS FUNDAMENTALLY AND MECHANICALLY BROKEN!

_childDocuments_.review: I wished I would love this game as much as I loved the previous ones.Do you remember Randy Meeks from "Scream" and his rules of how to survive a horror movie? Do you remember watching a horror movie and going "Oh, I would be so much better at this"? This is the idea of this game and it's ABSOLUTELY AMAZING, as it gives you the ability to be a part of an horror movie and to play it better. As it was announced - it was like a dream come true for everyone who loves horror movies and horror games. This game makes you a part of this horrifying experience, is set in an absolute perfect place, great scenery with traps you can't predict and music that fits the atmosphere...that gets destroyed due to the INCREDIBLY predictable jumpscares, you already know are going to come, and a relatively boring gameplay, achieved through interactions with characters who are part bland-part unpleasant. It's really hard to get invested in people who you forget immediately after meeting them. The couple in the beginning? I was hoping they would survive, because they were authentic and awoke sympathy.The main cast? They were constantly getting on each others nerves for no particular reasons, except of being mean and self-absorbed. Except of Erin, she's a sweetheart you wanna save at all cost. The rest just reminds me of my attempt to eat kohlrabi soup with no spices and immediately deciding to give up (don't repeat my mistakes - if you want, just eat fresh kohlrabi or use it in a salad with some sour cream and pepper - it's really tasty). I unironically would love to replay it some time later and see whether different results will bring me more joy. But in the meantime I'll just go and replay House of Ashes for the millionth time (such an amazing game, absolutely love it).

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to previous titles, the animations in this instalment are sub-par and frankly somewhat lifeless, albeit previous titles did suffer from lifeless expressions from time to time, however this title in particular is very bad. Almost the entire cast look as if their faces are painted on. Animation pop-ins occur time to time and for some jarring reason the animations in cut-scenes sometimes finish abruptly resetting models/expressions to the beginning, loads of t-posing occurrences and missing textures on animations within the cut-scenes. One example being ,girl being slashed in the throat has no cuts / incisions on her throat but there's blood gushing out from her neck with zero indication of wound.Regarding cinematic and ultra-wide resolutions, most previous titles have 21:9 and on wards support for various screen ratios, this game is locked at 16:9 with a couple of scenes being letter-boxed on both horizontal and vertical views. It baffles me to this day that a cinematic game cannot get this right.The UI is extremely buggy, if you're going to use mouse and keyboard, be prepared for a sloppy user interface experience, all previous games were polished and worked really nicely. In this title, lots of text, icons and items are cut off or need to be "scrolled".What I gather so far, the story seems engaging and rather fun, from the little I've played I'm quite engrossed already and looking forward to the story and how it unfolds. As always, visually the game looks amazing. No gripes here on that, from lighting to art direction, to how they model and animate most of their games look fantastic. Another plus here, the audio, music score and voice overs are fantastic, lively and accurately animated in, I have no gripes here.I would personally wait a week or so for the developers to drop a few updates to address a few of the issues, I hope in due time I can experience this game with the right additions as I've been waiting for this game for some time now and love how Supermassive narrates their titles.

_childDocuments_.review: I was very skeptical of the game due to the rest of the reviews saying that their experience of the game was completely ruined due to glitches. That being said, I wanted to try it out anyway as this series is one of my favorites. To touch on the glitches front, there wasn't any that made the game significantly unplayable. There were times where characters just stopped moving (extra ones that were tagging along to the player in control) or like glitched through walls, but those were not game breaking. The worst part is actually even just opening the game. With my double monitor set up, all I can really say was it was a pain the butt. Sometimes it would be half of one monitor, half on the other. Sometimes it would just switch monitors. Every time I tried launching the game it would take like 4 tries to really get it going. Once I got past the loading screen it was fine. (For context on my PC specs, I have a GEFORCE 2070 at 16GB ram). The game does offer remote play together, which was a little difficult to figure out too but that was more my fault. Regarding controls, they were a little frustrating as sometimes my character would just jump off of the box I wanted them to stand on top of, but it wasn't the end of the world. The characters in this game move much faster than the others (not at walking speed, but with the running option) I think, so that made it much more bearable. Highly recommend controller, and you can change the settings to accommodate PS buttons or XBOX.Now, for the visuals. Beyond the times it would glitch, this game looked fantastic. The lighting, textures, and everything was really pleasing. Best one visually yet.As for the story, I think this is my favorite of the Dark Pictures Anthology. The characters were the most likable of any. Also, I personally thought this was the scariest one of them all (well, I never played Little Hope but I did play House of Ashes and Man of Medan). It was also probably the most interesting of them too because it's [/spoiler]Overall, I would recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoyable serial killer cat and mouse interactive movie in a hotel that is manipulated by its mysterious architects whims. Drawing on the history of HH Holmes this (so far) is the most grounded of the Supermassive games. We have the usual scour for the things in the dark. some light puzzling and the usual quick-time events to preserve a bunch of not totally dislikable characters from meeting their grisly end. The atmosphere is eerie enough and I was caught out by the occasional jump scare. And did we actually lose our character to death-trap X? That was kind of fun.The new "gameplay" mechanics are forgettable. You're only allowed to jump, duck, crawl when the game contextually allows you to. No free running here. The 'hide' mechanic is literally pressing a button where prompted and doing nothing. As for the inventory .... it feels unnecessary and seems to be a button press just for the sake of interactivity. There's also a  sense that last minute button prompts on QTE's are a little too fast and weighted against the player (or at least players whose reactions aren't what they used to be). Of all Supermassive's games (save House of Ashes - unplayed) this is the one that I've probably enjoyed as a slasher B-horror movie shlock the most next to stuck in a creepy town with some malevolent entity in 'Little Hope'. Unfortunately the script seems to lose some of it's pacing once things move outside the hotel with far too much wandering around in dark environments with one of my characters kidnapped off-screen when I had been playing them moments before. Despite that I still enjoyed the game overall.It does leave me wondering where this series can go (Casting of Frank Stone is on the play list). Rather than lean into the  current 'new mechanics' the right direction would be to focus more on choices and impact on character interactions. There's a lot of directions Supermassive could go with the horror genre and the hint is they're going to do exactly that. Great news as a move beyond young adults/teens in peril would be welcome.

_childDocuments_.review: WARNING: DO NOT BUY THIS GAME IN ITS CURRENT STATE IF YOU'RE INTERESTED IN PLAYING SHARED STORY COOP!A friend of mine and I have played every Dark Pictures Anthology game in Shared Story mode on launch weekend so far. The last few years, we did encounter some issues, but the games were perfectly playable. This time, that's not the case. There's a lot more jank than there was the last few years, like characters teleporting around for one of us, or people randomly doing animations they're not supposed to do in a given moment. If that were the only thing, it wouldn't be good, but at least playable. What made us quit in the middle of the playthrough was when we noticed that important QTEs are entirely broken right now. We encountered one QTE we restarted several times, and each time, we would both succeed, only for both of our games to show as that the respective other person had failed their QTE. In a game where QTEs decide if your characters live or die, that makes the game unplayable. It clearly should not have been released in this stage, and I am appalled that most critic reviews don't even seem to mention these flaws despite them being glaringly obvious.The game has potential, and if it gets fixed and turns out to be actually good, I will change my review. As of now, DON'T BUY THIS GAME FOR MULTIPLAYER.Edit: You might be wondering whether the game works better in Co-op now. It doesn't. My friend and I gave it a playthrough this time, but we still ran into several gamebreaking issues. And, well, even disregarding these: This game is far weaker than its predecessors. The last third of the game feels incredibly rushed and poorly thought out. There are cuts where entire segments of the plot are just summed up within seconds. One player might find themselves in a high-stakes chase, while the other player just wanders around aimlessly. There is a point where a character enters an empty house, feels (for reasons unknown) compelled to hide in a box, when suddenly the killer arrives and... fails to find you. At the exact same time, the other player might be running from the exact same (!) killer in a completely different location. It's bad.

_childDocuments_.review: All my experiences are based on the Co-op element of this game on Keyboard and Mouse. This game is by far the weakest in the series so far. The game mechanics are terrible, the controls are very bad and either non responsive or have some weird delay on keyboard and mouse most of the time, which has resulted in failed QTE sequences despite proper key input. the characters are traipsing around in dark areas and have a light source, which is completely pointless because the light sources point everywhere except where you are aiming. it periodically moves from left to right whether it's the lighter or the torches, and the camera flash as a source of light is bad because all you're doing is just taking snapshots and then stuck in darkness again. its like the game's trying to trigger some dormant form of epilepsy in you. The game features some mini-games and puzzles such as trying to turn on a fuse box in the right order, but trying to complete that minigame on KBM was so painful because the controls are extremely unresponsive or your cursor doesnt go where you want/need it to. The game's visuals are pretty nice, and the FPS was a solid/stable 60 (it was higher, but for the sake of stream i lock all games at 60 fps). the lighting and environmental lighting looked fantastic. The character models were also well made, but there was something about the faces, especially during conversations where it just felt... off. either sometimes they'd have sync issues, or their face would morph into shapes that don't fit the words they're speaking, so that broke immersion.Navigating around the world was painful. you're slow, everything has a collision box the size of fat Albert, including the other characters, so more often than not you'd get stuck on terrain or on walls and even small rocks. the controls were also so janky that you'd not go where you're trying to, with some form of sway to the left or right to navigate through the map. Playing the game in co-op had it's own problem as well- if you or your partner were too fast to complete the "objective" of that particular scene while the other person was still exploring, you get cut off mid action and teleported to the next cutscene. I was trying to solve a puzzle to open a safe, using different codes. the last code ended up working and just as the safe got unlocked, i got violently yoinked away from the safe and my character ran to the next story progression point without being able to stop/do anything since my co-op partner had moved on to the next part of the game's story. While I understand that this is part of the game and experience and has been around in the previous games, the previous games were developed alot better where you were actually able to explore at your leisure while still completing the story without feeling like you just got denied/punished for exploring. While the theme and source material for the basis of the game was an interesting choice that had potential, the storytelling itself was a bit... predictable as well as the jump scares. Something in the closet that jumps out at you, some loud sounds playing as you go around a corner etc was all expected, and the game feels like it doesn't even try to put effort into trying to scare you, but instead it feels like just generic "jump scares" that were added in with very loud sounds for the sake of trying to scare you. Having said all of that, I had some hilarious moments on stream playing with a friend because of the amount of jank this game has and how much of a buggy mess it was. Having one of the characters' head spaz out from left to right like it's an episode of Dr. Who was incredible for example, so with the right company you can definitely have fun with the game. The Devil in Me could perhaps have done well with a lot more time in the oven to bake so that all the issues could have been worked out. I just personally don't think the game is worth picking up full price- perhaps on a sale, if you're looking to kill time between games and have money to burn/waste.

_childDocuments_.review: As a long time fan of these games now, it absolutely pains me to not give this a good review. Me and my friends (we've often had 10+ people around to play these close to launch night) regard DPA releases as events unto themselves and are always incredibly excited to play them.I can appreciate that Supermassive games attempted to reinvent the wheel with this release, and add more 'interactive' elements. I don't really read much of the online discourse around this series, but is this something that was actually requested? I feel like the charm of these games is that they're essentially movies where you can dictate the direction of the story and who survives. The implementation of these elements were unfortunately very slapdash, and at least 3-4 hours of this game's ~7 hour runtime consists of the player(s) having to run around, solving pre-school level puzzles with no build up of meaningful tension whatsoever. The quicktime events were few and far between, and upon completing the game, there were a considerable amount of people in our room who didn't have a single decent action heavy section.The introduction of coin collectables was an absolute joke, and contributed nothing to the gameplay. There was a collective groan from everyone in the room in the second half of the game when we inspected a shine, only to discover there was a coin. Replayability for the dedicated achievement hunter types maybe, but as far as the 'viewing' experience goes, it served only to distract and lower tensions even further.Spoiler free of course, but we felt several death scenes we encountered were unintuitive and that the game almost sought to reward you for making nonsensical choices.As far as positives go, the graphics were awesome, just as every DPA game has delivered on. No issues with the sound design and setting. The characters were vibrant and interesting, with my personal top picks being Charlie and Erin.Overall, we were immensely disappointed by this release - and hope that this was simply an attempt at experimentation by Supermassive that they will learn and iterate from in the future. The game could have easily been 2-3 hours shorter and it wouldn't have taken from the experience in any way. Uninspired platforming / exploration sections heavily detracted from a setting that by all accounts should have been incredibly terrifying and dread-inducing. We wanted anxiety and scares, and instead just found ourselves bored stiff!

_childDocuments_.review: If there is one thing I can give  credit for is having the potential in being the best Supermassive game since , but realistically it falls short of that standard.When it comes down to it after a disagreement in some design choices I simply can't recommend this game because it's buggy and not at all optimized. You will have textures pop in and out of place, light sources consistently glitch particularly switching between cutscenes, cinematics and gameplay as well as not knowing if all the assets for the level are going to load properly - i.e. characters not having flashlights although you see it on your D-pad inventory (controller) and it shows being on, but your character simply doesn't have any light. This is not a PC or bad hardware situation, it's a game which was delivered in an unoptimized state. Still better than Cyberpunk at launch, but buggy nonetheless. I would say wait until a good summer sale or until Supermassive patches most of the launch bugs - if they ever do. They're not a developer known for delivering a lot of post launch support for their titles.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is like a strange mix of Saw x F13 x House of Wax. The story is good, based on a real serial killer. For my playthrough it was either me or my friend T-posing in random places teleporting around, oddly placed invisible walls, flying mid-air when having to balance over something or having a character in game holding an invisible item and then there are some clunky character movements or questionable camera angles here and there. It made me giggle more than that it was annoying and it wasn't disturbing for our gameplay at all. The Devil In Me has a lot less of a horror/thriller aspect than the other Dark Pictures games.  Also, the deaths of the characters are a whole lot less memorable and gorey.I felt like I had a lot less (smaller) choices to make and I missed to interact and have conversations with the character my friend was playing. We often played in seperate environments/areas not seeing each other and unable to interact with each other.The big minus for me in this game was the fact that I got 'pushed forward' a lot. Since my duo was processing a lot faster than me, I didn't get to fully explore some of my rooms and places. It just made me skip in a small cutscene towards the next place. I rather have it that you have to wait for each other. It felt a bit like I had to speed through rooms in order to see everything before I would be skipped to my next area. (+ For me its a bit story killing seeing the same faces reused in every Dark Pictures game. Fliss of Man of Medan is way too similar and gives off the same vibe as Jamie in this game and I noticed I sometimes confused their characteristics and behavior. New face actors would be a lot nicer to kinda have a fresh view so the characters can grow independently on the player without past memories of previous Dark Pictures adventures)Either way, its a good story and enjoyable to play, even with the current goofy but harmless bugs that most likely will make you giggle as well :)

_childDocuments_.review: First game in the series to be refunded. I had to give up after just one hour. I actually liked the last parts despite their flaws, but this one doesn't work at all.The animations have always been a bit... strange. For me personally, it's always been a thorn in my side when the characters put their chin on their chest and look upwards in a strange way when they speak. Nobody talks like that unless they're embarrassed or something. But in this part, the animations are even worse. They look unfinished and spongy. Sometimes even jerky. The head always has to move. Arms have to be thrown in the air. What the hell does it look like in the developer studio when a normal conversation is taking place? *head jerks to the left* Hey, do you want to take a break? *head turns unnaturally to the side, but eyes remain still**throws arms in the air, pulls shoulders up* Sure, let's go *head tilts forwards*????maybe you should film a conversation and then you'll quickly realise that facial expressions and not head movements are the key here. The damn heads don't have to be permanently moved in extremes!This in turn means that nothing can be taken seriously. Even during the prologue I had to say to my gaming partner "Sorry, I can't take the game seriously. I'will mock it." because you simply have to make fun of every movement!As with the animations, the developers don't seem to be able to get by with just one second of silence. While you are "exploring" the area, the accompanying NPC always has to make a comment that is as high quality as a brain fart.In general, the dialog is meaningless, embarrassing and annoying. Uninterrupted.This also means that you are more likely to laugh or grimace in shame. Or, in the worst case, you simply stop listening at all. Especially in the prologue, which is set in an earlier era, "hip & modern" words are used...Nobody talks like that!All I can really say is: WTF?Who thought it was a good idea to put so much time on climbing and crawling around when you're putting in controls that must have been designed by a drunk?! And yes, I'm talking about controller controls here too!At the same time, the developers seem to think you're stupid. At every ledge, edge, gap or object, you get a great hint as to which button you need to press to interact with it (spoiler alert: it's always the same button!). Instead of simply saying "with A / SPACE you interact with your environment".Also, the markers for interactable objects only appear when you have already walked past them.Supposedly you can also control the light you're holding with a trigger. No matter how much I turn, the character only moves his stupid head, but certainly not the light.This makes "exploring" a pain in the a... - especially as there's nothing to explore!After three games, you would think that the quality of development would improve. But no. As already mentioned, the animations are even worse than they already were.Textures - especially on the characters - are terrible. They look dirty & greasy & lack depth. Just look at the fabric of the clothes in the prologue and you'd think you were playing a game from 2008.The brightness setting is a constant up and down. However, it should be mentioned here that I played on a TV. Nevertheless, the game was either swallowed up by darkness and individual light sources such as the sun or lamps blinded you at the same time. Or everything was so bright that it hurt your eyes as if a nuclear bomb had just gone off.And for some inexplicable reason, the game causes motion sickness.I honestly can't say much about it, as I gave it back after an hour. In itself, the topic can certainly be exciting. But the first hour was tedious and boring and didn't make me curious for more. Probably due to the other points.This was the last game in the series for me. _childDocuments_.review: The Devil In Me is the latest installment in the Dark Pictures series and the only one I hadn't played yet. It takes place in a modern-day recreation of serial killer H.H. Holmes' notorious 'Murder Castle'. The narrative commences when a group of documentary filmmakers receive an unsolicited invitation to this sinister abode, only to soon discover upon arrival that they are being watched and manipulated by an H.H. Holmes wannabe.While the story was really interesting, it had major pacing issues. The first 3 hours of the game felt more like a walking simulator than a horror game. It had a few occasional jumpscares, but I literally felt safe in the murder castle. However, the game becomes significantly more interesting and unsettling in the second part, though the pacing issue remains noticeable with long segments of walking around. I must say, I really appreciate that there are no supernatural elements, which for me personally, makes the game scarier. They really did a good job at making you feel trapped and hopeless. The gameplay is somewhat similar to previous games, except now you can jog and shimmy and overall the movement felt more natural. The game still suffers from the issue of bad facial animations and dead eyes that plagued all of the previous games. Performance-wise, the game had a lot of stutters, and my character froze multiple times, forcing me to reload the checkpoint.I feel like this game had a lot of potential. I'd even say it had the most potential out of every single Dark Picture game, but they really didn't handle the pacing well and released a broken game at launch.

_childDocuments_.review: Frankly, this game was not finished. The bones are there, and if you're willing to squint it can be something great. I play each of these with my brother and there was rarely a segment one of us weren't suffering from immersion ruining glitches. Like, I've been gaming for 20+ years and I've, without exaggeration, never experienced such a glitchy mess. No less than five times in our first playthrough we had glitches fatal to even playing the game. The character would lock up and be able to move in any direction without being able to move the camera at all. When there are items you have to interact with, that you can't look at, it becomes impossible to advance the game. At times one of us would permanently be stuck in a loading screen while the other would play through most of a segment. The loading screen would never resolve. It feels impossible to address the numerous other smaller immersion breaking glitches when those above were so common and so damning, but here's a rundown. Characters wouldn't exist in cut-scenes, they'd be postured like they were holding their items when they weren't, my coop partner couldn't see my flashlight, necks would swivel 180 degrees around and stare between their shoulder blades, the fuse box scenes didn't allow you to control the hand as intended, etc.The premise of this game was great though and the interaction between the characters was better than in previous games. I loved the item application in the quicktime events. I'd like more opportunities to choose between dialogue or multiple items as a kind of alternative to just having the base actions. Some of the decisions lead to consequences that one could never reasonably foresee, but that's the nature of these games and I kind of support it. If the game runs cleaner and can be described in some manner as "polished" in the future, I'd love to change my answer to recommending this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I can see why this game has mixed reviews but it is interesting. Would I pay 40 dollars for another game like it? No. Do I want to finish this one to see where its going, yes. I am about 5 hours into the game and the majority of the "game play" is walking around to find the next cutseen leading to a few dialog options with objects that you can interact with in between. some objects will change the story, most wont, and a few are collectibles. Its more of a choose your own adventure move then it is a game. Its designed to keep the player interacting as filler until the next branch option. It was likely intended to be replayed for multi story endings depending on choices but I am unlikely to go back to it once finished. The story itself is loosely based on HH Holmes. He is more the inspiration or theme for the setting, and is used as a sort of mascot. This has disappointed my true crime obsesses girlfriend who request I stream this to her. She likes the setting and fact that the jump scares and horror is not overly done or gory, meaning that its a spooky game, but not a super scary one. there have been more simplistic puzzles and platforming then horror.The controls are very sluggish and was clearly meant for console.  its mostly quick time events when action is happening, and decisions on dialog options are timed. Ever action has to be taken and not in a good way. if you want to look at a sheet of paper, you have to first zoom into it, then press a button, then look at the back and front. You alwase ready an action before doing it, hovering your hand over the object so the player has to interact multiple times in what should be a quick action. Sometimes you need an item to open stuff, but for the most part you need to attempt to open it first, fail, then are allowed to use it. This would not be that bad if opening a draw didn't take three interactions from the player to first fail, then have to redo the entire action along with a small puzzle to get it unlocked. for instance there was a book that was up too high to reach and a tool tip shows that you can use an item to get it. You first need to zoom in to inspect it, look up at it, try to reach for it, realize you cant reach it, do a different action for getting out said item, interacting with it to push it down, interacting with it to look at it, interacting with it to open it, interacting with the pages, and then interacting to put it down plus a quick time event you had to pass to catch it to be able to open it. The control systems just feels like easy puzzles made harder by shotty control styles that make things take far longer then they should. Its was likely designed like this to highlight details, but it makes actions annoying. The hoverhand is also not trying to give you a choice for interaction: if there is not multi choice on screen with a timer, expect that item action to be required to progress, at lest in obvious situations like a big red button. when interacting with environment you tend to have a moment lag on actually moving if it requires you to interact beforehand. This happens on stairs, platforms, and edges causing the already very slow walking/ running speed to be even more noticeable. The voice acting is good, but what is said is kinda strange sometimes, plus the  models have a uncanny valley thing to them that is slightly unsettling. It was likely mocap done, and the majority of the budget went into the player models. it might just be my graphics settings but the player models stand out from most of the surroundings. the most notable one being during a dinner scean, the player models look really good, and the environment is rather well done, but the wine in the glasses they are holding looks like hardened epoxy. Everyone's eyes are also super wet to the point where its distracting, in part because they often do not move then as much as they should for how realistic they appear.  This also goes for general body movement, as it seems very emotive in some instances where it wouldn't be and oddly rigid in others where it shouldn't, just leaning more into the uncanny valley issue. It reminds me of this one SciFi B list movie from 2001 called Thir13en Ghosts, but set in Victorian hotel. In fact, due to the narrator that it pans out to sometimes, its sort of like Victorian twilight zone. All in all its like a sold 5/10 game saved by its environmental design. I do not recommend buying it at full price but mabey 15. the best part of it was the intro song.

_childDocuments_.review: I've been in love with Supermassive Games since I first played Until Dawn, and I've played all of the main games they've released since. Unfortunately The Devil in Me is a major nosedive in quality compared to the rest of the series.I've seen a lot of people complaining about bugs, but I didn't have many of those, probably because I waited 7 months after release to play the game. But just because they fixed most of the technical issues does not mean the game is good.The biggest problem with the game is the shift of emphasis from character, story and choice towards platforming, "puzzles", and exploration. The whole reason people love these games is because they let the player be the star of an interactive horror movie. That's what makes these games unique. You are in control of how characters develop, who lives and who dies, how different characters feel about one another. The emphasis of every single prior game has been on long cutscenes, dialogue, and important choices. Not so in the Devil in Me. With this game, Supermassive have ditched character development and meaningful choices in favor of turning the game into the worst platformer of all time, the worst puzzle game of all time, and the worst exploration game of all time, all in one!The majority of the game is spent wandering around dark environments with a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ flashlight (if you're lucky; most characters don't even get one of those), pushing crates, jumping across chasms, solving monkey brain puzzles, and getting hopelessly lost because everything looks the same. The pacing would suck even if these sections were taken out, but with them in the pacing is just nonexistent. Any small amount of tension that could be had is mercilessly killed when you have to wander around an endless series of dark corridors looking for some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ puzzle you have to do to progress.Characters now have inventories also, which is completely pointless and only serves to make the game longer and more boring. In one of the previous games, if you found a cabinet, you could open it. It's the same in this game, unless you're playing Charlie, in which case the cabinet will always be locked, and you'll have to use your "special ability" to unlock it. ♥♥♥♥ off.Immersion is also nowhere to be found in the Devil in Me. In all the previous games, regardless of their flaws, you always felt like you were in a horror movie. Your characters felt like actual humans and (for the most part) behaved like normal humans. In the Devil in Me, within five minutes of getting past the prologue you're jumping across chasms, climbing up cliff faces and crawling through caves, all wearing just casual clothes. Utterly breaks immersion, right from the start. Every single one of the platforming sections does absolutely nothing other than waste your time and remind you that you're playing a (♥♥♥♥) video game. And it's not even fun or challenging either, just boring. So. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Boring.I haven't even mentioned the story because frankly it's not worth mentioning. The concept is... acceptable at best. Everything past that is a joke. Most of the characters suck; they also aren't clearly established in the beginning like in the other DPA games. In all the previous installments, you were introduced to each character one by one, which made them feel distinct from one another in the early game. Not here. All the characters are introduced at the same time, making them all blend together. The writing and acting is at a low point too. The only actor who seemed like he even kind of gave a ♥♥♥♥ was Charlie. Everyone else acts totally chill and calm while their friends/lovers are getting murdered. Oh, that reminds me, the romance is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ awful. There are two romances that happen, and both reach their peak in the same scene that they're introduced.Also, the choices suck for the most part. There are only three real Saw-esque traps in the game, and the solutions to two of them are stupid and really just require you to get lucky. The third gives the illusion of a choice, but doesn't actually have one.I really hope this was just a fluke in the Anthology, and they take their time with the next game. House of Ashes showed the potential that this series has, but man. This is a low point for sure. The only explanation I can think of for why they pushed this horrible platforming/puzzle solving ♥♥♥♥ is to pad for time. Either that or the game director didn't have a clue what makes these games special.Here's to hoping Directive 8020 can redeem the series.P.S. Rereading this review, it is very, very negative - as it should be. But it wouldn't be fair to say that there's no fun to be had in the game. There are a (small) handful of cool scenes. Charlie is cool, and I liked Kate alright as well. Sometimes it does venture into the realm of "so bad it's good" which makes it fun to laugh at. And there was one scene that definitely got my heart rate up.

_childDocuments_.review: As a massive fan of Supermassive Games work when it comes to the branching choices genre of games, I'm sad to stay that this entry in The Dark Pictures Anthology is a massive failure. Alright, I may be slightly hyperbolic, however, The Devil In Me severely lacks polish and the general oomph of all previous entries. The problems I encountered early on were simple, texture related bugs, characters looking high-res in one camera angle and looking lower in another. As the game progressed I experienced a game stopping bug. I was required to pick up an item to solve a quest in a dark area. My character was using a flashlight. When I picked up the required item it would blink and disappear from the inventory, making progressing further impossible as the object was also now gone from its original spot. Reloading the save was pointless because the game saves as soon as it registers that you have picked up the item. After several attempts I discovered that having the flashlight on when picking up the item would cause it to disappear so I was able to finally progress.The story itself, about H.H. Holmes is fun, but it's marred by weak writing and inconsistent voice acting. It all seems very rushed. I felt the plot points need to be fleshed out a little more and some of the "connections" were tenuous in my opinion. Were it not for all the bugs and other inconsistencies, this wouldn't have been as much of a problem I feel.  If you're a fan of this series, wait for a future patch to fix the myriad of problems. If you're new to the series, start with a different game, unfortunately for this game, they're all better. Such a shame. Do better Supermassive Games, I believe in you !
