_childDocuments_.review: I've co-opped played every one of these titles with a friend around when they launch. You'd think after this many years, we'd learn to wait a while. However, even that said, this is a weak entry in this series and I think Supermassive really needs to take at least an additional year before releasing the next ones.Despite being the fourth game in this series and running on the same tech, they always launch with issues, especially with the online co-op. Until the first patch (which took weeks), this function didn't work at all. After the patch, we were able to start a session, but regularly had to quit out and restart a checkpoint because one of us wouldn't be able to interact with anything in the environment or one of us would get stuck in a loading screen. In fact, we had to purposefully get a worse version of the ending we should have been able to get because the game would get stuck at a loading screen if we pursued that one. All of these kinds of bugs existed in prior installments in the series. There is no excuse for them continuing to come up every single time, especially with how little patch support these tend to get.On top of that, this installment is just plain boring and felt very rushed. The premise is fantastic, being based on an actual historical serial killer. However, most of the first two thirds is either slow, plodding conversation or wandering around samey hallways and small rooms that are so dark, you can barely see what you're doing. None of the characters are likeable, nor do they have any kind of good chemistry. This isn't the fault of the actors, who I think are trying their best with the script and direction they had. Most of your choices lead to the same conclusions and there are lots of awkward cuts between sequences based on different choices because they weren't seamlessly put together.The final third has more action and more interesting situations, but it's largely standard stuff of quick time events and once again, being presented with choices that largely don't matter or the character taking the choice you made and undertaking it in the stupidest, most counterintuitive way possible. The only way you'll complete the game with all the characters alive is if you frequently make the opposite choice you would in real life.My friend and I really love the idea of this series and playing through our own schlocky horror stories. But Supermassive has clearly bitten off more than they can chew with their yearly release cadence here and I've been burned too many times. They need to take at least another year to get the next game polished to a shine before they ship it. I definitely won't be buying at launch again and unless the next one ships in great shape, it'll be a deep sale purchase for me.Get your acts together.

_childDocuments_.review: My wife and I have played through the entire series so far, including playing through The Quarry in Movie Night mode - while the story is interesting everything else is the worst out of the bunch though. The entire first hour of this game beyond the prologue is slow, tedious platforming with nothing of interest happening - while when you get to the hotel things start to pick up, there are far too many segments where you are just wandering around rooms, picking up things which are completely inconsequential to the rest of the game or the story.Besides that, the Co-op experience of this game has been the worst of the lot due to just how buggy it is: QTE prompts will fail for no reason (still having half a bar on the timer left), heartbeat prompts will fail despite getting the timing and rhythm down-pat and knowing you hit them, some of the more interesting ideas in co-op can drag the game down for one player while you just sit there waiting for the other to complete a section on their end or just outright screw you over (such as monitoring the cameras to keep track of where the killer is while the other player lures them through the corridors) and result in character deaths as the killer and your partner seemingly teleport around the map.Combine this with general Examine points not appearing sometimes and the game soft-locking itself because of it, or having scenes jump randomly as your off-screen co-op partner completes objectives in a completely different scene this game really can just leave you feeling annoyed and frustrated.Finally, when this crap happens to result in a character death and you realise you would have to go through all of the tedious parts of again just to have another go at not getting bitchslapped by another bug at a critical moment to save someone you lose any and all desire to finish this game.The positive I'll give it though: we both played through this on a Steam Deck each (one OLED and one LCD) and the game runs great at 11W TDP limit and a 30fps lock.

_childDocuments_.review: The Devil In Me is easily Supermassive Games' best work since Until Dawn. Of the 2 games Supermassive has released this year (The Quarry being the first) this game stands out as the clear winner among the pair. The Quarry felt too much like it was trying to one-up Until Dawn and it (super)massively failed to do so, there was a LOT of things that could've been better about that game (like having an ending for starters.) The Devil In Me takes the established Dark Pictures formula and really perfects it. I might be biased because of my love of slasher films, but the fact that this was a real genuine slasher instead of a creature feature (like every other Supermassive title so far) really seemed to work wonders for this type of game. I hope in the future we get more from the Dark Pictures and Supermassive Games like this one. On the negative side, they have to do something about the Keep Calm sections - either give us the option to disable them or to turn them into regular QTE prompts. Little Hope and House of Ashes managed to make them much easier somehow compared to Man of Medan but it seems they're back to being as difficult as possible. Sometimes you'll hit the button spot on but the game seems to think you've hit it too early or too late, which can lead to you being prematurely moved on from a scene or worse - having a character killed, leaving you to feel more annoyed than anything because in those moments it feels like it wasn't your choices that caused that as much as it was the game's wonky timing. Aside from that minor gripe, The Devil In Me is a gem among horror games and interactive movie style games and I highly recommend you try it out!

_childDocuments_.review: Not really sure why anyone "not recommend" this as it's really just an improved version of every installment in the series unless you just blind bought it and had never played The Dark Pictures series before.Intro (not the prelude) was slow and ROUGH. It took over an hour before I started to really get into the story. The only reason I kept going is because this series has built up a good reputation with me. I'm glad I stuck with it because I found the story to be interesting, disgusting and engaging overall. Graphically it's the best one by a wide margin, even better than The Quarry. Unbelievable detail to the characters. Playing with a 3080ti and could run evereything in 2K with max settings or 4k with a few things tuned down. It's super dark and gory, way more than any other game. Some genuinely messed up stuff throughout. I was probably more anxious playing this installment than any other game Supermassive has done, including Quarry and Until Dawn.There are few things that don't make sense, like every one of these games, due to how it's edited and put together. For example I had one character obtain a weapon and they never needed to use it, it just kind of disappeared. Super weird. I must have missed something along the way. Even though I kept everyone alive I missed about 4 secrets and apparently a whole section of the game given that there are several ??? unlockables still listed. If you like this series, I think this is the best one yet. I didn't really "like" any of the characters but I also didn't dislike any of them. I think the series has gone away from the "try to keep this person alive even though you hate them" formula and you just kind of try to keep everyone alive. I don't have a problem with that, it's just different.

_childDocuments_.review: I have never been more disappointed by a game. Having played all the previous games in the anthology (and thoroughly enjoyed them) I was incredibly hyped for "Devil in me" when I saw the trailer for the first time. The entire concept of a murder house, dolls made of human body parts and death games seemed like a great concept for this latest installment. I started playing the game way back when it was first released in a double player co-op. That's where the first disappointment comes in. It was absolutely not playable. Glitches prevented successful hiding and scenes could not be completed. Frustrated we decided to stop and wait for a bugfix update.The update came and we decided to restart. After all, we hadn't even made it into the house yet.This time we made it about half way I guess before another bug prevented us from going forwards. Restarting the scene didn't help as, you've guessed it, bugs caused the entire game to glitch as apparently scene restarts in multiplayer weren't an option.Not having much of a choice and at this point thoroughly fed up with the game we abandoned it for multiple months praying for yet another bugfix to be released.We've now made it all the way through. Did I enjoy it? Not really, no. The storytelling fell flat, had holes, and big ones at that. How come a character suddenly gets dragged off to their death in a cut-scene (through absolutely no fault of the player) just because the other player has apparently reached an all important point in the game and continued too far too quickly? If this is a thing maybe communicate it? Have visible timers or warnings? There were many instances where it felt that it didn't matter what one did as a player as the game would simply force us to be in the places it wanted us to be. Suddenly having keys we've never collected just being one example of many.To sum and wrap this up: Did I wholeheartedly look forward to this game? 100% yes. And yet I could not in good conscience recommend anyone to spend their money on it.All I can hope for is that the next installment will be better and live up to the predecessors in this series. I have, however, learned my lessons and will not get my hopes up too much and also give it a solid year before even attempting to play the upcoming game.

I want to preface by saying I've never played any of these DPA games in Co-op.This game has some awkward moments where characters can look lifeless (I.E, moving their heads around while not moving their eyes/blinking), one scene where the audio has issues, and scene changes can be pretty quite goofy (E.I Kate in the locker on the roof after hiding successfully).  Despite prior issues mentioned, the game runs pretty smooth and the horror aspect is top-notch.  As a Chicago native and horror/history enthusiast, I went in without reading the description for the game (as I've played the other DPA games) and was pleasantly surprised that the horror element relied on the imitation of H.H. Holmes Murder Castle.  This game relied less on the supernatural or fantastical elements that prior games did, it's a slasher game.There's also a dog.

_childDocuments_.review: This game suffers from the success of its predecessors, making it the least compelling entry in the series so far, with its expanded gameplay elements left unsupported by a bland and predictable narrative.The Devil In Me features more elements of interactivity and player engagement than any of the other entries in the Dark Pictures Anthology - doing so at the expense of other parts of the experience, like pacing and narrative. For example, the first 45 minutes after the prologue of the game are spent climbing cliffs, balancing across fallen trees, jumping across short gaps, shimmying through tight spaces, and pushing around climbable objects, all while the characters have very little meaningful dialog between them. This sequence culminates in a 15 second cutscene where the characters continue to say nothing meaningful and then decide to return to the base of the cliff that you've just spent 30 minutes to an hour climbing. 5 minutes later you are doing the exact same thing with two different characters in a largely similar environment. These sections add nothing to the story or characters, and purely exist to show off the game's new interactive elements. Isolated, this wouldn't be nearly as big of an issue, but unfortunately this sets the standard for what many other sections of the game feel like further in. Furthermore, this game is the shortest of the series, making these drawn out sequences of linear interactivity feel less like improvements to gameplay and more like a waste of time for the player that detract from replayability. Previous entries would have spent the early moments of the game in more meaningful ways - developing the story and characters, allowing the player to get a handle on relationships, motives, and temperaments, but throughout the entirety of  game character development is kept to a bare minimum. Emotions during dialog seem to swing wildly, with dialog and actions often feeling disconnected from one another. Characters are incredibly dumb, even for horror standards, and coupled with those awkward emotional swings, it often leaves the player frustrated and surprised at actions taken by characters outside of player choice.What  surprising is the story. If you know anything about H. H. Holmes, you can likely tell how this story goes without playing the game; its veiled simplicity is paper thin. The story's delivery is dry and relentlessly repetitive despite its short completion time. For a series whose focus is, first and foremost, to provide players with an engaging story that has gripping and meaningful choices and characters that matter, it leaves  to be desired.

_childDocuments_.review: This is without a doubt the worst of the entire series thus far. And that's coming from someone who has excitedly awaited every title up until this point. So bad, in fact, that I don't want to finish it, and honestly would rather just get a refund.The pros:* The story is related to one that any horror fans should know of.* It is a fourth game in the Dark Pictures series.The cons:* Animations are buggy and badly polished.* The characters aren't just unlikable, they're downright annoying.* Choices either don't make sense or don't matter.* Motion capture is all over the place, with no one even appearing to look in the right direction.* Voice acting is unbelievable, in a bad way.* New mechanics are added that didn't add much to the game, and I would personally argue, make the game more difficult. This isn't in a way that's enjoyable, but rather how it would be more difficult to drive a car while handcuffed to the wheel.* The online multiplayer is an absolute mess, and is buggy if you can even get it to work.All in all, this game seems like a badly created mess that had no real heart in it, and feels like it was rushed out the door half-baked. Normally, I wouldn't be so harsh, but I've come to expect significantly better quality from Supermassive Games. Never thought I'd give this to one of their titles, but this is a 2/10. Buy one of their other titles, and stay away from the dud that was the season finale.

_childDocuments_.review: I played CO-OP with my friend. (She hosted the lobby). We have played Man of Medan, Little Hope, and House of Ashes with little to no problem, but that was not the case with Devil In Me. There were frequent crashes on her end. Both of us experienced issues like QTEs, or Choices not showing up in key moments where they were supposed to be (One of which caused a character to die in our first playthrough). Camera angels were off in a lot of places. While using Mark's camera to take pictures I noticed it would flash green in some places as if there was something to take a picture of even though nothing important was there. The issues that really ground my gears the most was that we were unable to finish the game. We came accros a bug in the very end We tried several different methods to try and fix the issue and could not seem to get past that section at the end of the game.That's a hard question to answer. I love the story, but I was still a bit disappointed. To me, none of the characters were very relatable, and it was difficult for me to build their relationships. Some of the scenario's didn't make sense. Although I admit I did not find all the collection clues in my playthrough, there were a few that were a bit confusing for me. The CO-OP experience was poor. It was too easy for one player to continue the story before the other was done exploring their section, and with the bugs and other issues, that made it worse. For now I am not recommending the game until some of these serious issues are patched.

_childDocuments_.review: The Devil in Me is a great season finale for the first season of the Dark Pictures Anthology! If you haven't played the other titles and are interested in checking them out, then I recommend starting here or Little Hope. The Devil in Me has shown how much the team at Supermassive Games has grown and what the future holds for the series! They were dealt with the obstacles of dealing with a confined play space after handling mostly open-spaced titles. The story was by far the best, that is if you are looking for less of a twist and more of a straightforward serial killer drama. Any true crime fan will be interested in checking this product out!Overall, if you are even a little interested, then I recommend playing it. However, if you do not like paying full price for games, then just wait. (You were going to anyway! XD)

_childDocuments_.review: The game feels unfinished and without any real love given to it. Odd because these games just keep getting more expensive but worse at the same time. The first Dark Pictures games were 20$ but now we're up to 40$ and a game that is worse than all the others.(Spoilers will appear)>First of all, animations are reused. Instead of having some different shimmy animations they all use the same. It's like this with other animations aswell, wall boosting for example. It's quite immersion breaking when characters are leaning against things that dont exist. One scene the comes to mind is when they're going to shimmy through a chain link fence, you could easily just swoop through that no problem. Instead you have to to a whole shimmy animation where you lean against nothing. It simply does not feel like a game that has been given enough time.The running animation in this game is god awful and same with the jumping ones, they feel to comical and sped up. Look how they run in Devil In Me and ask yourself "Does a normal person run like that?">Characters: are decent but nothing compared to the older games, I simply had no attachment to them and couldn't care less about them. You dont get to know much about them if you dont go and read books around the game.>Graphics: The graphics in my opinion are pretty good but even on the absolute lowest with a decent setup i only had around 45fps. I had 30 on Ultra but the visuals didn't change that much. There is no motion blur option so that was a huge negative, turning the camera too fast made you dizzy.>Gameplay/Mechanics: The mechanics in this game are pretty much the same as you've seen in the previous ones. The only new mechanic is the "Hide" when you have run and find a spot to hide. Personally this feature was pretty lacking and made no sense most of the time with no feedback when you're supposed to reappear from cover.Even though this game reused mechanics it had minimal QTE events and more choice events. This was a huge problem with how the game treats choices. Instead of giving you multiple options with maybe only one being the safe and right one it only gives you 2. In the previous games if you choose a really bad choice you had a chance most of the time with hard QTE, In this game you don't even get to redeem yourself.There was 2 points in the game where you have to choose between killing 2 different characters. Its complete 50/50 chance if you pick the right one because there is no way you could know. For example, kill Erin? she dies. kill Kate? Mark goes on a rampage seeing her die and just rips the whole room apart saving both of them. How is a reasonable person supposed to think about that? Jamie or Kate? it all depends on who has the screwdriver and who presses the button but HOW are you supposed to know the right choice when Jamie showed previously that the screw driver had no effect on the glass. My best quess was the she would open the panel she had on her side and hotwire the thing or something since THAT IS WHAT SHE DOES. If the glass was breakable why not show Jamie actually damaging the glass the first time she hits it.>Jumpscare and intensity: The game did not feel as scary as something like House of Ashes or Until Dawn with intense situations where you would clench your ass. It was mostly stale except for the ending where there actually was QTE and it felt like you could die any second.The Jumpscare were pretty predictable except for one that actually got me because it was well made.>As usual this game is not really made for Movie Night, one player gets more playtime than others but i guess thats expected in a game like this and with such few characters.One thing I also disliked with this game was how other people can get your character killed. Since this game is a primarily singleplayer i can understand it but it was quite annoying when you get to play 4 times only to get killed because your friend made the wrong choice.Lastly, this game needs a HUGE epileptic warning in the start of the game because WHY DOES IT FLASH SO MUCH. Everytime you pick something up and turn it around the game does a flashbang on you turning the entire screen white. WHY, GOD OH WHY. The previous games also had this and i don't get why, it doesn't add ANYTHING. It's a horror game, of course I'm going to play it at night in complete darkness, SO WHY DOES IT DO THIS.Will most likely update this post with additions, this is just from the top of my head.

_childDocuments_.review: I am a big fan of Dark Pictures Anthology and have played all the games (Little Hope is my personal favourite). Still, I would not recommend playing this one. I will try to be brief in explaining my reasons:The biggest one is that neither the behaviour of the villain nor protagonists make sense. The Villain is omnipotent, omniscient serial killer who can control hundreds of contraptions with shear power of his will. This would make sense in the world of Little Hope or Medan, but not here.The characters on the other hand behave like complete lemmings. One minute they talk about how they should stick together and in one second they just scatter around running and getting in random death traps. Moreover, this happened not on one, but ON TWO SEPARATE OCCASIONS. They run into a room, door closes behind them. They look surprised. Ridiculous.The game is also boring. There is more walking, crouching, crawling around (pretty boring) locations than in any of the previous games. And it barely makes any sense, it seems it was added for padding only as all of the walking/puzzling sections are linear (which is fine by me). There are also sokoban-puzzles!! I guess they forgot all the backlash Broken Sword 3 got for its box pushing.The only explanation for why this game is so much worse than the first 3 is that the best people in the studio were probably making the Quarry at the same time. The Quarry ended up an absolute masterpiece, this game is the opposite. Sadly.

_childDocuments_.review: I dont know why this game is getting MIXED reviews, so here is a POSITIVE one for a change.This story in the Dark Pictures Anthology is inspired by the real life serial killer Henry H Holmes, who was notorious for creating a hotel, in which he killed his victims with elaborate traps, and disposed of their bodies in the basement. The hotel was dubbed the Murder Castle, and was speculated to have been used to claim the lives of 200 people. You play as each member of a film crew that must escape from a recreation of the hotel, and the mysterious killer who controls it.Kudos to everyone at Supermassive for consistently improving upon each game. The setting and story are interesting, and the characters make a change from a group of teenagers. Relationships are touched upon, but don't take up too much game time, preferring to focus on survival and sleuthing.The puzzle solving aspects are more physical this time around, feeling on a par with Soul Reaver or Ubisoft's Prince of Persia series. Exploration is aided by additional items that are unique to each character - one has a pencil that can be used to trace over indented writing, whilst another has a business card, that can be used to jimmy locks open. There are also cameras and microphones at your disposal, but unfortunately these items do not appear to be utilised much. I hope that features such as this will be improved upon in the next game.The atmosphere is incredible, and is certainly up there with the second story, Little Hope. The scale of the murder castle and the island it rests on shows Supermassive is very confident about creating environments that are just as overwhelming and unsettling as the horrors that inhabit them.The acting in this game leaves you invested, and it feels as if Supermassive is getting to a stage now where they are able to get a greater variety of actors to star in their games, who move away from the "teen horror" setting.All these features make me keen to see what happens in season two's first story, Directive 8020James Franklin 27/11/2022

_childDocuments_.review: Despite a few visual glitches on my run through I can't complain about the games stability or graphics but I will say the DX11 version is more stable on my rig.The gameplay loop is the familiar Supermassive Games/Dark Pictures formula of interact with cutscenes by making choices, explore an environment, pick up items and secrets that expand the story and lore then throw in some QTEs.One or two additions this time round are inventory items you can collect and use in the world and in some cutscenes, and the need to run and hide at certain times in the game.The story was interesting loosely inspired by the real life killer H.H. Holmes and taking place in a recreation oh his murder hotel featuring a villain styling himself on Holmes, unfortunately the characters while serviceable aren't sparkling company and they're interactions seem to lack the familiarity of those from Supermassive's other games like The Quarry or Little Hope.Overall I'd recommend when it's on sale for a fun B-movie experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Man, I gotta say I'm pretty disappointed. I had really high hopes after playing House of Ashes with my best friend. The puzzles and QTE's are pretty well done and engaging, however playing co-op is like playing with >100 ping. Half the major events end up failing on my end because I didn't 'react' fast enough to the host's connection, however on my side it showed I did it correctly. Moments where I need to hide would show a cutscene as if I didn't hide, and within a second change back to me hiding. It's really immersion breaking and unfortunately ruins a lot of the gameplay, and changes the outcomes that could be prevented. That's the main issue with the story bugs, not to mention in a lot of the gameplay loops, my characters head gets locked and twists around, characters lagging and sliding when they're shimmying, facial expressions blank or lagging. I'm not sure if it's the co-op multiplayer that's bugged but it takes away so much from the game that I can't recommend buying in this state. If they bring some hot fixes to work on these issues, then it might be.

_childDocuments_.review: I've now played this game on my Steam Deck and on my PC. (PC has an overclocked 5900X and 3080 in it with 32GB of RAM) The graphical difference was definately stark, but I'll say that I intentionally locked the game at 60 fps at max graphics with Ray Tracing and all enabled with zero dips. I've experience no crashes, and overall have had a good experience as far as stability goes!However, as with all good comes some negative. The game itself is actually not a terrible one. But in the same vein, I'll say that the story is a bit....Lacking. Thankfully this one doesn't have the same long pauses as The Quarry did, but the story sure did seem to try something new and I don't think it worked for me. While creepy, I wouldn't say it fell into "terror" for me. Beyond a few jump scares (which I hate, and only look past if the horror elements actually work) there just wasn't really any feeling of dread throughout the story. The death scenes also lacked a certain dramatic flair, they seemed to just be simple.Can also say that I don't think the new "coin" mechanism quite did it for me either. I come to this game type looking for basically a movie that I can change the outcomes of. Something where my decisions ultimately have some say in what goes down. Instead, I feel like I spend quite a bit of time simply walking and hiding as opposed to watching anything. I feel like the tension gained from the scenes is lost from the fact that I just endlessly wander. I suppose this would be a pacing issue?Overall, the game is okay. I don't think it's amazing, but I do think it could've used a bit of refining. I'd say snag it on a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: The Devil In Me is the fourth game in the Dark Pictures horror franchise. When a group of film makers visit a recreation of the “murder castle” used by America’s first serial killer, it turns out to be more real than they were expecting.•	If you’ve played any of the previous games you’ll be familiar with the gameplay loop. The player controls a different character in each scene, and must make dialogue choices during conversations with other characters, and perform QTEs during action scenes.•	Each character will live or die based on your choices and your success or failure with the QTEs, as you try to escape from the killer and their deadly traps which are similar to those seen in the Saw films. Some of the choices are really tough, especially when the killer is close, and you need to decide whether to try to fight, hide, or run away.•	There’s also some basic exploration where you can find secret items to add more background detail to the story, and some basic puzzle solving such as finding keys to unlock doors, or moving boxes to climb over walls.•	The pacing was really good. The first couple of hours are spent setting up the story and getting to know the characters, and then when the action starts, it felt like they were in constant danger in almost every scene until the end.•	In my version of the story, one character died because of my bad decision in what I think was their first possible death scene. And towards the end of the game, I failed a balance beam section which caused someone to fall to their death, and about 10 minutes later I made another bad decision to lose a third character. With only 2 characters left, my heart was seriously pounding during the final scenes, but in the end, I did manage to save them both  . This was exactly the experience I was looking for during Halloween spooky season.•	The killer and the murder castle setting are interesting.•	I didn’t really like any of the playable characters. Most of them are annoying, and constantly arguing with each other. It didn’t help that the character I thought I might actually like  was the one who I lost first. However, I do believe that horror is the one genre where annoying characters don’t necessarily ruin the experience, because at least you might be able to enjoy their death scenes.•	Voice acting is very good.•	It took me 7.5 hours to complete the story, although it could take longer if you keep everybody alive because you’ll probably see a few more scenes.•	I didn’t have any problems with bugs, crashes, or framerate, while playing the singleplayer story.•	Before I bought the game, I read a lot of other reviews which complain about some significant game breaking bugs, but I did notice that most of these reviews mentioned they were trying to play the coop version.•	I’ve mentioned this before in my reviews of other Dark Pictures games, but I don’t like how these games regularly pop up a “bearing updated” message in the top corner of the screen when you make a choice. And this game also regularly informs you of “special feature unlocked”. I feel like these messages are distracting and immersion breaking, which reduces the horror experience.Devil In Me’s overall review score is quite low, but my own personal experience was extremely enjoyable. I suspect this could be because I played in the single player mode, so I didn’t suffer from the bugs which seem to affect the coop mode.I think this game is definitely worth buying on sale, if you’re a fan of the franchise or the horror genre.1)	House of Ashes (best characters, best monsters)2)	Devil In Me3)	Man of Medan (story depth is limited by being the shortest game)4)	Little Hope (I really hated the ending twist)

_childDocuments_.review: I love this series, but this latest game is absolutely horrendous in it's current state, and I cannot in good conscience recommend this game until they do a MAJOR update to it. It was beyond buggy on a wide scale from start to finish with very little redeeming the bugs in my eyes. The camera would stop working for us, the characters hand's would literally *invert* and point the lights at their own face versus where it should go (and yes, it did make the light useless as a result!!), the antagonist would get stuck in walls where it would totally halt progression and we had to reboot the game over 20 times (no joke!!) just to get passed things like this. This resulted in having to restart entire chapters even though we were at the end. We could not reload from the current save point on several occasions because the dude would be stuck in the wall again. The way the game is designed is forcing players to play the game multiple times, but dealing with the constant rebooting makes even one play through absolutely painful to get through. We almost rage quit at the Director's Suite chapter because it kept bugging out, and we had to reboot that *entire* sequence alone over 10 times. It accounted for the majority of our bugs, and the other part being with Mark/Jamie in the Interrogation sequence. Either Jamie's side would totally glitch out or Mark's side would over and over.Aside from that, if you do the co-op Shared Story version of the game it would *constantly* cut off cut scenes and make both sides miss out on entire story lines. At the end we were confused how characters knew names and sets of information we never saw at all, but they just magically learned in the pieces of story we were not allowed to see. The little coins are not shared by both parties, which caused a big problem in one of us being rich and the other not having enough to more than 3 or 4 dioramas by the end. We just picked them up as we both saw them and noticed half way through that they opted not to share the coins when it really should be a shared item given the costs of each diorama. Also, the premonitions and secrets were not shared as they were in previous games, so we were unable to share what we discovered that could make a big impact on decisions either of us might make to save characters potentially. I didn't get to see any of the premonitions my co-op partner found, but he could see mine in his menu while in game together. After we finished the game we had zero credit for the other's Secrets and Premonitions that we could not get to ourselves due to the nature of the game being structured with diverging story lines at the same point in time.Outside of the game mechanics and the directing of the player, it really relied far too much on jump scares to get any sort of "fear" or engagement from the player. I was more afraid of what dumb thing they were going to have pop out of no where that zero to do with the story than the actual killer coming out and trying to go all Jason Vorhees on me. They really dropped the ball on the story line and the horror element in this game and its disappointing considering they had such a good depth of history and story to pull from. Instead they kept throwing in things popping out at you to scare you versus having the fact there is a serial killer on the loose with you in a murder house. TL;DR: Don't buy the game in it's current state. It was more frustrating than enjoyable and adventurous. I will still buy the next one, because I love the series. Man of Medan was coded better than this one, and that says a lot.

_childDocuments_.review: This game blows. Genuinely the most disappointing "Dark Pictures" game so far because conceptually I think it's got some fun ideas. But execution wise? Oh man.Out of the gate you'll notice how atrociously buggy it is. Characters holding out items in cutscenes when they shouldn't be, randomly failing quick time events and don't breathe sections in multiplayer, animations missing / being skipped in co-op. The camera freezing in place and needing to restart a section. At one point one of the characters was straight up missing their arms - Rayman style. Which to be honest was actually pretty funny, but it’s not a great look for the game.Plus it suffers a lot of the pitfalls of the other Dark Picture games - frustratingly sluggish controls, same stupid logic at times, pointless 'trait' updates. I appreciate them trying to add more mechanics into the game with pushing / pulling boxes, fuse box 'puzzles', hide mechanics, vaulting walls and small obstacles, an inventory, shimmying, balancing, yadda yadda. Ultimately though, despite making the game more gamey, it in turn feels bloated and slow. I don't care about watching Charlie push a heavy box into place to climb over a wall. I want to watch the interactions between the characters and the story unfold. Which might I add felt weirdly cut together at times. Jarring, even. Often it was very obvious that decisions made had no impact, at least in dialogue. I know this has always been the case with these games but it's painfully obvious in this one.I will say that this game does do a pretty good job at establishing the likeability of the characters. As in, this might be one of the first games where I didn't just think everyone was an ass. However multiplayer probably helped in this way with conversation manipulation.And I'm glad they toned down the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ QTEs. That at least feels less frustrating.In summary:It's atrociously buggy and very inconsistent in co-op (events somehow played out differently between players?); all round messy. So many poor developer decisions and often weird pacing in conversations. The Devil in Me is sadly and strangely the worst one yet due to all the technical issues present, despite being really interesting narrative wise in concept. I only found it bearable due to multiplayer, but was the experience worth 120 AUD…? I’d personally say definitely not.Main selling point: the 60 AUD game doesn't go for too long...Just watch it on YouTube or watch a mate play. Or at least wait for them to patch out all the issues.

_childDocuments_.review: I have been playing video games in one fashion or another for going on 20 years now.  I've never (to my knowledge) left a review for a game on here before.  I'm going out of my way to do this because of how terrible this game is.  I've played games in an Alpha phase with more polish than this.This is the most disappointing game I've ever purchased and it's not necessarily close.I'm generally not too hard on games review-wise.  I can deal with some bugs or graphical issues and story telling loop-holes.  But this game is unplayable.  I saw reviews before purchasing that included comments about the game being buggy and hard to play and I assumed they were being slightly over dramatic.  They were not.  DO NOT PURCHASE THIS GAME.Negatives:-The frame rate drops made the game very difficult/impossible to play.  For reference I have a 3070 and the previous DPA games played perfectly fine on my old 1070.  This is a matter of optimization with this game alone.-Movement on mouse and keyboard is terrible.  Legitimately the worst character movement in any game I've ever played.-Character models completely disappearing during important scenes-Character just appearing in different locations after a cut scene starts-Sound files bugging out and not playing/playing over each other makes the game hard to understand-Dead characters appearing in scenes (yes, characters that you previously watched die just randomly appearing in future scenes).-CHARACTERS BEING ALIVE FOR ONE PLAYER AND NOT THE OTHER DURING CO-OP-Camera constantly snapping random directions made movement near impossible-Constant game breaking bugs requiring a reset every 30-45 minutes-Multiple instances where you were not able to tell if you died because of a mistake or a bug-QTEs not working.  Multiple instances of getting a green indicator signaling a completed QTE but then also a failure noticePros:-Story is okayThis game was unbeatable by me and my cousin because of what I assume was a disconnect between our games regarding which characters were alive. This game is not worth a $5 purchase as it stands.  If you're interested in the story then watch a Let's Play online.  Do not purchase this game in its current state.  You will regret it.  It is bad.  Very.  Bad.

_childDocuments_.review: If I could give the game a mixed review I would. The game isn't bad per say, but isn't great. I did not run into any bugs, issues or glitches of any kind unlike some reviews so I cannot comment on these issues. Game ran very smoothly, no noticeable clunky animations, no crashes or bugs limiting my progress.The story wasn't very strong in my opinion. There wasn't much of a real backstory or context. You get some backstory to the idea the story is bringing to the table, but nothing is detailed to truly explain a few key points. The end had somewhat of a twist, but it also did very little to explain anything going on. The best context you get is wandering around aimlessly trying to find clues to piece together the story and details the best you can. I don't need everything spoon fed to me, but a lot of clues were very random and hard to understand the context when the game gives you very little to go off of. The game is not scary. There were a few cheap jump scares that startled me slightly, but otherwise its a load of QTE's with pretty predictable twists and moments. The game is creepy and in it's own way pretty messed up when you sit back and think about it, but there was a complete lack of any sort of tension throughout the game. No real chase scenes, hiding was nothing more than holding a button at a certain area in a room that was clearly marked. The antagonist would act like he was about to find you only to randomly walk away while the characters would mutter to themselves, breathe heavy or cry. Lets be real, anyone with ears would hear these people hiding. Lacking in suspense and tension that makes a horror game truly gut wrenching in my opinion.The game is not difficult to save everyone. There are 3 or 4 moments where your choices actually have an impact and can kill of a character. Most were pretty obvious which one was the right decision. The rest of the dialogue choices aside from one near the end had zero impact and did not make a difference in the story. This game is far from a choose your own path and more of your choices slightly alter the linear story in front of you.This game is 60 percent cut scenes, 30 percent quick time events and walking and 10 percent actual game play. If you enjoy watching cut scenes every 30 seconds mixed in with walking/running, crouching/crawling, moving boxes ect, or mashing buttons this game is for you.All in all I give this game a 6/10. Was not a bad game by any means. Just lacked any true tension or fear and was very much filled with QTE's and walking.

_childDocuments_.review: The Devil in Me is the fourth and final instalment of the Dark Pictures Anthology, the horror series released by Supermassive Games over the span of four years. As the last title of the first season (season two has been already confirmed) I was expecting quite a lot from this game, also considering the improvements I have seen in the recent . The Devil in Me starts in 1893 at the World’s Fair Hotel run by H.H. Holmes, one of the most famous serial killers known in American history. After a brief tour of the hotel playing as a happy, but soon to be dead, married couple, we are moved to the present day in which a small film crew is hired to shoot a documentary about the serial killer inside a replica of the World’s Fair Hotel, which has been built on a distant island by a mysterious fan.For obvious reasons, the story can be quite predictable, as we immediately understand this isn’t just another hotel replica, but a real and dangerous Castle of Horror. Those who unfortunately don’t understand it are the five protagonists: the film director, the TV host, the camera guy, the key grip and the sound engineer. One step on the island and we already know it will be impossible to empathize with them. First they do everything they are told to (even giving up their own phones), then they start to investigate the place like some sort of detectives but when things start happening, they take forever to realize they are in danger. I could make many examples of illogical behavior, but those would be spoilers, so I will just say that this cast of characters is probably the weakest I have seen in a Supermassive production in terms of writing and development. The constant death jokes, the flirting and the rivalry between some characters has been widely abused in these games as we are reaching a point where every relationship is narrated in the same flat and boring way. Characters’ facial animations aren’t very expressive either, perhaps the weakest of the entire Anthology. That is not to say they are bad, but they aren’t what we have been used to with Supermassive games and there are some ugly “robot face” moments here and there.Another big issue with the story is the lack of a strong antagonist that provides pure moments of horror. From the start, we already know who we are dealing with, so there isn’t any surprise around the corner and the Castle of Horror simply becomes a set of death traps, some of which are also used multiple times, like the common  “save A or B character” type of game. There are many cheap jumpscares and some still got me, but other than this there aren’t any particularly memorable thrilling moments. Considering the setting, which is actually “fun” to explore (yes, I love hotels), there could have been space for more death rooms and sick games, but the quantity and quality of these are rather low.Now the gameplay greatly mixes cutscenes, choices, exploration and action sequences that include multiple quick-time events. Throughout the story, we will play as each protagonist at different times, facing moral dilemmas and struggling to survive. There is a moral compass that allows us to make choices within a short period of time; these are divided into rational (mind symbol) and emotional (heart symbol), greatly affecting relationships and the chance of survival. Compared to the previous games from the series, exploration has been further improved and there are many more open areas to explore, looking for documents, secrets and collectibles. There are also some new gimmicks that make exploration more interesting, such as the ability to run, climb, crawl under certain obstacles or jump over gaps, as well as the need to find a spot to hide when the situation becomes more dangerous. Another interesting addition is the inventory system. This time characters own different items (related to their work) that can be used during particular circumstances. For example, Erin (the sound engineer) is equipped with a directional microphone that allows her to hear through walls. Mark (the camera guy) is equipped with a camera for taking pictures at anytime. While this inventory system is certainly refreshing, it also seems to be very limited, as not all characters have meaningful items that make the difference during gameplay. I was taking many pictures with Mark’s camera, before realizing there was no point in taking them as nothing was happening. I’m certain there must be hidden scenes connected to the items’ usage, but those aren’t really that obvious. A few items can be crucial during some puzzle solving sequences, like in the case of Jamie (the key grip) who is equipped with a multimeter, used to rewire electrical circuits. Graphically the game is really beautiful, with superb lighting and very detailed environments. To my own surprise, the game runs flawlessly even at max settings, so the optimization is great and there shouldn’t be any issue even with older hardware. Unfortunately, there are still some bugs and glitches, and some moments feel more unpolished than others. It took me around 11 hours to finish the game by saving every character, exploring every single corner and collecting almost everything. I also had to reload the same chapters a few times due to unexpected bugs that lead to my character’s death, like a quick loading screen starting during an action sequence that involved multiple QTEs, or a bugged QTE that started right after a “smash the button repeatedly” sequence (and I was still smashing that button when the new QTE suddenly appeared). I was also forced to restart the ending credits due to the achievement “Hope You Enjoyed Your Stay” not unlocking, but I don’t know if there are other possibly-bugged achievements in there that I missed.The Devil in Me could have concluded season one in a more convincing way, but it still delivers the full Supermassive horror package, with some welcome additions. It is probably the weakest entry of the series to date, as characters don’t do much to keep the story alive, despite the fascinating  scenario and the infinite potential for  death games.

_childDocuments_.review: I really can't recommend this game, even though I'm an avid fan of Supermassive Games and I've played each of them multiple times. The game has serious gameplay pacing issues that really get into the way of the story and halfway through it, I really just wanted to rush through things and get it over with. Hell, I even quit the game a few times since those parts were extremely tedious and buggy/clunky that I just felt annoyed. No idea how but they managed to create some of the worst animations they've ever did. The constant moving gaze of the characters, staring into emptiness when talking to people, having little to no reaction when you most expect it, lip sync being poor, glitching into objects, textures in some background being very low resolution and just overall a worse quality than their previous games. I'm sure the actors did the most with what was presented to them but there were some questionable voice acting sequences that just didn't present the situation at hand and fell flat or just sounded like b-tier VA. The main antagonist was quite possibly the least scariest person I've ever encountered in a video game. The  constant jumpscares were poorly done and just tasteless, coming at you almost every 15 minutes until they just become an annoyance. The main characters you control have to be one of the most incompetent people in history since they couldn't do anything except run and trip instead of trying to fight back a man that looked less intimidating than most of them. None of them were very likeable except maybe Erin but even she gets annoying towards the end and I couldn't care less if I saved any of them or even bothered to listen to what they had to say.The music was just tense for no apparent reason while you scoured the empty rooms and hallways to try and read a bunch of useless information that was thrown at you while you tried your best to navigate with the awful controls. There were some things I liked that were, again, ruined by the slow and repetitive gameplay but at least I appreciated that were introduced. Running, climbing and similar actions are welcome and the use of inventory was sorely lacking in previous games but still.. poorly implemented.All in all, I feel like this is their worst game and I feel utterly disappointed since I know Supermassive can do so much better. Step up your game, guys!

_childDocuments_.review: Had a lot of fun and personally find this to be my favorite entry in the anthology so far. I feel that each installment has improved, and the new gameplay features such as balancing over thin walkways and the inventory were nice additions. Personally, the tone of the struggling cast with their job and career dilemmas was my favorite cast so far. This was also my favorite setting from the hotel to the outside tooAt the end of season one of The Dark Pictures Anthology, I personally find the final act of "House of Ashes" to be the most exhilarating despite this game being my favorite in the series so far. I enjoyed the longer runtime and played it over the course of four days to enjoy it slowly. I also found it to be the easiest anthology game for me personally after failing miserably at saving characters in Man of Medan, Little Hope, and The Quarry due to a lot of overthinking on my part. And while I've read some comparisons of each installment to Until Dawn, I really enjoy the anthology because I find a few moments that stick with me for a long time, and often those moments are really special. It took me some time to warm up to the cast, but it quickly became addicting around the dinner sceneLastly, the worse ending is actually my favorite regardless of the choice you make in it. I received a good ending with 3 alive and 2 dead, but watching the worst ending on Youtube afterwards made me love it the most. The biggest thing I loved about the game was how certain things were not confirmed before cutting away from the scene and coming back minutes later to surprise you. I won't give specifics on the scenes, but one happen in the mid-game and the other at the end of the worst ending

_childDocuments_.review: After "House of Ashes" which hit all of the marks of being scary, exciting, fun characters, and having big set pieces it was nice to see that the upcoming game, The Devil In Me, would focus on just a normal human serial killer while hopefully keeping the game exciting, scary, and having the fun characters minus the big set pieces in favor of smaller, more tense moments. However, it seems most of the really scary things happen before the game starts and you find or hear about them in written or audio logs. This is probably the weakest game in the series for me, along with story and pacing issues it was marred with technical issues (the faces do indeed look a lot worse in this game, the game pretty much wants to force you to use a controller over mouse and keyboard, QTE commands dont work all the time (particularly the button mashing) as well as a truly unlikable cast of characters. It was hard for me to finish the game with everyone surviving, not because that was difficult in itself but because I wanted most of the characters to die. There were also instances where all survivors are together and could take down the unarmed killer with probably little to no injury but all five of them run from a seemingly middle aged guy. The pros for this game are: 1) The actual main story thread between the games in the anthology which is what the heck is happening with The Curator? 2) Each character had a special ability or item they can use, this needs to be expanded on and refined in future games 3) The killer has a cool hat. 4) Received this game as a gift so I didn't have to pay for it, thanks Dave.

_childDocuments_.review: Finally, I made my way to playing The Devil in Me. Let me start off by saying that my absolute favorite of the anthology is House of Ashes, but I enjoyed each of the others... this is the exception. The story-line isn't compelling or very interesting. The characters are so unlikable that you don't even care if they live -- and I say that as someone who was able to have the entire group survive on the first (and last) play-through. The "scares" relied entirely on jump scares, which you come to anticipate early on in the game due to them being incredibly formulaic. I won't mention specifics of the story or plot line because I don't want to spoil it... but it is singularly uninspired. I remember at the end of House of Ashes seeing this trailer and being so pumped for it to come out. I waited quite a while to play frankly because I saw the reviews and didn't want to pay full price for a subpar game. If you like Supermassive, you may get a kick out of playing this but do yourself a favor and wait until it is heavily discounted. It's not worth it otherwise.

_childDocuments_.review: It still baffles me that you have to download a separate application to play this game co-op. If "It takes two" can do it, you can do it too, it's not rocket science. Just have one God d*mn game, not this intricate system of two games, with a CD-Key that you have to pass on to one of your friends, just so you can play ONCE. It's done just to restrict players by having them both buy the game or wait for Santa to come along with a f*cking one month period extra special mega suck me dry opportunity for you both to play on a single copy of the game. God forbid we make it accessible on a permanent, free friend pass that boosts the player base and spreads the word around. That's the only purpose. Stop it! Get some help!Another thing that baffles me is how in the God forbidden f*ck you have so many people working on a ~ 5h game with mid to high graphics and really average storyline, yet the bugs are so obvious Stevie Wonder can finger his a*shole with both his hands while tripping b*lls on acid and still see them? The f*cking credits were longer than some gameplay loops, you had quite a lot of testers, what the f*ck? What were they testing? Their nerves on how much desync they can handle? Even if they were playing in single-player mode only, the amount of times characters would just reposition themselves like f*cking Flash zooming across the screen was more than irl Ezra Miller's felony charges for molesting young girls.The friend pass thing was less of a pain in the a*s than previous titles.Story was fairly average, the Saw aesthetic was decent but the f*cking character development across acts and the decisions you had to make for these brain dead characters, oh my! It's like playing Bully but all the kids were in special ed. How in Christ's long nail f*cks do you write characters so brain dead, so out of touch with their surroundings, so bafflingly ret*arded? It's like watching a cross over of Scary Movie and some f*cked up TikTok TV Series. For example, in one scene There seems to be a lack of.... everything when it comes to animations. Motion capture, while it sounds good in theory, it's not really avant-garde when the best description for the facial expressions in this game is a comment I read on youtube: "The characters look just as lively as the mannequins".It seems that with every iteration of the Dark Pictures, Supermassive really outdo themselves on lowering the quality. I like this type of games, I really do but it's painful to expect greatness and be let down by the lack of perseverance in someone's craft. I don't expect perfection, I don't think anyone does. I just expect for characters not to Flash their nuts across the screen in predictable jump scares, saying their mediocre lines which can very well be replaced by "bro lol no cap" and the killer T posing, saying "fr fr no cap bro" and the whole story would stay the same.To summarize this game, imagine the Scooby gang but..... Velma. Just Velma, the new show. Just imagine that, it encapsulates this game perfectly. Soulless, predictable with a lot of prospect for a good story which eventually dies like a rabid dog. I liked it but I feel like I liked it only by necessity. So I can lie to myself that there's still hope for this series. Man of Medan was good, Little Hope was.... in retrospective it wasn't that bad. House of Ashes was interesting but this one? I can't recommend it, man. It's just not that good. Story is average, plot holes the size of my a*shole after a spicy shawarma, animations that might as well be AI generated and character development that rivals TEACCH. If you plan to get it because of friend pass offers, don't do it at full price. It's not worth it. On a decent discount, yeah, go for it, you do you, king.Oh and I had to let the game run for a while so I can write this review because all my "good" hours were on the friend pass version which nobody cares for when it comes to reviews.

_childDocuments_.review: So once again I wish Steam had a middle option, somewhere between yes and no. A "yes, but..." button. First off I want to say that I love this series. I love the style and I love the mechanics for the most part. And the stories are pretty good as well. But this, being the last one in this "season", is a bit disappointing. Not bad,  just a little underwhelming. Especially considering how good House of Ashes is. Personally I didn't come across the technical glitches people have been complaining about. I did notice that the character modals look not as good as in previous entries. Can't put my finger on it, but in other entries they looked more alive, more real. Also it doesn't help to relate to the characters when they are profoundly stupid. When you are an hour well into the traps full mansion and your characters are still asking "what's going on?!" when they find a locked door, it makes them seem moronic.Story-wise, the story is not bad, but, like other entries, while tributing a lot of classic horrors (Saw, House of Wax, Nightmare on Elm Street 3, to name a few), they also fall into the realm of cliche. A tribute is a dangerous business. The line between it and just lack of originality is very fine. It takes a lot of time to get to a point where it really hooks you. I found myself waiting for it to become good in the first 4-5 hours or so. I'm also comparing it to another horror in the same style from Supermassive Games - The Quarry - and also compared to that one, this one falls short. But it does have some good moment, a terrific atmosphere if you are a horror fan, and all in all it's entertaining enough for the price tag. I'd say in general this one is definitely worth picking up, now or during a sale, and I look forwards to see what's next from Supermassive Games. Hopefully a season 2 of the The Dark Pictures, where they have learned from what the fans respond best to and have made some improvements.

_childDocuments_.review: Newer Review after recent update:Gone back to cannot recommend. Decided to restart the game since there was an update.Even after the update there's still a lot of issues.First chapter/scene with the Hotel, camera issues appear to have been fixed and the QTE/heart-rate seems to work, this was off to a good start, there was a sign of... little hope :).Co-op - When it switches to the crew, first playable section when crossing the log it desyncs and cannot resync even with the workaround, so one player is stuck on the log. Very off-putting as it's in the early stage of the game.I really hope the devs can fix these issues while working on the next dark pictures game so that they can incorporate these fixes during the development of the next game to avoid these issues in future.Original Review:The game is ridiculously buggy, can't change camera views, can't turn with the character, the aim and trigger event doesn't always register, just to name a few bug encounters on the first section of the game. VERY very sad, was looking forward to playing this, but will wait until they patch it which will hopefully fix a lot of the issues, then I'll re-review.Second Review:So didn't end up waiting on any patches and decided to playthrough, this is still a mixed review rather than a positive, but a little more positive than negative.A minor work-around *sometimes* is to pause the game, wait a few seconds and then resume. This sometimes fixes the de-syncing co-op issue (characters remaining next to you, floating in air), but not always.Camera can still bug out at times and I encountered one crash (Cut scene of Jamie entering a Red Room, didn't crash when I was able to walk there myself). Other times the character's head looks odd, like they would focus on something while walking and the neck would twist unnaturally. Honestly much better than House of Ashes, still doesn't beat Little Hope or Man of Medan though, but a good return to what we know The Dark Pictures Anthology to be.EDIT: Haven't revisited since there has been no updates to the game.

_childDocuments_.review: "The Devil in Me," the latest installment in The Dark Pictures Anthology, presents a mixture of engaging elements and notable shortcomings. Pros:- The game's setting, inspired by H.H. Holmes’ notorious murder castle, provides a rich and atmospheric backdrop. -  The introduction of an inventory system and character-specific tools like Charlie’s lighter and Erin’s microphone adds variety to the gameplay. - The game successfully delivers a take on a new element of horror, this time focusing on the Serial Trap Killer genre.Cons:- The main cast of characters lacks depth and relatability of most of the titles.- Pacing and Gameplay Issues: The game suffers from pacing problems at the beginning.- While the introduction of new gameplay elements like the inventory system are positive steps but it feels like they were scared to fully commit to them and get he most from them.Conclusion:"The Dark Pictures Anthology: The Devil in Me" shows growth for the series, particularly in its setting and the introduction of new gameplay mechanics. However, it falls short of being the best in the series. Players should be aware of a potentially distressing scene involving a dog, which might be a trigger for some. Despite its flaws, the game is a step forward for the series, showing promise for future installments and gives me hope for season 2! I give it 3/4 Tales of horror.

_childDocuments_.review: While the creepy atmosphere in the game was amazing (I was truly scared and jumpy during and after playing this game lol), it could have done better in two areas. Firstly and most importantly, with the characters themselves. There was little to no (internal) conflict nor resolution of any sort. I didn't connect with them like I did with the characters in HoA, nobody endeared to me nor did I cheer someone on. So when the Curator summoned their accomplishment at the end, it left me baffled and questioning the Curator (I know, how dare I). In HoA you really felt like each character was unique and added something to the experience, but most importantly 'learnt' something during the game. I just missed some kind of conflict which would have made survival more difficult or challenging. They did try it regarding the issue of loyalty, but how fun would it have been if someone else from outside the group was a playable character and the question was whether that person was also in on the whole thing or not. Lastly, there was no explanation regarding some supernatural or surreal details regarding the 'hotel owner'. It seemed like that person was either invincible or could clone themselves. But maybe that was the point, lean hard towards the slasher genre and not per se fully thriller. Overall, my second favorite form DPA, but HoA remains nr 1.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to recommend this game because I don't think it's as bad as it's been made out to be. I've played all the other games in Season 1 and I would say I enjoyed this more than Man of Median but not more than Little Hope. What separates this one from the other episodes in a positive way is each character has different abilities which I really liked. They all have different items in their possession which can be used to find secrets, etc. (For example being able to unlock drawers or reach in high places). Some things worth pointing out: Don't bother collecting the coins on the ground. The curator says he will "make it worth your while" to pick them up but they can only be used to unlock "Dioramas" which are basically like still art of certain scenes or characters, most of which don't even look good and some are even out of focus. Additionally, the curator is barely in this episode for some reason whereas he is very much present in Little Hope. Some of the textures are extremely low res but most look fine. The game gets a bit repetitive and is constantly a game of cat and mouse while learning clues and backstory about the man trying to kill you. No, we never see his face or hear him utter a word, he's very 1 dimensional in that way. The mannequins take a long time until they are actually creepy, and only towards the end of the game are they actually interesting. Some scenes rely on character's relationship level to be able to survive so the stakes feel real in that way. I like that there is a diverse collection of characters in this game. The game has an inconclusive ending and for some reason a cliffhanger even though the story is over? Kind of unsatisfying but I enjoyed the game overall, I'd recommend it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm normally a fan of this series, despite some of its shaky installments, but this one is definitely one of the worst, rivalling Man of Medan. Story:I think the biggest problem is just how sloppy the storytelling is; it's even more egregious than what you might expect from a B-tier horror movie with characters making the dumbest possible decisions *constantly* in service of the plot--decisions which are completely out of your control. This is a huge problem in a "choice" game, especially since the "choices" you are given are often completely arbitrary; so many choices are A or B, and A is the "correct" answer, but nothing in the game really supports that being the correct answer, until you see character B get brutally eviscerated in some stupid trap of another that they should never have decided to waltz into in the first place. But of course they do in a cutscene, so you get dumb choices like: kill character A or kill character B, but if you choose to kill character A, you've made the right choice, because that room happens to have a flaw in its construction that allows *both* characters to survive, whereas if you choose to do nothing or kill the other character, they die. This is not influenced by prior choices, or evidence you've collected. It's just binary with no input except *maybe*, *in some cases*, meta-textual input like "this is a bigger star and has more interpersonal connections so is probably less likely to die"; it's like you're daring the game to kill a character it goes out of its way to keep until the end, which is the only place they can *really* die, so by choosing to "kill" them you have made the "correct" choice and both characters live. This is a HUGE problem with the game that the writing exacerbates by often being nonsensical. Other times, these binary decisions can only be solved if you happened to make an extremely *minor* decision earlier in the story, which I find equally stupid as that toy in Quarry.Another huge story problem: if you play with a friend, the secrets that reveal the mystery of the killer are paced TERRIBLY. There are some segments only one person sees, and some segments in which you are both playing different characters--which is cool! This is one of the positives normally. But these all-important clues can be found mostly in these segments which only one person sees, so you have to communicate to each other what the clues are, talking over the story moments in Discord or whatever, or else you end up leaving confused. Most likely this happens anyway; I certainly left with a feeling of "okay but who the ♥♥♥♥ was that dude" even though I had like half the evidence and my friend explained the other half. Meanwhile, some of the sections in which you both participate are just completely barren of clues. Literally why? Those clues should be *mostly* in those sections! Also, there is progression gating that sometimes invisibly propels your friend forward in their segments so that they sync, unlike in say House of Ashes where you would just wait. This is super annoying. This also seems to happen sometimes in single player, for no discernible reason? It's really annoying in both instances.Another problem--I played on PC, and the controls are absolutely terrible. The UI in particular does a terrible job of explaining which keys to use, sometimes displaying joysticks for balancing on logs (when really it should be A and D, but not the mouse or arrow keys), and the arrow keys for items (but not A and D), etc. Sometimes it even displays the *wrong* prompt and just waits for you to figure out why you can't progress. All of which leads to a very frustrating experience.Graphically, it's fine. The eye tracking is awful but the facial animations are decent overall; the water textures are very, very bad. I get that they're very hard to do but the game invests a lot of weird time looking at them which was a bad decision because they are markedly worse than the surroundings in all cases.Every other aspect of the game is competent or even good; the sound design is pretty good. The lighting is very atmospheric, if a bit too dark at points, and the environments are nice if a bit repetitive after a while.

name: inbento
detailed_description: inbento is a chill pattern-matching puzzle game where you prepare Japanese lunch boxes (bento) while enjoying a cute story about parenthood and growing up. Recreate over 120 puzzling recipes, master tricky mechanics and learn about the life of the kitten family as you pour your love into the food you create. SOLVE THE RECIPES In each puzzle you start with a limited number of ingredients and a picture of the final result - rotate, move and insert the food in the right order to rediscover the original recipe and make a delicious dish! A HEARTWARMING STORY Finishing each chapter will reward you with interactive illustrations offering glimpses into the life of a cat family and the ups & downs of parenthood. 120+ MEALS TO PREPARE Over the course of the game you will encounter new mechanics that allow you to swap, remove and copy ingredients in order to make the puzzles more exciting! ZERO UNDERSTANDING OF COOKING REQUIRED You don’t need to be a pro chef to play inbento - the game’s relaxed pace and textless tutorial will offer all the guidance you need to have a great time!

_childDocuments_.review: Simple 2d blocks puzzle game where you follow a recipe to create a ‘bento’ lunch. The game is accompanied by an adorable story about a single cat mother bringing up their child.Each level you are presented with the goal you have to reach, a box which may or may not already contain ingredients, and a selection of ingredients and/or mechanics ready to be added or used by dragging them into the box. This works in layers, so dragging one ingredient on top of another will make that one disappear. Mechanics vary from being able to rotate, swap or move ingredients already placed in the box.The difficulty starts off very easy but quickly builds up a challenge. With 14 chapters each consisting of 9 levels it felt rather padded towards the end but still a worthwhile brainteaser.

_childDocuments_.review: is another great puzzler from the people behind the excellent . in this one you have to recreate the layouts shown on the right by placing and manipulating food inside a box. in 14 worlds, with grids as small as 1x2 and as big as 4x3. there are always 3 unsolved levels available to play in a pack and the next world opens up once 7 of the 9 levels in the current one are done. the last level is accessed from the credits after the whole thing is completed, just like in .click and drag pieces to place them in the box, left click before picking them up or right click while they're being held rotates, if they're not locked, that is. pieces can be put over others, so order matters. e.g. you can place two half-white, half-yellow in the box, then another full white over the yellow section to create an entirely white box, but if the goal is half a box of yellow, you'll have to place the full white first so that the yellow comes out on top.later on you won't only be placing food pieces, but also modifiers that switch two squares in the box, move them around, take them out to use elsewhere, or replicate them. almost all the mechanics are introduced in the much easier first half, then things get tricky (and there's a new type of tile in world 13). , the move limit is the amount of pieces and actions you're provided with, and while stuff can be taken out of the box (last in, first out), there's still . besides the usual (non-rebindable) hotkeys for bringing up the menu, menu navigation, reset and undo, arrows move between available pieces, tab rotates, enter places the piece into the box where you can move it around, place it with another enter or take it out with esc. with many games unable to nail a single control method, this is a surprising amount of attention to detail from a mobile port.the graphics are nice, , but all the necessary basic settings are in place. separate volume settings, windowed mode, resolutions, v-sync, and some languages, even though there's barely any text in the game.settings are only available from the main menu, and initially only swiping or holding (not pressing) the hotkeys worked during cutscenes. they still do, but clickable arrows got patched in fast, and moving the mouse around makes the parallax effect more noticable now (or simply noticable, as I completely missed it in the bad old swiping-only days). I'm glad they listened to feedback, this way the game's mobile origins don't linger that much anymore, leaving a bad smell, much like cats.loved the food theme, but as always, leaving felines out of the whole thing would've made it a lot better, even humans would be an improvement. luckily, they're only present in end-of-world cutscenes, and other than everybody using the same animal in every game ever, it's excellent stuff, not too expensive either ( though), .
