_childDocuments_.review: The more I think about this game, the more I find aspects of it I can nitpick. I enjoyed FAR: Changing Tides. I really did. Not as much as I did with the first game, FAR: Lone Sails, but nevertheless, Changing Tides is as close as it gets to a Jules Verne novel in the gaming medium. Like a Jules Verne novel, Changing Tides is brimming with imagination and wonder. In seven hours, Changing Tides never failed to show me vistas that I would like to see for myself, explore and get lost in. It kept me wondering where I will see next in this post-industrial/post-steampunkish universe and I really am a sucker for some good steampunk art.Unfortunately, unlike a Jules Verne novel, and unlike the first game Changing Tides never manages to convey the feeling that there is a real, existential threat present at any part of the story. The tension subsides after two hours into the seven hour experience and all there is left is a serene voyage into the unknown, with pitiful attempts to reignite the tension here and there, most of them failures.Maybe replaying Lone Sails just before starting Changing Tides was a mistake as I was able to see that all the pitfalls of a brilliant short story rewritten into a novel is present between two games. Quite simply put, both games can be compared to two different pieces of knitting, made with the same amount of yarn. One is obviously smaller, but tighter and stronger. The other is larger by a significant margin, but you can see the gaps in the weaving.There is a larger variety of biomes in Changing Tides. There are more gameplay mechanics to control the vehicle. Now it doesn't limit itself to above the sea level, we also go underwater too (because underwater levels are not the most ridiculed levels in gaming history!). The ship itself is larger, covering most of the screen unless you zoom out. There is not just one ending, . There is more music. And I hate this saying with all my heart but I'll say it. Sometimes, quite unfortunately, less is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ more.Only larger variety of biomes feel like an improvement on the first game. More mechanics mean there is more stuff to do, especially when you just want to sit back and take in the view. Engaging with them usually produce underwhelming results, if they are not absolutely required to make progress. Underwater parts feel like padding and as usual in games (apart from ABZU) there is almost nothing interesting or eye catching to see there. It was easier to connect with the smaller landship of the first game, and I have no idea how they managed to make living quarters of such a large vessel so devoid of soul and character. Even its colours are more bleak and generic compared to the rest of the ship. The soundtrack does not hold up to the increased playtime of the game, yes it manages what it sets out to do when it comes in but those occurrences are few and far between. The ending needs a separate analysis. The ending of Changing Tides is perfect on its own. I have no doubt that anyone who enjoyed the first game will be left satisfied and emotionally stimulated upon completing it. The issue is that at that point, I just wanted the game to end.  Puzzles started to get boring and wow factor, one of the strongest suits of Changing Tides, started to diminish. The end might be perfect on its own, but the pursuit of more left it crippled, invoked relief when it really, absolutely shouldn't.Still, I loved this game. I'm hundred percent sure that if you look at the screenshots on the Steam page and like them, you'll like playing this game too. I cannot go on a voyage in a post-steampunkish, apocalyptic world even though I really want to (there is work tomorrow). But I can fire up Changing Tides, commandeer my majestic ship into the unknown and get lost in its beauty and as my dear comrade Harrier Du Bois says, "Beauty, don't abandon me in all this ugliness!"I want a third game with a zeppelin and steampunk skyscrapers/10
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: Far: Changing Tides is NOT a bad game. There is beauty, and the sublime comfort of traversing a broken world in your little mobile home. Exactly what FAR: Lone Sails boasted. However, it does just about everything somewhat worse than Lone Sails, which is why I have to give a negative.The only advantage of the game is its mechanical complexity, still not huge, it is still meant to be relaxing at times, but there are more things to do, more mechanics to interact with, and the very light 'puzzles' found in your environment are more time-consuming to do.However, vistas are less visually interesting, less striking, the wonderful music is also less, and the whole world is significantly larger and slower, although this was hidden well. The whole game feels more pointlessly bloated, while simultaneously having lower quality beauty to fill that void. Moving from one setpeice to the next takes much longer than in Lone Sails. It's never egregious, but Lone Sails keeps you enraptured and never bored from the start, while Changing Tides has me frequently craning my neck to see farther forward because I've had my fill of this giant rock 3 minutes ago.It's a shame but it feels very much like the soul and spirit of the game is being poorly mimicked, while filling that same void with more mechanical complexity. The mechanics were an excuse to behold the beauty, not the other way around.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: With just under 6 hours of playtime, this ends up being about twice as long as its predecessor, and yet somehow emptier than it. It feels like it actually had fewer, simpler, puzzles than Lone Sails. I picked it up for about $14 during a 30% off sale, and it feels like it might be worth that, but as with Lone Sails, I feel it also doesn't really command its full list price.Tides is pretty much a direct sequel to Sails, and for the most part,  will serve you again, here. The primary difference is that instead of a rolling machine, you're now on a floating machine. The precise mechanics have changed a little bit, but in general the same muscle memory will serve you here.  You're still going to be balancing energy and heat and motion with rough tools. You're still going to stewing in a miserable, lonely, post-apocalyptic world. You will still crash your sail into something off the screen that would not be surprising if you weren't locked into a side-on view.You will not suffer as much for energy sources this time around, but you'll still be anxious about it. You won't have to worry about exploding barrels this time, but you will still pick up items that seem like they shouldn't be burned. There are even /more/ overly-lengthy just-go-right sequences, that contribute to the game's theme of loneliness and loss.  It simply isn't a game to make you feel . The end-of-game payoff is just 'meh'. In the end, it was good for three days of slogging across a gloomy landscape. I recommend you pick it up if you enjoyed Lone Sails and Tides is under the $15 mark. Actually, wait for the inevitable bundle where you can get both for $10. But it wouldn't be a huge crime if you were to miss this one, either.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: FAR: Changing Tides is the follow up game to the Indie Gem FAR: Lone Sails. Once again you take the role of a nameless individual in a, nearly, empty world.No other humans around, just some animals and you. Like Lone Sails, Changing Tides has no narration, you discover the world, and make your way through the ruins of an old civilization, trying to figure out what might has happened.   You explore the world with a ship this time, which works like the Octomotive from the first game. You need to collect fuel to fire it up, or set the sails when the wind is with you. Every now and then, you come over ruins of the Ancients, which are the puzzles of the game, and often give an upgrade to your ship. The puzzles are not too hard but still very enjoyable to do.   I’m personally a huge fan of the art design, but if you’re looking for top the line graphics, this won’t be your game. The soundtrack is, once again, phenomenal and underlines the game perfectly.    If you played the first game, FAR: Changing Tides is a must play. The first game isn’t needed thou to enjoy Changing Tides, but it adds to it if you played it.  If you’re looking for a relaxing game, that won’t give you much hassle, and has a very atmospheric world, FAR: Changing Tides might be the game you’re looking for, to keep you busy for an evening or two.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: So here's the thing. This game is unique, and beautiful, and we need more games like it. It's a short, cinematic experience that plays with concepts of loneliness and desperation and hope. Mechanically, and even narratively, I had some gripes, but maybe my expectations were too high given how much I loved FAR: Lone Sails.So going through it - The ending has a sweet tie to the first. I have mixed feelings about the arc as a whole. The puzzles weren't particularly impressive, and because the game lets you sail on the water, or submerse below them, I found I often felt like I was missing out on content only seeing one or the other. That said, it's a blast maintaining the ship. The upgrades were cool and made me feel like I was going further in the game, though I would have ultimately liked to see more, and more use of them. The last upgrade for example is only required once. The music and landscape was such a central component of the first, and somehow both felt less in this go through. The ocean, the OCEAN, ultimately feels a little empty. There's wreckages and stuff, but this felt like a missed opportunity for MORE. There's a really long sequence where you're walking over an ice shelf, and I wasn't sure if I was going the right way, and it was ultimately a flat portion of the game. In FAR: Lone Sails there were numerous sequences where you solve a puzzle or something dramatic happens, and you have a significant decompress time of 'ok, time to sail and just watch the land slowly roll by and the music swell', and it was gorgeous and felt cinematic. That was fairly absent here - maintaining the wind in the sails makes it a little harder to watch the landscape, and again, the oceans felt fairly empty compared to the post apocalyptic wastelands of FAR: Lone Sails.Ultimately I loved this. It's a gorgeous trek, and I applaud the studio for their work. I hope we see another FAR game, and I hope they tighten some of these mechanical and narrative arcs, expand once again on the sailtankboat, and show us the next stage of the journey.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: If you haven't played the original game: Far: Lone Sails, go play that one before this one. But if you're a returning player looking for more Far content, and greatly expanding on the universe and lore of the first game, I highly recommend this to you. I personally find the gameplay loop less fun than the first (not much time to look at the world when you've got to adjust the sails and feed the engine all the time, and it becomes a bit of a platformer with such a large vessel), but the scenery and visuals completely make up for it. The water looks amazing, the clouds are amazing and partially hand-painted (some are 3d, which look bad imo, first game was 100% handpainted), and the mood and pacing is spectacular. The puzzles are significantly harder than the first game, but that makes it all the more rewarding. It is also a longer game than the original, but with less variation on biomes. This and the original are tied for my 2nd favorite game. Overall it's an exploration vehicle-focused chill game.

_childDocuments_.review: FAR: Lone Sails was a fantastic atmospheric experience. The soundtrack, artwork, and relaxing gameplay all came together nicely. You could sit back and marvel at the sights as the Okomotive drove through the plains and deserts.Changing Tides however, while still an atmospheric game, doesn't quite share in the same meditative and relaxing experience, simply because you just don't have much time to sit back and really appreciate the world around you.The sail has to be frequently adjusted to capture wind, or moved around to avoid it getting damaged by background obstacles. The background obstacles in particular are of quite an annoyance, because it introduces 3D mechanics to 2D gameplay, and I could never really tell if my sail was going to hit some random boulder in the background. It also didn't help that having to climb up an annoyingly tall mast each time to unfurl the sail was just unnecessarily tediousOn top of that, there's also the water depth you have to worry about when you're submarining. While I enjoyed being able to traverse on both above and under the seas, the submarining part required a good amount of active depth adjustments to avoid sailing into obstacles; more so when moving through caves.Don't get me wrong though, I enjoyed the many different mechanics and longer playtime. But Changing Tides has a much greater emphasis on active gameplay. Because I had to frequently adjust the sail, depth, fuel, and engine temps to meet the various demands, I actually took less than half the screenshots I did in this game as compared to Lone Sails, despite it having 3x the content. It actually took me a second playthrough before I actually got to notice elk/moose in the background.On a side note, I vastly prefer the "painting" art-style of Lone Sails to the blocky, polygon art-style of Changing Tides. It still looks good, but  as its predecessor.While not as relaxing as its predecessor, Changing Tides is still a decent atmospheric game, and an enjoyable experience. Fans of the first game would likely also enjoy the ending of this game as I have.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: It's generally alright, but you really want to get FAR: Long Sails instead, or at least first. This is a somewhat diluted rehash with Denuvo DRM that won't even let you boot the game without internet connection. Would have considered a recommendation otherwise.It kinda scratches the "I wish there was more" spot, but it's just not as good. Doesn't hit you in the feels, doesn't elaborate on the world-building. It might hit different if you played this first, but not so much as a sequel. You really kinda know the mechanics, so there's little joy in discovery.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: After playing through both the FAR games, I have decided to write one review for both as I would really recommend both and this way I can treat them as one product. FAR is a simple game with relatively easy puzzles which tend to be more aimed at telling you about the world the games take place in, than to make you feel like a mastermind. That is a pretty important distinction as pretty much everything in this game pushes the steampunk atmosphere to the forefront and keeping it there. Music is absolutely bloody fantastic. So let's get into the separate games.  (Land-Based Okomotive) is the first and a little more rudimentary. The animation feels more indi (not that it is bad in any way, shape or form) and overall, it is a little simpler. The feeling of utter loneliness really hits pretty hard. In some ways the simpler machine means that you spend more time actually appreciating the absolute gorgeous world you roll through.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: Unfortunately, it does not reach the high bar its predecessor set.Don´t get me wrong, FAR: Changing Tides is not a bad game. I did not encounter any bugs, visually and auditory its very nice to look at and the mechanics/ managing your ship works decently. The Ending is very heartwarming too. But often it just feels so bland and artifically stretched out to meet a higher hour-count to finish.Many times you find yourself travelling in desolate areas, constantly micro- adjusting your sails to travel at marginally faster speeds than usual.  Not even the OST playing for parts of this makes the world seem so empty. You get bored incredible fast when moving at a snails pace and having the exact same mountain or ruin in the background for 5 minutes.Talking about speed, your ship never really feels like it's moving fast(er), even when using all available sources. Sails need constant adjustments, oven constant refueling and re-starting, boost is nice to look at but didn´t seem like it makes any real difference to your travel speed. In the first game, you were also quite busy handling things, but could always spare a few seconds to take in the beautiful world around you.Now, you constantly get artifical speedbumps like low fuel, random overhangs to damage your sails while you are in the engine room etc.The OST is nice, but somehow never felt as empowering as the one from FAR: Lone Sails. TLDR: If you played the first game and want to dive deeper into the world i can recommend it. But don´t expect a better game than the first one was.20 bucks is also way overpriced for what you get. Better wait for a sale.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: with games of this scale, bigger is not always necessarily better. familiar yet fresh concepts work well.  far changing tides exemplifies this, feeling both familiar and novel.the vessel you board is quite different from the okomotive in far lone sails. it is more complex, making resource management trickier. while both games feature sails, they have distinct characteristics. the colour palette also differs. lone sails used a largely grayscale palette with occasional bursts of color, whereas changing tides maintains a definitive color palette throughout. another significant difference is how changing tides handles off-shore issues. it introduces underwater mechanics and more land-based activities. a great portion of your time is spent solving problems off-shore to get your vessel moving again.the two far games aren’t interconnected, allowing new players to jump right in whenever they please. however, I recommend starting with far lone sails for a broader understanding before diving into changing tides. overall, changing tides is a good game, though it didn’t captivate me as much as the first one did. I still recommend it to fans of the first game. I haven’t finished it yet and can’t say so I might at all. take my words with a grain of salt; try it for yourself and forge your own opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm confused. FAR: Changing Tides is a sequel of sorts to FAR: Lone Sails - everything is bigger, more complex, more advanced... but for the most part it's the same kind of experience. And back in 2019, I loved Lone Sails! And yet here I found myself bored pretty quickly. Is it because it's too similar? Is it because my tastes have changed? Or perhaps it's only superficially similar?My answer would be all three. It's too similar in the sense that it's still a game about maintaining a vehicle as it keeps going to the right, while enjoying the sights and clearing roadblocks. It might seem like having a more complex vehicle - a transforming boat - would make for a completely different time, but it truly felt like I was suddenly transported back to 2019, and not in a good way. Bad kind of nostalgia? Strange.The changing tastes thing is debatable and personal of course; but let's be honest. The last few years have seen indie games reach a cosmic level of variety, quality, and general artistry. We've been spoiled (also by Lone Sails)! The downside of that is that whatever was considered good in 2019 is probably not that good in 2022. Although I'm not even sure about this, lots of older indie games still shine today.As for superficial similarities: well, I guess that must be the "most true" of all those reasons. Yes, you still drive a vehicle to the right. But now it's a sailing vehicle. A boat. Maybe open sea and flooded forests and cities don't make for very exciting scenery - there were moments where the world looked fascinating, but for the most part I found myself not caring all that much. That also means that when you have to leave - and of course you do, to get fuel, items, decorations, whatever - you'll have to swim. Dive. And diving was fun in Subnautica, but here... meh, I had more fun in wandering the wastes of Lone Sails.In general, everything felt like a less interesting rehash of something I've seen in Lone Sails. That's incredibly strange, considering that the vehicle is objectively more complex and has more stuff on it - perhaps this is one of those "less is more" cases? Who knows.I didn't get to the end. Even as I kept unlocking new pieces of the boat, it all just felt like fake complexity. I don't know. Maybe it's me. I'd say just play the first game, but who knows, maybe that one's not good by today's standards either. If nothing else, it's rather pretty.

_childDocuments_.review: And here we are again with the "I wish there was a rating between recommended and not recommended."I'll have to say it is a beautiful game, with an interesting aesthetic. Certainly different than the first game in the looks department, but equally pleasing. Expect your typical side scroller from point A to point B indie title. rich, immersive world, endearing soundtrack, fun and simple game mechanics with some mild puzzles. This game has it all. A story that tells itself through visuals.However, I have mixed feelings about this one. I just don't... feel it's as good as the first game, Somehow it feels lesser, despite it shows a much more vast world, even adding verticality to the original title's purely horizontal plane. I don't know. This game is just missing the flow that the original had. That sense of awe whenever you advanced to the new area.If we take away the verticality of being able to submerge the game is just a bit barren and without much soul. At the same time, I feel the whole submarine add-on takes a way from the immersive experience, as in some points you are trying to figure out if you should just sail away, or submerge. Often this will lead to situations where the game probably intended you to just sail, even giving you an inspiring tune as you depart from the previous area, into the next one. But you went through the process of submerging your ship, just to find out there was absolutely nothing underneath the surface and you broke the natural flow of the game.In my opinion, this game should've stayed in on the surface, with shallow waters underneath that you could explore for resources without having to go out, and mild puzzles underwater as well.Also, some transitions are unnecessary long. Going from one place to another that are pretty much the same, or really don't have anything of interest.In conclusion, I applaud the devs for trying to expand from the original formula, but for these types of games, it just does not work. Gotta keep them linear and simple.Do I recommended it? If you like these types of games, like Limbo, Inside, the original FAR, then yes. It's worth having. Is it better than the first FAR? No. I don't think it is.

_childDocuments_.review: It's rare for a sequel to blow the doors off of the first game in the series.  This is one such case.Pros:* Much longer game. (maybe ~1hr of my 7.3 hrs is AFK)* Lots more biomes, and much large variation of terrain. (no, it's not "all water")* Excellent music as always.* Large improvement on the "keep the player busy maintaining the vessel" mechanisms.* Excellent overall improvements in vessel design.* Great at making the world seem bleak and devoid of almost any life.Cons:* Game locks your view when upgrades are installed. (eg: Install an upgrade, wait a moment and nothing happens, so you move inside  - and then the game does its thing, but you're well away from there so you only see a wall)* A cpl annoying jumps inside the ship. (1. Jump to install the hose, and fall down two ladders into the "basement". 2. Jump at the ladder to the hose, miss it, and instead hit the "load fuel" button - even if the tank is full)* Why's this game's end-area so relatively full of life, when ?Meh:* No longer able to just drive over fuel to pick it up - which is good and bad.  Good, in that it makes you explore more.  Bad, in that if you're sailing, you're not always watching  for items.* Repairing is now via consumable repair tools - some dislike it, I enjoyed the change.* Still only ~6-7 hrs long.TL;DR: If you like the voiceless-protagonist-exploring-the-world genre, it's maybe worth full price for 6-7 hrs of playtime - and if not then get it on sale for cert. If that genre's not your thing, avoid.

_childDocuments_.review: If you are interested in FAR: Changing Tides (CT below) but have not yet played FAR: Lone Sails (LS below), the prequel of CT and the natural starting point of the FAR Universe, you definitely should. Not that the story is closely related, but LS is a gem itself that deserves your attention. See my review of LS here: .If you have played LS and want more of it, then CT is undoubtedly for you; and if you do not enjoy LS, then you would not enjoy CT either. As a worthy sequel, CT has almost the same mechanics, gameplay loop, lonesome post-apocalyptic vibe, every-scene-is-a-wallpaper-pretty art, great atmospheric soundtrack, etc, as LS. Here are some comparisons:* CT is around 50% longer than LS. * The vehicle in CT is more versatile and complicated: it has sails and engine like the one in LS, but it can also . As a trade-off, the control and maintenance of the ship requires way more platforming, traversals, and cumbersome manipulations, making the game less relaxing or tranquil than LS and leaving you much less time to enjoy the scenery of your journey.* Although the movement is still 2D, the game looks way more 3D than LS. The scenery is, in general, sombre and tenebrous, giving me frequently a déjà vu of another great indie puzzle & adventure game called Inside.* It has improved zoom-in and zoom-out functionalities and camera movement, which surely helps you to better soak in the scenery.* Some fuels are now lying on the seabed (which therefore take considerably longer to load into your vehicle) and you have to keep an eye on the radar to find them. And no more auto-collect as in LS!* Puzzles are less intuitive and half of them serve as a blatant tutorial of the components of your ship.* There are more uneventful and dull moments, during which the scenery does not change much.* CT seems much less optimised than LS, perhaps due to the inclusion of Denuvo? Moreover, CT no longer supports macOS and Linux.* This is perhaps purely subjective, but the bond between the protagonist and his vehicle is less strong than in LS, and I feel less emotionally attached to the vehicle in CT.In short, CT is slightly below the high bar set by LS, but that does not detract from my recommendation of this game to all those who love LS. Also, it is so heart-warming to  at the end of the journey in CT. I am really looking forward to a sequel !

_childDocuments_.review: Truly a step in the wrong direction from the first game. The first game had a feeling of speed, momentum, and a reason to keep moving forward. This game though, is nothing short of a slow, tedious, vapid game that does not respect your time or have anything it wants to show you. Its a series of set pieces crudely spaced out by vapid tedium.In the first game, your upgrades helped you keep moving and help to a degree reduce the tedium of travel allowing you to spend more time appreciating the game, the view, and the motive of escaping a land with clearly hostile weather and terrain ravaged by what appears to be climate change. It was a compelling experience that respected your time and only had a handful of unintuitive frustrating puzzles. By the end of it you felt you had escaped and accomplished what you set out to do from the start.This game.... you start out wandering, you continue to wander, you are berated by tedious tasks all while you have no idea why you are even bothering to keep going. The weather poses little threat to you as you can just go under the water and now thunderstorms cease to be scary. The game also made the mistake of making repair supplies limited, meaning it CANT BEAT YOU UP to give you that feeling of intimidation from the environment anymore. It cant threaten you because it wont give you the means to recover readily. And do you remember that one part of the first game where you have to hook your locomotive to a hand cart and tediously jump to tow yourself? Remember how obnoxious but short lived that mechanic was? That's the WHOLE GAME NOW. It never improves. Remember in the first game where you got an upgrade that picked up items for you so you could focus on the story and environment over the tedious box moving? Not this time, now you gotta stop the ship to go search for trash and bring it back ONE BY ONE for the entire trip.This game has no respect for your time, it has no reason to play, it has no message, it took all the tedious and wrong parts of the first game and drowned the art and messaging that made the first game good. This is just a disappointing waste of time.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr If you loved FAR: Lone Sails, just get this. You'll love it.FAR: Changing Tides is a well-designed, well thought out followup that, for some players, misses many of the marks of the original but it is still, in my estimation, a wonderful game in its own right.The art style has changed in subtle ways, becoming much more of a full 3D rendered world presented in a 2D view with a lot of color and detail. Gone are the extremely desaturated, nearly monochrome colors of FAR: Lone Sails with just the pop of bright red from time to time. The end result is much more of a 3D game as opposed to the "living in a charcoal sketch" quality of the original. This is the first of many instances where this game appears to lean more into being a game and less an art project. This is neither good nor bad, but it is undeniably different.From the first moments in the game, the experience is much more game focused. Whereas Lost Sails starts us with the protagonist in a beautiful farmhouse, slowly heading outside and grabbing their mailbox as a memento before boarding the vehicle and setting off on their journey, Changing Tides starts with a very simply done tutorial sequence that teaches players how to swim, jump, climb, and move objects. There's a small bit of world building with some background paintings and a flower, but mostly this is just Tutorial.Once the game really gets going, it becomes clear that there is A LOT more content this time around. Whereas Lost Sails could be finished in under 99 minutes (for an achievement), the equivalent achievement in Changing Tides is 220 minutes. While Changing Tides could be completed in one sitting, it's long enough that playing it over 2-3 sessions is much more expected. In addition, CT focuses much more on active gameplay, giving players a lot more systems to manage on the ship all at once and a lot more freedom regarding which path to take. Whereas Lost Sails spent more time just allowing you to exist in the beautifully drawn world, with just enough gameplay to give you something to do, Changing Tides demands much more attention and activity from players. This is not an action game by any means, but neither is it the Zen-like digital storybook that Lost Sails sometimes felt like.In the end, it's a different game, with a different feel, and a different world, and a lot more activities to do. Either way, it's a world well worth enjoying. And if the ending doesn't make you at least a little bit misty eyed, you ain't wired right. :)

Consequently this game should really only be played after completing the original and not be seen as a standalone title.Similar to games that narrate the story 'silently' through its environment its interpretation leaves a lot of room for speculation and can arguably be a bit too vague. _childDocuments_.review: This game does a fantastic job of making you feel small, weak and insignificant amongst this vast, gigantic region; and yet you still feel like you have some agency over the world around you, even if to a very small extent.Everything from the first game is improved here: visuals, soundtrack, gameplay. The Vessel dwarfs the first game's Okomotive and the mechanisms inside of it are even more interesting and fun to deal with.I was fully immersed in the universe and the story, despite the game not having a single line of dialogue. It was relaxing, somber, crushing and hopeful. Beautiful.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: Similar to the first Far game you manage your ship, burn fuel, set sail and more in a distopian steampunk world with a playtime of 2.5 hours +. Gameplay was improved with smoother mechanics and good new ideas. The upgrades don't just make your life easier, but each add another aspect to the game, which is an improvement from the first game. Storywise it sadly did not deliver as good of an atmosphere like with the subtle background views in the first game. Though I have to say, it did not dissapoint, and left me satisfied in the end, even if not with that sense of awe and sorrow like in the first game. I do not feel a want for another game, which I interpret as it being a good round end of the story.

_childDocuments_.review: I have completed the Lone sails a couple of times and consider it as one of my all time favorite games. I was extremely excited when Changing tides was announced, whishlisted it as soon at it was possible and purchased the game on day one without hesitation. Therefore, it is almost physically painful to thumb down this game. But I am afraid it has to be done and below you will find my reasons why. First of all, the ending of the game is brilliant. If you have enjoyed the ending of Lone sails, you will surely enjoy the ending of Changing tides. Adding verticality to game gameplay also feels like a step in a good direction. Sadly, this is where the pros end and the grim painful cons part begins. I was one of those who asked for a longer Lone sails experience. Therefore, I will accept partial blame for what we have in Changing tides. Clearly, the developers tried to make the game longer than the first installment. This resulted in switching to mostly 3D assets instead of the artistic 2D assets we had in the Lone sails. Adding verticality to the rout pushed the amount of the required assets even further. As a result, the game visually looks less appealing. 3D requires many vertexes to match 2D art visually. Most likely, water shader was demanding a great chunk of the performance budget, so we ended up with mostly bleak 3D stones with blurry textures. A major issue in a game with a large emphasis on admiring the environment. Gameplay is yet another place where it feels like the developers have dropped the ball. Operating the ship is more tedious and boring at the same time compared to the machine in the Lone sails. It is a bit difficult to point out what went wrong, but I have a couple of theories: 1. The sense of speed got lost. In Lone sails the faster you go the more the camera zooms out. Which adds to the sense of speed. There are more objects on the ground you are passing by which also helps. In Changing tides the camera doesn't zoom out until being told to do so by the script or toggled manually by holding a button. Constantly moving water is also not a good speed indicator. No matter how fast you are going, it always feels the same. 2. Nothing to stimulate your brain while in motion. In Lone sails you had to think when to open the sails, when to burn fuel, how fast to go, wherever to engage brakes to stop and pick some crates from the ground or keep the momentum. It was a less complex system mechanically, but a system which allowed you to make more decisions mentally. In Changing tides you don't need to think about how fast you go, you don't need to brake to pick something. All you need to do is to look at the flag (which is also a distraction from the scenery) and make small adjustments to the sails when the flag is out of the perfect position. As a result, you end up mindlessly staring at the flag, making the micro adjustments and getting bored while waiting for the next thing to happen. Don't get me wrong, Changing tides is not a bad game. If you are into mindless relaxing experience or just willing to kill some time, it is a perfectly good product. But other than the ending, you won't remember much from this game. Which is a shame considering how much Lone sails had to offer. I think I would enjoy more replaying the Lone sails for the third time, than I enjoyed playing Changing tides for the very first time.

_childDocuments_.review: FAR: Changing Tides is a beautiful world to look at, but it's a far cry from Lone Sails when it comes to gameplay.Lone Sails is a world where you're in constant danger from both the environment and the puzzles you are frequently stopping to solve.  Changing Tides lacks all of this, and instead places you in a very large and open (yet still completely linear) ocean.  There are far fewer puzzles, and these are all very simple.  Nothing can kill you.  And everything is VERY far apart...  the majority of the game is spent sailing forever, waiting for the next anything to do.  The travel distances should be cut in half and it would be twice as enjoyable.Pretty disappointing, given how much I enjoyed Lone Sails...  and how well the game is being rated by others.  The ending, though, is a truly great moment; so if you do play, stick it out through the end.  Just be warned that you'll be bored throughout.

_childDocuments_.review: Game is about 6 hours long. The first 3 and last hour was fantastic.But between those there is a 2 hour section with a lot of just travelling with not much to do or even look at. Yes, there is a bit more feeling of being in control of the sails, but not enough to justify at least an hour of busywork. In the first game there was almost always something interesting to look, but this game has a lot of open ocean with not much around except maybe some ice flows in the foggy distance (especially in the second half). It would have been more bearable if the game was fully scored, but the music, excellent as it is, is doled out in very small doses at key points.Compared to the first game, the puzzles were fewer and further between. They seem to involve a lot more just moving around (swimming, climbing stairs, walking... often relatively long distances) and less making stuff happen. If I went in the wrong direction or fell off a platform, it was a tedious having to retrace my steps. 2 large puzzles left me feeling both bored and frustrated rather than giving me a sense of achievement and I came close to giving up on a couple of occasions. Even though the payoffs were objectively spectacular, I did not enjoy them, I was just glad it was over.Ultimately this could have been an absolutely fantastic 4.5 hour experience but it has been stretched out to 6 hours presumably to avoid criticisms that the game is too short to justify the price. Well at 6 hours it's too long regardless of the price.I only recently played the first game. I won't say that one is better than the other, only that the first one left me wanting more and the second one outstayed it's welcome. But despite all the criticism, the devs have done something truly original and clever with both games so It's a thumbs up from me.

_childDocuments_.review: Changing Tides is an excellent sequel. While Lone Sails travel across a dried-out seabed with your unique vehicle, Changing Tides is all about the wonders of a flooded world, rife with mystery. This time, you pilot a vessel. Gameplay is very similar to "Lone Sails," with you controlling and repairing your vehicle, collecting fuel, get upgrades along the way, puzzles, and enjoying beautiful scenery. But now that you're piloting a vessel, you can dive into unknown depths. I really like the new core gameplay, which involves maneuvering the vehicle.You can use the sail or steam power or both of 'em. They've designed it very well. To use the sail, you need to raise the mast by pushing a large button with your character, similar to the one from FAR: Lone Sails used to throttle the engine. Then, rotate the sail by moving a lever to capture the wind and if you manage to keep the wind long enough, there's a white flag that if it reaches the cyan rope, grants two additional side sails for a burst of speed. As the sail finally catches the wind, that sound of tightening cloth... But be careful, your sail can collide.The other maneuver is similar to FAR: Lone Sails but with new mechanism. To operate the steam power, you’ll find a control on the platform above that will move your vessel. To the far left, the ship will move left, and to the far right, the ship will move right. If you place it in the middle, the ship won’t move. Obviously, you need fuel to run the steam, and you can fill it with stash you found inside the ocean. The steam can overheat, and you can use the hose to cool it down. The hook system makes it easier to refill the fuel. Attach the stash to the hook and then press the button below the hose platform to load up your fuel.Along the way, you find an upgrade for your vessel that can go underwater whenever you wish. Once you got it, you can attach the hose to the ballast pipe (just to the left of the hose) and fill the hose with water by pushing the lever to the right to descend your vessel. If you push the lever to the left, it'll get you up to the surface.Lots of improvements from the previous one and it's truly an excellent sequel and excellent journey. I really recommend to play Lone Sails first, then Changing Tides for best experience.I wonder if they would make a new one that features a Co-op mode... FAR: Lone Sails

_childDocuments_.review: Not as enjoyable as the prequel Far: Lone SailsDifficulty ★★☆☆☆☆☆☆☆☆ (you damage your vehicle often unintended, with limited repair torches)I was an absolute fan of the first part. A calm puzzle game with atmospheric scenery, and a vehicle which was fun to control. What I got in the sequel was in the first half of the game just a mess to get the hang of. After I rage-quitted the game after repeatedly damaging my sails due to bad overview and control mechanics, I returned to the game to try it once more.This time I just kept on crashing and moving forward, and as soon as the game lets you travel by other means than just sails things get a lot smoother. Still, the core issue with the sailing still remains. The second part in the game is also much more interesting than the quite boring beginning.* atmosphere and sceneries later on* different ways to move your vehicles later on* the solitude musical tunes* the story twist at the end* diving and was an awesome idea* bad sailing mechanics. You need to walk to the nose of the ship to see further, away from controls, so you have to return regularly by changign winds. Or you alternately need to press and hold zoom out button and camera panning to the right manually. Both is annoying* limited repair torches (you usually find enough later on, but the game mechanic adds nothing to the game only being annoying)* general forwarning time to avoid collision is not well made. In the prequel the camera auto-panned by speed, which was way better* the emergency brake systems (driving an sailing) are taking too long. Unplugging the hose and set you pump to estinguish the fire, or unhooking the sails and retract the pole manually is really annoying* some objects don't produce water effects (balloon, the rudders then they are not moving but the vehicle is sailing, etc.)* there is not damage for direct hits in objects like in the prequel. If the devs did a better camera panning, and emergency brakes they wouldn't needed to do that in the first place* despite diving was quite cool, it felt that the devs didn't used this game mechanic to its full potential* I missed typical metal pressure noises while diving and raising, would have added a lot to the atmosphere* I always expected that water leakage may occur which you then have to fix and drain the water with the water pump (a real missed chance)* speedrunning in this the game was not as fun as in the prequel. The reason is that there is no kind of a vaccuum device to pick up stuff while driving (you only had to stop for story puzzles i nthe prequel). Travelling felt too much interruptive in this game for the speedrun achievement* because the game does play mainly above and below the water surface, travelling always felt like I am missing something important in the water or on the surface, depending on where I was in that moment. I, for example, permanently wanted to jump into the water to look if something is down there to collect or not. This feeling was very unpleasent. It took some time to get myself to a level I didn't cared anymoreThis game is barely reaching an "ok" level, but it missed a lot of good chances to do better. I still don't get it why the devs decided to give the player only limited repairs this time, or made some of the mechanics in overview and vehicle controls so awkward. The second part of the game was fine though, much more interesting, but getting through the first half was just tiresome. I hope they learn from their mistakes if they ever go for another sequel. if so, I will check before buying this time, if it will be worth my time.

_childDocuments_.review: It's... fine.  I enjoyed it.  The wordless story still works well.  I loved the previous FAR so I jumped on this one as soon as I was finished with the former.  It's a worthy successor in many ways but it makes more obvious misses.  For instance, while there is far more verticality to levels (and here a couple of slightly tricky puzzles), this often results very easy puzzles that require a lot of running around.  There are more ways to move the vehicle and some are really cool but that also means there are more buttons to press in different compartments; therefore, gone are the chill moments of just gliding along enjoying the view.  With that, some of the "just go" sequences are too long in my opinion.Then there are a couple of missteps that are bandaided over and that's a bit of a shame.  For instance, the controls are awkward and it's way too easy to accidentally feed unwanted fuel into the engine, therefore, there is so much of the stuff scattered about that it's difficult to be excited about exploring every nook and cranny looking for items.  Then this weird mechanic:  repairs are limited and that's cool, but the view perspective makes collisions annoyingly frequent, therefore, necessitating frequent repairs.  Rather than do something about the unnatural FOV, there are just a ton of repair kits around.  To me, this seems to undo the whole "repairs are limited so be careful" thing.  There is a point where the movement is expanded vertically, and, rather than making it easier to avoid collisions, the vehicle just stops taking damage in those segments.Anyway, the issues are minor and I enjoyed the game.  A bit pricey for something so to short but I don't feel too bad about it.  In fact, I feel like it should have been a bit shorter.  There is a fairly climactic false end which is followed by another hour or two of gameplay that was anything but.  Plus, like, they're just going to starve to death after this, right?

_childDocuments_.review: What can I say that hasn't already been said. It did it's job, in being a sequel to the first one. The first couple of hours I spent here were beautiful: I streamed my entire experience and I believe I showed how much fun it was. Unfortunately, it kind of stopped being fun. I don't want to say it was a bad game overall, because I did enjoy the challenge it posed in the beginning, but **and spoilers ahead** when you gain the ability to go under the water with your vessel, it goes downhill, no pun intended. **end of spoiler**I was really liking how it changed up the way to move the vessel, as any good sequel does, it shouldn't be exactly like the original. I liked the sailing mechanic as a whole. I will say, the gripe I had with the original about not really warning you with proper time that an obstacle was coming and to lower the sail so it doesn't get damaged was, also, a thing in this game. I wished it was something the developers learned to fix, but, alas, here we are. **spoilers again, sorry** Once you gain the going underwater mechanic, it hurts the game exponentially. What was once a back and forth you learn from the beginning becomes a "stop the vessel several times so you can put the water in the going down hole, but you also need to pump the vessel so it goes somewhere or you'll be wasting energy" kind of thing. Maybe it goes to show that I'm just not good at this kind of thing, but I was able to fully master the back and forth of the first game relatively quickly, so I think it was just poor placement of the items around the ship. I had a huge problem, and I mean HUGE problem of hitting my head on the button that placed another energy thing in the furnace, making me waste several items and once just trying to get up a ladder. Again, I think this is poor placement. What was once a fun upgrade to the manual moving of boxes and items became a crutch that I eventually just stopped using.About halfway through, you raise up what appears to be a generator about 80 times bigger than your ship. I still don't know why we did that besides just wanting to get through. I did encounter a wall clip on the entire right side of the map at this point, nothing major, just allows you to go a bit beyond the wall and around the map. Again, not a huge deal, I imagine most players won't be going over there, but, to play devil's advocate, I had no idea what I was meant to do here and spent more than half the time wandering around, trying to think of something I could do to progress. This part was the biggest hurdle and, honestly, the moment I checked out. I was so sick of the underwater controls that I just wanted the game to end. But it didn't. In fact there were still a couple of hours left. I won't bore you too much with the game after this point, because it ended up being all the same complaints, until the end.The ending specifically got me truly upset with the game. Everything was passable, within reason, up to this point. It confuses me to all hell. It kind of under plays the ending of the first one. What was once an open ended close to a fun adventure now left more questions than answers. Why were we there? Why did we blare the horn? What was our goal? What was the first protagonist's goal? Why did they do all that just to sit at a dock for what probably equates to a couple of hours?I won't say it's a bad game, I can't, because I loved what they were going for in the beginning. Unfortunately, the first game was just too good and too simple with just enough challenge to make it amazing. This one falls short in being too long, having too many upgrades feel like an excuse to add a gimmick rather than feel like an upgrade, and just being not as good as the first one. If it's on sail, and you keep your expectations low, this is a fine, fun adventure. Oh, and, also, take some breaks in between. I feel like maybe if I had taken a couple of days to rest between playthroughs, it would've been better, but I don't even want to say that'll fix it all. However, that being said, I don't want to recommend, as putting these kinds of handicaps on a game to make it "passable" is not a good sign. But again, if it's on sale, and you keep yourself from expecting a proper followup to the original, by all means.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Improves on the sequel by introducing many new concepts while also being a slightly longer experience. Highly recommend especially if you've already played the first (play it if you haven't!); it's a great, fairly relaxing experience.Having just finished the game, I can say without a doubt that FAR: Changing Tides is one of my favourite indie games of all time, surpassing its prequel. It improves on a handful of aspects while also keeping the same atmosphere and feel the original presented so well. The vehicle this time, a boat-submarine hybrid, is noticeably larger than the Okomotive in the original game, and felt a lot nicer to move around in, while also introducing a number of new mechanics.Changing Tides is also a slightly longer experience, with a completely different repertoire of environments to sail through. Being a fan of anything engineering/big machine related, I couldn't help but smile every time a new mechanism was introduced for me to play with.And of course, the soundtrack is incredible once again, and lead me to tear up more than a few times.While I've seen some people say that you don't need the first to enjoy this one, I personally highly recommend playing through it first, as it does tie in to the 'story' of Changing Tides.

_childDocuments_.review: Writing this review after marathoning through the game yesterday.Beautiful graphics, atmosphere, and animations. I've been highly anticipating this game ever since I finished Lone Sails and I'm happy to say it delivered on all levels. My most notable compliment is that the feeling of piloting a vessel has been realized even further. It's hard to put into words, but there was a powerful vibe to scurrying up the mast and rigging the sail, especially when I had gotten used to the basic rhythm of maintaining velocity and started being able to read wind direction. It was interesting feeling out how the ship's engine and controls functioned notably different from the vehicle in Lone Sails, . Even as I write this, I'm considering booting it up just to go at a storm one more time, this time without it hitting me while I was in the middle of trying to get the king of the world achievement.The controls are a bit floaty as per Lone Sails. It's still hard to react quickly to events, but I found the environments and interfaces seemed much more suited to it and I generally noticed the floatiness much less as a result. It feels like the devs have taken note of what worked from Lone Sails and focused on it.A notable addition to Changing Tides, I feel, is the sense of threat and risk. Lone Sails always felt like it was inevitable that I made it to the end, but I caught myself genuinely worrying sometimes in Changing Tides that I would get stuck out at sea without a breeze or fuel, or that a storm might deal more damage to my ship than I had repair charges to fix (yes the repair tools are now a consumable). The inclusion of non-linear fuel collectibles on the sea floor also forced me to think about more than just pushing forwards.I recommend Lone Sails to friends as a fun indie game for the atmosphere, the animation, and the relaxing nature of it. Changing Tides has all of these, but I can firmly say that I'll be recommending it as a gripping, fully-realized puzzle game that took everything I liked from Lone Sails and enhanced it. I excitedly await to see what else Okomotive creates.

_childDocuments_.review: I would say this game is pretty good for the most part for a simple game. Lone Sails did a bit better job, I think, when it came to things like the overall progression and introduction of the narrative (immediately it gives you the characters motivation), and navigating your vehicle was simpler and less frustrating at times, and I personally think the layout of the vehicle was a lot more sensible and intuitive when it came to navigation and placement of the utilities. There was just overall less frustration involved, allowing you to enjoy the ride more. _childDocuments_.review: This game makes me sadI loved the first game. I bought the soundtrack, because I loved it too. But this is just sad.I don't know why I should play this game anymore. It is so slow that I at one time just held down the left joystick to keep my flag up for about 15 minutes. I constantly run out of materials. The music is just SILENT. I really liked the soundtrack you got in the first game when you got your machine running. None of that here. It is all just silence, music is VERY scarce to the point where it simply couldn't exist and I wouldn't even notice. The game is extremely unforgiving, excruciatingly slow and surprisingly boring (what I mean by that is that you get a few very hectic moments succeeded by like 30 mins of nothing really happening).I didn't go into this game expecting something very exciting or fast paced. I expected something like the first game: Great soundtrack, great atmosphere, great environment-storytelling. It occationally gets the atmosphere right but the music is just either way too short or only a part of the real track (e.g. just a few of the instruments). The storytelling is still great, like the first game. The soundtrack is way too scarcely implemented for my liking,In conclusion I am very disappointed. While the game does keep the theme and artstyle, and is still made with incredible care in the environmental design, it feels like the game was made made with different goals than the first one in mind. It feels increadibly stretched with excrutiatingly long moments of nothing happening at all, the music does not deliver ingame (while the soundtrack itself is still great, if you listen to it on youtube that is), the game is surprisingly stressful when it decides that now something has to happen (mostly followed by you running out of ressources, making the game even slower).I loved the first game, and I wish I could replay it with no knowledge about it once more. This game does not deliver in any of the qualities that I loved about the first game.

_childDocuments_.review: I do not understand at all the "very positive" reviews I am seeing for this game. Perhaps others have a higher tolerance for everything this game is and is doing than I am. For me, this game could charitably described as "bland," and uncharitably be described as "boring."The whole pattern of the game is something like this:1. Solve a simple puzzle. The kind that legally, and technically counts as a puzzle, but doesn't give you any pride for "solving," because it feels more like putting circles in round holes. You know what you're supposed to do right away, then you do it, end of "puzzle."2. The ship gets a cool upgrade, to make you travel to another puzzle. This part is fine, though if you're the kind of person to ask things like, "why is there an upgrade for a model of ship that appears to be 'rusty dump made of trash,' laying about in a flooded grain silo," then just stop reading now and give this game a pass. It's the only achievement thing this game offers you in terms of an adrenaline rush, or flood of serotonin. 3. You "sail." This section will be too long by several minutes. Cool "mood" music will play in the background, and you will watch what amounts to a music video for it. Every music video's theme is "post-apocalyptic trash world," but the music is good. The problem though is that, Every. Single. Sailing. Segment. is aaaaaages long. And most of the time you just watch the dang rusty dump go by while hoping to see something on the horizon through a terrible camera designed to show you things you will crash into .5 seconds before you do, even though your character is staring straight at them. I'm not kidding about the camera. Every single picture in the marketing where the ship is at a 45 degree angle to the camera is misleading. This does not happen in the game. It's just a crap side-view with annoying camera movements the whole time, and a "swivel" on the camera that is just on the wrong side of useless. 4. You repeat steps 1-3 until the game is finished. Good things: Nice music. Looks decent. End of list. Bad things: All of the gameplay to play, and all of the boredom it produces.

_childDocuments_.review: FAR: Changing  this case I would have to say that the reviews were right and most of them were maybe too kind but hey, they don't pay for games. I did buy this game with Denuvo ( more on that later ) so I will try to explain why I found this game very boring and repetitive.I am a big fan of the first game so I was curious what this game has to offer. FAR: Changing Tides suffers from indie game sequel syndrome. It is bigger, longer, has fancy graphics and yet it fails to capture the magic of Lone Sails.Lone Sails was focused on the journey and your machine and that combination was a success if you ask me.                Changing Tides is trying too hard to impress. First of all you are controlling a ship, submarine, hot air balloon, some heavy machinery + the journey is broken by really boring and sometimes long puzzles and long periods of walking.The puzzles are basic stuff really like in INSIDE. The first half of the game is full of these puzzles and I really wanted to sail in this game. In the 2nd half of the game I got what i wanted, less basic puzzles and more sailing.The second part of the game is where the game fails because the sailing feels boring, even if you ignore your sails and use the motor the game is still too slow and bland. BTW you will still have to leave your boat and do some push the box and push few buttons puzzles. I thought the game couldn't be any slower but than I got the ability to turn my multi functional boat into a submarine........ok , I am confused now, I can't even describe how slow this thing is and how boring the sections are. So, the game play loop goes like this - control your boat, solve some basic puzzles (not on the boat), get upgrades so you can ride the submarine - solve more basic puzzles under water (you will have to leave your submarine of course) - sail for a long time and watch few extra long cut scenes- dive - sail - puzzles. Ok, you get the gist.They chopped this game into so many pieces and that is the ultimate flaw of this game. Like I said, Lone Sails great game, Changing Tides very boring. They even included other people.....ok I am done with this review.This game has Denuvo and my GPU was overheating like I was playing Metro Exodus. I really don't know why indie developers use this software when they made a name for themselves with the Lone Sails. Did this game sell better because of this best in class protection that tanks game performance ? Not a good look for small indie developer if you ask me.If you liked Lone Sails there is a big chance you will find this game boring. I can't recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: If you loved  then you would love this, too.More specifically, if you are doubtful as to whether the original game, as self-contained and narrowly-focused as it was, needed or would welcome a sequel then rest assured: this game really does add to and elaborate the formula in delightful ways. In short, it's not merely more of the same. Your ship is more complex, the puzzles longer, the world-building grander. And—without spoilers—it really does add charming elements to the original story.And it would also stand alone fine on its own. If you insist on only playing one of these games (why?!) then this is the more fully realized one.Some of my original complaints still stand. The zoom system is silly and annoying: you need to keep buttons pressed to zoom in and out, and so you might spend much of the game with buttons pressed depending on how much detail you want to take in. Also, I'm sad that with its gorgeous color palette it does not support HDR. With  I could turn on Windows 11's auto-HDR, and it worked very well, but this game is incompatible with that feature and so we are stuck in SDR.

_childDocuments_.review: An atmospheric experience for the journey, not the destinationAlone on the open sea, traveling an immersive and captivating world, Diving for sunken treasures, discovering abandoned civilizations, and managing a ship that is obviously meant for an entire crew. It's you against the opposing elements. The story is ambiguous but builds on top of the previous game. You don't know why you are moving forwards, but you know you have to. Maybe an allegory for life?The gameplay is "you" managing your vessel while you multitask between different tasks soo that you can sail through the tides. You also have to solve puzzles that are cleverly disguised as tutorials for the different ship mechanics. The music is a cross between jazz and classical and is excellent at expressing the spirit of a lone soul traveling a world taken by climate change. Far changing tides is the second game in the "Far universe." Does it hold up to the first game? "spoilers ahead"The first game does everything better than "Changing tides." and that's fine. Traveling the ocean is refreshing and new, but the landscapes are not as gripping as in the first game.  The feeling of danger never struck me as in the first game. If a storm appeared, you could Effortlessly submerge your ship underwater and wait it out. When driving the Okomotiv you felt exposed to the environment around you, hoping nothing alarming would happen when traversing the harsh world. I never felt my character was dependent on my ship. He had an infinite air supply when diving and could swim fast. It never felt like he needed the vessel for survival as in the first game. The music was less memorable, and there were a lot of quiet sections of the game. I have no problems with silent sections where you take in the atmosphere by listening to the ocean and wind, but it was too many of those sections for my liking. The pace of the game was peculiar, it took me 5 hr to finish the game, but the distance traveled felt shorter than the first game even tho this one is 2hr longer than "Lone sails." probably because of the similar unchanging landscape.The character design was too different from the first game. Lones character is hidden under her clothing implying that the world she lives in is harsh and brutal. But the new character's face is completely exposed. thematically this doesn't reflect the world he lives in (his hair also looks ridiculous.)I'm hard on the game because I want the next one to be as good as possible. "changing tides" is a creative sequel to "Lone sails." and is a worthy title of the Far franchise. I'll be sure to revisit the world again. Not for the destination but for the journey.

_childDocuments_.review: A really nice game. Visually a real improvement on Lone Sails. Although unlike Lone Sails, Changing Tides' addition of the 'space bar' to jump means moving the character around the vessel/environment can get a bit sticky and frustrating at times. You have to hit 'up' and 'space bar' simultaneously to climb ladders which, if you don't get it right, means you accidentally fall to the bottom of a puzzle or add more fuel to a near full furnace which can get annoying. There are moments where puzzles seems unachievable, not through difficulty but as if bugged. You then find that you simply have to connect 'this' to 'that' to move forward but haven't been previously introduced to that particular mechanic like the others.Lastly, although this is a beautiful game and journey, it felt like it was going on too long towards the end. A game like Changing Tides imo could hit a 3/4hr play through to hit the sweet spot (like Lone Sails).I'm rating a thumbs up because it is a really good relaxing puzzle game that really flies the indie flag superbly. Regardless of my little nags, people will enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: Then you'll find Changing Tides to be pretty much that game, but better in most aspects. It certainly looks significantly better, with a wider use of colour and a far more distinct art style. It has substantially more refined gameplay, featuring actual (albeit simple) puzzles and slightly more in the way of choice in operating the vehicle.Narratively, Changing Tides is a far less depressing game. The world is less obviously dead, threats are far fewer and farther between and an actual satisfying ending can be found at the end of the experience. It's also a far longer game, both due to longer travel segments but also due to a significantly larger number of stops and more complex activities at each stop. Basically, the development team took a lot of the advise players were offering about the old game and took it on board.Far: Changing Tides is a mostly linear "travel" game. You control a young unnamed protagonist in control of a large sea-faring vessel, escaping a disaster which destroyed their world by relentlessly sailing to the right. As you'll see from the screenshots, you'll spend most of your time inside the vehicle, pushing buttons, pulling levers and moving boxes - a core experience broken up every so often by puzzles requiring you to leave the vehicle and venture into old abandoned structures.This is a decidedly casual game. Difficulty is fairly low once you get to grips with the basic concepts, puzzles exist but are fairly simple and there are no real fail states. Nothing will attack you, you can't really die and you can't permanently wreck the vehicle. The intended experience is a long road trip alternating between relaxing sailing and unnerving obstacles, with a focus on the former.The concept behind Far: Changing Tides (and Far: Lone Sails before it) is fairly unique and I'd argue worth exploring even just on its own. Very few games exist where a small player character can traverse through and control a larger vehicle as their major core game mechanic, and this one in particular does so very well. I'd highly recommend giving it a try.

_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: It might be just me, but I absolutely love these kinds of games where you are an individual character maintaining and controlling a huge mechanical vehicle, like a train or submarine; 'FAR: Lone Sails' and 'FAR: Changing Tides' have perfected these specific niches. I would highly recommend this game, not only out of its fun gameplay and beautiful art directory and storytelling, but also for its uniqueness and phenomenal experience. 11/10 I hope they add more 'FAR' games to the series, it's absolutely wonderful.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a really good surprise. It's a story about someone traveling the world in a handmade ship. You get upgrades for it over time that extends its functionality and when you realize you are not just sailing, you are submerging into caves on deep waters, exploring abandoned places and technology while trying to survive your journey. A cute story with and cute ending. One of the best games of the genre that I tried!
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: This game is part interactive screensaver, part busy-work simulator, and part casual puzzle game, and very obnoxious about how long it makes you wait for things to happen. It looks amazing and is competently put together, but the amount of filler between puzzles is astonishing. You will spend literally minutes at a time doing nothing but moving a lever back and forth to adjust your sail, or jumping on a pad to keep your engine going, while admiring the pretty scenery going by. For all that filler it's also very short. It took me 6 hours to finish without rushing it. As it's very linear, there's unfortunately little replay value after the first play-through.On the plus side, the puzzles themselves (however few of them there are) and the different ways you can control your ship are good fun. It's a shame the engaging parts of the game are so padded out with busy work and scenery watching.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: Played the first game, loved it minus a few nitpicks. Such as it feeling like as soon as you get a good rhythm going you hit another roadblock.  That gets worse in this game.  God forbid I want to put the sail up, instantly another rockwall/tower comes along to smack into it.   The "story", such as it is,  feels a bit more present here though, and the ending has me hoping for another sequel.The design of the ship is baffling given how quickly the game expects you to move.  In the first game, the ship was designed around a central area, giving you quick access to everything at almost a moment's notice. Very good.  In THIS game you have to to sluggishly crawl from, say the engine, aallll the way around the bottom, back, and top to get to your sail, which at this point has likely already been damaged.  Such a design wouldn't be so bad, if you were given plenty of time. You are not.  Or if the throttle for the engine wasn't in the wrong direction, perhaps we could slam into reverse before an obstacle comes up.If you liked the tight control of the vessel in the first game, maybe give this one a pass.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: i would recommend this game to people that can actually play it.it looks like it would be fun. unfortunately it runs at 2 to 5 fps with 12 gig ram. even on low settings.character is uncontrollable at such low framerate. can't open the big door to get to the ship.half the screen is covered by green lines under water (on low settings) for no reason. makes the puzzles impossible and the jumping impossible to control.unfortunately i had to get a refund :( i know this would be a good game if it was playableyes i know it only came out today but the devs could atleast make sure it ran at a playable speed.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the hardest thumbs down I have given. As someone who loved the first game, FAR: Changing Tides was a bit of a let down. The game has undeniable great and beautiful moments, but the pacing was all over the place. There was something that made the first game special that's missing in this sequel. I'd recommend this game only at a discount and if you really enjoyed the first one.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: Usually games like this annoy the hell out of me. Those games, which are acually calusal puzzles, but pretend to have an actual world with some kind of lore. They usually come up with stuff like that huge machine in FAR:Lone road, the only purpose of which was to , and this stuff makes me facepalm.Usually games like this annoy me, but both games from FAR series don't. They are way too beautiful and atmospheric. For the whole game I was sitting there and constantly pressing that screenshot button to capture beautiful landscapes and intricate contraptions. And I didn't even care about how tedious the game's control scheme is.But no way I'm playing this game again!

Absolutely worth checking out!

_childDocuments_.review: Can't be played on an AZERTY keyboard.It's a shame - I was looking forward to this game. The predecessor could be played with the arrow keys, but here the character is controlled with the WASD keys, and you can't remap the keys. So it's impossible if you have a French keyboard.(The funny thing is that when you switch the language to French, the "controls" menu claims that  movement is now controlled by the ZQSD keys. But, alas, that's not the case. It's almost like the game is mocking me.)
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: "How do I sail a BOAT around a BOUY in the MIDDLE OF NOWHERE" is not a puzzle, let alone one that the whole game should be based around over and over again. The only puzzle here is how is the main character so stupid that they just HAVE to ram straight into EVERY BOUY in the WHOLE OCEAN.For an environmental storytelling game, this is immersion breaking and LAZY. I recall the first one being a masterpiece, but this one is too infuriating to allow the player to care about any background story. My guess is that the devs were probably pushed to shortcut their storyboarding process in the rush to make a cash grab sequel.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: It hurts me because I loved Lone Sails but no I did not enjoy this episode :(It's "longer" but not necessarily by additional content but by having more sections where you literally have nothing to do, it feels like whole half od the game I literally couldn't do anything. Just waiting for something to happen. Wind was blowing steadily and i had no fuel to burn so I couldn't even run the engine to make me travel faster.Overall it felt like they took inspiration from Lone Sails, the physics based puzzles, large machines, dramatic scenes with fitting music 👍, but sadly they doubled down on the irritating stuff, complex layout of the vessel, easily wasted fuel because you jumped and accidently hit a button, having to swim back and forth to search for and gather fuel, and like I already mentioned the passive sections where for long minutes there was literally nothing to do, with only environmental sounds keeping you company as the music stopped as well.Well I won't be playing it again any time soon, that's for sure.Technical notes:- runs great on Steam Deck (sometimes can feel a little bit choppy even when fps never dips, idk probably animation "stylex and not performance issue)
