_childDocuments_.review: This may sound like a pretty negative review, but believe me, I did really enjoy this game and I think that everyone who has played the first game should download this game immediately because some may find it a lot more enjoyable than the first, but in my personal opinion, it didn't really have the same effect on me that the first one gave. I'm going to go pretty in-depth in this review so the tldr will be at the bottom. :)So here are some pros and cons about this game, but in comparison to the first, so things I thought this game had over the first, and things that I thought this game lacked compared to the first.Pros:+Lovely and more detailed scenery than the first+The underwater submarine mechanics were amazing and were executed flawlessly+An amazing ending that ties up loose ends+A more clear and "universal" story (The text explaining some story details in the first game were written solely in English)Cons:-A molasses-like slow pace near the beginning of the game-A lot of waiting for stuff to happen. (In terms of micromanagement, the first game had a lot more movement around the ship.)-Moving boxes into the ship was excruciating since you could only push one at a time.-More animals and overall life (Trust me, I will explain this as best as possible later)-The soundtrack seemed more conventional compared to the first games' unnatural but extremely jazzy soundtrack.-A multitude of small bugs that the first game didn't have.ExplanationPacing issuesThe first of my problems occurred when I started sailing the ship. While in the first game, you had a multitude of buttons and levers you could mess around with from the start, the second game has you unlock more parts of the ship the further you go. The problem with this is that for the first 15-20 minutes of the game, you are stuck with just maintaining the sails. One lever, barely interaction, that is it. While I am patient with games, I can see how some people would be bored out of their minds and not give the game a second chance. I can see how this game is trying to replicate the lovely sailing sequences of the first game where there is no interaction, but that was different since there were only around 3 or 4 of those sequences in the entirety of Lone Sails. In Changing Tides, there was twice of that. Lack of MicromanagementChanging Tides does pick up its pace a lot after you get the engine, but even then, there is still not much to do. While you still have fuel to put into the engine, all you have to do is set a bunch on a conveyor belt and you can press a button so the conveyor automatically sends fuel to the engine, whereas in Lone Sails you had to manually put fuel into the engine by hand. There is also no chance of fires happening in Changing Tides, so stakes are slightly lowered, even if repairs are more scarce than in Lone Sails. One more thing: THE STORMS. By far my favorite things about the first game, they put your knowledge of your ship to the test and gave you tense and engaging situations. In Changing Tides, there are only about 2 storm with not much variety. How does this fit into micromanagement? Well normally, you have to make multiple repairs during a storm, and the first storm of Changing Tides was executed pretty well, the other one was abysmal. You can completely cheese it by going under water and evading it that way, sucking the suspense out of the situation. All you have to do here is sit and wait.Moving BoxesNot much to say here. In Lone Sails, you were on land, so it was easy to push multiple items at once onto your ship. In Changing Tides, you are in water, so you must pick up a group of objects one by one onto your ship, leading to mindless repetition for minutes on end.More lifeformsLook, I know how stupid that sounds, but here, the only lifeforms you encountered in Lone Sails were birds and a couple of bison. Everyone else was gone. In Changing Tides, that eeriness is broken a bit. The second game is brimming with all sorts of wildlife, both on land and in the water. You even see humans (But I'm not talking about the ending) albeit dead ones. What is bad about this is that there was no one, absolutely no one, in Lone Sails, making scenes a lot more tense, and you were able to ponder about what happened to everyone. In Changing Tides, you see people, and even if they are dead, they are still there, and that air of mystery is slightly gone. Soundtrack and GlitchesThe soundtrack wasn't quite as good as the first one in my opinion, but a lot of people might like it more than I do, and that's great! I just thought it was a bit more conventional with more of a stringed orchestra rather than a bunch of jazz instruments. However, there are bugs in this game, unlike the first. I completely ran through a solid wall and got stuck, causing me to restart from the checkpoint, and the camera clipped through many walls unexpectedly. The ship also clipped into many objects. ConclusionI think that both of the Far games are unique and fun experiences, (for the most part) but Changing Tides tries to add more, leading to a lot of ideas that are either executed beautifully or flop terribly. It is twice as long as the first game, but bigger does not mean better. It seems the developers were trying to make a prettier world than the first, and they definitely did. (Seriously, kudos to the level designers.) However, while it shows that they spent a lot of time making a great looking landscape, it seems that development was less geared towards the cohesiveness of the ship's mechanics, unlike the first. You probably spend more than 75 percent of the time in Changing Tides outside of the ship solving puzzles, which made me have less of a connection to the ship. TLDRFar: Changing Tides is still a great game, and adds some interesting mechanics and plot details, but doesn't feel quite as special or cohesive like the first one did. Still a must-have for fans of the series.8/10
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: FYI... this game is a follow up to their 2018 game "Far: Lone Sails." I'm not 100% sure how much they connect, and you're able to play this just fine without it, but I was slightly disappointed I didn't know about their previous game until halfway through this one. I would like to have played "Lone Sails" first since there does appear to be some reference to the previous game. I will be playing it after I beat this, but I wanted to give that warning so you can, possibly, start with the first game before jumping into this one. THE GAME:FAR: Changing Tides is an amazing 2D adventure where you play as a small boy that awakens in a flooded world. You venture around as this small boy, exploring sunken buildings and eventually find a ship. This is where the game gets interesting. You operate the ship by physically pulling down a sail and adjusting it's position to gain speed and momentum. There's even a lower deck with more gadgets and features that will eventually help with navigating the world.My first thought playing this game was how original it was. I've never played something like this before. I really love how you move around independently as a person and physically operate the ship. You can also jump overboard and explore the ocean depths, plus various ruins and buildings you encounter on your journey. The puzzles themselves, while they're not difficult in any way, they're still fun and enjoyable. This is definitely a more relaxing adventure with nothing overly exciting. A couple storms and upgrades to your ship kept me interested, but there really isn't anything overly intense or dramatic about this game. It's just a nice adventure with stunning visuals and a peaceful atmosphere. It was very relaxing to play.GOOD (Maybe BAD?):If you're looking for a challenging puzzle game... this isn't it. While this game presents you with some unique challenges, the puzzles are very simple to solve. I only got stuck on one, and even then... it only took me about 5 minutes to figure out. It's also not very exciting. There are a few scenes (lightning storm and tidal wave) but ultimately, this is just a relaxing atmospheric adventure with some easy puzzles mixed in. Many may find this game slow and boring, but I surprisingly enjoyed it. The pacing is done well, and they throw in some interesting things at the right time. You also unlock some really unique features for your ship (without spoiling anything) that add some different gameplay mechanics. This game will be a hit or miss for most players. For me... it was definitely a fun experience that I don't regret playing.GOOD FEATURES:*Beautifully done visual game with amazing atmospheric backgrounds.*Original concept on a 2D platforming adventure.*Explore on and off your ship. Physically control your ship by interacting with various gadgets.*Fantastic music and ambient sounds.*Story told visually through the atmosphere with an important message we can relate with in today's current world.*Water looks amazing and you're able to explore above and below the surface. Lots to explore!BAD FEATURES:*Ladders can be a pain to ascend and descend. Feels a bit clunky.*Beautiful environment but sometimes the foreground gets in the way, making it difficult to line up and navigate.*Game's length & price. It's just too short and overly priced for that.The good definitely outweigh the bad, and if you're looking for a slower paced (easy) puzzle adventure game, I highly recommend this. While the puzzles were very simple for me, they may also be a challenge for some. I recommend giving this a try... just wait for a sale ;)
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: Equally as good as the first game; FAR does not disappoint. The concept was pretty much the same the first one, but they added some new technology into the ship that makes it a blast to play :) Highly recommend this game for a chill experience and good puzzles. I did get stumped twice just because it wasn't entirely clear on what you were supposed to do, but ended up figuring it out. I felt that the 6 hours that I got out of it was worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: I was a fan of Okomotive's Far: Lone Sails and was excited to finally get to play Far: Changing Tides. The gameplay is very similar to Lone Sails and the music makes the game very soothing to play. I would recommend picking up Changing Tides if you enjoyed Lone Sails. The game has good puzzles and the soundtrack is beutiful.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: Bought immediately due to my absolute love for the previous game "Lone Sails" unfortunately i feel as though the sequel ever so slightly misses the mark.The Artwork, music and ambience is absolutely incredible; praise which continues on from the previous title.However I really felt like at times I was fighting with the gameplay mechanics just a little too much. Admittedly, very small annoyances that cropped up time and time again. I couldn't jump onto the mast's ladder because I found the platform too short on the left side and kept running off. The radar isn't accurate and can leave me searching for things it has pinged miles away thinking they're close by. And the bloody hose xD i put out the engine trying to cool the boiler more times than i can count.It's still an incredible game for the price, I just prefer Lone Sail's more simplistic mechanics that let me focus on the art style, environments and narrative more. I will definitely be buying the 3rd game, if one gets made.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: This game is even better than its prequel and much more relaxing. In general the game is more balanced in terms of puzzles and travelling times. The graphics, the sound design and the overall atmosphere are great and will definitely help you to unwind on a rainy Sunday afternoon. Also the story, events and cutscenes are very well made and if you played the first part you will find a few easter eggs here and there. Would rate this game with a 10/10. There was absolutely nothing that was annoying or frustrating, no bugs or crashes or anything else to complain about. Just a very well made game that lives up to the expectations. Well done Okomotive.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: The universe of FAR games is amazing. I'll start with the background of my acquaintance with FAR universe. I first got acquainted with this game on YouTube in 2018, when the first game of FAR universe was released. From the first frames of the video, I was amazed by this game. I love games in which the player is required to fully interact with the vehicle to walkthrough the game. FAR: Lone Sails was no exception. I immediately turned off the video and purchased the game in steam. During its walkthrough, I received as many emotions as I have not received in other similar games. The ending of the first game made me cry. After that, I went through the game several more times, looking for new details, and with each new walkthrough, I found more and more interesting details. Then I created a public in which I shared my thoughts and details. For several years I have been wondering if the second part of the game will be released? And, 4 years later, the second part of FAR universe was released. I don't think you can imagine my expression when I saw FAR: Changing Tides on sale. I immediately bought the game before its release to the public. I waited a few days in anticipation of what would happen in this game, I specifically did not watch the trailer of the game. After a while, FAR: Changing Tides releases to the public. From the first minutes of the game, I was delighted again. I played the whole game with my open mouth... From the ending, I experienced and still experience indescribable feelings. Simply put, my inner world turned upside down, from how the Developers were able to link 2 games into one or... I do not know how to express my feelings, but... This is definitely a masterpiece of the gaming industry, in my opinion. This applies not only to the second part of the game, I'm talking about the FAR universe in general! When I played these games, I had only one wish, that they would not end. I can say with confidence that FAR universe has become a part of me.At first I thought that these games would not intertwine at all. But fortunately, I was very much mistaken. I have already noticed a few details in the second part of the game that may provide answers to some questions that may arise during the walkthrough of the first part of the game. I won't spoiler. I hope this is not the last game from Okomotive.It is an honor for me to be familiar with FAR universe.My respects to the Developers.10/10
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: This game is stunning. What an absolutely gorgeous and fun successor to the original FAR: Lone Sails game! Releasing during the same week as Elden Ring is certainly going to impact play-time, but I need to express that I took a break from Elden ring to try this game, ended up playing it all day and am back for more. In it's own right, an absolute gem, and I fully intend to play it again on Steam Deck.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Lone Sails, then this is more of that.  I'd say it's about 3x longer than the first game with more challenging puzzles.Not quite as tight as the first, but certainly close enough to not let it down.  I just wish they would do more to make me emotionally invested.  Neither of the games really try to make you feel anything other than the bleakness of the environment.I still love these games and will be looking forward to what Okomotive does next.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: FAR: Changing Tides is a direct sequel of "FAR: Lone Sails". And like Lone sails, it tells you a story of a child found in the flooded streets of what may be presumed as an urban landscape completely deserted. Your only friend is the machine that drafts you across wide expanses of water, and in forming this bond you feel a sort of freedom that pushes you to relish in the beautiful art the team at Okomotive poured countless hours in. It is widely apparent there was much effort and care put into this narrative.FAR: Lone Sails and FAR: Changing tides tell the exact same story. Glee, bravery, longing, solitude, fernweh, loneliness, while being completely in mystery. (Why did everyone leave me?)If you've a creative mind, or one that relates to melancholic stories, this game is for you.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: It is just a beautiful game. Overall aestethically pleasing, with great music. I especially loved the underwater parts of the game. Water actually seems quite real, the way the waves move, the light effects, the way the avatar interacts with water, especially on and near the surface. It has a pull and weight to it. Best of all: NO tutorials. No "To do the thing with the thing, do this.." Just the game mechanics and trial and error. There are ques, and a very limited range of objects to interact with, but you have to work it out for yourself.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very special game series. I definitely recommend playing the first game if you havent before you play this as it will make this game more meaningful. Its a very quiet thoughtful journey where you solve some environmental puzzles and enjoy the scenery while managing your vehicle. I wont say more than that for spoilers but its a really touching amazing game that reminds me of why i play and enjoy games in the first place.  This is one of my all time favorite game series. I hope they continue to make these for many many sequels ill buy them and play through everytime to the end because its such a great journey.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Lone Sails, you'll probably like Changing Tides—it's fundamentally more of the same with some cool new mechanics and more glimpses into the FAR world, which is exactly what I wanted from the game. My only minor gripe is that the pacing can feel a little sluggish at points. Lone Sails only takes 2 or 3 hours tops to run through, while Changing Tides clocks in around 5-6 hours. That's not a bad thing, but some of that runtime comes from some repetitive puzzles and sailing sections that drag on a liiiiittle longer than they really need to.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the first game, FAR: Lone Sails. This game is a worthy sequel. It's beautiful, it's gloomy. It's sad, it's hopeful. It's simple, it's complex. It's art. If you're looking for extremely difficult puzzles, this isn't for you. This game is an aesthetic experience that you have to bathe in. It isn't high octane. Don't dread the stretches of time where you aren't actively doing a lot, you're missing the point. When it's quiet is when this game really shines. Sit back and let the beautiful post-apocalyptic, landscapes blow by. Most games jam music in to drive the action or force a mood, but the music in this game fits perfectly whenever it's used, which isn't all the time. Sailing wing-on-wing across a vast ocean will suddenly be punctuated by the fluttering sounds of a small string orchestra. It's really something to behold. The art style, the animations, the feel of this game, it's all perfect. Five stars. Two thumbs up. 10/10. I couldn't love it any more. I only hope I don't have to wait so long for another game, if there is to be one.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: Can't not give it a thumbs up. Took me roughly seven hours. Despite lacking any spoken or written story, it still manages to tell one. Great visuals. Only encountered one progress preventing bug which fixed itself after loading a save (story progression save system, very nice never too much progress lost) No other bugs encountered (that i noticed).
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: Well done sequel. If you like Far Lone Sails you'll like this one too. Playing with controller recommended.+ A relaxing, but emotional journey.+ Operating and taking care of the ship is fun to do.+ Immersive experience thanks to a complete lack of UI.+ The evolution of the ship is well done.+ Art style is beautiful and unique.- It's too short (mainly stems from the desire to play more).- Puzzles are too few and simple.- You basically can't fail.Much like the first title, this is a fun and relaxing ride. I feel this is best exprienced knowing as little as possible going in, but I can recommend playing the first game (Far Lone Sails) before starting this. It's definitely not a requirement, though.I loved keeping the ship going. The physical interactions with the boat are very satisfying. I appreciate that there's no UI whatsoever while playing, not even button press prompts. Normally, that can be a dangerous design decision, but the game's controls are simple enough that this doesn't ever become an issue. (Can't speak for inexperience gamers, though). In this case, it really helps with the immersion and atmosphere.Since I hadn't read any of the texts on the store page, I wasn't aware that the ship would eventually be capable of diving. That made me feel genuinely happy and excited when I realised I was about to unlock that ability.  That goes for basically all the upgrades the ship goes through. I was constantly wondering what would be next.The art in this was also very well done. A lot of story telling with no words spoken or written. There's a very consistent design language to the ship and the world itself. The music also helped pushing the emotions even further.While I enjoyed the game a lot and I can only recommend it, there's also a few things on the negative side to mention. All in all, all those points ultimately stem from the desire to play more of it, to experience more of this world, to keep sailing on and on.- The puzzle sections were too few in number and too simple.- Some features and mechanics you unlock during the journey are hardly ever utilised. Some you basically only require once right after getting them (i.e. boost module, crane) and then never again, really. All in all there could have been done a lot more with the various ship components in terms of puzzles, specifically having to combine different capabilities of the ship (and Toe).- You can't fail. There's too little sense of danger, even when there's a dangerous situation. The fact you can't drown or die from falling takes a bit away from the experience. The ship is your safe haven, your lifeline, your partner and in many ways the true main character of this. You get some sense of comfort and safety being with your ship and operating it, taking care of it. However, the fact nothing can really happen to you, dimishes that feeling a lot for me. I also would have loved to see flooding on the ship. There's a hose you can pump water out, so why not.- A few times there were some silly situations where an obstacle could simply be avoided by going around it. So, being limited to 2 dimensions was sometimes a bit jarring. Also, I often found myself wanting to go other directions just to explore that 3rd dimension.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a real gem.... played both parts, loved every minute of it. Nothing is being said in the game, yet so much is being told, what an epic tale. The ambiance created through fantastic graphics and all the sound and music is so well done. What a game. Epicly done. The puzzles weren't too hard, but very well made. Even without any clues and sometimes a bit lost, but if you notice the subtle hints you can continue on your way. Graphics were stunning. Combined with the music it was fabulous. What a gem.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: I loved the first game and I love this one too; however, I do have some issues with Changing Tides. Compared to the character's jump in Lone Sails, this character feels more cumbersome to control, i.e. a very fast drop speed after jumping. This could just be due to this character not being able to glide like the last. Another issue I have run into is ladder climbing. Ladders seem to have a terribly small range that you can grab onto if you are at the base of the ladder. This is not an issue if you jump onto a ladder higher up, but is a problem if you are trying to maneuver quickly through the ship to lower the sails or deal with overheating the engine.This problem is not related to the game but is related to the soundtrack. The Steam player for the Changing Tides soundtrack will skip songs upon starting and will not let you play the skipped songs. The player, in my case, immediately skips the first 5 songs and will skip back to song 6 if I attempt to play the previous 5. If I select song 7, the player will skip to song 24. If I select song 25, it loops back around to song 6. Is anyone else having this problem or are the files corrupted?EDIT: The soundtrack works on my default pc audio player, so it seems to be a Steam issue.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: This really didn't grab me in the same way as the first one, still ~ok however.The story didn't really feel like I knew WHY I was doing anything, why I was on the move. There are a few key moments I still remember from Lone Sails, even now I think there is only one I'll remember from Changing tides.However the game never really was a drag, at worst a resounding meh.My biggest gripe feels petty but the credits were a slow crawl, with no way to skip, and no way to quit. I was pretty tempted to just force quit the game once I was watching the open font license slowly scrolling up the screen with somber music. If you like the first game and want more, this is more! For anyone else I'd recommend going back to Lone Sails and giving this a pass.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, it's hard to put into words just how much I love this game. The music, the atmosphere, the art style. It's all just gorgeous through and through. Like the first game, a lot of the story telling is done through the environment. I have a few mixed feelings on the story as whole compared to the first game, but whatever issues I have are honestly minor nitpicks. Genuinely, this game is such a rare treat. It's beautiful in every sense of the word, and I recommend at least giving it a try.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: Truly a masterpiece! I really liked the first game, but this one was amazing. The soundtrack and art were just surreal and made the experience completely worth the trip. The ship is really cool to use and i'm glad that there is more control over the vehicle than the first one. While this game is not for everyone, I personally had fun from start to finish.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: Having played 'FAR: Lone Sails', I was hyped as soon as this sequel was announced. Usually not a fanboy, but the first part had touched a nerve... Therefore, I was looking forward to this with some degree of apprehension - would the second part be able to catch the spirit of the first without simply repeating itself?After my first playthrough, I must say - 'FAR: Changing Tides' delivered! Even if it has some lengthy parts during which I kept asking myself "am I missing something?" - the mix of light stress keeping everything running, amazingly beautiful and artful presentation and simple enjoyment of the voyage is once more perfect for me. The puzzles were mostly less technical than in 'Lone Sails', but the pure scale of the adventure and vessel is much larger.And then that ending... pure gold! For this alone I urge anyone who hastn't first played 'FAR: Lone Sails' to do so! It is not strictly necessary, but you'll miss out on an emotional punch if you haven't... I was close to tears at THAT moment...Thanks for a wonderful sequel!
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: Man what a full circle.Play Lone Sails first if you haven't as this connects back to it.The music that perfectly goes with the events and sets the mood.The gorgeous graphics that looks like its straight out of a paining.The atmosphere that's relaxing but lonely at times.The ending that is so very much fulfilling.Much like its predecessor, Far: Changing tides offers a unique experience that tells a story without any narrative. A story that steals your heart from the start. I don't usually leave reviews but if the devs are seeing this, Amazing game!Now excuse me while I go and buy the sound track.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, very chill. Loved that this was longer in length than Lone Sails, and that the vehicle was a little bit more complex (but not to the detriment of gameplay!)I really liked the story and world building. The ending is great and really satisfying.The only very minor detractor is that it is hard to choose when to dive underwater. There are a lot of indicators in the game that hint and guide you but other than the sonar, nothing really lets you know if there's any cool scenery or interesting things underwater.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: If you are looking for a relaxing puzzle game, this is a great choice.  I found the game to be both relaxing and engaging.  I very much enjoyed the art style and found that it created a beautiful world and added to the puzzle experience.  A few puzzles had me stumped for a bit, but never to the point of needing to Google the solution.  In a few months, when i can't quite remember all the puzzles, I'll be replaying the game.Occasionally the movement controls got a little wonky.  This usually happened when I was trying to rush for no good reason.  However, since nothing in the game is time based, that was never really an issue.  Also, on a few occasions while trying to figure out puzzles I ended up outside the games geometery, which often forced me to restart from the last checkpoint.    All in all, i found it worth more than the price and would suggest anyone looking for a relaxing puzzle game to while away some time pick this one up.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: A relaxing and nice game, had a few moments when under the water that i heard some odd or ominous sound and briefly thought this game was gonna introduce an aggressive entity trying to sink your ship but it didn't seem to be anything, it has been a interesting journey trying to piece together a story from the background. A small part of me wishes that there was a coop as this game seems like it'd make for a pretty neat coop experience and such could of probably worked considering the larger size of the vehicle, if there's a third part of me hopes there will be a coop, those who have also finished will know why
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: I can't stress how much this game, and the previous one, are both beautiful pieces of art in all aspects. Absolutely stunning visuals, heartwarming music, simple yet intuitive game play. In both games, I became emotionally attached to both the main characters and (probably even more so) to their respective (L)Okomotives (play them and you'll understand). Fully recommend both titles, and be ready for a roller coaster of emotions. Especially if you play both games back to back, which I did (admittedly I've played the first game many times over). I promise you, the ending is of the second game is so much more gratifying if you do play them back to back, it had me smiling and actually laughing at the final artwork during the credits.Absolute gems.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: after just buying and loving the first game, when I saw that a second one would come out in a month, i was so happy. this game is great on so many levels. in the first game you could only go back and forth, but in this game you have so much more freedom. it feels great to play and watch the amazing art style pass by. this world really makes you feel tiny when there are way bigger things going on around you. i just love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: FAR: Changing Tides is for the people who likes games like Journey but more interactive.For those who are familiar with the principles of sailing the control of the sails according to the winds are spot on. Wind does not comes from a single direction ,it always changes so you have to adjust to that. It is immersive and engaging. I liked most about this game. The artwork and background is so lovely and distracting that one can bump their ship so many times while looking around. While underwater I was looking for the whales but could not find them. Did you hide the whales?=)Story wise; I was on the edge of my seat because the Lone Sails was a little depressing so whenever something unexpected happened I felt a tingling feeling on my stomach but the second game is not as sad as the first one. Everything comes together in the end.Soundtrack, best regards to Joel Schoch. My favorite song was Colored Engine from the first game. I will pick my favorite as I play this game again. I hope Okomotive sees this and sleep well knowing that they did a great game.Couple of things(may contain spoilers):- Entering to the ship from below always requires usage of the ladder on the left and right sides, you cannot jump at that place.It is a little bit annoying. -When trying to pick up crates on the ship just at the horizon sea level you cannot see the main character although you zoom in. The waves hinder the sight.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my second review on Steam, so I guess... here it goes.I have to agree with many other reviews for this game.While I do recommend it, it wasn't near as good (rich story or more information about what's happening) or unexpected like the first one.I hoped that I would be again blown away by the cool music and I would be able to hear it constantly throughout the game, but either I am missing something or it was intended to not have music during some events in the game. Also, I strongly believe the first game's music and events/actions that triggered the music were just perfect.Anyway, I ultimately did enjoy the game and the ending is quite interesting. I feel that a part 3 would make sense in order to close the plot and explain everything?

_childDocuments_.review: Simply amazing. No spoilers:The atmosphere games like these can create as you play through a post-apocalyptic Earth is simply stunning. Though I prefer the atmosphere of the first game, mostly because in that game you get to take in a lot more scenery, as opposed to just sailing in the ocean trying to constantly min-max how much air your sails get.The gameplay mechanics are quite similar to that of the first game, since this is a sequel. The only thing I would criticise in terms of the mechanics is, that sometimes figuring out what you need to do can take quite some time, and repeated attempts, although  considering this game takes double or triple the time it took me to finish the first game (~2h), so around 4-6 hours in total, it makes sense that it's more challenging in that regard.Overall, very worth it. I would absolutely recommend this game, though . Otherwise, you won't get the ending.

_childDocuments_.review: Brilliant successor to Far: Lone Sails (buy that one too, it is currently on 80% sale).The graphics of this game are luscious, the controls and game experience is supersmooth and detailed, something a lot a of developers could use as inspiration.As an ultrawide monitor user I am a little dissapointed in the lack of ultrawide (21:9 , 32:9) support. In the previous game the option wasn't officially supported but could be tweaked. To play this beautiful game in ultrawide settings is to launch in unison with the Borderless Gaming app which can also be bought on Steam. It messes up the game menu's a bit but the game  is playable in ultrawide mode in this manner. Would like devs to consider native ultrawide support.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game on its own,not as good as its prequel, sadly.Pros:- StoryGreat additions to the previous story, a lot of things make a lot of more sense now and it was a lot of fun to play.- Amazing MusicI really enjoyed the Music, just like in Lone Sails- Great Visuals- PuzzlesChallenging and interesting, sometimes a little confusing but my own 5head could be at fault for thatCons:- ControlsIf you re-played the prequel beforehand, like i did, the new controls are pretty hard to get used to. Them being customizable would have fixed that.- Game Length / VisualsI think the Devs traded some Visuals with Game length, making it a lot longer than its prequel. I think the prequel length was great as it is, and i would have wished for more astonishing visuals similar to Lone Sails.- "Enjoyment rides" (Parts where you sit on top of the ship and enjoy the view)While they were indeed very chill, there were too many, and they were too long. Getting pretty boring at some points.All in all a great game, switched from being more of a relaxing game to an adventure game with "long loading screens" (referring to the enjoyment rides). Definitely still worth the full price.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: A sequel in the truest of sense, FAR: Changing Tides takes what made the first game great and memorable and adds on it. The whole management part of the game is much more seamless and intuitive now and I felt a lot less frustrated with the whole retinue of game mechanics than Lone Sails. Mechanically, Changing Tides is more complex than Lone Sails but easier and more enjoyable to interact with. The art style is still amazing and breathtaking. The adaptive nature of soundtrack in my opinion let it down a bit as there were large swathes of the game without any music at all. When the music does play, it is absolutely spectacular and beautiful, its just a pity you do not get to hear a lot of it. I enjoyed the plot and world building a lot more in Changing Tides as it constantly kept me hooked and curious. All in all it was an extremely enjoyable experience, developing on the foundations of the first game and delivering a more enjoyable and memorable  product.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: This title is an absolute triumph.  While largely sticking to the premise of the first title (FAR: Lone Sails), the vessel is endlessly more dynamic, the story more impactful and the art direction is somehow even better.  Some seem to favor Lone Sails, but I found the complexity of the boat far more rewarding to master, as well as intuitive to learn, with each mechanic being taught very tastefully with hints and demonstrations. This game is short, a thorough, but well paced play-through should last about 5 or 6 hours.  Due to the linearity, I believe it will be a one and done for most, or every few years when you get the itch or for achievements.  However, do not let this detract from the value, this is an artistic masterpiece and well worth the cost of a movie ticket or a decent Taco Bell order.  My last recommendation is to play both, in order.  DO NOT play this game without playing the original first.  FAR: Lone sails is good, but it makes this game infinitely better.

_childDocuments_.review: This is, hands down, my game of the year. It may have bumped off ME as my favorite game of all time and I'm not really sure I can articulate why without spoiling the story; and that's really what this is is a story to be experienced. There's no violence, no romance, no earth shattering decisions or real player agency. Instead there is an incredibly well thought out narrative told entirely throughout an expressive environment without need of a single spoken or written word in the entire game. The developers took the same elements we use to teach children basic facts about life and laid them out in a patient story with rewarding puzzles and a stunning visual design and somehow, someway, made a world I connected to without any of the crutches of a character creator, voice actors, or really any input besides move the story forward or stop and explore. The smile that split my face when I got the cultivation achievement still has my cheeks hurting. The level of excitement I expressed shortly after "Now What" when the color scheme switches from foggy to sharp ice blue had my partner bemused and my at an utter lack of words to explain how good the transition looked. I just had to show her a few times. And the clever writing, between "Now What" and "Sound Familiar?" plus the new mechanics for exploring this world, it really feels like I could spend more time writing about my experience than the eight hours it took me to beat it. This game is only $20, from a hands down incredible studio, and it is the best $20 I've spent this year. You should buy this game.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

_childDocuments_.review: Played the first game the day it came out, and had to play this one the day it came out as well.There's a certain awe to both of these games that I haven't found recreated in any other work in any other medium. I think it's one of the purest examples of "the sublime" as far as its definition in the art world goes... That is, the specific quality of greatness you feel when looking at a painting of a small silhouette in the shadow of a massive mountain, or something of the like. In all honesty, I don't know how else to put it. Despite being locked on a single path in mostly a single direction for the entirety of its duration, this game conveys a world with a sense of pure grandeur and scale that no other artwork challenges.The sound design is exquisite. I never get tired of wandering around the ship as it sails, listing to the waves crashing, the sails flapping, machinery creaking and rattling, and cables clinking on the mast in the wind. it makes a concept that would otherwise seem absurd feel so real and believable. The vibes inside your cozy little ship are a perfect contrast to the vast, open, and uncaring world outside of it. It's just so nice.Oh man, and the music! God, the music is just absolutely perfect. So lush and tactile. It's sometimes beautiful, sometimes ominous, and always strangely motivating and uplifting.Also, I love a game that conveys a good theme or simple story. Here, even more so than the first game, I get this beautiful story about perseverance. there's lots of world building and stuff that contribute to the larger story of both games combined, but I just love the way it stands on its own as a tale of someone defying all odds in a cold empty world.Anyway, in conclusion, I adore this game. Be aware that it requires a certain level of patience to get through the whole thing, but it's worth it. Don't just watch the game on Youtube or Twitch or something. You gotta play through it at least once. Play it when you're alone, and savor it. It's not the same otherwise. also, support the devs cause I love what they done so far and I want more outta them.
_childDocuments_.name: FAR: Changing Tides

name: World's End Club
detailed_description: Twelve kids. 1200 kilometers. One epic journey across Japan! Brought to you by Zero Escape series creator Kotaro Uchikoshi, and Kazutaka Kodaka, mastermind behind the Danganronpa games. With twists and turns aplenty, this mysterious, captivating tale of friendship and adversity will have you hooked from the get go. Dive into this easy to pick up fusion of puzzle platforming and choice-driven story adventure, and surround yourself with a cast of charming, quirky characters as you set off on an unforgettable trip! In an elementary school in Tokyo, a group of oddball kids from across the country have banded together as the 'Go-Getters Club.' Reycho and the rest of the Go-Getters are, to say the least, a little different to the rest of their classmates. One summer's day the group is riding the bus on a school trip when disaster strikes. They wake up to find themselves trapped in a rusted, long-abandoned underwater theme park. As they struggle to get their bearings, a sinister clown appears out of the blue and informs the Go-Getters that they'll be playing a 'Game of Fate'—pitting their lives against one another in a desperate struggle for survival! Bewildered and confused, prospects look bleak for Reycho and the gang, but when all hope seems lost, out of nowhere, strange powers start to awaken in the daring Go-Getters. What in the world could happen next!?

_childDocuments_.review: Finished the game already on Switch half a year ago (took me about 17 hours with all collectibles).It's a decent game, just not what you'd expect from the creators of Danganronpa and Zero Escape.It's more kids-oriented and naive. That's not a bad thing just, well...i'm not in this game target audience, it's too childish for me. That said, it has some good plot twists (as expected from Uchikoshi and Kodaka) and nice characters. Definentely can recommend for kids 10-14 years old, and well, you can get some pleasure of it even if you're much older.The gameplay is...fine, i guess, can't say anything particularly good or bad about it, the graphics and music are very nice.PC port had some problems with AMD CPU at the launch day, but now they're fixed. Overall, PC port is OK, "it just works", as once was said by wise and mighty Todd Howard.Edit: Looks like there's still some problems with amd cpu's later in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: I kinda already knew this game's reputation by the time I got around to it but was curious enough to sit through it anyways. It's not... awful, but it's absolutely a disappointment considering the creative team behind it.The story is... ehh. The overarching story is a bit cliche of a humanity vs. AI narrative but it's solid enough on that front, the main issue is just... the writing makes it impossible to take seriously. All sorts of forced wackiness, extreme logical long pulls even for the reputation of both zero escape and danganronpa, a lot of creepy & out of place sexual jokes/romance mixed into the really kiddy vibes - kinda gross honestly, and while there are some -okay- plot twists it's very easy to see a lot of things coming too. Also gotta shoutout the especially blatant product placement of Karamucho chips and Lifeguard energy drink, both of which are so flagrant even kids would feel insulted by them and the way they're delivered. Especially so since these seem to be primarily japanese snacks/drinks and while I'm sure it's possible to get them over here, they're not gonna be everyday market items! The plot mostly fails because it's hard to get emotionally invested in it - there's a subplot about a character's older sibling dying that is introduced and then resolved in like a half hour with no real prior indication and no real buildup, it's just a thing that... happens, and then the game just moves on from it and never mentions it again. There's also another important character death that's spoke about in hushed tones for a lot of the game and then you get to see the moment they died and not only is it incredibly stupid at the time, it gets even worse with additional information given later. Even the "fate game" at the start has fairly low emotional stakes because of how fast it's barreled through - so much so that the demo of the game contains the entirety of it.It's also really hard to get invested in the characters when nearly half of them suck. Like, there's a choice towards the middle of the game to either follow all the interesting characters or all the incredibly obnoxious ones, split riiiight down the middle with like one or two off to the side, and the choice is so obvious by itself that there's absolutely no reason any sane person would choose the obnoxious crowd. I hate Kansai. I hate Chuko. I hate Tattsun. I hate Pai. And I ESPECIALLY hate Mowchan, who is the most stereotypical "haha fat kid likes food" character I think I've ever seen. You cannot make me get attached to these brats because they accentuate the "kid" part of their personalities too much to be remotely likable or endearing. (Well, okay, Pai is mostly annoying just because of how unnecessarily slow she talks, but, whatever, it's still obnoxious.)The game also has, like, gameplay, and it's just universally bad. Poorly thought out gimmicks for each character that are introduced, used in the most basic and banal ways possible, never developed upon, and then very briefly brought back for the very end of the game where they go underused. Most of them feel bad, the gameplay is sluggish, the platforming is weighty and unsatisfying, the puzzles are undercooked, it's almost not even worth commenting on the gameplay for how much of an afterthought it feels like. You spend maybe three hours of the 15-16 hour journey actually playing the game and the rest is standard VN stuff.So yeah, no, I respect the attempt to do something different but this is pretty lousy from every angle, so much so that I almost have to question if it's intentional parody. There are definitely moments it gets so absurd it wraps back around to interesting, but it's a shallow story padded out by tedious dialogue, uninteresting characters, excessive amounts of forced romance, bad platforming, and a general lack of real surprises or engaging writing. Considering how much I love Zero Escape and Danganronpa (and A.I., looking forward to that sequel next year!) seeing these two team up for something this mediocre is really frustrating. But I only paid $20 for it so whatever.
_childDocuments_.name: World's End Club

_childDocuments_.review: Please play this game without expecting another Danganronpa or Zero Escape. I think that's what ruined it for a lot of people. But for me personally, I absolutely adored it. It was a delightful, well written, heartwarming little game. There are things to love for fans of their previous series, as World's End Club has a story with the brilliance of Zero Escape and well written characters like Danganronpa, but it's entirely new and they're done very differently here. This is obviously a game for families but there's something to love for adults and kids alike. I wouldn't recommend it to everyone, especially people who are here for the gritty, mature themes from previous games, but if you keep your mind open and willing to embrace something completely different without lowering your standards for the story and characters, you'll have a great time.My only complaint is that some of the gameplay can be hit and miss. I played on easy and, for the most part, I did enjoy the mechanics but there are some wonky hitboxes and annoying controls that are the difference between life and death in some places, so I found some sections very annoying. I didn't mind too much, as parts of the gameplay I thought were straight up bad were few and far between, but keep in mind that it is a bit unpolished in places. I cut them some slack for not having done a game like this before, and I encourage everyone to do the same here. I've played games with worse mechanics, so it wasn't as bad as it could have been.Regardless, I hope World's End Club takes off and builds a fandom. It was obviously made with a lot of love and it's fun to play. If you're willing to look past dark and gritty adult themes and enjoy it for what it is, I think you'll like it.

_childDocuments_.review: 100%'d the game and gathered all achievements/collectibles, I am having a hard time recommending this game. Not having a Nintendo Switch, I highly anticipated this game and tried to avoid any spoilers. Although I enjoyed bits and pieces of this game, there could definitely be some improvements.1) The black screen bug still isn't fixed (at least for me), which lead the game to become rather tedious, replaying acts that I have already played. The only way I was able to fix it was essentially quitting and re-starting.2) Screen resolution options are very limited; 1080p or 4K, and I don't have a 4k monitor. Being that I have two monitors, this made the game very wonky and I was only able to play the game in full screen (which is not how I always intend to game). As a result of this, it caused my game to freeze and black screen way more often.3) Graphics wise, the game wasn't much of anything special. I didn't notice much of a difference in gaming quality or performance when changing quality (leads me to think that it really doesn't matter at all). Additionally, the screen resolution made no difference to the graphics or appearance.4) The story wasn't too bad, but it is far more linear than it appears to be. I went into this game under the assumption that the first hour of game-play was going to be the entirety of the game, but was wrong about that. I can definitely see some aspects of Zero Escape and Danganronpa, but this game left me feeling a bit disappointed. It was very obvious that they took several elements of Zero Escape/Danganronpa, copied and pasted those same elements into a different game. The rest of the game is basically a side-scrolling action, and the only reason I played through the side-scrolling action was to see how the story would play out. I felt that from the beginning of the game, I knew what was actually going on, the mystery wasn't really there.If you are interested in purchasing this game, I would highly recommend waiting until there's a sale because IMO, the game was not worth full price. I feel like I paid for a copy/paste of Danganronpa/Zero Escape that was tailored for children, with little-zero new elements added. The side scrolling wasn't too difficult, but having to repeat parts of the game over and over again because it is not optimized properly was frustrating for me, thus I would not recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute delight! I highly encourage anyone who enjoys weird, heartwarming, bizarre anime  hijinks to give it a try!That being said, that recommendation comes with a few asterisks.Firstly, if you're a fan of the Zero Escape and/or Danganronpa series like myself, know that while the creators of both are behind this game, it is nowhere near as dark or challenging as any game in either series. Which leads to my second warning: it ASTRONOMICALLY easy in terms of actual gameplay. It's just a platformer with basic puzzles. Nothing more complex in the actual game aspect that that. Exactly one puzzle stumped me, but it was entirely due to my own inability to follow the game's logic, everything else was so obvious and basic I could handle it while half asleep.Despite both those points, it is still what a game should be at the end of the day: fun!The story is intriguing and features several twists and turns I could easily predict but a couple that completely caught me off guard, the characters are lovable and memorable, and Yuki is best girl.TL;DR: It's game for babies, but it's a game for babies that made me feel warm and fuzzy inside and kept me hooked.

_childDocuments_.review: World's End Club is definitely what I expected and I was a bit hesitant to try it out at first but due to it's recent discount, I have finally decided to pick it up. Definitely not what you'll expect from creator of Danganronpa and Zero Escape. It's fun, it's cheerful and heart wrenching for sure. Kind of like slice of life anime where you journey across Japan on post-apocalyptic settings. It scratch an itch i never thought i had.For starters, the game is pretty much a visual novel with some action sequences sprinkled in here and there. That's fine but the overall story isn't that interesting but I'd say it's still overall pretty enjoyable. It's clearly more light-hearted and tailor towards children. Again, something which I didn't expect coming from creator of Danganronpa & Zero Escape for sure. My only grip is that the end game of the story is really bad. It reeks of plot convenience and sometimes leaves me wondering what exactly is the villain thinking? Aside from that, the story is pretty straight forward with 2 branching endings and a flow chart where you can jump from 1 point to another similar to Zero Escape style. The graphics are nothing to shout about either with the game capped at 60 FPS and some scene capped at 30 FPS. That's to be expected as it's a port from mobile/nintendo. The game is also poorly optimized even to this day. I have experience some issue throughout my gameplay such as unresponsive controls and buggy menu. There's this issue where my entire game will just black out after I access the collection menu. I'm not sure what triggers the issue but it pop out a few time during my gameplay. The OST are great, I really like the soundtrack and the songs in the game. I think the composer did a great job. Last but not least, the voice actor/actress also did a fantastic job. I played it in Japanese Dub which is the default.Overall, I'll give this game a solid . It's fun, cheerful and certainly a change of pace. I definitely advice against getting the game at full price as it usually receive regular discounts throughout the year. If you like lighthearted and adventure-ish visual novels then this game is worth a shot.

_childDocuments_.review: mostly because one of the paths lead to a game breaking bug where you can’t progress and there aren’t any time-considerate alternatives. There are some accessory things that weight the game down a bit more, but because of my very narrow experience, some things don’t have an opportunity to be improved on.In World’s End Club (WEC), you primarily play as Reycho, a silent protagonist in this mystery/adventure side-scroller game. In this game, you are one of several children in the Go-Getter’s Club, and on the group’s way on a field trip, something crashes down from the sky and they crash. When they awaken, they’re found far down in the deep blue at this underwater amusement park. From there, the adventure begins and where it leads you, I can’t quite say, but from the glimpses I’ve seen, it’s seemingly a wild ride.It’s worth mentioning that WEC was originally released for the Apple Arcade in April of 2020, then the Switch in May in 2021, then finally, here we are for the Steam release. I brought this up because it clues in on the simplification of controls (Apple Arcade) and that there is an established working version of the game found on the Switch, and that’s even where some of the support for this game has stemmed from.Anyway, in addition to WEC being a side-scrolling platformer, it does feature some mild action, some light puzzle solving, but it mostly seems to emphasize on the story aspect of the game. The gameplay could be summarized as being as simple as possible without being a walking simulator. As you play the game, the children discover abilities that they have which allow them to progress and aid their friends on their adventure. WEC features a  of dialogue, for what I’ve experienced, but I wouldn’t consider it a visual novel. If it's of any merit to anybody, the game does appear somewhat self-aware.Anyway, that’s about all the foundation I can talk about, so let’s move onto what I liked.With the limited playtime I had, I really only got to enjoy the artwork that was featured in the game. The environment is nice and the character designs are unique in their own way. The only bit about the art I don’t like are these highly saturated comic panels that capture either actions or recalled memories — they don’t look great a lot of the time, and on their worst day they make whatever they’re trying to display mostly unrecognizable. But these panels don’t show up  often, so I can mostly overlook them in favor of the rest of the art.However, many things that could possibly be neutral or positive didn’t have time to develop given my circumstances, so we’ll move onto what I liked a little less.To start, the game does have some performance and frame rate issues. This does cause some stuttering or lag; while the community has provided some solutions, I myself didn’t try them because I feel a bit silly trying to fix something in a regularly priced $30 game. In a way, the frame rate issues weren’t bad enough to heavily hurt the game, but it does make some sections play out a little bit worse than others given what might be happening on screen.Next up, I found myself having to laugh at how the characters are portrayed. It’s not uncommon for characters in a game to lean into a trope heavily, but they are really shoved into that mold. This is the inverse of the game not wanting to have forgettable main-cast members, but since I could only reasonably experience a little over three hours of the game, the impression they left was really poor. The worst offender in Aniki, in my opinion, because he fits into that  trope and leads with some laughably cringy lines. Though, everyone, even Reycho, falls into their carved out trope, and since I couldn’t progress beyond an early act, the characters don’t really get a chance to de-flanderize themselves.Lastly, and what I’ve been alluding to in a few paragraphs now, is that there’s a game breaking bug on a specific path in the game. Early on, there’s a choice to go one route with one group, or the other route, with the other group. I think I’ve chosen one of the less popular paths, since there’s a good number of reviews on here with 12+ hour playtimes while I’m sitting at my nearly four hour one. None-the-less, if you choose to go to the , you’ll eventually have to play as a character whose power doesn’t work on melting the ice that’s impeding your progress. I referenced a walkthrough and some Let’s Play videos from the Switch, but nobody seems to be doing anything special to melt the ice. Then there’s at least one community post that indicates they’re stuck as well.In most cases, I would have just opted to go the other path, but the game doesn’t allow you to change your decisions (rightfully so). While you can play the other route, you can only do that option once you get to a future section of the game. If you wanted to try and restart, the game doesn’t allow you to skip most cutscenes and dialogues if you hadn’t seen them, so you’d just mash your buttons to try and get to where you once were. Pielope does give you a chance to advance you to a later portion of the game with a quiz, and depending on your answers you could be dropped in later on in the game  if you insist, after the first act in the game. Unfortunately, the first act is still probably about an hour plus away from the  (Steam censors the other town lol) decision, so the time investment for the correction is just hard to justify when I spent so much time trying to figure out what I was doing wrong and how to overcome it.Well, that’s about all I’ve got to say. I feel like the developer will fix this issue pretty quickly, but by then I’ll have moved onto another game. I’ll come back and finish the review eventually, probably after a couple of patches have passed since the game does get some love from those who have enjoyed it and I’d like to see this presently poor port push a profit.

_childDocuments_.review: I knew coming in that the death-game at the tutorial is only a fake out, and what the game was really going to be. I thought I had my expectations low, but I guess they weren't low enough.This game is very basic puzzle platformer. Each level I've experienced is pretty bland. The game has very stiff controls, that don't fit a platformer at all. Some cinematic in the past used slow, methodical scheme, like Another World or Flashback. This is not that. It's just stiff and clunky. Characters get stuck around the environment, or glitch around. It's not pleasant to control at any point in time, even if you are just moving to the right. Then there are puzzles, which are simple, but painful. You see the solution instantly, but you have to slowly execute it. And I would like to remind you that controlling this game is just awful.And then there's "unforgivable" tolerance for mistakes. For example in one of the first levels I had to jump over the cards while running away from a giant dog. I missed one jump, the character got "stuck" on the roof of the car while not falling, and not being able to climb up, apparently not knowing what to do with itself. It took about 1 second to figure out that I fell. I jumped at the car again, then trough the whole set of cars, but alas, that one mistake meant I wasn't fast enough and had to do whole chase sequence again. It's not much, as the game always puts you only a few steps away from where you died... but you also have to watch lengthy game over screen each time. Would it near-instantly respawn you like in Ori etc. it would flow much better. But slow and junky is the name of the game here, you can't expect anything to flow fine.The story is the only thing that kind of interested me, but I just don't feel like continuing at this point in time. The mystery is alright, but not strong enough to keep me there. It doesn't help that the kids are spending hours wondering if the world has ended, while the game title already answers that part. Is Tokyo destroyed? They will talk about it, and talk, and talk, while you were already shown the answer before that. Makes it hard to get invested. Maybe they were looking to introduce a bit of dramatic irony there, but it didn't work.I also don't like silent protagonist in this game. It looks like he is supposed to have plenty of personality, as people discuss him, and he acts on his own in cutscenes and does heroic things... But he doesn't speak. You don't even get dialogue choices, or anything, so the character fails as player stand-in, and also fails as silent protagonist. Each time he appears on the screen is just creepy, and it takes me out of the story.Looking at achievement ratios people either quit around where I do, or play up until the end. I guess I'm in the first camp.

_childDocuments_.review: Playtime: 15 HoursSynopsis:Twelve kids. 1200 kilometers. One epic journey across Japan!One summer's day the group is riding the bus on a school trip when disaster strikes. They wake up to find themselves trapped in a rusted, long-abandoned underwater theme park. As they struggle to get their bearings, a sinister clown appears out of the blue and informs the Go-Getters that they'll be playing a "Game of Fate"—pitting their lives against one another in a desperate struggle for survival!Bewildered and confused, prospects look bleak for Reycho and the gang, but when all hope seems lost, out of nowhere, strange powers start to awaken in the daring Go-Getters.What in the world could happen next!?Brought to you by Zero Escape series creator Kotaro Uchikoshi, and Kazutaka Kodaka, mastermind behind the Danganronpa games. With twists and turns aplenty, this mysterious, captivating tale of friendship and adversity will have you hooked from the get go.Plus:+A refreshing story form duo uchikoshi and kodaka writing+Short and solid story+Full Voice JP and ENG dub+The character growth for each cast of Go-Getters Club+Saturday Morning Cartoon vibe+Character Illustration by Take, one of artist who always work in pokemon gamesMinus:-Platform segment is janky -Character specific achivement steam ver is very troublesome to achive-enemy placement/pattern in some stage is RNGMixed:=Lot of Loading screen because the game origin from mobile/apple store=Sound mixingthe game is very anime-ish episode adventure story with a great character and lot of callback from all games uchikoshi and kodaka wroteits have a kodaka character style writing with some weird information style dump of uchikoshi...and of course their love of meta twist too

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely sad this game didn't get as popular as it should've. (SPOILERS FOR THE LIKE FIRST HOUR OF THE GAME) Not only does it do a fake-out where they make you think it's another murder mystery, Danganronpa-esque game where kids are immediately okay with killing each other, but the actual rest of the game is great, only getting better the further you go through the story, with the characters progressing and (most of them) becoming more intricate than how one-dimensional they start out to be. You do have to suspend your disbelief at some cheesy moments, but these are moments the game deserves to have due to everything else, in my opinion.By far, the best trait here is the phenomenal voice acting of the English dub, making already emotional scenes become even more heart-wrenching than they have any right to be in this innocuous-looking gameOverall, if you're someone who can appreciate a cute story that's not really deep but still enjoyable, with characters to get invested in, and a sh*tload of wild plot twists that are hinted at from the start of the game, I highly recommend this game...But if you're expecting great gameplay, then I'd suggest to uh, not do that. It's passable at best and frustrating at worst, only really used as a tool to move this Light Novel forward in the storyOverall, 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: A great intro to the creator of Zero Escape and AI: The Somnium Files for the young or just young at heart. Twelve - Yes twelve pre-pubescent kids with superpowers lost in an empty world with no idea what became of their home and all of humanity. Masters of rugged survival, machine repair, complex AI logic, motor vehicle operation and any other skill the circumstance needs them to have, they'll risk it all to save the world with the power of friendship and plot twists! An anime cliche with a lot of heart, side-scrolling puzzle gameplay with light combat elements and a script to rival a modest RPG, Worlds End Club will have you doing whatever it is you do when you play this type of senario. As a plus - for me at least - nearly the whole game is fully voiced in English and Japanese. The english dub is cringy, but more due to the scenario  than the actors doing a bad job. Except someone should have given Pai some direction. She's too much. I have no doubt it's just as fun ti listen to in Japanese, but I applaud the developers for putting in the effort. Also, this story is complete; no Apple Arcade cliffhanger.

name: Crucible
detailed_description: Dodge your way through the crucible of fire! Crucible is a top-down shooter game made by three DigiPen freshmen for their GAM100 class project. You control a magical dragon in a trial by fire against an older, stronger dragon. Your goal is to dodge through an onslaught of colorful bullet patterns without getting hit. There are twelve patterns in all; you win by lasting through all of them in a row. See the true ending by completing either difficulty without using any continues! Each bullet pattern can be cleared either by reducing the boss's stamina to zero or lasting until the pattern timer reaches zero. If the player is hit by a bullet, they can prevent themselves from losing a life point by reacting with a fireball burst attack. The player's score increases every second they're alive and whenever they come close to a bullet without touching it. Full controller support Full keyboard support Two difficulty settings This game was developed as a student project at DigiPen Institute of Technology and was created for educational purposes only. Please check out our publisher page for more information.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm one of the developers for this game; I produced the game, put together the overall design vision, and programmed the bullet patterns. This project was an incredible learning experience, and I'm thankful to my team for making it such a fun and fulfilling time. It was my very first game project, and very much a passion project.Things that went well:- For a six-week project between three freshman-level developers, I'm proud of how much we squeezed into the game.- The game is extremely short, but is a complete experience. The player can win and lose, and there is a progression in difficulty (if imperfect). - From a mechanical point of view, the colors used for bullets vs. backgrounds provide good contrast and make it easy to read the battlefield. - I think the bullet patterns are pretty cool, but I may be biased. :)Things that could have been improved:- Accessibility. This game can be a good time for those who are already into bullet hell games, but it is pretty unforgiving/confusing to those less experienced with the genre.- Player feedback. Lots of players have reported being confused about whether they were damaging the boss, and the player's primary weapon could feel more satisfying to use. - Visual cohesion. The art is of good quality, but I could have done a better job designing prompts that supported a central style/theme.- Game identity. This game was derived in large part from the Touhou series, and it shows. In the future, I look forward to creating games around more original ideas.Overall, this game has plenty of faults, but I'm proud of what my team accomplished. It is by no means a masterpiece, but it is a good first foray into game development. I hope that it brings enjoyment to somebody, somewhere!

_childDocuments_.review: I'd recommend this game, if you are good and familiar with bullet hell you'll find a good challenging game, if you are not you can also play this game because there is continues which allows you to keep fighting.That way you can improve and aim towards using no continues to get the true ending.The smooth music fits really well, the controls are responsive and regarding visuals it's really well made even with all that's going on the screen you are not overwhelmed by colors and objects, you can see clearly where you are.There are two difficulties, one which should be reachable for the majority and for those who seek more challenge.The only drawback would be the fact there is only one boss (with twelve differents patterns which really differ and makes sense) but considering that it is a student project made in a given time it is understandable.Overall it was a good experience and a good student project, might be a good way to introduce new players to this genre.

name: Dread Delusion
detailed_description: The world is broken. Its surface seethes with an undead curse, while humanity clings to flying continents in the sky. From mushroom forests to undead mausoleums, strange places and people await you. But will you find a way to heal this world - or seek power and profit for yourself? Uncover a rich, interactive narrative through the game's quests, or pick a direction and explore by yourself. Carve your own path. Towns offer a needed respite for a weary traveller to sleep through the night, trade goods, accept quests and speak with the locals. A keen mind or charming wit can prove just as useful as a sword; and your decisions will shape how the story unfolds. Welcome… to Dread Delusion. Key Features: Embark on a world-spanning quest to decide the fate of the land Build your character to face challenges the way you want. There’s always an alternative to combat: charm NPCs, pick locks, harness forbidden knowledge and more… Explore a world full of unique characters, creatures, challenges, and treasure Use Smithing and Alchemy to upgrade equipment - turn a rusty blade into a Master Crafted Clockwork Sword. Gameplay inspired by classic RPGs of the 2000s Wield a variety of powerful spells and potions to bend reality to your will. Join or Oppose various Factions as they pursue their own goals A beautiful retro 3D aesthetic
