_childDocuments_.review: Far from a frequent reviewer, but I had to put this out there. I was looking forward to playing this game for a long time, and waited for its full release to do so. I'm glad I did. This game's vibes are unmatched - mixing the best of Morrowind, Zdsislaw Beksinski, and PS1-style imagery to create a visual cocktail that feels like it was made specifically for me. The tone is matched by its writing and themes, which are excellently executed in this game, and make quests consistently morally engaging. Maybe I'm biased, as it also feels like this game was written for me 😅This game is not without its shortcomings, however. Regardless of them, I am impressed and delighted with what is here, and absolutely bulldozed through this game. Firstly, it seems to me that this game suffers from two challenges: firstly, being a small indie team, and secondly, possibly being a largely inexperienced one. Despite that, it is quite obvious that they were aware of the limitations they had, and had the wherewithal to take what they could accomplish in the time they had and polish it to a fine point.If you've read other reviews you'd notice that the consensus is generally that the gameplay is somewhat shallow, and the world is somewhat barren. This is true, though that is not to say the game isn't fun. I too came in with some lofty expectations (perhaps the constant comparisons to Morrowind don't do most games any favors 😅), but these were tempered fairly quickly and I found myself able to enjoy what is there. This is not a game for those looking for a mechanical challenge. The RPG systems and related resource management, to put it briefly, lack depth. But they are laser-focused in achieving an engaging means of progression with as little overhead as possible. Considering the sheer scope of the game, I think the team has done a wonderful job of balancing the core gameplay loop and the progression systems within, even if I feel they may have balanced it too far on the easy side for me. I consider it to be a success, and enjoyed it. There are some mechanical/technical missteps that I could go into as well, including the discomfort of flying your airship, the awkwardness of how the bow's fire rate works, etc. But these hardly matter.The game world is also quite large, and can be pretty boring to re-tread repeatedly as you explore and quest. I HIGHLY recommend a high-agility build, possibly with a sprinkle of magic to use a speed-boosting spell. I don't think the game hurts for content, and I wouldn't scale down the game either. There's a million ways this problem could be solved, and all of them require a TON of work, which is unfortunate.There really aren't puzzles either - no more than "find the hidden item" with the Lore skill.Now that I've explained what it doesn't have, let me try to convince you that what it DOES have is more than sufficient to justify spending your time in the Oneiric Isles.The exploration/navigation mechanics are a wonderful compliment to the often shallow world contents and quest mechanics. They're really well thought out and are a pleasure to engage with. I love discovering places for my map, using my compass, creating a mental map of all my various teleportation opportunities, and flying through the map in this way. Once you get an airship, it adds a whole new dimension of exploration - one which I wish they did more with, but I was happy with what I got.Narratively, I didn't expect to care so much about what this game has to offer. Clearly the opposite turned out to be true for me - the game is not shy about confronting you with the horrors of the world you're manipulating, and regularly presents the most extreme existential moral questions one would expect from a world so agonized. Rarely ever feeling contrived, and often surprising and delightful despite how dark it is, the game's narrative themes shine bright in its quests and match perfectly with the tone set by its art and audio.Unfortunately, the quests often boil down to "go here, talk to this person, then go here and talk to this person" while hunting for hidden places/objects along the way. This bothered me at first, but with my agility and speed spell I was not bothered by this. The subject matter carried the quests further than one would assume they could for a game of this scope. They've done a really excellent job of managing a large, complex narrative with branching dialog that feels believable, even if it doesn't branch very much in reality. And they also managed to make a few characters along the way that you really love, even if your time with them is incredibly short (I need me some more Rasmussy 😩 and the flesh thing). I found myself deeply engaged with the morality and convictions of my decisions throughout my trips from point A to B - the best gameplay is in the mind 😏I could go on and on about this games strengths and shortcomings, and while I'm sure another thousand words or so would be really great to read, I'll leave it at this: I love this game. For better and worse, this game will stick with me for a long time. I want a poster to put on my wall, and I want more games to revisit the horrors of my worst nightmares as concisely and boldly as this game does. It's a horrifying world with a ton of heart, and if you're on the fence, you should try it. My "completionist" run took about 32-35 hours, and I feel like I only liked it more the more I played it. There are multiple endings, but I can say that my ending was surprisingly satisfying. Your actions do play into the ending that you get, so try and make the right choices, whatever those are :) I cannot wait to see what this team does next, and whatever they do I hope they choose to build on this incredible foundation.PS: I want to be besties with the Goblins. I wish they were a proper faction. If anyone knows something I don't, please let me know D:

_childDocuments_.review: A delightfully stylized simple RPG with an engaging plot and interesting world filled to the brim with things to explore. Also the innovative, exploration-based leveling system deserves recognition.Before getting this game, I worried that the grimdark, everything-sucks, aggressively low-poly, permanently-red-sky kind of art style wouldn't be my cup of tea, but slowly I got used to it. It certainly is a very bold style choice.That said, combat is sluggish while also being too easy, and of the handful of skills in the game, three are obviously much better than the other five. Also a certain power-up gets teased throughout the game, but when you finally get it, the game is practically over.Even despite its flaws, though, Dread Delusion is a solid package considering its asking price and absolutely worth getting for the twenty-something hours of entertainment that it provides.

_childDocuments_.review: Fresh from my head ramble.As of writing this I have 14 hours on record and I have done just about everything available in the game so far (I think, there are quite a few secrets).As this game is an early access game there is not a whole lot of content available but the way the world is set up there is a whole lot that can and will be added in the future.The story and the lore are SUPER interesting playing with different themes about the human condition, psyche, and morality, I have some theories but its too early in the development cycle to really pin-point what the story is a statement on but I am very much looking forward to getting more.The game play loop is very Legend of Zelda-esq mixed kinda with The Elder Scrolls in a more Immersive-sim like package, I was mostly reminded of Majora's Mask while playing through this game.Also the combat is stupidly easy, I had no real problems with it, the challenge of the game is the puzzle of figuring out where to go and what to do next.Certainly worth the price as it is for me, and certainly worth for the excitement I have for future updates too. Though if you want more hours of content than 10 to 15 consider buying later down the development line.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion is unbelievably cool, a heck of an achievement for an indie team, harkening back to days of weirder & wilder RPGs with aplomb. I've seen plenty of comparisons to Morrowind, but I caution against approaching it as such - the commonality is mushrooms & oddities. Dread Delusion does not have significant character building, a near-overwhelming bevy of alignments and choices, or quite the same sprawling scope. What it *does* have is an imaginative, gorgeously rendered world like nothing you've quite seen before, an excellent layer of presentation for the terrific worldbuilding. There are many things directly depicted that made me say "oh wow" and even more implied that left me fascinated by this world and the characters in it. From the coffin-interred representative of the anti-god Apostatic Union who gives the player their orders to the Clockwork Kingdom run by a rampant mechanical king to the Endless Realm of immortal zombies, from the top level down it's all bangers, full of arcane lore that calls to mind Book of the New Sun or Gormenghast more than traditional fantasy mainstays. There is also, as befitting a game, Gameplay here. I would not recommend this if nothing I said above piqued your interest - the gameplay is Good Enough more than Good, centered largely around basic slash, guard, parry mechanics. There were only two points in the game I encountered any significant difficulty, my rise to power assisted by rolling a character heavy in the lockpicking skill and therefore able to open nearly every door and immediately overstuff their pockets with goodies. It doesn't feel bad by any means, but it is fairly simple, and even the climactic encounter plays just the same as the first time you flail a weapon at a baddie. There are a few things that feel slightly irrelevant or busted - a tab lists faction relationships that mostly seemed to fluctuate for reasons unknown to me with little impact on my game (do goblins always hate you? is there anything to do BUT fight them?) and at one point, when asked about my approach to violence, I answered truthfully that I had only killed in self-defense and was undermined by being told I was, in fact, a hyperviolent monster. There's also a little weirdness towards the tail end of the game where it turns slightly vague and directionless when an airship was bestowed upon me, causing a few glitches as I wandered a little aimlessly to find the pathway to the finale.But slight problems aside, this was a delightful experience that will stick with me for some time, one of the more imaginative worlds I've encountered in recent memory.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: The audio design of this game is terrible, it's eerily, maddeningly quiet. There's an insanely repetitive meditational BGM going on infinite loop. It just goes on forever regardless of what's happening, whether you're exploring or fighting, the BGM is the same constant loop. Apart from that, there's barely any sound effects. You don't even have footstep sounds, nor do the enemies. In fact the only sound enemies make is the grunting when you hit them, otherwise they're entirely silent. And NPCs make absolutely ZERO sound. It's as if you were talking to cardboard cutouts. After 1,5 hours, it felt like I was watching a muted gameplay footage, while there was a yoga ambiance playing from a different source unrelated to the gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: A review for those who are "holding off from playing Dread Delusion until it's fully done because it looks kinda like Morrowind and you don't want to ruin whatever amazingness awaits you":From my experience (played it months ago) I recommend you just go for it and play it for a handful of hours and then maybe every once in a while as development moves forward, months later etc.That's what I did and I do not regret it at all. I've thought about why and realized that games like Morrowind are endearing to people like us because of their "texture and atmosphere" and the "experiential emergence" we have when interacting with them. Put more simply, you want to play Dread Delusion because you hope it will make you feel like Morrowind first did (or still does) thanks to its certain combination of aesthetics, textures, overtones, sense of atmosphere, alien / hostile sense of exploration, bizarro lore, etc.But I think the people who hold out are doing themselves a disservice unless they know 100% sure they're the type of person who seeks "no-spoiler big production experiences that aren't about the immersion but instead about the excitement, the experience, the emotional rollercoaster, the edge of your seat thrill ride that makes you feel like you just got out of an amusement park"If you ARE that type, then yes, wait until development is finished. But if you still like Morrowind 22 YEARS AFTER ITS RELEASE I can almost guarantee you're not that.If instead you're the type to want intermittent immersive experiences of foreign-feeling science-fantasy and don't care about graphics so long as you can get caught up in a strange world's strange lore and become a decision-making part of it, at your leisure, as you decree, in the small pockets of time (or 4+ hour sessions, ya never know) where you crave those but with something new / different than Morrowind and its similarly-ancient contemporaries, then get Dread Delusion sooner than later.Another factor to consider is that the longer you wait, the more built-up your expectations will be, and therefore the more let-down you're likely to be, and when you remember that Dread Delusion is made by "essentially 1 person who has amassed a small team of helpers" and not "go big or go-home late 90's Bethesda Game Studios with every bit of budget they had left", you'll inherently feel less-satisfied about the game.Playing it while in early development, for me, gave me a connection to the game that makes it feel like an old friend who I don't think is all that great as a person but still like having him as a friend (if Morrowind was a cult classic celebrity that I still hope to meet someday).I think holding off from playing a game that is objectively far-lesser than Morrowind in most ways (other than being made in 2024 and thus being a part of today's relevancy Zeitgeist, and being creepier / weirder, and invoking Playstation 1 nostalgia, and other smaller superiorities I won't spoil pending what you find interesting) can only contribute to it feeling subjectively far-lesser than Morrowind when you finally do play it while wielding your far-built-up expectations.tl;dr: Dread Delusion is a "get your hands dirty" sort of creative force: in how it's being developed, in what its backing lore is, in its gameplay, in its art style, in its presentation, in its marketing, in its inspirations — everything about it screams "don't give any ♥♥♥♥♥ about me, I'm warning you" and to then give a ♥♥♥♥ about it as if it's worth saving until marriage on its eventually release day is not only a sure-fire shot at being a bit disappointed by it (IMO) but also kind of antithetical to the entire philosophy of the developer, who operates under the name "Lovely Hellplace", the name of which should be indicator alone that if you wanna take a dirt-bath in a weird world for a while, just do it now!In fact, I think if Bethesda was hypothetically making a Morrowind II, and it was an actual faithful continuation that would turn out to be good (and not a streamlined sack of neutered pandering meant to satisfy stakeholders' endless financial hunger), I'd jump at the chance to see its early alpha / beta access instead of holding off and waiting until it's all done. I think Morrowind and things it inspires is based in the philosophy of "♥♥♥♥ sucks, have fun"
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: You can feel the love put into this.Buy this game if you are interested in a fantasy world built with meticulous attention to detail. There are so many things to do here, I couldn't help but get lost in the sauce. 60+ hour experience that could easily be cut to 30 if you never explore- but why wouldn't you?A true gem for the adventure community.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of First-Person, Open-World, Action Role-Playing Games and the likes of Bethesda aren't giving you your fix anymore. Then I highly recommend Dread Delusion to you. It's mechanics are a touch simplistic (four stats, eight skills, with "hit abomination with sword" being a fairly decent strategy most times) and the gear distribution could be a bit more generous (if you want to play a ranged warrior or a combat mage, you're going to want a guide, because they do NOT give you a bow or any offensive spells to start and no one seems to sell them. You have to find them). But if you just want an expansive land to explore and scour, this will do you just fine.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the game overall. The exploring is fun, the world is very interesting, i loved the overall style, the quests where interesting, but the main Story a bit boring. The soundtrack has really good tracks, but they are way too short and are just looping over and over which made it pretty boring after some time.The biggest weakness of this game is its combat and difficulty. The combat is veeeeery basic (a bit like morrowind/oblivion) and waaaaay to easy. There is no challenge, nor does it feel rewarding to fight anything in the game. You get loads of healing potions from exploring and buffs/upgrade mats, so over time the game gets even easier.But i like exploring, i like the ideas, so i had a lot of fun and haven't seen everything the game has to offer, i'll save that for another playthrough sometime with a different built. I wouldn't say there is much replay value, but the fact that you cannot really level up everything makes it interesting to try different things and find different solutions and outcomes for some of the quests
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: while its very, VERY, rough around the edges, what youll find in the center is a unique and rewarding story and experience. The style and art are the obvious draw and they deliver in spades, and while some things do suffer for this (the combat is a bit clanky, some jank is to be expected) what you come for, you leave with, as it brings fascinating worlds and situations with some very nice choice making connecting them in quest and story.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most unique and fascinating worlds I've ever come across in any game.  The islands are packed full of secrets and surprises with small environmental puzzles which require you to pay attention to your surroundings to find switches or hidden pathways around obstacles.  The quests build on the game's story and sometimes ask you to make difficult decisions which will affect the ending.  Highly recommended to anyone who wants to immerse themselves in a weird and imaginative alien world.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: After 18 hours and beating the game this was a great game. Really fun just exploring the world and its lore which is very interesting. Combat is okay not really engaging which is fine as it was more exploring and seeing what kind of items i can find. Give it a try if you just want an interesting world to explore
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I would love this game if the combat was just slightly engaging. You can honestly just avoid combat a majority of the time and run past enemies, but when you do engange them it is a complete bore. The artstyle is great and the characters seem cool and well written but the combat being such a slog ruins it for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion is a mixed bag of good and bad, so some will love it, some will dislike it. It has a certain charm to it, with the grotesque art-style, dark setting, and calming atmospheric music. Its main focus and strengths are world-building and lore, whereas its weakness is its combat.LoreSide-quests and main-quests delve well into the lore of DD and they reward you with meaningful upgrades. Side-quests have adequate flavor and there were only a few instances where I felt disinterested. I found the lore to be very interesting and well thought-out. This is a gem for players that like reading dialogue and books. I talked to most npcs, read every book I found, meticulously searched for secrets, catalogued points of interest.ExplorationUpgrades are locked behind exploration and many secrets can only be accessed if you have leveled certain attributes enough. Most quests have attribute checks that affect the result of the quest, so the game does discourage investing heavily into some attributes early on. The map is absolutely full of secrets.The game does give you several different ways to travel if you complete certain questlines, which eliminates most back-tracking and the game respects your time.CombatThe combat is laughably easy on normal, slightly engaging on hard difficulty. Think of it like melee in Skyrim, except you can sprint while jumping and swinging, and sprinting takes almost no stamina, so you can hit, step back, hit, step back, repeat. On a plus note the game heavily encourages stamina preservation, since remaining stamina affects your damage.Few gripes I had are:Dialogue rarely changes as the story progresses, so you still have some random npcs saying what they said at the very start of the game, even though you beat the game.The faction systen is extremely bare-bones and has nothing notable besides specific buffs.The most fun form of travel is introduced almost at the very end of the game, meaning you don't get to use it much. On the other hand if you had it earlier, you could cheese many questlines, so I can understad why it's accessed near the end.Too few spells for spellcasters and some must-have spellcaster-items can only be accessed at the very endgame. Make sure to pick the mage starting skills if you want to be one.Personal note:I loved the experience of Dread Delusion and haven't played through such an interesting world in years, and as I don't mind the janky combat, my personal score for the game is 9/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Do you have fever dreams about old old games like Arena, or Daggerfall, Morrowind, or Kings Field? Where you know the Nostalgia makes your memories so sweet even though you know the games aren't that good? Well this is the game that the nostalgia promises you. It has the looks and some of the intentional jankyness of that era. But with all the Quality of life that one expects from modern games and stories, with a beautiful world and art. With Quests that make you stop and contemplate your life, with the best ending ive ever seen in a game honestly.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: First things first, ignore the game journalists calling this Morrowind; it's not, and that's just lazy shorthand for "it's a fantasy RPG from the first person perspective that is lore deep, is weird and has mushrooms". The similarities begin and end there.Secondly, this game is not challenging. If you are looking for a challenge combat-wise or puzzle-wise, look elsewhere. If you're familiar with cheesing RPG systems and exploring every nook and cranny of the game world to do so, you will have zero trouble cheesing this game. Hell, if you don't even go out of your way to cheese it, you will still have little trouble throughout. The combat functions at a basic level and is serviceable, which is the nicest thing I can say about it. With all of that being said; I LOVED this game. My playthrough post 1.0 release took just over 24 hours and would have been longer had I not diligently played through every update in Early Access and thus knew what to expect.If you are, like me, the sort of gamer that loves immersing themselves in a rich and detailed game world, if you love reading pages and pages of lore, if you love exploration and meeting all the weird and wonderful characters a game like this contains, figuring out how they fit into the world and how to solve the meaningful moral choices they present only to have your expectations subverted time and time again, you will likely love this game as much as I did. In spite of its flaws, in spite of the numerous instances where it falls short in the face of over-ambition, in spite of the sort of jank you'd expect from a small dev team producing a game of this scope, this is the sort of game I will remember for a good long while. It's the sort of game where, even after 50 hours of inhabiting this world, I'm left wishing it was just a little longer, wishing that there was just a little more to explore over the horizon, because although left fulfilled by the journey Dread Delusion has taken me on and satisfied by its conclusion, I don't feel ready to put it down and move on and THAT is worth more to me than many a 'triple A' game has failed to provide.Of course, your mileage may vary; this feels like a game that was designed for ME and, sure, there are a lot of things I would love to have seen improved, done differently or expanded upon, but exhaustively detailing the numerous ways this game falls short of the mark will do nothing to alter the fact that this game resonated with me in a way that few others do. THAT's the way in which Dread Delusion is most like Morrowind - unapologetically weird, purposefully cryptic, steadfastly refusing to hold the players hand and imbued with a sense of wonder, mystery and subterfuge that begets a deep fascination. I'm immensely grateful to have played through it, and that it was even made in the first place. A remarkable game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Aw man, this game is amazing. Amazing visuals and solid lore, game mechanics and exploration that are engaging and satisfying without being overwhelming. A good story to top it all off. Few games lean into the fantasy elements and art direction like this one does. The game left me at the end wanting more. I look forward to whatever Lovely Hellplace have planned next.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Me: "Devs tell me some stories."Devs: "Hold my beer."For real though, this game tells stories wonderfully, and the sense of exploration is very Morrowind-esque.  The combat is the weakest point of the game, but if you skip Dread Delusions because of that, you're really going to miss out on a wonderful experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Even in this early state, Dread Delusion is a unique experience. It presents a surreal world of floating isles and twisted monsters under a blood red sky.Compared to its contemporaries, the RPG systems are simple. Each stat covers a couple skills. Might for melee fighting & HP. Guile for stamina, lockpick & movement speed. Wisdom for MP, knowledge & magic. Persona for charm & barter. There isn't much to it, but it's as complex as the game needs it to be.The world is fascinating and visually enthralling if you're a fan of "retro" graphics paired w/ unique art direction. It presents a world ravaged by magic, where gods were hunted and killed (supposedly) by a militant and atheistic humanity that now enforces a ban on worship with zealous oppression.You were a prisoner of the enforcers of this ban, the Inquisition, and have been tasked with hunting down the leader of a rebellious faction of mercenaries. You're free to decide your approach and have a huge world to journey through to find her (at least once the game is complete).
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I feel conflicted about this game, it's not bad enough for me to not recommend it but also has decently big problems. First of all this game is not like old school rpgs, it has a very surface level stats system that just determines what rooms you'll be able to unlock and what dialogue you'll pass. The biggest problem with this game is the combat, it's too simple, and the enemies are too easy to avoid and circle around. They also are effectively the same with basically two types: they're either close range attack enemies or long range ones. However the game's art style is very good-looking and the world in general is very interesting, both visually and lore wise. Storywise it's kinda mixed, I enjoy the premise of the world and some of the regions and factions but I think the themes and allegories are too heavy-handed and simplistic. The house and ship systems I think are pretty good and well implemented. I bought this game back on Early Access and while I don't hate it nor the direction the devs took I also don't think it was fully satisfactory.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This feels like a strange mix between Morrowind and a niche PC adventure game you played once as a kid and could never find again. The setting is great, it hearkens back to old Elder Scrolls where the themes and lore and some grit to it, it's darker and weirder which is awesome.The gameplay is a lot simpler than that of old Elder Scrolls, but a lot more accessible as a consequence, it definitely feels like a first person graphic adventure game with a bit of RPG injected into it, but that's still pretty good! I'm not sure how long they're planning to make it or if it will go beyond the base archipeligo shown in EA, but I've more than gotten my moneysworth already so I look forward to 1.0 launch.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing experience for old school RPG fans. It's quite simple in gameplay, amazing writing, world building, and atmosphere. The combat is as simple or complex as you want it to be with the magic system and items to give you special abilities. Tons of branching paths in quests that make you consider the consequences, that all tie up neatly at the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a paradox: It simultaneously feels like a labour of love  a store bought template with very little added in.Yes, the graphics are great, but everything is static. Off the top of my head, your only interaction with the world is: opening doors (smashing, hidden switches, lockpicking), talking to npcs, killing enemies, opening chests. You can't affect the world in any meaningful way, nor will your actions be ever reflected in game (with a few cosmetic exceptions).Yes, the lore is unique, but most dialogue is bland and generic. Your mileage may vary, but I was glazing over dialogue for the most basic of knowledge I needed to have after the first town. Some dialog is good, great even, but it's interspersed by a lot of generic and mundane text.Yes, the game world is huge, with 5 distinct biomes, but it's mostly empty with the same dozen assets or so sprinkled around the barren landscape. Level design is.. let's say, interesting, but you'll spend half your time running around in circles, trying to get yourself oriented in the very specific direction to your location because everything looks the same; a regular penrose world hub, if you will. Yes, enemy design is great, but actual combat is non-existent on a practical level. All you do is swing your sword a couple of times, maybe kite the enemy if you're feeling spicy and then they die. This doesn't change even with the final boss of the game. Rewards for kills are generic and don't grant xp, which is why the dominant strategy is to walk past every enemy in the game. None will ever pose a threat to you, and killing them is more trouble than it's worth, even if you do want the meagre 2 gold or throwing knife their decomposed corpse will give you.The story is hard to get going, and it's a huge wasted potential if you ask me. The gist is that you need to apprehend an outlaw, and for that you need to recruit her four former companions. The way you go about this is learning their location then doing a fetch quest for them. Sure, the fetch quest has layers and exposition along the way, but it's a fetch quest all the same, aggravated by the need to traverse the confusing landscape several times over. The game presents an "assemble the team" format and then does nothing interesting with it!Sound design: What sound design?! There's two music tracks as far as I'm aware: regular 'crystal like' sounds and the adrenaline pumping battle track. If there's more than those two, I did not encounter them, nor will I ever encounter them because the regular music was putting me to sleep, no hyperbole. I have no idea what triggers the combat music, because it was absent from my first three hours of my gameplay, after which I put something else to listen to in the background. Everything else is equally as mindnumbing, but serviceable. Potions have a potion sound and swords sound like swords... whatever, next.Bugs: There are bugs, and I'm not talking about the mechanised spiders. But the devs are working on them, so I don't have any complaints in this department. Making games is hard!All in all, the game was not ready for release. You can put all sorts of subjectivity arguments, but I won't be convinced. It feels to me that the supposed '1.0 release' was to get a few more eyes and a bit more funding going. I can't fault the devs for making ends meet, but that screams 'marketing ploy' to me. What's there is great, it just needs a  amount of polish and refinement. If people enjoy it (and it seems they do), that's a good thing. Me, on the other hand, will be kept wondering what this game could (or will, hopefully) turn into will a little more work and thought put into it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: TL:DR - Great New-Retro GameThe game is great for players that like to explore the world and turn over every stone in the kingdom. It`s a great combination of old-school exploring mechanics ( player-crafted map, compass, road signs) with modern quality-of-life  features. Also , there are many moral decisions that are not so obvious to deside for.  The world is like one of the feverish dream and I find it amazing and refreshingThe only bad thing in the game is combat- it is very linear and primitive, you can literally run around your opponent and backstab them constantly, so if you like a challenging combat - you will be dissapointed
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: One of the best and most promising Indie games I've ever played.Well worth the price, with a hugely engaging world and combat and levelling akin to Morrowind. I love exploring this grotesque landscape and delving into whatever puzzles and monstrosities may be waiting.For an Early Access game, it seems very promising and I look forward to the future updates, but here are my nitpicks:The map quest is fun, but the current map system is next to useless, you aren't marked on the map and the markers are quite vague so it's a bit confusing to navigate with the map.The combat at the moment is a bit simplistic, with your character being able to sprint and evade at a speed that enemies have trouble catching up withCrafting and Shops are quite bare-bones but the Developer is working on thisThe music can become a bit grating, some variance or ambient sounds would be much more pleasant, but I imagine this is coming in a future updateBig ask, I know, but surely also add a photo/no UI mode and maybe third person player models with customisable characters? Would love to see my funky man wearing his Fancy HatOverall, I am very pleased with this game and the Developer behind it, would highly recommend
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: An exploration focused experience with some phenomenal music, writing and environments. This game really is something special.First though, the biggest issue. The combat is quite lacking, with it feeling simply functional; though the weight & swing of the melee weapons is very satisfying. Would prefer a slight increase in the variety of enemies early on (ranged/spellcasting goblins for example), as later combat appears to have encounters setup far better than in the earlier game or in general exploration. Also, there needs to be easier access to the weapons available. I'd rather not have to head into the Clockwork Kingdom just to get the only dagger in the game when I already have a 'mostly' upgraded greatsword. Additionally, the more interesting weapon varieties (such as the rad clockwork greatsword) only being available towards the end of the game, doesn't help the combat fatigue that'll set in sometime in the mid-game. An additional firearm ranged weapon, a couple more spells (and again making it so they aren't just loot found in a single late game location), maybe even a few more melee weapons with unique functionalty would also help greatly.Side quests and even the main quest itself, having meaningful & difficult decisions to make is so nice to see when many open world RPG's tend to just fall into Black/White morality. The overall lore of the setting is incredibly interesting, and finding tidbits of it is always a pleasure and reason enough to explore for me, though the lack of decent loot (most of the time) and somewhat empty locations (again not always) might put people off as time goes on. I dearly hope that we get some further content for this game, or even future games in this setting. There's unique elements and ideas here that stand against some of the best that games have had before.Had a few bugs during the game, though thankfully nothing game-breaking. Music occasionally overlapped, and it was noticeable that as the game went on towards the later stages more minor bugs with collision detection and dialog would occur. Again, nothing too serious for me, but it does get a bit buggy later in the game (the devs appear to be making a concerted effort of bug squashing as of now so this should get better in time).tl;dr Honestly, this game is the inverse of something like Starfield. It has a major focus on the details, feels wonderfully handcrafted in the writing and environments especially. Combat is nothing to write home about, but a high Agility character can avoid a lot of it and zooming around the environment is very fun anyway. Highly recommended. This game will stick around with me for a while, and I look forward to whatever comes next.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion is a wonderful game. It is exquisitely imaginative with the characters, creatures, locations, and history. While in a mixed fantasy setting, its writing is more like sci-fi given all the questions it asks you. Dread Delusion does not demand hundreds of hours from you to enjoy it. I think this is a good thing - it makes the story digestible and helps keep the content of the game inspired.I believe any fans of fantasy action RPGs should play this game as a way to reignite your passion for the genre. I will be using this game as inspiration for a D&D campaign next year.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I don't get the Morrowind comparisons and that could lead to a lot of unmet expectations. If you have to make a comparison to a previous game, it reminds me most of Divinity 2 (the 3rd person one, not Original Sin 2). This game is wonderfully janky, pretty simple mechanically, has a confidently unique art and writing direction, and doesn't overstay its welcome.Played entirely on Steamdeck and it was a great experience with zero problems except for having to increase the sensitivity.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: The game is definitely interesting and draws you in, but things like enemy density and variety is extremely lacking. Definitely fits the concept of early access but I hope the dev reads this and applies more danger and variety to the environment. Progression is kinda meh honestly. While it's great to level your skills via stat points only, it really seems like it was a shortcut to not having to have skills and stats progress separately from each other. Nearly everything is unusable as a new character and limits me so greatly that i cant even open a basic secret door. This is just frustrating to me, and from what I can tell in the other reviews, I am not the only person with that issue with the game.If these two issues were fixed in some way, I would rate this game a lot higher. As it stands now, I still want to give this a thumbs up, but the hopes that the dev fixes some of the progression and enemy interactions/variety seems.... unlikely :(. I would be happy to provide the dev more direct feedback over discord or whatever just so these concerns can be better elaborated on. However, I am doubtful that the focus on design right now is in this direction. I'm definitely not the only person with these issues with the game and it needs some fundamental reworks on the 'RPG' aspects of the game for it to be better.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: The only thing I can say: get it, hold it tight and really appreciate the love & care that went into this. I sincerely hope, the developer of this game has more ideas, more projects to work on. I could lose myself a thousand times over in this well-crafted and immersive world. Haven't had such a pleasent experience playing a game in a long LONG time. if you are hesitant - don't be. It is worth the modest price you pay for hours of play, intrigue and fun. PLS keep making games!
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE: So I originally bought this when it came out. Unfortunatly, due to a game-breaking bug my safe got lost. The delevoper also never bothered to fix said bug or respond to any comments about it. Regardless I decided to give it a new go and see how it goes.What I really like about the game is the premise. It is very bizzare, but the world does feel internally consistent, which makes for a great setting. The open world is also well done, beeing open enough to let you explore, but small enough to feel handcrafted. The same can be said for the quests, which are unique and offer some surprising twists.What really drags the game down in my opinion is the combat. Not only is it incredibly easy all the way through. It is also not very satifying to play. While this might not matter to everybody, by the time I went trough the main islands, I was just running past enemies, because they dont give xp anyway and I totally lost interest in fighting them (PS: they did include a hardmode, but it doesnt help, it just turns every enemy into a crazy damage sponge).Something to note, is that the RPG mechanics are also very surface level. You get like 4-5 stats and they all do one thing. You do can play a mage or a fighter but thers not much depth to any playstyle. Same goes for the skills-checks the game loves to use. Like a door which needs to be lockpicked, or a person which needs to be charmed. The systems of the game just dont go very deep, which gets kinda stale over the playtime.Overall I´d say for the price this is offered at it is still an easy recommendation. It is a uniqe experience with some suprises in it. Altough the gameplay does get kinda stale towards the end, you do wanna see rest of the world and the story. My review isnt meant to be negative, I just listed some things id like to see improved in a new project since I do see alot of potential here.

_childDocuments_.review: This is like being on a date with a really attractive woman who is the most boring person alive.Sure, she has a lot of lore going on, and she presents herself in a way that should be entertaining and help you to fall in love,but for some reason this woman just reminds you of your ex, and you sit there and think, "Why don't I just fix things with my ex, why am I here?"TLDR: A shockingly boring nostalgia trip, drenched in style with no substance.Pros: Looks real goodHas interesting lore and general atmosphere,Not very hard, casual gamethe "Lore" skill is a very cool concept for finding hidden sections of areas on the mapCons: The music is badthe general sound design is nostalgic, but nothing specialThe actual gameplay is either boring, or non-existent.Lockpicking is a "Skill" but not an activity, unless you consider watching a luck based dice roll an activity.Magic is pointless, unless you use the return home skill.The world is empty. And I don't mean the cities, I mean, getting from one city to the next, I only ever felt encouraged to just run from one place to the next.There are no secrets worth findingThe combat is swinging a sword or using pointless magic of throwing knives, you can stun lock most enemies, so most of the time you don't even need to move around.leveling up is lame, you find these blue skulls that eventually give you one skill point that you can put in a skill, though lockpicking and stamina are pointless, magic is pointless, so you basically put points in health or lore.A personal gripe, I absolutely hate that you have to "earn" a map. _childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Still not goodI want to start off by saying that while I do not recommend this game, I want to see it succeed very badly. I've been excited for this game for a while now and I can't wait to see where it goes.The visual style is beautiful with obvious inspirations such as TESIII Morrowind and a personal favorite of mine Arx Fatalis. The retro-style graphics options are a nice bonus and nicely give an old school feeling without feeling like too much or looking like lazy filters. The UI is crisp and compliments the PSX aesthetic nicely. Inspirations aside, it appears that Lovely Hellplace has done a great job at creating their own complex and interesting weird fantasy world.The majority of gripes I've experienced are concerned with gameplay. When I think of great open world RPG's the favorite ones that come to mind incorporate freedom as early into the game as possible while allowing for seamless optional tutorials. For example: In TESIV Oblivion you quickly escape the sewers and are welcomed into a large open world that is fully explorable. BUT, when you are let out into the world the devolopers point the character straight to a small dungeon that is completely optional but the player is enticed to go there since it's already straight ahead and so close. In New Vegas you leave Doc Mitchell's house and can go wherever you would like. Many players go without realizing that Goodsprings is an optional tutorial disguised as part of the open world. These types of beginnings in games allow for significantly cleaner replayability allowing the player to choose if they want to complete that first Ayelid ruin, Goodsprings, or Seyda Neen. Dread Delusion felt as though it was going that direction and nearly has it nailed barring a few things. It would be great have other options of escaping from the initial island as it would help demonstrate how different options are always available. Perhaps smuggling yourself off of the island somehow? Maybe you forge a pass to get over the barred bridge? Find someone on the island willing to barter for a pass? There's so much potential with the start of the game I would love to see fleshed out.The combat so far is not great. dodging is fairly useless as sprinting backwards to strafe and kite enemies is significantly more effective. The use of stamina in this game is not good. You're maximum stamina decreases it's size the more you use it. The only way to get it back is by resting. On paper it doesn't sound that bad until you realize your stamina bar is cut in half after defeating a single enemy. I won't dwell on this topic that much as I've already read a post that a developer replied to stating they are looking into improvements to the stamina system. Magic is unfortunately significantly weaker than melee. In my playthrough I put as many points as possible into making an optimal spellcaster and found that a missile spell that takes a chunk of MP did less damage to the games weakest enemy than a single sword swing with an empty stamina pool. This realistically means that if you want to have fun right now your best bet is to ignore your stamina bar and kite enemies with a melee build. I personally find that kiting enemies in melee is actually pretty fun, I just want there to be other optimal options to choose from for spellcasters. I did not play around with the stealth system so I have no comments on it. However, lockpicking is not very fun as it relies on dice rolls that are additional influenced by your main attributes and lockpicking. It would be far more fun and engaging to have a lockpicking minigame even if it's a rudimentary one.Dread Delusion is in need of a sound overhaul. Ambient sounds are minimal with the few I've heard only being noticed while in bushes. Having more ambient noises to compliment the beautiful visual design would vastly improve immersion with the game world. Other sounds effects being added would be nice such as a sound for unsheathing your weapon, interacting with many game world objects, footsteps, heavy breathing at low stamina/exhaustion, one-liner dialogue when interacting with npc's (not full voice acting), player character grunting upon receiving heavy damage, etc.There are of course bugs as with any early access release but I did not experience anything game breaking enough to warrant creating a new save file. The most irritating bug I experienced was an enemies model turning invisible during combat and having to fight them based on audio and their floating weapon.Dread Delusion shows extreme promise and I have no doubt that the developers at Lovely Hellplace will be working hard at making their vision a reality. The developers are already answering numerous questions in the steam community so they clearly are taking input to heart. Unfortunately, as of now the game is not worth $20 and I think they should have released just the tutorial island as a free demo before releasing the game into early access. I will be coming back to this game in the future and will update this review as time goes on.

_childDocuments_.review: Playing Dread Delusion is the closest you will ever get to experiencing Morrowind again for the first time. _childDocuments_.review: After my first playthrough of the game, overall Dread Delusion is an experience I would highly recommend to anyone that follows this genre. However, there are some large flaws to take note off. I'll keep this review as spoiler-free as possible for those looking to get into the game.Positives:-The open world. You're given a fairly large world to explore with tons of secrets to discover, and each area feels unique from the last. I was excited to explore any new place I found, and knowing I haven't found everything makes me want to explore the world even more thoroughly in a second playthrough. -Delusions. Rather than a traditional leveling system based on exp, you level your character using Delusions. These are a fantastic way of incentivizing exploration, as Delusions are earned through exploration and completing quests, among other rewards. -Visuals. The Oneiric Isles are stunning to look at, and the fauna you encounter throughout each region truly makes the world feel alien. It's been a long time since a game has made me want to venture through every corner of its world to understand it.-Story. From start to finish the story had me hooked. Every region explored and character met was interesting and the endgame (as well as the game's multiple endings) tied up all loose ends with them and their fates.-World building. As you venture through every region, you can speak to the many NPC's to learn more about their lives and the culture of their respective regions they reside in. On top of that, the game is loaded with environmental storytelling. Right off the bat you're given the sense that you're living within a world long past its prime, and almost every interaction solidifies that feeling.-Quests. Each region of the map contains multiple small questlines, and a major questline which ties into your ending. Almost every single one was interesting from beginning to end, with a fair amount of them having multiple endings. Some of these quests genuinely left me wondering if I had made the right choice.-Character design. Enemy designs from beginning to end feel greatly inspired and unique, even if they can become a little repetitive if you stay in one region for too long. On the other hand, any gods that I met throughout the game took the cake for some of the most memorable moments in the game, simply for their design alone. -Roleplaying aspects. Challenges will give you multiple ways of completing them; for instance using your lockpicking skill, you can simply unlock the door. Or, if Might was your chosen route, you can simply bash the door down and waltz through. Each stat, although some are more useful than others (looking at you, agility and lore), does serve a purpose for its respective role that is likely to help or hinder you at least once throughout the game if you have been leveling it up.SPOILER PARAGRAPH, SKIP THIS IF YOU DON'T WANT ENDGAME SPOILERS!!! During the final few quests to track down Vela, my character with an extremely high charm stat was able to make her second guess whether or not her goals were truly for herself or for the world. Later on in the final confrontation, she was so overcome with grief that I didn't have to fight her, and instead could deal with the threat she awoke with her. This, in my opinion, is the best moment I had in terms of roleplaying a character.Negatives:-The difficulty. Combat from beginning to end is just far too easy. Enemies stagger easily, allowing you to stun-lock them to death, and you can strafe their attacks far too often without the need to block or parry. On top of that, it is far too easy to land a sneak strike on enemies, which instantly kills almost all of them. Almost all of this could be solved by a difficulty setting that could alter the following:   +Increase enemy damage, health, aggression, and aggro range.    +Reduce stagger so you have to trade blows.   +Allow enemies to track your movement so you have to parry/block more often.   +Reduce or altogether diminish the bonus from a sneak attack.This problem with difficulty all comes to a head during multiple cases of dialogue, where NPC's doubt your survival and fear for their lives against hostile forces. Meanwhile, you go there and barely take a hit from a single enemy.-Resources. This is a bit of an interesting one, but there are simply far too many resources spread throughout the game than are needed with the game's current difficulty. I ended the game with a stockpile of over 100 healing potions, having not bought or crafted a single one.-Character creation tied to early game. Although the pieces of backstory are very nice to read as you build your character, it ends up feeling a bit null and void once you've entered the actual game. A mage character has no access to any spells until the second area of the game. A bow isn't accessible until the third, meanwhile you've been collecting arrows left and right. A warrior has access to the same rusty sword as a mage, rather than something like a greatsword. This all could be somewhat fixed by giving each profession a different starter's kit:+Might: a rusty greatsword and shield potion+Guile: a rusty dagger and bow+Wisdom: a rusty dagger and starting damage spell+Persona: a rusty sword and luck potionFinal Verdict: This is a game you'll want to play solely for the exploration and story. If you're looking for a game heavy on combat, at the moment this game isn't the one for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Having finished my first run of the game, I can easily recommend Dread Delusion and I can only hope more games like this are made. _childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion is a wonderful combination of floating islands and cosmic horror. Your in for a bout 9-10 hours of gameplay as it stands right now, which is a bit on the low end. Given these things, the current price of the game is a bit steep (I recommend waiting for a sale, or more content to be added), however, it is far from a scam. I can see the potential here and I hope that we can see the game expand to 10 times it's current size with more, complex quests and more secrets to explore. The devs are on to something here, and I think they are very close to creating a truly fantastic game.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me tell you folks, this one's a gem. If you're even thinking about buying it because it mildly interests you, go for it.Usually, when a game promises to be an oldschool rpg it comes with any combination of intentionaly bad graphics, wonky controls, unfair rng/difficulty and confusing quest design. Not this time, not here!The ps2 style graphics can be customized to make it easier on your eyes, you can turn off the wobbly textures for example. The controls are simple and never make a fuss, the difficulty rapidly decreases as you explore and become stronger over time and while quests have a lot of text to read that is worth reading, you could skip all of it and only look at your journal entries that boil down the useful information into one or two sentences.This game was brought to my attention by a youtube video claiming it feels like playing The Elder Scrolls: Morrowind for the first time again and after a full playthrough with only 10 achievements missing, all of which are for different quest outcomes and the hardcore mode I can confidently confirm the above claim.Beware tho, I am only talking about the feeling of it. The way you are dropped into this completly strange world which seems to have more mushrooms than trees, you know nothing yet, not even where north or south is. You aren't given a map, you need to make it yourself via a long quest that lasts pretty much the whole game. You don't get a questmarker at any point whatsoever, fast travel exists but is limited to only a couple of spots and is also unlocked via a quest at some midpoint.What is not like morrowind is that the roleplaying aspect of building a unique character is lost in the sense that you can put your skill points in different stats but you don't get a choice in the matter of what class you want to be. Sure, you can focus on strenght, agility, magic or charisma at first but with a maximum of 10 points in each stat you will find yourself leveling something else very soon. You also always have your spells in your off hand meaning if you want to go pure warrior you'll either never use your right mouse button or you cave in and buff/heal yourself with magic at least.As negative as this sounds, the game is very much built around the fact that your character will be versatile as there are many doors and obstacles that can be solved by brute force, dexterity or magic prowes but never all three at the same time meaning you would find paths that are inaccesible to you if you were to only go the warrior, rogue or wizard route.My only real complaint is that combat, outside of hardcore mode anyway, has not much going for it. You whack things with your weapon, shoot arrows at things or use a variety of damaging spells which are one of multiple flavors of projectiles with or without status effects to fight and that is pretty much it. You are allowed to get summoning spells to let a group of calcium warriors do the fighting for you however, if that's your thing.Now, as for the story without any spoilers I will say your choices actually matter here!Places and npc's change, new things appear or move elswhere based on your choices during quests, the main story has you assemble a mery band of missfits to stop the bad guy from bringing back an ancient evil which is something we have heard time and time again but somehow by the end I found myself wanting revenge for fallen comrades, longing for a better world for all the people I've met and helped out...There's no voiceacting in this game and npc's are barely animated at that, so the fact that I could get so immersed speaks for itself.That is enough rambling out of me, cheers!

_childDocuments_.review: This was a beautiful and captivating game.The art style gives it a nice old-school vibe, which adds to the effect of immersion, the map is huge - allowing for countless moments to get lost in the scenery and the ambience of each region, and if you take the time to speak to other NPC's whilst completing both main quests and side quests, it really begins to shape the decisions you will make moving forward. _childDocuments_.review: I was really looking forward to this game and I enjoyed my playthrough for the first few hours. However, my opinion has soured as I kept playing the game. The game has really interesting art and good dialogue writing, but unfortunately it feels disconnected from the rest of its gameplay elements. The combat is quite simple and extremely easy (Also with no difficulty options as far as I can tell) and often feels like a chore in the way of actually exploring the world. But even when I have actually gotten to the landmarks I wanted to explore, they are often just visually interesting loot/combat rooms. I don't think I've played an rpg missing this before so I had trouble at first figuring out what I didn't like about the game, but I've realized that its biggest issue for me was a lack of any environmental storytelling. While environments do look great, there is never a sense that you are stumbling upon some long history of events in the location. There are NPCS which will tell you about locations, but when you go there and just find a big room with giant loot floating about and no evidence of the history the NPC might have talked about, it kills that desire for exploration that I have had in other rpgs.If you're looking for something like a walking simulator/visual novel with light rpg mechanics, then you will probably love the game. But if you're someone like me who came to this game from rpgs like Morrowind or Fallout, you probably won't enjoy it.So while I really appreciate the work and unique ideas that went into this game. Unfortunately it fails to hold up as a great open world rpg, in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion has an amazing hook. If your a fan of old ps1 games or a huge fan of the Morrowind graphics then your in the right place.I believe the hook is the beautiful and yet horror hellish floating islands that are all completely open world for you to explore. It sounds funny saying beautiful and hellish as a description but Dread Delusion does it very well. I couldn't wait to explore the new regions just to see how different and unique the next hellish landscape would look like.The character building attributes system is simple and straightforward. Strength, Lore, and Lockpick allow your character to gain hidden areas with loot. Charm allows you to get more loot for rewards on quests. This is just a brief summary of the attribute system.The crafting system is a simple upgrade for your gear and creating potions with a variety of ingredients to gather and use.I love the retro symplectic loot pick-ups where there are no navigating loot UI containers, just pick up the item drop and keep going adventuring. This reminds me of retro boomer shooters' pick up system.The game play loop is very similar to retro games of the ps1 and Morrowind generation. First person combat with a variety of spells. Block or parry the enemy at the correct timing and set them in a brief stun then hack away at them or blow em away with spells or different melee weapons or shoot em at a distance with a bow. Pick up the loot and continue exploring. Gain levels by finding Delusion pick-ups. My opinion I love these styles of retro combat systems. It is for sure not a AAA combat system, but I don't need those complex features to have fun in a game. The AAA industry keeps getting to inflatied by having to keep adding more and more features which in the long run create too large of a scope for a game and then ends up in a disaster of a release due to being pressured by release dates. Sorry off topic.Dread Delusion is an amazing Indie game, it has inspired and given me ideas for future releases in my own studio. Small simple scope features can be fun if they are developed properly, and Dread Delusion nailed it. If a game can create ideas and inspire that makes it a keeper!The main quest is amazing, however when it comes to dialogue some players will be annoyed with no voice actors for the majority of the dialogue. I actually love reading the dialogue, which means I get to digest the communication at my own pace and use my imagination on what the character sounds like, this is due to my Pathfinder and Neverwinter Nights passion.I only played through the main quest before the 1.0 release and I do plan on restarting my playthrough due to the full 1.0 release. Looking forward to the new playthrough, can't wait to see the new unique content!I hope this review helps encourage you to pick up Dread Delusion. Thank you Lovely Hellplace for creating a memorable instant classic! This is definitely my top favorite Indie game of all time!

_childDocuments_.review: Edited Review: After some time putting extra hours into the game, I would have to say that there is a lot here that has suprised me and the game could be argued as an indie masterclass. I still stand by that the combat is a serious after thought with very little in the way of depth, but the world design and world building with a general good sense of exploration and progression does give the game a good sense of enjoyment. I still would not compare it to a lot of the games the fandom of this game compares it to, but it is good. Original Review: Despite the nostalgia drenched art style, interesting premise, and decently neat lore, the game is fundamentally boring typical indie Unity RPG snooze. Boring unimaginative enemies that you can run circles around and kite with no resistance what so ever. Dungeons are short boring fares that offer nothing unique in way of enemy encounters, boss fights, or worthwhile loot. World design has a lot to be desired and quest writing and general sign posting are not very strong suits either. I had a lot of high hopes for this small Indie RPG when a lot of comparisons were made to early Bethesda like Morrowind with the proto-soulys dungeon crawling aesthetic of King's Field, but none of this is really the case. The only thing Morrowind about this game is mushroom trees (only at the starting zone mind you) and the only thing even comparable to the other is the grim-dark surface. If you want to play the classics this game is trying to appeal to fans of, just play those games. Even with hard mode now available, its not much of an addition due to how the combat fundamentally is easily cheesed with its piss poor AI of enemies and broken sprint mechanic. Some will say, "well, now you see, combat isn't the focus its about the exploration". That be all dandy and all if combat skills and combat focused loot wasn't the majority of the game and if there was actually something interesting to explore except finding one off boring 2 minute long dungeons with only one enemy type or a boss. The sad reality is, this is another of those "Indie game that uses interesting art design to hide poor game design". Most of the new indie craze as of late I swear are made mostly of graphic artists and not actual game designers.  I say that there is a lot here that I can safely say there is a cool concept here. However, the poor and boring execution of it all makes the asking price feel like robbery. Just go play something better or wait for something better, because as the old saying goes, "This aint it chief"
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Good game but not great.This game needs more time in the oven:- The game's music is good, but it needs more tracks. In the final dungeon, there was no music; I don't know if it's a bug or if there just isn't a track for that part. Additionally, the experience of certain conversations would improve significantly with a change in music to a more dramatic tone. Another thing that would make a difference is having combat music.- The enemies have very little aggro and are very slow. They need to be a bit more aggressive, just enough so that the combat doesn't feel completely empty and inconsequential.- Sound design is lacking as well; it needs more crunch. The spells and sword hits sound muffled. A more distinctive melody when completing a mission would be a great help because sometimes, with the current sound, it isn't marked clearly.- The relationship with your crew is promising but never develops. You get to know the characters, their motivations, their past, and their way of thinking, but you never develop a relationship with them—only echoes of one. Perhaps an additional mission with each of the crew members, especially Bassalt, would be good. And yes, I know it’s asking a lot, especially from a studio and a game that has just come out of early access, but the relationship with the characters feels very empty.- The scale of the cities is accurate and maintains immersion, but it would be nice if some of them were expanded a bit to enhance the visual presentation.Nonetheless, here lies the infrastructure of a great game; it only needs some tweaks to shine. Despite everything, I recommend it because it is a very enjoyable game. Some good things as well:- Exploration and world level design are quite good.- The topics it discusses are interesting and raise thought-provoking questions, and the game offers thoughtful answers. It dares to do things that many games wouldn't touch.- The setting is phenomenal; the clockwork kingdom is amazing and full of detail. I love the representation of the decadence and stagnation of its society, which can be seen in its ambient narrative and the themes of the quests. Getting trapped in the escapism of dreams as a false balm for society seems like a great concept to me.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR – This game feels like it’s still early access. And that’d be fine if it wasn’t sold to me as a completed game. If you have the patience to play through a very buggy open world, give it a shot when it’s on sale. Otherwise I’d skip this, if this is indeed the finished product.I finished this game twice and got all achievements out of desperation to find something to make me love it, but had no such luck. The game on its face is serviceable; it’s an “open world” RPG, meaning you run around and get annoyed at a stamina bar in between points of interest. But it’s all the parts that make the whole which make it an ultimately unsatisfying experience.First the praise: The aesthetic and visuals. While many of the late game areas feel and look rushed, the early and mid game look great. The aesthetic and themes on display here really helped keep me looking for a game to love. Equipment especially looks really cool. The large sprites of the armor and accessories got me excited every time I found a new item. I wish the game play delivered on that vibe. Which leads us into the not-praise, which is unfortunately everything else.The RPG mechanics are confusing in that they don’t feel like they exist for any real reason. Dumping all my points into Might and boosting my Attack up barely ever made a difference, maybe resulting in an enemy taking one less hit to kill at best. Doing the same for spells had even less impact, to the point that my second run being totally decked out in max Wisdom, Spellcast boosting armor and all the ideal accessories still did less damage than just whacking enemies with my sword. Guile was a strange stat, as Agility had a clear soft cap for how much agile it’d make you, and Lockpick being bordering useless. Persona increased Charm, which was functionally just another means to open doors that also enabled some dialog choices, and “Regen” which only mattered very late in the game for some specific accessories, which still felt underwhelming to use at Persona 10. Oh, and Barter, which is useless because you can just sell the 2,000 throwing knives, shurikens, and ammo you find to get more money than you’ll ever need.I think this experience sums up my issues with the RPG mechanics nicely: Lockpick is an especially puzzling skill over the course of the game; my first run was 10 Guile, an averaged 5 picks to unlock the difficulty 5-6 doors (with the most ideal gear on, of course). My second run was 1 Guile, and averaged 3 picks to unlock the difficulty 5-6 doors (this time only with the Lockbug and Assassin’s Cowl). That should not be how things work out, and that general feeling of the numbers meaning nothing applies to all aspects of the game in which the numbers are applied. The only time I knew my stats worked was for Lore and Charm checks, which had flat requisites to be functional with a given check.The writing is all over the place. Some quests are fantastically written and self-contained. Others are comical at best and abrasively boring at worst. The main quest being yet another over done scenario where you are a prisoner given a grand quest doesn’t help this. The parts of the main quest that should feel grand and climatic felt flat and unpolished both times I played through them. If this were early access I could grit my teeth through it, but it isn’t early access. It’s just bad, unfortunately.

_childDocuments_.review: Held off on this one for a long while, but picked it up on sale for Christmas.  Glad I did.  Very fun, even though there's not much content for it yet.  I played 16 hours and reached the end of the available content for my first save slot.  I could run through again and ally with a different faction, and that would allow me access to some other stuff that I can't access right now.  But I'm pretty sure I've covered just about everything at roughly 16 hours.This game definitely reaches for an older style of gameplay, and it's something you don't see a lot of anymore - especially if you play a lot of AAA titles.  To give you an idea of the type of game, here are some highlights:The low-poly style had me a little concerned by the screen shots, to the point where I wasn't sure if I wanted to bother buying it.  But I'm glad I did, and I'm eagerly looking forward to the next major content release.  The overall world design reminds me of Vance's Dying Earth in terms of its fantastic aesthetic.

_childDocuments_.review: After beating the game, I can say the story is well worth it. I won't pretend that it's the most deep or intriguing thing out there, but it's pretty good for what it is. The lore surrounding the world helps build on that too. All in all, pretty rich game for an indie dev. However, something I have to get out of the way is that I would not at all compare this game to Morrowind like others. The gameplay mechanics are very simplistic, from crafting to progression and so on. I'd compare this game more so to a visual novel, with its great art style that just oozes personality.To round it up, while it doesn't succeed much as a "game," it is an excellent and immersive adventure that I recommend trying out if you're looking for a quick adventure fix.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel inclined to write a review now that this game seem to have become fairly dormant on the update side of things. The game is great, it has a lot of potential going for it. Charming graphics, amazing music that really leaves an impression paired with the feeling of a world in pieces. It is a very melancholic experience. I believe I read it was inspired by The Elder Scrolls 3: Morrowind and it shows. I had a lot of fun with it but 12 hours in I feel like I have done everything the game has to offer in its current state. Sadly it is quite shallow. I've done a few runs and quickly found the most effective way of leveling and exploring. From that point on I decided it is time to let this game catch up a bit development wise.So a big thing you should have in mind is this is EARLY ACCESS. The game is lacking in many areas, especially depth of mechanics. Now you need to make a decision whether you want to try it out in its current state or keep it in your wishlist, keep track of the development and buy it later. I had a lot of fun in it and I often think about revisiting it. But...It has been 4 months at least since the last major update. Minor fixes since and many bugs present at launch is still there now. In the activity feed on Dec 19 the "welcome home" and faction update appears as if it was recently launched. Which it was not. This is definitely giving me bad vibes about the games future. I hope I am wrong because this game has the potential of becoming something that'll keep you busy for a while. Just don't expect Morrowind kind of depth and that kind of hours spent in it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Playing Dread Delusion and it lives in a very special part of my heart: I've sunk several hours into it today alone without realizing it, all while exploring a strange, macabre, charming, beautiful, disgusting, and above all unique and imaginative world and story.This is a very, very special honor to hold for someone like me. This is the same place games like Morrowind, Oblivion, Grandia, STALKER, Journey, Inside, and few others live.My attention is notoriously hard to capture. This game has that, AND my admiration.The fact that this is an indie game at a steal of a value just adds to the good feelings I have for this, and is another solid entry in the Realms Deep library. If you worked on this game, congratulations; you did it, and you should be proud.The game is still in Early Access, but has hours and hours of content to explore in a mostly open world with a number of ways to play and influence the story. I'm just beginning. I HIGHLY recommend this as a purchase.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is not an immersive sim RPG in the vein of 3D Fallout or Elder Scrolls. Instead its more like an Elder Scrolls game boomershooter-ified. You'll rapidly bounce between reading books and taking quests in towns to exploring the overworld and pilfering locations of interest, with no voice acting and few scripted events to slow down your self-directed exploration. The three sets of character origin choices will essentially just determine which of the basic skills checks (Lockpick, Charm, Strength, and Lore) you have a headstart in, and little else. Dread Delusion is downright minimalist in compasion to the likes of Fallout: New Vegas, but what it does offer in full force is a strangely beautiful world with a fascinating history and an adventure that regularly examines your character's values as you strive to gain the power to save the world- or to change it
