_childDocuments_.review: I was convinced to buy this game by a friend who heard it was like Morrowind, one of my favorite games. I actually don't think it plays much like that game; Dread Delusion is less mechanically complex (there isn't really a crime system, you don't loot forks and expensive plates, the gear you get is less diverse) but it is still definitely an RPG with enough depth to be interesting and encourage many different types of builds. Three things convinced me to keep playing this game as I began to realize it felt very different than Morrowind (although I can believe it still pulled inspiration from that game). First, the world is really interesting. It's like a psychedelic fantasy setting, full of mushrooms, weird creatures, body horror, and more, without getting too silly or feeling unbound by internal logic. Second, the writing is very strong. There were repeatedly quests that presented interesting questions to me that I went far beyond the "hero" option and the "selfish" option you typically see in games. I don't recommend looking up how these quests conclude when you take different paths, as it is really interesting to face these problems and make these choices purely with the information you are given. Third, an RPG doesn't need to be as complex as Morrowind to be fun. This game has spells, leveling up, many accessories and armor types. It has a handful of weapons which work reasonably different to each other. Armor and weapons can be upgraded (which is pretty linear, except for the final tier of weapon upgrades). It's enough to encourage exploration and experimentation. If you want a game where your choices all feel important, right up to the end, this is a great game. It may not offer 100+ hours of gameplay like Morrowind, but it was certainly long enough to justify its price. Most of my real issues with it were very minor; there is a faction system where several factions seem to have very little way or reason to engage with them (I don't even know if you can make the Dark Stars like you and I don't think it matters to the story how that faction or most other factions feel about you) and there were some minor technical issues which I don't think ever impacted me enough to matter (I think I once needed to teleport when I got stuck in some geometry). If you want an extremely creative fantasy RPG where the stakes feel real and things are rarely black and white, then play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: The setting, writing, lore, and aesthetic of this game is incredible. This is definitely a fantasy world it's easy to get lost in. As of the time of writing, don't bother investing any skills into combat. All of the cool stuff requires you put skills into charisma, lockpick, and lore (magic detective skills). Honestly, combat is the only place this game is currently really lacking in. All you have to do is attack, back up so the enemy can't hit you, and go back in and attack. It quickly becomes a chore with few rewards. There is supposedly a block mechanic, though nothing I tried worked and I couldn't find any shields. There is a dodge mechanic, but I never needed to use it, because all I ever had to do was back up slightly and the enemy couldn't hit me.The writing and questlines present so far are fantastic. There is a lot of established lore, and many of the quests already present in the game ask you to make some really, really tough calls to decide the fate of an entire kingdom / people. You don't necessarily see the immediate consequences of your decision, but you know what's going to happen from a lore standpoint. I highly recommend this game if you like immersing yourself in a fantasy world with great lore and writing, and if you like uncovering secrets and interacting with NPCs.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I have been following this game's development closely for about 4 years now, and the wait was worth it! I think Dread Delusion is very much evocative of old RPGs such as King's Field, Gothic, and of course Morrowind, and is able to shape these influences into a unique and compelling world and aesthetic. The amount of potential areas to explore at any given time is pretty impressive, along with having some great writing that reminds me of some of the best of the genre. It's admirable what a team with such a small budget was able to do, and after all this time I'm very happy with the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Hard to put my finger on what exactly made this an instant buy from pics and description alone, but seeing other reviews mentioning Kingsfield and Cronenberg is a clue that it's either Steam's algorithm getting better or cosmic consciousness. One of the two, probably.Other reviews already cover a lot. One thing I'll add to the pile is that the feel is really nice. It has a fluid, frictionless movement vibe that makes exploration feel effortless. Definitely feels like it's going to be a good game to both chill out to, but also be rewarded with unexpected story and lore when you check out the nooks and crannies.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: You explore an extremely cool and original world, and visit all sorts of weird towns and people. If you like exploration, and a more 'laid back' gameplay style, this just might be for you. I felt it was a little lacking in actual RPG systems, and the "three skillcheck" system often felt like it almost never mattered except to gain access to additional loot. I was disappointed there weren't more opportunities for creative problem solving.The "final decisions" of a lot of the questlines are all very compelling and thought provoking, While the content of the quests aren't particularly stirring, I think the philosophy around them is very intriguing. Overall, a good game - very inspiring.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion scratches an open world RPG itch that's been bothering me since Morrowind. The worldbuilding is weird and beautiful in a disgusting way, jam packed with little secrets and humor and horror. Character advancement is simple but hugely rewarding, opening up more areas with every investment. Even in supremely early access, I managed to spend 10 hours sprinting around discovering things nonstop before running out of new places to explore. I can only imagine how incredible this game is going to be when it's finished.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Plenty to enjoy here. Crunchy graphics, moody music, and fascinating locations. If you're coming here for Morrowind, this is very much not that though. The only commonalities are the strange setting, low poly aesthetic, and open world. Dread Delusion is simplified. I would hesitate to really call it much of an RPG, because it's not really a good RPG. Combat is slow and generally only feels passable. The magic is similar, with a few good entries. There's not a whole lot of nuance to a playthrough, and its definitely not quite replayable. I personally found the simplicity to the game to be appealing. You end up zoning out and exploring, cutting down anything that gets in your way. I do with there were more traditional dungeons, but he combat isn't engaging enough to make that really work anyway.That sounds negative, or might imply I don't like the game, but my opinion couldn't be more opposed. I *love* this game with a passion. Its visually beautiful and crawling with cool little freaks and A+ designs. Exploration is rewarding too! It's a dense little open world, and I would eat up anything in the same vein as this. Excited to see where we go from here!
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I really like this game, there are so many fun things about it.I found myself wanting to know more about the story and the world.I enjoyed finding the secrets and deciding upon the fates of cities and gods alike.I enjoyed exploring every nook and cranny of the world and finding cool little items.I also love the art direction, the graphical design of this game and the little touches they've implemented make this game feel so nostalgic to play.Dread Delusion was a super fun experience for me if you can't tell, but this game also has what I would consider one major flaw.The biggest drawback is combat. Combat in this game is just kind of there to be there, it's rather anti-climatic. There's no enemy that felt like an epic battle or got me into a gamer position, enemies hardly feel that dangerous or even worth fighting. You get neat spells to help you fight, like summoning skeletons or shooting spells. But spells cost a lot of mana (which you want to save for secret doors and the best spell in the game which makes you move like 3 times faster), and skeletons have a collider box that makes them annoying to have follow you around. I was hoping that there would be at least one fight, that got me to use my items and think about how to defeat it, but there wasn't and sadly, I've beaten the game. This does not devalue the game in my eyes though but I'm sure it might turn some people off having worked for the chance to have an epic fight at the end of the game.I wouldn't say the game has more flaws other than this, sure there are bugs but hopefully those are to be fixed and I'm positive the dev of this game wants to make it even better than it is now, this game was clearly made with a lot of care.So I absolutely recommend this game to anyone who would love to explore a fascinating world, uncover secrets and decide an entire worlds fate.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: With all sincerity: one of my favourite games I have played in my life. Dread Delusion is a gorgeous combination of many countless underappreciated, as well as the well-established, elements from a variety of game genres and decades.The mysteries and engagement of the world are immediately thrust upon the player, to set a stage of big big philosophical questions and surprises. I am more inclined to consider the world sci-fi than fantasy, despite its typical fantasy-genre signifiers, for how complete and grounded the magic system is, as something tied into the same fabric of this enticing world.I do think, genuinely, one of the mot important things to love and appreciate about DreadD is how-- just-- FUN it is. It's a game that feels GOOD to play. The mechanics are smooth, simple, and are exactly as much as they need to be. As well, a player can make their own rules for themselves, to add their own challenges to certain scenarios and combat (upon my first playthrough I kept thinking of the new ways I could explore the small, but tight and exciting arsenal of mechanics to have a very different experience on my second run)! Also, I have never seen any RPG where "combat is optional", where combat IS optional. As much as I love certain classic RPG hits, all of them provide you ways to avoid certain combat in certain situations-- not an entire experience of a game wholly without it. Of course, having such a system gives you the extra sense that, with it being optional, your choice to participate in combat IS a choice you have made... a very small and standout sentiment done well.Beside all that, the physical world is exciting, enticing, and fun to move around in and explore-- full of tangible rewards for doing so! You can look at all of the magnificent landmarks, which all grab your attention, and know that nothing is stopping you from just Going. You are limited, practically, by nothing. DreadD is fun, it knows its fun, and it gives players the freedom to enjoy it being fun without arbitrary roadblocks or handholding.Lastly, and wow, DreadD is, as I have already said, gorgeous. But-- GORGEOUS gorgeous. Every detail, every design, every piece of the UI, every item, every sound, every soundtrack... One of the most laudable things in my book is that which is made with love, meaning, and intention. There was so much passion behind this project it overwhelms me. I'm not someone whose general affiliation for the arts brings me feverishly into a game and its development, but I was mystified by DreadD during its early access so much that, once I had finished my playthrough of just about everything to do in the game after its final content update before release, I found and watched each of the dev diaries to see how its creation came to be, and to hear the excitement of the devs in its process.My new playthrough I am enjoying in the company of a friend, to explore the world with me, as she, getting to see for only one evening during early access, was just as mystified and excited as I was (it's difficult to outshine The Endless Realm..). And I have hooked a few other friends into this world too. Play this game. It has all my love, top to bottom..

_childDocuments_.review: First time I tried it it didn't really hook me in, but I gave it another shot, and once I got through the tutorial stuff the game started to really shine, the beginning isn't as strong as the middle/later parts of the game so give it a chance. _childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I really like the idea of a non bethesda made first person rpg existing, and I like the artstyle and atmosphere of this game a lot, but there is a ton holding me back from appreciating this game in its current form, especially if it seems to explicitly hold as an aim capturing what makes those games compelling.- The map is terrible. I know oldschool games had bad maps, but they were an accidental not essential component of them. In a game awash with misshapen technicolor mishmash, not having any way to concretely pin down locations or landmarks and your position relative to them is incredibly painful.- I am not properly encouraged to engage with the world in any way other than vague quests or immediately visible collectibles. I understand wanting to make combat avoidance a viable way of progressing, but removing combat having any benefit at all, and making it so lockpicking, lore interactions, sneaking about etc. all do absolutely nothing, means I'm playing this game less like an open world arpg and more like Banjo Kazooie. The only way to progress is to collect Jiggies, and this is not fun both because it doesn't fit the game's intended playstyle and because I have no idea where they are other than ones I am apparently permanently content locked out of by not picking different stats.- Combat is barebones, it's like modded daggerfall in a bad way. I circlekite and wait for space, then hit the enemy once or twice. Especially considering even the most basic enemies take 10+ hits, and I in no way improve in combat efficacy by fighting them, this makes the combat a chore. Yes there are charge attacks, and they do pretty much the same damage. There's simply not enough here to make it compelling, and as of yet no area I've encountered actually permits stealth combat as opposed to just stealth avoidance.So this becomes my game experience thus far: I find myself aimlessly wandering around a mapless mishmash of color, making absolutely no progress of any kind regardless of how I interact with it. The world is bereft of cities, ruins, or locales, but merely has point of interest 'nodes' specked every so often. I come upon a POI node tower with a drunk soldier in it, my charisma check is too low to let me access the Jiggy held in the locked room below. The room is unlockpickable of course, and you are not allowed to kill or pickpocket him to get the key as characters don't have inventories and he's invincible for some reason. I make no progress and leave.I begin wandering aimlessly again, I find another POI node with a wheelchair bound man with memory issues in it. There is a locked door upstairs that can only be opened by having enough book smarts to tug on candlesticks, meaning I can never access the precious Jiggy inside.I go outside to a pillar and remember the man mentioning in bold that the pillar was made by people who hide things with illusion magic. I drink my truth seeing potion that specifically mentions that it interacts with such things that I found near a random lake nearby for absolutely no reason. Drinking the potion causes no changes to the pillar, it continues to not be interactable, but the sky changes color. The limited edition potion fades and the sky changes back. I make negative progress by wasting the potion and leave.I come upon another POI node that is a tall tower with a Jiggy in the bottom again. The door at the bottom is unlockpickable as it is apparently barred from the inside. I prepare to leave, but then notice I might be able to get inside the top. I use my typically useless high agility stat to get 0 EXP by jumping up to a ledge to let me access the upstairs. Inside are three macguffins that require the lore stat to interact with, and no way of accessing the bottom of the tower with the Jiggy in it. I make no progress and leave.I come upon a POI node with a wizard that has made several terrible spells and can't get into magic school. He tells me you need a letter of recommendation to get in. I get a quest telling me that people who can give letters of recommendation exist. Very oldschool, very cool. I make no progress and leave.I visit what I vaguely remember is the lake area where I got the forbidden potion of truth seeing that did absolutely nothing at the designated use a truth seeing potion location. I decide to fight the giant version of a smaller enemy that lives there. After 10 minutes of waiting till he attacks then getting singular hits in, I get 0XP and he drops nothing. A notification appears onscreen telling me that Goblins, who already attack on sight, hate me more than usual now because I killed one of them that was big. I make negative progress and leave.I do what I assume is backtracking but have no way to tell. I come upon a gap in two big rocks with an atheist soldier wandering about. He says I'm not cool enough to follow me around. I make no progress and leave.I return to the POI node with drunk soldier inside, I have gained ore from somewhere now and want to try interacting with the previously useless furnace inside. The ore I have sucks and doesn't do anything. I make no progress and leave.I wander aimlessly again. I continue to find arrows endlessly but no bow. I continue making no progress as nothing is lockpickable. I accidentally or on purpose retrace my steps constantly in a visually aggressive hellscape with no functioning map. I have not collected one single Jiggy aside from the one they use to explain what Jiggies are, I recall that I have not accomplished a single meaningful game act since the tutorial ended with the white haired lady saying my stat-penis was too small for me to be her sex slave. _childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion is a very good game with some issues. The world building is great, the setting is unique and the questlines not being build around questmarkers is a great choice. While alot of the quests are very interesting, there are issues with the payoff. A lot of quests will let the player make big choices that are said to impact the world, execpt that I never actually saw any of the choices have any impact. For example, I chose to uncover the secrets of the academy, which is said to major consequences, but nothing changed. This makes the choices feel flat. The game can also be a bit janky at some points, but I experienced nothing that couldn't be fixed by reloading the game.Overall very worth while, for anyone who likes Morrowind

_childDocuments_.review: I can appreciate what's in this game right now, i'm writing this review because the latest patch completely wiped my 9 hour save, which...really sucks. Though you're warned in the main menu this can happen, as a result i consider my time with the game in early access done for now and i'll continue playing when it's in a more complete state where saves wont be deleted by updates, which i assume will take quite a long time.If you decide to take the plunge and buy this game, then there is quite a big map to explore, there's a lot of polish left, and i believe one of the larger islands are currently unexplorable, but overall the atmosphere is quite rich, both in terms of the actual look and feel of the game, as well as the OST, it's clearly made by competent people on the artistic front.Gameplay wise, it's okay, i mean i did play it for 9 hours which means it's doing something right, i think it needs more smaller dungeon islands to explore, and maybe similar to Skyrim - some procedurally generated quests, like the Dark Brotherhood Forever quests for instance, but maybe more random? so not exclusive to one type of objective, i think having essentially infinite quests would make this game a lot more replayable, maybe they could be given by the leader of a mercenary group or an important character to the story or something, though this is simply just a suggestion and not a demand.Overall though? good effort, but please wait with purchasing untill the game is more complete, unless you just want to support the dev, or you don't mind maybe losing your save in the process, i can't wait to see where this game is another year or two down the road.Addendum 27/01/23:So i rebooted the game out of curiosity after the 0.6.04 update, and i'm not sure if it fixed my save, because i can now play from my previous save again, which is great! yay

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion was an unexpected hit for me. I came because I heard it was "similar to the elder scrolls oblivion" but it really does stand on its own. _childDocuments_.review: Sadly, no.+ Good writing, feels like characters actually have character+ Interesting lore, was curious to find out more+ Unique visuals* No fast travel that I can tell, a lot of walking around. You can teleport to last "save crystal" with a spell but can't choose which one. However, I've been told that you unlock the ability to travel between crystals later, so this is more of a early game annoyance than anything - Far too easy and simple, enemies drop lockpicks/money/potions/throwables like crazy and dying has no penalty. If the enemy is melee, you walk back when they swing, walk forward, swing, repeat. If it's ranged, you rush it to stunlock, or range it yourself- Stealth is very crude, there is no indicator for it, enemy goes from not seeing you to having seen you. Idea is to sneak behind them and get a hit in, but same can be done by running into their back, fast, mid-swing, I believe. Not that you ever need stealth to begin with- OST seems to consists of one ambient soundtrack which just doesn't do it for me- Game offers "multiple paths" like Deus Ex but these feel VERY artificial, since taking a "stealthy path" has no significance when enemies are no threat- No map initially, you can get a mission to write the maps yourself, but by the time you are done, you're intimately familiar with the area anyway, making me question why you'd need it after. Still better than not having a map, though- After some time there isn't really a reason to fight anything once you're stacked in consumables, given that enemies give no xp and only thing that gives stats is quest reward and/or found within environment- Agility is the best stat by far due to giving speed and stamina, which is not only QoL due to all the running around, but means you can outmaneuver enemies very easily, making them even less of a threatI can see someone enjoying this if writing/world building is all they care about, but rest of the game doesn't feel like it keeps up.

_childDocuments_.review: Very cool. However, I think players are doing the game a disservice by drawing comparisons between this and Morrowind. _childDocuments_.review: Absolutely fantastic game if you enjoy adventure games and exploration. Also one of the few games where you can realy feel the power scale difference compared to the start of your journey and the endgame. In addition to fun traversal mechanics and shortcuts, so you wont feel like walking around is a slog, game places at lot of unique treasure and items all over the world, so you feel invested to explore every nook and cranny. In addition a lot of story choices game throws at you arent obvious "good and evil". though there are some exceptions.There are some bad parts, like glitches here and there and some game mechanics late in the game feel "raw" but I am sure it will get ironed out later. _childDocuments_.review: It's a little rough, but still worth playing if you like RPG's with atypical aesthetics and unusual world building. You can tell a lot of passion went into the designs and writing, probably being THE strongest points of the game and the parts that will stick with me. It also feels great to have small NPC conversations and side content be recognized in their outcomes and ending but I wish that the main NPC's themselves would react more to the advancement of the story or events elsewhere, with most of them becoming static once they reach the base. Games like this with very open progression tend to suffer from losing focus on the main plot and this contributes to it, not helped by the fact that the main base is slightly awkward to get back into.The game mechanics themselves are also somewhat lacking. With the combat lacking depth, then becoming a slog by endgame with rooms full of tanky enemies and room layouts not really suited to sneaking, the stealth is also not great.The world itself can be nice to look at, but as the game goes on it begins to feels emptier as the actual level design of the overworld becomes less interesting, the amount of reused set pieces increases, and how often you will find yourself running back and forth across the same large areas. There is a spell in the second town that massively increases your speed, get it.It probably doesn't help that I played through Clockwork Kingdom just before getting to the final area of the game, meaning that my memories of the last half of the game are a blur of rusty metal, losing the charm of the earlier areas and likely souring my experience somewhat. Still though, any time I was reading a book, talking to an NPC or admiring some interestingly bizarre visual I found it very engaging.

_childDocuments_.review: I've extensively played this game in Early Acces, and have finished the full release.This game is very, very close to being great. The worldbuilding, graphics and the story (especially during the last 20% of the game) make a setup for a masterpiece. However it still has a lot of issues: Most gameplay elements are badly implemented - It is literally unnecessary to fight about 95% of the time, as you can simply run away from anything; Your movement is either too slow (in the earlier parts), making it tedious to walk across the map (which you will need to do a lot of) or too fast (in the end game, where you can speed through an entire island in less than a minute); The variety of items and equipment you can get is great, though realistically, most of it will never be used even once. Additionally, the soundtrack, although it's very good and effective in helping the atmosphere, is way too short and repetitive, making it seem like a track loops every 15 seconds. There are also a multitude of bugs (though since none of them are really game-breaking and relatively rare, they're not that horrible).I'd argue it's a decent 6/10, with huge potential to be an 8-9/10. I loved it, and you may too if you give it enough time - but it can be much greater, with changes to the problems listed.

I'm also glad the devs decided to include quite a few options to prevent motion sickness like the FOV slider. Overall it's definitely worth getting. The game seems to have a lot of content already and the foreshadowed updates seem to be quite interesting. Definitely a must-have for all old The Elder Scrolls fans.

_childDocuments_.review: What an amazing game. Sure, the combat isn't great. Swapping equip in and out in order to get the right bonuses for each situation can be tedious. Some of the late game stuff is amazingly crafted (creature island is incredible), but it's placed in a weird spot, at that point I just wanted to see the end but I felt compelled to explore everything. This are the only bad points I can find about Dread Delusion, and to be honest, they don't really affect what I think about this beautiful game.Dread Delusion is all about exploration. Exploration of the world, the lore and the characters. You get to search every nook and cranny of the finely crafted world, divided into distinct isles, each one with its identity, both in themes and graphics. You get to discover an amazing lore, through dialogues, books and the world itself. The way the information is presented always hits a sweet spot where it's not too much but also not too little. And finally, you get to meet and know interesting characters, explore their backstories, understand what drives them, their wants and needs.And maybe, you'll also end up exploring your own heart, what drives you, what moves your soul. As you progress through the Oneiric Isles you will have to take important decisions that will affect the lives of many people, and your own.And the best part is, all this points I just listed work together in harmony, to a degree that is quite rare to see in videogames. Themes, lore, world, characters, the decisions you'll have to take... these things are connected, they all add to each other, creating a captivating mix that gripped me untill the very end of the game.As a side note, I played the game on my steam deck, I didn't notice any huge problem, performance wise. It's true that the first area doesn't run too smoothly but it's far from being unplayable. This game is a really good fit for a steam deck, the handheld format reduces the distance between me and the game, in a way that I can't really explain with words.In conclusion, this game is a rare gem. If what I said about exploration resonates with you, you should really get Dread Delusion. You will have a blast.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion stands out as an endlessly compelling foray into a unique setting full of bizarre characters, interesting cultures and varied environments.While the combat is rather basic, and the old school visual presentation could certainly be seen as an acquired taste (Personally I love it), Dread Delusion offers a masterclass in writing, exploration, and most of all; world-building. The universe in which this game is set has a specific set of rules that form the basis of the history of the world, and I found it to be very thoroughly fleshed out. This information is handed to the player diegetically within the world, through dialogue and also some relatively scarce lore books. I usually can't be bothered with lore books, which might be a sign that I'm just not as invested in the setting as I could be - but Dread Delusion entirely the opposite case; I felt rewarded when exploring some esoteric location to find a book, allowing me to immerse myself more deeply into the setting. It helps that the writing is fantastic, highly original and often tragic. On performance, it mostly ran as smoothly as I'd expect, although I did notice a brief frame drop often when I entered a new area and the game loaded in a bunch of new assets. Not a deal-breaker for me. Aside from some voice lines not matching up to their text counterparts in the final cutscene, I don't think I encountered any other bugs. I also really enjoy the music - I just wish there was more of it, or the tracks were longer, as you'll definitely notice them repeating after a while. It's never intrusive, however, and always suitably unnerving.As a game developer myself, it's wonderful and inspiring to see a small indie team deliver such a gem. I really hope to see more games, or other media, set in this universe. I can see the similarities to something like Morrowind, but you shouldn't expect this game to eat 300 hours of your time - more like 50. The gameplay is also generally simpler by design, but the vibes? The vibes are glorious.

_childDocuments_.review: he whole setting threw me off at first but  drew me in the more I played, and I really enjoy the world that's been built. I like the open feeling and the lack of hand holding. The map mechanic was fun, and I ended up going through most of the game without the compass. Combat is okay, not stunning. The magic system is simple but still fun. The different buildings you can set up as your own base are pretty cool, but I'm bias towards any game that lets me customize living spaces. I think the Clockwork Kingdom was my favorite biome. It had the most gripping narrative of the three major zones, as well as a variety of NPCs that I really took a liking to, despite the few interactions you get with them.The bugs I ran into:In the Clockwork Kingdom several ramps lost their collision, making me walk straight through them. This prevented me from entering the main city there as well as the other areas.Every time an area loaded with the Agility spell, it would swap spells to something else. In the final area of the game an NPC companion continued to clip through the floor or would go through certain terrain details to combat enemies, but again this happened near ramps so, given the first bug I noticed, I wonder if there isn't some more temperamental code related to ramps in this game. :)

_childDocuments_.review: Seeing this is getting really bad feedback on the internet I hope I can make it clear that its neither GOTY nor as bad as some may want you to believe. It has nothing to do with oldschool RPGs like Morrowind and this is where the bad comments start.That being said, it has a very beautiful world to explore and map it which somehow is not a chore but actually pretty good,interesting spells to play with,player housing with upgrades,decent writing and it oozes atmosphere and probably you can buy an airship but I haven't reached that point yet. The negatives are that the combat is really poor, I have lvl 1 might and I can kill anything with the "fine sword" which is the first upgrade you make to the rusty sword you start with, and the music is really really poor and they should either scrap it or add lots more. I don't mind the dice roll lockpicking and I actually prefer it to a minigame but this last bit is merely a preference.On the technical side, it crashed once in my 9 hours and that was immediately after saving in Hallowshire so I didn't care.Unless they fix the combat and add some more polish and music I'd recommend getting it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a place of strange and alien beauty, of twisting and unfathomable horrors.This game is like someone bottled the feeling of wonder you got your first walking through Oblivion, that night in middle school before you knew how all the controls worked, before you knew what to expect from the quests or the rhythm of play, when everything you encountered was a new surprise. This game is one of the strongest arguments I've seen for why an RPG doesn't need to hound you with numbers or lead you by an objective marker, and it makes me feel lost in it's shattered titan skulls and the pulsating light of the Neuron Stars. Go play this beautiful thing
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: An open world RPG with a beautiful, unusual and engaging world to explore. It has an atmosphere I haven't experienced too often in gaming. It definitely feels reminiscent of Elder Scrolls: Morrowind in a lot of ways, it scratches a similar itch although I'd say the rpg gameplay isn't quite as detailed. (You don't level up through combat in Dread Delusion you collect glowing skull items called delusions so exploration is the main way you'll improve your stats) So far I'm really enjoying learning about the world, it's pretty odd and it's definitely a game that beats to it's own drum. If you love games that are kind of mysterious and you're constantly being surprised by things I think you'll find a lot to love with Dread Delusion. I haven't find the game all that difficult (and I think combat in general seems very "cheesable"), but I don't personally mind that as I'm more into the story, exploration and the lore. So that could be a positive or a negative depending on what you're looking for. As I said for me that was more of a positive since I can enjoy the story and the vibes.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: It has good writing! Very rare W, hell yeah. Combat isTrivial, but that's not really an issueExploration is quite fun and the reasonable length of the game means by the time you 'figure everything out' the game is almost over so it doesn't feel stale, and the game does a decent job of constantly developing your abilities in movement and such. Tackles mature topics quite well, has fruit in it
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, I haven't binged a game this hard in a good long while. Absolutely wipes the floor with Starfield and many other AAA big budget RPGs of the last few years. This very free-form kind of exploration designed specifically with not using way points in mind, interesting and detailed lore/world building, and always having something interesting going on over the next horizon will always be far more engaging than simply having modern graphics.The combat is too simplistic and overly easy, and I was a little annoyed at some bugs, especially "Map Marker indicator doesn't appear when you get to a point on the map that is clearly where the cartographer guild people were talking about" and "I can't un-crouch in my own manor for some reason," but I suppose those kind of bugs are to be expected with a big old open world RPG at launch. It's still a fantastic RPG well worth checking out, though.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Allow me to preface this by mentioning that this review takes the Early Access status of the game into consideration. Obviously there are many small bugs and a few questionably implemented mechanics, but the developers are taking player feedback to heart and are actively ironing things out as they come up. Apart from those few stumbling blocks, I can wholeheartedly recommend this game to those who enjoy old-school fantasy RPGs and will even attest to its uniqueness amongst that genre. I've had a few moments in this game where I entered an area or approached a creature and had to pause to admire the creativity of its bizarre design. In that sense, it reminds me a great deal of Morrowind (a comparison I am sure the devs are sick of hearing at this point, but I can think of no other game that captures the kind of feeling I am referencing here).With that in mind, do not expect a full on Elder Scrolls type experience with this game. If anything, the gameplay is closer to King's Field, though again that is not a perfect comparison. The focus, I think, is on exploring the strange world, and in that regard Dread Delusion excels. Please give this game a chance if the screenshots or trailer were appealing to you. I promise you won't be let down!
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Great vibes, fun story, interesting world building that draws you in quickly. Doesn't hold your hand with things like quest markers at every step, respects the players intelligence and so long as you explore, you shouldn't have trouble finding at least one solution to a problem. Had an absolute blast playing this game, Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an odd one. I found myself telling myself the combat was boring and it's riddled with minor bugs that kept taking me out of the game but the world, tone, and mood of the game was so intriguing that I wanted to see how my actions impacted the world and how far I could take it. At first I thought the god themes were just a backdrop but then discovered they still exist and this discovery alone probably is what led me to completing the game in it's current state.Positives- Music is great, if it wasn't for this, the game would feel empty and lifeless- The worldbuilding is great but introduced a little late. It wasn't till I started hearing about how theres more than one neutron star and the God War and the Cadaver Crusade that I realized there is history and background here- The writing in my opinion is greatBelow are Negatives, and honestly not sure I will play the game again unless most or all of the below items are fixed. There's just too many polish items missing in the game to warrant another playthrough unless those are added. As well as I just do not care about knowing the conclusion to the Main story since it's so disconnected from all the side quests and world.Negatives- Not enough/missing sound effects (Hitting walls/enemies... etc)- The Main story is the least interesting part of the game, The Emberian is way more interesting than Vela, the main story should be reworked to just revolve around her and the Emberians- The starter island is honestly just bad. Like legitimately bad, After 30mins to an hour in I was like oh... This is what this game is? And almost quit and refunded it. It's not till after you are done exploring the starter island and you move to the Hallowed Town island that you see the fun of exploring that the game has to offer. Part of the problem with the Starter Island is it's trying to force stealth mechanics on you when this game is just not a stealth game at all. As well theres just nothing really interesting to discover or find on the starter island except  There's one side quest which can be done in 10 mins and is probably the least interesting one.- Footstep sounds are too quiet- Combat leaves much to be desired, but becomes tolerable once you get 7+ Agility- Iron Ore Shortage is a serious and Odd problem (Prevented me from finishing the quest I was probably most excited to do, the Manor one)- dozens of very minor bugs (Nothing game breaking or blocking)- Armor, Trinkets are introduced way too late into the game- Missing Developer messages saying things are not complete-able this led to an interesting frustration I had where I would spend several minutes trying to find something just to realize.... Oh it probably doesn't exist. Which made me feel cheated and taken out of the game.- Clockwork Kingdom is not accessible even though theres screenshots of it on the store page- Factions don't have enough noticeable impact in the world and game- This is partially a bug and lack of content one: Dialogue ended up being one of the things I loved about the game and small outcomes after accomplishing something, so when I went and did something and then talked to one of the main NPCs in a quest and they acted like I hadn't completed the task or something else this was a huge bummer and took me out of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This game was fantastic. If you have a love for the old King's Field games, or just love games that scratch that exploration itch this is for you. The combat is trivial, and I wish there had been a touch more intent put into the AI and combat skills to make it more of a proper mechanic. _childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Terrible combat; never enough stamina to do anything and the best way to fight melee enemies is to walk backwards in a circle around them kiting so they can't hit you, otherwise they'll constantly get cheap hits in.  Fighting against a ranged enemy?  Enjoy getting shot in the face at point blank range while they just stand there and track you easily.The wobbly 3D sounds like a nice idea, but it makes enemies look like messy blobs of pixels past 15 feet so you can't even see what they are.I wanted to like this game, but it's not possible atm.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Recently dove into this purely based on the graphics and I'm really digging it so far. The world is huge, and with the most recent updates it's become much easier to navigate, although it can be a little sluggish and barren in the start while you figure out the game, but quickly becomes familiarized with upgrades and alternate means of traveling. That being said, it's easy to get lost and can sometimes feel like a walking simulator while you figure out next steps. But hey, it's an open world game, can't be thunder and lightning 24/7.Combat is very Morrowind inspired, but this really feels like it's own entity and deserves to stand on it's own two feet. Story is pretty interesting, definitely feels like whoever has creative control over this game has been thinking all this out for a while, both graphically and in text. Definitely had a few "wtf am I looking at" moments, and genuine bouts of uneasiness while finding something I wasn't expecting. I've barely skimmed the surface of Dread Delusion but it's quickly made its way into my rotation. It's nice to see that the updates coming out while this is in EA are not just minor surface level updates, but massive updates that actually increase the size of the game and introduce new mechanics so I'm not worried about this becoming abandoned ware. Really looking forward seeing where it all ends up. Fun as is. Worth the price.text1text2text3
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I completed the current available content in just over 8 hours, and it was probably the most fun I've had in a game for a long time. Dread Delusion has character, charm, depth, and lore that I just can't get enough of! This game is worth the money, and has had steady patches every day since release. There is so much beauty and fun to be had in the current version, and I am confident that future content releases will bring the same quality and character that I have enjoyed thus far.This game proves that graphics have nothing to do with enjoyment, or depth in a game. The simplified graphics pull you into a mysterious and terrifying world, where you can face challenges however you like!My only gripe is that the combat is very easy once you learn it. An hour in and the challenge stopped. This isn't necessarily bad, as the roleplay mechanics far outweighed that negative, but I would challenge the developers to find ways to make the combat more engaging, while preserving the simple hack and slack adventuring that they have created so far. I want to venture out with a little fear that something terrifying might kick my ass.

_childDocuments_.review: Rewriting this review for leaving early access- TL;DR, Dread Delusion is one of my favorite gamesI can't tell you how much I love this game. It's one of the best takes on the low-fi game aesthetic- I hate to call it entirely nostalgic, though, because it's very much its own style. It takes the aesthetic trappings of old games and makes them into a cohesive and new whole. It's absolutely beautiful, visually. There are some really delightful moments of nostalgic design, though- the opening dialogue is purposely compressed in a  way that threw me back into early-2000s childhood. That's not even getting into the writing. I love this game's story and themes- questions about Utopias, and the the utopian dreams that drive life in a violent world, and what you believe it's worth to try and attain them. I feel very pretentious saying those words in that order- but the game carries it off effortlessly, through worldbuilding and poetic dialogue. That makes it sound like it'd be a Pathologic-style slog but it's also a very funny game, with a full cast of weirdos that calls back to the early Legend of Zelda games and the influence they took from Twin Peaks, who speak in friendly rudeness, sparkling with a dry British wit. Getting into the gameplay- I'm a huge fan of the game's emphasis on exploration over grinding. I've been playing through my first 1.0 release character as a complete pacifist- not even killing monsters- and the game seems to want me to be able to do it. I can pick locks and sneak behind everyone- or just run past enemies chugging health potions- and complete every quest objective so far without ending a single life. And every life does seem to be counted- at first, I wasn't sure if monsters counted, then I saw the Goblins faction reputation ticked down every time I killed one- because of course it has the faction system that makes games like Fallout New Vegas and Stalker: Blue Sky feel like you're in the middle of a political struggle instead of the sole protagonist of a world waiting just for you, of course it does, it's too perfect not to. I restarted that save because the goblins are the cutest thing I've ever seen in my life, and I need them to love me, so- no murder for me. And this seems like it fits in with the game's themes- they've got a really solid ludonarrative going on. And importantly, every skill seems to be separately very useful. Lockpicking and Lore can sometimes- but not always- open a door that bypasses the other, and even speech can open doors that neither can- literally, in the cast of the skull-major-domo-robots that open some doors, and metaphorically in the case of talking your way past a guard. The new introductory area added in 1.0 showcases all these things nicely, providing a solid vertical slice of gameplay from the first hour of play, so you'll know if you like it pretty fast.I have played with the combat, despite the fact that I'm currently trying to outrun five bandits so i don't have to kill any of them, and while it's not the most fast paced or the most flashy- there aren't going to be any Skyrim-style decapitation cutscenes- I actually really like that about it. You can get some very cool combat spells, or you can hit people very hard with a sword, and in practice this plays out a bit like if Morrowind's combat system was intuitive. As a big fan of Morrowind, that's my thing! It might not be yours, but like I said- you don't have to do it. The game wants to let you avoid it. So if it turns you off at first, maybe give a stealth run a try.There's a few bugs- dialogue tree issues and missing text, mostly- but it's the kind of thing you'd expect on launch from a small team releasing what is a really very large game. I think it's more than forgivable, and I look forward to seeing the polish it gets after a year or two of bugfixing. And really that's the only negative thing I could possibly say about it.This is very seriously one of the best indie RPGs I've ever played. It's one of the best RPGs I've ever played, period! I hope the devs make a sequel- I want to see this setting fleshed out, see more stories from another part of this world. I genuinely think any fans of this kind of game should try it out. It's more than worth the price.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I saw this game at youtube and i'm very glad about it. I played only a couple of hours so far, but those hours have been very captivating. The devs created a fantastic world and exploring it has been pure joy. The artstyle is superb, the lore is great, the music and the sounds create a very unique and eerie feeling. All those points are supported by the missing handholding. So far there are no questpoints, i even don't have the map yet and it is very fun to just venture out and follow the descriptions of the npcs. I can definetly see some Morrowind influence here, especially with all the mushrooms around :) The only weak point of the game for now is the combat system. There is no challenge to it and it is also very bland. You just have to hit the enemies and can tank hits more than safely. I hope that the devs will keep adding to this game and maybe overhaul and improve the system, if it is possible.Overall it is a great experience, especially for that price. If you like exploring and getting lost in a strange world, you'll love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Finally a game that dares to ask "what if someone made an even weirder Elder Scrolls game than Morrowind, and removed most of the mechanical junk, and wrote an absolutely captivating story with best-in-class worldbuilding, and released it for the PlayStation 1?" Well, thanks to Dread Delusion, we now know that the result would be a pretty excellent role-playing game. It's not perfect; combat feels uninspired and there could stand to be more variety in the audio design, but the rest is absolutely exquisitely polished to a deep sheen.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion is going to be a game you are going to be able to tell that you are going to like just by looking at the images. It oozes style at every seam, and you wont find a world quite like the one created here elsewhere and its easily worth the price of admission. Buuut, at the same time, if the screenshots and trailer haven't grabbed you, I doubt anything in game would. Don't get me wrong, the world continues to be beautiful, and the writing continues to be great, but the act of playing it isn't that... fun. Combat, quests, and the overall gameplay loop is very simple, and not very engaging for a number of reasons, but the world is something so unique that you'll keep on playing anyway because the writing and art are so ethereal. If you're after something like kings field or this but modern and with gameplay, I'd recommend checking out Lunacid. Dread Delusion needs a lot of tweaks which... I doubt it actually needs, (don't get me wrong id love it even more if the gameplay was a lot better) because the style and the world are just that good that i'd recommend playing it anyway despite its glaring gameplay flaws.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I played the early access for all the content it had, and now I'm 10 hours into a very thorough playthrough for the full release. I will 100% recommend this game only because of its lore, atmosphere, and story. All 3 things meld nicely together to be fantastic in such a new weird way, that it feels almost like Morrowind, where every thing you learn is so weird and crazy and interesting, but it never ends in the best way.In terms of gameplay... well it's serviceable. The gameplay is very simple, very basic, and gets kinda stale later in the game. You can block/parry, strafe, dodge, and use a variety of spells, including summoning spells and spells that charm enemies to help you, on top of projectile damage spells and some that make you basically become the flash if your agility is high enough. While that may sound like a lot, it isn't complex in any way. It's just there to let you have more ways to kill enemies, and have fun. It's there to add a false layer of complexity that actually isn't there. While I am having fun with it, it would get stale after some time, but that also is ignoring the throw-able weapons, the ability to stealth kill enemies or stealth past them, a bow, a sword that works as a gun, and a double bladed sword that is kinda cool.Overall, I recommend because of the atmosphere, lore, and the story all working so well with each other that it makes a fantastic experience I haven't had since Morrowind, but the gameplay is serviceable and is probably the worst part of the game. Now if only the developers decided to go the extra mile and add mod tools. It'd add such an extension to the games life span.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: First ever morrowind-like I have seen. Despite first glance the delusion system, in my opinion, is actually fun. getting "exp" from exploration and quests rather than hunting enemies is something I quite like. (Though take this with a grain of salt as I personally find grinding in video games to be the most boring inane task ever conceived). You are also still rewarded for killing baddies, as they have guaranteed drops of coin, health, etc. Overall, I would highly recommend this game. Story is interesting, world is fantastic, and the system is fun. Enjoy :)
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't really the sort of person who grew up with the type of games that heavily inspired this title. Could never really get into Morrowind or games predating it, usually got pushed away by dated visuals (which depending on the title, could just be amended with mods but I was lazy). Something really clicked for me with this game though.Combat and the general mechanics are pretty simple + easy to understand, enough to the point where you don't have to be concerned with min-maxing. My first playthrough saw me specializing into melee, but after realizing how much I was missing out on in terms of Delusions by not taking Lore, I restarted about three hours in or so and built more around utility/magic. On this real first playthrough, I managed to obtain the achievement 'Iron Will' (iykyk) and honestly didn't face a whole lot of challenge until the last stretch of the game, by which I was more or less just handling cleanup before completing the game.If it was just the above, I might've gotten a smidge bored and not finished. The puzzles and searching around for discovering Delusions or progressing quests were fun, but as previously mentioned I didn't really find combat too engaging. If I had to note one thing, it'd probably be that the stamina cost for blocking, even for just trying to land parries, seemed a bit harsh and quickly deterred me from wanting to play around with it, instead opting for dashing in and out of enemy agro and rarely taking damage.But as I was going to say, the real strengths I got hooked on was a balance of the exploration/questing, writing, and beautiful artwork this game has to offer. Stumbling upon an npc at random among a crowd and setting off on intriguing side excursions from the mainline, which occasionally intersected, kept me engaged and wanting to move forward and see it through. The payoff for some of my choices was also pretty great, and I might even do another playthrough sometime to try out some of the options I didn't on my first time through. I was also pleasantly surprised to find that more often than not, I was able to find my way through quests just fine with the instructions provided in my journal, free of any quest markers.$20 was more than fair a price for this title, and I'd happily do so again.

_childDocuments_.review: Well... it's definitely interesting. But I can't pretend that I'm not disappointed.Blah blah blah Kingsfield Morrowind... Not really though. This game is incredibly shallow as both an RPG. and as a game where you explore, fight and loot.Play it for the lore and to experience the oddball game world. Combat is trivial. RPG systems are simplistic and don't matter much. Although I did find a couple cool things last time I played (which is unusual. Get ready for your 100th potion and your 1000th throwing knife).I can't help think that this game needs to be at least somewhat more tricky. The game we've got right now might just be the easiest open world game ever made. And also the most shallow open world RPG ever made, possibly?Hmm... I still kinda like it. But there's this pervasive feeling of "that's it?" permeating everything.UPDATED REVIEW: Changed recommendation to "no". The more I play it, the more I feel like it's a stupid and shallow game that completely fails to deliver on expectations. There is nothing else going on here than the visuals. Wander around and feel the vibes = alright for a while. Try to care about this as an actual RPG = Oof... Nothing about this is well designed. One starts to wonder if the devs have actually ever played any kind of RPG themselves. I saw some people throwing around the idea that this is gonna be the best game of 2024.R. O. F. L. M. A. O.'Nuff said.My personal vote for best indie of 2024 so far: Withering Rooms.And before anyone complains: If my playtime grow a bit after the review, it will just be me trying to stubbornly figure out what the devs are even trying to do. But I do think this thing is too far gone to be saved by patches. The problems are completely fundamental and can't be adjusted away.

_childDocuments_.review: A delightful hidden gem. A very nostalgic and cozy feeling game not only because of the games visual style but also the way it plays. The level design is thoughtful, the progress is thoughtful, the lore is thoughtful.As you progress the world gets both larger and smaller all at once. There is so much to explore it can almost feel a little overwhelming but the game design throws it at you in manageable chunks. The atmosphere keeps you engrossed in the totally unique world they have created.The game is definitely story and lore focused, so if you're looking for depth in combat mechanics this isn't the game for that sort of thing. I highly recommend this to anyone looking for a relaxed single player fantasy RPG.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: A great RPG in terms of story, writing, and exploration. The quests are great (there's about fifty quests in the game and I remember almost all of them step by step), the scenarios and envrionments are unique and interesting, there's a good sense of atmosphere, and the exploration mechanics (having to go to landmarks to fill out the map, having to use the compass to know what direction you're facing, etc) are a neat touch and feel rewarding.One negative thing I can say is about the Combat, since enemies both move and attack so ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ slow you can just run past them. It'd be nice if there was a hard mode added later on. That aside, i'd definitely reccomend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: The setting is basically warhammer 40k by way of jules verne, and the gameplay is pure exploration porn. It's the rush you get from a fallout or elder scrolls game where you see something in the distance and go "i wanna go check that out" but it's an entire landscape full of those cool (distracting) areas. Tons of weird factions with weird motivations, tons of quests with legit interesting moral dilemmas, and characters that i actually grew attached to by the end. The only cons are that the combat is weak (which is, to me, not that much of a dealbreaker in an RPG), and the game is still jank. One semi-major quest just straight up bugged out for me. But hey, in my eyes: thats just a good excuse to replay soon. Next go around im going full diehard steampunk space catholic. Death to all heretic gods.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Wow, what a gem this game is. Was looking for something to hold me over until Elden Ring went on sale and this has scratched that itch and more. The atmosphere is something truly special, the lore is incredibly interesting, and the loot loop is super rewarding. The map is dense and chock full of places to explore, puzzles to solve and, and items to find. It being an indie game it has it's limitations, but the charm with which it handles those limitations just make me like the game even more. I can't recommend this game enough if you're looking for an open world RPG!
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: The main strengths of the game are its exploration and dialogue, so if you're looking for a more challenging combat or puzzle game, you'll probably be disappointed. But for anyone susceptible to that blocky 90s fantasy charm, it's a hypnotic adventure that does so many things right. The dialogue is light and humorous, the setting is an interesting mix of familiar influences, and many story decisions are deep enough to warrant some thought. Character building elements do exist, but your limitations can be quite quickly overcome due to the abundance of stat-boosting items, buffs, and consumables. Given that there's little need or reward for combat, it quickly became simpler and faster to bypass enemies entirely. And so my Delusional Confessor became a sleep deprived Jitterseed addict and serial pacifist, spamming the Agility incantation to sprint-leap at Mach 5 over the heads of creatures and chasms, putting the world to rights one lockpick at a time, and only ever dying to the real boss of the game: gravity.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Bite sized oblivion. I cant get enoughLove the streamlined systems like crafting. No encumbrance, no inventory management (I prefer not living in menus).The writing is phenomenal and doesn't flood you with a wall of text. NPC Characters are written so well.- Soldiers following orders recognising they are not the good guys as they persecute the farmers- Immortals living with the guilt of harming loved ones- A rude person in the room who has a very good reason to be bitter about their lot in lifeThe world is weird and interesting yet somehow the tone and dialogue of characters really grounds it all.I would pay for a DLC with more quests within the same map.The music really fits and I just want more of it. Melancholy and calming not triumphant Multiple endings and they nailed the choices matter epilogue.Combat is serviceable and is the weakest part of the game. Enemy variety is lacking most are reskins.The last part of the game can feel like a slog with corridors of enemies.I love this game so much and hope to see more from this setting be it books, dlc etc*I hope mod support is possible
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: The Morrowind comparisons are way off. There's not much challenge to combat, the levelling system is very simple, xp is gained through pickups and quest completion rather than skill use and, as far as I know, I can't craft a potion that turns me into a god. There is, however, an enticing world that's enjoyable to explore, and that's where Dread Delusion's strength lies. It's game about exploration and searching first, fighting second. In a lot of ways it's similar to a walking sim, only more involving because there's stat management, questlines and swordplay. Altogether it makes a surprisingly chill RPG experience. I'd recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I've had a hard time describing this game to people when I tell them I'm playing it.Gameplay-wise I tried to make comparisons to an Elder Scrolls game or System Shock, but I think it would be unfair to say its "Like <Insert Game Here>" as it stands out on its own.Visually I would try to say it has a PS1-era aesthetic, but again, I think that would be a disservice to the time and art that went in to crafting the world's appearance and feel.As for the writing and story, I was beyond pleased and incredibly surprised.  I came in expecting an Elder-Scrolls like sandbox where there's an uninteresting main quest and a million unrelated sidequests, but I found myself in a game that was focused on providing a compelling core narrative where the player's choices have a real impact in the world, even with the sidequests.This game is a work of art and love in a unique fantasy world. It is absolutely worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoying the game so far. I've done everything it seems I can do.HOWEVERI can't seem to progress the main questline for "The Hunt for Vela Callose". It seems to be stuck on finding the quartermaster, even after he is back at Vela's Ship. I've even gone and collected The Emberian, and she as well is back at the ship now. Please let me know if I am missing something, or if my speediness has created a bug of some sort. Otherwise, this has been a lot of fun. My desperation to progress should be testament enough!
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Its biggest selling point is by far the atmosphere: the first area and its insufferable music aside, the strangely compelling alien world is a treat to explore and learn about. There are lots of creatures, factions and landmarks that have interesting designs and lore, it's all very enticing.However, and i say this with no hesitation,  Simply put, combat might as well not exist in the game because it offers no challenge. You can easily defeat every enemy in the game without any combat focused equipment or stats. Foes all follow the same pattern of running at the player and standing still while attacking, which makes them easy to dodge. The tutorial puts a heavy emphasis on stealth, but you will never need to be sneaky or avoid combat.As for the character building aspect, Dread Delusion simply puts too much emphasis on equipment rather than stats. After only a couple hours of playtime, i had at least one piece of iequipment that significantly buffed every one of my stat; in layman terms, i never felt the need to build my character in any specific way because if i ever needed to, say, pick a lock, i would simply equip the "+10 to lockpick" hat.Dread Delusion succeeds at being an exploration game but fails at being an RPG.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: A very, very good homage to the open world RPGs of yore with an acid/weird fantasy twist.This game is not perfect, there are a myriad of small technical issues I encountered, but none of them really took away from my enjoyment. Great visuals, fun quests, weird scenarios and characters. Buy this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I wonder if anyone mentioning this game and Morrowind in the same breath have actually played both of those games. I feel a bit misled by a lot of the community feedback on this title. To the dev's credit, as far as I can tell they AREN'T the ones out there making these comparisons. Either way, if you're looking for a RPG experience in any shape or form, then this isn't the game for you.This game does have a lot that I want to like. The art is unique and interesting, there is a decent amount of lore to sift through, and the world promises to be compelling to explore. But the experience just has no connective tissue -- the combat may as well not exist, quests don't have alternate paths to complete, the magic is uninteresting to engage with, and, for all its promise, there doesn't seem to actually be anything interesting to FIND at the end of all the exploration. At the end of the day, I'm glad I tried the game out, and I MIGHT come back to it. However I don't think this is a "hidden gem" that I can honestly recommend to anyone.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This is a game that has burrowed into my skull. It lives in my thoughts growing and changing. I love it dearly. It is a beautiful nightmare. How often I find myself questioning my own ways of thinking. This creature causes such wonderful stress, as I stare into the void of decisions I must make, who's ramifications feel endless. I beg thee, share in the void. Let it fill your soul.TLDR: Its a good game I like it. Good job.

_childDocuments_.review: absolutely amazing game, the gameplay and graphics is early 2000s but the world building and story is ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ amazing. i find myself exploring because i want to learn more about the lore of the world not just chasing a level up or for the sake of exploring. 9/10 game (not a 10/10 because i don't believe in a perfect game) would definitely recommend to anyone.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I got this game due to me hearing it compared to Morrowind. Morrowind is by far my favorite game and with that I don't think this game deserve to be compared to it, for it is so much more than that. Dread Delusion has such an amazing art style to it, it's story is extremely well made, every single NPC is unique and really contributes to the overall atmosphere of this amazing game. I have no intentions of ever dropping this title and I do intend on preaching this amazing game to everyone I know. It is worth the money spent, i love it with all my heart.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty darn solid, overall. The gameplay is *decent*, to be honest. Combat isn't all that deep, interesting, or challenging at most parts, but I've still got a bit more to explore and unlock, so that may change.What *is* interesting, however, is the world and aesthetic. This game nails the look/feel and has a really delightful take on more than a few concepts and ideas. If you like the look of the game and can get into it, and aren't super turned off by combat and other such that's more serviceable than novel, then you'll likely enjoy it. I also really enjoy such a creative take on divinity, magic, etc., none of it is too out there but, at the same time, it's original enough to draw a lot of nice thoughts and ideas into the world, especially when you make choices.Also.. the squirming godlets are staggeringly cute, and make me miss someone who would adore them.Edit: For once.. I think I'm actually quite satisfied with the ending - I feel like the writers came at the world, and the ideology and ideas around it, from an interesting perspective and did a good job keeping with that and leaning less into a 'right'/'wrong' choice that fit very well with the game's vibe and world. Definitely enjoyed this overall despite the bit of gameplay nitpicks.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This game has its charm. Cool visuals, interesting and deep lore. It's really fun to explore the world and unravel its secrets.But there are so many flaws that harm this experience so much that it's really hard to recommend it, especially when it's actually out of beta.For starters, combat is nonexistent. Yes, it has some mechanics like parry or block, but why bother. There's really no point in fighting unless you want this chance of a rare picklock drop when you need to bust some locks. You always outrun them, outdamage them, and outsmart them.The levelling system is really dull too. Theres almost no difference between levels. Basically, you feel no real impact. And on top of that, when you finish your first tutorial island you already have enough delusion to max out one of the stats, so yeahAnd, tbh, most offender are the main quest. Usually the main quest are the centrepiece of the game, the most quality writing and all and sidequests just provide additional worldbuilding and stuff. But for some obscure reason in Dread Delusion things are in reverse. The main quest has the weakest writing.I think this has to be the problem with the antagonist. I feel what they meant to do, but Vela is such a boring character, I literally cant care less. Paeguth questline feels more memorable than this.Dread Delusion tries so hard to make player pity Vela, but then again, do nothing but always remind them how awesome and strong she is. And there is no character building, no suffering to overcome, no stakes, nothingJust like Vela is so cool and kind, but also strong and deadly. And then she became bad. Not evil bad, but cool bad. Because she has trauma. But not because something happened to her personally, no no. She is strong so nothing can happen to her. Someone close to her died. And she's actually not bad at all, but no one just understands her and believes that she can do things right.Do you see what I mean? There is literally no motivation at all to take on a quest with writing like that, its borderline too silly to take all of this seriously.Especially when you actually have a chance to meet her later and have your first boss fight to be a literal cutscene with autodeath. Why? Because she is too powerful of course!Idk man what happened. Some quests like clockwork kingdom were hundreds of times more engaging and interesting which I really enjoyed compared to this mess.So yeah, idk if I can recommend this game. But if you can look past the main quest and pretend this is some cool atmospheric walking simulator you actually enjoy it a lot.But as it stands, Dread Delusion is far, far from being out of beta. So yeah, whatever
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: The gameplay is definitely simpler and easier, and the game does suffer for it. However, if you like world/worldbuilding, lore, exploration, and your favorite part of Skyrim was just wandering around, you will like this game. It is definitely more Bethesda-lite than Bethesda, but it is very engaging in the comprehensive world and story shown.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion is a walking simulator trying and failing to be an rpg. I haven't played an rpg with combat as shallow and uninteresting as this. This might sound like a negative (it is) but for Dread Delusion there is no reason to ever fight anything. Enemies give no exp or items of value, so luckily there is no reason to engage with combat. Its too bad every other system in the game is as shallow and worthless as the combat. Only foe that I actually felt the need to kill was because it was on a tight stair case and it was easier to just kill it then run past it for once (still could have). Its not like it had a unique effect, attack, or strategy, it was just a chore. Magic and stealth exist, neither are worth using but they are there.The only skill check that has a roll or isn't just solved by leveling the exploration skills is lock picking and the game somehow made rolling a die for a skill check terrible. Your lock picking skill only changes how high you need to roll on a roll of single d6, no modifier, no real mechanic, roll a d6 and see if you roll above a 3. A bad lock picking mini-game wouldn't be so bad, but its the only worthwhile system that progresses the game outside of the level up screen. Not unless you count walking around a 90% empty world with a stamina bar that decreases size unless you nap. The story and setting seem interesting, but the few quests I did where the biggest nothing. A quest might seem interesting at first but every quest I played was as shallow as everything else. You don't actually do anything interesting, go to a place, talk to people, and then skill check. Everything about Dread Delusion is somewhat interesting on the surface but an utterly shallow shame of wasted potential barely being propped up by aesthetic and promise. The dev might be able to rework every system before full release into something worth while, I highly doubt it but its not impossible ¯\_(ツ)_/¯*Edited spelling a grammar.**I didn't realize the game officially released when I wrote this, yikes.***Also I ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ hate how the skybox looks, its an ugly blur of red textures, the neutron star or whatever it is was cool for 5 seconds before you realize half the screen is red at all times. Might seem minor but its something your going to be seeing for 95% of the game and I never wanted to look up because all I would see is an ugly mess of red over an otherwise diverse and colorful world. The other zones might have a different sky box, its been a few updates since I was outside of the starting islands but I don't care to trudge through the game again.
