_childDocuments_.review: Open RPG where you can customize your character with basic stats and traits. Strength will mostly improve your ability to withstand damage (useless, i will explain later), do more damage (practical but really not required) and break some doors. Agility will allow you to lockpick (godtier at first but you can easily go by with low amount invested once you find the lockpick hat), movement speed, jump height and max stamina. Probably the single best stat in the entire game. Int will allow you to cast more overpriced spells your mana potion can barely keep up with, their damage and cast speed, but also the ability to unlock secret mechanism. Kinda mediocre because the cost of magic spell is too much in general. And finally charisma will help you unlock a few specific mechanism, find shortcuts in dialogue lines and a bit of money management.The game starts rather linear but once you reach the main city of the game it becomes pretty open, and relatively fun to explore in order to find more delusions (exp) and some side quests that give xp and sometimes some items. I usually finish the games i play and review but i decided to stop after finishing one of the small region for one of the part of the main quest. Part of why is because while i had fun exploring the main area, this small region in particular felt empty, barely rewarded you with delusion or items... an issue in general with this game, there's barely, especially for weapons... and felt like a mindless back and forth fetch quest, most of the POI being locked behind the progression of one of said quest. This region at the present time of this review also had several annoying bugs, such as an npc that didnt work but also locked you in a weird position where your character would be forced to circle strafe around her until you either killed yourself or restarted the game... or a path near the final small dungeon that is blocked off so forces you to die. This region just wasnt fun to explore, although the overall lore was interesting, and i was told the second one i had to go through was not any better. Add to this the atrocious combat, with enemy being perma stunlocked as long as you hit them with stamina and i just found myself spamming the super speed spell to avoid fighting, only use of my maxed wisdom stat honestly, and trust me, you pretty much become Sonic. This is actually the only thing that kept me going but even this loses its charm ultimately. This is why more hp or damage is ultimately kinda uneeded, the weapon upgrades are good enough for damage, investing in more stamina means stunlocking for longer which is all you need, and more hp is useless with how little damage they do and the ridiculous amount of hp pots that drops. The music is also far too repetitive, it changes at times but you will mostly be hearing the same few track for hours which is a crime personally.I do appreciate the effort done on sub quests, or npc dialogues making the towns less dead than most game (although far from how i felt with phoenotopia), the main are of the game feeling fun to explore, on the overall visual aspect of the game and weird universe that was created, but it was far too mind numbing for me in the end. I was basically left with a somewhat charming, janky and buggy at times rpg with horrible combat, a lack of gear but relatively fun exploration at first. Thinking back to it the most powerful enemies on my journey were the lockpick tests that were stuck at 5-6 until i finally found the hat that would carry me to victory. The horrible second region killed all my motivation to continue the experience.I wish i could but ultimately i will opt to go against recommending this game. I wish this would have been a smaller scope game that focused in making one cool region filled with cool or useless loot, instead of dividing it in one relatively good region and what seems to be less rewarding and interesting ones. Or have the same amount of polish for them all. Ultimately it's the lack of reward that killed it for me, and the few i would get such as exp for leveling up were far to rare outside of the main region.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Ive been following the release of this game for a while Ive been so excited to try it. TLDR: Storytelling and quests INSANE HUGE BRAIN GAMING. Sound is a little weird (looping music and occasional amibient sounds). Combat is really nothing to write home about but the games focus is storytelling and world building. HIGHLY RECOMMEND IF YOU LIKE EXPLORATION AND GOOD STORYTELLING HAS HUGE POTENTIAL. The GOOD:art direction: Its incredible and immersive while sticking to a retro old school feel (you can even turn off some of the SUPER retro settings to make it feel a little more modern). Storytelling: BOY LET ME TELL YOU. Its top notch, as you explore this bizarre world you start piecing together a bit here and there and things start connecting. an NPC can say something that makes you realize something within the landscape. or give you a hint about something later if you can remember the information. characters are Vague but interesting making you want to learn their secrets. you can tell the dev is a masterful storyteller that knows how to put you right into a situation. as you start learning about all the factions and people living in this world you start realizing the internal conflict among all its inhabitants and yourself. i want to learn MORE.Quests: This goes along with storytelling but there is something to say about the quests in this game, When you get the AH-HA! moment or something unexpected happens its always an awesome experience.Exploration: its good. Not incredible but good, if you aren't actively doing a quest you're trying to stumble on one. there are things to explore and find like weapons and items to aid you ( the couple i found felt a little game breaking like the No fall damage ring and the lens that can make you see magic objects). But i found myself wanting to explore to see what i can find next or the next crazy quest ill run into.Earning key items: THIS IS ALWAYS GOOD. Obviously this is always a thing in games but you don't start with a map. You earn it from a quest. You don't start with fast travel. You earn it from a person studying it, and its only from one portal to another. that type of progression always feels awesome. I was rewarded for exploring so my reward is to make exploring more efficient. ISSUES:Sound design is a little weird if you focus on it. Music, which is very good, is on repeat the whole time but you are still on a song loop for hours. the tutorial zone is really noticeable, almost overwhelming ambient noises: They are not quite there but they are? the best way i can explain this is that the music is on loop and you hear the occasional mushroom gurgle and stuff but it needs to have moments of silence with just ambient world noises (which it needs more of) Combat: It's very simple. BUT it is clearly not the main point of the game. If the combat was a little more exciting and there was more danger and enemies to make the world feel like a dangerous, scary living place it would add to the already immersive experience. maybe i haven't seen the dangerous enemies yet but more on that later Stat caps: There needs to be a movement speed and jump height stat cap i know this sounds fun but with very little gameplay i was going gamebreakingly fast .All it took was a few points into agility and the agility cloak plus the Agility spell and i was the flash. the world did not feel like a world it felt like a bunch of landmarks that i broke the sound barrier to jump and fly to. no need to fight anything or get lost. if you've ever played the FPS Tribes im not kidding i was doing the same thing in dread delusion.Stealth: there is a sneak feature but there doesn't seem to be a use. Maybe its intended to be implemented later but as of right now maybe its for avoiding enemies? A back stab mechanic could be cool. Dropped items: I had a LOT of potions and money. enemies drop potions too frequently, you can craft them and they are randomly scattered around the world. i had so many that i don't think i would of died ever. Money was never an issue, enemies drop it, and again its scattered within the world making buying any of the items kind of unrewarding. not all enemies need to drop something.

_childDocuments_.review: Released from a prison, you get to taste what it's like to regain freedom while exploring a mythical wold that keeps opening up to you with stories behind every tree.(+++) Quest-driven exploration. Traveling from point A to point B is a game aspect in itself. Any building/monument/POI can be reached and has a story to tell, even though it might not seem so at first.(++) Choices matter.(+) The world is easy to read and if you get lost, just looking around will give you enough of a hint how to proceed.(+) RPG mechanics play a role as you'll have to solve problems according to your build's strengths.(+) Great progression with the world slowly opening up to you. Feels very rewarding.(+) Interesting story constantly rubbing on the grand philosophical topics.(+) Great on steam deck (apart from the intro video that cannot be skipped without summoning a keyboard [ESC key])(+) Visual variety of biomes and creatures.(+) True open-world as you can get literally anywhere and beyond (once you purchase a flying ship)(+) Pretty chill.(++) Game was made with passion and it shows.(-) Everything could use a bit of polish: inventory management, combat, stealth, collisions, dialogues,...(-) Some bugs (incl. quest progression)(-) Although creatures vary a lot visually, there are very few differences in their behavior(-) The game has optimization issues leading up to some major stutters (esp. at region seams) that were resolved by the industry (by easily implementable solutions) good two decades ago (but are not used here).

_childDocuments_.review: This game is an absolute treasure.The story is fascinating, the setting is awe inspiring, and the whole thing gives me a sense of wonder.I actively enjoy and look forward to finding books, and asking questions that explain the lore of the world.Once you're in it and acclimated to the visuals the game is beautiful, though I personally prefer playing with the wobbly effects off.I'm only about 13 hours in, but still haven't yet completed the currently available content. I'm already looking forward to more.Traversing the open world is fun in and of itself, with being able to discover and fill out locations on your map. There's no loading screens, every interior is built into the world almost seamlessly. There are a few mesh bugs and odd clippings, but over all they are easy to look passed.The magic system is simple, but highly practical. There are a couple offensive spells, but most are used for non combat. There's a super speed spell, a spell to pass time, to teleport home, to name a few examples.Speaking of home, you can buy and decorate houses which is always a huge win for a game in my book.I am very excited to see anything and everything coming from this game in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: An rpg with very impressive scale, writing and worlds worth exploring. Not a single quest I took and finished felt unnecessary, or boring. There isn't much I can say about the story and exploration because I don't want to spoil anything, but these are absolutely the biggest reasons you'll want to play the game. The game is a bit long, maybe longer than I would've liked, and parts of it sort of drag on. But it really picks up near the end with a few last surprises and a strong narrative ending, the details of which depend on your choices throughout the rest of the game.Its most lacking aspect is easily gameplay, combat and builds. These three aspects are intertwined and I think need some work. For example, I started as a mix of agility and intelligence, I ended up leveling up intelligence and charm purely for the sake of lore skill checks and NEVER actually using spells for offense. The truth is, the melee weapons are too good to warrant using spells. Even without significant investment in the strength stat, you can deal enough damage through power attacks to kill most enemies in 1-3 hits. Why would I spend MP to do less damage, even at maxed intelligence? Bows at least have very abundant ammo that is used solely for it. MP can be used for more useful spells, like haste. Throwing knives and stars are not even a factor. They are quite frankly useless from the start of the game and remain so until the end. I basically just sold all of the throwables I found for extra cash. I'm fairly certain this could all be improved with some relatively simple balance adjustments:* Make stats matter more, I want my spells to deal big damage if I maxed out my intelligence, maybe increase that scaling.* Agility in general needs a buff, as far as I know it does not affect combat at all save for how fast you move, how high you jump and maybe how much stamina you have? You could make ranged weapons scale with it maybe.* Also, make it so that enemies are worth killing. I understand and appreciate that you wanted to make combat optional, but I think you still need to make it rewarding. It is decently fun as it is now at least so that's good.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: The developer of Dread Delusion has put the right amount of emphasis on both story telling, as well as gameplay. While the story and writing tries to ground the player in a fantasy setting, this is still the kind of game where you can put all your skill points into agility and then sprint across the map so fast you can almost fly. Probably 10-12 hours of content right now, all of which is enjoyable. I'm sure much more will be coming in later updates soon.Mood-wise there is an otherworldly and somewhat sad feeling that bleeds into the world of Dread Delusion. The atmosphere that these feelings create make it a world worth thoroughly exploring, which is a feeling I don't experience often enough in video games today. Highly recommend checking this one out!(∩ ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)⊃━☆ﾟ. *

_childDocuments_.review: This game has been wrongfully identified with The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind. This comparison is inaccurate in virtually every way other than both games' tutorial areas are vaguely similar-looking. That being said, Dread Delusion is a fantastic open world game with a very smart progression system tied to exploration of its gorgeous and layered world. It isn't a particularly long or deep experience, and the number of quests is very spotty (there are lots around Hallowshire but very few elsewhere), but the quests that are present are all of fantastic quality - every single one in the Endless Realm presented genuinely interesting moral dilemmas where it didn't feel like the developers thought of a single "correct" answer. This is a game that has serious problems sticking its landing, but the early and mid-game are so incredible that it's hard to walk away with anything other than a great impression, especially with how fantastic most of the writing is. If you're the type of person this game would appeal to, you probably already know that (I am too), so rest easy knowing that this really does offer exactly what you're looking for.

_childDocuments_.review: If Morrowind and Paradise Killer had a baby, this game would be it. Fun to explore, good narrative, and interesting side quests. There are some minor bugs, but nothing game breaking in my experience. The biggest drawback to this game is that the combat is extremely basic, easy, and boring. I have died only twice in the first ten hours of the game and both times were due to fall damage rather than enemy encounters. Still, I think this game is worth the price, especially if you can get it on a discount.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't know about this game until its full release a few days ago, but it captivated me to the point where I beat the game and finished the majority of the quests in just 3 days.  That being said, there are some minor gripes and complaints I have.ProsExploration is both fun and rewarding.  About half of the armor and basically ALL of the useful accessories are found at random places on the map rather than in stores (there are one or two exceptions though.  And the locales are diverse enough that 9/10 times you'll know exactly where you are without having to look at the map (for late game the map is still incredibly useful for long-distance traveling, so it isn't just a waste of space in the inventory), and getting where you need to go is almost no challenge at all.Stat are primarily for explorationWhile invested stat points DO make combat easier (more on that later) I've found that they mainly serve to increase your exploration abilities.  For example, strength is the most combat-oriented stat, increasing your attack, defense, and max HP; but having a high strength stat lets you break down damaged doors as opposed to lockpicking with your guile stat or puzzle solving with your wisdom stat.  on the other end, Guile is the most exploration-oriented stat, increasing your lockpicking success chance, your movement speed, and your jump height (maxing this out will let you zoom around the map at mach speed, try it, its fun)Worldbuilding, lore, and theme are all on-point and consistentI never felt like the story ever contradicted itself or created any plot holes that don't get explained.  The bleak, "light at the end of the tunnel" is present all throughout the islands, with each faction having their own different flavor of depression, and the NPCs deliver this not just in their dialogue, but in the quests they give as well (I don't wanna go into it because spoilers but trust me on this, its all super immersive and I genuinely cared about the decisions I made in this fictional story)ConsCombat is a little TOO easyEven the heavy weapons are faster than anything the enemies will throw at you, add in that you don't stop or even slow down movement when you attack and you can pretty easily beat the game without ever getting hit.  Seriously, I only died twice and that was because I fell to my death.  I can count the number of times I was actually at risk of dying in combat on one hand.  But honestly, it might be best to keep this where its at due to the simplicity of the combat system, since increasing enemy stats would just turn them into damage sponges, so all things considered I'm not too upset about this at all.ClippingOn some of the outer islands after you unlock the final mode of travel there are issues.  On one of them the game spawned 2 of each structure on the entire island (I could tell because of the planefighting on the objects) which prevented me from entering any of them (thankfully this was only on the one island that wasn't super important).  On another island I accidentally softlocked myself by clipping into a structure that had no exit (this was a simpe fix as exiting to the title screen resets your position to the last revive point).One specific piece of armor isn't upgradable for some reasonThe last piece of armor equipment which is basically the best armor piece in the game isn't showing up as upgradable for me, which is strange because its matching helmet IS upgradable, and the armor has "damaged" in its name.  This is, strangely enough, the thing I'm dissapointed in the most out of what I'm going to mention in this review.One last minor con is just that one of the end-game NPCs pulled the incorrect dialouge from a different NPC.All in all, this is a super fun exploration-based game with an amazing story in a very well-written world, with an emphasis on playing your way (you can even convince the final boss to not be a boss lol) with ok combat.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: Second Review: Takes around 8 to 10 hours to finish everything I could find, running into a couple story line dead ends. I love it and I'm looking forward to more. Could use some polish here and there but it's pretty solid. The combat isn't amazing but the world building and lore is so much fun to go through. The little puzzles and exploration rewards all over the place feel great. If you're really on the fence about it, you might not like it - it's a very particular niche. I can't wait for more!First Review: I'm loving it so far. The worlds is bizarre and fascinating and the more I learn about it the more excited I am to push onward. I've smuggled illicit goods, done favors for elder gods, picked locks and trespassed for profit and power, fought strange creatures across a very odd land, and I feel like I've only scratched the surface. Definitely check it out, especially once it's out of early access.

_childDocuments_.review: The trippy visuals draw you in and make you curious about the world you are exploring, but the lore, worldbuilding, and philosophy of the game are what really make it stand out.  Combat is basic to enable faster exploration and keep the story moving at a good pace.  Itemization and character building is also very bare bones for the same reason.  Combat only rewards you with money and consumables you use for combat.  Stats are mostly only important for skill checks that will let you access treasure and delusions  you spend on more stats.  The game leans heavily on its strengths, and lets you mostly skip its weaknesses without engaging in them very much.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: As good as this game is all-around, I want to give specific praise to the lore and writing of the world. The creativity and the detail are truly remarkable, and the execution of telling it to the player is very good as well. The gameplay and story itself were good in their own right, and I enjoyed them both to varying degrees, but the writing of the lore and setting had me captivated the whole way through! Excellent job on that part of it.Overall, a very solid 7.5/10. My biggest wish is that there were even more to explore of it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: The combat and the mechanics are simple and the difficulty is low, but that's not the point of Dread Delusion. The World Building and exploration is what in my opinion make this game a wonderful RPG, and I had so much fun exploring the Oneiric Isles. I quickly got hooked in deepening the lore of this small gem, something that reminded, as other players already said, of my runs on a The Elder Scrolls game, expecially Morrowind. There are yet some bugs and minor problems, but nothing too annoying. If you want a challenging or complicated combat there are better choices, but if you are looking for an RPG with a great and original open world to explore and discover his history and secrets, Dread Delusion will deliver a great experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: After being disappointed by Bethesda with the last couple Elder Scrolls releases, finding an entry in the open-world fantasy adventure genre that would let me fall in love with it is a godsend. Dread Delusion isn't perfect by any means. It's also not finished yet. What  there, though, implies that the finished product will be just as good, if not better, than the games that made me initially fall in love with the Elder Scrolls. That same sense of adventure, very little standing between you and the Great Outdoors when you start a new file (such as following people you have no reason to care about yet through Generic Sewer System #5 or listening to Imitation Nordic Guy #23 talk about Imitation Nordic Stuff for what feels like forever before following someone through Generic Dungeon System #3 and Generic Cavern System #8)... it's wonderful. The opening area that the game  trap you in for the "tutorial" is far more interesting than anything Bethesda's done since Daggerfall; things that are happening  me can very easily start happening  me, and there's enough extra fluff that I still feel in control of my path. Really, it feels more like a sandbox to get a few delusions (levels?) before going into the greater wilds than a tutorial area.The game knows what it is, and it doesn't try to be anything else. I can't wait to see what it looks like when it's all fleshed out and the planned regions are added.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I feel really bad for the people who look at this game and see the graphics, and then skip it. The world is so beautiful and dark, and the lore and atmosphere are so well done, it is insane. The style of the art direction and settings are incredible, too. There's so much passion and love put into just one small section of this game's tutorial area than 90% of modern games. It's a little difficult to describe what this game is, but if you played games like Lunacid or older ones like King's Field from FromSoftware, you'd understand what this is. You "create" your character, decide upon its stats and whatnot, and get pushed right into the storyline. The stats play important roles, not only in combat, but outside of it too. The Charm skill to charm people, agility to jump high enough to reach those suspicious looking places etc etc. There's smithing and alchemy, factions and AI for it, side quests and challenges...it is truly an experience I hope everyone gives a chance. 5/5
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: It's been a while since i've played a single player game that has really drawn me in and demanded my playtime. This game has very strong inspirations from games like Morrowind, Doom, and other various retro rpg/fps's. The world is really really interesting and fun to explore. I personally find myself wandering around trying to find every little secret scattered through the world. All that being said, I could see why people would not like this game. It is not high octane, intense gameplay that a lot of people are used to now-a-days. The combat is extremely simple, and there's really no skill involved. Also, I do wish there was more skill expression/skills to level. If you do not like classic RPG's, you will not like this game. If on the other hand you enjoy classic RPG's, you will probably love this game and I can't recommend it enough.

_childDocuments_.review: Optimization is insanely bad. Game looks like a PS1 game yet runs at 20-30 FPS on Steam Deck, and like 90FPS on a 7800X3D+4090 desktop.I understand some may argue the low frame rate works in the game's favor given the PS1 art style, but the game should be ABLE to run at high frame rates if desired, and just include an option for a frame rate limit for those who desire that experience.Can't comment on the actual game itself because I'm not gonna risk passing the 2 hour mark for a game I know I'm not going to be playing in its current state. Hopefully they optimize the game via updates in the future (It's happened with other games before, so who knows)
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: The game is good. It has a great world, fantastic art style, even the basic strike/block/parry combat can be fun. I really REALLY want to recommend it...But its FAR too easy. I picked up a ring that increased my defense, and I decided to take it off because the damage enemies would do to me was so little it became pointless to parry. You can find potions galore within a few hours, and more than enough resources to upgrade your gear to the highest tier. The game needs a hardcore mode. I'm not asking for Dark Souls levels of hard. I just wish the average encounter was a threat rather than a mild inconvenience. Reduced item spawns, reduced item effectiveness, doubled enemy health, damage and attack speed, and a death penalty would go a long way towards making this game actually fun. If it were harder, it'd be an easy 9/10. But as it is, its a 6/10, Good concept, poor execution. If an update comes along to add difficulty options, I'll happily updated my review.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I've been playing since Alpha v0.1 and this game has changed and evolved so many times over the years that it almost feels like I played multiple different games. However, I thoroughly enjoyed every single version.Since the very beginning, this developer seems to have had a very solid vision of what kind of world they wanted to create. While lore and locations have been altered over time, the visual design and feel of it all remains just as intriguing. Every conversation has my full attention because I don't want to miss any small details about how certain factions treated others, what caused certain areas to be devastated after so many years, or who built some of the weird structures in the world.This game isn't exactly the most in-depth or intricate with its mechanics but it's trying to mostly tell a story of the world you reside in and how it became the way it is. Who these people are and why they do the things they do. There are some mild RPG mechanics like skill points and multiple dialogue options but I feel the main focus is on immersing the player in the world and making you want to keep learning more.If you're looking for "the next Morrowind" or something akin to that, this might leave you a bit disheartened, but if you want a solid experience in learning about a disheveled world and its occupants, I fully recommend this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This is such a unique game. The writing is great and the world are some of the most engaging have seen in years. Most of the quests will reveal more of the games lore and are worth it for the journey alone, though you are always rewarded with material goods to help on your quest. It is important to note that the combat in Dread Delusion is not good. It is floaty, slow, and easy. The highlight here is the exploration, and I think the devs knew this when they made it so that the explorations and quests alone give you experience points. Most enemies can be skipped entirely and it will not change your experience. The world here is large and crapped with something to see in every corner. Hidden paths and rooms litter the countryside and reward those who take the time to seek them out. The regions of the Oneiric Isles are vastly different, keeping the game feeling fresh as you hunt down the pirates. The lore is dark and at times verges on depressing, but it is always interesting to see what the game will throw at you next. The comparisons to Morrowind feel misguided, as there is not a lot in common with your typical elder scrolls, but to any RPG lover you can not go wrong with a journey through this trippy landscape. I feel like saying any more about the game will spoil an experience that is best had as blind as possible. Also, might is a useless skill.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Seeing an RPG of this scale and quality from a small indie time is REMARKABLEthis game is really phenomenal. it's incredibly rewarding of different play styles, encouraging problem solving and critical thinking on the part of the player. the worldbuilding is freaking awesome and the writing.... ouaghi mentioned morrowind in my review of lunacid, which I got this game in a bundle with, but if you like morrowind or daggerfall I can't recommend this game enough. It's smaller of course, but all of the content is just. so good.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Despite the negatives surrounding this game, I absolutely adore it.The gameplay leaves something to be desired, and exploring the world isn't as exciting as it could be.But when it comes to the lore, world building, characters, writing, atmosphere and art direction: It's phenomenal.I genuinely loved the story and its ending, and it felt like a fantastic journey getting there. Bravo Lovely Hellplace.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This game has wonderful worldbuilding with plenty of interesting characters and situations to experience. Love the choices in all the side quests and the main story was great. Really enjoyed using the different skills to get through areas and find secrets, and would definitely like an expansion or sequel. There's still so much to explore related to the world that Lovely Hellplace has built here.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Liked the lore of the game, felt somewhat fun and an enjoyable environment, until I found out that in order to beat the game you need to pass multiple different stat checks. I had a lot of fun leveling agility, going fast is fun! but because I decided I want to have fun, I didn't level lore/charisma, making me unable to open some dumb doors that gate keep switches to progress the last quests. Oh and if I wanted to level up multiple times to god knows what level to get more lore, I cant just fight enemies, I actually have to find specific hidden areas or complete sidequests to get any form of exp. Bad game design choice, sorry not sorry.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: A neat little gem of an RPG that is light on game mechanics but strong on exploration and story telling. The world is fleshed out through dialogue, visual storytelling and lore dumps in the form of books scattered throughout the islands.If you enjoy a deep combat system and challenge, you will not like this game. It is rather light on the combat and equipment you can find (everything good needs to be upgraded). Indeed finishing this game, I had just ONE truly difficult combat experience where I almost died and that was with an abnormally large pack of random mobs. I killed the final boss without even realising it is the final boss. This was on Normal difficulty so perhaps Hard is more of a challenge. There is also not a lot of variety in weapons and armor. Technically all good weapons are crafted (which is nowhere near as tedious as in other games), with the final craft being a choice between 3. But to get all 3 you would have to find a lower-tier of that weapon (not super easy, vendors often don't sell them. For some i think it would be impossible to find 3 in the whole game) If you enjoy a good story and rewarding exploration, you will like this game. The world is laid bare in great detail and going off the beaten path will often mean you come across abandoned houses or hidden caves all brimming with potential loot.The consequence system is rather light, however. And the game is clearly not as free as more traditional RPGs (to give you an example, many NPCs simply cannot be hit). There is a faction standing system but unless I missed a major quest hub it's almost impossible to stray from befriending certain story-centric factions whilst making enemies of others.One thing I strongly disliked about the game was the save system. It has one of those "save at a save station" kind of systems, which also acts as a teleporter. Meaning if you want to keep your teleport to a main city, you cannot use any save point you find in the world. A minor gripe sure, but nevertheless I would have much more enjoyed having a normal save-file system.To make up for it though, the game has no carry limit. Meaning you can pick up anything you find in the world; something which I very much liked.Overall I liked Dread Delusions and might even consider a replay if and when a DLC is released for it. Solid 8/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This is a sad negative review coming from me.The game has excellent visuals, a cool setting and good background information. However it completely fails as a game. Gameplay is functionally non-existent, with enemies existing solely for the sake of existing. Player input and expression is similarly non-existent, with there being little to no character building choices or quest choices. Quests are startlingly uniform, with few or, most often, no alternative outcomes despite situations where they are clearly foreshadowed. It might not sound like much of a complaint but when there is no actual gameplay, having the ability to make choices about the outcomes of events you take part in is the only real method of player expression left and it fails on this count.It feels like something that has the bones to be good but failed in being a game. As a player, I felt like me being the one participating in the game did not matter - anyone could have done exactly what I did and I would have even gotten the same experience if I had watched them do it, because my input was in no way meaningful or calculated nor was there any way for it to be. I would describe it first and foremost as a walking simulator, as the only real appeal it has is in exploring the landscape and discovering new areas. I don't think this is a particularly bad game, but I do think it is very poorly labelled and am disappointed with my experience with it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like this. Indeed for the first hour or two I did, appreciating the retro visuals and nifty atmosphere. But the more I played the more I came to realize that that is pretty much all there is. So in no particular order I will list out some gripes that put me off.-Combat is utterly meaningless. There's no experience points or get-stronger-by-doing systems here. You level up by collecting skull items out in the world. Since the enemy AI is absolutely brain dead and they move super slow the best thing is to just run past everything unless absolutely required. Snoozefest.-The faction system is utterly meaningless. Being favored in one doesn't seem to cause any benefit other than giving you a free safe bed to sleep in. Excepting for when even this bugs out. I am "loved" by the Union and there is a bed in the first big town that the guy standing next to it says you can sleep in. Well, you can't because it says it's owned by someone else. Oops.-The respawn system doesn't make sense. You'll pretty quickly find one of these shrine things and understand that it is a respawn point. However there is no rhyme or reason as to which one you will pop out at when you die (and you probably will a few times from falling through the world if nothing else). At one point I was venturing way down to the south and figured I'd death-warp back so I jumped off the edge of the island. The game decided to respawn me back at the Blinding Light fortress actual in-game MILES away from where I was, and most definitely not the nearest point it could have used. Since there's no death penalty of any kind there's no reason there shouldn't be one of these things on every major landmass.-The world economy makes no sense. When I rolled into the first town I had the steel sword and one piece of iron. Upgrading it to the fine sword would take 3 pieces of iron. The weapon shop conveniently had 2 pieces for sale... surely this would be the best way to upgrade right? Well no, those two pieces of iron together cost about 20 coins or so more than the fine sword which was also sold in the same shop. I don't think I have ever seen a game where component materials cost more than bespoke whole items.-The map desperately needs a zoom-in button, especially for those of us playing at least part-time on the Deck.There's just too many friction points and half-baked systems that should interact with each other but don't. Like, I can't even comment about the magic system because I've not cast a spell a single time. I've got a few but they don't seem particularly useful. Woe betide the magic build enjoyers, I guess.I'm ultimately glad it's not the developers themselves who drew attention to this game by saying it's like "Kings Field" or "Morrowind" that I could see. Instead only fans and articles about it use these as descriptors because it is a massive hit of copium. The only thing in common it has is a first person perspective and a stamina bar.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: You can easily lose yourself in this game. I highly recommend it. It's such a gloomy, interesting... really weird place that just draws you in. And the story is honestly pretty good.One minor annoyance is that I started the game without any offensive spells, so I felt a little bit gimped at the start having picked lore and spellcasting as my two main attributes. This may have been a design decision made on purpose: perhaps the spells are too powerful for the enemies in this area and it may have trivialized everything.Everything else is just so well done that I didn't mind this much. Just be aware that those looking to wield the powers of magic may have to search for a bit before they find some spells to sling.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Pros:Visually this game is cool. It has a dark fantasy punk aesthetic with ps1 style graphics. You can tell the devs had a specific vision when you look at the settings and see an options for "wobbling". There is rad world building and you should absolutely steal it for your next dungeons and dragons game.Cons:Bad unrewarding combat. Seriously save yourself time and stamina, avoid as much combat as you can. Character progression is stunted and tied to collectibles. Underdeveloped magic/spells system. 6 hours in and i only have one spell slot, but thats okay, I only have 3 spells. One is a teleport back to your last checkpoint (the only practical one), another is a projectile that does less damage than the throwing knives littered through out the game, and the last one is supposed to make enemies allies but its not really all that useful, as none of the enemies are a challenge, again because the combat is so poor. At 6 hours i have only the starting sword still, although i have upgraded it twice. I keep finding "ammunition" but i haven't found a bow or gun to use it. The game map is tied to a quest and you have to actively use the compass like you would a potion, so navigating isn't great. It could really use a minimap or a quest marker system. Hell if it had a better fast travel system, maybe i'd consider using the other spells.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: It has been about 2 years. The game came out. Final opinion right before I go into the final encounter: Game is a wonderful exploration and secret hunting game with some good worldbuilding that suffers mainly from not expanding enough on said worldbuilding. The other parts you might expect in an RPG, mainly progression, quest design, and combat, are basically not there, but I cannot stress this enough: I didn't mind one bit! My biggest gripe is that I just want more stuff to explore and do to really fill the boots made by the lore! More islands, please!Right now it has a LOT of bugs and probably needs a few more weeks in the oven to hammer those out. Nothing gamebreaking, but a lot of little things that take away from the experience. Still a very good time!The combat, as many have pointed out, is entirely optional, and not that fun even if you try. I feel the need to emphasize this: it was a clear decision from the dev from the very early alpha. All delusions(levels) are earned from items on the map or quests, and combat earns you nothing but consumables. No quest has hard required combat, and dungeons tend to have paths that avoid most of the enemy encounters. All encounters can be bypassed by just... running around the enemies. I actually like this, think it was a neat decision by the dev, and my only complaint is that the enemies should probably be faster in later areas to pose at least some sort of threat. Right now, any agility score above 30-ish makes it impossible for enemies to close the gap and hit you if you don't want them to, and ranged enemies have yet to hit me once in 15 hours.The quests provide good lore but aren't really good quests because the major quests always boil down to one of two options at the end, and while they impose interesting moral choices they don't have any real gameplay effects besides maybe a different reward. There was one quest with 3 outcomes (I think, I know there are two but I didn't click on the option to give myself the third in case it locked me into it), and there are also a lot of more basic quests with exactly one outcome. Again, mostly vehicles for lore and exploration, which is where the game shines.When I wrote the review only the center island was done, and that bit hasn't changed much. There are now 3 new major areas including a reworked starting area and a handful of minor areas. The new starting area is... okay. You'll spend maybe 2 hours in it but the map is huge! The reworked fortress does feel like a real fort, and the starting area immediately after it but before the first passport gate is pretty small and an... alright if kinda railroady start to the game. You can skip this first quest, that is just a lesser version of the Paeguth quest(and the game acknowledges this), but either way you can get to Hallowshire in about 2-3 hours. The clockwork kingdom is probably the best part of the game with lots to see and do while the endless area is probably the worst just because it's actually rather empty(although it has some sick false wall action). There are 2 required minor areas that are... mostly enemy infested linear areas with a doohickey at the end. I think the dev listened to player feedback and added areas with a combat focus, but since running still works and the combat hasn't changed fundamentally for these areas it feels like wasted map to me.Some specific fixed things in my review: The faction system really doesn't matter and you can kill things at will if you really want. You miss out on a quest if you kill bandits and... that's really about it. It's not even a good quest. Very late game there are complete no-penalty kills but by then it really doesn't matter anyways. The wobbly effect is much less painful now and I even turned it on for a bit! Upgrade materials are still a little weird, I ran out of iron a LOT but never higher tiers of ore. Money became a non issue eventually, especially since this time I went full Charisma build. I think I've bought everything I could possibly want and I still have near 4 digit gold. Edit stops here. Buy game! Is good!----------------------First things first: Go into options, disable wobbly everything, spare yourself the headache. Trust me. The effect is... unique but makes me feel like I'm crossfaded.I think I've done pretty much all the content available. Overall: Solid. Not as Morrowind as the comments would make out, it has some smacks of Dark Messiah, of all things. Lots of hidden rooms and fake walls to poke around in. I really like exploring, and this game really scratched that itch.Game still needs a lot of work, this is no DOTA2 permanent beta. If you want a finished game, come back in a few years.Pro strats: Melee builds are trash. Go magic or just avoid fighting, so far it hasn't been required. Lore, Lockpick, Agility, Charm would be my choices. Levels are not hard to get, but each level in a stat only gives 5(?) points in each skill, so you can't cap a skill without really trying. Clothes make the difference here. Upgrading clothes gives more skill points in the stat, which is VERY good. Especially the charm hat you can buy, +30 charm for ~20 gold with 1 upgrade is super useful.Don't bother upgrading weapons, the fine dagger you can buy is more than enough.Don't bother making basic heath or mana potions either, just collect those.Some gripes: The faction system really discourages you from killing anything. Not even bandits and goblins are safe, no penalty kills. So I ended up just running around them, but then I had to kill bandits to open a door, with no other way past said door. Upgrade materials are really thin. A lot of things require iron to upgrade, and I actually ran out of iron. There is a mine dungeon, if I could collect from the walls like I do the alchemy plants that would help.Money is also kinda tight. Maybe because I never killed anything and had low-ish barter, but consider making house upgrades cheaper. Yes, I can alchemy treasure, but that's a very specific solution.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Loved every second of it. Combat wise, it's pretty rudimentary but you probably won't mind as you'll be too busy being charmed by nearly every other aspect of the game. Some characters are a little shallow, but others make up for it by being excellently complex. Many quests have multiple outcomes that you'll have to stop and think about; they have genuinely  interesting premises and sometimes philosophical quandaries. With a several vast islands to explore, there are secrets to be found most everywhere. And something I think gets glossed over a lot, the dialogue is well written. Honestly, it's a crime the devs are only charging 20 bucks for this. Support small (and good) devs, this game in particular is worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: So yes, I played for a pathetically small amount of time, about 20 minutes. In that 20 minutes I sprinted from enemy to enemy, barely reading any dialogue or flavor text, just hitting things and failing skill checks.It's hard to explain why...but I feel incredibly validated in my purchase. This game has room to grow, certainly. The heart however, is absolutely there. It's such a strong FEELING this game gives me, that 20 minutes earned my money AND this review. If you're on the fence just...check it out... You might get the FEELING too.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I really wish I liked this gameNow, I knew going into this that it was supposed to be an exploration-type game, and I've not been one to shy away from these types of games in the past, but typically if a game gives me the option to focus on a melee combat class/stats, I'll do so. I started off the game picking melee combat as my focus, with Agility and Lockpicking as a secondary and quickly ran into a few problems.1st Problem: I realized very quickly that combat was going to be a joke regardless of my melee stats because enemies get staggered when you hit them, and it is incredibly easy to move in and out of range of enemies while swinging your weapon, especially if you have high Agility.2nd Problem: Every single locked door that I came across can be opened by Lockpicking, Lore, or both. Some doors flat out lock you out of being able to access them without a high enough Lore, and there was only a single door I found in the first couple of hours of playing that you could bash down with enough Might, but you could still just pick the lock instead, which further makes physical prowess next to useless.3rd Problem: Ultimately, not having Lore and having a bad lockpicking skill caused me to miss out on chests that I never would have been able to get, so I decided to restart the game and focus on Lockpicking and Lore so I could access all of the chests I was missing, and what was in almost all of the chests you might ask? Ore. Not the most exciting thing to find tbh.4th Problem: Lockpicking is entirely RNG and the Lore puzzles are incredibly obvious.Honestly, just not for me. I don't even know who to recommend this game to. Don't just take my word for it, look as some positive reviews and determine for yourself, I just personally can't recommend it based on my experience and perspective. Just don't expect this game to be like Morrowind or King's Field like some others here are suggesting, I have no idea what they're talking about.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I really tried hard to like this, but a combination of a complete absence of any sort of difficulty in the combat and the game tending towards woke writing and THE MESSAGE tarnished the experience too much.The game starts off really strong, and the opening areas are grand. But as the game goes on the DEI aspects of the plot start to become more apparent combined with game systems just seeming unfinished. Notably the airship, which has a shop you can buy upgrades for in each town, but only one actually sells you anything and it's just one straight upgrade for each of the ships three slots. A few other things like this had me checking the forums and it seems the game was pushed out the door early, which does show in the game unfortunately.I'd give it a middle of the road holding my hand palm up and waggling it side to side, rather than a thumbs up or down. Sale fodder. But I must choose up or down, so down it is. The DEI/sweet baby inc. stuff always weighs too heavy on the scale for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This game will struggle to hold you at the start and definitely needs some tweaks in the combat and leveling system so players don't feel OP at the start of the game. I just felt that right away I could defeat anything I came across until I ran out of stamina which could easily be circumvented by waiting a few seconds. Leveling up only helped to extend this period of godly strength and when pairing this with a lacking in enemy combat mechanics, fighting anything just felt dull. I didn't feel like continuing to play because I was not being challenged. Granted this was a while ago but from what I can tell from other peoples reviews, this hasn't changed much. This game does excel in having a FULLY fleshed out world with lore accompanying it. Wherever I explored not once did I feel like there was excessive copy and pasting of assets. It feels like extensive time was put into the world and where everything is placed. What really kept me playing was finding books and talking with people around the world to find out what happened in this god forsaken hell-scape. Questing also helped in explaining what was happening in the world and was VERY enjoyable. If more time was being spent on improving combat i feel this game could attract and retain more players. I will be keeping a close eye on this title though.

_childDocuments_.review: [Final Update] There's lots to like in Dread Delusion, but one thing  bears mentioning. Something very misleading, said in reviews and by the devs alike - that the game is similar to Morrowind in some way.It's definitely not Morrowind. You should probably not play the game expecting a modern version of Morrowind, or you'll do the game a disservice.With its wonky, thick and blocky aesthetic, ridiculous run speeds, and floating collectathon pick-ups, DD resembles... i don't know. Zelda, maybe? Banjo Kazooie?? The player character is so short and fast that it almost feels like first person Sonic. It's disorienting, and takes a while to get used to.Unlike Morrowind, I don't get the feeling that you're supposed to "live" in the Oneiric Isles. There are no usage-based leveling systems, which means that there's nothing that drives you towards engaging with any gameplay systems beyond the plot, but... that is also where the game really shines. The story and worldbuilding is the highlight of DD, and the remainder is "the stuff you have to do in order to progress in the story."I wish the game either developed the combat more OR removed it entirely, because as it is, combat means one thing only: losing time and resources. I think a lot of the problem comes from there being only two weapons, really - melee and bow. No big chunky hammers, long range spears. You use the same two attacks throughout the game. The problem is compounded in Hard mode, which literally only makes the game worse. Luckily, there's not much in terms of mandatory combat (afaik, only three encounters). Yet there's so much to like in DD! The Clockwork Kingdom is a particularly good example of lots of things done right. You get the feeling that the devs, by the time they got to the Kingdom, had started to really understand how to make an interesting region. In a world crammed with gods (spawning from every crevice, peeking through the cracks) there's one place where the revolt against the gods resulted in the citizens scraping up the pieces of their dead oppressors and building a God for the people, out of cogs, quills, and ink... A god which, slowly, tick by tick, gets more and more corrupt. Wonderful place. Some incredible thematics.Though... it's almost a bit difficult to recommend Dread Delusion to people. Fighter-type players will be bored, and story folks will have their enjoyment tempered by the enemies. Honestly makes me wonder if Lovely Hellplace should've gone for a different formula - maybe not an open-world RPG, but... something else. A Dread Delusion metroidvania would be awesome, and if they take that route next, I'll support them as much as I can.I'll remember Dread Delusion fondly.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I have lots of mixed feelings regarding Dread Delusion, to begin with the art direction of this game (especially the 3D one) is just abhorrently beautiful and i really dig it, they sure know how to create an attractive and unique looking world for you to explore however when it comes to gameplay this leaves a lot to be desired, combat feels mediocre and sluggish, several game design ideas that do feel poorly executed or even underdeveloped, making it an issue for me to fully enjoy this game (Many of these mistakes could be fixed, which makes it even more dissapointing)The plot isn't anything out of this world but don't get me wrong, it truly is interesting and good nonetheless, but there is this one issue that keeps on bothering me regarding how the many NPC's of this world (and game's lore itself) tell you about how you are entering a really desolate and cruel world but once you play it... it doesn't translate at all into the game difficulty and overall experience, causing a huge dissonance between the two.Dread Delusion left me dissapointed but i still cheerish the work that was put into the final project. You can tell this people are passionate about their craft and what they bring to the table (specially, again, the art design) they just need to learn to take advantage of their pros and look how to work on their cons.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Just when I thought I've discovered everything, I find a new secret area. This is a game crafted with love and passion. It's not perfect, but I haven't loved getting lost in a world like this in forever. The art direction is incredible and the whole game just oozes atmosphere.But it's not perfect, my biggest issues with it are:1) Enemy AI. Enemies fight harder thanks to recent updates, but they don't open doors or chase for very long. I also think a sort of indicator of how well you're hidden while you are crouching would make stealth more engaging.2) Too many Delusions. I have maxed out 2 stats and am well on my way to max out a third and I've barely set foot on the second island.But these criticisms aside, this game is thus far for me the best open-world RPG of the 2020s. The writing is deliciously engaging, and I am already hyped for a potential sequel when this game hasn't even fully released yet.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This game is very interesting, its world, at least to me, feels vivid and full of secrets, it is in early acess of course, but the amount of content already available is vast, i do recommend you buy it, and as a tip, i advise not to kill wikkans, goblins, and specially not outlaws on sight, as you can improve your relations with them and make them friendlier.

_childDocuments_.review: Missing a lot of content, but a solid 9 hours in here already. World and limited story elements are worth the price just to experience. Graphics settings for wobbly ps1 style are cool in concept, but they aren't pulled off too well yet and just give me a stomach ache when looking into the distance. Cliche to say at this point, but a whole lot of potential, and whats here is quite polished.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, the developers definitely put a lot of effort in both the written dialog as well as thoughtful environmental storytelling. I will say I don’t know if it’s my astigmatism or what but I find that something with the graphics messes with my eyes making it hard to keep the game in focus, messing with some of the visual details does help but I have to stop playing after about 2 hours.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I went in not knowing what to expect or how much I would actually play. Ultimately though, I'm loving the entire experience. There's something to discover around every corner, the writing is excellent, and the music (while limited) is perfect for spending hours exploring one of the most unique worlds I've seen in a game for some time. I can't wait to see where the story goes from here and can't recommend this game enough.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to make it brief because i'd speak for too long otherwise. Fantastic game, perfect art direction, atmosphere and worldbuilding. Music is spot on and helps with giving a distinct feel to every region of the game. The main characters are alive and brimming with spirit, true companions on this journey.The gameplay is mostly exploration based, and while I'd like for combat to be a touch more interesting given the sheer amount of enemies you could potentially fight, but it's not a dealbreaker. I'm honestly in sheer awe of the imagination and passion that went into crafting this game and its lore, it's truly a joy to just be in it, explore and try to make sense of it.Great job. 9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I've pretty much done most of what there is to do now in Dread Delusion, but this is a basic, spoiler-free take on the game and my experience with it: It's got the shell of a really good RPG. The tone and the atmosphere are dense with character, but much like the game itself, and as to be expected from an Early Access title, it feels very, very unfinished. Most quests end in unsatisfying dead-ends or via largely incomplete, anti-climactic ways. There are a few story beats you'll come across that give you the flavor of something amazing, only to abruptly end before you realise it truly has ended. You can affect the world, but the effect is relatively shallow, and right now I'm chalking that up to it's incomplete, Early-Access status. No real glitches to speak of, some janky, clunky bits of game play or dialogue at best, it feels relatively polished despite it's being Early-Access, and for the price it's a steal. That said, it needs a lot of work, and if you're looking for another 50+ hour RPG Epic, this isn't it, yet. Combat's difficulty curve stops the second you find a weapon that's better than the rusty blade you start with, bows are largely useless, but magic and melee of middling progress crumbles most enemies quickly. Combat as a result devolves quickly into flailing weapons or blasting magic a couple of times until whatever's moving stops moving. A high agility means you outpace every enemy in the game, a magic rogue build practically breaks the experience, nothing can hit you. High Armour means little to no damage outside of some bow bandits with godly aim. The challenge drop-off is quick, but when it happens, it noticeably makes the gameplay far less compelling. Right now for the price you're paying it's worth playing, the what there is to experience is worth experiencing if you already like this sort of game, but if you're on the fence? Might be worth at least waiting until there's more fleshed out. It's an experience, but not a complete one, and because what it gives you is so good, it's disappointing when you run into those walls.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Game is a pretty good time if you can look past a lot of the quirks. You can absolutely feel the "indie" in this game. The end of the game in particular reveals a lot of the seams of the game in ways I didn't expect - not in good ways. Lots of very obvious bugs and oversights, though this could be fixed with some patches though with time.The game shows its cracks more and more as the game goes on, but even still I enjoyed experiencing the world and story of the game. If you're the type of player who can look past some rough edges I think you'll find some value in this game. Just be warned, this is definitely a "story first" kind of experience imo.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This game is good as it stands, worth the money and entertaining and beautiful. I hope more variety of weapons and equipment comes with development, which I'm sure it will.  Do not go into this expecting Elder Scrolls, it's an experience all it's own. Definitely get in early as to buy the game cheaper and to give these guys support to finish this beautiful and entertaining open world game. It's a trip to play, like an acid trip, with some pretty decent acid.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This is in so many ways a wonderful experience, with the game side not having any flesh on it. I still think, if you want a fun visual experience and narrative, this is a wonderful way to spend your money, and I am glad I supported the Devs in that regard. but unless there is some semblance of game play it really is just a "go here and look at this" simulator, as the experience is, so painfully easy that you don;t need to be mentally engaged. As pretty as the world is, I find myself looking for other things to do. I sincerely hope this improves and will change my review if so.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: If Skyrim and Lunacid were smashed together into a surreal experience. Disclaimer** The combat is not the focus of this game. Look elsewhere id you are looking for an RPG with a deep combat and leveling system with branching skill trees and the like. What this game does excel at however is the story, dialogue, world-building, lore, atmosphere, etc.**Dread Delusion brings the player to a world so unique and rich that it is impossible to put down while exploring for the first time. There is so much attention to detail in this game it is insane. The choice of graphics are very intentional, and give the game a more atmospheric touch because of the style it brings. This game is just bursting from the seams with fresh and creative ideas and stunning visual displays. I would recommend this game to anyone as something to just experience because of how original the whole game feels.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: No, sorry. This is one of the few games where I feel bad about giving it a "not recommended" but after about an hour I really didn't want to continue on with it. I like weird, I like old school and I appreciate what the game is trying to do. For some people this is going to be a home run and I'm happy for them. At first it felt like maybe I was going to get an old school Elder Scrolls game mixed with something like King's Field, but that wasn't the case. I can't get past a few things:Large, open areas with almost nothing in them. I see so many comments about Morrowind and I don't buy it at all. In Morrowind you could set off on your own and find a cave filled with mysteries and gear and my god that stuff was so addicting. Here, I don't have that. I have potions. Potions everywhere. Potions and lockpicks. That's all I found in an hour. No mapping until you find a map. Does this mean you can start mapping things once you get a map or does it mean you can buy maps to reveal areas? I don't know and didn't go find the map merchant to find out. I can't believe this game, where everything aesthetically looks so similar, doesn't allow you to have a dynamic map from the get go. Music is ambient sound and on a loop. Yes, I can turn it off. I'm not a fan of turning off music.You can't climb on anything, not even a box that is like maybe 2 feet off the ground. Nope, that's an obstacle now. That's one of those ultra annoying things that just breaks immersion for me every time I encounter it. I so wish there was a demo for this. You'll know really quickly whether or not it's for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Don't go into this expecting any sort of successor or something adjacent to Morrowind or an Elder Scrolls games. They are both open world RPGs with a strange setting, but that's largely the only things they have in common.The game's more similar to something like Deus Ex or Arx Fatalis: You've got objectives, you've got various tools to complete those objectives. Which in practice means you can run faster than god and do drive by dagger-stabbings on steam locomotive spider things.The game's got good dialogue, the quests are full of those morally grey choices that kids these days love, and you can climb aboard a giant farmhouse on treadmills and be told that if you speak in uneven numbered words it'll cause the thing to explode. If that's not up your alley you need better metropolitan geography.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I just finished it, and already feel homesick.Amazing game! it's like Skyrim on crack, but very cozy and immersive nonetheless. This game's appearance resembles a rogue-lite or like, but it's actually very friendly towards player. You can build your character any way you want and will always find something to do with skills you invested in and combat is simplistic but not primitive.Story is engaging and on top of that is sprinkled with dozen or so choices.Game may be underpolished sometimes (rarely so), but that does not ruin player experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: It's great. I love it. It could be so much better. Dread Delusion is what you get when you combine the dark fantasy of Fromsoft games and the sagas of the Elder Scrolls, shake them about, and then give them less money than they truly need. The good aspects of this game are, by far, its world and its quests. You get a genuinely fascinating setting, coupled with a series of missions that you almost want to lose yourself in forever. Some missions, like the Missing Persons mission, feel like a kick to the gut in the best possible way. There's a bleakness, a sense of hope, and a desire to explore forever that absolutely pervades this game, and it's the greatest thing I've seen in a very long time indeed. The downsides almost entirely consist of its jankiness. Some of said jank is caused deliberately (the lack of map early on is a bit of a nightmare. Some of us have no sense of direction). Other parts feel weird and bad. Oftentimes when you fire off a spell, it doesn't seem to even materialize. There are parts of the game where textures just straight-up should not be there. The entirety of the final act, save for the final-boss mission, kinda feels like an afterthought. You can really feel where the budget ran out, as much as I'm loath to say it. There are some mediocre as well. If you're looking for a genuinely deep combat system--actually, if you're looking for that, why are you here? Go back to the Soulsborne games. They're REALLY fun and have  a lot of replay value. Why are you here with us dweebs? There's a lot of QOL improvements that could be made. I'd really have enjoyed a slightly better fast-travel system, for instance, and the time-skipping leaves a little to be desired. That being said, it's hard to think of another indie game that does quite as much amazing stuff as this one does.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I just arrived in the last of the three main areas and I have to say: This is a lovely little RPG the likes of Morrowind. Not only the graphics are reminiscent of Morrowind, the story about gods, magic and metaphysics also play a major role. The inherent strangeness of the isles and their inhabitants make for a lot of fun exploring and completing quests. Even if there are no big puzzles or challenging gameplay elements, the quests are particularly captivating due to their storylines and world-building. Up to this point, I've mainly played because of this surreality and the story. And this is also the biggest point of criticism so far: if you don't like the setting and all the metaphysics, then you won't have much fun with the currently implemented combat and equipment system either and probably won't find a reason to play the game further than the first area.This is partly due to the fact that it is designed to be quite short for a open world RPG. You find resources such as healing potions extremely often and almost never need them, as you are able to finish off most enemies with three to five blows. Even if you are hit, the damage you take is almost nonexistent.The game really is all about the quests and exploring the game world. If that's enough for you, I can highly recommend the game at its current price, but if you're looking for challenging combat and a complex level system, you should go for other oldschool RPGs such as Gothic or Morrowind, the latter of which this game draws some heavy inspiration.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game a bit, but I dont like it enough to continue playing beyond the 5 hours I've put into it.I really like the aesthetics, the writing is good enough, and the weird twists on things are a significant plus - I've really enjoyed those parts.But, the actual gameplay is just too boring, compared to other games I could play.  This looks like a game from 1999, which is great, but it also *plays* like a game from 1999, when I really hoped it would be more engaging than that.  The combat is too easy, the quests are too easy, stealth feels either easy or arbitrarily hard but is always overshadowed by how easy it is to fight or run through everyone... the skill checks are not interesting and the platforming challenges or environmental puzzles are only mildly interesting.  Walking around a castle to find a backdoor to the castle that lets you go through locked doors/traps with your lockpicks instead of going through enemies with your sword is fun the first time, but not the third time.I wish I had played this game 15 years ago, when I had lower standards.  Right now, the aesthetics aren't enough to carry the rest of it, for me.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Conditionally recommended. This is very much an old school RPG in more than just appearance. If that's not something you enjoy, steer clear! Otherwise, read on for a more detailed assessment. Likes:* The writing for the dialogue is quite good, especially for an indie game. I'm so used to awkward and error-laden NPC dialogue in smaller indie games that I was pleasantly surprised at the quality of the writing I have seen so far.* Combat is simple but well implemented. I got the hang of parrying pretty quickly. Attack animations are varied and well telegraphed so that parrying feels "right."* The visual style I like for the most part. I turned off the PS1 style wobbly 3D but kept the wobbly textures on. That seemed to be a good balance for me. Most importantly the visual style is *consistent.* A lot of these kinds of games can run into issues where the VFX or some other elements look out of place because they're clearly higher fidelity than the world they exist in.* Price: The game seems reasonably priced for the amount of content it has. After 3 hours I've only recently made it to the first large city.Dislikes:* Not a huge fan of the lockpicking system. I started dumping points into Guile despite being a "mage" because the need for lockpicks was overwhelming and constant. And those points seemed to do little to reduce target roll on the d6. IMO this would be much better with a d20 roll. It has become bad enough that I am seriously considering starting a new character just to nab the lockpick bonus at character creation.* Early game spells are too well hidden. I finally had to look up where to get the first attack spell. It would be nice if this spell or a lesser version of it was automatically granted to those who pick the spellcasting perk at character creation. Also the damage per mana it does is kind of bad. At least in the early game you'll need to spend a large amount of money on mana potions if you intend to do the majority of your damage with spells.* Pacing is a bit slow at first (consistent with old school RPGs, to be fair). Not sure if things pick up later as I am still early in the game.* I'm not a huge fan of the method of character advancement (hunting down "Delusions" which are just powerups usually behind locked doors or otherwise hidden), but I get what the developer is going for here. So this is more a personal preference than a critique.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: The game is great. The atmosphere, the lore, quests and characters -- everything is crafted with attention and love. However, I have to point out, that this game is in development, and currently there are several issues with game balance and some quests. The most noticeable ones are: - Combat. And the problem is not that it's clumsy. It's... pointless. The developers write, that the combat is never the only option, which is good. But the point is that it is simply not an option in many cases: a lot of quests require high lore and charisma checks and do not allow combat ways of completing them. The experience gained through collecting blue skulls (which are called delusions) is also often locked behind lore / charisma skill checks, and killing monsters does not contribute to levelling up. I made two saves and put around 4-6 ours in each. My "Warrior" was level 6 and my "Mage" was level 27. I really hope that the developers will fix this. - Bugs. I experienced only one bug which was persistent through game reloads and locked some content from me: the interior of the Golden Typhos was completely empty, and there was no characters or interactable objects. Otherwise it's just some minor things: floating trees, holes in textures, etc. Also no crashes at all. Oh, and also (I don't know if it's intended) you can jump into the zone which is currently in development -- Clockwork Kingdom.All in all, Dread Delusion managed to exceed my expectations and has really good potential. I will definitely check out future updates. So if you like open-world exploration games, feel free go grab this one.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: While development is not as fast as I would like- they do add content from time to time and what is there is unique and enjoyable to experience. There aren't really any games out there that I can think of that are quite like this- yes the graphics are old school in nature but if you can look past that and just enjoy it is a very good game.
