_childDocuments_.review: Love the open world and many play style based choices at each location.Captures the same vibe i get from playing morrowind, with getting lost in a strange world full of unique landscapes and life.Only problem is that my laptop has a hard time running some areas, but otherwise really can't recommend it enough
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I have "beat" the game when it was EA (which was just completing the main storyline of the 3 main areas)And I have beat it now that is is full release, and I'll mention this was for V1.0.2.2 in case problems I mention are patched out later.Altho I am not recommending this game, I will try to describe what the game is before I start going into my experiences.Dread Delusion is a First-Person RPG Adventure visually set to the retro aesthetics of the PS1 (complete with vertex wobble). You are set upon a world that is 400 years post-cataclysm which has left the world to be only scatterings of floating islands in the sky, as the world below is uninhabitable to any and all life. The world is vibrant and cryptic.Now I'll start to describe my experiences with the game:--Gameplay-Character Creation and Attributes+SkillsAs mentioned this is a FPS RPG, when creating your character you can pick 3 traits that "describe" who you are, benefits you such as what your starting attribute is boosted, and what secondary and tertiary skills are buffed. I don't mind this, seems pretty standard. And without spoiling too much, there are secrets and puzzles that DO require you have invested in certain skills and/or attributes (which also increase related skills, Say Might (att) will also increase Attack and Defense (skills)) However if you feel like you've made a mistake at character creation, I will inform you, you can get gear and upgrade them up to a +30 for various skills, So you won't be locked out of secrets, however you will have to remember were they were to return once you've levelled up enough and found said gear-CombatNot very Engaging, however I believe this is the game leaning heavier into the PS1 retro experience, and also into a more narrative/story based game. Now some would call this a walking-sim which doesn't make it a bad game, but if you're looking for a FPS RPG with engaging combat, this is not it.You have the option to use melee (Sword, then you can find a Greatsword, and a Dagger), Ranged (This will be a Bow, throwing knives/shuriken, explosive potions, and a handful of ranged spells. Including summons (skeletons)) and Magic (mentioned combat related, but also many utility, like speed up, healing, skipping time (if you don't want to sleep), charming foes to fight for you)Most enemies will as simple AI would, is move straight for you when they see you, attack when in range. And if they are ranged, shoot at you, if you get close, change to melee and if you leave melee, return to ranged. Don't Expect much challenge if you've played many games like this, as any of the tried and true tactics will get you through this game, you can also be a pacifist too, you don't need to kill anything (outside of dialogue) to beat this game.-CraftingThere is crafting in this game, the main part of it will be combining raw ingredients you can find/harvest on your own, which do regrow, or you bought from the few vendors that do sell it. You can't craft weapons, but you can upgrade them, such as the starting Rusty Sword can become a Iron Sword, which can become a Fine Sword, and that can be upgraded again, and this version can branch off to 3(2 actually) final versions which about mid-late game you can find said ores.But most crafting will be for potions, and upgrading gear you find/buy-Secrets/InteractionsThese are heavily reliant on your Lockpicking, Lore skills and Might attribute. If you have a high Lore and Lockpicking you can solve 90% of puzzles, and there are a few in which you need brute force to smash through (As there is nothing to investigate (LORE) or to pick to open). And Lockpicking is simply a dice roll (1d6) your lockpicking skill can make the required number to get or exceed lower, and there is an item that can further help make lock picking easier. But it's just a dice roll, and invetigation objects are just a Lore check (are you skilled enough? yes/no, do you have enough mana? yes/no (if no drink a mana potion)There are a few that do require you have a key, which is mainly found around the world in a chests. And some doors a key is only give due to it being quest related.--StoryNow this is solely going to be how I felt about it, I want to avoid spoilers for those that do want to give this a go if they are looking for a game to explore and interact with that is calm or "tame" for challenge.I really like the theme of this game, which is a bleak setting in which several struggles are happening at once. And you can help solve them, with a choice that you can determine is right or wrong. A decent amount of quests have Choice A and Choice B even changing what the rewards are. However I found there is some that just rail-road you, and the inability to kill or harm NPCs (unless it's a dialogue choice) can make some of these rail-roaded experiences kill the immersion that we have been given from previous interactions, it just makes you shake your head at the choice to make a "solution" be singular when so many other issues have given you plenty of ways to complete them.Now did the above really bother me, not too much, it did (why else mention it) but what bothered me was that some quests tried their best impression of Dishonored. You can Kill something, and it's morally wrong and horrible stuff happens, Or you can do this other thing, where now that something is eternally suffering, and horrible stuff happens but different from the murder horrible stuff. I don't mind if there is basically "bad or bad" but there is quite a few. Like minor spoilers for 2 quests. 1st quest you can kill this one person, but then a plague is released, killing everyone. Or you can poison their son and they both suffer in eternal agony, there is no plague, but now people are mutating into tentacle monsters. 2nd quest you can help a god take root in the land again, and the ground becomes fertile again and people can eat and live, but eventually the people will mutate into monsters. Or you can tip the god-hunters off, which will try to deal with the god, leaving the land to become infertile and the famine continues killing more people. Very Dishonored-like where sometimes killing the target is the more merciful option, and the "pacifist" option they can live, but ooooh are they not going to be happy, for a loooong time.I can forgive some other minor things that happened in some quests like a character that stutters, at the end is talking quite normal. Or some cases a character has the wrong name or even the wrong dialogue (was talking to a robot, and it was using the same lines as a goblin earlier in the game)If I had to rate the Story, I'd give it a 7/10 most of the writing is serviceable, the good ones are brought down by some plot-holes. But most of it is propped up by the sheer setting and theme, It's a really interesting world, which is what made me push through with ignoring a lot of the issues (issues to me) because the core of the story and the world is just that good.TL;DRGame is like an interactive visual novel that lets you pick a majority of outcomes for situations, which also seem to reflect on the ending. However the project might have been a bit too ambitious as some parts of the story feel very on-rails and this may have been due to time constraints which lead to these choices.Story is very interesting (Theme and Setting) however as much as I enjoy retro throwbacks (which art-wise, nailed it 100%) the gameplay could have been more modernised which leads me not to recommend this (plus the bugs I faced in 1.0.2.2) for a release, it still feels Early-Access. However if you like old PS1 FPS story driven games, mechanics/gameplay and all. Treat this as a recommendation instead, but if you're looking for a game that plays like a "game" this won't be for you, and it wasn't really for me, but I vibed with the story.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I love everything about this game. It scratches that nostalgia itch for me, yet everything is new! The story is interesting, and rather dark. I normally don't care much for lore in games, but found myself enjoying absorbing it here. The endless crusades are my favorite so far. Some still like the thinkin stuff. Exploring is a bit daunting but as I ran in circles I passively learned the layout. Once I got the map it was a lot more clear.  The combat is a a bit too predictable, but you get tired and have to rest or take potions anyways so I still get the sensation of self care I guess. long story short, if you like the macabre, lore, exploration, dark atmosphere and mild combat this will probably make you happy.Only spoiler is you can buy the iron sword not too far into the game, you dont have to waste iron to upgrade. Iron is scarce and important.I already have about 8 hours into the game despite what the record says.

_childDocuments_.review: Took me 8 hours to complete all of the content currently. One island you still cannot access yet and you can't complete the main quest. But it was a fun 8 hours regardless since, although it may look poorly developed, it really wasn't. There was a lot of really good writing in the game, the game play felt smooth, the map mechanic was interesting but I quickly got used to it. 1 very important thing to note is that the compass currently does not work, use the directions shown in hollow town instead. I thoroughly look forward to further updates

_childDocuments_.review: Very fun game, somewhat simplistic in its combat and leveling systems but still extremely fun to explore and soak in the world. It is like morrowind in that the world the devs have built is unlike any other. Very strange and otherworldy with very cool lore. Cant wait for the full release. _childDocuments_.review: While fairly interesting to explore and learn the lore of the world of Dread Delusion, I'll be honest - every time I think about continuing playing this game, I just get annoyed. Because the devs decided that if players want to continue playing they will have to start back at the last magical crystal thing they've touched. And those are sparsely scattered around.Need to close the game in the middle of exploring or doing quests and do some other stuff? TOO BAD! You'll have to run all the way back to where you were from a "checkpoint".It makes even less sense considering the game saves all the progress all the time... but still sends you back to the crystal, instead of just allowing to continue playing from where you left off.To make things worse, player's movement speed tied to agility stat. So if you start the game as a non-agility focused character, you gonna move around with the speed of a slug. And if you're thinking on making a magic caster character - you gonna have miserable start of the game because it doesn't give the player any offensive spells to work with for hours (except for charm spell that is tied to charisma). I had foresight to pick "+20 damage with any weapons perk" during the character creation. Otherwise every encounter would be a slog.The art style is... interesting. It's unique for sure. However the graphics are ugly. And this will put off a lot of people, I feel like. My friends, for example, looked at the screenshots and said that the game looks horrible and that they don't want to play it. Can't blame them. If you gonna invest time into a game you should at least tolerate the way it looks.The music is repetitive. From what I gathered it has one endlessly looping track per region. It gets old very quick. Sounds are lacking. Mobs don't have any sound when they aggro. Or footsteps. So one could run after you for a while and you won't even notice until it hits you in the back.Combat is simplistic. Enemy AI is very dumb. It is extremely easy to "cheese" them by simply doing heavy attack and backstepping. And in 5 hours playing I haven't even encountered a single enemy who would damage me for more than a pixel off my healthbar. And I didn't even have any armor! Ranged enemies get completely neutralized by strafing.Lockpicking and trap disarm is pure luck based. A lock or a trap has "difficulty" represented by 1d6. And you can't know the difficulty unless you click on it and spend a lockpick (if you fail to roll 1d6).In 5 hours of playing I only encountered two, I think, dialogue options that did charisma check (not counting tutorial that can be passed by default). And in both cases I didn't see a big enough reason to invest level ups into charisma, which would gimp your character in other areas.My personal issue - no option to disable vignetting. It's subtle, but it's always there. And it gives me a headache if I play for a while. Combine that with having to start from the crystals when I want to continue playing, and... yeah. Can't edit config either - there's none. Only some parameters in windows registry.Overall, it's an alright game. There's not much competition in "morrowind-esque" niche, so I can see why people would like it.

_childDocuments_.review: It is amazing. On the front of options and exploration this game ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ delivers. there are different entrances to the dungeons for example like backdoor that has less enemies but more traps. The world is so bizzare that it forces you to accept itself and I can't wait to play more honestly after writing this review. This game captures the 3 most important aspects of morrowind, less hand holding, fleshed out bizzare world and exploration. It in my opinion isn't as good as Morrowind which is my favorite game ever but actually manages to scratch a similar itch while unmistakably having it's own identity making sure that this game is more(much more) than just "being similar to morrowind"

_childDocuments_.review: This game had all the hallmarks of a big success: real atmosphere, good world-building, and pieces of other fiction (Warhammer 40K, HP Lovecraft, Michael Moorcock, etc.) assembled in an interesting manner.Why do I not recommend it?IT IS BROKEN.Rarely is this game updated in a meaningful fashion. When it is, things are entirely reworked to the point of being almost unrecognizable, and everything you were used to has changed. That or all new, game-breaking bugs are manifested. It's MY FAVORITE type of "early access": We'll finish it whenever.DreadXP are actually HORRIBLE developers. Why do I say this? Look how many irons are in the fire right now. How many see the anvil? That's right, you have several TINY teams doing barely anything to multiple titles. JUST STAY AWAY from DREADXP. Trust me. It's not worth it. You'll wait years to see a half-@ssed piece of abandon-ware.All in all, Dread Delusion is a wonderful setting and a great idea, allowed to languish and wither on the vine before it even ripens. A true tragedy.

_childDocuments_.review: A first glace of screenshots, this game doesn't seem like much. But once you start playing it you get hit with such nostalgia from the graphics and music, as well as that sense of wonder and exploration you feel the first time you played the Elder Scrolls games. This game makes you want to explore every nook and cranny, and does a great job at hooking you into the story and lore of this really fascinating world.The only thing I will mention that may turn some people off is that the combat and movement are not complex. This game is more for the exploration and story than mechanics. Regardless, I think the options you are given are very fun (and the flavor texts on the items are cool too) so you shouldn't let that stop you from trying this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Everything about this game is exciting and attention grabbing, and I can't wait for more to be offered. The lore of the game, the organic quests, the story, the people/gods, everything is great and it makes you feel like every decision you make matters, which isn't special by itself anymore, but this game let's you know when you're about to make an important decision and makes it clear that your choice matters and is subjective as to what you think is right. Even with only the early access sections of this game available, I feel like I got my money's worth.A warning however, this game isn't complete yet, there are bugs, unfinished quests, inaccessible areas, and many other developmental issues (some NPCs don't have fully integrated dialogues either; one NPC said to me: "text1, text2, text3"). So, if you're not ready to get started on a game that you can't finish, then you should just add this to your wishlist and check up on it every now and then. And who even knows if this game will be the same when it's fully developed. My play style had me running around with max stamina, avoiding combat, using spells to make myself run even faster, and I had a blast, but it might turn out that this play style gets nerfed over time, so if you're not ready for that, just wait.Great game for me regardless, solid 8/10, maybe 9/10 or 10/10 when it's finished.

_childDocuments_.review: Wow. Just. Wow. I haven't finished playing Dread Delusion, but I'm going to throw a review up to show my support.*******Be sure to read HOW TO GET AN AIRSHIP ASAP further down in this review.*******Lemme give you the pitch:Welcome to the Oneiric Isles. Several maps worth of individual and unique biomes. A land ruled by a race of immortal dead men. A kingdom run into ruin by a mad clockwork king. A jungle of mushrooms. A nation split into those who illegally worship gods, and those who hunt them. And your goal? To hunt the mad visionary, Vela Callose, leader of the Dark Star mercenaries, who seeks to create a new world, and possibly destroy what's left of this one.The world of Dread Delusion is fascinatingly unique. It oozes potential and intrigue. It begs to be explored. Floating islands and manning airships, headed towards adventure across a strange horizon, with a star of magenta radiating otherworldly light overhead. Its simply magical.So, what is this game even like?Is this a heavily stat-based RPG? No. Builds, classes, and playstyles are not really the selling point here. I mean, I wouldn't even say the actual combat/magic is the real draw. If you're going to buy Dread Delusion, understand that this is a finely crafted STORY and LORE HEAVY experience. This is a world, filled with ideas and characters, on a whole other level, really punching above its weight, easily rivaling the thorough and thoughtful world design of any mainstream, big-budget RPG. I am constantly blown away by the conundrums I am asked to solve, the dreams I am to share in, the crises of a world on the brink of madness and destruction. The WRITING IS KING.Unfortunately, while I usually don't really ever notice the drawbacks Indies work with on their budgets and scale, the writing really contrasts with most of the actual game play.Quests are amazing! The maps are huge! Dialogue is compelling! The art direction is fantastic! The scale the devs were working on, the genius that went into the crafting of this world, it is so very compelling.But, combat is simple, as is enemy AI. Its really simple. Magic is fine. Stats are barely a worry. It all works, but its almost sad how much the actual game play pales in comparison to the creativity that went into narrative and visuals. Half of the experience is incredible, while the other is... there. Not being particularly compelling. This is something that keeps the game from being an easy recommendation.Although I had a Lovely (Hellplace) of a time with this game (consistently amused, befuddled, and hooked) I cannot really say this game will appeal to everyone. I could really see some people being turned off by just how simple this game is. Personally, I feel the game play could have used more development, and at the very least, I would love to see an even more ambitious sequel to set things straight. I want to see more, of this world, and from the developers.Minor notes:I also would have LOVED for major characters to have received voice acting. It would have done SO MUCH for the experience. But, again, whether it wasn't envisioned or they didn't have the budget, this is one of those things that sort of stood out to me as a real limit. The game's writing was on the level of some of my favorite RPG experiences of the past. But, none of it is allowed the added depth of a convincing VA, really there to sell me on the characters and their struggles.I also found, while a lot of time and attention was given to visuals and describing the appearance of even minor characters, NPCs in themselves are fairly one-note. They have simple "retro" designs that are regularly reused and don't match aforementioned character descriptions. In contrast to all the love the writing was given, I'm surprised a little more variation or attention wasn't given to NPCs. This, in combination with essentially one or two animations, and all the reading, results in characters that seem more like paper cut outs than the three-dimensional people the game wants me to see.AIRSHIP TIP:I will end my list of gripes with a warning. If you're anything like me, you'll play the majority of the game's side quests before pursuing the main quest.DO NOT DO THIS.Sure, smell a few roses on the way, but I ended up burning myself out running hither and thither over huge maps, increasing my Guile stat and chugging stamina potions. Play the main quest until you unlock the airship. Please, do this. There are fast travel points that you can activate anywhere (only one per spot recently visited), and set fast travel points you unlock later (giant portals). But, please, get an airship. These do not really mitigate the amount of walking you'll be doing without one.CONCLUSION:If you're to buy Dread Delusion, you're buying it for the pure, unadulterated, creative drug that is this game's world building and narrative. The decisions you make, the people you meet, the problems you must solve. Its all so very potent and thought-provoking. Buy, play, and enjoy, for that. If you're looking for an action-oriented, unique fantasy RPG with perks and play-styles... you're probably best looking elsewhere. But, for those looking to share in some truly dreadful delusions... please, partake and enjoy.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not Daggerfall, nor Morrowind - its very much its own thing: An openable, open world with a focus on exploration.There is no character appearance customization or outfits. Instead of exp / levels, you acquire and obtain Delusions that are spent on one of four attribute style categories that help shape how you play the game. There are items (potions, lockpicks, coins, et cetera) scattered all over the map to find while exploring, as well as various Points of Interest to investigate. It's also choice driven, allowing the player to select their responses to dialogue, as well as different routes for completing a quest, which may or may not have various consequences.The music is nice. The world is fairly sizable. This won't be your 'final game' but, its definitely worth the playthrough(s), esp. at the price. And, if you're concerned over the red sky, its not much of an issue when you're in game and on the ground, as there are a lot of environmental objects and hills blocking the view. There are also some options in the options menu that allows you to disable some of the settings that may be annoying.The weapons are fairly basic - no advanced weapons like a giant mace or halberd, unless i'm missing it. There are a few gear pieces for different styles, heavy armor v light. You can upgrade your gear with ores / threads. There's a plethora of spells. There are various jewelry pieces with effects to supplement your build. There's a simple, two ingredient alchemy system. Home-ownership. Airship ownership! :DHere are some points that some may find frustrating:You will constantly be picking locks, retracing steps for locks / 'Lore' check locks that you didn't have the skill at the time.The map is more for a person that can memorize and familiarize themselves with landscape, through exploration. You uncover the map as you explore, and there is a compass that will mark your location, but there's no HUD directional compass, that i noticed.There have been some complaints about combat being too difficult - this may be the starter build people have selected, or potentially something else on their part with attacking / dodging attacks. But, i picked the attack / defense route and haven't had issues or died. My only death during Early Access was not looking before i leapt off the edge of the island.The visuals - the art style and effects may be too much on certain people's eyes. There are the options in the menu that may help.Other than that - its an enjoyable, unique world that's meant to be taken in and appreciated.

_childDocuments_.review: An indie attempt at capturing something along the lines of the original Morrowind. The main draw is the narrative component; while the main quest is fairly linear, the worthwhile side quests are for the most part complex and ambiguous moral dilemmas. While there is dungeon delving, it's far more about exploration than a fairly rudimentary combat system- this can occasionally backfire (key spells to play a mage are often impossible to find and loot is often not the most rewarding).The game doesn't have the same depth as a Bethesda title as the faction reputation system is borderline meaningless and there are very few optional dungeons past the initial zone, but given the development team size and actual soul in the game it more than makes up for it. If a Morrowind throwback with modern touches and good writing would appeal to you, definitely check this out.

_childDocuments_.review: My first 4 hours with Lovely Hellplace's  were in two contrasting words: Confusing.. but Lovely. I should immediately follow this up with my playtime of 44 hours, a time in which I experienced all the game has to offer (achievements included).  is now firmly one of my favorite RPG games in the past few years. So, what challenges did I face in these first four hours that many players (including yourself, prospective buyer) also face? The game begins with Character creation, which consists of choosing a set of stat traits that simultaneously govern respective backstory info on your character. There is no avatar creation, as the player's appearance is never revealed. It is understood quite quickly that all level progression and experience points are gained through completing questlines and collecting "delusion skulls" spread across the map. Combat only rewards the player with various materials such as coins, lockpicks, etc. Leveling up consists of four traits which max at 10: Strength, Guile, Lore, and Charm. These four traits influence aspects such as damage, defense, stamina, lockpick skill, spellcast, charisma, barter, environmental puzzles, and so on.. All equipment also adds respective edges to player stats in the form of helmets, clothing, rings, and belts.With our gameplay bearings in place, the tutorial area opens up into the first zone of the game: Pwyll. This small town and its surroundings can be thought of as a breed of "soft launch" for the overall game and its ideas, a slight expansion on top of the tutorial. Moving to new zones requires (in most cases) a one-time use passport to lower the bridge and progress to the next town. The problem with this ease-in approach is it proves as simultaneously provoking.. but underwhelming. Lovely.. and confusing. This is not helped by the fact that the overworld music does not really change unless there is a switch in zones, and this (ONE!!) track begins to grate at around the 2 hour mark while you're still exploring Pwyll, its people and its oddities. I changed to playing my own fantasy music for the next two hours, the game itself would be improved by a more dynamic rotation of music when staying confined to one area for long period of time. After advancing beyond Pwyll to later areas of the game, music tracks change much more as you are able to explore at a more breakneck pace.After leaving Pwyll, the game subverted all my expectations and transformed into a creature that began to catch my every interest.Here will discuss the gameplay loop and all its isles offer. If so far has been about the first 4 hours of the game out of 44, then this section comprises the remaining 40 hours. Let's begin with the bulk. There are roughly six zones in  each with their own respective island(s). Commonfolk, as well as the world's empirical faction The Apostatic Union, populate two of these zones: Pwyll, Hallowshire, and their governed Union surroundings. A town of undead folk lie to the west in the Endless Realm. To the North-East are the Soviet folk in the Clockwork Kingdom. Underneath these islands are the Underlands, which is simply describable as a land "before time" as the player exists in the new world above. What remains are a collection of sporadic islands that populate various self-contained enclaves and stories, I collect these islands all as a big one despite being a small many. This is the operable game board that will be explored in your time with  The gameplay loop consists mostly of obtaining passports to explore, fight, and decide in the next zone, progressing the story. 's handling of themes such as totalitarianism, dogma, love, and identity are so well-measured it almost became quizzical. The game itself seems to place moral judgement closely within the player-reader's hands. Scenarios simply Are, symbols conveying many meanings, contradictory breathing Things. You will see!If we are to deduce the kernel of pleasure in the RPG genre, it would be nothing less than a sum of its moving parts. What does this collection of islands and its peoples oscillate around? Choice of faction is a large part of the storytelling underway  in the isles, and each persuasion of leaderships over this world make compelling arguments that will lead the player to emergent changes in morals and what they believe is best for the world as a whole. This aspect of  is one of 's strongest pillars it provides to support the player. Each isle essentially produces some breed of faction conflict underway, and the player character is just the correct weight to tip those scales. You aren't special, just special enough. The script for all characters and the twenty-some books that populate the islands is impressive, but it requires a player who is willing and able to engage with the story on this basis of reading. Asking critical questions such as "what does this person want?", "am i being tricked?", "what  they telling me?" are meaningful when engaging with this world at the level it is presented at, within its own historical contexts provided. This is the attitude that is conditioned for the game's lengthy list of quests. If you don't like reading or find it unsavory from a gameplay perspective, it will be a little harder to enjoy the game outside of its story. I think this is where the greatest schism is located within the playerbase. Lovely Hellplace's approach to storytelling decenters combat for top-shelf atmosphere.You may remember when I said exploration and quests governs experience, whereas combat is solely in the backseat for loot needs. I think this immediately and understandably turns some players off. For instance, I am excited as a player to be more heavily rewarded for exploration in comparison to combat. I can empathize with those who want a more combative experience. Thankfully, a difficulty slider has been added! Now, combat can be fresh. With that being said, the game can be effectively played as a pacifist. There are even unique dialogue options and consequences for the pacifist choice. However, I only recommend this option for a second playthrough, as it is less rewarding than a standard approach. Faction notoriety is greatly affected by combat activity, which reinforces some exploration opportunities with safe house buff rewards and endings. The game scales up wonderfully and provides a challenge at lategame.What scared me most about some reviews and discussions on this game before buying was the loose use of "broken questlines".  Here's the deal. In my experience, quests do not break. The only break I found in the game was a bug where the inventory menu stayed open, which required me to return to title and reload the game. This is a totally inconsequential bug as the game saves after every action you take. It is virtually impossible to lose significant progress with a save feature as tight as this. Sometimes completed questlines remain in the active quest tab, despite you completing and receiving EXP for them. I say big deal. In my three playthroughs, I only had issues with the inventory, which is literally just because I use steam overlay too much back-to-back. No issues with saving or progress. Dread Delusion does not have any game ruining bugs that I have seen.

_childDocuments_.review: It took me a long time with this game to figure out whether I could ultimately reduce my opinion to a thumbs up or thumbs down. My recommendation with of this game after getting to know it fully is heavily qualified. Everything you can read in negative reviews is true. This is NOT Morrowind. The item, spell and skill variety is as limited as you would expect in any low budget indie. Different skill choices barely impact play as they mostly determine which method of opening doors you use. The combat is extremely simplistic, and mostly avoidable just by running around the enemies. However, I ultimately decided I didn't regret purchasing it, and would recommend purchasing it to myself if I had a time machine, because even after the impact of the gonzo aesthetic wore off the game still managed to get one thing right that made it fun, which is that it rewarded exploration. I had fun with it just wandering around the map seeing what new stuff was just over the next hill. Even if I didn't NEED the loot or XP awards for anything, it was still fun to get them.I would recommend this game to you only if all of these criteria are met:1. The monetary cost is completely meaningless to you.2. You have time in your schedule where you are going to be playing some kind of video game anyway and are always looking for new video games.3. The aesthetic appeals to you.4. You enjoy exploration and finding new areas in game worlds just for the sake of exploration.

_childDocuments_.review: This game lies firmly in the realm of indie developer confusion. It's quirky, unique and displays some degree of technical skill, but ultimately doesn't really do anything well. It feels like a title that got spawned as a hobby project between a few friends: "remember those wobbly 3d graphics due to low precision old consoles? Let's make a game about that!".For Dread Delusion to justify the medium it either has to do well in immersion or provide a challenge. The game does neither well. Combat is... well, I personally would not even call it passable. No design effort was put into this aspect of the game - it exists because it had to. You strike an opponent, walk back a little as they whiff, strike them again and repeat. Sometimes you get to mix it up by shooting a projectile. Stealth is again the bare minimum; enemies raycast up to some distance to detect you - no other mechanics are involved.Immersion is a total flop as well, even though I would personally not touch this angle with a 10ft pole either; established RPGs are notoriously difficult to compete with - especially with such a limited amount of resources. Similar to the combat any form of immersion enhancing functionality seems to have fallen by the wayside; they wanted to make a game and come hell or high water that game would be released somehow. NPCs just statically walk over predetermined paths if at all. You cannot interact with the environment beyond the occasional "click button to collect plant". The whole thing feels like an empty set-piece. A draft of a game at best.The things the game seemed to have put effort into are all tangential to the experience; the environmental design, the lore, the amount of assets and dialogue. It's like a very, VERY dry piece of chicken seasoned excellently. You can't save it if the fundamentals aren't there.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the better 3D RPGs I have played in quite a while.If you can stand the graphic, which i kinda adore, you will find a semi Open Word to explore, filled with strange and sometimes horrific things. You will have to read quests and ask questions to figure out what is going on in each region. But I still never really felt lost or aimless. While there are no compass markers for quests the quest giver and journal usually describe pretty well where one has to go.With all that said, you should not expect content equaling a morrowind. The main story is not that long if you know where to go, each region usually only has a couple sidequests, most of them telling a small story over multiple quest steps. The amount of weapons and spells is limited.A couple of (upgradeable) weapons and a decent chunk of spells. Most of which are of the utility kind, which I quite liked. Rings and Trinkets allow further customisation.All of these are sprinkled over the whole map. Usually only one of each can be found or bought. So if you want to play with a specific weapon or spell, you might not find it until quite late in the game. Most of the Exploring rewards are Usables (Potions, Throwables), Gold or Ingredients to create Usables, and sometimes Glimmers of Delusion (XP).Unlike most other games, locked away rewards can usually (but not always) be retrieved through multiple methods, eg. pick the lock or bash the door.The Leveling system is quite Fallout 3 / NW ish, just with only main stats. Skills are increased by the main stats and equipment.There is also a Faction system, which felt somewhat underutilized.  Exploring near the end of the game also was strange and i had to look things up, as some (seemingly) not implemented things were left in the game, resulting in me looking into them more.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Solid world building, side quests, exploration, and surprisingly likable NPCs. Brought me back to the old days when RPGs weren't afraid to experiment and be weird. Finished it in about 27 hours, which is really solid for an indy RPG like this one.The endgame has some bugs and missing content after leaving EA, but besides that, the serviceable combat, and the over-importance of lockpicking, I loved my time with the game.

_childDocuments_.review: A warning to potential buyers:Most mechanics, I would say aren't lacking as a design fault or the game being unfinished, but purposefully simplistic. When people start a RPG, they expect to be learning all kinds of indepth systems, and/or really getting involved with their character. This game does not do that. Combat is extremely simple and easy. Magic is very straight forward. Alchemy has a little to it, but not much.If you like the look of the game enough to consider purchasing, you will be compelled to continue playing because of its setting (lore & location). And that's that.It is easy to wish for more out of the game as you would with a more traditional RPG. In understanding the game's purpose of storytelling over mechanics, the only gripe I have is how combat has no challenge at all. With all of that being said, I am getting my $20 worth. And having a fun time exploring this fascinating world in short play sessions.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread delusion in its current state is understandably in need of some polish and shine. But I cannot recommend it enough for it's captivating world and whimsical stylistic choices. This is the first game I've stumbled across in a long while that's exciting to see new content for, and can make me jump up from my errands just to explore the world over and over.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: Become kleptomaniac hero/villain ex-convict while exploring mad psychedelic broken world littered with dead gods(?) with a spell to run like drug addled blue hedgehog and being oppressed by a militant inquisition who turbo hates gods.I think it is great homage to RPGs of yore with certainly unique style and great lore and character (especially Clockwork Kingdom part) but rather falls flat at combat.You can ever just PARKOUR! and slash your sword to kill just about everything.As for comparison with big M, I can't say much because I'm not that old but this game does put you in weird artsy alien world.Definitely try if you like willy-nilly exploration stuff.

_childDocuments_.review: Update for 1.0:The newly designed intro has great pacing, clearer presentation and easily held my interest past story points that escaped me the first time around. Excited to revisit the world, characters, and see the new content!Original review:Played for ~45 minutes when I first got it. Seemed cool, but wasn't immediately engaging for some reason. Picked it back up on a whim and played for 13 hours straight. It's good.It's got a unique style and voice in its design, so might take some getting used to. Combat is indeed basic, but it becomes fast after the intro and it was plenty fun exploring builds. If you like exploration and story, especially with a world-building and character focus, give it a bit longer than the intro to get going and you might find it captivating as well.

_childDocuments_.review: I had been keeping an eye on Dread Delusion since first seeing it in the Haunted PS1 Demo Disc a few years back and being taken in by the eccentric writing and visuals. Having finally played the full release I’m pleased to see those elements were carried over and expanded from the demo, elevating the otherwise competent but mostly unremarkable RPG-lite foundation.What you should know going in is that this is very much a narrative and exploration-focused game, with combat being the weakest element by a good margin. With that said, I wouldn’t call it bad, just not particularly engaging - your attacks are responsive and have a solid feel, but enemies are almost universally very easy to defeat. The developers have attempted to address this more recently via the introduction of a hard mode and reduction of the hit stun your attacks apply, but with how well telegraphed enemy attacks are the basic loop of attack, backstep to dodge, repeat will still get you through basically the whole game.I don’t think it would be fair to call the combat an afterthought, but given the relatively low density of enemies and the fact they don’t award XP, it’s definitely not the primary focus of the game. To that end I wouldn’t bother with the hard mode, as going by the list of changes it applies the game would simply become more tedious to play.Apart from combat there is an abundance of different mechanics like speech checks, lockpicking and so on, but they are all relatively simple. Your character has stats which will influence or gate some of those features, but between levelling up and finding skill-boosting equipment most of those limitations can be overcome within the same playthrough. Ultimately, the game shines most when it’s somewhat divorced from those mechanics, such as when exploring a new area for the first time or conversing with the various inhabitants of the Oneiric Isles.To that end, the worldbuilding is some of the most fleshed-out and interesting I’ve seen from a game recently. While intertwined in various ways, each sub-region you visit has its own distinct culture and history that shape your interactions within. For me this peaked with the Clockwork Kingdom and its artificial Clockwork King's descent into madness, where the writing was at its strongest both in terms of the bleak questlines and overall setting. The quality in both respects was quite high for the majority of the game, with the colourful, often humorous narration of NPC actions interspersing their dialogue being one of the highlights.Given the team size, the scale of the game is very impressive. The open world may not be the most dense, but there are plenty of landmarks to see and exploring will reward you with XP (as will completing the many quests to be found). There are some fast travel options available to reduce transit times, but you can still expect to be doing a lot of running around. Along those lines, while I enjoyed the music I feel the game would have benefited from a few more tracks as you will be hearing the same songs a lot.I think there is an argument to be made that the game could have done more on the mechanical front, but as it is the gameplay could have been significantly worse and I would still recommend it based on the quality of the setting and writing alone. Just be aware of what its strengths are going in and set your expectations accordingly.

_childDocuments_.review: is an action-RPG with strong exploration and excellent writing, although the character development system is minimalistic and there is no visual customisation, there are still several options for the avatar's background, which affect the stats. The setting is distinct and consistent - an archipelago of floating islands under the light of a neural star, shortly after the local deities were slain by the newly-formed human alliance, the Apostatic Union. The world is consistent and self-contained (i.e. no out-of-game information is required to make sense of it), while different islands and peoples are very distinct from each other, with the quest lines affecting them. Both the background lore and the actual plot are clear and well-developed. The topics discussed vary from practical to philosophical. Additionally, the story and the setting are very LGBTQ-friendly. The exploration is rewarding and the few new equipment pieces are enjoyable and welcome to find. So are the NPCs and quests. In particular, the equipment is rare (possibly, too rare) and unique enough to be meaningful. The bonuses vary from quantitative (e.g. +20 to Stamina) to qualitative (e.g. no fall damage). The loot is distributed well, even if a lot of it is gameplay logic, such as potions and coins lying on the ground, the locations of clothing, spells, minerals, and plants make sense in a more general way. Additionally, the crafting materials can be spent actively during the game on house upgrades (there are several houses for purchase), which allows them to remain desirable throughout the playthrough. Regarding crafting, though crafting or consuming potions rarely was necessary, the armour upgrades can make a significant difference in one’s playthrough, while the collected ammunition allowed to defeat The combat in general is very optional and rather basic, with a strong focus on positioning, though making melee encounters engaging with the first-person view is always incredibly challenging. The controls are rebindable, 5-button mice are supported. There are also several options for the visual effects.There are also several negative aspects and I doubt that all of them will be addressed. The saving system is rather poor - there are 3 save slots, one per playthrough, with automatic saving at certain events and upon interacting with the checkpoints. Windows Explorer still allows better save management and it is strongly recommended to make a hard save every 30 minutes due to the bugs. The bugs vary from clipping through some objects to NPCs incorrectly recognising quest outcomes and actions to getting softlocked because a main quest was reset. The latter I resolved by modifying the save file via a hex editor and it was not exactly a user-friendly thing to do. The last issue is that very few quests are connected to each other or have complex non-linear structure, while the NPCs are impossible to kill at will, so the thread of the prophecy will not be severed. Overall, it was an enjoyable experience and I highly recommend the game.

The various creatures inhabiting the world are as bizarre and wonderful as I had hoped, excellent designs with that good good low poly crunch. I would say if you want to play a mostly satisfying short game and then observe its wretched pulsating metamorphosis over time, buy it now to boost the devs' resources. _childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion, as of the time of writing, is pretty buggy. While I have not crashed during my playthrough, I have encountered flickering textures, voiceover during the narration cutscenes that do not fit with its subtitles, floating objects and nonsensical hitboxes, and worse yet, falling through the world twice. This is particularly noteworthy, as dying for the first time is tied to a plot event.Undeniably, one of Dread Delusion’s most striking features are its visuals. Featuring a self-described “retro 3D aesthetic,"  the low-poly art style matches the brokenness of the setting the game takes part in. Nevertheless, this choice of visuals is a two-sided sword; on the one hand, it provides equally unique designs for enemies and the gods much of the story revolves around, as well as adding to the haunting atmosphere, but it can also often blend architecture together a bit, making certain locations a bit confusing to navigate.A real issue is that the game loads pieces of the overworld in chunks; however, this is rather similar to TES: Oblivion, where it’s dependent not on the distance of the player but on predetermined loading zones. This can lead to situations where there is a barely textured house right in front of you, and taking a single step forward suddenly lags the game as everything loads in.The sound, while good, is largely limited to a handful of ambient tracks for each region. Thus, over long periods of questing and exploring, it can add up to feeling a bit monotonous. Combat SFX is similarly lacking, and the game does not feature voice acting of any kind outside of very limited narrated cutscenes.The world is shattered apart by a cataclysmic event. With the surface world uninhabitable in the aftermath, a faction of humanity has taken upon itself to wipe out the remaining gods that had once blessed humanity through contracts and allow the remnants to fend for themselves. On the Oneiric Isles, the player is forced into a hunt after a Sky-Pirate who is after an artifact that promises to be able to change the fate of this shattered universe.There are two major conflicts on the Isles that the player gets to explore. Firstly, there is the hunt for Vela. For this, the player explores the various kingdoms, which have their own stories to follow. Among them, for example, is a kingdom of undead, whose undeath is accompanied by a constant hunger for flesh and whose true inability to die is affecting their internal politics, which the player can explore. While the story of Vela concerns itself with navigating the player through these factions and exploring the events that have led to the sundering of the world, the second major conflict is one of humanity versus gods. In Dread Delusion, gods used to be abundant and have contracts with humanity, offering them blessings at a cost until they were hunted to near extinction. Most of the morally strongest writing comes from interactions between the remnants of such entities and the implications of supporting or annihilating them.Quests can feel a bit linear at times, but this is made up for by how impactful the choices the player can make are. Furthermore, very little is gated behind Charm (Charisma) Checks, as RPGs so often like to do, and instead Dread Delusion relies on the player reading and following through according to genuinely what they think is best in the given situation.DD features a fairly unique, but ultimately obtuse, stat system in which each of the stats you can increase by collecting Delusions, governs a set of skills; for example, the stat Guile governs skills such as lockpicking or agility. Ultimately, however, due to the aforementioned balance issues, the player’s stats only matter insofar as you want to meet relevant skill checks to continue exploration. Furthermore, gear applies vastly greater stat bonuses than leveling up, further devaluing player progression via their chosen stats and background.Combat is likewise disappointing; magic is extremely underpowered in comparison to melee, and that issue is compounded by the monotony of enemy types. Meaning that while there is decent visual variety in the monsters you encounter, all of them are tackled the exact same way: weaving back and forth and hitting them with whatever you may have. Even with minimal Might investment—governing melee damage—I could comfortably one- to two-shot even late-game enemies.Ultimately, DD suffers from stats simply not being meaningful as they are irrelevant for combat and can otherwise be “forced” to meet certain stat requirements to continue your exploration or quests by keeping up-to-date with your gear. It is a means to engage with DD’s setting, but sadly, it is not competent enough to recommend it to people who may look at DD in search of a strong dungeon-crawler.Dread Delusion is unique. It has some of the most interesting fantasy concepts I have ever seen in a game, from syntax-based magic to its incorporation of factions, but I think it is this ambitious world that also simply rubs up to the limits of what an indie game can provide, as the endgame feels almost rushed—not unfinished, but clearly aware as to how lackluster the actual RPG systems become the further the player is going. It’s a great experience if people can stomach the look and the somewhat slower pace and are willing to engage with a story first and foremost, with gameplay serving more as a vehicle to experience said story through.

_childDocuments_.review: is an open world RPG in the vein of Morrowind, Gothic and King’s Field. Although, I assume most people with eyeballs figured out that there was a retro thing going on just through the screenshots. Specifically, it tries to put an emphasis on the old-school kind of exportation where you have to find your quest objectives through directions and a compass, rather than a marker floating above your head. Really, exploration is the bread and butter of this game. The world is vast, but is segmented into gated-off isles that you get access to as you progress through the story. I guess I could explain the story structure, which… it’s just Morrowind. It’s hard to discuss the quests without bringing up the setting, which is a world located inside a literal galaxy brain. There are gods that look like insects, ancient civilization that was just Victorian England and an empire of militant atheists that run around stamping out the last vestiges of god-worship in any territory they control. And while the quests follow the trolley problem structure, they still operate on blue-orange morality axis. For example, one of the quests is based around the ethics of eating a giant pile of flesh that managed to assemble a Holzman brain throughout the centuries. A pile of flesh that’s used as a food source by undead that normally can only survive off human flesh.One of the major conflicts in the setting is between the Apostolic Union, the large antitheistic empire and the remnants of the pagan cults, dubbed Wikkans. The thing about the latter is that the old gods are neither monstrous (although there are a few that are just that), nor entirely benevolent. Gods are creatures of primal animalistic desire and nature, so they often do not have human interests at heart or at least tend to wildly misinterpret them. You have to balance that with the fact that you eventually start meeting deities that started to emerge after the “god war”, those that tend to be far more human in both their interests and fallibility. While you can balance the various faction interests, it’s difficult to be a heel or truly virtuous due to how grey the general moral spectrum is throughout the game. A grimdark setting this is not, but it certainly is dark fantasy.As for the combat system, it’s middling at best. The games the developers were referencing were never renowned for their combat system. That being said, it replaces Morrowind’s dice-rolling hit registry with the one used in King’s Field. I upgraded my health once during the entire game and just used mage robes and I died in combat only a single time. It’s not great, but it’s not impeding your progress either.There’s one stat that’s low-key mandatory to upgrade if you want to go through the game with a lot less stress, which is Guile. Essentially, it governs your movement speed (which is important as there will be a lot of walking), your stamina and your lockpicking. The lockpicking minigame is literally a dice roll and with low Guile you will be running out of your lockpicks fairly quickly. It doesn’t help that there are certain story-mandated areas that can only be accessed through picking locks. That or you can upgrade your Wisdom stat to spam the Agility spell as your traversal workhorse. The biggest flaw in the Early-Mid game is that the world opens up, but a lot of quests rely on backtracking large distances. That and the faction that gives you fast-travel between continent is easily missed on your first playthrough unless you know where to look. I genuinely respect the developers for making fast-travel restrained until late game, but a few more Dark Souls-esque environmental shortcuts would have been appreciated.As for the character dialogue, it ranges from decent to great. Characters do not beat about the bush, yet show a lot of personality. My only complaint is that some of it feels a bit too modern for the setting, so it resembles less Terry Pratchett and more of a Twitter convo. There’s also a great deal of variety in backgrounds and the way they communicate. In all honesty, the more surreal parts of world building were the best parts of the game, so I actually would have appreciated if there were a handful more infodumps from some of the NPCs.The last nitpick I’d say is that the sky can be a bit tiring to look at after a full playthrough. You get used to it, but there’s something about looking at different shades of red and purple for a 20 hour campaign. I’d just wish the different isles had a bit of a different colour grading. That being said, I highly appreciated the cutscene art and illustrations by Artyom Trakhanov, who has this highly geometric style that really works with the low-poly visuals of the game. It makes the game really come together as a living storybook.In conclusion, it’s a good RPG if you want to get your Morrowind fix. The various flaws can’t really detract from the amount of imagination and passion the creators clearly had when working on it. Honestly, I just wish they would keep working on it for a while longer. There’s some minor features they forgot to implement. For example, I spent an hour looking for an ore that didn’t exist in the game yet. That and a handful of glitches that need to be patched out. It’s not for everyone, but that’s alright.I’m really looking forward to seeing what Lovely Hellplace makes in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: I knew this game looked good as it took a lot of inspiration from Morrowind, and it's much better than I even expected. Obviously the worst part about Morrowind was it's combat system that was limited by the technology of that era, but this game has a pretty good combat system on hard mode, requiring you to avoid attacks with high movespeed or block/parry. The game is moderately challenging, it's certainly no Dark Souls but it has more of a skill requirement than elder scrolls games. You will not have access to a large number of equipment/spells for a while, as most things are locked behind quests or secrets. You can buy base gear from merchants which can be upgraded with ore you find. The spellcasting is probably my favorite mechanic of the game, the game doesn't overwhelm you with a bunch of useless spells (lightning bolt, fire bolt, ice bolt etc). Instead you get a few very useful spells such as teleportation or extreme athleticism, spellcasting not only deals a lot of damage but is very functional as well just like in Morrowind, it's drawback being that you need to build for it and it's very resource intensive since you'll be needing lots of mana potions. The map and world design are beautiful, a unique blend of 2d, 2.5d and 3d artwork. It takes place on a series of floating Islands which are the only remaining habitable landmasses in a very alien world. Eventually you will unlock your own airship which allows you to easily explore different islands (regions). I'm impressed they made the game look as good as it does with the retro graphic style, which looks even better when you're on a vantage point looking at the whole region, also very impressive that you can see the entire region and landmarks from across the map to easily get your bearings. Surprising amount of content and map size with different regions, the game focuses on exploration and quests as the only way you level up is by finding Delusions from completing quests or discovering them hidden around the map.The story is actually interesting and original, and the quests have choices and moral conundrums that make you think, though I am not sure how good the ending or even mid game is as I still have a long way to go. So far it has only gotten better the more I have played. Every important quest has a stealth option where you don't have to fight, either for moral reasons or just to save resources. If you aren't observant, you may kill a bunch of people who you realize after the fact really didn't deserve it. This is a very good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: The art direction is there, the gameplay isn't. Currently the combat is very, very poor, and I say this as someone who enjoyed Morrowind's combat out of the box. The world is very interesting, the flavor is nice, the art direction is top notch, and the game runs very well on the steamdeck. Currently refunding until it seems like the game is in a better place. Hoping it gets there eventually!
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I got mixed feelings about this gameI kind of wish you could fight Town NPCs that could lead to consequences, lack of this feature ruins big part of atmosphere and immersion.Stamina bar mechanic is annoying when exploring the world.The art is incredible tho.I love to explore the games world but combat is way too shallow and easy that I end up avoiding enemies entirely.I wish that this game would get a simple but deep combat mechanics with extra polish.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic, the art style and direction of the game is fantastic. I especially like the magic system which is very similar to early Elder Scroll titles such as Morrowind and Oblivion. The faction feelings towards you is a nice touch, like Fallout New Vegas. The creature design is truly amazing to behold. Creepy and crawly, every creature is very distinctive with fighting styles to match. Very good game.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic gem of a indie game. Harkening back to the "retro" N64/PS1 days. Akin to OOT exploration wise. Giant map with plenty to discover. The art is very well done. I love the fact that you can turn off the wobbly effect. I do like it, but it seems easier on my eyes with it off. Excellent game, grab it if you can.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusions borrows ideas from many classic RPGs and blends them up into something lighter, more digestible for a modern audience. It’s like The End of Dyeus, but focused more on being an Elder Scrolls like. It might look like Morrowind, but it only has the depth of something like Skyrim. You wake up as a prisoner and quickly learn that most factions in the game are disliked. That being said the game world is incredibly engrossing and I enjoyed scouring each floating island for delusions, the things that level you up. However, that brings me to my one real complaint about the game so far – it’s incredibly shallow as of right now in Early Access. The gameplay loop is simple - seeing a building on the horizon, killing or sneaking past enemies on your way to the building. Then killing something in the building, charming someone in the building, or using lore to use switches. Then upstairs or downstairs there’s a delusion and a chest containing some sort of monitory loot. Of course, this doesn’t apply to every house or tower in the game, but it’s a majority of them. Later in the game you find yourself looking for ore to upgrade your armor and weapons, and some NPCs hint that you should check out the mines that dot the countryside. You get excited to explore some abandoned mines – only find out that they’re just a hallway and a single room with no enemies that sometimes spawns ore.EDIT: The dev just added an update with an actual mine and deeper faction systems! It’s a great game world that just doesn’t have a lot of variation of activities right now. Still, these are minor complaints that I hope are addressed in later areas. It’s a good game, and I’m excited to see where it goes.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I see a lot of people saying this is a spiritual successor to Morrowind, but the post-apocalyptic setting and large number of ethical problems the game asks you to solve made me think more of Fallout 2.EDIT:All bugs and glitches I encountered have now been fixed (according to patch notes). And while that doesn't change the fact that the combat is very easily skipped with any investment into movement speed or kinda boring when you do bother with it. Everything else about the game is pretty great.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: While the game is (at time of writing this review) unfinished, there is still so much to enjoy in Dread Delusion. The world that James and his team have & still are building is so full of love and care, blurring the lines between insane, disgusting & beautiful, and having a bizarrely wonderful marriage between dark and neon tones. The lore is at times genuinely frightening and enchanting but still with enough light and air to keep it lively and even funny at times. The core gameplay is simple, think Morrowind with a Lovecraftian edge that bleeds Slimer from Ghostbusters, but still offers enough variety to stay interesting and keep you on your toes whilst you explore the Oneiric Isles, learning through trial and error but never feeling unfair as you get the hang of it. Even the music & sound design are so far beyond what you would expect from an 'indie' title, sounding more like the work of a more prolific and storied developer. I truly love this world and all its crazy, kooky and positively spooky denizens and I hope you will to. Dread Delusion is absolutely worth your time, whether you find it full-price or on-sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: UPDATE: FINISHED THE GAMEIt was absolutely as good as I expected it to be. Weird, beautiful, wacky stories. Some genuine philosophical issues that left me really considering my options. Amazing game, get it.----Updating my review after 14 hours of play, still in the Early Access stage.tl;dr: game good, combat wack, story good as hell, the child of Morrowind + Cruelty Squad, literally better than Starfield. While the game suffers from a few bugs still (endlessWriter<English> lmao) and combat that's just a bit too simple, it is an incredible experience. It is an exploration RPG set in an absolutely bizarre world, and I found it wonderful. Combat: 4/10*I give this a low score because combat is just slightly TOO simple -- almost all encounters are won with by simply kiting the enemy, doing some easy parries, and launching some re-branded magic missiles. HOWEVER, I want to be clear that combat is not the main component of the game! I personally would like for it to have been designed differently, but I also played too much Sekiro, so... I wouldn't let that stop you from playing this game. It doesn't have complex combat because that isn't the point, and they were right to make this decision. Exploration: 9.5/10While not every location is as rewarding as it possibly could be, exploration is this game is incredible. Everything is spaced pretty much exactly how I felt it should be, nothing seems just impossible to find, and what you find in most locations is... incredible. bizarre. There's several times where what I found caused me to shout "What in the name of God!?" and I was stunned and enthralled by what I found. Also floating sky islands cool as hell.Story and Quest Writing: 9/10So far the stories and quests have been fantastic. Lots of interesting, and sometimes tough, decisions to make. Some good twists and stunning moments that have stuck with me. Several quests have made me wonder if I made the right call, if I shouldn't have gone the other way. I feel compelled to understand the world more and the people in it. RPG Elements / Character Customization: 6/10The RPG elements do slightly less than I want them to in the world, but nothing is particularly wrong about it. It's not that hard to level enough that you can just pass most checks without a problem, so sometimes it feels like my character's traits and history don't really matter -- then again, maybe that's okay. I wish I could customize more aspects of my character, but the game's not hurting for its absence. Average and serviceable, does what it needs to do without bloat or frills. Dialogue: 7/10Above average. There's nothing wrong with the dialogue, and it's certainly not bad -- but there's not a lot special about it. Characters have some personality through their speech, but it's not major. Setting and Worldbuilding: 9.5/10Insanely well done. I am blown away by how interesting and weird this world is. Everything is wacky and strange, but in a way that doesn't feel like someone spammed ideas that were incoherent, or didn't play well together. The world is a manicured combination of fantasy and insanity that feels internally consistent to an incredible degree. The history all makes sense and is fascinating. I wonder what it means, the Neuron Star and the Dreamers and the Gods -- and who caused the World Rend? How and why?Graphics and Art: 7/10Now, I personally love this graphical style. The old-school version where things relied on color and silhouette design, rather than samey "realistic" graphics where you can't tell what the hell is going on. There's a few things that I think could use a re-texture or a better model. Some of the animations could probably be reworked, as they are simple and stiff even for this art style. Music: 7/10Pretty good music! Enjoyable, but repetitive. None of the tracks are very unique, but they do fit the setting and tone well, and so far it feels totally consistent with the world and helps its vibe.My final score: 7.4 / 10. Play this weird freaky game.Also it's LITERALLY better than Starfield.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Weird ethereal blend of HP Lovecraft, Berserk following the Eclipse, The Elder Scrolls II Daggerfall, Morrowind, Arx Fatalis and King's Field. If that appeals to you, buy it now because I highly recommend it. I'm just barely scratching the surface of the game but it's huge and there's a lot to do and a lot of ways to do it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Has very strong vibes of old ps1/n64 era 3D games. Exploration is the name of the game. The world is wide and there's lots of loot and quests hidden out there. Deep dungeons, puzzles, tricks, secret passages in the walls.The moment to moment gameplay isn't exactly hard, but your hand is not held at all. It's up to you to find the quests a figure out what needs to be done. It's up to you to find the loot, find cartographers, chart your own map at vistas. Most quests have multiple options for completing them, sometimes with drastically different results and rewards.The story is very interesting and engaging, grim at times. There's no voicing, as one would expect. The worldbuilding is fantastic.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: So I'm only a few hours in, but I'm less than enthused about what the game really has to offer, what at some points feels like it could be a fantastical world rife with all sorts of fun things to discover is in a word: Empty!The reward structure for this game lies in its exploration. You are incentivized to poke into nooks and crannies of the world and get really stuck in, finding rewards that level you up, and disincentivized to participate in combat since you don't get all that many rewards from it. This is a good thing, combat in this game is boring, and uninteresting.What is not ok is how very little there is to really get your hooks into with exploration! The world has huge potential, and the art direction is unique enough that I can appreciate it even if it isn't entirely to my taste, but the environmental story telling kinda falls through with this game. There's a whole host of ruins mines and abandoned crap shacks that dot the land, but they're just kinda... there, and they end up blending into one another, with no ties to anything that goes on.I still plan on finishing this game, but I've reached a point now where I realize i'm not exactly engaged with it.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I rarely take the time to review games, but since I'm part of the early access buyers, I thought I should help however I can.I've been itchy for a Morrowind type game (which was a masterpiece IMO) for quite some time now. I remember fondly playing Morrowind with my older brother, being confused and amazed by this alien world that is so rewarding to tame and explore.Dread delusion scratches that itch. It uses concepts from Lovecraft/ eldritch horror, uses Morrowind as a framework for building the world exploration, it also rewards heavily free exploration, all delivered in a very charming visual style. Sure, there are a few downsides and weaknesses, but I'm sure most of it will be fixed by the full release. I won't be giving a note since it still is in early access, but I definitely recommend to anyone whose eye it catched. If you feel like it's your kind of game, buy it. You won't regret it. Plus, the price is reasonable.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I was initially apprehensive about recommending this game, but having found myself thinking positively about it months after finishing it, I now realize that I enjoyed it overall. In summary, it felt like experiencing Morrowind for the first time, but with an added layer of bizarreness - like playing through a dream. The world, the atmosphere, the story, and the quests are all deeply engaging. Even the interaction with the quite static NPCs was enjoyable. My only issue (and the reason I hesitated to recommend it in the first place) is: the combat.On "normal" difficulty, encounters were far too easy. That's disappointing, not just because of the lack of challenge, but because the game offers so many creative ways to approach encounters. Unfortunately, these options feel wasted when straightforward combat works too well and has practically no risk.  Overall, it's a fantastic experience in a remarkable world. Just be sure to crank up the difficulty when you start.

I really enjoyed this game and it not a 10/10 for sure but idk even with all the floors in it the fun i had running around and doing quests and seeing this world make up for it for me.Its not a game for everyone but a game never should be.
