_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion is a solid RPG with an very interesting setting and strong atmosphere; especially for the price of $20 US. I really liked it all throughout my playthrough, but I do have some complaints about it. I would recommend this at full price, and I look forward to future games made by this developer whether that be a sequel or something new. I did buy this during the start of early access so my time is actually closer to 30 hours to complete both the main story and all side quests, as well as secret hunting.As with the vast majority of RPGs, you have various stats and skills that govern what your character can and can't do. However, this game is heavily streamlined when it comes to how many there are and the range of equipment and weapons. You have four main attributes that then determine two skills each. Whenever you level up, you increase one attribute by one point to a max of 10, but there isn't enough experience points in the game to max out everything, so be careful when leveling because you can't respec. I both like and dislike this setup. On one hand, each skill is more important and each can have multiple uses such as Might being used to determine max health, melee weapon damage, and breaking down destructible doors. On the other hand, many skills are over powered and under powered such as the charm skill is the only skill used to persuade characters which is really strong, but the Defense skill is worthless because Agility increases movement speed and you will easily outrun any enemy attack and never be hit. Skills could have done with a minor rework such as incorporating more skills into dialogue, and give agility some other function like boosting attack speed by a small amount. You then have equipment which comes in a few categories: A head slot, chest slot, two rings, two trinkets. You might think that's a lot, but it feels underused. Sure each piece gives a unique effects and all of them have a use which is great, but there isn't much, or too much for specific niches. For example: there is a hat, one of 6 in the entire game, that increases charm and a trinket that give you a small chance to pass speech checks, but there are a lot of equipment for controlling or summoning monsters to the point that I think you can fill out every slot with just those. I did like that you could upgrade your equipment, but this wasn't universal, and you had no reason not to which results in your armor sections looking sparse.As for the rest, you get two weapon slots, six spell slots, and six item slots. These are fine, and I think the options are serviceable if limited, but combat poses no challenge to you after you level up a little. There is only one difficulty for the game, and it's on the easier side with me only dying due to falling off ledges that I rocket off of due to my insane movement speed. Ranged combat is especially broken since melee enemies can't catch you and you can easily dodge ranged attacks. You'll also be drowning in items such as healing potions or skill buff items since the game is littered with them in almost every turn. Speaking of items, you can also do some limited crafting which ranges from making new potions to upgrading the quality of the treasure you find, but the economy is broken once you figure out what makes what.It's about time I should mention that this is structured as an open world, exploration focused, game in which the only way to level up is by finding secrets and completing quest. Enemies only drop items upon death. I actually really like this system since it doesn't penalize you for sneaking past enemies, and reward those who put in the effort to explore. Your only limiting factor for exploring the world are bridges that require an item to pass, and very late game areas being locked behind story progression. To further incentivise exploration, fast travel is limited to a select few spots throughout the map and require starting a quest in order to activate them. There is also a player house system where you can buy an upgradable house in each of the three regions, but I would recommend mainly using the mansion which will be the first one you come across. There are also other fun systems such as , but I'll stop myself here. Except, for one last note, the game auto-saves often with no option for manual saves, but there are multiple save slots for separate playthroughs. This might be a deal breaker for some, even I question it, but I don't think it hurts the game much since if you get stuck/quit or die, you'll automatically re-spawn in a safe location.From the above, you might think this game doesn't sound too good. Admittedly, the gameplay is unbalanced in your favor, but its still fun to play. It can be fun to run around the country side at mach 5 and summoning multiple skeletons to fight enemies for you, and so on. In other words, the gameplay is broken, but not in a way that makes it un-fun like damage sponge enemies or mindless grinding in other games.This section will be light on details since I don't want to spoil anything aside from the setup. You wake up in a cell and are given three choices to determine the starting stats of your character. You're then released from your cell under the condition that you help your former jailers to track down and capture an extremely dangerous criminal, and you don't have the option to run way since your trapped on a series of floating islands. From here, the story branches out in a non-linear fashion in which you are given your objectives and you can do them in any order you want. In addition to the main story that'll take you all throughout the world, each of the three regions have their own overarching quest line that effects your ending, and various side quests to complete. I really enjoyed the quests and main story since they do a fairly good job at fleshing out the world and its character, as well as posing moral and philosophical questions for you to answer. The setting is very unique and well built for you to slowly uncover as you explore, read books, and talk to people. I only have a few minor gripes with this section. That being, I think most towns were a bit on the small side, except for  which was the only one I felt like was a good sized city with numerous NPCs. Ironically, the region with that city also felt the most sparse with quests and most arduous to traverse since it was so big. Additionally, I felt like some quests could have had multiple endings, but didn't for some reason. One in particular, , irked me since it made you do something stupid to progress the quest and because of that, makes you do one of two bad options to finish it. That quest is still interesting with a hard choice, but the road to that wasn't the best.Again, I want to reiterate that I recommend this game and think its really good, even with its faults. I wish I could go into more detail, but I don't want to spoil too much. My desire to not spoil anything should be a good indicator to how much I liked this setting and the stories within it.I wish this wasn't the final section I was going to end on, but I want to note that the above is more or less set and are a larger determining factor in getting the game than the bugs here which can be fixed. And the dev has already fixed some since the release, and none of these stopped me, or made me have to reload, so I consider them mostly minor. here's a few: I have had enemies not able to hit me, rare path finding issues, objects rotated at weird angles such as an elevator platform turned sideways, a late game optional area being inaccessible due to collision, and two achievements not triggering. The most common issue I ran into was load zones that would pause every time I crossed them.In short, this is a fun RPG.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I've been going back and forth on my opinion on this; I considering refunding at the 2 hour mark, but decided to push through. But there was a specific point that pushed me over the edge, so let me paint a picture.In the middle of a quest, you have to step through a portal to enter some weird void dimension or something. As I interact with the portal, excited to see what's on the other side, my character just... keeps standing there. Text starts appearing, *describing* what's in the portal, never actually going through. My character finds and has a whole conversation with a character in the void dimension, and not a single visual is shown.Now I understand using some flavor-text to help where visuals might be too difficult (ex. character expressions and whatnot). But to not give any visuals to what's happening here just rubbed me the wrong way. Couldn't we be warped into some void-texture skybox or something, at the very least?Like I said, this is just a detail that pushed me over the edge; it's not some dealbreaker. But it kind of put in perspective that nothing is really keeping me hooked in the gameplay loop, and I don't have anything to look forward to.There's two fundamental flaws that break the gameplay loop.1. Combat is braindead simple. You will never be killed by an enemy, or by anything really. My one and only death was 10 hours in after falling of a cliff and not activating a spell to save me in time.2. There is almost nothing worth exploring. Either there's nothing there (besides potions/lockpicks/ammo), it's a locked-off location for a quest, or a 1/10 chance of it having an actually unique and interesting item. However, since combat is so easy, anything you find that's combat related is essentially useless. Who cares if you found a better sword if you can just kite everything anyway? (Oh wait I lied, I have the same sword I started with (upgraded)). Or better yet, just run past literally every enemy since they don't drop anything useful and don't give experience.So the only thing left to do is quests, but all the quests are just "go here", which is usually a giant unmissable location solely dedicated to that quest that's like a 5 minute walk away. But all you get out of quests are usually random junk. So it's like, what am I even walking across all these empty areas for?I don't know. I want to believe there's more here, but I feel like I can't get back in the groove with this, now that I'm aware of the gameplay loop problem. I just wanted to fly a flying pirate ship :(Edit: I continued to play into what I assumed was the final area, putting all my stats into agility + using the run fast spell so I could run at 200mph. After completing the area, I finally got the flying ship, which was pretty underwhelming. You can fly and drop anchor anywhere in the world, which is cool, but the problem is that *I've already explored everywhere". Quite literally the only places left to explore are the two airship-only islands (one of which is currenty bugged and won't let me inside the main building) and the final area.So unfortunately I was right; there was nothing for me to look forward to.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Would I recommend this game? Yes! Are there problems? Yeah.But first, the good:- The artstyle is fantastic, the world is cool, vibrant and strange- Visual designs of creatures and structures are all amazingly creative and beautifully executed- The atmosphere is also great, it's very easy to spend hours upon hours just exploring this strange world.Now, to the problems:- Big stutters when loading between areas. This is being addressed, I believe.- Various small collision glitches. The end game suffers from it the most, it seems.  - Finally, some of my own opinions, which are just a matter of taste, I guess.- The writing is not exactly in my taste, but it's still pretty good. Some characters were enticing.- The fighting is incredibly easy and easily avoidable. - Some people had a problem with skill checks, but I kinda like them. - The notion that the world is barren, which you will find in many negative reviews to this game - well, there is a lot of space without structures, just hills and trees, especially in  This is sort of mitigated by your high speed and several teleportation methods. Also, most places, even empty, usually have a stunning view.All structures, are, however, fairly simplistic. There are certainly creative ideas, especially near the beginning and middle sections of the game, but generally they are very straightforward and feel linear  In my opinion, what this game gains in breadth, it lacks in depth. Which is understandable, given the limited resources.- Finally, there are some parts, which were obviously not finished. Despite all this, I had a great time playing the game. It's very expansive, that is why there's so many things to critique and much many more to praise. It's just that when you're criticising something, it's easy to have many individual points, but praise usually addresses the generalities. Still, I hope these issues get fixed. Good luck!To the consumer - buy it and try for yourself! I loved it a lot.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Judging by my achievements, no one has actually played this game.That being said, I like it. If you like Morrowind vibes, PSX graphics, interesting story and lore, and exploration for exploration's sake, this is a really good game. Some areas also have a real MediEvil vibe to them. If you want complex rpg elements and deep combat, this probably isn't for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Works well on Steam Deck. Some find that it doesn't run well for them, but I got a consistent 40 FPS.I really like what this game does with its presentation and world building. The world on display here is so much fun to learn about, and I wish I could have learned about it even more. Unfortunately, the game just wasn't that much fun to play. I think this game would be a great novel, or a great video essay. But PLAYING IT, I found myself consistently frustrated by the complete lack of challenge and worthwhile rewards for exploration.The main driving force behind exploration are level-ups, which you do not actually need as the game is ridiculously easy. It really doesn't need to be this easy. Why is it this easy? The places you stumble upon themselves are sometimes worth a visit, but sometimes they're kind of just boring paths to level ups. It was much more fun to rush the main story for me. That's not a great sign for me in an RPG.The presentation is great though. I love the design of the enemies, the design of the environments, and the sound design! For a fan of RPGS, I wouldn't recommend this game. For a fan of VIBES, I definitely would.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This game feels like the developer(s?) played arx fatalis, deus ex and some of the older TES titles, liked them, did not understand *what* it was that they liked about those games and decided to use them as a source of inspiration for their own game. It feels like there was a lot of effort put into the visuals and lore/worldbuilding/writing, but literally nothing else.I got into this game with mediocre expectations but they fell pretty steep when I encountered a certain guard tower just a few minutes after finishing the "tutorial" part where I could see loot in the bottom part of the tower, locked behind a gate. Despite this game having lockpicks and a lockpick mechanic with RPG elements like many games of this type do, the lock cannot be picked. So I walk around the tower and don't see any other way in except maybe up the stairs. I go up the stairs and there's a drunk guard of a faction which attacks me on sight telling me "eh, whatever, i wont attack you, but i also won't give you the key to downstairs."In literally any other game of this genre that presents you with such a scenario you would be able to do atleast two of the following:In this game? Have a charm skill of 40 or above or give up. For some reason this drunkard >hostile< guard of all people is invincible and there is no other choice presented to you despite this being literally THE type of early game encounter you should use to show people that multiple approaches can work, which SEEMS like what the game was going for based on the lockpicking, loremaster and stealth sections of the tutorial. Exploration in general is very poorly rewarded, all you ever find is these ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ flasks/throwing knives/arrows that you'll have 50 each of within 10 minutes of playing. Melee combat is just leftclick spam and basic backwards walking to not get hit.Based on the other reviews, it seems like very little has been done throughout almost 2 years of early access to address any of these points in a significant manner and I saw a notification recently saying the game is coming out of early access soon, but I do not know why. This game has an incredibly weak start, is very bland and feels like it was made by people (or one guy i dont know) who were interested in making cool 3d designs rather than people interested in making a game, let alone an open world RPG. no recommend from me!
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion is a great example of a game where the developer has really poured a ton of detail into every part of their lovingly handcrafted world. The map is already pretty sizable, and it's not even finished yet. But the real draw to this game (for me at least) is how there is a secret around every corner, and also buried under that corner, and maybe also on an island flying above that corner. There's a lot to see, is what I'm saying.I have nearly 10 hours played so far in the game, and most of that was in a single play session, because I was very motivated to see what there was to see in the next area I was running to. The story is interesting and leaves you with a lot of Actual Choices (imagine that) which do have real impacts. Definitely a game worth experiencing for yourself!
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't want to give a negative review.  This game has many of the things I value highly - unique setting, original story, unusual aesthetics - but it also contains multiple dealbreakers - real life politics, inconsistent writing, idiotic quest conclusions.The frustrating thing is that the START of each quest and storyline is solid, only to be fumbled right at the finish line.The good:You can tell from the store page alone how unusual the world is.The mediocre:Gameplay isn't good, but not terrible.  With a good story to drive it, the gameplay would be adequate.The dealbreakers:Real Life Sexual Politics.  In a world that's suffered massive depopulation due to past and ongoing apocalypses, you would think that same sex relations would at a bare minimum raise a few eyebrows.  Instead, you not only have multiple same sex relations (as common if not MORE so than opposite sex relations), you also have formerly heterosexual widowers taking same sex lovers without raising eyebrows.  I'm not saying same sex relations are unrealistic or that they should be discriminated against, but in the context of a totalitarian fascist cult vs an anarchist religious cult, it's a bit weird that such relations have zero consequences, without any worldbuilding justification.  There's also a token trans, token parapeligic, ALL of the 'strongest' and 'smartest' characters are girl bosses... With good character writing or good worldbuilding, this would be a positive, but without that it's just unimmersive tokenism.Inconsistent WritingThe biggest example I've noticed is the Last Emperean (emberian?) has some dialogue spelling out that she's lived only a single lifespan, but other dialogue saying she's lived multiple generations.  It's like the backstory of the characters was rewritten multiple times but the dialogue never got updated to reflect that.  Idiotic Quest ConclusionsFlesh Farm Quest: There's no moral dilemna.  Obviously, making one sentient flesh farm suffer non lethal nibbling is better than untold hundreds of peasants being permanently devoured.  Why the suffering of one creature is considered equivalent to the murder of hundreds is beyond me.  Worse, there are likely better solutions.  Would anaesthetic alleviate the suffering of the flesh farm?  What about booze?  And why am I not allowed to attack the leader who things eating innocents is morally justified?The Hand: Gee, it never occurred to this genius to mention what her missing daughter looks like?  The Crystal: I have to choose to worship or destroy this being... but its priest gives me no information.  What deal does it offer?  What fuels it?  What does it hate?  Who will it 'help', and what will it's 'help' look like?  It can 'speak' to randos who aren't even it's priest, so obviously it COULD talk to the PC if it wanted to.Nurgles Castle: If one suffering dude isn't enough, and two suffering dudes are unbearable... what if every single resident shared in the suffering?  Wouldn't that bring the suffering down to a minor annoyance?  Also, has anyone considered... leaving the cursed castle?Nurgle: Which is more likely, people get sick without Nurgles help, or Nurgle makes people sick to force them to worship him?  There's no way to even ATTEMPT to find out which is the case.Clockwork King:  What's up with this all or nothing mentality?  Can't we have a 'dumb' clockwork king instead of having to choose between an 'insane smart' king or a dead king?  Also, why can a single depopulated city produce enough faith to warp the reality of the entire cosmos?  Also, why didn't the surgeon stick around long enough to uninstall the ticking time bomb implanted in the PC's skull?Cursed Statue: Why can't I turn in the obviously cursed heretical statue to the inquisition?Wikkans: Supposedly they help broker deals between mortals and supernaturals, but not once has any of them helped the PC understand or make a deal.  For such a major faction, it's weird that they never do their job.  Say what you will about the inquisition, at least they actually live their ideals.Destroy the Undead Island: Even being burned to ash doesn't cure the curse of immortality, so what makes these geniuses think falling at terminal velocity would finish the job?  The Inquisition: Seriously, can I side against these guys? Without joining a cult that's even worse? Say what you will about Fallout 4, but I appreciated having a faction who's only deal was 'we don't have a deal, we just live here.'

_childDocuments_.review: People keep saying this is a "Morrowind like something something" but only the first area has that many mushrooms. There are three kingdoms with their own problems and which ask fundamentally different questions.Gameplay is relatively simple. You walk around and interact in the world with three key skills: Lockpick, Charm, and Lore. Item balance and game design is good enough that you can't really lock yourself out of something by focusing on a single skill first.Lockpicking is a D6 die roll based on stamina and lock picking skill. There are tons of items to manipulate this into your favor.Lore is a treasure hunt for interactive objections. There is an item to help make these more visible.Charm is just a flat "You go enough?" and you get it persuasion. I have not found a Charm skill you could not retry, which is good because I forgot to equip the right hat many times.Combat is simple but not the focus of this game. You can speed past enemies, hit them with status effects, summon skellies, or just swing the big sword good.Storytelling is where this game shines. It has a well developed world with a story to tell and questions to ask the player. Is it okay to make a deal with the devil? Should we embrace our selfish instincts if it betrays our culture's social morality (RULES OF NATURE)? Is there a such thing as a good tyranny? And lots more.I've plugged like 25 hours at this point and am close to the end game. I'm going back to old areas and rediscovering new things. I've found a gear set that I enjoy and also choices that make me want to go through a second playthrough and see what my opposite actions do. There are parts where the immersion breaks with obvious fades to black while NPCs shuffle around. The world can change based on your actions but so far I've only witnessed one region does so mechanically. I like how you can upgrade several things so progression is more lateral.If I had to ask for something, please let me put pins on the map. I saw those doors I couldn't open. I can open 'em now. Please to make me remember where they were. I'll just cheat and look online cuz I already found them before.Storytelling is 9/10 - very interestingGameplay is 7/10 - mechanics seem simple yet effectiveGraphics + Art Style is 10/10 - ignoring the retro aesthetic, the art design in both 3D and 2D are excellent and uniqueAudio + Sound is 8/10 - music is minimal with a few non-atmospheric tracks, sound and atmosphere are greatLevel Design 8/10 - areas are sprawling, only a few complex dungeons, lots of natural pathing to stop you from getting lost, finding secrets is more on your spacial awareness, curiosity, and paying attention to landmarksGame Progressions + Pacing 8/10 - I never felt under powered and delusions aren't the only way to make yourself more powerful. Lots of good gear, spells, and items to assist with all your tasks. Plot didn't plod along. Talking to NPCs actually felt rewarding with nuggets of lore and side-quests.Replayability + Longevity 6/10 - You'll be able to complete everything in one go except for plot choices, so you may want to replay once or twice to see the effects of your choices. Gameplay is diverse enough to entertain different builds.Technical Performance 7/10 - They are working on it but sometimes I felt like achievements weren't popping (they have some specific cues) or I couldn't pick up an item or treasure chest unless I ♥♥♥♥♥♥ around trying to trick it into letting me. There is noticeable slowdown when LOD items transition out (and the game saves at the same time). Sometimes stuttering. This isn't bad and hasn't destroyed a save file or my enjoyment. Just not perfect.Game gets a total score of 8/10. I'm an old man dad dude in his 30s who doesn't want to put more time into something unless it gives me something back. This game is worth at least a single playthrough. Achievement hunters won't have a rough time. If I sped through it, I could have finished the game in probably ~10 hours or less but the game made me want to stop and smell the mushrooms, feed the sky dragons, and read the books littered about. Game made me think and mull over stuff. Not the same way as Undertale or LISA, not because emotional investment, but rather because of esoteric questions and personal quandaries.GAME IS GOOD

_childDocuments_.review: This is an old-school first-person RPG. Unflinchingly old-school.  old-school. If you can't look past clunky systems and stiff combat, you probably won't like this game. If you can put up with relatively frequent goofy breaks in kayfabe and an abundance of early-access jank, you'll find some of the most striking visuals and gripping world-building from pretty much any indie game I've ever played. My main criticism is actually towards the sound design -- specifically the ambient tracks. They can be pleasant, but they're very, very repetitive for how often they play. And how loud they are. I think it'd do well with the minecraft-style fading in-and-out audio style, but for the time being, turning down the music slider to almost zero fixes it well enough. It's a shame that I have to do that, but the audio doesn't follow up on the ambiance that the skybox provides. I think that all of the criticisms you'll read in the negative review section are both valid and unfair at the same time. Perhaps the devs should have made a better map, perhaps they should have made combat more dynamic, perhaps they could make it more linear, perhaps they could make it less linear...but the thing is, that's a conscious choice by the devs to evoke a certain feeling.  I very much value a games that are made with a specific, unflinching vision. Dread Delusion sticks to that vision with a rigid fanaticism -- knowing very well that it will  alienate some players. It's encouraging for an early access game to be filled with that much love; the passion that the devs have on display towards this game gets me excited for its future! And the rest of my playthrough, of course.

_childDocuments_.review: You know how there's some open world RPGs where you can get lost and but you'll often be saying to yourself: "Where the ***k do I go?"  So you either rage quit or alt-tab out to read a guide because it feels like you aren't going anywhere?Well this game is nothing like that. Whenever I get lost or side tracked, I find secrets, I find loot, I find upgrades and best of all: I find new quests and things to do. Then I can either try and figure out where to go next or just get lost again and find more secrets, loot, upgrades or new quests. Several hours later, while being lost, I'll accidentally stumble upon an old quest I picked up awhile back and complete it.All of this is done in a really beautifully designed world with PS1 stylized graphics and with relaxing fantasy music. You will often backtrack, but it's going to be worth it because there will be areas you couldn't access before that will now be accessible and reward you with rewards to make you stronger.Like many other reviewers have already pointed out, the game feels more like a walking simulator than a RPG. But if I have to put numbers on it, I would say it's a 60% walking sim and 40% RPG. I'm 10 hours in and I think I'm only halfway through the game. If the game is really only 15 hours long, then I will explore and find every tiny secret this game has to offer because I DON'T WANT IT TO END! This is one of the most fun indie game I played on Steam this year so far.

_childDocuments_.review: B-tier walking simulator most of the time.  Morrowind's influence is obvious here, but Morrowind is just a better, more refined experience to play through.-Single/very-small dev team, so most of the issues get a pass, with a big kudos for representing a genre currently lacking originality.  It's a great first step that's missing quality of life features and some better direction.  To get the most out of the game, you really have to want to oblige their vision and have some interest in the setting.  In that regard, the world and its lore are both fascinating and the quests are humorous and inspired.  You'll need to read your quest logs to know your terms of completion, but be warned that some of those logs are fubar.  I.e. log told me to head to the forest in the west, but the place i needed to go was on the other side of the map in the northeast...wasted 45mins aimlessly wandering until I stumbled upon my destination.  You get lost and stuck wandering a lot, especially considering the map does not label anything (like towns or houses like "mine owners house").  Questing is your primary focus because it's the only way you level up - combat is worthless.  You get nothing from killing, which is fine.  If the focus is on questing, at least they're cool. -Experience soured for me at the end, where the game pads itself out unapologetically.  Climactic finale ends in a twist that sends you back home to start the real series of events to start the finale.  This sends you on a goose chase to get access to the final dungeon.  But you can't get what you need to access it because the door to the dungeon before the final is locked, but you can't open the door because your lore skill is too low to undo the locks so you have to go grind out quests to get a higher lore skill....really?  Say what you will but not many would like to indulge in all that nonsense - would have been more fun just to have the machine being something a monkey could operate, keep that last little push to the end flowing.  The device itself is no more than a single button, so it shouldn't exactly take a PHD in mechanical engineering to activate.-I'll be letting this one go without completing it since I don't feel like obliging those last few requirements through however long they drag on for.  I'm satisfied with what I saw and implore you to give it a go if you'd like to experience something palatable and Morrowind-flavored.  But I'll have to deny this one my seal of approval.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion is a crazy thing to talk about. It might well be one the of the best games ever made in it's genre, but it is also extremely indie, and for the genre(WRPG), very short, and in places, incomplete(I'm looking at you, godsires and crystal goddess quests). I could probably write 12-15 k words on just the writing in the game, its very very good, some would say, exquisite. While there are some problems the plot is striking in quality, even if the game is a bit railroady later in the title, I blame this on the budget. Characters and zones are 11/10 best in the house. The Lore books are all of truely perfect quality and feel as though they came from multiple authors in different times. Characters are a standout in the genre as well. Graphically this game is a HEAVILY flashy 2001 game and its a style you have to enjoy already to appreciate. Animations in this game run the full gamut of amazing and kinda stock, to just bad. The game uses crazy lighting and colors to make up for this, and frankly, it works. the style of the game is very consistent and powerful. The music is somewhat limited, but the tracks composed are perfect for the settings and the gameplay around them. Sound effects are top notch and very diverse. Very crunchy sound design help build the large complex worlds you will travel in. Things can feel sparse as you get farther in the game, but overall, sound ties the room together well. Gameplay is uh, complecated to talk about. The short version is that this game is very committed to the power fantasy and choices matter core beliefs of WRPGs to a degree where you can really make the game break in half. While this undermines the writing somewhat, I really like the commitment to being able to run around the map at mach 1 and also throw insanely powerful spells and hit like a truck. the decisions are the main purpose of the gameplay loop. This isnt bad, but it makes things *too* easy, while maybe this is solved moreso on hard mode(I played on normal), the game really wants to ask you questions in different ways, and you really can solve them any way. Stats and equipment are really cool, but they tend to work kinda like disco elysium equipment, making the core skills better and kinda carrying you through checks. I'm not a huge fan of this but it's fine.This game is legendary, make it a point to try it. 1 of the GOATS, and the main holder of the WRPG mantle. Keep Lovely Hellplace on your radar, because anything they make after this is gonna push boundries.

_childDocuments_.review: I got recommended this on the basis that it was like Morrowind and King's Field, but this was not the case. Not only is this game nothing like either of the aforementioned comparisons, but it is simply not a very good game, something I decided my feelings upon once reaching the Way of All Flesh after running through much of the sparse content.As for the comparisons, it lacks the build variety (or builds at all) of Morrowind along with any form of roleplay, it also has no real sensible world progression and there is a severe lack of depth with npc interactions and its writing. In the way of King's Field, it lacks, pretty much entirely, any of the qualities of exploration and puzzle solving which made that series and its worlds meaningful as this world is not only completely static but effectively dead.As for the game itself isolated from these comparisons, its art and music/sound design are both inconsistent in direction with a wide variation of quality in their execution. Combat is far beyond monotonous and spells offer little in the way of variety or depth for it. For example, there is no strategy with AI and dodging is worthless as you can crouch and backpedal to get them stuck in a loop of trying to approach as you wail on them from safe distance. The world is nearly entirely linear with very little life to it, and its scale is lessened greatly by the visibility of it all from the get-go (though the leader of the Inquisition does state it is a small island). The quests are not really "quests" so much as an on-rails story the game gives you regardless of choice, and there is no flexibility to how they are completed that I experienced running through the game. It is worth mentioning that there is a faction relations system in the game, but atm it is primitive to say in the least assuming it does anything at all. This game is simply under-baked, and what is halfway done here follows what is imo a design philosophy that is antithetical to the idea of fun in games of this style. I know this is early access and I appreciate the developer allowing us to view the game at the point it is at, but what has been offered is too flawed for me to recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is utterly fascinating and addictive as heck....if you know what you're getting. Thing is, I think people expect a PS1 era aesthetic Morrowind, and it's not. Think more Playstation 1 ARPG cult hits like Shadow Tower and King's Field, or maybe old very early 3D CRPGs like Ultima Underworld or a non-bad version of Descent to Undermountain. You're getting a really slow paced, chill, somewhat easy little exploration game with a veritable crap ton of cool lore and fun puzzles to solve. It's not going to impress you if you are looking for something uber difficult or has you mauling baddies every tick of the clock. It's laid back, relaxing, and has a weird vibe that you're either going to never get enough of or absolutely detest. Watch some youtube videos first, and if you loved Shadow Tower on PS1 like I did, I think you're going to love this too.

_childDocuments_.review: To start out, I had a blast playing this game. This showed up on my recommended because it's compatible with steam deck so I watched the trailer and was interesting right away. The graphics and the atmosphere were nostalgic and well made. It feels a lot like Morrowind. The combat is fairly in-depth with multiple weapon types and ways to go about combat (or not if that's your style). The story is well written and interesting, if only a bit short (25 hours to finish while doing a lot of exploration and side stuff). However, I do really appreciate how little the game tells you about the story, next objective, and characters without exhausting all dialogue options. It really makes you invest yourself in the world and the characters and makes you pay attention to little details. Especially with how little there is in terms of a wiki for this game (which is a good thing), missing a key dialogue will set you back some time and you really have to go searching for certain quest objectives. Exploring the world was probably the most fun I had playing this game because there are multiple "biomes" you can explore that all have different enemies and locations to discover. You start out not having a map at all and not knowing anything about the world which really helped immersion and you're able to take your time exploring.  There are a few points I want to cover: - The main story is really short, the endgame especially. You could probably finish it in under 15 hours if you only focussed on it. Not really a problem but when the story ended I definitely wanted more. I felt like I was just getting invested in the characters and then the story just ended. - There is a faction system in the game for some reason. I'm not really sure if there are any boons or banes to being on the good or bad side of any of them. At one point I was liked by the outlaws but the outlaws in the world still attacked me which would lower my rep with them. Then, after killing a ton of them I became hated but the outlaws still interacted with me and sold/bought items as if nothing happened. Some more quests or side objectives to do to get in their good graces besides  would be useful. Storylines exploring each faction would also be cool. There are a couple factions where you just see in the menu that you have almost no idea what they are besides monsters (i.e. goblins). - When you get to the late game you get to buy  which is awesome except that you only use it for about 3 hours before you finish the story. It would be awesome if there were more outside islands and territories that had side quests on them that you can't get to otherwise. The world is so interesting and fun to explore that I feel this was a missed opportunity. Also I was only able to find standard and endless cosmetics for the ship, not clockwork or mushroom or anything else. Not sure if that was intentional or if they are unlocked somehow. I would recommend this game to anyone that likes old style graphics and minimal guidance. I had a very positive experience with this game and definitely feel it is worth the money. The devs did a great job on this and you can tell a lot of work went into every aspect of this game. My only complaint was that it wasn't longer.

_childDocuments_.review: I changed my review after finishing the game. Everything i said in the original is still true for the first 2/3 of the game. But the last third is great, quest are much deeper, it still relies a little too much on skill checks, but at least now quest are pretty long, you have to move around the map and talk to different npcs, and it finally achieves the feeling of having multiple ways to solve problems. Even if those solutions end up being single skill checks. Airship is fun, but the segment is short, and story finishes in a great way, there's great vibes and atmosphere and i really enjoyed the last few hours because of improved gameplay *and* writing. This would've genuinely be an amazing rpg, if the first 2/3 were as good as the clockwork kingdom and the end of the story.original review:I wish i could recommend this. It's very close to being a good game, but it's just... lazy? I don't want to use that word for an indie game, but that's how feel after almost every quest in the game. Because it's never actually interesting, it's always lockpick/lore/charm and it instantly solves every problem. It's never "charm opens up a new side quest that you need to do in order to gain trust of this character that then will help you do your thing" it's just "pass this skill check to solve the thing completely". Every battle is extremely easy even without leveling any battle skills, and then you have items that improve your skill checks, and they improve them a lot. Like you get 5 lockpick skill per level put in dex or whatever it's called, and the hat gives you +30. That is 6 levels. I'm level 15 after 12 hours of gameplay, and these hats just cover 6 levels in respective stats each. I already have all three for main skill checks, and most of the time i don't even have to swap them, because even my third worst stat in charm is almost always enough to pass a skill check. And yeah, you pretty much always have multiple solutions in the most boring way possible. Chose this skill check or the other one, to instantly solve the problem. There's no depth to any of these quests, no thinking involved. You just run for a few minutes, ignore the enemies, skill check, done. Maybe run back to finish the quest. There's a lot of writing, and it's pretty decent, but it's so hard to get interested in it, when you do the same thing over and over and over again. Honestly i don't see how having 7 quests of the same nature that are solved by a single skill check is better than having one solid quest that actually has multiple engaging solutions. I understand that the game would be a lot shorter this way, but that would also make it way more intersting.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has an amazing atmosphere, compelling setting and the sort of mystery and intrigue that's very reminiscent of Morrowind. I can't in good conscience recommend it however, because of its rather subtle but insidious woke nature. While it doesn't embrace the fringe political nature of many modern triple a games, still the story seems infected with your typical modern politicking. -The strong fighter characters of course a woman; in fact you will find that all major characters are women,   except for one male character who is of course a crippled skinny nincompoop because you can't have threatening male characters anymore. -the story is presented as a philosophical one, however you will find that most of your choices revolve around an emotional spectrum and not a logical one, thus making many of the choices seem flaccid in the end, especially when there are no real repercussions.-only two relationships really pop up in the story in a meaningful way, and both of which are of course homosexual/lesbian. -there's the addition of a few characters in the story that don't seem to fit in the world, for example there is a city that is all mechanical themed, everyone there is Slavic-ish with a hint of 40k mechanicus styled flair, but the king's right hand man and most trusted advisor is some Indian guy with a turban?-of course there is the addition of a few characters who used compelled speech pronouns, and while you never have conversations but any other character in the third person, the developer of this game felt it necessary that you refer with every line of dialogue that you choose to them as "they/them" even though they are clearly women, even the character models are not ambiguous, it's just straight up bald female models.-I noticed that the vast majority of characters who recall traumatic events, such as family members killing one another, or civil war, etc. is almost exclusively the female characters that overpower the men, even in one case a little girl who overpowers her father. Now of course this is a universe with magic, but that falls a little short of compelling considering the clear bias of the developer. All in all, this game has a very beautiful setting and it would be nice to see a sequel done with more focus on better gameplay and perhaps having a professional writer continue the story without all the personal political agenda of the developer. It's been decent to play, but left a bitter taste in my mouth, with all the potential here I feel devastated. Would give it a solid 7/10 if not for the woke agenda, only a 3/10 as it stands. Perhaps get it on sale, and be aware of the aforementioned issues I listed above.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion's strong suits are exploration, world-building and decision-making. The combat is understimulating, however everything else carries the game so hard that I was not left wanting a deeper system. Exploring, doing puzzles, and reading lore books was more than enough for me to feel immersed and intrigued. Dread Delusion has some of my favourite premises of any RPG. There are existential themes at almost every turn, and I found that very appealing and refreshing. The aesthetics are other-wordly to match. All in all, a fantastic RPG!

_childDocuments_.review: For only 15 or 20 bucks you can get a solid 7-10 hours out of what's currently in the game. The combat is pretty plain, so don't go in expecting much in that department. The writing, choices, and lore make up for it. It's a really unique world. I played about a year after it was released into early access and it still isn't complete, but comparing what I've seen to a year ago they are in fact making progress.

You may get these bugs only ten minutes in and be lucky enough to generate a new save and fix them. You may get these bugs six hours in and only then realize the questline you chose softlocked your game because you happened to get the bug which spawns merchants with no items, and the only way to progress is through buying an item from a merchant.Whelp, it was good while it lasted. Thank god I got it while it was on sale because I will never be playing it again. I get early access and all, but if most of your playerbase is having the exact same issue with your game, that being massively game breaking bugs which they cannot be aware of until it is too late, then maybe you should fix your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game instead of trying to update and create new areas. Areas we will never get to explore because a large portion of players experience bugs which prevent them from reaching these areas but don't realize how poorly programmed the game is until it is too late to refund.Just buy Morrow instead. _childDocuments_.review: Genuinely cannot recommend this game enough.I guess, before anything else: Combat is... serviceable, and the game is fairly easy and only gets easier the more stuff and weapons you collect or upgrade, but where the real focus lies is the big, *incredibly* well crafted setting, written by someone who clearly cares deeply about every aspect of it.Characters I wanted to talk to, to get every little line of dialogue out of, to learn more about the world and the people in it. Little things to find in the wild, hidden doors in houses, books and historical documents, a lot of everything, everywhere. An incredibly well executed main quest with memorable characters in every major location. Genuinely conflicting moral choices, expertly built-up to. A visual feast of gorgeous & gloomy environments and grotesque and sometimes strangely beautiful creatures and gods. Big Mushrooms.I dunno what to tell you, this game just hit me in all the right places. And there's so much of it!! I ended up somewhere in the mid-30s, hour-wise, after doing every single sidequest, 99% of the main quests, and exploring until I was vaguely satisfied and felt like I'd seen everything there was to see, and I sure didn't expect it to keep me going and invested for nearly that long, but sure enough!! it did!!As I write this, I only have (what seems to be) the very final main quest left to do, and that makes me genuinely feel a little melancholy, because it means there won't be any more things to discover, but, heck, I'm also incredibly happy to have experienced the game at all - sure as hell didn't expect it to be possibly my favorite game I played this year, but here we are!!

_childDocuments_.review: This game, Dread Delusion, is .When I started the game, I expected a relatively linear first-person RPG experience on par with similar titles that are vaguely "King's Field"-like. What I got was something more open-ended, like a smaller-scale Elder Scrolls with less freedom but better writing and world-building.Dread Delusion has a certain vibe to it, an impeccable ambiance that could be likened to a particularly strange dream. Most characters have a few lines of dialogue at most, but altogether they sell the overall story of the environment around them, of a backwater series of sky islands, shattered by war, famine, political maneuvering, and magic perils, be they man-made or divine. These people may have killed their gods, but their influence lingers as various factions try to restore or suppress them.While combat is common in this game, I wouldn't say it's a major focus. It's simplistic at best. You're better off leveling Guile, Wisdom, and Persona over Might. Where Dread Delusion truly shines is its lore and questlines. Take some time to read the descriptions of potions and magic spells and you'll find humorous and thought-provoking descriptions.The game often has choices at the end of most quests. The outcomes and rewards may be superficial like other games do, but what's actually impressive is that the choices are legitimate crossroads that make you pause. Moral problems to reflect on your thoughts. How far do you value individual rights over the needs of the many? What determines the value of one entity over another? How many lies are worth preventing a massive tragedy?You won't get much out of this game if you're only here for gameplay; you need to commit to immersing yourself to get the most out of it. There are no quest markers; you have to figure out where to go from quest descriptions, signs, and dialogue. That means reading! Exploration! The game rewards you for paying attention. Secrets are hidden everywhere, and the way to find many of them is to remember what NPCs say or what the environment interactions tell you.I became interested in Dread Delusion based off its similarities to another game I recommend, Lunacid. While they are comparable, they play differently enough to stand on their own merits as excellent games. If you liked one, chances are you'd enjoy the other.

_childDocuments_.review: It's hard to describe why this game resonates so much with me, but playing it, exploring the world, talking to the NPCs and leveling my character gave me one of the most fun experience with a game I have had in a while.It's a relatively small RPG, especially compared to most RPG experiences nowadays. But it knows what it wants to do and it's doing it well. The world is filled with content and details. It doesn't unnessesairily draw itself out. Combat feels comfy and you can experiment quite a bit between different weapons and spells. It's not hard or complex by any means but it's fun and that's what mattered to me.Exploration is at most times rewarding enough and the fast and responsive movement makes it fun to just speed through the world. I was enticed by the story, the design, the aesthetic in general and wasn't let down at all.All in all this game was incredibly fun in the best ways and it surprisingly scratched the King's Field itch I have in a similar way that Lunacid did.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion is my favorite walking simulator.Jokes aside, I played this for the narrative plus worldbuilding and it did not disappoint in that regard. The game would feel fight at home with RPGs of the 90s and early 2000s. It's presentation is intentionally retro with small textures, low-poly models and low fidelity audio, and it combines fantasy, science fiction, horror and a dash of humor. Exploring this strange, sometimes unsettling world rewards you with alternate paths and shortcuts, books containing lore, or even floating skulls that serve as experience points. All your attributes can help with exploration: you could pick a lock or break open the door, find a secret way in or talk someone into letting you through. Also, there's no quest pointers, you gotta work for your map and you must actively use a compass item to orient yourself. The spells Agility's Addendum and Return Home are especially useful.Your decisions throughout the game's quests influence the ending and I often had to think about what might be the right choice to make, as they're not usually black-and-white. The dialogue has an amazing humanity and some parts even got me emotional. The actual quests themselves are a bit linear but that didn't take away from my enjoyment.If you're looking for interesting combat, you might be very disappointed: while there are multiple options to deal with enemies via blades, arrows, throwing knives and bombs, I found it a lot more exciting to sneak or run past enemies and avoid combat altogether. This might be an intentional design choice to encourage you to not simply fight your way through problems, however. If all this sounds up your alley, you should consider giving it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: is a ps1 style take on Morrowind that'd genuinely be better off as a regular adventure game. The combat is simultaneously dreadful and mind-numbingly easy ( does this kind of King's Field-like combat a lot better). Roleplaying system is barebones. There's only three useful spells in the entire game and none of them are combat spells. Exploration and searching for secrets start off strong until you get into a habit of hypersprinting to swiftly check every nook and cranny, and realize most hidden secrets only require pressing some hidden switches, rinse and repeat ad infinitum. Save system is annoying, if you ever close the game you get teleported to the last activated check point half a world away.   is a horrible, janky take on Morrowind. I liked it a lot.Delicious weirdness and enchanting strangeness permeate the world of . Learning the inner workings, politics and customs of Oneiric Isles was a joy, From sprawling hallowed mushroom grooves to dystopian bureaucracy of Clockwork Kingdom, it gripped my curiosity and never let go. Story and characters seemed perfunctory at first, but by the end I was fairly invested in the bittersweet drama of it all. Some side-stories and situations are incredibly memorable. . Writing's pretty solid, too. Also, I am an astonishingly literary dog and I appreciate writers stuffing the game dialogue with Borges, Brecht and Butler references. Please, be impressed with my refinement. And while my natural instinct is to mercilessly hate on PS1-stylized graphics, this art style suits the tattered world of flying islands perfectly. was a hit for me, but it'll probably be a miss for a lot of people, and for good reasons, too. I wish it was a more self-contained adventure game instead of an open world RPG, though.

_childDocuments_.review: This is by far one of my favorite games of the year, and I wasn't expecting much when I picked it up.Dread Delusion is a first person RPG, and it's not a complicated one at that; you will not find complex character builds, nor a myriad of status effects, equipment or a sprawling combat system you have to master. Indeed, these mechanics are simple, and I found that surprisingly refreshing. The usefulness of your major attributes are limited to lockpicking doors, finding switches (which is frankly just another way of unlocking doors), charming people and security measures (you guessed it, unlocks doors) and the usual combat and spell casting. It might sound tedious, and it might have been, if this particular gameplay was the focus of the game. It is not.In fact, the way the game distills these things into easily digestible information allowed me to relax and focus on what it actually does extraordinarily well: worldbuilding and story. It's been a long time since I have just opened a random game and found myself captivated by the creativity and prose as I did with Dread Delusion. The gods are dead? Why? How? Who is Vela Callose and why should I care? It actually delivers. Nothing "just happens". How were the gods like when they ruled this world? How did people structure themselves around it? How were these wars fought? While it sometimes tells when it could show, it tells extremely well.And while the quests do not have a myriad of choices and  variables, ending more often than not in a pick between A and B, they have depth, and meaning, and are supported by amazing writing and actually believable characters and situations. I can recall several times where I froze for several minutes just deciding what I wanted to do when I started said quest with a pretty clear picture of how the cookie was going to crumble.Another big selling pointing is just how cool everything looks. It has that retro aesthetic to it, which I personally like. But that aside, everything is so colorful and just interesting: the sky is trippy, the vegetation with fungi and weird stems, the islands floating on the red horizon, the environment changing between the islands. It's fun, and the world acknowledges it and makes it believable instead of being just little quirks for the sake of looks.The soundtrack isn't very varied. It pretty much different themes for each of the main areas, with a few exceptions, and that's it. I found the themes of the starting and main islands particularly good, though, with a great blend of mysterious and soothing, making it enjoyable and not taxing on the ears even after several hours, and adding a lot to the experience of exploration.The combat is simple but serviceable. A few charge attacks and most everything will fall, making it more of a chore than a challenge. I appreciate the fast running speed and agility boosting magics, too, because the game, while having a few fast travel methods, is very restrictive in that regard. The map, too, is clunky and not very useful at all. This is one of those games where you kind of end up memorizing where everything is; which is not that hard, since the maps are deceptively small once you start running from one place to the other.I had some amazing 35 hours with Dread Delusion. This feels like a world someone carefully crafted for years before successfully transposing it into a videogame, and it shows. It's an easy recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion asks the question: how much detail and complexity can you strip from The Elder Scrolls and still have a compelling experience? The answer: quite a lot, actually. A chunky, accessible RPG that boils down open-world RPG adventuring to its essentials and weds those systems to a weird realm of gods and steampunk beureaucrats, Dread Delusion is an engrossing game that feels like Morrowind if Morrowind wasn't such a chore to play. It's not especially difficult, however, so it's easier to recommend to people who like to explore fantastical settings than those who want a deep, challenging role-playing experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: An enjoyably unique romp through a creative and bleak world. The worldbuilding is interesting all throughout, and the character writing builds in confidence and quality as the game goes on.The combat is ranges from simplistic to trivial, harkening back to King's Field in a way that is a bit less than interesting for today's players. But, while there are plenty of other games that do combat well, few handle the world as well as this one does. Just know what you're in for and don't expect it to be something it's not.I enjoyed my time with this, even with that caveat. It scratched that Morrowind itch in my brain very well in terms of aesthetics and vibe, even if not in gameplay, and I really want to see more in this vein.

_childDocuments_.review: An explanation of playing for 27 hours then leaving negative review: I played through the Early Access last year, before the Clockwork Kingdom update and of course before the 1.0 release. I enjoyed it at the time, and in fact I still enjoy Dread Delusion. But serious bugs and performance issues mean I feel like I have to leave a negative review in order to be fair to the people who are considering a purchase. Internet hubbub and other reviews see Dread Delusion compared to both Morrowind and Lunacid. It comes out alright in the comparison. Like Morrowind, there are mushrooms and freaks; like Lunacid, there are banging tunes and an attractively low-poly "retro" aesthetic which never really existed, but feels like it could have. I think it's worth pointing out that Dread Delusion has even fewer RPG elements than Lunacid — it's really an adventure game at its core, with a veneer of RPG elements to help give a feeling of progression and gatekeep some cool toys behind speech checks and locked doors. It's only "souls-like" in that it imitates Kings Field (which if you haven't heard of it was an early Fromsoft game and a precursor to the Dark Souls series). It also  isn't a "metroidvania" at all, but I've given up on the battle of defining "metroidvania". Combat is also extremely simple, so the main draw of Dread Delusion is wandering around the weird environments and talking to strange people.Unfortunately, a game which depends on its walking and talking is going to be seriously hurt by any issues with its walking and talking. I don't recall too many crippling issues with the 10 hours I played of Dread Delusion in EA, but in the 18 hours I've spent with the 1.0 release almost every major quest has failed in some way. Some of them were benign — sidequests turning out the wrong way because the dialogue tree misfired isn't a major issue — but others have essentially rendered the game unfinishable. The game didn't recognize when I attained the passport that let me out of the starting area; it didn't recognize when I recruited the first major NPC in the first major area; it didn't recognize me entering the Clockwork Kingdom or allow me to recruit the major NPC of that area; I have no idea what happened in the Endless realm but I'm pretty sure it broke entirely. Even the fairly simple faction quests in Hallowshire managed to hardlock themselves when I recovered quest items out of order. So, that's the state of things. Hotfixes have addressed some of these issues, and I hope those continue to be released. For the moment I'm going to post this review and then set Dread Delusion aside. I'll circle around in a few months and see if these problems have been resolved. I hope they will be. Dread Delusion is a game worth playing, and for you it might even be a game worth buying, but the issues are too numerous for me to ignore.TL;DR good game, shame about the bugs, buy it in 6 months when it works.

_childDocuments_.review: As of June 2024, this game can be janky at times. There are clearly bugs that need to be fixed, and I would ideally like a save system with a safety net in case of save file corruption.This game is definitely something special. I cannot think of another open-world RPG - scratch that - another RPG that evokes the whimsical and sometimes grotesque melancholy of games like Majora's Mask and American McGee's Alice. The world building and writing are both grounded and full of personality, the exploration is fun, and there are few open world RPGs that are so frictionlessly immediate.The game is pretty easy if mind your spacing, but the developers resisted the seemingly ubiquitous urge to inflate HP numbers to compensate. As a result, the relative ease of one-on-one encounters never stretches nearly far enough to become tedious.Though it's smaller in scale, there's a lot to like here for fans of the writing in games like Fallout: New Vegas. There are very few clean-cut good vs evil dialogue choices here, instead focusing on factional allegiances and differences of opinion on methodology.I hope Dread Delusion gets more polish in the coming months, but I'm also 100% on board for whatever the team at Lovely Hellplace wants to tackle next.

_childDocuments_.review: An open world RPG with more soul and character than most anything else that's coming out these days. This game takes some clear inspiration from Morrowind, but very much creates its own unique world that stands on its own, and that world is incredibly fun and rewarding to explore. It takes place in a realm filled with chaos and conflict. There is the inquisition, freshly victorious after the war, and quick to impose their rules and punishments in the interest of preserving what little remains of the world after the tumultuous conflict. And there are the gods, twisted entities stripped of most of their power, but surviving nonetheless, and offering power and stability for their own peculiar prices. The tension between these forces drives much of the structure of the game, but there are many cities and places to explore, each with their own rich culture and history to discover. Graphics - Beautifully drawn retro-style pixel graphics that perfectly suit the tone that the game is going for. It's sometimes surprising just how intricate and complicated some of the designs are considering the medium they were working with. The overall effect of them creates a totally unique atmosphere that doesn't feel like anything else I've seen or played before, which is a rarity these days and very exciting to find. Gameplay - A balance between combat, exploration, and some very basic puzzles. Combat is somewhat bare-bones, more existing as an aside to the true focus of the game; exploring the world and discovering the stories there. The exploration is perfectly executed, no matter where you find yourself looking there is always something interesting to find. Story - The game has a strong central narrative with good pacing that always feels compelling, as well as numerous individual side-stories scattered around the map waiting to be found. The world they're situated in feels real and lived-in, which adds weight to the choices that you have to make to resolve the dilemmas that come up. You often have to consider what you're willing to sacrifice, or who you want to side with, and every choice has consequences. Overall an amazing game and a great experience. Would highly recommend this for any fans of the weird and strange, or of RPGs focused on exploration and discovery.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: As of 1.0 all previous save files have been wiped, so this entire review could change. Time to start over?Dread Delusion is a retro RPG, often compared to Morrowind, but don't be fooled, this is not Morrowind 2. There are no complex mechanics, groundbreaking visuals or intense combat. This game however is packed with cool stuff, a VERY interesting world and storyline, fun quests, cool items... all in that retro package. Feels like Morrowind, with a dash of Deus Ex and some Thief, stuffed into that late 90's aesthetic.I really feel like I'm in someone's super creative D&D campaign and my choices matter. Admitted at first and I had no clue wether or not I was making progress in any quests because there's no real way of keeping track. But I just kept going, exploring, talking to people and everything just fell in to place and started making sense. If you're not into slow paced gameplay, don't worry: questing is very rewarding, as some quests will unlock massive quality of life options, further speeding up your gameplay, and leveling up will make all dialogue or lockpicking checks way easier. Maybe a little too easy? I think I have one or two islands and a bunch of quests at this point, and I'm nearly maxed out meaning I can persuade anyone and pick any lock, smash any door and solve every puzzle, thus making progress super fast.Maybe that's the kind of stuff that's gonna get some balancing when it leaves early access. It doesn't feel bad right now but what was challenging at first is now a stroll through the park.I am going to give Dread Delusion my upvote because it's a real loveletter to oldschool RPG's, and the unique world, factions and lore really make it fantastic all together.Take your time, read dialogue, soak in the atmosphere.. I hope you enjoy it as much as I do!
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Story/lore is great. I also like the gameplay, but I do understand why it might not click for some people. _childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion is not a perfect game; it has its flaws, mainly related to its gameplay. The RPG elements are very negligible, the difficulty is very easy (if you go exploring), and some gameplay elements feel a bit underdeveloped.However, the game is absolutely fantastic in its style and atmosphere. First of all, the art style itself is very unique, and the way buildings, landscapes, and interiors are designed provides great visuals. It strikes a good balance of feeling retro while also providing a decent amount of fidelity. Building on that, the sounds and music are very good too, and together with the narrative background, it creates a unique atmosphere that lives up to its name.Content-wise, Dread Delusion offers a decent amount of quests and exploration, but personally, I would've liked fewer open locations in favor of a more polished general experience and straightforward level structure. Additionally, the Early Access development is rather obvious in the narrative structure of the game, as the different zones feel quite separated. Nevertheless, this also allows for very different sub-plots and themes to be developed independently from each other, and it works especially well in the Clockwork Kingdom, which is truly amazing in its world-building, themes, and designs.All in all, Dread Delusion delivers a very memorable experience in regards to its atmosphere and design, but unfortunately cannot match that in its gameplay. 4/5

_childDocuments_.review: This is a hauntingly beautiful journey that will sate the wanderlust of a patient and story-driven RPG enthusiast. With a strong focus on creating atmosphere and immersion as you traverse the surreal and supernatural environments, while leaning into a vintage retro dark fantasy aesthetic that might remind one of King's Field or Morrowind. The sound design is excellent, from the bittersweet melancholy of synth waves paired with the alien ambience of your surroundings. The writing and characters are so grounded into the world, you really feel there is a history and culture to be explored as you unfold the mysteries of the myriad bizarre places you might visit. There are philosophical undertones and themes that I find very intriguing. The game design loop compliments this well by giving the player agency through travel with features like cartography, airship travel and using an actual compass instead of a gamer GPS. The combat isn't overly challenging, but it is fair and quite functional. Having a stamina and fatigue system will limit your expeditions and make you plan your rest accordingly, putting a focus on preparation first. Magic is rewarding to discover and seems to have some alternative uses aside from combat, but I'm still a novitiate spell caster. Have yet to finish the game but it leaves a very promising impression. I feel good about supporting this dev because this is a work of passion. It's refreshing to see creative and unique ideas manifest into this morbidly obscure and abstract art.

_childDocuments_.review: Much has been said about the rich worldbuilding, the excellent writing, the joyous exploration, the fascinating art style, the boring (but fortunately deemphasized) combat, and the currently unfinished state of the game, but here's what really needs to be said:a.) the game is an incredibly immersive voyage into a world you've never seen before;b.) there are a lot of systems that are sort of underdeveloped; andc.) I made my character drink some wine I made by alchemically combining two throwing knives and then adding a third throwing knife.I really wish you'd find things in hidden corners that aren't just one of half a dozen potions, but I got sloshed on knifewine, and you can't put a price tag on that.
