_childDocuments_.review: Knights, goblins and dragons.Ok, standard RPG staples that is…Giant mushroom trees, the goblins are weird fluffy beasts.Ok, so more Morrowind territory then so…All on flying islands and a very trippy, colourful PS1 aesthetic and different realms including one run by a giant machine that demands tea.Alright, I’ll relent!Dread Delusion is one of the more interesting RPGs that has popped up in recent years, sort of similar to Lunacid with the strange throwback feeling of late 90s and early 2000s RPGs similar to Kings Field or Morrowind, being both low poly and very strange in their presentation. It is one where the world and the aesthetic trappings are absolutely the selling points and, if that is your kettle of fish, it is certainly worth looking at. Just beware as the general mechanics feel as dated as the visuals, for better or worse.To cut a long story short, the aesthetic, world and story of Dread Delusion is the selling points it has over all else. Take one look at any video or screenshot of the game and it is very clear how distinct it is. While it does use the overdone PS1 style, texture wobbles and all (can be turned off), it certainly makes it its own thing, from the hyper saturated colours, the strange floating world or the huge, mauve neutron star in the centre of the world.An aesthetic alone is not usually enough to sell a game, and thankfully the lore, story and writing do very well in that department. Taking place hundreds of years after a huge cataclysm, you have been roped into chasing down a sky pirate who seems to be trying to change the world, potentially in a more destructive way than the last disaster. On the way you will pass through mushroom villages with harvest issues, meet members of a godless union who are hunting down worshipers of old gods and even end up in an undead kingdom and one run by a huge clockwork king who wants you to make tea. Rarely does the writing or quests give a clear-cut “correct” side to fight with and most of the time everything is very grey. Side with the godless union and cause famine, or side with the gods and risk society being played with by inconceivable beings who may just turn 500 people into maggots for the hell of it? That is the trolly problem for the player.While the world and the story are a huge selling point, Dread Delusion falls down slightly in how the mechanics work. It does feel very mid 90s experimental, and sometimes this approach works and at others, it devolves into very boring combat.A key point is how levelling works. Unlike other RPGs, Dread Delusion has no XP. You gain levels and stat points by embracing glowing skulls or completing quests. These are dotted around the world in key places and in secret areas that usually have a few ways at which you can approach them. Have a high lockpicking skill and you can spend a minute trying to pick the lock, or have a high enough might skill and just smash down the door? Perhaps there are some candles or paintings that are at angles in the environment that, with a high enough lore skill, you can play with to open the door? Maybe there are people you can charm to open the door. This really is a game where you can use any number of ways to play through it where you can even forgo combat entirely. This is somewhat interesting, but the practical methods of actually doing these things usually just involves clicking on bits in the environment or, with lockpicking, rolling a dice until you hit the required number that opens the door.This flows into the game’s combat. As there is no XP gains, killing enemies only gives in game items to use. Also, the combat is obscenely basic. Think less Morrowind’s waving arms about until you get a high enough skill to attack. Instead it is more like a 2D Zelda game, with simple attacks going back and forth, only here you simply attack the enemy and then back off before they attack back. The difficulty is so trivial and the combat so simple that the only times I died in the game was due to falling off the edge of the world. While it is certainly functional, don’t go into Dread Delusion if you are looking for meaty combat, as it is absolutely the worst part of the game.Weak combat aside, Dread Delusion is a title I do advise to people who want to spend about 20 or so hours in. It is intriguing and mesmerizing in its world building and lore. Just don’t come in looking for very refined gameplay when it comes to the mechanics, as it is very 90s in that respect.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: What a breath of fresh air. I knew from the character and environment design, and the UI that this was going to be a great throwback to the early 2000s style of 3d. I didn't realise just how faithful it would be in the gameplay sensibilities though, and boy am I grateful. I wasn't at all surprised when I learned that Lovely Hellplace were the devs who made my favourite of the Dread X Collection games; "Shatter".With modern open world rpgs getting increasingly bloated with "content", both in character progression and in equipment, this game pares things right down and makes every new piece of equipment, and every upgrade feel meaningful again. I explored every corner of the world, not because I felt obligated to, but because I enjoyed the act of exploring and discovery. Every nook and cranny of the game has some new and fascinating piece of worldbuilding to show you, and likely another moral quandry for you to agonise over. The world is dripping with atmosphere and every person whose story you listen to feels real for the post-apocalyptic fantasy world the game takes place in.I felt the main character got a bit lost in the colourful cast that you assemble along the way, but I also realise and appreciate that was likely a deliberate decision which also harks back to the style of player characters being a blank cipher to better immerse the player and allow them to feel that they're taking on a role.I do hope we'll see more from Lovely Hellplace that follows the creative worldbuilding and visual design that they've put on display so far.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game, love the style, atmosphere and music in this game. I can't wait for the rest of the story to be added.Edit: Played the full release and man, I loved this game. The music was incredible, the world building sucked me in and above all else the story was fantastic. No choice is ever easy, and neither are the outcomes you get and I love that. The game really had me grappling with moral issues. Dread Delusion made the outcome of quest endings somehow both hopeful and melancholic. It really fit the tone of a world standing on its last legs. I can't say enough about how much I've enjoyed playing this game. I really hope to see more stuff like this come out

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve been playing Dread Delusion since early access and that’s something I rarely do. Most of the times I wait until 1.0 release, I don’t like unfinished products. Not this time - I was waiting for every coming update. This should be a recommendation on its own. This game has its unique charm and now, when it’s completed, I can wholeheartedly recommend Dread Delusion to every old school RPG fan.If You look back on games such as Morrowind or Gothic with fond memories - this is a game for You. _childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I am very conflicted about this game. I wish I could set it to be a neutral review, neither good nor bad, but I definitely don't think this game is a recommend for everyone.This game had a lot of potential. I saw a lot of people comparing it to Morrowind, and I can understand why, the crazy wacky atmosphere and world design is very similar. However that's where the comparisons stops.If you are thinking of buying the game and want something similar to Morrowind, you might be better off not getting it. The game is barely an RPG when it comes to combat (the stats may be there but they're relatively irrelevant except for lore and charm that unlock doors or convince NPCs to do something they wouldn't do in the regular dialogue tree). You can cheese every single combat encounter in this game because there's only two types of attacks the enemies will be doing: very slow telegraphed melee attacks or very slow and easily dodgeable ranged attacks. You can go through the entire game without leveling might or stamina and you'll be able to do decent damage to all enemies in the game as long as you upgrade your weapon. You don't even need to fight any enemies as you can just ignore them all (except one possible boss at the end if you picked the "wrong" dialogue choices).I understand some people (myself included) like to try and do pacifist runs, but in this game it's entirely meaningless. Not because it doesn't change anything (as far as I could tell it only changes one specific NPC dialogue) but because there's no actual risk in going pacifist. You don't need to try and be stealthy, you don't need to use your wits to outrun your enemies. There's no way that enemies will realistically ever get close to you unless you approach them yourself. This means that doing a pacifist run has NO risks envolved, and in fact I found myself naturally avoiding enemies because there was no proper reward or reason to kill any enemies. You level up by finding skulls around the map, so there's not even any experience incentive to killing anything.As it stands, it feels like the entire combat system was left in its early stages as a placeholder and somehow someone decided "this is good enough" and launched the game as is.The story is actually surprisingly good, and can be very emotional at times. You really care for the characters in it and it raises some decent questions about life and your place in it, with the only negative aspect of the story being the quests and stories in the clockwork kingdom, as they seemed to have been rushed or left uncooked, The exploration of the map is fun, but one of the things I was most looking for was visiting the floating islands that you need a flying ship for, but sadly there's only 2 islands that are noteworthy, and the other 2 have almost nothing in them. I was hoping that unlocking flight would have given me a lot more places to go, even if they were optional, but in reality its just a small segment before you reach the end of the game.Overall I did appreciate my time with the game, but it's definitely not for everyone. My initial reaction when I started playing was that of disappointment when i figured that the combat wouldn't get any better, and even worse when I realized there's only three main weapons you can get in the game, and no class customization for starter equipment besides the stats you pick at the start of the game. I hope the devs use the experience they got from this game and make a better, more polished game in the future, that can go more in-depth on some of the barebones systems shown in this game.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game in the tradition of Arx Fatalis.When you first play it, the game is legitimately painful to look at. You can turn off "wobbly 3d" and "wobbly textures" in the options menu and it makes a huge positive difference.Dread Delusion has a cool world and setting, and everything thematically works. It's not weird for weirdness sake. The more I play the more I like the world. There are tons of hidden secrets, and it really makes you want to explore and find as much stuff as possible.There are a few problems with the gameplay. There are 3 main "builds": combat, magic, and thievery. The problem is that if you equip the best thief gear and put all your stat points into it, you just get faster movement and not the real experience of any stealth play. Another issue is that the map seems pretty empty. Because there is no lighting in this game it is very easy to see long distances and avoid enemies from far away, so there is no feeling of threat while exploring or traveling the world. There might be a dangerous room with a bunch of archers, but you have 100% control over whether to engage. The creatures are not proactive, they just wander very small patrol areas with very limited perception.Dread Delusion solves the reload and repeat problem of most single player RPGs really well. You can only save at certain magic crystal locations, and dying will bring you back, but it will return you to altars of a specific god. This is all explained in the game lore and it means you are actually using consumable items instead of just hoarding them for a big fight that never comes.The game is early access and my recommendation comes with some caveats; I'm really enjoying it but I think the game needs a lot of work before it reaches it's full potential. My recommendations to the dev:1. More enemies in the overworld.2. More alert and aggressive enemies.3. Thief items and character builds should reduce enemy aggro range instead of increasing movement. Or maybe have a sneak mode that costs stamina and makes you move slower and reduces enemy perception.4. There are way too many lockpicks! There are probably too many health and mana potions as well.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Summary:You're getting a decent RPG with, at least for me, about ~20/~23 hours of content. One way to describe the game mechanics would be "TES-like", but don't get me wrong - this is no Oblivion, of course - don't expect AAA-level quality from an indie title. What I mean is that the game "feel" is similar: you have your levels, your attributes and their effect on the overall gameplay.In terms of open world content, Dread Delusion prefers the "low volume, high density" approach - you don't have a very large map to play with, but the POI density is much higher.Combat is functionally okay. Melee combat doesn't feel great - it's not bad, but it's not very good either; you have cool stuff like coatings for weapons, multifunctional weapons, etc. but the feel of the fighting itself is not great. Ranged options are better, especially if you're playing a mage, since mages can utilize a variety of offensive spells effectively.Pros:- Story is good - even with a fairly basic premise, the execution was captivating from start to finish.- Setting is AMAZING. This is often overlooked, but in my opinion it's one of the most important components for a game like this.- Quests are, for the most part, very good - many quests are not basic "fetch-me-that" or "kill-this" quests, and involve thinking. Although there are a couple of fetch quests as well.- Decent RPG mechanics.- Densely packed open world.Cons:- If you're doing a Might (Strength) build (basically warrior), your movement speed is atrocious. It feels like you're on a wheelchair for about 1/3 of the game. Note that this can be mitigated in mid-game and late-game by chugging mana potions and recasting the agility spell again and again, which gives you very high speed for a short amount of time.- Minor bugs are still present in the game. Save often, and do not ALT+F4 from the game.Personal Preference:- Melee combat feels clunky at times.- While the game gives you the ability to play as a very bad person, you can't take a route of an outright schizophrenic sadistic psychopath, which is rather unfortunate. It would be fitting to have a kind of "Kill Everyone" route where you basically kill everyone on sight and/or erase the entire remains of the world, but it is what it is. SPOILERS: This is a breath of fresh air in between the AI generated slop that is being offered to us at the modern game market (yes, Starfield, I am looking at you).
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: All you people comparing this game to Morrowind only make me want to change the review to negative. This is blatantly lying to other customers. This game is inferior IN EVERY ASPECT to Morrowind. It has much less story, much less loot, much much simpler combat, less spells, no spellmaking, barebones "factions", worse graphics, worse everything. STOP comparing this game to Morrowind as it simply doesn't deserve it.Yes, the game in itself is good. If you want a RPG-lite Quake 1 experience.EDIT: I have changed the review from negative to positive. The GOOD:- The story is quite good, an intriguing world, with interesting lore, NPCs, believable goals, basically the only thing that makes me want to play further. There are even quests with multiple outcomes.- Level design, Quake 1 was one of my all time favorite games, and I get some old old and good vibes from how the terrain is made. It feels big, amazing and refreshing. It is all one big level but stretched in space (floating islands).- It runs smoothly.- There is a map. And you need to work for it.The BAD:- Poor levelling system. You don't get any EXP from defeated enemies. And with the loot (lack of), defeating enemies is a chore, better to evade them. You will get *some* progress from collecting Delusions, but that's very rudimentary and feels poor.- Weak combat. Enemies are basic so far. Very basic. I'm not a good player in FPS games, but I wasn't challenged even for a moment. Combat feels basic. Spells are gained very late, the first combat spell I got AFTER I cleared the first area as I missed it and only read about it in a guide. So beware of taking all mage perks.- Graphics. While I like the level design, the colors and textures are plain ugly. There is a reason there ARE modern Quake 1 engines. I played Quake 1 since 1997 up to this year, and modern custom made maps look better. I did praise level design, yes. But the overall effect feels ruined by the choice of colors and textures. A shame.Loot is a mixed bag. I have written a negative first review as I simply didn't find ANY armor during first 5 hours in which time I cleared the first area. Later though I found the first real big town and I gained a better sword, armor pieces, a bow etc. Feels like the game opened for me. So pacing is clearly an issue, as for 5 hours I have only used a rusty sword and throwing knives besides being a mage.Overall, the level design is interesting, the story is interesting, and I want to play more.

_childDocuments_.review: At the time of writing, the game is still very much a work in progress so you'll reach a point where there's no way to progress, because the rest of the game doesn't exist yet. With that caveat out of the way, I've had fun with Dread Delusion so far. It reminds me of Morrowind, in a good way. The setting is dark and strange, there's no clear good or bad faction, and even the navigation is resolutely Morrowindian - very limited fast travel, no quest markers, not much of a map. You don't even get compass directions - if you want to know which direction you're facing, buy a compass and then get it out and look at it. So far, the game's systems are pretty simple. Combat is hacking away, plus a small number of spells. Supposedly there's a block, but it never did anything when I tried to use it. Lockpicking is a roll against a target number. Every now and then you get to improve one of your attributes, and although they don't produce any fancy special powers or anything, they do make a noticeable difference to how you perform in related tasks. The stamina system is a pleasant little wrinkle. It's a bit like Morrowind, in that your stamina depletes when attacking (though mercifully not when running), but there's more to it than that. Over time, your *maximum* stamina gradually declines, meaning that fighting tires you out more and more easily. This is addressed by sleeping in a bed, so every now and then you do have to stop for a rest. There are some bugs and oddities, as you might expect from a work in progress. The collectible 'godlets' often cause control to freeze up (fixed by pausing and unpausing), there's placeholder text and weird formatting in places - but all to be expected. If you don't mind it being a bit rough around the edges, and the fact that there's no way to get to the end yet, it's worth playing even now. The atmosphere is a big part of that, with the game offering up this bleak, warped world for you to explore fairly freely. There are also a few occasions where you have more than one way to resolve a situation, depending on which belief system you want to align with. It's good. It's dark and doesn't hold your hand, but it also doesn't leave you feeling completely lost and clueless. I enjoyed it. I expect to enjoy it again once it's finished.

_childDocuments_.review: Full Video Review:Short Text Version:Dread Delusion is a first-person open-world RPG taking place in a horror-fantasy setting consisting entirely of floating islands. That's a mouthful, but how does it actually play? Well, fans of Morrowind and Oblivion will be very familiar with the game mechanics here. Despite being in Early Access, you're given a pretty large world to explore, multiple classes, stats, and abilities to experiment with, and a handful of quests to complete. Although, unlike RPGs of old, you don't gain experience from repeating actions or killing enemies. Instead, stat points are awarded directly for completing quests or reaching secret areas. This means you can't really grind for character progression, and are instead required to complete the optional content to grow stronger. It's not a bad idea in theory, but it does make fighting enemies feel almost pointless. Sure they can drop a coin or a potion or whatever, but money isn't super hard to come by. Combine this with the ridiculous run speed, and almost every fight can be avoided easily. So if you already have the best gear from the shop, why even bother fighting anything?When you do fight, the melee combat ends up being lots of slashing and backing up before the enemy can land a hit. Much like it's predecessors - so I can't really complain. That said, magic is pretty strong, allowing you to one or two-shot most enemies from a safe distance. Not that you really need to fight at all with a little bit of agility.Speaking of agility, I love that they let you level it up to gain speed and jump height. Just like Oblivion, it lets you absolutely break the game by skipping important triggers or jumping out-of-bounds.Anyways, there's a decent amount of content to experience in the Early Access, in varying states of polish. Some of the quests kept me engaged, while others were just straight up stat-checks with little else behind them. The main story was able to keep me interested throughout, but I could barely recall most of the side-quests I ended up doing. The best non-story quest I encountered was joining the Thieves' Guild. Subtle introductions, secretive NPCs, and hidden passages throughout the city brought me back to the old days of RPGs long-gone. While not a very long quest, it stood out as a promising step forward for where the game could go in the future. Learning about the different factions and choosing sides was a nice touch to make the world feel more alive. Although the factions are pretty barebones at the moment, mainly just sporting slightly different dialogue and aesthetics.Which brings me to probably the most recognizable part of the game - the art. The game throws back pretty heavily to the graphics of the PS1 era, with a bit of modern design sensibility. Most people I see talking about this game picked it up for the art, which is totally understandable. It definitely feels like it was made with visuals at the forefront, while the gameplay is a little less fleshed-out. Personally, I feel like PS1 graphics may be a little overdone at this point, but this is definitely one of the better-looking ones. No real complaints about the art here. It seems to be the main selling point of the game for a good reason.The whole idea of taking on a massive open-world RPG project with a small indie team is already pretty wild. It's nice that they're trying to accomodate a breadth of gameplay and build styles, but there's only so much they can really do within a realistic scope. Open-world RPGs thrive on offering a wide variety of optional content that many players will never experience. Take away those options and the world feels lifeless and dull. It's a huge task, and I can't imagine the tough decisions they have to make on what features to cut constantly. But they seem determined to take a swing at it, and it is a promising start for a small team.If you can take it for what it is - a small indie game with some cool art and ideas taking on a big concept - then you might just dig it. But if you're expecting the next "Oblivion Killer" I don't think this is going to satisfy your desires. Then again, it's still in Early Acccess. If they focus on their strengths and polish the core experience,  instead of trying to add too many surface-level features, they might just have something here.Pick it up if you feel like supporting the devs through their rough journey. As for me, I'll be putting this one down for now, maybe giving it another go when it's fully released.

_childDocuments_.review: Go in blind, don't level might, and explore wherever you can.Combat is simple, and even on hard difficulty, trivial; if build-making, challenge, or mechanical depth are what you look for in an RPG, this isn't it. The world-building, writing, and atmosphere are what carry this game - and they carry hard. You're here to explore a tumultuous, alien world, and navigate all the gruesome moral dilemmas that exist within - not murderhobo your way to glory. Ultimately combat is not that important, and is in fact wholly optional.This game is brilliant, although not for everyone. Well worth the full price, and a total steal if you catch it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sadly gonna have to NOT recommend this game.It has a lot of potential, the base for worldbuilding and the graphics are really awesome, and that's where it mostly stops.The audio seems lackluster(?) compared to other games of its type, the story tries to create multiple choices, but it all brings to a straight line when it comes to tangible progression, as you may choose to aid other factions and their direct enemies won't bat an eye and do as more as to insult and threaten you, with no real outcome.The combat is EXTREMELY trivial, I've made a full stealth build and in 30m I found out that there's basically no point in sneaking behind enemies as they:1) Deal absolutely no damage2) Can be infinetly kited by just backstepping3) On the case you fall asleep on your keyboard and they kill you, you'll respawn with nothing lost, which completely destroys the stakes of a combat encounter.I've personally, as many other ones, never used an healing potion, as I've never been in a life-threatening situation.If you're in for a walking sim or a showcase of a very good artistic design, buy this game, but don't mistake it for anything else.

_childDocuments_.review: Summary:  Absolutely amazing game, with my full recommendation.  A very exploration and adventure heavy game with some combat thrown in to keep you on your toes.  Almost everything about this game was top-notch.   Bugs aside, my only complaint is how easy the game is with its combat, but even then combat still functions more than sufficiently, and it doesn't detract from the game to impede my high praise of it.While the game is easy (even on Hard Difficulty, I never died once  ), combat is not the focus of this game.  It's about the adventuring aspect, what choices you make in each quest, exploration, and learning about the world around you and what effect you may have on it.I'm sure some people will look at the graphics and find them to be a bit "crusty", but I find them strangely charming and more than sufficient for this game.The audio and music work well in this game.  Game sound effects work just fine, and all the music fits well and is never grating.Combat in this game is too easy.  On top of that, I found the "lowered stamina reduces damage" mechanic to just be unnecessary.  I understand why people keep making comparisons to Morrowind, and they are both right and wrong to do so.  I wish I could elaborate on how its both right and wrong, but my explanation would be an essay all on it's own.   Regardless,  I consider Morrowind to be one my most favorite games of all time, so to see many comparing this game to Morrowind is high praise in my mind.Despite my love for this game and my full recommendation of it, I have 2 issues I hope the devs address before moving on to whatever their next project is.1:  While I myself never experienced any game breaking bugs or corruptions of save files, others have.  Please ensure this game remains as stable as possible.2:  PLEASE fix the kill counter to not count kills done by others I had no part of or control over.  I noticed my kill counter went up even if i witnessed 1 NPC kill another that I had no involvement with. (at the beginning of the game even!)

_childDocuments_.review: Ever since I bought and really got into the game I could not stop thinking about it, it´s truly a masterpiece of its own caliber.The story caught me immediately and I got really attached to all the main story characters. The story is genuinely absolutely incredible and if you are into story games and/or play games for their story, this game is more than perfect for you. It has a decently long main story with a large variety of side quests, some long some short. The worldbuilding also is incredibly well done with a lot of different areas to travel through and experience. The atmosphere of every different area is spot on and really makes for a great time playing especially for a blind first time playthrough. There are a lot of secrets to explore and discover to make sure that even when you are done with the story, you still have other things to keep you engaged and entertained.This game is really something that I would call nearly perfect but there is just one big point that a lot of people have been pointing out already that, for me personally, is not a huge problem but it would´ve definitely been nice to have, and that is a good combat system. While there are a few weapons you can choose from, that are also upgradeable, the enemies are never really a problem what so ever. With every enemy its basically always the same routine: Attack - Back off - Attack - Back off - Attack, so it can get tiring after a while. Among other things as soon as you have aquired a bow you can just shoot enemies from a far distance to ensure you always deal critcal hits and if you are far away enough (which is not even that far to begin with) the enemies wont even take agro towards you. So basically if you like games for their combat, this game will most likely be not of your taste.In conclusion, while this game does have minor things that could be polished, in its entirety, it is a fabulous and fantastic game that I can only recommend further to most. I love this game very dearly and would love to see something like a part 2 of it or just a game with basically everything Dread Delusion has, as in art style, music, world building and story.

_childDocuments_.review: Let me preface by saying this: this isn't a good game. What it is however is a wonderful and imaginative world, with decent storytelling and good exploration. However the combat is incredibly simple, even by "retro" standards and bosses as awesome looking as they are, are incredibly easy. You're only going to die if you run off the edge of the world. There's a lot of baffling game design decisions. A lot of the good and fun things to find are found way too late into the game. It often feels like a game that had a checklist of "RPG" mechanics that needed to be included to be a good RPG. The box is ticked but these mechanics are barely implemented. Most stats and skills are somewhat useless, sneaking barely works, factions are completely redundant and player choice boils down to a dialog option at the end of a quest usually. There's a lot of great ideas here but the implementation is either unfinished, buggy or just poorly done. Some of the writing is questionable, while other is great, and the quality is all over the place. There's a lot of bugs and it feels like the game was pushed to V. 1.0 to meet a release date rather than the game being finished. Having played it in early access the biggest difference to me is the fact that the main quest now is complete. (But boy that's a whole 'nother can of worms) So what does it get right and why do I recommend it? This game is a work of art, visually and worldbuilding wise. It has so much potential and so many great ideas. I'm really looking forward to what the devs will do in the future and I think they deserve funding for it, because they are destined for great things. However there's a lot to be fixed here and I don't think Dread Delusion will unfortunately ever be a "good game", it plays like a prototype for a GOTY. I hope they take more time and pour in the same amount of enthusiasm and passion that has gone into this and actually get some QA testing done before shipping. PS: Stop comparing it to Morrowind, there's a few aesthetic choices that are reminiscent of the TES classic but they are nothing a like and it is a disservice to both games.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion is an open world rpg that focuses more on exploration, world building and story than on the combat mechanics or even the depth of the rpg mechanics. I need to emphasise the fact that if you're expecting challenging combat, exciting fights and intricate builds, this is not a game that can deliver that. Still, I find that Dread Delusion is nonetheless an engaging adventure in a weird yet beautiful post-apocalyptic world, and it features some well-written characters (some more fun than others) and a lot of impactful choices you can make all the way till the end. The ending itself is determined by what you've done up to it and by a dialogue choice, after which you'll see and hear the result of all of your major actions. If it counts for anything, I really enjoyed both the journey and the ending I got, which was pretty much perfect.First and foremost, I have to say that you may encounter a deal of annoying bugs in this game, and some can definitely detract from the experience. I only found a few glitches here and there throughout the vast majority of the journey, such as an issue where only a certain piece of the OST was playing instead of the intended one, and some buildings clipping into one another, blocking passage until I restarted the game. Overall, it wasn't a buggy game, but the ending area reallyy needed some more polish. And the OST bug happened there too, so I was listening to the very first track in the game, at the very end. I don't know if that was an artistique choice or not, and I didn't mind it too much, but it did make me rush to the end due to the fear of the game breaking further.The gameplay and rpg stats I find were tailored to complement your exploration of the world, but more on that later. Melee and ranged combat are really really easy, and combat magic isn't really needed unless you'd like to roleplay a wizard or sumfin'.  All 4 main stats affect different attributes, and they also give you one specific option of getting past a certain obstacle: you can break or lockpick doors, you can charm people or machines into opening them for you, or you can look for certain items you can interact with using mana to open a door or a secret passage. If you explore enough, you are guaranteed to be able to open every single door in one playthrough I feel. I think I only found one door that required 10 in a certain stat to open with no other alternative, but there wasn't anything game changing behind it. Besides level-ups, you can upgrade gear (helmets/hats and clothes/armour) and receive stat increases from it, and that can help you reach a threshold needed for checks that your base stats can't meet the requirements of. There are some different weapons in the game, but you can stick to 1 and upgrade it with ores you find around the map and it will never let you down. I had 2 or 3 points in the combat stat during the entire game, and I never had any issue dealing with enemies in CQB. I was focusing entirely on the other 3 main stats, yet I saw no point in stealth-attacking and I used my mana for other things such as You can go fast in this game; really fast. The maps aren't too big, and there are ways to fast travel, but speed-maxing exploration using a certain spell you find decently early on was one of my preferred ways to travel. Putting points into Agility also increases your jump height and speed, so that can help you turn Dread Delusion into a parkour exploration game, to an extent at least. I think there is a cap on how fast you can get, but don't quote me on that. Either way, zooming through the maps while gulping mana potions and trying to make far jumps or simply bouncing from rooftop to rooftop never really got old. Just to touch lightly on the spells in the game, there's a decent variety of them, but not a great number. By that I mean that you have buffs, debuffs, summon spells, offensive magic, convenience spells (teleport home, change time of day), but not a whole lot in each category. I feel like that is a bit disappointing, since you'd imagine that such a royally screwed world like this would have some wild, bombastic magic to have the time of your life with. It's true that from a lore standpoint, a certain major faction regulates the use of magic, but you often find hidden spells which I think are illegal, but they still aren't that much crazier that the more common ones. The legal magic missile is a blue slow moving projectile, and the illegal fireball is a slow moving projectile that has a little area of effect and some fire damage. I hope this was simply a limitation imposed by the budget or deadline that the devs were working with, and that if they decide their next project to be something in the same genre, we'll get to commit some magic instead of just casting it.As I mentioned in the intro, the main meat of Dread Delusion lies in its world: inhabitants, villages, towns, cults, ruins, they all have a story behind them, and you can most likely change them forever. Your character is a nobody undeserving of a name, and you never see them, but there's a lot in store for them. The setting of Dread Delusion seems to draw comparisons to Morrowind, but I have never played that game, so yeah. I'll let the game reveal most information and background about it, since I consider that part of the journey, but I can at least say that an apocalyptic even ruined the planet 400 years ago, and some decades before you start the game, a certain jolly global God War took place in an overall very religious and spiritual society. You can try to fix it, if ye want. Or you can wreck it even more! I chose one of these two options for my first playthrough, and I think I'll try the other at some point in the future. Oh, I meant to say something else about the combat here! I have even gotten the impression that this game didn't really even need combat, to an extent. Not as a gameplay element, at least (there's not even a difficulty modifier; I think this is another factor that points to that). It feels more like a narrative element, there to show you how dangerous this world is, and how inevitable bloodshed is within it. In addition, this may have been a conscious decision to make the game more accessible. I could recommend this to someone who has never ever played a video game before, and I think they'd be able to have a grand old time with it (that is, if they enjoy reading books lol) and not have to worry about not being enough of a god gamer to deal with the combat system. All in all, to me, this game is quite unique. It's one of the few games my always-online zoomer-brain ass has been able to finish in the last several years, despite its lack of a proper, meaningful combat system (which is something I myself need in order to enjoy a game. Not anymore, I guess? I must be getting old). I think I'll remember it fondly, alongside the ending I got, some of the characters I liked a lot, a good deal of the locations I visited and, of course, the sillier moments that were inevitable in a game like this. I rate it a big number out of a slightly bigger number.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: The simple definition of gaming is to give some challenge to the player. This game, either it was designed to show the player this very artistic world or to tell a certain story, is lacking the challenging aspect which makes me think that for now Dread Delusion is more of a simulation/presentation than an actual game. If I can conquer the whole world with a simple steel sword, something is not right. I purposely went for a full charisma build to see how challenging the combat could be to me, it wasn't at all. This is so weird because, from how it looks, the whole game is trying to convince me it has some energy of old Elder Scrolls games or old Thief. Players that know these games are used to the very high level of difficulty. Instead of giving something to this group of players, developers decided to make it even easier by, for example, creating more rest points. Were they ever interested in attracting this kind of players? I have no idea but for I can't enjoy it. In this form it's not for me. And if there's another group that want it to me as easy as it is now, there's actually a way to make both groups happy - by creating a different difficulty level, let's say the 'classic' one, where fighting and crafting would be much more challenging. Dread Delusion has its gorgeous look, I do care about this game but I don't want my review to remain unnoticed, and I don't want for the game to remain at this state. Thumbs down, for now...

_childDocuments_.review: I don’t do reviews very often but this game caught my attention out of the blue. I have no nostalgia for the morrowind era of RPGs which is what I’ve heard this game compared to very often. That being said the world built here and the ideas explored sucked me into this retro fantasy world almost immediately. There are some deep philosophical issues that are presented to the player that even with such a cartoonish art style the decisions I made really made me question the morality of them. The world building is very similar to that of Wizard101 funnily enough which sucked me in as I’m a major fan of that game while the looting, combat, and exploration all were very satisfying for the systems they emulate. The fast travel system is one of the best in any game I’ve played as it forces the player to work toward it and is very necessary as you get later into the game. I feel like the one thing I would have added would have been voice acting but even without it I felt enraptured in the dialogue. Overall I just really enjoyed this game and the vibe it sets for the player.

_childDocuments_.review: I see many call this a Morrowind-inspired game and label it as open world. If like me this is the main expectation that pique your interest, then you might be disappointed.With a retro-style game like this, everything comes down to gameplay, it wont woo you with its high tech next gen candy. However, I still need to address the elephant in the room. The graphics. While I do love retro-style graphics, there is a big difference between good retro style graphics and bad. This falls in the category of the developers did not really have the skill to make modern high quality graphics, then tried to cover it up by making it "retro" instead. The problem with this is that bad graphics is still bad in a rawer pixel form.I know this is a bit harsh, however, there are too many sloppy mistakes you would not see in a high quality retro game. Sure, we accept pixelated textures and low polygon everything. But, rugs that are not aligned with the ground, graphics clipping through where it should not, the lack of variation with copy paste the same stuff a million times so you barely know where you are, the overly saturated color palette, animations that are not just retro but simply bad, boring and forgettable monsters. No shadows, fog or any kind of remotely polished effects.. It all is a pretty big eye sore, the world seem fake, dead and uninteresting.  Even the real retro RPGs looked a lot better than this, where the developers had to manage with almost nothing. No pre-made game engine, no GPU, no assets or open source code, almost no RAM or harddisk-space. I would not mind all this lack of graphical polish actually, if the game is great. A lot of retro style games more than compensate by having great gameplay, atmosphere and story. This is not one of those cases.First off, I can accept the poor retro graphics, but a poor retro game design is harder to swallow. For example, there is no mapping function from the start. Getting the map is one quest, and then you need to locate special mapping points and add them to that map. You also need a compass that will show where you are on the map. However, small things annoy. Like you wont see the direction you are heading on the map. You will need to take out your map. Then, separately, take out your compass to check your heading. Immersive and realistic? No, it is just tedious. Why let the player waste so much effort on mapping, Also, the fast travel mechanism is really tedious as well, you can only go back to the last fast travel point you touched. I get the retro idea, but it can be retro and not tedious. Maybe this will improve later in the game, I guess I will never find out, I wont play this game again.It seems like the tedious travel mechanics is a coverup to hide the fact there is not a lot of content in the game, and by having the player to spend more time on mapping, memorizing and cover the same ground a lot they can stretch out a short game and make it longer. Then there is the game design. It is very basic as well. Again, I want to emphasize that I feel making a modern retro-game is not about recreating all the shortcomings of past games. Take a retro-style game like Rimworld, it has basic graphics but seemingly endless complexity underneath that would have been impossible to pull off in the retro days. Retro games to me is taking the best ideas of classic games, keep the style but pump in a lot of additional depth and where you save development time on graphics and game engine development, you just fill it with details and interesting features. Dwarf Fortress is another example, sure, on the top it is basically ASCII, but if you can get through that and start enjoying it you will find more content than you would imagine is possible. I was hoping for a Dwarf Fortress depth in a Morrowind open world setting. This game is not that. It looks simple, it plays simple. You will constantly find some bonus pickups behind something where you would not normally look for example, like some algorithm just processed the map and put stuff where the player would be unlikely to look at first. It is tagged like open world, but I found it really linear, and the world completely lacks personality, like an endless boring walking simulator in poor graphics without anything interesting going on. There are some forced concept of choices, like you could fight the monsters head on or choose the secret entrance filled with traps. But, it still seem like you are on rails. And most likely you would do both anyway, to make sure you get all the loot.The characters you meet looks overly synthetic. the world is dead. There are no NPCs going around making the world alive, anything moving is there to fit a shallow purpose. The story is flat and uninteresting. The lore is forgettable at best. Combat is just awful. Too much walking around to do basic stuff like have a rest.Oh, and then the sound. I turned off the music, as it was not my taste, but then I was left with something like three sound effects. The sounds were not synced properly to the action, and the game world produced some random weird noises just playing over and over to somehow make you feel the world is alive. This terrible sound design just dragged me right out of any immersion still left. My recommendation is to save your money, replay Morrwind maxed out with mods instead if that is the game that you thought you would get here. The most positive thing I can say about this game is that it is cheap, and it probably will run well on any potato computer. I really tried to like it, and played wishing I would be able to see past the poorly designed everything once I got deeper into the story, but failed. Maybe if you are truly desperate for an old school RPG, this could scratch that itch somewhat, but then why not rather play those old games and get a higher quality game experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusions is one of those games I can perfectly understand people not enjoying, and I myself find it pretty difficult to evaluate. It has way too many shortcomings and it's pretty repetitive as far as gameplay is concerned, but it's such a home run in terms of world, atmosphere, lore and writing that I really enjoyed my 20ish hours with the game, so I recommend it for sure.Many said that Dread Delusion is indie Morrowind. I didn't play Morrowind, but from what I understand the comparison sort of stops at "it's a weird ass setting with mushrooms in it". The two games certainly have little in common as far as being an RPG is concerned. DD is a very lite RPG, with characteristics such as attributes, stat checks and factions, but they all range from "kind of shallow" to "absolutely superfluous". It's more akin to Lunacid (no surprise that the two games shared devs) and felt pretty much like a dungeon crawler translated into an open-ish world RPG format.Dread Delusion immediately flexes its muscles with its charming PS1 style presentation (very authentic-looking, complete with optional effects such as warped textures and wobbly 3D) which complements the bizarre art style giving the game a unique weird and oniric quality. The music is also great and does wonders for the atmosphere, but there's too little of it, so it gets looped ad nauseam and I can see it getting grating for some.The setting kicks in soon after: basically, almost everyone in DD lives on these floating islands (the Skyrealms) that orbit around neutron stars after an event called The World Rend devastated the surface of the planet centuries prior to the start of the game. The player starts as a prisoner forced to work for the Apostatic Union, a powerful organization that wants to establish order by hunting each and every God still roaming the land after the God War wiped out most of them fifty years before. This is the setup of Hallowshire, the first of three major islands that constitute the better part of this game. Then you have the Endless Realm, the inhabitants of which are all undying cadavers after a ritual conducted by the previous king gave them all immortality with nasty side effects hundreds of years prior, and finally the Clockwork Kingdom, a sort of bureaucractic dystopia run by a mechanical king looking sort of like a grandfather's clock powered by magic and numbers. This all ties in with your mission: the overarching hunt for Vela Callose, a notorious mercenary who is looking for something that could potentially rewrite the entire fabric of reality. I can't keep writing about this or I'll end up just summarizing the plot, but suffice to say that it's an incredibly unique and captivating world, with drastically different cultures that feel believable, rich in history, lore and secrets and that you can explore in detail through frankly brilliant quests, often posing you some kind of moral dilemma with every side (almost) always having a point relatively to the context of this twisted society. It's genuinely interesting stuff and great writing, with some surprisingly emotional moment as well.The gameplay definitely isn't up to par. The combat is entirely superfluous, basic to the point of boredom and completely useless as none of the enemies pose a threat of any kind and you can easily outrun everything. Plus, you don't get EXP from combat, but only from solving quests and exploring, so engaging in battle has really nothing to offer. This hurts the otherwise good exploration, because you often find healing items, consumables, equipment or spells that are supposed to help you in battle, but it's going to be useless to most players. Plus, while exploring is compelling, it's very repetitive with few ways to discover secrets and opening doors repeated many many times; you also have to run everywhere forever, with fast travel points awkwardly placed, leading you to spam the speedy magic and chugging mana potions for most of the game. Stats are pretty meaningless, seeing as combat is a non factor and that you can get gear that boosts specific attributes far more than level up does, so you just end up swapping hats to do certain skill checks instead. There are various other annoyances, but the gist is that DD would have probably worked better if it was an adventure or a different kind of RPG-lite.What we got is a deeply flawed video game (and quite unpolished technically) but it's so unique looking and with a fantastic and memorable setting. This, coupled with the writing, makes it an experience I'd recommend to most people with a few caveats. It's also a very fitting companion to Lunacid, they're pretty different but they seem cut from the same cloth, and I enjoyed them both.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; This game pays homage to what I think is a neglected era of action rpgs and even though it's in early access I've thoroughly enjoyed my time with it. If you liked games like King's Field or Thief: The Dark Project or even Strife I would recommend checking it out. I paid 20$ for it and I feel it's a fair price. Kind of early in but I'm really loving this game so far. It manages to capture the feeling of those early pc/psx era hybrid RPGs perfectly. The dreamlike loneliness of King's Field combined with the world building and design of Thief/ Half Life really makes it stand out.  The lore and backstory of the setting is interesting enough, and I found that the characters had a surprising amount of personality given the limitations of the retro-style. The combat is serviceable, it doesn't really stand out but it's not bad by any means, it feels a lot like the old school Elder Scrolls combat without the dice rolls. The ability to block and parry is welcome, but ultimately I was able to beat pretty much everything by just circling and poking it to death. Ranged enemies were also a bit inconsistent, as there were several times an enemy with a bow was able to loose an arrow 180 degrees through their own body to hit me when I was behind them which made things seem a little too jank. As the game develops hopefully they'll focus on making the combat more rewarding, adding some new abilities or giving you more of a reason to focus on parrying and stuff would be very welcome. I haven't messed around much with magic yet but it seemed likewise pretty simple. I found one soul-arrow spell and was able to find enough mana potions to spam that whenever things got dicey. Again not bad by any means but I'm hoping as the game develops they're able to flesh out the magic system a bit more. The decision to tie character progression to exploration makes a lot of sense, as exploring the world was probably the best part of the game for me. The art direction and character/monster design has a very unique dreamlike feel which made exploring the world even more engaging. I was constantly finding upgrade points and resources as well as some new characters and side quests, which is even more incentive to get out there and explore. I don't want to make this too long so in closing I would like to recommend this to any fan of old school rpgs and I look forward to seeing how they develop the game from here.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This game is super promising. I've played a little under 5 hours so far and am really impressed with it. The combat is a bit shallow at this point and reminiscent of kingsfield, that's not to say it's bad only that there are limited options and most encounters are just hitting and dodging around enemies. That being said I still had fun with it despite its simplicity. The world and quests are pretty awesome though I love the dynamic of lovecraftian god beings and the apostatic union, the factions, and the bizarre world to explore. On that front I see a lot of morrowind and shivering isles in its dna. I really recommend Dread Delusion games this unique and creative are few and far between these days and devs should be encouraged when they make great games like this.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I will start by warning that this is an Early Access game, one that really feels as such, as  --being a single-player rpg-- the lack of content is obvious. The main story stops right after the tutorial and, although the big side quests on the accessible areas on the map can be finished, their repercussions haven't been implemented.But the base game itself is still wonderful. A better successor to Morrowind than Oblivion or Skyrim (albeit in a way smaller scale). It is a masterpiece in the making and it will be a wonderful rpg when it is complete. It's atmosphere is the sort of weird that you got from it multiplied by three and adding some eldritch horror to the mix. The only big gripe that I have with it is that it's combat is quite basic and easily exploitable. Although, just like in the Elder Scrolls, combat isn't the reason why you play this game. You play it to explore the world and experience its stories.So. I highly recommend this game. But only by understanding that this is an early access game that might not be fully developed.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Overall: really nice game. The graphic palette is just really nice and nostalgic. Lots of unique visuals and things going on in the game. It doesn't have the sort of RPG depth of character building or crafting that you get in some places, but the fun is from the strange things in the world plus the uniqueness of the story. Having to slowly draw and add locations to your own map and use an actual compass or telescope gives a nice sense of pixelated immersion.The music, sorrowful dialogue and visuals really give you a sense that this world is broken and has been bleeding for a long time. It makes it really nice when you're able to see or affect changes and accomplish your quests.Can't really go wrong considering the price tag unless you simply dislike adventure and exploration games. The RPG/and action elements are a little bit secondary, for better or worse. Closer to a Zelda kind of game than a Morrowind RPG.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Dread Delusion is mostly compared to Morrowind; mushrooms, clockwork, and writing strong to make both count. Both build up uniquely alien takes on fantasy which are absolutely enchanting. There's one aspect that compares more controversially: both games have awful combat.Dread's is too simplistic, usually too easy and, at best, can only be called serviceable. It's only better than Morrowind in that you don't have a to-hit% chance (and you can power attack? You could count that. Maybe.) But I'm barely criticising here. You don't play Dread Delusion for the combat, you play it to get drunk on exploration, intoxicate on atmosphere! Astonish at its world. The fighting feels vestigial, but, the game is so creative, I actually find that charming.Not everyone agrees--some of us need our daily dose of fun-for-its-own-sake action--and that's respectable! I like good combat too; those criticisms are absolutely something to take into account if that's what you're here for.But for anyone craving that weird immersion into something different? This game is a love letter.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This might be the best game I've played this year (2024) so far (August 13th). It was only because RPS and some YouTubers I like championed this game that I decided to play it. I bought it years ago while it still was in EA.The graphics are simple, but the style is very striking, much more memorable than many other photo-realistic RPGs. The combat is also simple and I'd describe it as serviceable, but I actually found a rythmn I enjoyed with it. This isn't Elden Ring or even Skyrim, but then combat really isn't the focus here.The focus, friend, is STORY, ATMOSPHERE, WORLD BUILDING, CHOICE. Dread Delusion excels at all of these. The writing is to the point without being basic: there's plenty of personality and character here. The choices presented by the quests are for the most part really engaging and way above the tired good/evil dychotomy. The choices make sense in this world: they're not some artificial options manufactured so a game has replayability or some other metric. Like Dark Souls, this game gives you enough to set your theory crafting brain on.That such a great game was made by so few people is astounding. I'm afraid it didn't make a bang in general like other recent indies like Dredge. I do hope you'll give this a try: it's worth every cent and every minute of your time.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: I think the team has something special here. I really enjoyed this game as Morrowind throwback, but the world, characters, and lore here is really interesting. I think with some additional time this could make for a really great franchise. Adjust the combat to make it more layered, give enemies movesets, make a few adjustments to how information is presented and i would lose my mind. On its own this is a great game, but over time i think it could be INCREDIBLE. Recommend y'all play it.

This game knows how to tell a story, how to make exploration feels unique. When you understand the Delusions of hope, of dreams, of a better life, you can empathize with the survivors of this lands. _childDocuments_.review: So overall I like the game and enjoy the surrealist open world setting. The floating islands and strange gods all work well to make the setting interesting. Most of my criticism comes down to, what I hope and assume, are things that are simply unfinished.While I heard other people complain about it, I think the combat system works fine, at least in melee (though it's fairly similar to Daggerfall, a game I love, in how the combat feels, so I might be biased in that regard). Currently ranged combat is terrible, though all that would be need to done to fix this is: 1) include an aiming reticule, and 2) Make it so the drop on projectiles isn't as much as it currently is.I played through the game as a mage, and currently that playstyle seems to leave much to be desired. There don't seem to be a whole lot of spell options (and none that aid in combat unless you get creative with the haste spell), and I was fairly surprised to find that, upon gaining access to the mage faction, that there wasn't a single spell there to learn. This likely is just because the devs haven't yet implemented all of the spells yet.The only thing that I disliked about the game that didn't boil down to the fact it isn't finished yet, was one particular quest (spoiler warning going forward): The quest regarding the fleshfarm that has gained sapience, and which can communicate telepathically with living beings like the player, but not its undead creators. I get that it's trying to present an interesting moral dilemma: Kill a single, unique life form, or endanger the lives of many? However the execution of this quest is... kind of a mess. I think there are massive holes in the plans of, like, every NPC involved...So basically it boils down to a conflict between two people: The mage who invented the fleshfarms who wants to kill the sentient flesh to cover up its existence and thus preserve the moral alternative to the Endless needing to kill and eat people, and the evil noble who wants to return to the old ways and who wants to use the fleshfarm's sapience to prove that the moral alternative to the Cadaver Crusades isn't so moral after all, and use it to argue for a return to the old ways.The noble's plan doesn't make a whole lot of sense to me: Even arguing that the fleshfarm is sapient, the flesh farm would still provide a moral alternative to the Cadaver Crusades, given that using a fleshfarm requires the suffering of one being, whereas the Cadaver Crusades would cause the suffering of multiple. And even without arguing morality, the fleshfarms could be argued to be more practical. The Endless do not reproduce, so gaining your food via warfare, where Endless are at risk of dying, will cause their population to decline.However, even if we take it on assumption that the noble's plan will work, that all he needs to do is expose the moral gray of the fleshfarm in order to convince the populace to return to the Cadaver Crusades, then the head mage's plan to cover up the fleshfarm doesn't make any sense.She wants to use a species of insect to completely and totally destroy the sentient fleshfarm, thereby getting rid of all evidence of its existence. However, I see two issues with this plan:1) If you just destroy the fleshfarm, the noble could argue that there was a rather blatant and obvious cover-up. He can still argue it was sapient, and point to its destruction as evidence of that fact. However, what's even more of an issue is:2) The noble is quite open about his intent to hire a human to say WHATEVER he wants about the fleshfarm being sapient, regardless of the truth of the matter. There are more fleshfarms than this one in existence according to the dialog. So if the mage and the player kill the one sapient fleshfarm, then the noble could STILL hire a human, take that hireling to a non-sapient fleshfarm, and then that human could make the EXACT SAME CLAIMS about how that fleshfarm is sapient and capable of talking to only living creatures, and the Endless populace would have the same level of proof as they would have had he gone to the real sapient fleshfarm and had his hireling actually made contact with the real sapient fleshfarm.So ultimately, once the genie is out of the bottle, once the noble has the IDEA for telling people the fleshfarms have become sapient and that they can talk to other living creatures telepathically, then it's all over. Killing the sapient fleshfarm doesn't solve the issue, since he doesn't care if they are truly sapient or not, and can just shift his claim to claiming a DIFFERENT fleshfarm is the living, sentient one. The only true solution at that point would be to kill the noble, which isn't possible within the game, or to destroy every fleshfarm in existence so he can't claim any are sapient using a bought human, except that just forces a return to the Cadaver Crusades anyways...And so, given all the above, it feels like there's a lot of dialog options missing from this quest. However, I must stress, this is the ONLY quest in the game that I found lacking in this way.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: While this game isn't particularly difficult - it is without a doubt pure Flavortown. The world and the characters are charming and interesting, and if you're the kind of gamer who enjoys travelling and finding exotic locales, this game is chock full of them. Good mission design with some twists, and some interesting morale choices too. Good music too, sets the tone nicely. Because it's not a full fat CRPG, it's not asking you to hyper-optimize your build and you're not going to miss content if you're somewhat wise about your level up and gear choices (acquire skill gear from shops, upgrade it quickly). It's a solid 20-30 hour experience, well worth your money.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: An interesting, colorful low-poly first-person action-rpg with good controls and some convenient features. I'm told it reminds people a lot of The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind, which I have not played. Atmospheric, melancholic, and strange, Dread Delusion made a singular impression on me.Set on a flying island chain called the Oneiric Isles, beneath the red light of a "Neuron Star", Dread Delusion is a strange fantasy tale of a lone adventurer who begins as a boxed crook of the Apostatic Union's Inquisition. You have been given leave of imprisonment in exchange for the task of hunting down and apprehending the rogue mercenary Vela Calose, whose ambitions could threaten reality as you know it. To that end, you must track down former members of her mercenary band, the Dark Stars, scattered across three island nations and surrounding smaller islands, some only accessible in the very late game after an important purchase is made. Along the way you'll encounter various monsters, sidequests, small dungeons and other points of interest, acquire an arsenal of weapons, armor and supportive accessories, and locate Glimmers of Delusion- the game's experience points, some obtained from quests but many more found by exploring the world. When you gain enough of them you gain an attribute point to spend on strength, agility, intelligence or charisma, which in turn raise your ability to pick locks, solve lore puzzles, charm NPCs, and break down doors- as well as your basic stats of health, mana, stamina, attack damage and the like.One might call Dread Delusion a "bite-sized" version of a game like Elder Scrolls, relatively- it took me about 40 hours to finish everything, which is a pretty full game. That is about the same amount of time I played Skyrim, but I didn't do two the Dark Brotherhood or Thieves' Guild questlines, the war questline and probably the majority of sidequests.Dread Delusion's combat is notably easy for the genre. I was able to melee my way through all encounters with a relatively low Might stat, only rarely needing to use a health potion and never requiring any of the fancier buff potions or Elixirs. I wouldn't count this against the game, the appeal of it for me was the exploration and aesthetic- but there have been complaints.I would however count the game's many bugs against it, though since I began my playthrough many of these have been patched. By the time I finished the ones I encountered earlier had all been fixed. Notably one of these killed me by falling through an elevator- and I might not have died at all in my run otherwise.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: 11 hours and most of the available content later... yeah, it's still good. A sentient lump of flesh gave me an existential crisis, 10/10. A wonderfully weird mix of King's Field and classic Elder Scrolls, with a bit of Lovecraft/Cronenberg and a PSX aesthetic dashed in for flavor.  If you enjoy mid-90's styled action RPGs, I think this will be right up your wobbly-textured alley.The game starts fairly linearly, but after the initial introduction (roughly half an hour or so?), the map opens up significantly. You'll come across towns, merchants, NPCs, skill checks, and quests aplenty. There's a surprising amount of lore to the world, and a fairly straight-forward leveling system.All-in-all, absolutely worth the $20 price if retro action RPGs and strange, almost alien, worlds are your thing.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: The good:Great story telling and world building. I loved exploring the world a discovering every nook and cranny I could find.  It's been a few months since my first play through and I can honestly say coming back to it for a second play through, I felt nostalgic the same way I would for a game I played in my childhood.The bad:The combat is unfortunately very simple and bland (especially if you don't use magic) and if you're trying to increase your reputation with as many factions as possible, you're basically punished for participating in combat at all.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most hesitant and difficult Thumbs Up I’ve ever given. Dread Delusion does so much right, and a lot terribly wrong. I'll go over its problems in brief, then detail its successes.- There is no risk in combat scenarios and combat is flat-out boring.- Key gameplay elements (such as magic projectile attacks) remain broken and unusable.- Tacked-on, ham-fisted LGBT content breaks crucial sense of immersion at critical points.- The music is a repetitive, terrible drone that distracts when it needed to evoke a sense of wonder.This is the fullness of my list of unforgivable complaints; there is so much the game does better than any other contemporary of its genre.From the opening scene, everything about the setting is brilliantly surreal and totally engaging. The game simply shows you one of the most intriguing, engaging, and bizarre settings you can possibly imagine, shocks your system with its absurdity, then plays it off as totally normal, expects you the player to figure it out, and it *works.* As you explore and encounter bizarre gods, fly an airship to visit a neuron star, understand the history and terror of a failed utopia, make gradual sense of the Shattering, it feels like a mystery that you gradually unravel and make sense out of until it becomes fascinating, yet familiar.I have never seen exploration handled so well in this genre, except maybe hardcore mode of Kingdom Come: Deliverance. An Elder Scrolls style map fast travel would have killed this game by simply allowing the player to not engage with its best content in a meaningful way.  Enabling only the use of a manual compass independent of a map and navigation system forces the player to learn and become familiar with the local geography in order to become oriented to the most prizeworthy element of the game; its bizarre and beautiful open world. Efficient navigation instead requires piecing together a convoluted series of fast travel techniques including airships, portals, magical devices, potions, items, and spells that makes exploration and a mobility in this open world game a part of the puzzle itself that the player has to unravel. This feels incredibly rewarding when you finally become its master.To the writers’ great credit, generally the characters were as surreal, bizarre, and interesting as the rest of the setting. It has been a long time since I encountered a game in which I did not simply skip through all possible dialog, let alone seek out any more than necessary. Conversation with characters were almost never uninteresting. While the times that these interactions were wooden and forced stood out enough to be immersion breaking, this is perhaps a testament to how well the writing was handled with the overwhelming majority of characters and situations. It stood out to me how frequently I was actually interested in what characters had to say and what the outcomes of their stories might be depending on my choices made. In addition to clever and interesting writing, the lack of hand-holding when it comes to quests forced me to have to pay attention to what the characters had to say, which led to the enjoyment of an aspect of the game that I would almost certainly skip over otherwise. Critical for an open world, immersive game of this nature, the developers nailed how to do a proper ending. While I'm not Philosophically sold on some of the possible elements of the ending, the sheer variety of possibilities and the free choice to make decisions that might doom an entire realm (because the player sees that it might actually be the best possible outcome) felt incredibly liberating and again, necessary for this genre of game. A forced, rote ending would have left time and energy spent on important choices feeling wasted. Instead, the game presents a multifaceted ending based on the free choice of the player's decisions, allowing the player’s interaction with the world and time spent in it to feel meaningful. (Also, any of these endings were better than the ending to Lost , so kudos to the writers for that too.)This review has gone on so long that I'm positive that nobody is reading anyway. While its sins are significant enough to be jarring detractions, the elements of this game that pass through the fire are overwhelmingly superior to any open world game that I have played since I'd have to say Kingdom Come: Deliverance. I will predict now that this game will be remembered by the few who play it as a far more memorable, interesting, engaging, and competently handled experience than Elder Scrolls 6, and I hope the developers are recognized for the bizarre and beautiful thing that they have crafted.
_childDocuments_.name: Dread Delusion

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed Morrowind, odds are you will enjoy this.Like navigating a nightmare, the visuals are a bad trip after reading Gothic Horror and Lovecraft. These visuals are what makes the game stand out. The atmosphere is the best part of the game.  The lore and dialogue are alright. They probably need to polish this area as recycling and combining cliches doesn't exactly create a memorable experience. Audio is alright, but the repetitive music is on a short loop; it feels like it repeats every 15 seconds depending on the area you're in.As mentioned above, the experience is very similar to Morrowind; this holds true for the combat as well. Fairly easy to master, this grows fairly repetitive after the first few encounters. It is currently unbalanced in favoring a melee build but it appears that will change. There's clearly some kinks that needed to be worked out (lag time of enemy drops, enemies disappearing, items not working) but all things considered the game is still enjoyable even in early access. It would be easy to be more critical but there is a lot of potential here and it so far deserves the benefit of the doubt.

_childDocuments_.review: This is just me putting my thoughts into words as they occur so it might not be the most readable but anywayI 100%d the game (afaik) and the lore and fluff was interesting, but mostly it was a slog. this game is basically all world building and lore, no focus on gameplay or consequences. it might as well be a visual novel if theyre just trying to tell a story, which wouldnt be a bad thing, at least it would be honest then. its honestly hard to put how i feel into words with this game because i do enjoy the world and the stories it tells but everything else drags it down so hard. i would wait for the combat rework/hard mode i saw teased in the newest announcement before playing this, and if it addresses some of the problems i'll probably change my review to positive, but it'll be reluctant because theres still the problem of quests lacking any consequence or changing the world state in a noticeable way, until the end of the game where its just a slideshow.my two least favorite quests are the one with the mines in the endless realm (who is the god, what do they stand for, what do they want, why? left unanswered), and the one with the diseased duchy (where you put the duke out of his misery or leave him to suffer) where there is only 1 subject and they just die of disease instantly if you do that path, its almost comical how instant it is, also the question of why weird fungal humanoids are attacking the duchy and castle is never answered afaik. just disappointing

It's atmosphere, gameplay, story and visuals are on point with the chosen art-style and design. The game itself made me look for every secret, try to solve every riddle and think on every decision.
