_childDocuments_.review: I never knew how badly I needed "survival horror without horror" as a genre. Horror is, of course, subjective, and there's imagery and dialogue in service of it. Still, I find the whole game's tone heartfelt, hilarious, tense, and otherworldly rather than scary. All of that is in service of the core gameplay, which holds its weight in gold and encourages repeat playthroughs.The environment and puzzles are the major stand-outs here. There are shortcuts in shortcuts all over the place, which makes backtracking a breeze, and space is well-spent when peppering the map with consumables and key items to stumble upon. Sometimes you'll find solutions to puzzles several areas ago, or unlock a new shortcut you can chain and skip minutes of walking from place to place. New enemies appear on repeat visits, and certain puzzles can entirely remove enemies from the map. When your game is 5 hours on a casual run, it's all killer no filler.I've seen feedback regarding the combat as "one-note," but I think that misses the point; like the oldest games in the genre, this is an adventure game first and an action game second. I find the most fun in routing to use as few resources as possible and keeping up the chase while exploring. Of course, if you value combat complexity on par with the RE4 remake or similar survival games, you're gonna be left wanting.In short, this is a breath of fresh air for the survival horror genre and honestly transcends the moniker due to its unique tone. Is there even a name for the gameplay style independent of its tone? "Survival?" That sounds stupid as hell, sounds like you're talking about ARK or Rust. I dunno. We'll figure it out!
_childDocuments_.name: My Friendly Neighborhood

_childDocuments_.review: Is it possible to do something new in the mascot horror subgenre?  proves that everything is possible and breathes new life into the tired old formula. Although it has horror elements and a generally eerie theme, I wouldn’t really classify it as a ‘horror-only’ title, as it features a lot of comedic elements and dialogue paired with a deep and meaningful narrative. + A deep and meaningful narrative that is worth exploring+ Fantastically designed levels, paired with puzzles that actually require you to think+ A vast cast of quirky characters, all with unique personalities and funny voice lines- Sometimes the solution to the level could be overlooked easily, as the game generally doesn’t provide much help On the surface, 's story isn't noteworthy; nevertheless, as you dive deeper into the game, you'll discover the extensive backstory that surrounds it, as well as make decisions that could change the conclusion. It was a pleasant surprise for me that the plot felt genuine and not like an additional feature, which is something unusual in the mascot horror subgenre.A long-forgotten children's show called My Friendly Neighborhood appears out of nowhere on local television, even replacing the news. The city, of course, is not pleased, so they send you, Handyman Gordon, to remedy the problem.The aforementioned show originally drew many children to the TV years ago, depicting the daily lives of puppets living in the neighborhood in a humorous and educational manner. However, when the youngsters grew older and became adults, their popularity plummeted, and the show was eventually canceled.The once-friendly neighborhood, subsequently, soon transforms the puppets into something altogether different - something wicked!When you arrive at the long-closed studio, two things become clear: first, you will not do this task quickly, and second, you are not alone! Comedy is an important component of the story, and it really enhances the experience - throughout the game, you will hear numerous hilarious discussions, and the overall tone is more humorous than threatening. There are no major plot twists, mysteries, or exciting sequences, yet the game manages to provide a comprehensive experience.  Characters are one of the key reasons this formula works so well: you'll quickly realize that their aims aren't always to murder you but something altogether different. Their odd monologues and chats are really entertaining, but by the end of the game, they become a little repetitious.A notable feature to mention is that the game is fully voiced: it is amazing to listen to all of these quirky voicelines! It may sound strange, but I believe is a more laid-back horror title: as I previously stated, the narrative is primarily intended to be amusing, and I believe the same is true of the gameplay.The game does not explicitly urge you to die and suffer as much as possible - in fact, it is the exact opposite! You need quite a few things to survive (and considerably more if you can't aim properly like me), but health and ammunition are easy to come by in practically every area. The guns themselves are on a whole other level: your handgun actually shoots the letter of the alphabet; how awesome is that?Another thing to keep in mind is that there are no jumpscares in the game - only one sequence is 'heavier' on the horror side, but aside from that, the gameplay mostly revolves around carefully considering your next move, managing your health and ammo in the most effective way, and remembering all of the puzzle's locations in order to backtrack them later.Navigating through the studio might be challenging, especially when you don't have a map. However, I can fairly say that a lot of effort has gone into the environment design: practically every building is related in some manner to another, and there are a plethora of shortcuts you can (and will need to) exploit in order to continue.It's worth exploring all of the studio's nooks and crannies because there are several portions concealed in each segment. These rooms could have more loot, a new shortcut, or even a puzzle!I also like the fact that there were moments when I had to return to a location numerous times (for example, to retrieve a key for a door that was initially closed), because it gave me the opportunity to collect items that I had missed the first time.The puzzles in  are fairly simple, yet they can be difficult in some circumstances. Backtracking is a feature, like it is in other titles in the genre, which means you will need to return to previously explored regions one or more times. In practice, this implies that there will be many locked doors, boxes, or straight up portions initially, but as you go, you will progressively open them all!The puzzles themselves are fairly varied: in one, you must collect particular materials and arrange them in a specific order; in another, you must defeat a puppet in a tabletop game; and in yet another, you must print out codes to open a door! The developers did an excellent job of balancing the complexity of these puzzles, although one relies heavily on RNG, which means that if you're unfortunate, you can be stuck for a while.In general, all of these puzzles are simple to solve, but if you get stuck, your best bet is to look for a guide, as the game offers no tips. is an exceptional, one-of-a-kind game. Both the narrative and the game design deserve praise, especially the fact that the game balances comedy and horror in a completely new way. The story is engaging and worth diving into, while also succeeding in being emotional. The Szymanski brothers never disappoint!Final Rating: Very GoodYou can find my review chart

_childDocuments_.review: "My Friendly Neightborhood" is a survival horror game where you explore the dark version of Sesame Street, solve some light puzzles, and shoot letter-shaped bullets at human-sized mascots hell-bent on hugging you to death. It's very, very fun and quite well designed, and about as scary as you would expect from a kids' TV show: so if you are put off by really intense horror, this game might work for you. I would recommend it to pretty much anyone, as I found it to be both deeply engaging and easily approachable, which is not always true for traditional survival horror. The gameplay and the aesthetics are just spot on. There's also a surprising amount of optional stuff to do. After my first playthrough I've certainly missed a ton of content, judging by the number of locked doors I left behind in the hotel. _childDocuments_.review: In these last years, we've seen the rise of what some call "horror games for cowards". They are survivor/inventory management games that are not so crippling scary, being more accessible to larger crowds and even children. I have seen even "Alien: Isolation" being categorised like that. The thing however is that this is not a derogatory term; it's more like a genre made for people who want to experience the mechanics usually involved in these games without the nightmares. And in this genre - if we can call it that - goes "My Friendly Neighborhood"."MFN" is one of the best survivor horror games I've ever played. It's really a game that can be easy if you want to, but challenging if you want the famous "true ending" - the term we use for the absolutely happiest ending, the one we're willing to crawl over broken glass to get.The first thing about this game is that it's somewhat straightforward - there's not a lot of backtracking involved in it at first. The game introduces levels to be visited in order: in each level, you get a tool that will open the path to the next one. The thing however is that, once you get a key, it can open certain doors in places you've already been. And these doors lead to special objects that can change the course of the game - and are directly related to the "true ending".Enemies are mostly either human-sized dolls or hand-puppets. The human dolls simply stand in any environment you get, and when they see you, they walk towards you. Walk, I say: you can outrun them until you reach a new room, therefore avoiding fighting, wasting ammo or injuring yourself. Bear in mind that some puppets can be more resilient than others in an arbitrary form: some can be put down with little effort, while others take a lot of hits before going down. Hand-puppets appear a bit later on the game: they're very weak, but they move when you're not looking, meaning that to ignore them can be dangerous. You can pass by them if you keep them in your POV until you're at a safe distance.But sometimes, there can be a lot of foes in a single environment, and you have to dispose of them in order to better explore rooms. The thing however is that you can't kill enemies: you can knock them down, but once you leave a room and come back, they'll be back on their feet. So if it's a place that you feel you'll need to come back to a lot, you have to tape them down once they're unconscious, therefore stopping them for good. There's only so much tape you can find, however, so you can't just go around taping down every enemy you defeat.Besides those, you'll find level-specific enemies that can't be tapped, and can be quite obnoxious. The way to dispose of them is to help them from their issues. For a giant bird, it's finding her eyes; for a trio of dogs, it's giving them food, and so forward. Once you do that, they'll stop pestering you, making levels easier to navigate. You help them with the special items I was talking about earlier.This brings me to an important aspect of the game: inventory management. There's just so much you can store, and sometimes, you have to rearrange your items for new ones to fit in. Luckily, there are safe rooms in where you can store some of your findings, and you can retrieve them at any other safe room. You can even storage weapons from your inventory if you feel you're not using them. Also, once an item has done its job, or a key has unlocked all doors it had to unlock, you can dispose of it, making things easier. And as it's common to some horror games, the act of saving your progress is not given to you on a silver plate: you'll find coins that save your progress or to heal yourself in safe rooms. So use your coins very wisely: try spending them every four times you do something major in the game.There aren't many weapons: you get a wrench at first, then a pistol, a shotgun, grenades, and if you play your cards right, a machine gun - each with their own ammo. You'll also find health drinks, and some chocolate bars that can make you faster, evading enemies easily. Which reminds me: there's no sprinting, crouching or jumping in this game. It's pretty basic in what regards movement. There's no hiding behind places or sneaking: this is not "Amnesia". It's not a game about hiding from your enemies, but finding ways to deal with them. Eventually, you'll find two bosses: I don't want to spoil anything important, but neither of them are hard. The first requires a lot of ammo and aiming at weak spots, and the second, close to the end, just requires evading.When you get at a new level, you'll commonly find a map very early on. And maps are extremely kind, showing you which rooms you have explored or not, and if you "completed" them - that is, collected everything on them. My only issue is that your pin location doesn't show which direction you're facing, but all things considered, that's asking a bit for a lot. Notes in this game can be accessed with F, but the game doesn't make it clear. So I'm making this clear now: press F to see the notes - some are important for puzzles. The game also features a lot of unlockable cheats and challenges that invite players to return once they're done, such as an ending score, a speedrun mode, a horde mode, or alternative endings.Visually, it very much is an Unity game. The visuals are beautiful and simple, focusing on art direction rather than graphics. The game conveys perfectly that you're at an once flourishing studio which stopped in time somewhere in the 60's or 70's. It really nails that "Sesame Street" vibe, and you can see developers did their homework. The voice acting is also amazing, particularly for the dolls: you can identify they're near by their sounds, as they blabber nonsense (one of them sounds a little like Kristen Schaal). But the thing that surprised me the most about this game is the heart: the developers really took seriously the main theme of the game. This is not some Adi Shankar-like subversion of a wholesome theme; it's a story about a broken world, in which people lost hope, and while the dolls may be out of control, your actions can save them. And yourself.I don't know how Jim Henson would react to a game like this, but given he wasn't a stranger to darker matters ("The Dark Crystal", "Labyrinth"), I think he would feel "My Friendly Neighborhood" did him right.

_childDocuments_.review: I was sceptical at first. I was not sure if this game, with its 3-4 hour story, would justify its price. However, after playing through it, I can confidently say that it does.The story is okay, but not the strongest. This game stands out more with the puzzles, with some horror elements and crazy humor. I have often heard that it is a pairing of "Sesame Street" and "Resident Evil" and I think that is very accurate. Sesame Street because of the visuals and also the humor and Resident Evil because of the puzzles, the enemies and the lack of ammo which can be a real problem if you're not careful, but there's actually a cool "solution" for that, which you have to come up with first but I do not want to spoil. (And maybe a slight touch of "high on life" with the continuous babbling that is let off there, which you can easily ignore at some point.)Besides the story, there are also many other small tasks that you can do, which can simplify the further course of the game, but also give it more depth. When you have played through the story, you get a new tab with modifications & difficulties for a new run, which are divided into modes and cheats and with each play through you get more and more of them, which greatly increases the replay value, because there are sometimes crazy and interesting things that change the gameplay.In my opinion My Friendly Neighborhoot is the best "mascot horror game" that has come out in years and I hope that it won't be completely exploited like every other game of this 'genre' with seven more sequels, films, and pervasive merchandise advertising.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: A perfect survival horror experience with an AMAZING and fully realized premise! Liminal space and "mascot" horror games have been done to death, but somehow, My Friendly Neighborhood combines those ideas and transcends them both. Also the storyline is oddly touching. Don't be too concerned with how the puppets are alive, though. The game doesn't care about that question, and frankly, answering that mystery is way less interesting than the path the story takes. What it IS concerned with is the idea of escapism for reality through entertainment. Is it healthy for us to just see the cruel world reflected back at us through the television...and when does burying our heads in sunshine and rainbows become just as problematic?THIS GAME MADE ME THINK, DUDE. And I got to shoot Elmo with a shotgun that fires books.

_childDocuments_.review: Another flawed entry in the Mascot Horror subgenre.My friendly Neighborhood is a survival "horror" title about a maintenance worker that was sent to turn off a broadcasting antenna at a studio (where they used to film a knockoff version of "The Muppets Show") that was interfering with news broadcasts.Alright, let's acknowledge the Snuffleupagus in the room. This game is NOT scary. The only horror that the game has going for it is a couple of frightening designs and buckets full of uncanny valley, which does not a horror game make. It's difficult to be on edge when every single monster is talking loudly in an annoying high pitched Elmo/Barney the Dinosaur/Kermit the Frog voice.The gameplay is pretty nice though. You have multiple weapon options and a grid based inventory system which is always nice, the weapons feel good to use, and all the animations are satisfying. I also like how you can stop the Puppets from respawning by duct-taping them.Being a game that parodies The Muppets, the fact that it's charming should be a given. The voices are annoying, but the psychotic ramblings of the puppets are very entertaining. I do wish that there were more than 2 character specific monologues while the rest were copy-paste across all characters. I also love how they got Arlo to voice Ricky, that is SO perfect.My Friendly Neighborhood IS a little better than Poppy Playtime with its gameplay, but not by much.

_childDocuments_.review: I only bought this game because Turbo Overkill's 1.0 release got delayed by a month. So the money burning a hole in my pocket went to the neighborhood and what lucky. This is a fantastic game. Mechanically satisfying as heck. Shocking given it's cleverly subverted genre of Mascot Horror. All of this game just comes together to make an oddly cozy game. It's not really a scary game. I jumped a few times and it has it's moments but the word that keeps coming to my mind is: Sincere. MFN is just oozing with charm and narrative vulnerability. The Devs weren't "too cool for school" to tell a sincere story and I can't properly put into words how refreshing that is. Obviously I bought this game with the Mascot Horror trend in mind but...I'm really glad they subverted that. It's all really much more innocent than it seems and that vulnerability in such a cynical period really spoke to me. I almost needed a story like this right now.  The old studio is laid out fantastically and sometimes when I'm walking around outside the game evokes Bioshock of all things. The level design itself is stellar but it's just the presentation that wows me. In summary I really can't give this a higher recommendation. This random purchase is honestly in the race for my game of the year. Also wow, what a soundtrack. I love the saxophone boss fight music.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played literally thousands of games in my 30 years on this earth. I've played more games than the average much-more-than-average person. I say this with my whole heart. This is the first survival horror game that I've ever finished. The first one I've ever enjoyed. The first one I've said aloud "Oh, I get it now, I get it, it's fun, I'm enjoying this."I have complex post traumatic stress disorder, so my brain has a really difficult time conceptualizing "scary" and "a good time" at the same time. I don't get the release of built-up tension like many people do - I stay in a state of extreme hyper-vigilance to the point of exhaustion and my frontal lobe is too locked up to be able to solve puzzles. I genuinely gave up trying. I blocked the tags "horror" and "survival horror" from Steam because I was forced to write off the entire genre as something that "other people get to play."This game truly found the absolute perfect balance for people like me, who WANT to play games like this but just... can't. I can't recommend it enough. This isn't "mascot horror" in the way that many other asset flips are - "Ooh no, the children's toy is actually a demon coming to get you JUMPSCARE JUMPSCARE YOUTUBE COMPILATION OF STREAMERS SCREAMING." So many games that look like this exist only to be streamed by people that react loudly when frightened (FNAF, Poppy), or to heavily market to children (Hello Neighbor). This is genuinely "what if Resident Evil but a $30 indie masterpiece."

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: A great survival horror game with fantastic combat and great puzzlesPros:- Gameplay: Akin to resident evil scrounging for bullets and dodging enemies with limited saves. Gunplay feels satisfying and ammo is neither too abundant nor too scarce (Playing on “Survivor” difficulty at least). Puzzles are at just about the right level of difficulty. - Graphics: Impressive especially for such a small team every character looks great, and the environments feel exactly like a once popular children studio with each area of gameplay feeling very appropriate too it’s setting.- Story: Some fun themes. A deliberate subversion of other mascot horror games. Nothing too deep but I liked its overall message and delivery. - Characters & Tone: Voice acting is great, and characters are fun. Game explores some interesting, if rather surface, themes with each character and the ambient dialogue of the base enemies is humorous (Though more context specific lines would have been nice) Neutral:- Length: Game ran me about ~6 hours. Perhaps a bit on the short side but overall, I feel the game used it’s run time effectively. - Enemy Variety: The base enemies remain consistent throughout with really only 3 enemy types (and one of those reserved for one specific area). More enemy variety would have been a nice addition. Cons:“Horror”: I was hoping for a few more scares. The game never really felt that scary which is unfortunate as some of the monster designs (as mentioned above) are very well done. Conclusion:A great game well worth playing for anyone who is a fan of the genre but don’t expect to be screaming in terror all that often.

_childDocuments_.review: A charming and fully-featured survival horror game in the style of Resident Evil, perhaps closer to the classics than even RE7 and RE8. This can be to its detriment at times, as bumbling through subsections of the game without knowing where the maps or save rooms are is sometimes a lot to deal with, and some wonky triggers on what the game actually marks on your map can be an issue. When I played the game save rooms were not marked on the map after discovery, making backtracking and shuffling items around needlessly tedious, and a critical red key door in the office tucked away in the corner of a disused floor was marked as simply an unlocked door for me so I ended up spending 20-30 minutes frantically running around to every conceivable location I could reach to check for progress. The game is also quite on the easy side, as the few times I died were either due to the inventory not pausing the game or having boxed my heals entirely to make more room - even on the hardest default difficulty the aforementioned progress block backtrack bonanza was the only time my supplies became remotely an issue, and by the time I discovered the hidden third weapon I had absolutely no reason to use it. Even so, exploration is quite a bit of fun, with an interconnected world full of secrets I mostly couldn't find and extra supplies I could, some cute 'sidequests', and the satisfaction of a strategic duct tape usage paying dividends again and again and again all throughout a playthrough is hard to beat. The store and lore files are interesting without being obnoxious, the visual and audio presentation are the perfect middle ground of appealing on a budget (except maybe Gordon's ♥♥♥♥♥♥-up hands and arms), and sprinting around already knowing where you're going while violently ragdolling puppets with a shotgun is just really satisfying. Not my favourite game in the world, but glad I supported it.

_childDocuments_.review: 2023 is just knocking it out of the park this year with amazing games... I can only get *so* erect.My Friendly Neighborhood from the Szymanski brothers (minus David) is an unbelievable love letter to some classic games while also taking some great steps forward on its own merit. The influence from Resident Evil and Bioshock is impossible to ignore, but they manage to give a nod to a lot of those classic mechanics without ever feeling like its ripped off. There is a Sesame Street-esque spin on every single mechanic borrowed from other games and its so stylized in the best way possible. Everything, even the weapons are turned into a kid's show friendly item. Letters get shot out of the "pistol" a rolled up stack of letter cards get shot out of the shotgun and you crumple a whole stack up to make the grenades (plus more I won't spoil). Instead of burning the bodies like in Resident Evil, you duck tape the puppets so they don't move, and they KEEP BLATHERING ON I mean holy sh*t it was so funny. I streamed this game and had to kinda stop myself sometimes from just sitting there listening to their rambling because sometimes its normal stuff like "bubbly bubbly bubble gum" and other times they talk about how they had their arms ripped off and replaced when the puppet was getting worn out, or how they like drinking the tears of their enemies. The perfect tone gets struck between silly fun and just a little spooky.Also, if either of the brothers ever read this review, f*ck you both for this jumpscare, I damn near ♥♥♥♥ myself: The complaints that I do have are pretty minor overall, and nothing that can't be fixed simply. One of them was that I picked up an item needed for a recipe, it was a can of polish, and the recipe I was making needed liquids that went in jugs. Even just changing the item you pick up from a can to a bottle would telegraph more what its used for. Other than that, I didn't actually get stuck at all which is remarkable because I usually HATE puzzles, but everything felt very good progression wise. There was always another step that I hadn't done yet I could return to and that always opened up the way forward with whatever I was caught up on. And on that note, I felt that the asset use in this game was very smart. It seemed to me that they spent the time on what mattered most so occasionally there was a weird looking thing (Gordon's hands... good lord what are those hands) but overall the puppets, the guns, the environments all look really good and the details all over are fantastic. The whole setting really is just ingenious and I can't believe that this is the first time anyone has tried turning Sesame Street into horror, but damn if they didn't nail the landing with this one. There was a really satisfying amount of side content to do, and I appreciated that there was no obtrusive quest log pointing out what I had to do at any point. For the most part that would kinda chill the atmosphere, and it also had me compelled to do everything even stuff that ended up being side stories, which I really enjoyed. A small issue, though, there's one part (same as the recipe from before) where you have to input a recipe code and you pick up a note that has the recipe on it. I did not know there was a files function before this point in the game, so having a prompt show up when you screw up the first time "F to open Files" wouldn't be too much at all, I think, because you don't use it before or after that point in the game.My Friendly Neighborhood seems intentionally designed for quite a few repeat playthroughs, even borrowing some of the same achievements from classic Resident Evil (pistol only, no healing runs) and I intend on returning to it eventually. That does bring up my only other gripe which is the price, and I'm torn because I really love whats here but 30 bucks is just a hard swing sometimes and I feel like 20 bucks would have a lot more people picking this up? I don't know, but I can say that I'm glad I grabbed it and I can't wait to see whats coming down the pipe in the future from these guys. Great game.

There's a few little blemishes that could be ironed out but nothing game ruining (could scale better with high end hardware for high framerate gaming or more pretty but demanding settings i.e. a better AA method as the only one available is incredibly weak and leaves a very aliased image.) _childDocuments_.review: MFN is a horror game in the style of Resident Evil where you must explore an abandoned "Sesame Street" esque film set and battle puppets who wish to kill you. IN MFN you take the role of Gordon, a repair man who has been tasked with shutting down a creepy signal being broadcast from an abandoned movie studio, upon arrival you realise that its not abandoned and the puppets who inhabit it want to hug you to death! Cue a very fun Resident Evil clone with lots of exploration, backtracking, secrets, puzzles and gunplay. There is a tonne to explore in this movie studio with lots of different puppets to meet and at times help so they realise you aren't a threat but a friend!The core gameplay  loop involves finding keys, opening doors in different areas to find items to progress in other areas and find keys, simple stuff but with the large amount of optional and secret content here exploring is very rewarding especially as you need to do it in order to get the best ending. Visually things look great the puppets and environments are clear and crisp and the stylised look to everything works well. Sounds are excellent with some great voice acting all around from all the puppets and great ambient background noise on the sets.I did come across some bugs when I played (on launch day so these may well be fixed), I had the guns randomly not shoot at times or shoot at random angles away from the crosshair, I also had saves not working properly (but I believe the save issues has been resolved) but it wasn't enough of an issue to stop me getting through this excellent experience. Well worth a purchase even at the relatively high asking price and a game I may even replay to find more of the secrets.

_childDocuments_.review: I despise horror games, but had heard that this game isn't really a survival horror game, and so I tried it.  Delightfully, while this game sort of appears to be some kind of horror game in the vein of Five Nights at Freddy's, it actually plays more like a System Shock game with a dash of Resident Evil puzzle solving.  It's the friendliest horror game you'll ever see.You play as a disgruntled New York Repairman tasked with shutting down a rogue broadcast at the old public access TV station host to a Sesame Street-like puppet show.  Predictably, the puppets come alive and you have to fight your way through to finish your job.  But they're not as threatening as similar games would have them behave.  Enemies are more like...obstacles.  They loudly babble to themselves so you know they're there long before you see them.  They stand in one place until you move close to them AND they see you, whereupon they try to hug you (it's unclear if this actually is harming you or whether the ornery main character just HATES hugs).  There's very very few "ambushes" or other unfair scare tactics.  Since the enemies act predictably, they're not exactly scary.  And most enemies can simply be avoided or run past.I do want to compliment the gameplay systems of this game.  Once "killed" enemies are knocked out until you leave the room, whereupon they respawn.  However, you can use duct tape that you've found to tape the arms of a downed puppet, preventing them from hugging you in the future and thus permanently removing the enemy from the game in that spot.  Since there's a lot of back and forth traversing the map, you can disable enemies in key spots that allows you to walk around without fighting much of anything.  There's also a super enemy in each of the stages of the game that can't be defeated and you have to avoid, but even they can be disabled by solving puzzles.The level design is really good with lots of unlockable shortcuts for your item hunting.  You also get a nice mapping system.  Rooms are highlighted in red if there's still an item to be found inside them, and green if they're all complete so while you explore you don't miss anything.  There's a modest amount of backtracking through the levels and you get a familiarity with the shortcuts and such.The story and worldbuilding is also pretty good.  The whole theme is really on point, a mix of Sesame Street, Muppets, and Lamb Chop's Singalong references peppered throughout and some accurately spoofed voice acting.I highly recommend.  This is a treat.
_childDocuments_.name: My Friendly Neighborhood

_childDocuments_.review: My Friendly Neighborhood isn't another mascot horror game instead it is an indie survival horror puzzle game about a repairman named Gordon who is sent to a film studio for a Saturday morning puppet show that is obviosly heavily inspired by Sesame Street. In it's core the game is „another“ homage to survival horror classics like Resident Evil 1. From RE4's inventory management, manual save tokens, puzzles, lots of backtracking, navigation(which was a big problem for me because I easily get lost in these type of games) it's all here. But this isn't just another poorly executed game which copies stuff from survival horror classics, no the devs added new unique mechanics or put their own spin on already existing ones. The game can very well stand on its own due to the fact that it's a mix between satire and horror. It also has a big interconnected map and you can backtrack most of the time so you can use your new found items or keys to solve puzzles or reveal secrets. I followed the development for years and I also played the demo, the one thing that bothered me is that the puppets don't have many voicelines. Some lines from the demo are still in the game, which is not a bad thing but since there are so few I can see that it could get annoying for some people. Luckily that wasn't the case for me, Norman( one of the puppets) teaching you to count by swallowing your hands so you know that you have two hands in your stomach was a weird but a nice way to break up the tension. This tension and the horror are both tied to the isolated and narrow corridors in which you can find yourself easily surrounded by puppets that all want to hug you. The replay value is also pretty big, you can unlock different cheats like infinite ammo or long arms, unlock different endings, solve unsolved puzzles from your last playthrough to unlock new secrets and yes there are a lot of secrets and some even haven't been solved by the community at the time of writing this review. Overall My Friendly Neighborhood is already one of my indie game highlights of this year and it perfectly balances horror, humor and satire and the mix between puzzles and fighting is very well executed.Copied the review from my   Profile⠀⠀

_childDocuments_.review: I have played this game for 15 hours in the first week I got it. I have been obsessed, so let's go over what makes this game amazing, and potentially the best mascot horror game right now.SPOILERS AHEAD (you should know that)THE STORY-LINEThe lore of this game doesn't take 9 years+ to figure out, and it's pretty simple too. The cause and effect is also great too, like how the war caused the city to become depressing and poor.THE GAMEPLAYThe gameplay is so good, I don't even know where to start. The voice lines were perfect and the combat system was good too. If you are someone who is new to shooters or not good at them, THIS IS THE PERFECT STARTING GAME FOR YOU! The mechanics of the puppets are very unique. The way that it's not just "Ahhh a scary guy that's gonna jumpscare me!" but it's a talking puppet makes it much more unique, and somehow even though the puppets talk all the time and don't have the scariest designs, they are still very scary! The puzzles are also a nice touch, because if they weren't there this game would be very bland and boring, but whats a game like this without a puzzle? The puzzles are all unique in their own way too, like helping the different puppets to get the secret ending... speaking of endings, that's the next topic!ENDINGSThe endings in this game are some of the best endings I have ever seen. Especially the true ending, it made me feel very happy and was one of the reasons why this is one of my favorite games. The bad endings can make you feel bad or sad, but any ending (besides the leave early ending) is really worth it. Though I feel that you should play for the gameplay more than the ending. (Obviously)MUSICThe music in this game is immaculate, especially the boss theme. The piano and the saxophone really carry that theme. The ending credits are really special because they decided to make their own song with the puppets that sing. If they ever make My Friendly Neighborhood a show, I really hope that's the intro or outro theme. The ambiance in this game makes you feel a certain way too, and they always fit the environment, which is my next topic.ENVIRONMENTThe environment is what makes this game... this game! Every section is on the line of realistic and cartoony, which is one of my favorite styles. I also LOVE how you can see the outside world through windows and when you're outside. You can also hear cars, and the traffic lights change when you can see them when climbing the antenna, which is a really nice touch that they didn't have to add, but did anyways! The environments are always different, but something about them always makes you know that you're playing "My Friendly Neighborhood" and some games cant perfect that like this game does.BOSSESThe bosses are really unique, the curtain one especially! Instead of just shooting any part of the curtain boss, you have to shoot the eyes of it, and it will shoot out puppets that attack you. This boss is different than a lot of other bosses in other games. The final boss isn't as unique, but it is a pretty good one!REPLAYABILITY The games items don't spawn in random places each time, they are always in the same place as far as I know, so the items will always be in the same spot in every playthrough. Though, this doesn't change the fact that the game is VERY replayable, with unlockable cheats you can use to make the game funnier and harder. And with noclip mode, they added in little secrets that you wouldn't be able to see otherwise, like the giant puppet leaning over the penthouse that cannot be seen when playing normally without noclip mode. These cheats and modes make it so the game can be replayed and have something different every time, let alone the different difficulties too.Now, time to talk about the things that I think could be better.MORE BOSSESThe curtain and the final boss are really only two bosses in this game (unless you count the janitor thing, the green dinosaur thing, the dogs, and the big bird. (lmk if I'm missing any), and I feel like this game could benefit from more bosses in some sort of DLC.BOSSES ARE WAY TOO SHORTBoth bosses can be defeated in less than 2 minutes, and I find it kind of sad. The final boss isn't hard at all if you have the conclusion gun, and the curtain boss can be defeated in less that a minute if you have enough bullets in the shotgun or if you use the grenade.COSTS MONEY TO SAVEI can understand it costing money to use the healing station, but it also costs money to save, which I guess makes the game a little harder and you can't spend your coins recklessly, but I feel like if you just got by a hard part and have no coins, you would have to replay that part again. But, most save rooms have coins in them, like the last save room before the final boss, so you should be fine.That's really all I have, sorry for going on for that long, but please, if you haven't already, PLAY THIS GAME!

_childDocuments_.review: Meh... It has lots of style and heart. However, the wonky hit boxes and lack of ability to precisely aim your weapons spoil the concept of a survival horror. Also, the different characters all draw from the same very shallow pool of voice-lines while seemingly having few unique pieces of dialogue. Not to mention, the puppets NEVER stop talking. This breaks immersion and becomes quite tiresome quickly. Finally, the duct-tape mechanic is just annoying. Especially with how limited the resource is. Having to take time and tear the puppets limb from limb so they don't just resurrect every time you leave a room would have been a better choice. Or, you know, once you've shot and or smashed them with a wrench roughly 6 to 7 times, they could just stay dead.Gonna finish it to see where the story goes, but the journey hasn't been that much fun so far.Edit: Not even going to finish... The repetitive slog of having to shoot and kill the same re-skinned immortal enemies over and over while listening to the incessant drivel about swallowing hands is too much.The sparse loot is also a problem. Most of it is just pistol ammo. However, even if there is room in the inventory, only 99 plus a full clip is allowed to be held. If you pick up ammo after that it just disappears into the void. One comes across no end of locked panels and doors requiring a plethora of different keys or tools to open, but whats in the next cabinet? Oh good, more pistol ammo I cant hold!The premise of this game is really very interesting and refreshing. Unfortunately, it is bogged down by poor execution and lack of polish.

_childDocuments_.review: I'd avoided this game because I figured it'd be something along the lines of Five Nights at Freddy's and the like (which really isn't my kind of genre), so I didn't think anything of it. But, while binging through a backlog of let's plays from a YouTuber I watch, I noticed that My Friendly Neighborhood was something altogether different.No, it wasn't the lack of gore, although I thought that was cool. I like horror games (Amnesia, Signalis, Dead Space, Resident Evil Village), but the elements I enjoy aren't enhanced by gore, so it's absence was surprising, given my assumptions related to mascot horror. Nor was it the humorous elements, for I wouldn't feel confident in categorizing this work as one of comedy (although many things about it brought me a smile). Instead, I would say that its very substance separated it as something worth seeing.At its heart is something I've not really seen in movies or games (at least, not done well), and that's the challenge of crafting a story that has some kind of moral, message, or meaning that is meant to transcend a trite aphorism. At the center of the story is Hope. Somehow, at least by my reckoning, it manages to articulate its purpose without descending into heavy-handed soapboxing or cheesy idealism.I don't know that I want to go too much more into detail on that. Partly for spoilers, but also because I think that something would be lost in reading my summary rather than seeing it unfold for yourself. The story, itself, communicates something that I would find hard to justify with this review.For some, I can see how this game might be a mixed bag: it's not scary enough for the horror junkies, not technical enough for the fans of precision-based rewards, and not graphics-intensive enough for those looking to push their rig to its limits. Some might hear the comment, "It's a game made with love," and assume that fans have simply decided to appraise the game with eyes half closed so as to see past its limits. But I would put it this way: "This is a game with character."It's a kind of excellence that budget can't buy: music that fits so seamlessly into the scene and overall game world; pastiches and callouts to other games--not as cheap laughs or obscure references for its own sake but for the simple joy to share them with fellow fans; puns and fictional poster parodies of Muppet movies. In short, a game made with care--not merely for itself, but for everything that it seeks to include within itself.I wish more games were like this; these are the ones I want to play and share with others.

_childDocuments_.review: "My Friendly Neighborhood" is a lovingly crafted homage to Resident Evil and Jim Henson's many works. The world of "MFN" is a joy to explore which is important in exploration based game. Each room felt unique from each other with little details and stuff to find. The world design kind of reminded me of "Luigi's Mansion" with how every room had a purpose within the world, as if this was a real production studio.  The exploration was also made more enjoyable through all of the unlock-able shortcut gained through progress, which really helped with back tracking. I loved the characters of "MFN" especially Ricky, who was voiced perfectly by Arlo. The cut scenes between Ricky and the main character Gordon are some of my favourite moments in the game. The cut scene in general are fun and sometimes a little heartwarming. "MFN's" story overall is very sweet and un cynical for a horror game which I found refreshing. I highly recommend My Friendly Neighborhood if you love "The Muppets" or "Resident Evil"8/10

_childDocuments_.review: My Friendly Neighborhood is essentially a condensed Resident Evil game with a Sesame Street Theme. There's tons of thought put into every room within every area, and many impressive details that proves just how strong the creative vision is. With just a little bit of polish, balancing, and maybe like 1-2 more enemy types, this game could easily be a 10/10 for the price. The final section of the game in particular felt like a missed opportunity since it introduces new concepts but only lasts for about 5 minutes before the game is over. Finding secrets organically felt rewarding and nostalgic. The game itself has a surprisingly heartwarming message although it left me with more questions than answers.The game length is about 5hrs if you are thorough, there's some replayability as well.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is everything I had hoped it would be and just a bit more. It's basically impossible to talk about the gameplay without comparing it to resident evil, because it's very clearly inspired by resident evil's formula, but this game does it so well that I'm by no means upset about that. The artstyle is very nice, the characters are entertaining to say very little, and the weapons and gameplay balance feels surprisingly good. As of this review, I've played 21 hours of this game and I've already gone out of my way to do all the things. The puzzles strike a nice balance of being simple enough to understand even for novice players without just outright handing the answers to players. Additionally, there's extra puzzles for more advanced players that require a bit more effort, which I appreciate. I also appreciate that the creators of the game went through the trouble of hiding secrets for those who want to look for them. Altogether, I'd say My Friendly Neighborhood is a well-worth-it experience and a gem of an indie game.

_childDocuments_.review: Sesame Street meets Resident Evil.I usually don't replay games. I find it tedious, especially if I just finished a playthrough. So, I want you all to know that I've played through this game 4 times in the past...however many days its been since release - I've been having too much fun playing the game to keep track.Let me tell you friends. This game. THIS GAME. What a marvelous thing this game is! A refreshing twist on Mascot Horror. No dead children's souls fueling the horrors, no unstoppable evil monster that was supposedly made for children but looks horrifying and commits murders. Instead, the reality of the situation is far more nuanced.I've stated before that I'm a fan of the intersection of comedy and horror, and My Friendly Neighborhood is right in that awesome, sweet place. There is some genuinely terrifying imagery in this game, but 90% of it is done with goofy looking puppets being weird. Imagine randomly finding the mangled body of Cookie Monster inside a locker with very little rhyme or reason as to why it's there. Then remember that in this universe, Cookie Monster is not only alive, he is a sapient entity that may or may not be capable of dying. You are simply left to ponder which of those possibilities is worse as you stare into the still, motionless body's googly eyes. There are tons of moments like that. I think my favorite are when you stop and listen to the insane babbling of your friends and they talk about doing things like cutting their friends into different shapes to sew them back together because crafts are FUN! It’s terrifying, but it’s absurd. And that's just the Friendly Neighbors - the ones who still want to be your friend and give you hugs, they're just a bit confused. There are other, darker things lurking in the Neighborhood.Another thing I really like about this game is the difficulty settings. Enemies don’t just take more damage or do more damage from difficultly to difficulty, there are a lot of other things that change. The amount of ammo and supplies you find can change, what enemies you even encounter will change, and sometimes the Devs will even play mean tricks on you, like taking something that in the lower difficulties that was just a statue or background element and turning it into an enemy. Your own expectations as the player suddenly play into the difficulty, and that’s awesome. And each of these changes may or may not be implemented from difficulty to difficulty, making each new run on a different difficulty a unique experience. It’s always really cool when a developer makes a game more challenging by doing things more complicated then just “making the numbers bigger”.The themes of this game are also inspirational. The themes of this game are nothing new, but the way the story explores those themes is pretty awesome. A lot of games touch on how kindness - true kindness - can be hard, for instance, but My Friendly Neighborhood says that even the completely unrealistic kindness of a children's TV Show is something worth respecting and aspiring to. That by poo-pooing it as something foolish and weak, we make ourselves weak fools. It’s a really cool take, especially in times like these where the world seems motivated by misery. It’s telling that in every ending where Gordon decides not to help the puppets, nothing happens. The broadcast is eventually stopped and nothing changes, and eventually the incident is forgotten – the Neighborhood disappears again. I think it’s meant to say that unless we deliberately make a choice to be kind, to sacrifice for others, nothing is ever going to get better. My only criticism of the game is that you can’t copy saves (which is really only a complaint I had because it meant I had to play threw it 3 more times to get all the endings, which I won’t be complaining about because it’s just that good a game), and that the health of the puppets seems really inconsistent. Maybe it’s the inconsistent bouncing of the ammo, but I found that I never really knew how much damage a puppet could take before it went down. The same exact puppet from one fight to the next could take 5 or 6 more hits. I’m not even sure how I feel about that one though because you could argue it adds to the horror elements of the game. Engaging a puppet is always a risk because you can never be entirely certain if you’re equipped to handle it or not, especially on the higher difficulties when ammo is scarce and most take a LOT of hits. I can certainly understand that as the point, and it definitely works if that’s what they were going for – I just wouldn’t have chose to do it that way myself because I’m one of those weirdos who doesn’t like waste. I also would have buffed the wrench, making it always a guaranteed one or two hit kill because getting close enough to the puppets to risk using it should be rewarded. But then the Devs gave me the Mega Wrench cheat and that’s literally what it does. What I’m saying is every complaint I could have is addressed. Part of me desperately wants more of this game and this world. But a part of me recognizes that at least some of those things might lessen this game. For instance, I really want answers to what in the actual ♥♥♥♥ was going on with the Unfriendly Neighborhood. But part of what makes the Unfriendly Neighborhood (and the Curt ‘n Call) segment so butt-clenchingly terrifying is how unexplained it is. It feels like it may even be a deliberate statement about how absolute, undistilled cruelty is at its core incomprehensible. If we explained how and why they came to believe that apparently doing things like sewing human teeth into their faces was a good idea and what the amalgam hoped to achieve by amalgamating itself – if that was even if its choice in the first place – we might lose that. Part of me wants an explanation for why the Neighbors even exist, but part of me knows what makes the Neighbors so interesting is how they’re not fueled by the souls of murdered children or whatever. They’re just puppets, and it feels like anything that answered how they’re alive and sapient might ruin that thing that makes them so unique in the Mascot Horror Genre if it’s not done with a lot of care. There are somethings, though, that I KNOW I want more of. I want more of Gordon being kind to the puppets and helping them through their problems. I want to see more of them being absolutely unhinged. I want more of them being that way while Gordon plays the straight man, even though he also does seem to, at least on some level, enjoy the chaos too. You don’t get to tell me he doesn’t when he sits down and plays a board game with a puppet who smacks him across the room whenever he loses or doesn’t follow the rules when he could just as easily blast the thing with his Rolodexer and take the key it’s protecting. If I were to make a sequel, it would be Gordon going around the studios to repair things and spiff things up while giving emotional support to the Puppets before clearing out The Unfriendly Neighborhood and learning things like where they got those teeth from. But that’s just what I’d want, it might not be what I need.TL;DR: If you’re looking for a fun, puzzley Mascot Horror game that does something new while being charming, creepy, adorable and occasionally absolutely horrifying, My Friendly Neighbor will not only satisfy, it will delight.

_childDocuments_.review: My friendly neighborhood is a fantastic homage to survival horror that somehow has no horror itself. A game that isn't scary at all yet still manages to be one of the better spiritual successors to resident evil.This game can easily be described as a mash up of Resident Evil 7 and sesame street, which sounds like a recipe for disaster but ends up working really well. This isn't a five nights at freddies jump scare simulator, this is a true homage to classic survival horror. You have limited inventory slots, limited saves, an interconnected world with a hub, a mechanic for dealing with enemies to keep them down permanently similar to crimson heads from RE1 remake and a crank. You play as Gordan, a disgruntled mechanic doing his last job of the day, he's sent to an abandoned TV studio to switch off a broadcast that basically plays sesame street 24/7. But once you arrive things aren't quite what they seem and the out of control puppets turn on you. Simply put, I loved every second of this game, it is short but most quality horror games know it's best not to outstay their welcome and instead fill the game with many options for replayability, and this game has that in spades. The world is so vibrant and fun to explore, I've seen many people say it has a bioshock vibe and I'm inclined to agree, the world is so wonderfully crafted and it really sucks you in.Overall my only real complaint is that it lacks the horror from survival horror and I feel they could've pushed this into a more messed up direction. It sorta gave me the same feeling as bugsnax. If you love old school survival horror this is a fantastic love letter to the genre in a fantastic and original setting, you won't be scared but you'll have a great time anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: My Friendly Neighborhood

_childDocuments_.review: Been waiting to play since demo and became even more excited after the PAX EAST demo. I loved the game. Seeing so many references to the Muppets and Sesame street was fantastic, getting to help the neighbors was delightful and the style was amazing. The game had FANTASTIC voice acting. Ricky was my favorite neighbor and someday if the game does well enough, please make a Ricky plush. The game is well made, I didn't experience any issues on day one launch. The characters, atmosphere, weapons and more were all wonderfully designed(the weapons had to be one of the most creative designs we got, they were so cool) The game was a mix of many amazing things many people love like nods to the Jim Henson Company plus mechanics from popular survival horror games we love like Resident Evil.Is it the scariest game? Not really. There were some on point jump scares and it had a wonderful overall atmosphere to the studio, Sadly with no actual directions given and just being handed pieces to future puzzles to solve, I felt that that the game was lacking in some way. After playing a run of the game in one sit down, the neighbors constant talking became very annoying(you can turn down the audio of the neighbors so you don't have to hear them.) At first it was very fun to listen to them but in rooms were there were more than 1 it became too much and I found myself wasting ammo just so I wouldn't have to hear them. I wish some puzzles had a bit more guidance such as Gordon(the main character) voices his thoughts a bit more. Gordon having more voice lines overall would have been very fun as well maybe so we could have learned more of his perspective to on the world as well. To avoid spoilers I'll be a bit vague, I wish that we had more time in the more scarier section of the game where we got to experience being in the dark with some majorly less friendly neighbors. More time there or if the game had more of that in general then I think it would have been a bit of a more frightening experience overall.Overall, I loved the game and would highly recommend it despite it not being the most frightening horror games. I think it would be great for those who don't do well with super scary games, Jim Henson fans, and those looking for a fun experience.I highly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: My Friendly Neighborhood

_childDocuments_.review: After completing the game and all the major side objectives, I can firmly say My Friendly Neighborhood is horror for kids not only done right, but done outstandingly. I also firmly believe that is a game, despite what many may feel about the mascot horror genre, is a game that can be enjoyed by pretty much all ages and demographics, offering genuinely engaging gameplay experience that requires critical thinking and a little bit of resource management and planning, as well as just an awesome visual style, atmosphere and story. This is a game made with an overwhelming amount of love, care and has been polished to near perfection, creating an overall unforgettable experience of a game. Mascot Horror has been progressively garnering a bad rep over the past 2 years or so, especially within the last year, but My Friendly Neighborhood shows it can be an outstanding genre if executed properly. If you're even remotely interested in this game, I 100% consider it worth it. It's a wonderful time, and as someone who actively engages with Mascot Horror as a genre, I think this might be one of the best things to come out of it, especially within the last few years.Read on if you want a more detailed opinion explanation.Firstly, I'd like to say I never really encountered any bugs. The closest you can call bugs are the janky ragdoll physics, which I think is 100% part of the charm of the game as you're fighting sentient puppet characters for the game's entire runtime, and comedy is pretty imbued into the core philosophy of this game. But other than that, it runs like a dream, load times are short as well and it overall functioned far more than every other mascot horror game I've played, well... ever, and I say that as a fan of the genre.The game's gameplay is a loving combination of Resident Evil, Bioshock and your typical horror game. The scares are present and tension can get very high as with all good survival horror games, but there's also plenty of genuinely charismatic and funny moments that help ease the tension. The game is able to masterfully balance this tone, creating a really unique atmosphere and gameplay experience. It's astounding, really, how engaging the gameplay is. Just be aware, you really should (and are expected) to explore whatever you can, and you will have to backtrack. However, the backtracking is far more engaging than many other games, especially since backtracking often involves going into new areas you haven't accessed, but can now. I would not say it falls into the same pitfalls other games do with their backtracking.The pacing is also fantastic. I never found myself getting bored, and I think the game's length is perfect. I wasn't left feeling unsatisfied or a negative feeling of desiring more, nor did I feel the game overstayed its welcome. It's just the right amount of length. The visuals are on-point, the character designs really do give a strong familiarity to the Muppets and Sesame Street characters without being too derivative and all the areas in the game having a very strong visual style and can clearly be separated from how they look. The soundtrack, when its present, is also pretty good and really does add to the atmosphere.I think what caught me off-guard was the story. It's simple, but unlike many mascot horror games, it's actually present, there's loads of genuinely interesting information about it you can actually come across as you play the game, and it actually wraps itself up all in one game. A first, in a long time for Mascot Horror as a genre. However, not only that... but it's a really heartwarming story. It's not the most overwhelmingly emotionally complex thing ever, but combined with everything else about the game, I did find myself very touched by the message the game puts forward. The story is also one of the main reasons I think this game is horror for kids is done right, as mentioned earlier in the review. It's good, it's quality, and it's far more appropriate for the main demographic of the genre while still being told in an interesting and mature way that even people my age (early 20s) and older could definitely appreciate. Seriously, some people don't know how nice it is to get a mascot horror game where the story is clearly communicated and self-contained in one game. I was so genuinely shocked this game wasn't obnoxious like so many others.Overall, My Friendly Neighborhood is a game that sets a new standards for Mascot Horror, providing a clear and concise narrative with something to say while also being both age appropriate for the majority of Mascot Horror's audience, but also being strikingly unique and maturely told for older audiences to appreciate as well, with the narrative itself breaking a lot of conventions of Mascot Horror for the better. The gameplay is fun and engaging, and exploring the map feels rewarding and solving puzzles and thinking your way through the problems the game presents is satisfying and fun. The visuals, attention to detail, and overall game performance polish is also amazing.I cannot recommend this game enough for both non-horror fans and horror fans alike. It's definitely something special, and I hope it gets the recognition it deserves.

_childDocuments_.review: That is how introverts see extroverts...-I am friend!!!-Don't touch meSo relatable.Also it's a good game, really like the style of it. The mix of muppets with resident evil. _childDocuments_.review: Casting aside the blood and guts that other games over rely upon, My Friendly Neighborhood plays like a G-Rated Survival Horror Classic. it feels refreshing for a game to manage to deliver a scary experience without having to wave around gore-caked cliches that feel tired and worn out. Instead, the game's writing, atmosphere, and gameplay all come together to deliver the thrills and chills of the genre. _childDocuments_.review: A game that gave me nearly everything I could have wanted from it. It feels like a love letter to survival horror but adds its own spin to a lot of it. I will say this right now, this game is not that scary unless you have some fear of puppets like the Muppets or Sesame Street. That being said it is absolutely worth playing just because it is that good. A solid point of reference is Resident Evil 7. You will go through an old studio while avoiding puppets that don't want to kill you but hug you for attention. Sadly they don't know their own strength and do hurt you so there is danger. When you damage them they don't die but come back as soon as you leave an area. To counter this you need to tape them up with a limited amount of duct tape. Combine this with a finite amount of ammo, healing, and saves you will need to manage everything to get through. If you are a vet at the genre you should have no problems beating the game but once you start going for all the achievements you will find a lot of depth to this game once it starts putting in more restrictions. On the hardest one you will find no ammo whatsoever so you need to know the game like the back of your hand. Now on to the story.  This game won't take you all that much time even on repeat playthoughs I only clocked in around 13 hours. It still was worth it to me at the full $30 just for the uniqueness of it but for those who don't much care for that I'd say $20 is more than fair.

_childDocuments_.review: Albeit with a few little issues here and there, performance was good I'm talking about game design, it was a great game.  My main problems stemmed from items being needlessly difficult to find at times, the inconsistent damage of weapons, the wrench being extremely deceptive with it's effective range, and a few places and items that were utterly redundant.  In fact, the entire last segment of the game really ruined the ending for me.  I won't spoil, but suffice to say the big fancy gun is pointless and you might as well go to that last stage with absolutely nothing in your inventory.It was a great game, but the ending was basically a wet thud because of the last stage.  I recommend it for people who like mildly tense survival horror, but don't expect to get more than a days worth of play unless you go for %100.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the Muppets, and I love Resident evil. This game manages to combine the two into an experience I wont be forgetting any time soon. In a wave of tried out mascot and "kiddie" horror games, My Friendly neighborhood manages to subvert this trend and stand above the rest. The game isn't particularly scary,nor does it really try to be either, coming off as almost seemingly as a Meta-Commentary on the state of horror games where Instead of relying on jumpscares or mechanics that revolve around waiting around for something scary to happen, the game takes mechanics from some of the best Resident Evil games to create a tense survival horror experience. Just without any of the horror...though there are some minor exceptions that I won't be mentioning, it would be a damn shame to have the surprise ruined like I did. (♥♥♥♥ you Youtube) Do not go into this game expecting five nights at freddy's or silent hill or you're going to be disappointed. However If you are a fan of Resident Evil gameplay, mechanics, and its endless replayability You'll feel right at home in the neighborhood.

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely good game with survival horror roots. The game isn't visually scary, but instead sets out to prove that strong survival mechanics alone can make for tense, scary moments. It also has a positive message at the end about the importance of bringing positivity and morals to the community, just like Sesame Street. I honestly expected this to be just another game cashing in on the mascot horror genre like so many others after Five Nights at Freddy's success, but My Friendly Neighborhood is not that. It's a powerful reminder that games can be good and have something to say. Highly recommended. Play this game. Survival difficulty on your first run is a must for the true experience.Edit: I went back and looked at some of the reviews and saw people calling this a mascot horror game, which is typecasting it in the worst way possible. Don't think of this as an attempt to grab kids and streamers attention like games in the mascot horror genre, the game is much more beautiful than that. When the game describes itself as survival horror, it really means it, and its mechanics are deeper than being labelled mascot horror.

_childDocuments_.review: +  From the iconic sounding pitter patter of footsteps on stairs, to the use of ducktape as a lighter replacement, to even the puzzle and color-coded keys - My Friendly Neighborhood wears its inspiration on its sleeve, and it wears it well. I was smiling very often recognizing how many ways this game was clearly influenced by Resident Evil 1 (like . But, it did not just copy from what came before: the carefree, goofy attitude of the puppets, mixed in with unhinged posing and dialogue, is unsettling in a way that is wholly unique from its inspiration. The game has a ton of heart that contrasts from the action horror movie vibe that Resident Evil originally had, and involves a much more personal story.+  The environments are bright and colorful, the puppets are cartoonish and cute. Your weapons are literature-focused, shooting literal letters at your puppet pals. All of it is a love letter to the age of Sesame Street and Muppets (Muppets especially). But the game very cleverly plays with your nostalgia for these cheeky and cute puppets -  with unnerving silence, unhinged and loud statements, jittery stuttering movement, eerily quiet environments... It's not a game with blood or gore, nor will it give you scares like Poppy Playtime, but there's something a little off about the puppets that will make you uncomfortable all the same.+  The thing that struck me the most about this game was how earnest it is. There are some genuinely sweet moments that don't feel hacky or forced. The overarching theme of the game - the loss of innocence, overwhelming cynicism and isolation in modern society, the horrors of war and how it affected Modern America's views on entertainment - none of it is preached to you, and it's all surface level. But there's just enough of it to where you really start to feel for the puppets, who feel like people simply left behind, unsure of such adult concepts and unable to grasp with them. Ricky is the only puppet that feels as though he might have some capacity to try and understand what happened, but the rest of them might as well be children themselves.+  My ingame playtime was ~5:30 for the first playthrough, with not an inch of fat (although a bit of backtracking, to be sure). I am surprised to learn that there were a few secrets I didn't find - which, usually, on a first playthrough, I try my best to do, but some of the secrets are intricate! Combined with two higher difficulties, optional gameplay modes (including a speedrun mode and a DUSK mode, which lets you bunny hop), several unlockable cheats and ranking/achivements to pursue, and you have a solid survival horror clone that leans into the replayability mechanics of RE2 and RE3.-  There are several ideas that feel like they'll lead somewhere but are never quite utilized well. The , for example, felt like it should've been a full zone with higher stakes and more unnerving scares. After all, it was a SLAM DUNK set up with how much of a tone shift it was from the rest of the game. However, it is a short area with one uneventful chase and a giant boss fight that isn't quite up to par with Resident Evil's iconic fights. There are other examples of playful and interesting mechanic choices, such as the , that are only used once in a standard playthrough and never again.-  "The war" is a phrase you'll hear brought up a lot of times in the game, as well as the concepts of overwhelming loneliness in a city and human cynicism and greed ruining the wholesome world of My Friendly Neighborhood. They tease at the subject being something the main character suffers from, and yet for all the talking Gordon does with himself and fellow puppets - we don't ever really learn anything about him. This would be fine normally, but the game seems to make Gordon's voice matter quite a bit in the way he talks with the puppets. In fact, Gordon has several incredibly vulnerable moments that can be a bit touching, which leaves you craving to know more about our hero. The Puppets are clearly about spreading joy in the world and the concept of "being a good neighbor", but Ricky and the rest of the puppets never quite return the favor to Gordon when he goes out of his way to help all of them out.  This, combined with , makes you start to wonder if originally there was supposed to be more of a back and forth - some sort of situation where Gordon received some of the hope that he desperately needed, or more backstory on why he lost a lot of the light in his life. This entire situation is a missed opportunity to really bring the game full circle on why .- : I really loved the direction of trying to get you to feel for the puppets, which it certainly did succeed in for the main cast - but it starts to unravel when you think about a majority of your puppet encounters. If I can , where do a majority of the other puppets factor into this? Do they feel bad for choking Gordon with their hugging grabs? Does Gordon just forgive them for that? -  I truly expected the enemies to have unique death/loss scenes, with how varied their way of attacking you was. For example, Gobblette's running hungry growling implies being caught will be an instant game over, but like all enemies, getting hit by her simply knocks you to the ground. Granted, we are dealing with puppets, yes, but even in . This is a huge misstep that is basically required in a survival horror game, because if the stakes are the exact same, why should I be intimidated by any other type of enemy? Imagine if the plant zombies in RE2 Remake didn't instantly kill you if you failed to get out of their grab, or the Hunter Gamma in RE3.-  While I felt like the gameplay wasn't terrible, it definitely lacks the feel of modern survival horror. Clean animations and sway that give real world weight to your weapons, for example, are nonexistent, and gunplay feels inconsistent - like I'm often shooting away from what I'm actually aiming at. You're left with gameplay that is okay, but could be better.This game was a surprise hit for me. It's definitely far from perfect - there are a lot of missed opportunities in writing and gameplay, where the game falls short on its full potential. It's not particularly scary, and lacks some of the elements of Survival Horror that make the genre so entertaining.But despite that, it was a game with a ton of heart that carved out its own distinct identity. It made me grin quite often with its references to Resident Evil. I enjoyed every second of it, and cannot wait to see what comes next for this studio.If you're a fan of Resident Evil or other Survival Horror, this game is a must play to hold you over and make you smile. If you're not, it can serve as a great entry point.

It's hard to know where to begin because it's a package of charm, excitement, and spine-tingling fear, among other things—huge kudos to the developers for their outstanding creativity. Truly unique.
