_childDocuments_.name: Frogun

_childDocuments_.review: Very addictive platformer that feels like a lost gem from the N64/PS1/Saturn era. The level design reminds me a lot of Pac Man world where it blends elements from both 2D and 3D platformers, and it has a touch of collectathon influence with collectable coins and gems along with dialogue boxes sounded with grunts like in the Banjo Kazooie games. The frog grapple gun is also very unique and adds a puzzle solving element to the levels.
_childDocuments_.name: Frogun

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute treat of a game. Plays great, looks awesome and the soundtrack bops. The colourful lowpoly aesthetic is particularly well-developed. I really enjoy the platforming, but what stuck out to me was the quality of the puzzles. There's a lot of optional collectables and you've gotta be observant and clever to get them all. Very satisfying when you clear a level and see that you got everything. Thoroughly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Frogun

_childDocuments_.review: Join Renata as she adventures across a world of mystical ruins with the titular FROGUN! Frogun is an old-school platformer with the soul of the PS1/N64 era, in which your frog-shaped grappling hook is a your best friend!. Renata's parents are world-renown explorers, archeologists and inventors that travel all over the world uncovering the secrets of the past, bringing her with them in their expeditions. However, in their latest adventure, they decide to leave her at the base camp - the Beelzebub ruins are said to be too dangerous. For three whole days she waits, her pride hurt and bored out of her mind, until she realized: if they haven't returned yet, something must have happened to them! In a hurry she grabs her parents' last invention, the Frogun, and heads to the ruins to rescue them, and prove that she's as capable as them!

name: SOL CRESTA
detailed_description: SOL CRESTA Complete Set Enjoy EVERYTHING that SOL CRESTA has to offer! Get the SOL CRESTA Complete Set at a great new price that offers the slick and speedy gameplay of the main game's Arcade Mode, the densely woven story of the Dramatic DLC, and the Legendary Fighters DLC that includes the legendary fighters from the CRESTA series. What you get in the SOL CRESTA Complete Set : - SOL CRESTA main game - SOL CRESTA Dramatic DLC - SOL CRESTA 'Legendary Fighters' DLC Set (CR47, Wing Galiber, Wing Galiber II included) Note: The SOL CRESTA Complete Set consists of the SOL CRESTA main game and all DLC packs that are currently available to purchase, with no exclusive content. Be careful of duplicate purchases. Prepare to Go Supernova with Excitement with the Dramatic DLC! - A parade of unique and expressive characters - A big-bang story penned by Hideki Kamiya, the force behind Bayonetta and The Wonderful 101 - A dense Database filled with images of and information about every friendly and enemy character, ship, and device - The continuation of the Cresta saga, which began with 80s classics Moon Cresta and Terra Cresta - A story that unfolds differently from Arcade Mode, with a true ending that awaits the truly bold! Enrich Your SOL CRESTA Experience with the Legendary Fighters DLC Set! Legendary fighters from the CRESTA series are back and yours to maneuver as you try and stop Mega Zofer’s conquest of the solar system. These 3 additional fighters can also be used for score rankings in Caravan Mode. The icon of the fighter used will be recorded along with your high score. Challenge yourself and see how much performance you can bring out of these legendary fighters, which are different to the Yamato fighters in many ways. CR47 The main fighter from Moon Cresta is back in all its former glory for you to pilot! Picking up a special CR47 Emblem will cause your allied fighters to appear. Dock with fighters II and III to power up your craft, just like in Moon Cresta. The CR47 can perform Charge Shots and perhaps even turn into a phoenix SOL CRESTA-style?! Wing Galiber The main fighter from Terra Cresta is miraculously back to fly one more time! Just as in Terra Cresta, dock with 5 of your ally fighters that appear from the hangar and experience a variety of different attack variations. Of course, the Formation Attack and phoenix are back! Wing Galiber II The main fighter from Terra Cresta II: Mandler no Gyakushuu, making its long-awaited return to battle. In addition to its Formation Attack and the legendary Firebird Attack, numerous special attacks have been carefully revived, such as Fire Formation, Formation Shot, and P.R.B. (Phoenix Rolling Bomber). Note: These 3 additional fighters cannot be used in Dramatic Mode included in the SOL CRESTA Dramatic DLC. Check the in-game manual for the controls of these 3 additional fighters. SOL CRESTA Dramatic Edition Trial Version This demo allows you to enjoy Stage 1 of SOL CRESTA's Arcade Mode, as well as a part of Stage 1 of the SOL CRESTA Dramatic DLC Dramatic Mode. *Scores from the demo version will not be saved or uploaded to online rankings. *Some aspects of the demo may differ from the full version of the game. *The purchase of both SOL CRESTA and the SOL CRESTA Dramatic DLC are required to enjoy Dramatic Mode in the full version of the game. About the Game PlatinumGames’ NEO-CLASSIC ARCADE series carries on the spirit and fun of classic gaming using modern technology, and the first project in this endeavor is SOL CRESTA. SOL CRESTA takes the docking and formation strategies of classic shooting games Moon Cresta and Terra Cresta and elevates them with the “free-form docking” system. The flagship Yamato, composed of the fighters Amaterasu, Tsukuyomi, and Susano can utilize various attacks depending on how the three ships are aligned. Docking, splitting, and reforming the ships as needed is the key to defeating the invading armies of Mega Zofer. Game Features Story Humanity faced a crushing defeat at the hands of the Mandler Army during their last invasion of the solar system. Losing the moon and being driven from Earth, they were forced to retreat all the way to Laomedeia, the 12th moon of Neptune. With the last of their hope, they formed the solar recovery squad SOL CRESTA, and placed the fate of the solar system with the Yamato, a cutting-edge docking ship. Free-Form Docking The Yamato, standing against the evil of Mega Zofer, is composed of 3 fighters. You’ll scramble with only one fighter at first, but pick up the right item and friendly fighters will appear for a power-up! Dock and split to change your attack properties and use different formations to access an amazing arsenal. Classic 80s-Style Excitement SOL CRESTA’s music is provided by legendary chiptune composer Yuzo Koshiro, and the game pays homage to the sound and visuals of the earlier Cresta series games, bringing back that arcade fever while taking it beyond mere nostalgia. There’s even a time limit, high score Caravan Mode, and online leaderboards. PlatinumGames' New Challenge What would happen if PlatinumGames, developers of satisfying and jam-packed action games like Bayonetta, NieR:Automata, and ASTRAL CHAIN tried their hand at shooting? This is the answer. The visuals are classic, but the originality and depth of the systems and gameplay provide a fresh and deep shooting experience that grows each time you play.

_childDocuments_.review: Alright, at the time of this review I've played this game for ~6 hours according to steam, which to me is a fair shot to give, especially to a shmup.Do keep in mind that this game may contain mechanics and/or visual design elements that I critique that are a throwback to earlier Cresta games, which I did not play. I'll question whether they were fun and good in my opinion regardless of their legacy and how they could, to some, shape the identity of the series.Also, opinions opinions everyone. Very few thing I say are hard facts.Honestly, I'd say that I am disappointed overall.I'll try to articulate that in the 3 sections below.- . It was composed and produced by Yuzo Koshiro, which I'd urge you to listen to. This is easily the most impressive thing in this game, not because the rest of it is bad ( although some of it is in my opinion), but because it is just that . - . The sol gauge makes scoring higher exciting and lets you unlock new attacks that can be unleashed with half circles, charge moves and full circle joystick motions (reminiscent of fighting game inputs) on top of more shield, more lives, more score and other exciting mini-objectives. Acquiring and messing with the formation, ship order and charge shots while managing your gauge is interesting and unique. I can't think of any other games that does that. Kinda reminiscent of wonderful 101 in a sense. - . There are no crazy danmaku mechanics with insane multipliers to be found, instead most of it revolves with playing the game safe and knowing when to switch to which ship to pass through colour-coded circles, hit cyan orbs with charge shots, hitting the right enemies with the right ship, getting the right formation coins and destroying crates with the right ship. This makes scoring a very different experience compared to just trying to 1CC the game .- . the CRT options might have alleviated that by making it not as noticeable, but the CRT doesn't look good either. Coins and shots also frequently clip and/or only partially get rendered, making it look like a really bad case of screen tearing (although it is not). It might be an attempt at emulating older hardware, in which case I'd like an option to turn it off. -  I'd like to see more CRT options, ways to toggle v-sync on and off, or other basic features, at least on the steam version.- . While not distracting and overwhelmingly animated or colourful, The greyish and monotonous looks of it really make the visual appeal of the game significantly worse. More importantly however, it completely feels at odds with the (not so crisp I admit) pixel art direction in game. It looks like a UI that would be stamped on a remaster edition with no regards for the game's artistic direction. On top of looking bad, I also think it does a poor job at making information easy to consult during play. Meter is spread out and a bit hard to get good grasp of where it's at until you stare at it directly, formations are okay in horizontal mode but really hard to make out which one you already collected in tate, and the sol gauge is just suffering from being too small, horizontal or vertical mode. Maybe displaying less, bigger icons and scrolling through them as you progress might have been better? - - , and feel kind of long. A playthrough is about 2 hours long , this discourages me from scoring it or playing this game long-term.- , this could have been a way for beginners and fans of platinum games that are not shmup players to put a foot in the door when it comes to scoring without attempting a full run, especially with loops.-   The formation slowmo is hard to control precisely, some patterns look too similar to each other and are a pain to "draw" (such as the triangle ones), the command inputs for shooting around you or on the sides are also kinda janky while still being fun and at times worthwhile to do.-  Too many moving parts with the game's pixelated (rather than pixel art) look in very narrow spaces can be difficult to make out. This is especially true when your ships are on top of each other and you don't have a clear-looking hitbox during slowmo. Also, while subjective, I do think that the background, boss designs and enemy designs are kind of too simple and repetitive. The T-rexes on terra felt extremely exciting as a byproduct of this monotony. - While you can just learn it (albeit in a 2 hour long run), this is still easily what kills me most after 5+ hours of playtime. At the very end of the game there is a portion where the scrolling becomes a lot faster and this issue can generate a lot of frustration as this portion will most likely kill you more than anything else in the game, at the very end of a 2 hour run... -  Hitting a wall or a door will kill you instantly no matter your shield, you respawn with 0 upgrades and just 1 ship and immediately need to dance around  the screen to get the 2nd ship medal and make your way to the ship that spawns. This makes dying a few times in 5 seconds when attempting to recover during a boss pattern quite frequent.-  This is subjective, But I would have liked the game to be a bit more open ended in how to approach a scoring run. This concludes my thoughts on the games. Overall, I Like the game for what it attempts and what it tries to do differently, but I dislike it because too many issues stand in the way of trying to seriously get involved with it. It feels much cooler as a precendent for the shmup genre and the industry rather than as a game to get involved with. As it stands, if some of the issues I have with the game get patched, I'll modify this review accordingly. At this time I'd say it's a  ratio for me between things to like and things to dislike. I am usually a shmup player that plays for hard CCs and/or score however, so this is coming from this kind of personal perspective.You might notice that I left the price point out of my review, as I believe that you'll make your own judgement on it after reading  and researching rather than take my word for it. However, I'll say that a lot of polish-related issues and the fact that the game is emanating from a well-established AA company seem contradictory with the price that is asked as it stands. patches and updates might change that in the future.

_childDocuments_.review: This great oldschool Cresta shoot 'em up is back with a new sequel!Survive through seven stages that are not only very challenging but also divided into different subsections that already provide additional replayability reasons.In most of these parts you will also have to compete against certain more difficult enemies that can be huge at times.Watch a short gameplay session here: You have three ships with which you will have to control the game, these ships can transform into different formations and according to which of the three is the head of the transformation your attacks will also be related to the main ship but nicely combined with the abilities of the other two ships.Although Sol Cresta can be very difficult to survive, there's no doubt that a fantastic vibe reigns there that will make you not want to give up too soon.Gradually acquiring the commando skills and bonuses in a stage as you score points is slick as it allows you to build and unload as the stage progresses. Docking goes both ways as it's thrilling once you're stripped down to just one small ship with a desperate dodge; try to rebuild. The visual style is very clear so you know what's going on at all times, as are the sound effects and great soundtrack.
_childDocuments_.name: SOL CRESTA

_childDocuments_.review: This game has some utterly amateurish display issues on every platform. The game looks like it was unevenly scaled with nearest neighbor scaling to some arbitrary low resolution and then upscaled AGAIN with nearest neighbor, so you get distorted horrible pixel warping, regardless of what resolution your screen is. It looks awful. There are virtually no display options, not even resolution. The only choice is a "scanline"/CRT filter that is genuinely the worst I have ever seen, and oppressively dark even on its lightest setting. The gameplay is... okay, but nothing extraordinary. You can reconfigure your ships for different weapon effects, but the system feels a bit cumbersome, and the weapon variety is not especially amazing. This game feels very rooted in late 80s arcade shooters, before all the bullet hell stuff, and that's refreshing, but the levels are long and not very interesting, and the game is very generous with damage so it can feel too easy, or at least it takes too long to ramp up. The music slaps, I'll give it that. But I was overall very underwhelmed by this game, and while I haven't played it long, I will probably refund it.
_childDocuments_.name: SOL CRESTA

_childDocuments_.review: I haven't had much experience with the previous entries in the series, but like many others my first impressions were mixed as if you were to play this like a typical STG "survival run" and not utilize the resources the game gives you the first few stages feel very bland. The later stages offer more variety and environmental hazards to maneuver around, but still nothing to really "woo" you over, especially given the aesthetics that aren't very screenshot friendly.I have since completed more playthroughs and things have really started to "click" on how the developers intended the gameplay to be.  After the first 30 or 45 seconds in stage 1, the design and placement of everything in the stage is VERY deliberate and there is a small puzzle element to maximizing scores with the different formations. It's enough for you to think but it's not so stringent that it ties you down to a single intended route/formation combo.The core of the gameplay and key to increasing score is very dependent on using the formation attacks, but in order to do that you have to:Then there are some smaller things that don't mean as much, such as command shots (the fighting game inputs) and going through colored hoops where your lead ship needs to match for some bonus points.In the end, on top of the standard STG gameplay elements you are having to constantly think about all of those things while applying inputs for formations and command shots where needed.Due to its differences from standard STG's a lot of people aren't going to like it.  For me though, the gameplay design adds a lot of fun and immersion.
_childDocuments_.name: SOL CRESTA

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend this game yet, I think it's very cool but there are clear graphic import issues, you can't move with arrow keys while in Formation Mode, let alone map any of your keyboard keys. The hurtbox on the ship is unfortunately quite big, but I will have to just deal with that. Also, the DLC they're offering should just be in the game from the start, I have never played a Shmup worth more than $20 and this game doesn't come very close to being an exception. Maybe it's because of Platinum Legacy but, who knows. And yeah, this game has the same """problems""" that every Platinum game has: Long Levels, Kind of Messy Graphics, and Tons of Mechanics. I don't say "problems" seriously because I knew this was a game made by Platinum and they just tend to be Extra AF so it's very hard to hate them because you know the effort is there. Those traits are common within every Platinum game I've played. That being said , the Messy Graphics thing is definitely the most harmful to a Shmup / Danmaku experience. And no, things being "all over the place" and "not knowing what's going on" do not have to go together -- CAVE games, mainly Dodonpachi, pull this off very well and have clear concise colors and you can tell what's a hazard and what's not.  The graphics issue in this game might be due to some nostalgia or whatever but I don't think it's working -- making things "look bad on purpose" isn't how dedicating stuff to the past works, and if it is, then I'm fine with the future.EDIT: Just realized they literally put the entire Story part of the game (dialogue, actual characters, stakes) behind a $10 DLC.......................why would you do this....................................................................................
_childDocuments_.name: SOL CRESTA

_childDocuments_.review: SOL CRESTA is a very solid and creative shmup, that combines old school sensibilities with modern gameplay ideas and mechanics.Behind the retro graphics and chiptune soundtrack (a marvellous and insanely catchy effort by the great Yuzo Koshiro, here in top form) hides a very modern and enjoyable shmup, full of creative gameplay touches, be it the formation mechanics (where detaching your three ships is used to trigger massive special attacks, and the order you reattach them in results in different primary and secondary shots), or the special moves (triggered by doing motions straight out of a fighting game, something unusual for the genre).SOL CRESTA combines the old with the new in great fashion, and the end result is a very solid effort.
_childDocuments_.name: SOL CRESTA

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very fun and complex shoot-m-up where the gameplay mechanics are pretty intuitive. It sounds old-school in a very charming way and it has the graphics look of the advanced 90s arcade machines (think Darius Gaiden). Especially the little bonus jingles sound so nice. As you can expect from Platinum Games it plays very smooth and modern. I'm personally a fan of shoot-m-ups, but I don't think it's exclusively aimed at fans of the genre. The difficulty is pretty accessible for the most part and the gameplay is not hardcore unforgiving. Once you get the hang of the transformations and make good use of them you can get further much more easily. It runs great on my machine and no problems in vertical mode. For the money sure you can get more bang for your buck, but I'm reviewing the game not a value proposition. If it's on sale it's a no-brainer to own.
_childDocuments_.name: SOL CRESTA

_childDocuments_.review: I've put in a few runs, hit 80% of the achievements, and so I think I'm ready to review.I disliked the demo, yet felt like there may be a bit more under the hood if I could ever get the whole she-bang for a decent price, and so I waited and waited and waited and waited till it was down to $12.50 for the complete set.Dramatic DLC adds very little. It being from an acclaimed anime writer, I thought maybe we'd get something memorable like that random chit-chat in Raiden V, but all you get here is cliche anime plot that'll make you wish the characters were discussing Brazilian coffee beans whilst in the middle of Armageddon (Raiden V).The story chatter is in Japanese dub w/English subs, and the characters converse during battle about stuff I care less about than coffee beans, and there's some odd emo feels they try to launder on you, but it doesn't hit the feelers. Most of the conversation is not worth glancing over in battle to read. The chatter should have been condensed rather than telling me that android girl is getting a tingling feel before Every.Single.Boss. YES. THAT. INCLUDES. MID-STAGE. BOSSES. lol.So for an extra $4, was it worth it? Well, yes and no. Yes, b/c you get hints of lore, and it gives you an idea of who the bosses are. And No, bc the story sux.Gameplay: The levels are a bit longer than typical. I enjoyed the change. I didn't time it, but est. 7-10mins per level. There are level hazards and collisions. By your 2nd play-through, they arent too hard to see or dodge. I actually disliked the hazards while playing the demo, but after running a lvl once or twice, I found I again liked the change of pace from doing purely bullet hell. Formations are aight. They add depth, albeit it is a bit hard to swallow the upgrade system/formation system during ur first hour, but play with it on Easy, observe, and you'll understand the system. You are required to change your formation's formation to increase score thru power-ups and drops, and sometimes a certain formation or ship gives you an advantage so the bit of strategy adds flavor. Spicy!Several ships to choose from so you get a bit of variety. The more achievements you achieve, the more ships you unlock (or if you get Complete Edition, then you get the Wing Galiber which is a very easy and casual ship to understand). I wouldn't call this a bullet hell, but in the later difficulties, be prepared for your deaths to occasionally stack 2 or 3 right after another as a new life starts with no upgrades, but has an upgrade ship drop from the top towards you. Unfortunately, you might be dead again by the time the ship descends to you at the bottom of the screen b/c a boss or environmental hazard is blocking you from quickly picking up the upgrade ship. So with ur pew pew shooter, ur just a duck in the water with everyone's guns pointed at you. Yet, the game is forgiving, and even on Platinum Hard, red ships often zoom by in boss fights which if red ship is shot, red ship will drop an upgrade ship so very fair.Speaking of bosses. They are very boring. 30% are just armored circles, 20% duplicate flying big boss ship with 3 phases, 40% is the same jet fighter (stage 1) that adds a second jet fighter in stage 3?, and adds a 3rd jet fighter ship in stage 5, then evolves to a mech in stage 6, 10% is the 4-phased final boss. So yeah, they are lame and feel like a 1st time indie devs attempt at a game. I wish more effort was put into them. However, given the level length, I almost don't mind the mediocrity that doesn't require much thought.Achievements: The first 80-90% of achievements are do-able with some effort, however, the no-damage achievements and the Beat 5-7 loops of the game as it increases in difficulty and without losing all your continues (max 10 continues if you earn them), seems almost impossible without max dedication. But I had fun chasing some of the no damage achievements.Well, that's that. I have enjoyed my time with the game, and I would recommend on sale even tho there are some glaring flaws.
_childDocuments_.name: SOL CRESTA

_childDocuments_.review: It is up for debate if this is a good follow up to Moon Cresta and Terra Cresta or not, and I cannot even participate in such. I didn’t play, let alone grew up with those games, despite being a big fan of the genre, I can only speak on how some element of PlatinumGames are implemented in here (formation change tends to be more interesting on paper than it is in practice). But as an overall package, this is way too stuck on its principles, putting it far behind the competitive quality for a modern STG. Not just visually (although readability can be a problem at times) but mainly on a stage design and enemy design standpoint. With incredibly uninteresting attack patterns and mixed quality in boss design. I don’t even want it to be a bullet hell, but looking at some games that push the genre just as hard without falling into that category released well after the previous cresta games, such as Gradius Gaiden, Salamander 2(horizontal shooting games but you get the idea), Radiant Silvergun, or even indie games like ZeroRanger, it is a bit saddening to see a game like this, with the audacity of being sold at such high price during launch, while also deliberately and/or arrogantly closing its eyes to any games released after the famicom era OUTSIDE of just PlatinumGames' own titles, which are not even in the same genre. I appreciate the price reduction but even at its current one, it’s a tough sale when even steam itself offers the latter two titles mentioned above for about as much or less, along with many others that are worth checking out over Sol Cresta. The fact this isn’t even trying to catch up to its peers makes this game at its best, an interesting capsule of ideas, and at its worst, a disheartening shooting game experience. And while it isnt entirely awful, it often ends up falling into the latter category.
_childDocuments_.name: SOL CRESTA

_childDocuments_.review: I have loved shooters like this for years. It's a great game however, I was disappointed with the bugs at launch especially as the game was expensive and created by a prestigious developer such as Platinum Games. I could not complete stage six part 1 (drama mode) as the game would crash. I am happy to report that since the latest patch update Platinum seems to have addressed this issue as I have now managed to complete the game.Pros: Fantastic pixel old school graphics.          Wonderful music by Yuzo Koshiro.          Lots of replay value.Cons: Hard to see / judge what objects you can collide into on some levels.           The Drama mode really needs localised voice overs as trying to follow the story with the            dialogue text is pointless when trying to concentrate on the gameplay (RAIDEN V Has a            similar problem).            Charging extra for the Drama mode is disappointing, the presentation is excellent            though.Would I recommend this game yes and no. If you like classic shooter games like this then you will not be disappointed. I would not recommend this game to players who find games like this difficult and are easily frustrated. I would say though you could start on easy mode and work your way up through the diffiiculty.Overall for me I would give Sol Cresta a 8.5 out of 10, Looking forward to playing it on the Steam Deck when I eventually get mine which is still a couple of months away :-(

_childDocuments_.review: As a  and  fan, this is confusingly disappointing, and hugely overpriced to boot.The graphics are ruined by the lack of a video mode that doesn't make them look like a shimmering mess of pixels, and the gameplay is a bit too gimmicky.The music by chiptune maestro Yuzo Koshiro is great though, so there's that.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like 2d rail shooters then you will love this game. It has tons if interesting mechanics, that make it a different experience such as the stacking system, and the separation supers. The heart of the game lies in how you master switching up how to stack your ships appropriately which is very fun. Would recommend
_childDocuments_.name: SOL CRESTA

_childDocuments_.review: I usually give breakdowns of games, but this game really doesn't deserve one, simply due to a single unforgivable feature/mechanic.  So I'll make a quick one.Pros- Good music- Fun gameplay w/ some interesting shmup mechanics I've never seen (I've only played a few)- First 2/3 of the game is really funCons- Graphics are not clear sometimes.  I'm reading ppl say they are too pixelated.  I suppose that is it.  Sometimes there's just too much stuff going on and you really can't tell what is what.  Too many times I've said "wtf hit me?"- The multi-ship powerups should NOT require you to fly backwards to actually connect to them.  They should apply right when you get the powerup.- OFF SCREEN ATTACKS FROM BEHIND.  Thumbs down just for this.  And I don't mean the ones that are easy to see incoming like in some other shmups.  Say hello to level 6 mid-boss.  Here, you are FORCED to hug the bottom screen, but there are still offscreen attacks coming from the bottom...randomly or semi-randomly (they're technically on an upward arc after going off screen from above).   THE most frustrating and unfair ♥♥♥♥ I have seen.- Also, random pop up hitboxes too!  Sure, this is part of the "learn the pattern" part.  But it goes into a bit of overdrive in late game.  Feels cheap.- It has a...3rd dimension aspect - height, but only for terrain things.  These things are falling above you or popping up from the ground.  Stuff hits you when it doesn't feel it should.  Plus it's overpriced.  But I try to not consider that a "con" per se.  It is what it is.

_childDocuments_.review: Because we've all talked ourselves into thinking that Japan no longer hates PC gaming, I think Metal Gear Rising and NieR Automata developer should be a reminder that they still hate our ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ guts, and the only reason they even give their half-hearted attempts at PC ports is because Steam's just way too big to ignore. However, if one or more of their games are allowed to fail, then they'll just use those games as excuses to only make games for consoles. This has been the case since 2013 with Nippon Ichi Software's failure of ClaDun X2, and with PlatinumGames focusing on games that'd only release on consoles moving on from 2017's NieR Automata, Sol Cresta and Babylon's Fall feel like a retreading of familiar territory, and I don't mean that in a good way.Basically, NIS' game back in August 2012 set the benchmark that most Japanese game developers follow even to this day, and PlatinumGames is no exception to this, since the failure of this game and Babylon's Fall will be their excuse to only make games for consoles. They expected their PC install base to like an admittedly barebones shmup along with a live service game that failed to drum up enough players to be profitable, and our punishment for failing to live up to the dev team's expectations is that they won't ever make PC games ever again. The most we can do moving forward is to remember that the need to "buy x so y can be on PC" is here to stay, though I fear that we've already lost too much in terms of Japanese PC support.

_childDocuments_.review: SOL CRESTA is the sequel to a game called TERRA CRESTA which is a sequel to MOON CRESTA. This is an 80's series that I strongly believe was popular in Japan but is not known globally like other shmups.Unless you're dumb as a door it's pretty obvious this isn't a hack'n slash, PLATINUM was very faithful with NieR:Automata (respecting what the original game meant instead of trying to make it a "new Bayonetta" ) and the same is true here: Very faithful to it's roots 80's arcade game style.And it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ good. Really good.But it's a niche game and honestly I doubt people who don't like old school shmups will really like it, but if you do...It's short, get it in a sale and just have fun with the CRT filter on.

_childDocuments_.review: This is about how long it took me to beat Normal mode. Good game. It probably isn't the best vertical shmup ever, but it's my personal favourite now. You know what's really important in a game? When you always have some ideas that you want to try out, so you keep coming back to a challenging stage, thinking, ! This is a good, worthwhile, challenging, varied, well-crafted game. Good job, Platinum.

_childDocuments_.review: Sol Cresta is a great game and one which has taken many years to arrive. Its a good game but one that has a fair few issues as well. The worst being that the story mode is hidden behind a day 1 DLC which just seems utterly insane to do and a real stupid idea as well.Its a great classic shooter but one which is exceptionally high priced as well and you cant help but feel that the developers are asking for more than what their realistically giving you.More details about the game and a proper review can be seen here
_childDocuments_.name: SOL CRESTA

_childDocuments_.review: Sol Cresta is an interesting example of a game trying to catch two types of consumer but pretty much failing to catch any. On the first hand its a sequel to a game which first entry was released back in 1980, also coming back to its roots after 3D remake of Terra Cresta, that killed Nichibutsu, on the other it wants to appeal to a new player that didnt played or didnt put much time into shoot'em up genre. By no means its not a bad game, more of a disappoitement perhaps. Maybe, its just me, a point of view of hardcore shoot'em up player that tried a lot of arcade titles such as Gunbird, Chouyikuu Yousai or Twinbee as well as new games paying omages to this amazing genre such as Touhou franchise, Sky Force or Raiden. To say i expected more from Platinum Games is like saying nothing, they did tons of amazing games after all like Vanquish or Legend of Korra, recently, they lost the good track and this is an example. Graphically wise game looks okayish however, i expected the ships to be much more detailed, it looks like a combination of psx/ps2 pixelart for backgrounds, snes/psx enemies and nes player models. It looks great for an eye but its far from the greatest. Gameplaywise though, i cant believe how easy this game is. Maybe i got better into this genre after my last attempts of beating ikaruga, but this game does not give me any challenge at all. Thats why i said this game targets a new to shumps user, because if you are new to this genre, you will like it, although the levels are too long imo. It serves good as a introduction to amazing world of shootem ups, ngl, but if your are an fan of this genre, this game will be like walk in the park for you. A very boring not suprising walk in the park. From positives, since to this point it was pretty much kicking poor fella, i like the ship combo system for ultimates, the fact that they do different type of damage based on how you combine ships and the fact it reffils based on your performance in game, unlike bomb system that is limiting your strategy in many other shumps. Voice acting and anime sprites are great too. Range of characters in story even though they are a bit cliche, same as story itself, is cute, on that point it really feels like a 90's game with these cringey death sounds or that one guy with a hamster. It have its charm and many may continue playing this game only due to it. UI is solid too, combining nier automata with darius games. Overall, although its not a masterpiece as i wanted it to be, its not a bad game either. Those who wants to get into this genre of games, will like it surely!
_childDocuments_.name: SOL CRESTA

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best platinum games, really loved how it implemented input commands like their other action games, like wonderful 101, but not as hard. It makes it for a pretty complex combat system for a shmup, it's kind of like Radiant Silvergun, tons of weapons that works for different kinds of scenarios, some are more useful than others. The score system is quite simple, defeat enemies as fast as possible to get more coins, which then become resources for your ship, like getting more meter, lives, shields and stronger bullets. It's pretty addicting and wish more shmups do something similar.The graphics are a bit rough but I find the artstyle kind of charming, reminds me of Saturn games, but I would say that my major problem is the visibility during gameplay, I find the background a bit too saturated which can make the bullets and hazards a bit hard to see sometimes and some of the hit boxes aren't accurate to the sprites which can make for some cheap deaths. Also, I find it a tad long for a shmup, it's around 1 hour for arcade mode which is a bit tiring in multiple playthroughts compared to other shumps that are 40 mins or less.Something that bother me was that the story mode was behind a paywall, they should have made it part of the base game since it is pretty expensive as it is. I recommend to buy it in sales like I did, while I find the game to be pretty good, I just can't justify paying more than $25 for it, compared to other shmups with the same quality that are around the same price. As for the storymode, it's the classic Kamiya kind of story, it shares a ton of similarities with Wonderful 101, it's good but I really wish it was dubbed, since the game is pretty frenetic it's hard to read the subs while playing. I end up playing on easy difficulty to be able to enjoy the story.I still recommend this game if you are a fan of platinum games or shmups, it's a ton of fun once you learn the mechanics and it is a fresh take on the genre, but wait for a sale to get a fair price.
_childDocuments_.name: SOL CRESTA

_childDocuments_.review: Very quality shoot 'em up from the action game experts at Platinum Games. Unique mechanics that involve swapping the order of the player ships to access different shot types. Solid presentation I think, while I know it has received some flack for it's appearance, I don't think it's a bad looking game. Granted it looks much better on a CRT display which I know the average person doesn't have access to. All in all a solid shooting experience for those on the hunt for a good STG!
_childDocuments_.name: SOL CRESTA

_childDocuments_.review: I love this game! I really recommend Sol Cresta because it contains combos that you can execute, the formation mechanic is amazing and last but not least, every spaceship has its unique "shot".Playing this game with an arcade stick makes it sooo much better in my opinion.However, I kind of miss a "training mode" and/or a "multiplayer mode" as well.Pros:- Formation mechanic- Combos- Ever spaceship is unigue- Levels are very well made- Easy to learn but hard to masterCons:- No training mode- No multiplayer mode- This game is kind of pricey

_childDocuments_.review: I Highly recommend this one if you're into shoot em ups both casually and for the hardcore there is enough here to keep you entertained and on the edge of your seat, its also slightly over a hour run to get a 1 credit clear, with some treasure-esque stage and boss design, really well done and worth the price.

name: Sins of a Solar Empire II
detailed_description: Purchase Options NOTE: Premium Edition content will be made available as it's released. About the Game Sins of a Solar Empire II is the sequel to the critically acclaimed space strategy game that seamlessly blends real-time battle tactics with the depth of 4X. As both emperor and battle commander you must lead one of six playable factions to victory against the threat of extinction! Real-time Tactics meets 4X Depth There are no turns. There is no battle mode. There is no strategic mode. It's all one mode and it's all in real-time. Instantly zoom in to control tactical engagements where every missile, turret, and ship is fully simulated and an important part of the battle. Instantly zoom back out to manage your empire where every asteroid, moon, and planet orbits its parent in a slowly evolving strategic landscape. Unparalleled Gameplay Experiences Sins of a Solar Empire II delivers sprawling empires, huge fleets, and completely new and exciting gameplay moments that can only be found in Sins II. The Surprise: Build a secondary fleet on a rogue asteroid and launch a devastating surprise attack when its orbit brings it behind the enemy's back line. The Body Block: Stall an enemy's home planet bombardment by using your massive titan to body block swarms of missiles attempting to knock out your starbase and its critical planetary shield. The Screen: Advance a screen of point defense flak frigates to protect your fragile long-range cruisers by intercepting incoming bombers and missiles. The Swarm: Maneuver your faster moving ships to pick apart unescorted larger ships. Their powerful but slow-moving turrets simply can't track your agile strike force. The Influencer: Influence a hostile expansionist Minor Faction to secure your border while reserving enough Influence to win an auction for a powerful item to install on your best capital ship. The Backstab: Protect yourself from a backstab by establishing a time locked alliance. But pay attention to the time - your “ally” may move his fleet to your doorstep just as the lock expires! Features A Dynamic Galaxy: Planets orbit their stars in real-time causing the galaxy's structure to slowly change, creating new battle fronts and new opportunities. Players can view the state of the galaxy up to an hour in the future to prepare their strategies. 3 Unique Races: It's War Year 35 and the emergent TEC, alien Vasari, and deviant Advent have been forced to adapt and evolve to survive. TEC: The inhabitants of this region of the galaxy, the TEC are humans who have joined together as the Trader Emergency Coalition to combat the alien Vasari empire. They rely heavily on trade to support their industrial base and augment resource income. Vasari: Ten thousand years ago, the Vasari Empire once ruled over hundreds of planets and dozens of sentient species. Now on the run from an unknown enemy they use their mastery of phase space to conquer and acquire resources to continue their exodus. Advent: A civilization of humans who were forcibly outcast by the Traders over a thousand years ago, the deviant Advent have returned with technologically amplified psionics and the power of the Unity - a devastating expression of their collective will. Each race features unique starting conditions, gameplay mechanics, units, abilities, items, and technologies. Their game changing new Empire Systems add a whole new level of strategic capabilities: TEC Trade: The new TEC trade system enables them to dynamically adapt their economy by adjusting the allocation of traded resources on demand. Vasari Phase Resonance: Strategically placed structures collect Phase Resonance allowing the Vasari to customize their global phase mastery effects. Advent Unity: Enables the Advent to harness the collective will of their population, unlocking the full potential of the Unity's global abilities. 6 Playable Factions: The parent races are further differentiated by unique sub-factions each with their own unique features and play styles that reflect their motivations and goals. For example, the TEC: Primacy is a xenophobic 'human first' empire focused on aggression and the Vasari: Exodus is willing to destroy planets to fuel their mobile empire. Combat Simulation: A detailed combat simulation adds incredible depth to tactical gameplay. Turrets with their own pitch and tracking speeds make firing solutions important in battles. Fully simulated missiles can be blocked by ships or destroyed by point defense. New mechanics around shields, armor and hull points give greater depth to units and tactical decisions. Empire Management: All planets and ships can now be easily analyzed, customized, and upgraded in one place without the tedium of finding and clicking through all units in your empire. The Intelligent Construction system will queue up the entire chain of prerequisites to fulfill any item, research, or unit build request. Fleet Management: The new fleet system includes the ability to request specific reinforcements on the fly. Requested units are automatically queued from the optimal factory and rallied to the fleet. Combined with Intelligent Construction this allows you to focus on the important tactical decisions and big picture strategy. Unit Customization: Planet surfaces can now be customized with special items that vary by race and planet type. Capital ships, titans and starbases can also be customized with race specific items to fill gaps in the fleet's composition or target specific strategies. Minor Factions: Numerous minor factions now inhabit the galaxy offering trade, auctions for rare items, and with enough influence, access to their most powerful abilities. Will you befriend them or annihilate them to keep your enemies from turning them against you? Diplomacy: New features include a new offer / counteroffer system, the ability to give or demand planets, and the game changing time locked cease-fires that prevent your 'ally' from backstabbing you until it expires - but keep on eye on the time! Multicore 64-bit Engine: The Sins II engine can utilize all available cores and RAM to maximize performance, now and into the future. Dynamic lighting, physically based rendering, higher resolution textures and more create a beautiful tapestry. 10-Player Multiplayer Support: A cloud based online system supports both 'join codes' and lobbies to make it easier than ever to play with others. Games can now be rejoined in progress if a player drops or has to leave; humans can even take over for AI players if a friend joins late. In-game Mod Support: Mod support has been integrated into the game, making it easy to discover, install, and share mods. Custom maps are automatically shared for multiplayer games, preventing the hassle of everyone downloading ahead of time. Easy to Learn; Hard to Master: With an elegant and intuitive user interface Sins II is easy to pick up and play. However, mastering your chosen faction will take true skill.

short_description: Battle for galactic dominance in this real-time 4X strategy game with unrivaled scale! You’ll explore, expand, exploit, and exterminate through military force, diplomacy, trade, culture, influence, and other underhanded tactics.

_childDocuments_.review: Great optimization and no to minimal bugs on launch? In this day and age? I'd almost forgotten what that was like.Compared to the likes of Stellaris and Endless Space, it's an easier 4x to get into than the daunting research tree might suggest on the surface. But Stellaris is frankly a different game entirely, and Endless Space is turn based with no direct control on the combat besides formations. I do find myself missing the bits of flavor that the latter game especially has; everything in this game feels oddly... sterile. There's also not necessarily a ton of gameplay diversity between the races, but neither was there in ES once you really dig into it.I would liken this game to the Command & Conquer of space 4x. You aren't managing the happiness of a population or handling bureaucracy and limited expansion or holding up supply lines between territories, there's no culture or wonder victories, everything you do is in service of military might one way or another. It's much slower paced than C&C, but it's almost as focused, albeit vastly more strategic than tactical.It's also got day 1 mod support, and SoaSE:R had some absolutely fantastic mods over its lifespan, so with any luck we'll see similar here.

_childDocuments_.review: Sins of a Solar Empire 2 is a sleek, well-designed RTS/4X hybrid that brings together the best of both genres, though appealing to a somewhat niche audience. It offers three distinct, highly asymmetrical races, each with two sub-factions that provide varied gameplay experiences. This results in a total of six factions, with a seventh one scheduled for release within the next 12 months.The game incorporates some 4X elements, especially in planetary management and strategic decisions, while maintaining the real-time action expected from an RTS. However, unlike many other RTS games where rapid actions-per-minute (APM) determines victory (e.g. starcraft, dota), Sins 2 provides a more relaxed pace, offering a similar strategic depth without the stress of ultra-high-speed gameplay. The amazing quality of life systems also help a lot here to reduce the volume of required user's inputs. Games typically last between 40 minutes to 2-3 hours, which makes multiplayer matches manageable and accessible compared to many other 4X games.At its core, Sins 2 is focused on combat—particularly fleet composition and tactical choices. While it retains some 4X features, it's more akin to games like Warhammer 40,000: Gladius than the more empire-building-focused Civilization. The game is built on a solid foundation of over a decade of experience from the original Sins, and each system forces the player to make meaningful decisions. For example, limited planetary slots and increasingly expensive upgrades require constant trade-offs, which opens up a lot of strategic depth and replayability. It is here, in this endless choice solicited to the player that "the build" you use takes place. Once the mechanics and overall understanding of the game is integrated, in some strange way this sort of "deck-building" system for every aspect of the game and races feels more like Heartstone than command and conquer. It's a key part of the strategic component.The three main races are well-balanced but extremely distinct, offering very different playstyles. Each race can dominate in unique ways, and their interactions create a dynamic system of counterplay that adds layers of strategic depth.A central piece of the game, which makes it "mechanic-oriented" is that there are no hidden bonuses (like simpler RTS). This means that X unit is not good against Y unit because of some hardcoded multiplayer somewhere, but all the combat takes place on equal footing for all the units. What makes a fleet composition good against another depends on the exchange it takes place based on this common mechanic. For example an anti-starcraft gun with no piece will have little effect against a starbase of 1000 durability. Or a heavy missile of 1000 pierce is kind of a waste against a small ship, and so on.Technically, the game runs superbly, handling large-scale battles with ease while delivering stunning visuals. The quality of life (QoL) improvements, honed over years of development, help streamline empire and fleet management. These improvements reduce the need for high APM and allow players to focus on the more enjoyable aspects of the game. As a result, Sins 2 is incredibly multiplayer-friendly, offering casual, normal, and expert multiplayer modes to accommodate players of all skill levels.Even if you're not typically a multiplayer gamer, Sins 2 makes it easy and fun to jump in (this was my case). Multiplayer is particularly well-implemented, with options that cater to different playstyles and levels of experience. In single-player, the AI is competent, though not groundbreaking, but co-op multiplayer against high-difficulty AI can be relaxing yet super fun.One of the standout features of Sins 2 is its welcoming and helpful community. As a somewhat niche game, the more experienced players tend to offer support for newcomers, helping them learn the ropes and improve their skills. This supportive environment is further encouraged through "mentoring" games and active discussions about tactics and strategies on the game’s Discord, making it easy for new players to feel at home and grow their expertise.WRT to the future, if history repeats itself, the developers will continue to build on this solid foundation, adding new content and improvements for years to come. It’s a great time to get invested.While Sins 2 has many strengths, there are some aspects worth noting:Gameplay Focus: * This is an RTS with 4X elements, but it’s not a direct competitor to Stellaris or a fast-paced micro-heavy game like StarCraft. It’s more in line with Total War or Gladius, focusing heavily on strategy over rapid micromanagement. Diplomacy is very limited* No Campaign (Yet): Currently, there’s no campaign mode, which might disappoint players looking for a story-driven experience like the frist Homeworlds. The focus here is purely on mechanics, not narrative.* Smaller Dev Team: The developers made smart decisions by focusing on core gameplay, but some compromises were made. For instance, music is underwhelming (consider puting it on mute and open a mix in youtube), and the soundtrack is set to be part of a paid DLC in the future.* Art and Presentation: The in-game art, especially for techs and items, feels somewhat generic. The AI-generated portraits, while passable in full screen, can feel cluttered and interchangeable as smaller icons, particularly for the Advent faction. There’s also a lack of visual coherence in terms of progression, as early-game and late-game techs look quite similar. On the other hand the art can be somewhat inconsistent within a race, having varying art styles that as a whole do not deliver a consistent look for the race.* Challenge Required: To appreciate the depth of the game’s strategic elements—such as fleet composition and resource management—you need to play at decent difficulty levels. In easier modes, you can win by simply clicking on everything, missing out on the game’s more intricate layers. There is some degree of subtlety on how the build playout, the good ordering for a given state of the game and so on.* Single-player vs. Multiplayer: While the developers haven’t explicitly pushed players toward multiplayer, the game’s focus seems to lean that way. Some of the creative freedom seen in other 4X games (like Hearts of Iron IV's crazy alternate histories, or endless space races) isn’t present here, as the game aims for balance and competitiveness in multiplayer settings.* The game is not exactly easy, even in middle tier AI difficulty levels. Being both an RTX and 4X can make losing somewhat frustrating. That is you invested quite a lot in a given build for maybe up to 2h, and due to some skill issue you get wiped out in 2 minutes. In a pure RTS if you are going to be obliterated in a run, this happens within the first 10-20 minutes and in a pure 4X, maybe being killed is even part of the gameplay (think governments in exile in HOI4).* The game is heavily fleet focused. Positioning is king, and if outmaneuver you can totally lose to a weaker opponent. Fleets take quite a while to travel and how to keep control on your empire or deal with other aggressive players is not at all trivial (and also race dependent). Finally in order to avoid stalements that happened in the previous game, the devs took the decision to make defenses in general kind of weaker with respect to the fleet. This means that in general building tall and turtling or trying to build an impenetrable stronghold is kind of a losing strategy.Conclusion (AI generated XD):Sins of a Solar Empire 2 offers a deep, well-balanced blend of RTS and 4X gameplay, perfect for players looking for strategic combat without the high APM demands of typical RTS games. While it’s missing a campaign and the art/music could use improvements, its solid gameplay foundation, thriving multiplayer community, and promising future make it a great investment, especially for strategy fans looking for a game they can enjoy for years to come.

I bought it because I grew up on SINS 1, but really for _years_ of development you get a very lazy remaster, with almost no novel features beyond some QOL and the new orbital mechanics. You can tell its an awfully lazy approach to development too based on their priorities. The AI art in the user interface has been mentioned, but really you can also see it from their focus on user generated content. When you have a game that is barebones (and this is barebones as a sequel, the core game is and always was good), and a lot of effort put into modding tools Stardock and Ironclad are expecting users to create the content they should have, as is usual.If you can imagine paying $100 for a remaster of a GOAT game, just to get a campaign (the first should have had a campaign too, it was controversal for its time) and no meaningful changes. Not to say that the campaign won't even be included in the base game and still isn't finished. Before you buy this game I _implore_ you to check out the reviews of anything made by Stardock since SINS Rebellion. GalCivIII and GalCivIV are essentially dead, unbalanced, shoddy games. Stardock has lost the ability to innovate and create novel products, please don't assume that because SINS is a strong IP that anything will differ here (in fact in some ways it's made worse with cut content and worse AI).Stardock is the Bioware for RTS games.Sheesh.

_childDocuments_.review: SofSE2 Is a game that could truly be great, but has some flaws holding it down that make it sort of middling. The game looks and plays fantastic, as the new ship models, physics system, and quality of life features added to the empire management system make the game appealing and easy for any skill level of player, but corners have been cut that stop it from being perfect. The ship on ship combat is really shallow, as even though the combat mechanics are extremely complex and nuanced, the game boils down to making just more stuff than the opponent, or getting a faction specific capital ship that ends the game. For example, their is a very light ship that the Vasarii faction can spam out in the hundreds early game that are extremely slippery so ships with spinal mounted guns have a very hard time shooting at them. The obvious counter to these ships are the dedicated anti light/missile ship, as they have gimbled mounts that should allow them to mow down these lighter ships.  This is not the case however, as you must build the same if not more antilight ships than the opponent has light ships to counter them, or else your fleet does almost nothing and you just lose the game. Did I also mention  the lighter ships are cheaper than their counters? Balancing issues like these (which have been present thoughout multiple updates) make it so that fleet strategy is boiled down to having one deathfleet that consists of one or two ships that are meta this patch.The other issue I have with this game is the usage of AI art for all non 3D art, as its just extremely shallow and takes away from the gameplay. The research icons and ship items are very confusing at first as there are so many of them and the art doesn't tell you what they do. In Sins1 you could glance at a research tree and easily find a jumpspeed upgrade for your ships, while in Sins2, if you dont know the tech tree by heart kinda have to rummage around and guess what computer hallucination means more jump speed.The game is fun, don't get me wrong, it just seems a little shallow at the moment. Hopefully balance updates and the great modding integration will fix it in time.

_childDocuments_.review: I know this game has a lot of fans from the previous version, and no disrespect to them... but to me it just felt like a kinda janky version of Stellaris, already bought that, ages ago. Movements of the planets really don't make any sense at all, so the whole feature is just that they do in fact move.  A little silly that our advanced space fairing civilization can only forecast the movements out to 1 hour in advance, considering lowly modern humans in 2024 can forecast that stuff out to thousands of years.. But whatever,  its a game thing.Anyhow, I'm sure for fans of the franchise, its great.  But for someone coming over from that other game, its not really a step forward.  Not in my opinion anyhow.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love it but it just feels soulless. All the art seems to be AI generated images and doesn't fit well into the game at all. A lot of it is hyper detailed and makes all the icons hard to read, if anything they should be simple to read at a glance, it makes it harder than it needs to be to learn the game. To top everything off the UI is so bland and ugly in it. Everything is blue and the icons are uninspired for each tab. They aren't easy to read at all from the choices they made for icon pictures. A lot of it feels like it was phoned in, and this is not what I expected from these guys as I adored the first game and them updating the game years later.I understand it's a new game but they have changed stuff up so much that it just doesn't feel enjoyable to play for hours and hours. I have played one game there for 6 hours and I think that's all I want to play. They tried to re-invent the whole thing too much by changing the mechanics and research tree, the whole time I was thinking that I would rather be playing rebellion, it just feels inferior. I told myself I would at least beat one game of it and I did and I don't find myself wanting to play it again. Another thing that I didn't like was the fleet system and how the units are displayed on screen. In the first game you could read on the sides of the screen what planet was what, who was in it, etc. Now it's way harder to read as it doesn't have the small easy to read icons for each ship and the fleet system doesn't auto update when you command group them. The whole game is just one step forward two steps back, who cares about all the sparkly stuff if it doesn't function effectively like the first game. I think it's the main reason why I dislike it so much, things are unnecessarily tedious.A few things that they did do right is the sound design and performance. It doesn't lag and stutter late game like the first game and it runs well on modern hardware. The sound design is great, the music is pretty soothing and fits well into the series by being similar to the soundtrack in the first game. There is also no deafening sound effects like in the previous instalment blowing your ear drums or speakers out. The graphics seem pretty decent. Everything seems like it has good texture modelling and nothing looks bad. I still think the effects from combat could do with an upgrade, the combat seemed a bit boring and could do with being a bit more visually interesting. Capital ships don't have a limit anymore and rely on special resources called "exotics" to create and upgrade them. This would be great if you didn't now share a "greater factory" with cruiser construction. It was better in the first game when they had they're own separate factory as you could build them separately than your fleet. They just don't seem as precious or as powerful anymore when you can just churn them out lol.The upgrade system for them is good but you have to click into more menus to click all these different upgrades and some of them only last for "2 uses" so you have to keep clicking into these windows on each ship to refresh them. It's just pointless micro management were it could do without. A couple slots for artifacts and a few easy to understand upgrades would have been much better, condense them into about 4-5 total and it would make Capital ships more powerful again and make it less tedious for the player. A lot of them you are guessing what they even do as well, there was no mention what "PSI power" does? I assume it makes your skills better but no where does it tell you that. Just another unnecessary mechanic and stat that would be been better if it wasn't even in the game. The game really didn't need all this bloat added into it making it more complicated to play, it may be just me though. If you played it and enjoyed it I am happy for you, at least someone got something out of it. Personally I just feel it went a few steps back on a lot of stuff. I really hope that it gets improved so it is on par with the previous game in terms of mechanics, if it was mechanically easier to play and they made an easier to read UI then I could sit and play it but currently it just isn't there.

_childDocuments_.review: *Note; at this time you cannot upgrade your copy of Sins2 to the Premium Edition, I hear that this is being worked on but really hoping to be able to upgrade soon as I want to support the company.*Greetings as always!  Sins of a Solar Empire 2 is a game I’ve been looking forward to for some time.  I loved the original (aside from the cowardly AI) and played it heavily solo and cooperatively with friends.  I was a bit concerned that this game would be another disappointment in sequels to my favorite games, were my concerns well founded?  Let’s discuss!War, War Never Changes:  I am pleased to say this game does not try to reinvent the wheel nor did it fail to innovate on it.  The basic mechanics are there still; build a fleet, conquer planets and expand your empire in the view of the macro instead of the micro.  Yes you can manage your fleets and probably get a decent amount of efficiency from them but the AI (of your own ships) is competent.  Ships engage what they are good at engaging, use their abilities when appropriate (mostly) and they even know what they need to do after a battle is finished (grab salvage, bomb planets, etc).  The Colors Duke:  This game is pretty, the sound is amazing, the music is great and the ships are downright sexy.  The particle affects are not to be outdone or forgotten either.  The game is just a better Sins, exactly what I hoped for in Sins 2.  They did add quite a bit to the game as well, some of this may have been in Sins 1 but it’s been quite a while since I last played.   First off the quality of life is amazing, clicking on most things will allow any needed research to be queued up, you can also add ships directly to a fleet from the fleet building menu, and they even join the fleet automatically after being built at a construction yard.  Items have been added to give a level of customization to Capital Ships, Starbases, Planets and even Titans, again you can queue them up if you don’t have the research already done.  The search bar on the research screen is also a great addition.  The game also allows you to interact with mini factions to acquire unique items, power ups or supports.It’s been a Long War:  Not all of it is good though, the game lacks a campaign of any kind and currently there isn’t much to do outside of skirmishes.  If you play with others that might not be a bad thing.   Custom mapping seems to be absent as well and we seem to be missing a lot of common map settings.  The game does a great job of explain many mechanics and providing you the data to make informed decisions but one thing I’d like to know is how to determine tracking speed, the game mentions and references, gives upgrades that improve it but I’d like to know what breakpoints are important, what turrets are fast enough to track what.  Other than that, the game is fine.  No bugs that I’ve been able to detect, no crashes either.Overall, if you are a solo RTS player this game may not have enough content currently but as long as you enjoy multiplayer in some fashion I think there is plenty here.  It does admittedly need more content outside of the factions such as new ways to play, a campaign, something because right now it just seems like a skirmish mode is all you really get.  Even still, I’d recommend the game to anyone who likes this style of RTS or has played the original.  Enjoy!

_childDocuments_.review: Having played several dozen hours across various alpha builds, and now had some time to experience all the changes and the extra layer of polish in the full release, I can confidently say that this is exactly the sequel I always hoped for. It remains fully faithful to the spirit of the original while evolving the gameplay in almost every way. QoL is improved across the board. Factions are more asymmetric. There are deeper strategic choices. Micro-management of fleets is more interesting, more rewarding, and more fun. New core mechanics like planet orbits resolve the issues with chokepoints and stalemates that could often happen in the original. The game is beautiful and incredibly well optimized.Maybe most important is the impressive new engine, and the mod support for it. Throughout development the devs have been very transparent and communicative with experienced modders from the original to provide the options and tools to bring their ideas to life. The incredible modding community extended the lifetime of sins1 well over a decade, and I am sure that with this new engine sins2 absolutely has the potential to eclipse that.

_childDocuments_.review: Like the first Sins game, but performance enhanced, what appears to be better AI (they have chased my fleet down across multiple systems instead of taking time to bomb an underdeveloped colony while you regroup), and the shifting jump lanes mechanic (which is optional) makes turtling far less effective (in a way that benefits the game, in my opinion).  Changes between Sins 1 and this (for example, requiring exotic materials to produce capships and putting jump inhibitors towards the end of the tech tree) make raiding with small fleets to simply wreck space stations far more viable.I only have one complaint- I wish the total unit cap per player was higher late game.  While there are some ways to bypass this (for example, using minor factions to call in allied defensive fleets), I hope modders expand the unit cap in the future. _childDocuments_.review: - Sins II is able to run very clean all the way through the end game. The originals suffered from a single core engine which caused major lag in end game scenarios. - The ability to join mid-game, take over AI, and pause the game are all great features that allow for a pretty smooth multiplayer experience. - The addition of planet orbit paths and the ability to scrub forward to see future orbits and how it changes hyperspace lanes is a very interesting change that allows for much more dynamic gameplay. - The game's settings are very minimal. So minimal in fact, that you cannot even choose your resolution. It should appall the consumer that a new release in 2024 lacks what has been an industry standard feature on pretty much every PC game for the past 25 years. - This was a problem in the older games as well. Don't get me wrong, the FPS does not dip in the late game, however closing out a game is still very time consuming and tedious. The final hour and a half of a very clearly won game is a lot of slowly forcing your way through systems while alt tabbing for a battle to go through and maybe reading a light novel on the side. This can be sped up a bit by the variable game speed control, yet still feels rather slow. - For what feels to be a remastered version of Sins I with a few tweaks here and a few content cuts there, learning that all of the  content will come at a later date in the form of DLC is rather disheartening. All in all it would bring a finished game up to the price of $100, much more than ambitious AAA titles and offering very little at that price point.  If you are like me and caught a bad case of vertigo trying to control your ships in a system with strikecraft, let me tell you a little secret. The game has a terrible feature that makes your camera follow a ship if it thinks you are looking at it. This means if you are trying to give your units commands in a battle (this is an RTS afterall, not Stellaris) you are left frustrated as your head is jerked all around the map. Remember those non existent settings we talked about earlier? Well, if you use ctrl-shift-s in the game, you can find the actual settings! Find"camera.snap_to_unit_zoom_target_distance_to_cursor"and lower the value. Changing mine to 100 fixed the issue. How this got through the beta without a single tester or dev noticing is beyond me. If you want to see tactical information such as shields and armor, you are forced to use the terrible outliner in the top right (that is system specific, by the way) or press and  the alt key. I would like to see more options that are just a toggle. If you are going to advertise your game as an RTS, then you should at least add in industry standard features for the genre.  The art for research and items is largely AI created. This AI art was trained on Stardock's art style, but it still stands out as pretty bad. Furthermore, the majority of voice lines in the game are recycled from the previous Sins games. Just for context, this is a game that they are expecting people to shell out $50-$100 for. EDIT (added context:): These voice lines, while reused, have been rerecorded by the original voice actors as confirmed by the developers. Overall, I would not recommend Sins II at the moment. It offers very little for the price point and does not strive to be much more than Sins I on a new engine. While it would be easy for the average Sins fan to praise it for not lagging like the predecessors, I would like to remind the room that this is 2024, and releasing a game with multi-core support is the bare minimum and definitely not a reason to excuse a half-baked release like this at the current price point.

_childDocuments_.review: Review:A complete upgrade on its predecessor, this game shines as a gem in the genre!Positives:Special Slots for Planets, Ships, and Titans:A fantastic addition that lets you truly tailor your strategy. Whether you focus on damage, defense, or unique abilities, this mechanic adds a layer of depth that’s incredibly satisfying.Planetary Orbits:A fun and impactful new mechanic that changes up both gameplay and defense strategies. Watching planets orbit adds a dynamic element that keeps you on your toes. Plus, for those who prefer a more static defense (looking at you, turtles), there’s the option to turn it off.Factions and Sub-factions:The division between factions and sub-factions is beautifully executed. Each one feels distinct, adding variety and fresh experiences every time you play.(Hope they change the visuals of ships so the difference would be highlighted even more)Smooth as Butter:The game engine runs so smoothly, it’s hard to believe. It’s a testament to the developers' efforts that everything feels this polished and seamless.Negatives:AI Art:Unfortunately, this is where the game stumbles. The AI-generated art feels rushed, with glaring issues like multiple fingers and inconsistent designs across the same race. It detracts from the immersion and leaves you wishing for a bit more care in this area.Endgame and Deathballs:The endgame could use some balancing. Right now, defenses and units crumble too quickly, making it feel like if you’re not massing your fleet into a deathball, you’re doomed. A bit of tuning here could go a long way in improving late-game strategy.Rating: 8.5/10Despite the few drawbacks, if these are your main concerns, then you’ve got yourself a good buy. The positives far outweigh the negatives, making this a worthy addition to any collection!

_childDocuments_.review: I feel that Sins 2 is a great remaster of Sins 1, they probably could have gotten away with only doing 3 base factions and essentially only replicated what Sins 1 had at launch, but they essentially implemented most of the Sins 1 + DLC features with some reworking of mechanics. The orbiting planets I can understand the controversy around, but I personally like them as they add a way for maps to evolve over the course of a relatively long session and can break up the planet hoping grind a bit.I also like the new minor faction mechanics which help make each game have different mechanics, even if you're using the same faction.Even with the minor factions and orbiting planets, replayability is rather lacking, with there not being too much difference between different sessions. The 2 TEC factions play pretty differently, but the Vasari and Advent loyal + rebel factions play essentially the same. The AI is also very finicky to do any diplomacy with and I really hope that diplomacy is fleshed out more in the future.I'm really looking forward to the mentioned story content and single player campaign adding new experiences to this game.Overall I'd say it's a 7/10, a perfect base for more features and content to be added onto.
