_childDocuments_.review: For now, I gotta (barely!) not recommend. On a pure gameplay level, the engine and such, the game feels very solid. It runs buttery smooth, the works. Albeit, for all of one game played can tell me. The game blows most others besides the likes of Factorio in optimization. Their code wizards are clearly level 20. This game really is good, under the shell of placeholder art!Problem is, like, some of the art. Ships are aight, albeit, you don't see much of them because they're much smaller in SOASE2. The problem's the music, and especially the UI. So I'm gonna rant about it. Because, why does a game that's had so much effort and love put in elsewhere have 0 put in over here? It's bizarre.The UI is straight-up worse than SOASE1. Everywhere. The ship icons have muddier silhouettes that're harder to read. Capital icons lack a certain boldness to make them stick out as, yes, obviously a capital. The equivalent ships of each faction don't really... match. Scouts are all different shapes, you can't just go 'yeah thats probably a scout' at a glance. They're the sort of icons you have to memorize.The other icons are by and large uninformative. Research screen icons, go show it to anyone who's played RTS and space games but not SOASE2, get them to guess what anything is. Can they? I doubt it. I know I found myself spending 30 minutes to read every single research. Likewise, structures, same problem as ships. The research screen is a bloated mess. Go look at a screenshot of the SOASE1 research screen - straight lines, colour-coded and everything. SOASE2's is, by comparison, spaghetti, which made worse by having to read everything to know what on earth it is. Yes, I'm blaming the AI use for it. AI does not, unfortunately, replace thoughtful UI design. Also, where's the soundtrack? I feel like I'm listening to a 4 minute track on loop! And it's not even a particularly good track! I had to mute the music after an hour. Specifically, it's that TEC_Early_Neutral track that plays whenever there's no combat, at least on smaller maps. That said, they could probably fix this stuff without too much effort. If this game hadn't already had forever to do that, I'd have let it pass, even. At this point, it's clear they're never actually going to do an art pass and flush out all the placeholder garbage. But hey, if they do it when they release in an expansion, hire some actual artists, hire an orchestra for a day to get a real soundtrack? Nice.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Improved version of Sins 1, feels like Early Access without the DLC contentSins 2 attempts to improve upon Sins 1 by addressing its major drawbacks, namely the outdated graphics, poor performance, and lack of a campaign. The graphics and performance are a big reason I had a hard time getting into Sins 1. Now they're great, even on a low performance machine on par with the competition. As for the campaign, it is not yet available.It plays a little  similarly to the original game. There are some gameplay changes, but most units and heroes are the same. This is another thing the DLCs are attempting to address with the unit packs and new faction.Gameplay options are varied enough that there seems to be enough content available to entertain/optimize for many hours even in singleplayer. I haven't delved into the multiplayer experience or high level singleplayer, but the fast update cadence is optimistic for a healthy game in the long term.AI art criticism seems overblown: it doesn't  but some of the art fails to make it clear what it represents. _childDocuments_.review: Nice iteration on Sins 1 that has phenomenal performance, some nice new wrinkles with dynamic planetary orbits, and new tactical possibilities from the way entities like torpedoes and turret rotation are simulated, though these systems aren't perfect. Everything is smooth and comfortable. Veterans of Sins 1 should feel pretty much right at home.The AI art is bad, though. Real bad. It has all the uncanny qualities that GalCiv 4's AI art generation does and then some. We're playing all the hits: portraits with uncanny smooth skin and unnatural shadow work, hands with the wrong number of digits, alphanumeric readouts on pictures of digital displays that have garbled nonsense text, the works. The most egregious use, though, is the armament tech images. Holy lmao. These images look like the AI was prompted to draw deformed crayons in the style of the Superman 3 fembot. Every single tech that features a picture of a missile/torpedo/bullet has a combination of nonsensical, overly detailed machine work, bizarre paint jobs, and structural deformations, because the AI doesn't actually understand that these objects not being vaguely banana shaped is a very important feature for them to appear real.I'm guessing that aside from some light auditing (e.g. prompting the model until something mostly acceptable gets spat out) the use of AI assets allowed for huge cuts in the art team for this project and lowered costs. The assets brought in and touched up from Sins 1 look mostly fine, but I'm assuming there was nobody on the team that was capable of dressing up these really raw assets so that at least the line work was clean and there weren't frank physiological errors with human characters, not that it would have made a huge difference. It is such a small thing, and yet it really cheapens the experience when you have a game with pretty cool lore and all the art is in the style of what is now clearly recognizable to most people as "AI generated schlock".

_childDocuments_.review: The GoodThe majority of the changes seem goodThe game runs buttery smoothThey have improved the UI+ They have made quality-of-life enhancements and generally made it really feel like SINS but an upgraded experience. The Bad-I think it was dumb to make mining facilities for metal/crystal take up logistic slots...this is a dumb change that really slows the game down-also regarding slowing the game down...you have to build 25 research facilities (50 if you include the fact you need both civilian and warfare oriented ones) to completely unlock all the tech, and there are separate upgrade milestones where it is not just enough to have the required amount of research facilities, you also have to choose to upgrade the next tier of research before you can actually start researching the tech you want (this is in addition to building all the research facilities). -building the Orkulus starbase, for example, requires level 2 warfare, but to upgrade it, you are gonna be hours into the game before you get the good upgrades...once again, the game has slowed down progression considerably.-although the UI has improved there are occasions where it is not exactly clear where the upgrade I need is in the research tree -it is also a bit weird to upgrade fleet supply now...they should have kept this similar to before with its own page and such-finally..the need for exotic metals to build a starbase means that there is yet another timegate on building just one starbase (each one requires exotic material). -finally, the one unforgivable change that I have noticed is that the gameplay options for a custom match are severely limited now. Before, you could specify no ultimate weapons...for example...well, options like that do not exist anymore, and I am completely mystified by this change...SINS 2 in most respects is an improvement over the original but for some reason they have gone backwards here and customization of your match is a step back from SINS 1. overall, I like the game, but I think they have made certain aspects of the game overly complicated, and personally, I think slowing down the gameplay was dumb. SINS was never a fast-paced game. It took hours to get through a match, but now it takes even more. It is up to you whether you think this is a good change or not. To me, it's not enough, but it is not enough to make me dislike the game. I hope some of the other issues I have mentioned will be patched/amended after players share feedback in the discussion forums (such as the lack of customization options for custom matches). Nobody will be happy with every change, but I think the vast majority of the changes were good. Just think some of them can be tweaked a bit to make the game more friendly for newer players and to help speed up matches.

_childDocuments_.review: Sins of a Solar Empire II is everything that the original game was, but better: a 4X game focused on ship-to-ship combat, now more gorgeous and immersive than ever -- each weapon on the ships is simulated independently and have different performances depending on the enemy ship type.Tech research is deep thanks to two extensive trees (one for civilian tech, one for military tech) which allows for different playstyles throughout your games. Speaking of variety, like in Sins 1 everyone of the six sub-factions that you can play have special units and/or abilities that you can peruse to gain the upper hand in your struggle for galactic conquest.Last but not least, the game engine's performances are quite remarkable, and despite the current lack of fine-grained tuning it will run well also on aging gaming rigs.Sins II is an example of a sequel done right, building on the strengths of the preceding game and expanding them instead of changing everything for change's sake. It is for sure a game that I will come back to time and again.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a good real time strategy game meaning everything is happening at once. Build your fleet, manage your resources and go smash the enemies right? No, that simple. There are three factions, 2 sub factions apiece. 6 choices in all. More on the way. This game is completed enough to enjoy the experience of playing the Ais or with friends or grouped people you get matched with. There is a great community on discord. The developers are listening g to the players while sticking to their vision of the game.The 6 choices are different in many ways and their play styles vary.. Its a steep learning curve with this game. It will take many attempts to get it down then that much more to master it, if thats even truly possible. THere is an extensive tech tree for each of the 6 groups. One can build defenses as you take over planets with the right ship, though. I play this game mostly on epic and the developers gave us a free copy to transfer here to steam. There are many voice lines and the voice acting is pretty decent. There is not story campaign, but one is in the works. The developers are very open at how they are going to be adding more features, patches improvements. The combat is pretty intense and as the point of these games, the bigger the army the better. There are clear stages to this game as the play progresses. There is a "culture spread" each player can do that gives boost to their own planets but gives debufss to opponents. THe constant struggle for resources is always a worth challenge to overcome. Capital ships are also brought with gems that are harvested or created in exotic factories. There are no micro transactions. It recommend to get the deluxe version as that guarantees that upocoming dlcs are already paid for. Thre music is pretty interesting and each group gets their own themes throughout the game. There is a wide selection of maps to choose from. There are smaller cpu controlled factions that provides an exchange market, harass players, and offer auctions using influence points that are earned by purchasing them on tech tress and placing  "+" influence points in planets. UPgrades for planets, defense starbases and even massive titans are available. Those become more advanced as research is completed in tech tress. The research can be expanded as orbital structures and planet items are purchased and a few of the "+" items are sold in auctions.The diplomacy options vary depending on how many players are on temas. Its possible to exchange resources with other players and allied Ai's. Even planets can be put up for trade. THis game is a fun and tough learning curve. There are tutorials available that help players learn. Even with that, it will take a few beat downs to learn what not to do and to do. This game is worth the challenge. Its still being made. The real fun feature is that maps are not static, they change and move if the players wish it. So where one of your planets is in one position, it can shift position when you are busy elsewhere. when you are not looking. This game is a lot to learn, yet the reward is excellent. You can run 1v1 on a tiny map or ffa 10 player immense map. THe choice is yours. Even the speed of the game and its various elements and game mechanics can have their speed adjusting. There is in an ingame chat with ping features.  The cake has no frosting, but what is there is delicious.

_childDocuments_.review: At first glance i was concerned that this was going to be a re-skin of the old game. Fortunately enough has changed to justify the games existence and improves on its predecessor in many ways. The NPC factions have been massively improved, each of the playable factions are far more unique in the way you play them than the previous game. The learning curve is steep and there is a lot to wrap your head around before you notice the differences between the old game. The tech trees are big and take a while comprehend. A quick overview to save you time: TEK enclave spawn massive free Defensive fleets that don't take up supply that can attack and defend adjacent starsystems. TEK Primacy focus on spreading Culture, spawning large free non supply costing fleets in enemy territory then supporting them with Novalith cannons that disable static defences. Vasari Exodus can produce ships from their capital ships and cruisers zip quickly from one side of the galaxy to the other quickly, Their titan at level 6 allows you to create new phase lanes to virtually anywhere on the map, fly straight to their capital, Weakest strikecraft, their corvettes are awesome. Vasari alliance are tougher but less mobile. Advent wrath and Reborns capitals level up quickly, have great strikecraft and focus on spreading culture to cast spells and use their superweapons to capture systems without committing any supply or ships. Wrath focus on capturing enemy ships, Reborns ships resurrect.

_childDocuments_.review: Sins 2 is probably one of the best RTS on the market right now. It seamlessly combines the grand scale and strategy involved in commanding a fleet of quite literally hundreds of different ships, while still staying grounded enough to let you care about the small scale as well. Very few games can let you zoom in and focus on a single fighter doing it's attack runs in the midst of the titanic clash involving dozens of frigates, cruisers, capital ships, titans, and even more, and still being able to give direct orders to ALL of them if you wish. Never did I feel overwhelmed by the sheer amount of stuff going on despite the sheer volume happening all at once. Seamlessly blending this feeling of massive fleets still being made up of individual ships that you had to build, command, and send into the fray is perhaps the game's greatest strengths over it's competitors. (Not that it really has many in it's genre) The visuals and attention to detail is incredible here. Every ship has it's own voicelines, with some even changing depending on their situation. (Smug, normal, and desperate) Every single turret, missile, and hardpoint has it's own tracking and firing arc that you can see in action every engagement and find on the unit card. Even the little trade ports you can build send out their own ships that you can then research escorts for, trying to make their way through a variety of different zones.As for the gameplay itself, it's more or less a direct improvement over Rebellion, which still holds up today in my book. The UI is MUCH better, with information more cleanly laid out and easy to access. The market system is far more in-depth, no longer just being an indefinite way of buying/selling different resources at temporarily increased/lowered prices depending on immediate demand. Exotics have been added as a way to make larger purchases more impactful towards both your bottom line and time spent investing. The new orbital system throws a ton of strategies on their head, with new curveballs being thrown at you constantly, (though thankfully, none of which can particularly sneak up on you due to the ability to see them an hour in advance) and previously safe planets now being thrown into enemy territory. Ships have much more defined roles and increased variety. And of course, each faction feels a lot different to each other compared to before.In the previous game, the factions all had their own unique structures, ships, abilities, and research, however there was a very large amount of overlap in how they actually played. Every faction had the same classes of ships that fit the exact same role, every single faction had the same type of structures and buildings, and even most of the research options had a direct analog in every single tree. Now, every faction has differences in almost every facet of their empire, whether that goes for how they gain their research points, the roles their ships fill, and of course brand new mechanics unique to every race. Playing as TEC vs. Advent is no longer akin to essentially choosing what ships you got and whether you were going to focus on culture or economy for most of the game. Vasari in particular play almost unrecognizably from both everyone else and how they played in the first game, in a good way.That being said, there are some nagging concerns I have with the game, both in how it changed stuff from the old game, and some new issues of it's own. Time-to-kill is much faster than it was in Rebellion, especially in large fleet battles. Losing 4+ capital ships and various cruisers in less than a minute is a much more common occurrence now, especially if your opponent brought missiles in large amounts. If your opponent so chooses, they can and will simply focus down your most important units and there will be little you can do about it other than bringing some redundancy and hoping you can do the same to him in the meantime. In general, battles are over much quicker, for better or worse, and also results in the smaller stuff not scaling very well into the late game and hard to get attached to. That being said, it's not crazy fast, and you  still have time to try and pull of some defensive maneuvers. The time-to-kill in Rebellion was also pretty damn slow, so maybe speeding it up was a given, but still, going from using capital ships in that game to this game will give you some whiplash.Defenses are also worse from what I can tell. Turtles are annoying to deal with in any strategy game, I know, but even a fully upgraded starbase will die to a fleet not even half it's time or cost to make, and pretty quickly at that. With some support from tactical structures, they will be able to hold off a raiding force or 2, but any sort of moderately sized fleet (~750-1000) dedicated to taking the planet will probably be able to roll over the average starbase and accompanying defenses with little issue. A far cry from their sheer power in Rebellion, and a bit of a tough pill to swallow for the likes of TEC Enclave and Vasari.AI is a noticeable step-up from Rebellion, but it still pulls some of the same dumb mistakes. Not pushing when it could easily win, randomly deciding to attack some random ship at the edge of the gravity well instead of bombing the planet to death, etc. Still, it's better in most ways.And of course, there are some balancing quirks. Certain units just seem to do the same stuff as others, but better in every way, certain units just have very few counters at the time they can be built, and every faction currently has some very unfun playstyles they can pull off. All that being said though, they are sure to balance the game in the weeks/months/years to come, and most of this can be fixed with some simple stat changes here and there.Overall, a very solid improvement to it's predecessor in almost every way that matters, and in the few that it isn't, it's sure to be in a year or two. They have a very exciting roadmap for this game, and it seems like it's shaping up to be an even more supported game than the first one, which came out 15 years ago and was still receiving updates as of this year. Lots of hope for the future of this game!

_childDocuments_.review: I played a little over an hour of the game and then refunded it.I loved Sins 1. Still play it to this day. I was hoping I could move to this one now because the multi-threaded performance would allow me to play on huge maps without chugging like Sins 1 does in the later portion of the game.1. I genuinely couldn't stand the AI art. This is beyond my ethical concerns with it as well. I actually grew to hate looking at it. It also made everything look the same. In Sins 1, I could glance at the tech tree and see a difference between all the icons and would know what I was looking at. Sins 2, all tech has that weird AI look and also has no real distinction so looking through the tree is a slog.2. No in-game map designer and very limited map choices. Another big one for me. What's the point in leveraging this multi-core stuff if I can't make a 6-Star, 250 planet map?3. Game setup choices are also massively limited. Can't turn off pirates or minor factions among other things.That's my big three. I also don't like how large the ship icons are when zoomed out on a planetary system, there should be a way to make that smaller. Sins 1, I feel, was better. I didn't see any diplomacy to speak of really either.In general, it feels like there's far too much missing from the game. There's just so much less game than Sins 1. Plus the AI art stuff is far too egregious.I hope there's a game I'd like to purchase here in the future but for now, there isn't.

_childDocuments_.review: If you liked Sins of a Solar Empire, you will also like the second entry. The main gameplay style is still intact but they have massively improved the graphics and the engine so even in super late game the game still runs smoothly. They have also added features such as orbiting planets which will change phase lanes over time to mix up the gameplay, and this feature can be toggled off if desired. Minor factions can also grant bonuses to complement your playstyle, adding a lot of replayability.The technology page uses a lot of AI art which doesn't look great. However since launch the developers have already fixed the readability of the technology screen and a good amount of other bugs, so it looks like they are working to make this game better over time. I can recommend this game to any RTS fans out there.

_childDocuments_.review: This is just a perfect sequel, or better: SOASE refurbished and modernized.So many QoL changes that i didn't even missed in the original but now don't wanna miss anymore.A lot of annoying mechanics gone and or replaced with better ones. Pros:- For example automatically losing colonies just to spread of culture, which is no more. So good. (and i play advent a lot)- being able to improve Capitals and customize them, so great.- Planets now have a LOT more importance, not only money wise but also orbis bonuses, mining and customization via different upgrades.- The secondary factions are not only an annoyance to anyone anymore, but useful too, if u spend the influence.- The game feels much more alive and responsive in general. I don't feel the need to use the game speed toggle at all anymore, even in the early game compared to SOASE 1 where i regularly had gamespeed on 2-4 x until later in the game. It doesn't get boring in ealry game anymore by just waiting for resources.- Wrecks are a good addition and also the rare resource system. It could have broke the SOASE experience, but it didn't. Well done.- The graphics are beautiful for an RTS and there are no FPS issues even in late game, not even in the slightest. Bravo. I, to this day, struggle with FPS issues on the predecessor.- Titans dont keep their EXP on death. Nuff said. That was just OP and made ppl suicide them all over as long as they get XP. Cons- Superweapons. It's an RTS, not a turtle an "fire artillery from safety" simulator.- On my personal feeling, balancing is still not good.- AI sucks Ass. IDK if they cheat, but their decisionmaking is just garbage. Don't get me wrong, i don't wanna play vs a supercomputer, but at least don't be hilariously stupid. I am by no means a good SOASE player, but i didn't even struggle vs hard AI, even if they seem to focus me.- Losing bid influence when u lost the auction doesn't sit well. it means if your influence regen is worse then enemys you can never win any, unless u miss out some. I don't like it.TL:DRThis is a great game and a great successor to the Original. Modern, faster in progress pace especially in early game but not overwhelming. Buy at any price. It's worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great game for people who like mobile games. If you played Starcraft PvP and that's what you're after, you'll get in real cozy with what Sins 2 is offering you. This is not a game like Stellaris, Endless Space, or the like. Everything about playing it felt like I was trying to square a circle, and that's on me at least as much as it is on the marketers. It's better than HW3's clear disdain for a deep story in favor of "let's make mobile gamers into computer gamers and mostly invest in skirmish-y scenarios", but if you want more than that you should wait on this.It's 4X, but other 4X have more depth to them. It's RTS, but other RTS have more strategy. It's gorgeous and runs smoothly, and seems really oriented around making it easy for you to simply build more ships and conquer more space to gain more of the same resources you already had. Your win objectives are build capital ships to defeat all your enemies - conveniently, you can build any capital ship from the start, but you need to research lesser fleet ships - and do it faster than your enemies, since that's their plan too. "But you just described all games!" - yeah, kinda, but I can keep describing other games that also fall into the 4x category or the RTS category or both, as Sins 2 aims to do. I can't say more about Sins 2, since that's all there is to it. That's why I compare it to a mobile game. Sins 2 is the kind of game that envisions you playing a session from beginning to end in a few hours, winning or losing, and goes grats-well done-same time time tomorrow. Some people want that; like someone said in the discussions, they put in thousands of hours into StarCraft multiplayer and never once played the campaign. That's their thing, and Sins 2 is their thing.But as another player said in their comment, this game can be boring - if you're looking for more than StarCraft Multiplayer-levels of depth, strategy, story, or immersion. I know a campaign is coming as a DLC, which seems like something I'd have launched with, so maybe when that comes I'll have a better review to give.So, it's not a thumbs-down because it's a bad game. It's not a bad game at all. It's just not the game it could be.

_childDocuments_.review: I finished 2 games on Easy and Normal with 5 AI's before reviewing. This took around 13h of play. I didn't play the original.It's ok, but not great. The biggest issue in this RTS game is that because of it's 4X design it falls to the same endgame trap as those - early and midgame can be fun and exciting, but endgame is an exercise in tedium.I think it's good enough if it piques your interest. Just don't expect an amazing game, this is just good at most.I also heard that it's not much of an upgrade over the original game, so if you played that - your mileage may vary.RTS with 4X design. You will explore the galaxy, colonize planets, improve your economy and production and command fleets against your enemies. There is no campaign, you can play skirmish vs ai or multiplayer.The map will usually consist of a number of stars connected by wormholes. Several planets/asteroids will orbit a star (yes, the planets orbit-move around their suns). Each planet/asteroid will be able to be colonized.A colonized world will have a static number of planetary improvements that can be built. These can provide various bonuses to many different things like resource generation, unit production, etc. You will also be able to upgrade with several passive upgrades that can increase orbital building slots, resource generation, trade and science. You have limited slots for civilian orbital buildings and military ones. Civilian ones will mine asteroids or trade, give you points towards unlocking tech trees, build ships and increase culture. Military objects will fire at enemies and defend your planet.Science is divided in civilian and military branch. Both of them require their respective science building to unlock further tiers of research.Fleets consist of different sizes of ships for different tasks. There are small ships for scouting and harassment, gauss ships that deal with large targets, carriers, torpedo ships, orbital bombardment ships, etc. There are also big capital ships of different classes and they can also acquire XP and level abilities and install upgrades to further personalize them. There is also a titan ship for each faction which functions largely like a capital ship but is bigger and you can have only one.Combat can be automated. When your fleet is in an area with an enemy they will automatically target things they deem appropriate for their role, so your torpedo guys will shoot at starbases while your gunships will target smaller ships. Your capital ships can use all their abilities automatically as well, so no need to micro at all. But if you want to - there's nothing stopping you from turning auto-abilities off and microing every ship in a fight.Game has some 3d elements and ships technically move in 3 dimensions, but it largely doesn't matter. You can treat this as a 2d game.Each fleet can be ordered to produce units and those units will be constructed by the most appropriate shipyard nearby. Likewise if you need to refine exotic materials for some building/upgrade/research - it will be done automatically as long as you have the means to do so. You don't have to manually switch to appropriate screen, queue up a resource, wait for it to finish and then start production of the thing you wanted - the game takes care of that for you and shows you full cost of each item that you will need, which is nice. Research/upgrades that require other reasearch/upgrade first will work the same way - the game will queue up what you need, letting you know beforehand in the tooltip.There are 3 factions, each having 2 variations with small differences between them.I've seen no major issues.Nothing special, but graphics serve there purpose. Big fights can look nice, but are pretty static.Biggest issue of 4X games is that you start the game with a set of options and have means to utilize them, but as the game grows, you get more planets, more ships, more fleets, more enemies, more battles, etc - the tools you are using remain the same as you started.It's good that this game has automation in terms of building/research queues and reinforcing fleets, buuuut...... it would have been nice to have an option to set a number of each ship type in a fleet and not worry about clicking production as they die. They could be replaced automatically to keep the fleet population at given size.Also once you destroy an enemy world and colonize it - you should have a quick way to queue full upgrades for it, maybe have a preset for each world size and type that you could quickly select upon viewing such world.Those 2 ideas should be implemented to make the game less tedious when you are snowballing, money isn't an issue and you just try to sweep the AI out of the game. Maybe some way to tell where the enemy homeworld is?As it stands - endgame is spent 90% of time clicking on build queues to have each world with appropriate defenses/etc, and the other 10% is sending your fleets to each world 1-by-1 followed by increasing game speed so that you don't die of old age waiting for the game to end.That's really not that much considering the game plays pretty simply. This is not like Starcraft where each race plays completely differently and it requires and rewards micro on a unit-by-unit basis.Games like Homeworld got away with just 2 factions because it also had a gripping single-player campaign with amazing story and many unique units not found in skirmish.Games like Endless Space have a lot of factions. Now, I get it - Endless Space is a turn-based game, not a real-time one and creating units that can move around, shoot and use abilities takes more time and effort, but still, the feeling is there that this game doesn't have all that much content.I like it for what it is. There are fans of the first game that complain that not enough was changed for this sequel, which to me means less because I didn't really playing the original. But it's clear that there is much less content here than proper RTS games with the lack of campaign or proper turn-based 4X complexity and race variety. The game is pretty expensive for what it offers.I'd give Sins of a Solar Empire aIt's about average, but considering lately RTS genre has been filled with duds (Stormgate, HW3, CoH3...) I welcome something that feels alright. I feel I would have more fun with 9-bit armies though and probably will at some point in the future.We'll see what is going to be added to this game later on. Better endgame automation would be a good start.

_childDocuments_.review: To start off, this game has potential. As someone who has played Rebellion for over a decade I have to agree with the majority of people saying that Sins 2 stays true to the previous games and largely does them justice. It has a solid base for gameplay but many glaring flaws. With that said...... Sins 2 doesn't bring enough to the table compared to Rebellion to be worth recommending for me. If you plan on getting the premium version then this is doubly true. I know some will disagree with me, but Sins 2 is mainly Rebellion with a new coat of paint and added stability out of the box. And, no, it still doesn't have a story mode after over a decade.What this game does right:It stays true to the previous editions and provides a solid experience that will be familiar to Sins veterans and be fairly easy for newcomers to learn. The game looks beautiful in its designs for ships, structures and planets. The music is good for fitting the feel and pace of the game in most cases. The various factions also feel a bit more unique with added mechanics unique to each race and faction. They don't feel as copy paste as in Rebellion. Economy is also not as simple as spamming trade ports and using them to buy metal and crystal.What this game does wrong:I have to point out the elephant in the room. The AI for this game is still eating the leftover glue it had from the previous entries of this series and seems to have found more. Aside from the absolute hardest difficulties it doesn't provide a challenge. AI fleets are rather lethargic until the later portions of the mid game and late game. They don't really build in response to your fleet composition and colonize rather slowly outside their starting star cluster.  As a friend of mine also pointed out and I noticed later, the AI will often run from a planet they should easily be able to take if it's defended.Diplomacy is bland. While it is nice that you can buy items and some ships from other factions, this portion of the game is rather stripped down and simplified compared to Rebellion. The previous level of depth just isn't there. This portion of the game really needs work.The planet orbit system in relation to the rest of the game...... I really want to like this mechanic. But it can kind of makes chokepoints useless and can really make defense tiresome. Not hard, but tiresome.  With the last game I played I probably spent more time moving my defenses around than actually moving my fleet.lolLastly, this game is in an odd limbo of wanting to be a RTS and a grand strategy game.  This was kind of true for Rebellion as well. It just doesn't seem to go far enough in either direction or marry the two in a way that feels quite right. Maybe I'm biased, but the flaws of Rebellion were just as amplified as its strengths in Sins 2.Conclusion:This game needed another year in development in my eyes. It has a lot going for it and definitely has points it does well. But many of the mechanics are under-developed and need further development.  I want to like this game. But I have to recommend avoiding it for at least a few more patches. If you do plan to buy this game then do it on sale and just get the base version. Don't pay for stuff that isn't even out yet.

_childDocuments_.review: Don't let the time played on Steam fool you. I've been playing the Epic Games Store version of Sins II since early access started there.Original Sins of a Solar Empire (all four iterations) was an awesome game. It's only downside was it's 32 bit single CPU core limitation. Which slowed the everything down drastically to a crawl during the late game (even on the most beefy of rigs).People wanted Sins to be ported over to 64 bit, and to utilize modern graphics.. Well guess what. IT HAPPENED!Sins II is basically Original Sins: Rebellion on Steroids! With a new UI, and some Quality of Life improvements. Along with some additions to capital ship, and planet abilities/upgrades. Some will think its just "more of the same". However after some recent game launch disasters more of the same is EXACTLY what we needed. Stardock/Ironclad chose to stick with the Original Sins game play formula, and IT WORKS.The Good:New 64 bit Engine. New Graphics. Zero Lag! Even in late game! Some new ways to 4X. Model details are Excellent. Planets now Orbit their stars changing the phase lanes, and the map overall. Plan carefully. Missiles are now targetable objects. Sins II AI is no joke, and will easily hand your @$$ to you if you let it. No "Brave Sir Robin" AI (In Sins 1 AI ran away at 1st sign of cap ship). SD/IC played it safe, and used the tried, and true Sins 1 game play formula.  The Main three factions (Six if you count the rebel factions) have changed game play wise, but are still very much the same factions as Original Sins.Sins II is going to be one hell of a Mod Platform! (Mod Tools released on launch day!)The Bad: (Just an Opinion. It's not really bad. Questionable at worst).The Backgrounds, and Environment. It's not just Sins, but it seems every space game lately is following the "Homeworld Look" of space backgrounds being bright Yellow, Orange, or Light Blue, and overly heavy on nebulas. If it were one or two maps i can live with it, but ALL of them? Good thing is we can disable the background, and mod in new skybox's.The Mouse pointer latching onto anything that comes across it. I focus on my battleship. Then a stray fighter, or missile crosses the path then Yeeeet. Gets pretty annoying when you try to control your fleets.Some issues with the new UI. Especially the research tree. Veteran Sins 1 players should have no problem figuring things out, but new players may struggle to get a grasp on things. Suggestion for new players, Play through all of the tutorial missions, and start on small two player maps with easy AI to learn the game. Hover over each research item to see what it does. Same with cap ship ability's, and upgrades. Again not really bad, and pales in comparison to the good.I think its safe to say we have another winner here :D

_childDocuments_.review: I've played hundreds of hours of the original game, and I am on my way to catching that number with the sequel. This is a great update of the original game and gameplay. They have stayed true to what made the original game great while improving upon it. I was a little concerned when I saw how similar the capital ships were to the original, but this has passed after putting in 25+ hours. The ship modules and additional planet customizations lead to new decisions for your fleet and empire. And the quality of life improvements are very welcome, my favorite being the new fleet system. This allows you to designate fleets and reinforce them directly. The game will then automatically queue ships from the nearest factories to rendezvous with the selected fleet. I also want to compliment the optimization of this game. My pc is entering its senior years and can still run 1000-2000 fleet supply battles full of missiles and strike craft. I've had to turn off some of the graphics options to do this, but it still looks great. I'm running a gtx 980 on a 34' 1440p monitor.  If you were a fan of the original Sins you'll be a fan of this. Same if you're a fan of RTS games. And ditto if you just want to see some of the best space battles you can get in a game.I'm really happy with what Ironclad did here and am looking forward to future updates. And I can't wait to see what the modding community does with it as well.

_childDocuments_.review: It's the original game, with all the DLC included, but with a face lift and a few new ideas. Modding support and a map editor ensure that this game has a high degree of replayability. Some of the UI choices will feel a bit dated, and I'm a bit disappointed by the limit on ships (2k Supply Limit or ~2-400 ships) given how far processing power has advanced since the original game was finished. I would imagine there will be mods to address this. I would recommend it, though I am hesitant to suggest the full ticket price. I am cautiously optimistic about future support, as Stardock has a good reputation; but, this is an old dog despite the most recent trip to the groomer. I'm not sure how many new tricks it has left.Definitely get it if it's on sale. If you're a hardcore RTS fan or truly loved the original (like I did!), you'll be happy even if you pay full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid sequel. Only minor complaint is the AI art for the technology screens. It's mostly fine but the thumbnails of it on the overall research screen is a tad hard to read and figure out at a glance. Otherwise, updated visuals, more distinct playstyles for each race, the orbital mechanics (which are not a gimmick but actually quite interesting and really change up the game), and nearly all of the content that Rebellion had, this is exactly what I wanted in a Sins sequel. Couple that with a big engine update that seems to never buckle even with hundreds of ships on screen, all shooting simultaneously, it makes great use of modern hardware. If only Supreme Commander would get this treatment.With the promise of more ships and an expansion for a fourth race, this is an easy recommendation for those of us who played Sins 1 back it's release over 16 years ago.

_childDocuments_.review: A near perfect game. _childDocuments_.review: Ironclad has done it again!Absolute master class in what a fun, 4x, RTS should be. The game is easy to learn, hard to master (if you're wanting to be good at PvP). Game is extremely enjoyable against other players (good community) and also just as enjoyable with bots, be it alone or with other players in a comp stomp. This is a step up from the original Sins in nearly every aspect with requested maps being ported over and an active dev community that actually listens to feedback and implements change accordingly.I recommend this game at full price as it is worth every penny, but on sale it is an absolute must have if you so much as think about wanting to play an RTS game. Diplomacy victories are possible with AI and players. The AI also doesn't backstab you if you treat them well which makes it possible to go into FFA games and actually form alliances that last until victory. Each faction brings its own flavor of playstyle from defense to offense, but doesn't divert so far from each other that the learning curve is steep.Hats off to Ironclad once again for making the sequel we've all been waiting for!

_childDocuments_.review: As it is in it's current state I recommend spending your money on Rebellion instead of 2, while there are major changes to the gameplay of each faction and new ships/abilities, I cannot in good faith say this is better than Rebellion . I also cannot abide by the ugly AI art, I get the dev team is small but surely after all this time you can temp hire an artist, there was one for Rebellion and previous titles, clearly. The AI art is ugly and has plenty of mistakes like too many fingers or texture issues - beyond that from a gameplay perspective the AI art makes everything very same-y and undefined. For example, when researching or using an ability, it isn't always clear what exactly you're researching or using unless you read the description. While this seems minor, in the previous game you could mostly tell what each thing did just by looking at it. I also don't like AI art in games I pay actual money for from a moral standpoint, it's not acceptable to me. I'd also rather have 3-4 portraits to choose from for each species rather than 10-20 of the samey ugly AI ones that all just kinda suck. Many of the voice lines and music seem imported from Rebellion - I've even seen icons from the first game. Again, its' been  since rebellion and this game feels like a testbed before a release. The game is NOT complete and while updates are coming, they focus on things that aren't as necessary compared to what the community wants. For example, diplomacy is utterly worthless in 2 - literally. You can send a million credits, metal, crystal, and other valuables and the AI will spit in your face even if you've never fought each other and are the same or otherwise traditionally friendly factions. You have to trade valuable planets to get maybe 5 minutes of a ceasefire they will immediately break as soon as possible even if you outnumber them 10 to 1. The AI itself is... not great. It's being improved as of this post, and from one game with it, it seems much better than before, but still has some issues that aren't nearly as bad as just an update ago. Defenses in 2 also feel massively worse than Rebellion, every defense just feels so weak now - I don't see the point in have a short range and long range turret when both seem to do about the same damage anyways and die just as quickly. There's also no mines to speak of, which as a defensive player is a massive letdown, especially when combined with the fact that they don't seem to have any intentions of adding mines for the foreseeable future. For some positives because the game has many, gameplay has received a massive change and update. Each faction feels actually different now, the TEC are addicted to money, the Advent have cool psionic abilities, and the Vasari have boosts they can give their ships to make them more powerful. On the smaller scale ships are more dynamic and have turrets or firing arcs for each gun, point defense can shoot down missiles, and the models (except for a single one) all look much better and up to date. One model that looks beyond awful however is the Advent rebel Titan, my god is the thing ugly as all hell. All other Titans have gotten a small facelift and along with starbases have dynamic models that change with each upgrade you put on them - but the Advent rebel Titan is utterly different and so ♥♥♥♥♥♥ ugly like damn what happened??? You had such a good design and threw it out the window for some fisherprice lookin thing. It really doesn't even look like it fits in the game itself, let alone the faction it belongs to. Nonetheless, while gameplay has improved generally, I still can't recommend 2 over Rebellion. At least not yet, if the game changed for the better I will gladly change this review because I  do want to see this game succeed.

My only reccomendation here is to make another tutorial mission which goes in-depth on research, how it affects certain things, and how certain trees work.On that same note, theres no mention of trade, or how that affects your growth, or how tradeships even work. _childDocuments_.review: After the massive disappointment that was Homeworld 3, this game really shows how to make a sequel. While the gameplay did not receive a big overhaul it was changed enough to feel fresh, and the focus was more on streamlining certain parts of the game in a way that adds to the experience, rather than just removing it to make it more "accessible".Rebuilding a fleet in previous games was quite tedious, because you had to manually recruit ships per planet. It was also hard to know how many of each ship you had, making it possible to recruit too many or too little of a certain ship type. They solved this problem by allowing you to create a fleet, and directly recruiting to this fleet. Removing the micro from a place you did not want it, and add it to the macro.This is just a small example of the changes that have been implementing, but shows the developers know their game quite well, where the tedium is, and how to remove/refine it. All the while adding new gameplay variations that don't intrude on the classic gameplay, like the orbit mechanics.Performance also had a massive upgrade, and the game plays really smooth even into the late game. Battles look impressive, and feel realistic. The small details of a shield showing a reaction based on where enemy weaponry hit it, weapons being blocked by ships/object because they are in the line of fire, are some examples of immersing you into the experience.Factions also feel more distinct compared to the previous titles. The new visuals really help to sell this, but also gameplay wise. Where the factions felt more like variations on each other, with little to differentiate them, there is now more emphasis on what these factions are supposed to be in this universe. I especially love that the Vasari now jump in with a capital ship and small escort, instead of just starting with a planet like the TEC for example.All in all I am hard pressed to find any faults with the new game, my biggest gripe being that the UI is not as readable as in the previous games, and feels a bit bland. Definitely a recommendation to both veterans, and newcomers.
_childDocuments_.name: Sins of a Solar Empire II

_childDocuments_.review: A faithful sequel to the original. The strategy layer is almost completely the same. Basically the same ships, basically the same counters. The economy layer is mostly different, overhauled, and streamlined. If you have spent any time in Sins I, you should buy this game. Especially since the big mods from the original game have said they want to port their mods to Sins II.I do have to dock the game for a significantly worse UI. While they did make an attempt to lower the amount of extra clicks you have to do to manage a fleet or empire, the buttons themselves do not quickly convey the information they need, you have to memorize many of the button placements rather than look for them. Additionally, a veteran Sins player will be thrown off because the default hotkey placement is different.
_childDocuments_.name: Sins of a Solar Empire II

_childDocuments_.review: For those of you who never played it: the first game is a beloved classic RTS that was on a little bit larger scale and had much slower gameplay than something like Starcraft or Company of Heroes. You don't need to be a 13 year-old hopped up on energy drinks to play this. There are some light 4X elements, but the focus is absolutely on fighting. Huge battles over multple planets with hundreds of individual ships. The capital ships and titans are huge and powerful center-pieces for your fleet, and they have special abilities akin to Warcraft. For those who HAVE played the original: This is the gold-standard for what a sequel should be. They took 100% of the stuff from the first game and just put it on a new engine. The only new thing (currently) is that the planets move around now and dynamically create new phase lanes--which is awesome! They are going to add more ships per race and a  4th race through DLC. At launch, it is just a direct transition form the first game. All of the old ships, voice lines, designs, etc are back. It is EXACTLY what we have been hoping for. We have multi-core support!!!

_childDocuments_.review: This game is mostly OK.   In fact, this game is mostly quite good.  It's basically Rebellion on a new engine, which is fine.   If you know what you're getting into and that's what you want, then this game delivers that very well.  Usually.The big issues right now are that balance swings wildly from patch to patch, the UI is an awful mess, and they put features in the game that simply don't work.   People were sick of seeing the camera rotated whenever they issued a move command, so there's an option that's supposed to address this, except it doesn't work.  How about you just add an option to disable camera rotation when I have units selected?  And then how about you make the option actually do what it says it does?  Really, I would like to just have the camera looking straight down at the map from above, and then to turn off rotation completely.   That would be great.   This is also apparently asking too much.There's an option for ships rallying to a fleet to avoid hostile gravity wells, except half of the time it doesn't work.   I'm not sure what the trigger is here, it doesn't seem to be the number of jumps, but it definitely happens, and it happens often enough for me to complain about it.   To quote my friend "Oh yeah, the option is there, it just doesn't do anything."There's an option to set your garrisons to defensive roam (they will travel to friendly gravity wells, but not hostile ones), except sometimes they just suicide into an enemy fortress world anyway.   Whoops!  Sorry!There are other issues, mostly related to game balance, that are just strange.  Missiles and strike craft are very powerful, which warps the early game into being almost unplayable for some factions.   TEC's point defense frigate is complete garbage, and I've witnessed a mixed group of light and PD frigates lose to even numbers of Advent missile frigates at around the 20 minute mark.  That's insane.  Obviously the solution to that problem is to play Advent, so that's what I recommend, but it's still a fundamental problem with the game.I'm leaving a negative review here simply because I notice that this game's online community loves the taste of developer boots.  Rather than trying to bring things up on the forums, I'm simply going to complain about them here.Cheers.

_childDocuments_.review: The Good:The gameplay feels familiar yet improved compared to Rebellion, offering a smooth and enjoyable experience.The Bad:The main issue with the new menu and UI is the lack of differentiation. The use of AI-generated images results in inconsistent, inauthentic, and illegible icons. Unlike in previous games, where icons clearly conveyed their functionality, the new design fails to provide immediate recognition of their intended purposes. This lack of clarity makes navigation frustrating.Additionally, several elements from the previous game are missing. Notably, the titan factories are gone, and now titans are absurdly constructed in standard factories, which is visually incongruent and confusing. The absence of these specialized structures detracts from the strategic depth and immersion.The tech tree is also problematic, requiring multiple investments before unlocking new abilities, which adds to the frustration.Despite these UI and design issues, the gameplay itself is engaging and enjoyable. I recommend the game with the hope that future updates will address the UI shortcomings and missing elements, improving the overall user experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a ton of time in the game yet but it seems like a straight upgrade to Rebellion. All the factions (with a hint of more to come) and they have greater differentiation than before.The core gameplay is largely unchanged, but the planet development has been streamlined in a good way, but also made more interesting with planetary buildings, a system that capital ships also use, allowing for fairly deep customization (and apparently some pretty broken combos). Interactions with minor factions seem rather limited, but there's more going on there than in rebellion. On the other hand, it'd be nice to have something broadly similar to the diplomacy/influence system of rebellion where you can forge alliances with AIs, or at least know what your standing with them looks like. My only gripe is with the AI 'art'. It's extremely bland and same-y (as it always is) and makes a lot of thumbnails/icons visually indistinct, taking the UI down a notch. I'd rather half as many character portraits with actual character than what we have now. Overall a minor gripe, just sort of odd to see. Apparently they have in-house artists, let them cook.Pour this down Blackbird's throat and have them re-approach HW3 plz.

_childDocuments_.review: Sins of a Solar Empire 2 is a genre martini. Mixing 4X and RTS elements with the coldness of space to chill both the glass and empty husks that once were your enemies. This is the second entry in the series approximately fifteen years later with the full release on Steam. How does this entry hold up to the predecessor? Asking $100 USD for the collector's edition is pretty hefty. The $50 USD for the base game with some features cut from the last iteration is a hard sell. I would only spend if you are a series fan or have no other game you are looking forward to. The launch week sale price of $40 USD for the base game and $80 USD for the collector's edition felt a lot more fair for the quality of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: A solid example of a game that didn't need to innovate with a sequel. All they effectively did was update the engine, make it substantially more stable, and improve the graphics. Sometimes that's all you really need to do. Seen plenty of times now a sequel to an older game try to remake itself and fail catastrophically by trying to reinvent the wheel, when what has happened here is really all the community that grew around this game wanted. Let the modders take the creative risks while you provide a stable platform for them play around with. Win/Win.
_childDocuments_.name: Sins of a Solar Empire II

_childDocuments_.review: It is hard to improve on what was already a nearly perfect game.  And for many years we told the devs what a sins 2 would need: Multicore threading, Turrets that turn, and the ability to link factory outputs to control groups.And they worked insanely hard over the past many years to give us exactly that and more.   They took the time to remake the old invisible and obtuse counter system into a much more clean and obvious durability vs pierce system. The crippled system is genius. (think negative HP in DnD)  They re-balanced and reshuffled all the capital ship abilities, and yes they did leave out some ships, but they added some others to fit better with the new systems.  The new voice lines really make things feel like the space opera you signed up for; it is unbelievably awesome and, in the case of a last stand, sad and depressing to listen to all your capital ship commanders reporting about how the battle is faring.And it runs so much better than Rebellion.   The last two nights I played a 10 player nightmare game (the AI basically all get infinite money, which means very quick maxed fleet sizes) , and all 9 hours were buttery smooth, with no crashes on my !!10 year old!! desktop.  And with the base game so great, expect the mods to be amazing.   If you have a sci-fi space opera you like.... look forward to experiencing it in sins 2.

_childDocuments_.review: The interface design of the game is very innovative and allows for a nearly seamless switch between handling the empire management (4X) and the combat at hand (RTS). The graphics are eye-catching and immersive, the scale of combat is what you'd expect from a galactic confrontation with large battles filled with massive fleets and hundreds of weapon effects simultaneously. The design of each faction is identifiable, creative and consistent across all units and structures. The voice acting is well done with many memorable lines and inflections, tones and urgency fitting the situation. The game does have some balance issues, which is to be expected for a game this young and there are some minor bugs and hitches but the development team is responsive to feedback and the community is spectacular! Strongly recommend!

_childDocuments_.review: "Our fleet has arrived at a Phase Jump Inhibitor and is now trapped!"Though this line gets old, the game does not! Sins of Solar Empire 2 is a fantastic, well optimized RTS that has a vast amount of depth in its tech trees, and some slight customization in its capital warships and star bases changing how you build and play.For new players, things can be a bit overwhelming at first when looking at the UI. But it doesn't take long before you start understanding each menu and how they can give you an overview of your growing empire and quick management tools to keep tabs on everything at a glance.Combat looks awesome! You'll spend time zooming in and watching things go boom often. It's really great. And building your fleets to support each other is key to winning.Modding support is awesome, and works in coop / multiplayer! Being able to save a multiplayer game with a friend or two and load it back up another day is fantastic and very much needed, as rounds can last many many hours.Other than some balancing issues, I can't say anything bad about the game. Really great and if you enjoy space RTS games you'll love this.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a recommend: 1) Serious problems remain between Sins1 and Sins2. some problems may be worse. 2) Major Imbalance in Tec Garrisons can make an end game literally impossible- An example of that later. 3) The Fleet Cap means the game severely stagnates at the end, and you cant develop your economy anymore so you just rack up infinite resources with nothing to spend them on. 4) Upgrades don't feel especially meaningful past the 2nd tier. 1st and 2nd tier tech is meaningful because you need to choose what kind of planet to develop/colonize when you don't have time or tech to colonize everything. Its meaningful because you can only pick to develop xyz defenses, or new ship types, or ship upgrades, as a way to protect those infant colonies. Your choices have meaning. 5) After Tier 2 however its just a bunch of spaghetti on the wall - develop this or that , it rarely matters very much, the point is just to max everything out. Which brings us to another problem with the tech6) There is no added replay value or dynamic A-Symmetrical warfare oppertunity : All techs get developed. The addictive formulas of games like CIV is that you can play 2 games , even with the same faction, and play them completely differently. None of that here. The addictive formulas of games like Starcraft 2 is that Tech Trees tend to become cemented and too important to jettison without consequence: EG, if you invest in what it takes to "Go Bio" army, you may not have the resources later to properly transition away to "Mech" unless you planned that transition in advance and what resources you would need.7) If by late Game you have infinite resources, by mid game the resources are already completely exchangable. The consequences of building this or that, because you had limited metal or crystal or credits completely, vanishes by time you have access to any of the black markets. 8) Late Game Vastly favors Defense, leading to dull cat-mouse game hoping the opponent attacks you, so you can find him in space where you likely have star bases and / or defenses. Example of TEC Imbalance: For me in one large game, AI's constant stream of units from at least (4) nearby garrison planets , + their fleet, can only be defeated if I sit over the planet jump landing. These planets have 2-3 factories EACH, they're pumping out constant streams of units beyond fleet capacity. I'm not TEC, I cant do that.  If I sit on the landing, I can stave off defeat by annihilating incoming units. If I move to try and destroy their factories or something, they over-run me. Its a no-win stalemate scenerio. Even When I try to move out, my 2000 supply , level 10 fleet, cannot overtake a fully defended heavily developed planet with a stream of garrison units from all those planets + their own 2000 navy, even if it is level 3 because I keep annihilating every ship to come out of jump. How to fix the game, mostly, in 2 moves:A) Take off the fleet cap. B) Neuter the TEC garrison so that they cannot travel outside their own gravity well. The Fleet cap is the most important thing to remove because it will turn the end at least from a boring whack a mole into a Ragnorock. It MIGHT reward a player with a larger economy a production advantage to press home an attack, instead of be knee capped and forced to joist on-equal-footing with the maxed out fleet of a smaller economy. C) Consider the Tech Tree to be something you pick a path through, instead of blanket get everything. Good Stuff: On the Plus it looks great & is easy to play.

_childDocuments_.review: I won battles against capital ships at least ten separate times and never blew one up - once you get past their shields, armour and hull points, there's another 6000+ points of 'crippled points' where the ships are fully functional and just escape to an enemy system seconds before I destroy them. Every battle is a huge slog, and since your attention is needed all over the map, you get mired in big battles and unable to build up your empire. Only to have the enemy capital ships heal themselves over and over, level up and escape to do it all over again half an hour lately. I really wanted to like this game but I'm bored of the cycle and done with it. Maybe someone will come up with a mod to disable the 'crippled points' thing. And maybe I've just had a few bad sessions and it's actually a great game. I'll click the thumbs up just in case. The graphics are really gorgeous and I like watching the laser beams blamming into things. Be better if they'd eventually explode though.     C+

_childDocuments_.review: A game with no single player campaign and a dead multiplayer community, Sins of a Solar Empire 2 is a beautiful RTS that offers less value than a 30 minute sitcom with about the same amount of replay value.Gameplay is not really much different than the first game, not enough to warrant the $50 price tag.As a 4x Space strategy game, it's got plenty to manage and should keep that left click finger happy for a few games. The sides are balanced for the most part, but against the AI the game is far too easy. That is the major flaw here, because multiplayer is essentially dead.This is a real time strategy game, and while stomping an AI opponent or two into the ground seems fun a few times, or while you are learning, it gets old quickly. No campaign here, so AI skirmish or multiplayer are your own only options. I can't remember the last time I personally saw an RTS without a single player campaign....But that is not the worst of it, they are going to add a campaign! It's a paid DLC. So you are paying 50 bucks for half a game here, one that ONLY provides you with skirmish mode, that has basically no one playing it.If you find the AI boring, or too easy, and you should after only a dozen hours, then you will have no incentive to play any further because that's all you're getting.All 22 of my hours came from AI skirmish, because finding a multiplayer session has had zero success.The game has nice visuals, but camera controls can be hit or miss. There are times when zooming in or out will have your camera completely away from where you expected it to be. It doesn't happen all the time, but a couple of times per session, and it's frustrating. Especially when it happens in combat.The scale of the game maps is huge, and it can be a slog trying to push from one start to another to find and eliminate the AI. You need to keep a fleet back to defend areas of space because if they somehow get behind you, it can take a long time to return to that area to stop them. It's not a major deal versus the AI though, as they are very predictable. Capital ships level up as they go, and unlock new abilities and passive traits. So keeping them alive is something you very much want to do, but the AI rarely shows any regard for this. They will toss cap ships at you, feeding your ships valuable experience and making your fleet level up and grow quickly. Rinse and repeat.Once you have a few Capital ships leveled up, those level 1 ships of the AI may as well just be dessert. Thanks for the free XP!The pacing is slow, which isn't a bad thing necessarily, but when you have all but beaten the opponents it becomes a tiring slog of warping to new systems to find and finish them off. It's not too hard to guess where their home planet it, it's just the getting there. You don't want to leave them with planets behind you, can't let them build new ships to slow you down. So you have to systematically destroy everything along the way. And you need to colonize the planet yourself, and build some defenses there so they don't recapture it while you're wiping them out. So, the game really becomes a boring mess, as you are just entering a new system, killing everything, capturing it for your empire, reinforcing it, and moving on. Rinse and repeat.The game can be sped up, but even at fastest speed it doesn't feel very fast when you need literal minutes to capture and build defenses in a given system.The average game takes at least an hour to compete, that's 1v1. If you have multiple opponents, add an hour for each one on average. If you aren't familiar with the faction you're playing, double that again. Once you have a sound strategy for that faction though, you'll be rolling along without much opposition.The tech trees and factional special abilities are hard to understand especially for new players. The tutorial in game is decent at teaching you how to build and move, but it does nothing to teach what the tech your researching actually does. It doesn't explain what those numbers mean. You research something, but then can't build it, and you can't find the answer as to why. A lot of games these days require you to have google on a tab ready to go, but in a REAL TIME game that shouldn't be a thing.A game the scale of Civilization should have an in depth encyclopedia available the same way Civ does, in session, with a search function that explains these things.But once you do learn everything, you'll know exactly what you need first, what ships you like, and then you're off. I have never once managed to play a multiplayer session of this game, so everything I speak of is based on AI skirmish only. Sadly, you don't need much in variety. In fact, you can usually roll the AI with only a handful of capital ships. It goes much faster if you DO have a fleet of smaller ships to assist you, but knowing how to position and take out the dangerous targets first means you can roll the AI with ease.But you won't be using just Capital ships, because that's slow and tedious. You'll build a fleet, you just don't have to diversify it. You can have 20 missile frigates, for example, and you can use JUST that one ship to back up a capital ship and win easily enough. Carriers are king in most cases, as fighters are replenished in combat, and they can fly off to attack targets without risking the carrier itself.The three races are different in their tech trees order and what they focus on in gameplay, but have basically the same ships and outside a few specialized tactics, they are identical. Where one faction may focus on trade to ramp up economy, another doesn't need cash at all and may collect scrap to build more ships instead.The major difference is their racial focus, but if you can play one you can play them all really. Once you understand the resources and tech tree, each faction plays relatively the same in strategy. There are two branches of each race, and each has a few unique buildings or tech research unique to them. But you can play them the same way if you choose and find victory.That's not bad on it's own, because it opens the game for you to change sides anytime you want and find success, but it also means that once you have a decent strategy for the game, you've seen all there is too see. And with the AI not putting up much of a fight, and multiplayer being basically empty....there won't be much reason to keep coming back.For me, if you own the previous game, there is really no reason to buy this one. While it is a small graphical improvement, and some map features are different, the game just isn't enough on offer to warrant that $50 price tag, and it feels insulting when you realize they are adding DLC like a single player campaign that you have to pay for on top of it.With new RTS games coming, some that just came out, for $20 less which offer single player campaigns, active multiplayer communities and the like...this game just can't be recommended at this price point. You can save some cash and go buy Sins of a Solar Empire Rebellion for less than half the price, and it at least has mods for when you run out of things to do there.As a fan of the first games in this franchise, this game feels like a cash grab. Fans of the series will jump on it immediately, as they have, but they haven't stuck around because multiplayer is dead. At the time I am posting this review, there are less than 1k playing the game, and 7 multiplayer games active, none of which are available to join. Game is barely two months old.If you REALLY like AI skirmish, then maybe this game is for you. But you can save 30 bucks by buying Rebellion instead, and get an almost identical experience.There are better RTS games out there, for less money.

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent sequel and foundation for the future.Highlights:- Slick, high-performance engine.- Genuinely cool planetary orbits feature, forces thinking on your feet and opens up new strategies.- Deeper faction asymmetry, with unique mechanics and entirely different approaches to building an empire.- Planet development is more restricted and forces you to make harder choices about the balance of your empire.- Excellent UI improvements which present relevant information in a cleaner, less cluttered manner.- Fat-trimmed Rebellion: It's like a cleaner, leaner foundation for future expansion.- Runs fantastically on Linux with Proton.Concerns:- Any expansion should be lateral. Rebellion was quite bloated, this is less so but they don't need to add more complexity. (The announced new faction is a good direction to go.)- There are ships not present from Rebellion; again, fat was cut and some people may not like that.- Currently (August 2024), a difference in platform string disallows Linux to cross-play with Windows. We need a fix, Stardock!

Immense amounts of QOL improvments from a more appropriate fleet management system on the main hud to a research finder really hammer the game feel so much better.Multi-threading, to make the game run buttery smooth even with all the graphics improvmentsPlanets move, creating unique strategy options in any game.Minor factions have new mechanics that make them more involved with the game, through an expansion of a more diplomatic style of gaining advantages through influence points. Ship upgrades and new planet upgrades give even greater opportunities to spec into various builds and ramp up in different ways. Each and every faction has had substantial changes that makes each further unique in how they play and win games, from TEC using trade routes and Advent using psy powers to enhance their ships abilities or use abilities that bombard enemy planets.I think it is unfair to Ironclad, who despite some egregious use of AI art in some of their research icons, have clearly put a lot of effort and development time into making Sins 2 feel similar yet so much BETTER to play than its predecessor to assert that they do not have the right to release it as a separate game.
