_childDocuments_.review: I'd give this an  perfect score except that the map variety to play on is too limited in my opinion. I don't mean the  of maps available to play; but rather the  between the maps available. I would really like a new random generator with multi-star systems (all randoms are currently one star that can have like 100 planets around it) for more stars with orbiting planets all for that true interstellar combat. They have planned future content which is also nice! I'm excited to see the upcoming developments and changes over the years, but as of right now this is a great sequel. The UI and development of player conveniences makes it so much easier to keep your fleets and systems organized as the game goes on. You can put your vessels in a "fleet," and when you select it, you can see (and build to that fleet) exactly what ship you'd like. No more individual factory selections, and then moving ships to planets one by one for twenty minutes only to realize you ordered the fleet to move twenty minutes ago to another star system! All of this is organized which helps focus on the tactical composition of your fleets and where they are in the galaxy.Orbiting planets its the greatest new feature for a space RTS I have seen. It is so fun and challenging. Opportunities to ambush, be ambushed, or have mobile super-weapons across the star system! The biggest limitation with this game is by players thinking that this is a new coat of paint on Sins of a Solar Empire 1. It has a fresh coat, but it has so much more rebalancing, ways to play the game, opportunities to prioritize, and rock-paper-scissors elements with each faction that keep the game interesting against the AI and other players. Ironclad worked on giving us so many new useful tools! Use them!Each faction has two variants that are overall associated with aggressive attacks or being more defensive/elusive. All variants have strengths and weakness that work against each other faction and their variants.The TEC have the best economy in the game and when fully kitted out have insane ship production speeds meaning they can always replace their ships. Expect losses when fighting against other fleets, as most of your vessels -- in lore -- are converted civilian ships for military purposes. But what does loss matter when by the time the enemy moves to the next gravity well they face a fresh fleet looking for conquest? The TEC can also gave automated garrison ships, trade ship escorts, etc. that artificially inflate the amount of ships you can field (at least for the defensive variant).The Advent focus on spreading culture (which does not, at first, appear to have military advantages) and using ships with shields and lasers. They have the best long-range options in the game, but can also be countered by point defense systems and focused assaults. Once their shields are down their ships fall quicker than other factions, but they have "unity" abilities to resurrect their forces. The Advent can use their culture to cause rebellions in other planets or flip them to their own empire. Culture spread decreases across each gravity well (so one planet can't force the entire star system to switch), so the best counter to their spreading influence is by convincing the planets spreading it to kindly stop via "aggressive negotiations". The Vasari have impressive punching and staying power, but their greatest ability is maneuverability. They can hit almost anywhere, retreat just as quick, and devastate enemy fleets. Their economy and culture isn't as good as the other factions, but their phase abilities make them competitive if you know where to strike (such as trade-heavy planets for TEC and culture/unity planets for Advent). The minor factions are still good fun and influence is useful for getting their help when needed. Although they are limited in many abilities (such as asking pirates to raid an enemy planet), as they will only perform fleet attack/defense operations a certain distance from their home planet. The total conversion mods with make this an absolute winner for all the Star Wars, Warhammer 40k, Battlestar Galactica, Stargate, and other sci-fi franchise lovers out there. These are not out yet, but the first game had an incredible and passionate modding community and I bet they are excited with the mod-tools Ironclad has already released (which isn't to say perfect, but mod-tools at game release is pretty cool these days!)Ultimate opinion for V1: fantastic game that keeps me coming back for more.

_childDocuments_.review: It's so shallow in every way compared to the likes of Stellaris, MoO and Endless Space, calling it a 4x is just silly. Unlike those games, however, you can complete a campaign in one or two sittings instead of 5 or 6.This game is an RTS, through and through, and a good one that includes hybrid warfare. Fully recommend.Edit:Having played more, I really have to push home how this game is NOT A 4X. It doesn't meet the basic definition of a 4x."The gameplay generally involves building an empire. Emphasis is placed upon economic and technological development, as well as a range of military and non-military routes to supremacy." From Wiki.1. Every empire already exists at the start of the game. You finish the game with the exact same empire you started with +/- some territory.2. There is no economic development. Collecting basic resources with zero depth does not count as economic game play. Resource gathering =/= an economy.3. The tech tree is alright, but very shallow, there's that at least.4. You basically win by supremacy, supremacy or supremacy. No tech victory, no culture victory, no economic victory, no story victory, ect ect ect.Still a good RTS, still recommend on the basis that it's a good RTS, but all these references to 4X in the advertising, store page description ect ect are false. Like calling an electic golf cart an F1 car or arctic lorry. Im actually kinda surprised Steam is allowing this game to maintain its 4X tag and descriptions as its kinda false advertising.

_childDocuments_.review: Compared to SoaSE 1, graphics are improved, game runs smoothly and the UI has been greatly improved. Everything is streamlined, for example you can upgrade items directly from the command bar. This allows you to focus on expanding and conquering, instead of going through spreadsheets just to get an upgrade. The capital ships can now be customized with ship items/upgrades and the same goes with your planets. There is an added feature which I always wished existed, and it is solar system rotations. It is a function you can turn off, but your planets are always moving, which can change the travel lanes. I'm even impressed with the replay function of the game. As soon as mine match was over, the replay was immediately available, like 5 seconds and I was watching it. You can click anywhere on the timeline and it will work its way to there, and unlike most games, it actually maintains the speed (10:1 second) no matter what. Also I didn't experience a single bug. Which is amazing. Overall, this was a worthy successor. After playing for 10 hours, I know I will want the expansions. It is also fun to play with friends.

_childDocuments_.review: PROS:Great game, brings everything over from Sins 1, but with a lot of quality of life improvements (creating ships from the fleet menu is a huge plus). PC did just fine with about 30fps when it was the most intense. Upgrades, upon upgrades, upon upgrades... You really can have an elite fighting force with the right upgrades. Tons of fun.Star bases are awesome, giving dynamic play to defense with ships to sit in the gravity field to give a homefield advantage. At least with TEC Enclave.CONS: The shifting phase lanes went from a cool concept to "well, guess another thing I have to keep track of".Some of the artwork looks AI generated which is a bummer.Old voice lines were re used, kinda cool throwback kinda bummer. meh AI can get too timid and turtle up causing a prolonged stalemate in some situations.Excessive upgrades can also be a con, as it can make the system feel bloated.Great game, going to sink a ton of hours into this one just like the first. Solid 7.5/10 making it a go to game if I have the time.

Some may balk at the price, but it's no different than the previous game for the amount of content you get, and given Ironclad's record, I'm more than happy trusting them with another 50 to finally add a story to this evocative universe. _childDocuments_.review: "Sins of a Solar Empire 2" is a triumphant return for fans of the original and a must-play for anyone who enjoys deep, strategic gameplay with a sci-fi twist. It’s a masterclass in delivering exactly what its audience craves. In an era where strategy games often overwhelm with excessive modes and features, "Sins 2" stays laser-focused on its core strengths—intense, tactical space battles without the clutter. For fans of the original, this sequel feels like a perfected version of the game you loved.While it may not cater to those looking for a story-driven campaign (at least for now) or a complex empire-building experience, it's perfect for players who crave action-packed skirmishes infused with deep strategic elements.Visually, the game is stunning. The upgraded graphics and breathtaking space environments make every battle feel grand and intense. The sound design, from the booming cannons of your battleships to the immersive ambient music, pulls you into the heart of the interstellar conflict.Ironclad Games has crafted a sequel that not only honors the original but also enhances it in every way. It’s a game that both newcomers and veterans will appreciate, standing tall as one of the best space strategy games available today. Highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: Really enjoy the game. It is Sins but with a lot of improvements and better graphics. The tutorial does a really good job at highlighting the quality of life improvements while showing you how to play the game. It doesn't take too long to get through the tutorial and it is presented in sections so you can skip parts you already know.The new mechanic with the systems moving around adds some life to the game. Systems that move around allow you to send your fleet in the heart of the enemy systems. The pirates weren't in your way one hour, now they are. Creating fleets and maintaining them has become so much easier. Left click to add, and right click to remove for a lot of controls. You can keep your fleets maintained by simply clicking on the ship in your fleet manager screen. The game will build the ships from the most time efficient shipyard and the ships will automatically join up with the rest of the fleet.I think the economy is just better. You aren't penalized for having more fleet potential, instead, you are simply taxed on your earnings. There are a lot more options at the start of the game with how much starting money is provided. The special resources are a good change to the capital ship/station requirements. You can build as many as you want as long as you have the special resources.I hope the voices from ships and the interface get updated or added to. I appreciate the nostalgia, but I would like to get some updates to the audio portion. Would like to see a fix to the carrier capital ship auto cast for the defensive missile platform, you have to manually place this right now.There is quite a bit of research, it takes around 4 hours to uncover most of it. Games will take several hours if you are trying to do everything. Perfect if you looking for a lengthier game that isn't over too quickly. Game is worth it if you are returning from Sins 1 or a new comer to this game.

_childDocuments_.review: sins 2 is a marvel for the rts and 4x genre. In recent years we've seen half-arsed remakes, bad sequals and badly managed series. Unlike, for example, the recent Homeworld 3 release they have managed to maintain the feel and look of the game play while enhancing things for the better graphics and computing power available today. They have also managed to increase the asymmetry of the 3 (functionally 6) factions by adding things to make them more unique. While there are still some balance issues, such as anti-missile ships lagging behind the amount that can be spammed, these are just early teething issues and seem to be aware of by those in the company interacting with us in the discord. Looking forward to the 4th faction, mods, story mode and hopefully more map options/randomization. well worth becoming your new "black hole on your time".

_childDocuments_.review: Sins II is Sins: Rebellion but with a lot more  in it. Beyond the obvious performance improvement and UI upgrades, the changes to Research, Planet & Fleet management immediately add a lot of QOL to managing your forces without radically changing the game. There's also just a ton more to invest in, from an inventory of items equipable on your ships and starbases to a broader range of research topics. Each faction's specific mechanics have also been more fleshed out. Influence replaces the past game's envoys and mission system and make interacting with Minor factions a lot more interesting. Auctions give you meaningful stuff to compete for beyond the Pirate/bounty system from Sins 1 (though the Pirate raids still exist as an option for their faction). The small changes to weapon simulation also make a noticeable difference in battle, as well as making engagements look more visibly interesting. Little details like being able to paint your ships in a wider range of colors is also welcome (though sad you seemingly can't use all the faction icons across all the races anymore).Really, it's a sequel that keeps basically everything that made the original great while further refining it. A rare and precious thing in RTS games these days. I applaud Ironclad for sticking to what made them great to begin with, here's hoping their future expansion plans are of similar quality to those of the OG.

_childDocuments_.review: First impression as a 4X casual is that the game is really good and really easy to pick up compared to other 4X games.   Everything about the UI and the economy feels designed to make things as smooth as possible.   Want to build a building but you need to do research first?  The game will just give you a total cost that includes the cost of the research and the building.  One click and both are queued up, no need to dive into the tech tree for that one tech in a haystack.   That drove me crazy trying out the original.   Want to build new ships and get them to the front?  Just keep your units in a fleet and you can simply order the ships from your fleet screen and they'll build from nearby factories.  No fiddling with individual factories and waypoints.   Without all that micromanaging Sins 2 turns into a game about outproducing your enemies and big fleet actions.  I'm to the point where I can at least keep up with a few medium AI after 10+ hours of gameplay.  That's faster than I expected to pick the game up, again as a casual player of these kinds of games.  But I still feel like I have a lot to learn too.  So the impression I get is "Easy to learn, hard to master" which is a good sweet spot to hit.  This is a great game, and I'm confident I'll be losing hundreds of hours to it over the coming years.  And with DLC promised including a campaign, can't wait to see the game's full potential.

If the game had a story that explained why the races are expanding into a wider universe that would make the game play far more enjoyable. - I think max fleet supply needs to scale with the map. If you are playing a huge map and you want to run 2 major fleets then 2000 seems too low. 2000 on a 1v1 is great! 2000 on a 1v9 map means you spend half your time jumping your main fleet from one side of your empire to the other. - The battles are great and I enjoy the balance between the races. However if you have an aggressive race it will just blob up a main fleet and constantly attack. A defensive stance will have the AI turtle and not expand fast enough to balance out the game. I only play against hard AIs and I dont know if the next two levels make this better or worse yet. In summary a fun game if you like skirmish matches with no real purpose or you enjoy multiplayer. If you play games as much for the story as the game play then maybe we all need to wait for the DLC.

I have a great PC but I hear this game runs perfectly on the Steam Deck and low-end PCs.This game plays more or less identical to the first game. Most, if not all, of the ship types, titans, etc remain the same and have the same names. The actual new features contained in the roadmap: new ships, a new faction, and a singleplayer campaign; will all be released later at a cost greater than or equal to the price of the base game, judging by the price of the premium edition.As this game currently stands it is more or less just the original game on a new engine. And unless you are buying the premium edition or plan on getting the DLCs (like me), I'm not sure this game is worthy of being called a sequel in and of itself. It's more in line with what you'd expect from a remaster or "enhanced edition" of an older game. Looks good, adds quality of life tweaks, but plays identical to the original experience. _childDocuments_.review: Sins 2 is a relatively straightforward in concept real-time-with-pause 4X game with a major focus on fleet compositions and maneuvers and a lesser but still extant focus on building a space economy on planets and asteroids.The game comes with a large set of tutorials which will take you about an hour. These focus on the very basics of the game's mechanics and fail to teach you anything further than that. About two thirds of the tutorials are functionally useless if you have the barest understanding of how to play a game like this (for example: right clicking the selected ship moves it). Most of your actual learning will happen inside your first game, which I recommend is played on Easy.The combat system is a rock-paper-scissors type affair. For example, small, fast corvettes can dodge the tracking of larger weapons and yet are incredibly vulnerable to carrier fighters, bombers, and point defence ships. A heavier cruiser, battleship etc. will have the armour rating necessary to basically shrug off lighter ships but will have a hole punched through it when attacked with a more specialised ship with higher armour piercing, which itself would struggle to fight off a fast corvette.With an economy constraining how many ships you can build and at what pace, this means that simply brute forcing your way through with more ships is not going to win the war. That means combat efficiency is the order of the day, and the power of reconnaissance should not be ignored. Learning what fleet composition your enemy is using and continuing to keep an eye on them while their fleet power develops is extraordinarily powerful and well worth the small investment.This is not the kind of game where you can only build one type of ship and coast to victory.There are three races in the game on release with two subfactions each. Each subfaction has its own unique mechanics which heavily influence how they are played which is very smart asset reuse. For example, the plain human race, 'TEC', has its own unique mechanic shared between both factions, but each faction has substantial differences. TEC Enclave are more defensive and get many upgrades catering to that including free garrison ships and a second defensive station per system (everyone else being limited to one) - TEC Primacy are much more aggressive; they get substantial bonuses from attacking planets directly, have the ability to recruit the pirate minor faction, and have the better faction-exclusive titan.Playing both 'wide' and 'tall' are viable depending on the faction but there are caps to how much you can invest into a planet and you will, at that point, need to make the decision between expanding or dying.There are a great many scenarios which offer very different experiences from a straightforward variety of 1 vs 1 conflicts and wider team-based or free-for-all conflicts too. The game runs great and looks amazing, and has no problem simulating war on a large scale. Individual game lengths run from between one and a half to 8 hours depending on the selected scenario. There is no meta-progression between games. A multiplayer component exists but I have not tried it.There are in-depth and complex post-game graphs and a replay function is also available which I found very insightful and would recommend that these are always looked at to help you learn more about the game. However, a lack of polish on the UI including usage of ugly AI/ML art is a huge negative which cannot be ignored. In addition, the AI tends to be quite vulnerable to headshots in the mid game and very much struggles to recover afterwards, at least on normal, if you manage to locate them in the right place at the right time.I only saw one bug during my time with the game which was a camera issue. However, the developers seem to have accounted for this without fixing the cause as when it happens (when zooming in or out in some situations, the camera disappears into the ether) a button pops up to recenter the camera for you.For these reasons, on balance, I recommend the game. However, the developers should focus on removing AI/ML art and improving the enemy AI.

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommend not playing or buying this game.  The game has fundamental flaws that make game play beyond 5 hours impossible.  You will be able to play at most on maps that have 2-3 solar systems and (small) map size.  Your fleet capacity is forever maxed at 2,000 and you will find you cannot defend more than 2-3 solar systems with that fleet while still going on the offensive.  It's arguably one of the most game breaking features.  Late game, your enemies learn the ability to jump right into your solar system, and you do not have enough capacity to have fleets in every solar system and you will lose all base before your fleets can get back.  It's a never ending cycle of you trying to defend while still go on offensive, it would be doable, if enemies could not ignore hyper lanes and jump right to your back-line.  This was my experience with a large map, and the same experience that hundreds of other players have exhibited. This games great but it's fleet capacity ruins the game.  You can't do it all with a capacity of 2,000.  You can mod but now you lose default game features so have fun with that.  Devs refused my refund because I played 5 hours (3 hours longer than you can refund) garbage game, garbage foresight, play Stellaris and save your money.

_childDocuments_.review: Initial early review after 3 days of playing.Overall I am very happy with what is delivered - I am already tending to the statement Sins 2 is already a better game than Sins 1 - despite it is not yet complete in all aspects and content and I always liked Sins 1 and spent 1000 hours or more on it. I would focus more on how the game stands toward Sins 1 (so sorry to people not knowing the franchise at all]:PROS:Perfect release on the technical part - not any issues, FPS drops only when zooming in to aircrafts in big battles, engine is completely new and very solid, utilize modern CPU to best - a big map with 8 players is stable 60 FPS from start to finish the session, really amazing job done.Also only very little bugs.Graphic and animation obviously, though not all models are to my liking - strongly believe there will be various mods for this soon.New modules and building feature - each planet, capital ship or titan has slots that can be utilized by various equipment (weapons, shields, consumable boosts..) and buildings allowing a very customizable approach. Those can be researched, found, won over the enemy, bought in auction or from various minor factions..Unique strategic abilities for each race. Vasari collect space resonances to utilize their mastery over phase travel, TEC has significant trade bonuses, Advent has unique Will abilities revolving around cultureA new fleet system allows easy production by defining the numbers of each ship in fleet and those are automatically produced from nearest shipyard and find its way toward the flagshipExotic resources - there are few new resources need for various advanced tech research and production (eg. for building capital ships). Those resources can be found, salvaged from destroyed enemy capitals and caches on map or bit costly produced in own refineries. Early to mid game it is an effective limiter for spam capitals and other stuff.Smart linking between production and research - by making fresh new construction (or ship, building module...) you see price for all prerequisite techs and exotic resources together and by one click you pay for all and all is automatically queued, researched and produced.In game mod support.In trade with other players you can trade for whole planetsCouple of new minor factions  offering different bonuses and items based on the new influence system, Devs are pretty active, acknowledging issues, sharing solutions and confirming fixes.NEUTRAL- no map editor directly in game, it is so far only as an external git tool- new planet orbiting system (it can be turned off and also depend on the map, somewhere it is more important, somewhere less) - planets move in time around their stars and eventually change the lines. This has 2 results: first planet can/will become connected to different planets than before. Second static defenses can be on a completely wrong position after the shift. Those can be moved but it need attendance and it is bit tedious. On other hand it remove stable static chokepoints and open new strategic options.- Pirates no longer raid as before, they are just one of many minor factions now. You can spend influence for them to form an attack (available for some other minor factions too) but it works only to small distance from their planet and the strength is not gradually raising through session.- no population on planets affecting income (instead there is building/modules system, condition of planets does not matter.- culture can not wipe enemy colony (though Advent has option utilize their global abilities for similar effect as before) - instead it make various positive and negative bonuses.- SFX like explosions could be better and with better sound- beside changes in features there is basically not any new content over Sins 1 - all races, ships, structures... most is there basically untouched both in abilities and visuals. New content will come with DLC and ofc mods.CONS (I have strong faith  most will be addressed, this is current state):- UI scaling is poor - only 2 states changing all elements and fonts alike. Neither of those 2 is optimal for me.- speaking of UI many options are there but hidden or need various keyboard shortcuts and are not toggable to be default as before.. (eg auto placement of new buildings)- lack of conditions for new run (no option to disable super weapons or variety in the setting of victory condition)- no diplomacy research and pacts- no upkeep, there is no transition to larger fleet for cost of economy malus. As it is all go for highest fleet supply asap.- broken super weapons that can not be disabledCOMBAT BALANCEI will say right away that I think about most new mechanics they are great but the result needs be balanced better. Shield mitigation is no longer a thing instead there is new system of durability vs piercing and hp/defense is split into shield, armor and hull. Shield is only defense replenishing during combat (outside special abilities or modules), Armor multiply its armor strength with durability and is the strongest defense line (though usually also not so big in absolute numbers)  and only once shield and armor are gone the hull is targeted (it go away very fast) even with full hull out, big ships come to cripple state where they can not use abilities or fight only move, only after this last level removed the ship is completely destroyed.Each weapon has beside dps its piercing value affecting how much dmg pass vs target durability.Also there is point defense system against missiles and bombers , making flak ships critical most of time.Many good Ideas but currently with no best result. Durability values differ per type (structure, fregate, corvette..) but otherwise  stay same for all races and buildings across board - eg all buildings has exactly same durability value, only starbase has highert. Also ship types are equal - eg all capital ships of all races has same durability.Weapons on the other side are similar way so each ship type have their most effective target up to starbase level. It is very clear and in basis good design (so you know why heavy cruiser is so efficient against light fregates), But even if proportionally lower all still do decent damage - this is most visible on missiles that have large dps values so even with  low piercing dont prevent them stack massive damage on the targets. PDs are hopeless against swarm of 100+ missile fregates that destroy ANY target in few salvos. Without shield mitigation mechanic eventually all need to eat way too big damage. You will see fully upgraded starbase or Titan go away in seconds. Playing as Advent against Vasari? Well one salvo of shield passing missiles go through thin armor and hull and give your capital ship goodbye before it can react. There could be something done about ranges of some weapons, starbases etc, but tune durability and armor to be by result closer to the shield mitigation experience the major issue  and improvement the game needs in my eyes.But overall it it is still great fun as it ever was and with patches and and new DLC content (we will even get full story campaign) i look forward great experience - and of course mods once they start flow in.

I love me some Stellaris but good gawd even small maps take for freaking ever. This one, a small game with me not remembering much about how to do things came in at <2 hours consistently.It's got just enough depth to give you plenty to keep track of, but not so much that it's unwieldy. They really found a good balance here.My only real gripe is that the AI's difficulty relies an awful lot on "cheating" for difficulty. I routinely wished for a version of SOSE that wouldn't get bogged down in the late game and that appears this is that game.

_childDocuments_.review: It's Sins of a Solar Empire. But better, and still could be better. A great game and the first RTS sequel in a long time that is actually good. It just needs some kinks ironed out.It has polish, Quality of Life features, better performance, visually fantastic*, and roughly feature parity with Rebellion. If you're new to the series you get this. If you're a fan of the first you get this (for the performance if nothing else). No need to reinvent the wheel when you can just take the wheel you have and make it better. There's only up in terms of future content expansion/post launch support. Ship and sound design are great too. There were concerns about TEC ships looking too clean, but they're now sufficiently greebled and if you don't want them looking bright and obnoxious you can tone their paint scheme down to mostly bare metal.Some things have been removed from Rebellion, but it's stuff that didn't really work out in the first like the trade/refinery placement minigame, or ships that were just never used or awkward like the envoy and command cruisers, or the TEC boarding capital (Corsev). Some mechanics have been folded into individual factions to further make them unique. The roaming outlaw ships were folded into TEC Enclave (Loyalists) as garrisons. The Novalith cannon was made exclusive to the TEC Primacy (Rebels),The bigger changes come with the combat and changing landscape. Missiles are now a distinct threat meaning those once useless flak frigates get an important niche for covering your capitals from torp and bomber spam. Likewise turrets being physical means there's more emphasis on where your ships are and how to get the most of their weapons. I really like what they did with Titans and capital ships requiring special resources which can be salvaged from destroyed enemy capitals. This with the items system lets you fine tune each ship and adding rare artifacts makes them into proper murder if you get good synergy. The orbiting planets are also huge, chokepoints and lanes can change. A player who pays attention can take advantage of these changes. A new backdoor into a now vulnerable planet can bypass a TEC player's unbreakable wall of guns and starbases. In a long game this can break a stalemate.The UI is great*, it's fairly intuitive and the QoL features makes research and outfitting ships and planets easy. Fleet management is so much easier and reinforcing them is a breeze. There is information readily available to be seen. Clicking on the desired ship queues up research to be done automatically. Though there's room for improvement in the QoL I think. Scouts die very easily and queuing up another dozen over and over made me wish I could just ensure there was always X amount of scouts. If one died an idle factory somewhere could pop out another. Fleets could work the same way, if I have a specific composition I'd like to keep I'd rather my factories kept up so I'm not over producing in any one fleet when at supply cap. Ditto with Refineries. When I have the resources to spare I would like it if they could automatically produce to top off my stockpile. It's like queuing up farm reseeding in OG Age of Empire's 2 and going back to requeue only when you get the notification you're bone dry, it's a bit of a chore. I also wish there was a way to decide whether to reinforce from the closest factory or prioritize speed (if there is I'm not seeing it), if I have a system filled with factories I'd like to be using that one instead of getting them one at a time from a slightly closer system. One thing that is VERY annoying is scouts jumping into systems with inhibitors and getting spammed with the voiceline/notification even if I have the tech for them to ignore the inhibitor field.The UI presentation is not so great. Here is where I rant.The AI art makes it feel very cheap and while you get used to it and tune it out it can take you out of the otherwise great game when it rears its misshapen head. When Pirates come attack a colony I don't want to see green ghost rider in the notification. The research menu is the worst of it. Nearly every icon and image is AI art, it's white noise that blends together. Take a look at the icons from Sins 1, there is a very distinct progression and theme. Sure they're simplistic but you implicitly understand that brighter laser and bigger missile are upgrades from dimmer laser and smaller missile. You understand that the little flag on a planet means it's a colonization tech. Things that had the metal graphic in it improved metal production, likewise for crystal.It feels as there was very little thought put into it and slapped in last minute. All the images of people, weapons, technology, cities etc. don't mean anything and doesn't tell us anything about the setting. It's not an Advent weapon tech, it's glowing scifi thing. It's not a Vasari starship engine, it's glowing scifi thing. It's not a TEC factory, it's glowing scifi thing and the guy is welding with his bare hands. When you have actual icons side by side to the AI stuff, it's night and day like the icons unique to the starbases or titans. Even more jarring are the few attempts I noticed to edit them, there's one from a cockpit view and there's a Cobalt photoshopped in that looks out of place.Then there's the portraits. Like cool, you got several dozen Vasari portraits, but all of them are this samey swooped metal dude, maybe they have something resembling a horn if they're daring. You look at one and not once do you recognize any distinct portrait as "oh it's the scrunchy bug face guy with the staff" or "the red one with the really big crest helmet". None of the Advent portraits stand out like the one resembling the Pathologic Tragedian with the blank white mask or big religious headdress lady, they're all the same plastic blue glowing person in a white robe + 2 scifi robots. None of the TEC portraits stand out like arrogant looking woman in front of a flag or that shady looking ♥♥♥♥♥♥, just a bunch of people in vaguely scifi clothing.It's just a visual mess, and I'm not even one of those people who think AI is electronic satan. AI art has its merits, just not as a final product you're selling people. I hope they get it replaced with actual art—with thought put into it—as development moves on.It doesn't impact the stellar gameplay at all. Sins 2 as a game is very good like its predecessor, it just sticks out like a sore thumb when the rest of the game is polished and well put together and make me ask "why?".

_childDocuments_.review: FOR THE UNITY! I adored the original, and this game takes that and really improves on it.  The menu option to help manage the empire is amazing. _childDocuments_.review: As a huge fan of the original game (Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion), I am loving this game. Truly a worthy successor to a legendary title. It is everything an fan could ask for. The game looks beautiful, runs buttery smooth, and stays faithful to the original game-play will tweaking old mechanics and adding new original ones (an obvious standout being the orbiting planets). In addition, quality of life improvements such as the in-game mod browser/manager (which supports BOTH locally downloading mods and mods downloaded from the browser (I am looking and you Bethesda)) is amazing and shows the devs appreciation for Rebellion's outstanding modding community. Can't wait for what Ironclad Games and Stardock have in store with the planned DLCs. Every penny well spent and every byte well used.

_childDocuments_.review: Sins of a Solar Empire II is what a sequel should be: a fresh and progressive improvement to the original game. The gameplay doesn't radically differ from the original, and if you played the first you will be immediately familiar with how to play. However, all of the gameplay loops, units, graphics, and performance have been improved and modernized. It looks beautiful. It runs buttery smooth. It's Sins of a Solar Empire, but better in just about every way: hence, Sins of a Solar Empire II.My singular complaint is that it uses AI assets. Some of the images have too many fingers or otherwise just look a little off. Thankfully, it seems to be an ethical use of AI, trained on in-house art rather than the huge models that scrape (steal) art from everywhere.

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Sins 1, you'll like Sins, too. That's why I like it. I'm one of those "got Sins when it first released" people.This is a very good "boring" RTS game. By boring I don't mean bad - I mean that it's a slow paced game where you watch strategies and movements unfold over the course of a long period of time. It's like StarCraft if you overdosed it with opioids in that everything goes by much slower and macro/micro doesn't require a ton of clicks. Opioids also make you chill out (allegedly) - unlike StarCraft where you're just immensely stressed and on coke. You can always increase Sins to 5x speed if you want to play it like a YouTube short though. Not recommended - it's a chill game and it's fun to see things unfold at the normal speed.You have different factions, all with varying strengths and weaknesses, and synergistic strategies with fleet compositions. I'm not a TEC guy so I can't comment on those lego blocks, but Advent are shield and ability heavy with a lot of cultist conversion abilities, shield projections, teleportation and buffing/debuffing one another. Their ships are also smooth, shaved and lubed up for all to be blinded by due to the shine. Vasari are chain-smoking aliens that are running from some unseen threat. I think they're tax dodgers because if there's one thing you can't escape, it's taxes. They basically play as a hit-n-run faction. Expensive ships and generally smaller fleet sizes but very chunky armour and they hit pretty hard. Their tech tends to be all about making their own private phase lanes so they can warp into your back line, depopulate a planet with enforced climate change and then bail before you can get there. Economically they also don't use currency, just metal and crystals. There's no money left after what the tax man did.There's more to the game than what I just wrote, but this review is getting long. You take planets, build an economy and create fleet compositions and defenses that outplay your opponents. It's fun, and watching fights unfold is spectacular. Wonderful death and blinding lights. Some abilities are stupidly powerful too. Giant cannons that wipe planets out immediately from 50 million light years away, or titans that vacuum entire fleets. It is an excellent amount of stupidity.Some cons - AI can be a bit of a d!ck head to fight. They often bail very quickly and sometimes they break in the late game. Unfair difficulty and up are recommended but not for beginners.- I dislike how sensitive right clicking is for camera movements. Sometimes I want to right click to move a ship, but it'll assume that because there's a slight movement in my mouse, I am rotating my camera. Stop that, you stupid bastard.Otherwise, it's a very good game. Thumbs up for good, feature complete sequels.

_childDocuments_.review: Personally, I would like to rate it as right in the middle of positive and negative. And because of that I have to rate it negative. The main reason for this is I feel the game does not do enough to be considered a sequel-- essentially the devs played it too safe with the release. No visual state change when adding modules to ships, or star bases. Build animations still leave a lot to be desired Sound design is poorNo new factionsLess ships than RebellionCulture system rework is poorSome ships lack a sense of scaleSkyboxes are often too brightLimited game settingsAI is poorI feel they have a solid foundation here to build on. Something that would be a mid to late early access type game but not a true full sequel. The main thing I think is the visuals and missing new faction. For star bases for example they could have made them visually grow in size and style with the new modules that you install. How cool would it be to actually be able to see what you have added to the starbase. Same with ships, if I install a new weapon, I should be able to see that on my ship in this day-and-age.  Beyond little flame and spark animations I would like to see damage states with ship models and better explosion animations. I should be able to see in detail fighters and bombers landing and taking off of the carrier ships instead of them just appearing out of the hull of the ships. Same sort of thing goes with trade ports, I should see the ships landing and taking off. Gameplay is generally ok but it often feels like: build good eco, build big fleet, win. It could benefit from some more unique ships or win conditions. Making the Vasari no planet strategy realistic, improving culture (see above) and making an advent culture victory possible, adding a unique human win condition could improve this. All in all, solid start, but missing graphical improvements and something that sets it truly apart from the previous.

_childDocuments_.review: Sins of a Solar Empire 2, developed by Ironclad Games Corporation, is the long-awaited sequel to the critically acclaimed original. Blending real-time tactics with the depth of 4X strategy, this game has a lot to live up to. However, while there are some notable improvements and new features, the game also falls short in several key areas, making it neither a resounding success nor a total failure. I'd rate it as a neutral experience, one that has potential but is still lacking in many ways.At its core, "Sins of a Solar Empire 2" retains the engaging real-time strategy elements that fans loved in the first game. The ability to seamlessly zoom from overseeing your empire to managing individual battles is still as captivating as ever. The introduction of new mechanics, such as the dynamic galaxy and enhanced fleet management, adds layers of strategic depth. However, the AI still needs significant work. Too often, it makes baffling decisions that can frustrate rather than challenge the player. This issue hampers the overall experience and diminishes the strategic satisfaction that should be at the heart of the game.One of the most glaring issues with Sins of a Solar Empire 2 is that it feels incomplete. The music, while initially fitting and atmospheric, quickly becomes repetitive due to the lack of variety or we turn into a pirate adventure mid way galaxy battles. This could be improved with additional tracks to keep the audio experience fresh. Furthermore, the absence of Steam achievements is a missed opportunity for rewarding players and encouraging replayability. These missing elements make the game feel less polished than it should, especially for a sequel with such high expectations.The use of AI-generated content in Sins of a Solar Empire 2 is a mixed blessing. While it might sound innovative, in practice, it feels more like a sci-fi gimmick that doesn’t quite belong in the game. The AI-generated research elements often make no sense and detract from the overall coherence of the game's design. Additionally, some of the upgrades are confusing, with icons that are hard to decipher and descriptions that leave you scratching your head. I can only hope these are placeholders because they currently add unnecessary complexity to the game.On a positive note, Sins of a Solar Empire 2 runs exceptionally well. The game is stable, and the new multicore 64-bit engine performs admirably, even in large-scale battles with numerous ships and structures on screen. The dynamic lighting and higher resolution textures make the game visually appealing, and the smooth performance is a testament to the developers' focus on building a robust engine. This technical stability is one of the game's strongest points, ensuring that players can enjoy the vast space battles without interruption.Sins of a Solar Empire 2 is a game that sits in the middle of the spectrum—not bad, but not particularly great either. While the core gameplay and engine performance are solid, the game is marred by incomplete features, repetitive music, and an AI that needs significant improvements. The AI-generated content, while interesting in concept, feels out of place and sometimes detracts from the experience. Fans of the original may find some enjoyment here, but the game still feels like it’s missing the polish and depth needed to make it a true successor. With some updates and refinements, Sins of a Solar Empire 2 could reach its full potential, but as it stands, it’s a neutral experience at best.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the few good sequels of the modern era. The combat system has been updated to include armor and armor penetration, fleet adding ships to fleets is much easier with each fleet having a "build ships" option, a new system of "items" allows for customization of planets, capital ships, and starbases that wasn't possible before.Each of the 3 races now has its own unique mechanic accessed by building a limited number of orbital structures: TEC has trade (which can now be customized to produce metal and crystal), Vasari has phase resonance (which grants buffs for a short time after arriving in a gravity well), and Advent gets access to magic powers like teleporting fleets.
_childDocuments_.name: Sins of a Solar Empire II

_childDocuments_.review: New engine, some new mechanics, nothing too far off the beaten path of the previous game. I'm excited to see what modding can be done with the new engine and what more the devs will add to the game over time. I really like the extra depth in planet development, I feel like that was missing from the previous game. Planets now feel less like control points, and more like an actual part of your empire. Being able to specialize ships and planets more with the added planet items and ship items puts more nuance into gameplay too. There's some minor gripes I have about the UI, but not significant enough to tell if it's not just from having to adapt to the new UI. Otherwise, this is basically exactly what I wanted sins 2 to be.

_childDocuments_.review: Sins of a Solar Empire II is a unique RTS where you need to expand and colonize planets in order to conduct research and build up your fleets, ultimately facing off with your opponents. I put in hundreds of hours with the original game and see myself doing the same with the sequel. If you enjoy the RTS genre, if building up your empire and fleets before going after an enemy is your jam, if you enjoy the space setting; I highly recommend trying this game.SoaSE2 is the original but better. There is nothing that I miss from the original. Big UI and QoL improvements, it is far easier to manage a large empire and multiple fleets. New graphics are pretty. There are plenty more layers of decision making with ship and planet items. These are extra upgrades that aren't just gimmicks but can really impact the game. The addition of all planets rotating around the sun and phase lanes connecting and disconnecting on a time scale of hours adds much more strategy to those longer games on bigger maps.This game does use AI art, more so than what the disclosure would lead you to believe. Currently all the research icons are very obviously AI art. There aren't any extra fingers or anything but the composition or perspective doesn't always make sense and some parts of the images have way too much detail while other parts look out of place. The buildings and vehicles look nonsensical at times. There is zero coherence and no real art direction to all the icons. Hopefully this gets replaced with properly done art in a future update.

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, meh, the units, capital ships, titans, buildings, all the same as the first game which is very disappointing. The only difference mechanically is the planetary building slots which are kinda cool I guess, and there's some minor factions that you can get underwhelming bonuses from. Visually it looks great, and it runs smooth, but realistically this is basically just a remaster of the first game, with upcoming DLC getting slapped in for features that should be included in the base game, such as a new fourth race, some new units and a campaign, these should be part of the game itself to set itself slightly apart from the first SOSA. I thought the orbital mechanics might be interesting, but running on 10x speed to get 7 hours into a game and the systems barely move, so that's turned out to pretty meh as well. To summarise, incredibly underwhelming for a sequel that I was really looking forward to.

_childDocuments_.review: What a fantastic sequel, everything I hoped for. I highly recommend if you are a fan or you are new to the 4x genre.Graphics and Visuals:The game’s visual upgrade is striking. The ship rosters have been completely redesigned, preserving their iconic shapes while incorporating additional details and character. Gameplay Enhancements:One notable addition is the rotating turrets on ships. While it’s hard to gauge the impact on gameplay, this feature certainly enhances the visual appeal and immersion, which is crucial for a game on a new engine.Resource System:A new resource, Exotics, has been introduced. It is essential for high-end technologies and structures, including capital ships, starbases, titans, and Novaliths. Initially, Exotics can be obtained by looting derelicts in orbit, but later, players can refine standard resources into Exotics using new structures or mobile refinery capship items for Vasari Loyalists.Customization and RPG Elements:The game now includes numerous new items for planets, capital ships, starbases, and titans. This system is similar to previous starbase components but adds customization options for capital ships and planets as well. This enhancement introduces more RPG elements, increasing depth and strategic decision-making.Minor Factions:Minor factions have become a more integral part of the gameplay. They now offer black market functionality, with their destruction removing the market. Each minor faction provides unique abilities or items that can be unlocked and purchased using influence points. These points, which can be boosted by additional planetary structures and culture, are also used in auctions.Overall, these updates and additions offer a wealth of new features and improvements, enhancing both the visual appeal and strategic depth of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe more of an expansion than truly a sequel, but it's an excellent upgrade so it worth the money. Rebellion was already a titan in RTS history, with less obnoxious apm based micro but instead a greater focus on ability usage and cleaver positioning that set it apart and made it so, so much more fun than other games, and this improves upon it in almost every way. Diplomacy is fairly gutted and I enjoyed working towards pacts but I can see that coming back later if Stardock continues to support the game.To actually explain combat a bit, your ships have real guns on them, and thus have to be positioned properly to shoot them with maximum efficiency. You can't shoot through your own bridge. In addition each race gets 5 capital ships with 4 abilities and each subrace gets a unique titan ship with abilities of its own, so there's a lot to do to be efficient. As stated above none of this is micro intensive and success will be based more on knowledge and decision making than anything else, so don't be intimidated. As far as story, there is none. There are some cinematics explaining the setting in Rebellion (which you can find on youtube), but ultimately you're not here for story so don't come in with that expectation. The future campaign is nice for fleshing out the factions but this is a game, not a movie or a book. If you like that or not is up to you. I love Stellaris, but there's no way I'm buying a $10 story pack that will be fun to read once or twice before being skipped in every game.Mentioning Stellaris, since that's where a lot of comparisons will come in simply because they're both space 4X games, they're a completely different package. Sins is combat and conflict first and foremost, so go in with that expectation or you'll be disappointed. I find it more rewarding since  the story based pop ups in Stellaris get skipped after you see them once or twice, but Sins combat will always be engaging.Buy game have fun

Each faction has a more defined uniqueness, with Advent having their own unique faction abilities and the Vasari starting the game phase jumping into a system rather than being an established presence.I've only played a handful of hours but it has been excellent so far! If you enjoy real time strategy, this is a phenomenal game to play!Very much looking forward to the DLC!!

_childDocuments_.review: My group of friends are huge RTS nuts and have been fans of the original game for many years now.For those of you who don't know what to expect, this is essentially a "remake" of the original game. Don't let that fool you though - in addition to a myriad of improvements there are entirely new sets of features the original game did not have that drastically improve the experience.Overall this is one of the most exciting releases of the year for me. There isn't much in the RTS space, and even less that is accessible enough for even non-fans to get into.Some of the highlifghts.1. User interface 10/10: Not something I'm a stickler about typically, but they deserve a shoutout for one of the most clean and readable UI's I've ever seen in a game. Everything from the font to the text size, to the button arrangement, to the tooltips is phenomenally and skillfully done. Information is available and accessible when needed.2. Gameplay 10/10: The original game is already a fantastic RTS, but they've added so much depth in critical areas that remove much of the "genericness" from the game. For example - now you can customize your capital ships as each one has multiple slots  for upgrades to fit your strategy/playstyle. Additionally, planet management has much more depth as you can devote worlds to specific types of resources or economic functions. You can now build planetary research facilities as well so you're not completely limited by your orbital building capacity. These changes and more have added a level of flexibility and customizability for the player that will dramatically increase the replayability of this game. I'm eagerly awaiting strategy guides, youtube videos, and more when players figure out optimal build strategies and start sharing their unique approaches.3. Stability 9/10: This can't be overstated. Players have come to expect extremely crappy levels of stability and performance these days, and it's not acceptable. Ironclad nailed it here. I haven't experienced a single bug or stability issue. I'm sure they're in there, but they are not diminishing the experience at all.4. Multiplayer: The game lobby interface is solid and easy to manage. Multiplayer is stable (although I've heard they're having capacity problems - a good issue to have!) I've played about 5 games so far and they've all run very smoothly with no issues.There is so much potential for this game in the form of DLCs, patches, and expansion of the content. This is a *chef's kiss* moment for games and specifically RTS - a pretty desolate space at the moment.Zoom in and watch the space battles unfold. The visuals are amazing and the ship models look beautiful. This is an absolute must-buy for space fans, RTS fans, or anyone looking to try a new game from a devoted group of developers who've demonstrated their passion over a decade.
_childDocuments_.name: Sins of a Solar Empire II

_childDocuments_.review: Before you buy this, know that this game has a high amount of AI-generated images.Art:The 3D modelings should be original designs by the devs, but most of the 2D images look very much AI-generated despite the devs saying that they are original designs and only went through AI processing. This causes the overall interface to look fancy in an uncanny valley feeling but lack a thematic feel to it. Different tiers of the same type of research can look unexpectedly different, whereas normally in games with original art, they would look mostly the same but with additional effects to indicate upgrade levels. Overall the game art style does not feel intuitive to look at.Gameplay:Macro seems to be the way to go, as in the ability to jack up your economy and vomit as many ships as possible trumps micro-ing individual battles. This means you will be playing in zoom-out mode most of the time. Likely the micro-ing part only comes to shine in multiplayers. As an offline single player gamer, a few hours of gameplay already made me realize there's not too much depth to both the 4X and RTS elements. Here's to hoping that as more content is added in and when campaign comes out, SoaSE2 will show its true potential.To summarize, I'm disappointed in the devs' heavy handedness in using AI art. I understand that this trend is only going to snowball and become a norm in the gaming industry, so SoaSE2 does made me pick a stance that moving forward I will be choosing to support games that have original artworks. I'm tempted to refund this game, but I won't for now. There is still room for the gameplay to be improved into a proper 4X RTS.

_childDocuments_.review: I had a blast playing the original and have loved revisiting it throughout the years. As a fan of the original I was excited to try this new edition. The new one just isn't what I hoped for.The Problems:1. It's Not a New Game: It doesn't even come close to meeting the standard to be called a new game. Essentially it adds irrelevant tweaks that mostly do nothing or make things worse. The new resources are the biggest change and the only effect they have is slowing the game down and wasting your time. There was no creative idea that improved the game, instead it felt like they just the absolute minimum to be able to sell the same game over without putting any actual effort in.2. Pacing: It is just a more tedious game. A lot of the changes make it harder to progress as quickly and just less fun. Too many of the features just distract from the core gameplay and end up being time wasting. The influence system is probably the worst offender for me.3. Endgame: It is now significantly harder to finish off enemies in the late game, often feeling like an endless slog on the highest difficulty. If your allies let you down it is very difficult to make up for it. You need your full fleet to move together which leaves you vulnerable because the defenses are far weaker now. The endgame was much more fun in the original where you could annihilate the other side with a maxed out fleet in the way you wanted.To be clear this truly isn't a bad game. It is a very lazy copy of the original but the gameplay itself is still fun. What it comes down is that I see no reason to ever play it when it doesn't do anything to improve the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: If you played Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion, you know whether you will like SoaSE2 or not. It is basically the same game with huge upgrades regarding the game engine and many quality of life improvements. The actual gameplay is still the same.If you haven't played Rebellion: This is basically a very condensed version of Stellaris (for better or for worse). Sins does not even come close to the ways you can customize your faction, but I personally do not miss anything. In Stellaris, if you decided to play a certain style (domination, tall vs. wide, etc.) you were basically locked in how you want to develop your empire and race. While you had many options, there was usually an objectively best solution regarding the situation and your play style. In Sins, you decide at the very beginning what race/faction you want to play with focus on influence, trade, defense, attack, ... and then have mainly access to gameplay mechanics that focus on that play style. This leads to streamlined gameplay and games that you can actually finish in one or two sessions. The number of options is reduced but that allows for decisions with more impact.The game also heavily focuses on quality of life in many areas. When you select a fleet, you can directly build ships for that fleet from the fleet screen. It will automatically select the most suitable shipyard(s) to build the ships and rallies them to your fleet. When you miss a research or item for something but have enough resources to build/research the requirements, the game automatically queues up everything you need. You can also toggle the option so that the game automatically goes to the market and buys/sells the required materials. Micromanagement is therefore reduced to game systems that require actual gameplay decisions (e.g. what do you want to build in the limited orbit slots around a planet? More mining? Research stations? Shipyards?)However, I do not think the game is worth the full price, as it is more of an engine upgrade and sandbox for content and mods to come. It is very competent in that area but 50 € is imho a bit much for that (I bought it with the 20 % release discount). Definitely wait for any kind of discount or sale. Especially as additional content might be behind another paywall in the form of future DLC (as it is included in the quite expensive premium edition).
_childDocuments_.name: Sins of a Solar Empire II

_childDocuments_.review: First and foremost, I want to say that the game itself is really great. A lot of what made the predecessor so outstanding can also be found in the second installment. I definitely had fun with Sins of a Solar Empire II. However, there are many things I have to criticize, and one thing, in particular, that really bothers me. Keep in mind that I'll definitely change and update this review, even changing it to positive if appropriate. I WANT this game to be absolutely great, don't get me wrong.The first thing that will please everyone is that the game now runs smoothly all the way into the endgame. The new engine delivers on its promises. No more massive slowdowns like in the predecessor. However, there is stuttering and performance drops when zooming into larger battles. The annoying part isn’t the frame drops themselves but that the sound sometimes completely stutters. Still, the game runs quite stable overall, and I haven’t experienced any crashes so far. Graphically, it also looks pretty good, even though some effects still look unfinished or end abruptly.I also like how they didn't try to completely reimagine the whole Sins of a Solar Empire gameplay. They sticked to their bread and butter and the gameplay loop itself works extremely well. And now we come to the topic of "unfinished"... This game is a hidden Early Access, and a significant portion of the content is locked behind a very steep paywall. But what I find even more outrageous is that none of it is even close to being finished. The game comes with a sufficient framework, so to speak, but a lot is simply missing.Another topic I want to address is the user interface. It just doesn’t look good, feels completely outdated, and is sometimes utterly confusing. Putting something like this into a finished game is not ideal. But what I find particularly bad is that many elements of the UI were generated with AI — and you can tell. The tech tree, for example, is pure, chaotic confusion. Hardly anything clearly tells me what it is — I often have to check two or three times, which was hardly the case in the predecessor.Another point that bothers me is the starbases and the defense of planets in general. To be honest, starbases now feel completely interchangeable and get destroyed incredibly quickly. Defenses are overrun so fast that it just annoys me to have to rebuild them every time, knowing they will be destroyed again in five minutes by just a few ships. The starbases seem to be made out of paper. I particularly notice this because of how easily I can overrun the enemy's defenses. It shouldn't end in complete stalls like in the old game but defenses should be stronger.Then there are a few things that I find quite sad for the high price, which further emphasize the “unfinished game” aspect. There are no Steam achievements, not a single scrap of story (only behind the paywall), no German voice acting (which was really good in the predecessor, and I think it's outrageous to cheap out on this at this price), and you now have to zoom in much closer to see your ships. Additionally, the automatic camera tracking is sometimes way too sensitive compared to the predecessor.I also noticed that I find the notification system very chaotic, and audio cues constantly block each other. In the predecessor, I could immediately tell which planet was being attacked by whom. Here, I only see it when I look at the planet itself. Many notification icons are very abstract and uninformative. The auction info in between is also quite annoying and sometimes covers critical information that should be delivered to the player more quickly.Oh yeah, items for capital ships? Honestly, pretty good; however, not the upgrades, which simply break after a certain number of charges. It doesn’t feel good.Seriously, a lot is still missing for a positive review here. Sure, I'm having fun with it, but you can't forget the price here, and I don't think it’s appropriate to release the game in this state.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really good game.  The visuals are fantastic, and they have even patched in more variety than what it started with.  Honestly the visuals are so good I sometimes fail to play the game effectively because I'm busy zooming in on the pew pew in screenshot mode.The game has a lot of depth as well.  So much so that honestly I'm a bit overwhelmed by it.  Not just tech tree research, but also everything down to which weapons are modeled as turrets or not, and how fast those turrets can track smaller craft.  I guess you don't really have to worry too much about that stuff if you are just playing single player against AI, because a balanced force will perform well enough... but if you want to play as smart and effective as possible, this is definitely something to think about.My only gripe is how fast paced the game is... that's a strength for some, but for me I feel like I'm always behind the 8 ball.  I can't click around fast enough or even think fast enough to really keep up, and I end up using the pause function a LOT.  I also wind up with huge caches of resources because I cannot figure out how to spend them at the same rate that I make them.  You could spin that as a positive if you like that challenge and call it a learning curve as well, but for me I bounce around a bit too much between games to focus in on it that much.Overall I'm very pleased with the game and am enjoying playing it on easy difficulty.

_childDocuments_.review: Oh boy, what a sequel.I've 500+ hours in Sins I and loved that game. Earlier this year, when the news about this dropped, I could not wait to get it. Usually, I never buy games on release. That is mainly because every other game is released a mere beta version with tons of bugs and missing stuff. Also, 30€ was my hard limit to buy anything.I made an exception for Sins II, because of how much I enjoyed the first installment and how long Ironclad Games kept putting out content and fixes for this one. So paying 30+ is a thank you for the support for Sins I and an investment, I know they are gonna put out stuff for Sins II for a long time.Regarding the game: I love the way they put in new stuff while keeping the old mechanics mostly the same. The factions are so unique and still balanced, it is insane how well it all works. Whenever you want to build an item/ship/upgrade you have not researched yet, you can now just start the prerequisite tech right there, it is queued, researched and once finished your unit/item/.. is build. You do not need to search the tech tree. It makes things much easier and you can concentrate on expansion and warfare. The graphics are not out of this world, but still brilliant. The performance is great, using a double fleet supply mod, I still achieve 50+ FPS in end-game battles. My rig is not bad, though; some people might experience some more drops. But its a totally different level than the old, single-core game.I look forward to the new fraction they want to introduce with the first DLC. Man, this base game is a perfect platform to give us new content over the upcoming years.

_childDocuments_.review: All Hail the mighty TEC, the game has been modified a lot under the covers.   Races ships "Especiially Capital ships" are weak as Fudge.  TEC cruisers beating Capital ships.  TWO TEC star bases in single system...ridiculous.  Limited civilian points so much you cannot defend a system.  TEC basically rolls over everything.   Dont even get me started on the nerfed Titans.  Examples.  Newly built Starbase from AI has ALL upgrades...yours starts with nothing.  The point I stopped playing was 7 capital ships, Titan and starbase along with 50 other cruisers were utterly wiped out by invading TEC with no Titan of their own.  Ships being built no longer have bars showing progress.  Absolutely hate the exotic materials BS they limit so badly you cannot build fleets  under an hour.   Totally and completely ruined the fun factor of the game.  No matter what race you play.  Go one on one with your capital ship and one from the AI and you lose 100 percent of the time.  Tried every race.   You want fun.  GO with the old version.  Advent mothership was a blast going around and destroyed things early game.  Titans were feared and Captial ships were strong and could be built reasonably if destroyed.  They beefed up some attacks like the magnetic or rupture blasts and made plasma nerf ball attacks.  Solar systems suck.  Choose 107 planets, delete all but four players and it is still a small map overall "I think they lied.     And whats up the the crappy primordial planets?   Just like all sequels.  Game looks the same but plays completely different.  Not worth the money unless you are a TEC fan and just want to easily kill everything else once you get the numbers built up.  Cant go without talking about how they killed the economy...no shortcuts, need more attention to build and over an hour just to get things rolling.   You need about 8 or more planets to start having the money to build things and then you lose them because you have limited points to defend them and build research towers.  Many astroids leave no room to build after harvesting resources.  Just a constant headache and rush to expand then build one large fleet while to conguer a system while losing three others of your own.   Not FUN, not the same and not worth the money.

_childDocuments_.review: I only have a few hours in it so far but it's an amazing followup to one of the greatest RTS's of all time. Nearly every aspect of the original game has been brought forward and in some cases improved upon. I have nearly no complaints, everything looks beautiful graphics wise as wellThere are some things that aren't great, however, but they're not game breaking or enough for me to care that much. The player (and some of the research) portraits are AI-generated and therefore generic and ugly. In this case honestly they should have just used the same ones from the original game. _childDocuments_.review: I don't recommend it right this minute. It's actually a really good game... other than the camera logic, which Needs Improvement.It never zooms the camera in or out in a straight line; I get dizzy because it never quite looks where it ought to, and that's the least bad thing. Worse is when I'm trying to zoom in for a view of a battle and it suddenly dips and swirls because it randomly decided to focus on a fighter. And, no, there's no setting to tell it not to do that crap.But the real kicker is, sometimes it just goes absolutely bananas and whizzes away from everything. They even know this can happen because when it does, a 'focus on homeworld' button appears at the bottom. So they know, and decided not to fix it, which is a kick in the teeth.So yeah. Camera logic Needs Improvement really bad and I won't recommend the game until it gets it. But once it does, this'll be a real winner.Ending on a positive note, this is one of the best performing games I've seen for its level of sheer beauty. I just... really hope they fix the cameras.Update: It looks like the 'not going in a straight line' problem was caused by the game being in zoom to cursor mode. Instead of zooming straight in and out to or from the cursor, first it zooms in or out from the center of the screen, then adjusts sideways to center on the cursor, which causes a very weird feeling when I look at it.'Zoom to cursor' mode also seems to automatically focus on the nearest ship to the cursor, which is bad. If it says 'zoom to cursor' I want it to zoom TO THE CURSOR, not to something else nearby. This also causes the 'randomly focusing on a fighter' problem, as when you're zooming in towards a battle, there's usually going to be a fighter somewhere near the cursor. So zoom in to focus on a battle and whoosh, your point of view is flying off into the sunset.Not sure if the 'PoV whizzes off into nowhere and I can't find anything' problem is also related. I'll have to test it more.

UI is improved and management is much easier which is quite useful considering all the extra things that were added. Economy is mostly planet focused instead of resource asteroid focused with special planetary buildings that can add special abilities/effects to a planet. Planetary are pretty neat though I haven't played enough yet to see it be game changing (they can also be turned off if you want). It's optimized quite well though the graphics options do leave a lot to be desired. It has almost no graphics settings you can change. _childDocuments_.review: A worthy successor of SotSE: Rebellion.The game is streamlined, but not to a detriment of gameplay. You have limited options to customize planetary buildings, capital ships and even trade.The pace of the game seems a bit slower, though you will eventually end up with massive fleet battles and starbase sieges. The fleet command cap is gone and so is increased upkeep - instead, you require rare resources to build capital ships and advanced upgrades, which are produced in your refineries. Rushing titans is harder than before, since you need more military research labs to research the tech.Another interesting mechanics is that the "core" planets periodically change place around the sun (they orbit), so suddenly you can end up with enemy planet at your reach or your planet isolated, which creates interesting scenarios.If you are a fan of big ships going pew-pew and economy and building management thrown into the mix, this is the game for you.At this point, I would give it 10/10, but I admit I am biased and haven't fully explored everything; however, based on hundreds and hundreds of hours spent in SotSE and one victorious playthrough as TEC, this is the game I have always wanted. The king is dead; long live the king.
