_childDocuments_.review: The game is exactly what you would hope from a sequel (with some exceptions); all the features of the previous title updated to work on a modern engine with modern freedoms and visuals BUT with excellent quality of life improvements. A list:- The game looks amazing; watching the guns on your ships track enemies is fantastic. - The 'build-to-fleet' feature is such a dream. When your fleet loses ships on the front line, simply order more from the fleet menu itself, your empire will then work out the best place to build them and they'll be sent to rendezvous straight away. - Want to build a ship you haven't researched yet or don't have the exotic resources for? No problem, click the ship build button and the game will queue up the necessary research or exotic creation and get your order filled. - Late game lag seems to have been completely eradicated and the game has never felt so smooth. - Research has been expanded so that you actually need to think a little bit about how you get the requisite number of research labs. In the previous title, you need 8 of each type of lab to max out the research tree; this could be done on a handful of planets. Now you need 25 of each at the top tier so expansion is required. - I know I have said it already but the game just looks incredible. I have spent much of my time so far simply watching the ships fly around one another and tracking fighters and missiles as they scream to their target. - I also cannot stress enough (and some may see this as a downside) that this really is Sins Rebellion in a better engine. With the exception of the quality of life changes and the new research trees, it almost plays exactly the same. It will feel so familiar. Another list- Leading off my final point above, whilst it is great the game is so familiar it is a real shame it didn't launch with the 4th faction. rebellion was all about setting us up to prepare for the unknown faction that had chased the Vasari to Human space. You would naturally expect the next game in the series to continue that story. (Note they are going to be added but you really would have expected them at launch). - Most of the voice lines are great, some are less so. The pirates being "oo-arr me hearties" in the first game was cute, now it is just silly and doesn't fit the tone of the game at all. The less said about the Harcka's "russian" accent the better. - There are no steam achievements on launch. Many won't care, many will. I did. - Building off the point regarding the 4th faction; the game has launched with no new ships. Well, not entirely correct, there are some new ships but they replace existing roles. There are no new roles; could have easily added a titan-tier mobile factory ship for example. (Again, the game's greatest strength and weakness is that it is just a shiny new skin on the previous game). Now, despite my second list, I absolutely recommend this game. It is an incredibly smooth and bug-free experience that is a visual treat. Ironclad knew that Sins was not going to beat Stellaris in the 'grand strategy' element of the game so they doubled-down on the real-time strategy and it absolutely pays off. You won't be spending your time managing your vast empire - that management is simple - instead you will be spending your time moving your ships to strike from an advantage and timing your ship abilities to ensure a decisive victory.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR : If you liked SoaSE this is a must have , if you are new then its still a very good experience. 9+/10 game.Main perks - holds onto what made the first game great and the new innovative additions work well.Each faction has a dynamic gameplay element now - TEC: trade stations allowing the player to amp credit/metal/crystal generation (customisable) , advent: unique psy abilities which if invested in can be hugely impactful, vasari can amp their fleet speed/weapon dmg/ antimatter usage whenever they phase jump.Each ship/spacestation and planet has item slots which really help the player tweak them to their needs - a super tanky cap ship or one more utility focused for example.Moving planets and moons - Really good chaos - also can stop turtle gameplay and enables surprise attacks.A major shift in how all ships work/counter each other and do damage compared to the first game that makes it much more dynamic.  Positioning ships so they take the hit (body block) the focused target is one example but there are lots of other things like this in the game.  If you can counter missles, you counter missles.  If you dont then watch your cap ships melt.Performance is wonderful.Visual looks : new model detail and ship design is 10/10 , especially on advent - the giant gun and boot from the first game are no more.  Particle effects and sound design 11/10 , @the devs (the marza dreadnaught commander line about debris and cheese made me lol)On the AI usage:  I can tell there was a LOT of manual effort put into all the art here within the game.  I've worked with AI enough over the last 2 years to know how easy AI can get things wrong.  There aren't enough mistakes (there are a couple out of hundreds of assets) to suggest they simply shunted the concept art out of a bot in 5 mins.  Besides the art concepts themselves are cool and add to the direction the devs want.  Request to the devs though : those small minor mistakes, fix them please.As for the reviews saying "its all AI therefore its evil".Those people are simply getting too immersed in the game and pretending to be Advent acolytes - dont let them mind control you.

_childDocuments_.review: The originals Sins of a Solar Empire has been my all time favorite RTS (even my Steam avatar is a Vasari). The new game is good. I don't know if it is better than the original, I have so far played 2 full games, but it is a bit different. I enjoyed some of the new features and am happy that the creators have left most of the old ones. So I'm going to leave a list of Pros and Cons for the game in my initial experience with it. Pros:+Game is beautiful. The developers have really improved visuals. +Soundtrack is as awesome as before. +The new tech trees are really impressive and provide some more advanced features than before. +The scale of the game remains the same, but feels a bit better in terms of massive battles. +The constant pirate raids have been removed and instead you need to become friendly with the pirates to bribe them to attack other players. Also raids are more realistic as they are not with monstrous armadas as before, but a more manageable ones.+The economy has been really improved.+Now planets can house research stations and gather resources different than credits. +While planet management seems to be similar, it is a bit more advanced. +I like the exotic resources feature. You cannot just spam battleships, but need some more specific resources to build them.+Minor factions are managed easier than in the original game.+Titans are available later in game. +Some more advanced defensive structures are added in the game. +You can have patrols between systems. +The changing phase lanes are an awesome new addition, but for those who don't like it - this can be disabled from the menu. +The 3 races are a bit different, but retain their main characteristics. +The new health system is quite interesting.+I like that it is more difficult to advance in tech tiers than before.Cons:- There are some minor bugs, which I'm sure will be fixed relatively quick.- Super weapons are no longer available to all races.- Star bases are extremely easy to build, upgrade and yet are difficult to deal with. - Leaving wreckage and waiting to collect it to gain experience seems a bit too much. Maybe if it is just for resources it would be OK. - While Artifacts are still available, they are not listed in a specific section and is quite hard to find what kinds you have. - The Tech Trees are now combined. I think the original ones were sorted better as they would separate defensive from offensive abilities and fleet capacities. Currently Tech Trees feel quite heavy. - Still no information on the factions. Any campaign will be awesome. I read somewhere that you need the deluxe edition for this, but it is still not much. If that is the case, that is not a good decision. - Some features from the original game have been removed - such as pacts. Also only the original battleships are included and not the ones from Rebellion. - I think everyone was expecting the 4th race to be added. You know the one that has been heavily speculated as the reason why Vasari empire collapsed. It would have been great if this was added. - Rating was a very nice system where you were able to see where you are placed compared to others during a specific game, but for some reason is now missing.- Achievements are also missing.My personal rating for this game would be 7/10. If the developers of the game decide to add some more features it can easily get to a maximum score, but I guess it will take some time for that.

_childDocuments_.review: For those new to it, Sins of a Solar Empire is a 4X game that lets you really enjoy the game with just the basics, while giving you more complex details to play with if you wanted to up the difficulty. You can play against 3 easy AIs with just capital ships and still feel like you're commanding a space empire, with mechanics that are engaging in the beginning but not obstructive later in the game. Once you're familiar with the game and the different smaller ships and structures, you can increase the difficulty and start to get dynamic fleets and battle plans. The simple mechanics now require more attention, so the skills you learned for fun you now can put to the test. Features that seemed unnecessary on easy now become your lifeblood, but since they were simple to use before you'll already know what to do. For the veterans, in many ways it's just an updated version of Sins 1. However, the improvement to the engine lets you have the large scale galactic conflicts you always wanted. For someone like me, who absolutely loved the original game, that alone makes it worth it. More content is being added regularly, showing the studio isn't just doing this as a cash grab, they really want to make the game as great as possible, even if it takes time.Newcomers to a 4X experience will love it, the old guard will love the improved performance, and for the stragglers who don't want to buy a new game that still feels like their old way, just give it time. They'll give you the new content you want, and you can buy it then. All in all, I'm happy Stardock is releasing content again, and that it still has the fun and easy to jump into feel of the original.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't believe it. This game has managed to beat my expectations from the original.Sins 1 slowly had things that improved over time, starbases & mines (entrenchment), diplomacy, and culminating finally in Rebellion. I know things will be the same here with Sins II9.5/10Diplomacy is kinda handwaved out here for now (no more pacts or missions for the other players), while minor factions are in a significantly more strategic role, helping with upgrades and free attacks or defense. While there aren't pacts or missions for the players, the treaties are much stronger. I expect more of the older design to come into play in the future since I believe they have mentioned that diplomacy hasn't really been worked on that much yet.Combat, the backbone of Sins. I cannot believe how absolutely cool it is to have all these individually tracking turrets and damage I can body block with my starbase or any of my ships. Not only did they manage to take it and improve it, they managed to do so while keeping it fresh, adding a new armor/hull system that flows really well. Some of the same old abilities are here, but new things like ship upgrades and planet upgrades keep it very interesting. Exotics have a new twist, and fleet comp is way more important, with even tiny ships needing to be used to make sure your capitals don't die. PD is no joke against the Advent. I am not sure how I managed to get this far without mentioning orbital paths. It is super cool to see them, and there's options to see the paths all the time.Economy and Building have been changed for the better by exotics, I was skeptical, but it made survey more interesting, while also allowing you to focus on what exactly you are going after, and you can hamstring yourself with it too, and just get more from killing the enemy capital ships, titans, and starbases. Research feels a bit weird, but mainly because I haven't gotten used to it being in segments. Also Fleet no longer ties into the economy.UX: Everything is so much easier, I think the only thing that is slightly less easy than the original is the market, but I can now hold alt-shift-ctrl and buy and sell 5000 at a time, so that is super useful. Building from the fleet, being able to upgrade, and see which one of my ships has their armor down all are just some of the UX changes I have instantly noticed. Building on planets is significantly easier. Some things I wish showed up a bit better, like the orbital structures. I ignored the tutorial on that and wondered for a bit where it was when I selected the planet, but I found out rather quickly. Pause is still here, still bound to the actual pause key :)It doesn't feel like Sins is my favorite RTS game anymore, now its Sins II

_childDocuments_.review: Sins of a Solar Empire returns in all it's glory with a brand new engine, extensive modding tools and upgraded graphics alongside new mechanics and units for all original factions.For those who haven't played the first game, what is this all about ? It's a slow paced space empire builder with extensive space combat going on, from the humble Corvettes that rely on their agility to survive to mighty Titan class warships that dwarf any other. Capital Ships will duke it out with Cruisers all the while your Flak ships will gun down missiles and strikecraft in this lovely cinematic scene. However, the battle is not all for show as each ship has it's strengths and weaknesses alongside abilities that can change the tide of battle !It follows the standard 4X formula. You can expect games to last on average 2-3 hours, however they can go on for MUCH longer. There is extensive modding tools incorporated into the game and devs are highly supportive of modding. In fact, a good portion of them are former modders from the first game that got hired ! There is a multiplayer PvP scene, but it is not the core of the game. This is a sandbox game with lose ties as to why each faction fights, ready for your own narratives to get fired in.For those coming back to the series, it's essentially Rebellion, but better. New engine, better core processing, not more minidumps or crashes because the game is trying to run on a single core. And even better, we're getting DLCs and more after the launch. The devs are very responsive and talkative over on the discord, so feel free to hop there and have your questions answered.In short, I highly recommend this beauty of a game.

_childDocuments_.review: SoaSE was one of my all time favourite strategy titles.  I found it equal parts engaging and relaxing to sit back and oversee an ever expanding space conflict, sending my fleets down jump paths while I tweaked production and planned my next engagement.  It absolutely didn't hurt that you could assemble a huge psychic choir to convert a planet instead of bombing it.  Sins was full of metal ideas like that.I'm well into my first Sins 2 campaign, and I'm happy to say the magic is absolutely back.  This game looks, sounds, and most importantly: plays great.  The orbiting planets system addresses what my biggest gripe with the original was (it getting too easy to defend chokepoint planets) and makes maps a little more dynamic.  There are some really nice UI touches here (like quick placement of orbital structures, and the ability to easy queue up ships to add to a fleet directly, without having to manually handle the logistics of choosing which factory to build which ship) that help keep that feel of constantly making interesting decisions without getting too caught up in the mechanics.I will update this review as I continue to play, but my early impression has been one of delight.

_childDocuments_.review: Moderate letdown. They would have done better just rereleasing SoaSE: Rebellion with performance improvements. There is almost nothing added, and what is added is not significant. The new orbit feature is fine, but nothing outstanding. One new ship per faction is really unimpressive.  The scenario selection and random map generation is really lacking. They launched with almost no graphical options, and what options there were were shoved into a developer console with a million bizarre options nobody would ever touch? Really baffling, that one, hard to imagine how they could be so disconnected from what PC players want.The new 3D art is just boring, the old art had character and detail and the new art doesn't. I see people saying things like "they're going for a more sci-fi aesthetic", and that's not a defense. If that's what they decided to go for, then they made a bad decision and the results are bad. The AI art for icons and portraits is noticeably random, uncommunicative, hard to differentiate at a glance, just uninteresting, and kind of an odd decision. How much money are you really saving on tiny static art for icons and leaders, in exchange for controversy and underwhelming results?Big fan of the original. _childDocuments_.review: The Games Great! Overall I would say it's about an 8.5/10 This is a True Successor to Sins of a Solar Empire and it's Expansions. The fact that the Game-Play Loop is about 90% the Same with the 10% being very important and helpful Quality of Life Changes. You really do get the feeling of spending more time focusing on the Strategy aspects and less of empire management as well as not being punished by your expansion. Gone are the penalties for building a big army faster and getting out paced in the economy by your enemies. No longer do you worry about is it the right time to grab this planet, as you no longer lose income by having more planets! Go Forth and Conquer; Expand Your Solar Empire!Things to Improve:-- Achievements. There are currently now Achievements upon the Release of the game; not in the game, nor on steam. This is a big factor of a negative Score. -- Key-Binds and UI Elements and Toggle Options. It seems that in the First Game we had all sorts of different seemingly useless toggles and key-binds that maybe a small % of people would fully utilize; however, when slimming down I think they went too far. There are Some Toggles and Key-Binds that should just exist to allow players a more customizable experience. Notably; The Auto-Place Structures key-bind / UI Element is completely removed in this game. While you can do a few things to still Auto-Place Structures there shouldn't be the need to have to click an additional button every time unless you want to have that limiter on. Some of us just want to have structures placed at the click of a button and not have to do a work-around for this experience. -- The Faction Selection Screen showing the Pro's and Con's of each Faction and Race was Better in Sins 1 however, getting into a game is much easier and more akin to other RTS games so it's more familiar with players in General. Some Key Benefits:-- The level of "Micro" that you have to do in this game on the Management side of the game has gone way down. -- The choices of upgrading your planet in Sins 2 make the game feel like less of a Burden to own multiple planets and keep up with each one; though you do lose a few bits of the quick Customization between Planet Type A and Planet Type B you retain those Key Differences in the Planetary Upgrade choices you get that are determined based on Planet Type and Research and can even grab some unique ones from your Minor Factions NPC's that remain Passive throughout the game. -- I found building an Army of Ships was also relatively easy though I didn't do much of the "Squadrons" The fact that you can easily click a Squad add ships and they would automatically rally to wherever the Squad was at was really cool. Instead of needing to manually build ships, and remember to grab them and take them to the Destination System only to leave them behind when your squad changes the destination before they get there. Though this system can Lead your Titan into enemy Territory and get caught in a Phase Jump Inhibitors Range, it's overall a good way to keep Expansion going. -- Conquering the Universe while being able to quickly Build Ships, using the Interfaces to Manage multiple planets, systems, starbases, defenses at a time also makes for a really easy time spent focusing on your Battles and expansion rather than the Management of your empire.

Sins 2 feels remarkably smooth.The bad would perhaps be for people who wanted to see a Sins game with combat closer to the Homeworld series. Understandable but for me I am glad they preserved the basics of the combat. I was a bit less pleased that it feels like the culture/propaganda aspect is less relevant. There is no culture victory or using culture alone to keep the enemy from colonizing at time of writing. It's not world ending but it would be nice to see that aspect expanded a bit. While a lot of the compressed or altered features are a plus, this one feels like a step back.Overall this is my favorite strategy game I've played this year. _childDocuments_.review: Certainly gives another dynamic to the franchise with the systems that are able to move around, they also changed up some of the bonuses that the ships have to make it little more difficult to win so easily.  Below are the positives that I have noticed with this new update.The Advent used to be my "go to" race and having so many aircraft made it easy to wipe out all enemies quickly, however the changes made to them have made it where the fighter craft still make a difference but you can offset this with other races.  They still do an amazing job at their culture expanding much faster than other races so this will help you with some bonuses.  The Vasari now are an actual "traveling race" and have a lot more starting resources, this helps with being able to get more than one capital ship at the beginning.  This sometimes makes them a lot harder as enemies and makes them a cinch to win with if you play as them.  Their warships are still strong but not over the top like they used to be.The Human race is always great at a defensive war and if you like protecting your territory while building up your fleets they are still great!!  They are also the only ones that have trading ports in this new iteration which makes them stronger when it comes to getting credits, however the other races have bonuses that you can get which negates this.If you loved Sins of a Solar Empire then you will love this new update, just remember that the Pirates and certain races will attack you anytime you get a direct line to their home world.  This keeps the game a lot more interesting than putting a bounty on other people.

_childDocuments_.review: Very solid successor to Sins1 on a completely new multi-core 64bit engine.In consequence the game runs absolutely buttery smooth and looks absolutely fantastic while doing so. Frankly from the technical side this might be one of the more impressive RTS games I have seen. Add to that powerful modding tools with ingame mod.io integration and I can already see how various mod teams will have a field day with creating full conversion mods for this.The game itself iterates and improves upon the Sins1 gameplay, streamlining some of the more cumbersome parts and comes with a overall (imo) nicely sorted UI. The only real critique I have here is that the UI symbols could be better accentuated, especially in the research tree, but this is honestly a nitpick.The AI is (imo) overall more competent than in Sins1 (it expands aggressively and doesnt suicide tactically) but probably wont make too much of a challenge to any RTS veteran or player who eventually knows how to play. Much like the predecessor, Sins2 will shine most when you can play this with friends or just generally PVP where you face opponnents that can think outside the box and make the most of the ships abilities. For more casual Singleplayer players various different maps, aforementioned mod support aswell as the planned campaign mode will offer plenty of good stuff too though.The devs have also proven to be rather responsive reacting to community feedback quickly, shipping some QoL and balance changes within 2 weeks of the release, which makes me rather hopeful for the future of this game.Overall I can recommend Sins2 to anyone who seeks a straight & honest RTS experience with 4X sprinkles or just likes duking it out with cool looking space ships (again the game is pretty).

But given the amount of effort these Developers put in, I’d like to give them their well deserved praise.This is my first time playing the series, and I regret not getting into it sooner. It really is a great game that knows exactly what it is trying to do, which is refreshing when a lot of modern games are trying to do everything and fail at most of this. This is a hybrid 4X/RTS game and it pours everything into optimizing that fact. I normally don’t like those types of games but they put a ton of effort into minimizing the tedious aspects of those genres on both the micro and macro scale while still providing a large amount of options and choices that ensure things never get boring or too easy. I was able to understand most of the game after the (great) tutorial and one quick game; that is the fastest I’ve ever gotten into a game like this.Performance is great, in particular I’d like to call out Steam Deck performance. Despite the Devs saying they haven’t done any work on Deck optimization or controls, it runs fantastically out of the box and controls are easily configured to make it very playable. It comes with a decent control template to start which you can customize a bit to add/remove functions as desired.Overall, really a great offering and a development team that is committed to supporting the game for the long haul. More content is already coming in the short term, and they intend to help facilitate a robust modding community in the future. Price is fair, IMO, at around $40 for current game content. The game is ultra polished and has pretty robust simulations going on - ship battles can get well into the hundreds of ships all with unique mechanics and stats and it tracks all of them without really dropping performance - that’s better than a lot of AAA games these days which are priced double this game. I’d highly recommend giving it a shot if you are on the fence. It’s really a deep, polished, and beautiful game that is only going to get better over time.

_childDocuments_.review: Sins 2 takes everything I loved about Sins 1, and builds upon it in really satisfying ways. It maintains that stately grand pace of the original, with visually epic fleet battles, and now just bigger everything thanks to the new engine, and modern PC hardware. A lot of long-awaited sequels tend towards re-imagining the whole game into something totally new, and in the process losing the essence of what made the series great. I'm very happy that Sins 2 held true to its roots.Planet orbits force you to rethink your defenses and routes of attack continuously. And the minor factions actually have real gameplay boosting utilities that really can offer meaningful advantages in the mid/late game. And holy cow the new editor and mod tools! People did crazy things with limited tools in Sins 1, I can't wait to see what they come up with given everything IC has provided to radically change the game.If I had one quibble, it would be the tech tree and the use of the scaled down header images as icons. Even at 125% UI scale, I find the images too busy when scaled down to be able to quickly scan the tree to know what's what. This holds true too for other image-as-icon UI sections like planetary and capital ship upgrades. I'd like cleaner, simpler iconic images for readability.I've been playing the game through it's tech test, and have really high hopes that Sins 2 will evolve much like Sins 1 did over the years, going from an outstanding game, to a true GOAT of the genre.Disclosure: I worked on the original Sins of a Solar Empire from the base game through the early development of Rebellion. However I have no connection to the developer/publisher anymore. I'm simply here as a fan of the franchise at last.

_childDocuments_.review: It's good. It's really good. It's awesome in all the ways that Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion was awesome, with some very welcome changes. There's lots of quality-of-life improvements across the board, particularly the new fleet and planet management sytems. It's now fantastically easy to order a batch of new ships and have them sent straight to your fleet upon completion. No more messing around with rally points. Ditto for planets - the planet management screen lets me look at all my planets and their infrastructure at a glance, so I don't have to do constant zooming in and out clicking. Nor do I have to contend with a horribly overbloated empire management tree in the left of the screen. Nor do I have to manually set my scouting ships to auto-explore mode.I'm free - free! - to zoom in and out, not to do busywork, but to appreciate the pretty colours and the spaceships shooting the stuffing out of each other. Pew pew boom.All the content from Sins: Rebellion is here, including the cool stuff like starbases and titan supercapital ships. And Rebellion's content was itself drip-fed into the original game over a series of expansion packs. There's also some welcome tweaks and additional features - notably the the capital ship modules, upgrades that you can equip your capital ships with to make them extra powerful. Interestingly, there no hard limit on capital ships like there was in Rebellion - the limiting factor is the new "exotic resources." If you can scrounge up enough exotics, you can build as many capital ships as your overall fleet supply can support (though you might also want to spend the exotic resources on other things, like certain planetary infrastructure). Sins 2 has a proper 64-bit, multi-core threading engine, meaning it performs like a dream and doesn't suffer horrible framerate drops on bigger maps with higher unit counts like Sins 1/Rebellion did. And it's so *pretty.* A key part of Sins has always been the spectacle of turning off the UI and watching the spaceships go pew pew boom, and Sins 2 absolutely delivers on that.The sins of the fathers never felt so good.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm sure I will update my review in time but right now I'm on the fence if Sins 2 is worth it (leaning towards no).I am a long-time Sins fan and have been waiting eagerly for this to arrive on Steam. Sins was one of the main games I played with friends when in school and I’ve logged countless hours in it (I played when you had to use the Stardock client and bought it at a retail store when disks were still a thing). It's a special game that was among my favorites when it came out and that includes the additionally released DLCs.Sins 2The good:Performance is greatIt looks decentThe new engine offers a better level of detail with ship weapons, shield reactions and damageNew tactics with moving planets/asteroidsA great modernized engine for Ironclad to build upon with future contentThe bad:It's too expensive for what it isGreat to not so great AI artworkVoice-over mistake "builds more" instead of build moreMissing story contentVery minimal graphic settingsBugsDe-sync errors with Linux/Deck when playing multiplayerJoin via steam friends with an invite not working (not sure if this is a system issue or game issue)To me, it feels like they’re asking too much for too little. This should be $30 for the introductory price and $40 for the game given its current state (and the fact that they will add much more paid content at a later date). The fact that they chose to release Sins 2 on the epic store first (for beta and EA) seems to have hurt the game’s development and quality control. There are several bugs and mistakes my friends and I have found, which clearly shows they didn’t have the diverse player count needed to properly find and fix bugs/game issues.Bugs include... Some of the AI artwork has issues with faces or does not match the aesthetics of the other AI artwork.Playing as Tec and clicking civilian tier 2 when having insufficient resources plays a voiceover that says “builds more” instead of build more (the other tiers seem fine). The camera gets lost (in deep space) and stuck when zooming the mouse wheel in and moving the camera (Fixed by clicking a button that pops up which centers you back on the planet you were zooming into).Unable to connect to my friends playing on Windows because of an overly restrictive architecture check that fails the connection when a mismatch is found (Linux system showing as AMD64-WINE and Windows systems showing as AMD64). Client de-sync when using the workaround of manually setting the architecture to AMD64 in the settings file to get past the architecture check. Can’t join games via a Steam friends invite. Multiplayer does work long enough for testing this but I can only join with the in-game join with a code feature. Joining by right clicking a friend's name or through an invite causes nothing visible to happen in the game. Sins does not try to load the lobby or show an error message.I am having fun but I think there should be more meat on the bone. I hope they sort out the bugs, touch up or redo the AI artwork, fix the voice line and support Linux/Steam Deck with Proton QC checks.I want to love this game and live in that modern nostalgia with my original friends I played the game with so many years ago. But right now I cannot recommend the game unless you are so into it you can look past its flaws. We will have to wait and see how the game really turns out but right now I’d still call this an EA title and it should be priced as one.

_childDocuments_.review: Sins of a Solar Empire II is the definition of not trying to reinvent the wheel. Often second parts of games try to do some "new" thing and in the end it has basically nothing to do with the first part anymore - Soase II is quite literally the first game with a new engine, new graphics and some quality of life improvements. Good:- As mentioned above, this game is VERY similar to the first part, down to the ships names, voice lines, faction names etc. (this can be positive and negative but since soase I is an excellent game I am happy that they stayed close to the original)- The game runs butter smooth and my PC is more on the mediocre side of things- Additions that were made to the first game are very good, for example items slots that allow to construct buildings on planets and specialize your capital ships- In general, the game puts more emphasis on planetary development, orbital mining is something that you actually have to research. Planets now actually feel like planetsNeutral:- The portraits of players and research symbols are obviously AI generated. I personally do not have a problem with that but some people might be annoyed by this.The "new" research is now more compressed, in the first part you had multiple windows and many researches could be done multiple times - in soase II all research is compressed into two windows (civilian and military) and research can only be done once. While this definitely helps cleaning up the UI a bit and makes research "simpler" I still preferred the older, more complex system. But again, thats personal taste.- While the graphic is quite good, combat is a bit dull. No impact animations, no debris, no parts ripped off from capital ships, it's a lot of pew pew and explosions. Especially with bigger ships and starbases I would've expected a bit more detail.Negative: - Sometimes the similarities to Soase I are too great. Especially when voicelines are simply reused it gives the feeling of copy&paste for the sake of saving money. Not a lot of negative things to say here, there are a few questionable gameplay choices (like capital ships having a "hidden" health bar that pops up once the main health is depleted, just why?) but this should not influence a review. The game runs smooth, played multiplayer without any kind of issues and there were no bugs, crashes or problems I could see. If you liked Soase I you will like Soase II, since there are not a lot of differences between those two games and most of the new implementations are positive ones. Especially the new engine will give plenty new options to the modding community, so I am certain we will see lots of things there in the future as well. The price is okay-ish but considering the fact that lots of voice lines were reused and I art was used I would've hoped for a price that is a bit lower. But I can recommend buying the game.

_childDocuments_.review: If I had to summarize this release in one word, it would be YESNow, don't get me wrong, there are some things I wish were better.Art style is kinda meh at times, especially all of the AI generated stuff - not because it's bad, but because it creates a lot of visual noise without any clear direction. It would've been better if research was visually coded in some way, for example. As it stands, it's very hard to visually intuit things, I have to look at the descriptions a lot.Fleet is occasionally being dumb - I wish the ships could position themselves 1) at their maximum range, and 2) avoiding being in firing range of close range weapons, if possible. As it stands, a dreadnought, which is supposed to be a ranged capital ship, will occasionally try to get into the meat grinder instead of staying away. It's much better than in SoaSE: Rebellion, but still I have to occasionally micromanage my fleet quite a bit in order to not lose my capital ships. Target prioritization is better as well, but still not perfect, and I wish my fleet was smart enough to e.g. target starbases and capital ships first, and then try to destroy factories or corvettes or whatever.The fleet reinforcement mechanism needs work as well: it is much better than before, and for the most part reinforcements correctly avoid enemy sectors, but when the only path to reinforce is through enemy sectors, I wish they picked the less dangerous sectors first. I lost many ships because they were opting to go through the only sector which had an enemy starbases in it, for example.The minor factions are IMHO not very interesting and they can be ignored (I usually just kill em all), but it would've been nice if they could just be turned off (it's not going to happen because the markets are tied to them). Which raises the question of, why does every map call out "minor factions" as turned on when you can't turn them off? Plus, if you're going for minor factions, you might as well include pirates and outlaws.Another annoyance is the fleet size - 2000 fleet is just enough to build one big fleet, but not enough to build two or three that are capable of penetrating enemy defenses. A 800-sized fleet isn't going to kill a starbase and remain viable, and without that, a fleet is basically useless. I would've loved it they increased the cap. Still, on the whole... The update is exactly what I expected from the sequel: it's basically the same game, but better in every way. Economy is better. Fleet behavior is better. UX is better. Less micromanaging, more fun stuff. It's not a generation leap or anything, but it didn't need to be.

The game has so many things under the hood which help you going by even though you may struggle at first. The ai is really good in helping you out, automatising targets and filling the micro managment gaps that sometimes transform RTS games into pure stress. Not so much here. Make a good fleet composition and lay down to experience the spectacle of it.Basically the game has three ressources and you need to amass more of them to build bigger fleets. There are hero ships, titan ships and rock, stone, scissor small ships. Everything is pretty self understanding and that is an achievement for this type of game. This is going to be a, let's play a small and quick round of Sins of a Solar Empire 2 game. I am not a fanboy but sometimes I feel the urge to pick up a good RTS, where you need to think but you can also automate lots of stuff. I may only be five hours in but I already won against the first ai on medium difficulty, overwhelming him with my fleet. That was great fun. If you have power fantasies, this is the game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: I have plenty to say about this trashfire product, but suffice to say all that the shills and bots are talking about is that this is the first game but modernized...and that's the problem.The original Sins was a largely lifeless game with no strategy beyond "build more ships than your opponent" and if there is only one strategy, there is no strategy.True, this is a game that LOOKS to have a lot in it for a new player, but I promise you; everything hinges around spamming resources to spam ships to steamroll opponents. If you enjoy doing that, well I can't stop you from purchasing this game, but I promise it'll get old quickly. No nuance, no real tactics.Building different ships and bigger ships and more ships is all, at the end of the day, building ships...Where is the "economic victory" or "science victory" or something else? For those few who don't know, Sins is a setting in which, ultimately, you are fighting over human worlds, be that as enslaving aliens, telepathic cyborg communists or hypercapitalist humans. Why not...use that? Maybe a victory condition could rely on you finally showing enough of the local human populace you can finally win this 35+ year war and they all side with you, pushing out the opponent? I shouldn't be better at this than a game's own developer, man...For you experienced Sins players, what is really new here? Some ships look different, some ships have been altered, there are even some new ships, like the railgun frigate. At the end of the day, again, all you do is build stuff until the enemy is steamrolled.The only new feature of worth is that some planets orbit around the map. This could be cool, if you could make use of it, but all it means is that some interplanetary transit routes shift every so often. You can't really "upgrade" your fleet to make use of less stable routes to open up raiding or sneak attacks.Other changes include "exotics" but all these are are some rare materials you can find or, eventually, manufacture that need to be consumed for some more advanced technology, ships and upgrades. All they are, though, is just a roadblock to progress. You're already managing creds, metal and crystal resources, but finding these exotics is largely chance and making them when you get refineries just consumes resource you have, anyway. Who. Greenlit. This?Sure, the game runs better than the "first" game, but the minor changes have done nothing to truly add to the gameplay. All you do, everything you even can do, is just in aid of an interstellar starship sumo wrestling match, just like the first game.Further, Stardock has shown itself to routinely alter games down the road, so there is no guarantee that this game, even if you buy it, will be the same in a few years. Maybe they'll make it good, but I do actually remember GalCiv 3, so I'm not holding my breath. Add to that the fact that there is nothing really guaranteeing that they'll ever release the "premium" content, there's no guarantee that the community will ever see a campaign or the "fourth faction" which is probably not even more than a collection of sticky notes on some interns computer at this point.This game? It's worthless. Base is 50USD, for a graphical remaster, mild rework and the addition of moving planets. Pathetic.Don't waste your money. Ignore the shills and avoid this game like the apathetic fart in the wind that it is.Edit: Mere moments after posting this review I deleted this game off of my hard drive...it took almost eight full minutes and that's just when I started looking at the clock. I hope Stardock, Ironclad and their malware "financial supporters" enjoyed all of my unique and interesting choices in both music and smut..."There is no middle finger big enough!" -Benjamin "Yahtzee" S.G. Croshaw

_childDocuments_.review: The engine improvement is immense and is by far my biggest praise in a sequel, and I'm looking forward to seeing what the devs and modding community can do over time. I feel this took a significant step backward from Rebellion. It's no longer 'clean' for lack of a better word. I can no longer simply look at the info-cards and quickly find what I was looking for, and instead have to scan the whole thing to make sense of what I'm looking at. This sort of philosophy in the UI is everywhere. It's likely subjective, but I'm not a fan. I'll be downloading a classic-esque UI mod as soon as it becomes available.- The Research Panel. Still sort of UI related. I miss having the research condensed into one area where you had your Military with your Combat and Defense techs, and the Civilian with Civic and Diplomacy. Now they are split into 2 different menus where the tiles are huge and you have to scroll down the tree to see everything. I also don't see different ranks in Tech, which I became a fan of using the expanded research sub mod for E4X in Rebellion.Overall, this is a solid launch, and will easily become my preferred sins with a few mods or patches.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game that got so many things right in terms of game design and execution right out the gate, but horribly plagued with game breaking bugs in the control scheme. I've never seen a game with so many bugs with the controls that even if I liked it, I cannot play a serious game on it because of all the random things your ships will be doing that will make you pull your hair out. I only have 8hrs in this game and here are the bugs I've encountered so far:Bugs:1) Fleet Control - When you are zoomed in enough to see the planets and the other celestial bodies in a system, select your fleet and right click on the planetary body in the system. What will happen is your capital ships and any other ships that can target a planet will move into that system and the rest of your fleet will silently do nothing as you told combat ships to target a planet, which it can't. If you are not watching the result is you just sacrificed half your fleet to the enemy for no reason and probably threw the game.If you zoom out all the way to the system level, this won't occur, your whole fleet will move into the system (it targeted the system not the planet). In general it is not uncommon to tell your fleet to do something, where half your fleet will do one thing and the other half of your fleet does something completely different, sometimes moving into a different system.2) Broken fleet stances - Stances are very janky at the moment, for example for carriers pretty much all stances are broken, I advise you not to use carriers until this is fixed. If you have carriers in your fleet and you set the stance to hold position, it will cause the strike crafts to idle and not move. On top of that, your carriers will just sit there and not engage even if there are enemies within the strike craft range. With engage all stance, when you right click attack something, the rest of your fleet will go to the minimum range for its weapons and start shooting, your carriers on the other hand will suicide move in right next to the target infront of your entire fleet and get wiped out immediately.Ultimately this is because it tries to use the weapon range to figure out where it should move to, where for unupgraded carriers they have no weapons, only strike crafts (so it has a weapon range of 0). With a weapon range of 0, it will never target enemies in hold position, and will move in directly next to the target in engage all.This makes carriers completely unusable until this is fixed.Note: Some capital ships seem to also do similar things despite having weapons, notably the Marza dreadnought who on hold position will dive in suicidally right next to the target despite having long range missles.3) Cancelling players orders - There are many situations where you've given the fleet an order, and it will get distracted by something and completely ignore your order. For example, if you are trying to move your fleet right up to the hyperlane to setup a perfect jump with your capital ship in front to tank, if an enemy scout ship comes into the system before it gets to the hyperlane the entire fleet will start chasing that enemy ship despite you telling it to move somewhere. This can be fixed by manually commanding your fleet again to move to that spot (seems this only happens once, when you manually give the fleet another command it will follow that without chasing).While I get that this game tries to automatically do alot of things for the player, it is entirely inconsistent when it chooses to do that, and when it will completely override a players command (which it should NEVER do).4) Unable to override pathfinding - When you tell your fleet to go somewhere, this game seems like it will always pick a specific path, and you cannot override this path NO MATTER WHAT. Given a scenario where there's a primordial planet one jump away from your system, but there's another way to get there by jumping to another adjacent system, and then jumping from that system to the primordial planet. Now imagine that system in between is a crystal planet with massive fleets guarding it, there will be no way for you to get to that primordial planet without going through that system with the crystal planet, because the game has decided that is the path it wants to take there. I've just ragequit a game because of this where I could've had an easy start with a primordial planet next to my home planet, but I cannot get there because of this forced pathfinding.5) Broken Autocast - Autocast breaks halfway through a game, I will have everything on autocast and nothing will be autocasted, even though the border is flashing indicating it is autocasting. I can click the skill manually at that point and it will use the skill no problem. This makes your fleet not work at full potential unless you personally micro everything. This happens to the colony ship as well, who will sit infront of the planet staring at it doing nothing, until you manually colonize.6) Useless static defenses - Less so a bug, but static defenses are basically useless in this game. You can build all the static defenses you want, but the enemy can come in and skirt around the outside of your system to avoid the defenses, and just raze the planet. Once your planet is taken, your defenses just dissapear, making them completely useless. Of course, you can build your defenses right infront of the hyperlane you think the enemies will come from, but guess what, the enemy can move their fleet right pass the defenses to the other side of the system where its safe, and raze down the planet. At no point do you ever have to acknowledge the static defenses, you can ignore all of them (only the bot will try to take them all out before taking your planet). To fix this, simply change it so that you can't attack the planet until you clear the defenses.-------------------------------------------------------------------------------I've found all these bugs in 8 hours, this is unacceptable given this is an RTS game where controls have to be the highest priority. If I can catch all these bugs, your QA team should've caught at least half of them in the time they had to QA the game. And yes I've verified all these bugs in the bug report forums.tl;dr - This game is a buggy mess, maybe good enough to play against bots but way too much game breaking bugs for pvp against other players. I actually really like this game but I cannot enjoy playing it due to the above bugs, and won't play until they are fixed. I'm happy to flip this review to positive if the bugs are fixed, but at the moment its not playable

_childDocuments_.review: Where do I begin.Alright, I know.What did you expect? Were you checking out this game because you remember the good old Sins of Empire days, spending at times entire days fighting over a massive map with fleets happily filling up entire planetary sectors with enough gunfire to make the Orks blush?Well, let me tell you, you have come to the right place.This, this I say, is what a Sequel to a, by now, old Game series ought to be. No, has to be.Taking from the old and making it new. not necessarily changing things but twisting them to make it fit a more interesting and engaging gameplay style, something that the old games struggled with just a tiny bit at stages. Giving you all kinds of quality of life improvements, from more Comprehensive menu's to better tooltips, over to the joy of clicking the button to build a ship or a building and having it research the stuff you need for it for you. Gone are the days spent looking through the, now extended, research tree to find that one damnable thing that unlocked a certain upgrade you want, or ship you desire. To the enjoyable Upgrade system, letting you upgrade both ships and planets more easily from a menu for either, while making additions with more extensive and intuitive plantary and ship upgrades on top of the powers, giving you even more customizability and capability to adjust things to your needs or expand upon necessities.And all that is without mentioning the changes to old game things like the capital ships now being made with so called "Exotic". making way for the slightly clunky feeling of the extra, seperate, supply system they had along side the normal fleet, which they also drained along side it, making it all a bit simplistic, if more direct.Now forget that extra research dump, no, now you get these new fancy exotics by exploring worlds, salvaging ships, both yours and those of your enemies, or simply making your own in the old well known refineries. Yes, those are now simply for forging exotics for you, automatically if you build something that needs it or manually if you wanna stock up on some. Which is nice. I rarely ever build the old one, but now? that stuff is necessary and ads to the more interesting trade offs your plantery logistics menu provides.Having to weigh your options with plantery specialization feels far more extensive here than it did in the older games, maybe I imagine it but sacraficing mining efficiency for a broadcast center can be a grading decision, that and once again having to go short on research stations so i can ramp up production.Oh, side note, gone is the days of building mining bases on asteroids. thats now also done through plantery upgrades.I like it, maybe some dont, you can still build upgrades on those asteroids but that does cost logistic slots so its once again a trade off.I could go on and on here.I did not even go into the minor factions and their mechanics, the mild changes to the market, the visual overhaul omg the visuals... I cannot say anything on it because i would be here all day but this game is as gorgeous as i remember the old games being, which i assure you are only that pretty in memory. this isnt. I didnt yet mention a thing about the trade changes, the escorts, garrisons, so on so forth, i mean god i did not get into changes for the good old battle stations yet or faction mechanics.So much more to say, but, this is already long enough.So, its best I give a tiny little short version.This Game is, to me, a rare but appreciated 10/10. This is a Sins of Solar Empire game. It is what you expect and nothing less, a bit more and certainly all around greater than the last, nearly. This is a sequel done right, and I think the Devs deserve some real pride for what they have delivered here. Few could have pulled this off. They did and I am here for it. ironclad, if you read this. Sins of Solar Empire Rebellions is one of my all time favorite games. And I swear, I think you just kicked it off its throne with this game.

_childDocuments_.review: After 100 hours I can confidently give this an A.  It's weird that on its face, the game just looks like Sins HD, but in practice there have been a ton of improvements to the mechanics and interface.  No longer are there hidden mechanics, everything is grokable without much research, though I do wish there were some better tools in game to see some details about the units, upgrades and mechanics, like an index or something.Mechanically, every single gun and bullet are simulated, you can literally zoom in on individual turrets tracking individual missles, it's madness.  It's also sort of Warcraft 3 but 4X in space?  The Capital Ships are effectively heroes, with abilities, leveling and items, both those you purchase and those you discover.  The item system is also an elegant way to handle planet and starbase upgrades.Epic game, ton of fun, ton of depth and options, creative mechanics, best in class user interface (auto-queuing is a godsend) and jaw dropping space battles.  I don't know what more you want.

They've made some obvious efforts around play balancing, but ultimately I can't recommend this until they issue some improvements / updates.

_childDocuments_.review: Stardock took a previously good game and expanded upon it. And that is just what the game needed. The orbiting mechanic is awesome. Planets orbit suns and planets can have their own moons orbit them.  This allows for an evolving space map which you can utilize to attack opponents in new areas. Each race feels unique and adds on to their lore. For example Vassari start the game jumping onto a planet in the system conquering the world vs the TEC who starts on a planet.
_childDocuments_.name: Sins of a Solar Empire II

_childDocuments_.review: Everything I wanted from a sequel. Keeps what made the original great and adds many improvements and mechanics. If you loved the original get this! For me other than waiting for mods to start releasing there is no real reason for me to play the original vanilla version other than for mods. Plays so smooth even late game to a point that I felt the standard 1.0 game speed felt too fast since I was so used to Sins1 late game slow down! If I were to give any criticism, is that the settings menu is bare bones. No texture, view distance, particle settings (with the exception of the hidden settings menu which isn't overly clear). You can't even charge resolution (at the date of this review). I also feels like this sequel should've arrived sooner (like 5 years ago). But minor critique aside, It's here now and its a great release! Considering the state of other recently released space strategy games, this is a fantastic release and has rekindled my love of the series.

_childDocuments_.review: Maybe I look back to SOSE with rose colored glasses when I was watching the dev or this and then into playing it.   I feel they went way too deep into the "space simulator" genre, and too far away from RTS mechanics that are fun, engaging and rewarding, especially for a "Ship battles" type of game. I find the lack fleet management / formations, setting defensive priorities and so forth feels like you have micromanager virtually every aspect of fleet interactions.  Jumping works well i suppose.   I find that even a game like Star Wars Empire At War, for a 20 year old game or whatever, feels way more immersive when it comes to how ships feel and behave together.  I find the transition before "tactical views" (like when ships are icons, etc) and the "real-time view" creates this void-space of immersion.  There's essentially just music and menu voices, unless you're basically dry-humping a ship.   You rarely get a good "cinematic feel" for the space battle, as it's either icons, or a very small viewing space of the battle view (on account of having to zoom in so far).Micromanaging ship abilities is not that much fun - but at least it's something, because otherwise it's just automated battle --- all you really do is chose the priority targets with the right countering ships.  Should absolutely be able to target ships equipment/technology instead of it just being a rinse and repeat of "take out shields, take out armor, take out health".Maybe just buyers remorse - i played SOSE 1 (along with the SW TC) for like 800 hours....10 hours into this and it already bothers me to play it.....  Anyways, bored af, and $70 bucks poorer for it.

_childDocuments_.review: The game starts out with all content that was released in SOASE 1 and its expansions. At least that's a good thing (unlike certain developers and distributors who like to make you pay twice....).It has been updated to a new engine and with some new features. Some are interesting, some are... less interesting or even annoying due to the limited selection offered within. One thing I'm really missing though is the artifacts which gave more story/lore background. Just like in SOASE 1 you can puzzle together some new lore from the research, development items and such, but those are relative sparse in what they tell.Sadly the most of the (new) lore has to come from the upcoming DLCs it seems, which is really a minus.The game just like its predecessor is fun (although the larger maps do feel a bit grindy, any map above 6 players is something more suited for multiplayer). The moving spacelanes and moving planet locations are one of the best new features, although it can be quite a headache with them to put up a big defense now at the right locations. _childDocuments_.review: This is a great sequel but not only does it bring back almost all the content from the original game and all its expansions but it also improves the whole experience with a new engine, upgrades to combat, UI, management, diplomacy and minor factions.True the price is high, there is some reused content from previous games, and some AI work that is quite obvious but considering the serious drop in game development and publishing standards this is above them all.The perfect mix of RTS style combat which even allows for some micro of units, with the macro 4X elements of expansion and empire building make it a unique sci-fi game which could really benefit from a campaign mode which it lacks now for a second time. It offsets this lack with great support for custom games, multiplayer, even LAN. And there is one feature which  makes it incredible versatile to play which is taking over another AI faction when you load up a save instead of continuing to play with your faction. This way you can jump into your own save from another perspective, go from a losing side to the wining one or test out other factions in a fully developed empire instead of starting over.The new engine makes the game run incredibly well with hundreds of ships in combat and dozens of planets to control and build up. The minor factions and the influence mechanics necessary to interact with them give you a wild card to play in every match and spice things up. Using CTRL+SHIFT+Z key turns off the UI and lets you enjoy battles like you are watching a sci-fi TV show or movie that you can direct and set up. The future mods will make this into any kind of sci-fi you like from Star Wars and Star Trek to Star Gate and Halo.If I didn't get it for free, I would buy it 100% then and now after playing it.

_childDocuments_.review: If you have played Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion, then you can jump right into this game and feel at home. There are the same six factions (two each for TEC, Vasari and Advent), mostly the same ships, many similar technologies, and what appears to be the same voice lines. Almost everything from the original is still there, with the exception of diplomatic and starbase construction ships (there are still starbases, they just get built like any other structure instead of by a designated constructor). However, there are some big changes, which I will highlight:1. Some planets now orbit their stars, which results in a changing battlefield where phase lanes shift dynamically, so a planet you conquered early on may end up deep in enemy territory later. I really like this mechanic, although it can cause some confusion as you look for the planet that has the shipyards.2. There are minor factions, and the pirates count among them. You have influence points that recharge over time and can be spent to gain favor of the minor factions and unlock special abilities. Minor factions will also occasionally hold an auction where they sell resources or artifacts to whoever pays the most influence.3. There is a lot more customization available for capital ships, titans, and planets (also for starbases, but they already had that in the previous game). Aside from regular planet upgrades and capital ship skills, you can also give them items.4. Planets have value on their own, regardless of their orbital structures. Planets will now produce not only credits, but also metal and crystal, and can be upgraded to house research facilities or generate culture, and a lot of other stuff. Asteroid mining got pushed back in the tech tree, so you can't use them right away.5. The different races are more unique. Vasari don't use credits natively. They don't generate it and nothing they build requires it, so their economy is simpler, but there are still ways they can get their hands on the credits and use it. Advent have Unity points they can spend to unlock special powers, and Focus they use to activate the powers. Advent always had a bonus to crystal extraction before, but now it's actually useful, because they can convert it into credits or metal. I haven't played TEC yet.6. There are rare resources now that you can gain from searching your planets or refining them. They are required for things like capital ships and some advanced upgrades.There are probably other changes too, but those are the ones that jumped out most to me. Also, on the roadmap it looks like we're finally going to find out what the Vasari are running from.

_childDocuments_.review: READ THIS:DO NOT BUY THIS SEQUEL YET*DEFINITELY* DO NOT BUY THE PREMIUM EDITIONI have just under 500 hours in Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion. it is one of my favorite games in my library, a game i keep coming back to. When i saw the announcement for a sequel, I was cautiously optimistic. When it released and i saw a flood of glowing reviews promising a familiar but improved game, i was excited to try it.40 minutes of gameplay later, I just put in my request for a refund - the first refund I've ever requested on Steam.If you already own Sins of a Solar Empire: Rebellion and its expansions, do NOT buy this game. Keep playing that one. Either Ironclad Games or Stardock has made the decision to cut features from the previous game and release them later for another 50 dollars. I will not claim it is altogether a bad game or that there is nothing at all new. As a matter of fact, Sins is a GREAT game, and Sins 2 includes some genuine heartfelt work to improve upon it. It's clear the development team includes people who care deeply about this game and want to see it succeed. I loved SoaSE:R. I have a lot of appreciation for the team that made that game and continued to update it over the years, so this is a hard review for me to write. My issue is not with the fact that the sequel is similar to that game. My issue is that the new game is not as robust as the old one, and most of the new features and mechanics are essentially things each faction could already do that have been shuffled around and recycled while most of the truly new features are either half-baked or not released at all and DLC-gated. My BIGGEST issue is that they are asking 50 dollars for a remaster they're calling a sequel and 50 dollars extra up front for a mixture of cut and resold old content and mysterious new content that hasn't been released yet that nobody is going to see until it is too late to get a refund.Missing from this 50 dollar sequel are several INTEGRAL features, like adjustable fleet sizes, that ruins gameplay on larger maps. All of the tooltips and portraits - all the 2D art in the game - are AI generated. i'm just going to take a guess at what the premium edition is trying to make you pay 50 extra dollars - a grand total of 100 dollars! - for:1. the unreleased single player campaign you won't see until it's too late to refund2. an unreleased new faction you won't see until it's too late to refund3. all the skirmishes they cut from game 1, not yet released4. the capital ship they cut from game 1, not yet released5. possibly one(1) new capital ship for each faction, or possibly a cruiser - not yet released!I have to ask you, reader, does that sound like a 100 dollar value, or does it sound like maybe the amount of content, combined with the new stuff in the base game, that would all together be worth a 50 dollar sequel once everything is released?my advice: don't even TOUCH this game until all the content is out and it is on sale. Honestly, I feel so suspicious at all the glowing reviews for this game, because i can't be the only one who feels cheated by what i paid for, and especially considering the AI generated content in this game is wildly unpopular everywhere else on the internet, the very muted hostility i've seen to it here in the reviews leads me to suspect those reviews are being artificially curated.You need to drop the AI generated art, you need to re-release the integral QoL features and start options you cut, you need to release some of the day 1 DLC-gated artificially-cut content back to the base game, you need to cut the price tag by about 33%, and you need to have all the premium edition content finished before advertising it for sale - period. Do at least most of that, and I'll try this sequel again. Until then, you've lost me as a customer and a fan.

_childDocuments_.review: So my thoughts on Sins of a Solar Empire 2. Its a extremely good sequel to the original game and you can clear see there has been a lot of work that's gone into the past 12 years of its development. The graphics and game play are top notch and its not trying to be vastly different from the original while still being different enough that you notice easily. It takes what was good about that and makes it better while addressing it's flaws and adding in whole new mechanics like orbiting planets and each factions unique mechanic. Is it perfect? No nothing can be but its got it's flaws. I thing some of units path finding is a little flawed and the auto structure placement is a flawed in a way that it just clusters everything as close as possible into one big higgledey piggledty mess as well as the game probably not being too new player friendly (but doesn't overwhelm them either thanks to its easy to follow tutorials). In short for a game that's a day old on release id give it and 8.5/10. Very good product that just needs a little more polish to shine brightly and i can't wait to see what the future dlc holds.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm going to give this a thumbs up because I love Sins and have waited for a sequel for over a decade. As it currently stands the game should probably get a thumbs down. It's way too close of a game to the original to be called a "sequel". It's more of a reskin with a few additional mechanics. The reskin however, is beautiful and the game runs so much better than it used to. The devs proclaimed to have mitigated the 'blob of death' mechanic but after playing a round it didn't feel much different. I was hoping with a sequel that we would get some additional unit variety but alas, it is exactly the same units as the previous. The modders are the main thing that kept the previous title relevant for so many years. The quicker we can get mods like Interregnum, Armada, Battlestar, Stargate etc. the better. _childDocuments_.review: If you like Sins 1 buy this. Nothing more to say about this group of people. It's basically Sins 1, enhanced in all regards.For those of you that did not play Sins 1, this is a 4X strategy game, in the broader sense. Do not expect grand schemes, slow evolving plans like in Stellaris or Civilization. This is more combat oriented, it's basically a blend between a classic RTS game with base building, armies gathering and storming each other in a satisfying cluster....uh...chaos, killing each other with the victor pooping all over the loser's base and a grand 4X strategy game where you have multiple tech trees, several resources and ways to get them, suited up in a kind of empire building that is reminiscent of grand strategy titles.It does both things well, strategy aficionados would in most, if not all cases, love this game. But do not expect a Stellaris level of grand strategy, nor a Starcraft level of combat micromanagement and quick gameplay. All in all an excellent blend of grand strategy and RTS combat that does both things well while not delving in either types too deep. It does have a lot of systems and a satisfying complexity, however. Also do expect to be amazed by the battles as fleets clash with each other, with ships maneuvering around to find firing solutions, beams discharged, ordnance of various types travelling to their targets, missiles flying with PDs desperately trying to shoot them down, shields stricken with a satisfying effect, ships exploding left and right, all those paint an incredible canvas of a dramatic space battle. I have found myself losing track of my plan(s) because I had to observe the fight. It's that good.

_childDocuments_.review: It is a sequel to a really good game, Sins if a Solar Empire: Rebellion (the og is way outdated). It also does exactly what a sequel is supposed to do: maintain the original game's identity in gameplay while innovating the mechanics and adding new ones.Staying in the 4X/RTS genres, the game maintains the same overall gameplay loop including phase jumping via phase lanes from world to world, colonizing and improving the new worlds, fortifying and destroying all rivals in the match.Mechanics like orbiting planets add a strong dynamic to the progression of matches as phase lanes can shift, leading to the same map not necessarily playing out exactly the same every time. The addition of exotic resources aids in limiting the players rapid military expansion while making exploration (now surveying) planet upgrades relevant from the beginning of the game and onwards. New combat mechanics get rid of armor types and dramatically reduce the amount of stats hidden to the player, as they are replaced by durability and pierce (which work against each other, durability lowering dps of weapons that get fired at it while pierce reduces how much durability lowers the dps - it follows a bit more complicated formula, but basically, a ship has a weapon with 100 pierce firing at a ship with 200 durability, the damage dealt would be about 2/3rd of what could be would the ship have only 100), also armor which many, but not all, ships have and is a regeneratable pool of hp that reduces damage dealt to it (with no counter to that). Capital ships/star bases/titans also go into crippled states; where all weapons and abilities are disabled but the ship isnt quite dead yet and can still be repaired.Missiles can now be intercepted by point defense, definitely adding to unit positioning, at least for pd-units. Every gun is now a turret (or fixed weapon emplacement), increasing the immersiveness and visual looks of the ships by a lot.Overall, the ship models are insanely well made and look very nice. The TEC are now the only faction to have trade (now a strongly dynamic way of generating all three resources as needed); whereas the Vasari get phase resonance (a rather basic global upgrade system generated by structures like TEC tradeports that provide Vasari military with potentially huge buffs); and Advent receive "Unity", a mechanic vastly expanding their culture game, very simply explained.All of this is supported by the "component" mechanic, which allows unique infrastructure to be built on planets or components on capital ships/titans/star bases. They add great depth by allowing unlinear upgrade progression and significant bonuses that are fully customizable, for a price of course.Some of the ui is unfortunate, to say it kindly, but it is always functional, even where it could be better. The 2d-art is... like it if you want. Ai made it, new art from the steam release probably due to time scramble not even getting touched by humans. It does mean the tech tree - because what is a space 4x without research - is very busy due to overly detailed art.However, if the worst complaint is bad art in the places you are going to spend less time overall in anyway, i think things are really good. And that is true, the gameplay loop itself is amazing and is very nicely expanded. This game perfectly fulfills it's purpose as a sequel. Oh, and talking about performance - huge improvements. Much, much, much less lag if at all, and this stability includes older hardware. The game is very optimized. Multiplayer, at the time of review, is a bit overloaded but this should soon be dealt with. Singleplayer bots work perfectly fine. Internet connection is only needed to download the game, mods (that are integrated into the game right away) and for multiplayer. Singleplayer is always accessible.Highly recommend this game, would give it a score of 7.5/10. (Losing 2 to the 2d art, as no game with ai generated art could be above 8 for me - and .5 to unmentioned bugs and ui.)As for the purchase options, buy what you can afford. The base game is great, the "deluxe edition" is purely adding content in the future (4 dlc; see the info graphic on the store page) and a soundtrack. They will be added to your account (if you do purchase deluxe) when available, which they arent yet (including the OST!)Date: Aug. 16th, 2024Played the game for a long long time on epic.
