_childDocuments_.review: I played all my runs in the hardest difficulty avialable and this review is made from within this point of view.The graphics are gorgeous like any game released in the last 5 years can be but not to the extremes where my 1070 couldn’t run it on High settings. The only main flaw I can point out, something I  dislike, is the “” that characters suffer most often than not when living in the cruel realm of Unreal Engine 4. Other than that, the world is as gorgeous or as scary as it must be. The characters look really good and seem to be believable human beings rather than ubisoft-eyed glitched androids. Developers certainly worked hard in making them to create realistic skin imperfections, hair, eyes, and mainly the eyelashes. Simply gorgeous work. The animations are sometimes weird, and Tyler’s beard is not their best product but this aside it’s all really good.The entire first chapter is a slow tutorial in itself, which takes about 30 minutes. Here you’ll get some lore exposition and character info along with the controls and basic mecanics for stats, crafting, fighting and interacting with the environtment. You will have to learn to guide yourself within the environment as well since there is no map. I would love to say something good about the tutorial but I 𝐟𝐤𝐧 hate when the player is made walk at a slow pace, while another character talks and a prompt to “PUSH E” appears in your face. I wish it was skippable, but it isn’t.Controls are good except one thing. The “throwable items” button coincides with the “exit menu” command. Guess who wasted a huge amount of precious limited throwable items ammo. Yup. I repeatedly threw my 𝐬𝐡𝐢𝐭 around while trying to quickly close a menu.The environment and scenery are dynamic and varied. Is one of the focus points of the game. You can go from a wide forest where the danger seems to lurk behind every tree and bush to a narrow and claustrophobic corridor. As you explore, you will notice the game gives you no map to check. This is because the world is designed in such a way you don’t really need a map. The signs scattered around is all you need to arrive at your destination. It is easy enough to guide yourself because the different zones are interconnected by rather simple multiple paths, some with a free surprise in them. Other players may call this simplicity a flaw, I say it does the job well, you don’t notice this “limitation” during gameplay and makes things all the more enjoyable taking away from the player the task of navigating a complex world. In some games having to open a map to guide yourself around may be a good thing, but in this game i believe they made the right choice, so to never break the tension and immersion.The sound design is excelent. The music choice is great, both for melancholic moments and for tense fights, for intrigue and solitude, and most important of all, the seemingly ‘random’ clues and foreshadowing sounds that something dangerous may happen soon.The character’s depth is one of the game’s focus points, which means they are well developed and you WILL get to know them, one way or another. I can’t enter into much detail without spoiling stuff, but I must say the characters go through an arch and solid development which makes them seem to have depth and sustance, each one of them. They are people with a heavy past, a turbulent present and a questionable future, it is your job as the player to find out why i say this.There is a good amount of enemies and bosses in the game. You SURELY won’t get bored in solitude. The design behind the enemies is also diverse. Each enemy with it’s own attack pattern and characteristic combat style. They enter your journey at a controlled pace, slow and steady. The bossfights are unique, no boss is repeated. No cheap reskin or recycled bossfights. The final boss is simple but great quality, although a short fight. It is challenging and coherent with the theme of the game and it is one of the highlights in my opinion.While the game may not be entirely unique in anything it does, it follows a set of well known rules of a working formula very well adding in it’s own twist. There is a level up by perk system to improve health, sanity and spiritual energy related stuff and weapons are crafted.There are some anti-cheese mechanics that make combat actually quite fun and engagin. You can’t just spam attack and be merry with it. There is a “cage stage” where you HAVE to learn to fight. In hardest difficulty this is engaging and challenging enough to keep you tense but not enough to frustrate you out of your mind and ragequit.  Choose your confrontations wisely. I had to go back a chapter once because I messed up my resource management. The AI of the enemies is not perfect, sometimes they may break due to weird pathing but nothing too serious. They are “on a leash” though, so you can exit their “leash range” and leave them behind, but keep in mind, you may have to go back where they are waiting for you in the future.Exploration is as rewarded as it often is in a survival horror title, quite minimal and only to gather some extra resources.There is a cool “panic attack” mechanic that will make you run for safety when it is prompted, it is an innovative thing i have never seen before, it is not like Amnesia’s Sanity meter nor is it similar to Daymare’s hallucination mechanic, its different.  Sadly there are no unlockable items, no extra game-modes or difficulty . The only incentive towards replayability is the multiple endings available to the player.  Despicable practice in my opinion. Most of the game’s lore exposition, as in most survival horror games, happens through written documents, but there is some good environmental story telling that if you rush through the game running you may unwillingly ignore. I would suggest paying attention to what’s around you. Like Ricky and Betty’s storyThe game launches you in a WTF situation, no real introduction no real feeling of the situation, you are just suddenly there and good-effing-luck my dude. The first chapter is an unskippable PRESS W simulator.It is hard to call this “Survival” when no savepoint is necessary. There are constant checkpoints even in the hardest mode that will undo any mistake you make every couple of minutes. Dialogue options are way too vague and feel a bit irrelevant.Weapon design is unique but underdevelped, in the end you’d wish for more possible choices.Once the intearction is over, NPCs just stand there watching the wall, in case it moves.I love this genre and I’ve spent countless hours in games like this one. This game ticks all the boxes for a great Survival Action Horror experience with an uncommon and original setting and tool-set.I may be running into a case of pareidolia, but i think there is a possible message to this game, about how we often give in to sorrow, how we fall victim of anger, and how we are conditioned by guilt or devoured by lonliness, blinded by pride & ego. How misguided we get from resentment, and how often, as we get to grow closer with people and to know them better, we sometimes carry part of their burden with us and share ours.
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: The Chant visually is enthralling. The eldritch horrors are designed wonderfully, and the boss encounters are fantastic to look at. Sadly, thats the only real plus for this game.The narrative, the characters, the setting/lore - its all incredibly predictable, to the point that when plot points come in they fall pretty flat. I wondered briefly if this was intentional, and the designers were aiming for a by-the-numbers story in order to either parody it (riffing on the old cosmic horror films of the days gone by) or to let the gameplay shine: neither of those things proved to be true. - The game has an interesting premise with your stats in that you have Mind, Body, and Spirit. Mind depletes in "terrifying situations" and once dropped you need to run away for a bit to recover. This can be restored through meditation or consumables, but using meditation depletes your Spirit which essentially is your mana pool thats used for the abilities you unlock (more on that in a moment). Finally you have Body - your health pool.Depending on your actions through the game (the items you find, the combat you partake in, the dialogue options you take), you'll be silently boosting one of these stats that determines which one of the three endings you get - this is a frustration simply because I dont wish to spend my time replaying the entire game to see what one of three 1 minute long endings you could get.The other frustration off this is that all the possible options you do have no perceivable effect on the actual story in game. - You're taught how to make "mystical" sticks to fight your enemies. If you run out of resources to make these, you can sort of "shout" at the enemies and that causes a small amount of damage.Due to enemies having lots of health, combat largely became about mashing the attack button with whatever you had to hand, dodging occasionally when they telegraphed their attacks.Mentioned above, but your Mind depletes in terrifying situations (typically in areas of "Gloom"), so some of the busier combat scenes become a race against the clock to finish off the enemies before you get terrified. Thats a kind of cool premise, but then when you do get scared it just means you cant attack for a bit till you regain control for a short time. In one of the final boss fights it was largely just a case of attacking lots, backing off, recovering, repeat.You do get spells however, but this deserves its own section: - For context, each of the characters has a different coloured crystal. When you get their crystal, you gain a new skill thats reflective of that person. The guy with self worth issues has one that allows you to cause huge spikes to explode out around you (pushing others away etc), the girl who feels largely used and unseen has one that lets you go invisible as long as you dont attack - so on and so forth.On the surface layer, this is a fun link but if you start overthinking it, its a bit rough. These are people, as two dimensional as they are, suffering from trauma in various forms. It feels kinda icky to be reducing that to a quick button tap spell. On a mechanic level, most the spells are rarely touched. I found myself using the spike one the most (and the game recognises this would be the case by making it cost more to use than the other spells), but quite often you find yourself unwilling to use the spells in favour of hanging on to your spirit to keep your mind topped up.When you gain the crystal of someone, you are tapping into their "negative energy". This has some cool moments when you're exploring their areas where you get to hear their thoughts, their feelings - this felt lik a vastly underused feature.Instead of simply receiving a spell, I'd have loved to have spent more time exploring their psyche, learning more about their situation (and a chance for the writers to push the boundaries on each of the characters past their cliched templates), and then feeling like I had earned the "spell" - I needed to call this out as one of the most frustrating parts of the game. At times, a mass of flies forming a human shape will appear and pursue you at a brisk walking speed. This is supposed to be a representation of your dead sister (the source of your trauma and reason for being on the island). You know this cause she loudly complains about how you let her die and so on, so forth. If she catches up with you, you can attack her to dispel the flies briefly, or she can grab you and kill you off. Because of how she moves, shes at best a nuisance that ruins any tension and makes exploring an area mildly annoying.It would have been far better to utilise her as a way to give more backstory - when she catches you, have snippets of the past play out. Instead of having her chase constantly, have her watch from afar, an ever present threat and reminder of your trauma. As it stands, by the end of the game its hard to feel any sympathy for the sister (though I hasten to add that its clear its not _actually_ the sister but the Gloom using that memory, but when thats the only side you see of the sister it turns her into an annoyance). - As mentioned at the start, visually the game is delightful and the end boss battle is a great reflection of that. Frustratingly however its just a slog, and if you die you have to start right back from the beginning of the battle - as a result the end battle become a huge chore.This could be acceptable if the end cutscene you received was impressive to balance the hard work. What you get however is a 30 sec-ish cutscene (mentioned further up, based on your style of play). All three endings are "downers" which fits the genre, but could have done with something more. Even if it was like "post events media coverage" while the credits rolled, or snippets of life of the characters before the island, anything really.The Chant, despite the detailed negatives above, isnt a _bad_ game but its largely forgettable. It feels like the team had a great idea they wanted to run with, but werent able to fully realise it for whatever reason. Coupled with a very high initial price point, I'd avoid recommending this game at least until it drops to something like £15.The game has numerous pacing issues, some scenes randomly cut short, though not too many bugs. A poorly implemented combat system hampers a respectable narrative, though the lack of twists or characterisation will leave you largely unsatisfied unless you're a strong fan of the genre.During the first two hours as I played, I considered a few times stopping to refund (I paid £35 for it), but pressed on - I regret not getting the refund while I could.

Sometimes you simply don't have enough resources to kill them all, and you have to run. But it takes a few deaths before you figure that out, since you think you stand a chance at first. That alone is bad. Trial and error is something to avoid building a game around. The Hitman series embraces this to the fullest, and can work in that case. But generally it doesn't. This is one such example.And then there's the toad "boss", which is where I stopped playing to write this. It's just a matter of luck if you manage to kill that one. _childDocuments_.review: A survival horror set in a cultic island convent. Pretty standard setup, which made me a little worried, but I feel like it did a good enough job fleshing out mechanics and working in lore that it was able to set itself apart from the pack.The storyline itself was a little... standard. Not bad, just fairly by the books. I can see flat personalities being a fault of the story; personally, I thought the characters had enough personality to pass as real and it was the story focus that left most of it on the back burner. But I could see people knocking that. The overall storyline of the camp and of the secrets of the island was pretty good though. I haven't found all the lore, so I don't have the whole picture. But that's the way it goes with scattered lore pieces. Jess's personal storyline... I can't quite tell if it could use a little more time in the oven, or if the story just didn't do it justice. It felt like they were trying to play to the mystery of the story, get it piece by piece, the way the rest of the island's lore is paced out. But we the audience had very little investment in the actual story, which means we weren't really encourage to stick with it, so that part of the story ended up feeling shoe-horned in and just... kind of there.The combat system isn't this game's strong suit, but it works well enough. It does the Silent Hill thing of having Jess swing her weapons around like an extremely normal person, which I found a somewhat effective way to heighten the fear factor. The actual mind/body/spirit mechanic was cool, and a decent enough theme for several mechanics to revolve around. I think there were ways it could have been made more effective, but in a survival game with limited resources, I don't blame them for playing it safe; then again, I only beat the game on the default difficulty, so maybe that was something they did on higher difficulties and I just don't know. Basing the endings off which of the stats was highest was also a pretty good move; means you have to worry about what dialogue options you pick, which monsters you take down, and how much of which resources you use. Lot of stuff to keep in mind is a good way to keep the player's brain working - and worrying. The prisms were a decent power system, though I found there was the issue of constantly running out of spirit, even after pumping some prismic crystals into my stats. The actual lore behind why they each did different things was interesting (and I have my own crack theory about why Jess was able to resist the gloom like she did rooted in that), so good on them for that part.The gameplay outside of combat was also cool. The map layout was well constructed, and I love the metroidvania-esk manner in which it opened up further and made shortcuts after getting more crystals. I think the gloom tunnels as the fast travel system were a decent idea, and would have been a very good mechanic... had the entrances been easier to find. The scavenging mechanics stuff worked well enough. And the collecting lore helping recover mind was a stroke of genius; great way to make players want to go after lore, even if they didn't want to read it, and a good way to ensure the player's mind is topped up. Great work on that front.I love, *love* the sanity mechanics of this game. I've seen some other reviews saying "oh, she can't stay in the dark for long or else she has a panic attack, how melodramatic." Except... that's exactly the way that it works. Speaking from personal experience, if you're in an unfamiliar environment, especially one that's more or less totally isolated, even the smallest thing can set your reactive lizard brain off - and in that experience I've had personally, I've never had to deal with unknowable eldritch monsters, but I imagine it only worsens the anxiety of the situation. Well established character fears are the only thing that really set her off outside of the gloom, and those established were also well shown by the story. Some of the things, like just coming out of a panic attack that quickly, were simplified for the sake of gameplay; I can't fault them for that. But for the most part, they did a very good job of showing a rather realistic side of those aspects.6.5-7/10. Pretty by the books stuff, with some interesting off-script ideas, a couple that didn't pan out as well as the devs probably hoped. But there was quite a lot of that 'by the books stuff,' which is more than most games these days can say.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a reluctant Thumbs Down.Overall, the concept is rather good.  It definitively is channeling Lovecraftian vibes.  Game ran well, no bugs that I could see.It is, however, not very polished.  Facial animations are rather stiff.   Voice acting is "acceptable".  There is no mini-map or quest markers so often you'll either have to hit the internet to find out what to do OR wander aimlessly looking for Quest Object A.   You're on a forested island covered in plants and I have to... go find a specific plant.  No markers, no location and only a general "it's over there" instruction.   Even Resident Evil games would have highlighted objects to show they can be interacted with and/or picked up.I did get it on a sale, but still refunded.  Perhaps if they patch this game OR make a Chant 2 I'll try it again.  Until then , unless you enjoy pausing and googling half the time, I'd pass on this game.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't play this game for very long, but I don't think I'll continue. This game is obscenely obnoxious and every chance it had to be scary, it chooses to be annoying instead.On paper it looks like a good third person horror game, you have the monsters, craftable weapons, documents detailing the story, etc. But you know what ruins it for me? That ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ sanity meter. Oh sorry, your "mind meter." Any time, well, ANYTHING happens, the stupid screen has to start going black and white, your character has to start screaming, etc. It's incredibly distracting and adds nothing to the game. You might think, "well, Amnesia had a sanity meter and that worked, so it can't be that bad." But with Amnesia it added a layer of depth to the game because you could not look at enemies directly, or else risk attracting the monsters towards you. Oh, and the things that would drain your sanity in Amnesia were actually scary. This lady will flip ♥♥♥♥ at a stupid flower just sitting on the wall. Or a swarm of flies. It's idiotic as hell. As mentioned before, the effects just distract from the game, and unlike Amnesia it feels like I am constantly low on mind power no matter what I do.You know what? If a horror game is doing its job, you don't need this dumb mechanic saying "Look your character is freaked out omg!" The protagonist is just the eyes to experience the horror from, not the person who should be affected by the horror. Now making a horror protagonist isn't hard, they just need to be sympathetic and mostly silent. Yet they managed to mess that up here too. The protagonist has zero charisma. She is not likable and I find her distracting and pointless, her swearing incessantly at any situation adds nothing.Just look at the most revered horror games of all time, what do they all have in common? They're games where everyone just shuts the f--- up and lets the monsters and atmosphere speak for themselves. We don't need the player character to chew the scenery to understand it's a horror game. This could have been a diamond in the rough like The Evil Within but instead it's worthless.

_childDocuments_.review: Adventure! Horror! Cults! Psychedelic drugs! Lovecraft? Psychology? You know there is such a thing as too many ingredients, right? I’m getting ahead of myself so why don’t we take a trip to Glory Island to see if the horror adventure game The Chant is worthy of a vacation to.ProsA pretty island settingCool creature designsFree DLC expansion that continues the story (more on this later)Solid opening that makes you think you’re about to play a b-horror movie with several good ideas howeverConsThe game takes itself too seriously by hopping into another genre while the other genres established take a back seat with said several ideas ending up being duck tapped together and as a result the game as a whole is a messSeveral of the games mechanics are undercooked and probably could have been cut out. There’s a few dialogue choice you are given which seem to only give you XP in one of the three stats rather than make any significant difference to the events of the story. There’s even a portal hub system that I completely forgot about until I stumbled across it again starting my second play through. The upgrade system also feels like an after-thought, outside of increasing how much you have of the three stats the rest seemed to make minimal difference to game play. Hell I didn’t even unlock the ability to upgrade my dodge until I was basically at the end of the main game.Combat consists of using craftable weapons/throwables/traps and powers you unlock as the story progresses with three different flavors of the enemy types. Using the appropriate one will deal more damage but there isn’t really a downside to using the incorrect one. Said new powers you gain from progressing the story I ended up finding that I barely used them in game simply because I just didn’t have enough resources to utilize them often and when I did I just used one of them. I got this same experience even when attempting a build based on using said powers and even then found myself mostly using melee attacks.The story feels like it was written by multiple writers who each did separate sections of the story with minimal consultation with each other and then they duct taped it all together. As a result of this, there are several moments that come off as unintentionally funnyThe characters, who are also bland enough I have a hard time remembering their names, sometimes come off as if having multiple personalities literally going from “everything is fine” to “I’m completely losing my ♥♥♥♥” the very next scene.There are three endings to the main game however it’s safe to assume that with the inclusion of the DLC that only one of them is cannon considering that’s how it continues. This might not be so bad if the ending for the DLC also didn’t leave off on obvious sequel bait. Speaking of which…Mini review for Into the Gloom DLCPros Combat feels slightly improved; I had more chances to use the powers you’ve gained from the prisms much more often but still resorted to using just one of the powers.A new craftable weapon and a new craftable throwable/trapCons  It plays vastly different from the main game, its less story focused and plays more like a rogue lite where if you die you just return to the main hub with only your XP and key items. Unlocked short cuts also remain unlocked when this happens and everything you’ve collected or killed respawns as well.None of your stats from the main game are carried over into this and same issue with the upgrade system I had in the main game seems to have carried over with even more fluff.So would I recommend The Chant? Not really, this game feels very much like a game by committee with minimal leadership. If it’s on sale or you’re curious, it’s a harmless enough purchase but this isn’t a game I would recommend seeking out. There is too many different ingredients in this dish to make it a special experience and there for I give The Chant 2 Glooms out of 5.

_childDocuments_.review: I give this a thumbs up, but it's with some caveats.Firstly, the story is good. Mourning the loss of her sister, protagonist Jess embarks on a retreat, where her friend Kim is already ensconced. Pretty soon you realise this retreat is not all it seems, where a chant goes wrong and starts affecting the group. You set off and figure out not all is what it seems with the group. You fight magical enemies with magical melee weapons to get through and figure out what's happening with everyone. As far as stories go, it's simple, but conveys the message well.The graphics are also good. Nothing AAA, but the animations, world, ambience, and lighting were all pretty good. I felt immersed in the world the game created. Also, I'll give props to the voice acting in the game, too. All acting was believable and conveyed the right emotions at the right times without any hint of force. Good job.I will also commend the game for its stability. I don't recall it crashing even one time. No stuttering, glitches, or breaks of any kind.Now here's where things get a bit shaky:Anyway, I know I listed all the stuff I disliked, but overall I do recommend this game. The combat is fulfilling, once you figure out what to do, and the puzzle elements are well integrated, despite me not being able to see them immediately. I got more enjoyment out of the game once I downgraded the difficulty. It's a good price for what it is, even without a sale.

Visuals and audio are good technically speaking, but art direction is great.As for cons, there are few. Animation is a bit off/yanky andfacial expressions of characters are limited. Fight mechanics are a bit frustrating at the beginning (but for me this just needed a little practice).Game also have free DLC with true ending, that's also kinda roguelite mode.Whole thing can be finished under 10 hours, but they are packed with fun survival horror themed in quasi cosmic horror. Overall this game deserves a recommendation, it is a hidden AA gem, worth of giving it a shot, especially on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: LDR: The Chant is a game that resembles an old fashion Resident Evil in 3rd in third person but peppered with a bit of crafting, leveling and melee combat. While the game has a very interesting premise, the execution is mid level. The DLC, at least to me, was fun(er).Story: Jess, a woman trying to both get away from a past trauma and rekindle a friendship, decides it's a good idea to go to a island retreat that reeks of cult within 2 seconds flat. And, of course, everything goes wrong and you summon the Upside Down from Stranger Things (The Gloom). You Will spend the majority of your time exploring zones that get progressively unlocked and as you go through the ''gloom'', you will hear inner dialogue of different NPCs, understanding their different traumas or better understanding their personalities, all the while trying to save them. Sadly, it isn't greatly executed and the story tends to take a backseat and make much less sense as it tends to make bounds and leaps.Gameplay: The game attempts to include dodging mechanics, melee combat, a sanity gauge, a leveling system and a few spells to boot. It's a lot for how small a studio it is, and while the main game handles it in an acceptable fashion, the DLC manages to do a lot better. There are resources to loot and they are scarce, making them very important, as they allow you to craft weapons and items to use in combat.There are 3 types of melee weapons to craft (each more effective towards a specific enemy type and situation) and 3 different consumables. You WILL want to switch a lot.It is important to use said consumables, combat will get much easier once you accept you can't just melee through the whole game.The gloom, a place that hosts parasites, a strange flora and enemies, is a basically the focal point of the story as it it locked behind many different colored gems that you will accumulate over the story, thus allowing you to explore further (and unlocked new spells). Though it initially feels like you can explore a lot, it's mostly linear and involves a bit of backtracking along with some light puzzle solving. Different spells will unlock as the game progresses, however the cost to use said spells tends to be too high, IMO.You gain 3 different types of XP (each go along with their respective gauges); mind, body and spiritual energy. Using restorative items will restore the corresponding gauge and give you a bit of XP, downing enemies with specific colors will also grant you respective XP. Even dialogue choices will give you respective XP (While it's probably the biggest XP amount, there'S like 5 or 6 times in the whole game you get to pick dialogue). Graphics: The gloom environment especially stood out with its originality and attention to details. It's no triple A game, but it looked good overall. I did not experience at glitches.Audio: The majority of the tracks fitted well, and the atmosphere is well executed. While not every dialogue flows in a manner that is logical, the voice actors did a fine job. I recommend it only if the trailer interests you, and try to get it under 20$.

_childDocuments_.review: Short Review: Yeah it was decent. The story is pretty good and the combat is simple yet engaging (very similar to Senua's Sacrifice tbh). I do recommend this game but heavily on sale; I bought this game recently when it was on sale for 80% off, $6,48 CDN. I would say that's all I'd be willing to pay for it, but the dev's have provided a free DLC with loads more gameplay which, honestly, makes me suggest to buy the game full price to support such a classy move.Long Review: I had fun shouting "Pocket Sand" and "Essential Oils" as I attacked enemies, I also enjoyed looking at the final boss and saying to myself "I ain't got enough sage for this". The game has a great lovecraftian story told decently well, but is also more comedic than it is horror with how much it ties in new-age spiritualist and vegan stereotypes as combat weapons and mechanics. The issue is that it's short, I beat it in 5 hours. There are 3 endings, but considering the game is 100% linear I don't think the story lends itself well to being played 3 times. The endings are also really anti-climactic to be honest.That all said, I know they offered a free DLC called "The Gloom Below," which is only available after you achieve the mind ending, and is a rogue-like version with new mechanics to encourage repeatability. I'm gonna be honest with you, I'd promote this game for that reason alone, it's a real classy move on the dev's part. Most developers would have charged another full game price for that kind of DLC, but these folks are just giving away likely 200%-400% more gametime for free.

_childDocuments_.review: The game is short, entertaining if not a bit predictable. Which isn't a bad thing I watch a lot of horror so I picked up on the plot fast and hoped it would deviate a bit but it stayed true if you like Cult horror movies and some survival horror on rails then this game is for you  SPOILERS: || I wish that Monroe was more flushed out or they did more with him, I honestly thought Tyler was going to turn out to be him or that he'd become an Ally once he was found instead of going immediately agro, given what you can learn from lore pick-ups. I also wished the game explained why things like your fear of flies happen. or why your sister appeared as a swarm of them. but in all the lore I found in the game nothing explained why that was a thing.|| I also liked how the three endings are tied to more controllable actions and gameplay instead of just dialog choices or simple A, B, or C choices in certain spots, which is a refreshing mechanic imo.

_childDocuments_.review: Just in the middle of playing 'The Gloom Below' DLC but I get the general idea and have played through the main game to leave my two cents on the subject.Not a bad little project at all honestly, nothing that will blow anyone's socks off and the whole thing is a bit of a cheese festival with very rapid pacing and easily forgettable characters, but you can see there is some love behind it, enough to make it stand out from other indie titles and make it worth at least one playthrough if you like weird, culty, almost Lovecraftian inspired ritual type themes. Its pretty short, even has an achievement for running it in 4 hours.There's a particularly heavy emphasis on combat, namely battering things with twigs and incense or casting what I guess is "mind/psi magic" that you channel through different coloured crystals, though I did come to realise later that a lot of the combat scenarios you run into are optional and you can just ignore them if you want to speed run the game...I imagine you wouldn't be at much of a disadvantage vs someone who has a fully decked out skill tree either. Beyond that you mostly run around this island in a fairly linear progressive path as you gain new powers and upgrade your abilities, occasionally having to solve pretty rudimentary "puzzles" or find keys while listening to the obnoxious inner thoughts of the others you meet at the beginning of the game as they all lose their minds one by one to the...whatever the ♥♥♥♥ it is you're fighting. Resources are somewhat scarce, and your usable items all have durability, so you have to keep crafting new versions with what you can find since they break quickly or have only a few charges at most so you gotta kinda use them wisely, but its not completely detrimental if you aren't min-maxing your choices.Its simple all in all, but has a certain charm to it that makes its a recommendation in my book. The DLC seems to be set after the events of the main game and appears to be a sort of rogue-lite situation where dying resets most of your progress but has a definitive end if you survive. I'm usually a bit iffy with rogue-lite games, not a fan of the whole getting real far then dying to some ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and having to go through 30+ minutes of content again immediately, but ill give it a run as it seems to introduce some new mechanics from the base game.

_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: This game ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ rocks. _childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: Honestly, I ended up enjoying this more than I thought I would. I mean, obviously, it has all the expectable AA jank (cheap animations and motion capture, graphical quality being somewhat inconsistent etc.). But I do admire it for its ambition, as it certainly strives to reach a level comparable to other big survival horror titles, which elevates it a lot above your average indie horror game.The combat and crafting systems are surprisingly complex, even though the upgrade system might seem a bit too simplistic. Additionally, dialogue choices and your particular use of abilities or items builds toward one of three endings, even though they are relatively short. There is even a fast travel system, and the unlockable areas do function similar to the classic RE system of backtracking for more secrets/collectibles. Some puzzles also sprinkle your way through the chapters, and in typical survival horror fashion, resource management is key, a well-implemented mechanic. The graphics is also very realistic in most parts apart from the facial details and animations.The story was intriguing in itself, and the atmosphere created was rather immersive. Leaning heavily into cosmic and psychological horror, it manages to give some depth to the characters and create a convincing setting. The creature design was also on point with the thematic, even though it's generally not disturbing.In general, it's a game I'd highly recommend to anyone who's a fan of survival horror. But do not expect an AAA experience here; it's obviously much lower-budget, which you can see from its price as well. It is very memorable, however.P.S. If you can, do try to buy the PC physical edition instead; it's what I did, and it's a great piece for collectors. Enjoy!
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: A cool little horror game that went on longer than I expected and maybe a little longer than I wanted. The setting, story, characters, and voice acting are all good, and the exploration was mostly okay. Environment graphics were good, the creatures were really good, and the faces were not too uncanny, with often excellent expressiveness. The body animation especially in cutscenes was not as good. This seems pretty common; I had a similar experience in House of Ashes recently.Combat was tedious and brought Spiders games to mind, though that might be a little pejorative since Spiders games are notorious jankorees. Almost all I did in this game, much like Mars War Logs long ago, was left click a few times then dodge and repeat. Occasionally oils, after remapping keys so I wasn't constantly wasting them by accident. Traps would have been way too much trouble. Almost never used any powers, because I never had even close to enough spirit to spend on them. I often didn't have any weapons because they burn out and crafting them requires rare resources that make you choose between which weapon to craft without knowing which you were going to want. Dropping crafting entirely would be no loss to this game at all. Also, in most cases which weapon you used didn't matter that much anyway, so either dropping that mechanic or making it closer to mandatory would be better. The RPG style upgrade mechanic would have been better if it were linear because I don't see how players would be likely to have different enough playstyles to warrant it.It took me a few sessions to get through The Chant because of the annoyingness of combat. I started out playing on hard, then didn't play for a while, then later on was very annoyed at constantly running out of resources, remembered it was on hard, set it to easy and was able to get through the story without tearing out too much of my hair. And it was worth it, because I enjoyed the game up to the end, if you consider the end to be the last scene before the three attribute-based endings. Attribute-based endings might have been a good idea in principle but I have no idea what "mind" had do to with the one I saw and I've seen other reviews bemoaning the others.Oh yeah, while the "tragic backstories," "exploitative cult with even more and uglier secrets than most exploitative cults" and "crikey, monsters turn out to be real and I seem to have a previously hidden talent for fighting them" aspects of the story were all in good fun, a chunk of the story I could have done without was the pro-vaxxer virtue signaling-style sermon that just went on and on throughout the disproportionately long green crystal chapter. I get it, you trust the science. I have various vaccines floating around in my system too. I don't need a medal for it. Let's move on.It's sincerely swell that the devs provided a free DLC which reportedly has an even endinger ending. I hear it's mostly combat, so I guess I'll never know, unless I come across a Let's Play video. Edit: I did but didn't learn a ton. Looks like combat got a bunch more complicated though, in a vaguely Dishonored-like way.Like every game ever and also everything else, it's better to buy this on sale. Does anyone ever not buy a game on sale?Summary: Mostly good, and I'll be interested in seeing other games from this studio.
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: While the game is mechanically a bit clunky as is a bit of the voice acting, overall this is actually a pretty cool little action adventure romp in a lovecraftian cult setting. I enjoyed it more, the more I played. The combat is mostly spent scrabbling on the ground avoiding melee attacks, but once I realised I didn't have to fight everyone I had more resources to spare etc and things were a bit smoother.Graphics are good, creature designs are very good indeed. I never felt like the powers I got really worked that well though - was just pressing the button but never felt like my powers were kicking in. The throwables worked but often resulted in me throwing more than one which is an expensive mistake.A good bit of cosmic horror for a quiet afternoon!
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: I had fun with 'The Chant', but I can't recommended this in good faith unless:1)  You're a big fan of Lovecraftian horror2)  You're willing to put up with low budget production value, janky combat, unnecessarily complicated crafting and occasionally frustrating auto-saves.  If this was a movie it would be one of Clive Barker's lesser ones.On the + side, I don't think I had any major bugs in the entirety of my play-though, and performance was never an issue.If both of those are true, you may have fun with it, but I'd still pick it up on sale.P.S.  The free DLC is better-designed in terms of mechanics than the main campaign, and provides a nice finisher to the story, it is absolutely worth playing through if you make it through the campaign.
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty fun game. My biggest issue is I got lost a lot. Had to look up a guide for one particular section but since guides are free online I won't count that against anything. The enemy designs are nice, the environments are nice, gameplay is simple but smooth and the combat doesn't feel clunky to me.  But I can only recommend this game at a discount. I know my play time says 11 hours but that's because I'm such a slow gamer and, as I said, got lost a lot. But looking at all that was accomplished the scale is rather small.A bigger complaint is story wise I never got to know any of the people who died. Which is what I mean by "small scale".  We go from 0 to "Oh ♥♥♥♥♥" so fast that by the time the first guy starts going crazy, the only reason I keep going is because I'm super interested in what happens next. Unfortunately the story is very insular and to me it feels like not even the notes reveal much. Could have used more time developing the other camp people.  So when they died I was like "Uh...well bye."  I kinda liked Maya, her story felt the most tragic at least. So tl;dr, a decent game, buy it when its on sale. Also the concept of sage and essential oils being your main weapons against evil inter-dimensional demons is hilarious af.
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: SOME SPOILERS AHEADI think this is a solid horror title compared to the crap we usually get these days.  I would describe it as Silent Hill meets Stranger Things.  It is a rather quick playthrough, but at least the gameplay is coherent.  You get used to the crafting stuff quick.  I played it on hard mode and it's not all that difficult, just as long as you understand how to dodge enemies.  The main thing about this game is the story.  I wouldn't say that it is very deep, but it does have a lot of interesting elements that all work together.  I really like the "prismic energy" cult thing, along with the alchemy stuff.  The design of the island and the lore behind it are all good too.  Like I said, it's nothing that we haven't seen before, but it's put together in a coherent way.  It was a little goofy that all of the characters interacted with Jess in intimate ways despite her only being on the island for a few hours, but I guess it can be kinda explained with plot points in memos. I felt that the endings were a little shallow, not sure if the DLC ending is opening up for a sequel or not.  To be honest, I think if they were to continue on, they would be way better off with a prequel back in the commune days (they completely set it all up).  I love retro stuff, that would be fun.  When this game originally dropped, I watched a live playthrough of it by SHN; he really disliked this game, but I felt like I wanted to give it a chance myself some day.  Unfortunately this game has been undervalued by the horror community, which is a shame because it doesn't feel like some cheap cash-in like most horror games these days.  Obviously some love went into this game with the writing and I hope the studio keeps up with what they are doing.
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: The Chant hits the right tone for the genre. The look, the sound, the sense of panic and the limited resources. The sense of foreboding before your desperate plans inevitably turn out against you. Exactly as it should be.In retrospect, the game is very linear, but it doesn't really feel that way for most of it because of the great level design that twists and turns back on itself like a knot.Bonus that a free expansion is available with everything from the base game except a plot :D
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoy psychological horror games that rely on the narrative and environments to slowly introduce a sense of growing dread as you play. The chant absolutely does that while introducing some welcome new mechanics to the genre.It's not a AAA game so lets get that out the way first. There is a certain level of AA jank present most notably in the facial animations. Its really not bad either, just that our standards are so high because the benchmark in games is so high these days. I will also add that in horror AA games are always far more scary than ultra polished AAA titles as the jank adds some rawness to things.The story feels like its something out of the early 90's. In a good way. The setting and themes are unsettling to me. It's sort of a cosmic supernatural horror that you aren't so used to having to deal with.The combat reminds me a little bit of the first Alan Wake game but with more variety and choices. You can also choose to run and avoid many of the encounters if you prefer. I like the fact you have that option. Some things do force you into an arena of sorts but alot of times if you are low on resources its better to run.The pacing is good. The narrative flows at a good pace and it feels like you are always moving forwards. The story bookmarks its self in specific that let you know you are making progress or have completed a 'chapter' and make it clear how much you have left to do. All of this is built into the narrative presentation.Overall i had a really good time with this game and played through it a couple of times. It's one of those games i will keep going back to replay every few years just because i enjoy the genre.More importantly i'm really interested to see what the developers do next. There is clearly a talented team behind this that have done an incredible job at delivering something that feels unique and fresh with limited resources.
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: I was not expecting to enjoy this game as much as I did! They really went all out with the spiritual enlightenment story arc AND mechanics. Having a mind, heart, and soul levels to help stay alive in any given situation in the game was something I was not expecting but was very much pleased. Game looks and feels great, story isn't amazing but it's a full story (although the "Spirit" ending I got felt super rushed and really no explanation). Runtime of 8-9 hours is pretty good, but perhaps the typical price tag is a bit higher, as I did get it on sale. If you see this game on sale and enjoy adventure games with some combat and a little bit of crafting/lite RPG elements, jump on it.
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: A fun survival horror with truly unique idea and combat. The story is thin though and after the first boss fight the rest of the fight might feel a bit repetitive until the final boss (final boss was fun!). None of the characters are likeable save for the main character lol but the game is not about story or character development anyway. It's just a fun exploration of a mysterious island while trying to survive against demon from another dimension. The graphic is very good and some locations are very beautiful. Animation is great, i especially like the dodge animation. The weapons and stats are unique and refreshing. There are 3 different endings depending on your stats. I'd say not really replayable but it was quite a fun journey from start to finish.
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: WOW! WOW! WOW! The Chant is amazing. I mean, it is a game with a strong heart. It might have lacked some final polish (and budget), but despite that, it feels and plays amazingly. The only thing I can complain about is the combat, which feels kind of good, but lacks some “juice”. The models and environments look amazing. Personally, I didn’t like the soundtrack. I understand the choice of the synthy vibes, but it didn’t sit with me all the time. Like in the finale, I expected some monumental and memorable tunes, and there weren’t any of those. I love cinematic narratives in video games and The Chant really could have used more and a bit longer, moodier cutscenes. There were some of those, but like the final cutscene was too fast for me. The UI designs are worth noting because all the menus are simply gorgeous. I love the 3-stat system, especially with the panic attacks. But I think that’s kinda limited, especially because the game is very linear (well, semi-open, but with me kissing all the walls there was no need to go back anywhere). If your next game happens to be another horror (which is my silent hope) I would love to see that mechanic expanded in an open environment (like the Baker’s House from RE7). Nonetheless, despite its flaws, I love this game.
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: The Chant is surprisingly good! It's short and pretty easy, I beat it on the max difficulty in under 9 hours, and while there's a little room for secondary completion replay and achievement hunting, there's not too many extra hours of gameplay left in there. That said, what is there is cool. You beat up cult people with sage sticks and get lovecraftian style super powers, that's pretty rad. The story is a cool in a, you've gotta suspend your disbelief and just enjoy the ride kinda vibe. It's super campy and doesn't take itself too seriously, while keeping things just creepy enough to actually be really cool. There's definitely a big stranger things influence in the art and horror, and it works for sure. Every one of the wild upside-down style monsters you go up against are honestly incredibly well brought to life. Worth a play for sure if it looks good to you on the outside, what you see is absolutely what you get, and then some.
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: Overall the game started off good.I was intrigued by the story of the game, but as the game kept progressing everything was so cliche and started to become bored of it.  As I approached the end of the game, I felt the game was just dragging on, the combat system very slow and annoying, I also found myself running out of inventory extremely quickly. (I was playing on regular mode)The only thing making me want to complete the game was because, I wanted another game to be checked off as complete.4/10
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: Wow this game really is something special. a hidden gem and a game people will find, overtime, to be better than this has any real right to be. The combat is most enjoyable on harder difficulties i feel that they were going for a souls-esk feel to combat with stun locking enemies and dodging out of the way of their patterns or dying horribly. not something i expected to be implemented so well. the story keeps you on the edge of your seat on you uncover the mysteries of glory island and its crystal science. a great blend of lovecraft and prismatic "science" that nonsense crystal magic, brings to life a story that is a deep dive into madness, great visuals and engaging gameplay. very cool of the devs to release free dlc that adds onto one of the endings. this they seem to up the difficulty a bit, as you should be use to by now and they add in rouge-like elements on what was already there. very ambitious and rather interesting. i find the game fun to even come back to after awhile to see the other endings. i highly recommend this game i wish they make more lovecraft inspired work. cult classic for sure.

_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: I just spent the last 7 hours binge playing this game till I beat it. I did not mean to but I got pretty wrapped up into this game.Things I like: The story concept and characters: though predictable it was still engaging enough to where I didn't skip through anything; The monsters and combat: Quite a variety and different ways to approach things can even run from most combat if you want to. The skill tree was a surprise too but it did encourage me to explore for upgrade materials so I liked that. I think I got the majority of the collectibles and I did enjoy the story written out in the notes I actually read each one. This game is also visually gorgeous with the environments and colors big fan. Things I didn't like(Spoilerish if you are interested in playing I encourage you to play and give it a shot before reading this) One hit kills. Just no. That's always eternally frustrating especially when you hit that load screen too many times because of it. I feel the story could have been fleshed out a little more with the whole compound this game kinda feels like a prequel to something bigger especially once you hit the endings. Which there are 3 endings but none of them really affect much they all feel like short sequel bait which could have been done better. Also I did get lost a time or two a small map would have been cool and more reasons to use the teleporting.Overall though This is a great game and a fun run. 7 hours of play if you muck about and collect things like I did. I'd love a second game to delve more into this cosmic horror.
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: I will recommend this game, yes. However, there are issues with it.The crafting resources you need to craft the main weapons; mainly sage, branches. Are unnecessarily rare. I never found myself without a weapon, but there was a time or two where my only weapon was fire oil. I also wouldn't call this game 'Scary' or 'Horror' theme. I would call it suspenseful. That isn't a bad thing, but I don't exactly know what it's missing that would have made it 'Horror'. It's missing something though. My loading times were also not very good. Not the in-game loading. That was quick. But the initial load INTO the game was pretty excessive for me.One more thing, I found it difficult to distinguish between the three consumables when they were bottled, due to the dark nature of the enviroments. A nice quality of life update would be displaying the name of the resource on screen when you hover over it instead of wondering what it is and it just telling you your inventory for that resource is full.  I found myself several times consuming lavender to try and free up space to pick it up, when it was actually ginger or spirit caps. - - - - - - - - - The enviroments were beautiful though. Every area felt unique and I never felt bored exploring them. The enemies were also beautifully dark. That's the way I would explain them. The fact that a lot of them were flora based was a wonderful idea and it reflected in their design. Combat was fluid too. It didn't feel janky or sluggish. The weapon wheel was easy to navigate and switching between them didn't feel cumbersome at all. Overall, I would give this a 7.5 out of 10. Not a bad game, just needs a little polishing

_childDocuments_.review: I’ve never heard about The Chant until it suddenly appeared at the storefronts and something about it made me curious. And now that I’ve finished it, I’d still call it “curious”. A pleasant variety of curious, though, and quite likely worth your time if you like horror themed action adventure titles of the survival action-esque variety.So yeah, it’s not a horror themed adventure game or a title where you run and hide all the time. The game knows that it’s, sadly, a big deal in modern times as well and establishes that it has combat in a short introductory section way before there’s any real danger. In fact, the game is surprisingly swift and concise with a lot of the things. It doesn’t really rush through the story as much as moving at a constant and confident pace, discarding a lot of the superficial and building up “just enough” of anything before letting you try it out for yourself and move on.It does help that the main mechanics are quite simple, as you have a very primitive combat with a dodge and a push options, simple crafting of weapons/tools and an almost unnecessary upgrade screen. It all works well enough, even though apparently there is a perfect dodge and a perfect push, since there are abilities for it, but the game never explains how that works and whatever timings I’ve tried I never saw them trigger. But even with that somewhat undercooked idea that slightly reminded me of Resident Evil: Outbreak (and Illbleed) works just fine and after some time in the beginning, where you might be tight on resources, you will learn to manage them well soon after.The story is also really well done, with characters addressing everything you’d expect them to, having some fun banter and also not shying away from some unexpectedly heavy topics. But not the ones that are often touched upon in horror, which also felt fresh. The game constantly balances out the ridiculousness of the cosmic horror that’s going on with pragmatism of the characters that feel grounded and it works fantastically.That is, until almost the very end. For whatever reason, the ending 20 minutes of the game or so are just non-stop trash fire with poorly designed bosses and an ending that just happens, seemingly because the developers just didn’t know what to do. It’s a real shame because – as mentioned, the swiftness of things felt completely controlled and intended up until then. And then suddenly the game just falls flat on its face so hard you’d never expect it coming.Nevertheless, I genuinely enjoyed my time with The Chant. It’s a really fun survival action-ish title, with cool story and characters and a pretty neat soundtrack. Don’t expect it to blow your mind, but do expect to be pleasantly surprised by just how good this game can be.
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: I was impressed to begin with. Then I found out this was the studio's first game. Really looking forward to good things from this group. The story is solid, with interesting characters and plenty of lore to root around for while exploring the island. The game isn't long but it isn't short either. Sort of hits that sweet spot where it doesn't overstay its welcome but it also doesn't make you pissed you spent the money, plus the three endings should add to replayability. Simple but cool combat system that evolves at a steady pace, keeping things from getting stale as you play. Fun puzzles. Lovely environment. A few little moments of jank here and there but you get that in AAA games, too. So what if a person's hair occasionally wiggles or their clothes ruffle strangely? I like that the game uses inter-dimensional, cosmic horror as a metaphor for the ways people deal with or don't deal with their emotions. Trauma is a big theme in this game. Nice to play a female protagonist. I love seeing equal representation, especially when it feels natural to the story. A few minor issues with pacing maybe? The opening felt a little rushed but I guess they were trying to get to the conflict. I like a lazy, slow pace when establishing characters but I guess that bores most audiences. There's gonna' be a point where you think you're at the end and you'll be like, "Oh this feels like they had a deadline to meet..." but then it's not over and you go, "Oh... Nice!" and keep playing. Honestly, I really loved the game and plan on playing it on my stream soon.

_childDocuments_.review: I like the overall vibe of the game. However, the game appears to suffer from either a budget issue or a gameplay creativity issue. A lot went into the visuals (creatively speaking) but the gameplay falls flat and is a little too simple. I was playing on the highest difficulty but when you realise the dodge button has massive i-frames it makes it far too easy to just dodge and move on from just about every enemy in the game. The AI isn't very smart at all which means that despite playing on the highest difficulty, the game was far too easy. I think the game had potential but it fell short of what I personally like. That being said, some people may like this game and I could see it having some time of cult following (no pun intended), but if you do want to try it. I suggest getting a cheaper key from a third party site or waiting for a sale. I cannot recommend it at its price point when the gameplay gets boring and the playtime is only about 4 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: I was a bit skeptical of new age and 'cosmic horror' as cults, rituals and weird symbols are the least interesting things about cosmic horror. I did get a weird (unintentional?) sensible chuckle over using burning sage and essential oil to fight monsters from other dimensions, but somehow it works and the vibe I think works. The old school survival horror exploration and combat is done well.  Characters and acting are done well. I really am enjoying this game as a decent old school survival horror with some modern treatments.  It obviously doesn't have the production values of resident evil, but I think the devs did a great job and it exceeded my expectations.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a bad game so far but I have to point out that if you are looking for a horror game this ain't it and it's more of a combat oriented game with some monsters and a weird plot. Even though the game is more combat oriented and you have to dodge like it's some Souls-like game and beat the devil out of the monsters you are not even forced to engage with the enemies, you can just walk past them grab the items you need or want and get out so the monsters will just despawn and that's about it.As for the story I'm not even sure, you meet with a cult like people drink some magic tea and things just happen very quickly to the point you don't even have an idea what is going on anymore cause things just happen quickly and makes no sense.Performance is also all over the place where there's random FPS swings for no particular reason and no matter how much I fiddle with graphics settings it's the same but besides these swings the game works well and keeps a stable frame while also looking quite good. Oh and try not to change graphics while in the game and not in the menu cause that can mess up your game and you might need to restart it.I'd say pick this up on sale cause it's not bad and I like the janky look and feel of the game and nothing has to be perfect to be enjoyable.Oh and lastly all the combat is done with a lit up weed in melee and there's no guns at all.

_childDocuments_.review: After over 2 hours playing I can say: I LOVE IT! The Chant is a fantastic, atmospheric and thrilling occult-horror thriller with esotheric bonds. The game is VERY well voiced, at least the German voice actors do a great job.Grafic, atmosphere, gameplay, story.....this all is done very well in my eyes.In the last few years it has become clear to me that it is increasingly worthwhile to look at the games of smaller indie developers. And with The Chant it shows me once again that I'm right about it. The game is definitely worth the price, and when I see a game that has been developed with a lot of love and effort, I love to appreciate it. While the big studios give me the feeling that they are working more in the interests of some hardware manufacturer than in the interests of the players, I prefer a technically not quite as perfect game as The Chant a thousand times, and I would rather pay a full price for it a thousand times . To me, The Chant is a better than average game, and there haven't been many of those lately.

_childDocuments_.review: Optimization scared me at first. Although it is wild. This game needs more then one would think. Not saying the game looks bad, I think it is fine for what it is. Sometimes easily topping EA/Ubi games in the facial expression department. That being said, I did get it to run near perfectly. Still, I wouldn't mind a patch. There are stutters here and there that instantly take you out of the immersion. This game is wild. Straight acid trip. Only difference here, you actually have some kind of control. Combat isn't bad. Still, I am playing on the hardest difficulty. Rubber banding can and will happen. Although not the easiest to spot because this isn't the Arkham or a Fromsoft game. Jess (MC) doesn't side step a couple of yards. However, she will stand up during an enemy attack and take damage all the same. Still, I watch others play walking simulators. I need combat and I appreciate it here. But a slight touch up would be nice. Still, what we get is serviceable. Actually pretty good compared to other indies I've played. I do have to give credit though. A game about a retreat / cult / people. They nailed it with your mind body and spirit. The three categories everything hinges off of. Conversations and how you answer will give exp, even finding lore (expanding Jess knowledge) will give exp. It is a very cool touch. Only downside, it may force you to answer in ways you wouldn't normally want to, just to get a certain ability unlocked. Still, nice way to go all in. Not the hardest, not the scariest (subjective, I know), but definitely unique. Within two hours you'll get a feel for everything. Careful though, you could pass it running around too much, but I think most will be OK. I am usually the slower player. Most smoke me in time. So you should be alright. For $40, give it a go. I think it's worth a shot.After beating (Spoiler)Fun game. I like how unique it is. Sticks out in its own way. However, the final boss is not fun and annoyed me more then challenged. Also, I got the mind ending. Made zero sense. Took ten hours to beat. I am not going through again for another ending. But if I had to guess, the multi ending is just a way to help marketing of the game. I read every bit of lore and watched all reels. Never once did it bring up water. So I just assume the boat got pulled in? What did it mean if so? We don't know. Not a big fan of this. In the end, fun game. Still, I have to admit, the unique side of it, is 70% of the recommendation. Final boss, story/lore/ending, could use some work.
_childDocuments_.name: The Chant

_childDocuments_.review: I really enjoyed the overall story of the game, every character in the game had at least a little more than what could be seen on the surface and added to the overall plot in a good way. The side stories appeared in the game through the collectibles was also a nice touch and helped tell a stories that added to the main story in a nice way.  Overall the game was very pretty, the enemies all had something unique about them and were, although in a sort of grotesque way, beautiful to see. The shadows worked well to create the creepy ambiance that was intended. I felt like the combat was kind of tacked onto the game after the fact. It felt very clunky and unsatisfying to me, while also being a little too easy, it boiled down to "If glowing do not hit, if not glowing hit because they will be staggered indefinitely." The combat just didn't really add anything to the game in my opinion and I think having a stealth mechanic, , would have felt better in the world created.  Although the story was great, the overall progression was very linear, but it gave a fake sense of choice while also railroading you. There would be areas that you would want to explore (an open passage way, a door,etc) but when you walked up to it the door would either wouldn't be interact-able or there would be a wall that you couldn't go through until later in the game. This may be a little nit picky, but it was a gripe that I had. Also, there's a fast travel mechanic but there no real point to it besides going back to the first location... I don't know the fast travel just seemed tacked on again... If you want a good story, this game has it. If you want combat enriched horror, this ain't it

_childDocuments_.review:
A single-player, third person horror action-adventure game set on a remote island spiritual retreat. A peaceful weekend soon turns to dread after a group chant opens The Gloom, a psychedelic dimension of terror that feeds off negative energy. Interact with a recurring cast of characters, untangle the complex history of the island, and witness terrifying revelations about the cosmos. Only you can fight off the creatures, reason with the survivors, and unravel the legacy of a cult from the 1970s to reverse the ritual.

Features:

* EXPLORE AN ISLAND FILLED WITH COSMIC DREAD: Interact with the other members of the retreat as they slowly become consumed by their own negative energy.

* Survive against an array of prismatic creatures and cultists released from The Gloom as you piece together the weird history of the island.

* FIGHT OR FLIGHT: You must choose your fights and battle for survival with spiritual weapons and abilities. Collect, craft, and manage your resources to take your chances in close combat - or succumb to panic and flee.

* MIND BODY SPIRIT: Balance is everything. Steel your mind against horror and panic; Protect your body against physical threats; Elevate your spirit to meditate and access supernatural abilities.

* MODERN PSYCHEDELIC HORROR: Inspired by the psychedelic horror of the 1970s, experience a landscape of colored lighting and an electronic rock soundtrack, composed by the award-winning Paul Ruskay.

name: Citizen Sleeper
detailed_description: One of 2022’s most acclaimed indies, the Game Awards-nominated Citizen Sleeper is a Tabletop-inspired narrative RPG set on Erlin’s Eye, a ruined space station that is home to thousands of people trying to survive on the edges of an interstellar capitalist society. You are a sleeper, a digitised human consciousness in an artificial body, owned by a corporation that wants you back. Thrust amongst the unfamiliar and colourful inhabitants of the Eye, you need to build friendships, earn your keep, and navigate the factions of this strange metropolis, if you hope to survive to see the next cycle. Inspired by Tabletop Roleplaying games, Citizen Sleeper uses Dice, Clocks and Drives to create a player-led experience, where you choose your path in a rich and responsive world. Each cycle you use the dice you are dealt to choose what to do with your time. Make or break alliances, uncover truths and escape your hunters. Survive and ultimately thrive, one cycle at a time, and sometimes against the clock! The station plays host to characters from all walks of life, trying to eke out an existence among the stars. Salvagers, engineers, hackers, bartenders, street-food vendors, each has a history which brought them here. You choose which of them you wish to help, and together you will shape your future. Eventually, you will learn to use your dice to hack into the station’s cloud to access decades of digital data, uncover new areas and unlock secrets. This is your unique power, and with it you can change your future. Corporate secrets, rogue AIs and troves of lost data await those willing to dive into the depths of the station’s networks. Essen-Arp: to them you are just property, one more asset in a portfolio that stretches across the stars. You are the product of an abusive system, in a universe where humanity’s expansion is marked by exploitation and extraction. Escape the makers of your decaying body, and chart your own path in a richly imagined, deeply relevant sci-fi world which explores ideas of precarity, personhood and freedom. Citizen Sleeper uses Dice, Clocks and Drives to create a player-led experience, where you choose your path in a rich and responsive world. Each cycle you roll your dice. Assign them to vast range of actions available on the station. With every action, choose what, and who, matters to you, shaping the lives of those around you, and ultimately the future of the station. Clocks track both your actions and the actions of others across the station. From becoming a local at the Overlook Bar to protecting a friend from Yatagan enforcers, clocks allow you to track your own progress and the influence you have on the world around you. Follow drives not quests, allowing you to pick and choose the stories and activities that matter to you. As you do, you will shape your character's five skills (Engineer, Interface, Endure, Intuit and Engage), unlocking perks and bonuses that reflect and change how you choose to live in this world. Citizen Sleeper now includes all three post-launch DLC episodes FLUX, REFUGE and PURGE, which expand the game and introduce additional characters and locations to Erlin’s Eye in an exciting new late game storyline. ABOUT THE DEVELOPER Jump Over the Age is a one-person game development studio founded by Gareth Damian Martin (they/them). Gareth is the winner of GDCA and Indiecade awards, and has been nominated for a Games Award, multiple IGF Awards, a GDC Award, and four BAFTAs. They have been named both “An accomplished world-builder” (Edge Magazine) and “one of the most exciting indie talents around” (Eurogamer).

Salvagers, engineers, hackers, bartenders, street-food vendors, each has a history which brought them here. You choose which of them you wish to help, and together you will shape your future. Eventually, you will learn to use your dice to hack into the station’s cloud to access decades of digital data, uncover new areas and unlock secrets. This is your unique power, and with it you can change your future. Corporate secrets, rogue AIs and troves of lost data await those willing to dive into the depths of the station’s networks. Essen-Arp: to them you are just property, one more asset in a portfolio that stretches across the stars. You are the product of an abusive system, in a universe where humanity’s expansion is marked by exploitation and extraction. Escape the makers of your decaying body, and chart your own path in a richly imagined, deeply relevant sci-fi world which explores ideas of precarity, personhood and freedom. Citizen Sleeper uses Dice, Clocks and Drives to create a player-led experience, where you choose your path in a rich and responsive world. Each cycle you roll your dice. Assign them to vast range of actions available on the station. With every action, choose what, and who, matters to you, shaping the lives of those around you, and ultimately the future of the station. Clocks track both your actions and the actions of others across the station. From becoming a local at the Overlook Bar to protecting a friend from Yatagan enforcers, clocks allow you to track your own progress and the influence you have on the world around you. Follow drives not quests, allowing you to pick and choose the stories and activities that matter to you. As you do, you will shape your character's five skills (Engineer, Interface, Endure, Intuit and Engage), unlocking perks and bonuses that reflect and change how you choose to live in this world. Citizen Sleeper now includes all three post-launch DLC episodes FLUX, REFUGE and PURGE, which expand the game and introduce additional characters and locations to Erlin’s Eye in an exciting new late game storyline. ABOUT THE DEVELOPER Jump Over the Age is a one-person game development studio founded by Gareth Damian Martin (they/them). Gareth is the winner of GDCA and Indiecade awards, and has been nominated for a Games Award, multiple IGF Awards, a GDC Award, and four BAFTAs. They have been named both “An accomplished world-builder” (Edge Magazine) and “one of the most exciting indie talents around” (Eurogamer).
short_description: Roleplaying in the ruins of interplanetary capitalism. Live the life of an escaped worker, washed-up on a lawless station at the edge of an interstellar society. Inspired by the flexibility and freedom of TTRPGs, explore the station, choose your friends, escape your past and change your future.

_childDocuments_.review: Heartily recommended for all who want to confront themselves with the question what it is to be human. The game is not long (16.3h) and not really hard or overly complex; kinda straightforward. But it gives a fresh turnbased approach to you managing your stay at a spacestation. It gave me a really relaxed time enjoying the general atmosphere and pondering about decisions needing being made. The narrative is well put and stays to the point. It offers to the interested a gentle ethical framework about choices.Does my own life matter to me? And someone elses? What about life in general?The pulls in life of greed or power machism. And not only how that affects some people directly, but how that shapes society in the long run. What do you wish upon yourself and the human race in the coming millennia?Think BIG, expand that horizon, and when that's nicely clear, you will experience satisfactory confirmation in even the littlest of deeds or choices, knowing that you live toward something worthwhile. SciFi can get your compass needle inwaverable. And as long as they are in your right direction, also the babysteps will get you there. And me. And others being maybe less brave, or persistant. We are many. Your path and yours alone
