_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is a great atmospheric story game. Basically a visual novel with a bit of resource management and the dice mechanic to take actions it draws you into its world and makes you feel for the people you encounter on the eye, a station abandoned by its company that has become a haven for those looking to build their own future.Gameplay works well to support the ambience, but this is not a strategy game or anything close to it (even though it would also be interesting to see a game in this style that focuces more on the choces of where to use your time and where to risk using low dice). As such I don't think that there is much replay value and if you don't like the feeling of the world or the stories that unfold there, this game has little to offer. Also note that there is no voice acting (this allows a lot more story threads and is fine, but since the trailer has voice overs, it should be mentioned that the majority of this game is reading).For me the world of citizen sleeper was a great place to relax for a few hours every week.

_childDocuments_.review: It's a game that is a really good paper RPG simulator, much like Roadwarden. Speaking of Citizen Sleeper itself, it is an amazing adventure in a Sci-Fi setting. The game absorbed me and for the 2 days I played it I was simply in another world. I was the Sleeper and got to know a part of life on "The Eye". There are many characters here and their depth is incredible, while I have to admit that my heart was stolen the most by Mina.A good finish to this game is, of course, the brilliant graphics, music and sound design.In conclusion, if you are hesitant to play it, I definitely recommend stepping into Sleeper's shoes and seeing for yourself what it's like.

_childDocuments_.review: A thoughtful game. It reminded me of Disco Elysium and Fallen London, both in good ways. The character art is stylish, and the music atmospheric. It reminded of me of cities when they are empty at night.Interestingly, I was able to do almost every storyline in a single playthrough, without having to reset or do any save trickery. _childDocuments_.review: One of the most striking aspects of Citizen Sleeper is its dreamlike atmosphere. From the moment you dive into the game, you're transported into a world where reality blurs with imagination. The art style is minimalist yet incredibly effective, with vibrant colors and ethereal landscapes that shift and morph as you progress. Accompanying the visuals is a hauntingly beautiful soundtrack that perfectly complements the surreal nature of the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I think anyone going into it should know that this is mostly a visual novel, with some light dice-game and resource management on the side. The gameplay is mostly there to pace the story, but it is clear that most of the focus went on the narrative.It's a good thing then that the writing is good!The game basically tells relatively linear stories of various characters which are separate threads you can progress by using your dice on them. At times the stories overlap, which was very neat. The tone is bittersweet with glimmers of humanity and hope, but thematically the game stays true to its Cyberpunk roots.The ambiance of the game reinforces the stories nicely, with superb character art and good music / soundscapes. I would have hoped to perhaps see more 2D art depicting the environments beyond the 3D space station that functions as your 'game board' but what artwork is there is very nice.While the gameplay is light and mostly 'fluff', it does do it's job in pacing the story, and creates a "one more cycle" element to the gameplay as you spend your dice and rest to get them back. It is just robust enough to not wear out it's welcome.

_childDocuments_.review: So just initial impression. I really wish I didn't want to get this game refunded, but I do. Some things are just kind of irreconcilable to me. _childDocuments_.review: Honestly it's a good game. The gameplay itself isn't particularly difficult. The start of the game you have to manage your resources well, but you can use context clues from the dialogues to figure out what to do to help yourself in the long run, and you should have enough stuff going to make it in the short term. There aren't too many resources to manage and it is pretty straightforward in how it works. I like that. Let's talk about a few of the other aspects though.-InterfaceIt's good visually. The rotating through the ring is pleasant and in general the visuals here are sleek and communicate most of the important details. The things that aren't communicated are found out relatively easily through trial and error. This is both an upside and a downside. Because there's so much gameplay information readily available a lot of the uncertainty is taken away. There's a time pressure and the characters don't know if we can make it in time? Well I can see it's only 6 slivers and I get 2 slivers per successful action so that won't be an issue. You can't fully expect what the rewards are going to be from different drives (quests), but that's about it. The last thing I want to say about it is that at some point having to repeat an action over and over again makes it annoying that it takes time to resolve. This can feel jarring.-ArtworkAll-in-all I really like it. The character design is great and in general the artstyle is evocative of the themes of the game. It fits a very cozycore vibe somehow to me. Nobody in this game is really cozy or comfy, but it made me feel like i could really connect with these people. The sounddesign and music set the mood perfectly as well. Honestly I can't immediately pick out any tracks or sounds that stood out to me, and unfortunately that's how it often goes with soundscapes. If it's doing its job well, you don't really notice it.-WritingIt's good. The characters have motivations. They lie when they feel they have to, and often leave things to be inferred. You need some emotional intelligence to truly understand most of them, and that's good. They feel like people rather than just characters. The storylines are understandable and provide twists and turns. Nothing you can't follow along in the moment, but most of which I could not have predicted. If anything I don't really like the implication that you're special EVEN FOR a sleeper. That said, nothing inherently wrong with that.Overall I really recommend this game. I got it in the humble bundle, but it's fully worth the price regardless. If you like moral dilemmas set in a dystopian scifi future with some mysteries to solve, and you like games where most of the interaction is reading dialogue, this game is for you. If you tend to focus on the challenge of the mechanics rather than the story though, you might end up a bit bored.

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely adore this game. I love the entire story and all the interwoven stories within. I love the characters, it would be so hard for me to choose a favorite character. The dialogue was really easy to invest myself into, I didn't find myself skipping any of it. I love the time/resource management, IMO it was easy to get the hang of and fall into a rhythm with though it can be a little unforgiving with choices sometimes unexpectedly. I love the music, I could listen to the soundtrack all day on a loop and I'd never grow tired of it. I've actually pulled up the soundtrack to listen to in the BG while I work from home. The representation was the big cherry on top as well, with a nonbinary character, Sabine, who goes by they/them pronouns. You could also technically count the robot/entity characters as well, which were really fascinating.In addition to the main story, they actually continued to update and add more free content with new characters and world building. I just heard about the sequel and I can't wait to play it!

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is not really a game, but more like an interactive story. But that's okay, since that story is great. _childDocuments_.review: have had my eyes on this since it was revealed, and has been one of my most anticipated games of this year (up there with Coromon, Cult of the Lamb, and Have a Nice Death)--and hot damn if it isn't excellent. but what's so good about it?:+ the writing is most likely the first thing you'll see folks mention as being a standout element of the game. this is for good reason, as the writing is superb. really captures the tension and emotion of the story and its heady themes.+ also not a particularly deep point of praise would be recognizing that its visuals are slick as all get out. not only the illustrations (which are phenomenal) or its colors (which are bold), but even with regards to oft-overlooked matters such as typography. yeah, the fonts in this kick ass.+ its soundtrack is great, and worth picking up on its own if you enjoy lofi synths.+ while most will feel the inclination to label this a text adventure or moral management title based on screenshots, it in actuality is a text-based RPG based on pre-existing tabletop RPG mechanics, as I understand it. how they are implemented, however, thanks to the tactile nature of Citizen Sleeper is that they elevate the more cathartic elements of the game. it's very easy to find oneself enjoying filling out quests.+ I greatly appreciate its themes of anti-capitalism and gender identity, among many others. it largely handles these themes very, very well with some accidental stumbles that I'll get into in a second.- while I dig that the game has a diverse cast of characters (which is another point on the board you could give to it, but I was gonna mention it here anyways), and the presence of nonbinary characters--I did find at least one instance of a character (namely Sabine) seemingly being misgendered (I have to presume accidentally), as they are always referred to by they/them pronouns, except for one panel which refers to them by "she". maybe Sabine as a character is (in the fiction of the game, obv) copacetic with both they/them and she/her, but this is not established much, from what I've seen. so maybe I've just missed something, in which case I'd absolutely double-back from this particular critique, naturally. I will be sharing this to the official Fellow Traveller Discord server and find out--but I wanted to post this user review right after my first 3 hour long session so as to give an extra thumbs up to the game. I don't think this is a major sticking point except for enbyphobic reactionaries, as it is either an old line that got missed in editing, a pronoun mix-up, or just me missing that the character prefers they/her rather than they/them exclusively.- there is a minor typo here and there. I'll try catching exact screenshots for those and sharing them for the devs on my second playthrough, as I missed them this go-around due to my screenshot key not working at the time.- as for something a little more substantial as an (entirely subjective) issue I have with the game, at the point I'm in the story now, there are A LOT of choices which can lead to analysis paralysis and feeling like you don't know what will open up an important path for you. it's still nbd, you can still seek a guide if you really need it, but I found myself getting momentarily lost once or twice, personally.all in all, I think this game rules. it's intriguing in all the right ways. highly recommended.for more thoughtful recommendations of the best games on Steam, check out my curator, .

_childDocuments_.review: I'm grateful to the person that recommended this game to me because otherwise I would not have ever heard of this game.  Immediately immersed into the story and the world that is lived on the eye.  Characters are great, with a story that entices multiple playthroughs. You are a sleeper that awakens in an unfamiliar place known as The Eye.  This place could either be one that you must escape from or strive to make a home of.  Should know right off the bat, the gameplay here may not be familiar to you.  It involves a set number of actions.  Each action has a value to it (you have numbered dice that affects the chances of a positive result vs neutral/negative).  With each action, you make progress towards the current arc you're in.  Some events have a time limit which are measured in cycles.  One cycle is a day and in each day, you're given five or six dices. You are also at a disadvantage as a sleeper at the start.  You need to make connections in order to get repairs for yourself.  Your condition worsens over cycles which will limit the amount of dices you have which in turn, will limit how much progress you can make towards the goals.  This game is very unique to me and I look forward to the next one as the ending leaves me wanting more.  You should also know that this game consists of mostly reading and there is no voice acting.  Also, no cutscenes.  What you do get is stills where you can appreciate the art and well written dialogue.  You spent most of the game with an overview pov of The Eye.  Traversing deeper into the ring where you'll find new people, businesses, and opportunities to manage your condition and hunger.  I recommend seeing a quick video on the gameplay of this to tell if you'd enjoy it.  I for one, really like the storytelling, characters, the gameplay mechanics, and the damn sound design!  The futuristic lofi soundtrack and the ambiance of being on the eye, really gripped me.  I can't really share any negatives to this game considering that the price of this game is reasonable and I genuinely enjoyed the amount of time I spent on the game.  If I were to nitpick though, perhaps this game could've used some voice acting but honestly, it didn't cost me much to read.  If it was crappy dialogue, that would be one thing.  But it's well written.  Can't say much more, other than treat yourself to this game and cop it!  I look forward to Citizen Sleeper 2!
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This game isn't bad and it intrigued me enough to keep plugging away at the dice game to see what was coming next. But honestly, there's one thing that's leaving a bad taste in my mouth and it's specifically the comparisons to Disco Elysium. Specifically, some people are claiming this game is better than that game.And you know what? That's just like, your opinion, man. But I can't help but feel that objectively, Disco Elysium is a much more significant game than this one. I can't get this comparison out of my head. Now every moment I spend playing Citizen Sleeper, a game I was having an ok time with, I can't help but think "...people are seriously saying this game is better than Disco?". Why couldn't you guys just leave Disco out of? Let this game stand on its own legs? There's room for the both of them.But yeah, now I have this feeling (or expectation?) that I'm supposed to like Citizen Sleeper as much as Disco Elysium and honestly, I do not. And that's a bummer. Whereas Disco Elysium's writing fluctuated between beautiful prose, comedy, and engaging dialogue with a very colorful cast of characters, Citizen Sleeper just feels like a stream of text. I find myself skipping a lot of it. I haven't really connected with any of the characters at all because I don't feel like there's any reason to. My actions don't feel like they carry any real weight either. Maybe I'm also a bit spoiled by Frostpunk, a game that really doesn't have anything to do with this one except that Frostpunk will show you immediate and long term repercussions to your decisions. Sleeper Citizen feels like that's what it's going for but I never really felt like I was in danger of losing the game or that I put anyone's lives at risk. That may just be a consequence of it being an easy game, I don't know. Maybe there are consequences and I just skirted around them with ease. There's also the gameplay itself, you just scroll up and down and drop dice into activities for the day. Dialogue choices are limited and aren't reflective of your character's personal growth the way they are in Disco Elysium. I mean look, games are just an illusion of choices and decisions and sometimes the illusion is so well crafted it's hard to see past it, but I was pretty aware that my actions meant very little. Disco still has me wondering if there's stuff I missed because seemingly every action DOES matter.I feel kind of ♥♥♥♥♥♥ for being the dissenting opinion and probably a gatekeeper but I feel like I had to say something. Maybe view Citizen Sleeper for what it is and if it works for you, cool. And comparing it to Disco Elysium is fine but it feels kind of audacious to suggest this game is better, it's not, sorry. Maybe I'll flip this to a positive review later and I'm just being salty and needed to rant. But whatever.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an exceptional game. The story it has to tell is one that many people would benefit from hearing. You have to choose, to make your choices regardless of your desire for an easy solution, but the game gives you an opportunity to do so and see the consequences quickly and safely. This is a game that has great pacing; you can focus on sidequests and not run out of time, despite the potential concern otherwise. It really gives each tone, feeling, and scenario the time it needs to fully develop. If you like stories and compassion, play this game. If you like conflict or choice-based narratives, play this game. If you aren't sure if you want to die, play this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: It's a narrative game with a light resource management layer on top that has a tabletop RPG feel. I had a great time with it. I wish the resource management part was a bit harder, but it's just not that kind of game. In any case, exploring the Eye and getting to know its citizens was amazing. The OST and the overall mood were amazing too.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. Just finished my first run in about 8 hours-ish. I branched out into every direction I could story-wise and managed to see three different endings in one run. Highly immersive despite being mostly text based and the characters you meet are great. Gameplay is not too hard as far as I can tell but I might have just had good RNG. The gameplay also manages to be almost perfectly paced with the story so there's always something to work towards. It only got just slightly tedious near the end when I had already amassed enough materials to not have to do anything but wait for certain timers to run down. This was after unlocking two endings so I don't blame the game though. I am not sure how replayable this game is yet but I'd say it's worth.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I had fun, though I don't think I want to do a second playthrough. Other player characters don't seem to have any real difference aside from a very slight re-allocation of a few skill points. They do not have anything unique to them other than starting with a different bonus (which can be obtained with like, 1 skill point on the other characters). My first run was so successful I already completed many questlines, and got halfway through many more, despite spending the first 10 days or so not realizing that I could do more things. I imagine that I could've absolutely crushed the game if I had done things right from the start. Once you know what to expect, the game is fairly tedious, with slow scrolling speed, transitional animations that must be done multiple times per day and can't be skipped, and little sense of tension in the late game. That doesn't mean it's a bad game. It was enjoyable for about 6 hours. I loved the game opening up over time as I unlocked new areas. I'm just not sure if it was worth 20$. I'd recommend this for maybe 10$.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I'll start by saying that I have a 14 month old daughter, so as soon as I saw Lem and Mina I knew I had to do everything to help them. I went with their ending. I got emotional several times throughout my first playthrough to the point where I'm not sure I will play the game again. When I chose to leave the Eye with Lem and Mina, I got teary-eyed at the epilogue text after making the decision.This is a wonderfully written game and the writer, Gareth Damian Martin, should be incredibly proud of themselves for the art they have created. 11/10
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Some of the best writing you'll see in a videogame. Amazing soundtrack from the composer for the Kingdom series, another of my favorites. Art and design that is low-budget but executed with intense care and eye for detail. An atmosphere that is at the start overwhelming, but by the end you will feel melancholy for leaving as the Eye slowly zooms out of view.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a very long game, but it's a solid world to inhabit. You're on a ring station, in a body that's running out of power and slowly degrading. Fortunately you can get energy from most any kind of food, but maintaining your body is harder. You roll a number of d6s every morning based on your body's condition and allocate them to various station tasks.In addition to getting money to buy the things you need to maintain your body, you'll also affect progress clocks with your work. Maybe you need to have a few drinks at a bar before you're recognized as a regular, maybe your side investigation into a wreck your salvaging is racing the actual progress of the work.It feels Forged in the Dark as all get-out, in other words, and the writing's pretty solid too.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Started so very promising, but by midgame it was just a bunch of chores and to be honest no choice making.So many dialogues are between yes and yes. If you try to change anything in the narrative you find that you kinda can't really do anything in there, also the DLC or update or what have you disappoints in the most hollywood/netflix way, containing the one-dimensional angry strong woman cliche and other banal boring stuff on a game I was excited about.It held up for a bit for sure, and I don't know what level of either self-absorption or pandering was involved in creating the characters, the quality at the beginning doesn't survive midgame - but you might like it!
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: A kind of CYOA-style game akin to The Life and Suffering of Sir Brante. Sleeper offers more gameplay by giving you a set number of dice per day to allocate to various tasks you can find in your environment. It's simple but works well to provide the player more of a sense of control and decision making. There is no combat of any kind for those who need that sort of thing in an RPG.The core question with a game like this concerns the story, and it is pretty captivating, involving questions about the nature of AI, humanity, and consciousness, but told in a very down-to-earth way. Everything is wrapped up in a cyberpunk, sci-fi dystopia set aboard a decaying ship which is a kind of mirror to the main character. It's easy to get lost in the atmosphere and prose. The main weakness, as is often the case with a game like this, is the mechanics. Too many clicks are required to perform tasks that ought to be more streamlined. You sometimes have to click to enter something, input an item, leave, then return to do a dice roll. It's a little annoying. Beyond that, it can also be difficult, at first, to figure out what you're supposed to be prioritizing or why, which may lead to some players losing focus or getting lost. Some parts of the game, like the matrixy shadow realm where you can steal data from agents also felt extremely shallow. There are a few interesting quests connected to it, but then it just becomes a source of infinite money with no consequences. It felt like a missed opportunity. I guess another issue is that the game felt very "top heavy" with its content. There isn't really an end game, and it all comes to a head extremely quickly, with things getting easier the further you progress. I think I prefer the style of Sir Brante, which starts out very simply and ends in an extremely challenging final scenario, instead. I suppose this may be subjective, but having a frivolous end-game seems to cheapen the difficulty of the early parts. That said, Sleeper does a great job building tension in the early game. It's too bad it fails to keep that tone throughout.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This writing is fantastic, compact, and the gameplay compliments it. With a few dice each day you get to decide where to put the best you have and what gets the dregs, and frankly, what gets nothing. You often don't have time for everything you want, sometimes even what you need. You wake up in a cargo container, escaped, but hunted. You need food, medicine, connections, and you run into people solving their own problems, getting beaten down by forces much greater than themselves. What a flawed world to live in. Expect visual novel levels of text. The writing is very well done, but reading is the game, don't come here looking for something else. The game starts and ends . The music, the characters, the writing all mingle into something great.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: In all honesty, what drew me to this game was the fairly common statement from other users' reviews that "Citizen Sleeper" was the sci-fi cyberpunk equivalent of Disco Elysium. After having played this game, I must say that I disagree with this statement, however, this is still in my opinion a very good game. I found the gameplay mechanic to be unconventional yet interesting and intriguing, the artwork is a definitive testiment of the love and creativity invested into this project, the writing is quite good and the setting is gripping. The game on one hand partially gave me a Blade Runner feeling, only the player is actually the synth on the run, on the other hand had a Ghost in the Shell vibe with the discussions of the definition of sentience. In fact, many interesting sci-fi topics are present, and while some of these aren't particulary new or original, I would still consider this sci-fi of a higher quality. Recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: A nice little game that is under 10 hours if you do almost everything available, yet, feels much more satisfying than other games of similar length. Quality over quantity. I described it to a friend as "like Disco Elysium with less self loathing". The dice mechanic is pretty neat. The one thing I don't fully enjoy about it is how much injustice goes on and how rare justice is. But it fits with the narrative. It's not a downer game or anything, there's a lot of positive different endings.I think it's funny that the credits will roll every time that you decline to leave the station. Feels like a bug to me.I recommend it to anyone that enjoys narrative focused games and RPGs.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I'm glad I got this on sale because it's not worth the full price. I don't know if I'll finish it. With the amount of praise for narrative and writing, I was expecting a lot more. Sad to say it did not meet expectations. The prose bland and insipid. It was very hard to get invested in any characters because of the lack of universe building and depth. Hilariously, they come with descriptive subtitles like "cynical mercenary", as if the developer knew the writing was lacking and needed an explicit description to properly frame them instead of being able to rely on the strength of their characterizations. I looked them up out of curiosity and am shocked they have a PhD in Experimental Literature - was it an intentional choice to make the writing bad and I am just too small brained to appreciate it? You are a "Sleeper" on the run from a company hunting you. Your body is breaking down constantly, you live in an empty cargo container, you are trying to stay alive and figure out what's going on around you. Yet with a few exceptions it seems like everybody you meet is a gaping maw of need who constantly demands your time and energy with no personal consideration, and every time you think you've hit a milestone, it turns out it's just more demands for you to fulfill. Apparently they all are powerless to advance their own goals and need to rely on an android who's practically a stranger to get anything done. Conversations are railroaded. It's not just the characters, even the game itself has this problem - you can invest a significant amount get your own apartment, except for all intents and purposes it's the exact same as your old cargo container aside from being able to feed stray animals. As a game, it's bad. Imagine Stardew Valley, except you can't improve anything. The UI gets repetitive, I don't want to have to go between multiple screens just to advance the cycle. There's just about zero reason for it to even exist in the current form, it's not as if there's even a map for the player to traverse and explore. It's a very formulaic "use dice, advance" system with little to reward the player as they progress or break the tedium.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Wonderful. Though listed as an RPG, this is really an RPG-lite text adventure with a very simple but effective gameplay mechanic, a well-written story, a clean UI and a genuinely INCREDIBLE soundtrack. There's no voice acting or character models or anything, it's simple in execution, but the excellent writing and art direction of the hand-drawn characters really help to realize this world and your Sleeper's struggle.I loved this game, you should play it if you're into story-based or RPG text adventures.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: A phenomenal delve into a world I've seen done before but with characters who I genuinely cared for. We've all seen the cyberpunk classics - a grizzled cigarette-smoking trenchcoat detective, the horrifically over-modified gangsters and muggers, and the recently-born android with the naivete and intelligence of a 10 year old.Citizen Sleeper disregards all of that, and makes new a new high standard in its place. I was infinitely more intrigued by the story of an altruistic doctor whose clinic is funded by an underground mob, of a working man and his daughter trying to earn a better life through endless struggle, and of the artificial intelligence that (for reasons beyond its own understanding) attempts to savagely hunt you for the crime of daring to break free from technologically-induced slavery.Additionally, I'm not someone who beats their chest demanding more representation in games (for reference, I'm a bisexual man saying this) as I often find that inclusivity for the sake of itself often hampers good and genuinely well-written characters with moments where a gay/trans/ace/so-on person feels the need to awkwardly reinforce to the viewer that they're part of the LGBT community, or where racism is suddenly shuffled into a story out of left field so that megacorporation developers can claim to be progressive. Jump Over The Age is not one of these clueless developers haphazardly tossing characters with minority traits into a story in the name of a quota, but instead writing genuinely fascinating and proper characters who happen to be any of these things. Almost everyone in the story is a minority yet it doesn't feel forced for a quota or a desperate plea for progressives to buy the game, instead JOTA has made characters who I feel are infinitely better representations of real people by actually feeling like sympathetic and complex human beings not defined by being gay or trans or black or asian or what-have-you. THIS is something that absolutely deserves reward.The soundtrack composed by Amos Roddy is an absolute wonder that helps me whether at work or home instantly feel like I'm back in the harsh and complex station of the Eye, attempting to survive amidst threats of recapture into slavery and helping people not too dissimilar from people I know and care for in my real life. It shocks me to my core that the soundtrack of Citizen Sleeper isn't brought up as already one of the best of the 2020's, competing with Cyberpunk 2077 and other marvels of composition for truly breathtaking work. I'm absolutely looking forward to what Roddy composes next.I cannot recommend this game enough, and I have great empathy for JOTA in their new challenge of having to make their next game surpass the high bar and legacy that they have created for themselves with Citizen Sleeper.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: You are a Sleeper. Not quite human and not quite machine, sleepers are a product of corporations trying to bypass regulations for AI, as well as labour protections for humans. Having escaped your "employer", you don't belong anywhere, and try to find a space for yourself in a space station.It is rare to find a text-based game that is so well-written that you really find yourself stuck to the screen. Citizen Sleeper is such a game.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: 10+ hrs on another platformWhat a fantastic experience. Draws you in from the first few minutes, with immersive art, sounds, music, and excellent writing that all work together to create a complete, vivid world that you inhabit, with nuanced and complex characters you get to know and live with for a while. A sensitive, well-crafted story. Quite an achievement for games as an art form, really.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: beautiful, amazing game about precarity and hope in the face of uncertainty. Building a community in the face of adversity, uncertainty, and exploitation. It's about so many things, but fundamentally about our shared human experience. One of the most beautiful games I have ever played, and it will run on pretty much any system. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a risk for me. I don't consider myself to be a fan of text adventures or visual novels, and I was wary of giving this game a shot. I am very glad that I did though, because while it is a relatively short experience, Citizen Sleeper is one of the most compelling, engrossing games that I've played in a long time. The sort of game that you really can't stop thinking about, even after you've put it down for good.Even as I type this, I am fighting the urge to start a fresh save, both to optimize my decisions, undo my mistakes and see how playing with a different class would change things. I'll save the second run for the when the rest of the DLC comes out.Excellent worldbuilding, writing and characters. Don't sleep on it. An Easy Recommendation.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: What a fantastic gem. To me it feels like a visual novel and the story telling is excellent.The only thing I genuinely missed is voice acting. The trailer voices were what captivated me and just a little voice line here and there would be great. Although the game it self doesn't need it, it all feels right.I never write reviews but this deserves it.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Really good writing and a clever user interface and mechanics based on tabletop games like Blades in the Dark. Tells a really interesting story about themes like living with  disability and building community in the wreckage of capitalism. I was worried the story would be a bummer, but it's not! It left me feeling quite hopeful.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Not as good as Disco Elysium, but by the same token this game damn near brought me to tears! If you like dice rolls and choose your own adventure books, this game is for you :) *My friend gifted this game to me because I helped them move house, so technically didn't receive it for "free". It was an honest days work*
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: First of all, the game's got pronouns, you're welcome :)Why I recommend it? The writing is prety good (not on the level of Sunless Sea/Skies, but still), the vocabulary is larger than the standard dumb texts we get. And the resource management game of dices is very interesting.Of course, you must understand, that this is 90% text, so if you don't like reading, skip this genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This game combines all that is needed for a good game. Its interface is unique, the dice chance are a concept used rarely, it design is elegence in simplicity and all of it many stories are intertwined and beautiful describing emotions from happines to sadness. Simply put I already are waiting for another game from this studio.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This is a very short game that still takes too long to end. Most of the content has run out but you still have to go through the motions until the rest of it eventually wraps up.Only the very beginning has mechanical decisions, very quickly every class levels up into a generalized mush that can accomplish every goal.I'm unsure to what extent I could call this a role playing game, you don't get to decide your characters choices or values, the writing forces opinions onto you frequently.A lot of the choices/endings don't make sense. Choices often don't matter, and the main threat Not having my choices matter, or my build matter, or getting to decide my own opinions, having the survival element be extremely simple to overcome, it just feels like this isn't a gameplay challenge and there isn't roleplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This game, has grabbed hold of me in a way I was not expecting. I randomly saw an ad for it on steam. Liked the poster, watched the trailer. Seemed to tick my sci-fi boxes, and although I literally have no time to play now-a-days I bought it... And basically couldn't put it down. Most RPGs with walls of text put me off quite fast as I just want to progress, but this was something entirely different. It is written superbly, characters have had lives before you came, have stuff going on, priorities other than you, but you have the option to gradually get involved, help them out, pass judgement, foil plans... but things are not always as straightforward as you might think. It is both a shining example of good writing from a developer's point of view and humility as playthrough experience. It basically threw me 3 or 4 curveballs while playing it, as I was expecting it to be over, but no. The stories are intertwined to a degree, and previous actions are very well handled at the end. I rarely get this caught up in characters, but jeez, this game... it pulls on your heart string some fierce. The ambient soundtrack and sound design is captivating, It's mechanics are easy to learn but rewarding, there's very little grind, there's some challenge in the beginning, but after that the story just takes over, yet doesn't overstay it's welcome. I honestly want more games like this. Thanks for making it.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: In its limited scope, Citizen Sleeper is a well written little game that offers a very interesting story that mixes creativity and clichés of the genre. You are a Sleeper, some kind of android, in search of his humanity, past, and future, after stumbling on a barely functioning colony deep in space. To survive, you'll have to earn your keep, meet people and try to navigate through the troubled reality of the colony. The good: The concept of dices that shape the odds of succeeding is really interesting, especially if you don't take a perk that helps you anticipate what's going to happen if you don't.The writing is probably where this game shines the most.The endings are worth the read, there are quite a few of them and they are all touching.The badMost of the choices don't really matter. It might lead to some people skipping walls of texts and useless decisions.You can continue your quest after an ending, which is really neat, but then you can achieve most of the game in a single playthrough, so replayability is really low. The game is rather short and you'll go through most of the content in +-8 hours.You have a choice of 3 different characters, but ultimately it doesn't matter which one you choose. Once you have figured out how taxing it is to lose dices, you're all set up to do everything in your power to avoid losing them, which leads to the main negative thing: You can't really fail or die. You think the game will punish a bad decision, but it never really does.So in the end, it's a visual novel with some gameplay features. Don't get any of this wrong, it's really well done and I recommend it. However, for such a short visual novel, the price is a bit steep. I'd wait for it to go on sale.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful art, great soundtrack. The world and atmosphere are engrossing and the characters are complex, diverse and have interesting motivations.I really enjoyed the die management system and I expect other devs to adopt it in some shape or form in future games.The only thing I can criticise is character upgrade paths at the beginning are cool, but I felt they don't have enough depth, . One more tier of upgrades would've probably made it so characters feel more unique and encourage replayability. All in all, I can't wait to come back to Citizen Sleeper on a fresh save and see how different choices pan out, one of my favourite games released this year.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Really well made. Music is great and the story is well writen. Characters are fine too. The interface sequences are better than I expected as well. Very solid. All in all, I recommend this game.I do wish we had voice acting, but that's a bigger fish for a different day. Hope you all get there. I know you will :)I also wish we had some more ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ choices, like i'm really OK with some of the more 'negative' options out on here, and on a ROLE PLAYING perspective... I sincerely hope you take that into consideration. Sometimes, people just want to play the bad dude and say "Yeah, f**k them, I don't care what happens just give me the cryo."
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I've played a bunch of popular indie titles before and while I thought they were amazing none of them compare to the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ experience that is this game. The game plays like an incredible novel except you are the main character. If you love reading this game is a gem. The narratives build stakes in such a subtle way that before I knew it I was just repulsed by some choices and felt like some choices were a no brainer. I came to think like a sleeper. I understood my place in that cruel world. When you help someone in this game you are left feeling great. The threats feel terrifying and beating them feels insane. The true sense of freedom when you manage to find you footing is simply unmatched in any game I've played so far. This felt like an experience.The soundtrack is also something else. The feeling when you wake up in your old container and the music hits is just my god. I have no words yet I'm compelled to write a review. This is the first game to make me get off my ass and write a proper review. If anyone sees this buy the ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ game it's ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ worth it. Trust me.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Very similar to "I Was A Teenage Exocolonist" with a joyfully unique perspective on the cyberpunk genre. The content is easy to digest, so much so that I ended up logging 15 hours into the game within 36 hours of starting it. The stories are very enthralling and the collective story is very fulfilling.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Nothing but good things to say here. If you like cyberpunky space games with fantastic writing? This is what you want.If reading isn't your thing, this game isn't for you. If you're searching for super high intensity mechanical skill and gameplay, this isn't for you either. You make choices that matter and get to see what happens, and that's the whole gameplay loop.It's great. Good choice for Deck, too.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is a great game. Read the other reviews for more information on that.I want to draw attention to the music. The songs in this game bring the setting to life in my imagination in a way that no other game I've played has achieved - not even Disco Elysium. 'Signal Haze' in particular manages to be emotionally resonant and introspective while at the same time pumping an absolute banger of a bassline. Incredible work by Amos Roddy.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: An incredibly well written story that really captures the day to day struggles for survival in a hostile reality.  You find what you need and you find people to connect with along the way and maybe you can help them with their struggle while you wrestle with yours.  Maybe you can't.Outstanding soundtrack.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This game is underrated. The story, engine, and gameplay are all top notch. The futuristic cyberpunk themes blend well with the art style and mechanics. The overall game itself is focused on the story progression, so it's not a sandbox experience. I highly recommend this to anyone who enjoys exploring the themes of what it means to be human, and how corporations may influence humanity's journey into space.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Not bad, but kinda lacking.The theme is nice, but with how easy it is to bootstrap yourself from less than nothing to a safe, stable and secure life, the game is not only lacking tension, but fails to deliver any of the critique it attempts - "things are hard for everyone, but with a bit of elbow grease you can get by, disability is no excuse" is probably not the message the game was going for. But it is what the game keeps saying.The game pushing you to leave the one place you can reliably get the medication you quite literally need to live, and seemingly refusing to wrap up until you do, also feels really poorly thought out. Again "even when capitalism is no longer a threat to you, it's better to kill yourself than live under it" is probably not the message the game was going for. But it is what the game keeps saying.And despite meaningful choices being pushed as a selling point, I don't see it. More often than not, any time the dialogue offers a choice both options have the exact same outcome (sometimes the one paragraph immediately after changes to reflect the option you picked, but sometimes not even that. Everything beyond that is usually unaffected). And there are barely any meaningful choices in the gameplay, because you have enough time and resources to do everything you need and then some, so you eventually end up seeing it all anyway.The plot is bare-bones. The characteres are better, but still kinda flat, not helped by how you only ever get to see them from one angle (see: lack of choices). The mechanics, difficulty aside, are more interesting to think about than to actually use, carrying the vibe of a game that mostly finished development before anyone thought to playtest it.I don't actively regret getting this game, but I expected better, and I leave with little reason to ever think about it again. Avoid unless heavily discounted.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This one's a gem. I'm wordy as usual but check the last paragraph if the rest is too much for you.For those who have had the pleasure of them, this game plays like a game book, only with the bookkeeping automated so you don't have to track flags and variables, sift around through pages and deal with all that overhead.  This is a good thing because, beyond not having to do that extra work, it allows for a lot more flexibility to pursue threads concurrently or in whichever order you choose, rather than being limited strictly to branching paths. It's less one story you direct towards one of several ends and more several intertwined stories that you can choose to progress or ignore as you discover them.  That said, being able to jump around between things isn't without consequence.  If you're the type to try to do it all, or at least maximize what you experience in a run, you'll find it fairly easy to bounce around between things and focus on checks you're good at rather than really suffer your weaknesses until you earn enough points to grow out of having any weaknesses at all. This isn't necessarily a horrible thing but know that if you choose to taste all of the stories, you'll soon find you've outgrown having any real challenges to oppose you. It is satisfying to be able to establish yourself like that and transition from merely surviving to thriving though. It allows you to climb the ol' Maslow pyramid and move beyond a survival mode and engage with the other characters more personally as an individual and friend instead of just a desperate fugitive beggar. You can repay those that helped lift you out of those more challenging times and that makes their stories really hit home better than your typical RPG quest line not just because of the growth but because you have the agency to choose whether to do so or not.I likened it to a game book earlier because that's really the core of the experience: reading a book whilst making choices and engaging in light dice placement and basic survival mechanics along the way. The trailers imply at least some voice acting but be aware there is absolutely none in the game itself.  That's not a bad thing, just something to keep in mind if that's important to you.  The story itself is very well done, with a rich world and characters you can't help but feel for. For a game I've repeatedly compared to a book, it doesn't disappoint in the critical aspect of writing.  The art is quite refreshing and the music is unobtrusive and subtly enhances the experience.  The interface is clean and fairly minimal but does its job and feels right for what it's trying to be.  A big part of that is the 3D map of the station that serves as a backdrop for it, the two work well together better than I think either would on their own. All in all, the game presents itself very well.It's a worthy experience for sure and an easy recommendation if any of the info on the store page catches your interest at all.  It has some real Eclipse Phase vibes for those familiar with that. It nails the themes and a very similar setting, offers a compelling story, great writing, enough mechanics to provide engagement and avoid being just another visual novel and wraps all of that in solid presentation.  We need more games like this. I sincerely hope this proves successful and we get more like it in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Its short. The challenge of scavenging for survival and fighting against the clock with your precious few actions disappears after the first couple of hours and settles into a routine without threat or danger. The choices don't mean much and the endings lack the sort of weight they should have. Questions remain unanswered and the central struggle of your character goes unfinished. Whatever you do, whatever happens, the Eye will never stop turning. But its not a game about the Eye or the corporations or the universe beyond, its about the people that call it home. You'll finish the game and get almost all the endings in less than six hours (I did) so if you're looking for a long lasting, hundred hour RPG look elsewhere. But if you want to spend a night meeting the strange new characters living in a strange new place give it a go.Worst comes to worst, its short enough you can refund the thing halfway through.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the coolest, most unique games I've had the pleasure of diving into in a long long time. Locked me into my chair and had be anxious for what was around the next cycle, planning every move and hoping not to get unlucky with my rolls. What a fantastic game, also the first game that I've ever purchased the sound track for, because it's just that good. At one point I just stopped playing and closed my eyes and listened to the music for a solid 2 minutes, lost in the synthwave alure of this dystopian future that we are rocketing towards ever faster.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Will someone feed my cat? 🥺I really didn’t want to leave… but I completed almost everything, tied up all the loose ends, stocked up on stabilizer, and an old friend offered me a ride. A beautifully written cyberpunk adventure on a space station with the character of a beloved city and a life of its own, literally if you can’t Neoven-er “navigator” : )
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: The first part of the game was a lot of fun - thrilling, very high tech, very low life, mysteries and interesting characters.Then everything sort of... fizzled out. And it did so particularly fast after survival stopped being a problem - it should never have turned into routine maintenance.So I'm not sure something actually changed about the quality of the writing, or I just found it more tedious because I wasn't in mortal peril anymore. But in the second half of the game I started finding most quests boring, most characters flat, most text full of fluff. I think that sticking to the basic information being transmitted is important even in wordier games. Scrolling though long columns of character reactions, character background stories and common metaphors got old quite soon. Sometimes a more metaphysical mystery or revelation popped out of the fluff, and then I became invested again. Then we went back to personal dramas of various not-particularly-interesting side characters... Briefly put: great concept, lovely experience during the first half of the story. Aftert that it became tedious. Sticking with a core cyberpunk-heavy mystery and a find-resource-or-die gameplay would have preserved the enjoyment and engagement level from the first half.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: It's been so long since a game made me get teary eyed. This was such a beautiful experience. The writing is amazing. It's not particularly showy but it's beautifully crafted. The music is haunting and perfect for the setting. The visuals aid in the storytelling without taking center stage. The story itself is one of the best that I have ever experienced.If you have any appreciation for story-driven games, then you owe yourself the treat that Citizen Sleeper represents. You won't regret this experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen sleeper is an outstanding experience and great game. Strong recommendation.The world building at display here is simply excellent and the way the setting is presented to the player is expertly crafted. The writing is very engaging and the characters are varied and interesting.In my opinion the game is at its best in the early game, where the mechanics present an intense resource managing game that constantly keeps up the pressure (). That pressure relieves a bit once you make some progress, which is at first a good thing as it allows you to explore more. However, unfortunately at some point that tension completely goes away and the "game" portion becomes almost trivial - but the story still kept me pleasantly engaged nevertheless.Citizen Sleeper (as many other RPGs) also does that thing where you can go down all the story directions at once - regardless of the character's specialisation (at some you will have so much experience you can be decent at everything). While this is a natural choice to allow the player to experience more of the stories in one play-through, here in particular this feels very much at odds with the time constraints the game mechanics try to set.If I could improve one aspect of the game, I think I would wish for the different plot points to be a bit more interconnected. Each of the separate mini-stories is well written, clever and engaging. Many of them even feature dramatic choices in the context of that story - but there is no effect whatsoever on the overarching situation or how other parts of the story play out. I think a stronger focus in that direction could have brought this from a very good game to a must-play classic.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I love, love, love the world building, the characters, the narrative, bgm and art style. For a good chunk of the game, I was so intensely immersed into it's world. Everything worked so well together that I was basically glued to the screen. The characters you meet all feel so realistic, and the friendships you develop so warm and accepting.The gameplay however really outstays its welcome. During the endgame where you just want to finish the last remaining goals, the dice, and cycle mechanic devolves into a waiting game where you're not really doing anything meaningful any more. Which sadly kills the pacing.I would implore everyone who wants to try this game and reads this to take this game more like a visual novel than a game where you can play a role or where the dice rolls mechanic has actual consequences. The start implies these two are possible, but they just really aren't. Due to the dice/cycle mechanic, I'm glad the latter isn't a thing because restarting over and over again after a bad luck streak would have killed this for me.Every playtrough (there will only be one unless you want to 100% it) you will be a lost, broken soul that finds new hope in a hostile place by connecting with other beings, building friendships and fighting against oppression.Which honestly still is an amazing message.The package in total is really wonderful and while I wished the gameplay had more fine-tuning towards the end, I cannot recommend this enough for everyone to try.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Before I start justifying my thumbs down, here's what I liked: The art, the overall setting,  the UI, and the mechanics. The mechanics especially, I felt, made fertile ground for creating compelling, organic, and personal stories.Now everything else. This game is essentially a visual novel, a genre about making choices and living their consequences, with little in the way of choice or consequence.There's never a time where you're really in danger. There are few times that you're allowed to antagonize any character you meet. There are few times where helping one character comes at the expense of another.That last thing did almost happen, once. Two NPCs tasked me with getting them some item called a "shipmind." One of them loaned me a lot of money for it. I obtained a shipmind, but handed it over to the other NPC instead. What happened then? Did I get in trouble with the first NPC for betraying her trust?Well, no. There are timers in the game that count up to some outcome, positive or negative. There was no timer associated with either of their requests. After I handed over the first shipmind, I spent a few in-game days accumulating enough resources to buy another, and now everyone's happy.But that was a quest (a "drive" the game calls them) without a timer. What happens when you let one of the negative timers complete? Do you die?Well... no. The game tells you that your body is corporate property, you have illegally escaped employment, and so there's a bounty hunter after you. The associated timer makes a full circle, the bounty hunter shows up, and then effectively just lets you go free. I haven't tried letting my health bar reach 0 yet. I would hope it's something tragic, but I doubt it. The game seems allergic to letting terrible things play out.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is a game that has RPG, Survival and visual novel elements, with a great art style, background noise and music that made my experience MORE IMMERSIVE which is quite odd because usually immersive games are first person view(there are exceptions).Citizen Sleeper has an emotional deep journey"story", and it was a unique experience that I want everyone to experience, because it provide a great story (that the player shapes), with some difficult options(at one point I thought maybe surviving isn't the right option), and if you think that wasn't enough to buy the game then let me tell you that the game has a beautiful "cyberpunk" world building and characters that have their own struggles and that they "breathe life".The only thing that I think would make the game better is if they used pictures in the background that resembles what being described (it would make it more immersive IMO)Citizen sleeper is a game that I don't want you to sleep on, and its a must try game.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful story, beautifully told. The writing really brings each character to life and it doesn't take long before their wins feel like your wins, their losses become your sorrows. A wonderful and touching sci-fi adventure.I only wish there could have been more depth to the central game mechanics. The optimal choices for each cycle are often very easy to determine and after around the 4 hour mark, the simplistic decisions and upgrade tree start to lose their charm.However the writing is so strong that there's no way you won't see this one through to the end.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This was fun. The game tells a short but compelling story in a world that it manages to portray quite vividly. While the dice and skill system is simple, it's a sufficient vehicle for what the game wants to do. The game has an odd melancholic undertone that every so often get's shaken up by high points, with the music contributing well to it.All in all a nice gamefor around 7 hours. Definitely an experience different from a lot of games and - for me - worth it.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: The game is barely a 'game' and more like a visual novel.And sadly the story is boring and not well narrated, especially as it's only available in english and use the pronoun 'they/them/their' a lot for no reason to make the pointless dialogs confusing.I don't understand the good reviews about it, the gameplay is boring and any book has a more interesting story than the one in this game.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Good game. Though kinda expected something related to a story of surviving on a slowly dying ship, like Orphans of the Sky, but it went instead into a blend of Neuromancer and your general cyberpunk dystopia in open space. The gameplay is builtright in this context, when in the beginning you're on the edge of dying as you  appear in the story and gradually acquire connections, resources and abilities to make RNGesus less important. Lacks underhanded options for the protagonist and kinda too linear, but still a great story. For Visual novel sci-fi lovers there somethingto consider
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is an amazing achievement for immersive storytelling. I was sucked into the story, and I just HAD to know how this was all going to play out. I'm personally not one for visual novels. I've tried a few, and they are just not my jam. This game however had very challenging and though provoking writing that really puts the player/reader into actual mindset of role-playing as your character. When it says inspired by TTRPGs, it's the style of writing that really evokes that feeling, rather than completely open-ended choices. Your choices really reflect the order of events and nuance, with a handful branching story chains that you can explore. I don't see this as a bad thing, I see this as a thematic choice by the creator to have the player explore the concepts of identity, community, classism, and determinism. I would say this is where the marketing for this game does a disservice-- the writer's beliefs are transparent, not heavy handed to strong arm you into a specific cliche anti-capitalism conclusion. The actual game-play is comprised of dice rolling and resource placement/accumulation, which will be very familiar to any modern board game player. It felt like a very intentional connection to the emotional themes the creator wanted to you to notice. You are feeling that your outcomes are completely random, up to luck and fate, but as you progress you start to forget how difficult it was to begin. You take for granted the progress you've made and it feels easily mastered by the end of the game-- the time in which your character has to choose to stay in comfort or explore the unknown. Overall, I was very surprised by how much I was drawn in and enjoyed such a curated experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Gripping narrative, well crafted economical design, and atmospheric setting. This reminds me of a much better written "choose your own adventure" book from the 80's.  It's a text heavy RPG adventure with character, story and a  rich world at its core. Refreshingly,  unlike so many games the prose is always beautiful, lean, evocative and affecting - none of it feels superfluous.  A stressful "survival" opening gives way to resource and health management mechanics that lose some of the initial urgency but continuously unlock the breadcrumbs of branching narratives. I found all of them worth pursuing.  The speed and simplicity of the UI go a long way to minimising the grind - here less is more and the more abstracted  "board-game" design keeps things super snappy.  I'll admit It's short with a limited replay value but as a gamer with a time budget I appreciate that.  I powered through it in 2 sittings  - 8 hours total and loved all of it. I'd rather have that than an artificially padded run time. Finally - there should be an option to copy saves so you can less anxiously commit to any of the many multiple endings!
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Pros: Immersive worldChoicesChance influenced outcomesClasses & statsMinimalist cyberpunk styleIncredible emotive storyCons:Character build becomes irrelevant if you choose to play a certain wayRequires reading which is not for everyoneHeavy topics may not be for allYou wake up on a space station not knowing who you are or how you got there. Your choices will determine how you navigate all of the questions you have. It’s time to explore who you are.​Writing a story about what it means to be human may sound like one that has been written all too much, however, many do not manage to capture the experience of being human quite like this. This story does not gloss over the difficult situations that we must navigate and the heavy consequences that sometimes entails. These are not the black and white choices, this felt like a real representation of our decisions in a beautiful sci-fi setting. There are moments in this game that evoked such deep emotions from the small interactions with characters or environments, a great reminder of how those small moments add up to such meaningful events over time.Citizen Sleeper manages to maintain a very difficult balance of keeping you on the edge of your seat, but also giving you a sense of safety within the choices that you make for your character. This is a great dynamic of being held responsible for the consequences of what you decide. You may find yourself starving, but this will be because you made a decision to sacrifice energy over something else entirely.There are four simple mechanics at play. You have a set of dice that you use to obtain items, learn information, help others, and finish your own goals. Choice based narrative, a simple yet very effective system that is deeper than it seems. You must medicate your body and maintain your energy levels by sleeping, eating or finding other ways to do this by exploring the station.The levelling system is very simple and easy to use and play to whatever build or approach you have in mind, though the character class starts to feel a bit irrelevant towards the late game sadly. Your character eventually has stats to be able to do everything without negative stats if you choose to play this way.Your character is one of many classes you can choose from, each with their own unique skill bonuses. The bonuses impact your dice rolls by adding numbers, or adding bonus stats such as gaining energy or items. The ambience of this game is subtle yet it is deeply engrossing and evocative. The music sets the tone, while the 2D/3D visuals allow for a more interactive UI rather than just a straight 2D approach as visual novels have. You can look around the world easily just using the mouse wheel and it is very satisfying to discover new areas you unlock along the way.With subject matter such as corporate ownership, AI sentience, exponential gains over lives, this story will hit you in ways that you may not expect. This may be set in a sci-fi cyberpunk future but feels incredibly relevant to our current modern world we are all trying to navigate.This game will make you laugh, keep you on the edge of your seat and surprise you where you least expect it. You may even find yourself crying at 9 a.m after finishing your first ending of the game, and have the game pull you right back in again.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Very good writing and surprisingly simple game mechanics that work really well. If you want about 10 hours of an interesting sci-fi story that, naturally, ponders a lot of existential questions, then this is a good game for that. The premise and world-building here are great!However, I do have to say that the narrative and gameplay kinda fall apart halfway through the game. For the first 5-6 hours this is a quite thrilling survival game. The player character needs to get certain items to stay alive. There is also an external danger to them that gets ever closer. But then you complete a quest that eliminates that danger and all the items you need for survival also become abundant. When this happens, it feels like the main quest is complete. But the game goes on, expecting you to complete "side quests" before you get an ending. At that point, the game kinda started to drag.People have been comparing it to Disco Elysium, Tyranny, and Life is Strange. This comparison is what drew me in. The writing here certainly is top-notch like in these games. The gameplay is different here, more minimal, but still ok. This game was made only by a couple of people and I think they found a really good approach for it. So, don't expect the breadth and complexity of game mechanics from these other games. Most importantly, all these other games kept the motivation and pacing up until the end. Things connected together in these games, all lead to some culmination. This is missing here. At least it was for me. The storylines are mostly disconnected and after you get rid of the main danger to the player character's survival, there wasn't anything equally or more important to take that place in the story.Still a very good game and a memorable experience though. Nice stylish look.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: A personal favorite of mine for story driven games. Some of the mechanics of keeping the character functioning can be a bit boring, but the story is fantastic. It drives you to keep going, and forces you to make choices that have no good option, or sometimes both options are so good it is hard to chose one.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: A story of finding one's place within an unknown, cold and scary environment, and within ones unknown, cold and scary body. It might seem on the nose or strange of me to say this, but I found this game a lot more like Outer Wilds than Disco Elysium (though it still is a lot like DE), through its theme, the way it handles characters, and the general mood while playing, it somehow deeply reminded me of the same amazing feelings I had while first playing Outer Wilds and experiencing the games story for the first time.The greatest strength of this game is it's writing, specifically in the fact it's able to convey such warm and pleasant stories and feelings alongside crushing melancholy and sadness. It hit's mostly all cyberpunk sci-fi tropes, but I still found every character endearing and enjoyable, and all of their storylines concluding in interesting and satisfying ways. I don't think this has ever happened before, but I genuinely for a while not decide which ending I wanted because they were all so good for different reasons.The music brilliantly compliments everything I wrote about the writing, the entire OST is able to hype up or highlight the mood of every single aspect of this game. I'm writing this while sitting in the main menu after finishing it and the feelings I had while playing are put right back into my brain as the music idly plays.In terms of gameplay, it's not the deepest systems, it is quite easily min-maxable, but that puzzle in of itself is still enjoyable to figure out. And if you are struggling, it adds to those moments of freebies that you're giving from good people in the story willing to just lend a hand, further fueling the want to build upon those relationships. The best part of the gameplay was how satisfying, clean, and intuitive the UI is, it's just fun clicking around.There definitely needs to be some QOL changes some character portraits would switch when not supposed to or some menus would bug out, but nothing too terrible. I think the greatest fault of this game is the lack of either narritive clarity or visual/gameplay clarity of important decisions that you get locked into, sometimes I would get a warning, sometimes I wouldnt. If those we're non-decision decisions, then nevermind but then I have different fault with that.9/10
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Like for the soundtrack and art alone.If the 'one man' dev team is responsible for the worst parts of the game should it really be praised aside from its ambition? Is the game loop purposefully one dimensional as a comment on the monotony of your characters existence working dead end jobs to survive and the only colour is the human interaction with NPCs? Given that the dev is a self professed anarchist maybe but idgaf its mid and you dont feel pushed to consider your choices in dialogue or dice rolls.Would've been better suited as a rogue-like with harder balancing, but that wouldve taken focus away from the self aggrandising writing covering age old scifi tropes with the poise of a YA novel. Given that the 2nd game seems to be taking more of an FTL approach there's hope yet.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: An incredible and immersive story told in an interesting way. The game is relaxing at times but I was always debating what decisions to make as you often have limited information about the situations in which you find yourself and I always wanted to do the best by my newfound friends. The end of many characters stories are very emotional and as I spent more time living on Erlin's Eye I came to realise that whilst the systems of the Eye might be cold and callous, there was compassion and humanity in spades to be found amongst its inhabitants. I don't want to spoil anymore but if you enjoy a good story, some light ttrpg mechanics and have an interest in anything philosophically cyberpunk or in the struggles of people living in an uncaring system then you should play this game!
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: "And to persist is to believe that a future, any future at all, is possible"One of the best narratives in a video game I've ever experienced and one of the few times that a video game made me cry.Pick this up now, it's worth every penny spent.Plus the soundtrack by Amos Roddy is so thoughtful yet relaxing.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is roughly a sci-fi narrative solo boardgame set on a space-station. Each day you're given a limited pool of dice to spend on various task. Some of those task keep you alive and healthy enough to survive the next day, while others move along various plots you can involve yourself with, and some do both.The initial stages of the game feel like you're desperate to survive, and the dev has talked a lot about this aspect of the game. The gameplay elements, with ways to manipulate and spend dice, traits that change the mechanics slightly, work well. Unfortunately, the narrative elements and gameplay feel like two separate games. As you progress in the game, that early desperation reveals itself as mostly superficial. You can easily accumulate resources and stats to relegate most tasks to background paperwork. The narrative changes from a single homeless individual trying to break even, to someone who can basically solve every problem from fighting a government to scientific breakthroughs. Your character-creation choices become meaningless as they're overwhelmed by the abundant quest rewards.I understand it's difficult to make a fun game at the same time as telling a story about abandoned parts of society, and the two halves of the game are both good in isolation - the combination in a single game misses the mark a little.Otherwise, writing, sound, and art are all excellent.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly, it's important to adjust your expectations. They say this is supposed to be reminiscent of a pen and paper RPG, but I'd describe it more as a narrative focused adventure/worker placement game. Your starting character class really only matters for the first couple of questlines you complete, and you can easily complete all game content in one playthrough not accounting for differing endings. I didn't end up doing this, as it just didn't feel thematically appropriate from a roleplaying perspective, but it's an option. It's also important to note that they added free dlc that took an extra 1.5 hours or so to complete, and ends the game completely. Most endings that do not have the player leaving or otherwise being incapacitated allow you to keep playing, but the DLC endings end the game completely. So sum total, DLC included, I completed all but 2 questlines in 7 hours.The game is a lot of fun, the worker placement systems work well for the most part and the game is well written. I was sucked in enough to finish the game in a single sitting, which it pretty high praise. That said, the game doesn't feel very rpg-like due to the low character diversity, and the skill options you do have are not balanced so repeat playthroughs will likely see similar skill choices. These are minor issues however, and it's very easy to recommend the game to those looking for a narrative focused experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper
