_childDocuments_.review: Very enjoyable game!  Kind of a meditation on life, what's important, what you'd do for a friend, what goals are worth pursuing.  All wrapped into an engrossing cyberpunk story, with real elements of pathos at times.  It took me a little to figure out what was going on, but that's kind of the theme too; you wake up disoriented on a space station, in an android body, and have to navigate your way through a lot of decisions, all told through branching conversational text options.  You meet a lot of people along your journey, some of whom become friends, some colleagues, some just worth knowing because they are amazing cooks and bartenders.  Highly recommended for a calm, quiet, meditative type of game.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: If you like story driven games with a little time and resource management, this is the perfect game. The replay-ability is a little on the lacking side since the choices don't really effect the overall story, but there are multiple endings, which is nice. If you are into sci-fi element story games, it is definitely worth the price for a play-through or two.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent table-top style RPG/lifesim. You'll traverse a rogue space station as a dying android making life or death decisions. Decisions are made by applying a set of values generated via random dice rolls to actions throughout the day. Your decisions are lightly modified by your stats. The story is gorgeous, the art is gorgeous, and it has one of my favourite video game soundtracks of all time. It becomes a bit easy in the end, and it's short in length (not a detraction from the overall experience), but it's still one of my favourite indie game experiences in a long while.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent mostly text RPG. Uses a clever daily dice mechanism I haven't seen before. Those random dice, along with energy and health, let you push your characters story forward. Lots of paths to follow. A nice cycles mechanism gives a sense of a world going on around you.  Altogether a very novel and satisfying  RPG game mechanic. Lots of paths through the story. I played the three  different character classes, and their stories felt sufficiently different. Played the new Refugee story addition, and was disappointed by that. My choices seemed to make no difference to that story. But the game is well worth playing for the original content.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is a text based RPG with a sci-fi/space/cyberpunk theme.  I know I'm going against the grain on this review, it does happen rarely, but there's reasons for it which I'll get into now. There's an overwhelming amount of mediocre Visual Novel/E-book style scenes in this game.  So you'll spend a huge amount of time not playing the game, but clicking through endless lines of mediocre VN text cutscenes because the developers couldn't work out how to relate their narrative through the game mechanics, and decided instead it would be better to compete with reading a book for your time.  We're here to play games, not read books.  This is almost enough to be classified as a book rather than a game.It's important to remember games don't exist in a vacuum here... this is on the same platform as RPGs like the Deus Ex series, Cyberpunk 2077 and Baldur's Gate 3.  In fact, this is priced not far off those games, but it's offering more of a Steve Jackson's Fighting Fantasy gameplay experience than a truly interactive RPG.  Most of the gameplay is just Choose-Your-Own-Adventure book navigation.  The examples I cite show that the PC is capable of much more dramatic and immersive gameplay than this mostly-text game offers. So, should you buy this game?  Is this one of the best of the 100,000+ games on Steam?Citizen Sleeper has the gamer gouging price of $20 USD, for which you could easily get any number of older AAA games.  Given the defects and quality issues with the game, coupled with the unrealistic price, this is impossible to recommend.  For comparison, the $20 asking price for this game could get you games like "Rise of the Tomb Raider", "Wolfenstein - The New Order" or "Kingdom Come Deliverance", as well as many excellent, fully interactive RPGs.  This is 3 times more expensive than Skyrim can be bought for!Unfortunately Steam reviewers aren't presented with a "Maybe" option... if they did, that's what I'd choose.  This isn't a completely bad game, but it's also not one of the best.  As always, if you read my review and you can overlook the negatives I've called out, or they just aren't important to you, then by all means go ahead and buy this.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This game broke me emotionally. I have never experienced anything like this. This game draws you in so quickly into its bustling landscape and compelling side quests, that most of the time i didn't know what to prioritize. But be careful, don't forget to eat or do your Estrogen injections or you will wither away, like the pharmaceutical overlords of this world designed you to. The artwork is gorgeous and the music let's you forget everything else. 10/10
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Just a really beautifully constructed and realized game. I thoroughly enjoyed experiencing this game with my girlfriend and having philosophical conversations about the people and world of Citizen Sleeper. I fully plan to revisit it years in the future to re-experience some of it and shoot for a different experience/ending
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: The game is really good! An interesting story. Fantastic writing. Fitting soundtracks. Look nice. Overall, quite pleasant experience! However, not without its flaws.- The interface of The Eye is not convenient to interact with. It took time to understand and get used to scrolling with the mouse wheel all the time. - Needs some quality of life improvements. For instance, returning to your "home" to rest in one click, or proceeding with a dialogue by pressing something on keyboard instead of manually clicking on an option.- Kind of repetitive. Introducing more of time/situation-limited opportunities can fix it. So that you have to think how you'd better spend your dice.- Lack of challenge. It doesn't seem to punish for making poor decisions, and there's hardly a chance to miss anything. It also leads to poor replayability - picking other class doesn't add anything unique to the gameplay, the storylines can be covered in one playthrough, and pursuing some things doesn't prevent you from tackling the different ones later.Overall, could have been more engaging. Still, I enjoyed the game and would recommend it for the story - a good read.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper will disparage you, throw you into a small ring-world ripe with deadlines, demands and a constantly decaying body that is you, but not you. Trapped inside a mechanical quasi organic body that dulls the senses of outside touch, yet even then, those around you function better in the long term than you do. And to top that off, a situation that wants to gut you from the outset.But. It'll show you there is more to living than those sensations of touch, more to feeling than the base desires you feel at your finger tips. And that, is valuable.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is a quite a special game I think. It is a tense lonely cyberpunk dystopia that isn't full of guns and noise. It has some quite wonderfully powerful moments and a set of systems that are so familiar to me as a tabletop gamer but which are still fascinating when presented in a videogame. The ideas, the images, the soundscapes are all excellent. Definitely play this.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: let me get this out of the way right now. i dont like visual novels. i find them boring and slow and a waste of money.this is none of thosethis is the best 12 bucks i have ever spent on a game. i cried during the credits because it made that much of an impact on me. i will admit, i missed a few quests before leaving the eye but i still felt like i helped the people there.the games music is second to none in my opinion and the art style and character designs are perfect and resonate with me for some reason.i would fully recommend getting the game at full price. it is one of the best games of all time.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I got this because it was nominated for a BAFTA... the slow burn worldbuilding, meaningful relationships with the people you meet and the influence you have on the community as a whole are what sets this diceroller apart from the pack. Get it if you like adventure games like Disco Elysium or any of Failbetter games' games.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Highly recommend. Super atmospheric and deeply moving. I was super roped into every character and determined to chase all their stories to the end as soon as I met them. Choices certainly matter, and often wrap back around in a surprising way that makes a ton of sense when you get it to it. The game does a pretty good job explaining mechanics & basic resources while not overexplaining itself, so there are some secrets & resources you'll have to do the work to uncover the best ways to utilize).Don't spoil yourself, don't look anything up. Just jump in and join the cycle.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper delighted and surprised me. It's wonderful writing and character design bring the story to life, and the tabletop RPG-style resource systems reinforce the feeling that your character is barely scraping by in a Cyberpunk dystopia on the frontier of space. I find myself constantly thinking about the situations and people I met along my first journey on Erlin's Eye, and I can't wait to start another. And another. And another (I am actually on my 4th playthrough). Do not miss this one!
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Engaging, thought-provoking, and emotional.Successfully made me cry, which means I was invested enough to care.Something that sits with me after I finish playing it.Love the style of the visual art, music, and writing.Played it during a Game Pass free trial, bought it on Steam.They've added new content since then, good stuff, just like the rest!They're also working on a second Citizen Sleeper. Excited!I think it's worth your time :>
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: a Wonderful , Beautiful Journey through a Sci-Fi cyberpunk world where you get to experience struggle, kindness and the human nature ( in any of the ways with which you may understand it ). its a gorgeous game of stories, feelings, thoughts and ideas. its world building is exemplary , its story telling smooth, its writing elegant and its gameplay effective at helping you through this. Honestly one of my favorite Indie Games. absolutely love it.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely one of the best pieces of media I've ever consumed. I cried the whole way through. The visuals are so pretty, the concepts are interesting and thought provoking. There were points where some of the writing was a bit stilted, grammatical errors, or something was just lost in translation. But even with those hurdles, I can not name another piece of media that's resonated with me the way Sleeper did. Thanks for the mushrooms.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: The writing and storytelling really engaged me.  Through it I was swept up into a place that I felt like I could touch  and see and smell in my minds eye. Even though I knew I would never get to see or experience it anything like The Eye, it brought me to a place where I could reflect on where and how I am - and we are.The music in this game is 100% spot on. It can drive you forward and can halt you dead in your tracks with washes of doubt and fear as each story progresses.The dice mechanic, similar to a worker placement system (like the board game Euphoria: Build A Better Dystopia) is engaging and makes you consider each action carefully to get the most out of each precious cycle.I really enjoyed this game, and I look forward to additional playthroughs after a bit of a break.If you like story based games, you will enjoy this title.Hats off to the Developer, Jump Over The Age.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: It is a text story game where choices matter.Since I have found zero (0) bugs, including the background sound-loops, this alone makes this an automatic thumbs up. This is quality work.Already decided this needs a second play-through at some point.The worst part of this game is that I can't read.Edit: This is one of the best story games I have played. Highly recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic game that I got on a whim, the mechanics are simple, but the story is very rich and complex. I started blowing through it fast cause I like getting 100% achievements in games, but I noticed that I slowed down after about a half hour and just started reading and enjoying the story. My only criticism would be that I would like a bit more options for leveling, but otherwise, it's simply a well-written story and entertaining game.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Touching game about carving out an existence for yourself on the edge of galactic civilisation that is let down by dry gameplay. Ultimately a resource management with very light RPG mechanics, the most engrossing part of Citizen Sleeper is the writing for encounters between the gameplay loop of spending your daily dice rolls in the most optimal ways available. Really great music. First free content update has been very good and looking forward to the next two. Always feed the stray.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Mechanically the dice system is incredibly unsatisfying, and makes it so you can be rewarded for mechanically smart play, but rather the fact you just got lucky that day. The story also is fairly dull, and even when a story line does seem to be more interesting the game constantly forces you to take breaks from that subplot so you can't even pursue it how you wish. Sure it is more "realistic", but if I can't even explore the world I want, and the sole mechanic of the game is luck then I can't say it is worth playing
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I actually played this entire game (and the available DLC) while I had a free trial of Xbox Game Pass, so I technically was able to complete the game for free, but I still wanted to buy it here on steam so I could own it and play it again (and also play the next DLC episode : D)It's a beautifully written story. I loved the protagonist character's backstory and the path they take going forwards. There's the right amount of melancholy and potential for hopelessness at the outset, to help demonstrate how powerful it is when a character keeps trying their best to live and make the most their situation, day by day. The diverse cast of characters was also a delight. Each of their side stories was very rewarding and illustrated the many dimensions of the game's world in a variety of ways. Some stories were action-suspense: anti-corporate activism, a monster lurking in cyberspace, etc.  Other stories were on a smaller scale, focused on the personal trials and also victories of everyday life. There are a variety of story endings--my favorite ending genuinely made me cry it was so good.Also, the game's OST is VERY good. It perfectly characterizes and also enhances the game's atmosphere and emotional journey.Definitely my favorite game of 2022. Highly recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: narrative roguelikes rock. roll the dice to see what part of the plot you open up next, but also to progress through traditional character development skill trees. this is what the choose your own adventure reading system always wanted to be. no resolution scaling though so i'm going with the switch version instead
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This game has made me feel, the art is great, the music is spot on, the setting is interesting. The story and characters have made me angry, sad, happy, the jokes and references have made me laugh, I've cried both for the "goodbyes" and the "I'm still here's," I've felt powerful and influential, and insignificant. I've been hunted and afraid, also welcomed and made to feel at home. I've been pushed to act quickly, and encouraged to take my time and make a home on the Eye.I know I'm gonna replay it at least twice to get the endings I've missed. An amazing story, worth the price of admission, and I wholly recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: "Citizen Sleeper" has a game play loop is reminiscent to "Disco Elysium's" dice roll system and "Cloudpunk"'s point to point activity to expand the narrative. Each cycle (day) in the game the player gets a number of dice dependent on your health to use for any activity in the station of the Eye with your stats acting as modifiers to those rolls. This turns the game into a management of your dice and resources to figure out how best to use them to keep furthering the narrative. Some objectives are a race against time, however, so planning ahead and deciding what is important to you is a must. The more you explore the station and work with other people and factions, the more of the narrative and world lore opens to you. The narrative is cyberpunk in feel with it's SciFi capitalist dystopia, but with a sense of hope in a hopeless situation at its core. Gamers who are interested in a more narrative focused experience would be the key audience for "Citizen Sleeper".
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Good, but short-lived. The writing was nice and generally pretty good. The characters were somewhat interesting but rarely surprising. Very much a visual novel; the gameplay is largely absent, just selecting dice which gives you some percentage chance of a bad thing happening. The "quests" themselves were largely just a series of "do you trust this person or not". It only took me 4 hours to beat and I don't regret my time with it, but even with only 4 hours it started to get tired by the second half.Overall an interesting story, if short. Best part of the game was the soundtrack by far, but I appreciate the aesthetics
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: The game has a "choices matter" tag, but your choices do not matter. You get the same story results regardless of which choice you choose in any given story event. Not only that, but any time you choose to stand up for yourself or even just try to escape a situation and don't choose the "comply humbly / give up quickly" option you get punished for it. It feels like a "get bullied" sim and it's really not enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This has to be one of the best TTRPG games I've played. It's original, in the world of COD, AC, Rogue Lite remakes it's nice to find something original. The story had me pulled in from the get go. The dice actions were unique and not knowing the consequences of some things made it all the more real. Like "should I really do this?". If you like story driven games this one is a 10/10 I can't wait for CS2.     My only complaint is one character the game keeps referring to as "they" which is confusing as hell. Its obviously a woman just say she. No need to bring this woke genZ nonsense into the game, which I assume is what the makers were going for. It is a distraction every time I had to interact with that character. And confusing. There's no 3rd gender. You'd have to be brainwashed to believe so. Leave that nonsense out in the 2nd game please.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I've never seen a 'choices matter' game where you have such little control over how things play out.No matter which dialogue option you chose, things will always end up the same way, with the only volition you have is to park a story thread and refuse to complete it.Case in point: At one point in the game, a Bounty Hunter tracked me down. Rather than kill me and send me in, he decided on some slave labour to buy him off temporarily. After a bit, he tires of it and tries to kill me. (None of your dialogue choices can change any of this). After failing to kill me, he comes back a week later and asks for a favour. You can't tell him to bugger off, much less attack or kill this monster. You just have to accept his quest, and maybe just decline to spend resources helping him.Choices matter? Bah humbug.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Really good worldbuilding and atmosphere, and Amos's sound design is great. I wasn't expecting it to be so text-heavy but once I adjusted, I was there for it. I kept playing because I wanted to see the end of the character stories.Gameplay-wise the mechanics side of the resource management really shines in the first half of the game. It's not  but it does feel tense and limiting and makes you feel like you're struggling to get on your feet. You have a lot of possible options but only get to choose a few.Regarding the writing and story, the focus is definitely on the characters and the world. Your own personality and story is mostly through the eyes of the characters you meet. You don't really say much and you have to construct your own head canon. It's a style that reminds me of a blend of tabletop roleplaying and interactive fiction. When I put myself in that mindset, I really enjoyed it.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is a great game. It's one of a kind and if you fully listen to the narrative you will love it. Its survival aspect is not overbearing and the game gives you lots of room to explore other outcomes. However, I mostly beat this game in 7 hours. 20$ for that little game time is not worth it in my books.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best games I have played having well written story lines and compelling characters.  This truly is a game where decisions matter and affect outcomes.  Many other games advertise that but still have very linear story lines where "decisions" don't really matter.  For this type of game the graphics and artwork is I would best describe as elegance in how it conveys the personality of the characters and the atmosphere of the game's universe.  The soundtrack - amazing!  I have listened to the soundtrack in its entirety many times while working.FYI, if you end up really liking this game try "In Other Waters" from the same developers/designer.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is a melancholy little gem of a space dystopia RPG. You play as a "sleeper", an android with an emulated mind, who has escaped indentured servitude and now must eke out a way to survive while you are hunted by mercenaries and your body slowly degenerates from its engineered obsolescence. Major themes include "the downsides of capitalism" and "it's lonely out in space". Like a lot of other cyperpunk and futuristic space capitalism narratives, the kernel that keeps these downtrodden characters pushing through are the friends and relationships formed with people who have it just as tough. Citizen Sleeper can be compared to Disco Elysium. They both have themes of capitalism and social dystopia. They are both RPG's. Citizen Sleeper does not have the same size or features as Disco Elysium (a voice cast would be really cool for Citizen Sleeper), but the descriptive writing in Citizen Sleeper carries the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome game, with an awesome story. Tremendous writing throughout, with characters that feel fleshed-out and nuanced; if i have any complaints, its that i only got to spend so much time with them all.This game is sincerely incredible. Mechanically speaking, its very clean and neat; no need to worry about QTE-like timers or precision gameplay; everything is done in "tuns" and even the Clock mechanic is generally pretty forgiving. But really, the selling point is the narrative. I haven't felt this deeply about video game characters in ages, and rarely if ever for characters i've spent only a few "indie game length" hours with, which speaks to the writer's skill at engendering empathy with their audience. I know i'm late to the review page, but seriously, if you havent played this, do so. It's worth every single penny, and then some.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: (the Clock system is particularly a standout in it's use!) There is not necessarily a ton of replayability but nevertheless, I thoroughly think it's worth digging into if you want a table-top roleplaying experience but singleplayer. There is a chill vibe to the music and the familiar flow you get into each 'cycle' as you re-roll your available dice and take on a new day.Side note for the devs; I would really dig a Hacked in the Dark set on Erlin's Eye!
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: The writing is sometimes good and I liked the worldbuilding, but overall I was disappointed. People compared this to Disco Elysium, but it's really nothing like that game, other than being a dialogue-heavy RPG involving dice. There is very little player agency in the average conversation - the dialogue "choices" are usually like 1) nod, 2) "okay", 3) stay silent. Or maybe someone asks whether you like something and you can say yes or no, and that has no effect on anything. There are a couple of different endings but the game in general feels quite linear, and as though very few decisions actually matter.The gameplay isn't challenging or particularly interesting, and I wasn't a huge fan of the writing or the character art style. I was just invested enough to finish the main plot, but overall would not recommend.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I've never been compelled to write a review, but this game more than deserves it. Is hands down my favorite game that I've played this year and maybe even longer. Amazing narrative and art style which keep you invested throughout whichever path you take despite the simple game mechanics and lack of difficulty levels (somethings I think could've enhance the experience).There's a lot of dialogue which I initially had my skepticism about but the quality of the writing in this game makes the game so worthwhile. As someone who's normally impatient to get to the action in real life and games, the lead ups to the climaxes of the storylines and perspective given made me fall in love with the characters and the world. No matter what genre of games you're into (and even if you're someone who fast forwards/skips dialogue), it's worth whatever time you put into it. Hoping and praying for more content so I can explore this universe more.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: A sensitive, intelligent, emotional, and spiritual masterpiece of a sci-fi game.This is not a game you fight for hegemony. You play as a new form of life, or an android, so to speak, a discriminated, chased, and overpowered.The worldview is inspired by anthropologist Anna Tsing's brilliant book The Mushroom at the End of the World. I was impressed by the setting and details of the characters and factions, technologies, and spirituality neatly thought out by the creators. Obtaining sustainability that does not depend on money in the latter half of the game, for example, apparently shows the idea of de-capitalism. Citizen Sleeper exceeds the scope of a game. One of the best games I have played ever in my life 👏👏👏
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing 10/10 fantastic game.Light survival mechanics layered on top of excellent nonlinear branching story. And after finding one ending, you can pick up immediately prior to completion, choose the other path, and continue -- so it's possible to see most of the storylines to completion in one playthrough. Can't wait for the second DLC!
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I do not review often but this was such a well done experience.  I can see it not being everyone's cup of tea but the stories were well fleshed out and if actually let yourself get lost in it you will not regret it.  You will really feel the tug of your decisions even if you like or hate the outcome of them.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: So immersive. I really connected to the story, it's thouught-provoking and I often think about it, and what it says of who we are as people in relation to the systems around us. The free content update is very nice, I can tell the developer really loves this game. The game doesn't coddle you. Success is earned. You co-create this story. There's enough with the images and actions, with the text, for you to create your own relationship to the story. I've played through twice
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: You start off, just scraping by, surviving by the skin of your teeth. And at the beginning, you'll only want to leave the Eye. By the end though, you'll find that leaving is harder than expected, because you'll have to leave behind everything you've found here.Remember: no love, however brief, is wasted. And kindness will always be rewarded.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: There were parts of Citizen Sleeper I liked, but overall I can't recommend the game to others like me.  If you like a Choose Your Own Adventure, text-heavy, game-mechanic-lite game, you may like this one.  I prefer more of a challenge, and after a bit this game becomes a Progress Quest.  Where you just progress the plot by clicking some stuff.It starts off a little challenging, but after stacking some upgrades and re-rollability, the challenge is removed.  The mechanic of your body degrading is easy to defeat, and energy is rarely a problem.  Negative results become easier to avoid.  The text story seemed on rails to me, where the few Either/Or choices felt unimpactful to the story.  The story itself, and the details of the Sleepers, are unique (to me) and pretty interesting, but the story itself isn't enough to outweigh the funlessness of progressing it.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: What a beautiful game!The story is well written, the mechanics are simple but fun, and the music fits perfectly.The pacing/difficulty can spike if you happen to chain too many quests lines together, but even at its worst I could handle it. My only complaint is that some endings requires multiple playthroughs, and I think the magic of this game happens in the first one so I won't be getting all the endings. But other then that, there's no regret to the choices I made and the branches of the choices felt genuine and meaningful.As a side note, there are a lot of people comparing this to Disco Elysium... and I don't think this is anywhere near that level of polish and depth of DE. But it's very good in its own way and deserves to be considered as an unique entry, not a copy of something else.Absolutely worth my time and money, and I think if you like good stories, don't miss out on this gem!
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: For how much the two get compared, I don’t think Citizen Sleeper has much in common with Disco Elysium. It seems as if people have an innate desire to label everything, either to understand it better or to dumb it down. Themes of class struggle? Check. Disheartening atmosphere? Check. Into the Disco pile you go. However, I do think there’s a comparison to be made, just not in the pompous, overarching way. Both games begin with the same: darkness. In Disco Elysium, a detective wakes up half-naked in a messy hotel room without an ounce of memory; in Citizen Sleeper, the protagonist comes to in a claustrophobic container. But unlike the distraught cop, the Sleeper has no way of retrieving their memories. They are an android infused with a human soul; although they can talk and move and sympathize, there’s always that distinction: the fleeting memories of being human, the realization that that time is gone, the alienation from others…  From the beginning, the alienation is at the center. After escaping from a life of relentless work at a corporate facility, the Sleeper is on the run, on the lookout for a proper life. They arrive at the Eye, a circular space station of gigantic proportions. Previously a corporate structure, the Eye now serves as home for all kinds of drifters: the poor, the rich, those in between. Although many settle there, none are satisfied. The Eye is a reminder of an unkept promise, a desire for something better.  This is how we start: the distinction. After these paragraphs, you’re offered a “choice”—to reminisce on the body you’ve lost, or to forget it. Choice is a bold term, because no matter which option you pick, that body isn’t coming back. It’s lost to time, a memory, and while you can shovel through the earth and gravel and soil of your mind trying to remember what it was like, how it  to be human, you cannot  the body back. This is the tragedy of Citizen Sleeper: it’s a story about harsh truths and the hopes that carry us onward. It’s a story about being human. Before diving into this world, I looked into its inspirations. In an interview with , developer Gareth Damian Martin stated the following: “For [cyberpunk] to be effective, I find that it needs to draw on something about now (…) We should continue to make cyberpunk work about the moment we’re in, not the moment that they were in or this awesome imagined future. I think cyberpunk is about now.” —this is etched into the storytelling, from feeling lost in a world where the individual is suppressed, to corrupt conglomerates, to people trying to eke out a living and form communities in the shadow of capitalism. Some of these are staples of the cyberpunk genre, but it’s the depiction that brings with it a sense of modernism. Gone are the towering mercenaries and infamous rockers trying to bring down the corporations in a blaze of glory; this is a game about the little folks, the overworked engineers and chatty street vendors, the market doctors and gamblers. It’s a game about you and me. Unless you happen to be one of the rich folks. Then it’s only about me ;)This sincerity resonated with me, and I’ve found that it’s these stories—stories about the idiomatic conditions and experiences—that make the deepest impact. It’s when the writer embraces their personal sensibilities and rids themselves of any pretense and grandiloquence that their story transcends words on a page and becomes an experience, a statement. Good fiction is truth; bad fiction, a lie.In contrast with the vivacious and immersive writing, the visuals are impersonal, mostly static shots of the Eye with only hints of the life coursing through it. It is a dichotomy that highlights the staples of cyberpunk—the illusive, grand structures juxtaposed with the ugly reality; the people in the skyscrapers and the people below; the cold and the warmth. You could even say a fight between the three-dimensional viewpoints and the dialogue box takes shape, as one side of the screen reminds you of your insignificance, and the other of your acquaintances. Of course, this was not the intention and likely a result of development constraints, but not all artistic qualities are achieved with deliberation. Sometimes, it’s the flaw—the wrong stroke of a brush, the shoddy camera angle, the missing line of dialogue—that completes the work. Think back on the number of times in which a mistake of yours, or lack of notice, led to fortune; why shouldn’t the same apply to art?The gameplay stays true to the suppositions of the narrative. Unlike Cyberpunk 2077, where we’re led to believe V is an underdog until they’re mowing down gangs like overgrown lawns, Citizen Sleeper incorporates the risk and thrill of life on the Eye into its mechanics. The game happens in cycles, each ending when the Sleeper hits the sack and beginning with the assignment of a set of dice. A die is then used to perform actions: the higher its number, the better the chance of success. You must also keep your condition and energy in check. To ensure the Sleepers don’t escape, their manufacturer has given them a need for a rare drug; without it, they’ll meet a slow death. As such, the biggest challenge in the beginning will be to procure this medicine while also making progress around the Eye. Where the game stumbles is in its choices. A great way to enforce the harsh truths would be moral dilemmas, decisions that determine the matter of life and death; as far as I could tell, however, none of mine had repercussions. Furthermore, the layer of verisimilitude starts to crack once you discover that there is no death. Should your condition reach 0, you will be unable to perform actions and will lose one of your skills. A temporary setback, nothing more. To be different in a world that does not tolerate diversity. To risk not having a roof over your head tomorrow. To go for days without food. These are problems relevant in both our current climate and the future of Citizen Sleeper. We tend to look at futures in too ways—utopian or dystopian. Life on the Eye is neither. This is a story about now, and now is neither of the two. And therein lies the question: why? Why keep on existing in this world of pain, sorrow and hate?A powerful concept in Citizen Sleeper is the rhizomatic network that connects the Eye’s structures and people. As an android, it might be possible to upload your sentience onto this network, to become one with the stream of data—but at what cost? You might escape the challenges and the prejudice, but you would also burn the relationships you have forged, the people that bring you joy and console you when you need it most. You would be reduced to something impersonal, a tiny ball swept across the ever-expanding sea of the net. Citizen Sleeper argues that there is purpose in this struggle: no matter how intense the longing gets, we should keep on going and appreciate what we do have. It teaches us that the world is cruel, but also that it can be kind. And in that, there is meaning.

_childDocuments_.review: So I have mixed feelings about this game. Especially since it has "Overwhelmingly Positive" reviews which is why I bought it. The character design/writing, story, and sound design all get a 10/10 for me.But the actual gameplay is around a 1/10. There are some design decisions that are so annoying that I've considered not playing the game anymore rather than restarting my run for the 3rd time. I have to do this because there are no saves, only autosaves. Normally this wouldn't be a big deal, except the core gameplay isn't fun, more tedious. The reason I am playing this game is because of the story, so a restart/new game is just me re-reading the same content until I get to the places I'm actually interested in or matters. And so far there isn't enough variability to the story and dialogue to make this interesting. There also needs to be some quality of life updates to the navigation. It's slow and frustrating to try to find the right locations. For some reason, even though the graphics are not hardware expensive, you have to click through a location to move between certain zones. Just put all of the locations on one map. Those transition locations have zero purpose except to make turns (cycles) feel longer. I'm confident that any modern computer could handle all of those location nodes in one map. Like I said, I love the story, but can't stomach the tedium in progressing that story. A part of me thinks I would have enjoyed this more if it was a book. Some of the quest lines aren't written to account for where other quest lines are in progress, so it makes for some awkward dialogue in places. Also, would have liked to see have seen more text variety in some of the redoable dice actions. Getting the same dialogue every time is boring. I think it would have given the game more life if each one had a dozen or two randomized responses.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I played, pretty invested in the "unique" path I thought I was going through. But that's not really how the game works, despite how people are talking about it.The game is basically a bunch of pins on a map. Depending on your skills at that time (which get increased with every completed goal), you put completion points into those places. These places usually have characters associated with them. The outcomes for these completion points are either a) a consumable item b) more map pins or c) character story.I love character-building, but I feel like most people's stories are just filled with so much lore jargon that it's a bit hard to appreciate where they're coming from (emotionally or otherwise). They talk AT us, and because everyone is engaging with you for their particular story, they're just listing a bunch of facts about their situation EVERY time. And because they don't connect to other characters, we get a new set of information every time as well. You don't really engage with characters outside their immediate needs, so it's just you reacting to that - there's no sense of real relationship outside of maybe 2 characters (2 characters who still drop out of the story after you finish their quests).The outcomes of these character dynamics is either that something happens, or doesn't. What I mean is that either you don't bother finishing the task, or you do and you get a "thanks, we're friends now" option that will impact nothing beyond that task. I wouldn't mind as much if there was more gameplay, but this is essentially a visual novel that has a binary outcome for everything: do the thing, or don't do the thing. I was specifically trying to find a choice-matters type game, but this was not that. Plus, the character is literally a shell for the player's personality. I LOVE that, when you get actual agency. I like when I can decide on my character's personality. But you don't really get a choice for that either. You are designated as a bland, generally amiable person who everyone feels about the same level of affection for over time. And it's pretty boring. If my choices were going to be so constricted, I rather have a super-defined and interesting character. Wouldn't it have been interesting if the person you were occasionally conflicted and grappled with the person you were trying to be? I felt that this was a strangely overlooked aspect of the story. There are a lot of existential questions suggested and never really explored.Citizen Sleeper feels like a competent mini-game in a bigger game - like the map quests in Dragon Age Inquisition. If you're into just reading, it's fine. But I feel like relationships are too basic (you help me, therefore we're friends; you don't help me, we stop engaging). Events - even world-changing ones - are isolated to their plot lines. Specializing is only useful in the first hour or two of gameplay, after which you can broadly put points in everything without consequence.I think there needed to be more dead-ends, more options to specialize not just in skills, but in people and their factions. Why have more than one game option when you can do pretty much everything in one route?
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Fun gameplay loop, but no difficulty increase means after a few hours you treat your character like a sim. Get food, get some cash, make sure you don't die. All good? Keep doing plot for a few cycles again. Taking care of your character slowly but surely becomes a chore.Was not a fan of the writing, the dialogue options don't matter and your character's perspective on things is very one-dimensional (Corporations bad, small commune good).While the game starts strong with an interesting premise, a strong emphasis on managing your time and resource to both survive and explore The Eye, it ends with you grinding mushrooms because you're doing good on all resources and waiting on a new plot point to be done.

_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I can't recommend this game enough. I enjoy the gameplay and main story a lot (although the dice mechanic does become somewhat trivialised later in the game by your upgrades), but it is the characters, writing, and feelings this game is able to invoke that will make you fall in love with it. _childDocuments_.review: You know when you're looking for a feeling and you can't find it, and everything is just a little bit wrong, like how people who design affordable women's clothes seem to have this procedure of making a normal garment, then adding some dumb frippery or ugly v-line which ♥♥♥♥♥ the whole piece in a subtle way; or simply making a normal dress out of horrid, coarse plastic faux-gauze. And it is all ♥♥♥♥ like that: an un-terminating thrift dive of not-quite-right ♥♥♥♥... Everybody seems to know the feeling, but they are simpletons emulating the feeling badly. They don't understand what it even is they're interested in. "Flying cars... Just like it, don't I. Yeah, androids. Neon. Yep. That's what I like!" 😒But then, ah, there's a good piece at the bottom! _childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I enjoyed this game for what it is.  I hope the creator will develop further games with a lot more depth, because there is great potential here.  However, a small warning to those of you that have read other misleading reviews and threads in the discussion forum:- As the developer has stated, this is a STORY.  This is not a Bioware or similar publisher style game. You are along for the ride and your conversation choices, and other game play choices, in general, mean nothing.  The story unfolds as the authors intends it.  There are no romances. Think of this game as a well written comic strip with some light game play features. - The game play features of Sleeper are simplistic at best and tedious at worst (particularly in the later part of the story).
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is an instant classic in my books and a must have video game. While it may be a short by many peoples standards (I got roughly 15 hours out of it) the amount of wealth you get from its personal and driving storytelling more than makes up for it. The way events are written and choices are made build this up to an impossibly well executed game making it a must buy.Storytelling: 12 out of 10I haven't been this moved by storytelling and character development in an incredibly long time. The listlessness of existence in a place eking out an existence on the edge of human extremes. A space station in full decay barely habitable but bustling with people trying their best just to survive for wages that are paycheck to mouth let alone keeping a roof over your head. The empty burnt husks and shells of people who survived corporate warfare on the living rights of man and claiming them as property and not as people. The attempts to break free from the bonds of servitude even after set free and to keep the demons of control at bay. The sad reality of watching the wool being pulled over your eyes for hard efforts and hard work, dreams of colleges and friends being dashed by the time aged tradition of favoritism and cronyism. Escaping sad destinies for brighter futures even if it isn't your own but that of a poor and scared child who can break the cycle of servitude.Gameplay: 6 out of 10 There isn't anything ground breaking about the game play but dont let this distract you from the way the game plays. The merit points here are based on the life cycles of existence on the Eye. Early urgency to keep a failing husk of a body operational while trying to discover the reality of your own existence. Will you be able to produce the results needed to repair your frame or get the nutritional needs to keep synthetic organs operational all while avoiding attack programs set to find and eliminate entities like your own. So if you read this, give the game a chance and have no expectations on where it brings you... just that it does.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: awsome worldbuilding. the eye is a beautiful place you will love to explore and learn about. the gameplay is really nice as well. you roll dice every round and use them to to do actions (work, investigate, explore ect.)  you also collect recources and data you need and manage events and ticking clocks (they tick every round, no real time clock). the good writing makes the world believable and i never knew who really could be trusted.great experience overall.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is a remarkable work of tabletop-influenced narrative with an emphasis on relatable characters and an engaging setting that qualifies as a character in its own right. Dealing with themes of structure vs freedom and other complex topics while simultaneously being an engaging narrative, I would describe Citizen Sleeper as one of the best-written games I have played in quite some time. Its dice-based component creates simple yet meaningful gameplay which complements the story without overshadowing it as well. Overall a firm recommend to fans of narrative-focused games and even first-timers to the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Of all the games I've played in recent years, this is the one I enjoyed most.  It's so immersive and atmospheric - you will care about the story and especially the people you meet.  It's a journey of self-discovery.  The music and art are exceptional.After you've finished your first playthrough, try it again with a different archetype.  Make different choices.  Explore other stories.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Not a bad game, mixes point and click with dice progressive RNG and visual novel elements. Interesting concepts all around the Sleeper Mythos. Visually, the game centers around the an outerspace Torus Wheel and a whitewash hacking filter for additional gameplay. It has some ASMR style feel good music. Wished there was a little more illustrative immersion between the sleeper as it is deceptively much more text based than it seems. The consequences in different Sleeper choices doesnt seem different with some individuals it chooses to interact with. Maybe there is room for improvement in later updates.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: The game is, at it's core, one about resource management. I don't think other reviews have stressed this enough, but it's also mostly linear; there are a handful of different endings to be found, but the routes leading up to them don't have any forks. The allure of Citizen Sleeper is its writing, which is good and interesting. I can't help but feel it's a little overpriced for what it offers, though
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: The joy and beauty of Citizen Sleeper is in it's simplicityWhile the environment of the game is not that big, it manages to feel larger than life and more complicated through the art direction and storytelling. Every character has their own motivations, values, and personalities, and the choices you make matter. There's several story lines and endings to follow as you figure out why you're on the Eye, and where you'll go from there. A highlight of the game for me is that you can explore multiple endings in one play through, as you can continue from where you left off. It's still quite fun to go back and start over with different choices, and I've played through this game several times at this point. I also loved how most of your choices do matter in the long run, and affect the outcome of the game and your relationship to other characters. One thing I'd like to point out before you get this game--it's reading intensive...If you don't like to read walls of text, then you will not have any fun with this. I personally thought the writing and dialogue was fantastic, so it wasn't a dealbreaker for me, but it's important to know for those who may not be looking for that experience. Overall the game is amazing, and I look forward to all the updates the devs have been adding to the story. Every run reveals details and choices I never considered before, and I find myself enjoying even the dull relaxing moments in between. (Note: I originally played this game for several runs on Game Pass first, so my total playtime is more like 20 hours instead of 10--I loved it so much I bought the game and art book here :^))
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: It was the moment I met Lem (And Mina). Just get the game.The music, the art is all so beautiful, the story is addicting and the characters are charming.Its all reading, I hate reading, I completely forgot I was reading when playing this. _childDocuments_.review: this is just OK.i enjoyed bookwalker or pentiment much more as far as recent visual novels go. the RNG factor can straight up ♥♥♥♥ you around for something you've spent a few hours slowly building up and working towards, it adds nothing to the game besides frustration.i couldnt get invested in the characters at all, i didnt find them interesting. there is very little in terms of visuals or sounds as well, barebones. no gameplay to be heard of besides clicking on icons.what it does well however, is set up an interesting atmosphere, allow for player choice, and an addictive "gameplay" loop. i was very willing to start each new day after each new day. still recommended, but only on heavy sale, this game gets too much praise for what it is and there is much better competition.

_childDocuments_.review: The start of this game is fantastic. Honestly, up until half way, it's one of the better games I've ever played.The problem begins after that. Every single quest you finish tells you, the player, how you should feel, how you should react - It feels awful, and it's incredibly disingenuous and disrespectful to the player. However, if it was just the end of the quests, I'd still recommend this game, just while mentioning the caveat that the end game is extremely poorly written.The problem, however, is the new content (episode: REFUGE update). They dropped the pretense completely; it isn't even posed as a story anymore. It reads as a manifesto on the developer's views on refugees (which make no sense when applied to a very limited space station with severely limited resources).Allow me to quote a line from the intro to it: "Even calling them 'refugees' is just a way of turning a lot of scared, desperate people into a single, monolithic group."This isn't a game anymore, this is someone's twitter feed. You have no option to combat the people invading the station, no option to try to stop or mitigate the issue, only a quest to help them invade the station (you are also supplied with zero motivation or reason to assist them).Maybe grab it when it's for sale at ten bucks; first half is still worth playing.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: It's okay, but it's not for people who like Disco Elysium.But it's not awful, in some places its quite good, but comparing it to Disco Elysium is like comparing Divergent to Hunger Games. One is written by a much more experienced writer than the other and its obvious. If you played Disco Elysium first you might not like this as much.Narratively, it's not really breaking any ground or saying anything new, which isn't a problem unto itself but... I don't feel like a character in this world. I'm not uncovering a story so much as someone watching cyberpunk/dystopic sci-fi tropes exist in front of me. There's something about the writing that makes these characters feel flat. It's got that inexperienced DM's "the barman looks you over and ask's you what you'll have" quality to every interaction. Which is not a bad thing unto itself, but the reason that works for a TTRPG is because the players don't expect a compelling story told to them, instead they want to dictate their own story. But you can't do that in a video game because of the limitation of the medium. (Unless you're specifically exploring that kind of meta-narrative relationship like in Inscryption.) The game writer *has* to give you options, you cannot just write your own and have the game respond meaningfully. So if a game writer has to do that work they also have to do the other work a TTRPG player has to do, like build a character to play.Part of the difficulty of a video game that wants the player to do some serious role playing is giving them a character they *want* to inhabit. The thing about games like Disco Elysium or Planescape Torment (who both do this very well) is that they give a player a fully fleshed out person to play and then carefully dole out that info to the player. When done really well, it lets the player become this character and in the process learn more about themselves and their worldview.Citizen Sleeper does not do that. The Sleeper is a blank slate for the player to jump into, but that means that the player is now required to make up so much of the character that it's impossible for a writer to know anything about how they might react. So they can't be specific or take the player anywhere personal. Much of the player's dialogue or reactions to things are generic so as to fit many possible player reactions. Sometimes it reads like a "choose your own adventure" novel and at other times like a "y/n"-insert fanfic. I don't feel like there's a strong narrative or story here beyond "things happen around you, some of them are connected". Others have talked about issues with the design of the mechanics and difficulty flow, but I felt that with stronger writing they wouldn't have been issues at all. Some of the balance of really feeling like picking a class mattered could also be solved with stronger writing and more robust narrative design.Overall an okay game, but not one that I would recommend.On the technical side: the game often gets stuck loading new games or save files so it's also been hard to pick back up after a break.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is a great game. Pros: +Dripping with atmosphere. The music, the ambience, the setting - they all contribute to a futuristic, bleak, but very human vision of the future. You are an insignificant speck in this vast, unfeeling galaxy of people. Your struggles are not unique, your life - short and disposable. Even then, you still exist. You are here, and you are human.+The art direction and artstyle are great. The portraits could be a little bigger on the screen though.+The writing and worldbuilding are great. Cons:-The writing is very exposition-heavy. It can come off as dry and rambly at times. The game is going for a Disco Elysium-esque surrealist/introspective writing style, which it mostly executes well. However, Disco Elysium is also immensely witty and funny. It uses the absurd, light-hearted moments to hold your attention captive, then hits you with the sad, surrealist stuff. In Citizen Sleeper, the sad, surrealist stuff is all you get. There's also a lot of exposition and technobabble that you as a reader could not care less about. Disco Elysium has exposition dumps too, but it lets you choose to either listen to those or just go straight for the plot-important stuff. In Citizen Sleeper, you WILL read the exposition, whether you like it or not. It was bearable at first, but after 10 hours of game time and still being hit with more exposition, I was getting tired of it.-RNG. The game, by nature, is dependent on RNG. This is good for an authentic tabletop roleplaying experience, but bad for your sanity. Sometimes, you'll get a time-sensitive important questline that you really want to complete, but the game requires you to specifically roll natural 6's and 5's multiple times. Nothing will ruffle your feathers more than seeing a questline fail purely due to bad RNG and through no other fault of your own.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: If you want a perfect game, don't play this game.But if you want a rich, beautiful game where every character has a backstory and every choice matters, you might eventuelly want to buy this game, replay through all the choices and quests, and end up breathless for a moment upon finishing.That's not what I expected from the game, yet it's why I don't regret buying this game despite being early access and flawed in few minor spots.A huge praise to the people who made the game by the way.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: 8/10world is unique and interesting. the characters are even better, having different motivations and goals that lead them into your path. the idea of you being a sleeper makes the story more complex, as you are not a real person. one problem i have is that after you finish their respective quest or story, the characters completely disappear from the game, except for brief appearances when you go to their location. there were a lot of cool characters that i wanted to talk more to, like tala or emphis, but once i finished their quest they were completely gone. maybe not worth $20, wait for sale, but had a fun time.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: A wonderful narrative experience. It's greatest strength is it's incredible writing, I found myself genuinely caring about the characters, both love and hate. Its greatest weakness is the almost complete absence of challenge. I'm sure people will suggest simple fixes but really the game would need to be reworked from the ground up to create a fair and entertaining challenge. But that's okay, the experience of Citizen Sleeper is not worse because of it, only different. Highly recommend this game as a short but well written cyberpunk space story.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: While I do recommend this game, I highly recommend you watch a lot of gameplay videos. The trailer oversells the sound quality of this game. While it is not inherently bad, it is bland. There is no voicing at all (and a lot of text), music is entirely forgettable, and there is really little in the sound department that elevates this game.What is fun is the gameplay. I like the loop of trying to build your life on a space station, balancing a few survival stats while trying to invest in systems on the station to develop your story and get closer to true freedom. You start each day with some dice rolls. These determine your success on various tasks you can do. High rolls are low risk, and low rolls present a greater risk. If you roll low, maybe you do some safe tasks for the day. Roll high and go for those more difficult tasks that offer better rewards or development.The storylines are interesting in general, but when you get into interactions I found that it is far too text-heavy. I skimmed a lot of it. But I still found myself interested in continuing the stories and getting deeper into the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: The setting and story of this game REALLY resonated with me, and I'd love to see more games with a similar setting and themes. The character art is very good, but I do have to wish there was more of it, since it seems most characters only have one or two portraits and that's it. The gameplay itself is easy, and once you know what you're doing, it's really no challenge at all, but that's okay in a story focused game like this. All in all, I can solidly recommend this game, and I'd love to see more like it.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This is an amazing game.I formed a real connection with the story and characters, and the music and artwork form a perfect backdrops. The dialogue is all text based and the mechanics are quite abstracted / 'point-and-click' but it works very well with the style and feel of the game. This game is about the story, the RP and seeing how different paths play out, and it's does that very very well.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: The game is okay, I'd probably give it a 6 or 7 out of 10. I liked (most of) the writing, but the game itself often just feels very shallow. I think another playthrough would hardly be any different. As I said, I think it's OK, especially if you like visual novels, but in my opinion it's certainly not a "overwhelmingly positive"-type of game.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is a wonderful homage to tabletop RPGs and an excellent lesson in both world building and character development. The world is fascinatingly complex and every character on the Eye is memorable and lovable in their own way. The variety of choices and endings makes for an emotionally fulfilling experience regardless of who or what you choose to invest in.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: To the devs: this is a beautiful thing you've built here. Thank you.I'm grateful for the ride, the care that went into this world and experience.In the late game (~10 hours in, for me), you'll find a handful of  well worth pondering.In these late hours, I found myself capturing half a dozen screenshots of memorable conversations with NPCs.The game systems support the narrative very well.I'm not in the least interested in the conversation about AI sentience.I liked that in this game, I could see sentience almost as a decoy, a gateway to these other themes I'm glad to have explored: identity, self-determination, belonging, community.(Also, for Metal Gear Solid 2 fans: if you've enjoyed MGS2 for its themes, do play Citizen Sleeper!)
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This game is hard to place, genre-wise. At the beginning of each day/cycle, you roll a pool of dice, then assign each result to the various actions that are available to you. You'll collect money and items in various ways, and you have a health and hunger meter that are reduced each day. Your resources are very limited, but you usually have enough to scrape your way through.There is a very good story here (so far), and I enjoy the feeling that disaster and ruin are just one or two bad decisions away. Some of the dialogue options reference people and events that I haven't encountered, or that took place along some dialogue branch that I didn't take. But overall, everything is very well written and the resource management is tightly balanced.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This game is amazing.  The story really hits me deep.  I've never identified with a character more in all of the games I've played because of the all the real life themes set in an awesome futuristic dystopia with all kinds of intrigue and fun chance-based gameplay.  It's not difficult to play and the story shines through.  The art, game interface, and the writing are very good.  It builds up tension really well.  I look forward to finishing the game! Anyone with a health issue or is or has been marginalized in any way in society will find this game cathartic in a cool futuristic setting with fun gameplay and robots.  I always love stories about sentient robots! Sentience: An Android's Tale is a fun game too that's like this but this one feels more like real life.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: A real indy gem. The graphics work well and really grow on you (after you realize that you can rotate the map and that the points of interest are actually represented on the map).The many little stories are well written. The characters are vibrant and feel much more real than your average NPC.The "game" part of it all is where the game struggles a bit. It all works but it is a massive case of an inverted difficulty curve. In the beginning, you are desperate to find ressoures to survive and your skills are bad, so you fail a lot. The longer the game goes on, the better your skills get (you even get a reroll) AND the better your choices to gain ressources (locations). So it gets easier and easier. In addition, there is not chance to guess which action should be performed with priority (mostly) so you are stumbling along blindly. The latter is a problem from the "game" perspective but it helps the story and the immersion in the role.All in all, it is a very nice SciFi setting with a few cool ideas for the story (and a poor bad ones, of course) and a few good NPCs. It feels like a hybrid between a game and an interactive novel. Like a choose-your-own-adventure game that succesfully adds a bit of grind.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: A few years back I played 2 of the Hero of the Kingdom games in which you collect many different resources with mouse clicks, energy system, and basic character progression and use those resources to progress dozens of tiny quests. One of the good tools they used was displaying very clear progression bars (showing the items and energy levels you need) to give you the constant feel of moving forward, hooking you in.Those games are very simple, and a bit grindy, but while they have cute fantasy backgrounds and are short and sweet, they suffer from having the most basic narratives that shouldn’t be used as anything other than a placeholder. So while they feel great while they last, they left me empty as I was constantly wondering if it would be possible to merge their alluring gameplay loop with a stronger narrative.Citizen Sleeper is that, and also more. It complicates things by giving the player an additional layer of character skills (instead of treating every possible stat as an item), a more interesting energy system, and by inventing a very strong time flow that both paces out various quests and forces the player to sometimes react to threats, losing the luxury of being constantly in control.At the same time, it involves actual worldbuilding, 10+ hours of content, story choices affected both by dialogue options and the way you spend your energy, interesting moments of writing, a dose of creativity and - most importantly to me - a heart. The art style is beautiful, if restrained, additionally supported by the stylish SF-looking interface, background animations, cute music bits, ambient tracks, and sound effects. It managed to merge what I feel is a very strong gameplay loop with great storytelling, adding a new quality to the lacking formula. I’m now envious of the dev’s design skills.One thing I didn't enjoy was the obscurity of some of the game's rules, especially one attached to having a an option to reach the end credits quite early in the game. Without googling, I wouldn't know if I would have an option to reload the game and play further.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Amazing.  Immersive, without earth-shattering graphics - although the artwork is stylish, and evocative, and guides the imagination.  It is the words, the story, the setting and the the character that grip you in this beautiful experience.  I first played it one day before posting this, and I've just completed it for the first time, and I thoroughly enjoyed every part of it. Value for money far beyond many expensive games.  I hope you enjoy it too.  Not for combat-junkies!  This isn't a fighting RPG, this is an interactive story with RPG elements.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This game gives you the illusion of choice, no matter what you do, the only real choice you get is how you end the game, and if you want to end the game instead of exploring the other story lines. The game promises that the player will have to make tough choices throughout the playthrough to survive. After the first couple cycles, I don't think I ever felt the pressure of losing, ever. I ended up completing every mission the game gave me. Only reason I don't have the game 100% is because I chose to stay rather than go with  instead of going with them to get the achievement and just reloading to do the other endings. After that I decided it wasn't worth my time to 100% the game.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: The best narrative experience I've ever experienced in a video game. I'm not normally one for story-driven RPGs, but this one gripped me from beginning to end. I felt rare emotions, and quite often many different emotions at once. I repeatedly made choices in this game that were objectively bad for me (in gameplay terms) simply because I was moved by the emotion of the moment. This might be my game of the year.

_childDocuments_.review: I know I haven't finished the game yet but I would still highly recommend it. Really engaging and unique gameplay with great characters. Good story, interesting lore, and it appears to have lots of replay value. I've been locked out of events or pathways that seem really cool and it makes me want to go back on a new character. _childDocuments_.review: First thing I will say... Regardless of my opinions of the political slant of the writers, I feel this game has a (mostly) well-crafted world, and an engaging gameplay loop. It caught my interest well enough that I stayed up far too late, and ended up clocking my current gametime (13.6 hours) over a day and a half. (Yes, I'm an addict. Sue me.)The Good: The setting carries the game, you have to choose which risks you will take to move forwards, and the game keeps enough pressure on you that you do feel like you have to take risks to keep ahead of your inevitable demise. The ticking clocks and the need to balance resources against your dwindling piles of dice, alongside the mission timers, means you will not feel comfortable until the last 1/3rd of the game. The game gives you choices that, in most cases, you can guess what the best and worst outcomes are, but the writers are perhaps a little too in love with 'but then they decided to do something else' as a way to get out of a bad situation. (Glares at the bounty storyline)The 'Meh': The twists. Bounty Hunter decides to take you in? He's thirsty, and he wants you to pay his tab... and now his bounty agreement has been cancelled... but don't worry, someone worse is coming, but they are a long way away... so you have time to solve this. Good Luck!It's not 'BAD', it just begins to feel a bit 'meh' when you realise that the game is happy to railroad you down a path... and as long as you aren't stupid, you've got time to get out of whatever stupid series of mistakes you made.Two playthroughs, and I didn't die in either of them... I'd probably not be looking at spinning up a 3rd playthrough if I'd cottoned on that I could easily load the last autosave after each of the 'endings' the game offers you... and just go 'no thanks' without it even being a sad ending... except for waving goodbye to the young lady on her way to what will probably turn out to be a hellish life as a 3rd class citizen... but that's related to...(I'm about to talk about politics. If you don't care about politics, and everything else sounds awesome, you should buy the game, either on sale, or when you have the money aside. I think it is worth the money, but the next part is one of those 'it irritated me afterwards'... bits.) Still here? Last chance...The Bad: One-eyed political slant. Yes. Corporations will do what is going to get them maximum profit. No, they don't care about who they destroy on the way through. Yes, corporations will use dirty tricks and the fine print to screw you over. Unfortunately, Communes don't tend to tolerate people who suck at work, and given time, they'll stop feeding you if you consistently fail to complete tasks well, regardless of the effort you put in. Criminal enterprises tend to do crime, rather than organise community projects and peacekeeping patrols. Police being 'just a sanctioned gang' is a take... Corporate boot-lickers will always tend towards corporate boot licking, but the criminal organisation being painted as one of the more ethical sides, even more so once their corporate puppet master is removed irritates me. Addendum. If people using plural forms of address to avoid referencing sex or gender annoys you? probably give it a miss. It's not 'in your face', but it's there. Don't care, but I am talking about the entirely subjective politics side of things.BUT. I will repeat. I'd probably be happy recommending this game to most people. It's a few hours of fun, and I'd say it's worth a few bucks.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a solid little CYOA visual novel. Your enjoyment will depend on how much you like the characters you interact with, but since very few of the storylines are intertwined you can feel free to ignore a character you don't like to focus on the ones that you do. Having gotten access to several endings and finally chosen one I think I would have preferred a more focused narrative, the slice of life aspect has you going all over the place and you can get some tone whiplash. But overall a solid recommend if you like these sort of games.
