_childDocuments_.review: To be clear: I love sci-fi, I love reading, I love choice-driven narratives and I love simple but addictive game mechanics.  That's where I'm coming from, so if you don't like those things, fair warning!  This game pretty much maxed me out on all those fronts.  The narrative is deep and branching, while still allowing for a strong main through-line experience no matter what you pick.  The game mechanics start out very simple, but over time as you add more objectives and try to juggle more Drives it really involves some tactical thinking on what is truly worth your dice that day.  The writing is excellent all around, and in some cases truly phenomenal -- sometimes even showing how a perfect description can outshine the most expensive cut-scene in the world in terms of emotional and imaginative impact.  The soundtrack is just superb as well -- highly recommend playing the game on headphones for this reason alone.  I kept playing after the credits several times just to tie up loose ends and stay in the world a little longer (don't quit out if you see credits rolling!  there's a good chance you can keep going!)  Really looking forward to the DLC episodes; I can see a ton of potential directions the story could go from here, and I am absolutely ready to go :D.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: An excellent environmental story marred by poor gameplay pacing and a lack of late game goals.The early game captures the feeling of being an unwanted, dying asylum seeker very well. Your options feel limited by the resources and barriers in your way. Questions arise of whether it's worth paying a toll to a new area or joining an enterprise and whether that will cut too deep into the limited resources you have, preventing you buying essentials like food or the essential medicine you need. The lategame works too, in a sense, you certainly start to feel like you've achieved your goals without the game ever explicitly saying so.However the flaws are there, there's very little actual decision making in the game past the first 30 minutes, the progress clocks in the game are never sufficiently present to force a meaningful choice between them and many promising character stories simply cut out after a few scenes. This doesn't leave time to build a real attachment to the characters and there's certainly no real conflicting choices between them. The result is some early characters (Tala is a great example of this) kind of peter out as you build what you're told is a great relationship with them only for them to become a non entity in your characters life. You can be close to a gang, a fixture of a local bar, a regular inhabitant of the lowends...but none of these are part of the "official" endings, they're transient even though their mechanical benefits continue to be available (and roughly equivalent to the benefit of every other option you'll come across with most jobs paying pretty much identical amounts). The endings themselves also suffer because of this, most of them are abrupt and simply elect to ignore that your character needs medicine every week. They also don't feel very earned. The game relaxes those tight resource limits quite early on which means most endings are pretty much determined by you putting the minimum number of actions in then reading the short dialogue sections, roll credits. This wouldn't be a problem if there was anything to stop you just plowing through a task in one game day but there really isn't after those good 30 mins at the start. It feels like there's the idea of a management game here but in reality there isn't and  the gameplay is just a formality to make it feel like time is passing.At the end of the Day Citizen Sleeper feels like a wasted opportunity, it needed more time in the oven and a tighter focus on the gameplay for fun and replayability. That said this game is easily one of the more atmospheric games I've played in a while and I would absolutely recommend it on that basis alone.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: The game touches on some really deep cyberpunk and sci-fi themes such as: AI bodies with the consciousness of other people ; industrial / capitalist exploitation of workers ; indentured servitude. This is a strong point and some of the stories are really touching and hit hard.However the game fails at what it is supposed to be - a game. This is in fact a Visual Novel with very light gaming elements in terms of dice and resource management. Very close to a digital version of a table top. A game is divided into cycles, normally when you use all your dices on different actions you can end the cycle and advance various event counters (as you advance there is more of them), the next cycle your dices will reset and you will be able to use them again. As you progress you also get more ways to spend you action dices e.g. new people you meet, new events pop-up, etc. However that doesn't take from the fact that in the end you are reading a lot of text and then deciding where do you use your dices. The whole cycle takes a few minutes at most, then it's a repeat.The whole game at a leisure pace is less than 4-5 hours, way faster if you already played one path and are rushing to replay the other ones, which devolves into you knowing where to go and which events to advance, and which ones to ignore completely. Yes, the game encourages multiple playthroughs with this approach but at the end of the day the system never develops from selecting the events, applying the dice rolls and advancing the counters.Might work for some, didn't work for me.

_childDocuments_.review: From start to finish, a flawless peek into a flawed world, not too far from what ours could be, a couple hundred years into the future. Believable characters with their own motivations that intersect, and sometimes collide with yours, gorgeous art and a great soundtrack.The best part? This game respects your time and can be played over a long week-end, and will not require you pour 80 hours into it to appreciate it (looking at you Witcher 3).At 20 bucks it's a steal. At any price point below that, you'd be foolish not to give it a try.

_childDocuments_.review: How story driven games should be. It had those old-school-choose-your-own-adventure book vibes, and I loved every second of the 8 hours I spent as I binged the whole thing in one sitting. There will be a few complaints, however they are vastly outweighed by how wonderfully the environment and characters were drawn out.The whole game is beautiful with wonderfully fleshed out characters. You really feel like they slowly become your friends as the two of you learn to trust each other. The setting is great. Who doesn't like depressing futuristic corporate hells set in a space station? You can really tell the devs really wanted to make the players feel certain emotions, and it really shows.I feel like the game kind of suffers from being a libral dream and seems to be trying to get a point across with all the bad guys being comically niche captialist, money hungry pigs or just an evil corporation and some of the good guys being literal communists, but it doesn't ruin it. I don't know I just feel like it was a cheap way to try and get a political point across but maybe that was the point. I mean you are in a futuristic corporate hell after all.The choices don't really seem to matter. Sure, there are the final choices for each of the characters story lines that result in the different endings, however the majority of it just seems like filler responses that will result in one different line of dialogue and then move on to the core of the storyline which will not change.$20 seems like a steep pricetag for a game that most will get 4-8 hours of playtime on, but the experience was well worth it in my opinion. I had a good time, and I think most people would agree.Overall 9/10, would save the single father and his adorable daughter again.

_childDocuments_.review: I accidentally did an entire playthrough in a single five hour sitting which felt nowhere near as long as that. That alone makes me certain I've gotten my money's worth.The game is definitely in a vaguely similar vein as that of Disco Elysium, and I'd definitely recommend it, but choices are mostly confined to how you react to certain events and which event paths / questlines you follow - there isn't a whole lot of customization or variety beyond that, and your starting 'class' mostly determining your first two hours of gameplay.Taking on all the quests you can leads to inevitably failing some and being timed out, as you have limited resources and turns to do some of the more sensitive ones, with bad rolls possibly screwing you out of a productive turn. This happened to me occasionally during my first playthrough and especially towards the end, where I mostly settled on an ending that presented itself as a result of me over-committing to Lem and Mina's questline earlier than I maybe should have in the game, pressured by Maywick's timed appearance. While this was a satisfying way narratively to end the game with where I was in other questlines, what I had explored, et cetera, there was clearly more to the game I hadn't seen and it was obvious, and I fully intend to give the game another playthrough just to see it. I can see this being a tedious process for some when now the first few hours of content is made redundant by having already seen, and little in the way of differing paths for how to pursue different questlines, and minimal options for expanding your perks and skills - gameplay in that sense definitely seems intended in a simpler, Old-School-Revival style of RPG than Disco Elysium's expansive systems.Would leave Ethan in what is definitely not bartending at gunpoint again.

_childDocuments_.review: 8.5/10I recently finished one of the games 8? endings after playing through and not finishing the game once before right after its release. It is a rare game that is worth every penny of its price tag at launch. _childDocuments_.review: What an experience through and through. The game sells itself on storytelling and it delivers in industrial amounts, genuinely an ingenious take on the TTRPG genre. The only issue I can think of is the fact that there are rather few decisive choices that lock you out of things, no matter what, so long as you search for everything, you will be able to do everything, there are virtually no mutually exclusive storylines, on my first playthrough I managed to do all endings, or at least get to the point of doing all of them, which while it feels liberating, also undermines the brutality of the game itself. It's not a difficult game, it's meant, after all, to be an experience. Gameplay-wise I had very few gripes, perhaps the fact only 1 item or action dice can be inputted at a time on any given destination is somewhat annoying, but besides that, an excellent game that immerses you into a strange and wonderful, yet brutal world where moral dilemmas abound and attachments thrive despite adversity.

_childDocuments_.review: Mediocre story, poor game. Fans of visual novels might get something out of this, as this is even less of an RPG than something like Disco Elysium, which is already fairly light on RPG mechanics. In Citizen Sleeper, there are really only 3 mechanics to speak of:1. Modifier dice (randomly generated every day)2. Condition (a health stat that determines how many dice you get)3. Energy (another arbitrary bar that dictates condition loss)Keeping all three optimally topped off by juggling money, resources, and time forms the core of the gameplay loop. This would all be well and good if it didn't feel extremely easy to optimize within a few days of in-game time. The beginning of the game had me hopeful that I would have to make some tense decisions, perhaps even sacrifice my health or hard-earned money at crucial junctions without any re-dos. Nope. By the end of the game I was flush with cash, resources, and modifier dice, and felt perfectly equipped to take on any challenge the game threw at me, and I wasn't trying to minmax the game.Ordinarily, that wouldn't be a problem if I was looking for a cozy experience, but Citizen Sleeper takes great pains to remind its players of how HARD life is on the Eye, and how everybody is just DESPERATE to survive. I couldn't help but snicker every time my character muttered something like "I'm getting by" when I was drowning in chits and had never come close to death. It's a dissonance that only grew stronger the further I went through the game.It doesn't help that there are barely any choices to speak of. Most dialogue options are three variations on the same response for a character that lacks significant customization (and unlike Disco Elysium, a significant backstory to explore). You pass your checks, and eventually you'll get a binary choice to make at the end of some, not all, storylines.And the storylines themselves are... okay? I personally thought that the themes of reconstructing one's identity, outlining the relationship between body and mind, etc. worked best in the AI subplots. Most of the other plots involve blue-collar workers in some degree of distress because of faceless, hilariously callous corporations that you never interact with. I'm fine with bashing on capitalism, but this is really shallow, surface-level stuff. It's very easy to take a hardworking dad and his adopted daughter to say, "Look! Look at how poor and downtrodden these workers are! The corporations promised them so much!" It's a much harder task to dig deeper than that, and Citizen Sleeper, with its vignette approach to plot, doesn't seem interested in doing that.And if you're not interested in very brief, nuance-less stories about how capitalism is bad, well, there isn't much else in the game. There is no central plot, and after a certain point the stats and dice no longer matter. From that point, you're left with merely reading about how corporations have brutally plowed this poor space station six ways to Sunday. Your choices mostly concern what ending you pick, and rarely extend beyond a couple paragraphs of expository text. Since there isn't an overarching story or any branching paths, I just meandered to a stop after 9 hours and took the first ending that seemed appropriate, like taking the first exit off a highway because I was running out of gas.All in all, it's a firmly okay experience, but I was expecting a lot more from a game with "overwhelming positive" reviews. Fans of other narrative-driven games might find something enjoyable in this, but they should go in knowing that the story will largely be told to them, not delivered through gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Well written, emotionally driven Sci-Fi story supported by a simple but yet a strong dice-based game-play loop for you to chose you're actions of the story.The people on the Eye are fleshed out characters with their own, each unique personality that makes them feel human allowing all the emotion of the story to shine through these people.But what sells it for me is the art-style and sound design that went into the game. This feels like the developer and there team took the time and effort to make this masterpiece.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper brings you a short yet amazingly written narrative about a foreign body waking up in an unknown location without a memory or a chit to their name.Citizen Sleeper's 'Gameplay' is a series of pre-determined dice-rolls at the beginning of each day or "cycle" that you use to perform tasks. At first, it takes a few cycles to gain your bearings as to when and where to place your dice. You may feel like you're missing something or you're not utilising your dice correctly. Thankfully, it doesn't take long to work out that most things you can take your time with and eventually you can come back to it at a later point or you can slowly widdle away at it.Even though this may be the case with most, there are timed tasks that require a bit more consistent effort or you will miss out. Thankfully again, or not so thankful to some that desire a challenge, the game is pretty generous in the timed events as well as the dice rolls never really being heavily weighed against you.This may be the only flaw to this game. Eventually, at least for me, I found myself so overpowered that I could just skip cycles to hurry up certain tasks as I had nothing else to do and to open a new section of story I had to wait a set amount of cycles. The difficulty after the first hour or two drastically goes down when you figure out where all the best things are to keep yourself from dying, which you can repeat over and over with a spare die or a small fee.That being said, the characters, the world building and stories albeit small, are delivered so perfectly that I didn't mind the visual novel-like gameplay as well as how easy the game became. No one really overstays their welcome but are around long enough to get to know their stories and grow attached. I found myself wishing that after I had finished one of their stories I could continue to at least see them about or pop by to say hello.On that note, finishing any of the MANY endings this game has, I felt empty. Hollow. But in a good way. The endings are so well crafted that they make you think about different perspectives and self reflect. They are all somewhat open ended and allow for personal interpretation which I enjoy yet still supply a satisfying conclusion if you don't really want to think about it.TLDR; I recommend this game if you love character development, story-driven games that don't have much to offer in terms of gameplay mechanics. Think point and click choose your own adventure.Safe travels and stay warm.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I just want to say: this game is fantastic. The atmosphere is such that you find yourself being drawn in straight away. The game play is engaging without being repetitive and the dialogue is exceptionally written. All in all, I think this a great, contemplative game that I'd recommend to everyone.

_childDocuments_.review: I genuinely loved this game. So much, in fact, that not only did I 100% it in the span of 2.5 days, I'll definitely buy the sequel.Let's start with the writing, since there's plenty of reading to be done in this game. I personally really liked the prose; it flowed well. On top of that, the text got broken up into small paragraphs, which made it easy to read through.Plot-wise, the game was really interesting. I don't tend to gravitate towards sci-fi (I generally prefer fantasy), but this one grabbed me by the throat and kept me there. I just had to keep playing to find out what's really going on the Eye.What surprised me the most is that it's perfectly possible to fail "Drives" (quests) if one isn't careful enough and the overall story will simply progress in a different manner. Some of the failures may even end up having consequences way later in the game. Some do straight up cut content, but even then, the changes made in comparison to a success state are interesting enough to keep playing.The setting of this game is detailed enough to be understandable but mysterious enough to be interesting. There's a lot to explore in this wolrd and I really hope the sequel will capitalize on that.Gameplay-wise: the dice system this game uses is very engaging. At first, it may seem like a lot, especially for those who don't play tabletop games, but it's intuitive enough to grasp quickly. Quests progress through filling out "clocks"; each action fills up a portion of it, but some have the option to backfire based on the dice used. I found filling the clocks out very satysfying, it scratched my brain just right.Overall, it's a very good game. I can't recommend it enough — and I can't wait for the sequel!

_childDocuments_.review: it's almost an example of "leftist meme with too much text" in a videogame format but it's done pretty well (and also it's fairly standard fare for rpg filler text), the storytelling is great, the characters are realistic and well written, music is great. gets too easy after the first hour other than the endgame episodes, but still fun even when it's basically checking boxes since you want to know what happens

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is part visual novel, adventure game, and tabletop RPG. The core of all these things is a narrative and Citizen Sleeper has a good one.The gameplay takes place over a cycle--an in game day. During the cycle you click on different locations and have different actions at each location. Perhaps you need to hack into a governing body's network or help a mercenary fix their damaged ship. You complete these actions by spending your dice, which are rolled at the start of the cycle. The higher the value, the higher likelihood of success on that action. The amount of dice you're given each cycle is determined by your condition, which you need to repair throughout the game in a variety of different ways. Completing actions can progress story lines, provide you with items that can be used in a bunch of different ways, repair your condition, feed you, etc. Once you have completed a quest, called drives in the game, you are given a skill point. Skill points give your dice +1 or +2 depending on the type of task, new abilities like recharging energy at home, rerolling all of your dice, etc.Citizen Sleeper isn't an action game. The gameplay consists of scrolling through the space station, clicking on different locations, reading what actions are available at a given location, reading and choose your dialogue entries with other characters.If you are a fan of adventure games and tabletop RPGs you will probably enjoy Citizen Sleeper. If you don't like visual novels, this game likely won't change your mind. However, it isn't strictly a visual novel. It might be a good starting place if you are curious about the genre.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Absolutely amazing!Beautiful narrative, beautiful characters, good storytelling and overall a very immersive adventure into this world.The gameplay serves the purpose of telling the story, but the game is surprisingly engaging because of the dice mechanic that I personally found quite interesting, it allows you to choose what you want to do and when, and if it happens that some quests are timed, which is often the case, it forces you to make some choices about what you want to do in what order. It's nothing revolutionary and gameplay wise the game remains relatively easy to get through, but it spicies things up from a more traditional narrative driven point and click type of game. It definetely makes you feel in control of your own choices, eventhough towards the end most of our basic needs are easily met.SPOILERSI, for example, would've preferred that the vials for our condition would've been harder to get. In the middle of the game it is almost a constant stress, you don't have many and they're expensive, but towards the end you start to get a lot of money very easily and you can go from buying them cheap from the medic to making them in the Greenway for crazy cheap. Maybe it would've been cool to have the medic be able to hand out only one vial per X cycles, so you know that even with the money, you will have to wait for the next shipment. And then in the greenway maybe make the vials more expensive, even by a little, not to make it a hard thing to manage but maybe just so it still is a relevant aspect of the gameplay. In the beginning the game makes a big deal about your condition and all the problems with it, but it never really reaches a point where you're struggling, at least i never did. On one hand I like that the game focusses more on the story, but at the same time it would've been nice to play around a bit more with the actual mechanics of the game (maybe having difficulties? Story enjoyer difficulty and Seasoned Sleeper difficulty where vials maybe don't full you up completely? Idk).Overall tho I'm not complaining, this is a very good game that I loved playing and would play again.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: While I have yet to complete this game, I will say it's sucked me in with it's unique atmosphere and story. Trying to find yourself and your purpose as a Sleeper on the station, while meeting all kinds of unique characters makes for a sci-fi world you can almost lose yourself in. The implementation of dice rolls and how they let you interact with the world is charming as well, and makes you consider which actions or events you want to take, with the available dice you have left each cycle. It's a nice game for when you're traveling, or when you've got a lazy day where you want to lose yourself in another place...
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Finding a Job in Space is Harder Than on EarthEver dreamed of escaping Earth's hustle to bask in the solitude and silence of space? Well, "Citizen Sleeper" offers a reality check – turns out, the cosmos still has rent due. This game is not just about seeking self amongst the stars; it's a simulator of gig life on a space station.As a runaway AI, you strive to carve out a life on the space station Erlin's Eye, seeking freedom and belonging. Yes, you heard right – even AIs need jobs to survive here, clearly indicating the future isn't as automated and carefree as we'd hoped.The game shines with its rich narrative and character development. Each choice you make closely impacts the unfolding story, revealing a world that's both beautiful and brutal. But importantly, it reminds us that job hunting remains a challenge – especially when you're software.In summary, "Citizen Sleeper" is an exceptional role-playing game for fans of deep stories and space station life simulators. Even if you're not an AI, there's fun and challenge to be found in this game. Highly recommended!
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: 9/10Amazing writing, really good usage of DnD like elements, multiple endings to experience and overall a very concise and tight knit experience easily in my top 10 in 2022.Only con would be that at a certain point, the need to balance dice rolls and the risk associated with your lower rolls kind of fizzles out at a certain spot as there really isnt a clock to push you to finish the story lines. But apart from that, for the type of game it is this was a near experience and personally a much more preferred one than Disco Elysium. Also with all 3 free DLC out now, you can experience the true ending of the game without waiting.

I spent more to go to the theatre this week, and that movie was less than 2 hours.Worth your time and money if you are looking for a narrative about what it means to be alive in a future remote part of the galaxy.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: It gets a lot of comparison to Disco Elysium, and I think that's entirely understandable. It's an entirely story-driven game with a lot of point-and-click adventure, and classic rpg elements. No real-time combat in either as well. I think other comparisons to Disco will hurt this game though, as it's frankly no where near the same level. The writing, while soild, is often quite flat. It fails to be properly reactive to the order in which you do certain events and storylines. It's also just completely bogged down by having *too* many good story ideas. It implies a main quest, with myriad of side quests, but in reality it feels like several main storylines poorly connected to one another. When the one story ends, you get an achievement, then reload the save file and continue. Rinse and repeat until you clear the last of the (free) DLC chapters. It's poorly constructed, and my hope is the recently announced sequel will focus better on one singular, satisfying narrative.That was a lot of criticism, but I want to stress that this game is largely very good. The writing, when it works, works very well. The art is utterly fantastic, and I'm left wanting even more of it. The gameplay loop and progression, while simple, also suit the game very well. This is the kind of game that's easy to recommend, but please don't set your expectations too high. If you enjoy narrative games, you'll likely enjoy this.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: The style of the character art is just a tick above CalArts dreck.  The gameplay is reminiscent of flash RPG's I played on Newgrounds 18 years ago. The story(and its accompanying politics) are of little substance--a sickly pastiche of much better sci-fi stories.Many people liken Citizen Sleeper to Disco Elysium; God knows why.

_childDocuments_.review: Gripping story. Time pressure combined with resource management make for somewhat challenging gameplay in the beginning. This lets off later though and at that point unskippable animations which play regularly become annoying. Overall, I really enjoyed this game, though towards the end I only played to see all endings.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of tabletop RPGs, I was interested in Citizen Sleeper, but didn't get my hopes up. Most games in this genre aren't very interesting or engaging.Aside from one or two issues, this is one of the best TTRPG (or visual novel) style games I've played in a long time!The story is great, the art works, and I'm interested in the DLC or replaying the game to see the other endings. All that's holding me back is the awkward control scheme.So, you don't walk around the map, but use the scroll-wheel to go up and down the station. Occasionally you have to click two times to reach harder to access areas (and this is after scrolling all the way there). You can increase the scroll speed, but I really wish there was a better way to handle movement. Right now it can feel slow and ponderous.Second, the UI isn't intuitive when you first come across it. You'll get it, after a fashion, but it could use some work to be more user-friendly, if they make a Citizen Sleeper 2 that is.Last, the fact that the physical goods and data goods are kept in two separate menus is awkward, especially because you're often switching between the two for different missions. A contextual menu that only shows items you have on hand for any area you enter that can be used in that area would be better, imo.Other than that, great-great game! If you're reading this, then I guarantee you're the sort of player who will enjoy Citizen Sleeper. Hopefully they'll make more games in the future, and iron out the weird UX stuff.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I absolutely love Citizen Sleeper!  It's a resource management game with a compelling story and interesting characters.  You play as a Sleeper, a being with memories emulated from another, who is on the run.  Can you make a new life for yourself on The Eye or maybe escape to some other future?  The game play is simple yet addicting.  You roll dice for each daily cycle and apply them to the tasks you choose to complete and further the story.  It is easy to get sucked into "just one more cycle" and play much longer than expected.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper had been recommended to me multiple times by friends in the Fallen London community, so I had to check it out. If you're a fan of Failbetter's games, then I can't recommend Citizen Sleeper enough!So I played through the entirety of Citizen Sleeper in one (nearly) 13-hour session.I definitely hear some of the negative reviews noting that the gameplay loop becomes a bit of a clickfest in the endgame, especially once resource & risk management become irrelevant. So why did I stick around & persevere to reach the end? It's a stunningly well-written game, the characters are a joy to discover and learn about as you progress in your journey around the Eye, and their stories weave together a world that I'm eagerly awaiting to learn more about in the upcoming sequel. Plus the art is cute!I'm also a big fan of the dice system used to introduce risk to your actions, and how it blends naturally into the character's state/wellbeing. It's intuitive, and as others have mentioned, makes you really focus on just surviving in the first few hours. The economy is fairly well-balanced, and you'll feel like you're barely scraping by for quite some time until opportunities that offer long-term stability crop up. Your struggle mirrors the struggle of those around you on the station, which is a good basis for adversarial or collaborative relationships to feel natural - something a lot of other narrative-based games often spring on the character with no rhyme or reason just to progress the story.My only criticism is that the soundtrack is a little generic for a sci-fi game - it fits nicely as background music, sure, but I'm not left with a strong impression of any of the melodies.Do I recommend that others play this in one sitting? Absolutely not, unless you want square eyes. But was I hooked? Absolutely.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I put every waking moment of two days into finishing this game, and I regret nothing. Feels casual and low stress, but engrossing, engaging and emotional. And the sales pitch is true, it does feel oddly similar to actual tabletop RPGs in a weird way I can't describe. The pool of d6s probably has something to do with it.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This game is charming. As of this review I have played through one time, taking me about six hours. I feel like my money was spent well for that. Looking at the achievements suggests that I've seen a little under half of the milestones within the game. I could play again, but I'm not sure I will. Going into the game blind made the experience especially meaningful. There was a constant sense of tension, of worry, of things slowly falling apart, of there never being enough time for everything I needed to do. And that survived to the very end of the game, perhaps because of the ending that I reached. I won't spoil anything for anyone, but I had the opportunity to do something kind for an NPC that I particularly liked, but by doing so, I would give up the ability to help several other people, some of whom I also cared about. But the first NPC... emotionally, it was a foregone conclusion. Forced to pick, I picked them. I could see the ending of the game coming, because of the commitment I made to them. I tried to help everyone I could before I could no longer, but it wasn't enough time. I ended the game by confirming the choice I had made, simultaneously regretting leaving behind the people I had to, and still knowing that I made the right decision.That's hard for a narrative game to achieve. I can't guarantee that you will have the same emotional experience. You might have different feelings about the characters in the game, or you might unlock or pursue entirely different paths. Maybe you'll never even meet the character to whom I made that promise. Or maybe the game won't resonate with you. But it could. And that's all you can ask from this sort of game. You should give it a chance, and find out.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Great game with a few issues.Pros:- Interesting story and characters. Vibrant lore and world. All around beautiful game to experience.- Great action and resource system. Very unique yet easy to use as well.- Become a Fungus Fan and grow mushrooms so that the coolest character in the game can cook them up for you and swap stories <3- There is a ton to love about this game, with little details and secrets that are worth finding so I won't spoil it. It lacks some replayability in my opinion, but that was still a fantastic 10 hours I spent getting through most of the content. I could probably stretch it to 20 if I wanted to be completionist and get all the achievements as well, so the price seems about right to me.Cons:- A lot of bugs. Nothing game breaking though, as you can reload an autosave and it'll all be fixed. Very rarely can it screw you over, but it is annoying regardless. But there was one drive (mission) I completed but then was told I failed it, for some reason? Weird stuff.- The difficulty curve is very high at first, which was pretty cool, but then it just drops off into oblivion once you've gotten your feet under you. A significant portion of the game is spent on easy mode just trying to get any content you've missed along the way.- Some of the character storylines feel kind of rushed. Like you have a handful of limited character interactions with them, then suddenly you unlock an "ending" scenario with them like you're close pals and it just feels forced. I'm also super disappointed in the female mercenary plotline, as it takes a hard left turn that makes no sense and just does not translate emotionally through the text. I left that scene bewildered and feeling a strong disconnect with my character.So yeah, other than a few issues, I had a fantastic time and would definitely recommend this game.

_childDocuments_.review: This review is a tough one, and a case where I had a more-neutral option to select between positive and negative.Citizen Sleeper is, in essence, an interactive novel with sometimes-diverging-before-recombining plot lines. A system of mechanics laid on top of it makes it feel like more of a game than many other interactive novels, but the gameplay never evolves enough in complexity or difficulty to make for an interesting gameplay experience. From a story point-of-view, it is well-written and has a lot going on. At times it even feels like there is too much going on--it is easy to get overwhelmed by the number of plots and sub-plots you are juggling at any one time, making it so that none of them really have room to breathe.Ultimately, though, there are many places where it's evident that your choices don't meaningfully matter. Most options presented in dialog don't have any lasting impact, and the gameplay is never tight enough that making an error feels like it will have long-term consequences. In short, this game feels good as a novel, but fares worse as a game.

If nothing else than to experience The Eye and its locales.Also ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ the characters are so hot. Like, ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. They got that spacer drip.

_childDocuments_.review: So.I'm not really ready to rave about the game, to be honest. Not that it's a  game, mind. Throughout the entire time playing this, the emotions that were stirred up weren't intense, but just a slow buildup of emotions until you get moments of catharsis that just make you sit there for a bit, before nodding, and buckling in for... more of the same.The system in itself is very well constructed. While it is possible for you to get into the position where you never go below flickering, and that it's possible to stockpile materials to a significant degree, you're never far from reminded that you exist in a body that not only needs to be nourished, but one that is constantly,  falling apart, where a single moment of inattention will cost you a single dice, and even if you're well-fed and full of stabilizer, the RNG can  bone you by giving you a cycle full of nothing but 2s and 3s, and when you reroll (if you have the perk), you might end up with 1s and 2s instead. Some cycles aren't just worth it, and as someone who struggles with chronic issues and mental health, oh boy that's relatable.That being said, the systems evoke a lot of the precarity of life under capital, but don't exemplify it — they're gloss that once you've dug through, reveal what essentially is a visual novel. A fairly non-linear one, where you're not compelled to a single path, but in the end there's no real point in avoiding everything the game offers. You can end up in the end, especially digging through the DLCs, with a character that's for +2 in every stat, who's survived being hunted, rejected digital heaven to become some kind of bodhisattva, helped a dude and his daughter find a new life, own a damn bar and save the station several times in a row, it seems just sensible to unlock all the game has to offer, or very close to it.. but you'll only do it once.If you're a fan of quiet, reflective moments, especially interspersed by a struggle to survive that starts out very bitter but ends up being... doable (a nice change to adulting IRL honestly), this is really the experience for you. Just don't dig too deep into the system that it uses to bring those feelings, they're there to help with the immersion, not be a deep simulation.

After playing through the game three times I am left with the feeling of disgust, aggravation, disappointment, and anger. _childDocuments_.review: Short version: Wroth it, although maybe wait for a sale. Longer version: The game is a very immersive experience, that takes you on an unforgettable journey through the life of a station on the edge of society. Throughout the game you try to find out more about yourself, and meet new people on the station which you can help, if you so choose. The systems that drive the game, becasically the dice, stat system is pretty easy to understand so anyone can pick it up imo, but beware that if you really want to enjoy this game, you should prepare for a lot of reading. You can with multiple playthroughs get around 15-20 hours of gameplay here, maybe more. The graphics, art in this game are absolutely mesmerizing. There are a lot of hidden details on the characters, and locations that you can observe. The station even changes, as you progress through the story. Following this I think the UI could use some work as there were some minor issues, like the name of locations sometimes going out of screen. There weren't that many, but pretty noticeable, although they did not have that much of an impact. SoundThis is one of the strong points of the game. It's sound, and effects are absolutely on point, and can keep you engaed. Even during dialogues it changes as the tone of the text changes. Never got bored of it, and even listened to some after putting the game down.GameplayNow here as I said before we have the dice system which is really intuitive, but too easy in my opinion. It seems hard at first glance, but after figuring it out, it seems way too easy, but at the end of the day that's not the purpose of this game. It tells a story. Late-game the gameplay can get a bit tedious if you want to finish a couple of character arcs, which kinda put me off a bit. One of the reasons it was tedious is that later on you can travel between some sections. Without spoiling anything the travel between these gets really boring after you have to do it a couple dozen times. StoryYour personal story is pretty alright, but it was overshadowed by the multitude of stories of the characters you encounter on the station. There are multiple endings, and you can try more of the out in a single playthrough although not ALL of them. I have cheesed the game somewhat I admit, by making a backup of my save games before making crucial decision. These decision you make are pretty obvious so it wasn't an issue.  One of the reason I did this is that currently only the ending of some the character arcs is different and I did not really want to replay everything just for the last bit of dialogue. The game loses a bit of mystery after the first playthrough, which could be improved upon. ConclusionAll in all even with it's issues this game is awesome, and an experience you won't forget soon, although maybe for a bit cheaper and not ~16 euros which is the price in my region. My score for this game is: 7 / 10

_childDocuments_.review: As a general rule, I try not to frame games I'm reviewing though the lens of other games, but  is one of those games that wears its influences so obviously on its sleeve that it's hard not to talk about it without acknowledging those influences.  In short, the pitch of  is that it's a computer RPG riff on Weird Age's tabletop RPG , which positions itself as an explicitly-polemical, anticapitalist cyberpunk tale that presents a community-minded take on the titular "punk" rather than the selfish, lone-wolf nihilism of the genre's heyday.  's setting of Erlin's Eye bears more than a passing resemblance to 's Grand Cross Station; each is an 'RPG Adventure City' based on a decaying space station under threat from the looming spectre of megacorporate capitalism, a capitalism that has already irrecoverably ruined Earth (or in  case, the 'Core Systems').  Stories are not about raging against the machine so much as they are about rehabilitating the machine, through radical acts like community gardening and public awareness campaigns.Lest this sound overly dry and polemical, it thankfully isn't because  wisely structures itself like a series of overlapping CYOA stories, each centered around the human core of some interesting personage from the Eye.  The titular Sleeper -- an escaped corporate slave who's been scrubbed clean of any indentification or personality, the better for the player to transpose themselves into -- flits into and out of the lives of bounty hunters, bureaucrats and botanists, changing their story for (typically) the better through radical acts of anti-authoritarian kindness.  These are rendered through exhaustively long, novel-length dialogues presented in a snappy 'chat field' UI format, reminiscent of s second and likely most obvious inspiration, ZA/UM's .  Despite the bittersweet nature of the dystopian setting, I found  to be filled with the kind of realistic hopefulness of , owing to that polemical core of empathy for the working-class that both games share.  That's not to say that  is quite on par with : it's quite obviously a freshman affair, with a lot of room to grow, but the moonshot was there.It is in how these stories are resolved that Sleeper's third, and probably oddest, inspiration shows its head: another TTRPG, Evil Hat's .  This trendy storygame is much-beloved within the pretentious "fishblade" indie TTRPG circles that I frequent for how smoothly its mechanics model the structure of a heist movie, although I must admit I'm at something of a loss regarding its inclusion here.  In , all dice rolls and actions advance a 'clock,' a sort of pie chart of doom that counts towards either a success (the gang makes off with the Euclid Jewel) or a consequence (the Bluecoats arrive with truncheons in-hand).  The clocks are a visualization of the constant plate-spinning that a heist crew has to manage, and they really help to sell a sense of precarity.  Here, clocks are used to track progress and consequences among the many dozens of storylines, which isn't a perfect fit when the stakes are frequently less making off with the jewel and more talking to an old man about how the untested corporate mods his employer saddled him with gave him early-onset osteoporosis.  Despite the narrative framing device of a race against time where the Sleeper is constantly dying and must obtain rare serum to survive, most of the story structure is considerably more laid-back and character oriented, which makes the Sleeper desperately sprinting from task to task across a scattershot of storylines feel tonally less like you're an escaped slave and more like you're a harried Millennial gig-worker bragging on a groupchat about being "soooo busy."  It's a weird mechanical fit that makes a game that's theoretically about anarchism and mutual aid feel more like a celebration of "the hustle"/"the grind," which undermines its own polemic.I'm giving the game a hard time here, but in truth it's because I hold this new breed of story-based RPGs like  to much higher literary standards than video games of the past, which I used to give a sweeping "they're video games, they're allowed to be bad stories for idiots that don't mean anything" handicap.  I enjoyed  as both a video game and a work of literature, which is the highest praise I can give.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr - Citizen Sleeper is a 10/10 for haunting music, incredible visual design, and characters and writing which will stick with me forever.At times nail-bitingly intense, laugh-out-loud funny at others, and always with an undercurrent of melancholy, Citizen Sleeper sits in a very special category of my favorite games of all time: games which made me feel something.Like with all of my favorite stories, I sat in silence for a while after finishing, letting the lingering notes and last lines settle into me. I'll be pulling apart the threads of the story for a long while to come, examining how it made me feel and why it made me feel those things.My recommendation: Sit with Citizen Sleeper like a good book. Make yourself a nice drink (I'm a Rum and Coke person myself), put your headphones on, and let the game wash over you. Make yourself vulnerable to these characters, to their struggles and hopes, give yourself a chance to reflect on the choices.***** SPOILERS *****Each time I was given the option, I chose to stay on The Eye. And each time I said goodbye to a character or characters who I had grown to care about. Whose journeys I wanted to see more of. Who I felt genuinely sad to be leaving. Who left sometimes with a hug and a sad smile, sometimes feeling betrayed or hurt that I was abandoning them. But I kept falling in love with these characters, helping them, and saying goodbye to them because I wanted to stay and finish the work I had started.For me, Citizen Sleeper is a meditation on letting go. What it means to let go, how different people react to loss and grief, finding comfort and happiness in people and in yourself, and understanding that even things which seem permanent have an end.10/10. Can't recommend highly enough.

Game also worked great on Steam Deck, with only few minuses being some text being quite small or obscured by the small resolution and some issues with map navigation (toggle L1 twice for a hot-fix if you cannot point at a certain place).Absolutely recommended and can't wait for the updates!
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Sort of a tepid recommendation -- the characters are frequently paper-thin and the writing gets cringeworthy with fair frequency, but I did enjoy the core gameplay loop and felt relatively satisfied at my ending (encountering a few different opportunities to leave the station but in the end deciding to stay). Buy on sale unless you're really into visual novels.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I love the non-combat take on an RPG, where time is your true enemy. There are a million things calling for your attention and only so many dice to use in any given day.Quite heavy on the reading, so if that is not your thing then be warned. Think Disco Elysium. The writing is solid and with the free DLC bundles it took me about 15 hours to play though the whole thing.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a great narrative and wonderful world building, they did a great job making this world feel alive. Every character was wonderful and had a ton of personality. I highly recommend this game, but I will issue a warning: this game only has about 9-10 hours of content in it, which I personally don't feel is justified with a $20 price tag so maybe wait for this one to go on sale if you value time investment.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Cyberpunk. A story of resilience thriving under the weight of callous corporatism. I love seeing how science fiction can be a powerful ambient space for slice-of-life narratives. A space to extrapolate stories about ourselves. I want to stay with these people living ordinary lives in extraordinary settings. I would recommend this to anyone who enjoys Andriod: Netrunner, Edgerunners, or any solarpunk story focused on community-building. + Love the use of spice and mushrooms; the taste of a matsutake is an apt symbol of rebellion and living+ The ending passage of the free DLC story was poetic+ Favorite characters were Tala and Riko, I am glad they were part of the epilogue+ I like how every character could grow; your actions could see them be redeemed or fall short of expectations.+ Good length. 7 hours and 4 hours to finish the main story and DLC- I wish the Sleeper's avatar appeared more often in scenes, and not just in menus- I wish it were easier to achievement hunt
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: A deeply touching game about community, sacrifice and second chances. Almost every character had an avenue which I could approach them with empathy, something that's quite rare in most modern games and left me wishing that I had more time with them. I can't say much more without spoilers, but I loved this experience from beginning to end and the epilogue of my ending left me in tears. Transcends the label of just being a video game, nothing short of art in motion and music.
