_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper follows the story of the titular Sleeper, an android with a “human” consciousness who fled to a space station to escape slavery. The Sleeper is now faced with the harsh reality of survival, and of navigating an unfamiliar and occasionally unfriendly space, while also learning to make friends, to trust, and to become who they choose to be along the way. Citizen Sleeper is difficult to place in any particular genre. It has some survival elements, though these are light and fade away by the mid game. It veers close to a visual novel, though it has more interactivity and player agency than I would ascribe to a visual novel. Even though it has some degree of character customisation, it’s not quite an RPG either. It is, much like its main character, a blending of a variety elements into something wholly new and intriguing. The game’s mechanics are similarly unique. The player has a set of dice that they can invest in actions, though how they choose to invest these, and the risks they choose to accept in doing so are wholly up to them. Indeed, the dice themselves are not the point. They are a vehicle to get to the story, and to see how the world around the Sleeper plays out.The story of Citizen Sleeper is one of survival, but not necessarily exclusively in a physical sense. While there are initial survival elements, these become easy to overcome, to the point where I was flush with every resource I could ever need, except time. Time became the sole limiter of what I could do, what I could accomplish, and what crises I would actually solve. Survival became not a question of survival of the physical, but of deciding how best to use the time allotted to me to do what I saw as most meaningful. In a sense, Citizen Sleeper became a mirror of the fundamental human experience - to make the most of the time given, knowing that it is finite.There’s an irony to this being expressed in Citizen Sleeper. The player character is a Sleeper, an artificial body infused with a human consciousness, giving it the durability of an android, but the mental flexibility of a human. The corporate entity that created this particular Sleeper made some modifications to the mind - very few of the original human’s memories survive, for instance - though what those modifications are isn’t entirely known. That mind can be duplicated and placed into any number of bodies, rendering the mind as a whole immortal, even if any given iteration of it is not. The concern of time and making of it what we can isn’t one that necessarily matters to this mind, though it does very much matter to this particular Sleeper. This Sleeper seeks survival, though what form that survival takes is up to the player and the choices they make along the way.One of the themes of the game is that exploration of humanity, and what actually defines humanity. One of the prevailing questions undergirding the game is that question of whether the Sleeper can ever truly be human, or if that’s even something the Sleeper wants to be. While there are multiple endings, how the player understands the humanity of each is entirely depending on a foundational understanding of what it actually means to be human in the first place.The idea of uploading consciousnesses isn’t a new idea. It’s existed in science fiction for decades, and for some, is seen as increasingly within reach in reality as well. It’s often coupled with the idea of immortality, that, with a consciousness uploaded, an uploaded person is effectively immortal, as they are no longer reliant on their body for survival. For some, then, the idea of uploading a consciousness is an enticing one. It provides the ability to overcome the physical, to be the ultimate expression of mind over matter, to move beyond one of the most fundamental aspects of humanity and become something more. Digital immortality represents the ultimate expression of transhumanism, and the potential of humanity to move beyond our earthly shells. This is an optimistic vision of the potential of consciousness uploading, and one that I think already disregards a certain degree of the human reality. Uploaded consciousnesses are vulnerable. They are able to be tampered with, to be manipulated, to have done to them the same things we already do to any number of programs or simulations. To be disembodied is to be stripped of rights and protections, as our current body of laws and rights understand consciousness and humanity as requiring a body. In any world where the consciousness can be removed from the body, new laws and new conceptions of rights would need to be implemented. To do that, we would need to conceive of these digital consciousnesses as still being human. We would need to understand a copy as being as deserving of rights as an individual, or that something artificial can still be sentient. We already struggle with the idea that non-human animals are deserving of rights and protections - the idea that we would believe that a digital consciousness has any rights at all is a laughable one.And that’s before considering the role of capitalism. Citizen Sleeper examines all these questions of rights and laws and how humanity is viewed through a post-physical lens, but it takes the brilliant extra step of considering not just the role of morals and ethics, but how those are warped by capitalism. Citizen Sleeper is a deeply anti-capitalist game. The game is set on a space station abandoned by corporate overlords when it became unprofitable to maintain, but whose existence is later threatened by a different set of new owners when they, again, view the station as unprofitable. Multiple characters tell their stories of engaging in employment in good faith, only to be chewed up and spat out by a system bent on profit at all cost. The Sleeper themselves is a consequence of the intersection of capitalism and technology. The Sleeper’s ur-human uploaded themselves for cash, analogous to how someone today might donate plasma. They condemned copies of their consciousness to slavery so they themselves could survive. These ideas are presented through a science fiction lens, but they are not science fiction. Neighbourhoods, cities, or entire areas are decimated through the drive for profit. Amazon warehouses, digital sweatshops, and the endless sea of low-paid workers fed into the tech economy are stellar examples of how people are reduced to resources on a spreadsheet, to be disposed of without thought or consequence. We sell our bodies and our selves for survival, knowing in doing so, we are feeding the very system that seeks to destroy us, but continuing because we have no other choice. It is this or oblivion.The dystopia of Citizen Sleeper is not because of capitalism - it is capitalism. This is the story of Citizen Sleeper. It is a story that explores what it is to be human under capitalism. It frames this through the lens of a Sleeper deciding their own humanity for themselves, but it is also a journey experienced by the player. In playing through Citizen Sleeper, I thought a lot about my own experiences, and the choices I’ve made. There is no question in anyone’s mind that I’m human, but does that mean anything anymore? I am a writer, but I can’t write as quickly as ChatGPT or SEO optimise for Google’s algorithms, so my writing goes unseen. I’m a photographer, but Midjourney can craft entire worlds in seconds, using the images it’s stolen from me, so why would anyone look at the originals? When I browse the internet, the value I present to the sites I access is not my thoughts or interest - it’s my engagement, my data, my ability to give them what they need to craft algorithms that can better engage people like me. I give them my soul so they can, in return, try to sell me things.

_childDocuments_.review: I love narrative-driven games and this one is a hell of a masterpiece, one of its endings made me really emotional, and I don't doubt most of them would. Furthermore, the mix between gameplay and story made the pacing so enjoyable, totally changing my first glance at the game - to be honest I thought I'd be soon bored by its simple nature. I could keep writing on about what I love in the way its narrative feels so natural as you progress to the game, but being honest I'll just say that if you love intense narrative-driven games with compelling characters with strong stories, but also with fun rpg-like gameplay, I'm sure you'll love this - especially if you are a collectivist, such as myself. If, otherwise, you are unclear whether this game is for you or not, we also have Lem and his lovely daughter, Mina, which is really all the reason you need to play this game. To finish, I have to say that I haven't played Citizen Sleeper enough to talk about its full experience, but, so far, I couldn't be more happy that I did play it.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I recently reviewed another game, claiming that it was a wannabe-game that handled more like a visual novel due to its lack of compelling gameplay. This game, however, is the opposite - it looks like a visual novel, but it adds just the right amount of something extra, something to differentiate itself from others. Its music is easy-listening, its story compelling, its art polished, and it adds enough interesting gameplay to keep one thinking about their next move without overcrowding it or making it inaccessible to those who just want to relax with a good story. A well-deserved positive review from me!
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This game is absolutely beautiful, not just visually. I cried at almost every single resolution of a storyline. This game paints the darkest, bleakest, most horrifying picture of the far future that you can imagine, and STILL manages to make you cry tears of joy and feel human empathy on a level that you never expected. Truly a work of art.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: I completed my first run a few days ago and I've still been thinking back on it, which is usually a good sign. Here are some thoughts.I expected the game to be more punishing than it actually was, but that actually ended up being something I appreciated. I do like games that require a lot from the player, but I ended up noticing some of the things people have been pointing out in other reviews that the game is actually very hopeful. The game presents you with challenges, but it also presents you with (generally) clear solutions, even if you can't get to them right away. This left me feeling generally like I was growing stronger and more adept as the story continued which was a nice change of pace from lots of bleak narratives. I wasn't able to complete all of the story lines in my first play through, which seems like an obvious statement, but also at the same time it felt oddly fitting. Without being to spoiler heavy, by the end I felt very self sufficient and the sort of resolution I ended up with wasn't necessarily one that felt empty and lacking, but felt fitting at the same time, which again was something I haven't experienced before.I will definitely return back to this game in the future for another run with a new character outlook. This is one of those games I suggest paying full price for if you're considering it because its well-crafted and smart in its storytelling and simple gameplay.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is a beautifully crafted story with deep tones of nostalgia. The mechanics drive a sense of urgency creating a prescient need to keep going, "do the right thing," all while battling the clock. Time is of the essence and managing your strengths and weaknesses is key to survival. A five star emotional play-through that has multiple definitive ends.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever wanted to live the life of an escaped slave whose body is deteriorating faster than the current world economy, living off of burger king foot fungus for 15 chits, while trying to escape a hitman coming for him? No? Neither have I but this game is good anyway.+Your choices do matter to some extent and there are multiple endings, some of them are even good. The characters are well written and you can bond with them, so you kind of care for their safety when they get in danger. Cannot say this for every character though. The illustrations are simply amazing. I can safely say that the art style of this game is what sells it.-My problem is with the dice and the difficulty. There is no voice acting but the writing in this game is good enough to ignore that issue in my opinion. Your early game progress is purely determined by the numbers you can get by rolling the dice. It can be a breeze or a nightmare depending on the dice. Late-game, on the other hand, is so damn easy that I could finish the game in at least two different ways before the assassin shows up. I almost maxed out my stats and the numbers didn't mean anything. I'm not saying the game should be harder but it could be more complex so the endgame does not feel like a visual novel. I don't know how I would fix that, though, so I won't harp on this too much.All in all, good game and worth its price. If you compare it to Disco Elysium, it is going to fall short, however.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: If you like Pen & Paper RPGs (or TTRPGs), Science Fiction, good story telling or just a chilling game, THIS IS THE GAME FOR YOU!!!!I really loved this game. Also, that you can see almost every ending and get almost every achievement in one playthrough. I missed two trophies but with a guide I could have done everything in one go.So if you wanna do stuff in one go, you can!This game is brilliant and I don't wan't to spoil anything.Just.. experience it!
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: it's a choose your own adventure story on a computer. your overall choices are affected by some dice rolls and player character skills that level up when you complete storylines.it's fantastic. much like the old choose your own adventure books where i just read through them to see all the possible endings, i played until i got every single ending. one was a bit obscure and hidden behind some dialogue, but with a guide you can beat the whole game in 8 hours.good soundtrack and the story is immersive. excellent game for chilling and clicking.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: The mechanics are interesting and your choices do indeed matter. The concept is great. The world-building is fantastic and I haven't even finished it... The art is amazing and the descriptions paint a clear picture in my mind. It's the concept that really sold it for me. These are the reasons that I think people should play this game.However, the story (so far; I have not finished it) has been disappointing to me (as a writer & consumer). Nothing interesting happens unless you choose the "right" option, and if you don't, the storyline with that character just straight up ends. There's no warning as well. I feel like if this game's story and each choice was delved into more deeply, this game would be more fun to play.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: This review is written on the first day of playing Citizen Sleeper, which goes to show how much this game hooked me. I'm not really a fan of text based story games, but mannnnn. The writing is amazing yet not so long that if you're like me, you won't get bored just clicking and reading. Beautiful world and message.The mechanics are simple enough to grasp that by the time you reach the three bonus chapters, you have mastered them and are prepared for what comes(THAT BEING SAID, WAIT UNTIL YOU COMPLETE ALL QUESTS AND HAVE BACKUP MONEY BEFORE YOU START THE NEW CONTENT, DO NOT GIVE THEM THE MUSHROOMS, I DID DURING WHAT I THOUGHT WAS LATE GAME AND I WAS SO WRONG)What I love about the game is that it makes you feel like you are at risk and that one wrong step spells doom, but it is very lenient when you do inevitably make that wrong step. More games need to be like this, instead of just saying "Lol you died" and booting you to the home screen.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: A very well written and emotional collection of Sci-Fi stories.   The dice system is much more forgiving than other text-based RPG's. With your roles predefined, you're free to prioritize tasks instead of getting random, often frustrating results (such as Disco Elysium).  Hour count may vary; I completed all the story paths in a little over 10 hours, my brother in 18.   The soundtrack and art are also both fantastic.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Citizen Sleeper is not what I was expecting, to be perfectly honest. Instead, it is a tightly knit story where you have to decide for yourself what constitutes a "good" or "bad" ending... or even what constitutes an ending at all. Each character you meet in this game feels fleshed out, leaning into the strengths of their archetypes while subverting them in delightfully surprising ways. Everyone has a purpose for existing, even the shop vendors (try the fungus, it's worth the investment).It's a game about tough choices, with no right answers, and that gets reflected in the survival elements of the game as well. The daily routine feels meaningful throughout the game, and while you can get ahead of the forces of entropy for a moment you'll never be totally free of the tension inherent to the game. The stories this game tells are rich and challenging, and hold themselves to an impressively high standard. Citizen Sleeper is one of those few games where I have sat back after a playthrough and genuinely thought about what I just played. Flux and Refuge, the two free DLC packs that have been released so far, add another few hours of gameplay, a heaping handful of memorable new characters, and the promise of a third pack in 2023 is a welcome one. The quality of the DLC story lines is held to the same standard as the rest of the game; indeed, if there wasn't a text box explicitly saying where the DLC pack started (one of my very, VERY few gripes with the game's choices), you might never realize this wasn't part of the core experience.Short answer: Sign me up for more.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: The soundtrack alone makes it a recommendation. Solid writing, an interesting setting and fun gameplay settle the matter for me. Very little to criticize overall, though sadly a bit short. Quality has its price I guess.Surprisingly grounded and believable scifi, which is very rare honestly. Lots of attention paid to details and very few inconsistencies. I have never seen such a detailed and well-made representation of a large rotating habitat.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

_childDocuments_.review: Great writing. Still on first playthrough so I'm not sure how reactive the story to my choices but I'm in love with this game already. I'll a little sad but just so it can have some great characters who overcome their problems. Great cyberpunk vibes though it's a lot more of a calm vibe then something like cyberpunk 2077 or the ascent. I haven't seen any sort of combat system in this game. It's a lot like paper's please in that you main goal is just to eke out a living. My only criticism is after running into a few negative timers I'm a lot less worried about a game over and that has taken away some of the stakes. I would recommend the dev sprinkle in a few more ways to screw up badly to keep pressure on.

_childDocuments_.review:
Live the life of an escaped worker, washed-up on a lawless station at the edge of an interstellar society. Inspired by the flexibility and freedom of Tabletop RPGs, explore the station, choose your friends, escape your past and change your future.
LIFE ON ERLIN'S EYE
An abandoned station on the edge of a system in crisis. Run down, chaotic, unruly, and alive—it was founded by idealists in the shadow of a corporate collapse. Now it is held together by anarchic alliances, ramshackle factions and a shared desire to be free from the gravity of corporate control.

DO THE WORK. GET PAID. SURVIVE.
Every cycle you get up and choose what to do with your time. Toil in the yards, or take a bar shift. Search the markets for rare components or grab some street food. Make or break alliances, uncover truths and escape those that hunt you. Learn to survive and ultimately thrive, one cycle at a time.

TURN UP FOR YOUR FRIENDS
The station plays host to characters from all walks of life, trying to eke out an existence among the stars. Salvagers, engineers, hackers, bartenders, street-food vendors, each has a history which brought them here. You choose which of them you wish to help, and together you will shape your future.

ACCESS THEIR SECRETS
Hack into the station’s cloud to access decades of digital data, uncover new areas and unlock secrets. This is your unique power, and with it you can change your future. Corporate secrets, rogue AIs and troves of lost data await those willing to dive into the depths of the station’s networks.

YOU WERE MADE TO DIE
Essen-Arp: to them you are just property, one more asset in a portfolio that stretches across the stars. You are the product of an abusive system, in a universe where humanity’s expansion is marked by exploitation and extraction. Escape the makers of your decaying body, and chart your own path in a richly imagined, deeply relevant sci-fi world which explores ideas of precarity, personhood and freedom.
_childDocuments_.name: Citizen Sleeper

name: The Last Worker
detailed_description: WISHLIST MEOW! 😻 About the Game The Last Worker is an immersive narrative adventure centered around a lone worker’s last stand in an increasingly automated world, with a unique blend of work simulation and stealth strategic gameplay. The game is set in a lonely, oppressive but strangely beautiful environment, with characters designed by comics legend Mick McMahon. Kurt works for the world’s largest retailer and is forced to choose between capitalism or activism. Having dedicated his life to work, Kurt’s loyalty is put to the test when a group of activists ask him to dismantle Jüngle from the inside. Aboard his corporate issued flying JünglePod and armed with his multi-purpose JüngleGun, Kurt dispatches countless products from a fulfilment centre the size of the sunken city of Manhattan. Kurt (voiced by Ólafur Darri Ólafsson) has dedicated his life to Jüngle, with only his co-bot, Skew (Jason Isaacs) to keep him company. But when S.P.E.A.R., a group of activists, asks Kurt to help dismantle Jüngle from the inside, Kurt is forced to discover his employer’s dark underbelly. The Last Worker delivers an emotional, thought provoking and inspiring story with rich characters performed by an all-star cast starring, Jason Isaacs, Ólafur Darri Ólafsson, Clare-Hope Ashitey, David Hewlett, Zelda Williams and Tommie Earl Jenkins. Hand-painted 3D characters and environments based on concepts by comics legend Mick McMahon (Judge Dredd, 2000 AD) Hours of narrative, immersive gameplay in a giant hand-crafted environment. A story worthy of the big screen - A collaboration between writer/director Jörg Tittel (The White King, Ricky Rouse Has a Gun) and VR pioneers Wolf & Wood (A Chair in a Room: Greenwater, The Exorcist: Legion, Hotel R’n’R). Rich characters performed by an all-star cast in a story filled with heartfelt drama, biting satire and intense action. Starring Ólafur Darri Ólafsson, Jason Isaacs, Clare-Hope Ashitey, David Hewlett, Zelda Williams and Tommie Earl Jenkins. Composed by Oliver Kraus (Sia, Adele, Florence and the Machine), with vocals by classical music star Jakub Józef Orliński Playable in either flatscreen or in VR!

But when S.P.E.A.R., a group of activists, asks Kurt to help dismantle Jüngle from the inside, Kurt is forced to discover his employer’s dark underbelly. The Last Worker delivers an emotional, thought provoking and inspiring story with rich characters performed by an all-star cast starring, Jason Isaacs, Ólafur Darri Ólafsson, Clare-Hope Ashitey, David Hewlett, Zelda Williams and Tommie Earl Jenkins. Hand-painted 3D characters and environments based on concepts by comics legend Mick McMahon (Judge Dredd, 2000 AD) Hours of narrative, immersive gameplay in a giant hand-crafted environment. A story worthy of the big screen - A collaboration between writer/director Jörg Tittel (The White King, Ricky Rouse Has a Gun) and VR pioneers Wolf & Wood (A Chair in a Room: Greenwater, The Exorcist: Legion, Hotel R’n’R). Rich characters performed by an all-star cast in a story filled with heartfelt drama, biting satire and intense action. Starring Ólafur Darri Ólafsson, Jason Isaacs, Clare-Hope Ashitey, David Hewlett, Zelda Williams and Tommie Earl Jenkins. Composed by Oliver Kraus (Sia, Adele, Florence and the Machine), with vocals by classical music star Jakub Józef Orliński Playable in either flatscreen or in VR!
short_description: The Last Worker is an immersive narrative adventure centered around a lone worker’s last stand in an increasingly automated world. Kurt works for the world’s largest retailer and is forced to choose between capitalism or activism.

_childDocuments_.review: The game isn't bad but I desperately hate the hacking minigame. It's difficult to control with a mouse and takes too long to complete within the time constraints provided. When I reached to a point where it wanted me to hack twice, one after the other in within a single hacking time limit I closed the game to come back to later. _childDocuments_.review: This game is a fascinating tongue-in-cheek look at what a dystopian future late-stage capitalism holds. This is especially poignant when the news is filled with stories of mass layoffs amid soaring corporate profits.A man wants to keep his job so he sacrifices his health and mental well-being in order to subject himself to humiliating corporate trauma. Have you ever had to win a productivity race to keep your job? The main character of this story has - and his reward: He gets to keep sacrificing his health and mental well-being, but is given a 20 second lightshow while a holographic projection of the CEO of Jüngle commands him to "Dance!". It falls somewhere between 'surreal' and 'something that a corporate "enthusiasm coordinator" would come up with'.The tone really captures the feeling of being ground down by capitalism and smoothly shifts between ennui, emotional vulnerability, despair, and cautious optimism as the story progresses.The story is clever, the art style is captivating, and the characters' motivations are all believable. Other reviewers may complain that they were expecting "anti-woke messaging" in this story. Those reviewers are COMPLETELY missing the point (and don't understand the concept of 'woke'). The game description tells us that the main character is "forced to choose between capitalism or activism" in a "fulfilment centre the size of the sunken city of Manhattan." These reviewers not only miss the point, but they themselves puppet the sentiment of lowest common denominator anti-intellectual bigoted media mouthpieces. If anything, that should be a solid indication that the game might be worth a look for anyone who has been paying even the slightest bit of attention.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Worker

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game on the interesting premise it presents, yet sadly it doesn't seem to do much with that you would expect. Throughout the game you are forced to make assumptions about why things are happening, but don't get any closure on any of it as when you start to think critically so much doesn't seem to make sense or is just a missed opportunity.While I was playing I came up with one word that I felt best described the game, and that was still true at the end. I felt the game was disjointed, where at the end I just didn't know what to make of it.Maybe it's just me where I over time have been growing not to like games where the story itself is left be left open-ended or specifically written to be as such, though if you are like me then you probably won't enjoy it either. On the other hand if that is something you like then there is a good chance you will enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: (THIS IS FOR THE VR VERSION OF THE GAME, AS IT IS BY THE 31ST OF MARCH 2023. THIS MAY NOT BE RELEVANT TO THE 2D VERSION RIGHT NOW)It breaks my heart to say this but if you want to play this in VR, like the game was initially promoted as being before they focused more on the 2D version in marketing, you may have to wait a little longer before you can enjoy it. Right now, the VR side of this game is bugged and badly needs fixes to play nicer with VR controllers while also ironing out some peculiar behaviours that proberbly weren't supposed to be in the game from the get-go.I'm really excited for this game and when they fix things up where the VR side of this goes, I'm stoked to try it out again but unfortunately the bugs are bad enough that I have to regrettably hold off from really diving into it until a later time. The bugs are as follows (Note that while I obviously used SteamVR, it was used via the Pico 4's Streaming Assist app, which works directly with SteamVR and usually has excellent support and compatibility. I also played in Seated Mode):- It freaks the Chaperone out into becoming visible as if I'm in a tiny box-shaped space, which happened during startup, during menus and while being in the space where I had to watch the intro video (had to turn Chaperone to "Floor Only" to fix that for myself as it was very distracting)- The title screen, opening menus and logo images are slanted at an angle. Keeping my head as still as possible as it launches and holding the "Re-Centre" button on my controller didn't fix that- The mirror in my vehicle isn't sitting at the right height for my character's face to be visible, only his head up to below his eyes. The position of his head is also weirdly to the left of the mirror too, so that's not more centre neither- (Specific to playing the game seated) The box I have in front of me after the first section, that you open up to access its contents before it triggers the intro cutscene, is *way* too deep into the middle of my reach, so I had to uncomfortably adjust myself so I could interact with the box without punching my own body by accidentAnd last but certainly least- Controlling the movement of the vehicle is incredibly finicky, inconsistent and largely ineffectual which is *crazy* given the actual instructions are incredibly simple (turn by flicking the analogue stick on the left controller left or right to turn that direction and upwards to go forward). Turning left or right isn't so bad, even if the way the game Snap Turns (if that option's turned on) leaves a little to be desired in its current state, but going forwards is utterly ridiculous. I could only accelerate and move forward the vehicle for 1-2 seconds at a time. Getting it back up requires pushing the stick up enough times before the game decides to go forward...for another 1-2 seconds before stopping. Or at least, that's how it is some of the time. Other times, I've found that when tilting the stick up doesn't do anything, pressing the A button after trying *does* make it go forward, again for another 1-2 seconds. It's an incredibly frustrating time and like a lot of the VR portion of this game, very badly needs bug-fixes with many things that charitably should've been quashed days before launch.The way I was introduced to this game, I was alerted over it being playable in VR on top of it being available for platforms that are non-VR. This game launched pretty suddenly with little fanfare to me as well, aside from Nintendo releasing the Launch Trailer on their YouTube channel for the Switch version. I really, really want to dive into this game as it seems super up-my-alley: a unique take on an immersive, 3D puzzle-platformer ala the "Portal" series that uses bold and necessary commentary on the (sadly, still barely unchallenged) way mega-corporations screw over their employees for their own selfish interests as a launchpad for an intriguing adventure. This also being playable in VR only made me *more* interested. But while I hope those playing this in 2D have fun, I'm gonna have to still wait a little before I can dive deeper.TL;DR: Excited to play your game in VR as you've given us that option, guys, but my *goodness* please look into a lot of these bugs that're plaguing the VR side of things before you risk having this game land on people's bad sides in the VR community rather than what you may wish instead. And good luck elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: The Last Worker is a narrative-based adventure game centered around the reign of a corporate giant in a grim dystopian world. The narrative follows blue-collar worker Kurt (and definitely not Bill from The Last of Us) as he is thrust in the middle of the years-long battle between world’s largest retailer Jüngle and activist organization S.P.E.A.R. Kurt is a warehouse courier in one of Jüngle's "fulfillment centers," and works as the company's only remaining human employee — as the company's activities have since become automated and its former employees "terminated" — under the watchful eye of secretive Mr. Jüngle (who bears a marked but totally coincidental resemblance to a certain real-life businessman). In his journey, Kurt befriends the sarcastic robot drone Skew with a pottymouth Scottish accent and the S.P.E.A.R. drone HoverBird.The story is played out in the first-person and involves moments of actual play, making it much less like a Telltale journey and more like The Stanley Parable. It features a well-designed mix of stealth exploration and riveting courier work to tell its story, as Kurt slowly uncovers the deepest and darkest secrets of his employer of 25 years. Simple puzzles are integrated into the various interspersed stealth missions which, while increasingly difficult through the course of the game, are relatively simple.Despite its well-executed story, actual gameplay can sometimes feel like a chore as the stealth portions are frustratingly obtuse and the work simulation sections are painfully boring and long-winded (though I suppose that is the intention). Both halves of The Last Worker are completed by the game’s primary mechanic: the trademarked Jüngle gun. The gun is issued to all courier employees and is intended for transferring and dispatching boxed products and tagging damaged or incorrectly-labelled parcels, though the player earns some non-standard S.P.E.A.R. upgrades to the Jüngle gun throughout the game.The bulk of The Last Worker is confined to the Jüngle shipping center Kurt works at, with well-designed levels that — while feeling more designed to fit the progression of the game’s tale than reliably mimic actual facility layouts — have a sort of eerie and fatigued The Stanley Parable-esque beauty to them. With its cel-shaded comic book-style aesthetic, the game is able to really hammer home its intended nihilistic tone. Complementing its themes is its haunting string ensemble soundtrack, delightfully eerie in just the right moments.The game’s voiced dialogue is actually enjoyable (a feat that many narrative adventures can easily fail to accomplish). The voice acting is almost impeccable, a mark of a proper cinematic experience. I love the strained chemistry between Kurt and Skew as they form an unlikely friendship, and the constant bickering of Skew and the HoverBird provide some welcome and much-needed comic relief throughout the game’s undoubtedly stress-inducing plot. Another humorous element involves the parcels that Kurt dispatches and recycles as part of his daily tasks at Jüngle. As Kurt delivers each parcel, the player is shown the comical products inside: a coronavirus desk lamp, octopus head massager, selfie hairbrush, and branded knock-offs like a “Fartnite” pro gamer chair and “Zodick the Hellhog” plushie. (There are 110 unique product designs in the game to find.)These enjoyable elements are somewhat dampened, though, by The Last Worker’s subtle but ever-present technical snags. There are too many load screens which, while short, are a startling jump out of the game’s immersivity; it’s painfully easy to softlock the game when messing up a task; phasing out of the map when interacting with the game’s various moving objects is almost a guarantee during a stealth mission; and scene restarts are unbearingly buggy. While the game is supported in both traditional PC widescreen and VR modes, the sluggish MKB controls — though passable enough to be playable — let slip its obvious preference for the VR experience.Despite its absurdist premise — Kurt works in a rundown shipping facility the size of Manhattan and the height of the Empire State Building, is accompanied by a Scottish-accented robot drone, and dispatches the most whimsical products imaginable — The Last Worker takes itself as seriously as much as any story can. Fun at stages though drawn-out enough to feel dull by the end, the game’s redeeming qualities lie in its exemplary voiced dialogue and humorous retail products more so than the chilling narrative it tries to tell.

_childDocuments_.review: A very weird, unique experience that I heartily recommend for all.Pros:* Great voice acting and music* Excellent puzzles and timing to keep gameplay fresh.* Absolutely hilarious "products".Cons:* Had a few times where the game bugged out and erroneously failed me, but I was able to get past them.* The warehouse work took a few tries before the rules made sense.  Controls are also not shown long enough - had to peruse the key bindings to grok them.Meh:* Not one, not two, but THREE rounds of Flappy Bird?  C'mon... :P* Living in Bezos' hellscape.* One part was artificially contrived to be evil.  Meat isn't universally considered to be murder. :P* A few times the action got a bit heated, but my lackluster reflexes pulled them off after a cpl fails.TL;DR: Great game, hilarious from beginning to end. 9/10

_childDocuments_.review: A short game, for sure, but an interesting one with a clear message which, while a bit clumsy on occasion, told the story it wanted to tell and gave you the choice so play the part you wanted. I really thought it was going to try and both-sides the situation - attempt to say the idea of revolution is as bad as the Capitalist mode of working forever - but it did present a third option or doing what you feel is right and escaping the paths put forward. Was it perfect? not entirely. It did stumble on it's plot in places and I think some exploration of exactly what corrupted SPEAR would have definitely helped deepen the narrative. It did, however, show those things as not inevitable and you can defy hierarchy if you need to. It may not end in the idealised world we want, but you can carve out a space for those you care about. Oh, and the package sorting is fun, just let me turn packages around so I can see the labels please and thank you.

_childDocuments_.review: Effective use of VR to create an atmosphere that feels lonely, desperate and grim. The world-building leans on the familiar, collective consciousness of Amazon warehouses...of monotony...of following instructions...of idolizing figureheads that represent something we want to believe (btw, saw that ending coming a mile away). There's too much motivation to apply the adjective of  “cynical”; not enough humour to say it is “sardonic” but there's an uncomfortable truth being expressed.

_childDocuments_.review: ~ DIFFICULTY ~🔲 My 90 year old grandma could play it✅ Easy🔲 Normal🔲 Hard🔲 Dark Souls~ GRAPHICS ~🔲 MS Paint🔲 Bad🔲 Meh🔲 Graphics dont matter in this game✅ Good🔲 Beautiful~ MUSIC ~🔲 Bad🔲 Not special🔲 Good✅ Eargasm~ STORY ~🔲 This game has no story🔲 Like playing Temple Runners for the story✅ It's there for the people who want it🔲 Well written🔲 Epic story~ PRICE ~🔲 Free🔲 Underpriced✅ Perfect Price🔲 Could be cheaper🔲 Overpriced🔲 Complete waste of money~ REQUIREMENTS ~🔲 You can run it on a microwave✅ Average🔲 High end🔲 NASA computer~ LENGTH ~🔲 Very Short (0 - 3 hours)✅ Short (3 - 15 hours)🔲 Average (15-50 hours)🔲 Long (50-90 hours)🔲 Extremely long (90-110 hours)🔲 No ending~ FUN ~🔲 I'd rather watch paint dry🔲 Hard to enjoy🔲 Repetitive✅ Actually pretty amusing🔲 Ride of your life~ REPLAYABILITY~🔲 It's a one-time experience🔲 Only for achievements✅ If you wait a few months/years🔲 Definitely🔲 Infinitely replayable~ WORTH BUYING ~🔲 No🔲 Wait for sale✅ Yes----------------The Last Worker is a dystopian view into a grim future run by end stage capitalist monopolies. The game puts you in the shoes of a lone worker, Kurt, who has to survive alone in a harsh and oppressive environment, while also finding some joy and humor in the mundane tasks.The gameplay is great, there are multiple items to keep in mind when dispatching products, and you need to be careful, as your boss enforces a zero tolerance policy!  The controls feel nice and smooth, allowing you to move around JFC1 with ease and precision. The art style is beautiful, with a hand-drawn aesthetic that creates a contrast between the bleak setting and the colourful details. The music is also very good, being nice and calm at the start of shifts, to pushing and loud when your shift is about to end.The only letdown is the story, which has a great start but seems to lose itself halfway through the game. The game really begins when Kurt meets a mysterious person that guides him through areas his superiors do not want him to see. However, as the game progresses, the story becomes less coherent, too rushed and doesn't really have a satisfying ending. The writing decisions seem flawed, as in one case Kurt will state he will be ending his time at the company, but then after act 2 just completely reverses that decision and decides to stay after an action that should have had significant repercussions for his actions . The humour is pretty good though, with most of the jokes landing well.Overall, The Last Worker is a fun and engaging game. It has a lot of charm and personality, as well as some solid and unique gameplay that keeps you hooked. The story could have been better developed and more consistent, but it does not ruin the overall experience, but fortunately the gameplay more than makes up for it.The Last Worker gets a 7/10.For more reviews check my Steam profileHope you enjoyed my review, god bless you

_childDocuments_.review: I remember playing the demo for this game, and initially i thought that it had a great deal of promise but after completing the game and completing all three endings i was largely disappointed, not to say that it is a poorly made game, the art is very well done and its voice acting is brilliant, however i managed to finish the game in less than 5 hours (managed to get the game on another site) which is not great bang for your buck as many people subscribe to the 1 dollar per hour idea.To sum up the story, its rather meh. A very prominent anti-capitalism theme, which isn't a criticism of the game, its actually done rather well, but the game play can be compared to a 3d papers please (a horrible example i know but all i can come up with) with checking contents and a secretive power trying to decimate an oppressive system, but the game play gets very repetitive very quickly as you devolve into simply rotating a box and throwing it with there being no increasing difficulty of this arduous task, and the later sections of the game turning into a game of hide-and-seek.i think many of the other people who left negative reviews agree on this aspect but a lot of its commentary is rather on the nose, blue-bird saying how she was raised so she wouldn't need to rely on a man, as well the political commentary in the game does not so much as make you want to roll your eyes and scoff, but it is a largely unnecessary and a mildly irritating inclusion. However skrew (or whatever the companion robot was called) did an excellent job of playfully dismissing blue-birds comments without it being an awkward of confrontational exchange and was in general a very much needed source of comedic relief from certain portions of the dialogue. The game could have spent a larger portion of its time going over these themes in a different manner that wouldn't have come across as being pretentious, it doesn't seem that the developers wanted this to be the case but that was simply my experience of it.Seeing the developers comments on the negative reviews it does not seem that they were trying to push a narrative and were in fact very respectful of criticism so huge props to them.The endings themselves were largely unsatisfying as all you needed to do was hold W for 3 minutes before making a choice that would lead to one of three endings******* spoiler alert*****in one of the endings the jeff bezos wanna be is dead and in the other he is alive, that massively threw me off, as it made me think that my choice did not matter at all and that the developers were trying to nudge you into choosing another option. which has to be the largest of my personal gripes with this game.all in all i think there are a lot of other games that tackle these themes a lot better and offer a more satisfying game play experience, i wish the developers great success at their future endeavours but i do think it would be worth their time to look at the criticisms of this game and try to steer clear of them in the future.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Worker

_childDocuments_.review: Enjoying the game a ton early on! I'd usually wait a bit longer before reviewing, but with some various takes out there want to give my own.Playing without VR. The controls are fine and the HUD works A Okay. The only real issue I've had is that I feel the tutorial doesn't do a great job showing off how to ID package size and weight. It tells you that you have to, but doesn't really line it up with the controls you'll need. Maybe it's just me, but trying to work that out took me a bit.If you're having issues with that (using mouse and keyboard) hold the package and rotate it with Z and X to check the labels. They're what the package is supposed to be. There'll be two labels, one for size and one for weight. You've got to check those are right: the small medium large thing is how it compares to the storage area on your pod, the weight on the label vs the weight on your Pod's HUD once you've put it down. If it matches, post, if not tag and recycle.Story and graphics so far are a treat! The intro cutscene got me, the environment is really well done... I plan to update more later, but don't worry about controls. This is a great game and worth your time! Any questions, just ask!
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Worker

_childDocuments_.review: The advertising for this game made me interested.I was here for the anti-establishment, anti-woke, pro-human messaging the advertising put front and center. It's a type of game that emphasizes the story, and it is clearly attempting to tackle real-world contemporary and near-future issues. This game could have been pro-human, anti-automation, and anti-monopoly while remaining relatively a-political. They have chosen to tackle real-world social and political issues, so it is fair to evaluate it from that perspective.Playing the game I'm getting the impression that the advertising does not match the message of the game.Just an hour in I'm getting "capitalism bad", "meat eaters bad", "muh climate change". All establishment, woke messages, in a game that advertised as anti-establishment and anti-woke. I'm getting the impression that it lacks self-awareness, like all 'woke' things. One of the characters has a throw-away line the implies the problem with the Bezos character is that he uses his rainbow hair to fake being progressive. As if "fake progressivism" is the problem. Reminds me of how they say "Nat. Socialists weren't really socialists!" or "Real communism hasn't been tried!". Gimme a break.The main character calls the color pink sexist, and a Trump doll "What an a--hole", they toy a little with masculine/feminine pronouns of robots. This is all within the first hour.It has not established the context required for irony. Therefore it is sincere. Therefore it is cringe.If it IS irony, it has not "paid off" in the short period I have played the game. I would like to fully evaluate the message of the game, but I want to stay under the 2 hour refund limit.I will wait for reviews so that I'm not funding a message I disagree with.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Worker

_childDocuments_.review: Received a code via Dare Drop, but would have grabbed this one just for the premise alone. And Skew. I would have played just for Skew. Story was great, voice acting was on point - my main gripes were with issues controlling the audio, which when you are streaming is awkward. The death sound and the sound of the big bad robots was deafening at times and no matter how low I had game audio, it blasted through. Wasn't a fan of all of the mechanics, but honestly, didn't hate it enough to stop playing. Overall I'd give it a 7/10. Enjoyed my playthrough, solid game - just a few small things made me grumble.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Worker

_childDocuments_.review: I'd played the demo at EGX 2022 and the introduction animation and tutorial had me sold before the release. Luckily the game lived up to my expectations and then some. The Last Worker is the sort of narrative tale that games do so well. You live within the world and experience the daily grind of a warehouse 'Jungle' worker as he begins to question the nature of what he is doing and what he has sacrificed by doing his job. As with many narrative tales, gameplay is limited, being split between timed delivery runs (with various mechanics) and some stealth selections. These are fun and work well but it's the story (and characters in particular) that keep you engaged. The Last Worker tells a poignant and emotional tale well, filled with comedy as well as drama. Special mention should be given to Jason Isaacs in the role of Skew - a foul mouthed assistant robot that largely steals the spotlight every time he enters the story.There are some gameplay elements that take sometime to get used to - it is easy to fail the delivery and stealth sections and at times the controls can feel a little clunky. I only played this outside of VR on PC and Steam Deck (which ran perfectly btw) so I can't comment on it though it seems suited to a VR environment. At a little over 4 hours it never feels overly long and tells a story efficiently with no padding.A must for all narrative game fans.
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Worker

_childDocuments_.review: The Last Worker VR - A Game of Package Delivery, Capitalism and Activism.This is one of those games that really surprised me. I never knew I would find another package delivery game (Death Stranding) that I would really get into. The Last Worker is an excellent story driven game, with amazing voice acting, narrative and plot that keeps you wanting more. At the same time, it is also a really fun package delivery sim.We play Kurt, the last human employee of the world's largest evil retailer, it's like an evil Amazon. We and our robotic mate Skew take packages from a city sized warehouse environment and deliver them from point A to B. Listening to Kurt and Skew go on as you play is humorous and entertaining. The world is stunning with its cell shaded graphics and feels very immersive. The game also has lots of humorous items and things in the world to see. The world changes for Kurt when he is approached by a team of activists asking him to help bring the company Jungle down. This is where the story gets you drawn in and wanting more. The characters are well done and creates a love for each one of them. The story is well written and could be a movie itself. The gameplay its really fun, and the world and gameplay fit the story perfectly. The game had me digging for more. If you enjoy a great story wrapped into an interactive game, this one hits all the right boxes. Watch my preview here,
_childDocuments_.name: The Last Worker

_childDocuments_.review: The Last Worker is less the managing package shipping game you might expect at first. The story quickly takes over the game, and I think that's a good thing. We follow an interesting story using the game elements presented to us at the start of the level. It may be a bit easy in many corners, but in this way it prevents moments of frustration, allowing you to focus on the story. I recommend playing the game in VR, as it makes it easier to control and allows you to dive deeper into the game. But The Last Worker was also playable on screen with mouse and keyboard without any problems.+ VR support+ interesting story+ excellent voice actors+ many game elements- presented elements too less used

_childDocuments_.review: Unsure of the games origins being a duel flat screen/VR release, seemingly the latter? If that wasn't the case, The last Worker is one of those that would have been commented on asking surely it would make sense.Make sense it really kinda does. The motion controls work well, button mapping feels intuitive, there's the sense of presence with you being able to look around, you're even able to look at your own mannerisms in the mirror during the dialogue captions.The game itself is fairly simple, not much beyond moving boxes from A to B. They've mixed it up a little with the box itself requiring you to either tag it as damaged, being overweight, or out of season. There's a definite jeopardy simulation in play, one that'll only get more difficult as you progress through the game.I feel the games greatest strength is in the narrative and overarching story. From what little i've seen going through the opening chapter, there's a requirement for you to get involved with that. The voicing cast is mightily impressive, the art assets look great, i appreciate the graphical style. Not much seems cheap here, it's a well produced game.If you're looking at this for a middle of the road VR game, this is a good one.Extra note: They don't list the Pico as a working VR device, absolutely 100% working here on my Neo 3 Link.

_childDocuments_.review: The Last Worker is a first-person narrative adventure centered around our struggle in an increasingly automated world. Combining a hand-crafted art style with uniquely immersive gameplay mechanics in an epic setting, The Last Worker delivers an emotional, thought-provoking, and comedic story packaged with rich characters performed by an all-star cast.

name: Gunbrella
detailed_description: Gunbrella is a gritty noir-punk action-adventure set in a world dependent on a rapidly diminishing natural resource. Fill the rain-soaked boots of a gruff woodsman on a quest for revenge, entering an unfamiliar town armed only with the titular Gunbrella, a high-caliber firearm that doubles as an umbrella. Your hard-nosed investigation soon becomes entangled with the inner workings of a creepy cabal of ghouls and gangsters, cops and cultists, and the fallout of corporate exploitation. GAIN MASTERY OF THE GUNBRELLA Engage in thrilling, side-scrolling action making full use of the Gunbrella's unique maneuverability and close-quarters combat capabilities. The Gunbrella is more than just a weapon - use it to glide, swing, dash, and dive around the world and discover seemingly unattainable secrets along the way. LEAVE NO STONE GUNTURNED From a small town menaced by cult kidnappings to a junkyard fortress ruled by a ruthless trash gang, explore a diverse assortment of unusual locations and interrogate bizarre characters on your quest for answers. Keep track of findings in your trusty notebook, and remember to retrace your steps... RETRIEVE. RELOAD. REPEAT. Salvage scrap and spare parts to trade for different munitions and upgrades for your impermeable arsenal. As your search deepens, and you conjure increasingly ghastly agents of the supernatural, you'll need all the help you can get.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a pretty hard not recommend to make. The artstyle and music is charming and the movement/combat is very satisfying; but the level design, bosses, and story is so simple every single chapter will make you go "...That's it?" The gunbrella allows for some quick movement and great jump control, but you almost never need to do it. Bosses at most have 3 attacks and don't do much else other than get shot by your gun. Your gun can fire different ammo types but you never feel the need to. You get only burst rifle shots for most of the game which don't do the damage your shotgun does. The other ammo types you start getting near the end where you're already fully upgraded.There's other reviews saying "Cave Story drawn with crayola" and "LISA with no bite," and I think it does fall into that. It leads to a lot of potential interesting exposition and story but ends a lot of it by directly telling you the exact arc every character has and exactly how the world feels. It feels afraid to have some things require thought, as harsh as that sounds. The main character is a vehicle for the world as a traditional silent protag with the most being that he has a sad backstory. This would be cool if the rest of the characters were more than just telling him exactly everything they feel with no subtlety. A cool thing with the story happens around 85% through where I thought this structure would change, but *very* sadly, it didn't. The villain is a laughing stock and the main character does not get a conclusion to the moral question he gets asked. It's like an abrupt cut and I really hope it was just production issues. I can't believe this is what they wanted out of the script.
_childDocuments_.name: Gunbrella

_childDocuments_.review: 4/5+-6hA good shortish twinstick action platformer In short :- Shallow writing that feels incomplete+ Veeery fluid platforming+ Satisfying although generally easy combat+- Bosses that range from challenging, skilltesting and fun to absolute pushovers- Wish there was optional difficult platforming-centered challengesMy main gripes about this game:- Setting is underexplained and there's a major plot holeI don't really mind if story is bad or generic though as a lot of games I enjoy even have even worse stories. This one just ends up generic but with missed opportunity to stand out more- There's a lot of different ammo typesThey mostly end up clogging your inventory as I found half of them worse than the infinite default one and the last 3 I kept for bosses only.Most importantly- I wish there was more and more challenging optional contentI did all sidequests to my knowledge and it took me 6hThis is a shame not because of how short the game is but because I wish there was much tougher platforming challenges that required me to fully master advanced gunbrella platforming.The movement is very fluid and interesting and reminds me a lot of Celeste. Smooth walljump, airdash, floatSadly the game ends without really asking you to challenge you to masterfully chain these actions. I wish like Celeste there was optional challenges to get to after I beat the game but wanted more and was ready for tougher.Using the gunbrella is really fun and it's impressive how intuitive but multi purpose it is (Hold to block, tap to dash, block just right to reflect, use it to dash downward or float slower down)Moving fast becomes addictive and fun but is sadly never a challenge required by the game
_childDocuments_.name: Gunbrella

_childDocuments_.review: 7/10 game. The platforming is excellent, controls are tight and responsive. The combat starts off fun, but never really evolves beyond getting a few different ammo types that have slightly different properties (rifle rounds travel further, throwing stars have a higher rate of fire and bounce, etc etc), overall a mild disappointment. The story is a little corny, a trope-ridden and hamfisted cliche-fest about capitalism and classism. The music absolutely bangs. The art style is fine, nothing to write home about.So basically, every element ranges from "great" to "fine, I guess." Which means overall that's a pretty good package! My first playthrough was about 6 1/2 hours, I'm fine with spending $15 for that, but if you need to wait for a sale, hey, it's your money.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok, we all know there is no middle ground on Steam. This review is actually not a thumbs down but also definitely not a thumbs up. I have mixed feelings about the Game and I should also state that this is a) purely subjective and b) I have to admit that the thumbs down part is also because of my expectations for this Game that were flat out wrong (this was not false marketing or anything, I just expected it to be a metroidvania - which it isn't -  based on the indeimaus Video)Let's start with the good:- It can be fun movement wise- Gunplay feeling is good soundwise- Pixel Style is okayish, nothing that I have never seen before, it just does the job- Music can be okayish (also this is down to preference, it was just not what I like)- The atmosphere was kinda good - The ending was ok- It was short Now to the negatives, at least for me. (Also let me stress that I usually like almost all Devolver Published Games, this is just not one of them)- Gunplay is boring, you just shot that one Gun 99% of the Time, I didn't need to play with the other "Ammunition Types" at all- Movement can be wonky sometimes controlwise. You can pull it off easily but also at the same time it feels clunky from a control scheme, especially when you move around in the air and have to shoot- The Game itself is 60% Story (talking) and 40% Combat, not a good ratio for my taste when it comes to sidescrollers- Story could be boring at times- Bosses were way too easy, no challenge at all- The whole Game was way too easy that I sometimes wondered why they put combat in the Game at all- You can have 3 upgrades in the Game, that's it. It really felt super barebones and thus I felt there was no variety at all- I was getting annoyed a few times and wanted the Game to end. Don't ask for a specific reason, it just didn't come together well enough for me.With all that being said, I don't think it's the worst Game of all time or really just bad. I just have mixed feelings about it but I'm leaning towards a "Not recommend".

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely short (My play time is potentially half-2/3rd of what my actual time shows, since I reset half way through because I picked an accidental dialogue choice I didn't want to)., but the game is a delight to traverse through. That being said, I played hard, and barely needed to worry about any of the bosses (stun locked two of them), never used any of the other ammo types, and basically didn't engage with the consumables system. Difficult it ain't. Story is serviceable, not bad or good, and the art is pretty dang primo.I'd say buy it if you're really into indie games, or buy it on sale if you're mildly into indie games.
_childDocuments_.name: Gunbrella

_childDocuments_.review: Beautiful pixel art, fantastic movement, and great feeling combat, but everything that surrounds it feels very underdeveloped. The devs are clearly a talented bunch, but they really should have either kept the scope smaller and delivered a more focused action platformer experience, or gone all out and made a fully-fledged metroidvania that takes full advantage of its mechanics. As it stands, it just sits in this weird middle ground where it feels like it's unsure of what it wants to be.

_childDocuments_.review: I cant recommend this game. Because i am pissed with it. Look, this game advertised with its gameplay in every video of it before the release. All of its videos on Steam page show gameplay, not dialogue parts. Plus, it doesn't say anywhere on the steam page that its a ''narrative driven'' game, it says Side Scroller Action Platformer (and idk why cuz its not, yet still it says ''roguelike'' and ''metroidvania', its not). Nevertheless, it progress heavily on story. So, i dont mind a game being short, on the contrary, i prefer short games these days bc of the content richness. But this is different. In 4 hours of lenght of it, only about 1 hour of it is pure gameplay. The remaining 3 hours are full of dialogues and going here and there for the story.I was very enthusiastic towards the game at the first hour. ''Gunbrella'' was really fun to use, and i thought it is a great/fun idea. Mechanicaly, its like Katana Zero, like dashing with katana in any direction. Except, in this one you have a ''GUNBRELLA'', a shotgun and umbrella combination. You can dash in any direction and deflect enemy attacks using umbrella and shoot enemies with shotgun obviously. Its so fluid to play, its simply fun. Maybe not long-lasting as it is but fun for a few hours. It can also be enriched with more mechanics. The problem is not that anyway.Besides Katan Zero, it also has some Celeste vibes. Its art is great with cool visuals and a little repetitive yet stimulating musics. Frustratingly, by the time goes, that enthousiasm of mine died slowly towards the game because of its eagerness to tell the story. Look, its story is NOT intriguing. Its not deep anyway, narration going more like funny-ish and in a frivolous way, its a revenge story, simple. And it is not intriguing, is just a banal story, not like Katana Zero or Celeste in this term.Idk why the hell but they chose to tell that story at all cost, at the cost of making pure gameplay about 2 hours less than it. Not just with hour lenght, even most of the level designs contains safe areas in which you talk with npcs. Only the short routes we use to get to the safe zone contain enemies, that's all. Its like a joke but you dont even have enough space to play the game. I really dont understand this motivation. They have a great tool gameplay wise, it could be so much fun if levels are designed and cherished more for it. There is some health and weapon upgrades as rewards for doing side quests mostly, but they dont mean much since the gameplay is already too short and kinda easy. The game has 4 or 5 bosses and they all are too simple with so poor attack patterns. You have 3 health at first and can also easily die but in 4 or 5 try you can beat them without much effort. So they are not satisfying.

_childDocuments_.review: I think this game is more of a proof of concept than anything. The developers have something special with the main moving and shooting mechanic but I don't think they quite hit a home run....yet.The only reason I'm still recommending this game is cause i want it to do well enough to warrant a sequel although I think its a lil more expensive than it should be. For a sequel i'd like to see:*Longer combat set pieces with much more enemies.*A lot more secrets, especially while traversing.*The game should be much harder as well. I played on hard and i barely broke a sweat. Give us masochists a challenge.*Cut out some of the pointless dialogue and if not hire a writer with better comedy chops.*Different ammo types specifically for different situations.*Lastly, some light puzzle elements.Maybe wait for a sale on this one but I would definitely say I'm glad i played it and I hoping Doinksoft can really expand upon a pretty neat start.

_childDocuments_.review: After Finishing Gunbrella I overall had a positive experience. Definitely something I would expect with the great teamwork of the dev who made Gato Roboto and Devolver. Though I can imagine there was a lot of pressure put on the development of the game I still really enjoyed myself. However I feel that there was few things lacking. And it really ties itself to the whole "Gunbrella" gimmickHere is some suggestions I believe that could be/been added to improve the games overall performance.Now I played this game on "Normal" difficulty but even then the game felt to easy on me.- Lack of Enemies - most areas you will be wondering and you will barely in the early stages of the game have anything to shoot. I would really loved if rooms had more than 2 - 4 enemies in them and I would sprinkle some more fun pointless things to shoot and use my gunbrella for!- Spongier Bosses - I have to say the main premise I found with the bosses were that they were waayyy to easy to kill... Really like even early on I barely had my gun upgraded and it still killed them way to fast.- Beast Boss - I mean... cmon man that just made me feel bad killing the mother and leaving the cubs alone to probably starve ;x; I wish I could just not done that.- Ammo is practically pointless - The idea of the ammo for your gunbrella is fun but you are A) Always low on ammo or B) Have so little storage for it its honestly better to sell it for other more useful and practical things, not to mention how the base shotgun damage is already enough- More Parachute gimmicks - Through out the game I only encountered ONE falling segment with the umbrella and that feels like a waste of opportunity.- New Game Plus? - I feel like this game could really use one after beating the game. Overall I would just like more of what already is in the game, if rooms and enemies were more sprinkled around and I had more reasons to shoot or jump with my gunbrella around more I would had less annoying time backtracking. But in the end the game was great and I only wish it had more of what it already offered.7 / 10 - Needs MORE Gunbrella Action

_childDocuments_.review: It kinda sucks to leave a negative review on this game since i was hyped up for this since it was revealed but after finishing the game I just had a very mediocre experience.Difficulty is incredibility easy that you shouldn't even consider easy or normal when playing it for the first time, yes, it's THAT easy (why there is a "difficulty" tag on the game baffles me).Don't be expecting to go in and start going guns blazing on every enemy you see, the enemies are very spread apart per room and you will either 1 or 2 shot them, very lacking combat.Bosses are honesty the most disappointing part of the game. Once again, very easy and they are just bullet sponges that are not even that spongy to kill.Story is alright I guess, has it's up's but it wasn't able to carry the lackluster combat paired with it. Ending wasn't satisfying and ended up falling flat.The art and the OST for the game is really the only thing that made me go "I like that". Art is clearly done well and the OST really does set the atmosphere well.Very nit picky thing for me but in order to get all the achievements you need to play the game a minimum of 3 times (1 full playthrough and 2 partial playthroughs around 75% completion). Having guaranteed missable achievements really just suck to earn and I may just not bother to finish it because how lacking my first playthrough was.If you are looking for a badass game where you are a dude shredding everything with a gun-umbrella like me then this game isn't going to cut it, it really felt like a "talk to this person then go to point A to point B then repeat" type of game because of how lacking the combat was.Clearly there is love and passion poured into this game and I do hope it gets better over the following months but as of right now, I don't recommend it at its full price.

_childDocuments_.review: Gunbrella has a super fun core mechanic but the rest of the game falls short creating a game that feels satisfying enough to finish but as a whole isn't fun enough to be worthwhile. The gunbrella itself is used both used for combat and movement with the former being basic but visceral and the latter being the game's strongest point. The controls feel tight and responsive and dashing around the place is engaging. Gently gliding down with the gunbrella or using it to ride a zip line is also fun. The wall jump on the other hand leaves something to be desired but the gunbrella's dash is so versatile that you don't have to rely on it as much. Level design as a whole doesn't push the gunbrella's movement set far enough, with most rooms being very simple in terms of layout and hazards. There were only a few rooms that gave some harder parkour challenges which were the most enjoyable levels in the game. The rest of it felt very basic and unremarkable also due to the fact that the levels are extremely linear. I even went in thinking this game was a metroidvania but it's more of an action platformer with some minimal backtracking and side routes. The game also recycles a few areas with the passage of time creating several points of no return, further limiting the open world feel and making the game feel claustrophobic. The game also just has many small rooms in which to fight enemies, with barely any room to maneuver.As stated before combat is quite impactfull, as point blank blasting enemies in the face with a shotgun literally explodes them across the room. Which can give you some very cathartic enjoyment. However the combat is basic and enemy variety is severly lacking. Bosses don't fare much better either as their movesets are uninteresting and due to the consumable nature of healing items often very easy to beat first try. There's very few enemies or bosses that are interesting enough to be memorable and the final boss felt out of place and completly random. In fact some of the story payoff is quite weak for a game with this much dialogue.The narrative has a cool premise but the pacing feels poorly done, and the writing drawn out. You spend a LOT of time talking in this game, probably more than you do fighting which is odd for an action platformer. Gunbrella feels like a mismatch of conflicting genres. With a story you'd expect in a cinematic puzzle platformer, movement that fits better in a metroidvania and combat that feels at home in a fast action platformer. The payoff for none of these is great though as the story falls flat, the movement is great but frontloaded without any progression throughout the game and combat that is unrewarding.The music is nice though, all the tracks feel right at home in this game and some of the more soothing jazz tunes evoke a noir feeling. The visuals are gritty but quite basic in terms of pixel art. There's also this annoying film grain that is reenabled every time you boot up the game. Like the game forgets your options everytime you quit, this got really annoying by the end. What was also annoying is that the game fails to recognize your controller if you unplug and plug it back in without rebooting the game. This paired with the softlock and crash i had made me have to reset the film grain over a dozen times. Poor QoL in conclusion, but at least there were no mayor game breaking bugs or lag.In the end Gunbrella's movement, while great, isn't enough to alleviate the other pain points. This game would've been better as a fully fledged metroidvania or a more condensed action platformer but now it just sits akwardly in the middle. This is one of the first devolver titles i didn't fully like, but it's still better than most AAA publishers. So if you're craving a game that isn't terribly long, with fun movement then you can get this on a deep sale (40% or more) otherwise play any of the other amazing devolver titles. Death's door especially is a great time! But carrion, gris, cult of the lamb, astroneer and titan souls are also amazing titles! Gunbrella isn't a stain on their catalogue but it doesn't reach the heights of its peers.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like it, but ultimately the game kinda fell flat for me. I got past the middle point of the game before giving up, partially due to bad directions from the game (I was asked to find an NPC, Francine, without any guidance to where she might be, and despite looking everywhere that came to mind, I couldn't find her).The game isn't a *bad* game. It does a lot of things right. Graphically, it's quite nice looking, reminding me of old flash games from Nitrome, and the music is really good. Another thing I'd give praise to is the movement-- your controls are pretty tight and dashing, floating and swimming with the gunbrella feels really nice. Unfortunately, at least from what I played, none of that movement ever really feels... necessary? The game is very easy. Even on the hardest difficulty. Given the movement the gunbrella gives you, you can effortlessly outmaneuver any and all enemies, as well as pretty much all environmental dangers in the entire game. It feels... full of potential that just never get tapped.The combat was alright. But again, you never quite feel the need to make much use of the various tools you get. Generally speaking, mashing your shotgun up against enemies over and over gets you through all fights without difficulty, and while different ammo types exist to add variety to the gameplay (sawblades, rifle ammo, grenades, etc) swapping between bullet types feels a bit unintuitive and crucially, the cost of ammunition is so expensive you never really feel like you can 'afford' to experiment with different ammo types when you have infinite shotgun ammo that does the job just as well if not better than the other options. (Particularly when the ammo cost competes with upgrade parts which you'd much rather spend money on)The story is alright. I appreciate the character dialogue, and how different people talk... though I have difficulty explaining just what i like about it, I suppose you could just say it's charming. The worldbuilding is alright. There's a couple innovative concepts. I was surprised that there were a few points in the story where I could make a significant choice that had consequences. I suppose that's a plus-- there might be more in the parts of the game I didn't get to.But ultimately, the lack of challenge in enemies and bosses and generally uninspired platforming segments meant I wasn't too thrilled to see what was around the corner, and the lack of walkthroughs and guides meant I couldn't move past the hurdle of poor signposting with finding the NPC I needed to progress the main story. Maybe get it on a sale?
