_childDocuments_.review: Alrighty then! Just over 70 hours and the first playthrough is over.There´s a few things to unpack, but I´ll keep this as spoiler free and to the point as I can.Overall I´d say I had a good time with this game, and I´d say it warrants a score of about 7.5/10.Is it a flawless masterpiece? Absolutely not, but there is a fair bit to enjoy, plus the promise this game shows gives me a lot of hope for the developers and their future projects. The story is simultaneously fairly standard fantasy fair, but intersected with sprinkles of originality that had me invested for periods of time. So there are definitely a few things there to enjoy. In terms of basic layout, the story feels like it would be quite at home in a Fire Emblem game, but it still manages to slip in a couple of surprises here and there.The world itself feels simultaneously lived in and fairly sparse at the same time. While the locales and different battlegrounds start to look a bit similar after a while, again there are little nuggets of gold in between, that stand out so much more for it. The characters are a fair few and are either hit or miss. It feels however as if the developers really gave it a shot to give each character a story, hopes, dreams and a personality (mostly) all their own. Some are unfortunately a miss for me, others could have used a little more time in the oven to cook, but a fair few actually managed to pull me into their stories as I interacted with them through the story. Like a traditional Fire Emblem game, you build up ''Rapport'' with different characters by spending time with them, and as your bond grows you gain access to character exclusive support conversations that mostly do a good job fleshing out each one a bit and giving them more dimension, as well as give a bit more insight into the world of Lost Eidolons.Unfortunately, I did catch myself zoning out a few times during these conversations, as they can drag on a bit with meaningless chatter. The characters have fairly distinct looks to tell them apart, but sometimes the animations can feel a bit limited and/or stiff. There is another issue in terms of story and characters that I ran into quite frequently, and I´m not certain whether this is a genuine issue or if I just screwed up somewhere along the way. After you finish about a 1/3 - 1/2 of the game you reach a transition point in the story. All of a sudden characters started to reference concepts, events and objects that seemed to have already happened and/or were happening but I had seen no previous mention of many of those concepts.The titular Eidolons are the worst offenders here, with characters frequently talking about them but with me having absolutely no context, so I ended up having to piece together the basics from just listening to the conversations that were available to me at any given time. I truly hope this was just me being dumb, or mabye I just zonked out during a relevant conversation or missed out on some optional material. The gameplay is very familiar to anyone who´s played a grid based, turn based RPG. So experience with Fire Emblem,XCOM and the like will make you feel right at home. You will spend your time jumping in between your camp (hub world) and various battle maps. There are a few activities to undertake while in camp, such as optional quests and battles, building rapport with different units, and training each units skills and abilities with certain weapons and armor. Any unti can theoretically become any class, but some are clearly better suited for one rather than another. You can also spend time while in camp to have a chat with certain units after each story mission, although as the number of units increases this can become a bit tedious. As a result I ended up only chatting with units that I felt would have something worthwhile to contribute after any given storybeat. Mabye that´s where I went wrong with my earlier problem of lacking information, as it seemed as thought there were a fair few pages missing from the in-game codex by the end.I was personally a huge fan of the variance between each of the different classes, and how none of them feels overpowered or obsolete, so props there. My absolute favorite aspect of combat was that some of the spellcaster classes have the ability to alter the terrain around you to some extent. Different magic elements interact with each other in various ways, that allow for all manner of strategy like calling down a localized rainstorm to soak the field and soldiers as a means of crowd control, damage increase or decrease by utilizing a soaked unit´s vulnerability to lightning spells, or using the same condition to shield your units from fire damage. Dark magic offers all kinds of interesting debuffs and control abilities as well, and when combined with certain elemental magics can lead to some fairly lethal combinations. Light magic falls a bit flat in terms of buffs and amounts that can be healed at a given time, but nowhere near enough to take away from the experience. Class specific combat skills ensure that each class has something unique to offer, and mixing and matching your to discover your favorite formations was quite fun (I personally love variety and adaptability, so I mixed in a little bit of everything). Don´t sleep on a class just because they don´t work out as well as expected from the start. Take some time to level them up and unlock their class abilities and likely your opinion will change as a result.The music does a decent job highlighting the mood at any given time, although no tracks particularly stood out as good or bad to me. The voice acting for what it´s worth is quite nice overall. With only a few stilted and cliched performances overall, the cast does a pretty decent job of bringing each of the many units to life. Although some will most likely stick with you more than others, particularly the ones that stick with you through most of the game, as is to be expected.To summarize, I quite enjoyed my time with Lost Eidolons. While there are a few rough corners here and there that could use some smoothing out, the game as a whole is an entertaining and somewhat engaging experience. I can absolutely recommend any fan of turn based RPGs to give this one a go. Those with little or no experience I imagine could find a few things to enjoy, but I would recommend approaching this one with an open mind, and try not to let the few rough edges sully the overall experience.

_childDocuments_.review: Currently at chapter 8*I don't understand why the reviews are mixed at the moment, but this game has been a great experience so far with some minor hiccups, and the dev team seems interested in expanding the experience with player feedback.Combat is quick and smooth. Animations look great but are a little one note, especially with the physical classes generally having 1 attack, as well as dark magic looking a little samey. I'd say magic is a lot more interesting than the physical classes as well, with magic having an effect on the terrain similar to Divinity Original Sin 2 (wet units will receive more damage from lightning, and freeze when hit by ice). Class customization starts off pretty shallow, but where I'm at I've already reached the 3rd out of 4th tier classes, so you move quickly and each unit really falls into a specific niche (though less distinction between knight/warrior, knights feel less tanky than they should be, this may change with progression). Zone of control is also a great addition here, and map design is looking pretty good. There are some boring open field sections, but the terrain effects add more depth than nothing.Story-wise the game is a standard rebellion against an oppressive empire. However, all characters are interesting in their own way. Voice acting is great with some recognizable voices, though at times they don't exactly match how the character looks (Gabriel comes to mind). The recruitment mechanic is also a neat addition, I'm hoping they expand on that and the rapport system. The main character is also pretty likeable. Eden is known to be a smooth talker, and it really shows in  the dialogue, of which there is....a lot. It doesn't bother me, but I can understand how it can feel slow in the non-combat sections of the game.The negative reviews so far have all mentioned the turn limit, which is honestly a non-issue. Playing on normal and with permadeath on, I haven't come anywhere close enough to worry about losing a battle because of the turn limit. You are also given a generous amount of undo's very early in the game, so a stray crit or bad call isn't going to ruin things. A casual mode also exits if permadeath isn't your thing.This game has been a great addition to the RPG scene, especially with how disappointing the AAA entries have been lately. My biggest criticism has to be how jarring the beginning of the game is. Being thrown in the tutorial (in the future, of course) and then spit right back out to humble beginnings is a little strange and not much is explained. However after the first couple chapters things really get back to a normal pace.

_childDocuments_.review: a lot of effort went into this, which is respectable. but you ultimately just play the same battle 40 times. there are technically different classes, and equipment, and skills, but they are all so minor as to be functionally irrelevant. your units and enemy units maintain strength equally the entire game. which means you can never count on a unit to one shot an enemy, there must always be 2 on 1 to finish an enemy off. this is also true of the enemy, but since they always outnumber you by a significant amount, every battle plays the same. advance cautiously, peel off a few enemies, pounce on them, repeat. it's the same thing every time, doesn't matter if you get new characters or anything. it always plays out the same. pretty boring!

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Skip this conversation?Some good ideas but holy smokes the endless, pointless, vapid dialogue. I thought this would kind of be like Kingdom Under Fire or something, but it isn't really. The writing is cheesier than a Green Bay Packers playoff game, and there's SO MUCH OF IT. If they'd only put more time into the combat & tactics, and less into this pointless gophering around your camp, I'd recommend it. But the battles aren't quite good enough to have to waffle through all the mindless chatter and silly camp fetch quests. Oh another guy lost his book. Great. Since I'm... you know, leading a rebellion, I'll go find it for you.If you want to write THIS much dialogue in a game, hire an actual writer. I could even get around the bad dialogue if there were some interesting characters, but it feels like the cast of a bad soap opera or CW show got trapped in a video game. I've never skipped so many cutscenes in my entire gaming life, and I'm freakin' OLD.The battles are... okay, but could be so much deeper, tactically speaking. Like, it's a grid system but there's no flanking mechanics or attacks of opportunity. Archers can shoot two whole squares. All kinds of spells but so far haven't seen any that target more than a single enemy. Character customization is non-existent, and I think was a huge missed opportunity, especially when the models look pretty. Almost too pretty.Somehow, I'm going to push on and try to finish this, but it's a bit of hot mess. There's half a good game here, but it could have been so much better.

_childDocuments_.review: So I held back on this one for a while after reading some of the negative reviews.From what I've seen at just about 8 hours into the game, they are unfounded. What I would guess is that those people who wrote those reviews were expecting something different from the game than what they got.This game is for folks who enjoy the tactical combat, definitely, because it's fun. Character development in terms of class/skill is akin to something like an XCOM. The combat itself is, at this point, not overwhelming but deep enough to be engaging and keep you on your toes.But at least half of your game time will be spent in camp, managing the camp, and developing the lore and story with the host of characters, soldiers, and workers of the camp. This makes it reminiscent of a game like Valkyria Chronicles, and in a sense during those parts like a much, much better looking and "open world" visual novel.The voice acting is good, imho, but only "quest" interactions are voice acted fully. Just chatting with the various folks in the camp, is done in a typical VN style with some generic sounds, sighs, affirmations etc overlaying the text. But I find learning about all the people in the camp fun, especially given the story being portrayed and the events that thrust everyone together. Plus, random chats occasionally open up new options, or even the opportunity to recruit new folks to your camp.So as for now I can solidly recommend this game to anyone who digs tactical games that are more akin to Valkyria Chronicles than XCOM. If you liked the first or both, you'll like this a lot I think. If you only liked the second, and not the first, this might not be for you. You will spend a lot of time in camp management and building relationships with characters via gifts, chatting, having meals together etc...all of which you have limited chances to do between chapters, meaning you have to choose who gets to spend time with you, and who doesn't.I'm enjoying it though. Really like the story, it seems timely given our current world, and the game looks great, plays well, and is well voice acted and written.Edit: Now about 30 hours in, on chapter 20 of 27, and the original review is still holding up. If you enjoy the "social" part of games like this, talking to people, building relationships, and seeing them develop for better (or worse) this game has a lot of it. One thing I will mention is that at chapter 17, there is a BIG leap in difficulty. You will be forced to manage your troops much more efficiently than in the prior 16 chapters, and experience a battle that is way above those prior. Other than that, the review stands as is. I will add a final bit once I complete the game, but they definitely focused on character/relationship development and creating an atmosphere and lore. There are moments that made me smile, as things occurred that had been talked about for many chapters prior, or just things you learn from picking up and reading correspondence written by characters in the camp to their family or friends back home. The devs definitely paid attention to the little things, it's fun to watch relationships develop in unexpected ways.And of course, there are sad moments, but with seven chapters to go, I'm already starting to wish there were more than that. We will see if the ending can carry the weight of the story before it.

_childDocuments_.review: Starting with the TL:DR, because I know I wall of texted below.  This game is very frustrating because it's very close to being truly excellent, but there are many flaws that keep knee-capping it in that regard.  I feel it does enough right to be worth a look at least, and if the team makes a sequel, I'll definitely get it because the problems here are fixable.  It definitely feels like it's aping Fire Emblem Three Houses in particular, and unfortunately that hinders it to some degree.  I overall recommend it but there are definitely caveats.  Onto the list.Pros:- Map design is pretty good.  The game generally does a good mix of movement-impairing, movement blocking, wet terrain, and so forth so that it creates a lot of natural chokepoints and differentiation.  This combines with the Zone of Control mechanic so that you can tactically position people to protect vulnerable injured members.- The Undo Mechanic.  This is basically Three Houses' divine pulse in that it lets you rewind turns.  This is just a nice mechanic to have since it means that random errors right at the end or surprises don't force an entire map restart.  - To add to the map design point, the game does some pretty decent storytelling with map events.  It's one thing for the story to say that the enemy is a great tactician or what not, it's another for them to set the woods ablaze as a delaying tactic or to set up ambushes.  Generally, the Undo Mechanic allows the game to show that the enemy is competent at doing that kind of thing without overly penalizing the player with surprise moves.- Magic System: Overall I like the magic system.  All the magic types have a purpose, and I'm using all of them, which speaks of good balance there.- It looks good.  Movement and animation is fairly crisp, when combat zooms in it even tracks if you set the nearby woods on fire or something.  - Camp movement is very convenient.  it lets you use the map to teleport precisely to people for whatever purpose, and with minimal loading times in between.  This is the part that it learnt the lessons from Three Houses.  Doing its part to reduce the tedium of running around the camp is important.So-So:- They removed misses entirely, and replaced it with blocking.  I somewhat support this because in FE, this reduces the band of RNG, so it makes it easier to tactically plan (and easier for the devs to precisely design their maps).  However, it kind of makes it so that the only stats that really matter are Str, Def, Mag, Res, HP.  And then the other stats functionally don't matter and end up as white-noise.  - Map restarting: In a map, you can hit restart map and it'll start you off right at the beginning after the point you hit deploy.  Pretty nice.  Except that for some reason, they don't allow you to save in the unit deployment screen, so if you decide you want to change your setup, you have to redo all the changes that you wanted to keep for that map.  This is such a weird mix of a convenient feature followed by a bone-headed inconvenient one, and that kind of mixing is what the game does a lot.  I'll preface the cons by saying I realize that this section is longer than the pros, but there's more to say.  The game does a lot well, but that's why it's easier to be frustrated over what it does wrong.Cons: - I'll start with the camp.  Like Three Houses monastery, it's neat in theory.  However, it also gets repetitive just like Three Houses.  However, due to the above-mentioned convenient movement, it reduces the irritation from 'tediously game killing' to 'kind of annoying'.  - Intro: Simply put the intro sucks.  It hits you in-media res, gives a random flashy no-context cutscene, gives another cutscene of showing the parade where the empire is evil, and then bludgeons you with world-building you don't give a ♥♥♥♥ about because it hasn't given you a point of view to actually care about.  I'll tell you right now that I don't remember a thing about what their world-building said.   - Bug: There's currently a bug where if you finish the map condition with the last person who can move on your team and it triggers a map conversation, the game seems to softlock.  I think it's because it's trying to transfer turn to the enemy and trigger the dialogue at the same time.  If you do trigger this, it's a map restart because the game won't go forward, so consider this a warning.  - Unskippable map conversations: Just... why?  It gets worse if you undo before the action that triggers it because it repeats itself.  The weapon swinging in conversations just looks dumb too.- No short animations: There's either full animations or skip everything.  There's no short animation option where they swing their weapon and it shows the damage number on the combatants.  They already have the stupid weapon swinging in conversations, use those animations.  - Characters are super interchangeable.  The only question is are they physical or are they magical?  The level-ups in theory look like they're random, but they're pretty obviously weighted depending on if the character is slightly behind or slightly ahead of the curve.  You can swap the spellbooks of the two starting mages (and oddly enough this is actually an optimal move to train a 2nd light caster) and they'll function exactly the same as how the other person was fighting.  They learn the exact same spells at the same skill levels.To add to the point of interchangeability, pretty much any two characters will kill a generic opponent, and most of your non-tank designed dudes die in two hits to most of anything.  The numbers can vary from an attack leaving a person close to 50% or almost killing them leaving them at 20%,  But that's kind of set dressing overall.  There's a few exceptions, mainly with boss enemies, or stacking archer damage so that they can one-shot mages.  What's not helping is that class mastery skills vary from 'useless' to 'optimal'.  All physical characters benefit from Flaming Arrows for a 3 range option if they're not going archery as a final class.  All characters like having Swap to have something to do in off-turns where they aren't hitting something.  Same thing with 'Movement' which is basically just Shove.  And then, the rest of the masteries don't matter that much.  Maybe you use the +6 HP.  Sure, whatever.  - Class Tyranny: If a character is a class, they are basically just doing what that class role is.  This is most pronounced in the final set of classes, and in the beginning commoner class.  Commoners can't equip tomes and weapons at the same time, or they're always one or the other before the mage/physical class split that just hard-enforces that.  The final set of classes enforce it by basically only breaking the skill caps of those specific skills, so you're disadvantaged for using other weapons or tomes.  To mix with the character interchangeability, going into the tanky Squire line is the thing that generally allows a unit to survive more than 2 hits, but literally anyone going into those classes do it the same.  - Too many recruited characters.  Basically a person goes to your camp, you do whatever their initial quest is, then you shove presents down their mouth until they'd say yes to join your party.  This already isn't the best start since it's pretty samey.  It also inflates the cast too large for their writing team so that each individual character gets shafted somewhat with lacking development. So this mixes with character interchangeability, where everyone having similar stats and little personality development.- Optional battles: They suck.  Literally copy-pasted fighting underleveled enemies, but the game also mechanically incentivizes you to do them with the prestige quest system.  At least it's fast.

_childDocuments_.review: I must be over 75% of the way through, but am now sufficiently frustrated with Lost Eidolons that I won't finish it.Overall I found Lost Eidolons to be a good, but not great game. Players who enjoy themes like the horror of war, the corruption of power, or the choice between bad and terrible will likely enjoy the story more.Some features I appreciated:+ Fast travel within camp. Being able to open your map and click on a character to move straight to them for conversation was a big time saver.+ Monster battles. Needing to match specific attack types to specific cells in multi-square monsters made for a good mix of interesting moments.+ Boss units. Having to defeat all the minions before the boss would take serious damage added an additional tactical element to these confrontations.But more features I did not appreciate:- Dull strategy moments. For 30+ hours of my play time I've only needed one strategy: agro a single squad of enemies at a time and fight each group of enemies with overwhelming numbers.- Cumbersome character management. When changing equipment, skills, classes - I found no way to select characters from a list. The only option was to scroll through characters using prev/next buttons. This was ok at the start but became bothersome when the order of the 20+ characters kept changing.- Unclear scaling. Choosing power level 2 spells instead of power level 1 spells only does 1 more point of damage. When units have 20-50 health, this difference is irrelevant. I am not sure what attributes did contribute to relevant changes.- Idiot character moments. "We need to post lookouts" "Our allies might abandon us" Next cut scene: We've been ambushed because we didn't post lookouts and also our allies have abandoned us.- Unsatisfying character growth. The only character who clearly changes over the story is the villain. Among your allies - the tactless character continues to be tactless, the ambitious character ambitious, the naive character naive, the worried character worried.- Unexplained end game mechanics. There is a red path and a blue path for your end game choices. You can find these choices in one of the Steam guides. When the first choice arrived I was confused because (1) there are no similar choices in the first 35 hours of the game, and (2) I had no context for the red/blue paths.

_childDocuments_.review: As an avid fan of SRPGs like Fire Emblem and FFT, I would have to say this game is very, very solid. For its price, you get a very big game with a story that is unfortunately a bit of a slow burn- but when it really kicks off, gets very engaging. The Characters are likable while not being as quirky as FE characters tend to be. Now, in terms of gameplay, the easiest way to think about it is an evolution of the general combat of Fire Emblem 3 Houses- Your units are Malleable and unlock classes based on weapon rankings which leads to a lot of replay-ability and lets you try weird builds. There is some Character individualism, but it only, unfortunately, comes in the way of singular passive, unlockable passives/actives through 2 specific final tier classes, and lastly their own ability as a "pair up" for lack of a better word, not really comparable to the pair-ups of FE fates or awakening. I kinda wish there was some other ability that let characters from your original party members shine at around chapter 13, but that might be a little much to ask for. I really like all of the different types of magic, and had used all of them throughout my whole campaign, but kinda wished there might have been to some extent, personalized spellbooks like how it was in Fire Emblem Shadows of Valentia, but obviously, there are way too many characters to have that.Now, I will stop with the multiple comparisons to fire emblem games and talk about the Difficulty. Currently, I am on chapter 20. I'm playing on Hard, Manic, and limited turns. I did this because of all the FE I have played and figured it wouldn't be so bad to get through and boy am I pleasantly surprised. The game isn't super evil, It is quite fun! Now, I would admit that it did take me longer than I would like to admit to understand the zone of control mechanic, but I feel like it is a very welcome fit. The multiple damage reduction effects on bosses initially seem unfair before you understand how to play around them, and then you feel really powerful with how you can bend the game to your will, especially with the 3 x 3 fog that slows your enemies down that the Dark Mages get, it is really fun to use and play around with. Speaking of Dark Mages, I felt like they were a staple on my teams. All of the massive amounts of support they provide along with specialized offense really helped me pull through. Now, here are my actual gripes about the game: Most of these vary from actual issues to nit picks, but here they are.-On the steam deck, it runs REALLY well, but when you are at camp and you move through menus, the lag is unbearable. -On the controller/steam deck, the same button that toggles ranges is an end turn button for a unit when selected- Not a major gripe, I would just like to state it because I used a few too many turn mulligan's to take back a fat-fingered turn end. -Battle Preparations is kinda clunky. The unit selection list would benefit from being a 5 x 3 box of multiple names so that more names can be on the screen as the list gets pretty long in the late game. Whenever you are looking at the map, you cannot select units on the map and swap places around on the map itself, you have to specifically select whichever units you want to reposition, and hit the position option. I honestly would just never set my positioning myself because of this, it was really aggravating -I'm really glad that there is a "danger zone", but I really wish you could highlight certain units, say, a boss, to make it to that their movement and attack range is more specified while showing the others. aka, I kinda wish the danger zone was a Lil bit like Awakenings.-Aggro lines, their inclusion is very, very nice, I just think it would be cool if it showed the damage that unit would do so I wouldn't have to go in the opponent unit menus and look through all of their skills and abilities make sure that placing a unit there isn't a reset.- minor nit-pick -Maps. The map designs are pretty great, especially with all of the elemental integration, but I wish there was a way to pull back and see the whole map, or quickly move through it with your camera.-The camera. Because when you rotate the camera, it bugs the inputs you put in for moving on the map, this is the most minor of nitpicks, I just felt like it was important to the state.I love this game. This is a promising debut for Ocean Drive, and a great 35 bucks spent, buy it. NOW!

_childDocuments_.review: If you enjoyed FE3H you will probably also enjoy this game.The story is very linear though and while the game sometimes pretends like you have choices they dont really matter untill the final bossfight, where you can either pick the red options to make the fight a bit easier but get the bad ending or go with blue to get the good ending. Either way the endings arent that impressive anyways and I wouldnt recommend replaying the game just to get the other ending. Luckily the story itself is pretty good. The 27 chapters each consist of a storybattle, some time to interact with your companions in the camp and one optional battle. The optional battles are pretty generic and sometimes reuse maps, but they never repeat. The storybattles on the other hand all have unique maps and scenarios (straight forward battles, monster fights, ambushing the enemy and getting ambushed, sieges and siegedefenses, running away and chasing the enemy,...). Additionally some of your companions will sometimes go off on solomissions towards the end forcing you to try out some different units (of which you will have enough).I enjoyed getting to know all the different characters and their backstories. There is a core of storycharacters that you get automatically. The rest will typically show up in the camp where they will stay for a chapter or two so you can reach the first supportlevel with them to then recruit them. Some of them will be enemies from the previous map. Every character has one personal passive skill and two more abilities they can unlock by mastering their prefered classes.There is a kind of a weapontriangle, but it gives weaponeffectiveness against armortypes, not other weapons (Swords>Leather, Axes>Plate, Spear/Bow>Cloth). The different classes require certain weapon and armor skilllevels to unlock, but they do not force you to actually use that equipment (Berserker requires Axe and Leather skills, but you can still use swords and platearmor to train up those skills to unlock the Vanguard-Class). The exeption is magic, which can only be used by classes that can equip grimoires. There are classes that can use magic and weapons though and some legendary weapons have elemental attacks.Magic is divided into Dark-,Light- and Elementalmagic. They are all good and usefull, a personal highlight of the game is Elemetalmagic because it interacts with the terrain. Firespells (or arrows) will set the forest on fire and waterspells will put out that fire again or turn the ground into mud. Units in wet terrain will get wet themself and take less firedamage but can get frozen by icespells (or arrows). And so on. Basic stuff that should be in every game of the genre, because it connects the attackanimation to the map and lets the player actively change the environment around them.

_childDocuments_.review: Is this game a masterpiece? No, but it is still a rather good turn-based fantasy RPG with tactical fights (and boring conversations). After the old conquerer king vanquished, brutal soldiers began to rule and terrorize the land in his name. You have to lead a bunch of heroes in a rebellion against the corrupted servants of the emperor.The core game element are the turn-based fights in scripted battles. Seems there is no real grinding, just a fixed number of battles. And they are quite good. The battle interface is one of the best I have seen in a long time, it is easy to move your troops and give them commands. Before the combat, you can select which troops to use. Then you begin the battle. I was a bit surprised they used a square grid and not a hex grid, but it works fine. There is a zone of control that makes it impossible to run through the enemy ranks. Your own troops are not hindered by their friends, which allows you to move a unit from behind a row of your own soldiers "through" them to the front line. The environment is also important, we all know that standing in a water puddle might be dangerous if the enemy knows how to cast an electricity spell... Attacking from behind (backstabbing) is not very effictive. Disengaging from melee is possible without getting backstabbed. There is no overwatch command. Archers do not shoot very far, just two squares, which makes them a bit vulnerable. Different waepons have different effects against different armor. You can move your troops in any order, there is no such thing as "initiative". After you moved your troops, the enemy moves his troops. Executing the turns shows a battle animation (can be turned off) - but it also shows the sourrounding fight going on. Quite cool, I haven't seen such a feature before. The visual presentation is not bad for a turn-based RPG, just a bit dark outside the combat. There are constant conversations during combat, but they are faster and less annoying than during the combat-free parts of the game. You do not have forever to achieve the winning condition in those fights, there is a turn-limit. This limit quite generous, though, you do not have to make the perfect moves at every turn. As long as you stay focused, you will rarely lose a fight because you run out of turns. Units heal between fights, magic mana is fully restored.Between the fights are long, drawn-out conversations (skippable) that tell the (cheesy) story. You will also have to recruit and train your army. It consists of heroes and of various troops, they all have unique skills, spells, and passive abilities. There is a friendship system to improve your relations with other characters, but it is limited (by the available ressources) and you cannot upgrade all your relations (and recruite everyone). This might be a pain for completionists. You run around your camp in 3D, talk with the occupants in multiple-choice.Not everything is perfect, though. The game does not support 21:9 ultrawidescreen, 2560x1440 is the highest resolution. Seriously? Everything is streteched when using a 21:9 screen, and there are things cut off on top and on the side. Yea. Even if you don't have an ultrawidescreen monitor today, chances are good your next one will be one. The font is tiny, completely unreadable. You might be able to read it today, but believe me, after 30 years of playing computer games you will be as blind as I am today thanks to reading such tiny things. At least the conversations are fully voiced so you don't have to read everything. My rig (Ryzen 5600, RTX 1070, 32 GB RAM) begins to sweat loudly after playing a bit... always a sign of great optimization. My PlayStation 4 controller does not work, the XBox One controller works fine, though.Turn-based strategy RPG that still has a few children's diseases.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my favorite genre, and I was really looking forward to this title. But I also understand its a small team indie title, so I kept my expectations in check. I am glad to say, I wasnt dissapointed for the most part although when you see how close this is to being a masterpiece, it can leave you both enjoying it for what it is and frustrated at what it COULD be. Story is fantastic especially after a mid game twist. Its not without its flaws though....PROS1) Amazing story. I went into this thinking it was going to be its low point, but surprisingly  it is very good.2) Music is decent.3) Battle animations are very nice but (see cons)4) Likeable and interesting characters, and a ton of them but.... (See cons)5) VERY capable AI.6) Great voice overs. In fact, you will recognize quite a few of them if you played Fire Emblem, 3 houses....CONS1) Experimenting with classes is kind of off the table, since XP is very limited (one battle per chapter, and sometimes one optional battle). A game like this should have grinding for people to play around with classes and skills. You will find that you may as well just leave them in their starting class and progress with whatever comes in the line, and thats sad because it has potential and is a great system w/carry over skills and some hybrid magic/warrior classes that are ridiculously tedious to unlock, and by the time you DO unlock them it will probably be the end of the game.2) Not much variety in the battle animations. They look good, but its not enough of a good thing. Finishing moves/flashy critical moves would have gone a long way. Gore would have been nice as well (to match the more realistic look of the game).3) The friendship system is a pain. You will have a hard time just getting a couple people up in ranks. And you are limited by both leadership points and gifts which are rare and hard to come by (You mostly get them from the rare goods shop which sells about 5 of them every 3 or 4 chapters) it costs points to give gifts (5) and do activities with them (15) the latter of which raises the rapport about as much as a compatible gift does (which isnt much). So to raise a character 1 rank, you have to do about 5 activities with them or give them about 5 compatible gifts, and there are 3 ranks. When people visit your camp, you have a chapter or two to get them up a rank to recruit them (which means saving all your gives/points for them). I REALLY dont know what they were thinking with this set up tbh. Your leadership points to spend start at around 60 or so....And your probably going to need to spend 15 or more of those for your quests.....And in a game thats around 27-30 chapters long (I think) that just isnt going to put much of a dent in this many characters. Yes, they tell you you wont fill up everyones rapport, but that is a questionable thing to do, as completionists (like me) arent going to like that at all....Whats worse, some characters leave or die mid and late game via story, so any ranks with them are lost. Again, dont know what they were thinking.If they just made "common" gifts unlimited or high in quantity for purchase and removed the leadership cost for gifting, that would probably fix the whole mess. Some characters/secret items/mounts are tied to some rapport with some characters as well, which really adds pain to the mix.Some mount variety other than just plain old horses (Maybe a monster mount or two, and some armored mounts), unlimited optional battles for those who like to grind and customize, and fixing the rapport system (no one wants to replay a game over and over just to see all conversations....Thats not enough of an incentive) would do WONDERS for this game.If they fixed these issues, this game would be on par with fire emblem. Its really a good game, dont get me wrong....But its just shy of greatness.Its worth what they ask for though. And with a few tweaks could well become a classic franchise in its own right.

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to update my review due to the recent patch. One of my problems with the game was the turn limits. Developers acted immediately and soon came up with a satisfactory solution to this problem. Their communication with the community was excellent. Even though they built a lot of mechanics around the turn limits, they understood why players were unhappy with it and made it optional. They are the developers we want to see in the industry; devoted and hardworking.Lost Eidolons is an ambitious game: with its story, characters, voice acting, mechanics and gameplay, it reaches for the sky. However, sadly falls short for the most part. While there is a decent story in the game, I'm not sure it's worth all the time players spend on it. Music is there, but nothing noteworthy. Voice acting is all over the place with its' highs and lows. I enjoyed the combat but getting to it was always a chore.Even though I cannot recommend Lost Eidolons, I am very excited for Ocean Drive Studio's future games.(my old review regarding to turn limits: Combat and story is decent but hard turn limit is a bad game design. I heard developers planning to make the turns longer but they still gonna keep the hard turn limit for some levels which is still a deal breaker for me. _childDocuments_.review: Looks like game of thrones smashed together with dynasty warriors, but the writing feels like an incredibly juvenile and cheesy anime with voice acting to match. The combat is effectively fluid and easy to grasp, but anytime you are not in combat you are drowned in a constant barrage of cinematic dialogue with a nauseatingly shallow script. I'm not even an hour in and I have to take a break because of how dry the story and acting are. Every character is an overly pretentious trope, and I am struggling to care about any of them. The good news is, I got it heavily discounted, and it feels like I got what I paid for. Go for 60% + off.------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------After playing a little longer, I'm still pretty much of the same mind. There's a few companions that have better voice actors and are essentially just bros you don't mind having at your side in war, but boy howdy do I find the main character and all the other companions annoying. The Fire Emblem inspirations are apparent throughout the entire game, which is a good thing, but the game feels kind of shallow because effort and resources were poured into things like graphics that really do nothing in the flat and static way dialogue is handled and dominates the majority of your play time. The time spent on those animations feels like they could have been replaced with character portraits and the resources devoted to polishing other aspects of the game. The story's biggest flaw is that it's too idealistic and grandiose, making it fall apart and collapse into nonsensical plot twists and surprises, and then get hurried along just to propel the story without any real explanations. It seemed like they were so focused on making a giant sweeping epic, that they overlooked the many inexplicable interactions and small plots along the way that developed holes. Marchelle, for instance is an Inquisitor of the Emperor seeking out corruption, and apparently her word is worth so little that she inexplicably has to turn traitor and go on the run. What is the point of having an inquisitor if the governing body isn't even going to trust their testimony? It isn't like she was contradicted by a superior or peer either, but by someone she was there to specifically investigate. This idea is absurd and could have been handled more rationally, but instead the story takes the most extreme possible route to advance the plot because it was quickest and easy. In a complete contrast to this, the main character is lackluster, and completely uncompelling as a leader. His only real strengths are luck and plot armor, and is terribly unremarkable otherwise, but is made essential by happenstance and is only ever a driving force because he just happens to manifest some latent powers out of thin air when the story needs him to. His leadership just amounts to him making overly simplistic statements, and then everyone around him being compelled to side with him because the story demands it. He could have told enemy armies that the sky was blue and it was a lovely day out, and they would probably just throw down their arms and decide to become pacifists. My eyes rolled every time he started to give a speech. Companions such as Robere, Leon, Gilbert, and plenty of others have better dialogue and acting, with more relatable character traits and end up overshadowing Eden. I found myself wishing the story was based on their perspective, rather than Edens, because they were ordinary people thrust into extraordinary situations. This made them look at situations with displays of rational thought that is otherwise absent in the game, and they behave like a normal sensible person would; by slowing down and trying to think or talk problems through instead of just winging it as if the knew they were essential to the story. Ultimately, the game is a good way to burn some time and distract yourself, but I mute it any time the main character speaks and just focus on subtitles. If you're more tolerant of such things, there's plenty of foundation for a good game beneath that.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is currently in the Humble Choice for September 2024, and this is part of my coverage of the bundle. If you are interested in the game and it's before October 1st, 2024, consider picking up the game as part of the current monthly bundle.A Tactical battle game. Lost Eidolons is a tactical RPG. Players will move their units and then allow the enemy to move themselves. With the option for permadeath and more, it reminds me a lot of Fire Emblem or Symphony of War, only without the anime style. There’s a weapon swap system and the armor the opponent wearing matters more than the weapon they are wielding, so for heavy armor you’d want to use an axe. Unfortunately, so far, the game is straightforward. Combine your attack with others to overtake one enemy at a time. Eventually, you start getting magic that will heal your party and I assume there’s a camp system mentioned a few times right around the corner. However, Lost Eidolons also feels a little weak. The game has good lip sync for the characters, but not a ton of animation, so characters feel static while talking. Outside of battle, characters talk in a group but it looks weird seeing only one character speaking at a time, where this could have been a cut scene or just showed four characters talking. I also hope the games are much more tactical. At the current time, it’s pretty easy, but this is a 60-hour game, and I’m just scratching the surface. Finally, there’s a cool feature in the opening battle where it looks like the player is in a large riot, and that hasn’t come around again in the first three chapters. I hope there are more clever tricks like that. Pick this up if you’re a fan of tactical games, especially unit-based ones, and of course Symphony of War, Fire Emblem, and maybe even Wargroove or such. This has a lot of tactical potential, but it also will depend on how aggressive the AI gets or the level design is. Still, it’s a meaty campaign so those who give this a shot will have their fill, whether it’s something they enjoy or if the luster wears off. _childDocuments_.review: is a game base on the Fire Emblem series but with a more grounded style and located in the West that uses clever map design to differentiate missions from one another. From assaulting castles and keeps to pursuing enemies, defending from wild monsters, or dividing your army into two fronts, there is a lot of variety in objectives. The game is also more reserved due to the story's focus on medieval times with magic, and the characters have enough actions to make the gameplay worthwhile while staying true to its setting.The story centers around Eden, the leader of a mercenary gang that, due to circumstances and bad luck, finds himself at odds with his kingdom, The Empire. The nation is a mere shadow of what it used to be, crumbling over with citizen disdain, traitors, and a low workforce, but despite that, it is still a force to fear. The title centers around "Power" and how it can be a great tool at one's disposal, albeit with a heavy price. Characters' dialogue centers on how having power can change a person, justify cruelty, and determine who justice is. It is up to the player to follow Eden and see whether he can remain true to himself in all the chaos.The voice acting is superb, it starts a bit reserved, but the characters will get more pronounced as they develop throughout the story. There are intense moments that give villains and heroes the spotlight, and the diverse cast in terms of units makes for a merry band at camp. It is a shame that not all lines have a voice recording, which is more evident when talking to optional recruits on the base during chapter intervals.Thanks to the intricate map design and the units, the gameplay is enjoyable. While that might sound like a bad thing, it is what allows the title to become more tactical. Your characters are ordinary soldiers, so a few bad decisions will see them perishing on the battlefield. The game divides classes by colors, ranging from Vanguards being blue to physical attackers such as Berserker and Assassins being orange or Archers being green. They have a good amount of variety, but by the end of the game, one can feel a bit lacking in promotions. Dark mages were my favorite by far. Their utility and damage are a force to be acknowledged. They can shape the battlefield by slowing enemies on tiles with dark mist, stealing health from them, or even silencing enemy mages, making it so they cannot cast spells for one turn. Meanwhile, the elemental mage focuses on controlling the terrain and creating interactions, making your enemies wet to electrify them or using chunks of ice to trap them on the spot.Archers are godsent when assaulting keeps, as your forces will have to endure rains of arrows trying to get inside. They can pinpoint targets and take them down, thus making the assault more bearable. In addition, they are a great unit to use to get rid of enemy mages. Melee classes are the less exciting but have a solid defense and can take quite the beating. Assassins are good for diversions, while berserkers are useful for dispatching monsters. Finally, our vanguards can lead the army and make risky choices while feeling safer, and they can even learn a bit of magic, depending on the class! Each unit has a role that is important to determine victory. Remember your healers too!The game's strong points are the story, gameplay, and voice acting. All together creates an exceptional environment that begs you to explore it and see how the tale will develop in the next chapter, mainly because the party finds new trouble to face every time. The map design elevates the gameplay more, featuring missions that don't feel similar and even expand on it, such as a map where you have a spy, and you can try to make the workers revolt against the enemy forces!The title needs to include a bit of polishing, and it is not surprising considering that this is the first time Ocean Drive makes a game of this caliber (it is also their first game, if I am correct), but it is an excellent strong entry! I want to see more of what they can make. Classes could have used a couple more promotions. While it is nice that they try to make everyone viable by having similar overall stats in distribution, fans of the genre love to see those special units go bonkers and distinguish themselves from their peers. Other than Robere, Eden, and Stella, everyone on the roster is similarly strong (Robere being a weak unit and Eden and Stella being strong ones) I played with a controller; it sometimes felt a bit clunky, but it was responsive. The graphics card was RTX 2060 at max settings. I could not get 60 fps on the main camp at max settings, hovering at 45-ish, yet on maps and battles, having locked 60 fps. Some maps run better than others if your machine is not the best tech, but overall a pleasant experience performance-wise. Some topics take a good chunk of length in the storyline, so there might be some burning out near the end. (getting tired from the story dialogue) is a fantastic first entry from Ocean Drive and a title that gets that sweet soft pot between being modern and classic. No crazy units to go bonkers is a bit disappointing, but at the same time, it allows the tactical aspects of the game to shine more easily. The strong story and plot twist have you guessing what will happen next, and the tale's conclusion is satisfying enough to warrant a sequel. If you like strategy games, this a buy. Sorry for the lack of screenshots; writing the review got complicated as I moved out!If you enjoy and find the review helpful, please follow my curator StarsDeck!

_childDocuments_.review: "Fire Emblem-alike but not anime and on Steam" is an interesting proposition for friends with a distaste for anime and for those that don't plan to buy a Nintendo console. Three Houses in particular is a huge inspiration for Lost Eidolons and it shows so much in the gameplay/story.---The Good: (Some) Improvements to FE CombatLost Eidolons improves on FE's magic system, with the magic types playing into their flavor for mechanics. Light Magic here is all about defensive buffing and healing, Dark Magic focuses on crowd control and offensive debuffs, and Elemental Magic focuses on environmental combos. This is some much needed depth compared to FE's typical magic system where magic is functionally identical apart from some slight numbers tweaks and which animation gets played.I found it interesting that Ocean Drive mostly removed the % hit system. Instead of dealing with the frustration of losing units due to misses, if you're in range of an enemy, your attack will always deal damage. The only RNG based rolls are critical hits, which are what you think, or Guards, which act as your "misses" and your attack deals reduced damage (functionally closer to Dodges from XCOM 2). A very interesting innovation for a FE alike game that reduces some of the luck based elements.Lastly, cavalry juggernaught-ing is not a thing. Horses are rare, Canto is practically an endgame skill,1-2 range weapons don't exist, dedicated armored tanks are useful with actual taunting mechanics, archers are no longer bench material due to their long range and reliable chip damage, and enemies keep pace with your units unlike most of the Gameboy FE games. You will need to actually use your units in a team, which is great.---The Neutral: The story/aesthetics. The FE anime heroic fantasy aesthetic is replaced by a low fantasy atmosphere, which is a double edged sword. Everyone is practically dressed and the story takes itself more seriously, but the gloomy mood can get grating due to ludo-narrative dissonance (oh no we're losing the war despite the player winning battles with ease) and the atmospheric music fails to stick in your head unlike FE music.Plotwise, I didn't care for the story, as I didn't care for most of the characters and I tuned out of the plot by Chapter 10 due to how many tired old FE story beats Lost Eidolons uses. Like "overthrow the evil empire as a band of plucky rebels", "headstrong fighter from humble origins becomes a leader in the rebel army and has to deal with prejudice from snooty nobles", or "a betrayal during a pivotal chapter kicks off a timeskip and plunges the world into more war". Mercifully, Lost Eidolons avoids the "evil dragon cult ran by an evil wizard orchestrating the war for reasons" story beat, unlike a majority of FE games.Familiar story beats aside, I do admit that there were a few moments that made me chuckle, like that on generic soldier who writes an unflattering song about Klara or Levana's dialogue about Eden's special destiny possibly being related to being a corpse for someone to trip on.---The Bad: The things Ocean Drive .Ocean Drive didn't learn from 3H's monastery, as the camp segments are as similarly grating and annoying as the monastery. I hated having to stop after every battle to check up on everyone, just in case I missed some quest that would give me some support bonuses (or worst yet when the questline/dialogue yields some rare weapons). There's also the "optional" battles which may as well be mandatory in some cases due to being tied to sidequests, leading to additional fatigue in just getting through the camp sections.Ocean Drive mostly copied the 3H class structure, where anyone can spec into any classe and the role being fixed per-class, rather than the character being fixed to a role. Although the normalized class role approach fixes a FE balance problem of some units failing at their intended role (see: FE10 Aran or Meg failing to be the tanky walls the Dawn Brigade desperately needs), it also creates the new problem of me not feeling anything about the units and then not really caring much about them as characters. I can't distinguish between Karin or Stella or Robin or whoever else gets nudged into the archer line when they all perform practically identical for shooting enemies from long range. As bad as FE gets, I can at least remember units for their quirks, good or bad, like FE6 Gonzales hitting hard but having ridiculously bad accuracy, or Conquest Arthur for being one of the only units in the series where a bad luck stat actually is relevant.A really infuriating aspect of Lost Eidolons is the way they handle some of their best loot and ,  as if the devs wanted to sell you their $30 hardback strategy guide. For example, you can miss out on a special sword intended for Eden in Chapter 17 if you don't deploy Francisco then save your special Venezeus power for the chapter boss. It is entirely possible to miss this if you dislike Francisco's dumb muscle character and benched him or used up your Venezeus power on the earlier enemies. A good portion of these awesome rewards are locked behind certain support levels, which effectively constrains you to only supporting Leon, Robin, Albretch, and Linard rather than trying to get to know other units. And worst of all is that some of these support bonuses aren't really all that good, like Gabriel's extra training slot when most units stick within their recommended roles, or Stella's 20% discount in a game where money is for nothing.Another annoying thing that Ocean Drive didnt learn from 3H was making varied map objectives. The first half of the game may as well only have rout as the objective, since all of your objectives are killing every last one of the enemies or killing the boss. Except that the kill boss maps may as well be rout, since Ocean Drive gave the boss enemies a passive that reduces boss damage by a large amount unless you kill all the small fry first.  The second half of the game is pretty much all defend maps. Even a few of the kill all enemy maps also played like defend maps, since the game expects you to use some of the natural chokepoints on the map to funnel enemies through and the game in general lacking anti-turtling incentives, unlike FE's villages or fleeing thieves with treasure. The lone exceptions were the three (three and a half?) escape maps, since you are now on the clock to advance through enemies instead of just funneling enemies through chokepoints.A very specific annoyance was the  The game either expects you to pre-prepare everything in the camp or only use the same squad for the entire game (which is otherwise impossible due to some of the story beats removing certain characters from the team). Otherwise, if some issue or another pops up and forces you to restart/exit of the game (which was common for me, be it bugs or real life issues), you lose all of your preparations and need to spend more time re-setting up your army. ---Overall, I found the negatives of Lost Eidolons to generally outweigh the positive gameplay overhauls Lost Eidolons has made to the FE formula. With some more polish, I can see Lost Eidolons standing as a worthy alternative or new player's dip into Fire Emblem, though seeing as the game hasn't gotten any updates since 2022, I highly doubt those core issues will be addressed.

_childDocuments_.review: A good Fire Emblem inspired srpg made with love but marred by a few head-scratching design choices and unsatisfying resolutions to some plot elements. Lost Eidolons could have benefited by taking more inspiration from Path of Radiance rather than Three Houses.In my opinion, all of the main characters are well-written and I actually became attached to them throughout the game's runtime. The main character, Eden, was a bit generic as the "do-gooder hero" archetype, though he did start to become more interesting near the end of the story. Sadly, the plot points that start to give his character more depth are kind of just glossed over and forgotten about by the time the credits roll.In theory, the post-battle camp was a good idea that visually showed the player the scale at which things were changing, however, it was poorly executed. Running around camp after every battle became a chore and I would have rather had a menu that allowed me to directly converse with people instead of fast traveling to their location.\I still recommend the game and (mostly) enjoyed my time with it. I hope that Lost Eidolons does well enough financially that Ocean Drive is able to make another game with a larger budget while taking player feedback into consideration.

_childDocuments_.review: Putting this at the top just for clarity, this is NOT a full review so please don't consider it to be that. The only reason I am reviewing this is to provide some counter feedback for the devs and anyone looking to buy this game because when I looked at the reviews, I saw a lot of people either lying about the game or or saying things like the following direct quote.Also, I yet again wish I could put a thumbs middle rather than just up or down, this isn't a horrible game but it definitely has some pretty significant hiccups, so having to choose I lean towards a thumbs down."I played for storywriting. The story in this game and its background lore is so great you can tell this is a very carefully and dearly crafted piece of art!"Spoilers, the story is not a dearly crafted piece of art lolThe pacing alone of the cutscenes is like watching paint dry, which is a damn shame because the characters are animated as they speak (the lip sync is really bad though) and every line is voice acted VERY well. The big shame is that the dialogue just kinda sucks, the story just kinda sucks and it feels like a waste of time. This is where that disclaimer at the top comes in, it is entirely possible that as the game goes on the story gets interesting, but I can tell you from the in media res start that whatever the story was leading to is at the very least confusing. Now the reason that I'm spending so much time on the cutscenes here is because that is most of what this game is. The few level headed reviews I saw seemed to be complaining about the same thing, this game is death by cutscene. There was one cutscene where they legitimately spent 2 minutes going, "Huh, I wonder what we should do?" "No clue, I really wonder what we should do..." between 3 characters. For 2 minutes. That is just a waste of everyone's time. I really hope they either get new writers or the writing team learns to be a bit snappier with the pacing of their story. I think that it would be a bit more bearable if the dialogue in the cutscenes moved faster too but the strength of having animation on the characters also slows down the game because sometimes a line will end and then the character keeps moving for 3 seconds which holds up the next line of dialogue. As far as the combat goes, there was a lot more to it than I thought there was going to be, this really is a pretty good approximation of Fire Emblem style combat. It's not quite the same, and I think the level design is where this one suffers a bit. When you play Fire Emblem there is a level of polish on the difficulty curve that just isn't there in this one (at least it wasn't in the first couple hours). They had an interesting mechanic with how they handled weak spots but I'm not sure how that would play out in the long run. Another note on the combat, the animations for all of the attacks and spells are really nice, and in general the game doesn't look bad considering it being a first time entry from this dev and a relatively small budget.What I'm trying to get at here is that JRPG fans and SRPG fans in general have a much higher tolerance for BS and mediocre quality than most gamers, so I wanted to provide a review from someone who doesn't really have any attachment to the genre. The game is... fine? But its also really slow, and I think that paying 35 bucks is definitely too much on the consumer end, although for the work put in its probably a fair price from the devs. I just don't think there's quite enough polish on this one. Its one of those games where whether or not you end up enjoying it will largely be down to your jank tolerance, and there is a good bit of it in this game. Best bet is to go watch someone actually playing through it so you can see what I'm talking about with the pacing. Check out a stream or youtube video without cuts so you can judge for yourself.I don't normally do reviews with this little playtime but I figure a non biased opinion would help a lot for this one. I have a curator page if you're interested in long form reviews from games I've actually beaten lol. Thanks for reading

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game, with some very obvious flaws.I'm currently at chapter 5 or 6 (I can't remember), but I think I have a decent understanding of what this game is by now. The game can be dividend into three parts:1. The gameplay -- turn based tactical combat, with rpg leveling and unit management.2. visual novel style dialogue3. 3rd person camp management and relationship building.1. I think that the main gameplay, the tactical battles and the rpg mechanics are all very solid and mostly well implemented. The graphics are good, the battles are fun and so far have enough depths, though I'm missing a few skills here and there.Mage units seem a lot more fun overall than the rest of the units though. Mage units have a grimoire, where you can select a combination of spell for that character to use. And there a few types of spells and spells even interact with one another. Make and enemy wet with water making, followed by using ice magic, and you freeze them. Pretty cool, It works really well and is a lot of fun. The rest of the units seem to just get some fairly basic skills though which seem to hardly do anything. I for one would have liked some more relevant skills here and for them to allow me to chain/combine skills, just like they did with the (elemental) mages.Class selection also seems a bit minimal. There is a single starting class from which all advanced classes branche. There isn't really all that much choice to be had though as far as I can see. Because characters seem to have a clear optimal path, with maybe a single additional option if you really want to do something different. No clue what the pay off is going to be here though, since I'm not that far into the game yet. So far it all looks pretty scripted and one dimensional though.2. The dialogue. This one is a big no-no for me. I like visual novels, though the way it's implemented here is really weird and feels really inorganic. Beside a few more cinematic dialogues -- which are okay-ish -- most dialogue is done with a single character in screen. Then that character fades out, after which another fades in and says something. The down time between the fade in and out, makes conversations feel really weird. Especially since there barely is any other environmental sounds. It feels like two soundboards are talking to one another. Start clip 1 -> pause -> start clip 2 -> pause -> ...Just doing the anime visual novel style would have been way better and probably way easier/cheaper to make. 3. than we have the 3rd person walking around in camp. This too feels pretty sub-par. They should have probably just left this out, in favor of management through menus or 2d graphics, and put more time and money into creating more skills and classes or improving the sub-par story and dialogue.Overall, while #2 and #3 are not absolutely horrible and by no means make the game unplayable, they are poorly implemented at best. #1 however manages to save the game. The battles are fun and if you're into turn based tactical games, you should probably give this a go. Don't get this for the story though; you'll regret it.

_childDocuments_.review: Lost Eidolons is a masterpiece of a tactics game. Not because of the astounding, beautiful graphics. Not because of the plethora of classes, skills and builds to choose from. It's also not the amazing and engaging story. Those are all traits that Lost Eidolons have and make the game great, but the most amazing aspect which makes it a work of art is that it's actually hard to play on hard difficulty settings. You'll get people complaining about how challenging the game proves on some chapters (especially 18 and 27) because they feel like they are entitled to succeeding on the hard difficulty setting even though they're not playing out the map right. Hard difficulty is where you need to get out of your comfort zone, and change tactics often, try to work with different classes, in some rare cases make squads out of low level characters that are suitable for the mission, and not the characters you like the most. And surprisingly it works, even with low level characters with the right class. So ignore people who claim that it's impossible to win this game on hard. I've done it on hard with maniac mode on and I assure you it is possible and very fun.Pros:- gorgeous graphics- voicing is next level- character design is amazing- dozens of different characters with their own stories- the game is extremely long, has 27 main chapters, camp activities with side quests inbetween them and optional battles- difficulty settings are suited well for people who don't know how to play tactic games well (lowest difficulty is super easy) as well as have an actually hard to play hard difficulty where it's up to the player to use strategy and tactics against the foe which has major damage bonuses- different endings- option to revert moves (limited number per battle)Cons: - some conditions for missable side quests and objectives are vague when it comes for requirements on even starting the quest and then there's also stuff like the game telling you to test Eden's power but then it turns out that he was supposed to wait and use it on the final creature that shows up after the regular ones are beatenI highly recommend this game. I didn't expect such an amazing story and characters and it's extremely fun to play.

There are also some non-voiced moments where the animation still goes as if their talking, which is kinda like why bother?It's a diamond in the rough, and I really wish the developers would come back to polish it up

_childDocuments_.review: I would give this game a solid 6.5 out of 10. It was clearly created by fans of the more recent Fire Emblem games and they took a lot of the mechanics/gameplay from Three Houses and incorporated them here. Off the top of my head, here are some similarities:- the combat takes place on grid map. Similar turn-based combat as Fire Emblem.- FE has sword/axe/lance matchups to get advantages; Lost Eidolons does something similar with weapon/armor types. - This game has a large cast of characters that you have to form relationships with. - Like 3H, you have to raise a character's opinion of you to recruit them. - In 3H, you ran around the school, picking up gifts, talking to the cast, and doing side quests after each mission. In Lost Eidolons, you run around your camp, picking up gifts/books, talking to the cast, and doing side quests after each mission.There are other similarities that would spoil some things, but, just know, that you are getting a slightly more adult version of Fire Emblem 3H. This includes all of the grueling, tedious tasks/cutscenes that you are required to get through in order to actually play the game.However, I would be remiss if I didn't point out that this game is a downgrade overall compared to Three Houses. The combat is fun, but not remarkable. The characters, though, fall flat. They are all one dimensional caricatures of a common trope. The story is decent, yet predictable. They introduce some mechanics late in the game that influence which ending you get, but they literally show you what the best options are so you can't really go in blind. There are also 2 chapters in this game where the combat difficulty increases tremendously out of nowhere. Overall, I would still recommend this game if you are a fan of turn-based combat games, like me. I thought it was a solid effort, and I look forward to what the developers come up with next when they iron out a lot of the issues. This game is probably worth $20-$25. I'm not sure I would pay full price for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Like others, i want to give this a fair shake from a lot of the "turn limit" negative review this has been getting lately. I may add a story and progression review when i complete the game, but feel it needs praise for what i have experienced so far. (See add on below)I am by no means a hardcore gamer myself, but i enjoy a challenge. On the normal difficulty with "maniac" selected, I have yet to come close to the turn limit (current chapter 6 or 7).The turn limits only stop you from dawdling. This promotes using each unit on the field efficiently as well as keeping the pace. The game even rewards you for finishing the levels quickly with more experience for your units. Can confirm the turn limit did not become an issue during my play-through. The only times I found it "unnecessary" was a mission where you had to survive a limited number of turns, as well as one where you had to escape in a limited number of turns. The reason it was unnecessary was because the turn limits i believe were longer than the designated timers.So far I have many good things to say regarding the combat system. Like fire emblem it is easy to pick up but still has it's own unique feel by adding equip-able armour types. Unit movement feels balanced, and I very much enjoy the "area of influence" mechanic allowing you to spread front line units out a bit to truly surround opponents when used properly. (This is all still true my only complaint is that the game only gives you a total of 4 horses to improve movement)I do have a few criticisms of course, but I do not feel these take away from the game enough for it to be considered poor. these may be simple oversights or issues due to limits during development.-Pre-combat phase (preparation in fire emblem) should have a save button. Being able to only autosave and manual while at camp is a bit frustrating. Being able to save your unit positions and adjustments means you can prep the next battle for the start of your next gaming session.-Conversation sections with 3D avatars are fine, but having the avatars phase in and out with each line of dialogue is pace breaking in the conversations. There may not be enough room on the frame for everyone In sections with many characters, but only phasing characters around as it requires is preferable to what we currently have, Using a highlighting system and keeping active conversation participants on screen would be preferable.-Small thing but the first few camps feel too dark. I understand they are at night and I can just turn up brightness, but every other seen has been fine without adjustment. (Patched)-Camera during certain cut-scenes is tethered to focal characters. This looks a bit jarring and less cinematic than it should, again likely a development limitation Not to big of a deal.TLDR:-Good balance so far very much like Fire Emblem-Don't believe the turn limit hate, you have enough time-Small issues with conversation pacing and times you can manual save.Additional notes from after completion ****(Spoilers Ahead)****The story felt very well put together with multiple forks that influence your endings, i was quite happy with the one I got. The adjustment of who is friend and foe as the war plays on is not the most unique plot, but it was still very engaging. Starting the game with a sub-level mid story, did give away some major plot developments, but it didn't stop me from humanising an ally even knowing they would become the villain. The turning point for friend to foe is for very real, if a bit unfounded reasons. Some early plot points felt predictable in the first half, especially with NPCs without plot armour.Be warned because this blindsided me, you get "Aerith Gainsboroughed" in this game .... TWICE. (If not more depending on choices). Your rag tag group of freedom fighters feel tough but well rounded. All in all very liable with actual character progression. Losing characters you get early hit me in both emotions and unit development. I had spent time and resources making my main party what it was, then they rip out a core player at one of the worst times possible. So here is the hard lesson, not everyone comes home from war. This conflict felt grounded, even in a fantasy setting. People fighting not for kings or honer really, just for the people they want to protect from the horrors of war at your doorstep.My biggest complaints about the plot are 2 specific points. The first one was required for the story to play out, but it still felt a little forced even for the reasons given. The Second felt like cop outs and keep certain characters around.-The villain, once turned could not be reasoned with. They came to a conclusion and refused to reassess it even when allies from their own camp counselled against some aggression. They turned into something worse than the thing they swore to take down and blamed the world so their actions could be justified. Yes I know tyrants exist, even ones surrounded by good people. Those people need to try harder or stop following a lost cause.-Villains allies (even when alone) have plot armour. The amount of times you defeat the same enemy generals gets annoying fast, especially when you actually want to see some of them dead for their arrogance. These ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ have to be defeated so many times it doesn't feel fare. I lose a unit forever if i make one misplayed step, (undos not withstanding) but these guys show up behind enemy lines, get cornered in cities or just out in open battle fields. Then just walk away like they are going home to cry to their dad about those bully rebels. With the villain we had, I really doubt they would accept failure and should have killed them for retreating in the first place.Final Words:For an indie game, and especially at its price point. This game is an absolute Gem. I remember being interested when first glimpses of this project appeared to me, and I can safely say Ocean Drive Studio rose above and beyond the call of duty with this project. All the best and good luck on your next one.. (Thank you for coming to my Ted Talk)
