_childDocuments_.review: Basic premise/StoryIn the world of Strategy RPGs(SRPG) we need more games akin to Fire Emblem(FE) and Final Fantasy Tactics(FFT). This year we had Square Enix’s Triangle Strategy and in the summer another indie RPG called Symphony of War. Just last year we had another Dark Deity. And now thanks to Kickstarter backers we have another indie RPG. Much as the games before created a new spin on the FE/FFT formula. Lost Eidolon's also has something share. And boy oh boy does it pack a mean sword to the throat. However, just because we have a new SRPG the question remains. Is it good? And most importantly worthy of your time? Well, let’s see. Unique GameplayFirst, let me be clear I love FE games and FFT. But I'm certainly no expert in either of these games. Lost Eidolons(LE) shares many traits as the games mentioned above and has new tricks up its sleeves as well. One of these examples is how integrated the camp is. You won’t see it early on. After several chapters, it’ll show up. I spent a lot of time talking with my companions and visitors that would pop up in camp. Initially, I was a bit skeptical of the camp system. But after continuously talking to everyone in camp after a main chapter battle, it became an enjoyable routine to do. I’ve even taken the liberty of buying gifts and gifting them to my companions in the hopes of building more rapport with them. One main feature I adore in the game is Rapports. Basically supports from FE games. Build enough rapport with a character and you can recruit new units from visitors. Unlock new conversation topic. Net you items such as rare items/legendary weapons/useful potions or other features like new training slots and even a horse. As someone who likes to peruse through a lot of support conversations, I took my sweet time seeing as many rapport conversations as I can. There are also different tiers to keep in mind. Going from Peers, Acquaintances, Close Ally, and Trusted Friends. Everyone starts at Peer. But rapport can also build from key story/sidequest conversations. So it's not solely on gifts to build rapport. Conversations feel realistic and immersive, especially after the main chapter battles. Providing an excellent breather so to speak to converse with my allies at camp on what went wrong and what went right. Countless times I wish we had a post-battle summary and my units reflected that each time here  which I love. As well as providing additional context and new elements.  This isn’t the only way to recruit allies. Sometimes they’ll ask to join or after completing a sidequest. Speaking of side quests there are a bunch of them and worth doing to build rapport with each character. Along with cool useful rewards. I want to say I did more than 95% of them since some side quests are locked behind the 2nd/3rd tier of a character. And I couldn’t get 100% rapport with everyone. It’s not possible. So I only did as much as I possibly could. Love how every class is unisex. So I could outfit one of my units as either class. In Fire Emblem Three Houses there were certain classes you could not change into because they are locked into gender-specific roles. Here we don’t have that problem. Useful since you have a large assortment of characters to choose from and mix-match. Aside from the praise, let's go straight into the critique.Optional battles could use an overhaul. They reuse the same map and enemies again and again. There is no differentiation, no randomized generation of troops, and no selection of different maps. It’s always the same. Some side quests do use optional battles. But these are very very few and about an allied units rapport tier in the 2nd/3rd tier. So those are worth doing. But if you’re doing optional battles for the sake of doing it. Don’t waste your time. Thankfully the devs are going to work on it. So look out for an upcoming patch. Perhaps add in grindable procedural generation maps to allow grinding for players if they want? I didn’t need to grind, but the option would be welcome.Papers on the ground/on top of barrels or desks need better visibility. The small light-emitting on top papers are hard to see in the daytime. Perhaps a small radius on the minimap to detect where they are to see new lore and unlock new dialogue with your character’s units it relates to. I had a bunch of missing pages in the codex since It’s a chore to run everywhere in camp looking at every nook and cranny each time. Despite the fact, I could fast travel to anyone. Just a small suggestion.The game could’ve used elevation more to make use of hills. Or adding side objectives(this might be a bit of work, to be honest). Granted there are moments when you can go atop wooden/castle ramparts to snipe at enemies. However, these moments are few. I feel the inclusion of hills and more elevated areas would spice up the gameplay on maps. Didn’t have a problem with the maps in general since a lot of them were fun to do. Final thoughts/RuminationsI’ll be frank, my first couple of hours with the game didn’t impress me a whole bunch. I wanted to see the camp immediately. I wasn’t interested in the main character(Eden) and the company he keeps, especially since they were one-note characters. But after I got to the camp and had a little bit more battles under my belt and started to see more rapport conversations I turned an immediate 180 on everything. The soundtrack started becoming more epic with instruments conveying emotion and a cool tempo during intense clashes with the enemy. Along with tranquil tracks that soothe the soul during breaks. Voice actors are also pretty good with some notable voice actors from Fire Emblem: Three Houses here. Playing major roles too. Loved the cutscenes in the game since there are so many. And shows how much care the developers put in. I didn’t expect it at all considering it was an indie game. But I was pleasantly surprised since the animations reminded me of the first Witcher game. A plus in my book. In the end, what ultimately sold me is how the game’s story in battles and sequences started to affect my characters a great deal. Resulting in each of them getting strong character development throughout the game. From the beginning, middle, and until the end credits rolled. I was impressed by how far Eden develops in the story and his companions alongside him. Even the allies you recruit receive similar treatment of development and strong rapport conversations. There are multiple badass female characters with strong development too and I'm glad it’s not just Eden who gets the spotlight all the time. His companions all receive varying degrees to shine and the game reflects that not just in cutscenes. But through dialogue and in battles as well. It’s a worthwhile journey to see what Eden and his mercenary company have gone through in the low fantasy, civil war-torn nation of Benerio. There are plenty of shocking turns and twists I didn’t expect. But for most of the game, my suspension of disbelief was held at bay. A remarkable achievement where other games can send you off to unknown parts of unrealism and disaster. Lost Eidolon’s goes bold with its ambitions and sticks the landing to convey a realistic and mature story I haven’t seen since Final Fantasy Tactics and Fire Emblem, particularly the Tellius games. A realistic story matched by a strong likable cast. Lost Eidolon is a must-play for those looking for a quality SRPG. And only priced at $35. An absolute steal. For what you get. Honestly, I think the game could’ve sold for $60. And I would be 100% fine with it. Score: 8.5/10Total Times Beaten: 1(Normal/Casual)

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome game made by a great team. Hard difficulty feels perfectly balanced. Unlike other Fire Emblem-alikes, Lost Eidolons has modern quality of life improvements such as rewind and enemy targeting indicators. Gameplay and animation feel smooth but impactful.Only things I would improve would be music and facial animation. Battles can be eerily quiet besides sound effects. The character models are extremely detailed, but their eyes and mouths don't seem to move much. It would be better to reduce model fidelity or increase animation detail.

_childDocuments_.review: I hate to leave a negative review. I have no choice, because I've lost the will to play the game so early.This is not a bad game, but there are a lot of really bad things woven into this game that unfortunately make the good elements really difficult to enjoy. I am still going to watch this studio because if they can get away from some of the garbage below I think they have the potential to make a really great game.The story for this game starts out pretty uninspired and very rapidly becomes a hot mess. The characters in the game are all very one-dimensional and spend an obscene amount of time talking about absolutely nothing related to the plot. They are trying to build in-depth relationships, but the characters are so deeply unrelatable that by a few chapters in I am slamming my escape button to skip the dialogue and move on. I finally just stopped playing the game because I lost all interest in the story and characters. This is separate because it must be mentioned that the way that the aforementioned story is told is through a really disjointed conversation system with characters fading in and out of the dialogue. Every time a character fades in to say something, you have to wait a few seconds. The conversations have clumsy stops and starts that damages the pacing in a pretty significant way.I almost fell out of my chair when one of the first quests I was given in this game was to do a 3rd person free roam around a camp looking for a lost book. I was insulted the first time they asked me to do it, and so far I've been asked to do it twice more before the end of Chapter 8. This is a completely unbelievable waste of time and should be criminal for existing as a gameplay loop in a game like this.Furthermore, other quests send you on insensible adventures to talk to multiple people throughout the camp. The conversations are essentially, "Oh, that's a great question, you should go talk to Robere about that." Why add tedium to an already tedious idea and force me to move from character to character? Ultimately - the game has built in time wasters that pull you away from the gameplay loop to waste your time constantly and it shouldn't be encouraged.Nit-picky - but if this game would just flip from a square grid to a hex grid the combat would be much more interesting. I hope that doesn't need an explanation, we should all be enlightened enough to know that Hexagons are the only way to tile games now.The combat is above average. It is not innovative enough to pull the rest of the game with it though. I would genuinely like to play more with the class system and the combat options that are available here - they would be enjoyable to play with, but I finally decided that it was not worth smashing my escape key for 10 minutes to move through dialogue sequences that are beginning to give me physical pain.Take some story-telling cues from games that have mastered pacing in their story-telling. Take a look at how Hades introduces rich story-telling in between its gameplay loops and you'll see a game that understands pacing and respects the player's time. Even in that system, it has optional written information a player can read through at their own pacing if they want to enrich themselves further. There are countless other examples even from this genre that do their story-telling in a variety of ways, but in most cases they slowly feed the player story-telling and don't drown them in it constantly.Do not insult the player with monotonous garbage like fetch quests.Don't lock unit recruitment and player bonds under a wall of optional mundane dialogue and character back-story that is burdensome to keep up with. If you want to build scarcity around your recruitment options, put a price-tag on the recruits, give us a budget, and allow us to quickly make our decisions and move on. I shouldn't have to court recruitment options 4 times between missions to work through their personal issues of whether or not I am pretentious enough for them - slowly building up some arbitrary relationship meter.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is my favorite tactical RPG of 2022. Lost Eidolons offers a nice mix of story, combat, loot and general amount of content.You play as a head of small mercenary company, slowly moving up in the world, recruiting new heroes in your band, meeting new friends and enemies, and ofc doing a lot of battles along the way.Between the battles you can rest in your war camp, do some minor side-quests, build rapport with your heroes, buy/sell equipment and do some training. Each chapter features 1 story battle (total of 27 chapters), some side-quests, 1 optional battle (not right from the ch.1, its unlocked a little further into the game).PROS:+ very good main story tactical battlesEvery map is different, enemies provide enough challenge to be interesting, AI is not retarded (or at least not as stupid as in similar tactical RPGs)+ surprisingly pleasant story While the plot is ofc not on Games of Thrones level (and has a lot of typical tropes), it still manages to be interesting enough. The characters in general (with a few exceptions) are feeling alive, not some cardboard placeholders with boring dialogs. They have coherent motivations for their actions and most of them are grown up, mature ppl – big plus for players like me, who are tired of edgy teenagers world-saviors you encounter in most modern games.!BE AWARE! That the game has A LOT of cutscenes and dialogs (all skippable). For me it was a good thing, because it helps you to actually care about the heroes, their troubles and struggles.+ a big variety of viable combat strategies, decent level of troops customizationYou have a big variety of classes to train your troops, mix them and make your own combos of units. Every playable hero has customizable gear, abilities and some unique traits/skills.+ nice difficulty curveIve played the game on hard with permadeath, and it was difficult enough to be challenging, but not overwhelming.+ English voice acting is 10/10All main story dialogs/events are fully voice acted and some of the side quests as well, but a sizable chunk of additional content isn’t (side quests, rapport dialogs).CONS- optional battles are not goodThey reuse only 3 different maps and become old very fast. The rewards are generally not inspiring as well, with a few rare exceptions (quest-related).- rapport rewards are not very balancedIn the game you have a limited resources to build up rapport with allies, where higher tiers of rapport give some rewards. However some characters absolutely outclass everybody else (unique items rewards) and by comparison characters with lower-tier rewards are feeling like a waste.TL;DRA musthave game if you like tactical RPGs. While it ultimately doesn’t add much novelty in terms of game mechanics, Lost Eidolons is certainly a pleasant story you will not regret participating in. It has some replay value as well.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll give it up a thumbs up, but just barely. Most everything is mediocre. All the positives I could find were all balanced out by negatives. There are too many decisions that were made that left me wondering if anyone there has ever played a turn-based strategy/RPG or if they were just "making" a game. I feel like the game starts off heading in the right direction and then somewhere takes a turn for the worse. Value wise, price is just barely acceptable for the play time.It is a game not a show. Needs to be more game and less filler. There is less actual game time than "other" content.The game is repetitively linear. Really took a lot of enjoyment out of the game.Story is a gritty and grim take on war and human nature.Choices and RPG wise, 3 main decisions each for 3 different end game scenarios/accomplishments. That's it.There are a few random pop up monster that were enjoyable. The optional battles are awful. Same 2 battles over and over and over.The main battles are about 50/50.  Visually the game looks very nice and runs smooth at 4k ultra - minus some shimmering in spots.Fully voiced cut scenes are good. The rest of the random sayings and "noises" need removed.The music was wonderful. Timed and toned well to the story. I didn't stream anything in the background the entire time I played.Fast travel in camp, loading and saving is superb - if you are using a NVME.Controller for this game is nice and smooth. Keyboard and mouse is jarring while panning.Only 1 freeze/crash the entire play through. By today's standards that's excellent.Overall if this is a first attempt I'll give it a meh. If you like the genre worth a try, if not save your money.
_childDocuments_.name: Lost Eidolons

_childDocuments_.review: The tactical combat was decent, basically your paint-by-numbers rock/paper/scissors with a few skills and spells thrown in to break the monotony. It throws you right into the action with a flash forward, then returns to your humble beginnings for the game start (not a spoiler, this is literally the first five minutes of the game).Honestly though, the writing really turned me off. I'm fine with standard fantasy tropes (chosen one hero, bruiser brother, kid archer, sassy female fighter, etc), but the cut scenes were not only painfully written, but PRODIGIOUSLY long. Like I would skip through a cut scene only to have another cut scene, followed by (you guessed it) ANOTHER cut scene. I'm fine with this sort of thing if the writing is novel or interesting, but if we're just talking about a rehash of standard tropes (evil duke, ailing emperor, plucky rebels) without problematizing any vanilla fantasy elements...yeah, I'm out.The animation is polished, if a bit clunky. Like I'm not sure why they felt the need to close up on characters or focus on cutscenes when the characters' lips don't really match the dialogue. It's a Korean/American studio, so maybe the vocal animations match the Hangul words? Not sure, but it was distracting.This isn't to say I hated this game, it was...fine. But if I'm going to choose this over more tightly-plotted, character driven RPGs, you're either gonna have to give me better writing or ease up on the cut scenes.
_childDocuments_.name: Lost Eidolons

_childDocuments_.review: As a long time Fire emblem fan this game is right up my alley. It takes heavy inspiration from Fire Emblem Three Houses one of my favourite games.The combat is fun and challenging but not super hard as of yet (played through 5 chapter on hard Difficulty)The characters seem a little bland in the beginning but it gets better once you get to know them.Almost everything is voice acted and its good!The mechanics are easy to understand once you take a closer look at skills and stats its not hard to anticipate how much damage you will deal and take.I really wanna keep playing but have to go to sleep...I can already say I'd highly recommend this game to anyone who likes tactics games and micromanaging an army.Props to the devs!
_childDocuments_.name: Lost Eidolons

_childDocuments_.review: It's honestly a very visually appealing turn-based game, graphics and art wise. Cinematic cut scenes, while get repetitive over time makes it different from other games. However, the story was really rushed - I didn't really get what it was about due to the lack of detail. Dialogue was also all over the place. I'll still make efforts to finish it but yeah, nothing to rave about.If you're simply here for turn-based combat this game is great. If you're here for story, character development, choices matter consequences - then no. This game had so much potential to do so but is wasted. For example, we have way too many party companions which means none of them have a proper backstory, personality or special contribution to the game. I ended up making them all 'aides' to other characters during battles.Each companion has a friendship system but I didn't know what the point of it was considering the game is linear. Everyone is on the same storyline.That being said, I love their fast travel system within camp to talk to all your NPCs - so no need for mindless running around to find people and same goes for their quest tracking/map.
_childDocuments_.name: Lost Eidolons

_childDocuments_.review: This game was a blast to play, really itched the fire emblem vibes. The gameplay was fun, the difficulty was good and the characters were interesting. While I did enjoy it (Hard and Maniac), the two main things that I was not a fan of was the "boss" mechanic and characters leaving your playable party for story reasons. I get wanting to do it for story but it really sucks when one of your best units is not useable for a few chapters but luckily the aide system does help with this. Overall though this game is a solid 9/10 for me and can't wait for future updates!

_childDocuments_.review: In general it is a good entertaining game. Pros:fast travel to everyone in camp - only limited hunt and seek.The ability to roll back turns a limited number of times in battle - first time I used it was because I accidentally fire balled one of my own people.Graphics are good - but for play-ability turn off the  combat graphics - ok the first couple of times but really slows down combat.Voice acting I thought was good.Cons:story a little week I thought.Would like to have more control over the character development on leveling uplast couple of battles were tough - especially if you have not been power leveling your troops.After you get the ability for aides - make sure your healers and elemental mages have spells with lots of use numbers and then just cast them every turn you can - they level up fast and so do the aides.

_childDocuments_.review: Strategy puzzles with a story. Came for the strategy, stayed for the story. Clever re-do system removes much of the frustration of this kind of puzzler, and there are easy ways to skip the story if you need to. Pleasantly good looking animations give some drama to combat, but when they become repetitive they can be skipped too. Try it, it's customizable in the way you can go through everything, and there is a bit of build depth in the latter part of the game by the looks of it.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game in the fire emblem/tactics playstyle. _childDocuments_.review: The art, music, animations are good. However, everything else feels basic.The combat tactic is basic. What kind of military leader keep getting surrounded by bandits? Yeah. In the end, you are just bunch of bullies who go through enemies because your army quality is way higher. The game only reward players who rush the combat, and the only way to rush it is to one shot basic every enemies with a crit after a weapon swap. Movement doesn't matter, encirclement doesn't matter, flanking doesn't matter, What matters then? Friendship??The resource management is basic. What are those gifts for, if not a hinder to storytelling? How often do you use potions? I bet never? Training is limited once a battle? Gross.The game start extremely slow, and the first 10 hours are just chores and tutorials.The story only has a general good direction of development. The narrative details made no sense. For example, everyone's conversation is just plainly outright rude. What the heck is "Sera told me to tell you that so you felt guilty". I'm not sure if it is something lost in the translation, but I quickly lost interests to most of the characters who just want you to ♥♥♥♥ off. Another point, in cut scenes, the whole voice casting direction doesn't match the narrative. The emotion and energy of wrath in the voice feel off most of time. They are often filled with arrogate anger and uncalled frustrations.The plot twisting also made no sense. High command made one mistake and got killed off by the plot. Yet, somehow the army with no leadership was not falling apart thanks to ...huh.... plot? I just want to get it over with half way through.You know what? If delicately balanced it might be a classic in the 1990. However, these arts cost way more than the thoughts in the work. I feel the execution of this product is a result of a lot of nit picking from people who lacked the view of the whole picture. You can see that from an artistical UI that does really basic management function.

_childDocuments_.review: Turn based based games are one of my favorite genre's. LE has great graphics in all areas of the game. The combat system is also very easy to understand. However, right out of the gate you are subjugated to a story line that presented several issues for me. At first is was so slow I almost quit. I understand setting the stage, but there was just to much up front. The writing also has its ups and down. Sometimes I was immersed, but more often that not the dialog seemed like an awkward conversation between to teenagers. So much unsaid or worded poorly. to many of the conversations also added little to the story or your understanding of the characters.The next issue for me was the Character development. We are allowed to see the path from commoner to whichever level is next. There is however no real instruction given for how to obtain it. The could have easily been a part of the story line, a part of our instruction. After all were just a bunch of lowly mercenaries who need instruction aren't we. To complicate the problem we start enlarging our retinue, only what are we to do with these new members? Oh yes make them advisors or some such thing to our other players during battles. Of course we've received no instruction as to how that will benefit either of our crew. Despite all that I found myself still enjoying the game and the story enough to continue playing. That is until the dynamics of the battles changed so significantly that moving forward just doesn't seem worth the trouble. I've read a number of other players thoughts and lessons from the game, and yes it sounds like they figured a number of important lessons out, that kept them prepared to finish the game. As for me when a game lets a player wander down a path that leads to mediocracy and expects your A team to show up to win. Well that's a big lose. I don't mind a hard battle for making a few mistakes along the way, but having to go back and start over to get there. Well that just isn't going to happen. Lastly and maybe the games biggest flaw is that there's no reason to replay the game. Each time you play your going to get the same story, the same characters and the same exact battles. The DEVs need to take a lesson from a number of other very successful games in this genre on their next venture give us a game we want to play over and over. That's what makes us look forward to the next installment or their next game.

_childDocuments_.review: Came for the tactical battles, stayed for the story and the characters.That being said, I enjoyed the battles - they weren't overly complicated, not too hard, not too easy and yep, I sat through the cast/fight animations every time. Love how the soldier cheers when you heal someone and the spell animations, hahaI would've wished for more battles against monsters, I liked how they worked and monsters are always cool.That being said, the optional battles were... a pain to do. Because there are basically just three of them. And seriously, always the same composition, the same way they are standing, the same map etc pp.The first 70 minutes of the game were very confusing to me. I had no option to pause the dialogues, I had no clue what was going on, I didn't know if progress would be saved in battles and basically just jumped from cut scene to battle to cut scene to battle, being confused as hell until I FINALLY was standing in the camp and could move on my own and press Esc and SAVE. (it has been addressed and should be fixed now though.)The armour and character designs over all are absolutely awesome, which is why I bought the Artbook, something I usually don't do. However the female characters really got the short end of the stick here. Except for a very few, they all look the same. Like a bunch of twin sisters with different hair styles. And all of them are like 20. Where are the older ladies? Why does the game gives us a wide range of male characters but such an absolutely boring and bland bunch of females? There are a few interesting side female characters that have a bit of a more different and interesting design, but even those are all just 20-somethings. Are only young, slim girls fighting in the war? A similar problem I found in the way they were written: most of them are obnoxious b-words, specially among the main characters. Only one female main character was, imo, likeable. (on this side: the romances are so light, why only offer one male romance but 5 female options? Would one more male really hurt so much?) BIG shout out to the Voice Actors. They all did an amazing job. With the lack of facial animations, it was them who had to deliver the story and boy they did. They really did.Overall:one can see that it's an AA game, but it's an AA game with lots of love being put into. And the devs really listen to feedback of the community which is amazing btw and you can see that in the way they implemented NG+

_childDocuments_.review: If you’re a fan of tactical RPGs but not crazy about the stylings of Japanese games then this is one to check out.  It has its flaws but for 30$, it’s a solid game worth the money. On harder difficulties, this game is very puzzlely. Combined with the camp elements this game feels a lot like Marvel Midnight Suns crossed with Gladius from the PS2. The story is solid but it’s a massive slog to get through. Every cutscene is way too long and could have really benefited from another round of edits and refinement. Even though I want to enjoy the story, find myself skipping through large portions just to get to the point. Just like in MMS the camp is very cool, but can be a bit repetitive at times, and there is no way to skip through the fluff tasks and jump to the next mission. Overall it’s a good game that would have really benefited from further refinement. The bones of this game are so good that I look forward to the sequel, where they will hopefully iron out some of the slow parts of the game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a fun turn based game, and unique because it combines third-person gameplay in between battles. As with all the based games, however, the battles can very long and tedious. The turn-based mechanics are good, but not as good as they could be, and there was a glitch that prevented me from finishing an achievement that really irked me. That said, the ability to develope relationships with your fellow party members is fun, and the limits on gift-giving makes every interaction matter. They also offer a "New Game+" mode after your playthrough, but I haven't gone back to it yet (getting through 27 chapters was exhausting!).

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't impressed with this at all.  Feels like they put a lot of time into the cutscenes and combat animation cutscenes but not into making the combat fun and interesting.  The overall gameplay and controls scream "mobile game" quite loudly.The combat animations are just miniature cutscenes and seem to include a bunch of people fighting in the background of the scene that aren't there when you're in between combat animations, this is a turn based game and they just... disappear after the combat animations play.  It's jarring and unwelcome.You can shut these off, and I did because they're annoying and only slow down the game (you can also speed them up but then the look silly), but then characters just kind of move toward each other when they attack and... well, that's about it.  A few numbers fly up on screen and their health changes, and that's really all you see.  It's too bad combat animations weren't done properly from the same camera view as the rest of combat.  That would be a big step in the right direction but I don't think that would be enough on its own.The graphics really fell flat and I didn't like the writing (story and dialogue), and some of the voice acting wasn't very good.  At one point your main character says an enemy character's name like they are surprised to see them but they called that same character by name during the dialog in the previous combat turn so they already knew that person was there.  Things like this show a lack of attention to detail, and a lack of care.I highly recommend you look into this one very carefully before making a purchase, I'll be refunding - it's not for me.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm a few chapters in and for an indie game its pretty good. The normal difficulty keeps battles challenging without having to reload just to avoid tactical dead ends. The multiple routes of advancement through social and side quest events in your camp should be familiar to modern Fire Emblem players. It introduces the rapport and social systems slowly though, which I like, so I dont feel your killing the pace between battles running around looking for peoples underwear.   I do think the game could have used just a bit more polish in the presentation department. The lone mouth rigging and stiff static hands during conversations make the characters lifeless. Dialogue is also a bit "naive JRPG protag" heavy to the point that it clashes with the seriousness of the plot.  If you like turn based tactical rpgs and can deal with something not quite AAA, then I would play this.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is such a failure if you compare it with other similar turn-based games (like Fire Emblem, Symphony of War...). Here's my thought:Graphic: this is the only part that is better than other games. You already saw it in the trailer, so I think I don't need to say anything about it.Gameplay:- The game has a potential to be good at the first few chapters, I was expected more classes, more skills... for the freedom of building your squad. But what you see at the beginning was probably 70-80% the games has to offer. Later of the game, there are more classes to come but they're just an upgrade with higher stats & very few active skills unlocked (a lot of passive skills though, but I didn't even care about them because the affect was too small).- Main stories battle are somewhat interesting with few map had unique objectives, but they are very few, more than 60% map was just wipe out all enemies (the main goal is to defeat the boss, but actually you cannot kill him/her until you cleared all the mobs because of the stupid dmg reduction mechanic). Optional battles are the worst, they were just reused 3 or 4 maps and raise the level of enemies, that's all!- Enemies, especially human enemies, are boring, just a bunch of mobs with same skill set in every chapters. Especially when you get to the final part of the main stories, you will see the same enemies, same bosses in every chapter. - The camp activities is the only gameplay I found it unique compare to others. But the quests they gave you are just stupid, mostly just running around the camp and talk to people.The stories: I think most of players will find the story are just bland with a lot of plot holes & clipphanger. And I think I know the reason why:- Actually, if you familiar with Chinese history, around the period Han-Chu Contention, you will find the stories are extremely familiar. Yes, they was just copy all the events in that history period & paste it to the game, with some modifications to match with the settings world:-- Eden is actually an idealist Liu Bang-- Balastar is Xiang Yu (with more friends than the historical character)- But the most stupid work they did was that: they did not go deep into the detail of the events, and cut off all of the strategic parts. So you will see the characters in the game usually make stupid decisions with vague explanations, and some big battles was skipped (maybe they are too lazy to do the research).In general, if you're new to turn-based games, this game may worth your time & money if you just... wait for it to sale, then buy it and give it a try. Otherwise, the price is just not worth it.

_childDocuments_.review: Not a good game. It looks awful, with a color scale that goes from light brown to dark brown; the writing is bad, with stuffy and corny, but far from charming, dialogues and a plot that hinges on a series of non sensical, sometimes downright impossible "clever" ruses; the protagonist has a bottomless pit where his charisma should be and is as bland as it comes. Other characters blend together and have no visual, mechanical or statistical traits that really identify them in direct gameplay. It also suffers from the same problem as 3H does, where characters are far too flexible and versatile for their own good, and there is very little incentive to try new characters when all of them are roughly interchangeable within some limited parameters.Still, it has some good stuff. The magic system and spells are not original, but certainly well executed. Same goes for active skills, and the exclusion zone is a good iteration on this sort of game. There is a good spread of objectives and the levels are largely decently designed, though the enemy spread and distribution holds some of them back. OST is a bright spot in a game that is severly lacking in visual beauty.As for difficulty, it's ok. Playing on hard, maniac, turn limits on, I had to reload a few times, mostly very early on a level after realizing that I would need a specific item or spell I hadn't equipped. A special ♥♥♥♥ you goes to the last boss, who regains all of his health twice, with no previous signs, and introduces, as the last enemy in the game and after a one hour grindfest of a level, new status effects, mechanics and abilites the player has never seen before.Ultimately, the game might scratch the itch to anyone who wants more FE but has played all/can't access them, but I would strongly recommend Dark Deity, Symphony of War or Vestaria Saga instead. I definitely wouldn't have played over 50 hours of it if it weren't for the fact that I'm trying every FE clone out there.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid 7.5 or 8. play if you're desperate for a new fire emblempros- voice acting. Balastar's voice actor is the highlight- story/characters- engaging combat mechanics and weapon triangle- flexible classes- good difficulty with a lot of options to tweak it to your liking. i played on normal, perma death, and limited turns and i felt sufficiently challenged- the game has a pair up system that gives the tag along buddy 100% of the exp which lets you have a massive barracks of well trained soldiers for flexibilitycons- the "monastery" is tedious and repetitive- the class system is convoluted at first and you want to plan in advance what you want or miss out big time later- to get the full amount out of the story, the game expects a lot out of you. a lot of talking to people in camps or reading book pickups- the middle of the game kinda slogs. its 27 chapters long and chapters 10-15 are a slog. (so 5 chapters total, not 15 bad chapters 🤣 )- the recruitment system is strange. people come to your monastery for a few levels and you have to shower them with limited gifts to get them to stay- characters come and go from your party, sometimes for multiple chapters, requiring you to always have a backfill. basically, if you have a templar on your team don't only have 1 of them in your reserve cause that templar may leave for a bit. i found that system more frustrating because you had to make sure you kept an eye on the bench warmers so that they were leveling into good slots you may need

_childDocuments_.review: I originally bought this game because of all the weird negativity surrounding turn limits in the game. The developers also seemed very nice and communicative so I wanted to support a new entry in one of my favorite genres. I honestly didn't expect to like it as much as I did though, and it seems like a great game from what I've played so far. Fire emblem is one of my favorite game series and I can definitely see the influence it had on this game. In fact there are at least a few fire emblem games I would say that are worse then this. I think the worst thing I could say about is that it's a bit on the simpler side. Most of the game is just positioning your units well and knowing when to attack and defend. From what I've played so far on hard it seems to be pretty enemy phase focused with combat abilities being the main tools for making things happen either defensively or offensively. My opinions on the game might change as I get farther in but honestly I feel like this game should be getting a lot more love than it is. It's a shame that a single mechanic turned so many people away especially since it isn't even badly implemented.

_childDocuments_.review: So I am a huge tactical RPG fan. From my uncountable play throughs of the original FFT on PS1, to Yu Yu Hakusho tactics on my gameboy, to every fire emblem I could get my hands on. I have played a lot to say the least. My biggest challenges are lack of diversity in character customization and, admittedly particle effects (i am a sucker if it looks cool). I hate when a game boils down to every character, stat wise, being bland or lacking choice. I want my party to be MY party. I always use permadeath when available, but on normal difficulty throughout different games. I can say that this game is a fantastic Indie game that hinges on trying to be  a AAA game and that is a good thing. We get what benefits we can from that. Is it a AAA game? no. But I think it does have some pretty great cutscenes, and voice acting that usually come from bigger budget games. The people complaining in the reviews have not gotten into the game enough to really give it a fair review. There is a lot more to the class system customization that is brought in more and more as you progress. It looks shallow at first glace. Just give it some time and trust and abilities unlock and characters start mastering classes. This game is VERY fire emblem the 3 houses gameplay. The camp you have leadership points and you have to do what I think is a bunch of nonsense complete quests and interact with characters (same as 3 houses, not my cup of tea in that either). This isn't really a crutch for my as I played the crap out of Fire emblem by skipping the nonsense voice lines. The story cutscenes I actually watch and enjoy.Also particle effects are pretty good and varied especially for the magic. Deff give this one a go and you are going to be pouring some hours into it. _childDocuments_.review: Anyone remember a cheesy historical movie from the 80's called Hearts and Armour?This is what this game reminds me of. Hearts and Armour was an Italian-made movie that was released in the late 80's, starring about half the cast from the then-popular soapie, The Bold and the Beautiful. I can't remember much about the movie, except that the acting was bad, the fight sequences even worse, and everyone walked around in shiny plate armour most of the time, flashing their pearly whites while trying to look wistful or imposing.Honestly, I think this has been one of the most boring CRPGs I've ever played. I reached chapter 7 and just couldn't take it anymore. You play the role of Eden, a mercenary captain who, in a nutshell,  ends up fleeing his hometown and gets drawn into a rebellion, doing a series of missions while levelling up and attracting more companions to his mercenary company along the way. The core gameplay loop consists of fighting a tactical battle, sitting through some or other cut scene showing developments before and/or after the battle,  then spending time in camp where you do some small quests, talk to your companions, buy or sell equipment, and occasionally deal with other new developments that may happen. The story is effectively on rails as there is no exploration and you have no choices in dialogue. You watch a cut scene, do a battle, return to camp, finish your activities there, then watch another cut scene after you exit the camp, then do the next tactical battle. Rinse and repeat. Despite the country being gripped by war and rebellion, everyone looks ridiculously clean cut and immaculately groomed, like they all just walked off the Bold and the Beautiful set after filming. Eden himself has this elegant early 90's off-centre parted hairdo, which never looks remotely ruffled, even after the most brutal of battles. The women all look like they're all dolled up  for a night on the town, rather than a battlefield. The writing for this game is awful, as everyone seems to talk like modern day teenagers while constantly harping on about the completely obvious, and having to sit through the various utterly banal conversations with people in camp will make you feel like your brain is melting. It would probably be a bit more bearable if you were in the 12 - 16 age range, I guess, but probably not by much. What makes it worse is that most of the other characters are generally either snarky and/or disrespectful towards Eden, despite him being in charge of the mercenary company. He just takes it all on the chin and tries to be diplomatic towards them, and it can be frustrating to put up with this as you have to sit through the scripted dialogue without being able to select a response.Regarding the tactical battles, I really think the system needs an overhaul. Before actually starting a battle, there is an 'Explore' option on the menu, but this seems utterly pointless as all it lets you do is pan the cursor around the battlefield (which also moves too quickly but you cannot adjust the pan speed). You can already pan around the battlefield anyway after the battle has started, as it is turn based anyway. All spell casters and archers seem to be short sighted, as you can generally only cast a spell or shoot an arrow at enemy units a couple of squares away, which seems a bit strange. This makes fighting larger enemies like the hellhounds really annoying as your archers and mages have to move within their attack range to attack them, so always end up getting targeted by the hellhound on its turn. Your units can either move and attack (or take another action like drinking a potion) on their turn, but they cannot attack first and then move, or move twice instead of taking any other actions.  There is no cover system, and enemies can still target you with ranged attacks even if you're behind an obstacle. If there are enemy bosses present, you are forced to deal with their minions first, as they apparently take greatly reduced damage from your attacks while any of their forces are still nearby. The enemy forces are typically divided into a number of smaller groups, so you will usually end up using the same tactics, in this case moving in 1 or 2 of your tank type units to aggro the nearest smaller group, deal with them first, then move onto the next group. Again, rinse and repeat. I've only reached chapter 7 or 8, so I can imagine later battles get extremely time consuming to get through as your mercenary company grows in size and the enemies become more numerous.On the plus side, the game's graphics are very good for a game in this price range, with characters and their gear having an almost photo-realistic look. The game's soundtrack also sounds nice and somewhat epic, and complements the various battles nicely. However, I just can't recommend it because of the poor writing, dull linear gameplay and combat system.  If the developers could hire better writers, implement dialogue choices in the game, allow some degree of player exploration, and completely redo the combat system for their next game, then we might be onto something......

_childDocuments_.review: Not sure why Lost Eidolons is getting so many negative reviews -- methinks people are coming into it, expecting it to be something that it's not. The reality is that Lost Eidolons is a really good SRPG which has a few flaws here and there, but has a competent enough core experience that it's nonetheless a worthy recommendation to fans of the genre. In short: I'd say it's basically a more grounded, realistic version of Fire Emblem: Three Houses that's actually designed competently.You have a similar core gameplay loop to Three Houses -- i.e. battle, talk to characters, tackle optional battles, prepare your units for battle, cutscene, repeat -- except here it's executed with more finesse. The campgrounds (LE's version of the Monastery) is much more intuitively designed and easier to navigate, so it feels less cumbersome to play through. Your protagonist, Eden, actually talks and has a personality, which is how a story-driven RPG SHOULD be. Byleth, by comparison, is a silent cardboard cutout who has less personality than a wet tissue paper. Side characters have much more realistic personalities, and aren't just 1-dimensional anime tropes, unlike any given character in any given FE game after New Mystery of the Emblem.Sure, characters have less flash, but that's the natural consequence of writing realistic characters with realistic personalities instead of basing an entire character upon cheap anime tropes; there's a decent amount of depth to each character if you take the time to dig a bit beneath the surface. Lost Eidolons also isn't afraid to kill off important characters, which is a refreshing change of pace from the usual JRPG fare. Their deaths, and even those of nameless soldiers, is treated with seriousness and realism. For these reasons, Lost Eidolons has far more competent storytelling than shameless, fanservicey drivel like Valkyria Chronicles or FE Awakening. I have to say I'm still not a fan of the sandboxy nature of class advancement. Granted, it's better here than in Three Houses, but if a SRPG results in every character having 99% the same potential skills and abilities, then that's a fundamental failure of that SRPG. One of the joys of great SRPGs, such as FE5, Valkyrie Profile: Covenant of the Plume, Energy Breaker, World's End, Regalia, and Fae Tactics, is that every unit has a completely unique identity, resulting in unique and colorful ways to utilize them on the battlefield. But in a game like Lost Eidolons or Three Houses, any character can become any class. What's the fun in that? The harsh truth is that this is lazy game design and it's simply less strategic. (I blame Yasumi Matsuno for stealing from FF5 and introducing this sandboxy nonsense to the genre with FFT.)Another letdown is that the game could've done more to make its battles feel more grandiose. Every cutscene, and every battle engagement scene, will feature dozens or hundreds of troops in the background. Yet, none of them are playable. Lost Eidolons could've taken a page from Langrisser's book and incorporated troops into the battles, or it could've done more with support/bond bonuses. This was somewhat disappointing, but it's ultimately only a minor letdown. On the other hand, the game has a few ideas which are not native to FE. Spells with AoE ranges, taunt skills, terrain effects, equippable horses, and limited uses of combat skills make Lost Eidolons feel like a pleasant hodgepodge of FE, Shining Force, Berwick Saga, Bahamut Lagoon, and classic D&D. While Lost Eidolons doesn't have the greatest level design in the genre, its core systems are entertaining enough to keep the experience engaging. It's clearly FE-inspired, but it doesn't feel like a FE clone.The story and battles start off pretty nonchalantly, but everything gradually becomes more dynamic and interesting as you get further in the game. Lost Eidolons goes from "good" to "great" around the chapter 17 mark. Battles become tougher and more creative, the story gets more serious, and the campgrounds really open up so you can have some nice conversations with your supporting characters. Although I think Lost Eidolons could've done more with its systems and could've been more challenging, I was pretty satisfied when I delivered the killing blow on the final boss and saw the ending cutscenes. It's not a perfect game, but it's still a great one. I'm very much looking forward to Lost Eidolons: Veil of the Witch, and am curious to see where the developers take the series from there.

_childDocuments_.review: A must play for those who enjoy Strategy Role Playing Games(SRPGs) like Fire Emblem! The game and world are beautiful and the story is quite good. It does have its faults, such as the Management Menu system which is convoluted and slow, but even then, I voted it as Game of the Year 2022 as I enjoyed so much! The world building in this game is really good. The story itself follows Eden and his band of mercenaries who are pulled in to a much larger conflict. Throughout the story, notes, books and conversations with characters reveal more about the world of Artemesia as a whole which was really interesting. Character development is mostly done through a Rapport system where, in-between missions, you are able to initiate conversations with your units/friends. The first half of the game was well-paced and interesting, the latter half of the story is not as good, with the final battle being a bit frustrating and underwhelming. That being said, I still enjoyed it very much and feel like the emotions I felt during that part of the story, matched with the characters, which is interesting and, I believe, a sign of good story-telling.In SRPGs, the management of your units equipment and classes are just as important as the actual battles. A good management menu is integral to the game and my thoughts on the management menu is not as positive as other aspects of my review. The user interface and user experience of the Management menu is only passable, but not great. I found myself struggling to find key information, while also finding the text quite small. On smaller screens such as the Steam Deck the game may not be playable for many, while on my 4K, 27 inch monitor I still found myself wishing text was larger. On slower hardware, such as a Steam Deck, the Management Menu is slow, cumbersome and causes the game to drop from 60 fps, to 15 fps. Especially when selecting your equipped spells for your grimoires. On my gaming desktop, it was better, but even then, I could tell my computer was working harder when in the Menu Management system, then at any other point in the game. I believe the main culprit for the performance issues in the menu system is that the game continues playing in the background while in the menu. As such, the game has to render 3D assets such as the characters, or the grimoires in the menu, as well as the game environment in the background. Hopefully the Menu Management systems can be improved in the future, with an option to increase font size, improved performance and a focus on improving how information is presented.The battles in Lost Eidolons are challenging and diverse. Each character class has their own strengths and weaknesses, and the map itself can be used to your advantage. Burning enemy units in a forest tile, or drenching them in water, only to shock or freeze them with a mage is quite fun and adds to the strategies available to the player. Up until recently, there were turn limits in every mission, I never found them to be problematic and honestly thought they added a lot to the game, but if you did not feel the same way you can now remove the turn limits. Honestly, I have nothing but good things to say about the graphics. The game looks visually amazing. The characters, environment, weapons, armor and clutter in the game all look great! I personally love the armor design of the game the most. I believe it is pretty clear that I thoroughly enjoyed Lost Eidolons. It is a fantastic game, with a great narrative, and beautiful visuals. For those who enjoy SRPGs, I believe this is a must play and whole heartily recommend it.  Outside of the few complaints I had above, I hope to see some improvements in the future for this title, or for future titles by the developer. 1. More diversity. Many of the playable characters are white and I think that it would feel more immersive with more diversity in the characters. 2. More customization. As stated, the armor design is beautiful, but many characters end up looking exactly the same when they are of the same class. I would like to see a weapon customization feature such as in Fire Emblem and even perhaps an armor customization feature so that we can make characters stand out. 3. Some sort of end-game content. I believe in the future they plan on having a new-game plus. This would fit that criteria and add some extra replayability to the game.

_childDocuments_.review: Took a fast look at Ocean Drive Studio's ambitious Lost Eidolons. Let's get to what I liked and what I feel needs improvement. What I enjoyed:Dynasty Tactics: This is Dynasty Tactics set to a medieval fantasy story-line. A honorable homage to those classic KOEI games.Controls: sounds, action, is pretty straight forward and simplified. Controller friendly indeed. SmartHonorable work: A lot of action sequences, solid surrounding support model inclusion, and solid atmosphere gives Lost Eidolon a good solid presentationPretty: Everything is pretty in its looks and customization that you can create fun looking characters.Combat Animation: Like Dynasty Tactics, the execution to end result turn animation from magic, to swinging attacks executes well.Music: Fits the mood and excitement of the game.Timid: For those who do not like a lot of blood and gore in a game that is suppose to be brutal in its combat, pretty timid by those standards. Defined roles: You know your heroes from your villains, no real pressures to save the world.Expandable: With a solid straight forward base game and mechanics, additional DLCs can expand easily from its core. Upgrades: Simple straight forward defined implementation of classes, roles, and classes.Iron-man Mode: You don't mind a brutal experience, afraid of losing members, then Ironman is for you.Camp: Nice idea, in the old Suikoden mode. Despite its rigid straight line. It does have potential to expand if the developer is creative enough to give alternative results. What I feel needs to improve:BAM: A gamer's term used to describe Bad Anime Motion. This is constant unnecessary movement in your models after each sentence phrased. It takes away from the emotion of your story.Story Dialog: Out of the genre. Bad cliche dialog and catch phrases do not fit the fantasy saying your are doing. "You man!" and "what's the old cliche saying" does not inspire a great story, but belittles it.Common Sense Issues: Gamers that follow story plots should not ever question character's motives and actions in a game. Tactics: This is Dynasty tactics, not true board strategy, of combining attacks. The Strategy is taken away from you in its straight forward combat points. Spotty: In some of the modeling it gets spotty with the hands, grabbing items, and movement.Final initial thoughts:If you loved the Dynasty Tactics series from KOEI, or Suikoden, then you may enjoy the work put into this game that simply alters the genre from ancient China to fantasy Medieval. It doesn't quite pull that off, for looking Medieval doesn't mean it is. You can tell from its story sequencing that felt out of sequence at times. Modern slang English does not work for that period. Even in a fantasy Medieval anime setting.  It does give you a lot for the price, but may want to wait for a sale. See the video game-play above the discussion page to see if this game is for you. I commend the publisher for the hard work put into a game that honors an old anime game play. My score 3.1 out of 5

_childDocuments_.review: STORY :The story of this game is inspired by the history after the Qin dynasty unified China, the rivalry between Liu Bang and Xiang Yu or in history known as Chu-Han war.Although there are some storylines and relationships between characters that are slightly different, the main plot remains the same. GAMEPLAY : - Two Mode : Battle and walking at Camp (similiar to The Abbey in Marvel Midnight Suns)- Party-based : can use 10 characters in battle. another 10 characters can be used as support to buff each character.- Battle Map : quite a variety of battle maps in each chapter, except for side missions or optional battles.- Relationship : can raise relationships with many characters in the game but the rewards are lacking.- Character Progression : Equipment, Skill and Weapon Mastery. we can't increase attributes other than through equipment.- Voice Acting : all important conversations that relate to mission and story have voice acting.Unique Features : UNDOwe can undo the action taken no matter how many turns have passed. Of course, undo has a usage limit but we can increase the limit.I finished this game on normal difficulty, when compared to other TBS games I've played, I think this game is quite easy and not stressful (thanks to Undo Features).now let's wait for the sequel which is about to be released.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall a very enjoyable game. There's some rough edges that could be smoothed out a bit though:1. not sure if it's a gap in the voice acting budget, but the minor side quests don't have full dialog -- instead employ canned one liners that are rather jarring. (and no option to disable these, at least that i noticed)2. the class (job) system is great, but not immediately intuitive. i wound up restarting on chapter 20 over this.  Basically I wound up gimping a few characters by not leveling up things like elemental or light magic, thus making unlocking master classes much more difficult than it should have been)3. kind of dovetails into #2, but the way the battles go (including optional) means you have a limited window in which to level up your characters.  Other RPG's use grinding as an equalizer for this (along with skill, if a battle is too hard, you can just go level up until you can win. not so in this, you have your chapter battles, and then one optional battle per chapter.  there's no grinding at all.. (and dammit, i never thought i'd look at that as a negative..)4. the story is very linear, you're basically on rails versus your decisions affecting the outcome (think triangle strategy)5. The unit cap per battle is 10 (whether this changes later on, i'm not sure, only on chapter 20 or so), but you have easily double that number of available units, though this is mitigated somewhat by the aide system.6. scripted events in battles, if you undo a turn, you get to sit through the same speeches again, and again, and again. (and these can't be skipped!)7. Leon. :(It might look like a list of negatives, but i'd still whole heartedly recommend this game to anyone who likes strategy games  The characters are all interesting (francisco in the early chapters is a minor exception.)  There's huge potential from this as a franchise or IP due to the well written backstory, characters you feel invested in,  and geography.

_childDocuments_.review: Lost Eidolons takes you on a grim ride through a linear medival war story centering around a band of mercenaries. The turn based combat with its rock-paper-scissor approach is fairly simple but enjoyable through the class progression system. As it is a party based game, you will spend about half your play time in and around the immersive party camp, talking to the large cast of interesting characters, while doing basic (side) quests and optional missions and equipping your growing warband.Enjoyable:* Immersive, atmospheric war camp with a large cast of believable written characters and dialogues* Simple but motivating turn-based combat due to the class progression and variety* Interesting medival fantasy story with unexpected twists.* Atmospheric (ambiance) music* Nicely detailed character, weapon and armor models as well as spell and battle animations.* Immersive battle action cameraShould be improved:* Optional battles get repetitive and boring quickly -> more map and enemy variety* Somewhat repetitive and slow progression between chapters 10 to 17 -> maybe add some more unlockable skills for each of the basic classes?* Chapter 17: Advised battle plan makes no sense in "maniac mode" -> make it clear to the player where the devised strategy leads* Later Chapters: Defeating certain characters in the turn based battles over and over again without any influence on the overall story makes it less believable.Wishlist* More banter dialog for each character in camp.* Voiceover for all dialoges.* More to come in the universe of (the) lost eidolons.

_childDocuments_.review: Normaly i do not do reviews but i want to give this game a push for 2 reasons:1. This is more or less a copy of the combat system from the fire emblem series2. The game overall is for a AA/indie game well done and deserves the supportTL;DR: This is an indie/AA Fire Emblem game on PC with real graphic (real in the sense that it is not anime graphic). If you like fire emblem three houses chances are high that you will like this game aswell. It is an indie game and that shines in the complexity of the class system and the storyStory and Voice acting:So far: the story is standard mage and knight and evil empire stuff, the characters are clicheed and the voice acting ranges from decent to: how did this get into the final cut. Definitly the weakest part of the gameClass System:The class system is straight forward and you can see from the beginning what each class as as attributes and what you need to grind in order to reach that class, making planning your rooster very easy. Every character has a certain class and as far as i can tell you can learn every character the class that you want to, but of course each character has a natural tendency for certain classes (Like Fire Emblem Three Houses system but less complex)Combat System:If you have played any Fire emblem title you know this system, if not here is the short breakdown: 8-9 characters for each battle, each character has a class and a corresponding weapon and armor, making that class effective against specific armors (what is effective against what is always shown on the bottom right screen and indicated on the units aswell) there is a turn limit for each mission, the faster you finish your mission the more additional xp you get at the end.Very neat: weapons do not break and each character can have a secondary weapon so weapon choice matters.Social Aspect:Like Three Houses, you have a sort of hub in between missions. THere you can build trust with your allies, manage your equipment, do some sidequests, change classes, buy new gear/items ect. basiclly everything that is not fighting. My personal favourite part about this feature: you can teleport to every character in your camp!GraphicIt is ok, it is not a Last of us 2 or horizon forbidden west, but it also doesn't look like ♥♥♥♥, for a Double AA titel it is good in my opinionConclusion:Why do i compare it so much to Fire Emblem Three houses? Because i am pretty sure the devs looked at that game and said: "we can do that" And in the restrictions they had in terms of budget, manpower and probably experience aswell: they did a good jobThis game does not reinvent the wheel, but it doesn't need to. It knows what it wants to do and that it does well (except for voice acting and story probably)If you need to scratch your fire emblem itch until the new game comes out, this game is it, but don't go into it expecting a deep story and complex characters (but neither did Fire Emblem Three houses have those and the game was still awesome)

_childDocuments_.review: "I've come looking for silver, but found gold." - my initial review at ~30 hours or ~1/3 of the game. Now, after finishing the game, I can elaborate on that.This game is an amazing story set in Witcher-esque world, presented via enjoyable gameplay loop, told by a team of extremely likeable characters voiced by excellent actors and accompnied by a great soundtrack. Every chapter begins from exposition presented to us via character dialogues and/or animated cutscene, sometimes a monologue from the narrator, usually when a timeskip involved. It transitions into battle, which is very much "Tactics" turn-based RPG at its core. "Gears of War" or "Fire Emblem" Tactics would be decent analogies. Terrain plays an important role and could be manipualted by elemetal magic to a degree, which sometimes leads to a very satisfying combos. For example a couple of mages can tag-team: one summons rain, and the other brings down thunder electrocuting or flash-freezing the now soaking-wet opponents. After the victory you get to your camp, where you can talk to your teammates, customise their classes/skills/loadouts and complete simple quests for extra bit of reward and lore. Normally fetch-quests would be boring, but excellent writing and banter between characters make it more than worthwile to run around camp. Plus, there's fast travel option for your convinience available at all times. Once you're done, you proceed to the next chapter. None of the elements of this cycle outstays its welcome, so I was never bored of a dialogue, a battle or a downtime at the camp. It's a simple loop, but very enjoayble. Now, the game isn't without flaws, but they aren't many.  Update: Optional Battles have been reworked and don't feel so stale anymore. They're not as fun as battles in the main story missions, but have just enough challenge and varity in them to not be boring. Another problem is that while all curtscenes, main and side quest dialogues are fully voiced, miscalleneous banter at the camp is not. Which is a crying shame, because I want to hear more of those glorious VA's!So, to sum it up, this game is a great example of when the whole is more than just sum of its parts. Every single component of the game is solid by itself, but the magic happens when they're all blended together.Looking forward to any and all new content the devs will be able to provide. Update: New Game+ mode has been added for extra replay value.P.S. "Power of the Lost" is, as youngsters apparently call it these days, quite a "banger". Give it a listen even if you're not interested in the game itself.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR in case you don't want to watch the video:1. This is a straight up turn based tactical RPG with some strategy elements2. The visuals and sound design are great - as seen in its countless lengthy cutscenes.3. The audio visual spectacle is truly something to behold - but beyond the first 1 hour of gameplay and cutscenes, it breaks up the pacing of the game so often that it almost becomes a chore. Although its possible to skip and disable all of it, its crucial when it comes to the storytelling as well as the combat, so you're kind of left with little choice.4. Speaking of choice, the story makes you think you have some say init; but beyond some additional dialogue and choice in quest rewards, there is little to no influence over the overall narrative and character development of the game - which, by itself, may not be a bad thing as some players do enjoy a linear story line.5. Despite all that, the class tree, as well as the 'progress your skills the more you use them' style of character progression felt organic and fun, and did not shoehorn you into any particular playstyle. Sadly, all of that is overshadowed by repetitive combat encounters where enemies only get increasingly difficult with more health and damage.6. The turn limit that many others have mentioned, really only becomes an issue in the harder difficulties, and later stages in the game - but it still is an issue nonetheless.I would only recommend this to players who don't mind lengthy cutscenes, and a linear story line. And even then, I would have to recommend to WAIT for more updates and changes made by the devs.

_childDocuments_.review: Lost Eidolons [SRPG, FANTASY, INDIE, KOREAN] [8/10]Lost Eidolons is an indie strategy game made by a Korean studio. It is highly based on S-RPGs such as Fire Emblem among other games. Despite being highly based on mechanics and gameplay the game manages to be original enough to not be considered a copy and have its own personality.From a narrative point of view, the game manages to grab you in the first chapters, being its main attraction the narrative between the protagonist and the other characters.From a playable point of view, it is a fire emblem which has a turn counter as standard, forcing you to think about how to win in a certain number of turns. On the other hand the game has a camp, similar to other games of the genre is where you socialize with other characters, being its weakest point, sometimes being somewhat tedious between fights and somewhat slow to move through.In conclusion, it is a very promising game, with a rich lore, some charismatic characters, a terrifying villain, challenging at times and with enough merit to come from a small studio. Recommended purchase for Fire

_childDocuments_.review: A little clunky at times, but there is a lot to love. If you enjoyed Fire Emblem: Three Houses and felt like Engage took out all the good parts, then Lost Eidolons has my recommendation. It makes some changes to the basic Fire Emblem formula and adds it's own mechanics to the mix, but it actually flows better than my first impression had me believe. At first, the lack of dodging or doubling and units exerting a zone of control to restrict movement felt awkward, but that passed as I played further and I came to rather enjoy the combat. The story was also there, and I appreciated the attempt in the latter chapters to enact a morality system, but I felt that could have been fleshed out further.

_childDocuments_.review: A valiant attempt at a Fire Emblem-esque tactical RPG and very impressive as a first outing. The clear major inspiration for this is Fire Emblem: Three Houses, and fans of that I would outright tell to get this game. However, don't expect the same level of polish or depth. The combat is fun and simple, the graphics are pretty good too (only exception being some stiff faces and a few too many repeating assets), the voice acting is great, the lore and world are fun, it feels like a mix of Golden Age Berserk, GoT, and Fire Emblem. Likewise the characters I enjoy (mostly, a few I disliked, but like FE, characters are a major selling point of the game and very subjective person to person), a bond system, many unique dialogues, etc. I would love to see the framework of this game expanded upon by a sequel! But as it stands it is still a damn good game. Get it if it interests you, or you are dying for a Three Houses like game, or you wanna support a smaller studio making stuff like this in the future!

After the first few quests, you wish you could skip it all together. Characters are bland, and you simply don't care about them2. Combat - which is still the strongest point of the game is very basic, AI is dumb and very scripted, skills and spells are basically re-skins with small differences. There is a very little tactical approach to it. (not to mention, you can just shoot through walls). Feels like there was a better idea behind it, but in the end was very simplified.3. Camp/Team management - again, very basic. You get few simple things to do there, mostly you run around the camp to talk with all characters ( time-consuming & repetitive and poorly written), buy potions, and do some meager upgrades for characters. Overall game with underutilized potential, where the only good point is decent graphics.

_childDocuments_.review: For a few years now, I would often look to see if any PC game was coming down the pipeline that was directly inspired by Fire Emblem, as it is a series of brutal tactical games that I could spend hours trying to survive each battle. This is that game, and it is by no means a pale shadow of FE either. It has its own character while preserving the systems that makes FE so great. Definitely worth the price if you like a challenging, tactical experience. Hard mode, set to Maniac  (perma-death for characters) and turn timer on to preserve that FE experience! The story is great for a turn-based tactical game. Fans of the genre will not be disappointed.

_childDocuments_.review: A decent attempt at making a compelling turn-based tactics game. If you don't want to fail because of your AI allies' incompetence, I suggest you keep the difficulty on Normal or lower.The combat is polished and it's fun to pick apart enemy defences with a ragtag group of warriors and mages in the story battles. The optional battles are mostly big, dull squares of recycled terrain filled with enemies to slaughter. The fully animated story sequences and cutscenes are good. Each character has their own motivations and personalities... but there's so much of it that it dragged for me. So much time of my 50-hour playthrough was spent talking to people and fetching things around the same camp environment, it honestly became a chore for me 15-20 hours in.As grandiose as the story appears to be, it's basically centred on two guys who want to kill each other. It's well written, but I think the story could have been finished in half the time it took to play through.Playing Lost Eidolons, all I can think is, "What happened to bright colours?" Outside of the hand-drawn/painted cutscenes, I don't think it's a pleasant game to look at. Generally it's a mix of dark browns, blues and greys, which I guess helps make the magic effects stand out.Recommended only for turn-based tactics and fantasy fans like me, who'll overlook the things that'd otherwise put us off. If you're looking for an entry point to the genre, you're probably better off starting elsewhere.
