_childDocuments_.review: [Edit]After playing more, I have to give this game a thumbs down, even though it shows so much promise. There is a big flaw in its overarching game design, which is its camp. The camp conversations are long, arbitrary, linear (even though they appear otherwise) and ultimately add little to the game, because you get bored. The actual conversations and interactions are solid, the animations are on point, but it feels like they said "let's do one battle, then have forced roleplaying to build story and then repeat over and over". It doesn't feel natural, it feels gamey, and it takes you out of the flow- and too much time between the skirmishes, which are the highlight. I think their next game which learned lessons from this one, should be better. I still believe in the studio, they just missed the mark with this one.Previous review: This indie studio is something to watch. I'm excited about their continual development of this underlying tactics system, with good graphics, challenging decisions, and solid voice acting. While this game itself is an even 7/10 - I think their future games will only improve upon this. And if you're looking for a fantasy tactics set in a war where you're a commander, then this is a really worthwhile game to add to your library.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: A tactical RPG with a straightforward war story with a fantastic cast set in a medieval world with a hint of fantasy that gets better the more time you invest; highly reminiscence of modern Fire Emblem titles.The story starts slow, yet the characters are strong, except the main character who initially feels aloof. It does pick up considerably before the second half and becomes more engrossing, and the characters develop considerably, especially the MC. The story is heavier in the latter half.The art and theme are fantastic, accompanied with some fantasy tunes and a few cut-scenes. Each character has a unique look; however, the lack of facial expression hurts; the strong voice acting throughout the main story helps convey emotion. There are many elements that happen off-screen that I would have enjoyed seeing. I did enjoy the narrative stills that tie the larger plot together.The camp multiplies, and there is much to traverse. Wise decision to add fast travel; cutting the map into sections makes sorting companions easy. There are many camp actions between missions; for completionists, this is most of your time developing relationships through waterfalls of dialogue, training troops, and doing the odd side mission or battle. The game could benefit from fewer characters and a tighter cast.Classes and items are easy to understand and very minimal. Combat is a back and forth with the addition of limited-use skills and spells that affect the environment, and there is no weapon repair! Instead of a weakness triangle, it is armor-dependent, and giant monsters have rotating weaknesses. Some missions bring that extra gimmick or flair; each mission is well-tied to the story.Since the launch, Ocean Drive has made several improvements: New Game+, stability fixes, dialogue, and U/I. It's great to see the commitment. It's a fun time for fans of tactical RPGs at a solid price point; you will get your worth from this title, delving into solid combat and the superb character backstories. Their next title, Veil of the Witch, is in the same setting with familiar faces. I'm excited to see how the process has developed.

_childDocuments_.review: Would give it a thumbs up as the story is quite nice and the fights are good.Up to 20+ mission where there is a flood of bosses all having a "boss immunity" needing to kill trash mobs before you can really hurt them.I am now at a point where there are like 10 bosses around on mission 23.They hit like a truck and get only 2-3 damage if you do not clear the endless trash mobs first.And all you got is the never changing roster of 10 on the battlefield.The equipment you pick up during the campaign does not match the power creep of the bosses you meet later.And due to the "protected boss" mechanic they are are just walking tanks with a damage output which kills even your tanks in 2 hits.So now in chapter 23 it is like 10 bosses - even 2 unnamed mobs are promoted to boss status.There is a "escape" mission but with the mass on bosses around you are just getting trashed and swarmed by mobs and invincible damage NPC which ironically you took out several times over the course of the campaign.And you got two perma loss due to story of highly trained characters as well as probably a emptied roster of characters if you put this game on permadeath for battle.Don't use the permadeath option.It totally destroys ANY kind of accomplishment when due to story the enemy NPC just keep coming back due to story reasons and your roster is just perma-killed due to option that does not really fit a linear story driven campaign.It is already bad enough they kill of 2 characters story-wise until mission 23 (I think there will be more) but then never changing "only 10" roster as well as the inflated boss numbers with their immunity mechanic is not motivating.I enjoyed the game until mission 23 but it got really draining as the mass of immune bosses keeps rising.Sadly this really ruins a enjoyable game.Story is quite railroaded and there is really no meaningful decisions. The loss of characters due to story might be dramatic but if it piles up and there are no meaningful ways to change the narrative as well as have true decisions it gets frustrating together with the shortcomings mentioned before.Thus I am afraid I need to give the game a thumbs down as there is no mixed option.The monster fights are nice with their need to chain certain attacks on different angles.As for the bosses they should have gone for giving them more HP or anything other than boss immunities chained to mobs.Having also a GROWING roster of characters to USE would be also a nice thing especially given the flood of bosses later on.If you would have more slots to take into battle against this "boss flood" this would be a good thing in my opinion.But keeping 10 slots all the game is bad.And the bonus of "aides" you can attach to each characters are sadly a joke.+5 to accuracy and such thing does not in any way give you much better chances.So all in all a flawed experience.World building is nice and I will have a look at the follow up title.But here I really lost motivation to get to mission 23-27 which ends the campaign.

_childDocuments_.review: Fun game, smaller but you can feel passion went into it. Much like Fire Emblem.Update: So I have played a lot more since my first very brief description. I think this is a great game. Good combat, lots of interesting tactical maps, only one dog so far (I'm on chapter 20, so that is a very good ratio or good to bad maps). And really even the dog map was fine if you just ignored what they were trying to do and just took it head on (talking about the odd stealth mission storming a castle). Character progression is good, you upgrade each unit a few times - there is some incentive to minmax and level up different paths and take little tidbits here and there, but minmaxing is hardly required as there are several modes to play (easy to normal and I think at least a couple hard and harder modes). I like the balance between Tactical Combat and Base/Team management -- it feels like what Fire Emblem 3 Houses wishes the Monastery was, here it's a camp but it does not wear out it's welcome like FE3H did (for me, the monastery was the most disappointing aspect of that game).Good music. Good art. The story is not bad, with the usual twists and turns but going in blind you'll probably not see a few things coming. Fairly dark but not overly so. This is a very good game and if you are into this genre, it's absolutely worth checking out.

_childDocuments_.review: An SRPG that I had supported on Kickstarter. Solid mechanics with some interesting strategy and character class elements, a few cool features and enemies that unfortunately don't always amount to much throughout the full game, and a nice plot change where the often used terrible SRPG end goal of "let's fight our evil rulers who overthrew the monarchy and restore the power of the old monarchy in the process" doesn't go so well.You begin the game as the leader of a mercenary company with four of your friends. The current rule is in decline and a corrupt figure oversees the town that you are the local heroes of for your helpful actions and monster hunting work. Soon you end up being drawn into an assassination attempt, pushed to join an open rebellion with the support of a former inquisitor, paired with allies that seem like they might be just as bloodthirsty as the current imperial faction, and awakening to a destructive magical power that can be used in battle but that begins to corrupt its wielder.The game plays as a typical SRPG where you control up to 10 characters on the battlefield. Characters get the usual movement and attack options and will unlock skills and spells over time, unique legendary weapons might come with their own skills that can be used, and characters equipped with a shield can also take a defensive action that increases their guard chance. When a character is attacked a unit can counterattack them if they are within range but unlike a game like Fire Emblem your counterattack damage is greatly reduced from a normal attack. All attacks will hit but depending on character skills in accuracy and guard and on their equipment they might block which will greatly reduce damage, critical hits are also possible and it is possible for the attacker to crit while also having the defender block the attack. Magic using characters set spells in a grimoire before battle, the number of spells available to equip depending on their class, their know spells depending on their familiarity with the type of magic they are using, and the number of uses they get with each spell being unique to the spells themselves.Class wise, at lower levels each person starts as a commoner or noble. These two do the same things and allow for any type of weapon (two sets that can hold either a sword and shield, spear and shield, two handed axe, or bow), a single spellbook (elemental, dark, or light) to be equipped, and any armor type with each being stronger against certain weapon types or more defensive against physical or magic attacks (plate, leather, cloth). As you continue to use skills, attack, or take damage your skill rank in weapon, spell, and armor type increases as does your character's level. Eventually each characters skills will push them towards a promotion as a more damage focused fighter, magic using mage, or a more defensive and taunt focused squire. As you level up to the next tier you have the more advanced fighter and squire type but also gain access to class focused on archery and one for each type of magic. The final tier gets you access to 11 final classes that either favor certain weapon types, give you two types of archers, or allow for more unique combos like a duel sword wielding assassin, axe and elemental magic users, or a spear and light magic focused character. Each class has its own experience tree that will unlock skills as you level them up that will either be bonuses you always have as that class or as skills that you can equip to a character (you can equip five skills, up to seven in a new game plus run). Every character can become any class but some are heavily pushed in a certain direction by their set stat gains, each also has two master classes that will allow them to unlock an ability that they will always have equipped once you max out one of the two listed classes, they also each have a minor passive ability that is unique to them. As the game goes on you will eventually unlock up to four horses. Any character can use a horse with the horses sometimes adding to certain stats, adding two to a character's movement limit, and eventually unlocking an equipable skill that can increase your damage while mounted and allow you to continue moving after attack, though some terrain penalizes mounted characters more making the dismount option a helpful inclusion.For some of the more tactical features of the game. Your formation can be important as every allied character near you raises damage by 1 and character will block enemy movement as any unit moving next to an enemy is not able to pass them until the next turn if they are able to move on the side and then away from the enemy character (like an attack of opportunity system but one that only prevents movement). As you grow your army to much more than the 10 character limit you have on the battlefield, you will be allowed to assign aides to each deployed character for minor bonuses. The aide character gives their assigned character their unique passive ability and a bonus based on the class that they currently are. This feature also allows you to continue leveling up 10 other characters in case someone dies during the story, temporarily leaves for the story, or dies when you have permanent death options on. Elemental magic and some bow attacks pairs with terrain environmental effects and enemy status, for example, making enemies wet to slow them down, hitting wet enemies or terrain with lightning or ice to create AoE damage or to freeze enemies in place, hitting poison with fire to cause an explosion, setting trees on fire to do damage to units on the space that would otherwise have gotten bonus defense, using water attacks to douse fires, etc. Each weapon using character (or the two battle mage classes) also have two weapon sets they can swap between, though this is a bit less useful than it can first appear outside of giving everyone a bow for ranged attack in the early game.Enemy character basically play in the same way that your units do. They make use of most of the same classes and you will see them using the abilities that your characters get with those classes. They will take advantage of terrain and magic effects to freeze or set you on fire, they will use skills with their archers to keep them out of counterattack range, they will use knights to taunt, and their if you heavily wound one of their later game berserker characters they will punish you with very powerful attack skills that can almost one hit full health characters. Enemy commanders that take the form of unique characters don't have much difference than a normal unit except for being slightly stronger, their main difference comes from them taking about 90% less damage from attacks if they are within six spaces of any normal enemy unit, typically forcing you to take out their soldiers before going after them.Some battles change things up by having you attack or defend areas that are under siege. These missions will have gates that you or your enemy have to destroy by moving units next to them and using the action that orders your troops to hit them with a battering ram. Ramparts near the gates give archer units a bonus to their attack range when they climb stairs to take the high ground. This is an interesting thing at first but as the game goes on nothing gets added to it, and near the end of the game you start being the one on the defense and by that time the variety of AoE and terrain poisoning spells that you have access to allows you to wipe out enemy troops gathered around the same area so quick and easily that it tends to confuse the game's AI. Battles against monsters are an interesting though oddly minor change of pace from normal combat. Monsters only appear Full Review:

_childDocuments_.review: I would recommend this, with a "yes, but...."You need to know what you are getting into.The gameplay is very, very restricted.You have dialogue sequences that serve to drive the story, you have tactical combat with your troops and you have a very limited encampment part, where you initiate dialogue with your party, buy stuff from dealers, solve simple quests (very simple) and make upgrades.Visually the game looks great, much better than you would expect from a game with this small a developer team.However that comes with a price and the price is no customization at all. The characters have one look and only change the visuals of their armours and clothes once you change into a more qualified class.The battles are fun, if a bit stale, because skills feel very limited at the start. It would have been nice to start out with a few more. There are also limitations on the battle system, which are probably wanted. Fe. spells and bows only have a very limited range, so you don't have the usual advantages you get in round-based combat with them. I played the game around 3 hours and I had fun, but not so much that I wanted to come back to it, when I have other games with similar combat like fe. Warhamme 40k Chaosgate or Pathfinder.So, if you are a fan of turn-based RPGs and don't mind the restrictions the game has due to being a small indie title, this could be fun for you, but go into this not expecting more than there actually is in the game.

_childDocuments_.review: While I liked this game and I recommend it, I still have a lot of criticisms.First, the pros: I had fun playing it.1) The gameplay was fun. Like Fire Emblem, you find good positions to attack enemy units, you exploit terrain, you level up your units and choose particular skills. I enjoyed making terrain wet, then electrifying it with a lightning spell.2) I didn't find the characters too annoying. In some games, there are characters I just really hate, and you're not meant to hate them. Here, the good guys are discernible from each other. I didn't find them annoying, except sometimes the main character was tooooo happy-go-lucky or something. Oh, there was another character that sometimes disagreed, and while I don't mind disagreeing, the way the game portrays events made the disagreements seem illogical and silly.3) There's a hint of romance, if you're looking for that. They don't go crazy about it, and it just shows up in the end, with a conversation and an epilogue. So it's not intrusive or forced on you, like other romances. And you can have no romance, too.The cons...1) While they've started an interesting setting, they never really dive into it. Like the name Lost Eidolons. I have no idea about the Eidolons, and I could care less. The intro movie talks about a lot of interesting things, but then throughout the game, you can easily forget all that. All this to say, the storytelling is horrible.2) Similarly, the missions or chapters can get repetitive. You may win a battle, but then the story will say you lost and you have to retreat. And you will keep retreating and losing and retreating forever. I get tired when the villain says, "Coward, I'll kill you," and the protagonist says, "Just try," and the protagonist wins the battle but runs away in the story, and the cycle repeats. I feel like my actions have no influence on the story. You win a mission, and the story will still act like you're a loser. ...I guess this is more repetitive story than repetitive missions.3) There are choices, and I think they affect if you become a good guy or bad guy in the end. But the choices are so vague! One time I had a choice between being serious or making a joke or something. I made the choice, and then a message appeared saying something really vague. They never explain the consequences of my choice, and I have no idea if I chose the good or evil route. And again, the choice I made was be serious or make a joke. My choice wasn't execute a prisoner or spare a prisoner. That would be a lot clearer.4) The weapon system is a bit bleh. Supposedly axes have an advantage over heavy armor, and swords have an advantage over light armor, and spears have an advantage over cloth armor. But often, axes were used by light armor people, and swords were used by heavy armor people, and so even if you have an advantage in your attack, their counterattack will have the advantage too. So their weapon and armor advantage system was too... bleh. At least for me, maybe I'm just bad at the game. In the end, I often stopped caring. Now that I think about it, because of the classes that I like, I think I stopped using axes. Bows and arrows, swords, and spells. Those were basically all I used. Sometimes spears.5) Back to the world building and all, there are monsters in the game! And they kinda made a big deal of monsters existing, but it was just another enemy type to me. They don't really go into the story of the monsters. It would be nice to hear about the origins of the monsters. But nope, it's just, "Monsters are here! They're bad." "What, this one group can train monsters? How???" But you never learn how. The world of Lost Eidolons is too shallow!6) The camp part of the game seemed unnecessary. So, there's the battle portion of the game. Then, there's the camp part, where you can talk to people or search questions to find a letter or a thing. But after playing a few hours of the game, I realized, why not just make this a cutscene or list of cutscenes. That would spare me the time of finding random things, finding people to talk to, Despite all the criticism, I enjoyed the game, and put 75 hours into it in just 3 or so weeks. I kept wanting to play more and more, to find out what happened next. But because of the repetitiveness, it was a tough grind. Anyway, if the game is cheap and you're looking for a competent RPG tactics game, try Lost Eidolons out.

_childDocuments_.review: I have mixed feelings about this game...I have a bit over 50 hours now and lost the final battle twice.I guess i know how i can win it, as it was super close the 2nd time and i guess with the next run i would manage. At this stage I missed to reach the top class of the main games character, which would help a bit as well.Anyhow, I am hesitating to replay the final battle or even restart the game and play it on iron mode once more.Why is that?Overall the game in the current mode is too easy except the final battle. The last third of the game is a bit ridiculous as every battle has many enemy "king" units on the field - its managable. After 27 chapters the tactic part overall feels a bit repetetive but still fun tho. What keeps me (currently) away from replaying it, is kind of a very very very repetetive story part...after a while its just got boring for me.It feels like i was listening/reading the story part up to chapters 16 to 18 (or so)...after that i mostly skipped all talks as it does not change anything on the progress in the story. Its just to grab rewards. There are almost no relevant decisions to make, and the decisions has minimal to no effect on the story progression. It also doesn't require any thinking, following the story or decision to complete a quest, each quest is just a simple series of cutscenes and talks. This was fun for a while...but as you can't fail the quest, there is no challenge or replay motivation at all. THe prestige quests could be fun but are not - god rewards tho. Same counts for the optional battles. Its only few variants at the beginning, after a while its just the exact same battles as before, What disturbs me most - as it is a predefined progress and storyline - some of those battles were designed to be close and hard to win, so the story tells you that you were broken, almost died and so on ...this felt odd as I dominated most of those battkes, killed the enemies in a minimum amount of rounds and survived often barely touched with all units. So the battle results and the story progress were a complete (felt) mismatch. I normally don't care, but i often was like.."wtf, that's not what i experienced in the battle". In the overall campaign the economics seems not to matter, i always had enough cash to buy what i needed and still had always enough to buy more than required. The story told me often that I am broken and times are difficult....the situation itself doesn't felt like. Overall it's a solid game with a good foundation for a great game - some more relevance of choices (or better: any choices at all) which impact the campaign required, It would be fun to have impact on the grand strategy but you have none....the 27 chapters happen, regardless if you like it or not.  The grafics are good for such kind of games and nothing to complain about. The voice acting is weird, especially for everything which isn't related to the main story...it's just "uff, aehm, oh" noises....plus reading the lines. It's ok, as story doesn't matter :-)Gift system is a nice touch, and the only choices in the game you make (who will be a friend, who not). Anyhow. overall its a good game and entertaining for a good amount of time. If you can live with the above mentioned its a nice buy. If you need more than that, probably not for you.

Different facial structures, blemishes, scars, birthmarks, freckles, bumps in the skin. All tailored to the individual. The voice acting is pretty damn good. The fights do a good job of mixing up battle strategies from fight to fight. The combat is pretty easy to get a hang of and I had a lot of fun playing the game. _childDocuments_.review: I intend to go in-depth on my feelings about Lost Eidolons, but for those who are short on time or attention, here is the short version: Lost Eidolons is a capable strategy RPG with strong character writing, a grounded world, a comprehensible story, and gameplay that runs the gamut from decent to exceptional. It is a worthy entry to the genre, and something I would recommend to those familiar with Fire Emblem, Dark Deity, and similar. It has weaknesses, but overall if it's objective was to create a fun and engaging western take on the genre, it succeeded and then some. It is not merely "western Fire Emblem," It is a good game on its own merits. I played on normal difficulty, casual deaths (characters can die without being lost forever), and limited turns. I will occasionally be using Fire Emblem as a point of reference as well. There will be minor spoilers, and I will warn when they are about to appear.PresentationLost Eidolons is a time capsule to the early 2000s, when color was out of fashion and brown was in. The game's washed out color palate and battlefields are straight out of the Somme. Animations are functional but unimpressive and character scenes are still images of 3D characters posing at each other as they talk. Armor and character designs are generic western fantasy but fit well with the world and tone. Voice acting is present but reserved for plot events and quests. These things might turn people away from the game, and its horribly tragic if they do because the game demonstrates remarkable presentation otherwise. The music is solid and fits the context well, the voice acting has some phenomenal performances, and the still-art narrations are beautiful. It makes me wish they had cut out the 3D scenes entirely for art and voice overs because when present both are gorgeous. Strategy GameplayGameplay in Lost Eidolons has several substantial departures from other games in the genre. The most interesting of these are environmental interactions. Elemental mages and some special attacks can manipulate terrain. Bushes can be set on fire, wet enemies can freeze, wind can spread fire and remove clouds of poison, etc. Most classes also have special abilities like taunting, pulling, or marking targets for more damage. A clever player will be rewarded for using all the tools in their box so battles remain engaging throughout, even when concepts like attacking a castle are reused. Unfortunately the map design sometimes lets the concept down. Aggressive objectives and a 10 unit max in small battles makes fast damage and recovery a priority. Delaying tactics, traps, or DOT effects are undesirable because it is faster, more effective, and more rewarding to maximize damage and speed on 80% of maps. The remaining 20% are where Lost Eidolons truly shines, when the battles get larger and longer, and resource management is more important. Lost Eidolons also has issues balancing maps and objectives. This is partially due to the generous undo-turn system but it is mostly because the game never hits you hard enough or fast enough to make you sweat for more than a turn or two.  It undermines the tension of an escape sequence when I have slaughtered the forces I was supposed to be running from. Despite these lapses, the average experience is positive, and in the moments where Lost Eidolons hits its stride mechanically, it is some of the best TRPG gameplay I've had in a while. CharactersLost Eidolons' greatest achievements and tragedies are in its characters. With few exceptions, the writing and acting of the major characters is great. At first glance, Francisco appears to be the usual buff fighter guy, but he has many layers beyond that. Loyal to his friends and home, frustration and anger he channels into his songs and poetry, fear for others and of himself and how he's changing, and so much more. He is wonderful, and he sets the standard for characters in the game. The protagonist Eden goes through a good arc and is a great character in his own right. There are a few misses mixed in with the hits, but the character writing overall is fantastic. Which is why it sucks that most players won't ever see most of it! Much of the depths to these characters is locked behind Lost Eidolon's equivalent to the support system. You have a finite amount of Leadership to spend having conversations with and giving gifts to your favored characters. Talk/give enough, and you get a new support conversation with the character, a buff for them in battle, and sometimes extra stuff. You don't get enough money, gifts, or leadership to max more than maybe 6-7 people out of a cast of around 25. The only way around this is either replaying the game, or editing save files. I freely admit that I cheated in more gifts and gold to max everyone, and I feel I would have missed out severely if I hadn't. Despite this restriction, I still believe that the character writing of Lost Eidolons is its greatest achievement, and is excellent on its own merits. StoryLost Eidolons has strong character writing, but weak storytelling. The first half of the game has a cohesive plot that makes sense and does what it needs to do. The second half of the game mostly works, but had significant issues. Spoilers ahead.The issue is two-fold: indirect storytelling, and weak antagonists. Lost Eidolons has a serious problem of major plot events occurring off screen and relayed to you through narration afterwards. In one case "a legendary battle erupted, rocking the foundations of Artemesia itself." This event ended major characters, changed the course of the plot, was described as awesome, and neither Eden nor the player was in any way involved. Its hard to feel like a protagonist when the plot happens without you. The player can reasonably ask "why couldn't I *fight* the legendary battle, instead of being told about it?" This happens regularly, to the point where one of the major antagonists literally dies in a basement and is never mentioned again. The ending is also abrupt and lacks closure on multiple plot threads and many characters. *EDIT* A recent patch added in epilogues for the playable characters. This is a massive improvement, but still leaves threads dangling. The other problem is the Big Bad. Spoilers ahead.Balastar is a fantastic concept for a villain. The game tells you that Balastar is going to turn on you in the prologue, and because the twist is told to you immediately, it becomes a kind of mystery about how we get to that point. This is further supported because his team of named characters are supposed to be foils to the major characters following Eden. The end result should be what the plot presents: two diametrically opposed protagonist characters with their own loyal teams of followers. In theory, this is what you get. In practice, you don't have enough opportunity to get to know Balastar or his team so the foil element goes nowhere, and several are killed/captured off screen anyway. Balastar comes across as a paranoid loon that only got as a far as he did through universal incompetence. You hate him because he's frustrating, inconsistent, and bends reality, not because he's evil or opposes Eden. Worst of all, he makes Eden look worse by association.Their conflict is a narrative circle based on a false premise and subsequent revenge attempts. It speaks volumes to the strength of the main cast that this didn't kill the narrative.Overall, I do like Lost Eidolons, and hope to see this game thrive. I also hope that when they make the next game, they'll learn from the missteps, and refine the brilliant gem of character, art and gameplay that can be seen through the rough.

_childDocuments_.review: The main gameplay is decent and fun most of the time, especially if you like tactical rpgs. There are a wide variety classes and skills to choose from when building your characters and several maps come with their own unique objectives that provide a different way to overcome the increasing challenges you'll come across. Once you've finished the game, you get a very extensive selection of progress to carry over with ODS's recently added NG+ mode.The side gameplay involves running around the camp doing fetch quests, delivering messages, sitting through a stupidly long and unnecessary slide show of all the classes your characters have unlocked, and reading/listening to a bunch of boring exposition dumps. It quickly becomes tedious and although most of it is optional, you'll lose out on helpful rewards if you choose not to suffer. One of the only great features of the camp is the ability to slap whichever one of your characters is pissing you off at the moment via a sparring match.The story is generic as many major plot points are predictable. Something being generic doesn't automatically mean it's bad and I actually think it's fine for this game, but my main gripe is that the story is also somewhat lacking in details, to the point where the game never bothers to tell you why things are happening in the first place. Some plot points have little payoff and some go absolutely nowhere at all. And across the entire plot will be many characters you'll want to strangle, both friend and foe. I don't think I've ever wanted to real life slap so many fictional characters from a single game before in my entire gaming experience. Honestly, the story is best enjoyed if you don't take it too seriously and maybe laugh a lot on the way.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid first effort in the genre. Fire Emblem in a new setting feels pretty refreshing honestly. The voice acting is surprisingly good, and I'm enjoying the characters so far. I don't echo the sentiment that the game is poorly written, this is classic fantasy writing. Character models are top notch, even though they don't emote at all in cutscenes, honestly I really like the look of this game. The UX is pretty good during combat as well. The gameplay is structurally extremely reminiscent of Fire Emblem Three Houses, even including a monastery stand in between battles. Combat is very similar as well, but new mechanics freshen up the experience, notably a different and tactically interesting take on large enemies/monsters, a unit's presence blocking movement through surrounding tiles, and a weapon vs armor weakness system that both allows whacky things like tanky mages and also mixes up your offensive tactics quite a bit. It's a cool twist on the formula, and I can't wait to see more in the dev's next game. The class system feels like it's a bit too simple though, but maybe I haven't fully grasped it yet, and I wish the devs would pick permadeath or not and balance the game around that choice, or at least make it clear what the default choice is supposed to be. As it is now, with permadeath on there's a lot of spamming the rewind mechanic, which, while also in Three Houses, was not the most compelling part of that game in my opinion. I'm not convinced the game should even have that option if enemy aggro is this unpredictable. _childDocuments_.review: Lost Eidolons was a real surprise treat for me. I only heard of this game after it got a video preview from my favorite Fire Emblem content creator (shout-out to Ghast!) and I was not disappointed when I gave it a shot. Being the dev's first game, its definitely got some blemishes, but the heart that they poured into it more than makes up for them.- The tactical combat is a delight. With varied classes, environmental/elemental effects, interesting scenario design, and balanced difficulty, every chapter felt like a certified strategic accomplishment.- The writing when at its best is phenomenal. With a fairly large cast, some are bound to stand out more than others, but no one felt like fodder. They all bring something unique and endearing to your camp. Some of my favorite writing actually comes from notes that party members will leave around the camp, letting you in on some part of their character that they weren't yet willing to share with you in person.- The voice acting is similarly fantastic. You'll hear familiar voices from games like Fire Emblem: Three Houses, Persona 5, Sonic the Hedgehog, and Genshin Impact. The performances are all consistently good.- The game is DENSE. Between camp objectives and the typical tactical gameplay, there's a lot to sink your teeth into. If you're looking for something that will last you dozens of hours, look no further.- I also enjoyed the meaningful rapport system. You can give gifts to your units to increase their relationship with you and even do camp activities like eat and train together. These activities often provide some relatively lengthy conversations that serve to supplement the already well-executed support conversations. Rapport also feels even more meaningful when they unlock unique items, quests, features, and (rarely) unique plot occurrences.- Unit progression harkens to Fire Emblem Three Houses as characters promote based on the conditional of a level and an equipment mastery requirement (usually one weapon and one armor). There are few restrictions and the requirements are all laid out from the beginning of the game, so you can freely plan your army however you'd like.- The presentation leaves a bit to be desired. While serviceable, the game can get grating to look at. Animations are stiff during dialog, frames will drop during menu navigation and camp exploration, and facial animations will almost never convey even an ounce of emotion.- While I enjoyed the non-essential camp quests, they could benefit from more variety. They often involve little more than fast traveling to the objective marker on your map. In my opinion, though, the writing usually makes up for the monotony. *VAGUE SPOILERS START HERE*- The pace of the late game can be a slog. All of these maps involve a confrontation with the main antagonist which usually results in you fleeing to an objective. In all scenarios, though, you're fighting the same named characters. You usually end up fighting the less important ones and defeating them, just for them to show up again in the next chapter like nothing happened. While the scenario design kept each encounter fresh, there was too much dissonance with with repetitive boss encounters.- The plot similarly suffers at this point. The late game follows a predictable pattern of the big bad hounding the player's army, they concoct a clever scheme (with varying degrees of success) to escape, drama ensues, then rinse and repeat until the final chapter. The main antagonist's lieutenants are unfortunately downgraded to one-note repeatable bosses. I feel like it would have been much more effective to have one or two of those names characters lead the fight against the player by themselves in these chapters. This could lead to a better examination of those characters and their feelings about the conflict, why they remain loyal to the bad guy, etc. This is one of my favorite things in Fire Emblem (i.e. the Camus archetype, or good people who end up on the wrong side of the war), and it's sadly missing here.*VAGUE SPOILERS END HERE*- While I would otherwise praise the unit progression, there is a long stretch during the mid game where not much is changing with your units.- Many of my criticisms have a common theme of being a symptom of the game's length. A lot of players see a long runtime as a positive in and of itself, and while I admit that MOST of what the game fills itself with is good, I believe they could have benefited by shaving off a couple of late-game chapters in lieu of its repetitive boss encounters.It's worth noting that the devs have built up a lot of good-will with their fans as they've accepted much critical feedback from them and have already implemented some much-anticipated changes. Some of those changes even directly address a few of my criticisms, like the cutscene presentation and overall stability! We love to see dedicated devs!There's a lot more to dig into, but I feel like everything can be summed up by saying that Lost Eidolons is a fantastic tactical RPG that sometimes suffers under the weight of its dev's ambition. If it were just a few chapters shorter, many of the late-game grievances could be cleaned up and the dev's brilliant vision for a gritty take on the Fire Emblem formula would be able to shine even brighter than it already does in spite of those shortcomings. The devs got so much right with their first attempt despite some rookie mistakes. Nevertheless, Lost Eidolons has made a huge fan out of me.

_childDocuments_.review: Awesome game over all. The story is great the the characters have personality. _childDocuments_.review: For a first game, I found this to be a very solid start from Ocean Drive Studio.  I would recommend this game to anyone that enjoys games similar to Fire Emblem.Story:  I enjoyed the story segments of the game quite a bit.  - The story is linear, however, I felt engaged the entire way through the game.  - With the limited opportunities to gain rapport with the various characters in the game (some recruited and others joining during the story automatically), I felt like I was missing story and context relating to certain (mainly side) characters.              On the flip side, it will give me a reason (other than DLC) to explore other characters' side stories in             future playthroughs of the game.Graphics and character design:  I really like the graphics in the game.  - Sometimes animations weren't the greatest, however, it didn't detract from the visuals or the story for me.  - I appreciated how the characters and the class armors look in the game.Combat:  Grid-based and turn-based SRPG in the vein of Fire Emblem.  I greatly enjoyed playing through the missions for the main story.  - Side missions are mostly the same variation on 3 different enemy configurations, however, that didn't bother me too much in my playthrough.  - The mid-battle save, undo (rewind back to a previous character's turn), and ability to skip enemy and allied turns was helpful in the larger battles when I didn't want to sit through 2-4 minutes of enemies and allies taking their turns.  - Early reviewers mentioned turn limits: I didn't lose a single battle by exceeding the turn limit on normal + maniac.  This was with me taking things cautiously and slowly in battles.Overall I would recommend giving this game a try if you like tactics or SRPG games that are similar to Fire Emblem.Edit:  I also wanted to share my appreciation for the developer's post-launch support and responsiveness in addressing feedback.Edit 2:  I appreciate the New Game Plus that was added and will explore that feature in a future playthrough.

_childDocuments_.review: Overall I think this is a very good game, but there are a few things that keep it from being great. ProsThe characters are almost all well written. Even some of the side characters that you can recruit are fleshed out and you feel a connection to them. The way you can equip different spells on your mages based on their book which gives a great deal of customization to mages especially. you can have two different dark mages that do two very different things with one focusing on damage and another focusing on control and zoning. This is really well done.Even martial classes have a decent amount of customization based on the class they have allowing them a different level of skills. If you want you can swap some classes every mission to best suit what the level calls forThe overall story of the game in engaging and a lot of fun to go through. I do think it looses it in the final few chapters, but for the vast majority of the game it's excellent. The mission variety is pretty good. They only have a few different kinds of missions, but they do a good job dressing it up in different ways.ConsThe later stages of the game throw in some cheapness for added difficulty. Enemies that spawn in random locations that don't make sense story wise, and massive meat shields (Even casters) who take way too many hits from their "Counters" to be considered fair. The main story goes off the rails for no good reason. The game is like "Persons X just won this great battle" but how or why is never explained. Also there are too many "You won, but actually lost" missions. The in between missions while optional are needed for leveling are terribly boring there are like 4 differnet kinds and after the 1st time it sucks. Finial Grade B. I got almost 50 hours through my first play-through enjoyed the vast majority of it It's a solid tactics games and if you're looking for something to tide you over until the next Fire Emblem or a not as anime take on the genre this is a very solid purchase even at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT:While I still give the game a thumbs up it come with a really BIG caveat.The game has issues with overheating your gpu. The game will really work your gpu out during cut scenes. And some cut scenes can go on for ages.This is currently being reported by more players but at least the devs have stated that they will look into the issue.For this reason alone I would suggest holding off buying the game for now. Oh, and don't think having a high end gpu will help, as it is happening with those as well.Original review:A story focused turn based tactical rpg. Good points: Save mid battle (handy when the misses says "oh it's Aunty Mavis... come here and say hello"). You can pre move your characters to see if the attack you intend to do will actually work and if it doesn't just right click back to the beginning of your move.... oh I love that.Even if you do something totally dumb (like calling Aunty Mavis, Aunty Mary) you can just undo all those past moves and try again with no penalty.You can swap weapons with no penalty to see what damage they will do, and even swap them back again, and again, and... you get the idea.... with no penalty or lost movement points or whatever.The graphics are great (I am old though so my eyes are not what they used to be) and the combat sound effects are nice and thumpy when they need to be.The combat is what is to be expected for turn based tactical stuff, but there is no overwatch (oh I miss thee) but various land situations can be exploited.... wet areas can expand electricity attacks type thingy...... I think there was a Divinity type game that started that sort of stuff?Tactical combat is a joy to play. There is a bit of a learning curve with all the in and outs sorta stuff of character builds and the tutorial is somewhat lacking, but that's where Youtube actually comes in handy.Voice acting is for the most part above well above average and really helps you get interested in the characters, which is really a relief as there is quite a lot of dialogue in this game. Thankfully the story is worth listening to.Now the not so great stuff:The UI is somewhat clunky in places... not hopelessly clunky.... but clunky none the less. You want to see if you have the required mastery skill level for becoming a class you want?Go to the skill tree menu, check the mastery requirements. Then go to your character menu and select stats. Then see if you have the mastery level required. Make sure you remember what requirement is needed from the skill tree. Why couldn't you just tell me in the skill tree whether I meet the requirements... huh, well?Actually, that's the only negative I have with the UI.... the rest works a treat.The cut-scenes can really give your GPU a solid work out. My GTX 1660 super was getting smoking hot on Ultra settings. I had to lower down to Medium to get a respectable simmer temp. A shame that the game offers no separate graphic settings for cut-scenes, because the combat battles look great at ultra settings. To be honest after playing for some 52 hours at the time of this review I have no real issues with the game. The battles have been fun and not too difficult (Disclaimer.... I am a wuss so I'm playing on Normal/ Casual (ugh I hate that wording) but at least I have the turn limits option on, so there.Summary: Lost Eidolons is a turn based tactical rpg that should tick all the boxes for fans of the genre. The combat is fun to play and requires a good amount of tactical thinking. There is no RNG nonsense here either. You will hit the enemy, when you expect to.... unless their guard is very high which will lower your damage and..... well other things can come into play but basically you will hit every time.There is also a good story to follow, which a lot of these games tend to ignore.It's worth it's asking price and deserves more recognition. I give this a 4 Schooner rating.

_childDocuments_.review: I discovered this game through Angry Joe's video! It looked really good and I was really addicted to Fire Emblem: Three Houses at the time, so I decided I was buying the game. Luckily, the game released the same day AJ's video came out!Overall is this a good game? Yes! I'd recommend it for tactical RPG fans, especially if you played recent Fire Emblem games. It almost feels like a love letter to the Fire Emblem-style gameplay with how much features mirror FE, primarily Three Houses. You can even walk around camp and deepen your bond with your companions! There's various ranks/classes to assign your character, and combat is what you'd expect! What separates Lost Eidolons from Fire Emblem is the usability of terrain to your advantage. If you've played the Divinity Original Sin games, you know what I mean. You can set fire to bushes/trees and whoever's standing there would get damaged every turn. If the enemy is standing on water, you can use a frozen attack to freeze them or use lightning to damage whoever's standing adjacent to them.The story is good! Nothing outstanding, but I feel after playing this game, you'll be satisfied with the narrative. It's a pretty standard medieval fantasy war story but not too cliche that it's entirely predictable. You'll come across various characters that you can recruit and are also crucial to the main story. If you can use 10 characters in battle, perhaps about 14 of the recruitable characters are part of the main storyline, while everyone else is a random recruitable character that shows up in camp. And there are a bunch of them! Now there are some characters that will permanently die in the storyline. And you can only get back the equipment of one of them, due to the story letting you keep their remains. However for the other deaths, you're screwed. And I can't spoil who dies, so be careful with who you assign OP equipment and horses too. Now will you care about the characters? Maybe. Some characters are likeable, the others are pretty meh. The deaths are sad, but they don't really hit you in the feels except for one of them. I was pretty meh about one of the deaths, and another happens off-screen so that kinda sucked.Other negatives I can list down are- Characters dying off screen. Some of them seem like a big deal but they suddenly get killed off- Game can get pretty glitchy at times. The primary glitch I encountered was not being able to click on characters during battle, so I couldn't move anyone. Luckily those all happen at the start of combat, and autosave always lets you reload the beginning of the battle.- There is a turn limit on the game. If you exceed a number of turns, you'll fail. I feel like this is a dumb feature to have, especially if you're playing on harder difficulties. Luckily, the game now has a feature to turn that off. Though I do not know if you can do that on hard difficulty.- Maniac mode(permadeath when a character gets beat in combat) is useless in my opinion. Unless you want to get the achievement, don't play in this mode. I assumed this would be like Fire Emblem where the units really do die, but they still show up in camp to talk to. Kinda took out the immersion out of me when I purposely sacrificed units to save the main character in some missions.All in all I can say this game is worth the purchase! Buy this game if you like tactical RPG's and sinking 30+ hours in a campaign!

_childDocuments_.review: If you like fire emblem three houses and can't wait for fire emblem engage/tactics ogre, you may like this game as it is a very good alternative for it at the moment. But there are some issues with it currently.Story: The story is pretty good for the first part, good build up of the characters and meeting of new characters/setting/world/lore. The latter part of the game leaves me scratching my head as it starts to feel like the devs are trying to prolong the story for no reason. Support/Rapport: Pretty much like fire emblem three houses. You spend prestige to drink/eat/train with characters that you want to build rapport with. You can also buy gifts for them. If you want to recruit characters, you need to build rapport with them before they leave your camp forever. Unlocking some of the character's tiers gives their side quest and items. But not all character has them.Combat: Combat is pretty much fire emblem-ish. You can select an aide to assign to the character and change their jobs/class once you unlocked their requirements. You can change their weapons/armour to level up their mastery in them. One downside of this is the mechanic that if any enemy "boss" character is near an enemy troop they are literally invincible. This is a really dumb mechanic and shouldn't be in there at all. In one chapter when I was blocking the entry way with my vanguard/templar with sharpshooter/sorcerer/dark wiz killing any troops that comes. But once the "boss" type character approaches with their troops behind unable to target at due to range, I am literally stucked there with unable to deal more than 5 damage to the boss type enemies.Also for horses, they are limited to 4 only. I don't know why this is a thing but I think the devs should just go ham and let us have horses for all 10 characters if need be.BGM/OST: The tracks are pretty tame and mild and also pretty much lackluster and unnoticeable aside 1 or 2 tracks. Unlike Fire emblem three houses, fodland winds, god shattering star, the apex of the world and some other tracks will stick in your head.Difficulty balance: Neither here nor there, very bad on some chapter very easy on some others. The difficulty spike starts from chapter 17 and it feels like the QA/devs didn't have much time to play test and balance this for the difficulty settings. I have to turn down my difficulty from normal to story mode because I neglected some character's growth and still some later chapter annoys me to no end. There is even a chapter that tells you to do A but by doing A you literally cannot win the game because of the dumb mechanic as stated in the combat above.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid entry in the turn based tactics genre.  It's a budget game, and you can tell at times but still a good experience, considering this is the first game from this developer.  The game is fairly linear, and there is a ton of dialogue & cutscenes but the voice acting is surprisingly good, as is the music.  This is basically a budget version of Fire Emblem.  The developers are very active within the community are are consistently listening to player feedback and implementing appropriate changes.   8/10 - worth the $35 price tag.

_childDocuments_.review: I saw this game and was interested to give it a shot, without having many expectation. I was surprised by the interesting gameplay and an intriguing story. The first chapters explained the games but it's a bit after that the story become more interesting. The characters are well designed though I would like to have a bit more freedom in customization. That would have make me feel even more involved with them. I feel there's a lot of cool classes for everyone, except for those light and dark magic user. The option for permadeath is very cool, making your combats more meaningfull. The AI choice are very good and keep you on your guard. Mistakes could be painfull. I also like the music a lot. To become a real AAA game in my eyes: More customization, better romance options and some choice that could make the story going into differents directions (pretty linear right now). As for now, the studio is communicating well with his players and we really do feel like we're  getting on board with them and that is why I take time to write this review. Final recommandation : A solid game very fun to play who could become a very great game in a near future.

_childDocuments_.review: Solid story driven puzzle game.  However if you looking for a engaging, in depth turn based tactical then you will be disappointed.  The great graphics and voiced dialogue keep you interested in most of the story and rapport systems, though on my first playthrough the rapport did seem to be a bit lacking in terms of actual content.  I was pleasantly surprised by just how long the story ended up being.  The undo/restart buttons are amazing, especially going through on Hard/Permadeath difficulty.  The class armor is incredible and you really feel a sense of progression through them.  The UI and combat are snappy and tooltips are well done.  The other reviews mentioning turn limits are not accurate. I cleared the map on all but one of the missions that force you to fail/run away within the turn limits.  They are a non factor and I'm sure only exist to give a semblance of time pressure.------Extremely linear systems starting at the story and including classes, gear, stats, combat, camp activities, and even the abilities basically top out around 1/4 through the game.ALL units take two shots to kill, including yours.  There are exceptions in the case of 1 and 3 shots, but it always comes back to one rounding the enemy wave, especially ranged enemies.  And yes you will be undoing turns constantly where one of your units got focused by TWO attacks.  I stopped trying to make a tank viable half way through the game and ran all ranged damage dealers. Which is possible since you receive effectively duplicate characters as you progress.  There is very little to actually macro manage outside of combat which is where a lot of the enjoyment in turn based games comes from.  All the characters that share classes are nearly identical in stats, have the same abilities(based on class) and perform almost the exact same.  Gear is completely linear with VERY slight stat increases with tier progression.  There is also a Crit chance vs crit defense and accuracy vs guard system that cancel eachother out.  So for example my assassin(Andrea bae) with full crit set up and dual swords(two attacks) will see a critical hit about 10-20% of the time...which is awful.  If you want a turn based game that plays more as a puzzle than a combat grinder with great graphics and story then I recommend Lost Eidolons.  Perhaps in future updates or mods we will see health of units doubled and stats more relevant, among other things, but for now its been a decent playthrough with no plans of a seeing another run.

_childDocuments_.review: A fantastic game from a new developer, I'm assuming, because their webpage gives no hint of having worked on any other titles. Extremely well done strategy/tactical turn based rpg with all the right little additives to make it highly entertaining most times. The "gripping cinematic narrative", as described on their page, is hit or miss sometimes. Sometimes the narrative is fairly great. Other times it can take minutes to get through absolute drudgery concerning nothing of meaning. Still, it is well done. The character models are excellent. Weapons, armors, etc, all look amazing. Lip synching is shoddy most of the time but isn't the worst I've ever seen. Music is standard fare for this type of genre but it does have some great moments. Where the game really shines is the combat though. I've played about 80-85% of all the "great" and some not so great strategy/tactical rpgs. The combat really does have a "cinematic" approach to it and it is really, really fun to play through chapter after chapter. Leveling up your squad, getting new gear, learning new spells, etc. I don't recall ever seeing this kind of approach to combat in a turn based game before and it's refreshing on a whole other level I wasn't aware I needed. Quite fun and unexpected. I do get some jitters sometimes during these moments and even with Vsync turned on it doesn't seem to dissipate the effect of some kind of screen tearing happening at times or these weird jitters than can occur every once in a while. Hopefully the devs can patch in a fix of some kind soon. My only real gripes with the game are, to me, what seems like a ridiculous amount of time you take in between battles concerning yourself with others in camp at times. "Quests" are sometimes absolutely meaningless in nature and yet you get experience for them so a win I guess? It does get a LOT better the further you get into the game as the systems open up for you and you find yourself looking to do more to increase your odds of winning in battles, etc. Still, some of them are a chore at times. I find that the devs included fast travel to get to people in the camp a solid win against drudgery though so you can finish these "quests" fairly quickly later on. My last gripe is the that "loot" seems to be fairly stingy in this game. I'm at Chapter 5 or 6 right now and I think I've discovered a set of armor, a ring or amulet and a sword. That's it. Oh, and some money. Money never hurts. Still, besides buying some potions, items to use during battles, I've found absolutely no reason to really go spending my money. I'm hoping it gets better as the game progresses. Also, I should note that as your characters raise their level they can raise their class and BOOM they get new armor. Nice, but I'd have preferred to kit out my soldiers myself. It's hard to put my finger on where this game would fit in this genre. It's somewhere betwen M&M VII and, maybe, King's Bounty 2, except much better than KB2 in all the right ways. I've NOT finished this game but I find myself wanting to which says a lot. Battles can be harder depending on your difficulty, obviously, but a lot of the enemies don't hold back on you so come prepared, make sure you potioned up and make sure to use the "swap weapon" FREE ability during battles if needed. There's a lot more I'm not really going to go into but rest assured they've done a LOT more than I've discussed here. A solid 8/10 for me because I'm having a lot of fun with the game and I haven't been bored to tears, frustrated with bugs or had any crashes and the story is really interesting so far as to what's happening. Can't wait to finish it.

_childDocuments_.review: This is my review after finishing the game on Hard/Maniac deathless. The game's kind of a mixed bag and I found myself getting more and more frustrated in the third act due to a combination of story and gameplay problems. However, I had a good time with the game overall and can still recommend it with some heavy caveats. I'm gonna type 'til I hit the word cap cuz I have a lot to say. Not gonna talk about the presentation: it's mixed but leans towards good. Facial animation is awful.Story:Starts out meh, the middle act is pretty engaging, and the last act is rushed and unsatisfying. It starts as a pretty typical "mercs join a rebel cause", but there's enough surprising stuff that happens along the way and just enough of a semblance of grand strategy to make it enjoyable enough to go through. Characters actively worry about supplies and morale along the way, and it takes multiple battles for the characters to get to their goal. However, this starts falling apart by the final act. If I had to compare it with something, it would be the last two seasons of Game of Thrones. Armies start moving across the country in record time, being able to bypass enemy armies completely in the blink of an eye. Characters make dumb choices specifically to heighten drama and start arguing with each other over very little, with only one of these characters having a story reason to be acting strange. Armies suffer devastating defeat after defeat in the story due to said dumb choices and yet still retain enough strength to split up and have both armies still be capable of fending off the army that just finished stomping them. A ton of characters are introduced and dropped almost immediately in the last act, and there's a lot more cutscenes where the narrator covers a series of important events in a sentence or two so we can get on with the story. In the first two acts, these events would be playable. Not in the final act.The part that annoys me the most is the titular Eidolons. Frankly speaking, they don't contribute anything important to the story. They exist as a Deus Ex Machina superpower and an artificial way of forcing characters along their arcs. Characters:I think this game does characters better than Fire Emblem. On the surface, there are less conversations to have with characters, since there are only three support levels as opposed to Fire Emblem's max of five. However, they make up for this significantly by having much deeper ambient conversations. After every chapter, a good chunk of characters will have something to say about recent story events, and they all have their own attitude towards things. Hanging out with the characters, which is the equivalent to Three House's tea time, has you being able to talk to them about a bunch of topics. Whereas in Tea Time, they will only give you one line of dialogue, this game has full blown conversations about their topics. This all comes together beautifully and lets each character shine.I didn't like the main character for a good chunk of time, but he grew on me by the end. He seems like just a typical nice guy, but he's just relatably snarky and snappy enough for me to enjoy his interactions with the cast.Gameplay:  I like two of the things this game adds to the Fire Emblem formula: Zone of Control and the weapon-armor advantage. Zone of Control means that every unit will stop enemies from moving past the square that's adjacent to them, making formations much more impactful than they are in Fire Emblem and actually giving a purpose to tanky frontliners. This will also change how you approach fights, as you can identify that mage in the back as a major threat and you have someone that can reach them, but you also have to find a way to clear a route through all the enemy front liners to actually reach that mage.The weapon-armor advantage is a replacement for the weapon triangle. Spears and bows are good against cloth armor, swords are good against medium armor, and axes are good against heavy armor. This also adds more tactical depth to the fights, as you now have to be conscious of just slapping plate armor on everybody. Axe enemies can and will shred through you if you try to rely on heavy armor all the time.What I'm meh towards: the turn limit, monsters, and the elemental combos. The turn limit is barely a factor. I never even got close to hitting the limit, so I have zero opinions towards it. The monster fights are somewhat interesting. Monsters all have weak points that are also weak to specific attacks. If you hit anything other than these points with their weakness, you'd be doing chip damage. The problem is their weaknesses change every turn, which is extremely frustrating as there's no way to prep for that.The elemental combos are meh. Fire burns wood, fire makes poison explode, lightning does chain damage and bonus damage to wet enemies, and ice freezes wet enemies. My main issue is how fire is the odd one out here. You have to pray the enemies move into the woods, or use poison, of which only one class has access to (and it doesn't even do much damage). The enemy being wet is extremely important, but actually setting it up is usually not worth the turn, so you have to pray they stand in a puddle. It's nice when you can hit it, but meh.What I really don't like is the class system and the boss design. The class system looks like it has a lot of depth, but it ends up extremely dry. Whereas Fire Emblem has awesome (and frankly broken) capstone abilities like Galeforce, this game has...a one-use 3x3 spell that does decent damage. Or the ability to be more accurate when hitting axe wielders. Or move an ally a square ahead. Useful, but boring. The stat+ skills in Fire Emblem that you swap out for more interesting stuff in the late game are some of the best skills in this game even towards the end.And unlike Fire Emblem, it doesn't matter what character is in a class. They function pretty much identically. In Fire Emblem, you will notice if you assign a mage as a physical damage dealer, or notice the crap spellbooks physical aligned characters get if you try to force them into being a spellcaster. Not in this game. Everyone is basically the same.My biggest problem is how long you're stuck in the intermediate classes. You unlock them at chapter 6 and get advanced classes at chapter 17. I had the stats to get into the advanced classes by chapter 10. So now, I could diversify my classes, right? I found there was very little point in that. The things you learn in a class tends to only be useful for that category of classes. Why would I want to multiclass to learn diagonal spear attacks when the character is an axe user? Or multiclass into a different class of mages when I can only use one school of magic at a time anyways?And the boss design, my god. Bosses take minimal damage if any of the generics are in range, which is realistically all the time. This is on top of a 40% damage decrease if any of their allies are in range. You will do under 5-7 damage even into the endgame, which is a poor use of your action economy (duh). This was fine in the first two acts. CC the boss, clear out the generics, and then kill boss.The final act, however, will throw waves upon waves of enemies with bosses at you. You will regularly have to contend with at least two bosses side by side, accompanied by six generics. This is where it starts falling apart. All of these bosses are incredibly strong already, with them able to do 3/4 of your tanky unit's health on their own. Now, there are 2-4 of them, all with 40% damage reduction because they trigger each other's damage decrease, meaning you will never do normal damage to them. And this is on top of having a large group of generics that can all kill your units in 2-3 attacks and you have less actions to kill them because you need to keep the bosses locked down. And once you manage to beat them, there's two more identical groups after that. Infuriating.
