_childDocuments_.review: Twenty years ago, when everybody and their dog was hot on the heels of  and ,  did something new. It combined the base-building aspect of real-time strategy with the action of isometric RPGs, tipping the design scales closer to the latter. While it had nothing to do with Blizzard's heavy hitters,  was like a peanut butter cup of both. But seeing how, unlike in the early 2000s, turn-based games seem to get people going these days, THQ Nordic hedged their bets by taking a different turn to their genre hybrid.Set after the events of the third but before the original game,  is, in effect, a sequel to the prequel taking place after the Circle of Mages—a covenant of the most powerful magi on Eo—was established, but before they managed to shatter the world into loosely connected bits, and chainmail bikini was agreed upon as the required uniform for the resident female warriors.In the beginning, you are but a humble apprentice flocking to your master’s side only to find his tower in ruins and himself in the embrace of an untimely death. Armed with your wits, your master's magical hits, and an unshakeable grit to figure out what happened, you set about researching the secrets of the Allspark—sorry, Allfire—to carry on his legacy and establish your credentials as the hottest thing to hit the magic circuit since white rabbits. is less narrative-driven than its more RPG-like predecessors, and although the side content might be rather simplistic, it'll hold you tightly throughout with its writing. Some of those are simple affairs like attacking a roving group of goblins or leaving them alone, but others have moral choices that require you to weigh up risks and rewards. Nonetheless, everything you'll be reading here is of a kind that immediately paints a clear picture of the author's vision in your head. All quests and quandaries are text-based, yet they feel far more visual than dozens of movies can ever be.But before you set out on your journey, you'll need to choose just what kind of wizard you are. Alchemist, Necromancer, and Artificer are the archetypes that determine your approach to crafting and the schools of magic, such as death, enchantment, mentalism, nature, and so on. Want to enchant your way to customization? You're free to mix and match with the available options, too.On my first run, I opted for Necromancer because it seemed evil and macabre. Its strengths lay in raising minions from fallen foes and toying with the powers of life and death. Alchemists can distill various items down to their essences to brew potent concoctions, ranging from simple healing rations to bombs capable of wiping out half an army in a good throw. Artificers mine ores to forge powerful glyphs for their units, creating smaller but stronger armies that punch above their weight class. However, losing even a single unit could deal a devastating blow to their overall strategy. Whether you stick with the pre-made ones or summon your inner mage-maker, the only variations lie in a few spells and initial creatures available to them—sadly, no secret ingredients.It's hard work being a mage, having to search for a lot of materials for your craft, including your late master's notes. As you journey along, you'll find pages of his grimoire, and boy, did he have a fine taste for flashy books. Embellished with golden margins, elaborate hand-drawn art, and functioning bookmarks, the spellbook doubles as your tech tree menu that contains all sorts of incantations, from zombifying mortals to elemental summons and even water walking. The intricate art style of the spellbook seeps through to the UI, too. It's as if you've stepped into a world where magic permeates every aspect of life, from the book's pages to the very fabric of the game itself. Sadly enough, it's lacking an important feature for the time being, and that is a log to keep track of your expeditions.Whether on the overworld map or in the thick of a battle,  looks colorful and attractive. Its art style strikes the perfect balance between intricate detail and a stylized fantasy look. In contrast, the sound design falls a bit short of the visual appeal. The lack of voice acting and rudimentary audio feel like they come from a less polished game. The Celtic-inspired high fantasy tracks make for a pleasant soundtrack but aren’t strong enough to exist outside the game.Plenty of exploring, exploiting, exterminating, and extremely aggressive AI behavior lies ahead. However, building cities, advancing through complex tech trees, or creating a vast empire isn't among them. No, expanding isn't cut off entirely, but instead comes with a twist. Since sources of revenue, like gold, mana, and research points are finite and scattered around, you'll often have to pluck out your tower, the base of your operations, and fly it to unexplored lands, adding an extra layer of strategic thinking to the gameplay's loop.Of course, the AI shenanigans won't let you rest easy. The mages, more than other factions, have large territories, resources, and the ability to spawn entire armies from the very beginning, putting you in the common underdog scenario. They'll try to walk all over you from the onset, while any attempt at self-defense rubs them the wrong way. Although a couple of patches have aimed to reduce the difficulty spikes, your paths will cross sooner than later. With diplomacy nowhere to be found on Eo, you're in an uphill battle unless you decide to fall back on über strategies to cheese the fights.Speaking of fights, turns dictate the flow of combat on Eo. Assuming direct control of fights transports you to small hex-based arenas. It’s as simple as moving troops into one another and letting them duke it out while you cast magical spells like an all-powerful overlord; it's not all that thrilling but not poorly structured either. For the impatient, encounters can be resolved automatically, but the predictions are a tad off. In occasions where the game is adamant you’ll lose, you might be able to snatch a tight victory by taking matters into your own hands.Jarringly, stacks cannot unite to form larger armies, which reduces the sense of spectacle and importance in the engagements; however, gifted individuals can considerably bolster your forces through their special attacks and customizable loadouts once recruited. Heroes find their way to you, each having their own elaborate questline. Apprentices, on the other hand, know less magical trickery but are easily found in certain places.The main quest and major landmarks are set in stone in each playthrough. However, the map is procedurally generated, and the smaller quests and skirmishes are shuffled around each run. Problem is, the main story itself is somewhat incongruent with some of the design philosophies here, like how you're incentivized to do multiple playthroughs due to different starting locations and customizable difficulties on the offer. Yet, the "been there, done that" feeling remains.On a final note, my adventure to dominate Eo was magically smooth on my  at 1080p 60 FPS, with a few crashes here and there. Nothing of concern.A somewhat askew balance of narrative and sandbox content, a simplified approach to combat, and a far from stellar AI.  isn't risky or new, but the stories it has to tell are a delight. It's the type of game you'd want to play if you're fatigued by the glut of turn-based RPGs or can't dedicate to the intricacies of 4X titans.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a tough call.  There is a good game here, but it's hidden behind an interface I can't fathom.  First, to address some concerns others have pointed out:  It badly needs to allow retrying combats.  In a game like this where experimentation of mechanics plays a large part, it's not fun to keep reloading because a unit didn't function like you thought it would.  Second, this isn't a 4x game.  Professional reviewers who are also dense as lead like to call anything with a hexagonal strategic map a 4x game.  This failure to understand a game is echoed in players who label games as "like D&D" because units can equip swords in the game.  Conquest of Eo is an exploration/strategy game with stories, played on a hex map.  I won't even say it has rpg elements, but it does have story.  The happy buyer will be one who likes combat that is sort of like Age of Wonders, likes moving armies and making decisions, likes hand-drawn art and stopping to read text, and likes resource stockpiles and crafting.  Like every 21st century game of its kind, it has necromancy.  You don't have to play as a necromancer to participate in the necromancy, because all armies collect corpses (called "remains") as part of looting.  So you are always a necromantic dark hero, no matter what choices or roleplaying goals you make.  Your hero (who doesn't appear in the game, at least as far as I progressed) rejects the will of the ruling mages who forbid access to Allfire, the trademark resource of the game.  Never mind that Allfire magically lures people to touch it and thus destroy themselves.  So, yes, it's evil, and the mage council is actually protecting everybody, but we'll just imagine our rebellious, corpse-hoarding hero is justified nonetheless.  Ignore that bit of twisted philosophy, and the rest of the story is probably a good one.So here's the rub, for me:  I can't make heads or tails of the various crafting, research, and spellcasting screens.  I start a project only to find I've sacrificed valuable magic items to do it.  I research a spell only to find I've actually cast the spell instead.  I click with determination on every screen searching for an icon I remember seeing, then hope clicking the icon has the desired result:  Wait, no, that cancels the spell; I've just wasted 3 turns of prep.   The interface screens are artful, but I find it distracting.  I want very clear cause-and-effect, and this game doesn't deliver that.  For example, you can split troops away from an army, but the highlight on the selected troop is so light, it took me a long time to figure out they were selected.  Similarly, pressing F5 seems to have no effect, though I'm told there is a very fast icon somewhere, and it does in fact create a quicksave file.  But the culmination of many weak interface features is that the whole game takes a long time to understand.I haven't had so much trouble deciphering basic commands in a couple of decades.  Being certain of my instructions each turn means playing so slowly that the two-hour refund limit arrives before I've really learned anything about the game.  Caveat emptor.I played several early combats.  The best strategy given the units and resources I had was to have melee units Defend and missile units behind them Attack.  Any effort to have my melee units proactively inflict damage was met with death, failure, and the discovery of no combat replay and no autosave before combat.I write this seeing many positive reviews by people who figured out which thing to click.  And I do see good gameplay here, just it's out of reach for me.  Too much work and confusion to harvest whatever goodness the game holds.  If you find that a new interface is never a problem for you and that settings ignoring good and evil are the best (even though this usually means you're siding with evil without wanting to think so), then ignore my review.  If you're bothered by lost potential and flawed ideology, even though much of the game is quite playable, then avoid this title.

You have a little sorta fantasy warband trying to learn  new spells and explore like you would do like in Might and Magic where it would seem your arch rivals are the circle mages which ultimately you will need to face later in the game that sorta act like A.I players. Resource management of Gold & Mana is very important and the game offers a very harsh difficulty level for veteran gamers along with moderate settings. _childDocuments_.review: First wrote at 20 hours:An overwhelmingly positive review.Edit after finishing the game, 50 hours play time total:This one here is an exquisite piece. It combines simple to grasp, yet supriprisingly fun to experiment with combat on randomly generated battlegrounds with a multitude of contexts with a very reasonably built turn-based strategy world.The economy of the game naturally leads the player in their development, and the transitions to higher tiers are well-balanced as well. Behind every system, there seems to be enough thought to make it seem at least reasonable, if not down right smart.The AI is a computer. Let's not argue there. Still, it did manage to suprise me many times with good reactions and the ability to utilize positioning, resources and my mistakes. In a single playthrough on the balanced difficulty, I used more than 200 manual saves, because combat against strong units required actual strategy and at the beginning, some instances took multiple tries and experiments to actually discover how to deal with specific problems.I played the game as the necromancer, meaning my primary damage type was Death. The problem with this type is that is actually rather weak against other undead - and there are many undead in the world of Eo. I had to work around resistances, consider my reduced effectiveness and even alter my heroes to temporarily deal White damage that works against undead, so I get at least some sort of advantage against the higher-tier minions the AI somehow had in its disposal.The graphics are beautifull and easy on the eyes, no complaints there.The soundtrack is sufficient.The main point of my review, however, is the really entertaining design of the game. The world itself is set, so the regions and some of their important locations are locked. Many other aspects, however, are random and ever-changing. In every playthrough, the players is set against four powerful rival mages, but those are drawn randomly from a pool - and each of them has a different set of favorite minions, spells and tactics, none of them being particularly easy to deal with.Side quests and storytelling are lovely designed, many of their aspects are randomized. For example, some of the most important units of every campaigns are your mage apprentices and heroes. These are also drawn from a pool and they are significantly more variable than would expect. Each hero, on top of all that, has a mainstory of their own.Since the game is actually fun to play, challenging and entertaining at all times, and much of its world is ever-changing and developing, the replay value of this little piece here skyrockets.I give a solid 5/7 score.(Hey, developer, I know you're gonna read this, so take these suggestions:1) Let me name my stacks and allow me to organize them more smoothly.2) Allow me to enchant and disenchant units from the unit screen, always going to the Big Bad Book for every single enchant I need to is just not that great.3) I am a necromancer. I zombify my mortal units. I need to zombify my mortal heroes as well - but some of them would like to heal and their heals only work on other mortal units. That would be fine, but my heroes got zombified. And they fight for a zombie army. I need them to change to the Undead Healer class after I zombify them. Yeah? Thanks.4) I would very much like to draw and write on the map. Pins and locations....I might add to this list later. Thank you.)

_childDocuments_.review: Heroes of Might and Magic IF it had TONS of side quests, units gained experience and you can move your castle (in this case, a tower).Biggest gripe against the game is in the combat system. You have 3 action points per unit, but some actions are repeatable and use them all up when you may only want to use 1/2 of them. This can make combat frustrating/maddening.It's recommended to manual combat every fight too as the AI Auto Resolve isn't the best and will likely cause you to lose units.One more gripe before going into the good stuff: the font used in the story line window is a little jarring. For me at least, its not easy on the eyes to read. Maybe the font needs to be brighter, or with more contrast.The map is absolutely full of places to visit and loot, with roaming enemies, 4(?) enemy factions constantly pumping out units, and neutral cities that you can do quests for, gain reputation, to be able to buy units and consumables from the store.A unique feature is the limited resources: a mine might give you a ton of gold each turn, but only for a limited amount of turns before it runs out. You'll need to move your tower, and your heroes have the ability to make lodges which has a certain area of control, and any buildings within will be harvested from daily.The resource system seems to fit nicely together. Some resources are consumables that are used in combat, they can also be used to create glyphs which can either be attached to individual units OR be used to upgrade buildings in your tower giving special abilities (faster hiring of units vs being able to hire unique units). The most beautiful parts of the game comes in the side missions where there are hand drawn pictures, and the grimoire, which is both a quest tracker, achievement tracker and spell book. Unlike HoMM, you'll be earning Research each turn, which can be used to learn specific spells that can be used both in and out of combat (casting freeze on water sources, so you can traverse rivers).A great game, and if they take care of the action point-use system and the font, it would be perfect.

_childDocuments_.review: SpellForce: Conquest of Eo so far has been outstanding, a very pleasant surprise, at the current price, it's an absolute steal! I'm glad I purchased it, there are 143 units in the game. I was hesitant to buy it, thought the units and such looked too cartoonish, definitely not case, they look that way in the game upgrade screens, though on the battlefields they and the maps and terrain look great. I'm playing this maxed in 8K with an RTX 4090 and it's flawless from an optimization standpoint. I do wish there were more game modes, vice just campaign, though given the randomness of it, I can see there being a fair amount of replay. Some things are not well explained at times, I was at least 50 turns in one game, had wings went across the water with a six unit stack and that pretty much ended the game for me, I couldn't get them out of the now impassable terrain. Overall, I'm really looking forward to getting into this more, can't wait to see a number of other units outside the first starting area.You’re able to upgrade your units so technically no two are the same, they have a great path to customize each of them to your liking and what type of strategy you want to employ. I’m still a but confused on moving your tower, though it’s better to take your time and level your army some, don’t, you’ll be overwhelmed. The AI so far has been excellent, it functions as it should and chooses its tactics and approach better than most 4X games, it’s very capable and competent. This reminds me a bit of Age of Wonders and Warlock mixed, highly recommended!

_childDocuments_.review: Hi,Conquest of Eo plays amazingly well and captures a lot of spellforce 3 magic in it. I did enjoy it a lot trough out my time, even tho I do not like turn-based combat. I enjoyed being immersed in a fantasy map with multiple enemy factions, locations to explore, plenty of magic, multiple combat encounters, main and side quest. These are some negative notes I have gathered from my playtrough:-Combat: The turned-based gameplay does not have a lot of depth, battles take no longer than 10 minutes. I mostly auto resolved the combat encounters unless I was forced to play the combat manually which you are required to do if you want to take out enemy main towers. auto resolve seems to be the better 90% out of the time because if you play it manually you are most of the time guaranteed to lose at least 1 unit which the auto resolve wins you the battle without loosing any units. The issue being, combat encounters the enemy focusing on 1 unit and dealing all the damage on to one unit. Not be able to retreat or redraw a unit makes you loose a unit. or you play necromancer which is the best class and unit loosing or dying becomes the least of your problems. for the other classes getting units that you actually want is hard.-The Map is Huge and exploring does yield to new quest, items, factions, enemys etc. It offers a lot. Not exploring and not moving your tower to new positions is a huge negative so it somewhat forces you to take action to visit new locations, awesome right ? Yeah but: The movement is so minimal so short it takes so long to explore this huge map and get from a location to another.-The balance between the mages(classes) is questionable. Because the necromancer can summon powerfull units as much it likes, the only problem being the units upkeep. but you can also infuse your summon with the highest tier to get no upkeep cost. so having multiple death stacks roaming around the map is too easy. The other classes just dont do it, improving and infusing units with glyhps or potions is great yeah but the necromancer already does get amazing units with great buffs and these summon also can get glyphs and potions.-Recruiting units seems to be incredibly hard, especially if you want a certain unit to hire. you have find a town than do a lot of quest for them to get reputation with them to get a blueprint and that blueprint need to be build inside your tower room for several turns and than you can finally hire units of your liking. of course if you do not play the necromancer which you get what ever you want easily.-Spells and spell books: You get a lot of spells to cast, also a lot of spell pages to get even more spells which is great but as always but but but I found myself using only 3-4 spells most of the time, one being the extra movement spell the other being because it is forced the summon a spirit spell the get resources from the altar other than these two I do not remember any other spell worth mentioning. others are debuffs or buffs for allied or enemy units, some are even spells to impact the map to freeze water or to fly your units around etc.This game definitely gives you what it promises. Not being that expensive is another great aspect to it. I wished it was real time tactics. Give it a shot. (There are some modern aspects in the game in which you might not recognize any man or woman or other stuff.)

_childDocuments_.review: SpellForce: Conquest of Eo is fundamentally an RPG game played on a 4x-style map with tactical battles. It changes the way 4x games are played by tweaking the expansion and exploration aspect of the game, where expansion isn't the be-all-end-all, since you're limited in how far your domain can expand, and exploration carries throughout the game as you explore the map and find new quests. This isn't a Master of Magic or Civ-style game, so if it's what you're looking for I'd refer to those series, especially because the map is NOT procedurally generated, while quests, events, and some locations are.If you want to try a fun and engaging game with a variety of interesting mechanics and fun, quick tactical battles, this game is a steal at this price point.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of those games that makes me wish for a neutral review button, but since I have to choose, here we are.I'd recommend this instalment of Spellforce on a heavy sale. The biggest reason being replayability.There is one campaign, and no multiplayer. There are three factions as which one can play as, but since the story is about the same there isn't much difference from playthrough to playthrough.Also mechanics still need some heavy polish. Since the game is very reminiscent of the Age of Wonders series, it's a pity that the game has not borrowed the ability to bring multiple armies to combat from that series (at least I have not figured out how). Now, if one does play with a faction which is centered around bringing lots of little cretins to battle (the Necromancer), then one needs to send multiple sets of units to engage the opponent to whitle them down (at least in the early game), this is a clunky experience and makes the class less viable than the others when dealing with scripted events.Anyhow biggest gripe is definitely that there will be very little replayability. The lack of  more than one shortish campaign is not great and the lack of multiplayer is most frustrating, since the game is polished enough that it might be fun to play with/against friends. Now the game's content is mostly fire and forget. Hence I can't recommend the game for even 20€, even if the core mechanics are decent.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a work of beauty. I really didn't know what to expect from a Spellforce spin-off, but this is just a brilliant example that sometimes trying something different pays off.I would say this is loosely a similar genre as Heroes of Might & Magic + some elements of games like CIvilization, and it just couldn't be more fun. It's this increasingly rare kind of games that can either be absolutely relaxing, or a proper, in-depth strategy depending on what you want and the difficulty level. I don't remember when a game last sucked me in so completely, and pretty much all other really good games I've been playing have kind of fallen by the wayside since I installed it.And the interesting thing is that it has "just" the campaign, but it really feels like a smart choice - the campaign world is really wonderfully designed, and because you can play different "classes" of sorts and start in different locations, there's a ton of replay value, and I already know I will instantly jump into a second playthrough after I finish this one. Admittedly, some shorter "skirmish" mode or even "custom battle" would be cool, but it's clear that they had a specific scope in mind when making this game, and they did it perfectly.Oh, and if you played Spellforce 3, you'll meet some very familiar faces and it definitely brings a smile, but if you've never played any Spellforce, don't worry, this is pretty much a standalone story.

_childDocuments_.review: I was craving a replacement for MoM recently, and after realizing that the remake is not really anything new, I read many threads discussing the comparable qualities of various games such as AOW4 and Spellforce: Conquest of Eo.At first I thought Conquest of Eo was going to hit the mark for me - the early game is pretty fun with decent progress, the excitement of drawing new apprentices, smashing your enemies... but it runs out fast.Commanding troops on worldmap is frustrating. If you mis-click you waste your movement points on the day and I didn't see any way to undo it. Travel is slow and the speed of tiles is not made very clear so you are left with 1 movement point left and no obvious reason why you can't go that last little bit. It takes too long to get from place to place and random aggro units on world map attacking your light scout parties turns into tedium just trying to keep things on track.Commanding troops in battle has some of the same frustrations - a misclick and you've ruined the entire battle. Add to that the fact that there's no permanent fast mode so you have to click every unit's turn just to speed it up and the battles drag on and on. There are no spells for battle like in MoM so it's completely down to the particular units you had on hand and you as the commanding player have no way to influence the outcome beyond unit control.To have ANY kind of success you need to play very aggressively and have many units out on the map trying to mine/harvest/explore for new allfire nodes. This gets really frustrating and tedious trying to command them all, especially when enemy units can spawn any time anywhere, and screw you over. Yet again, we get into tedium and sapping the possible fun out of the game.Resource harvesting is finite, and having to constantly pack up and move your tower or lodges is incredibly irritating. The amount of resources given in each location's landmarks is too little, so basically once a week, two at the most, you have to find a new place to camp out, and spend multiple rounds constructing a new lodge.Since you have to constantly have most of your troops out exploring/conquering/completing quest items, your lodges and tower are essentially defenseless and the mana/gold gain balance is too poor to maintain a standing army and combined with overland travel being slow, you get penalized for the pillaging.Maybe I'm judging it too harshly for having only played 1 class in 2 tries so far, but I'm already disinclined to pick it up again to try another class because it's too much on rails, too grindy, and too tedious. I really wanted to like this game, but I regret buying it and spending any time on it at this point.

_childDocuments_.review: As a strategy gamer, I was on the edge of my seat from the moment I started playing SpellForce: Conquest of Eo. This is a game that combines the best elements of turn-based strategy and tactical role-playing games, creating a thrilling and unique gaming experience.From the moment you step into the rich fantasy world of SpellForce, you'll be captivated by the stunning graphics and immersive sound effects. You'll feel like you're right in the middle of the action, leading your army to conquer territory and defend against enemy attacks.The gameplay is fast-paced and challenging, requiring you to use strategic thinking and resource management to succeed. And the RPG elements, such as character development and dialogue choices, add an extra layer of excitement to the game. You'll feel like you're part of a living, breathing world, making choices that will determine the outcome of your story.But what really sets SpellForce apart is the customizable army and hero units. You'll collect and upgrade powerful spells, weapons, and abilities to make your army stronger, and your hero units will have unique abilities that you can tailor to your playstyle. As you progress through the game, you'll feel a sense of pride and accomplishment as you see your army grow in power and skill.In conclusion, if you're looking for a thrilling gaming experience that combines strategy, role-playing, and epic battles, then SpellForce: Conquest of Eo is the game for you. So grab your controller, strap in, and get ready for an unforgettable journey through a magical world!

_childDocuments_.review: Conquest of EO is very similar to Master of Magic, where you control a mage, explore the overland, research spells, and fight roaming map enemies both independent and with enemy factions. Overall, the game is well made with a good UI, well designed tactical combat system, a large map with a lot to do, fun magic, and an interesting story. The problem is there is no tension. As far as I can tell, the enemy factions either aren't seriously trying to defeat the player or the AI just can't figure out how to organize powerful enough stacks to do so.  While there is a lot to do, if there's no chance of me losing leveling up my units eventually feels like a chore because I'm just increasing numbers for its own sake, rather than try to overcome the competition. I'll still recommend the game as I played for 14 hours, but I feel like this could have been a lot better with better campaign AI.

_childDocuments_.review: This is an excellent tactical game with role playing elements. The focus on crafting, with three core different methods of crafting grants the game significant replayability. A persistent map between games does nothing to dull this aspect (despite what some online reviews might have one believe). At times, the randomly generated RPG elements can bog the player down in text, but it is easy enough to ignore these. They are perhaps the weakest element of the game.The tactical combat is very close to Age of Wonders 3, and it is well implemented, with several maps that can grant significant tactical advantages to a savvy player.  The combat is fairly basic with height, and cover for ranged attacks, as well as choke points being the most significant considerations, however it is functional. I am thoroughly enjoying the game, and the continued support in improving the game shows a commitment from the development team.

_childDocuments_.review: SpellForce: Conquest of Eo is the 16th or so release in the pretty popular but probably still underrated SpellForce series. Instead of an RTS/RPG hybrid as was SpellForce 3, however, Conquest of Eo is an interesting blend of turn-based strategy, tactical hex grid combat, and roleplaying elements, all of which adds up to an experience not unlike Heroes of Might and Magic... or whatever it’s called these days. Fans of that franchise know how long a campaign can take, and I’m equally excited slash exhausted to report that Conquest of Eo is no exception. Indeed, after 20 hours with the game, I’ve barely made it into what feels like midgame, and I am loving almost every minute...  As you’ve probably guessed by this point, Spellforce: Conquest of Eo is about conquering Eo as a pretty powerful and pretty pissed off mage who—early on and regardless of the starter path you pick—finds their way into possession of a book of spells and a floating castle. Well, that's a little generous, I suppose, as your spellbook or “grimoire” is empty on receipt and your tower is less a majestic teleporting Castlevania castle and more a dusty, disabled piece of ♥♥♥♥.  In order to get it off the ground, you'll need to accrue quite a bit of gold to hire and maintain an army, mana to then cast army-enhancing spells, research points to unlock new spells, and, most importantly, “Allfire,” a sort of omni-resource you can convert into mana, research, or “mastery.” Mastery levels up (literally) your tower and, with it, you! All the way from baby mage to BIG BOY MAGE. With each new mage level, your tower’s domain radius increases, you unlock new types of rooms for construction, and you can add additional heroes to the battlefield. These powerful units, each of whom has a personal quest, can then build their own lodges throughout the land. Lodges contribute to your domain’s area, so any resource they encompass, wherever they, are will add to your resource totals for each turn. If at this point you’re feeling a little overwhelmed by the game’s impressive list of  mechanics, rest easy—the game actually does a great job of introducing new information through its largely skippable tutorial, and things then stay quite intuitive for the campaign’s duration, in no small part thanks to Conquest of Eo’s wonderful . It’s responsive, it’s helpful, it’s easy on the eyes, and I don’t have a bad thing to say about it. That’s not the case for the game’s , however, as—at least this far into the game—most fights feel pretty much identical. Your quote “stack” of units spawn on one side of a small map, the enemy at the other. You’ll then maneuver to exploit the ♥♥♥♥♥♥ AI and, barring insurmountable odds, win. There are a decent number of buffs, debuffs, and unit abilities to learn and employ along the way, but it just never adds up to anything particularly fun. Luckily, the devs have slightly rebalanced the "auto-resolve" feature in the player's favor, so you'll be able to skip more fights than I was able to. This helps the game's playability.  Luckily, there’s an awesome variety of enemies on display here, and the map is so large and environmentally varied that exploring it and unearthing its many procedurally-generated charms is a true delight. Consider me currently amazed by Conquest of Eo’s rich  and impressed by its —in addition to the main quest, there are dozens of at least mildly interesting sidequests scattered about the land, and they change based on, for example, the heroes you use to access them, the items in your inventory, your standing with opposing factions, and the type of mage you pick to play. On that subject, the Alchemist can brew potions to aid you in battle. The Artificer crafts glyphs to do the same. But because hiring new troops typically takes so FREAKIN’ long to do in this game, far and away my favorite mage was the Necromancer. With its ability to summon cheap undead scouts, I was able to get further in an hour with the necro than I did in five with the alchemist on an easier difficulty level in an easier starting location. Not that your story will change much, regardless.   Finally, some rapid-fire thoughts on style. Conquest of Eo is a visually charming game and I never got tired of looking at it, though its  lack a WOW factor unlike SpellForce 3, which is (five years later) still one of the prettiest RTS games I’ve ever seen. The , meanwhile, is pretty plain—standard fantasy adventure fare, and the  are just okay.  So, in the end, Conquest of Eo is a mostly enjoyable experience that’s likely to please turn-based strategy fans. I’m giving it a subject-to-change aggregate MEGA score of 3.57/5 and look forward to updating this opinion closer to full release. Until then, this is Scope, and thanks so much for reading!

_childDocuments_.review: It pains me to give this game a down vote, as there are LOTs of great ideas in this game, and I'm going to keep playing it because I love to explore game mechanics.The main reasons I have to downvote it:1) Managing your economy is painful, and often devolves into your 'gaming' the system (keep starting stacks alive cos they have 0 upkeep for some dumb reason, enslave units, use boring wisps as their upkeep to power ratio is so good, etc...) rather than playing with what would make a fun tactical arrangement of units. Managing your economy is a real boring grind :(2) REALLY bad autocomplete fights. Game forces you to play boring manual fights just so you don't lose units.3) Necromancers (1/3 of the mage types) are a real pain to manage as their troops don't auto heal (lots of micro, even more manual fights, etc...). They can eat corpses during a fight... but why don't they auto eat them at the end of the fight? You're going to waste hours and hours of time just to get them to a point where this mage is fun.4) RNG placement of quests... even key quests that lock entire vital sections of the game's mechanics away (need adamantium but its only found in the far north and your in the far south, quests locked behind mountains/rivers/seas, etc....).But i will give a massive shout out to the key illustrator Dominik Mayer, his work is amazing!Also, slowly growing your spellbook out with spells and quest notes is quite flavourful.Again, so many great ideas held back by some really poor game design decisions that hamper it. Price point is also fairly ok for what you get.Edit: Played another 8 hours and a lot of things get better as you get more magical options. But unfortunately the game keeps crashing after key fights :( I think I'm going to uninstall this game and try again in a years time after more things have been polished out.

_childDocuments_.review: Full text On the one hand there are were few games of the specific Spellforce flavour of the RPG-RTS hybrid subgenre, and seeing the IP pivot into an already overpopulated genre sucks. On the other hand there are three first games, four+ second games and three third games, then there are some clones. The IP itself is pretty saturated and one spin-off is not the end if it. Hopefully.Though, from what i played, I’m not sure there’s enough lore there to have an IP not tied to the mechanic itself. All the writing was barely thrown together to prop up the unusual mechanic of the game. While the first story is solid, the plot and dialogues are pretty much skippable and forgettable. And yes i have no idea what is happening here story-wise and i really don’t want to read the random events mundane texts. Because the ones i read fully don’t add anything to anything.So instead of a Spellforce this game is a blatant mix of Age of Wonders and a 4X. Considering that AoW is already a mix between Heroes and a 4X, this new game is one step further into 4X away from a hero-driven TBS. Instead of a campaign of maps to conquer, you just have one giant map with territory control, production bonuses and upkeep. But all the battles happen with real mechanics on a grid instead of pathetic overworld animations of an onager sinking you air carrier full of jet planes in one hit. The auto-resolve is pretty balanced, i think. It can play way better than you when you have an advantage, yet your manual control can achieve a flawless victory when autoresolve expects and utter defeat.Despite it clearly being a 4X you can’t create cities or conquer them. You project your zone of influence from your Age of Wonders 2 tower that you can move around and from dachas your 5 not-heroes can build. (You can have one of the heroes with a mini-quest per session, but they can’t build a dacha). You can send a spirit to coit with a source of stem cell energy and there is a spell to plant a small building emitting influence. Your tower has a number of slots for rooms and you can fill most of them as you like with resource producing or global / unit enchanting rooms. The rooms also have slots for a choice of specific upgrades, so it is possible for you to fill you tower with rooms extending your influence from every source.But most of the resource nodes will be depleted in a ten or so turns, so moving your tower and dachas around with the scorched earth policy is your intended means of engaging with the game. I reckon more than half of the tower / room upgrades are about helping you or hurting the enemy inside your zone of influence. Only if you have proper nature spells you can forgo your nomadic lifestyle and create agriculture farms, generating most of the resources and some ingredients for you (that you can sell for other resources).The unique offer in this game is that you can pick your crafting profession. Alchemy allows you to stock up on potions which you can use 3 per turn per unit. You can pelt the enemy with elemental AoE grenades, or you can release bottled units that can release bottled units until every free tile is occupied by your forces. Necromancer is creating undead units requiring mana upkeep with inherent “swimming” out of souls and ingredients. Some souls create more resources than their upkeep, including the souls producing stem cell energy. Some souls remove all upkeep from the created unit. And /or you can fill the whole map with upkeep-free T2 walking corpses. Meanwhile artificer creates minor buffs, two, at best three, per creature and three-four per leader. The best you can get are peasant skills for your combat units, free upkeep, and world movement buffs to ignore terrain types. Necromancer still can buy potions and glyphs in the cities, meanwhile the other two can’t participate in necromancy.The magic is really powerful and you can collect and research spells that don’t belong to your initial school(s). You can remove upkeep from your human units, you can summon influence projectors. And you can grow the resource tiles inside your influence. Downside is that many of the spells require constant upkeep so they are not worth bothering with. Or that many basic buffs are cast per unit not per stack, which means you have to repeat casting ten times for ten times the upkeep. If your mana income is good you can activate some global enchantments.You don’t just play a session for 4X sake, there’s actually a something like a campaign. And it’s a bit more involved than the ones from Gladius. You make some minor decision in text-adventures instead of just working towards the stated goal. There are tiny text-adventure side-quests with branching decisions and solutions locked behind your attributes. Some are given by the cities, some by your rivals and you can step in some of them randomly generated in the overworld. But this is not entirely thought-through, since even your “peasants” can trigger them, not just your leaders. Imagine having to abandon a quest because your lvl1 workers with pitchforks can’t take on an approaching legion of deathdoom to save the travelling orphans. Your one random hero per session also asks you to do a minor quest, and there are five of them. Good luck trying to get each of them, which is also required for an achievement.The game is unpolished. It can look good on the screenshots, but it’s a typical mid-budget 4X production with a lot of pretty colours and jiggling keys but no substance to the presentation or storytelling. No cutscenes and all the text side-quest are tiny repetitive visual novels. The map “map” button is useless — it depicts it as a pointless parchment you can’t interact with. The edge scrolling is painfully extremely slow. When you pick your leaders from the leaders menu it doesn’t jump-select them and it always shows their dacha first. The list of factions doesn’t jump to them period. There is no list of active quests and quest-enemies can just run away into the fog of war. There’s no reveal all end-game spell either so have fun scrolling around for ages enjoying low FoV and no map, searching for things to do. And of course there is plenty of minor bugs. The game renders on 4//3 screens, but in >>the current year the GUI is unscalable and unmovable. Many of the elements overlap so you have to play widescreen windowed. The tutorials page is broken and displays empty buttons. There are some orthography errors and missing words. Sometimes the game gets stuck in the overworld or in the battles and nothing happens. You have to reload it. And yeah of course they removed the “load game” button from inside the battles for literally no reason, so you have to exit to the main menu every time.The achievements are mostly just boring, for completion and features. Also they all use the same boring pictogram. They also demand a victory at the max difficulty and to pray to RNG you will meet all the heroes. Because the heroes don’t come until you invested some significant hours into a session.All in all, i’ve spent 52 hours on a full-map run on the 2nd difficulty. The first ten were extremely enjoyable, discovering more and more ways to craft stuff. But once i got all the mechanics and could end the game any moment the map wasn’t yet fully explored and i had like 35 more hours of repetitive swiping in front of me.It’s kinda a great game with its unique properties, despite the flaws, but what’s next? If it’s successful i bet they will release some DLCs, but it being the same exact map, replaying it is not that alluring. It’s all the same units, all the same mechanics. Once they finish patching the bugs, i hope their vision for additional content would be other maps with different units, cities and side-quests. Even if with the same main “story”. But i kinda doubt it will go that way.

_childDocuments_.review: The game requires a lot of love and reworking.Building tower and crafting is really fun.The idea of mobile fortress is insanely great, i enjoyed every bit of it.But there is also a bitter part. You want to explore the map, scavenge resources, but your tower is constantly getting hammered by circle mages forces, beasts, demons, every unit on the map in the vicinity of your base. Eventually you unlock the recall spell, but because good units have very high upkeep, until you build your economy, most of the time you only have 2 doom stacks that can clear the map. Constantly jerking them to defend your base doesn't feel nice, you want to do quests, clear camps, etc.There is also a special part.The demon realm.Demons are fun to fight, but there is one but.This part of my review is dedicated to you, dear developer, who thought it would be fun for players to fight demons, who are formidable enemies among meteor showers.It seems to choose targets "randomly", but it doesn't.2/3 times it hits your backlines, you have to move your units, receive opportunity attacks, just not to die, because meteors hit very hard. Sometimes areas where meteors are going to hit are invisible, it also add fun to the game. Sometimes areas where meteors are going to hit in lava, so you also cannot see them. My main question, dear developer who was working on meteor shower, is why do you hate people?Games are supposed to be fun.Later in the game when your forces grow there is a bit too much micromanagement for my taste.It is a big problem for all games of this type.Least you could do is automate harvesting of resources and make navigation between quests more informative. After a couple of sessions i had big problems finding what should i do to earn reputation for one of the cities.Don't get me wrong the game is not terrible, it is really fun to clear it for the first time.But my overall impression from the game is bitter-sweet.In my life where i don't have time to play all games and have to choose, i wouldn't recommend this game.If you are starving for a 4x game that you have not played, you might enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: Alchemist review:  I played one game as the alchemist, and I spent 36 hours on it.Worldbuilding thoughts:-This is a massive world to explore.  36 hours and I know I didn't see half of what the game has to offer.  Quests, stories that could have multiple outcomes.  While over that time period, the different outcomes didn't play too big a part, sometimes finding a surprise relic was super exciting!-The story that's told is acceptable.  I did find myself reading the dialog, but I couldn't tell you what happened other than my Master was killed, and I never really figured out why.Unit thoughts:-There is a huge variety of units.  The different factors that make up the unit is often boiled down to damage type, damage resistances, and preferred terrain.  You generally don't have access to many unit types, so you can't easily build to counter the Death damage of the demons for example, you just have to not visit Demon-land or buff with potions/glyphs to counter.-The unit levelling abilities are excellent.  General abilities most levels are just a tiny increment better, but hitting levels 5/10/15 can add some really game changing abilities, and that's cool.Battle thoughts:-There is enough tactical variety in the beginning.  After about 5 hours, you've found about all there is, so get yourself a doom stack and autoresolve your way over the map.-Here's my best strategy: get 2-3 ranged units, add range glyphs, Eagle Spirit potion, sit them behind 4 tanks.  Watch the enemy come to you and be picked apart by the ranged units.  It's cool the first 5 times, but it got old doing this.  But if you don't want your units to die, it works nicely.Spell thoughts:The variety of spells is great.  I used many different spells over the course of the game.  Some are situational (befriend a beast in an enemy stack - turned the tide early on), others are required (Aid - heal my units more so I can conquer quicker)Resources thoughts:-The income (research+gold+mana) was well balanced throughout the game.  Excellent job with this!  I never got carried away with too much income, but I didn't have to scrounge up a few more pennies to keep my units happy all the time.-I personally needed more gold. -To get the most out of the map, you have your apprentice bases harvesting while they're conquering the next area, then move.  Explore, Exterminate, Exploit.  It means your forces are pretty well spread apart so that you can cover the most resource nodes.  Which is fine, I guess, but a lot of scrolling around the map.  Scrolling is too slow!  Give me a hotkey [shift] to scroll faster!Balance thoughts:The alchemist recipe that affected enemies weren't as useful as the ones that affected my units.  I'd always go for +3 range to my ranged units and they'd use that the whole battle.  Maybe some Golems if it was difficult, but rarely a debuff on the enemies, because a single enemy can be focused down too quickly for the debuff to have great effect.  And the largest enemies that I couldn't take down in one turn were often not affected by the debuffs anyway.Quality of life improvements that would be nice to have:A way to duplicate a recipe - when I want to queue up the crafting of the same recipe with the same ingredients.  Right now, I have to click all the filters to find the ingredients I want each time. A way to save most recently used recipes.  I found several potions that I used consistently, and it would be nice to queue them up with the last used ingredients. (or even put in ingredient suggestions for me to use or nix if I want)Who will enjoy this game + Alchemist?-somebody who enjoys the great unit diversity and tactical combat of Fallen Enchantress/Eador/Age of Wonder-esque games but on a grander scale-somebody who doesn't need a storyline with regular touchpoints-somebody who likes lots of summoning Golems :)Comparing this game to its siblings, this is an excellent example.  But this is a niche game - make sure you like this genre before committing.

_childDocuments_.review: Nice game!It continues the SpellForce formula of mix of strategy game and RPG very well, even when slightly shifted genre to turn based strategy instead of RTS.The turn-based combat feels like a mix of the best features of an Eador: Genesis and a Age of Wonders: Planetfall, which is a very good thing in my book :DThe AI is decent to good. It has some behaviors that you can exploit, but also can go mercilessly for any weaknesses you show and target focus units down.The campaign progression aims to prevent the "scope creep" that 4X games usually have as they conquer more land and more cities to manage and I feel like it achieves that.You can get a bit towards what is in other games refered as a "doomstack", making endgame battles rather easy, but often this limits your other armies enough to be a questionable choice. And sometimes other mages surprise you with doomstacks of their own! So fair game here^^Also the pacing at which enemy armies throughout the map become stronger feels spot on for their respective difficulty levels.As different professions and different spellpages encourage a different playstyle, some more territorial, some more nomadic, some very aggressive, and you don't have to explore all of the huge map in one playthrough, there is a good amount of replayability. Not endless, but for people looking for challenges like me, you can play it a good few times.The crafting is easy to understand but offers some nice mini-game challenge of combining in the most efficient way and gives incentive to look for specific material types in the world. Just how I want it. My complains here are only, that it lacks a filtering option, which at some point becomes definitively appropriate. And receipes could be added to the list upon discovery of the preview and not only on first craft, as it otherwise becomes a lot to keep in mind.Unit leveling options can be a bit hit or miss: There are for all units amazing upgrades in the pool, but it is not guaranteed, that they will be presented as choices. A third option as default might be suitable.Overall the core systems and their combination and presense in the game feel close to perfect for me and any expansions could solely focus on more content: (Even) Bigger map, more units, more characters, more high tier crafting receipes, more enemies, more factions!This is a very good spot to be for a just released game, I think! There are two things that frustrated me a bit: The first that explanations are very sparse and sometimes things like whether a multiplicator affects damage calulations before or after armor have to be discovered yourself. Or how exactly willpower drops due to high damage hits work.The second thing is auto-resolve. While it shows you when you can definitively clear a fight without losses, it requires an overwhelming power to be offered that. The auto-resolve seems to be working on a abstract formula rather than a quick AI vs AI battle simulation, like AoW: Planetfall does. And this formula likes to kill a unit at least, resulting in having to play a lot of battles yourself, that aren't interesting to play. The AI is there, just give it the second it needs to calculate the battle off-screen.The world and interactions and exploration give a very spellforce-y vibe :)The difference in how you perceive and encounter the circle mages in SpellForce 1, 3 and now this game is very interesting to watch :DFinal verdict: Gimme more!

_childDocuments_.review: Revised:So I forced myself to play the game through completion because I wasn't 100% sure that the 29 hours was enough to give the game a fair assessment.  I logged an additional 57 hours (86 total) and played it through to completion as an Alchemist on super-easy level.  I had played as an Artificer on my first game but didn't quite get the gist of what the ♥♥♥♥ I was doing.  So frustration set in and I just began to resent the game.  But the game is quite challenging.  As I played and learned more, I began to respect the game and the rules.The game has a TON of depth to it which resulted in a pretty steep learning curve for me.  Managing the resources (mana/gold) is one of the main challenges you face. There's never enough of either. Exploration is key as there are many potentially friendly towns you will need to engage in order to start compiling your "killer stacks" of units and a leader.  Growth is slow at first and learning the mechanics of combat can be frustrating but they start to make sense if you look at the details of both your units and the enemies.  Take note which of your units deal the most effective type of damage versus the enemy defenses.Suggestion for the composition of your armies:2-3 melee units for fighting up front1-2 archer units for plinking at weakened units 1 healer type (alchemists are among the best)Leader with as many HPs as you can stack whenever possible.  Those who have summoning spells are super powerful as they instantly add another body to the fight.Quick Fighting tactics:Use the Guard ability when you have 2 or more enemy next to your unit.  Let the other units help with DPs while to you try to keep that one unit alive.Spread out a little bit but not too much - keep your team within easy reach of everyone to support enemy fliers, spiders and bugs who can run around your front line.Use terrain to your advantage - buildings, fences, rocks, etc.  Choke points are key in many battles.I completed the game with an Alchemist archetype and by the end, it was pretty easy to deck my teams out with great equipment, glyphs and potions, potions, potions.  A few of the go-to suggestions for young aspiring Alchemists are below - if you take nothing else with you into battle, use these:Bottle of the Sealed Elemental - this summons a Lesser Elemental which is great cannon fodder for the bad guys on Turn 2 and 3. Place them one hex ahead of your forward troops and you can plink away with your ranged units for two turns almost without danger.Bottle of Eagle Spirit - increases the range of your archers by 3 (from standard 5 to 8).  If you need me to explain this, you shouldn't be playing this game.  :-)Potion of Sacred Water - this drops a ton of pain on up to seven undead/fantastic enemies in a cluster. Below is my original review.  I'll leave it intact for others to see and relate. Suggestions for improving the game-play:Travel is super slow mid-game to the end. Offering faster road travel could make the logistics of a large campaign less painful. I have two ideas:No-cost movement for units in their own domain. A road-building option for hired workers to increase travel speeds. Or an achievement in which you donate/sacrifice a number of workers on an ability which increases movement speed on a sliding scale. (Call it the Transport Improvement Union - each of those workers are then lost but their usefulness is felt throughout the empire for the remaining time.)Free teleportation between the lodges, the summoned towers and the main Tower.  This could make those towers a LOT more useful than just a 1-hex area of control.Units should have limited movement inside an enemy domain. Or there should be some kind of detrimental effect placed on them as they enter as a way to dissuade any trespassers. This should work both ways, for the NPCs and the player. ------------Original review:I've played the game for 29 hours so far.  It's sort of fun at first - lots of units, effects and abilities.  But the "same old, same old" starts to kick in pretty quickly.  You can't field more than 2 full armies in the beginning due to high unit costs. Jumping around trying to do quests, defend your areas, kill random stacks for XPs and replenish your troops becomes a nuisance. And by mid-game, you're struggling with getting and keeping income nodes (gold/mana) from the wandering beasts and enemy units. The combat mechanics are pretty cool and there are lots of synergies and tactics to learn and employ.  But the boredom kicks in and you just want to shut the game down because there are other things to do.  I really wanted to love this game (I've played 825 hours of Age of Wonder 3 and 784 hours of Warlock 2 - The Exiled so I'm super familiar with this type of 4X fantasy game) but it pales in comparison to those two. It just never got to feel exciting to me.If I could get my money back for this game, I would.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure what people are expecting here.  Some down votes because the game is turn-based instead of RTS like the previous titles?  Ummm, read the description and watch gameplay videos much?Other negative reviews have mentioned frequent crashes.  In my time with this game I have not experienced a single crash or even a stutter or slow down.  Loading times and gameplay have been smooth as can be for me.  Also, currently at $23.99 you can't go wrong.  Especially nowadays with companies charging $70 for a game with true issues and crap mechanics rolled into one.  Once again, not sure what people are expecting here.Others saying it isn't good because of little to no unit customization....  This isn't Skyrim or a true RPG.What is true is what others have said though.  This game takes a little from a few other titles like Age of Wonders and even Fallen Enchantress.  The unit models could look a little better for this day and age and yes, there could be more customization with your units but you can equip your Apprentices (Army leader) and Heroes (Army leader) with  armor, weapons, grimoires, and a trinket item.  I do enjoy that each and every unit in your army receives upgrades.  Your options are random at each level which makes for good variety.The gameplay is a lot of fun.  Over 5hrs in my initial play and I literally had to force myself to turn it off.  There's a ton to do and explore which gives it that "One more turn" vibe.This isn't a true 4x in the sense that you only have your one tower.  Once you've depleted your resources there you're going to need to move that tower via a spell to farm more resources, which makes exploration that much more interesting and necessary.The battles are good for a turn based game.  They do make you think and if you're not careful, you could be in bad sorts.  There are a few good videos on Youtube in this regard as it does have a unique mechanic with action points that deplete for your next turn if they counter attack a unit.  This gives it a fresh feel imo and makes positioning of your units all the more important.  Also, in this regard, the UI is very good and clean.  You're able to distinctively tell where your enemies can move on their next turn so there's no guessing.A lot of good things here.  It should be noted that there is no Sandbox mode but from what I'm aware, each game (On 5 different map types) is procedurally generated.  There aren't many options at all at start up either.  You can't select map size, number of opponents or most other options you'd expect from a typical 4x, which again this isn't.I was on the fence about getting this as I'm waiting another 3 months for AoW4 but I'm honestly glad I picked it up because it truly is soooo different but in a refreshing way.  It's almost like you're playing through your campaign and it's the first 100 turns for the remainder of the game if that makes sense.  Nothing is getting stale as I'm still exploring all over the place and turning up new locations, completing new quests and meeting new Cities and other mages.I hope this clears up some concerns people might have after reading some of the other reviews but they almost turned me away.  I'm glad they didn't.

_childDocuments_.review: What a ride. The early game is untouchable. Exploring the randomly generated world feels incredible, the mechanics are intuitive and easy to pick up, the crafting is actually fun (what the ♥♥♥♥?), and your troops and enemies feel moderately varied. I felt like a kid watching my older cousins play hotseat Heroes of Might and Magic again. The traditional D&D fantasy setting scratches that itch. You only have a handful of units so you spend a lot of time customizing their glyphs and abilities as they level. The game forces you to explore the map because of the resource depletion mechanic but you can sit your main tower in one location and explore with apprentices.There are some abrupt difficulty spikes in the mid game that actually caused me to lose my first playthrough (on balanced difficulty no less!). You will consistently have 5-6 units against 8-9 and there are a LOT of enemy stacks. The combat starts to feel a bit basic (the best comp is always 2-3 tanks and 2-3 ranged, move your blockers up, guard and use ranged attacks from behind them) but there is still some variety with unique units, abilities, resistances, and global buffs. The late game feels like a bit of a chore. There are WAY too many enemy stacks in my opinion. Thank god they implemented the auto resolve mechanic from TW. You basically go around cleaning up the remaining enemy mages, summoning golems and finishing any unresolved quests for HOURS. The late game is a problem in every 4X game I've ever played and I don't think SpellForce escapes this pitfall.Doesn't seem to have the replayability of Civ or Total War but god the early game was so fun, this is an 8.5/10 for me.

_childDocuments_.review: SpellForce: Conquest of Eo, Owned by Gravity's take on the series is a surprisingly coherent, bug-free package with a clear vision of what it wants to do. It offers both depth and simplicity depending on who is playing it without forcing you to act in ways you don't want to. One of my concerns going into Conquest of Eo would be the possibility of stale gameplay, but I'm glad to be able to say that this wasn't the case. Though I've mainly rushed through the game multiple times thus far to test certain mechanics, the times when I played it proper were all enjoyable, offering well-thought-out adventures that make you wish for more.I'm also elated to be able to call Conquest of Eo the first proper canon addition to the series since Dragon Storm, with Owned by Gravity taking extensive care to fit the story they want to tell into the world of Eo. It features many strong ties to SpellForce 1 and 2, making it a must-play for long-time fans who have, no doubt, been itching for an addition to the universe.For those new to the series, some friends of mine and I have created a fan website with all the lore content to bring you up to speed, alongside a lot of other useful information: You could criticise it for its lack of language support or the recycling of a few unit models, but considering the rumours of its budget being fairly limited, it’s hard to fault it for it, especially considering the game is fairly priced at only 29,99€ in a time where shelling them out for 70 Euro a piece.Overall, it’s a game I can wholeheartedly recommend to both old fans of the series as well people dipping their toes into it for the first time. It easily offers 30 to 40 hours of single-player gameplay that you can revisit multiple times for a different experience.❤ Audience ❤☑ Beginner☑ Casual Gamer☑ Normal Gamer☑ Expert☼ Graphics ☼☐ Bad☐ Alright☑ Good☐ Beautiful☐ Fantastic♬ Music ♬☐ Bad☐ Alright☐ Good☑ Beautiful☐ Fantastic☠ Difficulty ☠☐ Easy☐ Average☑ Easy to learn / Hard to master☐ Hard☐ Unfair§ Bugs §☐ Bugs destroy the game☐ Lots of bugs☐ Few Bugs☐ You can use them for speedruns☑ Nothing encountered☯ Story ☯☐ There is none☐ Bad☐ Alright☐ Good☑ Fantastic⚔ Gameplay ⚔☐ Frustrating☐ Sleepy☐ Boring☑ Fun☑ Challenging۞ Game time / Length ۞☐ Really short (0 - 3 hours)☐ Short (4 - 8 hours)☐ Few hours (10 - 20 hours) [if you focus on the main story]☑ Long (40-60 hours) [if you complete everything]☐ Very Long (61-100 hours)☐ Extremely Long (101+ hours)$ Price / Quality $☑ Full price☐ Wait for Sale☐ Don't buy☐ Refund it if you can

_childDocuments_.review: Similar to Age of Wonders but with a better interface and campaign. The best single-player experience I had in a while.Edit:Okay, I played for more hours, and now I can better formulate why I like this game more than AOW or similar titles. The unique side of this game is that while it has all properties of 4x, it feels like you play a single-player epic adventure. You solve mysteries, visit cities, meet interesting characters, craft things, and travel around. You can fly your tower over a mounting range. If 5 minutes ago you were fighting hordes of undead to get some magic artefacts, now you focus on harvesting resources for powerful potions while solving problems of local elves. And the art style, especially such nifty things as spellbook design, greatly helps immersion. I never had such an experience in 4x. Love it. Kudos to developers and game designers. I hope you have a remarkable career and bring us more unique experiences.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is at its best when you take your time. Free up your day, have some hot chocolate and pizza, and chill for a few hours. Appreciate the absolutely beautiful art, the fun writing, and the endless quests. If you do that and just let time get away from you, you'll have fun. The unit options are neat, and the mechanics are too.However, if you try to force yourself along and steamroll the AI as quickly as possible, you'll soon find the that game grinds to a halt. There's too much area and too many quests to cover with too few heroes. You need too many resources for your wartime logistics, and they run dry too fast.But, just don't do that. Chill out, put some YouTube on in the background, and have fun.It's a good game.

_childDocuments_.review: This is quite breath of fresh air in the fantasy 4x space. It plays as a bit of a hybrid game; a bit of 4x, a bit of RPG and a bit of adventure all rolled into one. It can sometimes scratch the HoMM itch, sometimes a Sorcerer King/Fallen Enchantress itch and sometimes an AoW itch. There is also more depth to the game than it first appears and there are some interesting mechanics to learn how to mange and exploit. So far, a really enjoyable experience.I do have some modest cons... having only one map and a somewhat linear progression with some of the main story elements might impact replayability, but when you consider the price it is still really good value for the game play that is in here.I hope this sells well enough to warrant some future DLC but in the meantime, I'm having a blast!And lastly, it plays quite well on the SteamDeck, especially with the ability to scale the fonts up (I wish more games did that).

_childDocuments_.review: EDIT: Updated review after 39 hours of play.The more I play this game, the more I have come to believe that it is at heart a RPG with heavy 4x elements.Like a RPG such as Neverwinter Nights, there is a known game world with fixed cities and deep, well established lore and units, spells, etc. You choose a class and then play through the story that is presented in this fixed world. There are multiple ways to finish the game that has procedural elements and you do quests and gain in power to face the story threat (Circle mages in this case). You have hero companions that have their own companion quests (I’m doing one right now).Once you finish the story, you can choose a new class (or customize your own) and then play the story again in the same world from a different perspective. In my mind, it’s a RPG/4x hybrid like we haven’t seen before and it’s fairly brilliant, imo. I think this may be why some folks going in expecting a pure 4x are disappointed or confused. It’s actually something new.ORIGINAL REVIEWI’m currently 16 hours into my initial play-through (Artificer) and although I’m doing fairly well, I still feel somewhat weak overall. I have 2 apprentices and a hero and 2 and a half armies. My hero has a couple of tier 2 units in it but all the rest are still tier 1. I just managed to clear a bridge being blocked (by a tier 2 army) with an apprentice (with tier 1 units). I just moved my tower for the first time (really cool mechanic) and have set up shop near the Shaper’s Secret tower.As in most tactical games like this, combined arms are key. In that bridge battle, my army had 2 melee, an archer, a shaman to heal and the apprentice can raise a demon as another throwaway melee. It costs him two stacks of bleed to call the demon but he got the Cleanse ability on one of his level ups so now he can clear the bleed in the same turn that he calls the demon. Enemies really hate that demon so he makes for a really valuable meat-shield while my ranged (archers, shaman, apprentice) units are firing away. I also stuck a spider web glyph on my archers so they can web melee enemies in place on hit so they can’t get near me until their buddies are dead. I love the tactical diversity you can have with this.Overall, this game is so great. At 16 hours into an AoW3 game, I’d be in mop-up mode. In this game, I feel like I’m hanging on by a thread still. I love how the quests and accomplishments you have to achieve before advancing further in power serve as a gate to regulate what typically becomes a mid-game rush and then a tedious end-game slog to kill everything with your OP stack or two. This feels completely different and compelling at all times.There is so much to learn and do in the game it’s just amazing. It’s so different from other 4X games I’ve played in many ways and I love it for that. It’s a breath of originality in the genre and very welcome. I was initially worried that a single map wouldn’t make for much in the way of replay value but I now think I was wrong there. This is not a game you can just cruise to victory in your very first run and I love it for that. The map is also absolutely huge and I’ve only uncovered a tiny fraction of it so far. I look forward to learning the ins and outs of all the mechanics, spells, tower abilities, etc. and playing as the other classes and customizing my own class.To sum up, this game may not be for everybody but it certainly is for me. I love it.

_childDocuments_.review: Its essentially Age of Wonders on a budgetFrom my understanding Spellforce is a decent brand so seeing the same stock icons i use for my mods without any kind of edit was a little taken back- if your an AOW vet you should have no trouble jumping right in here wit no tutorial- Too scripted, i tried a few of the races and the story arc happens the same, and you get the same hero with the same name. Eg goblin camps allow to produce units- Animations and spells are stiff, sometimes i cast and when you think its done it keeps going this could be trimmed- as its so unrefined it has kind of a charm, when i have a bit more time ill give it a better spinEh it deserves a thumbs up as its great to see diversity in this niche field but lets hope theirs ongoing development, random maps, multiplayer, random heroes, no scripted event, there is a good game here but it def needs more polish. _childDocuments_.review: Shockingly, this game has only one mode--scripted "campaign".  The map appears to be random, but everytime you are walking a single-player SRPG campaign mode with heavy guard rails and very arbitrary scripting walls.  There is very little customization option for your wizard, and you always start with access to the same minions.  So to be clear, other than picking the "world" type (five options iir), and a difficulty, plus your wizard (crafting + primary/secondary magic), there are no options to configure a game.  You can't select number of enemies or size of map or any such thing.  As a die-hard fan of fantasy 4x style games, this was a rather shocking disappointment.  If this was an EA title with other modes expected one might be inclined to forgive and suggest a wait and see attitude, but as it stands...

_childDocuments_.review: The game feels like a boring and frustating version of Age of Wonders. Poor balancing of the three classes, no randomization in the map layout and no casting of spells in combat. There is no option for diplomacy and as soon as you meet other (circle mage) factions, combat is the only option. Worst of all though are the annoying ticking clock elements in the game. Your reputation with the circle mages deteriorates with time regardless of your actions in the game, with only very rare opportunities to (temporarily) increase it by a bit. The enemy factions get free stacks of units spawning with time and the defense of their tower (main base) increases also with time. Enemy factions don't seem to need any economy to sustain their troops. Thus, taking a slower approach doing quests and exploring the map is not an option, since the hostile faction will always attack you and will have stronger armies and tower garrisons the longer you wait. This forces you into a rushed playstyle where you race against the clock to take out all enemy factions before they get to strong. Being forced to rush you campaign is a fatal flaw and deal breaker for a game in this genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Just beat the game on balanced difficulty. Honestly it is a very good game - will be even better after 2-3 patches! It is a bit different than I've initially expected - it is mostly survival/RPG game for me, not 4X, mostly because of different it is with expanding. You get apprentices who can build lodges and a tower which you can move to certain locations in order to gather resources - which are limited by the way! Overall I highly recommend playing on balanced or even exploration difficulty first to get the feel for the game. Combat is decent, I have found only one very cheesy spell in the entire game which can be abused if you so desire (not recommended because it ruins any fun of a fair gameplay). All age of wonders fans and seeking a bit different experience should find themselves in the right place! It is more about picking your fights very carefully and improving your units, rather than massive scale battles, You will have fewer armies, but if you play well you should have plenty of scouting stacks or armies who are able to defeat weak/medium enemies without your apprentices' help. I really liked tower expansion and unit leveling systems. Have fun! See you in the world of Eo :)
