_childDocuments_.review: In SpellForce: Conquest of Eo a wonderful fantasy world has been created that captivates you. The story behind the game is beautifully told and you're dying to find out what happened to the master. As the game progresses, new quests keep popping up that keep you busy and make you stronger. Combat is turn-based, and each unit has balanced abilities that only get better as you level up. Unfortunately, there are also some issues that can affect the gaming experience. Units can disappear when merging or worse, sometimes buildings are inaccessible because they appear randomly on the map and are separated from access by a river or mountain. There may be a spell that allows the whole unit to cross the river, but I haven't discovered that spell yet, even after over 4.5 hours of play. The sound is monotonous and could have been made more exciting in some places.All in all SpellForce: Conquest of Eo. An exciting strategy game with random events that at some points you can solve with kindness instead of just violence. Imagine tripping over a magical wishing well or lifting a curse from the undead. It's a real test of your strategic skills and a must-read for fans of the genre. While it already has compelling appeal, there's always room for improvement. So keep your fingers crossed for some electrifying updates and DLCs that will take your experience to the next level!"

_childDocuments_.review: Overall :: 85/100An excellent and low-price game that breaks down the 4X/Grand Strategy genre to its simplest and most fun components, removing most of the micromanagement that makes the late-game of many 4X a chore. Higher difficulties offer an actual challenge as well, something severely lacking in something like Sid Meier's Civ where your win is assured after the first few dozen turns. Plus, the developers seem quite involved which should mean updates in the future and DLC adding more of what this game needs.If you've never played a Grand Strategy game before but want to try & like the high-fantasy setting, then buy this game! This is an excellent entry point to the genre and I'm sure you won't be disappointed. If you've played a 4X before, this will be hit or miss but there's no real surprises. The game's well-made, if a bit lacking in variety and polish (units don't look very good, some audio and UI annoyances, minor things overall). The most important thing to recognize is that this isn't a traditional 4X game and it's $30 so it's a somewhat small/short campaign. Be sure to watch some gameplay vids and read a few negative reviews if you know what 4X is about. + Exploration is a huge part, which I LOVE. If you enjoy the early exploration of a new save in Civ then you should like how this game handles exploration. + Extermination is the core gameplay loop - you'lll be fighting constantly and, personally, I love turn-based tactics so I see this as an absolute win. + Exploit resources by harvesting them around the map and engaging in mini-quests scattered around the world. The way you engage with the world itself feels unique and fits this fantasy world perfectly. + Expanding your domain is a mechanic, but you only have your tower - you cannot have multiple 'cities' like most 4X games. Love it or hate it, it's how this game works.Aside from gameplay, just consider the setting: if you like wizards, magic, and fantasy then you're sure to enjoy this 4X! Just keep in mind it's $30 for a reason: there's not much meat to it yet.

_childDocuments_.review: Cool game. From what I can tell so far, it's a fairly simplified and linear version of Age of Wonders, but it does do some very interesting things - the main one being, I think, having finite ressources on the map. This avoids entirely the city spam problem that pretty much plagues the 4X genre since forever ; you only really have one city that you move around exploiting the different ressources. So there are no repetitive building chains or tedious economic micromanagement, but it's not so simple as you do have to plan out how you're positioning yourself on the map. I feel like this is a great concept that should be picked up by more devs, as really managing multiple cities (or planets) inevitably make these games more tedious as time passes. Nothing like that here. Otherwise, you get a linear tech tree and limited amount of troops per battle (4-5), so as mentionned, it works like simplied AoW ; there is a pretty involved crafting system ; also a quest system that gives the player direct goals to follow, which may limit the replayability, but it's pretty dynamic overall (the quests blend in the exploration and ressource gathering). These are mostly first impressions but I'm writing them down to support the game, it's a very welcome surprise, and the price really makes it a steal (comparing it to the Master of Magic remake, which really did not have the kind of new ideas we have here).

_childDocuments_.review: An absolute pleasure to play! It differs slightly from other 4x games in that it has way more focus on roleplaying and quests, which makes each turn so much more interesting and immersive. And the custom designed map, although fixed each playthough, oozes theme and charm.I also love the roaming tower, it means you're constantly on the move trying to make the most out of your surroundings. It maintains that exciting early game feel throughout the whole game.Only potential negative is the limited replayability, mainly due to there only being 3 main classes - alchemist, necromancer and artificer. Having said that, I've still yet to dabble with the necromancer and you can also create a custom class from different schools of magic (of which there are 6). Plus there are many different heroes and questlines to discover with each playthrough.I didn't think this one would capture me so much but I've been playing Age of Wonders 4 lately and the main feeling I've got from it is a yearning to come back to this, it just holds my attention so much more.Probably GOTY for me. Hopefully we'll get a DLC soon with more content!

_childDocuments_.review: This is way better than I thought it would be. When can I expect DLC? The gameplay is deep, instead of describing the key details that you still won't have a true feel for unless you play yourself, I'll try to relate things to popular titles in the genre.Civ element; Hex map, tiles that do all kinds of stuff, resources, cities, landmarks, forest/water/mountain tiles, havent come across any "nothing can get past here" spots its a good map, everything works how you'd expect if your familiar with the Civ series.Units; Again only been a necromancer but there's like 20 units I can create, but you can also take tiles that give access to all sorts of stuff, I had a dwarf hero leading an army of orc slavers that I sent into the goldenfields and enslaved bugs and goblins which I trek'd back to my domain as a free mass security force. Theres alot of diversity, really you can think Warhammer Fantasy style factions and units. You can also level up most everything aside from "fantastic" units, allowing you to mold them for specific purposes, theres really a ton that can be said about the units and stack assembly but you'll prolly actually need to play it and find the "theme" you want.Combat; Think top down turn based rpg, Divinity Original Sin 2 comes to mind. Make sure to read about the tile your attacking or the 4 tier 1 goblins are going to be backed up by 2 banshees, or its going to rain meteors etc. The actual battlefields aren't really decorated, more like a hex chess board in a way.Quests; There's a ton, ranging from benign to highly rewarding or debilitating, read carefully, but even then sometimes it's just dumb luck. Quests in tiles, encounter quests from moving, random quests from stacks, quests from your tower, etc etc.Story; I'll be honest, Spellforce is HIGH fantasy and it doesn't have a movie for me to watch to get it, Circle mages or something rawr gonna take them down I honestly have no idea, don't really care about that but I'm sure the work was put in and it is well done, that said I get the general idea of what I'm doing in regards to the choices matter quests so if you like a good story, I'm gonna say probably, If you're here for the RPG/tactic/Civ aspects you should probably just go ahead and buy it.Item crafting, spell book with pages, custom "mage" skills theres alot more but If you're to this point and not leaning more to a yes than a no, I probably lack the ability to convince you otherwise.9/10.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried really hard to like this game.   I like the world of Eo from previous Spellforce games, and I like 4X games in general like Civ, Humankind, Age of Wonders.  I just could not really figure out how to enjoy this game.The primary problem is how difficult it is to become powerful enough to achieve your goals, even on a relatively EASY difficulty setting,  That is because you are severely limited by your STACK SIZE or how many units you can bring to a battle.  You start with 5 and it grows to 6, but there it gets stuck at 6 for what feels like FOREVER.  You cannot "combine" armies like in other 4X games, they cannot assist each other in any way.  You also do not want to lose units, because you become heavily invested in them after they level up quite a few times after running around and completing quests.  If you lose a unit, that you've been leveling up for hours, in an unimportant battle, you feel like reloading the save, retrying the battle to get zero losses, or avoiding it altogether.  It feels like you're walking on eggshells even on easy difficulty settings.  So all in all none of the mechanics really work well together.  After 3+ hours in a game (after multiple restarts figuring out build orders) I had just run around doing quests with nothing much to show for it.  I don't think I was even halfway progressed through a game.  I could stomp pretty much any wandering army (easy difficulty) but the limited stack size prevented me from progressing past harder fights.  It makes ZERO sense to me why adjacent units cannot reinforce each other in a STRATEGY game.  This is such a huge frustration that I decided to uninstall.Update....I gave it another try, and I'm still discovering new critical game mechanics.  For example, I just learned late in the game that I don't have to leave my tower at the allfire nodes.  The game asks you to move your tower to the allfire node, but it's not obvious you can leave and still keep the node.  I also learned that the shield "resource" is actually reputation and you can build a lodge to gain rep, so unlocking major things for me.So overall, the game has a steep learning curve and it does a poor job of explaining things.  Expect to start over many times unless you consult strategy guides and videos.  Normally in games there is a "tech tree" that helps you plan.  Here, spells in the book "uncover" themselves gradually, making it hard to plan anything unless you consult guides.  Crafting is the same where you "discover" the recipes so you don't really know what's next or what's available late game.Other problems remain: I'm constantly save scumming, more so than in other 4X games, because losing experienced units unnecessarily is so punishing.   The fact that armies do not assist each other still feels heavily contrived.  Yeah, you can figure out how to "work around" (cheese) it, for example:  - Land your tower nearby and send suicide squads to soften the enemy up (units build for free and only require upkeep if they stay alive).  - Just sacrifice armies.  Later on your tower can rebuild armies quickly and even with starting XP.  - Dump tons of mana buffing each individual unit.  Diplomacy is really basic.  Placate the mages so they don't harass you.  But if they do, rush their main tower quick (sacrifice armies) to eliminate them.  No alliances it seems.In the RPG department, I think it also falls short.  My mage is not an actual character, in that there's no name, gender, voice or appearance (is it me then?).  All of the quest text references the mage as the main character.  Yet my apprentices, the guys I actually move around, they have no personality or story, save for one of them.  There seems to be a plot, but it's slow to reveal.  The plot here is... you are power hungry.  I think Spellforce 3 was excellent in the RPG department, the dialogue and voices were excellent, the plot of discovering the shapers' secrets was very cool.  That's not really here, at least ~4 hours into a game.All that said, the game has that "one more turn" feeling from 4X genre, and it's easy to rack up the hours.    The questing is actually a good and relaxing time, but once you face a challenge it's like OK is this worth sacrificing an army.  And for the time spent, I feel like I've neither built a powerful empire nor a powerful army.  Even my tower is not sufficient, I need to keep roaming to make enough gold to upkeep my armies.  I've mostly played whack-a-mole with every quest on the map, which was fun, but doesn't help the game be replayable, as the world map is the same every game.I do appreciate the entry into the genre.  I've been looking for another game ever since King Arthur the Roleplaying Wargame.  It is a creative game that just tries one too many new things, the most contrived of which is that units can't help each other.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game for the moment, clear interface, original beginning, attractive price. The music is discreet but effective. The campaign map is pleasant and does not lag for the moment on my modest PC configuration. Being able to have units by several means (crafting, recruitment and spells) is a plus. I appreciate having alternatives in events and having non-manichean choices.Some drawbacks though:-It lacks the ability to rebind its hotkeys and lacks shortcuts in general.-No possibility to disable the camera tracking in battle mode.-The noises in the fights are a bit disappointing.-I would have appreciated a French translation.Despite the fact that Age of wonder 4 will be released in a few months, I wanted to give Spellforce Conquest of Eo a chance for its aesthetics and the positive feedback from some previews and especially to support the developers for their attempt that changes from previous games in the series, otherwise I would have waited for patches and sales. I hope that the follow-up will be good and that some of the above mentioned flaws will be improved.

_childDocuments_.review: I was on  the fence about buying this game as Age of Wonders 4 was coming out, and the Master of Magic remake was not all that.  But the more I play it the more I am utterly captured by this game's charm and design.  The game does fewer things than a typical MoM clone but it does them very well.  Examples:1) The spellbook!  The spellbook is fantastic and includes not just spells, but tower stuff, hero stories, overall quests, etc.2) Unit creation via item collection (aka "crafting").  This is a very clever means of creating magic-focused units.  You gather materials from exploration, and grind them up for candy like your turning in Pokemon.  It sounds not good. But it's really good, trust me.  3) Economy unlike any previous game.  Some of your initial resourcces come from the map... but they run out.  So you have to relocate to keep finding materials, which is unlike a lot of other games.4) Combat.  Animations SNAP.  And the design is thoughtful.  This is not pokey Age of Wonders Planetfall.Anyways.  This game is worth checking out.

Early in this game is showing alot of promise. I get the feel of fallen enchantress, sorcerer king more than I would say might and magic vibes. So far a few different scenarios, types of magic and types of characters should give a few playthroughs worth of value. I have only encountered one game breaking bug so far, however I was unable to replicate it. I feel it was more of a freak coincidence.

_childDocuments_.review: Fantastic 4X, sort of, turnbased , crafting, building, recruiting, learning, moving around the good looking map, fighting battles with small armies of very diverse units that gain xp and level up. Heroes lead the armies but fight also.  Some tought battles. Your base is a tower, but as soon as your the resources in your domain get exhausted you must fly your tower to another place on the map where you can collect resources etc. Excellent game with quite a lot of choices and depth.
_childDocuments_.name: SpellForce: Conquest of Eo

_childDocuments_.review: I really want to like this game but it's just so chaotic and unorganized I barely understand what I'm doing/have to do. The crafting system is frustrating to no end because as a new player all I see is those little colored dots, I literally was making glyphs and then accidentally using those glyphs to make other glyphs because they appear as ingredients. I play as artificer and no mines appear, I play as alchemist and no herbs appear. The heck is going on in this game? I could get past all of that stuff until I realized my resources were limited and I had to constantly move my tower around, that's a big no no for me.I'd give this game 4/10, I rarely felt in control, promotions for units were random and 90% of them suck, enemies are god-tier stronger than you are yet you have to kinda invade one of them soonish into the game because you use up your resources so quick. I quit the game after one battle where the enemy had 2 of these like fire elementals that could just move wherever, have insane range + apply burning. I couldn't even reach them with my whole army before I was routed and everyone but my apprentice was dead.
_childDocuments_.name: SpellForce: Conquest of Eo

_childDocuments_.review: Starts off interesting, but early-mid game you're constantly desperate for resources. You eventually get overrun. You'd need to manually fight every battle in order to not waste time or resources (and this gets boring and time consuming). Otherwise, it's only a matter of time before your "economy" collapses. Just becomes desperate tedium.PS. I was playing the "hard" difficulty since I usually beat these games on the first go (obviously not this time...). I played a second run. A patch nerfed my runes and back to loserville I went. Still think the game bogs down with multiple circle mages taking turns sending titans your way. I feel like they released this game too early. There's potential here, but they probably should have tested and tweaked for several more months to create a fun, diverse, and balanced experience. As it is, to beat the game on hard difficulty, you'd likely need to cheat by knowing the map beforehand (it's always the same and trying to explore/discover spreads your forces thin), and very expeditiously concentrate your heroes on the few main objectives to get through the map as fast as possible before the circle mages gang...wreck you. One other complaint, recruiting decent units was a struggle. I created several slave armies, but slave units are inferior to recruited units.
_childDocuments_.name: SpellForce: Conquest of Eo

_childDocuments_.review: This is a great and underappreciated gem. So much play value at such a modest cost.The game is a great combination of turn-based tactics and RPG elements. Some have complained that there is "only" one map. That single map is massive, like the map of a complex RPG. Many quests and challenges will await you. I completed the game multiple times and I didn't get bored. I almost never replay a game like this after I have completed it the first time.
_childDocuments_.name: SpellForce: Conquest of Eo

_childDocuments_.review: I nearly deinstalled the game after the first hour or so. It seems confusing. random and like there isn't much to do in this game at all...Oh boy, I'm happy I stayed!!!This is essentially a 4X game with an unusual allocation of the focus of the different Xs:1)  = Very high Focus: Explore the land, discover quests, experiment with the really fun crafting system. This game keeps the sense of "I wonder what else there is..:?" going for a really long time. Excellent!2)  = Low Focus: Your territory does not really expand...it changes/moves. In addition, there isn't much to manage/optimize economy-wise.3)  = Medium Focus: Your stacks wander of the map to harvest/exploit resources. With creatures prowling everywhere, there is an interesting risk/reward to it.4)  = High Focus: You'll have a fight nearly every round. I find the fights to be engaging with some interesting new mechanics, at least one of which has the potential to become a new standard for the genre.of turn-based combat. Stiil, with so many fights I am happy that the auto-resolve combat function works reliably well.Overall, a great game with the potential to be a fantastic one once flashed out more: 8/10
_childDocuments_.name: SpellForce: Conquest of Eo

_childDocuments_.review: It reminds me of Total War Warhammer but: - With hex turn based battle - With hex turn based grand strategy - It is not a 4X, but more a 3.5 IMO: You do Explore, Exploit and Exterminate a lot, but the 'Expand' is not what you'll found in a 4X such as TWW where you snowball economically with territorial reach. - Economy is nomadic for the most part, this add a lot of (good) difficulty when you come from more classic 4XReplay potential is good, but not excellent: - The main goal stays the same, but you have multiple ways to accomplish it along the way - In each game you'll face 4 foes, they are picked randomly in a fixed pool of 12 or so. So you can't always use the same strategy. - You'll get one hero per game. with their own quest line. The hero is picked at random- The map only change a bit between each games: the main landmarks and topology doesn't change, but the rest is placed at random (for example, where bandit camp will spawn etc). So yeah, less discovery for the map: you'll know pretty soon where's what.The predetermined map is also a positive tho: it's handcrafted and takes place in an established universe, so it offer a nice and consistent experience compared to some game that are use more procedural.The game is really good, I do hope we will see more scenario added!
_childDocuments_.name: SpellForce: Conquest of Eo

_childDocuments_.review: I played this game for a couple dozen hours (mostly offline), but the long-term motivation just is not there. Without the economy-building aspects of a classic 4X, the game just feels static, and it doesn't really add anything to make up for it. Notably, the RPG aspect is only in terms of the story, you have no actual main character and the development of your apprentices or heroes is only marginally more expansive than for standard units.Once you have unlocked all the main mechanics as part of the story, the game just feels to grind to a halt. Turns get repetitive as your only way to progess is by playing through the story missions (usually some text based choice followed by combat), but constant spawning of enemy stacks prevents you from moving freely. So many turns are just spend fighting a bunch inconsequential battles while you inch towards your objective.The crafting system is quite cool and figuring out how to get the essences you need is rewarding. Map and story design are good, but this does not by itself hold up the game. The whole "master mage" aspect is underdeveloped. World map spells have low impact, and apart from some utility spells I mostly did not bother. A lot of it is single target for no good reason (why the hell do I need a single-target flight spell?). Having a flying tower base is cool, but apart from being a teleport hub you don't interact much with it.The combat is competently designed, but nothing that you haven't seen before. Ranged damage rules, as is common. Units have lots of abilities, but usually the simple strategies work best - avoid giving the enemy free shots at you and hit fast and hard. The enemy AI does not consistently "shoot to kill", and any heal abilities are thus very powerful. This game's "gimmick", which is that units that retaliate in melee loose an action for their next turn, is mostly inconsequential. It makes the melee fight more static, which means ranged units are even more important in deciding the fight.Overall, unless you find the story especially gripping, there is very little to keep you playing.
_childDocuments_.name: SpellForce: Conquest of Eo

_childDocuments_.review: Conquest of Eo is a nice blend adventure, strategy and RPG based in the Spellforce universe. Similar to the original Spellforce series which were an interesting mix of RPG and real-time strategy, this game provides similar experience by mixing turn based strategy with other genres. Conquest of Eo is somewhat similar to Age of Wonders (or Master of Magic if you want to connect to the ancestral origin), however there are nuances. First of all, you will have only one city/mage tower, secondly some of the resources will expire over time. So the game nudge you to move (levitate) across the map in a constant search of new resources to balance the expenses for your growing army. Small outposts can be established across the map not only to get resources but also to get new abilities and new types of unites for hire.In addition to resources there are multitude of different quests on the map (or even chain of quest). While the quests themselves are simple kill/fetch items, the stories connected to them are interesting enough for the strategy game making every playthrough an interesting adventure. Another interesting aspect is that not only your heroes evolves but every unit can be developed in a unique way, through numerous level ups and glyphs. This allows you to really fine tune every unit to your playstyle.And of course, you have large arsenal of different magical spells from enhance your army or even summon it. You can even make changes on the global map, for example freezing water will allow you to cross the ocean.Just look at this game not as empire building strategy (for that choose Age of Wonder) but as adventure strategy – then you will like it.
_childDocuments_.name: SpellForce: Conquest of Eo

_childDocuments_.review: I am a long time Spellforce series fan. Conquest of Eo is  like the previous titles, but that should be obvious. THQ made a bold attempt to come up with turn based strategy packed with so many events it almost feels like "choose your own adventure" game. I must admit, after playing for a while I almost felt like going back in time playing Master of Magic or Age of Wonders for the first time, so if you know these, you should be right at home. This game is clearly inspired from these titles while having some mechanics of it's own.My biggest concern was the lack of depth because the UI looked like a mobile game port. Luckily I was pleasantly surprised.  There is some basic base building, but you can find ways to improve your mage tower (for example make it fly!). You can craft glyphs and artifacts, research and cast spells, hire or summon units,  based on your mage affinity and locations in your domain. Events and quest give you loot, allies or lead to unlocking new features. Suffice to say, there is no fouding/conquering of new cities. It's just your tower, your domain and few methods to relay your domain in other places.Combat is fun, there is really not much to say, because it's all that matters. Units level up and you pick from two random perks every level. At levels 5, 10 and 15 you get to choose from two new abilities instead. And then there are the hero type units. You cannot make a hero-only army like you could in AoW series, because one army can only support 4 standard units (will improve as your power grows) and one hero. Also you are limited in how many these heroes you can have. Heroes have access to powerful abilites and can even equip artifacts. Conquest of Eo caught me by suprise and I am having fun for the time being. There is nothing groundbreaking, it's like having a coitus with a girl that looks very much like your ex (the sweet one you got bored with).6.9/10

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this on a whim, thinking that given the low entry price it would be a decent placeholder waiting for Age of Wonders 4.Turns out that I'm enjoying it a LOT more than I originally anticipated. The game is a typical 4X in the standards of its genre, but the production value is very nice, the UI clean and practical to use, the gameplay loop tight and there are even a couple of interesting twists on the concept, like the Heroes you can hire for your army being proper characters with a background story and a personal questline to go through.Frankly the only downside of the game in its current form is that is a bit sparse in terms of amount of content. There is only one (massive and extremely detailed) map, where you can choose different starting points and the specialization of your "Archmage in the making", but not things like what race/faction you control at the beginning etc.I hope it will do well enough to get some update in the future, because the foundation is extremely solid and there's room to make this become one of the "must have" in the genre.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not sure why people are saying this is not replayable.The map, admittedly a singular one, is really huge and it's unlikely you fully explore it in one game.The different cities have interesting quests and you can unlock many rooms for your tower and pages for your grimoire and again you propably won't unlock everything in one game.The game-mechanics between Alchemis, Artificer and Necromancer are different enough to be worth exploring and the different interactions with various Circle Mages are kinda interesting too.And each game you get a different Hero with their own questline to follow.So to make it short, I played it through fully with each of the major starting-builds and I had a couple of false starts too, since the game is not all that easy, coming out at over 40 hours of gameplay.Which is certainly not that much in comparison to some games, but worth the price and to me fun.Edit: I really hope the eventually bring in Demon Summoning as a main-skill similar to the three we already have. That addition seems obvious, but unfortunatly updates are coming kinda slow.

_childDocuments_.review: An AoW variant that *actually* hooks and is fun to play.So, right away, the franchise and setting is 'SpellForce', but the gameplay is actually Age Of Wonders, full stop. If you're looking for the next title in the SpellForce RTS franchise, this is not it.However, putting that missconception aside,there's an actually solid game here. The tactical combat aspect is pretty default AoW stuff, with small-scale combat between individual armies consisting of a few units each (starts out with 4vs4, but can escalate to 10vs10 in lategame). The mechanics are tried&tested, and work well, allowing a fair amount of tactical maneuvering around obstacles, heigh advantages, and particularly flanking, with fair power attributed to both ranged and melee combat, a tricky balancing act between using the innate advantage  of defense, or the higher initiative of offense, and all spliced up with magic and spellcasting (that is powerful, but with spellcasters also being the most fragile units in the game. Usually). The AI, on that tactical level, is a bit hit and miss though: It correctly understands the concepts of flanking and exploiting weak links in your defense, but also doesn't understand (de)buffs and resistances properly and will occasionally suicide it's troops in nonsensical ways.On the strategic layer however, the game shines: The game does away with your general bread/butter 4X playstyle, and also doesn't go down the route of presenting you a fixed single-player campaign. Instead, you get an asymetrical 4X-gameplay where you start as a small mage in the middle of nowhere, with four well-established and virtually infinitely powerful mages in the neighborhood. You can pick your starting position from five possible regions in the setup, and the map itself is static (including key locations like cities or landmarks, or which NPC factions are active in which region), but a lot of details are randomized: The locations for quests and the generic ruin/mine/whatever locations will be randomized, enemy spawners and the gradual troop movements of factions will differ each game, and most importantly you only ever get to face four out of a total cast of eight circle mages... and whilst they share the general theme of being overly powerful and generally a threat to you, they each use different troop setups and also behave differently: One necromancer will pretty much expand into your territory from the very start if you neighbor them, and ruthlessly march their undead armies all over your bases. Whilst the flirty enchantress will be pretty amiable, until you start refusing to comply with her arguably arbitrary demands popping up from time to time.And not only is the game initially dynamic via randomization, it also retains that dynamic nature as your campaign progresses: You don't build a fixed base or city, but only temporary outposts, with the core of your domain being a tower that may be initially stationary, but soon becomes a mobile fortress. And since ressources in a region are strictly depletable, you're naturally encouraged to migrate about, questing and harvesting region by region. The direction of which is determined by a number of factors such as where circle mages have set up shop (pretty much a no-go zone for you early on), where your quests lead you (again randomized and depending upon which profession / hero you pick up), and which regions' inhabitants you're well suited for fighting (i.e. a white magic beast army is great for murdering your way through a swamp full of undead, but might face an uphill battle when trying to fight through volcanic pits full of fire elementals).On top of that, the game offers three distinct archetypes, that change what your general crafting system looks like. The devs did a great job at making all three types use the same kind of crafting materials, and also interact differently with certain elements of loot, yet also generate distinctly different playstyles: Alchemists have the easiest time crafting, but they also end up crafting mostly consumables, that allow you to turn each battle not in a question of 'are my troops strong enough to win' but 'how many potions do I want to spend to bruteforce a victory in this battle'. The Artificer, for comparison, instead just invests into permanent troop upgrades via glyphs... but both does the Artificer also have access to consumables (just can't craft them themselves), and the Alchemist has access to glyphs. And then there's the Necromancer who likewise uses both of these mechanics, but also prioritizes crafting their own undead elite troops, whilst turning the city-recruited units (that the two other archetypes base their armies on) into undead cannon fodder.This leads into another two layers of gameplay difference: Schools of Magic and Troop Type. You start out with two selected schools of magic, and whilst you'll generally find random bits of access to any school whilst playing, you'll find more of those two, meaning they have a distinct impact on your playstyle. And whilst there are some obvious synergies (i.e. Death for Necromancer, Nature for Alchemist, etc), you will also find interesting combinations that aren't quite as standard (such as buffing up your undead armies with Light Magic, to go on a Holy Crusade against the other undeads).Likewise, the type of troops you focus on can massively impact your gameplay: Do you just craft your own Undeads as Necromancer? Or recruit sturdy Dwarves that will level up slowly, but become an unstoppable force? Or rather go for the somewhat less powerful humans that level up fast? Or just go with an orc-based build that is accompanied by large swaths of maintenance free slave armies? Whilst you can technically do all of that in a single campaign, the buffs afforded to you by the specific race's buildings strongly imply you to focus on one or two races, and consequently generates replayability.As a sidenote, graphics and sound are both fine, if not extraordinary. Seeing graphic assets from other Spellforce titles reused can either be marked up as cheap, or as nostalgic, that's up to you.Overall, three complete (and a few aborted) campaigns and 80hours in, I can firmly say that this game was a surprise hit for me. I've played a few AoW titles, and never particularly grew to like them. But in this one, the strategic layer with it's deep replayabiltiy, and the tactical level with it's tight and streamlined combat, come togather just right.Definitely a good title if you want to play a fantasy strategy game, bonus points if you like either the AoW franchise for it's mechanics, or the SpellForce franchise for it's theme.Final score: 9/10There's a couple balance issues that are actively being worked on, and are neither unexpected nor too much of a concern, but other than that, the game scores fairly high due to being simply good in all relevant aspects, with no negative aspects (such as the occasionally lackluster AI) affecting the gameplay too greatly.

_childDocuments_.review: More streamlined version of  Single Player AOW4(with minimal diplomacy), Very well done, very minimal bugs experienced.  All 3 types of characters excluding the DLC(I didn't purchase yet) Have very unique archetypes, where you decide to start on the map completely changes the next run that you play.  The end starts to drag a bit like all 4X games, but by the time you get there, you can usually push the final objective in 10-20 turns, instead of the 40-50 turns it feels like in other 4X games.  Lots of diverse strategies/unit compositions, with random events to make each run from turn to turn different.
_childDocuments_.name: SpellForce: Conquest of Eo

_childDocuments_.review: It's a solid game, fun for a quick exploration of the mechanics and setting.  It doesn't seem super complicated, but the randomization that's in the game (What little there is) and the multiple story arcs make it a fun little hero-squad adventure game.  It definitely has some small problems and the major thing it feels like the devs need to plan out sooner rather than later is wide expansions rather than tall, as it feels like the game's designed to end at a specific time and you can't really milk more from a fancy endgame, so yeah.  There's definitely room for improvement though, by adding in more mage classes, more possible tile markers and unit spawners, more enemies, and even possible catastrophic events that can just happen.  Overall, I like it, it feels like an honest, good game.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought the game with the Demon Sourge DLC. The base game and the DLC are worth it. The game looks great and the story is nicely told but doesn't force itself on one. Multiple different runs are possible, where most of the game is completely different depending on what archetype you chose at the beginning. On top of that, there are subcategories to choose from at the beginning and while playing.

_childDocuments_.review: good game, if u like the age of wonder series, this game is basically age of wonders 3, but imagine it as a massive mod overhaul.the biggest differences to other turn based strategy games in the likes of homm or age of wonders is thatu start with a squad size of 4+1(slot for hero/apprentice only) units, which can be increased to up to 9+1.the most fun part of the game is getting more pages for ur spellbook (each new page adds 4 new researchable spells for its spellschool) because there are literally spells for everything in this game, and the other fun part is building up ur towrs with new rooms (which also can be part of new pages) and upgrading those rooms for further boni.there isnt anything bad with the game or gameplay (maybe a bit balancing here and there but that is always an issue of discussion). in all my hours of playing i only encountered one bug where i was softlocked due to the game not accepting any commands (reloading an autosave from the same turn and ending/skipping my turn fixed it). asides from that there are 2 unit traits who dont work (which both basically work the same so prob just a single line of code not working) and one exploit which i wont mention so the devs dont patch it ou (xd).can only recommend to buy this game and hopefully there will be some dlcs for even more content (since besides a single wood elve unit, all elven (as in not monster/construct/undead) wood elven and dark elven units are missing from the game) also hopefully they change it, so that one can have more than one hero per run and also some kind of reroll mechanic for the lvl ups would be nice (since there are some units who reaaaly need some specific traits and it sucks if u dont get them).

_childDocuments_.review: This is a Master of Magic clone (which was the first 4x magic-based game ever, and still probably the best). This game's innovation is that your tower can move, there's a crafting system, you can put some of the things you craft on any unit (not just heroes), but they've significantly nerfed magic. For example, there are no spells that can be hurled in combat (what kind of mage lord can't huck a few fireballs?) There are few other small changes, like buildings you construct and permanent benefits from them, weekly buffs, and how the level-ups offer a few random improvements but no static stat increases (meaning you might get lucky or you might get poor choices, or make poor choices, which in itself adds some luck and strategy to the game), but that's just style...and honestly, it's been 30 YEARS since MoM came out, so shame if they didn't come up with -something- new.In any case, it's smooth and enjoyable, for the most part. The music fits the ambience. There are different schools of magic, and three different crafting professions. The world is always the same, so the "explore" phase of the four Xs can be somewhat ignored once you know the map. There are also a few glitches. So far, I've experienced:- When using the "Reputation Increase" spell to get cities to like you, if you then accept their quests, it can freeze the game completely. I've experienced this with three different cities. The only way to side-step it seems to be to get them to like you, accept their building (if they have one), save the game, reload it, and then you can accept the quests.- Sometimes, for no apparent reason (but usually late in the game, like after week 20 when there's a lot going on) you can freeze; the enemies can still move about their days, but your units lose all movement points, healing, progress on harvesting, and so on. You're given one option every day: "End Turn." A save and reload fixes this as well.- The battle predictor and battle calculator don't seem to match up. You can have numbers like (yours) 820 (theirs) 350 and the predictor says you'll be annihilated; you play the battle and wipe up with them. Also, you can usually use some simple tactics like tossing your archers/healers in a corner, putting your melee units around them on guard, and then shoot/heal/defend until the opponents die. Any thought at all lets you easily defeat the computer. That being said, you seldom lose a unit that wasn't predicted to be lost, and you often don't lose a unit which was while using auto-complete. Finally, there really should be a "speed up" option in battles.- Some quests are ignorable, such as the "into the snows" quest trying to get past the gate. Just click the choice to go another way, come back and do it again, and the quest seems to disappear. This is fairly typical.- More on that: I found some trolls and demons fighting in the mountains, and I helped the trolls. After the combat, a unit offered to join me. I looked at him, then went back to say yes, and the game froze. This kind of thing happens more often than it would if they'd adequately play-tested and debugged this game.- A lot of things don't really make sense. Like the Dragon Heart quest which only shows up if Gor is there; otherwise it seems to be a useless building for the whole game. Once he IS there, the quest shows up, which is essentially "walk in and take the thing, despite the region possibly being inundated by droves of his soldiers". If he's not, then you just get a message saying "turn up and take the thing," but it doesn't happen until so late in the game that it's not all that useful.- The ending screen is buggy. If you click too fast on the "next" button before it's finished drawing in the current text, the holes that appear when drawing in the next simply stay. There's a good deal of -that- too.- Sometimes the tooltips that tell what a potion does in combat will just disappear. When this happens, they're gone for that save, no matter how many times you save/close/reload the game. They're also gone for all other games you begin. I've uninstalled/reinstalled the game, and it's still a problem. I assume at this point that I need to delete all saves an uninstall, then reinstall to fix it, which I haven't done yet; nor am I confident that it will fix the problem, gamedevs. >.> This is a huge inconvenience!This game wasn't adequately play-tested before release. That's the kind of lazy thing companies do these days knowing they can patch it later. They also are adding DLC, which is the kind of greedy thing companies do, but again, sign of the times. All in all, the glitches can be worked around, and the game is enjoyable. I got it on sale, which I recommend. I wouldn't pay full price until they get rid of the bugs, and also I'd rather pay one full price for the full game and all DLC than this micro-pay crap.I give it 3.3 stars out of 5.

_childDocuments_.review: This game doesn't do a whole lot different from others in its' genre.. and yet does so much unique stuff. It's a 4X genre in the same style as Sorcerer King but with an Age of Wonders flair. However, the devs took an old franchise and leveraged it wonderfully to bring the game to life. The SpellForce IP isn't theirs but you can tell that they put in effort and care into paying respect to the IP, as little details about the kingdoms and archmages are noticeable.But gameplay wise, this is super satisfying. There's a degree of RPG elements that break up the pace the standard 4X macro-micro gameplay loop; fairly typical dialogue box narratives but they do it RIGHT. The frequency that they pop up is about right, although leaning towards a little much, but none of the boxes are unwieldly in their text length or sequence length. Text is kept to short one to two small paragraphs and two to three dialogues per sequence. So you get a narrative break without being taken out of the 4X gameplay. And you can skip reading the text and just implicitly understand the context from the choices accurately, which makes replayability reasonable.There's only three classes (artificer, alchemist, necromancer). Basically defines your core macro mechanics. Necromancers can create their own (undead) units and have an extra level of customization as the souls they use to make a unit tend to come with an extra ability. Making undead units can be fun as there's a level of strategy and customization in the mid and late game. Artificer can make runes/glyphs and items. Glyphs are special items that grant units a specific ability or bonus. Artificer are the only ones who can freely remove glyphs to be reused as well, everyone else has to permanently use the glyph on a unit. Items are standard RPG items (weapon, armor, trinket) with the obvious stat-ability stuff. Typically only used by your special units (heroes/apprentices), you can get units to level up and gain an equipment slot. Not sure how rare or restrictive that is yet. It is fun being able to freely make powerful glyphs to really power-up units late-game, although they don't seem to get any special glyphs to stand apart from the other classes who can find those glyphs as loot or in shops.I haven't played alchemist yet because it doesn't seem appealing to me, for now.This game has a heavy emphasis on mobility, completing quests, and managing your relations with the archmages (pseudo-gods of the game/lore). The archmages are all preestablished, maxed out nations who will destroy you if you make them mad... until you build yourself up. So there's a fun and rewarding mechanic of tiptoeing around these pseudo-gods who can feel intimidating, trying to not make them mad while building yourself up one day at a time. And that's really the core of the game. It's a Sorcerer King with a heavy emphasis on being mobile (your home-base flies) and diplomatic (there's no real diplomacy mechanics, it's just not messing with their territory or objectives, of which each archmage has their own objectives within).

_childDocuments_.review: Good strategy/tactics game.  No real diplomacy but a really nice set of interesting systems and an active decision space that feels meaningful.  Wide unit variety, and a really cool grimoire system that you use to unlock your spells.  Also a very strong crafting system that doesn't suck!  As an alchemist the potions you make are vital to winning difficult fights and your ability to craft them makes it feel earned without making you fall into the "better save it" and never use it trap.  The most interesting change is the way the mechanics force you to keep moving.  Instead of getting into that mid/late-game slog where you have an incredibly vast empire full of lame micromanagement, it keeps you limited to a small number of nodes that you move around to suck up the resources.  Very cool and creative solution to a long time problem in the genre. Definitely worth trying if you're a fan of the genre and at such a reasonable price point, there's really no reason to procrastinate.  I've already dumped several days straight into it and I'm looking forward to future playthroughs with the other classes.

_childDocuments_.review: I'll try to give some concrete advice so maybe more people get to enjoy this overall very fun and original game.1. Necromancer seems to be the mode most people choose first according to achievement stats. Imho it's both harder and less fun than Alchemist or Artificer. In fact, I think if I had tried Necromancer first, I wouldn't have played the game more than a few hours.Alchemist lets you build strong stacks and then be super flexible in battles because you have tons of potions that will give you just the exact power or boost you need at that moment. Artificer gives you mostly fixed buffs on units. Also powerful, but less flexible, so sometimes units have to fight enemies that hard-counter them. Necromancer gives you very little flexibilty, just more extra cheap units to soften up enemy stacks. Stack slots are limited and stacks without a hero are weak anyway, and crafting undead kind of competes with normal unit hiring because of upkeep costs. So my tip: Play as Alchemist, it's more fun than it sounds. The crafting is super fun - coming from someone who always hates crafting in games.2. The story and your powers and options advance on several separate tracks, which is very confusing at first. You can easily progress on one track but forget the other and then get stuck for a long time. Since the game world basically has a timer and will progress in difficulty and hostility over time, this can doom your game. Definitely recommend to play on low difficulty first, then you can be slow and confused without being punished much. Crank up the difficulty when you know how things are going to develop and what you'll need to have to take the next steps (then beating "impossible" isn't actually very difficult).3. Always start in Goldenfields. Other regions have way harder enemies which you probably can't handle at the beginning.4. Keep in mind that hired units cost upkeep per turn, but there is no initial cost for hiring them. Which means that you can just keep hiring new units and immediately send them somewhere to die. This is especially useful in the beginning. Hire goblin brawlers, use them as cannon fodder to protect your ranged and hero units, then just hire more cannon fodder.5. Create foraging stacks that just pick the countryside clean of herbs and ores. Even if you don't need all the ingredients for crafting, you can just sell them. This makes it easy to run a large gold deficit and still not go bankrupt. Four workers cost only 4 gold per turn, but can easily harvest multiple times that in ingredients.6. You don't need to rush to collect more spell pages from Shaper Ruins or even meld with a lot of Allfire nodes. This just makes the Circle Mages go after you. I won on Hard difficulty without having more than a few skirmishes with Circle Mages, and only towards the end. They are quite forgiving if you don't push it.

_childDocuments_.review: Conquest of Eo won't ever blow your mind with it's setting, but offers surprisingly good writing on par with Spellforce itself; generic but in a "warm and fuzzy" kind of way. Soundtrack is on point (the FX are a bit harsh though), and you have great visual cohesiveness throughout. Seemingly small elements like your grimoire have that lovely bit of charm in their presentation, and the overall feeling of being a renegade mage in search of his master's scattered, forbidden notes -- is very well done in terms of atmosphere, pacing and mechanics.You have a game that borrows the worthy mechanics from 4X-games, survival/pve-games and CRPGs. It's more scripted and campaign-like than most 4X-games, but as a result the map you're playing on is much more focused.It will force you to relocate your only base of operations because resources are finite: the first of many surprises. And when you realize this in your first play-through, you begin to understand that just when things about to get too comfy, you should expect the worst. This sense of urgency keeps you on your toes.The fact that your base is mobile, resources are finite, and quests are somewhat randomized, makes this game play out more like an "open world 4X-game", which as an idea is worth further experimentation. The replay-value comes from this mobility in a map that is (technically) not locked anyhow.You'll be doing quests; fight the wildlife that keeps eating your workers, hunt down thieves, search ruins and crypts, and even discover derelict factories of the ancient "Shapers". You'll use alchemy, necromancy or artificing to grow your power, each providing unique playstyles: Will you discover recipes for potions that will allow your peasants to breathe fire, craft your own artifacts and runes to empower your few and selected ones, or create your own unstoppable horde of undead monsters from the souls of fallen enemies?This is coupled with different schools of magic.Will you embrace death, befriend the local populace, focus on the divine, or become one with nature? Soon enough, you'll have to figure out ways to become relevant in this world already filled with bigger forces than you, for the revered Circle Mages won't overlook your attempts.A game that seems to reward your time, and your own exploration of it. I recommend the game if you like asymmetrical design; not something that is supposed to be ever balanced for multiplayer. It's the kind of game that rewards you for not looking up a single guide online, because I'm sure it's easy to break in many ways, if you're trying to min-max everything in a more scripted setting.The developers should be proud of what it is in it's own constraints -- the fair price-tag reflects this.Yes, there is still tremendous potential to push the game further. Adding more (mage) classes, more dynamism (the static city-factions are currently too static), more enemy-types, races and neutral camps. Even biomes like deserts and jungles, not to mention new maps!

_childDocuments_.review: Not a 4x and not explained.This game suffers from a problem that many games that try to do some genre bending, innovation suffer from. The game is marketed as sort of like something (4x) but isn't even close to how one plays, but then they offer no explanation within the game about how to play it.I played this game for over 9 hours and never got a good idea of what overall I am trying to do. How do I advance? How do I get new troops? What is it I am actually trying to do?It feels like it has the one-time playthrough time of an RPG (60 hours or so) but the brutal difficulty of a much quicker 4x, where when you don't know what you are doing, you just have to restart. The RPG portion of the game isn't really that interesting. It plays like a very simple open world RPG with quests that are all the same and repetitive. Go here to start mission. Go to 1-3 locations and do 1-3 fights. Get reward. Repeat.The late game tedium of managing your cities seems to have been replaced with a terrible crafting system. Many 100s of recipes that you have to randomly 'find' each play through. 100s of ingredients that don't mean much other than combining different color combinations. Someone might love this, but it is basically just a collectibles system.The combat is not bad in the game, fairly simple and quick. However, the auto resolve for battles is terrible, meaning you have to manually fight almost every battle. This is because even if your strength is almost double the enemies, you still could lose units, which you wouldn't even be close to doing in manual combat mode.One day the game might be more playable. I like that the developers are trying something new, but they need a much better system to guide you through how to play this game, especially with on the surface it seeming like a 4x (which it is not)

_childDocuments_.review: In general:- VERY well done story/campaign, written well- WAY more content than it's price- VERY deep mechanically, that means it is complex (moderate complexity for this genre imo)What this game's budget did not have time for:- Lore entries for units (Spellforce has multiple games in this universe)- Voice Acting- Some specific sounds (Walking on snow) do not fit wellDo you like the turn based, grid, RPG games a la Heroes of Might and Magic?If the answer is yes, here is what you should know:- The map is set, you choose where in the map to start- Well balanced combat system, you need to use buffs/crafting to beat the end game large enemy stacks - Crafting system based on loot you get, creating potions/minions/permanent buffs (Depending on alchemist/necromancer/artificer start)- You do not paint the map, and have a set number of tiles that you can control at any given time- Not as replayable as randomly generated maps/campaigns, but story/mechanics make up for itIf you do not like the genre, or do not like managing 5 different resources, or spending 20+ hours until you are able to handle higher difficulties..... _childDocuments_.review: I've played the other SpellForce games. This one is not nearly as fun.Overview  You can pick between 3 classes, Artificer, Alchemist, Necromancer. Then, you pick your starting location on the map which is meant to have an effect on the difficulty. Finally, choose your difficulty setting. I tried all three classes and several difficulty settings. The difficulty doesn't seem to have a significant change. There seemed to be more enemy stacks in the early game, but that was all. Mind you, there are about 6 difficulty levels from Story Mode (easiest) to Brutal, and that was the extent of the difference that I noticed. Classes  The classes are somewhat useless. You can learn any kind of magic regardless of what you choose in the beginning. The only difference is what you can create in your Tower. Alchemists create (mainly) potions. These potions can be a major help in battle, but take too long to make to use them in most battles. Necromancers obviously create undead minions. These minions have expensive upkeep and thus you can only maintain one or two stacks, rather than the hordes of undead that you are promised in the class description. There is little or no advantage to creating your own undead rather than hiring regular units that are available to all three classes. Artificer creates runes that are mostly "okay." The vampire runes and a couple other runes/items that can be made seem massively overpowered. The rest, well they don't hurt but are nearly useless.  No matter which class you take, it seems that simply waiting until you can train animals is the best way to play. You can upgrade all animals to have no upkeep so that you can finally have massive armies without going broke as well as keep them long enough to level them up.Difficulty/Battles  You are punished for advancing in the game. In the first two games I tried to upgrade my tower for the perks you unlock. The enemy difficulty is based on your tower rather than the number of turns that have gone by or the difficulty setting that you selected. The enemy stacks will be so strong that it takes 3-4 of the strongest stacks that you can field, attacking one after another, to destroy one enemy stack. Which means that it's incredibly difficult to upgrade a stack. So in the third game I avoided making any advancement until I leveled up my units, which then made the game extremely easy. There is no happy middle ground of "challenging but fun."Maps - only one Worldmap that isn't all that big.Autoresolve - If you don't want to micromanage every battle you can try the Autoresolve option, but it doesn't work very well. There is a power meter (don't remember what the game calls it) that shows the estimated strength of a stack and the individual units in the stack. This strength meter is useless. I've had stacks that are marked as double the strength of the enemy lose to that enemy. So I micromanage the battle and sometimes win without much difficulty, sometimes lose my entire army without taking out a single enemy unit. Same goes for when the enemy is marked as being much stronger, sometimes I can micromanage a win very easily, even though my units don't have any special advantage over the enemy units.Overall a terrible game that I don't recommend and does not live up to the previous games in the franchise.

_childDocuments_.review: Lack of basebuilding is just not for me. Conquest of EO focuses on troops rather than basebuilding.I think Spellforce works as a 4X title. It's just not very well executed. If you are making a 4X title, maybe focus on getting the mechanics that people like about 4X titles, into your game. I believe many people would have loved to build a massive elven, necromancer or dwarven fortress, instead of having a tower that later on teleports across the map, like the castle in Castlevania. Aside from the lack of basebuilding and the endless amount of pointless reading where the preforged story is getting shoved down your throat, they got everything else right. The scenery is amazing, the lore is great (just too much story in your face, leaving barely any room for your imagination), the combat is better than most 4X titles and has a surprising amount of depth to it. Also one has to love the little sidequests and choices you have to engage with and resolve them. I hope they get the chance to make another Spellforce 4X game, but then please with basebuilding. Basebuilding is handsdown one of the best parts about building your empire. Just like Sauron did in LotR. Having a sense of visual progression is vital for a game like this in my opinion.

_childDocuments_.review: The Conquest of Eo gets many things right, and those who enjoy 4X games and Heroes of Might & Magic should definitely take a look. I love the graphics. I love the artstyle. Simply beautiful to look at while getting addicted to flying around with your huge ass tower. Rating: ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️Since most quests and expeditions lead to battles, you always have the option to automatically calculate the outcome of a fight. An indicator informs you beforehand about the chances of success, but I no longer trust it: Several times, I let the game automatically resolve battles, only to suffer severe defeats. When I manually engage in the same battles, I emerge victorious without losing troops. That's why I've made it a habit to save before battles; since the last patch, there's finally a Quick Save and Quick Load feature. My advice: Use it! Because you can hardly afford significant defeats due to a simple reason: Your troops gain experience and level up through battles, acquiring new skills and attributes that can have a significant impact. Such experienced troops are too valuable to be squandered in automatic battles.In most cases, I fought my battles manually. It takes longer, but it's enjoyable and well-executed. All skirmishes take place in tightly confined arenas, with a limited number of troops.Battles unfold on hex grids and play out classically in the best sense. However, there's a lot to consider: Ranged attackers and mages, for example, must take into account elevation, sightlines, and ranges to effectively participate. Powerful flank attacks are crucial for melee fighters, but they can be mitigated with the right equipment or specific spells. Each unit has three action points per round, used not only for movement, attacks, items, or skills but also for defenders to counterattack. Conversely, it means that opponents can be "disabled" by draining their action points, which can often end in significant losses. Added to this are features such as resistances, different damage types, buffs, and debuffs - while not particularly original and familiar for 4X Players, they provide enough tactical depth and make it enjoyable. A clear interface and fast animations ensure that turn-based battles never feel sluggish; most fights are over in just a few minutes. God bless the speed-up feature.While Conquest of Eo explains many features in the game, some details need to be figured out independently. Once you've mastered that, the game plays smoothly and comfortably. However, long-term enjoyment is a different story: While the world map of Eo is expansive and beautifully designed, unlike most 4X games, the layout is predetermined. Cities and locations are always in the same place, with only quests, events, resources, etc., randomly distributed in each playthrough. However, even in my second and third attempts, I found some overlaps. And because diplomacy, alliances, and interesting AI opponents are completely ignored, the game loses its momentum after the first playthrough. For me, Spellforce: Conquest of Eo doesn't have the potential to be a long-lasting favorite. It lacks multiplayer as well and especially the already mentioned 1-Map-Only-Thing. I enjoyed playing it though, got hooked after overcoming some initial hurdles, and could hardly put it down for days. However, now, after the first complete playthrough, I feel my motivation waning. I'll probably pick up Conquest of Eo again, maybe even twice, if only to get to know the other mage classes better. But afterward, it will likely be removed from the hard drive. And you know what? I find that perfectly okay! For 30 euros, I don't expect a groundbreaking masterpiece that revolutionizes an entire genre overnight. What I get here is enough: a good, entertaining mix of turn-based tactics, 4X, and a dash of role-playing, which is eventually completed. So, a clear recommendation for that price.And the best part:After my first playthrough with the Necromancer, I initially set Conquest of Eo aside. Until now. Because now, there's a brand-new, demonically good DLC called Demon Scourge for just 13 euros. It provides fresh missions, story content, and spells, along with a new mage class that allows you to summon demons, break the spirits of your units, and infiltrate the entire realm of Hohenmark with your cults.

_childDocuments_.review: If Civilization 6 was an epic high fantasy roleplaying game, you get SpellForce Conquest of EO.You start off with a tower that creates a zone of control, and a few units.The tower can be upgraded and improved, and its your base of operations. Allowing you to research spells, Build rooms, and progress your search for magical powers. The game has crafting in a simple but smart combining of materials, where reaching certain levels of quality gives you different results.The units are unique, some cost upkeep, others are free. Its up to you how you want your army to look and fight.You can hire mercenaries or goblins, summon creatures with mana upkeep, and even pull creatures from the forest to fight for you for free. Each creature has its own abilities and damage/resistances. And each creature's level-up gives 2-3 upgrades to choose from, some upgrades adding attacks or utility while others are simple stat boosts.The map you play on is filled with different factions, some are neutral cities you can befriend. Others are enemies pestering everyone. And some are from a council of mages like yourself, who each have their own goals and might or might not tolerate you. You get to decide based on your actions how the people and other factions see you. As a helpful mage, a tyrant or someone who is in it for the rewards.The map is also filled with quest locations, loot stashes, and materials (renewable) that can be harvested. Some locations give rewards if they are in your zone of control, but most will run out of resources to give.The game has ''heroes'' in the form of apprentices with their own abilites that can lead an army, and even build buildings that give zone of control.You get to choose what kind of mage you want to play as, and what spells and abilities you focus first on. You can play a nature/alchemist, necromancer or artificer (crafter) mage. Or mix and match.The game has a few flaws where using a skill or item does not tell you it ends your turn, but in general i only found this problem 2-3 times. The tooltips are normaly accurate and detailed.Also the game is surprisingly well optimized. Even though the grafics look pretty good on the highest quality, the loading times are only a few seconds. So it never feels bad to take manual control over combat, instead of letting it auto-resolve.My first session was 9 hours non stop, and i had to be mindful to close the game at some point or i would have kept playing. Im surprised this game hasnt blown up in popularity yet.The game is worth its price, even without discount. 9/10.

(Review is currently based on a 6 hour preview, writing a full review after playing three playthroughs of each main crafting type) SpellForce & Heroes of Might & Magic... Merged together to make on hell of a game!The overworld map & story is amazingly interesting & the variations of events keep the game feeling fresh constantly without causing too much panic, the different difficulties & the custom mage option make for interesting multiple playthrough ideas. _childDocuments_.review: CoE is hard to talk about because there's almost nothing quite like it on the market. The closest thing is probably Stardock's nearly forgotten Sorcerer King: Rivals. Even though it's turn based as opposed to real time CoE does continue Spellforce's tradition of combining genres and what we have here is something akin to a limited scope 4X set in an rpg-ish open world. You don't build a large empire and paint the map in CoE. Instead you lead a small, nomadic, somewhat scattered magical kingdom moving across the map depending on your needs and goals as you explore, gather resources, allies, do quests and accomplish strategic goals. You don't face off against other rulers like yourself who are roughly on equal footing but the world itself as well as the Circle Mages who start off much more powerful than you forcing you to be careful about stepping on their toes too much, at least early on. As such CoE is a very assymetrical game where a lot can go wrong or right depending on your choices and semi-randomness leading to some fun (imo at least) unpredictability. Like it would be in an open world rpg a la Fallout or Elder Scrolls the large world map in CoE is manually crafted and not random as one would expect of a 4X but there is still randomization in the details like which Circle Mages you face and what kind of quests and rewards you find, which heros you meet, etc.Your victory conditons are modular. There are 6 "victory tasks" but you only need to complete three to win and which ones you choose will probably depend on your playstyle, strategic choices and/or roleplay and, if you want, you can do all of the tasks or even play indifinitely, you can proceed to the "victory stage" whenever you want as long as at least 3 of the tasks are done. Otherwise there's the usual things like crafting, hero equipment, unit training, construciton, magic, research, etc. The magic system is very similar to Master of Magic with "Allfire" in place of Power which you distribute between mana income, research and casting proficiency. Combat ocurrs on separate tactical maps and derives highly from the Age of Wonders series with unit action points determining movement distance and number of attacks. Combat is pretty involved with a rich system of active abilities, stats and passive traits and it highly encourages preparation and scrutiny. Choosing the right units, buffs and tools can be the difference between crushing your enemy with no losses and getting crushed yourself. One of my favorite features are the game's landmarks and exotic quests and rewards which can give you unique benefits like, for example, an Airship which works as an aerial transport and mobile magic domain projector which is completely unique and can't be obtained by conventional means.CoE can require a bit of getting used to due to how different it is from other 4X-like games but I highly recommend it to turn based strategy lovers, especially those who enjoy the combat layer of TBS.A few tips:- Prioritize befriending some of the towns in your vicinity (by doing their quests for example). This will provide you with more poweful units as well as room blueprints and economic benefits.- Magic proficiency upgrades your wizard tower and increases your army size and apprentic (hero) cap. Don't neglect it.- Don't sit in one spot too long and get bogged down. Be proactive and get those Allfire nodes, magic is very important.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm nearly 200 hours in and still loving it.  The best way to describe this game is that you are a wizard aspiring to become a master and join the elite of elite mages.  This game isn't about conquering or empire building, rather completing quests, research and gaining access to magical sites that help further these goals.  I love the concept of fantasy wizards and this game does a good job of putting you in that role.  Most games treat wizards like a shooter with a fantasy skin, you are just running around blasting things, not really doing "wizard stuff"  When I think of a wizard I usually think of either the wandering wizard in search of knowledge, or the wizard in a tower conducting his research and experiments.  In this game you play the wizard in a tower with apprentices that wander and lead your armies.  While the apprentices can throw fireballs and cast traditional spells, you are focused on far more powerful magic, spells that buff your troops or debuff the enemy, spells that change the world, impact entire cities, or grant abilities to everyone under your command.  If you are enjoy immersion and want to play a game that makes you feel like a master wizard, I would say that this one does a pretty good job of it.  I would be wary of negative reviews as many seem to be from people upset that the Devs have been very active since launch and work at balancing the game.  A few things have been nerfed due to them being so extremely overpowered that they completely removed all challenge from the game.  That said, the game has multiple difficulty levels which allows you to casual experience the story or find a hardcore challenge.  There is an element of RNG to the game that makes it very replayable.*Edit to add middle paragraph, forgive my inner nerd.

_childDocuments_.review: I have played a LOT of 4x games in my time, and i have to say that this has become one of my absolute favorites. It manages to be both innovative AND intuitive at the same time. I have enjoyed it immensely and will be adding to the "choir" chanting for some DLC as it practically screams for it. The core gameplay has so much potential to expand upon, and even though the 4x elements are not the most intricate or complicated (which can be both a negative and a positive aspect), i find it to have pretty good replay value with all the randomized events, starting positions and the 3 very unique playstyles. It is also very well written and that contributes to immersion. I am at a point of proficency now where impossible difficulty is no longer a challenge so i would very much like it to be even harder. I will not say that it is too easy and fault the AI, but at a certain point when you know the game well you have so many options and strategies at your disposal that an AI will become vastly inferior. And that, in a way, speaks volumes to the sheer depth of this game.If you are bored with all the other great 4x strategy games out there; give this game a chance and experience something that feels fresh to the genre. It is damn near a masterpiece for what it is, and scratches the "one more turn" itch perfectly.
