_childDocuments_.review: This game, in its current state, is not very fun.Its not bad in the regular sense; I havent experienced many bugs, it runs and looks ok, it has interesting ideas that put a bit of a twist on older designs etc. Im just not finding it very fun.Despite the tags, it isnt a grand strategy 4x game, though it looks like one and takes quite a few things from the classics like Master of Magic. You only have 1 "city", your magic tower which can move across the map. Resource nodes are mostly temporary, meaning you need to set up semi-temporary control areas with your Heroes to not waste precious mana. There's very little in terms of building, even armies, as you'll heavily rely upon magical creatures tied to your brand of magic (of which there is only 3 at the time and Ive only played the Necromancer). The crafting system for them is pretty interesting though. The game world itself is mostly predetermined, interestingly enough, forming a set stage where you do quests and explore and fight your enemies, both random "barbarians" and preset Circle Wizards who control many areas and who are essentially already made "empires", in the sense that you've shown up late to the party and the other players dont really give a damn about you.  All ideas seem pretty interesting, my only problem is the lack of a feeling of growth and progression. In a regular 4x game theres a beginning period of scrambling and having to squeeze every drop of resources, having to ration everything and then, after your main things have been set up, you have a chance to explore and exploit the various mechanics of the game. Here, this scrambling time never seems to end. My current game, on week 22 Necromancer (and the two shorter games I did before, all on the recommended difficulty) is starved for everything all the time in an endless cycle. My resource nodes depleting means I have no mana but I cant move my tower because Im trying to resurrect a hero to claim other nodes to speed the process and I cant disband my army to free up mana because a random event decided a Circle Mage now hates me and keeps sending doomstacks against my Allfire nodes and if I fight him he'll get even more mad and burn my tower down. Everything is too RNG based to be consistent and too infrequent to allow a buildup. I cant afford to tech up because I have to constantly deal with things out of my control that I cant deal with because I havent teched up. Progress is glacially slow and at every time the game might tear down everything you built and you're back to skipping turns as the game world seemingly scales up to the strength you had before you fell so you're not even at square 1 but rather -1. I have no idea how the harder difficulties are supposed to work besides savescumming and hoping you get good mats. tl:dr, the game is Functional but not Fun. Difficulty dosent make for interesting gameplay when it just results in grind.

_childDocuments_.review: Some spoilers in here if you dont want to read then pass this over...I've completed the game on explorer and the world map to all its borders - also cleared every stack on the map. First off stack power is reltively meaningless. I beat 90% of the enemy stacks with one stack - using only 1 member and I did this for ~75% of the game.First off the initial 50 - 70 turns will be slow, manual and frustrating as the game starts really slow - magic is relatively meaningless unless you get certain spell schools for early game - I would say the best 3 spell schools are Guardian (1st), Enchantment (2nd) and Mentalism (3rd).Guardian gives you a spell that costs 100 mana and raises all of your units by 1 exp level per cast and another spell being Immunity, which is 100% physical resistance. With Artificer as your crafting class you can get 3 rune slots and add 2 low level runes that give 50% elemental immunity (100% makes you take no damage) and the third rune of the vampire that gives life leech (50% of damage is restored as health). You now have a mob that takes no physical damage and no elemental damage - this one mob can beat any stack that only does these damage types no matter there level - even on auto calc - because it cant be damaged - do not use it for undead or any mobs that do white damage.Enchanting because it summons the best Titan in the game - Guardian Golem (I tested all the high level summons and this one is just so good). Further Enchanting has true teleport which makes getting around even easier and some essential p[arty buffs to get around the map faster - Speed is an essential stat early game but once you get teleports and own most of the map you just teleport everywhere.Mentalism - Allows for immediate revered reputation in all cities with one of its spells - which gives you really good tier 2 and sometimes good tier 3 units. Also has some good mid level summons (these are strong - medusa anyone);  and casts a really good spell that makes all mobs in the stack do minimum damage as well as mind control which you can use to whittle down stacks one at a time - costs a lot though 160 mana a pop. So once I got enough resources and the right spell pages to unlock the spells needed - I achieved 1 mob buffed with Invulnerable, Flight, Endurance and some other great fun stuff - that mob went out and killed everything which it could - this gave me enough mats to make the upgrades in the rooms that add white and death resistances. Mid game I summoned the Titan from the guardian tree as he has amazing death resistance and with the buff from Guardian school that adds 20% death resistance as well as a room extension upgrade from the tower he had over 100% - there is also an apprentice -0 the Orc Warden that can get 75% base death resistance - with the room thats 95% damage reduction to death - the hardest battles in this game are death units. He took me to most of the slayer ruins which then unlocked more pages in my spellbook. From mid game I summoned 5 Guardian Golems with all the relevent buffs, 1 Titan from the nature tree (he does the most damage - around ~50-60 per hit) and I kept the Guardian Titan cause I like a tad of variety. Nothing could beat this team and it was auto battle to the end. The end game from this point took me around ~8hours a I wanted to get every room upgrade, complete all quests and kill all mobs and take all mines and nodes.The max stacks you can get is 8. Although you can increase this to 10 in your domain - summoning chamber adds phantom knights and also a room extension upgrade adds wolves.The best hero hands down start to mid game is the earth mage as he gets earth shield that gives 50% physical damage resistence. Add two runes at 20% each to get to 90% and your on your way - watch out for elemental damage.Have fun

_childDocuments_.review: This came out of nowhere to be one of my favorite games on 2023. As others have said it's sort of a hybrid fantasy RPG-4X (more on the 4X end of things), but it adds a lot of its own nuances to those genres which meld together as something greater than the sum of its parts.Some of the unique aspects I've enjoyed:1. Probably one of the most engaging interpretations of a "spellbook" I've seen in games. It's not just a screen you add spells to - more like a recipe & scrapbook where you gradually piece together & develop different schools of magic, how to build your powerbase & other wizardly studies, & how you interact with the world & some of the characters in it. It's constantly evolving depending on your specializations. When you discover something new it's fun to see what other opportunities materialize.2. You choose to specialize in one of 3 very distinct crafting systems - Alchemy, Necromancy, Artificing - each of which provides a different playstyle. They have ingredients in common, but how you prioritize those ingredients & use the finished products will vary greatly. Likewise your chosen schools of magic give you very different toolboxes to interact with the world.3. Unlike most 4x you are not building a new civilization or settlements that set down permanent roots. You're a powerful mage who is to some extent seen as an interloper by the cities & towns, and to fuel your studies & military forces you essentially exploit the limited resources around you. So you are regularly moving your power-base (Wizard's Tower and apprentice lodges) to find more fuel for the wanna-be Archmage engine. It takes time & resources to relocate, and get the locals to trust you somewhat, so you can never get too comfortable - it's a good mechanism to encourage exploration of the map and keep things dynamic.4. Like other good crafting-based games, there are a ton of options & synergies to discover - it's not just "Craft studded leather armor which gives you +1 AP over regular leather!". Very satisfying to hit on a combo that gives you a significant advantage in a certain situation.Three main improvements I'd like to see:1. Better world quest tracking. Goals in your spellbook are well-described, but quests you get thru world encounters are just listed by title.2. A fully procedural map option. The world map is large & fun to explore, but aside from the randomization of certain quests, features, and factions, it's the same every time. I think this is essential for long-term replayability.3. Another overall balancing pass. There are ton of spells & crafting objects, but many with similar costs are clearly more useful than others.I hope the devs continue support it with main-game patches and maybe a DLC or two.Overall, this game really hit the sweet spot for me. Highly recommended for anyone interested in a new take on the 4X genre.

You'll get eye-stain and headaches trying to find the correct combinations because of a serious lack of organizational control. If they just allowed us to sort any combo of colours, it would have improved this game 10 fold. The battles are set up randomly and are mostly unfair. They could have a massive group of long distance fighters that are far away from your mostly melee group, making attacking difficult, or the opposite, you have a majority of long distance fighters and they'll throw in a bunch of melee that are already engaging your distance fighters. They always attack first and they always have the advantage. No real tutorial and it could really use one. Many quests are dependent on unknown, specific requirements that can be missed and you will have many uncompleted quests because of this. I  f u c k i n g  hate this! It's just shi tty game design. It's a game that had a lot of promise but failed to perform because of a few idiotic game design choices.

_childDocuments_.review: Very frustrating game.  Game balance is very poor, and after playing for a while you will be stomped buy a titan, and larger stacks than you can make.  It doesn't matter how many units you have in the game, if you can't put them all in the same stack, you lose.  One 900 point stack should not be able to kill 3x 800 point stacks in the same turn - but on EO they can!The power number seem random.  I have had stacks with a strength of 600+  vs an enemy stack of 300 and autoresolve says I will lose half my troops.The recommended strategy seems to be "don't annoy the other mages, all of whom are MUCH more powerful than you" (yeah, that's fun) but then all the things you need are on the other side of the other mages - who are camped out on the bridges with stacks far bigger than you can create. _childDocuments_.review: Conquest of Eo is a fun spinoff title for the SpellForce series.As someone who has played the series since the days of SpellForce 1 I can call it a worthy part of the series and its universe.It has to be kept in mind that this is a SPINOFF, not a full entry, so yes, it is another genre than what SpellForce is "normally" known for.If you are looking for a RTS/RPG mix game - then this game is not what you are looking for.If you like turn based strategy games that focus more on combat rather than diplomacy then this game is right up your alley.You are not building your empire but instead the focus lies on your Mage Tower - and the specific abilities of your class.The Necromancer raises the dead using souls and other materials, allowing you to create a wide variety of abominations - and playing with a proper Undead faction is something I wanted for almost 20 years in the SpellForce franchise.The Artificer creates items to buff your units while the Alchemist creates potions and bombs - I have not played these two a lot as of yet but from what I have seen so far they seem to perform very well.I recommend it to turn based strategy players and SpellForce fans without the shadow of a doubt - especially for this prize.My first playthrough took about 27 hours in total - and that was me rushing a bit towards the end, if I hadn't rushed towards the end, it might have been another 3-5 hours.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game. Not exactly your standard 4x, more like Thea mixed with Age of Wonders - text-quest-roguelite-4xlite-tbs. Sounds like some crazy cocktail, and it probably is, but it's good. You play as some upstart mage striving to get into the Circle and you have 4 craft mastery types (classes) and 7 spell schools to choose from. Crafting process itself is pretty similar for different classes, but results vary greatly and each class feels very powerful and unique in it's own way.Graphics and sound are good, but nothing to write home about (although illustrations are absolutely gorgeous). Story isn't particularly very exciting also, so don't expect to get some rich plot.Buy this one if you like to manage limited resources in dynamically random conditions and to optimize your playstile according to external stimuli and you won't regret it. Bonus points if you're fan of other Spellforce games and it's universe.

_childDocuments_.review: I can't stop playing this game, and I have been looking for something "new" for quite some time.First, this is not Heroes! Here, the main game involves a series of quests (main adventure and side quests) that have a large degree of randomness, which ads replayability and unpredictability.  The AI "opponents" may be friendly or hostile, depending on a number of factors, and you don't have to kill them all, at lest not that fast.The several game systems are remarkably well designed, with PC audience in mind. _childDocuments_.review: One of the best 4X games out there. The more time you invest in it the better the game gets. PROS-All 3 main archetypes feel very different. Yes their base game play in building units and resource collection is fundamentally the same but each one needs to focus on what they excel at while gathering their lesser resource or you'll be moving slower than you need to and you'll likely get overrun. Using the built in mechanic on your mage choice is also very important for a good clean run. Not crafting runes as artificer? Enjoy your units sucking and being weak in the mid game. Not making consumables as Alchemist? Your battle power is nerfed from where it should be. Is the game still winnable? Yes, but hamstringing yourself can have dire consequences if you've got all the circle mages mad at you. Units are varied and even T1 units are important for the flow of your game play. Managing investment into more costly units while still having roaming units or fodder out is critical. The T3/T4 units feel good to have and building good synergies can make you feel godly. Important for a sense of accomplishment. The spells! Because of how different your spell book can start out and end depending on what pages/Mages you beat your spells will change each run. This is really neat and very fun. Probably my favorite part of the game. CONS-Static map makes the game much easier on the next run. I totally understand WHY the map is static, but it doesn't change the fact that the major locations being know hampers the sense of exploration you get from the first run. Elemental Damage is kinda lame. I think breaking it up into Fire and Ice for battle variance would have been much better. I came across a few bugs that forced me to go back multiple turns off of things that were very normal. I would path towards an objective and once I got to it the game would auto crash. Would try moving from another squire and it would do the same thing. Would go back another turn and come from another angle and it worked just fine. This was very odd and happened enough times that it caused me emotional distress. Overall I loved the game, hoping for an expansion or sequel eventually with more of the good stuff. Please. Thank you.

You get only one hero per game, and they all play quite different so if this gives you enough motivation to play again, that's a plus, too, but what helps me to stay on a game for longer is random maps or at least a lot of different maps to explore.This is completely absent from this game. The map is always the same and needs to, for the story quests to make sense.The map it has is big and well crafted, but well, no diversity between games there.I've also read a lot of disappointed voices coming from previous spellforce games - it seems to have broken with a lot of mechanics from it's predecessors. _childDocuments_.review: Another game I really wanted to like. It feels like the Master of Magic game lineage just can't get a break.Combat is very inconsistent, which is at least in line with expectations from games based on Master of Magic. Units that have leveled up and received spell bonuses will behave quite differently from units with different level up bonuses. Fine.But units are given random choices for things to level into, and the usefulness of those level up bonuses range from "wildly, incredibly powerful" to "you will never notice this unit has this bonus." The same unit with ten different, random bonuses may perform quite differently.On its face, that sounds exciting, but when you have thirty units running around and four of them level up per fight and you have three fights per turn, it just feels like a time sink. Automatic, consistent bonuses for leveling up, or just not leveling up units, would be preferable.This is the tonal issue I have with the game. There is an awful lot to do to improve your odds, but there's a noise to signal problem. I can put my domain over some resources, but sometimes I can't get resources out of the thing. Sometimes that's because it's an enemy spawner, I guess, but walking on it doesn't give me an option to fight, so why are there resource symbols on it? I don't know.The numeric representation of enemies is often rather misleading. I have a stack worth five hundred. My foe has a stack worth 150. Predictable heroic victory. I leave it to the second group coming behind with a stack worth 400 so the first one can go fresh to the objective. 400 stack's prediction is *crushing defeat.*Unit and damage types can certainly have an influence on battle, but if the influence is that stark, the numeric representation of stack power is useless. Get rid of it or tone down your type matching.The game offers a slight balm with the regular progression of research and spellcraft, but it doesn't really tell me what I'm working toward. I have an objective nearby with a stack that I will never defeat with the stack size I have access to, so do I research more stack size? Well, I can't. I'm given a couple of choices every time I research something, and it's not really abundantly clear if this is a tree or not because the tech is organized into book pages. Are these connected by more than theme? I don't know, because the game doesn't do a great job of communicating.Tactical considerations are a little stifling. Attacking with a unit ends its turn, spending all remaining AP on attack. That seems a little limited, but fine, sure, they're busy in combat. But so do most other actions. You can move and make one action, period. It seems a bit silly that I can't shuffle my healer a bit after spending one AP to restore some hitpoints or offer a buff, and it feels like a strange bit of immersion breaking for a game that seemingly really wants to immerse you.Music is good. Art direction is good. Presentation is solid throughout, though I'd like to double down on the tech book being a bit silly. The outside is great but the substance makes me wish I'd given it a pass.

_childDocuments_.review: Spellforce Conquest of Eo is a 4x strategy RPG hybrid developed by Owned by Gravity and published by THQ Nordic. In this game you take control of a wizard, raise armies, fight monsters, discover quests, and deal with the powerful Circle of Mages as you try discover the reason behind your masters death and leave your mark on the world of Eo. As always the first question we ask is if this game is worth the asking price of 30$, and the answer is yes. The game provides a surprisingly deep tactical combat system and a large strategic layer with minor rpg elements. Being able to combine 6 different magic schools in various ways with 3 different production methods provides a decent amount of variation and replay ability. The graphics, music and story weave together well in a satisfying game that caused me want to keep going and lose track of time. Now there is limited replay ability. There is only one map, but your starting position determines difficulty. In addition as previously stated the fact that you are limited to only 3 production methods and 6 schools of magic does mean eventually you do reach a limit. While there is a decent variety of AI’s you can fight, 9 of them, you can only fight 4 at a time and there is no multiplayer. However keeping all of this in mind, for 30$ your going to get your moneys worth and I would strongly recommend giving this game a chance.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a pretty fun game! I want to enjoy the grand strategy games, but most of the time they're overly complicated and need excessive micromanaging. _childDocuments_.review: Ultimately, I refunded because of the core gameplay. I've put hundreds of hours into these kind of games and the necromancy focus interested me the most. The problem for me is I've played this exact game before...I ♥♥♥♥ you not, it's a diet Age of Wonders 3 with the unit crafting system from Iratus: Lord of the Dead. And I know, Spellforce is a franchise known for slapping two genres together and calling it a game, but I just can't justify getting this, even on sale, when I already own and have experienced all of this years ago. There is replay value with the multiple choice story events, 5~ different starting locations, different playstyles and enemy AI factions - which is great! And I like some of the artwork too. However, it's a story-focused game and the entire story is presented entirely through text boxes. The soundtrack is very forgettable. The unit designs are uninspired. There are less options in this game than the aformentioned games. And the necromancy gameplay isn't appealing compared to other titles in the same genre. _childDocuments_.review: What a surprise this game was. I didn't even know it was being made then it was just here on Steam. I haven't played loads of it yet but so far it is a lot of fun. A somewhat relaxing, single-player-focused turn-based strategy game (it has a bit of an age of wonders feel) placing you in the role of a wizard trying to make a name for themselves and defend against their rivals, with a surprising level of depth for a game at this price level. The idea of having the player choose a magical crafting class (necromancer, artificer or alchemist) that is used directly to upgrade their troops as well as two schools of magic makes sure that all players have incentive to explore the map and experiment a little to be able to defeat new enemies and provides a little variety (though I struggle a little to keep track of the side-quests). The wizard tower as a mobile base of operations that can both draw from its current surroundings and be built up into a stable foundation is a nice way of balancing stability and dynamism. I also particularly enjoyed the main quest (I think) being progressed largely at my own pace (with some nudging from the other factions) via the build-up of my character's tower and strength in magic.

_childDocuments_.review: Spellforce: Conquest of Eo (S:CoE) is a 4X/RPG hybrid that is clearly inspired by "Master of Magic", "Warlock" and "Age of Wonders".You play a wizard apprentice who controls a mobile wizard tower with the goal of becoming the most powerful wizard in Eo, the world of the Spellforce RTS series. Your enemies aside from random spawns are the powerful Circle Mages (independent wizards like yourself with their own tower, minions and magic expertise). They don't see you as a threat at the beginning, but the conflict escalates once you become more powerful.You can choose one of three wizard characters to play in the beginning (necromancer, alchemist, artificer, all with different gameplay options), but can also create your own custom wizard type.You command groups of minions which can be led by unique heroes, and you can have apprentices yourself which are a special type of heroes. Your groups have to collect resources and solve quests which include battles, but also choices you make in descriptive textboxes.As an aspiring master wizard you can of course research and use all kinds of spells.The map is the same in each game, but some of the side quests are randomized. In addition you cannnot only choose a difficulty level (5 choices), but also the start region (5 choices), which has an effect on starting difficulty, enemies encountered and minions available for hire. Since one of the early patches you can also choose the antagonists (rival circle mages) you will encounter.The game puts more emphasis on the story than the inspirations, from the beginning where you follow in the footsteps of your dead wizard master over the whole main quest and hero-specific sidequests.Your minion groups can consist of  a huge number of combinations of troop types, which can be either hired or summoned, but also enslaved or mind-controlled (from an enemy group). All troops can be equipped with magic glyphs and your heroes can also equip weapons, armor and magic items. Troops come in different ranks, from lowly goblin rogues clad in rags up to powerful plate armored elite units, bomb throwing or healing specialists and even huge monsters. Both heroes and troops can level up which allows them to choose perks.The graphics of the game are good, but not very optimized and quite taxing on the hardware.The game evokes the typical addictive "one more turn" feeling.If you like games like the above mentioned or similar games (Endless Legend, Fallen Enchantress) I can recommend this game for you.

_childDocuments_.review: Thumb up, but...Good game for masochists.  As this player is not one he cycles mostly between stress and rage quitting.  Sometimes things go as planned and it's great.  But some things will just screw you no matter what you do.  Though at the price point it's not a bad game.Some things are unique, for example your flying tower instead of the normal painting the map with cities and forts.  The crafting system is top notch, and some combat features are cool (e.g. you can capture "souls" from enemies for crafting troops as a necromancer).  Mostly combat seems a clone of Age of Wonder 3 combat with the added feature that auto-resolve is atrocious so yes you will want to fight almost all battles manually.  This may be incorrect but it sure seems auto-resolve does not consider the various combat perks and healing units possess.  A great feature is at least auto-resolve lets you know how bad it's going to maul your troops before you select it.Some serious flaws which frustrate me but will impress masochists really make me wonder.  No journal for quests is a big one others have mentioned.  I have no memory of what I'm supposed to do with some of them so they're basically dead ends.  In one case i couldn't continue a quest for a hero because the location disappeared or I had not discovered it on the map (and yes many, many turns were spent scouting for it).  On level up your troops get a random selection of perks to acquire, meaning you will find yourself in situations where a unit is hardcore nerfed.  Say for example your skeleton mage may never be able to heal or raise undead (which is the only two things they are needed for).One game ended early when my 2nd apprentice (basically an army leader hero) spawned in a tower across a river whose only bridge I found for crossing was guarded by an enemy circle mage (i.e. enemy boss).  This kind of thing isn't uncommon, so frankly this is by design and intended to be a challenge.  I'm sure many players handle it but some folk say screw that.  In another early game instance a major quest appeared in the lands of a particularly mean orc circle mage.  The troops ran in to finish it and get out to piss him off as little as possible but he declared "cold war" (which turns out to mean hot war) and let's just say the play through imploded quickly.  Why is this kind of thing happening in the early game.  A major gripe for many new players is that you are not going to know what you are doing for many hours.  Tutorials are a 2 sentence blurb on a major topic that really doesn't explain anything.  It's trial by fire which I don't mind so much as an unemployed bum there was free time to spend 35 hours getting a clue about what the heck was going on.  Surely though some guides will pop up soon enough to help newer players (and me).Note that currently there is no steam workshop.  There was one clever mod posted in the steam discussions for the game where the random troop upgrades could be re-rolled.  Purists will disagree, but Hallelujah.  Searches for other mods have proved futile.This game has gotten great reviews from other players so take this summary with a grain of salt.  This mostly pertains to experience in the early game.  Some of the issues highlighted are not concerns to many out there.

_childDocuments_.review: I already loved Fantasy General 2 (from the same developers) and this game has the same strength. It just feels well-rounded. Everything meshes together. The complexity is at just the right level for me. You can also clearly feel the love for the Spellforce world. I loved meeting the individual antagonists, whose diverse characters were captured wonderfully expressively in the dialogue along with the portraits. And the idea of playing a Circle mage aspirant on the way to becoming a member of the Circle, with his own tower, moving through the world in search of ever new resources and more power (which is really something new!), serves a fantasy that I found myself really pushing. I wasn't bored from start to finish - the typical endgame problem of 4X games, that you've actually already won but the game still keeps going for another 50 rounds or so, doesn't exist here because of the structure of the game.Of course, the game also has weaknesses or things that I personally don't like. But most of them could be improved relatively easily and pale in comparison to the overall impression.The only real weakness is the price. Because it makes me feel like a thief! I paid just about 22 euros with launch discount and community voucher. But even 30 euros is clearly too cheap. After about 50 hours, I have now finished my first run as an alchemist. And I will play through the game at least twice more, as a Necromancer and as an Artificer. What a price-performance ratio. Every potential DLC is an insta-buy! Thank you very much for this beautiful game.

_childDocuments_.review: THIS IS NOT A NORMAL 4X/AOW STYLE GAMEYou should really be aware of that before you buy.  If you like those kinds of games, I still think this is absolutely a winner, but don't go in expecting standard Age of Wonders 3 style gameplay. The battle is very similar, but there's some key differencesThings to note-1. You have 1 base for essentially the entire game. The game is designed around this, but you're not going to out econ your enemies and overwhelm them.  Getting your econ stable is important, but you're purposefully limited in how many heroes you get, so you're probably only going to have 3 or 4 super stacks.  This is not the kind of game where you just spam out Tier IV's by turn 30 (probably....).  That said, your base is mobile, and it's got mechanics to make sure you use that.  Picking up your base and planting it down where it's needed, or because you need to get space from a dangerous area, is a key and interesting part of the game.2. The game is in some ways a passive rougelike.  As there's a massive map (I've explored maybe 80% of it on a 15 hour run), and the topography/biomes/cities are static (plenty of other things aren't), I highly recommend starting on a lower difficulty (explorer/balanced) so you get time to learn about it.  As you get more familiar with how things work, you'll feel a lot better cranking the difficulty up to add the challenge back in.  On balanced or higher the game has the enemies ramping up and getting aggressive pretty fast.3. This game is asymmetric.  It's not resource cheating so much as they literally are playing a different game, and are supposed to be.  With that in mind, they're also not casting magic (sorta) or using a "craft" like you are, so you've go your own bag of bs to fight them with.  Again do not expect to ramp up exponentially quite like a normal 4x.  A lot of your power comes from your craft coming online and your smaller armies finding broken combos with that, your magic, and their skills.4. Discovery is a big part of the first phase of this game.  I really think you'll ruin a lot of the fun for yourself if you instantly dive into a full spoiler guide.  A lot of what makes this interesting is figuring out how to use the resources you've gotten on a run (again very mildly rougelike) to make something work.  This is not some "the timing for a tier III is around turn 20" thing (well..not as much at least).  Your starting stuff is always the same, but beyond that there's quite a bit of RNG in how things unlock and what you find.  It is VERY well balanced and i've never felt RNG screwed, more just that I wasn't using options I had, but be warned it's a thing.  The second phase is once you're discovering less, you can crank up the difficulty or shuffle up the start to get a new challenge.Again, as an avid fan of a ton of Turn based/4x games, this feels like a massive breath of fresh air and is easily one of my favorites.  It takes some getting used to, and the initial difficulty curve is probably too hard (something they just made a lot better in a recent patch), but this really is a one of kind game

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: A magical 4X game with RPG elements, recommendedYou are a mage taking control of your master's old tower, formerly his and now your seat of power. Your task now is to research spells to cast; create, train and/or hire troops, gather apprentices and heroes to lead your armies, go on battle-heavy quests (including the main story quest), and generally exploit the land. At the start, you choose what kind of mage you want to be. There are basically 3 "factions" and 3 primary (but not exclusive) resource types: Alchemists who mainly use plants, necromancers who mainly use souls, and artificers who mainly use ore; every mage has 2 additional schools of magic at their disposal.Exploration is a key element of the game, as this is how you find new cities to trade with and quest for, encounter the other mages on the map to try to get along with (or vanquish), and expand your magical repertoire by way of the hidden knowledge of the ancient Shapers. Territorial expansion is not as pronounced as in other 4Xs, you mainly achieve expansion by building small outposts and moving your tower around.There is no journal that logs your quests, rather, they are all displayed as items on the map, which unfortunately makes them at the same time easier and harder to keep track of.Battles are usually short and sweet, not too complicated but not too simple, either. The main thing to keep in mind is zones of engagement for melee units and distance/line-of-sight for ranged ones.All in all, I'd recommend it.

_childDocuments_.review: In short, i'd call this game a 100% spiritual successor to AoWIII. A grand tactical journey to another world, no less. Spellforce: Conquest of Eo, while having some flaws story-wise, in  terms of tactics and strategy is a real gem. If you played magnificent AoWIII or any of the "Endless" series garbage you'll love this game 100%. Pros:-Hardcore non-linear tactics AND strategy in one game. One of the best I've ever seen. It is just satifsying to plot your advancement here - there are no "hard ceilings" or "story bottlenecks", yet at the same time constant world progression always keep you on your toes.-Huge world, and you can pick a starting location that suits yourself-Always interesting to explore and make choices in various events with different races and creaturesSo-so:-Music is kinda ok. it is good but variety of tracks is small. Easy to get bored ofCons:-Game tends to be getting VERY tedious close to lategame, with the sheer amount of heroes and armies you have to micromanage each turn (but, again, AoW series veterans find themselves right at home with that)-Story is outright poor, because as usual with Endless and AoW games it is not character-focused. Yes you are a mage in search of your lost master and there are other mages who you can either fight or not fight. But thats pretty much it. World events are all set separate, they have no connection to each other and no real logic. -Apprentices are generic AF, if you expect Thea or Expeditions series level of character development you won't find it here. Aside from your 1st apprentice, there is about 10-15 random characters with no backstory or even lore regarding to "why are they here" ,no nothing, they just exist to provide you with a generic hero as you advance your "power"....-Same about units - missing lore pages, it may be a small detail but combined with other parts it really hits the atmosphere in a bad way-Also, as mentioned - your rival mages, you can either fight them or not fight. No diplomacy. There are sometimes some minor events featuring their minions but result is always the same - small tick one or other side on the "reputation" bar. If it goes low they attack you. Thats pretty much it.... No real consequences.Overall: 8/10 If you love hardcore strategy and tactics, as well as world exploration and conquest, as well as feeling of constant pressure - this game is good at it. Unfortunately, story and lore are not as good, and characters have no personalities, they just random pictures with stats - think for yourself if that is ok with you.

_childDocuments_.review: Firstly let me say that this is a really great game. I return to it from time to time and play through a campaign. Each time it is fun, challenging, and different. The game is more strategy than role playing, but the encounters and quests really add to the flavour so the experience is immersive.The mechanic where you can move your mage tower is something I've never seen before and sets this game apart as different from others in the genre. You also don't have to endlessly manage resources in each of the towns you visit which is, in my opninion, a welcome change from the norm.I also want to complement the developers for their support for this game. I've played it for many hours and just came back to play another campaign after a break. A patch had just come out that did a number of things including adding a quest log (the only thing I felt was really missing), and a new hero, Galtrak. I got Galtrak during this playthrough and he's a great hero, again interesting and different. For the developers to be adding new content this long after the game was released really says something.From the standpoint of balance I can't fault the developers either. The game is tough at the start when a wrong decision could cost you armies and apprentices, but if you invest a bit of time learning how to play the early stages it's not that hard. I found that I gradually learned what the enemy units can do and how to protect my units that were vulnerable to them. You can also customize the game to make all aspects easier or harder according to what you prefer. To summarize I'd say that this is a wonderful and lovingly crafted game that I will keep coming back to play. I wish more developers made games like this one.

_childDocuments_.review: I'm not one to write a review but this game was so much fun and unique that I feel compelled to do it.  This game is a wonderful combination of exploration, tactical combat and RPG like storytelling quests and advancement of both Heroes and Units.  Yes, you level up units as well, all the way up to level 15!  As to why I feel this game is unique, it's the exploration aspect of the game.  You see, there is no empire building in this game that can result in long, unwieldy turns that can lead to a boring "just finish the scenario/game" late game.  Instead, your "realm" is a floating tower that you expand and upgrade as the game advances, which can be supplemented by your hero lodges and certain spells/creatures.  Why does the game have a floating tower (beside it being cool)?  Well its because you must move around to find resources to pay for your unit/spell upkeep costs.  There are also unique locations that are unlocked by your tower, which adds the storytelling part of the game.  Speaking of resources, you might see some comments online/in this forum expressing annoyance or frustration about (most) of them being a finite resource that will eventually run out.  This is actually an important part of the game design, because winning the game requires you to explore the world, and it is a big world with a lot of quests, unique locations to explore and creatures to discover and recruit!  Being a big 4X game player who loves games like Age of Wonders this part of the game was a little stressful at first.  However, once I realized how big the world is and how much there is to do and find, I realized that it not only advanced the game but kept it fun and exciting.  The 3 unique classes also play very different, so combined with the very large map it brings some replayability to the game.  There is one part of the game that does need improvement and can be a little annoying, which is the quest log book...or rather lack thereof.  I suspect the small size of the team is the reason for this omission. but given how great the rest of the game is it's a minor issue (IMO).  All in all a great game that I strongly recommend any 4X or tactical player try!

_childDocuments_.review: Um... I want to recommend this game. Its's really great in a lot of ways. It has two major problems. One of which is going to keep me from playing it. 1. I'm getting some crashes. It doesn't happen a lot but it happens enough to make me stop playing the game for now. 2. Minimal varity. Campaign always starts the same. But within the small framework of necro/arcanist/alchemist there is still quite a bit of depth. It just needs to be fleshed out. Also, instead of being a faceless wizard you should be a character in the game. Customizable and with a particular race that you can choose. This allows more variety in the game. Ala age of wonders. Not syaing to be more like them in general, but more starting options would be great. #2 is not really game breaking for me. I got my money out of the game with the current variety set and would even still be playing it if it wasn't crashing every hour or so. None of my other games do this... :( :( :(

_childDocuments_.review: It's like a blend of the all the best Age of Wonders 3, Heroes of Might & Magic, Fallen Enchantress, Fantasy General 2. If you like any or all of those then you'll love this.Things I don't like aka negatives for me - 1) No random maps2) not enough info that's easy to find about many things.3) steep learning curve but not Dwarf Fortress level of steep. I'm going on my 3rd restart just because I made some bad choices and fell too far behind the AI. Not horrible because I like the game but some more info would be helpful (see #2 above). When some guides come out I'm sure everyone will avoid some of the basic errors that I've made so far.4) needs more options for individual games and for making custom characters.5) I had one game freeze event that kept happening on a certain event. It was annoying but the devs are aware of it so I'm sure it'll be fixed soon. I have had no other bugs but had to mention it in case any of my friends buy it and encounter the same thing.Things I like and consider positives -1) The price - In a time when most games are over charging for what they release and then killing you with a gazillion high priced dlc's this game is a steal at this price. I would consider this a deal at anything under $40 USD. So on sale for like $22-$23 it's crazy.2) Even though the customization options are very limited there is a ton of content here. I see myself probably putting in a couple hundred hours on what's already in the game.3) The games that I listed in the first sentence are some of my favorites and this one will fit right into that group. I'm sure there will be some dlc's and maybe even mods in the future so this will be a really huge game for years to come in my opinion.4) Super fun and fresh for me. I've needed one like this for a bit. 5) Xcom 2 style base building - This gives you some options. Most people will all build the same way but who knows? Sometimes I built a few of the same rooms in XCOM for faster research or production etc.. I like it a lot and hope more tactical games add in similar base building.6) One of the biggest positive for me is that it is not easy. "Oh I saw a streamer doing this and that."? Well they are pros and earn a living at it so they usually are far better than average players. I consider myself at least a little above average in tactical games of this nature and I've gotten owned pretty well so far. To me that's great because it keeps me coming back. Also it wasn't really unfair like just getting swarmed by AI or something. Just my parties weren't built right for the fights that I got into and some strategic global map opportunities were missed by me. All good, I hate when a game is too easy  and you just steamroll right through it to the end.Summary - The game is super fun. It should remain so for a long time to come. Based on the hours I see putting into this one it's super cheap with or without a sale. If you like the games that I listed in the beginning then do yourself a favor and buy this now. There's nothing horrible about it.

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to like Spellforce; Conquest of Eo because it contained many game elements that I enjoy; magic, multiple quests, mythological characters, and 4X structure.  But I quit because the game difficulty was dominated by the dearth of resources.  Additionally, the very limited resources deplete in the blink of an eye forcing the player to constantly (slowly) relocate his home tower and auxiliary lesser domain claims.  The player guides do make the promise that the resource limitations can be minimized with additional time and accomplishments, but I find the rewards and satisfactions significantly less than the frustrations to try and slog trough to that point.Quests are also problematic because there isn't a quest log which is complicated by another factor.  If a quest has multiple objectives and if one of the objective locations is in the FoW, the quest location becomes obscured and you have to remember where the location is. I found that it was best to limit each of my two armies (could not afford more) to a single quest to simply quest resolution.  Successful completion of the quests is very often essential to advancing the game to enable assorted promotions, level ups and access to powerful upgrades.  This game simply is not fun to play.
_childDocuments_.name: SpellForce: Conquest of Eo

_childDocuments_.review: This was as surprise.  I knew nothing about Spellforce going in.  And whereas AOW4 proved a huge disappointment this proved to be great fun from the start and all the way through my time with it.I like that's it not a traditional 4X, they took a risk with a new twist with the castle you fly around and it just works.  Exploration of the map is driven by a need for resources that deplete rather than some mad rush to stake out claims to territory because if you don't the AI does.  The explore portion in most 4Xs is nothing more than a land grab and all the more boring for it.The tactical battles are just crunchy enough to make them fun but not so involved you dread playing them out.  Looking at you AOW4.  And it matters that you keep your troops alive because you don't have a bunch of them and ranking them up and assigning them attributes matters.  Which is also where crafting ties in and makes a difference.I can't stand crafting, I loved crafting in this game.  Loved it, it's brilliant.The three main choices for who you play are sufficiently different the choice matters in how the campaign plays out and makes it enjoyable to replay the game as each class.  The art-style in this game is superb.  You can tell with your first glance someone put some heart and soul into it.  And thematically it all ties together in the appearance of everything in the game.The enemies you fight in the form of circle mages are mighty enough to prove a challenge and fit well into the lore of the game.Net it all out: This is my Game of the Year for 2023.  This feels like a development team who took chances doing something different, had a design vision they executed well and the result was something unique and refreshing.  I don't know what Owned By Gravity are working on next, I hope it's DLC for this game.  But I know whatever it is I'm there for it.

_childDocuments_.review: Conquest of Eo is a wonderful blend of Civilization, RPG and Dungeons and Dragons story telling.I really liked the combination of the quest system with the global turn-based strategy. _childDocuments_.review: update: so it looks like there was a patch that directly addressed my concerns/gripes/issues so I will remain very open to changing my review to a thumbs up as soon as I get the chance to play the game again. I do think it speaks very very well of them to so rapidly churn out a major patch that directly addresses balancing game play and letting the player customize their difficulty/challenge experience because this will only make things better for players desiring any difficulty level. Story mode seems broken. Did my first play on the level above that (explorer I think) and took my time figuring out mechanics, wandering around, and just being chill. Ended up against the undead dude who was handing me my butt on a platter so I did a restart on story guessing I had wasted too much time. Needless to say I was much more businesslike, went right to resources, immediately researched spells as soon as the storyline allowed it and same with hiring additional troops and building out my tower, etc. Within a handful of turns my tower was attacked and almost destroyed and the same tower quest that I had easily defeated with 1 fewer troops before now basically TK'd my army stack including my apprentice hero. Note: this total kill was against 1 unit, I had 5 units including apprentice hero. This was literally less than 20 minutes into gameplay when it was supposed to be introducing me to the mechanics of the games and there were tutorial windows popping up everywhere for things still.  I wanted something relaxing to grind on since the rest of life is stressful enough. While new to this game specifically I have gamed similar formats for a number of years. This is ridiculous. No point in making story mode at least 3x more challenging than the level above it. _childDocuments_.review: Spellforce: Conquest of Eo offers a good strategic part but its leveling system is very bad thought out and includes RNG on leveling your units / savegame scumming to net desired results, a very low level cap (15) and inferior functionality that wastes your time.For those that still remember Disciples 2, this game is basically a 3D version of it but watered down functionality. You could achieve level 99 with your heroes and you could import them from map to map in Disciples 2. Graphics-wise, Disciples 2 has a lot of well drawn units and combat while the 3D models for Conquest of Eo are somewhat lacking. There are only a few maps to choose from including 3 biomes: grassland, forest, mountains.Your base, a mage tower, does not expand as you gain power. Instead you manually have to expand your domain to reach father away resource nodes by placing buildings with a very small area of influence manually. You do this A LOT, its a real hassle. Hate to say it, but in Disciples 2 this area expanded on its own and you could concentrate your playtime on the Strategy/RPG elements. In Conquest of Eo a lot of your playtime gets wasted and its really only the Strategy experience you get.Cannot recommend.

_childDocuments_.review: What the game is not: it is not a full fledged AAA/4x title with randomly generated maps and throughly balanced units/abilities. It is not going to dethrone e.g. Age of Wonders or Caster of Magic.  What this game is: a lovingly crafted turn-based strategy on a hand-crafted large map with randomised parameters such as resource/stack locations. A neat simulator of an upstart mage trying to carve out their own place in the world where the Circle (uber-mages of the world) deem her/him beneath their notice. Last but not least, supported by responsive devs with a lot of good will towards adressing the community's needs within the limits of their budget.  Final verdict:Treat as a semi/indie title worth recognition and a chance to build on a very, very solid foundation through patches/DLCs or sequels. Worth it for the price.PS. Lore callbacks to previous entries in the series (the Circle, Tahar, Mugwa), reading the text adventures thoroughly pays :)

_childDocuments_.review: Anyone who has played Age of Wonders 3 is going to feel right at home here. The combat system is essentially the same, minus the ability to use spells in battle, and, also importantly, there are no multi-stack battles.Your Domain (territory) extends from your base in an X tiles radius, very similar to how cities worked in AoW3. None of the 'sectors' nonsense that came with Planetfall and AoW4. A Major difference in this game, however, is that you only have 1 main 'city' (your tower) ever, but that it is mobile. And you will be moving it - a lot. Resource providing nodes on the map are mostly not permanent - they expire after being collected for some time, and so you are thus highly encouraged to keep moving your tower to collect other resources that are not yet expired. Its also encouraged to move your tower because staying within its radius helps fight your enemies.Speaking of 'enemies', this is somewhat difficult from a typical 4x in that regard. Your Antagonists in this game (the circle mages) don't even pretend to play by the same rules that the player does. Yes, we all know they get all sorts of cheats in other games but functionally those cheats are numbers in the form of +X resources or some other buffs. In this game, the player is the only one with an actual 'economy' in any sense. Also because of this there is no form of diplomacy with the antagonists that you would see in other 4xs. You get events that let you get on their good (or bad) side, but not the typical form of diplomacy. Some circle mages are easier to stay on the good side of then others, though if you play long enough you will eventually run afoul of even the friendliest ones. You are not technically required to engage with any of the circle mages to win though, technically, though - although you most likely will take out at least 1 or 2 in a typical game. The game feels more rpg-ish in this regard.With regards to what you play as, You're given the optiion of 3 different (and very distinct from each other) crafting classes. Alch can create items, nec can create undead, and artificers glyphs, which are essentially a form of equipment. They are all well designed and fun to play as. Secondary to this is magic schools, which are again well designed and distinct.The game also (in its base state anyway), also contains only 1 singular map. This is good and bad. A Fixed map helps with campaign narrative on your first few playthroughs - something annoyingly lacking in AOW4 and planetfall, but the lack of random map generation massively hurts replayability in the *base* game. I say base game because random map option *was* eventually added, but its locked behind DLC.Overall however, its still a game worthy of playing. Just be advised that if you want endless 4x replayability - you're gonna have to pay extra later.

_childDocuments_.review: One of the best things about Master of Magic (the original) was all the little ways it made you feel like a mad wizard in a tower, from collecting spellbooks to tinkering with the power vials to the animations that played when you summoned strange creatures.  This game takes that part of Master of Magic, applies a AOW3 style battle system, and then runs with it.Things I've tried:  1) Levitating my tower, loading up a life-stealing paladin/golem doomstack, and flying it around the massive map like it was an assault carrier. Only needed one stack that game.2) Going all in on Nature magic and alchemy, coverting the Misty Coast to a maze of magical groves (which generate mana, of course), training dozens of stacks of no-upkeep bears (many of which were just decoration), building a ton of "elementals in a bottle," and then teleporting in teams of tactical elemental assault bears right to my enemy's door step.  Five bears deploying two elementals each = chaos, and that was just my first wave.3) Guardian Spells (+white magic damage) plus the structure add-on that decreases enemy white magic resistance by 50% in your domain.  That one was kind of math-y but hey it works.  Highly compatible with the assault carrier approach.I've also heard that slaves are good but that's kind of a ♥♥♥♥ move ya know?  Even for a wizard.5/5 - magic tactical assault bears

_childDocuments_.review: Edit: After months of silence devs updated the game. Some bugs were fixed AND new content added. So there is a non-zero chance for more content for the base game and perhaps DLCs. I still consider the rest of the review valid and I do sincerely hope for more patches and some DLC to fix what is subpar, expand on what is there, and add what is missing.I do like the game. Sometimes even love it. Other times I hate it with passion. Would I recommend it? No. It's a tough decision but since there is no neutral option I am going with negative.First, let me say that the game hasn't received patches, updates, or additional content for some time. That is not even a critique but merely a warning as to what to expect. What you see is what you get.Now what I like. The presentation. The entire theme of being a young mage, ascending to the highest circles of power where people use entire armies as a bait, or sacrifice without any remorse. You start with almost nothing, while they are already established. You are struggling to survive while they are merely playing a game half of the time.I adore the fact that so much is done through your magic book and you literally flip through pages as you add more. You also have a moving tower, and while other games have fixed territories you have limited abilities and have to make some tough decision as to what to approach. Generally you can either attempt to lay low and slowly build up your power or rush toward the next objective, knowing you will anger other mages and just hoping you get enough power to face them when the time comes... The reality operates on some rules and every time you play in the early and mid game you get a unique combination of ways to bend and break those rules. Fantastic. You also need to actively move around the map which is quite unique.Now why do I not recommend this? TLDR:The game is incredibly rough on the edges. It's a bunch of really cool ideas and concepts that ultimately fail to make a coherent whole. Do not treat this as a strategy game, it's more like an RPG with some strategy elements. It's your journey to become a powerful mage, but the 4X elements are half-baked. I finished 2 full playthroughs (one on the Explorer and one on Balanced difficulty) and made notes what I would change/add/remove and I have dozens of them. So many design choices make no sense and QoL features are missing.The long version:There is no diplomacy. You get random quests and dialogue options that are specific to each mage. And your response can either anger them, do nothing, or rarely improve your relationship. You can't send them gifts, bribes, conspire with them against others, intimidate them, nothing. You can merely anger them by intruding into their domain or defending yours against theirs... And once you slip into Cold war with them they will send units after you which means War is just a matter of time.Every time you get stronger, reach some important milestone, or post offensive memes on social media, the Circle will take note and this decreases the reputation. Which means you are on a clock. You either win before they get angry, attack first, or wait as long as possible and attack then.You can interact with neutral cities a bit more, but those are all spells. Like I get that pouring mana into a spell to improve relationship with a city is a spell. But giving money to a city to do the same is also a spell. Specific to one school of magic which you might not get for the entire playthrough... Otherwise killing bandits, doing quests, or having an inn within your domain improves relationships with that city.All research is done through pages so the spells you can have are set. You can occasionally buy a single spell from a merchant. There is no tech tree to speak of.There are also "neutral" enemy factions such as bandits, beasts, racist dwarfs, undead etc. Those hold buildings, randomly roam the map, or very much nonrandomly target one of your buildings.The enemies scale in power as you do. So the strategy element goes out of the window. They can also spawn units and structures randomly with no reliance on territory or resources (except spawn buildings). You on the other hand are bound to that (which makes the game very frustrating until you get recall and teleport spells) so you will need to defend multiple locations.You can't siege or surround an army or a fort. It's always 1 army vs 1 army. That makes weaker armies and harvesting/mining parties more of a liability than utility. And since the enemy doesn't operate on the same rules as you, the only one suffering from attrition will be you. They will, in time, simply spawn more.Music, units, and maps are... limited. Common maps you will fight on so often you will recognise the few maps very soon. And the fact that every mage tower isn't a unique map is just a sin. Also units have like 2 voice lines they usually use. Some share those 2 voice lines. Music isn't that pronounced but it's basically the same one theme of somewhat epic orchestral tune with zero diversity.The balance of some units is of the whack. And the only way to defend against that is breaking the game more.You can choose three "professions" - necromancer makes LEGO units, glyph smith makes permanent upgrades, and alchemist makes mostly consumables. While you can eventually find spells from schools of magic you didn't start with, this choice is permanent and one-time. I like alchemist the most because every single unit can use consumables with basically zero restrictions (a golem won't heal from a potion, but it can still use it on others). Do you know what an ancient shaper golem, an elf ranger, a wolf, and a goblin have in common? They can use the same consumables. So you can spawn a load of trash units, and have one of those who survive the next turn throw a silence potion on the enemy mages...And often you need to do this since the random pack of bandits that are outnumbered, on fire, and poisoned, will often target that one single unit that is hurting... It feels less like fighting a neutral army and more like you are playing against a game master that is your angry ex girlfriend... Aside from that enemies are dumb as bricks.Some units and spells reveal garrisons and their strength. Otherwise you might need to attack to find out, and then just retreat. You have no way of knowing (except prior experience) if this quest is a trash fight against two goblin units, or two battles against powerful beasts with no time for rest. And often quests and battles pop at random, so weaker armies will again get destroyed or you need to skip on loot and opportunities. The story clashes with the strategy elements often.And I could go on and on. Literally have dozens and dozens of notes. From what I gather from community channels the game didn't sell gangbusters so it will get only limited attention. So we will need to live without such luxuries as rebinding keys or the ability to set the number of competing players (it's locked to 4).It just pains me to see the potential this game has go unrealised. And I am not even talking about DLCs, expansions, sequels, more maps (you get one map where some things are set and some are randomised). I am talking mostly about balancing things, small additions/changes to existing systems, and expanding on what is there (like variety of combat maps).I went into this expecting 4X strategy not RPG with 4X elements. That might be the source of my disappointment. I still enjoy the game and will give it more time occasionally but there is a plethora of reasons why this didn't become the next huge hit (even among strategy games). And with the poor balancing and some awful or missing mechanics, and little variety in places you will see hundreds of times during every playthrough it doesn't have the staying power either. And that sucks because it nails the "just one more turn... oh ♥♥♥♥ it's 3 in the morning" feel perfectly.

_childDocuments_.review: This game kind of came out of nowhere to little or no discussion and has silently continued dropping cool DLCs and content updates. It's criminally unnoticed and I thoroughly enjoy it. It's a turn-based, 4x game where you play a mage and his tower slowly accruing resources, magical power, and an army while embarking on quests throughout Eo. Depending on your class you'll interact with the resources differently, whether it's necromancy with zombies, alchemists with powerful consumables, or artificers with glyphs and equipment. There's a few different ways to play up your fantasy mage as you contend with four randomly-chosen rival mages who resent your growing power, and you must either relieve them of their fears and be welcomed into their midst or simply crush them under your heel. It's definitely worth a peek for someone who enjoys a game like Age of Wonders.

Some of the unit acquisition and map movement can be painful, and playing the same map every time can get a bit droll; but this game is still fun enough to look past all of that. Complex crafting systems and mechanics string together to create a comprehensive and versatile race of Demonologist. It is so refreshing to play this game and see that there are devs out there who will take the time and not rush their game out, while also having the funding to do this.While there are a couple of personal issues I have with the game, I think this is still a very well developed game. You can tell how much love was poured into the lore and crafting system of this game. It also has a good bit of future potential (probably planned). It could be streamlined a bit more (shorten the length of the games by making traversing the landscape less painful is only one example). I also feel like the unit acquisition mechanic a bit more liberal. I really like the necromancy crafting system and I'm sad to see that only they get a unit crafting system. I have not yet played as alchemist so I don't want to speak about tower buildings for building units, but for sure I can say it's not as fun as crafting your units like the necromancer. _childDocuments_.review: This game hurts my usual AOW brain because it has inklings of that game, but is also entirely different in approach.It's a 4X game fundamentally, but moves well beyond that very quickly. You don't really expand, but levitate your tower to other places to siphon resources. You recruit units, but it's dictated by several factors: special events, places you have control over with apprentice lodges or your tower dominion, or if you're a necro, you piece together ingredients to create minions.Leads into core elements of the casters: it's an in-depth crafting game. I've tried the Alchemist a little, and he can summon some neat units alongside hiring, but excels when he uses ingredients to craft potions, bombs, berserk mushrooms, etc. You become a potion throwing psychopath, like the alchemist in Tales of Maj'Eyal. I like it. You have to discover the combinations of recipes, too.Necro is the same, but instead of crafting items, he puts the corpse of his wife back together in varying ways. 3 element ingredients mixed with a soul and you get yourself a skeleton warrior. Items and scavenging are for discovering recipes to build walking corpses of varying quality. It's interesting. I haven't toyed with Artificer yet.All mages have different spellbooks with different research trees. Necro can cast spells that allow you to cannibalize living minions in your stacks, feeding everyone else and raising a skeleton warrior in his place. You're playing the cannibal holocaust in-game. He can also siphon souls (core item for minion making) from cities. Alchemist have primordial trees and harvesting from the get-go. My playtime is mostly Necro, so that's all I know, but there's a lot of stuff in this game.The world is hand-made, very beautiful. It's always the same map, but you can choose different starting positions of varying difficulty. It has distinct locations from Spellforce lore which is nice, and variety comes from the randomized quests and events that pop up, with varying dialogue options. Doesn't feel stale whatsoever. Music is partially new mixed with echoes of Spellforce 3, which is excellent because Bastian Kieslinger did an amazing job and it's a splendid musical journey start to finish.Combat is polished and tight. Well balanced, but the auto resolve and some QOL issues make it slightly imperfect. Lots of extra buttons for confirming things - really should just be able to turn those off. Let me screw up and get mad at myself for clicking too many times because I'm an idiot.It's overall great so far. Performance has been fine, pushed it to 4k downsample on a 2060 and it's not an issue. It's pretty much bug-free from my experience. Grimlore carried through with SF3 and its expansions to deliver a truly special title (I have those on GOG), and Owned by Gravity are carrying the series through into a TBS game in a nice way too. It plays different and is delightfully pretty.Ace price too. Worth a buy.

_childDocuments_.review: This is a really interesting game that is *just* shy of truly something special.  That said, you should play it if you like 4X games and have played them all. I think one of the things I love most about this game is the single city nature.  You basically have one city that you fly around the map, plopping down when you find some resources, and moving on when those resources are exhausted. One of the great drawbacks of most 4X I play is the city management I have to do once I get big enough.  As such, I'm usually a tall player but I find most 4x reward wide playstyles.  I honestly thought I'd hate the one city nature, but it's really quite liberating and adds some additional stresses.  For instance, you may have your doomstack army many turns away from your tower when all of a sudden, a random horde attacks your tower.  You have 4 turns to get your doomstack back or figure out another way to deal with the baddies.  And speaking of doomstacks, the tactical battles are so important because losing a unit can be devastating when your ability to replace that unit is half-a-map away.  Not to mention that your doomstack is probably a doomstack because you have it stocked with max-level units.  Sure, it might just be a goblin archer, but it's a level 15 goblin archer.  You can't just print another one of those and so losing it can hurt.  I cannot tell you the number of reloads I've done in order to ensure my uber unit doesn't get trashed.  You are forced to really weigh cost versus reward.  I am also a fan of the different playstyles.  Artificer, Alchemist, Necro, and Demon all play differently and you better respect those differences.  Alchemist, for instance, doesn't have natively strong units.  However, you can pump out a dozen Sacred Waters a turn and become the ultimate undead killing machine. Or stock up on Elements in a Bottle and flood the field of battle with them. When you switch to playing artificer, you have to then figure out how you are going to deal with the hordes of demon and undead that seem to flood the land without your unlimited supply of Sacred Water.  The answer is runes, but it's a different mechanic that needs to be considered. I've played all of the different types and enjoyed them all. Now for the cons:The map is gorgeous but it never changes.  Every game, the same map.  Resources might be distributed slightly differently, but the big ones like Dragon's Heart are always in the same place.  The map is big enough that you can win by only ever seeing half of it, but it harms replayability.The inability to bring more than one army to a fight makes me sad too.  I am used to the AoW/Planetfall world where I could bring up to three stacks to a single fight and have these full on brawls.  I enjoy the tactical battles and missed being able to do it on a truly large scale.  I imagine I may be a minority on this one since the restriction does make the battles more manageable and less resource intensive. The randomness of magic.  Point in case, Recall.  Recall is one of those spells everyone gets access to eventually and let's you pull your doomstack (or any stack) from anywhere on the map to your tower.  Super helpful and gives you the security to move your stacks further from your tower.  However, some of the games I've played I've gotten it really early and some games almost at the end.  Anyway, these cons aside, hight suggest anyone with a love of 4X give this a try.
