_childDocuments_.review: TLDR; Started off decently strong, but as the game went on it moved further away from actual Trolley Problems and more into making you pick one of two (usually terrible and unnecessary) options, ignored any actual attempt to let you shape your decisions and character, and all the while it berates you for every decision and calls you a terrible person. 3/10.As a longer Review...Honestly, the first week of actual trolley problems were pretty decent (EXCEPT THE DOG ONE, SEE FINAL PARAGRAPH). Not a whole lot to say about most of them.The second week of hospital problems were also good, though I was rather annoyed from it Third week of car problems started to go off the rails as the game began deciding that you were That last spoiler'd bit is actually pretty representative of one of the two big issues in the game. Forcing you to make a tough decision and then commenting on the one you choose, as well as highlighting potential issues with it? That's fine. That's great even! It helps make you think about the issue more, and realize how little these situations tend to be black and white, so to speak. ...Except that's not what this game does. Instead, it constantly, consistently calls you a terrible person no matter what choices you pick, does its best to make you feel like a horrible person for doing so (even when you make the same choices as the dev, so at least it's not quiiiiite as biased in that way), and eventually starts gaslighting the player about being responsible for these horrible events taking place at all regardless of how hard you tried to stop them. That's messed up, unpleasant, and all around makes the game terrible to play. It's certainly also not what I'd call "The Narrator challenging your decisions".In fact, frankly that's just one bit of the many misrepresentative or outright  things said about the game on its steam page. "Review by Techraptor: Cuts deep with social commentary without condemning or attacking the player's actions" HECK NO IT DOESN'T, attacking and condemning the player's actions is  the only thing the narrator does throughout the entire game! And I did watch the rest of the game on Youtube, so I'm quite certain about this. At a later part I didn't personally reach the game  That's the opposite of what the second of the three "professional" reviews claims. I also disagree with the third review, that it's a challenge for your morals, as you're (as previously mentioned) considered and stated by the game to be doing the morally wrong thing no matter what you choose about 95% of the time (from the first question even)... and the first review? Thanks but no, I don't think I'm gonna trust  that it's "2022's most important game" either. It's true that the reviewers have the right to their own opinions, but the fact that the dev chose those three in particular (especially the second) feels rather dishonest. I also feel that the fact that the game basically ignores every decision you make goes against the idea that your choices matter and that you get to decide the fate of basically anything. There are... a lot of examples of this as you get further and further in.Finally though, I think the worst and most personally insulting thing about this game can be summed up by the 4th choice in the game, one I'm pretty sure a LOT of people take issue with;  I'm not gonna spoiler this entire paragraph, and it's frankly one I feel SHOULD be spoiled before someone buys this game. That said, if you REALLY want no spoilers you should stop reading now, since I've said everything else I need to say.The Dog Question; A dying dog is on some trolley tracks, but there isn't a trolley coming or anything. You're just told its dying, that you're in a hurry, and then the game gives you the option to either leave the dog to die alone or to put it out of its misery personally. There's no option to stay or try to help in any way other than just "killing" it. And then, from this point on, the game has decided you personally have killed this dog despite the situation not having been your fault in any way. It will give you "jump scare" flashes of a dead dog in a few places. It will have the dog be used as a reason others in-game consider you a terrible person. It will  This would be... upsetting but ultimately tolerable if not for two further things; There's actually an achievement for saving the dog, and that when you get to the results page for the question where it tells you how many other people agreed with you and whether you made the same choice as the Dev? The maker of the game, ReadGraves,  This isn't even a possible result for the player, either. You get the achievement by choosing to go back to main menu through the big red X button in the upper right before being given the two lethal options... and the game will NEVER credit you for this in any other way. You will still be told you killed the dog, regardless of if you've gotten the achievement, and even if you use the "choose a question" option in the Continue menu to skip the question entirely. And it will count it against you in the statistics as well; even if you pick the same answer for EVERY other question in the game as the dev did, it will always tally you as having "chosen" to kill the dog. It's not possible to finish with 100% agreement. I tried.This feels like a personal insult from ReadGraves. He's personally told you - to your face via both The Narrator and the "percentage of questions agreed with ReadGraves bar" - that you are a bad person  That alone is enough for me to thumbs down this game and ask for a refund. You can take your game and your "better than me" attitude, and give me back my money in return. I don't want either.

_childDocuments_.review: A good idea for a game, and not even necessarily a bad execution. But take that thumbs up as more of a neutral thumb. This game is very much a 5/10. Not awful, but enough annoyances that I would say to only grab it if it's on sale and if the concept intrigues you. Some of these "problems" are very heavy handed and obvious analogues for real life issues such as abortion, though the game is thankfully self aware about it. Several other portions of it, however. feel as though the game thinks it's much smarter than it actually is, while lacking that same level of self awareness. Sometimes it will chastise you for not making certain choices, despite those choices not being options at all. In several other sections, it makes assumptions on your choices that may not match up with what you said in the past. (IE, calling you ruthless and self interested if you made a series of choices regarding personal loss for public good.) The narrator will treat you like a piece of ♥♥♥♥ no matter what choices you make, which can get grating after a while.I enjoy how every problem is given a linked reference to somewhere you can read about its origin, too. That's a nice detail to have. While I had my fair share of annoyances with the game, I don't think I can write it off completely. Could probably make a fun co-op experience as you argue among friends. Don't refund it after finishing the whole thing though, even though its short. That's just a ♥♥♥♥ move.

_childDocuments_.review: This is something I would have expected to see on Newgrounds for free ten years ago.Your decisions change nothing except what the narrator berates you for.For example, the game will make you kill a dog, either through inaction or action. It will then keep coming back to this, saying you should have saved the dog.Spoiler alert, you can't save the dog. You can get an achievement for "saving" the dog by quitting the question, but hitting continue after that just puts you right back at that question, where you have to kill the dog.

_childDocuments_.review: "A game you purchase on sale for $9.89 USD promises to provide an interesting take on the Trolley Problem, a classic ethical dilemma. However, upon playing the game, you discover that it is not fun at all: many decisions aren't 'real' (with little or no actual choice), many hypothetical scenarios aren't honest about the circumstances surrounding them, and worst of all, the narrator complains  about  you make. Perhaps you expected a discussion of the responsibility one bears for making certain decisions, but you certainly did not expect someone to spin a negative narrative regardless of the choice you make; complaining is not discussing. You ALT+F4 in frustration at several points and, at the end, discover you have less than two hours of playtime.Upon considering a refund, you revisit the game's description (which you only briefly skimmed) and find a few facts. The description  that there are only two hours of true playtime and  note that every decision you make is challenged. Everything was right there in the text; you simply didn't see it. Regardless, that does not make the game fun, and you still payed $9.89 for under two hours of a negative experience. What do you do?"[-] Do you refund the game, playing into the systematic problem of people refunding short games, thereby hurting small-time creators and the game's developers, despite the fact you played through the entire product, solely because you didn't read the description?[X] Do you not refund the game, giving money to game developers who presented you with a frustrating experience, who wrote an unclear description, and who you could feel shouting at you throughout the entirety of the game's playtime?"So they took $10 from you and make you feel like an arsehole, and you're just going to let them get away with it? Wow, you really must be spineless. What are you going to do if someone mugs you, just hand them your wallet in a nice little box?How about this. Steam provides you with an opportunity to review the game. You could leave a positive review, reflecting that you think this genre and studio have potential regardless of this particular product, or you leave a negative review, adding your own negativity to the slew of complaints and shouting that is the internet. And, because choices are rarely binary, you could also choose to stay out of it, not leaving a review at all."[-] Give the game a positive review, disregarding your enjoyment for the potential the game and studio might have on the genre.[X] Give the game a negative review, disregarding the research that went into the game and the clear effort the team put into making it.[-] Do not review the game, staying out of any potential conflict."It's good to see there's  on the internet who isn't a just another Negative Nanc- oh, you left a negative review? Well, I hear some people don't mind verbal abuse. Maybe they won't take it too harshly. You're sure to be popular on r/AmItheAsshole..."For whatever it's worth, I agreed with the developers on about 42% of the answers when trying to answer from as Utilitarian a perspective as possible. I assume this means the developers and I hold very different perspectives, or perhaps we simply answer these sorts of questions in very different ways.

_childDocuments_.review: Got the game as a gift from a friend after putting it on my wishlist. It was an interesting concept, and I loved the idea of an expanded trolley problem game based on philosophy with a narrator that challenges you. What I expected was a game where you got several different similar "this or that" problems, and at any moment, the narrator might interrupt to go "hold on a minute - you made a choice that put the lives of the many above the lives of the few right now... but 3 choices ago you did the exact opposite? What about this set of circumstances made you kill people here, but not there?"The game gets nowhere close to being that clever.By "the narrator challenges you", what they actually mean is that the narrator will always disagree with your choices and berate you no matter what you chose. The narrator HATES what you're doing EVERY time no matter what! You diverted the trolley? "OH MY GOD YOU KILLER!" You didn't divert the trolley? "OH MY GOD YOU JUST LET THEM DIE?" If the narrator disagrees with you and berates you no matter what, that isn't having your ethics and personal philosophy about life be challenged, that's being yelled at by a contrarian.That isn't the end of how grating the narrator can be. On one early question, you are asked whether you want to force vaccines onto children (topical) BUT the catch is that this vaccine makes 20% of the kids vaccinated WAY sicker than the sickness it's vaccinating against. I've worked in the health industry and have several friends in it. A 20% "sickness-worse-than-what-we're-vaccinating-against" rate on a vaccine is horrendous and would NEVER be approved. Yet if you do the thing that the actual health industry would do in this situation, the contrarian narrator calls you an anti-vaxer. Cool. (Also brief side tangent here, no hate to the voice actress, she just read the script. It's not her fault the material is really awful sometimes)The biggest disappointment is that there's a lot of missed potential and some early questions show a lot of promise. As the timer ticks down before the choice is locked in, every 15 seconds or so, the narrator will pipe up and say something. In some cases she will actually make a point about the question that could change your frame of mind. For example, the second question in the game is just the trolley problem but the second track contains a named, 5 year old little girl. If you have the trolley head towards the 5 people instead, the narrator makes the point "How do you know there aren't any little kids in that group of 5 people?" which is a FANTASTIC point. You DON'T know that! In that case, her narration as the timer ticks down ads urgency and another ripple to your choice!Unfortunately, only around 5% of the narrator's "mid choice" voice lines are insightful, thoughtful things like that. The other 95% are either calling you an idiot or trying to say something funny (I did not laugh once.)If it sounds like I'm nagging about the narrator a lot, it's because the game is only your choices and the narrator reacting to your choices. She's 50% of the game and she's very poorly handled. The quality of the choices also diminishes as the game goes on.As for the "based on philosophy" part of the pitch, it fails that pretty badly. To give a quick example, after a choice later on in the game, there is a note that pops up on screen that says "this last choice was a metaphor for [one of the game's major themes]." If you have to put a literal sticky note on screen to say "that metaphor was a metaphor and this is what the game is about", you maybe should've considered getting that point across some other way.I was super disappointed, but if you're interested by the premise, give it a shot during a sale. At it's worst, it's a neat little timewaster, and I always want to support game devs branching out and trying something new. But don't expect something super deep and insightful. Expect to be presented a series of 50-ish "this or that" questions with a British lady whose name is likely Karen Karenway, who says you're stupid no matter what.

_childDocuments_.review: Ok so here's the thing.The game added some extra dialogues before and after you made any final decision for each choice.Some added confusing precondition to each dilemma, like "the young is probably drunk driving" in elderly vs youth question, which took away the original point of the scenario completely. But most importantly, every time each choice is made, the narrator is going to state all the frustration and drawback caused by your choice. The core of this type of classic dilemma is a value testing of the GAIN of the choice of sacrificing in an individual's value vs the LOSS. By taking away the first part and focusing only on the second, you didn't make people question whether they made the right choice, you made people question why are they making choices at all if they cause nothing but losses. Dev wants people to always question their choice, I get it, and I like it. But I am disappointed that they failed to present the philosophy behind them, only scratching the surface and thought "Oh it wants people to question themselves, that's about it".This, plus it asking for $10 for what essentially a powerpoint with ideas from others and a script. Not recommend. Buy a Japanese gal game instead since at least they have cute anime girls.

_childDocuments_.review: Completed, 4/10:Pros:-Everything up until the Secret Service section is entertaining, and the only reason I didn't drop the game afterwards was out of hope that it would return to that.-While few, the game did have a few joke problems to lighten the mood. My favorite example of this is 4.1.02 The Innocent Threat Problem.-The music was pretty good and worked well with the rest of the game.-While I don't have dyslexia, including a special font so those who do can still play was a nice touch.Cons:-The game looks very blurry with the CRT effect, and very dull without it.-The agreement with the developer meter seems like an interesting idea, until you realize that they don't actually have to answer some of the problems, as they just cheat. It could have been interesting, but ended up just feeling annoying.-The game starts off with simple, thought out problems, before going more off the rails the closer you get to the end of the game. This means that most players will only enjoy about half of the game.-Many of the hypotheticals aren't well thought out, and don't apply well to the real world problems/debates they try to comment on (Most of the abortion problems have issues that make them entirely different circumstances to the real world abortion debate, for example).-The game requires you stream on Twitch in order to get all achievements.-The narrator isn't really able to argue for all of the positions you can take. The idea of having a narrator that constantly disagrees with the player seems like an interesting idea in a game like this, but half the time it feels like the developer just didn't want to/couldn't think of arguments for one of the sides of a debate, and so they just call you a commie.-The game doesn't actually let you make choices. Even if you choose one option, the game's story may very well decide that they think the other option is better, and so it becomes meaningless, as you see the consequences of the other option play out, rather than your choice.

_childDocuments_.review: I love the Trolley Problem thought experiment. It's an interesting concept that makes you think and examine personal ethics.This game is just variations of that same ethical dilemma. The worst part is the obnoxious snooty Stanley-Parable-wannabe narrator that assumes your reasoning and nags you for any choice you make, no matter what it is. (I don't blame the actress however. She performed it how it was written.) It was cheeky the first couple of times but it's repetitive and becomes agitating quickly.For free? Maybe. For 10 bucks? Absolutely no way.

_childDocuments_.review: Good game for gifting a friend or streamer and see their choices.It took me 1 hour 26 minutes to get through all the questions.Based on scientific articles from past decades and philosophical questions going back to Plato.A really good introduction to the topic.I had read most of the questions before, but this is a great introduction to the real science which is also linked so that players can go to the sources.The storyline in the solo game gives the questions a twist making them more fun, but less objective.If you are curious about the topic, this is a good place to start.But know that this is not an original game, it is well known questions dressed in minimalistic graphics.

_childDocuments_.review: You open your steam app, and there is a notification. Two of the games on your wishlist are on sale. You do not have much money, If you buy one, you cannot buy the other. do you press purchase? Well, I did, and boy let me tell you, it was an experience. The hardest choice of this game is actually choosing whether or not I recommend it.by far the funnest part of this game was trying to guess what the dev actually bases their choices off of because it often feels like a coinflip and a lot of it doesn't seem to align with their previous choices. Quality over quantity? Quantity over quality? man, I dunno, but after maybe, I don't know, 10(?) questions, we just start delving into these completely absurd and made up scenarios that are so insane unlikely to happen, and nonsensical that they're not even fun to wonder about. I find it funny that the game is tagged as "choices matter" - they actually don't. everything you do, the game will find a way to berate and argue against you, with... "sometimes" valid points from the opposite view from yours. Your choice is *always* the wrong one. One thing that is interesting though, the game seems to keep track of your answers, and point out whether or not you're being contradictory. The game takes "inaction" as an action, and will not hesitate to call you a murderer for what would be essentially an accident that you were witnessing, just because the choice of interfering was there. Kinda weird. Game feels a bit loaded on these kinds of opinions, and it would be nicer if it was a little more neutral. Other types of bull included: unsolvable puzzles, wording things like there's no other way out and then implying there *was* a solution, and binary choices where things just straight up don't make sense:Well, That is not to say the game doesn't have its positive points, though. Overall fantastic job on the audio and voice acting, the visuals are very clean (even though I thought the jumpscares were massively unnecessary) and... I think this is one of those games that are more fun to play if you have someone else to discuss choices with. It gets tiring really fast.

_childDocuments_.review: Not worth almost £10, it should be half.I get what the game is going for, really, but it ends coming off a tad pretentious and forced sadly, which was a shame as I went in with high hopes.Harbouring on your game's self-aware nature doesn't make it innately smart or witty, which is sort of the tragic flaw here, there just isn't much past the seemingly faux-deep droll commentary and sluggish pace.There's definitely some cool ideas here, don't get me wrong, just felt very overshadowed by some odd texts and stance pushes which seem to go against the nature of the experience.Maybe I'm missing the point, here."This sounds like an abortion question... I don't like politics in my hallucinations."

_childDocuments_.review: It's really trying to be some deep narrative, but it's too sloppy to pull it off and instead just spends the game trying to insult the player but not even being consistent. There's a choice where you have to either kill a dog or leave it to die naturally, and then it spends the rest of the game shaming you for not saving it when that's not even a choice. I can't even get a refund because I waited too long to try to play it so I really recommend anyone interested in buying to just save their money. I got this on sale and it wasn't even worth it

_childDocuments_.review: *Note that I have only played single-player.Firstly, I think this game does do some good things:- It's good for a bit of mental stimulation and informing the player about relevant philosophers based on the questions being asked. - I think it'd be a fun enough game to play with your friends once or maybe twice. - The game has moment of creativity with it's visuals, and although simplistic at times looks nice.- As I put below the game has it's faults and stumbles here and there, I think at it's heart the developers tried something a little bit different with this game so props for that.- It's a cool feature to see what people voted for after you answer the questions, definitely would not have been as interesting without this.However, there are also some problems I have with the game:- I think the price for what amounts to 1-2 hours of content is not completely unreasonable, but perhaps a bit on the higher side. Pick this up on sale if it's not a big deal to you, I also think it'd be hard to persuade a group of friends that you wanted to play this to buy this for what is quite a short game.- I thought the game might be funnier and inject humour and fun into these thought experiments and philosophical questions and I don't think it did that, but tbf perhaps that wasn't it's aim and comedy is subjective- The game's overall conclusion and core message is that often times we don't have a choice, that is that we are put into positions where we have to choose the options available to us but being in that position might not have been something we chose. In this sense it questions our free will, it also show's that sometimes you can make what you think is the best decision available to you with the information you have and that can still be the wrong decision. I think people who are complaining about the lack of real choice, perhaps miss that it seems to be part of the game, I could be wrong but I think that was probably intentional by the developers. Although I think it might be easy to look at a game about making decisions and to think that those decisions will actually mean something or significantly change the game, so if you're looking for that, this game isn't really that. - My problem though, is that the ideas at the heart of this philosophy focused game are kind of a basic concept, that the game doesn't really go that deep into. As a result it's commentary on different issues and ideas, which it definitely has, felt a bit basic to me at the end of my run. At one point the game even admits that this message is unsubtle, when it gives you the option to either a) kill a person, or b) kill that same person.- Another problem is that the game doesn't let you make decisions quickly, it takes a longer time to play than it should, so that 1-2 hours is definitely drawn out, all whilst the narrator kind of nags at you no matter what you do. - Speaking of that narrator, I know it's been mentioned a fair bit by other reviewers, but I don't think it was done in the best way, it was kind of annoying for a lot of the game. Obviously the point of the narrator is to show you that sometimes no matter what option you choose there will always be someone that disagrees with you or a reason why it wasn't the best choice to make, but this get's extremely repetitive especially in the first part of the game. - I think most of the decisions players make whether considered right or wrong by the majority of people, will have been done for a reason or a thought process however flawed and this game seems to forget that and act's like you didn't consider your answer at all. I think a better approach would have been to question the thinking behind the choices and pose a question that challenges that view rather than just saying something along the lines of "You made this choice, too bad this could potentially happen or has happened as a result" when the opposite of that outcome was equally possible. I liked the narrator's performance I just think the writing they were given could have been better. - I think people's annoyance at the narrator's writing also has a lot to do with hypocrisy, where no matter what judgements you make the narrator will make comments about what right do you have to make that judgement or the potential consequences, making asinine comments that often conflict with what the narrator has previously said depending on your choices so the narrator as a character seems inconsistent. Also it's just like I paid money for this experience can you please leave me alone.All in all, I wouldn't mind seeing a similar game to this again it's just that this game doesn't really have enough content, that content is drawn out, the overall message and ideas for the game seem fairly basic, although I believe it's intentional this game doesn't have choices that mean anything if that's something that interests you, the lack of depth in exploring the ideas it touches upon means that the game leaves little impact. The game at times seems to try and guilt trip you, which it then seems to contradict later when it explores the idea that you had limited choices or options to begin with, creating confusion about the berating you've likely just received for the majority of the game. What could have been a thought provoking 60-120 mins is instead quite bland in what it explores.

_childDocuments_.review: Is it short.? Yes.. Is it good.? Yes.. Is it worth the price tag.? That entirely depends on personal circumstance and financial situation..It's about the cost of a film, similar length and probably more entertaining and engaging than most. _childDocuments_.review: Despite this game generally being considered quite mid, I thought I'd try it anyway as I enjoy dark humour. What I don't enjoy is jumpscares for no reason whatsoever. This is not the kind of game that wants or needs jumpscares. Jumpscares aren't and never have been fun or something people actually want in their non-horror games, and dark humour and horror aren't the same thing.I got a refund after the second jumpscare. Closed the game right there and put in the refund request. They ruined their own game with them.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: Great concept poorly executed. It feels like a great demo that was padded to two hours to reduce the chance of refunds.We spent most of the game waiting for the narrator to hurry up, or the arbitrary timers to run out. We answered some questions within 2-3 seconds, and were forced to sit around."Co-op". It's not co-op. You don't get to make independent choices, or independent anything. You just control the same pointer. It's equivalent to advertising a racing game as "coop" but you don't get separate cars, just one car that you can drive with controller A or B.Most questions are boring, repetitive, and lacked nuance. We gave up when the questions essentially repeated themselves for the nth time, asking whether we would kill someone to vaguely "save our reputation". It didn't make sense and wasn't interesting the first time.The writing does not carry this like it should. Most of the pre-question writing was vague and boring, totally cuttable. The meta-narrative was uncompelling, and was full of obvious false choices (no matter what you do, the next thing happens).The narrator complains about every choice you make, which get repetitive and annoying. It would have been simpler and more compelling for the narrator to have a consistent philosophical viewpoint. They praise you when you follow it, and berate you when you don't.Some of the decisions were framed incorrectly, showing a lack of understanding of the material. E.g. The abortion questions.Great voice work, and aesthetic. A lot of potential with a rewrite.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't want to say that the people who don't like the game kind of missed the point. But a lot of the negative reviews seem to be people that missed the point of the game. It's a fun, short game that I would recommend playing in one sitting. I do recommend getting it on sale though as the base price is a bit much for how short it is.Remember, there are no wrong choices, and all of your choices are also wrong.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: Trolley Problem Inc. offers players a journey into the depths of moral and ethical decision-making, wrapped in a veil of dark humour and philosophical intrigue.Initially, the game started strong with philosophical, ethical dilemmas based off genuine papers, although that changed quite fast. The game felt extremely dragged out (you are able to fast forward but that only increases it for a few seconds) and repetitive to a point I contemplated multiple times to stop playing. Despite this, the achievements kept me playing - all of which are pretty easily achievable (especially with the scenario picker). I honestly lost enjoyment after the first 15-20 minutes.Before playing the game, I read the reviews and am extremely confused. Firstly, the jump scares were non-existent. Having a "scary" picture appear for a few seconds, with no sound effects does not warrant a jump scare. These photos are consequential to your decision-making earlier in the game. Secondly, a lot of players had criticisms with the narrator condemning your decisions which feels misplaced, considering you are literally answering philosophical questions, where both answers put your morality into question. I understand it becomes berating and annoying at times, although I believe it is a self-given when you look at what the game is about.The premise of the game is interesting. Who doesn't love a philosophical game which questions your morals and ethics? With that being said, the game overall felt extremely linear, dragged on and inevitably lost its "put your moral compass into question" vibe.In conclusion, while my overall experience with Trolley Problem Inc. wasn't wholly negative, its prolonged and somewhat repetitive nature left much to be desired. It felt as though I was watching a two hour slide show with philosophical questions which progressively get more random, all while the narrator berates you for any decision you make. Despite its potential, the game fails to maintain its initial intrigue, making it difficult to recommend it, especially with the current price point the game is sitting at .
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: Unlike really anything I've played before, Trolley Problem Inc. is a great game for people interested in philosophical dilemmas.At it's core, it's a big collection of difficult questions played out through a narrative (featuring a well-spoken narrator questioning every decision you make) which goes from classic trolley problems, to bigger scale issues, and even some very abstract problems.The game is a little on the short side (the solo campaign is beatable in about an hour) but it's also pretty fun to play with friends and significant others on subsequent play-throughs. Would honestly love to see a bit more of this, be it more problems, a DLC, or whatnot.Overall, a fun little experimental game for people who love (incredibly difficult) decision making!
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: I think a lot of people would enjoy this game more if they realised there isn't supposed to be a right answer and it's more of a personality test kind of thing. The game even acknowledges at the end that it's placing you in unfair situations with no good resolution, and even implies that free will doesn't exist, which potentially could've been explored a lot more.It doesn't shame you only to be funny or make you feel bad, I think it's trying to make you challenge your own decisions so you can make a choice that really reflects what you would think is the best outcome.It does pretty well in posing what is basically the same question at different points but with different contexts. For example, saving 5 by sacrificing 1 is the same as saving a big city by sacrificing a smaller one, but you might find yourself taking a little longer to answer the second question after everything you've been through between the two.Good game, but get it on CDkeys for cheaper. Not worth full price for the length.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: The game takes all your answers in bad faith and has the snooty narrator berate you incessantly. I get the feeling this was supposed to come across as charming and witty somehow, but it does not. The game is inconsistent with your decisions and its references to previous questions (I was told "If only you had saved that dog", even though I never had the opportunity to save a dog, the choice at the time had been "let the dog die naturally" or "end its suffering by killing it"). Might be a good game for content creators (whom I suspect are the target audience for this anyway), as a single player experience I can't recommend it.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting game. Bought this on sale for £3.29, so it was worth it. Definitely only buy on sale. Only bad part of the game is the fact that the brain-dead allegories of Judith Thomson were included. Apart from that, the game gives you references to different philosophical and ethical sources from which the hypotheticals are derived, so you could read up more if you are intrigued.All the negative reviews seem to come from literal babies. Read Ecclesiastes.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: Even after reading all the reviews, and playing the demo, this game wasn't what I expected it to be and I ended up refunding it with very mixed feelings about it. Don't get me wrong; the ethical dillemas it starts of presenting are fairly fun, but then if it was just about these, that could've essentially been done on a webpage. It was about more. The game tells a story and tries to be funny with a sarcastic commentator that dislikes every decision you make, which is lovely, and yet...== Warning for spoilers ahead ==There lies the problem. You make decisions in this game that have incredibly grave moral and ethical implications, yet you have essentially no control over where the story actually goes, while at the same time making you feel you do have that impact, making it all the more disappointing when you end up realising you really don't in any substantial way, which if it hadn't happened anywhere before the last chapter, will happen very abruptly when you reach it and the story is abruptly ended to just take you into an abrupt, drugged up set of fantasy questions that reframe common day to day or culturally/politically relevant questions into the format of the game. All of this makes the game fall in this weird gap between being that far-too-long, but unusually interesting webpage you visit once to pass that unusually quiet evening, and a game where a player can feel in control, and may get notable additional value over being on that hypothetical webpage, and maybe even some replay value, and keeping that in mind it is just absolutely not worth the over-10€ price that is being asked for it. == All in all my conclusion can be summarised as follows: ==While the sassy voiceover was great, the game overall left me feeling disappointed, and that feeling was exacerbated by the steep price. I rate the game 2/5, I do not recommend buying it, not even on sale. == Specific comment regarding the developer: ==I am not impressed with the developers comment about how the price of this game compares "favourably with time spent at the cinema". - The problem here isn't asking this price for a game of this length, (even if this is fairly steep for such a short game when compared to the pricing of games with comparable playime,) It is asking this price for what this game does, where it falls short in what it's trying to do/how it's presented, how it compares to free to acces websites that talk about these same ethical dillemmas in interesting ways and allow you to compare choices that it has to set itself apart from, and how it compares in quality in general to games of comparable length that dó potentially warrant such a pricetag. This response to these critiques from the developer comes across as incredibly tonedeaf, as it places the problem behind the critique with the price with the customers by making it sound as if they just don't understand the comparative value of the money they are spanding, rather then the developer acknowledging why people might not value the game at the price he's setting it at.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the kind of game that makes me wish steam allowed for reviews without having to give a binary thumbs up or thumbs down (though being forced to pick one is very much in keeping theme of the game), because this game has an interesting concept and does something new and different, I also feel that it didn't fully accomplish what it set out to do and ultimately leaves a lot to be desired.Trolley Problem, Inc. is a game that is a series of no win scenarios where you have to make a choice one way or the other, like the Trolley Problem that provides this game with its namesake. Now the thing that makes these kinds of scenarios fun to think about is that you can go back and forth on what answer you want to give, and that's were I feel the game falls short of its own goals. The game only gives you a set amount of time to make your decision, which doesn't really give you much time to think about it, and the rebuttals to the choice you currently have chosen aren't always insightful into why the other option might be the right choice, oftentimes they are just insulting you, and if that was intended to be humorous then they needed to make those lines funnier.There are a few other issues, trying to connect each scenario into a single storyline is a huge stretch, and not every scenario presented is interesting. And while this may be a bit of a nit pick, but having one of your achievements only be achievable by playing the game on Twitch is kind of a crappy move.Ultimately I came down on the side of recommending this game, as I'd rather applaud the game for trying something new and falling short than condemn it for its flaws.

_childDocuments_.review: This game has a brilliant premise. I'm not sure it always digs into that premise as richly as it could, but I found it enjoyable and fairly thought-provoking.It reminded me of the TV show The Good Place and the youtube series PhilosophyTube, both of which are attempts by their creators to make philosophy (in TGP's case, moral philosophy specifically) accessible and engaging. There are a few places where I saw echoes of those two works, actually, so it's very possible Read-Graves was inspired by them. I have to say, though, that while this game reminded me of them and at times evoked that spirit, it never reached that brilliant blend of genuinely interesting philosophy and genuinely engaging presentation. The game starts off strongly, throwing difficult moral questions at you in the form of trolley problems (ie. "Let A happen, or do B"). But the game tries to neatly wrap everything up by making your decisions have longterm ramifications on the plot. By the mid-point I was the President of a country ravaged by a war started via my own actions in chapter 1, which would have been fine except the whole point is that those choices were, due to their being trolley problems, extremely contrived. Also, this desire to wrap everything up in a single plot actually skewed my ethical decision making: an interesting choice about whether or not to develop experimental AI became moot when the AI took over the game itself and caused disturbing errors and glitches, heavily hinting that I should *not* develop the AI.Some level of context is necessary for these moral choices, of course. ("Escape the terrorists or attempt to take them out" will obviously be skewed differently if I'm answering as the player - a weak man with arms like sticks - or as the protagonist, who has been trained to kill.) But I sometimes felt like I was given either not enough context, which made the choices feel arbitrary and random, or too much, weighing them down in plot contrivances that weren't really necessary.Nonetheless, I'm going to say that yes, this game is worth checking out. It's experimental, fun, has nice clean visuals, is genuinely funny in places, and the premise is interesting the whole way through. I think it could have dug deeper, and decided to either become a thorough attempt to educate people on moral philosophy OR a game that seems like that at first but is actually a hilarious joke. But at the end of the day, I liked it.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: The core concept of this game is good - throw some moral quandaries at the player and then have the narrator react humorously to the player's behavior, like the Stanley Parable.  Throw in some secrets and hidden relationships between the given answers that can change the later questions and it should be great.In execution, however, the dialogue isn't written well enough to pull this off.  The game has a timer for each question that you have to wait for, and this makes it drag.  I stopped playing after getting decision fatigue and feeling like it was a slog to keep going.  The hidden relationships are too hidden to notice on first playthrough, and the game isn't fun enough for a second.Instead of leaning into the humor, it instead leans into actual research on moral quandaries.  It cites research references for each question, which is great for further reading, but not for making the game fun.  Showing the choice distribution percentages is good, but including the author's answer to each question was odd.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: In short, fantastic game. Beautifully designed, fantastic voice acting, absolutely ridiculous amounts of research and care went into it and I'd 100% recommend it to anyone interested in a quick and accessible introduction to philosophical thought. Below is a more in depth review as well as  opinion on why I think a lot of the criticisms of the game miss the point entirely.My first experience with this game was, like many others, through watching streamers and Youtubers playing it online. I was intrigued, to say the least. I bought and downloaded the game, messaged a friend, and asked if they wanted to play through it with me. We finished the game over the course of two sessions.We've all asked or been asked the trolley problem question. I remember spending something like thirty minutes with some friends once talking about what the best option was. So when this game hit the deck, I had to buy it.Actually playing the game was quite an experience. It starts off with the basic trolley problem (citation included!) and then slowly, then not so slowly, gets more and more absurd. The game doesn't shy away from bringing real life news stories into questions or metaphor-ising pertinent political issues and questions. A lot of people like their games apolitical; I don't (nor do I think that's really possible). The game stretches the limits of your imagination, forcing you to consider ethical questions from angles you may have never come across and ones you may personally find to be unsavoury. The narrator feels like a judgemental, almost antagonistic, voice guiding you through the questions and purposely making you second-guess yourself as a crucial mechanic to drive the game's point home.A lot of the reviews of the game complain about the price, claiming it's too expensive for what it does. I completely disagree; having just skimmed the bibliography and having finished a dissertation very recently, I can attest that the game is very worth the price. There's citations to dozens upon dozens of references, both academic and non-academic. An Intro to Philosophy class at your local university or college is likely to cost multiple times what this game does, and is likely to teach you about as much. Collecting the bibliography alone is hours upon hours worth of work.The narrator being antagonistic is another complaint about the game, but that's the point. The game is Some reviews complain about the lack of agency in the game. While it is true that, save for a few exceptions, your answers to the question do not actually have a major effect on the "story line," I'd like to note that this lack of agency is a very purposeful mechanic of the game. As stated above below the spoiler bar,  The game is not a narrative nor a CYOA game, it's not meant to allow you a story, and the narrator is not really a character at all, but a metaphor.This game is, ultimately, an extremely cheap Intro to Philosophy class. It's a clear labour of love and the pursuit of knowledge by the creator and all involved, and is a fantastic way to get you started on your path to exploring your ethical and moral compass and ethics in a more general sense.

_childDocuments_.review: If I had to sum this game up in a word, it would be "shallow". Or, to put it another way: I wanted to like it, but I couldn't.Overall, I'm a big Yogscast fan and wanted to support this endeavour, so I bought the game despite having had mixed feelings when I had seen it played. I quite like games which force you to make difficult decisions and so I felt like a game about ethical dilemmas would be right up my alley. For me, at least, there is something lacking in Trolley Problem, Inc. and I realised I'd rather return it than to play through to the end.I felt some questions were overly contrived, and weren't so much of a dilemma as picking between two arbitrary courses of action. In these cases, I found myself wishing for an option c) to pick. For example, in a question about a rogue AI, the options were to a) fire 5 coders or b) say the AI is possessed; there is no option c) to take responsibility for the rogue AI yourself, it's either a) punish people who may or may not be responsible, or b) say noone is responsbible.Other questions seemed to have more plausible responses to choose from, but in these cases I felt overly rushed by the timer. There's no time to weigh up questions like "whether you have a responsibility of safety first to your customers or first to the general public at the expense of your customers" in 30 odd seconds, and so it felt unsatisfying to go every time with your gut response.And in other questions still, the lack of an ability to clarify the question lessened the experience. Do we know that pushing the fat man will save the others on the tracks with 100% certainty? Or if we choose to advertise to customers in our free driverless taxi service instead of selling driverless cars themselves, are we also collecting data about the customers, or are the ads just an annoyance the passenger has to put up with in exchange for the service? With the information given, it's hard to make a meaningful choice.The overall feeling, unfortunately, was of a buzzfeed quiz which at the end tells you which Harry Potter character you are. Except, it doesn't even do that. It would be great if there was some indication or tracking of which responses followed a more utilitarian philosophy etc. as you go through, but there isn't, and with the timer, I found it difficult even to think about whether I was being consistent in my philosophy.To end on a positive note, though, the reading list which links each dilemma to a paper on ethics is a great feature!Sadly, I would not recommend this game, but if you are looking for a "would you rather" game of ethical dilemmas, perhaps it could be for you. :)

_childDocuments_.review: Excellent game overall, great fun to play with friends. The setup is very clever, the philosophical problems are more detailed than they would appear, and there is a clever way of introducing bits of information as the timer runs down that just may change your perspective. One of the reasons I enjoyed this so much is because I have higher education in philosophy, and this game nicely expands on many of the problems I was taught - it has clearly been well researched. People arguing that the puzzles are too rigid are somewhat missing the point of these types of exercises. The whole purpose of these types of questions is to force you to confront morality in a fixed way, without hiding behind "unpredictable outcomes"Visually it is a little same-y, although there are some amusing and cute animations on some of the questions. My only real complaint is the graphical-glitch style towards the end, it is done deliberately but I think it goes on too long and causes a little eye strain
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: I will say first of all that I don't  the basic concept behind this game. It's a fascinating idea, taking the well-worn and well-known "trolley problem" and expanding it into not only a game, but a sort of entry-point to philosophical thinking. I just wish (and this is the one thing that drags it into a negative) that the game didn't  taunt you and guilt you after As the game page says outright, "every decision you make is challenged." By this, it means that you are constantly gaslit into thinking that every choice you've made is the wrong one. This element in particular was what turned me off the game - rather than serving as an entry point to philosophy, all this game did was make me feel like an idiot. Maybe I AM an idiot. But in the end, this particular element counter-intuitively making me LESS interested in the kinds of conundrums this game posed.I therefore recommend this game only if you've the thick skin to dip your toe into philosophy while being put down and berated at every juncture.

_childDocuments_.review: As much as it is a choice game and tagged as "Choice Matter" they sadly don't, it puts you up with a dialogue that wasn't appropriate for the choice and seemed like a forced work around to make the game linear.Spoiler: Example, you leave sick dog, it dies, you kill it well ... it dies, then you get blamed for it either way.I went through to see if your path changes slightly but from what I saw ... it hasn't despite picking opposite decisions.Another: You get an option for 1 or 5 as the classic goes but with a twist, on both occasions it says somebody you killed/let die was doing Vaccine research.I'm a little disappointed in it being that way since ... this exact game should show you how your decisions effect the world, yet it failed to do so.

_childDocuments_.review: i feel silly leaving an essay in a steam review for what can somewhat be summed up in, i hate the narrator to much to enjoy playing. although i will be fair in saying, a special interest in human morals and that "autism sense for justice" probably are what causes it. the black and white thinking she holds just being flipped so she disagrees with your choice no matter what just feels. too irritating. its probably meant to be the point and irony that she gives black and white stances for trolley problems, but i just despise it. basically if you're autistic and care heavily for nuance like me, you might wanna be aware that the narrator is not fun. but if you don't care much about that, or even enjoy the irony and find it funny, you'll probably enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: I was super excited to check out this game when I stumbled across it. What I love most is that each problem is a segue into a deeper rumination and/or conversation with yourself and friends (if you're having friends join along). You really take a minute to explore and reflect on personal values and biases, and the potential external influences for each question. AND if you have friends playing with you, compare and contrast answers, values, and morals with them. It's a great way to either a.) have a genuine dialogue or; b.) start a heated debate in which you never talk to said friend ever again. (And I bet it's because you opted to kill the dog.)I see that there are a lot of other reviews stating that it's not worth the $10 dollar price tag. I'd argue that it is. For a couple of reasons, the game itself, AND the reference list the dev(s) provided so you can read on the studies/cases that prompted each dilemma question. It would be entertaining at the end of the game, upon answering the final question to see a final tally with a breakdown of worldwide results. I love when games can tie together my nerdy psychology phd side and my gaming enthusiast side.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: The game's premise is interesting, and who doesn't love a philosophical game that questions your morals and ethics, but overall the game felt extremely linear, drawn out, and inevitably lost its "question your moral compass" vibe. The purpose of the game seems to be to provide a list of different philosophical/psychological scenarios with immediate pressure to choose the "right" option, then step back and analyze your actions. Then compare and contrast the "how" and "why" behind your answer as an exercise in philosophical thinking and, perhaps, introspection about ways you may not have realized you were thinking...This is where the game fails. It tries to put a narrative into these scenarios, which results in you losing the suspension of disbelief needed for the Trolley question to be effective in the first place (it's pretty hard to take my position as "President" seriously when I've just escaped from an AI-controlled, robot terrorist organization after being drafted from a failing company), which results in the later questions not being answered in any meaningful way because the player's thinking and response becomes "Well, there's no way that could happen, or it just seems silly, so whatever". I remember one question being: "Would you rather put your brain in a dog or flamingo?" And I was like: ????"This is very much in keeping with the voiceover's continual scolding of the player, which makes the player's decisions seem meaningless because they have no benefit or good reason for either choice, as the voiceover goes on before and after each question about how irrational the player is being. If this is done for the purpose of introspection, it fails, as it leaves most players feeling frustrated rather than thinking, because the narrator only ever acknowledges the downsides in ways that are communicated on a superficial level (example: The first Trolley Problem does not question the fact that by pulling the lever you are actively killing someone and the consequences that may or may not be present in your head, rather the narrator simply states "Oh my God you killed someone (some people), try not to do that mkay?" without going into the details of this example before moving on to "What if that one was an infant").Due to the constant berating by the narrator for situations that become incredibly unbelievable in a matter of seconds, most players do not engage in any level of thinking that the game seemed to be trying to cultivate, rather most players just begin to express their frustration at what appears to be a 2 hour slide show of "you're wrong" that cost them $10.Overall, this game seems to be a *really good* concept. It just needs a decent amount of rewriting to make it work the way it should. As it stands, it is simply leaving a fair number of players frustrated and feeling like they have wasted their money. Thus, at the time of this writing, it has a mixed review score.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

A lot of the moral dilemmas were really thought provoking and even funny at times, the ending also posed a great question that left me wanting more. Looking forward to repeat playthroughs of this little indie title to see if there's anything else hidden away! :)

_childDocuments_.review: What a disappointment.The game is so linear, which is kinda expected, but it hints at non-linearity that isn't there.For example, if you kill the child that wants to be a doctor, their portrait would flash in a later question signalling that saving the child would've changed the question or something. But it doesn't.Then there are collectibles that look like they have some purpose. For example, one question asks who to give a heart to, but in a different question you get organs and it specifically shows a heart. So, if you return to the question, nothing happens.I pretends to be thought provoking while actually just constantly yelling at the player. It kinda tries to be the Stanley Parable, but the dialogue isn't nearly as witty. Then out of nowhere it asks an abortion question. NOW you want to ask real questions?This game never really was about the Trolley Problem. It was never really thought provoking. The game acts smarter than it actually is, and you can tell they think they've accomplished it.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting and expanded take on the original Trolley Problem dilemma. I have played through it only once, but it was a generally fun experience, seeing how the story evolves around my choices. _childDocuments_.review: I'm a fan of thought experiments (to the point that it has become an inside joke around my circle of friends). About a year ago, I played another game also based on the Trolley Problem, and found its scenarios to be funny and quirky, but in an otherwise shallow experience. , on the other hand, goes into the opposite direction for the most part, trying to put an ethical and moral weight on most of its questions. When it succeeds, it can even get gut wrenching or give you a strong feeling of regret.I'll get to the finer points of what I like and dislike of the game, but . That's as bare bones as I can put it, but I don't think of it as a negative. If you get mileage for thought experiments and creative narrative, you're bound to have a great time with this.Gameplay:- You choose option A or option B for most of the game. There are slight variations tied to the narrative, but that's about it.- You can think of it as Choose Your Own Adventure, since there are some scenarios that change, and there are collectibles. Odds are that you won't get them all on a single playthrough.- That's about it, really. The meat of this game is not on its gameplay, but on it's presentation... and oh boy.Presentation :- Be prepared. This game will scold you, . This can be upsetting to some people, and I admit it was to me up to a point. But at its core, the original Trolley Problem is based on making a very difficult choice. The narrator, rather than highlighting the good that you did, tries to hammer down the idea of the negative consequences of your actions. Personally, I believe it helped highlight the gravity of each decision, rather than taking a more sarcastic or "washing-hands-off" approach.- The game's UI tends to reflect the scenarios, and starts innocently enough. But as things grow more serious, it'll get more erratic and even unnerving to highlight the point it's trying to make. When it's at full speed, it can feel very, very tense.-  is at its best when the puzzles make you wish you had more time to think about the answers (on default settings), and for me, there were a lot. In some cases, I even wished I had selected the other one right before I was told the outcome. Basically, the more polarizing the response, the most intense the problem. And the scenarios presented by the game, for the most part, were elegantly woven into a longer-lasting narrative, rather than independent, isolated cases.- However, in my opinion, the game is at its worst when the results you obtain are independent of your choice, or feel ineffective, or the scenario is oddly convoluted. This happens more often at around the middle of the game. While there are some scenarios that play with some ideas and can be excused as experiments or fun variations, some just felt out of place or outright frustrating. For example, the bottom of the barrel was - Mentioning this out just as an opinion: The narrator will try to dissuade you from your choices, no matter which. And sometimes even bring in some extra context to the scenario. My opinion is that this is a test of resolve, to try to force your hand into choosing something else. Some others could think that not saying these upfront might skew their choices. - Also, the game compares your answers with the average response to each case. That's a great detail.Bottom line, I do recommend this game to anyone that wants an interesting narrative experience that digs into one's soul over trying to tell one specific story. It sort of does, but the original Trolley Problem is less about finding a solution and more about exploring what would  do and why. The game is less about itself and more about the one that's playing it. But that doesn't mean that you should just find the script and read them on your own. With its presentation and tense atmosphere,  helps experience these fascinating conundrums in a creative, immersive way that, when it does its magic, makes you feel the weight of your choices.

_childDocuments_.review: The game presents itself as bearing moral problems. The issue is that many of its problems aren't. It's not even the classic moral philosophy issue of "well what if you choose wrong because you don't know all of the facts" - the questions that are most blatantly wrong and judgmental are ones where we know the facts clearly and in some cases the developer also manages to choose an option that NEVER EXISTED.The two earliest examples come in the form of the Dead Dog and the Vaccine Mandate. In the Dead Dog, you are given two options : "Do you ignore the sick dog and leave it to die, miserable, cold, and alone" OR "Kill the dog yourself to spare any suffering." Yet oddly the Developer credits themselves as having chosen to save the dog. That's not how absolutes work. In this choice system, we know, absolutely, for 100% certain that both of these outcomes end in death for the dog. Otherwise it would be "You see a sickly looking dog on the track, you know no trains will come today, do you ignore it or kill it?" By expanding the information, you guarantee to the player that there is no outcome in which the dog lives or can be saved.In the Vaccine Mandate, you are told that the vaccine with leave 20% of the children MUCH sicker than the virus would ever make them. From this we immediately know that the virus doesn't kill or cripple most people infected with it, let alone half. You can't get MUCH sicker than dead or having loss of organ/limb.. But then we are antivaxxers and directly responsible for the children getting sick from a virus we know clearly isn't that serious.These aren't moral questions, and they fail to even be virtue signalling. These are bait and switches.

Also the people complaining about the time don't account for the fact that it's purpose is to make you pause and think??? It's really not that long, I promise. _childDocuments_.review: I really liked the idea of a trolley problem game that can be played with Twitch chat, but sadly I don't think this one does it well.It starts pretty decent but the story behind it quickly just turns weird and unenjoyable and everyone was just wanting it to be done by the time we got to chapter 3. There is 4 chapters with 55 questions in total and it just felt like it was never ending by the end of it.So what is all wrong with it:- as I already mentioned the story/commentary is basically trash. I don't have any problems with the fact that you get presented with 2 bad choices with not enough info, that is the whole point. But everything surrounding that is badly done.- You can't just skip all the nonsense around it. There is no way to skip text and you can't just chose either of the options in the problem, you gotta sit through the whole dialog and wait for the time to run out.- The Twitch integration doesn't count the votes correctly. When a vote starts it post the instructions to vote in chat telling you to do "!a" or "!b" to vote and that comment gets counted in the votes in-game. It also won't automatically pick the side that Twitch choose, you have to manually select it yourself before the time ends.- The 3rd save file in the game just wouldn't work for me? I straight up couldn't select it, no idea what is up with that. Other 2 worked no problem.- Sound settings don't work correctly. Even if you completely mute the audio some sound effect still play anyways. And at some point I managed to somehow bug it out in a way that all audio played even when it was fully muted.- A couple of achievements are buggy and don't unlock correctly as they should. They all unlocked in the end, but it took some time and fiddling with it.There is also a couple of good things:- the first few questions make you think a bit, before the game gets stupid- the Twitch integration was super easy to setupI wish someone made a better version of this.The ProtonDB reports for the game don't look good, but the game actually ran without any issues for me on Linux with Proton (8.0-3).

_childDocuments_.review: Played this game onstream with friends. Our goal was to make a game out of discussing our thoughts on each Trolley Problem, but at the end of it we all decided that if we were playing alone and didn't have co-commentators to make fun of the game with, we wouldn't be having any fun at all.Trolley Problem, Inc. very quickly goes off the rails and misses the entire point of a trolley problem: They're only interesting because they're purely hypothetical toybox philosophy questions. These questions lose their appeal almost instantly if you're giving too much context for who you're saving or harming on the tracks, and that's exactly what this game does.The game starts out fine with simple Trolley Problems, but it quickly attempts to string together a "campaign" of interconnected in-story philosophy questions. In a vaccuum these might work, but the instant you add the context of "You are working for an evil company. Do you do an evil thing, or a good thing?" the game becomes boring. Of course you're going to pick the good thing. You'll pick the good thing every time.The game tries to be funny and snarky by mocking you for your callous choices, but it also clearly has no idea what choices you've actually made. Early on there's a trolley problem where you're given the choice to run over an old dog and give it a quick death, or let it live out the end of its life. There's no indication the dog is suffering, so we let it live. The game then accused us of DOG MURDER about 5 times afterwards despite the fact that we chose not to kill the dog?The rest of the campaign are just vaguely philosophical questions that the developer found by searching "PHILOSOPHY QUESTIONS" on google and then awkwardly reshaped into Trolley problems. Here's the thing though: None of them were Trolley Problems originally, so they don't work as Trolley Problems. They're all dumb. The context of the "campaign" makes all of the decisions infinitely easier and makes your choices feel useless as your character always seems to pick the evil thing. If you pick the good thing, the game just continues on as if you picked the evil one. The dev didn't even bother including any branching paths.Also, it must be said that this game gives off big "Fake deep" vibes. We played this on a stream with around 200 viewers and that was the conclusion the chat came to before we even put in any input. Whoops!Also also, the game puts in SPOOKY JUMPSCARES OF THINGS YOU CHOSE TO KILL (or not kill in the case of the dog we allegedly murdered). This is so cheesy it reminded me of 2007-era Newgrounds flash games that children would make for halloween.If you want a better version of this game, go to Neal.fun and play "Absurd Trolley Problems" instead.I'm not usually a "this indie-produced steam game is too expensive" guy. I understand how much time and effort it takes to make something. Even so, charitably this game might be worth $3. Maybe $4. It is absolutely not worth $12.

_childDocuments_.review: Before you is a runaway train, barreling down a track towards a group of 6 million Jewish immigrants. There is a lever before you that, when pulled, will divert the train away from the group, but in doing so, will be sent on a course towards a young Austrian teen from a troubled home, who has dreams of becoming a famous painter one day. He has just sent in his application to the Vienna Academy of Fine Arts, and is eagerly awaiting their response. What do you do?Oh, you pulled the lever? What a shame. While I doubt such a prestigious academy would have let in a commoner like him so easly, that boy would have grown up to be a leading researcher in the cure for autism one day. Poor Heinrich, if only he'd left his Airpods at home that day. Hmm? What? What did you THINK he was going to do?There; it's just 90 minutes of that, rephrased in different ways. If you want a game where your choices actually matter, look elsewhere.

_childDocuments_.review: Trolley Problem is a game that I really would have liked to have enjoyed, but it ended up being quite lackluster. The game has you answering different ways to resolve various situations. This is the entire game all the way to the end, and that by itself isn't a bad thing. However, the scenarios given start to become more ridiculous as you progress throughout the game, and the options you are given are quite nonsensical sometimes. On top of this, the narrator will berate you, no matter the choice you choose. Even if the choice is objectively the right choice, they will berate you, while later on contradicting themselves by saying you should be more objective when you make a more subjective decision. I get the narrator is supposed to make you feel bad about any decision you make in this game, but it becomes very annoying over time. Another thing to mention is the sad attempt to include "jumpscares" and creepypasta-tier imagery within certain scenarios. It just feels forced, and it adds nothing to the game. This game truly is a shame, as the concept is interesting, and the developers seem to have put a good amount of work into this. I really wanted to enjoy this game, but it just has way too many flaws for me to recommend it to anyone.

_childDocuments_.review: Disclaimer: I'm a sucker for nontraditional games like this. Artsy games, feely games, thinky games. I also "got the product for free" cuz I can expense games at my job.This was a really challenging game, but not the kind of challenge most Gamers™ are probably used to, hence why the mixed reviews, I think. A common theme in the negative reviews seems to be that some folks went into Trolley Problem, Inc expecting a more "fun" or "videogamey" experience, but this is something that isn't trying to be that. Nowhere is the game advertising that "your choices matter/change the game"... that's just an assumption that's been drilled into us by a lot of OTHER games with choices in it! There aren't right and wrong answers to these long-standing philosophical/ethical questions! This is more akin to an exercise, not a "game" that you can win. This isn't like doing a Renegade run of Mass Effect, the point isn't to unlock endings or whatever. It actually wants you to confront your biases, challenge yourself, and find some personal enrichment from having done so. And that's a RARE, neat thing that we don't get out of videogames very often (perhaps because the demographic doesn't often find value/entertainment in that kind of challenge, so it's not in a developer's best interest to take that route. I mean, look at the Mixed Reviews, there's not much reward in making a game that is this divisive.) The game has little nods to this demographic dilemma by including some fake little "collectibles" that don't matter, and a couple more jokey ethical exercises to keep the mood from being *too* harrowing. These were a little tone-whiplashy for me, but it didn't detract from the experience too badly, since I was honestly a little thankful for the breather.It's an excellent educational tool and a very neat (though stressful) time for anyone even a bit interested in ethics and philosophy. Got me to feel uncomfortable, got me to reflect on a lot of things, got me to write down "Try to reschedule that one hangout that got canceled with X a month ago." And I'd be a jerk not to review it nicely for instilling those feelings and actions in me.
