_childDocuments_.review: The game really makes you want to embrace moral abolitionism—props to that.Jokes aside, it's still somewhat fun. But in a way that is in a reverse position of what the game sets itself to achieve. Please take it lightly and go meta yourself; troll the game that tries to troll you. It can be the game that Socratizes people who didn't think much about these issues, perhaps? Not to mention, it'd be a damn hard task. I see that some people are upset, and that also had been asked to the dev in a Reddit Q&A. In a game like this, some people will be upset, and I think the dev has no problem with it, deducing from the fact that he clearly adheres to his 'Stand with Ukraine' agenda, and that is fine. It's his damn work, thought, art, property. Call it what you want. But it also should mean how hard it would be to create a game that is not affected by its creator. This is the Trolley Problem's problem. And you can ignore it.First and foremost, the game will whip you regardless of the decisions you make. It will shame you, defame you, belittle you. That's where its satire lies. Is it damn good at doing so? I will argue not so much. That's not something bound to the narrator and her excellent performance, of course, but the script itself. Philosophical doctrines themselves needed to be gamified to create a sensual and amusing experience, right? That might be the case, but tying scenarios together back to back and reminding you of your past actions unfortunately do not work in these types of thought experiments. Furthermore, any piece of information (even how much you agree with the developer—seriously, why should I care about that?) has the possibility to mess up your mind even at the slightest chance. In a game that needs to be ultra-minimalist (and somewhat achieves it), it's unnecessary information. I have no clue about the values of the dev, and as far as I know, he does not debate them in-game. It's still interesting to see the player base's statistics, yet you couldn't potentially know how meaningful the data is. It will be obviously skewed data that will accord to the players who probably play these types of games and have some familiarity towards philosophical/psychological dilemmas.Then, you need to realize that these scenarios are just safe havens for discussions with little to no real outcome. Even if these were real-life scenarios, there would be a damn incredible amount of context being pumped into your thought flow within mere seconds. These are intuitive guides, not ultimate criteria, intuitive being underlined.Reductive, oversimplified statements do not work well with thought experiments. Some will come out and say 'there are no right or wrong choices.' No ♥♥♥♥. But there might be more damn favorable decisions, even if not definitive. Or else, how are you going to defend 80% of the player population vouching for one certain solution? That's moral intuition, and what do we have to stick to other than common sense? It does not work always; maybe it does not even work half the time, but we won't always have the facts either. These scenarios need to be damn well thought out and communicated clearly. The game has a 'Suffering problem' in which you need to put a dog out of his misery or let him die, cold and alone (see how morally persuasive it is in language). You know that the dog is located on tracks; however, you also know that there are no trolleys today, so it will not get hit. But you are also in a rush. So... apart from the secret ending (where you click on the cross and actually save the dog, kek), he dies either way. What the heck? The game presents you with the eternal 'let nature do its thing' debate. It's no longer fun nor satire. Do we even know how the dog ended up there? No. We are in a rush, but we don't know the weight of the situation if we take some time to take care of the dog (whether it be actually killing it or trying to run him to a vet). These are not some irrelevant questions. As far as the question goes, it's damn obvious he'll die, but we don't know if there is a vet nearby or are we even equipped enough to try to save him or kill him without making his pain worse. Well, how are we going to separate the location strictly from the proposal of the question? Imagine the dog being just around the corner of a vet and you are not equipped well to assess the situation (THIS IS AN IMPORTANT INFORMATION). If he is needed to put out of the misery why not let someone else handle it with far more knowledge about it (after clarifying for doing so and knowing that the situation cannot be reversed so poor dog's gonna die eventually). Then what if you are stuck with the dog you were sent for a space mission in a damn space shuttle. Once again we take it granted that you are not well equipped and trained to save the dog meanwhile how such situation occurred also do not ultimately matter. Then imagine it's a dog dying in the middle of nowhere in a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ forest with no vets nearby. Now, the problem is there would be no matter what you do in the forest situation (kill the dog and walk away, kill the dog and even bury it, or just walk away and hope that some predator would finish him off) you are eligible to walk away either way. You can repeat the scenario within your head, but you won't be in the scenario. But being stuck in a space shuttle while the dog cries out loud while dying would be something else, and I don't think nobody would ever argue it would have the exact same psychological effects behind your decision-making compared to the other two scenarios. There is not much room to walk away, and obviously you'll need to dispose of the body either way so why not make it quick and put him out of the misery? It would be a far more damn favorable option most would argue; otherwise, it would be a huge distraction to your mission and your mental well-being for a certain amount of time. Time and location as well as any additional information might have severe implications on such scenarios.Anyway, if you go deeper, you would possibly find much more flaws in my thought experiments, and that is solely because as the old saying goes: 90% of the thought experiments are total ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥.You cannot damn separate linguistics from the questions either. So, to me, the game ends up being a damn useless exercise. It's not like we are all a bunch of deontologists, and the game tries to prove that there are relativist approaches with consequentialist frameworks. Realist people will play this as well as possibly quasi-realists and anti-realists do too. It's inevitable to find yourself questioning what this moral proposition aims to convey? Is it a damn mere attitude that's dressed up in moral language or does it actually claim a moral property? Bunch of stuff going on there, and I am not even well-read in meta-ethics. Just for the starters, I will say that we have no external measurements to confirm the moral 'facts.' Don't get upset, folks.The game throws you the never-ending 'commie' joke where you do not opt in for selling subscription plans to people. Does not mean anything outside that it's an overused joke.ps: Less about philosophical ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and more about the game itself: I'd appreciate if scenario select just included the names. They become available after you select act/week which is a complete waste of time.It's also weird that the dev went his way to flash images to regard your old decisions as sorts of jumpscares as well as altering the narrator voice in accord to some scenarios and/or try to visualize the game in accord to aforementioned scenarios. They are just distracting you and you steer away from the question. This game is about the questions. The dilemmas they present. Nothing else. BE MINIMALIST. Most of the cases drag the game down. It is what it is. The game excels at its very first chapter and then... Nothing. Because they are not founded upon well nuanced thought problems just some actual research papers.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: Do not go into this game expecting a Socratic seminar, and certainly don't enter the game expecting for every question to be "fair". You're not exactly sitting in on, or God forbid with some of these reviews, participating in a debate. For a good bit of fun for about 2 hours, ten dollars isn't a bad price. And it is fun. There's this expectation in gaming for your choices to "matter", but there are some games which are overtly attempting to tell a specific story, and therefore, player choice and the impact thereof has to be limited. In a game all about choice, those choices having minimal impact on the story at large might seem somewhat odd, but really, this isn't exactly an RPG, and it doesn't really have much of a "story" in the first place. Some of the ways the game presents certain philosophies are a bit off, but those thought experiments were mostly never meant to be presented as having only two answers. Providing each question with a source is a good thing, but some of the sources were a little vague, I've never read Confucius' Analects, and it'd have been handy to know whereabouts I might find what the problem is based on.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the concept. The execution, well... Not so much.Trolley Problem, Inc. tries really hard to be funny and engaging, and for the first chapter, I may be okay with it. But trying too hard makes the comical standpoint really, really artificial and not so satisfying.I've never really felt challenged or provoked by its implications on the player. The overall feeling is that each line of dialogue is really predictable, even though it should "provoke" you.Overall, if done in one sitting it may be worth it, but for me the campaign wasn't really interesting.Artistically, though, it is really pleasing. I appreciate the effort, and I'm sure that ReadGraves can make something really interesting, it's just that Trolley Problem Inc. wasn't as I expected.

_childDocuments_.review: Do you want to be a leader?Do you want to make the hard decisions?Do you want to feel bad and guilty for every decision because there's a downside to every one?Then this is the game for you!!The game is about 90 minutes of questions which test your moral convictions.At full price it feels a bit expensive but on sale it's more reasonable for what is a mostly linear experience.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: What a weird game. I can really understand why it got mixed reviews. For starters, I will say that the complaints I've seen about jumpscares are ridiculous and overblown. I scare fairly easily in video games but the jumpscares here are literally nothing. People are overreacting.The philosophy of the game is heavy handed, and that's a bigger issue. This is no Disco Elysium, and unlike other heavy handed philosophy games (ie The Forgotten City) there's no interesting and redeeming gameplay mechanics or good character writing to make up for it. Its even more problematic that the choices eventually become quite bizarre to the point that its hard to take them seriously. It also would've been great if there was a better designed way to fast forward through the game.Overall I think this game has a lot of potential, and I enjoyed a good bit of my time, but I don't really recommend this as an experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This isn't a terrible game. Well, it's not really much of a "game," but it does provide what's shown on the tin. With that said, almost all the problems presented are done in such a heavy-handed way that it makes the game almost impossible to enjoy at times. It's obviously meant to be tongue-in-cheek, but you will be mocked for every decision you make, usually in relation to things you had no control over. In some cases, you'll make decisions to prevent things, and have to deal with the consequences of things that should never have been able to happen in the first place...which is still philosophically meaningful, but doesn't feel like an authentic experience.The game doesn't do a good job showing you it has a fast-forward mechanism in place. As short as the game is, I frequently wished there was a way to speed it up more, and didn't discover it until I'd already finished every problem, purely because it had an achievement tied to it.There's no reason to spend money on this game. There are websites where you can do collections of Trolley Problems for free that are far more fun than this. They don't have voice acting, but I'd say that makes the free websites better, not worse.

But then, the game had to make a joke about how my decisions in-game meant I was getting cancelled on Twitter, and the game told me that there were rumors of me being involved in a human trafficking ring with minors. That's taking it too far. Jokes like that had better be really funny to make them worth it, otherwise they come across as insensitive to people who have been victims of such things. Furthermore, those jokes should never be made in the style of "this loser is you".Despite picking the game up on a sale for $3, I have never felt more compelled to refund a Steam game. _childDocuments_.review: This is one of the few games that I knew going in had Mixed reviews and still bought it without a care.It's a fun game, rather short for $10.99 and rather limited solo replay value aside from a second playthrough for achievement hunting. However, this game does come with Multiplayer, so you can discuss the ethical ramifications of diverting a trolley to kill a child and THEN choose and a custom mode, which I haven't tinkered around with yet, but from what I understand allows you to mess with timers and the like.This is a game that is entirely on the back of social commentary and philosophy, which makes it a rather niche game because it discusses themes ranging from acceptable losses, profit over safety, the value of another's life over one's own, etc. and I think that this game is quite important as a touchstone. This is a game that you get to thinking about questions over and forces you into a time limit so you can't sit on it for a few minutes and decide. You have to go with your reaction, and then see if you want to stick to it. You might find yourself thinking about questions after the fact.I look at the decisions I made in this game and I'd be willing to defend every choice I made and I think that's the best statement I can make. This game will have you thinking about your choices and willing to defend them because it is an accurate measurement of your ethical ideology. This game is a fun way to explore Philosophy and I'm happy that I bought it.

_childDocuments_.review: Not worth it.Basically, it's a personality/trolley-problem quiz game except with a heavy-handed bias on certain questions and an attempt to sell on a narrator whom seems like she doesn't want to be there or read these questions. The problem with a ton of these questions too are how they are presented and the tone shift what tries to be a comedy turn into a really bland and edgy attempt at "spooky" from the classic indie tropes.I'll just ramble off the bad things:1. The bias is almost laughable - When one question about smuggling refugees comes out, picking to save them from an unknown fate has you applauded and the narrator telling you how brave you are. Get used to this black/white style commentary as the game will constantly tell you about how Black people and women are oppressed on the daily by facial recognition AI and other fair-weather Twitter talking points that only the most bland of people enjoy.  Oddly enough, what you will learn from the stat tracker is that Read Graves is kind of a sociopath, so that is pretty interesting, especially when you see answers like "MAN I HATE RACISM! - But, at the same time, I would sacrifice countless unknown people to make corporate profits."2. Tone shifts - What starts off as goofy once again has to go back into INDIE mode and proceed to have the same tropes that we all know and hate. VHS static and tracking, glitch graphics, and other non-shocking and utterly moronic visual affects to give off a sense of dread as your imaginary man must face his imaginary body count and instead of being a joke proceeds to ask you about morality and free will with all the depth of that one stoner friend you hated growing up with that constantly got fired from Arbys for being too lazy.3. There is nothing of value - These questions and problems have been asked from the start of mankind and you could have further reflection and a better time discussing these questions with a drinking buddy at a bar rather than pay $10.00 for a game that can't be comedy, horror, or insightful.4. Twitch bait - "HEY DID YOU KNOW ABOUT ALL THE STREAMING OPTIONS?" Get lost, nerd.As you can see by my playtime, I did a run in an hour and have no desire to ever play it again. I'll be asking for a refund - You would have better insight, growth, and reflection for a horoscope reading. That's how awful this game is.

_childDocuments_.review: I honestly wasn't into it, but others may find it enjoyable and I overall support the Yogscast and its subsidiaries.In terms of actual review, here are my points:1. Complete lack of nuance. I get that a game based on binary decisions is ultimately lacking in nuance, no matter what, but then the game guilt trips you.2. The game guilt trips you. I understand that is the entire point, to make you face the consequences of actions, but it just misses the mark on that front. Especially with the dead dog.3. The dead dog. Honestly, this part of the game upsets me the most. You are presented with the choice of either Letting a dog die OR Deliberately killing the dog to put it out of its misery. Either way, the dog dies, but then immediately after and for the rest of the game, you are made fun of for killing the dog and not saving it, WHEN THAT WASN'T EVEN AN OPTION! I resent anything and everything that claims I did something when I very clearly did not do it, and so every single damn time it was brought up, I simply got angry. Screw my conflictions with nuance, you are claiming something which is factually incorrect, and that I cannot abide by.4. The language of the matter. A lot of the language just doesn't match up with what is presented. Like with the dead dog, the game presents that you killed it, but that isn't true, because allowing something to die, no matter its relation to me, is simply not killing it. If a deer dies of old age in a forest thousands of miles from me, I did not kill it, and if I do not touch the lever, I do not kill those 5 people. However, the moment I intervene, I am implicated in the matter and therefore become the murderer the game sets out to portray you as time and time again.The game doesn't just ignore nuance, it ignores facts and definitions. I did not enjoy my time in the classical sense, but I will take inspiration from it, as I do with all things. If you are less stringent than I, you may actually enjoy yourself.

_childDocuments_.review: While I like the idea behind the game very much (forcing people to make unpleasant choices to reveal the content of their characters) the game itself employs a lot of cheap gimmicks and faux moral outrage. In that view it's quite reflective of the modern consumer-subject; there's a lot of grandstanding, emotion but ultimately, quite little content even less contemplation and understanding. They player seems to be pushed to act "correctly" which is the cardinal sin of any choice-based games. It was probably not the intention of the developers, but the game comes across as preachy. I get the feeling that the developers of the game did not really understand the papers referenced, given the predictable conclusion of the choices.Don't get me wrong, the basic idea for the game was good and there certainly was a lot of potential, but it was not properly executed. I, however, do welcome similar initiatives in the future, if more effort is put into understanding that not everyone shares liberal western values. I want games like these to succeed which means that I will ask more of them. If profound is the goal, pseudo-profound does not cut it.Here are my (hopefully constructive and helpful) suggestions for the future:1.  When writing moral choices to the game, be always sure to consider the situation from the "wrong" or "unethical" point-of-view as well. It is typical to our contemporary times to believe in a very black-and-white way that there is a side who is totally good and incapable of wrongdoing and a side that is thoroughly evil and incapable of doing good. In the real world, even the "wrong" choices can have intellectually honest and principled reasons for them. My choice not to act should be understood as a valid choice too. One does not have to agree to understand2. visual gimmicks and lazy attempts to provoke and shame the player will only annoy the players who are truly interested in philosophical issues like myself. Gamifying such a topic is not easy but can be done.3. I would actually welcome overtly political questions to the game, and an opportunity for the player to explain his choice. That way people could discuss their choices and most importantly of all, the reasons behind them. Approaching a hot-button issue in a roundabout way is usually not going to work.4. I find it ironic that people who say that they are no right and wrong choices usually mean "you're free to agree with me". That's the impression I got from the game, especially in the early dilemmas. Try avoid doing that.TLDR: Could the game work? Absolutely! Does it work now? No.

_childDocuments_.review: Have you ever found yourself in a situation where there does not seem to be a correct way to proceed?  Where no matter what you decide to do, something gets solved, but something else gets worse?Sure, we all have, and it is a terrible feeling, just knowing that you can't fix everything, but still have to decide.  Heck, you might even have a job where that is a regular occurrence.You could be an emergency room worker, deciding who gets seen first, or when it's too late for someone to be revived.Perhaps you're a military commander who has to decide if they should drop a bomb on the terrorist hideout, even though a busload of school children are visiting for career day.Maybe you're a security guard who catches a little old lady trying to steal a can of cat food so she doesn't starve.Or god forbid, you only have a mismatched pair of socks left, and it's winter. Do you have unstylish but warm feet, or look good and get frostbite?If you find it hard to make quick decisions that alter, or even end lives, then have I got a game for you.  Trolley Problem, Inc will present you with a series of decisions where you must choose one of two options, and either way people will die.There is no winning here, and whatever you do, you will end up feeling as bad as you do after you've voted on election day.  You did what you thought was best, but damn, if only there had been some other way.I reckon the point is to make you think about difficult things, and not to simply see how many bodies you can pile up, though it does keep track for you, and the numbers are impressive.  I quite liked the game, and while I can't say I know the answers, at least I have learned something along the way.Stay the hell away from train tracks. Trolley Otter can't find the lever, and is a .

_childDocuments_.review: Let me start off by saying, this is NOT a choices matter like in a "choose your own adventure" game.  Choices matter in a lose-lose kind of way, meant to make you kind of go back and forth with yourself, or if you stream it like I did, with your audience. So if looking for a choose your own adventure, this isn't it.  With that said, I thought this was a well done game with the Trolley Problem as its base.  I played a little bit by myself, it's fine.  But with other people (streamed or with friends) I found it to be much more engaging. People have thoughts about the narrator, but I think she serves her purpose.  She's not really there to help at all, not a guide or a moral compass.  Just talks at you about your choices, saying out loud sometimes the thoughts that creep in the back of your head as you make decisions.  And sometimes, I was actually stumped and myself and chat had differing thoughts on some matters.I thought this makes a great streaming game and we had fun talking out all the choices. I like the feature that lets you choose how much time you have to make decisions.  Gave me more control on how I wanted my stream to run while playing this.  Is $10 worth? Sure why not.  Is it good to get on sale? Sure why not. People sat down drew visuals made a BUNCH of different "trolleys," (even changed the look of the mouse depending on scenario, a nice detail) and brought in a voice actress to ACT and read for us.  I think this game is worth being bought.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is preachy, but it's also full of misinformation about many of the things it was preaching about, leading to moral admonitions at the end of levels that were not just contrarian, but factually incorrect.The writers of this game don't seem to understand (and don't care) what capitalism is - apparently not wanting to offer a particular service is communism, and doing literally anything immoral is how to make shareholders happy despite the company portrayed being a publicly owned company, and trying to sell its products to humans, presumably with morals. They also have no idea how AI works, even watching a handful of Computerphile videos on AI safety would give you a better understanding of the topic than the writers of this game seem to have.In some levels, it appeared that the consequences of your earlier decisions were relevant (I chose to put the dog out of its misery, as it would have otherwise died of illness cold and alone, and Tyrone's evil brother came looking for revenge)In the AI section, however, I chose not to offer improved protection for extra money (which is communism, apparently) and still had many follow up levels claiming I had decided the exact opposite. At the end of the AI section, I was forced to resign in disgrace, despite every one of my decisions being in the public interest and displeasing shareholders.Several of the "problems" are just someone assigning blame to you for no reason, or overly reductive. Some of the options are not mutually exclusive - for example, waiting to see if a software patch is effective, and then recalling a product if it isn't.Some of the options are just two bad choices, ignoring an obvious 3rd choice, such as choosing which department to fire, instead of just disbanding a department and moving the employees into a different chain of command, or simply not firing a department in the first place.I stopped playing after the game told me my desire to become a flamingo instead of a dachshund was "awful", the humour wasn't landing very well after I had spent the AI section being told I was a communist revolutionary for not wanting to commit corporate espionage or kill pedestrians.

_childDocuments_.review: Trolley Problem Inc. is a pretty good narrative philosophical conundrum game. It starts with the titular dilemma, a trolley is going to kill five people unless you switch the lever, but if you do it will kill one. You have 30-seconds to rationalise and choose which outcome is better, but like with most of the options there is no choice that ends entirely positively.The game poses several of these binary choices to you over about one and a half to two hours, that use a variety of scenarios, starting with trolleys, and going on to health care, business, technology, privacy, law and the armed forces along with a few other surprises. Trolley Problem Inc. also wraps the package up in a light narrative arc, with the player going from job to job. It's knowingly absurd as you go from health care worker to self-driving car mogul and beyond. It's briskly paced and it gives you something to think about even though sometimes it can lead to frustrations. Quite purposely, though, every situation you encounter is a bit unfair, and that's where the presentation comes in. The choices are made on a white screen with symbolic art (think of the symbols on restroom signs or the symbolic tutorials in Portal) while an English woman narrates the scenarios, and questions and taunts you for your choice as the timer ticks down along with a visual timeline track. Regardless of what option you pick, she can always find the downside, there are no win-win scenarios here. The game does subvert this a bit, but if you find that basic formula hard to stomach it probably isn't the game for you.The game also has a full bibliography of references to where you can read up more on the scenarios and the philosophy behind them.

_childDocuments_.review: Alot of the questions in this are false dichotomies. At one point we're given a scenerio where every choice we make is going to be made public by an employee at a company we are in charge of. At no point is "I stand by every action I've taken and I will no resign. the board will need to fire me to get me to leave" an option. I have no qualms with any desicion I've made except for the one where I was confused what it was asking. Along with the false dichotomies it often forces your hand or outright ignores what you did and makes you deal with consiquences that make more sense for the other choice. The abortion metaphors late game also sometimes remove the specific circumstances that make abortion special or aren't clear enough; I make my desicions based on the situation you give me, I dont make some comparison to other things or look at metaphors. Specifically the one with the guy I rented the house to, the narrator said I was trying to make some comparison when I wasn't. Reminds me of old newgrounds games, definitely fun if you can get it on sale but I wouldn't bother buying at full price.

_childDocuments_.review: I never write steam reviews, but I hate watching this game get slammed for length. I played it all the way through and genuinely I adored this game. The writing was absolutely fantastic, with some moral choices I was never and will never be prepared to make and just funny and thoughtful dialogue on the state of the world. But I think here's the bottom line and what others will not say about this game: If you want to refund it, do it. The game is built to be done under 2 hours and even the game says you can refund it. I see the devs responding to comments disparaging the game for existing in a way they don't particularly like, probably because their choices didn't necessarily have the best outcomes, and being seemingly ok with the refunds. The game is free technically speaking, but I urge you to not refund this game because we need to support these shorter, hand-crafted experiences rather than find reasons why you should refund them. This game was made with love and care, and is decidedly worth every cent, not just because we should support shorter games, but because the game is genuinely good. Give this game the love it deserves and buy and enjoy it.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: the game is good overall but your choices do not matter and the author suffers slightly from bias interfering with writing.Interesting, overall good but almost certainly not worth the asking price for the amount of content. I played the game twice, one answering honestly, once attempting to be as evil as I could possibly be, in doing so I have seen most of the major content available. Two playthroughs took 2 hours and covered almost everything the game had to offer. In the game's settings you have the option to increase the game speed and enable a speed up button, I recommend you turn them on and use them to your personal taste, I found some of the waiting pointlessly long.At first glance the game seems like a straight forward philosophy questionnaire, then veers in the direction of making it seem as if your choices in one question will impact other questions. There seems like there might be some minor changes, such as the flashing of a spoooooky picture for a second on a few prompts, and some minor dialogue changes, but it is not as significant as the game might lead you to believe. The most egregious form of the lack of decision impact is in the self driving cars section, in which regardless of your choice, a single outcome always happens in a later question and the game treats it as if it was your decision that this outcome happened when you react to it. Minor forms of the lack of decision can be seen in transferring a trait between people who die, the vaccine guy will always die for example.Looking at other reviews, people seem to have taken issue with two major things about the game, its treatment of the player's decisions and the game's thinly veiled bias towards certain outcomes. The first point I think is unfair, the second is certainly fair but perhaps overstated. These two issues are also hand in hand to a certain extent.The game is clear that the narrator is hostile, they generally attempt to play devils advocate and flip the player to the other result if possible. Usually this is done by giving common arguments against your position, playfully insulting the player, inventing a strawman argument for the player or insinuating that the player is choosing this for reasons that are not as good as they may like to pretend. People who feel very strongly about a certain result may get offended by facing push back, I expect a decent number of negative reviews come from this knee jerk reaction alone. Seeing both results, you will see that in almost every case the game is equally critical of each result, such as calling you a filthy capitalist or communist depending how you react, but there are notable exceptions to the balanced insulting.The most notable exception and clearest display of bias is the way the game reacts to assisting illegal immigration during a war. The game will unambiguously say you did the right thing if you assist them, offering absolutely no snide comment to temper it, while if you do not it will be sure to let you know you are a hypocrite. This is abnormal in the writing of this game, if this issue was a sacred cow for the author, to the point that they could not even make a softball counterargument along the lines of "why should they get to be the exception" or something similar, the author should not have included it. The author clearly also has strong feelings about racial biases in AI visual training, but those do not impact your choices as directly, and are instead simply preached at you as an aside. Repeatedly. Despite the very clear liberal leanings of the author, the abortion adjacent hypotheticals at the end of the game are handled in a more even handed way. You can only barely tell that the author wants you to choose one over the other. The game is only two hours long at best, an hour if you are quick. It will be a matter of personal tolerance and taste if having twoish notable moments of bias flare up in what should be a non biased universal attack on your beliefs is too much for a game of this length.There are also a few moments, such as the heart transplant with the old and young man, where the narrator will introduce information at the last minute in a quip as response to your current decision. This information can certainly make the difference in the moral calculus the player is doing, and might be seen as unfair as you should have had all the information to start. The ending was a bit edgy, but also fun. I was surprised by how many people took the situation at face value and were willing to sacrifice themselves for the world. I thought it was fairly clear given the not at all subtle foreshadowing that the implication was that you were making a deal with the devil or being were deceived by them, but seeing the difference in interpretation of people is part of the fun. I really like that the game shows you how many people agree or disagree, it really elevates the experience.I imagine this game is much more fun for streams, but I am not a streamer so I cannot comment.I would have preferred if the game included links to the sources, rather than just telling you the sources, it would have been much easier for the player, but I imagine that would be difficult to get the rights to so I cannot complain.6.3/10, probably should have been 5$. I don't regret buying it, but I think most people would be better off watching someone else play it. Pretty neat for a playable philosophy paper.

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr - Not fun, doesn't make you think, doesn't actually explore the concepts beyond surface level, attempt at dark humor actually just irritating to listen to.Almost exactly what it says on the tin- if you know of the trolley problem and all of its variations, this is just listing through those variations one after the other with a little window dressing and 4th-wall breaking snide narration on top.The 'game' plays out by giving a version of the trolley problem - starting with pull the lever to kill 1 person or ignore it to let 5 people die, then many more increasingly complex variations - then gives ~30s or so for you to make that decision while the narrator derides your decision.Next, the game shows you a running tally of how many people you've 'killed', sarcastically derides your ability to make decisions again, and you move onto setting up the next trolley problem.The narrator constantly cheekily derides the player's decisions. This is meant to be funny (I guess to keep your interest) but it undermines the purpose of the thought experiments. Almost always, the narration did nothing to challenge what I was actually thinking about and just kind of undermined my desire to play and continue to listen to it.The problem with this format is that while it seems 'fair' to allowing people their own interpretations, it doesn't really engage with the problem meaningfully. The constant snide derisions from the narrator are not carefully placed to make the player question their decisions, make the player question their own consistency, or seek more nuanced exploration of why one decision might be more or less morally permissible or morally necessary.What we are left with is a 'game' that isn't fun as a game, doesn't do anything to meaningfully add nuance or understanding (at least ~15-20 problems into the game it hasn't) to the thought experiments, and doesn't actually challenge or inform the player to try to get them to actually question their ideas.

_childDocuments_.review: Had a lot of fun with this one on my Twitch stream. The Twitch integration works really well and gets chat involved. The questions are sometimes really tough decisions. You're not supposed to be finding the best solution to the problem presented, you're supposed to be discussing and analyzing the two decisions you are presented with and choose which one you might like better. It's also something you can get through in a couple hours (it took me 4 hours to get through the whole thing on stream with the timer speed set to 0.25x so you can probably get through it in an hour or 2 at full speed). This leaves room for multiple playthroughs if you want to try different mindsets and reasonings (also achievement hunting). I had fun. You might as well.

_childDocuments_.review: It's probably exactly what you would expect if you understand the title of the game. What you get in about 1.5 hours is a series of moral dilemmas answerable in the form of A or B choices, that are all connected by an absurd and amusing narrative. Everything is voice acted and narrated very well, and every dilemma has unique visuals that all help to prevent the experience from becoming monotonous until the end. Each choice is compared with the the community to see how many agree with you, and often the narrator will gaslight you, which is amusing and gives you the impression that you've picked against the games wishes, which ultimately ties into the point of the game which ultimately is . It's hard to recommend the game at full price as it feels steep for the length of the experience, but the voice acting and clever presentation do warrant value to the experience.

_childDocuments_.review: These questions, even if presented in a practical format like here, are not actually questions about whether you would kill 1 person or let 5 people die. That's not the point of the questions and you don't have to worry about that, not really. These questions are to provoke discussion, not to make you seem like a bad person. The questions are do you value quantity of life? Do you think you have a duty to do something, even if that duty might cause something bad to happen? Does quality of life compare equally to quantity of life? This game is about making you think about why you make the choices you do. Lots of the things you do are arbitrary or hypocritical when you dig deep. That's okay. It happens quite often, called Cognitive Dissonance. This is a game about the Socratic Method, about asking questions until you realize you don't really have a perfect answer, or even a good answer. And even then, you don't have to change yourself or what you do. It doesn't mean you're wrong for doing the things you do. It's a game for introspection, which is often very uncomfortable.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is by no means perfect, but it is fun. I probably wouldn't pay full price, but I did find it worth it on sale.Most of the negative reviews seem to take issue with the narrator berating you for your choices or attempting to put the blame of impossible situations on you. That is the entire point. You aren't supposed to take the narrators words at face value or even agree with her. The point is that many of the questions are only wrong answers. Personally I took part of the games message to be that our choices are often constrained to be only bad options, and it is up to us how much we choose to blame someone who has had to make a choice like that.

_childDocuments_.review: I hate to say it, but this game is kind of lack luster. I loved the ideas presented in this game, and I think there are a lot of great things about this game. I thought the writing was pretty good and the voice acting was not bad at all. It was also very nice that they give a speed option (otherwise it would be painfully slow).That being said, a lot felt lacking. Most of the scenarios (at least early in the game) did not feel like I had to think much on it. Maybe that is just me. A lot of it came down to do something very illegal and morally wrong or save more lives. And at then end of the day I was thinking my life matters too here. The writing made me feel like I ALWAYS choose wrong which really wasn't very fun in the grand scheme of things. I know the game wants me to always question my decisions but it always felt like I was being shamed for my decision. Which didn't make me want to keep playing.So I would sum this up to that this game isn't for me who feels quite firm in their morals and maybe put myself too much into these situations where I still bear the consequences of my actions regardless of what happens. Like who would actually push someone onto a trolley track to save 5 peoples lives?! I could never physically push someone to get hit by a trolley. And then I get shamed for my actions. I love the idea for this game I just think some of it was poorly executed while other parts were amazingly executed.

_childDocuments_.review: I returned the game after only around 10 decisions. It is unfortunate to see a cynical spin on what truly is a philosophically engaging problem: The Trolley Problem. I have no complaint with the price, 10$ to see where I stand morally compared to other gamers, casual, professional, and so on is a fair price for me. The part that was disappointing was the growing amount of variables (namely unpredictable variables) that taint the philosophical part, and turn the game more into a sorts of Impossible Quiz intuitive guessing type game. It is cut and dry to understand that (a) or (b) will have their own unique consequences. Whether or not you caused them, whether or not your inaction was an action of its own, and whether or not you are responsible for said inaction or action, regardless if you deliberately choose for less destruction. It is, however, not cut and dry to be put in a situation where you have to guess about the effectiveness of a vaccine in its future. It is unfair because you are not a professional in that field, because you do not understand know the severity of the illness, nor how it may or may not mutate BECAUSE you have no access to that information WHICH even if you did only plays to the strength of professionals in that field. Choose the vaccine which kills MORE than the virus it cures, or "do nothing." But nothing is worse because oh look you knew nothing about the virus, actually it was AIDS but airborne, oh ♥♥♥♥ everyone is compromised and dying GG WP. _childDocuments_.review: "Trolley Problem Inc." is a brilliant and innovative game that masterfully blends dark humor with deeply philosophical dilemmas. This game stands out not only for its engaging and well-crafted narrative but also for how it challenges players to think critically about their choices.The game's core mechanic revolves around the famous Trolley Problem, but it takes the concept much further, presenting a series of moral quandaries that are both thought-provoking and surprisingly entertaining. The story is incredibly fun, laced with wit, and often delivers unexpected twists that keep you fully engaged from start to finish.One of the standout features of "Trolley Problem Inc." is the timed decision-making. The timer is perfectly balanced, providing just enough pressure to evoke a sense of urgency, but not so much that it overwhelms you. It allows you to think through your decisions carefully while still maintaining the tension that makes the gameplay so immersive.The gameplay itself is smooth and intuitive, making it easy for anyone to jump in and start making tough decisions. However, don't be fooled by the simplicity—each choice you make carries significant weight, and the consequences are always intriguing. Whether you're playing alone or with friends, the discussions that arise from your decisions are half the fun, sparking debates that linger long after the game is over.In summary, "Trolley Problem Inc." is a must-play for anyone who enjoys games that make you think. It’s a perfect blend of humor, philosophy, and interactive storytelling, with a well-paced timer that keeps the experience engaging without being stressful. If you're looking for a game that will challenge your moral compass and provide hours of thoughtful entertainment, look no further. This game is an absolute gem!RATING: ★★★★★ (5/5)

I expected this so I wasn't too disappointed, but the writing itself was incredibly annoying.I genuinely do not like how certain choices in moral dilemmas are somehow linked to political beliefs.The game is also very clear about what beliefs the developers hold. It will berate you no matter what option you pick, but certain snark will feel a lot more genuine than the opposite choice. I'm by no means a religious capitalist, but whenever I entered the realm of supporting the idea, the game pulled no punches. When I entered the realm of socialism however, the snark was more akin to "Oh how *dare you* pay taxes", further berating more capitalist choices.Writers, Artists, Devs, etc. can insert their political beliefs into their works all they want, but it feels incredibly wrong when they are attached to moral dilemmas like the Trolley Problem, where there inherently is no objectively correct or wrong answer. The most fun I've had with the game was trying to cut off the narrator laying out the premise.I was also amused by the fact that the book "The Myth of Ownership" was recomended to me by a game I purchased with money. (and then refunded)Aside from this issue the game will assure you that they are no horror elements, depictions of violence or sex in it, but it will contradict itself and insert horror elements anyway. _childDocuments_.review: As someone who enjoyed Philosophy at University so much that I decided to do a masters in it just for fun as well as being the president of the Philosophy society at the university, I was incredibly excited about this game perhaps in the hopes that it would show the rest of the gaming community the fun that philosophy could hold.Unfortunately, it could not live up to those lofty expectations, the game quickly devolves from providing genuinely interesting (though simplistic) moral questions, with witty and comical replies from the game (which reminds me somewhat of the Stanley Parable, which is still one of my all time favourite games) into choices which offer little in the way of philosophical interest and instead are centred around somewhat entertaining yet entirely unconnected subplots.If this were not advertised as something philosophical I may have had lower expectations. As an interactive movie, perhaps something to watch for the first time with a couple of friends, it is a decent little game which gives an hour and a half good entertainment. However, as a game in and of itself (and one that aims to be philosophically interesting at that) it falls short of the mark that the price tag suggests. £8 for an hour long interactive movie, simply isn't a good value proposition to me but if it were on sale, perhaps 50% it would be far more palatable. Furthermore, it seems (as far as I can tell) that your choices do not change the future questions as I received numerous quips from the narrator that did not apply to the choices I had previously made.

_childDocuments_.review: I thought this was going to be a fun philosophical exercise and got the game to play along with a few friends.  After the first hour we were only playing to make fun of ReadGraves.  You learn pretty quickly that whoever was in charge of writing these questions left out a lot of vital information or just had no idea how things work in general.  My group was constantly laughing and asking things like 'Why would a vaccine even be mass produced if it had such a poor success rate?' or 'Didn't we just get put in a government prison, how are we fighting terrorists now?'  The 'story' goes off the rails so badly and so quickly that it's hard to follow along with, and often blames you for mistakes you didn't make. 'Why are we having to take the blame for the subscription service when we decided against it last question?'  Seriously the only thing that kept us going was the fact that after each question you get to see if your choice aligned with the developer (ReadGraves) or not.  His choices seem to follow no consistent moral compass of any kind, so we started taking bets on what he decided during the discussion time for each question.2/10 Only get it if it's on sale and you have 2-3 hours to kill.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: Questions were hard to understand, choices were meaningless, attempts at humour come accross as heartless while attempts at calling out any kind of actual injustice seemed mocking, almost any decision you make is treated as wrong with the narrator constantly berating you, and finally you'd find just as much joy from reading the wikipedia page for famous thought experiments with a stopwatch.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: It did not take me long to figure out that this game was nothing but a long list of false dichotomies and poor framing choices, as well as being rife with bias. Not to mention the whole "AI takeover" thing really detracts from what was already an increasingly terrible experience. Do yourself a favor and go buy a grand slam from Ihop with the money you would have used to buy this game. It'll be cheaper and more enjoyable than whatever the hell this was supposed to be.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't write reviews. When I do, they're rarely negative. But I have to write something about this.I hated it.It started off fine, with the normal questions you'd expect. Then it veers off into a wildly unexpectedly unadvertised tangeant throughout the rest of the game. There's also some weird paranormal effects throughout that I think you should do a better job about warning people. None of that is nearly as irritating as the narrator. Every single choice in the game is arbitrarily wrong, as far as I can tell, and she takes every opportunity to needle you about it. I was under the impression that this was a moral choice simulator, not a Portal2 style kick-him-when-he's-down narration every time a choice was made. Wildly frustrating narration, completely out-of-place social issues that - while important - were shoehorned in with no thought for whether or not it would actually improve the story, and general lack of honesty in the game description leads me to actually leave a stupid review. It had a lot of promise and it fell flat on its face. I don't even recommend it on sale.

_childDocuments_.review: While it is a good concept for a game, I don't like how it shoves politically aligned narratives into these problems without explaining the other side of them. _childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: I shouldn't have purchased it. I played it for 9 minutes too many. Fake moral dilemmas, pseudo-philosophy, false dichotomy. _childDocuments_.review: Samuel Read-Graves, I absolutely LOVE this game!! You clearly put a lot of effort together to make each choice not only interesting, by context of the situation, but also trying to convince me to change my mind. _childDocuments_.review: It's alright. Overall is good, but a lot of tiny annoyances. Steam really needs a 'neutral' option for game reviews. Not much gameplay to speak of, its just answering binary questions, so I'll just shotgun the rest of my thoughts in a single paragraph. Also your answers, save for a single one, doesn't matter and doesn't affect anything. I don't mind that aspect, but definitely something you should know going in. The game heavily leans into humor, which is does well for the most part. It's not as clever as it thinks it is when it tries to be deep. Can be a bit tedious when you know your answer right off the bat then have to sit there waiting for the timer to run out, even with the hidden fast forward option (It's A, by the way). There are at least three different abortion allegory questions, which I just find to be really weird. Once achievement requires you having a Twitch account, stream and integrate your game, then have someone vote on your stream. This is very stupid and a huge annoyance for achievement hunters and completionists. Also one achievement is buggy and not awarding it to me. I really loved the final stretch of questions, though.

_childDocuments_.review: This was a great little experience to have with my girlfriend where we could both discuss something tricky but also silly fun together. People should remember that this is a game. It's meant to be fun and there is no 'correct' answer. It's like a personality test, which aren't ever actually worth taking to heart anyway as concrete definitions of you in the first place. While completionists who do not stream will be miffed by the Twitch integration achievement, I think for the discounted price I got this game at (during a sale), my chaotic decisions to kill 5.6M people (and 1 dog) and own it even during divine trial were well worth the 2 hours of amusement. Get this game, get some friends together, and have fun!

This goes so quickly from 0-100, and had my nervous every time I made a choice, I would feel so strongly about a decision until something would happen. _childDocuments_.review: It's one of the smaller games designed to question your own morality. Later on it seems to get into metaphysics but the early conundrums are very interesting. The story is Telltale like, in a way that most of the choices are arbitrary, the story plays out the same and you are there as more of an observer (ironically).It's a pretty good game to get to know yourself a bit better. I mean the trolley problem itself as a concept is interesting - if you do not intervene and let the trolley run over 5 people, are you really responsible? Are bystanders responsible for deaths that happen in front of them? Good way to test your morality and see if your SO is a sociopath lol.Some of the issues are worded... well, in a "gotcha" manner (e.g. the dog one, you'll get what I mean if you play the game). Probably not worth the full price IMO but worth the time.

_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: Interesting game of "this or that" where every choice honestly sucks.I guess my one complaint is there are a number of scenarios where there is clearly a third choice but the game doesn't offer you that choice.My only other complaints are logistical. Takes too long to finish the choice if you make it early, and there are a couple where you really aren't given enough time.I know some have complained about the negative commentary about every choice you make, but to me it's all in good fun. I couldn't help laughing at most of those criticisms.There is a lot of social commentary here, and depending on where you fall on that line you might not enjoy the message the game is sending. _childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: Instead of making the questions feel as though each one matters or has a deeper meaning behind the choices, it just feels like someone asking you a question and then leaving it at that. Some questions also seem very lopsided, as if there is a right and wrong answer. Some seem to have a bias. Eventually many feel pointless. No introspection, no contemplation for the consequences of your choices, no thought provoking argument for the other choice, and in my opinion, no reason to buy. Just empty questions and an annoyingly antagonistic narrator as a pitiful attempt to get you to second guess yourself. Poor execution on an otherwise brilliant prospect with great potential.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: It was funny and very interesting, but incredibly short. You're limited with binary decisions to problems that can be solved by making a different choice, so that was very frustrating to be forced to decide on something when I knew a better option. A couple of the decisions I just didn't understand. The game also connects all the problems together, but in a very loose way. Sometimes this is funny or appropriate, but other times I felt I made a certain decision and the game ignored it and assumed I picked something different. The ending wasn't exciting and also the acceleration feature doesn't pop up when you're replaying specific problems and it doesn't pop up very quickly when you try replaying the whole game. Good for a laugh, psychology research, and some introspection, but just a little disappointing for an $11 game instead of a more appropriate, $1 or $2 game.

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed my time spent playing this game. It’s fun to play with others and gives an insight into how your thought process may differ from your friends’. It is streamer friendly, and though I’ve not tested it out myself, it appears to be twitch chat incorporative and allows them to also participate in making choices throughout the game. To complete a run of the game, it took my friends and I about two hours. There’s a collectibles feature that rewards you with certain items according to the answers you chose. I’ve only managed to gain three items so far. I don’t think I’ll be using the “Vegan Cook Book” anytime soon, however.With that in mind, there is a factor of replayability. Though, it may be more entertaining to do your replays with others.I also believe there is an implementation of the butterfly effect where your choice in a previous question may have a result on the dialogue used by the narrator or possibly even the questions you are asked. It does an outstanding job picking at your brain and morality with increasingly torturous and boggling dilemmas. The first question that you start from is the classic trolley problem and then continues onto questions that the developers seem to have conjured in relation to a famous or historic quandary. Every question has its relevant reference pop-up in the bottom left with the option to “mark” it in order to see further into it later if you wanted.Of course, the game is not all serious. The developers have done an excellent job including humorous aspects. Whether it be little jabs made toward the player by the narrator or one of the increasingly bonkers questions, I, along with my mates, had a great laugh at the absurdity of it all. Not to spoil anything, but the final chapter is a riot with how ludicrous the questions, along with the game functions, become.Overall, the game is well polished and I would recommend it to those with patience and a craving for surveys. It may be tortuous, though, to some people. It’s not a game for everybody; especially not for [REDACTED] who recently got a job as a [REDACTED] at [REDACTED].
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: Great game! The main thing that stood out to me is its marvelous sound design. If, like me, you love games with narrators (such as Bastion and The Stanley Parable) then this game is for you.There is also, very noticeably, great care put into the problem selection, with references for every problem. I'll definitely read some of them when I have the time :)
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: I tried killing as many people as possible.This game is great for both people who know philosophy and those who have only just started to look into it.The sound design and graphics (especially how your cursor changes depending on the situation) are very nice choices to add in. Subtle, but necessary. It's very immersive. The dog question really got to me though, since the game keeps pestering you about it (yes, it's done for a reason, but it still sucks). I wouldn't say this game is worth the price-tag, in my eyes it would have been 5 to 8 USD, but for an independent developer I understand why it's this much money.Would I play the game again? Yes, only to achievement hunt, though. The pacing (especially if playing with friends) is very slow and feels repetitive, so I found myself getting bored about a half hour in.(edit: Forgot to add that I appreciate a lot of the accessibility options put into the game- especially the ability to use the Dyslexic-Friendly font. It helped me understand the questions a lot better.)
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: It's not a big no, but I can't recommend it to people in my position. The game is not bad but it has SERIOUS performance issues. My laptop is not that good but it runs GTA V, DOOM 2016 or dark souls 3 with no problem in low/medium preset and this game isn't playable AT ALL. Too bad for a power point. Tested on Windows and Linux, on linux it's not even remotely playable and on windows I couldn't play for more than 40 min with like 15 fps.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: Incredibly underrated. It seems a lot of the negative reviewers are mad that you're constantly forced between two evils, and the narrator chides you no matter what you do - but that's the entire point! You have to deal with the consequences of your actions. You have to feel that guilt. This isn't a game you win.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: I liked the narrator, especially when you skipped her narrating.Now regarding choices, I did enjoyed most of them. However for a lot of the choices I couldn't make an "informed choice", because I didn't know all the details, but as in life you never do, so it was not a major gripe.What I did disliked is lack of Ultra-wide support in 2022, no resolution option and UI funkiness with my setup. I ended up fixing it with a 3rd party program which forces a windowed game to full-screen, because when I wasn't in windowed move, I couldn't click the right 1/6 of the screen.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: I can see how the narrator's snark could be annoying to some, but I quite liked it for the most part. There were a few choices where I couldn't shake the feeling that "option C" was the obvious right answer, and that was always a bit frustrating. But ultimately, the writing was good enough for me to recommend it anyway.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: I really liked it. Some people seem to not have liked the extra details and caveats they added in but personally I really enjoyed them. The extra caveats made me realise some of my own biases and it was interesting how changing a question in small ways made me feel very different about it even though from a moral perspective I still agreed with the same ansver. It's also a really funny game, which is always a plus.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: Best game I've found yet for masochists!I really liked it, though the fact that opting not to use the subscription service doesn't actually change the fact that in the story of the game, the service seems to end up getting used anyway. I did like the links to all of the studies that allows you to learn more on these topics!
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: There are no winners with this game. No matter what option you choose someone dies, is hurt, or disadvantaged. Its often the good of the many vs the good of the few or one scenario. Even when you think you have the best answer you get to feel bad about it. This game isn't for everyone, if you suffer from PTSD or depression I reckon I would stay away.You can see my first play at  - I deliberately only cover the first bit because spoilers :).
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: It was a great experience. I found this game accidentally and bought it without putting much thought into it. It's a simple and cheap game that won't consume a lot of time to complete. I would advise playing it with various friends to see the differences between you and yours thinking process.As to some negative opinions about this game. At this time, I can easily say that it's impossible to be surprised negatively by anything this game has to offer. You would have to be unable to read to feel tricked by the description.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: Neat little narrative philosophy game, that makes you think about impossible choices. Getting steadily more absurd as it progresses, it still deals with really interesting philosophical questions and provides sources so you can research further. It won't be for everyone, but if you've ever wondered how you'd deal with an impossible choice it's worth a go.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: Genuinely an interesting game that takes complex moral decisions many of us have heard of and strings it all together with a narrative that is comedic yet serious at the same time. The timing for each scenario leaves you not much time to decide which I feel adds weight to every choice you make and the way the game makes you question yourself as you play is very intriguing.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: So i don't wanna go into too much about the actual game as its more of an experience than a game but i will say that this game offers some interesting moral perspective and can spark some reflection on life that you may otherwise not think of. The game takes about 2 hours to finish but will leave you thinking for some time afterwards. If you enjoyed things like the stanley parable then this is probably something else you will enjoy.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: Very easy to tell if you'll have any fun with this one. It's a thoughtful philosophy survey. If you want an option to burn an hour and a half answering hypothetical binary questions for ten buck then just pick this up and have a go. It's all familiar concepts to me by now but I like the idea of having a consolidated list of my decisions on these things.The narrator gets a little offended if you interrupt the talking to get to the questions and that was fun, you'll read ahead of her anyway and just want to get to making decisions.I dunno, it is exactly what it looks like. A couple questions left me wanting to have more information and a couple were useless nonsense.   8/10   Delivered without blowing any minds. Going to recommend to anyone who asks. It's my jam.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: The game might be considered a little pricey for what you're getting, a 1-2 hour experience with questionable replayability. But I think the overall experience is a fair justification for the priceThe game is basically all about philosophical ethical dilemmas, so can glance against pretty tough subjects, but the game derides pretty much all of your choices, so it's not so much about passing judgement as it is letting you explore them. The game cites references for each problem presented, though there's no easy way to link to them (which is fair, as many of the references are books, or in one case, unsurprisingly, The Matrix).The game's done nothing to remove my distaste for the Trolley Problem model as a method for resolving ethical dilemmas, which I think is the point of the game, as it does demonstrate the pitfalls of only offering a binary solution to a problem, though maybe there are some actual philosophers that disagrees, who knows.In any case, this feels less like a traditional game and more a piece of interactive social art.Also appreciate a lot of the visual design in the game, which feels very "TfL design but not quite" and gets slowly more unhinged as the game progresses.Voice acting in the game consists of a single narrator, who you might find hit or miss, but I think was a good choice and does a good choice of switching between detached narration and increasingly deranged egging on.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: I recommend with a caveat. There is a lot of judgment coming from the game itself to make you feel faux anxiety for the questions. That was a little aggressive as the internal moralization of choices is far more exquisite than someone else who has no stakes in my life judging me for choices that honestly never matter anyway. Fate was my default choice and I will not go back to choose the other options simply because of the moralization the game attempts to convey.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: I feel like this game was designed to snark at people who would pull the lever, because as someone who would not pull the lever the next ten or so trolley variations were like... "literally nothing has changed for me"? Also the whole segment about self-driving cars is hard to make decisions within that framework if you already know why they're a terrible idea in the first place, which I guess it's good at showing. I don't regret playing, very easy to play game, only wish the reading list came with internet links. What even is a library?
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: I do think it's quite short for the price. The way I see it it's about the price of a pizza and I got about the same amount of enjoyment out of it. But I can absolutely see why some people don't think it's worth it.It starts out pretty basic, but gets more interesting towards the end. So basically don't judge it too early. I've only played it once (which took about 1.5h) but there seems to be a few branches so I'll probably try to 100% it at some point in the future, just to see what can happen.Arguing against the premise of the game or the questions is missing the point, by the way, so if you do that you're probably not going to enjoy it as much. I love that there's a reading list. Make sure you tag the interesting questions (click the little star in the citations) to know which papers and articles you want to go read. If you don't want to that's fine as well, but I think you'll get more out of the game if you're the kind of person who'd want to read at least a few of these articles.I have to mention that there are a few places where they could have done a little more QA, and there are also a few design choices that I disagree with. None of this distracts too much but it's a little bit annoying. Overall it's an OK game, and I'd recommend it if you have some money to spend and/or are interested in philosophy.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: I didn't expect this game can became demonic.Well.., it's kinda repetitive. BUT, every segment feels like have some weird unique idea that the game want us to feel.If you like to "interact" with the game with fourth wall breaking kinda thing, this is a decent game.Now i need to report back to beelzebub.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review: A fun, short game about philosophy and moral dilemma. I was looking forward to playing this since it was announced by Jim Johnson at the Yogscast Games Direct. I recommend this for streaming to get more interactions with your viewers, although I enjoyed playing this solo.The narrator was slightly overbearing at times, but I understand that they are there to play devil's advocate and instigate some internal discussion about something you may not have thought of.If you're after repeatability, you could get away with a few play throughs to get all the options and aim for the Collectors and 100% Achievements, however beyond that there isn't much. (Fingers crossed for some additional questions down the line!)*Update* As you can see I have managed to get at least 10 hours of gameplay, even playing the game more than once was somewhat enjoyable.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

_childDocuments_.review:
There is a runaway trolley careering down the railway tracks. On the tracks are five people unable to move. You are next to a lever. If you pull this lever the trolley will switch to a different set of tracks. However, you notice that there is a person on the other track.

Watch the situation play out and five people die. Choose to pull the lever and only one person gets killed - but by you.

What will you do?

Trolley Problem, Inc. is a darkly comedic narrative game based on real world philosophical papers, in which you are asked to make a series of impossible choices from two awful answers. Wrestle with your moral compass, decide the fate of millions - and compare your choices with the rest of the world.
_childDocuments_.name: Trolley Problem, Inc.

name: High On Life
detailed_description: SUMMARY Fresh out of high school with no job and no ambition, you’ve really got nothing going for you until an alien cartel that wants to get high off humanity invades Earth. Now, you and a team of charismatic talking guns must answer the hero's call and become the deadliest intergalactic bounty hunter the cosmos has ever seen. Travel to a variety of biomes and locations across the cosmos, go up against the nefarious Garmantuous and his gang of goons, collect loot, meet unique characters, and more, in the latest comedy adventure from Squanch Games! FEATURES Rescue and team up with charismatic, talking guns to become the deadliest intergalactic bounty hunter the cosmos has ever seen. Navigate dynamic and changing worlds that range from a jungle paradise, to a city built inside an asteroid, the hub of the cosmos. Leverage the unique skills of each gun to go up against a variety of criminals as you track down the nefarious Garmantuous and his gang of alien goons. Complete hunter challenges, meet weird, fun and hilarious characters, collect an array of alien technology, and more! FAQ Is this a VR game? Although many of Squanch’s previous titles were firmly rooted in VR, High On Life was built from the ground up for traditional flatscreen devices. What type of game is this? Single player? Multiplayer? High On Life is single player only. There is no multiplayer. Can my kids play? Can families play together? As this is a mature-rated title, we do not recommend it for children. What languages will High On Life be available in? The game will be localized (text-only) in English, French, Italian, German, and Spanish. Who is Squanch Games? Founded in 2016, Squanch Games develops comedic games for multiple platforms and devices. The studio’s mission is to create immersive content that people can lose themselves in for hours at a time, as well as shorter experiences that can be enjoyed with friends. Their latest title, Trover Saves the Universe, is currently available on PlayStation 4, Xbox One, Nintendo Switch, and PC, alongside other digital and VR titles such as Dr. Splorchy Presents: Space Heroes , Accounting and Accounting+ . Do you have any other games? Other games launched by Squanch include Trover Saves the Universe , Dr. Splorchy Presents: Space Heroes , Accounting and Accounting+ . Will there be DLC? The High On Knife DLC is out now! Available individually or bundled with High On Life.

To which you meet Morty, who is from a planet where evolution raised society as living guns. Together you become an unstoppable force to be recon with.
