_childDocuments_.review: So I bought this game as I saw it was described as basically Rhythm Heaven.  As a long time Rhythm Heaven fan and music game player in general, I immediately grabbed this game and played it excitedly.  But it has a lot of room for improvement before it can capture the charm of Rhythm Heaven.First off, I have a major issue with how the tutorials are set up.  In the beginning of the game, there's a massive info dump about all the control schemes when you don't even use the arrow keys or hold down Space until Nights 2 and 3.  The player doesn't need to know about everything at the beginning, it’s better to introduce them as you need to.  I also feel the tutorials for the minigames were confusing.  The text at the beginning of it doesn't help, and you're left to figure it out as you go along.  As it's Rhythm Heaven inspired, I think it needs to take a page from that game and have just a short description for each cue as you do it.I think it failed in taking advantage of the theme of the game: dreams.  The first few nights were the main character dreaming about real life, and not using the fantastical aspects of dreams.  I played long enough to get to the more surreal elements in Night 3, but I think it would lose the attention of most players by not introducing it that way.  The game could take advantage of the fact that these are dreams and make rather absurd elements or wondrous, instead of his day to day life.  Even “boring” everyday tasks like social media could be made more imaginative.The minigames themselves are rather repetitive as well.  Rhythm Heaven is quirky with its environments and characters, there's a lot of emotion and fun in how they express themselves.  In this game, the backgrounds don't change, the visuals essentially remain the same throughout.  In a few games, it will change, such as the Time one and the Dating one, but it's to make the game more difficult and IMO, doesn't make it more interesting.  The gameplay can be static: I think of some of the Rhythm Heaven games that are rather static, like Tambourine or Screwbot Factory. But even in those, the monkey and the robot are very expressive.  They'll jump around and smile brightly at you when you succeed, or break and screech at you if you mess up.  The sound cues make it more fun, with the robots going ya-ta! or the nice chime from the monkeys.  I feel you don't get any of that fun in these games.On that note, there's hardly any change in reaction when you mess up.  You get an Early/Late to show up, but nothing really happens past that.  There’s also no sensory reward for succeeding.  Only something happens when you miss, and that's only in some of the minigames.  I feel it's a problem where what happens in the minigames, missing the beat doesn’t visually matter.  Like the Nature minigame where you water, why don't the plants wilt when I miss?  Or why don't they grow into massive plants when I succeed, leaning into the dream aspect?  Another example is the dating minigame, where you can have more fantastical avatars to swipe from, such as a swipe left profile being a monster or Frankenstein instead of something you'd encounter in real life, like bots.I do think the gameplay itself is fine.  It matches what I would expect from the rhythm minigame genre.  If the visuals surrounding it were more interesting, even with the same sort of gameplay, it would be a lot more fun to play through.  And I think the graphics are very well drawn.  The music is a lot more subjective, but I found a few of the songs nice to listen to.Overall, despite my love for rhythm games, I found myself getting bored with it by the end of Night 3 and I couldn't continue.  It has promise, but lacking the charm and fun of the game it was inspired leaves a lot to be desired.

_childDocuments_.review: I received the game in exchange for testing and provided feedback on the game during development. However, I did not receive any additional compensation for doing this. The game runs great on the deck. The game includes a setting under "Display" to use colors calibrated for the steam deck's display, which I recommend using. You can also disable the deck's framerate limiter for better input latency (at the cost of more battery drain), but the game also plays fine with a 60 fps framerate limit. I would not recommend going lower than 60, as it's not worth the added input latency.Melatonin is a fantastic rhythm game. The art style and aesthetic look amazing. The songs, quite possibly the most important part of a rhythm game, are all great, and fit the mood of the game well. The theme of every minigame being a dream allows for some really creative setups, and it does a good job of tying the whole game together.This game is pretty clearly inspired by the Rhythm Heaven series and similar games like it. It plays at a calmer pace than some other rhythm games, never really requiring fast inputs, and only uses a limited number of buttons (three across the entire game, with most minigames using just one or two). One thing that I think is important to keep in mind if you've had experience with Rhythm Heaven is that Melatonin is generally shorter than most of the Rhythm Heaven games. Melatonin has 16 unique minigames and 5 mashups that combine previous minigames into one song. For contrast, Rhythm Heaven Fever on the Wii had 29 unique minigames (excluding the sequels) and 10 remixes. Melatonin does include a "hard mode" (where the song plays faster, and there are more inputs required) for all of the dreams, including the mashups, which does extends the length of the game to some extent. The game is still fantastic, and is appropriately priced for its length in my opinion, but it's important to remember that this is a smaller game made primarily by a single developer, and as such has a smaller scope than games released by large video game publishers.It's also worth commenting on the lack of things to do after completing all the minigames. You can always replay the minigames to go for more stars and rings, as well as try to get perfects, but there's not much else outside of that. The game includes a level editor, but , it's very limited.   In the about a year since the game came out, pretty much all of the promised features for the level editor have been added, namely the addition of custom mashups, custom songs, and steam workshop. This adds more you can do after completing the main game, but I also recommend keeping in mind that workshop levels are going to vary in quality a lot more than developer-created levels, and there are still some unfortunate limitations to the in-game editor that limits what can be done with custom levels.Overall, I think Melatonin is a fantastic game for what it is. There's a lot of creativity on display here, and I very much enjoyed my time with the game.

_childDocuments_.review: this so called "relaxing" game as i was told, that's supposed to lull you into a peaceful state. kiss my ass! I didn't even get through its first night without feeling like my brain was going to explode. It's advertised as this serene, dreamy experience, but let me tell you, it doesn't bring any melatonin production to your body. Instead, it makes you focus like a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ dog on steroids, eyes glued to the screen, heart racing, as you try to keep up with its ridiculous rythms. I mean, who thought it was a good idea to label this game as Melatonin?The whole premise is laughable. You dive into this pastel-colored world thinking you'll be gently guided into a state of relaxation. But no, it’s like being thrown into a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ pressure cooker. The levels are designed to keep you on edge, with timing and precision that would make even the most seasoned gamer sweat. There's nothing relaxing about frantically tapping and swiping, trying to hit these absurdly fast and complicated rhythms. It's like someone took a hyperactive metronome and decided to build a game around it.And don't even get me started on the Followers level. Whoever designed that must have a sadistic streak because it's absolutely impossible. You're supposed to follow these patterns and hit the right notes at the right time, but it's like trying to juggle flaming torches while riding a unicycle on a tightrope. It's infuriating! You think you're getting the hang of it, and then BAM, the game throws in some crazy twist that sends you spiraling into frustration. It’s like the developers sat around brainstorming the most maddening experience possible and then put it all into this one level.But here's the kicker: even after all that frustration, there's no point in trying to sleep. Somehow, despite the mad ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ difficulty and the stress it induces, Melatonin is addicting as hell. It keeps you wide awake all night, eyes burning from staring at the screen, your mind buzzing with patterns and rhythms. "No sleep" is an understatement. Once you start, it's nearly impossible to stop. It's like the game digs its claws into your brain and refuses to let go, making sure you're hooked, desperately trying to beat just one more level.So, you end up in this vicious cycle: you play, you get frustrated, you can't stop, and then you can't sleep. It’s a total nightmare. Instead of winding down, you're wound up tighter than a drum, lying in bed with your mind racing, replaying the game’s infernal challenges over and over. If you're looking for a game to relax and unwind with, stay far, far away from Melatonin. It won't help you drift off to sleep; it will have you wide awake, sweating bullets, and questioning your life choices. If you want to keep your sanity intact and get some actual rest, find something else to play. Trust me, your brain will thank you.♥♥♥♥ YOU MELATONIN!!!!(Game is pretty good if you get the hang of every challenge tho)10/10 would never play again (:

_childDocuments_.review: I wanted to like this game, I really did.Rhythm Heaven Fever is one of my top 10 games of all time, and the other 3 games in the series are also some of my favorites. I have perfected the whole series. Keep that in mind, this is not coming from a lack of experience or a dislike of this type of game. Quite the opposite.Melatonin started off wonderfully. Night 1 was everything I could ever want. Once I beat the first "remix" I was in love with the game. It seemed almost too good to be true. Unfortunately, I was correct.Night 2 was where the game went from nearly flawless to god awful, and it's all because of one small problem: Audio Cues.Audio cues in a game like this are not just *one of* the most important things for playability. They are *the* most important thing for playability. Melatonin ♥♥♥♥♥♥ them up royally.  Let me be more specific though.In Night 1, I only really had 2 complaints. The sound effect for dreaming about shopping when you swipe the credit card is a bit too soft and not quite percussive enough to feel super satisfying. It didn't make the game any harder, though. In dreaming about social media, the audio cues for jumping twice and continuing after a big jump are the same sound, but the former plays twice. It is a bit hard at first but it's doable.Night 2 is where everything fell apart. The first game in Night 2 is dreaming about working out. It's a call and response game. The call can include three things: Left arm curl, right arm curl, and both arms curl. You use the L button R button and both, respectively to copy it. In a GOOD video game, the audio cues would be distinct- maybe a "HOO" for left, a "HA" for right, and a "HOY" for both- just as an example, there are a million ways you could do it. What does melatonin do?There's one sound effect, pitched up or down slightly depending on the direction. No, I am not exaggerating even slightly.It gets worse.This review is getting pretty long so I'll ignore some of the other atrocious examples of audio cues and only mention the worst example: dreaming about money.Up until reaching this level, I got 3 stars on everything within 1 or 2 tries. It took me an HOUR to get 3 stars on the hard version of dreaming about money. Why? Because the audio cues are so bafflingly terrible that I question whether or not this game had any playtesters whatsoever. "Oh, just use the visual cues" except, you can't, because the visuals are designed specifically to mess you up. Dreaming About Money has 5 different things that can happen. A coin falling left, a coin falling right, two coins falling, a coin falling left and then wooshing to the right, and a coin falling right and then wooshing to the left.Do you want to know how you tell the difference? The audio cue is *exactly the same* regardless of which side the coin falls... but it is ever so slightly louder in one ear if you are wearing headphones. Not to mention if it's going to fake you out, lightning strikes and the thunder sound effect drowns it out entirely so you cant hear what side it's falling on in the first place.After finally getting 3 stars on everything in Night 2, I went to Night 3, hopeful that things would get better. They got worse. I stopped playing.If the devs ever update the game to fix the god awful audio cues then I will take away this review and instantly this game will be a thumbs up from me. It is literally so close to being a flawless Rhythm-Heaven-like rhythm game. They just ♥♥♥♥♥♥ up the most important part.All you have to do is make the audio cues distinct! That's it! If I can distinctly and easily hear the difference between two audio cues, then I can play your game. Unfortunately, your game makes me want to stab someone! Since my therapist has advised against stabbing people, I cannot play your game.

_childDocuments_.review: I don't know if it's just because I'm used to other rhythm games, but I was never able to get the hang of the timing of any of the stages in this game. Rather than being timed with the music itself, I noticed that stages tended to be timed according to the sound effects of the level. I ended up just turning the music off just so I wasn't instinctively trying to stay on beat with the music, so I was finally able to clear and perfect some levels. The calibration doesn't do much to help when it comes to timing, and fiddling with the other settings and accessibility options didn't seem to make that big of a difference either. I didn't want to believe the reviews that said this game relies more on its aesthetic and art style over gameplay, but I should've heeded the warning before buying. Don't get me wrong, the game is cute and the music itself is nice. But when it comes to playing the game itself, it's hard for me to think of an experience less satisfying than this. Such a shame.

_childDocuments_.review: If you're a fan of rhythm games like Rhythm Heaven, Melatonin is for you. Featuring 4 sets of 3 minigames, each with normal and hard difficulties, as well as 5 remixes, with the last one being the culmination of the whole game, although there isn't too much substance to the game (I'd say about 6 hours if you're looking to get excellent [but not perfect] scores), what is there is certainly fun. The art style and music are more chill than other similar games, and the songs contain no lyrics and are lofi-themed. The games themselves are very simple to play and fairly easy to complete, with only three buttons ever being used. Although I've never used it, there is a level editor for easily making custom songs, and levels made by others can be played through the workshop, so that's a feature to take note of if you're a fan of user-generated content. Overall, for its current $15 price point, it is a worthy buy, though if you're especially strapped for cash the short playtime can be an immovable hurdle, in which case waiting for it to go on sale is definitely the right call.
_childDocuments_.name: Melatonin

_childDocuments_.review: It's funny because when I think of melatonin, I think about how I tried taking the supplement for sleep and it turns out it would help me fall asleep but not stay asleep. I certainly did not want to turn into the addict who wakes up in the middle of the night and takes another one to knock themselves out again.Anyway, this game is a peaceful rhythm puzzle game that can be challenging but there are options to make it easier if you're struggling and it has many fun levels that pertain to moments of everyday life and our thoughts. _childDocuments_.name: Melatonin

_childDocuments_.review: Can't say I recommend it, and that makes me sad.As a diehard Rhythm Heaven fan, seeing a spiritual successor like this pop up on TikTok and the Steam storefront made me really excited at first, but after sinking less than an hour into it and completing around 80% of the game's main story, it's proven itself to be not my cup of tea.For starters, the game aesthetically is very stagnant. Whereas in games like Rhythm Heaven or Warioware or other Minigame collection type deals, what keeps them interesting to me is the sheer variance in presentation of every single game. In Melatonin, you're basically getting pastel pink and lo-fi for every minigame. And yeah, it's not like I didn't expect that or anything, the game is very clear about that in marketing, but I figured there would have been some other thing that would keep the gameplay loop fresh and new every time. There wasn't, really.On the topic of music, the soundtrack is actually pretty good. If this game were an album it'd be a solid 7.5/10 lo-fi record. Again my only issue is that it doesn't really give me anything more to work with. When designing game feel, ideally you want those peaks and valleys of excitement, while Melatonin just sort of feels like it keeps a straight middle ground the entire time. In fact, I KNOW this because I didn't even realize I was in the final world until I checked the achievement list to find out that there were only 16 minigames total. Overall I can't recommend this game. For anybody who saw this on TikTok and is looking for something similar, I'd recommend Rhythm Heaven Fever for the music minigame aspect, or Unpacking for the Cozy relaxed stress-free type deal.For existing Rhythm Heaven fans trying to find something to scratch that same itch, Rhythm Doctor is my personal choice.
_childDocuments_.name: Melatonin

_childDocuments_.review: I don't even know where to start lol. Everything about this game was just mind stimulating. It's been a while since I've literally had my eyes locked onto the screen. It was just beautiful all around. You have to play it to experience it yourself. _childDocuments_.name: Melatonin

_childDocuments_.review: For a game so aesthetically pleasing and with a great dreamy lo-fi soundtrack as this one, one would expect a chill experience right?Wrong. This is the most excruciatingly hard rhythm game I've played in my entire life EVEN with most accessibility options turned on. You hit a note 0.01ms early or late? You get punished. Your eyes are not quick enough to see that one frame that indicates you have to follow a very specific pattern? You get punished. Jesus Christ, most of the levels in this game were extremely counter intuitive. There were some regular levels that you can beat somewhat easily but most of them are just a mess in this aspect. Visual and audio cues are not visible enough and since you don't have an area or anything to press the buttons at the right time is up to you whether you do it perfectly or you're an effing loser.I seriously do not understand the total disconnection between the vibes of the game and the actual gameplay. Yes, it is very simple: just tap the key to the beat by learning different patterns en each level. Buy boy do they go hard at it. And thank god there are accessibility options in this one that make it slightly less complicated; otherwise I'd be still stuck into the first night.The game has everything to be a wonderful experience but it decides to treat you like garbage. UX needs to be redesigned completely to fix this, 'cause in the end it takes the whole fun and joy out of the experience.3/5 - The cutest nightmare.

_childDocuments_.name: Melatonin

_childDocuments_.review: First of, I've played Melatonin more than Steam has registered. I guess offline mode of Steam Deck messes with my total time. Anyway... Good stuff:- Very pleasant art style. The hand draw animation is gorgeous. - A very original setting for a rhythm game. Dreams can offer a lot of variety and unique gameplay- The controls are tight, gameplay is fluid. This is a must in a rhythm game and Melatonin nails it. - The game is fun. I breezed through normal mode in a single take and now I'm going for some hard mode levels and maybe perfectsBad stuff:- 20 minigames and 2-3 hours to beat them all on normal difficulty come off as lacking in content, specially for an almost 15 dolars pricetag- Music is not memorable at all. I get it, the game goes for a lofi soundtrack. Still, all of the tracks sound the same and not even a single one manages to stand out- The setting (Dreams) is very original and gives the game visual identity a lot of personality. But I think they could have done a lot more with it. Maybe a more expansive story? Levels that tell a more personal story of the guy dreaming? Maybe dreams could affect gameplay? Like... If you miss beats, the dream gets less and less lucid until you wake up (and lose) if you miss too much- Audio cues are hit or miss. Sometimes they are very clear and sometimes I feel like they could be a bit more unique and loud, specially in minigames with more than one cue. I know there are options to show cues like in practice mode, but that's not the point. The point is, the base game should be able to communicate better what it wants from you- Similarly, some sound effects when doing something right are way too weak both in volume and general feel, which in turn makes following the rhythm harder in certain minigames. Correct timing should be felt and percived by the player at all times- Minigames are cool and original in design, but just as the dream setting in general, I think there was room to be a lot more creative. The remix levels are specially disappointing, as they just mix the four games of the chapter, but without altering the visual presentationIn general, I think it's a good and entertaining game with a great personality, but with some gameplay problems, a sense that they could have done a lot more with the setting and a serious lack of content for the price they ask for. I recommend buying it at a heavily discount price
_childDocuments_.name: Melatonin

_childDocuments_.review: It sounds great, it plays great, it looks great, it's a really well done game. However, in my opinion, it commits the worst sin any rhythm game could: Having boring music.The game exclusively uses chill lo-fi beats for the music, which are all well made and sound great, but when every song in your rhythm game follows the same conventions, in the end all you're doing is making every level blend with each other. The levels in this game range from buying clothes, to shooting aliens using a spaceship, to catching dreams with a claw machine, to escaping from an active volcano... Every level has a distinctly unique theme from each other, and yet you could easily swap the songs with each other and i don't think anybody would notice. And when you're trying to make a game centered around fun and unique levels, this is definitely not something you want.This is what I would call an incredibly rare case of "Terrible idea, great execution"

_childDocuments_.review: I am extremely disappointed with this game. I didn't want to be, I went into this excited and optimistic, but came out upset and bitter. _childDocuments_.review: Pros:- Really nice music and art style!Cons: - The way the game judges whether you are "on time" or not seems to be based on when the animation ends, not when the beat actually is. This results in you either having to act before the actual beat or changing the calibration. However, animation lengths for the different songs are different so if you change the calibration you have to keep adjusting it for every song- Calibration is difficult to do--it's basically trial and error until you get it right, unlike other games where there is a bit more guidance- I find it a bit weird that the game basically encourages you to memorize the 3 set patterns per song instead of more variation with the beats- The practice rounds are not helpful because they teach you the rhythm by having you look at a big circle to see when you should act, but when you actually play the song the circle is not there and you are supposed to be looking at other cues to know when to act--very confusing!!

But because this game wants to be a cozy game, it doesn't really have either of those. It's just a little too easy and forgiving to be challenging. This game is so pretty and I wanted to like it so bad, but I think I'm just disappointed. It's not awful, its just disappointing as someone who really really likes rhythm games. Ironically enough, this game kind of puts me to sleep. Maybe that was the point lol

_childDocuments_.review: I will be completely honest here, I was sadly not the biggest fan of this game.While the visuals of this game are incredible and the music is top-notch, the reliance on visuals for most levels is really just a turnoff for me, especially some of the levels like Stress and Future which are nearly impossible to play if you aren't looking at the screen constantly.This brings me to my second issue with the game, there is a shocking lack of orchestration in this game, levels like Stress and Desire require you to react within an extremely quick time-frame in order to succeed, it doesn't help that most of the audio "cues" are the exact same (If it isn't obvious I am not the biggest fan of Stress).The music occasionally doesn't even line up with the prompts in some levels, I first noticed this in shopping where there was a beat in the song but no prompt in the level.And finally there is a huge lack in replay-ability, if there was a way to share your custom levels online (or make custom remixes) then this would give it a massive boost in replay-ability, the reason why the Rhythm Heaven games don't have this issue is because they have significantly more levels and said levels are longer and they give the player incentive to perfect levels. Overall, this game tries its best to be a Rhythm Heaven successor but there are a few glaring issues that are really holding it back.
_childDocuments_.name: Melatonin

_childDocuments_.review: Melatonin is short, sweet and an absolutely beautiful game. The ultra-attractive graphics and soothing music of this game would be enough to entice any player. However, the game goes above and beyond to engage the players through a set of unique mini-games, while tending to all the issues one might face during the game-play. From the access to visual and auditory assistance to the ability to alter calibration, to further ahead the interesting opportunity to customise the beats- Melatonin gives each player an experience of their dreams. Pros: Friendly UIAesthetically pleasing graphicsEngaging and Addictive Mini-GamesSimple to UnderstandCons: None yet; Half Asleep has done a great job at fixing any complaint-raising features beforehand
_childDocuments_.name: Melatonin

_childDocuments_.review: Melatonin is a rhythm-heaven-like with a unique theme and feel somehow brimming with new and unique ideas. Please buy it.I genuinely didn’t think that very different and new ideas could even exist in a rhythm-heaven-like, but here we are. There are genuinely types of timings and ideas that I haven’t seen before, and they’re fun as hell.The artstyle and general theming of the game, from what the minigames are representing, to the music, all has this kind of tired feel, which it pulls off really coherently and well. I can’t think of any games that have done this level of dedication to a theme, and this level of dedication this well.Speaking of the music, the music works fantastically and is great for keeping the rhythms to. If I were to say anything negative about the music it's that there aren’t any tracks with lyrics or even vocals at all. They’re also kind of forgettable, at least compared to something like rhythm heaven. Also, all of the sound cues are fantastic, and you would be able to play it off of them alone, which is good considering the type of game that it is.Also, if you’re worried about content because there’s not many minigames, I will say that there are hard versions of all the minigames and remixes, which in this case counts as content because they certainly would in rhythm heaven. They’re also super fun, which is great. :DMelatonin is exactly what I wanted it to be, exactly what it wanted to be, and exactly what it should’ve been.Oh yeah, and don’t forget to calibrate it.Objective - 9/10;Subjective - 9/10;
_childDocuments_.name: Melatonin

_childDocuments_.review: Although it's pretty short if you're not going for perfects, this was a great experience. The music is great, the minigames are fun, and the level editor seems pretty fun to use.My only complaints are that without "Wiggle Room" turned on, the judgements are WAY too strict for a rhythm-heaven style game. |There's also parts of certain minigames that make them annoying to perfect. For example: Dream about Mind's speed ups and slow downs aren't well telegraphed, and you only have 1 beat to react to the change in tempo.Dream about Desires is really unexpected in remixes, and doesn't give much time to react after the transition.Dream about Time requires visual cues because there's no audio indicator for when a portal is going to shoot multiple clocks.Aside from these few nitpicks, this game is great. _childDocuments_.name: Melatonin

_childDocuments_.review: As a fan of the Rhythm Heaven Series (which appeared to have inspired this), this game is a disappointment.The theme of the game has led to some weird design decisions that make it not a very good rhythm game.- The cue's tend to be drowned out by the background music- The scoring system is based on perfect streaks, more so than % hits.- The songs are all very similar and uninspired, every minigame has the same style, and that style makes the beats feel soft.- Some minigames are impossible without the visual clues. You couldn't play the game blindfolded without memorising all inputs. One minigame features 2 coin sounds meant to indicate left or right with a 1 beat reaction, however as they sound almost identical it is more a question of reacting to them appearing on screen. Another features portals, some as background setup, some as indicators for the next beat, but they have the exact same sound! You have to watch for them to turn blue to be cues.- Some “press every beat” games change tempo with no warning, which will cause you to miss unless you memorise where in the song they happen.- The practice modes use the same song as the score modes, which makes the game drag on a first playthough.- The game is broken up into chapters. While neat on a first viewing, it makes the menu-ing for replaying minigames longer than it needs to be- The Remix's offer not fun variation of background music or themes (no change in art)- The Final Remix (all games), doesn’t mix up the order between the chapters, huge missed opportunity for flowing games into each otherOverall, they mess up the fundamentals and produce a very samey and lack-luster experience.If your looking for the same experience as Rhythm Heaven, you will not find it here.
_childDocuments_.name: Melatonin

_childDocuments_.review: Buy the OST if available, that's what I recommend. The rhythm and beat feels very off. The dev was responsive, so hopefully they tweak it more for better space bar recognition. The tutorials are all fine but once you play the actual level, where you think you need to hit (the actual beat) and where the game thinks you need to hit (the off step) is wacky. I couldn't really play more than 15 mins which bums me out. The game looks adorable and I wanted to experience it.
_childDocuments_.name: Melatonin

_childDocuments_.review: I wish steam had an in-between option.A lot of the mini-games are generally bland, with syncopation never being introduced. Which isn't necessarily a bad thing, but it leads to uninteresting music sync and the difficulty progression being reliant on reaction-times, more buttons, more consecutive inputs, and/or memory. Some of the cues are not easily distinguishable from each-other, making you rely on visuals often. There are a few more nit-picks that wouldn't work in a general review, so I won't detail them here.But I will say that there's a lot of potential, and I hope Half Asleep will continue to make rhythm games. Hopefully with the intention of including more interesting rhythm concepts.These are all things that I noticed immediately and was surprised to see that there was near no discussion about it. Patricia Taxxon made an amazing video detailing a lot of my criticism. If you like this game, that's great! But I didn't find the enjoyment that it seems many others did.
_childDocuments_.name: Melatonin

_childDocuments_.review: I really wanted to love this game. I grew up on Rhythm Heaven and it's the reason why I'm so into rhythm games today. This game if very clearly inspired by that game series, and it nails the style of gameplay and progression. But this game doesn't come close to scratching that itch for a new Rhythm Heaven. The mini-games are alright, nothing remarkable though. I enjoyed about 30% of them. However, the music is where this game really fell off for me. Before each song, there a kind of "tutorial version" of the song. Just like Rhythm Heaven, these songs aren't meant to be bops. But unlike Rhythm Heaven, they don't get much better when you begin the scoring mode. Don't get me wrong, there were some good songs in there, like the Money Dream and Food Dream, but for the most part the music was kind of a snooze fest. Even when the songs try to pick up, I was almost always left with disappointment. There just wasn't enough "umph" to the songs, and that may be because of the choice of genre they developers wanted to go with.I will say, the art style is absolutely stunning. Whoever was responsible for the art direction for this game deserves an A+ and gold star. It's one of the big parts of this game that drew me in initially. _childDocuments_.review: As someone who loves the Rhythm Heaven series, it was great to see an indie take on that style of rhythm game. The overall concept is very clever, taking place in a dream. There's no need to try and explain why a guy is sitting in a flying chair while flying boxes with faces launch food at him. In turn the style and aesthetics are nice. It's definitely a very bright game, with light pastel colors and with settings befitting of a dreamscape. Each level had it's own look while still being cohesive and connected to the overall theme.The music was great. Just like it's inspiration, the kind of music throughout the game varies. Each song is heavily influenced by the level they're a part of. Like Time has the ticking of clocks or Technology being chiptune. My personal favorite had to be Money in combination with the in-game audio cues.The game isn't particularly long if you just do a simple playthrough of it. A single session of 4~ hours got me through it while going for 3 stars/rings for each level and a little bit of messing/testing with the settings. That's not to say there isn't replayability. Each level has the "Perfect" rank above the 3 star/ring rank which can be hard to master. I have yet to really try this yet, but I look for to my many failed attempts.There's also the level editor. Once you've beaten both the normal and hard modes of a single level (not counting any of the final levels of a night), you'll unlock the editor for it. It lets you go in to create your own version of that level, giving you full access to it's audio cues and tempo shifts. It is a tad limited in some aspects, like you can only change the tempo to preset speeds and if a level doesn't have offbeat inputs it simply won't have them available to try, like with the Money minigame. That aside, it's a fun extra that was a pleasure to mess around with.The many options this game has to offer is greatly appreciated. From your basic fullscreen toggle to a cam shake toggle and even a toggle that will change the colors more inline for a Steam deck. The audio having four separate sliders (master, music, sound effects and the in-game metronome) is nice as well. The accessibility options is very interesting. There's a toggle to make the practice circle show up during levels, the aforementioned metronome to play, for the window of error to increase to help with timing and even getting penalized less for early and late hits. These are of course all off by default and are there purely for those who wish to use it.One big flaw I see is the calibration option. While the option for having an offset is always a must for rhythm games, I don't believe the game has a big enough calibration range. It's a simple range of 50 milliseconds of offset, either positive or negative. This is simply just not wide enough of a range, as most rhythm games I play I need an offset of around 200ms for appropriate timing. It was most apparent when I played the Mind minigame as it was the simplest for me to tell. There's also the feeling of my input delay constantly changing, though I'm still not entirely sure why that is. On some games it was manageable, but for others I was having a harder time with it. Funny enough the Time minigame was when it really made itself noticeable. As of writing, I saw there was mention of adding an input test for calibration. I hope to see the range will be increased along with the implementation of the test.While the calibration issue is certainly one that can't be ignored, I still thoroughly enjoyed Melatonin. Its charm is captivating and the presentation is wonderful. I would recommend this game to any Rhythm Heaven fan or really any rhythm game enthusiast for some simple but tough fun.

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a rhythm game.That sounds disparaging, so let me elaborate. I was charmed by some advertising visuals in a YouTube Short detailing several levels and their gameplay. Melatonin was portrayed as a fun, interesting rhythm game with synchronized visuals and a catchy OST. It is not that.Don't get me wrong, the art is lovely. The animation is very smooth. The levels are fun to look at, interesting to watch move, and follow a very cozy color scheme. However, the gameplay is incredibly lacking.As you can see, I have 53 minutes on record playing this game for my friends to watch. We all shared the same opinion: this is not a rhythm game. There IS music, but it never truly synchronizes with the levels or the beats you're expected to time your button-combos to. This is especially evident in the "TECH" dream of Night One [Chapter One of the game], where the "music" is a low hum that barely registers and the "rhythm" is a single unrelated instrument suddenly playing out of sync.This issue is present throughout the game, where the background visuals and animation almost hinder the player because you're not truly listening to the game or trying to follow along with the rhythm. In some levels there is next to no visual or audio indication of rhythm to follow. The final "song" of Night One is just an amalgamation of all four songs in the level, mashed together and flipping through each other's beat-styles very sporadically.I had a perfect run on my first "SCORED" run of that mashup, then a no-miss run on my first "HARD MODE" run of said mashup. Each level was relatively easy to complete. This is not a testament to poor gaming skill or a ragequit scenario. The game is simply not fun [in my opinion], because it is not a rhythm game. I can't even argue that the visuals have a rhythm, because I spent so much of the game attempting to figure out what visual cues = a beat.If you want to give the game a try, I understand! But if you are looking for a "fun" "upbeat" "lofi" "rhythm game" or just something with an interesting OST, this is not the product for you.[Note: This game was a gift from my GF. It was not free, as I paid her back directly after, so I will not be checking that slot. Thank you for your time.]

_childDocuments_.review: Melatonin is a game that takes heavy inspiration from the Rhythm Heaven. It's a beautiful homage and a carefully written love letter to vintage rhythm games.  Melatonin is beautiful and the soundtrack is something I truly adore. If you're looking to chill and unwind I definitely recommend this game. The pastel colors and retro vibe this game off that truly held me. I'm a sucker for chiptuney songs and upbeat lofi.Any cheesy thing that has you reaching for the stars or smiling is truly enrapturing. This game does have that in its essence.Although the game leans to casual players, this doesn't mean veterans are left at the wayside. With an included hard-mode remixes it definitely can provide a challenge to those seeking it.What I do love most about this game is the accessibility it provides to those with disabilities. In the settings menu you can find there it has a subsection dedicated for options to make gameplay easier such as a timing circle, a metronome, and a wiggle room delay on hits. My brain and hands can be a little bit out of sync given tremors due to previous hand injuries and anxiety spikes. I will visibly shake when excited or in tense situations even more so if my old hand injuries act up. I can't help that. I found this to be a lovely feature and it's something that I wish more games did. All in all, very lovely game. I would definitely pick it up.

_childDocuments_.review: , developed and published by  is an indie rhythm game. The gimmick is, at least without turning on any assist options, that you are meant to sightread and listen to audio cues in many different dream-themed minigames. The game takes place in a sleeping cartoon man's thought bubbles, and every level is a thing (concept/place/activity) that the man is currently dreaming about. The theming and aesthetics are clever (even if the overwhelming purple of anything and everything in the game can be a little grating afer a while). The game is beautifully animated, the score is serviceable, better on some levels than others, but always at least a little clever.Overall, I recommend getting this one only on a sale, as the actual game mechanics can be somewhat frustrating and inconsistent. The game doesn't have industry-standard auto-calibration features, and the calibration that is there is... peculiar. Plus, the game just seems to read inputs weirdly, I don't know if it's latency or what, but calibrating with the keyboard was an exercise in confusion, as I continuously pressed the "c" button on my keyboard in the appropriate rhythm, as steadily as I could, and yet sometimes the calibration needle was flung halfway into orbit.The levels being different is fun, and provides some novelty, especially in the animation department, but unfortunately the audio cues and sightreading potential of levels is hit-or-miss, and this, combined with the previous point about calibration and weird, intrinsic input latency, just makes the package into a very middling experience that fails to personally keep my interest for more than a 30-minutes per session length of time every few weeks. If you pick this up, do it on sale, and check the accessibility options to make the jank of the game a little more bearable.

_childDocuments_.review: Probably the best rhythm game I've ever played. The visual style is incredible and the music is delightful, but what makes Melatonin so special is the way it presents the gameplay. There's no circles lining up or anything of the sort; instead each level has up to 3 patterns of audio/visual cues to memorize. This small detail made it the most immersive rhythm game I've played. (If that description scares you, know that there is an option to enable more obvious visual prompts and other accessibility options in the settings. The cues are also very well-designed and outside of 1 or 2 levels I had no trouble learning the patterns)My ONLY gripes with this game are as follows: 1) I wish there were more levels. The game is broken up into 4 nights and one morning. Each night has 4 unique levels and then one level that combines all the others. The morning has one level which combines all of the nights. For those counting, that makes 16 unique levels and 5 mashups for a total of 21 levels. Not a tiny amount of content, certainly, but I was able to 2-star every level and 'complete' the game in under 6 hours, including a couple of 3 stars and Perfects. I'll probably play more to grind out more perfects, but I don't expect to get much more than ~10 hours tops out of the content at hand. 2) I was underwhelmed by the level editor. It basically just lets you take the existing tracks and insert one of the patterns from that track on any beat. I was hoping for a bit more flexibility, and maybe fully custom tracks and Workshop support. I think they are working on improvements to the level editor though, so we'll see what comes of those. Overall, I thoroughly recommend Melatonin to anyone that likes lo-fi and thinks the style looks cool :)

_childDocuments_.review: This game is fantastic and wonderful. If you're a Rhythm Heaven enjoyer, I can't recommend it enough. It's so much fun!!! It has a bunch of quality of life features that you might be looking for, like being able to attempt Perfects whenever (with a Perfect-Only mode), a progress bar, actual in-level feedback in the form of if you were early or late, an actual honest-to-goodness restart button... I love this damn game. Night 1 isn't my favourite, but Nights 2 & 4 are absolutely fantastic. Plus, if you're someone with experience, every level has an immediately-accessible hard mode that makes meaningful and significant changes to the level beyond "lol it's faster now". Even the end-of-night Mashups have hard modes!! It's awesome!! A lot of care has been put into the visual elements to help you root yourself in the timing windows, and the game is *not* afraid to take some of that help away for the hard mode levels (which I actually really like). If you're someone without experience, don't worry! All the hard modes are optional, and their progress is tracked separately with their own few achievements.The whole game is oozing with charm, care, and attention to detail. It's the first game in a lot of years that I actively want to find new ways to replay, and I'm hoping that further updates to the level editor help me out with that. It's a lot of fun and I'm very happy I took a chance on this game. And if you buy it, I hope you enjoy it too.

_childDocuments_.review: I thoroughly enjoyed my time playing Melatonin, and I hope to see more content like this in the future! However, it's very difficult not to compare such a game to the original Rhythm Heaven games due to how incredibly similar they are, and as such, the shortcomings of this game become extremely hard to ignore. First of all, the elephant in the room: the duration. I beat the whole game in 2 hours. I'm sure that alone is enough to deter a lot of people. Did I enjoy my 2 hours? Yes, yes I did. It's why I'm recommending this game. But it did leave me wanting more.Secondly, there is some rough edges in this game. Notably, there are some moments that feel unfair or untelegraphed. Moments like the tempo changing without warning in a level where you gotta hit space every beat, little to no differentiation in audio cues for certain special interactions, and a few levels where every cue has the same starting sound which changes it from a satisfying rhythm game to a QTE game. Finally, the scoring system. There is absolutely no reward for getting any score above 2 stars (earned in normal mode) aside from progression. On top of that, the rings you get in hard mode have zero purpose, other than to pat you on the back and give you an achievement if that matters at all to you.All that being said, I did enjoy this game. Its subtle storytelling, its unique aesthetic, and it's calming and relaxing vibe, all blend together to make it truly something special. It's just a bit of a shame that there's not much of it to really sink your teeth into.

_childDocuments_.review: This game is great, but there are a few problems I'd like to mentionMy SINGLE BIGGEST problem with this game is that the calibration setting, one of the single most important settings in rhythm games, is maxxed out at a 50ms delay. Some extremely well-made minigames that rely on visual cues include Dreams about Stress, which was done quite well.The last little rant is that it feels too expensive for such a short game. But that's just me and my broke wallet talking.All in all, a really well-polished game, but the calibration delay being capped at 50ms really annoyed me.

_childDocuments_.review: Recommended, but only just. There's a lot to like about this game; the minigames are creative and interesting, the music is good. And there's the simple fact there aren't many rhythm-heaven-likes on PC at the moment.But, I don't know. For all the style the artstyle has it manages to lack personality. There's not a lot to be said about our ambiguously-gendered protagonist, nor the situations they find themselves in. The music, too; it doesn't really stray from the sleepy, Shawn Wasabi-esque electronica that it starts with. And it's good music, but it's all kind of the same music, even when it doesn't really fit.It's a shame too, that the conceit of dreamy minigames ends up getting used to create fairly bland situations and visuals. It's bizarre that it ended up *less* dream-like and surreal than Ko Takeuichi's work on Rhythm Heaven.Still, the gameplay is good, the timing is well-tuned. The scored mode/hard mode system allows for some fun minigames without creating hard roadblocks (Hello and ♥♥♥♥ you, Bon Odori 2). Overall...It's fine. It's not much more than fine, and there's a lot of wasted potential. But it's fine.

_childDocuments_.review: An indie game heavily inspired by Rhythm Heaven. It does it pretty well, while there are parts that could be improved a bit it is still very fun. If you've never played Rhythm Heaven, it's a rhythm based game with little to no visual aspects required. Gameplay generally requires you to press one or two button to the beat of the music accompanied with audio cues for shifts in rhythm, or complex rhythms. Easy concepts, and the main focus is staying on beat to the music, rather than heavily based on visual reading like in most rhythm games (Guitar Hero, DDR, Osu! etc.) The gameplay of Melatonin follows that exactly, you have 3 gameplay inputs L, R, and A (Left Arrow, Right Arrow, and Space).Some negatives of the game - the music, while good, I don't find to be as memorable to Rhythm Heaven's. Though I feel like this is due to me spending much more hours in those games getting perfects. I still think that Rhythm Heaven's OST stands out a bit more than Melatonin, and it can make playing it feel a little muddy especially when deciding on what level to play. The next is a small one but I think the timing windows are just about as tight as visual rhythm games, which given the visual aspect of it, you have an easier time determining on when to hit a note. Taking away the visual aspect of it and solely relying on the audio and still have that strict timing makes most Early/Late feel a little random sometimes especially when it's just a frame or 2. There is a setting to widen the hit windows, but I don't want to turn it on just to get all perfects. I do respect the option being included for the people who need the accessibility.The last negative I want to bring up is that some of the audio cues, especially Nature, are very similar to each other. It causes me to use the visual cue accessibility feature to see a visual of what I'm supposed hit cause the audio cues aren't good enough. In Nature, the little plants could have large variances in conjunction with the audio cues to create a better overall cue of what to do with visual telling you whether you're going to hold, or tap and audio giving a precise timing setup. Work is another one with that issue. There are 3 audio cues, while the actual sounds aren't that similar they happen with the same timings as each other, and it can take a little while to associate the sound to the proper button, and to do it with 100% consistency. There are visual cues in Work, but to discourage the use, the screen pans pack and forth causing a lot of eye strain with constant movement. Again, turning on visual cues and ignoring the game's own visual cues is the fix for it.While it seems that I've been ragging on this game for a while, all of that doesn't sway my enjoyment of the game. I still really like it, and will continue to go for perfects, hopefully getting them all. I think the game is still very much worth it. While it isn't quite as long as the RH games, it still has it's own unique charm. There are some great minigames in here, and with remixes. If you like Rhythm Heaven, you'll probably like this game. It's not long, with 21 total games including remixes and still feels really fun to play.

People who play rhythm games know that the worst part is the beginning where you're getting used to the controls, and the really enjoyable stuff is when you're fluent with the controls and can sightread the music track. Well this game spends a lot of time teaching you new "control schemes" and not very much time letting you just flex your newfound skills.Additionally, I felt a lot of the time it was just testing my ability to be a metronome.. which isn't the most fun thing.I had a ton of fun with the last level where they combine all the "minigames" into one track, but its just one level. If there were even 3 more levels like the last one this game would feel much better to me.The custom levels don't make up for this either. _childDocuments_.review: this game is pretty ok. and by that i mean "it's a great start, but if they made another that improved every complaint i had i probably would not go back to this one" type of ok. to start off, i'm gonna point out the mass amount of Pink and white used in the colour scheme. there is a contrast option, but there isn't a brightness one, which really weirds me out like at points on the overworld map (world 3 in particular felt the most bright) i felt like i was going blind, like i got up to get a drink and i was like "oh hello normal world, i see  my eyes have to readjust now".This next part is probably on the controller i use, but the rumble felt way too strong, and i had to turn it off. which is a shame, because rumble is definitely a good feedback for telling if you messed up a input, but it's only a on/off toggle, not a slider. this kinda leads into my next point too.Some of the games just feel like they don't match the songs at all. and the baseball just felt really wrong to me. like as a long time Rhythm Heaven Fan, having to do the windup feels really clunky to me, and the portals are not a very good visual tell either like i kept hitting the button on the first clock every time. Some of the games also really hit the mark on the head. like the one in the workplace is genuinely fun as and i wish a lot more of the games had cues like those where i can actually tell what button it is. There's a game based on "mind" that comes to mind when i say this next sentence: some of the tells just don't sound different enough to tell that it's a different thing you're meant to do.another thing that really confused me was the implementation of a star rating system. you need 8 stars to get past each world. but the issue is that me, a guy who's been doing the rhythm game dance for a long time, can pretty easily do that, and it more feels like a detriment to people who'd be new to this type of rhythm game, because all the games in the world you're on appear in the remix levels so why would you skip a game and not know how it works before going into a remix level? you'd think with all i've said i'd give a negative, but honestly i can't because the positives outweigh the negatives but i probably wouldn't play this game again unless they add a brightness slider like i can see the burn in just waiting to happen.good game, like between a 6 and 7 out of 10. probably closer to the 7.

_childDocuments_.review: The good:The game has great visuals and music. I love the overall style of this game. Each mini game is clever and beautiful. Each music track is fantastic.The bad: I had trouble with timing while playing this. I asked the dev what the size of the timing window is because it's either VERY SMALL or the notes are just offsync.A few of the mini games require memorization, especially in the "remix" levels. Other games in this genre handle fast transitions by giving you an audio clue before the note. This game also does that, but the issue is with this game you have to hit more than one button. You BARELY have enough time to react and stay on beat. You will end up memorizing certain sections of songs in order to get that perfect score you're striving for.I recently played through rhythm heaven and rhythm doctor, so I was very excited to play this. While I enjoy the overall feel and vibe of this game, some of the minigames and the sync made parts of my experience frustrating. If you are just looking for a quick rhythm focused collection of mini games to have a good time with, I would recommend this. _childDocuments_.review: It's a good game. A nice game even. A solid.... 7/10. Melatonin is themed well, and you can see the inspiration from the likes of say, rhythm heaven. A sequence of rhythm minigames.But... Very few of the minigames were... notably interesting. And I know none of them are meant to be super interesting. But quite a few I was just kinda left with a sense of boredom. And that might be because I was too good for the game? Which isn't really a problem in all honesty, just an audience thing.Sorta related to that, my biggest gripe about it is the over-reliance on visual cues. Like, the minigames are nicely themed, the music is often neat enough; but towards the middle, some minigames have no auditory distinction between cues at all. I always treat a rhythm game as, if you're really *really* good, you should technically be able to do every level with your eyes closed. Should you? Certainly not, but *technically* every distinct input should have *some* kind of distinct auditory cue, and that just wasn't the case for maybe half of these. Just left it a little unsatisfying.Additionally, towards the end, I did well, but I felt I had little to no reaction time for some of the inputs. The amount of time you get between between when you can deduce which cue you're getting and when you have to do the input is, for some minigames, incredibly small, and that also left me a little miffed.Now, with all this complaining you'd probably expect me not to recommend the game, but actually, I do! Again, not a bad game. I just have high standards, and it's not *perfectly* to *my* liking, but for particularly casual players, I think one could get a lot of enjoyment out of this. Heck, if you want to go for perfects, go ahead. I just didn't find it intuitive enough personally to want to play any level more than once on each mode, and I didn't have to to get at least 2/3 stars on each one.So yeah, solid 7/10. Not the best, most polished, awesome rhythm game ever, but a solid, fun experience that has cool graphics, neat music, and a lil bit of side story.

_childDocuments_.review: Extremely poor calibration compared to other games:* No tap-to-calibrate mode, you just have to fiddle with it until it feels right* No separate audio/video calibration* The calibration offset is capped at 50ms, which wasn't enough for me (on Linux with a low-latency audio interface)* The calibration tool is very hard to use to feel the beat because every time you tap it plays a delayed beep.All of this might sound minor, but led to me getting frustrated before I even made it through the first level. I could play by intentionally offsetting my keypresses, but I was unable to calibrate to a point where I could actually play by tapping in time. As a lover of significantly more complicated and precise rhythm games (eg ADOFAI) I gave up and asked for a refund. It's a shame.

_childDocuments_.review: I bought this game after seeing clips of it on YouTube Shorts, and I've always been a big fan of rhythm-based games, so I was really intrigued after seeing the clips online. The colors are very calming and the scenery for each level is very pretty, and each type of level has a fun premise. The music is also very catchy and calming, so if you love lofi music, you'll probably love this game even more. The game, which I haven't really seen in other rhythm-based games, gives you a lot of audible cues as to when to do certain actions along with visual cues. This is probably one of my favorite aspects of the game, as once you start the understand each level better, you can focus less on the visual cues and really focus on the music and listen for those audio cues in the song and appreciate the graphics. I really appreciate this as I feel like it helps you get more immersed with the music and appreciate each song in each level. Overall, I love this game and I think the name "Melatonin" suits it quite well as it is equal parts fun and relaxing! If you are thinking of buying the game, do it. It is well worth it!

_childDocuments_.review: it is a fun rhythm game, but meant for casual players. The gameplay is simple, as rhythm games should be, and it has some interesting ideas of fun challenges. However, the execution of those ideas is not always great, and given the other cons I point out below, I would say it is worth trying only if it's on sale, and I expect most fans of rhythm games will not enjoy it.The visuals and songs make it a nice casual game if you play it without caring about the score, especially if you are not looking for a rhythm game per se but just something to spend some time doing to wind down. Overall, I'd say it is a casual rhythm game for people who don't like rhythm games. Many design decisions make me think the designers themselves don't really play a lot of rhythm games. Pros:Nice visualsFun songsCons:It lacks the kind of feedback you would expect from a rhythm game - literally the only possible outcomes from a beat are "perfect", "early", "late" or "miss"The calibration is terrible - you can go on increments of 1 ms, but it is all manual, and you can't calibrate audio and video separately (even a "practice mode" with a simple 4/4 beat and that lets you see how far off beat you were instead of just "early", "late" or "perfect" (and perfect has a very big window) would be great, but no, that isn't a thing)The beat misleads you sometimes (not by being tricky, but by literally having the audio cue that means you should tap x beats later, but not being an actual cue, which you can only know by paying attention to the visuals)

_childDocuments_.review: I've spent the majority of my teenage years playing osu! and other rhythm games like the Project Diva series, but I never played Rhythm Heaven. I wasn't too familiar with the source material apart from acknowledging its existence, but when I heard this game was inspired by it and had Lo-Fi music, as well as a clean hand-drawn artstyle, i couldn't help but give it a try. And its one of the most wholesome games I have ever played. My name's Angel and today we're taking a look at Melatonin.For those who don't know, "Melatonin" is the name of the hormone in the brain that helps you fall asleep. As such, the game naturally will have elements that are deliberately designed to make you feel relaxed and could potentially make you fall asleep. It is a short and concise story about a sleep deprived man who struggles with insomnia and the only way we can get through the night is to help him in his dream sequences.Each level is smoothly hand-drawn with themes that match their dreamy visuals. From dreaming about food, to dreams about work,  and other surprises. The game also has some pop culture references which I believe are a self-insert of the developer (). As for the challenge, this is not a game that would ever be considered for that type of experience primarily. Although it is easy to follow with tutorials being straightforward and making Practice mode mandatory, there is a Hard Mode and Perfectionist options and achievements available for those who seek a challenge. But as for its main purpose, It is purely relaxing, which encourages you to chill out if you're having a bad day. I picked this game up when I was having a rough one and I was pleasantly surprised with the outcome, as it became one of my favorite rhythm games I've ever played.The gameplay consists of following sound cues and pressing the right keys/buttons on the beat, which play out like an interactive album with minigames. However, the way the game implements these cues is similar to that of the Rhythm Heaven franchise in everything but presentation. At the end of the level, you are awarded stars (or rings in hard mode or P's for Perfect) based on your performance. The better you do, the higher the score you get and thus more stars/rings. You have two kinds of levels in this game, for the sake of simplicity i'll name these Singles and Mashups. Single levels essentially play a song that is befitting of the theme. which can either speed up or slow down as it experiments with one consistent mechanic. There are 4 Singles each Chapter, while Mashups are a compilation of all the levels in that Chapter. In other words: Mashups are a combination of the 4 levels inside a chapter and each of them have their own individual song. The game runs smoothly without any bugs.I feel like the soundtrack of this game has been scientifically approved by a doctor to be the most relaxing music you'll ever listen to, accompanied with its visuals. It is filled with tons of catchy tunes and melodies that will keep you hypnotized. With enough plays you'll practically memorize each of the songs and eventually come back to listen to them more. It's very reminiscent of its source material in a way, but stands out on itself and it is the kind of game that will have you listen to the soundtrack in your subconscious.Melatonin helps us sleep, it is a much more needed reprieve that can aid us to continue a brand new day, and it is now a game that can help with both, whether in soundtrack or the gameplay. it is a must play for those who are a fan of rhythm games or looking for a game to chill out after a tough one.

_childDocuments_.review: TLDR: Try the demo. It pretty much contains 4 of the best levels the game has to offer.Melatonin is an interesting rhythm game, and I give it only a very small recommendation.There are 16 levels which have you input various rhythmic patterns following cues. Additionally, there are 5 levels which mix these 16 levels up with a new song, which requires you to quickly switch back and forth between interpreting the different sets of cues. These mixed levels are the highlight of the game, giving you a much more varied song to play, and requiring quick context switching, which is very fun.The level of polish is exceedingly high, with the game's aesthetics, sound, and music all being immaculately crafted, which results in a very well implemented game.My biggest gripe is that these 16 levels lack severely in variety. There's only two levels that I think are on par with the demo's first 4 levels, and at least a third of them I'd classify as "very boring". This is why I can't give this game a wholehearted recommendation. The content is relatively sparse, and not all of it is great, or even good.

_childDocuments_.review: TL;DR: I was hoping for a smaller, lo-fi version of Rhythm Heaven; nice beats, some relaxing gameplay and some challenge. I did not get that. Not only is this *barely* even a rhythm game, it's also trying to be the Dark Souls of rhythm games (and doing that badly). This gets a -1/10 for gameplay and frankly I would call labeling this a rhythm game false advertising. I will be refunding this game. Longer version:I'm pretty sure most people are with me when I say that rhythm games should be timed to the *music*, that following SOUND cues is the whole deal. They can be supplemented with visual cues, sure, but in my opinion a good rhythm game can be played almost with closed eyes while just focusing on the beat. The difficulty comes from that. So my issue is not with a high difficulty. It's with how *this* game achieves that high difficulty:Not only is the timing window for pressing buttons ridiculously short (think half of a second), the gameplay also NEEDS you to follow the visual clues...because the audio ones are totally useless. Or just nonexistent. Seriously, the first time I beat a level was when I *muted the sound*, playing only following the visuals. I had to play this "rhythm" game on mute to actually play it! That's just stupid. When I played trying to follow the music alone, the music just distracted me from the visual cues, while providing barely any useful sound cues that I could actually hear. The sound clues that did show up were also NOT properly timed to when you should press a button according to the *visual* cues (even accounting for syncopated rhythms). Also, I do like very minimal electronic lo-fi music, but even so some of the tracks barely qualified as "music" to me. They're often just some electronic noises played vaguely rhythmically. This game's soundtrack is the audio equivalent to a Windows screen-saver made from clipart. Also, I'm a disabled player, so I should be happy about accessibility options, right? Well, I was not. My disability does not notably affect my sense of rhythm or ability to use a controller, but that's not my point. My point is: I'm pretty unhappy about a game letting me try (and fail) the first (!) level a grand total of *three* times before it keeps shoving the accessibility options in my face. Imagine trying a new game for under five minutes and basically being told "Hey, you play bad - are you disabled?". Apparently you're not allowed to just be bad at a game you've never played? Clearly the devs think abled players can master the mechanics in under three tries. (eyeroll) If you're out of practice using a controller, congrats, you are now disabled according to this game. It's insulting at best and also feels vaguely ableist. (What, I MUST be disabled because I tanked the first level too hard?? Nonsense logic.)Also, to add insult to injury the accessibility options are useless in actually making the game playable or fun. Sure, the metronome overlay (called "audio assist") makes this *barely* playable while unmuted, but frankly if I wanted to follow beats to a metronome then I'd practice the piano. The metronome also blends in with the soundtrack far too easily, the mixing is off on that. It barely helps. And the "visual assist"...just gives you *another* BIGGER visual clue to follow. Which also means you pretty much look at the middle of the screen and no other part of the game. Wow. So I could probably have completed this game...by staring at a circle on my screen while following an often barely-audible metronome, not actually enjoying the graphics or soundtrack. Fantastic./s

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a disgrace to the rhythm game genre.I like to sort my rhythm games into one of two types: ones that can be played with your eyes closed because you can be carried by the rhythm (like Rhythm Doctor or the Rhythm Heaven games), and ones where seeing the game is integral for it to function correctly (like osu! or Crypt of the Necrodancer). These games also have very defining characteristics, like encroaching circles or other telegraphed signals which are always the same. Moreover, the most important part of these games is that you hit whatever you need to hit  ; hitting it slightly early or late doesn’t mean that you are going to get punished heavily.Melatonin throws all of that out of the window, and not in a way. The game markets itself on being a chill rhythm game with sleepy lo-fi beats which makes you think that you can close your eyes and drift off to Rhythmland, but the opposite is true: hitting the beat just slightly imperfectly? BOOM! The words “EARLY” or “LATE” get shoved in your face WITH an additional change in the environment making sure you feel like a loser. You can’t close your eyes to avoid this since most of the games have visual signals as to which button you need to press. The game tries to audially telegraph it too, but it just doesn’t do a good job of it.What’s the worst of it all is the art style. Though it being hand drawn is a neat touch and one of the games better qualities, who in their right mind thought A SLEEPY LO-FI GAME should have BRIGHT WHITES, PINKS AND BLUES and not darker tones that are easier on your eyes!? Couple this with an unattractive protagonist and it’s just a recipe for disaster. Building further on the lo-fi audio of the game, some of the songs used are weird, not lo-fi, or downright creepy and unsettling.I can’t recommend this game for the life of me and will be asking for a refund as soon as possible.

_childDocuments_.review: Melatonin is a rhythm game like no other. Each level has a different cue for when to press the buttons, similar to Nintendo’s Rhythm Heaven series.There’s not much story, just some short cutscenes every now and then.As mentioned before, the gameplay is similar to the Rhythm Heaven series. If you have played a game in this series before you will understand, but as mentioned before (again), you press buttons to a cue which is different based on the level. Sometimes these cues could be confusing, and you might need some extra assistance. There are 4 different options: Visual Assist, which shows a cue in the center of the screen indicating when to press a button. Some levels might make this more useful. Audio Assist, which always plays a metronome in the background. Most levels have an obvious beat, so this might not be that useful. Wiggle Room, which makes hitting a Perfect easier. If you are trying to perfect all levels I recommend this. Easy Scoring, which makes hitting early or late give more score than normally.In conclusion, I would recommend this game to Rhythm Heaven fans, and also newcomers to this genre.

_childDocuments_.review: Melatonin, a mesmerizing rhythm-based game, effortlessly blends dreamy aesthetics with engaging gameplay. It's not just a game; it's an experience that transports players into a surreal world of dreams and music, where every beat and visual detail feels meticulously crafted.Visuals & Art Style:From the moment you dive into Melatonin, the stunning hand-drawn pastel visuals immediately catch your eye. The art style is soft, dreamy, and distinct, making it feel like you’re navigating through a series of living illustrations. The color palette is soothing, with gradients of pinks, purples, and blues creating an ethereal atmosphere that complements the theme of dreams perfectly. Each level brings a unique dreamlike scenario, beautifully designed to immerse players deeper into the world of imagination.Gameplay:Melatonin excels in its ability to turn rhythm into an immersive experience. The core of the game revolves around synchronizing actions to the beat of the music. What makes Melatonin stand out is how it seamlessly integrates rhythm gameplay with the thematic elements of dreams. Whether you’re catching flying objects, hitting alarm clocks, or interacting with abstract dream elements, every movement flows naturally with the music, creating a satisfying harmony between visuals and gameplay.The difficulty ramps up gently, ensuring that players of all skill levels can enjoy the game without feeling overwhelmed. There’s a perfect balance between challenge and accessibility, making it ideal for both rhythm game veterans and newcomers alike. Melatonin avoids the pitfalls of overcomplicating its mechanics, keeping the focus on its dreamy ambiance and the player's sense of flow.Soundtrack:The soundtrack of Melatonin is an absolute highlight.
