_childDocuments_.review: It's another one of  things. Marching under the diminutive misnomer banner , mechanically pumped out of shovelware factories straight to your local internet hentai toy store. Perhaps 30 years hence too late I come with fury to bemoan the sheer banality of this little cottage industry. When I think of the uncritical, incestuous pit of death that spawns these products, it calls to mind a quote from Jodorowsky's masterpiece film, The Holy Mountain: "We feed the computer data of coming wars and revolutions. It tells us what kind of toys to produce to condition children from birth." Drooling youtube yesmen lap these things up and do disservice to their audience with seemingly no ability to take developers to task. When 9News inferred a certain relationship between Columbine and DOOM, perhaps they were retrograde correct, and the truth is that school shootings cause boomer shooters. The term is, after all, pure marketing, a strawman representation to re-sell you something  than the false remembrance of much better games. This is a game about shooting 9000 zombies in the head with a Chicago Typewriter. It would be disingenous to pretend that there is not a certain catharsis, i.e. -fulfillment in this activity, much as it was disingenuous on the part of the developers to cloak their unremarkable game with the writings of one Howard Philip Lovecraft. I think a little kitsch is inherent in this medium, but it feels especially apparent here  we have a badly r*tarded geek appreciation for the original stories they're cribbing. Ultimately, Lovecraft is just an open source skinsuit for the developers to insert flavor into their game with, along with Dark Souls references on the walls and the not-Steve Blum voicing the protagonist character. Something particularly tone-deaf about meeting Yog-Soggoth on E1M8,  unloading 4000 rounds into his face(?) whilst dodging touhou bullet patterns, all for a geyser of blood and a sign pointing to the next level at the end.I couldn't run Forgive Me Father the first time I booted the game; Unreal Engine demands some ludicrous system requirements to sling clipart enemies and bad noise filters at my native resolution. The comic book art, to its credit, is well-drawn, with some capable animations and (albeit still-kitsch) enemy designs. There are worse art styles to rip off than Darkest Dungeon. The levels are somewhat grounded in the now-mandatory spooky New England interwar setting. You can fill in your own commentary on the name, "Pestisville." Unfortunately, whereas a more abstract setting might get away with totally nonsense level designs, the sprawling "mazes" here don't really work for what is ostensibly an attic or a hospital. If you guzzle shooters down without even chewing you might not even notice the levels are too linear to require the conspicuously-absent automap. Somewhere along the line "old-school shooter" just became synonymous with the Serious Sam school of design, presumably right after a legion of Ritalin-humming children lapped up DOOM 2016. Let me know if you've seen this scenario before: you walk into a conspicuously-open area. A large pile of supplies gleams at you in the middle. The door locks behind you as you step on the Superhealth, and monsters spawn in behind you. Circle-strafe until everything dies. This is what happens when nobody involved in the creation, critique, and purchase of these products actually plays any of the classics they pretend to enjoy. Mechanically the game is similarly poorly thought out. "Madness" in this game just functions somewhere between a combo meter and Kratos' rage, increasing bullet damage as it fills and randomly emptying out if you don't see an enemy for too long. There's no drawbacks, much less the hallucinations that made "Madness" an interesting game mechanic in the first place. This somehow recharges your powers as well, though the exact correlation between madness points and when you got another charge of your Holy Water Mop was lost on me. Using your power to freeze enemies takes about as long as reloading, so you're better off just blasting away, but I guess they tried for variety. There's a half-baked upgrade tree seems like an excuse to play the game again with the female character, because obviously i wanted the overpowered fish shotgun instead of the health boost.There's little touches of inspiration here. Some of the written lore you pick up seems passably-written to make up for butchering the pace. A rat skitters across the floor with comic-book style onomatopoeia in the first level, never to be seen again. Ditto the rare dream sequences. The mimic barrels genuinely f*cked me up once or twice. Other than that though, these games are up against the thriving, living tradition of Quake, DOOM and Build engine. Nobody plays bad fan mods when the sheer iteration has arguably produced better maps than the actual originals, and you shouldn't accept it from these wannabes. Do you really want stale chewing gum, now with zany chromatic aberration? F*ck New Blood Interactive.

_childDocuments_.review: I play a lot fo these "retro FPS" games, they're just extremely pleasing to play. Fast paced, great music, fun weapons. _childDocuments_.review: Many of us millennials grew up playing games like Doom, Quake, and Wolfenstein, and are eager to recapture the simpler, nostalgia-filled days of our childhood. And since nowadays we're the primary consumer base for video games, publishers and game devs are more than happy to oblige.Forgive Me Father falls squarely into this boomer-shooter renaissance, mixing the mechanics of classical shooters with a pastiche of H.P.Lovecraft's literary work. The result is solid and enjoyable, if not too deep or creative.No, I mean it - if you've ever read one of Lovecraft's works or seen any piece of media he inspired, it's extremely likely you already know the plot of the game.The gist of it is this: the protagonist receives a strange letter from their cousin that compels them to return to their hometown. Immediately, strange things start happening as they are set upon by monstrous creatures. While investigating their cousin's disappearance and fighting for their life, the protagonist uncovers a sinister plot involving a cult, human sacrifice, and the obligatory return of an elder god.It should be noted that any Lovecraftian elements here are purely cosmetic. The game could have easily featured a weird science and occult aesthetic and it would feel like it was inspired by early Wolfenstein instead. The story itself only serves as a loose framework to tie the levels together. The entirety of it is told in cutscenes inserted between game sections, totaling about 5 minutes.There is also a fair amount of lore notes and similar expository devices that try to create the feeling of some sort of Lovecraftian conspiracy. This is ultimately pointless since you're playing a pretty straightforward shooter, without any elements of mystery or investigation.Forgive me Father features an interesting blend of graphics and visual styles. The general level geometry is rendered in simplified 3D graphics, while the details, textures, and sprites are mostly hand-drawn. Combined with floating sound effect prompts, this creates the feeling of playing in a comic book.The enemy sprites stand out in both design and animation. Enemy designs range from the standard zombies and ghouls to Lovecraftian aberrations of twisted flesh and metal, and the limited framerate of their animation gives their movements a jerky, uncanny look. The only issue is that many of them have a muted color pallet, which sometimes makes them hard to make out against the frequently drab backgrounds.Speaking of backgrounds, the game is at its best during early, smaller-scale levels, when you fight indoors or in the cramped streets of the coastal town. In later stages, the environment is mostly composed of low-poly models covered with less detailed textures. This is especially obvious during the end of the second section, where you have an arena-style fight in what is basically a circle of brown dirt, interspersed with gray rocks, under a dark sky.The sound design is nothing to write home about. The ambient noises during traversal are replaced by a rock score when combat pops off, but both are pretty generic. The sounds the enemies make are interesting and can be pretty useful to telegraph what's waiting ahead.Starting a new game, you have a pick of two possible protagonists - an elderly priest and a plucky young journalist. Each of them has four special skills, with the priest focusing more on healing and defense, while the journalist excels at dealing damage. Each skill has a certain number of max charges, which are refilled with madness points you gain by killing enemies.Besides the mechanical benefit, high madness also affects the game visuals, turning them grayscale with occasional red highlights for blood splatters. You can also turn this effect off or leave it on permanently in the game options.Like I mentioned in the intro, Forgive Me Father tries to replicate the gameplay and feel of old-school shooters - and for the most part, it succeeds. It follows the rules of "combat chess" - you have to constantly move to avoid taking damage and prioritize which enemies to shoot. This is helped in no small part by the protagonist's high movement speed and snappy and responsive controls, especially when switching weapons.This can also present a problem, especially towards the end of the game, where you have to fight on suspended platforms and pathways. Minding your footing adds an unnecessary level of complexity to already pretty difficult fights. I probably died from falling off a platform more times than I was actually killed by enemies. This is further compounded by the fact that ammo and health bonuses have an extremely small pickup area, which can be deadly when you're in the middle of an intense combat and trying to nail that health pack while running and gunning.The protagonists' jump height is also pathetic - a wasted opportunity to introduce more verticality and platforming or at least make the existing platforming more manageable.Breaking from the boomer-shooter tradition, the game offers the unexpected feature of leveling up the protagonist. You can invest experience points earned by killing enemies into upgrading the protagonists' abilities or modifying weapons. Weapon modifications usually fall into two categories: upgrading the damage and fire rate through mechanics and science, or combining them with eldritch organisms to change the way they work.From a level design standpoint, the game is pretty linear and consists of a series of corridors that connect various "gotcha" moments. These typically come in two varieties: arena fights where all the doors close and you have to fight a horde of monsters, or enemies jumping out at you from behind or around the corner. After a while, the game's antics become predictable, but this doesn't mean dealing with them gets any easier.The levels themselves are simply a collection of horror tropes with little discernible logic behind them. The game is divided into five sections ("worlds"), each comprised of several thematically connected levels.Also, later levels try to use darkness to ramp up the difficulty, making you choose between using a lamp and firing your gun. While this is OK in itself, even the parts of the game that aren't supposed to be dark are so dimly lit, it gets pretty difficult to see where the enemies are.They also feature enemies in seemingly random places, put there solely to drain an extra bit of your ammo and health before a more challenging fight. Removing these random obstacles would do much for the flow of the game.The one standout is an interesting underwater level, where you have to use a diving suit and are limited to the harpoon as your only weapon. Considering how difficult underwater levels can be to make, it's a bit surprising this one is a highlight of the game.Forgive Me Father may not offer many new and intriguing ideas, but what it lacks in originality, it makes up in execution. It features solid old-school-inspired combat and that certain X factor that keeps you coming back for just one more level.If, like me, you're a fan of both FPS games and Lovecraft lore, you'll probably get at least 10 good hours of fun with this game. A fast and loose boomer-shooter inspired by Lovecraft's work. Unique art direction and atmosphere, fast and snappy gameplay. Haphazard level design, barely any story.

_childDocuments_.review: Forgive Me Father is a very solid FPS with a great lineup of punchy weapons, fantastic visual design, and excellent level design.  A full playthrough takes about 12-15 hours, and the enemies' variety stays fresh all the way through.  It's weak spots are in the voice acting, which was honestly a little distracting because of how silly it was, and in the jumping puzzle segments, which thankfully are few and generally short.  Neither of these weak spots meaningfully damaged my enjoyment of the game, even if I wish they had chosen a different direction for the Journalist character.  The eldritch body horror elements of the visual design are great and the gore is phenomenally rewarding.  Lots of upgrades which are paced very well as you progress through the story.  The boss fights and late-game arena battles are REALLY hard, be ready for a challenge as you approach the later part of the game!

_childDocuments_.review: You know, I'm not the biggest fan of Boomer Shooters, but since I had **Forgive Me Father** in my library from a past Humble Bundle, I thought I'd give it a....ummm...shot.It's an enjoyable Cthulhu-ish game with really cool, kind of Darkest Dungeon style graphics and a fantastic metal soundtrack with some cool dissonant melodies. Rather, it's just me having my fill of this style game ATM.The actual gameplay is super tight, guns feel good and have fun upgrades, special abilities are rad, level design is consistent with the genre, new enemies are introduced pretty consistently through the story progression, and the story itself is fun Lovecraftian. _childDocuments_.review: Among the boomer shooter scene, which honours and continues the tradition of classic FPS, 'Forgive Me Father' doesn't necessarily innovate or do much that hasn't been seen before but if you're a big fan of this sub-genre then you'll likely enjoy it.If you're familiar with these types of games, you'll notice a weapons system reminiscent of 'Project Warlock' which allows for you to choose between 2 upgrade paths for your guns and 'spells'. During the campaign you'll also come across levels which feature designs that might remind you of other games like Dusk, Wolfenstein or even Doom. The game has a deep focus on H.P Lovecraft's Cthulhu mythos, which you could compare to Quake, but Forgive Me Father focuses in on the Eldritch horror a lot more, with grotesque body horror and viscera. The fast pace of the game will find you swapping guns quickly to avoid a quick demise, killing multiple enemies in a short period of time will fill up the 'madness' bar which makes your character take less damage. It's an energetic loop, but it is made by a small studio, so you can expect some of the usual problems in boomer shooters. Notably, bad enemy AI is present and a bit notorious at times; enemies can be easily cheesed by shooting them from a corner where they will not react unless you get in their line of sight or shoot them from a distance where they will be quite helpless. Your guns' range is likely shortened because of this, but even then it's not enough and you can simplify some sections by taking a distant approach. Regardless, some enemy designs are quite creative at times and make for some fun fights. You have an enemy that takes on the appearance of an explosive barrel, but should you get too close, it sprouts limbs and runs toward you to blow you up. Another, which shoots deadly green fire at you but can be disarmed by shooting its' weak point. Some enemies can blow up into smaller chunks that crawl towards you if you fail to kill them with a headshot. There's zombies which carry extra heads in their hands, so if you blow off their heads with a headshot they'll have a spare. These are some fun ways to encourage players to play smarter; by making them considerate of when and where to shoot and move.Secret hunting is quite fun in this, there is even a powerful secret weapon you can find for looking around. Unfortunately, I found myself looking for secrets less and less as the worlds progressed. The game's pacing and map design starts to take a nosedive at world 3, which is lengthy and features larger maps that can become stale after some time. World 4 and 5 almost felt like a solid change of pace but couldn't prevent the latter half of the game from feeling less impressive with its gimmicks due to the bloated middle. The game utilises lighting and effects, as well as solid use of ambience in the music to give certain scenes that great look and feel to it that meshes well with the comic book aesthetic. However, this is unfortunately undermined by the voice acting of the playable characters which ruins the mood. Now, to add fuel to the fire with a potentially controversial opinion. The game's ambient music changes to metal during heavier combat scenarios, and while I have enjoyed the presence of metal before in games like Doom, Forgive Me Father's metal tracks never really did anything for me and I would have preferred them to be absent or repurposed to fit the uneasy tone of dread more. Sure, you could argue that the fast gunplay can only really work with metal but it just didn't impress me nearly as much as the ambient music."Not like the other games" is a statement that might not hold entirely true for  but its' appealing style is noteworthy, and in some regards it benefits from sticking to its' guns.

_childDocuments_.review: I wasn't sure if to give Forgive Me Father a positive or negative rating. I eventually ended up going for a favorable review, even though I'd consider the game something of a mixed bag.What first catches the eye is obviously the artstyle. The comic book visuals while not entirely new are fairly unique in the shooter genre, and are for the most part fairly impressive even though some of the environmental texture work looks a bit on the simple side. Enemies, while looking like the part, are sort of lacking in the animation department making them look somewhat stiff. That said, the overall effect is still pleasant looking.Almost every encounter is signaled by the start of heavy metal music, and when I say heavy I mean HEAVY. The default sound volume in FMF is incredibly high, with electric guitars being played directly inside your head by cthulhu himself, probably, which gives every encounter the right amount of excitement you need to fight the hordes of undead and eldritch creatures the game will throw at you. The same high volume extends to sound effects, some unbearably so. The metal doors closing and opening themselves as you approach in I believe Episode 3 jump scared me more than other actual horror games. Please do something about those. Please.The game offers two playable characters, The Priest and the Journalist. Both are voice acted, with the first sounding more stoic and the second trying her best to crack one liners and jokes in the vein of Duke Nukem, Blood, and other similar main characters in old school FPS. Now, I've only tried the priest briefly and the voice actor seems to play his part well enough. My actual playthrough was with the journalist, which er, can sometime sound a bit off. Although the campiness eventually grew on me.Gameplay-wise characters are distinguished by their personal skills, each requiring the build up of "madness" acquired by simply fighting enemies. The more you kill, the less damage you take, and the more you inflict, which results in even more madness acquired. The skills are, in theory, a central part of combat, and can even be upgraded. In practice, they don't work as good as they should. The journalist's consists of, first, a blunt that somehow grants you a sword for a limited time which restores your health with every kill. Cool in theory, in practice the hit box for said sword is so small that you'll miss most hits, instead leaving you wide open. If that was not enough it will barely do any damage later on if left unleveled, so if saved as last resort to restore some HP it will in most cases have a counterproductive effect. Second, a camera that stuns enemies and stops them on their track. Nice, if not that the range of it is really, really short and in life or death situations will rarely be effective. Third, a voodoo doll that deals damage to all enemies surrounding you in a small area. Seems good at first, but again, it quickly becomes ineffective as the damage barely does anything especially in the later stages of the game. And lastly, what I found the most effective, cigarettes that slow down time for everyone except you for a few seconds, something that can actually affect the outcome of an encounter even in the latter parts of the game. If not... if not that it seems to be bugged and in some levels it caused massive slowdowns in such a way that made things harder to hit while active, making it effectively useless.Now, all of these special skills can be leveled up to level 3, something I have not done, and here's why. The game uses a skill tree of sorts from which you can upgrade your skills, weapons and maximum health and armor. Additionally, one of these skill allows you to get more experience points with each kill (protip: spend your first three points on this skill). And yet, even with this skill unlocked, leveling up becomes increasingly difficult as you go further into the game, even considering the large quantity of enemies you'll be put against in the last third of the adventure. In other words, you'll be unable to acquire everything and will have to make some decisions on what to learn, which in my case was mostly weapon upgrades. Which brings me to the next point: weapon upgrades often bring you a choice, a non reversible one at that (unless you decide to reload your save), something that in some cases will change the ammo type of the firearm, sometimes in one that is less common. The general feeling is that, while the system is kinda fun (the upgraded shotgun rocks), it's also in need of some rebalancing. Why would I want to upgrade my flashlight/lantern when XP is so limited? What if you decide to do so early on and realize it's a waste in the final stages of the game when leveling becomes slow as molasses and you are unable to upgrade actual useful equipment?Speaking of balancing, this is perhaps my biggest gripe with the game. If you've played lots of FPS in the past, old and new, and want to start the game at anything higher than the normal difficulty setting, don't. Save yourself the headache. Things start balanced enough until around the midpoint of the game, where it starts throwing enemy upon enemy at you, eventually reaching the final episode, where some of the most annoying critters I've ever seen in a FPS are introduced. The last episode loves, it loves tossing flying enemies throwing projectiles at you from far distances, and it loves mixing them up with every other type of enemy. It's hard to even tell what some of these enemies are, as they flail, bounce and trot uncontrollably left and right as they had just stolen one of your blunts and smoked it just before the encounter. High-as-a-kite-Kirby, I've called the little pink blob sliding all over the room shooting all kind of things in every direction. Perhaps an even worse enemy than the Kleers in Serious Sam, which I hate with a passion. But Serious Sam, though, allows you to save in the middle of a fight, and perhaps more importantly, it usually gives you enough ammunition to deal with everything in your way.As other people have mentioned, at times it's unclear if deep inside FMF wants to be a Survival Horror or a FPS. Ammo has a carrying limit (something you can upgrade to be fair), a bit too limited for some weapons, and if that was not enough the game gets incredibly stingy in making you find more in some of the late stage levels, essentially pitting you in forced encounters but then refusing to give you a mean to actually try to come out of it alive. This one level at some point required me to shoot a barrel to break open a wall. Enemies are hidden in the room, and enemies are also after the breach I just opened in the wall. I have 10 bullets left between 2 weapons. No, there are no ammo pickups nearby. I lost count of how many times I had to retry this segment, each time trying to use less ammunition or attempting to run past enemies (I pretty much couldn't).Now let's talk about the save system. Unlike old school FPS where quick saving was common, FMF takes a Turok approach to things and only allows you to save at specific points in the level (luckily, unlike survival horrors of old, doesn't require an item to do so). Initially this is not much of a problem, but here we are in the last couple episodes constantly backtracking to the save point after every encounter so I don't have to deal with Kirby on crack for the umpteenth time.If that was not enough, the game had this bug that made so the "reload checkpoint" option after dying sometimes would instead make you restart the level from the beginning, essentially making me waste more time between more loading screens. This happened to me over and over, effectively skyrocketing my hatred for stoner Kirby and his friends.Having said all of that, FMF is for the most part a fun game with a moment to moment action that keeps you going straight into the next level. That is, until the balance issues start crawling up.

_childDocuments_.review: FMF1 always looked intriguing but it was the sequel that excited me the most. I played the early access version of that and I was ready to play the official release until the discord community advised me to play the first game to follow the story. I’m glad to have completed FMF1, but I don’t know if the story was worth it as this is the game’s biggest weakness. It’s mysterious and it’s trying to flesh out the story through lore scattered in the levels but the lore chosen, the amount and relevance in that order is badly done. And you can’t look up that lore again. The main cutscenes before every act do look cool and they do a better job but a lot of it is flashy with little substance. It’s as if the story was an afterthought and only added after the rest was complete. The premise is very cool though and the ending does help you understand the beginning of FMF2 better. What is also most important is this kind of game being perfectly enjoyable without the story as it’s a boomer shooter and it’s a good one at that. The pacing is high and it feels arcade like as there is no reload animation for most weapons. You will keep firing until you’re out of bullets. There are 5 acts with different amount of levels, you can play with 2 characters that have their own special skills, there is endless mode that’s pretty fleshed out and there is new game plus too. The game is very good about the amount of content you have. The levels are short for the most part but they’re highly replay-able thanks to the skill tree and character specific skills. You earn XP and you can use it to upgrade whatever you want to create very different weapon upgrades. It’s incredibly satisfying to experiment and all those options are viable. The upgraded weapons have really cool designs and the animations of the skills are fire. The controls are good, the levels are mostly well designed, there is some iconic voice acting and some of the soundtrack sounds so nice. It goes without saying that the game has a distinct art style and it’s great. The achievements are also fun and fair. You’re basically asked to complete the game with both characters, do some skill related kills, level specific objectives and spend some time on endless mode.So we already talked about the story not being all that. The other con is the completionist aspect and how it’s done. You can find secrets and lore, you’re shown the amount during a level. But when you end a level, you’re also shown stats of total enemies killed and sometimes total barrels broken. I don’t understand why the rest of the stats are kept after a level ends. They should have been viewable at all times together with the secrets and lore. But not only that, the game doesn’t keep track of what you’ve accomplished in every level aside from the result screen after completing one. Also you can’t go back to get whatever you missed. There is chapter select but your current progress is not tracked or updated when playing them. This makes the whole thing pointless. It seems the developers were aware as there are no achievements related to getting 100% on every level aside from one specific level. Trust me, it’s the right choice here. It feels like a relic from the past (old school design). The game was very enjoyable, I spent over 25 hours getting all the achievements. It kind of kept me away from playing other games since it was on my mind often. Btw, I played it on easy which is not something I usually do with FPS games but normal got ridiculous quickly. You can change the difficulty at any point and I recommend you take a look if you’re having a difficult time. I also highly recommend you playing the game if you’re looking for a boomer shooter. Just don’t do it for the story or the completionist aspect.

_childDocuments_.review: So....I'd give a neutral if I had to give it a rating.Let's be clear: as a boomer shooter, at least first impression wise, it feels fairly tight, the weapons are interesting, the upgrades are...intriguing (as much as some of them are fairly useless imho, like the throwing knives), and as I'm reading about the Journalist does seem to have some issues balancing wise, but aside from that it feels *good* as gameplay loop.What I really am having trouble with, is the tonal dissonance. From the artstyle, reminiscent of Darkest Dungeon, to the name, to the description, it's sold as if it's a lovecraftian game, with tension, madness, terror, and so on.What it *is*, instead, is a boomer shooter with a lot of pop references (the DS bonfire, the Doctor's blue box, etc), with constant action movie one liners with a...let's be frank, not great voice acting, and the madness being just a sort of temporary buff/way to fuel some abilities. It's...I don't know, it feels like the 'H.P. Lovecraft' inspiration is only to put some monsters and tentacles here and there, without any sort of tone proper to the sort of stories I was expecting.So, do I reccomend this? Gameplay wise...yeah, I think I can, tad rough about the edges but yes.tonally? If you're looking for horror, nope. Not at all. I don't know if it's gonna get better going forward on that regard, but I doubt it.

_childDocuments_.review: What is it with the retro-shooter genre and not offering save game functionality? Does anybody really enjoy playing the same section of game 10x in a row because of a simple mistake that causes you to die, bad luck, or even (gasp) low skill? This game even has save technology fully implemented as you can save as many times as you want once you find the level checkpoint. They just often place the first/only checkpoint so late in the level that it's kind of meaningless. Let me decide if I want to save and when, don't force it on me because of some misguided idea about preserving difficulty and "game integrity". If i want to "ruin" the game by saving more often than the designer intended, let me have that choice!! YOU don't have to save if it ruins the game for you,  but not being able to save ruins the game for me.There is a workaround, but it's pretty dumb: change the difficulty level to super easy and blast thru the part that you've been stuck on, and then change back to your preferred difficulty. How is that an improvement over just offering a real save slot? But at least it gives you a way to get past a stuck point without repeating it 10+ times.Other than that it's a decent game, with hit or miss level design; at it's best it occasionally reaches amid evil/dusk quality, at it's worst it's project warlock. Still, I did enjoy it enough to finish it. There's a lot of frenetic fight pits where you have to kill a bunch of rapidly spawning enemies before the door unlocks and lets you move on to the next area.  Like 3-4 per level, minimum. Not my favorite design, I like being able to think a bit about how to approach a tough area, and whittle down their numbers. This is blind run and shoot, no time to think.

_childDocuments_.review: This is one of the most fun experiences with a game I had this year. It gives that taste of a dark horror game with a comic book art style that blends in so perfectly together. I love the comic book aesthetic, and it's not just with the graphics. There's words that pop up relating to the action, such as "BOOM" and "SPLAT". It's a little touch that goes a long way in giving the game it's own look and feel. The atmosphere is always dark and gritty, while also having colors pop out that helps the characters stand out from the environments.Speaking of which, the enemies are designed in such a creative way. All of them are these grotesque abominations that really show off how bad this world has gotten. There's zombie looking dudes, a chubby gangster looking dude, a hazmat squid looking thing... yeah, a little strange. But also so unique and fun to see. There's also variety in which they attack. The combat system is extremely rewarding. The main gimmick of this game is the Madness system. The more Madness you have, the more damage you do, which is fueled by more kills. This forces you to keep the flow of combat going, pushing you towards a swift and efficient way of handling this rather than slow and safe. There are also these special abilities that spend points that you only acquire when reaching a certain madness level. I started the game on Hard, which I am so glad I did. Each enemy has a different approach on killing it if you want to be as efficient as possible, and there are plenty of encounters where that could be the difference between life and death. Hard difficulty seems to force strategy onto you, which without it, might feel like just running and shooting through each section. The zombies are melees that run at you, but also have a mechanic where if you head shot them and they're holding a head, they put in on and continue coming after you. The chubby-gangsters shoot light balls at you and try to keep some distance, but if you don't head shot them, they split in half and crawl towards you. So remembering each enemies' mechanics is key to surviving throughout the levels.Which leads into weapons, which are more on the normal looking side of things. You have a revolver, shotgun, tommy-gun, so on and so forth. There is a leveling system, which is hard to tell when you get another level. There's an XP bar next to your character's picture, but I never noticed it until writing this review, so presenting it in a more clear would be nice. With each level you get a point to spend in upgrading a gun you have, upgrading your abilities, etc. The weapon upgrades are handled really well here. Instead of just boosting stats, it changes the gun entirely, appearance and mechanically. With the revolver you can either dual wield, which decreases accuracy and increases fire rate, or make it longer range. The shogun can either have more shells per shot or make the shells ricochet off walls. The way it's handled here makes each upgrade a choice in strategy rather than just making yourself stronger.I really have nothing negative to say about this game so far. The levels are designed extremely well, there's a ton of secrets to find. There's lore spread throughout the levels if you're into that. The whole retro feel along with the art style is a combination that works much better than I was ever expecting. If you are interested, please go give it a shot. Especially with the 10% off at Early Access launch. It is definitely worth $18, and $20 at that. A perfect price for an excellent and tantalizing experience.

_childDocuments_.review: This is the most fun I've had in a shooter for a long time.Gunplay is fun and rewarding, there's a decent push to change from weapon to weapon but the game doesn't outright force you every two minutes to change weapons, you have a lot of options in how to level up your character and change your weapons through skills.The weapons feel very rewarding, you get a nice flow of new weapons throughout. The recoil on each weapon feels perfect, very enjoyable and the hitboxes are some of the best in a game I've played in recent member. I thoroughly enjoyed the upgraded semi-automatic rifle to make it full-auto. Recoil is very much present but it can be controlled and fun to aim and shoot with. Lots of fun!The skill tree is decent and adds an extra layer of dept. You find that you have to stop and think about the skill points you use and potential impact each skill will have on gameplay, your guns and character. Skills aren't simple "+5 damage" or "+5 defence"(There are some skills like that) but more "This changes your weapon significantly, what kind of ammo it uses and how it works."The art style is very reminiscent of Void Bastards which was a great rogue like game I thoroughly enjoyed and found very visually pleasing.Levels are very well done and varied. You have a decent amount of corridors, tight corridors, open corridors and large open areas. Some of the levels are a real treat that you don't expect to come across in a game like this. I genuinely found myself saying out loud "That's actually so cool" simply due to the fact I wasn't expecting the game to change it's level design in such a way and change the setting so much between acts.This is a great game and I fully recommend playing it. For €20 this is a lot of fun you'll have in around 10 hours with some replay value in trying it on higher difficulties or with another character.Really good, well polished and enjoyable retro shooter!

_childDocuments_.review: tl;dr, good game at present, can be a great game with some improvements - solid 7/10 currently. I really liked it and I'm looking forward to more.Detailed pros, neutrals & cons below, but includes some spoilers as to content.Pros- Game controls very well. Character is fast and fluid, which suits the backpedal/strafe style required.- Gunplay is excellent, guns have good feedback and they feel effective.- Graphics are excellent. Enemy design is unique and enemy telegraphing is fairly clear. Level aesthetics are varied.- Skill points and active abilities add an extra layer of choice and playstyle.- Level design harkens back to Doom/Quake with key hunting to obfuscate linear design.- Leaning into Lovecraft inspiration makes for solidly tense and unsettling areas.Neutral- If you're expecting Lovecraft's 'cosmic horror', that isn't what you'll get. You're killing the horrors, not going incurably insane from them. If you want slow burn, look elsewhere, it's a game more influenced by Doom and its successors.- Game frequently uses item pickups to spawn enemies, often having them show up behind you. This can get frustrating if you're not a fan of this gameplay style.- In addition to the above, the general flow is arena room to arena room fight, with some run and gun corridor sections. Some people may find this bland.- Skill points can feel superfluous when some choices are 'must' take, and there's no respec option presently.- Game has no checkpoints between rooms, just save points so dying can lose a lot of progress.- Levels are, generally, short - 10 to 20 minutes long aside from boss levels.Cons/Issues- Music is... good? But feels very out of place at times, the heavy rock doesn't really fit the atmosphere. The music in the hospital and cemetery areas feel more suitable. I can understand that it's to 'pump' the player up, but if guitar is a must a stronger focus on drone/doom mixed with strings would develop the atmosphere further.- The first level is a very rough introduction due to enemy numbers and checkpoints, while I understand it's there to introduce a lot of the mechanics and ideas it could put a number of people off. It's possible to get to the save room, not save, grab the key and then get mobbed by enemies requiring a complete restart. With the narrow spaces and the way enemies can easily box you in, there are a lot of potential frustration points - especially the final room being so small.- There is a noticeable delay between being able to switch weapons, you have to wait for animations to fully complete before you can swap - this is especially noticeable on the shotgun - and can kill a lot of the game's fluid combat. Would much prefer to be able to instantly swap weapons.- The Rusty Vito feels superfluous, it has low accuracy and the basic pistol fires on auto anyway. It feels like a 'use this to save other ammo' instead of a weapon with a useful niche. Hopefully a rebalance or an alternate upgrade would fix this.- The G40 upgrade for the pistol is excellent for DPS and feels necessary as a sniper option, but is frustrating on low tier enemies because the -damage means it won't one-shot a basic zombie on headshot any more - they're left with a sliver of health. Adjusting this so it still one shots basic enemies would do a lot for game feel.- At least in current EA, if you don't choose the grenade launcher upgrade on the MP18 you won't have an explosive weapon. This can make things a lot more difficult since you lose a crowd control option.- The swamp level's visual clarity is awkward, where you have a lot of green enemies up against green reeds.- The Yellow Cultist's orb following you forever is not a fun mechanic. Nobody likes the Vore from Quake. Nobody ever said "My favourite enemy is The Vore and I want it to be in every game from now on." It needs to stop following you after a distance, be destroyable, or not do 90 degree turns around doors and walls. It was not fun design back in Quake and it's not fun design here.- The harpoon feels like a combination power weapon/sniper, but comes extremely late, especially when there are a number of longer ranged encounters earlier. Hopefully there's a sniper-like available earlier when there's more content.

_childDocuments_.review: The first thing I noticed about Forgive Me Father was the black screen it presented on boot. I searched discussions to find a solution, and did a few things on other monitors while trying to figure out how to resolve the issue. Before I did anything however, after about 10 minutes or so, the game picked itself up and displayed a launch screen. The game itself starts with a lot of story. I expected a comparable amount of story in-game, but the game at its core is a fairly basic 2.5D shooter. The game mechanics were innovative, but playing on default settings, I also noticed some of the worst screen tearing I'd ever seen. There is a VSync option, and turning it on resolved that issue, but that's not something that everyone is going to know how to do. If your game suffers from such poor screen synchronization, then you should have VSync on by default.All in all, I might come back to this game or give it a positive review if the system was more stable. After booting it up for the second time and being confronted by a second black screen, I decided that the game wasn't novel enough for me to keep dealing with these tech issues. A 2.5D shooter similar to old DOOM is very much a solved problem and I expect any game implementing one to be a far smoother and glitch-free experience than this one is.

_childDocuments_.review: A thrilling and unique retro-shooter that combines all the hallmarks of epic 90's shooters with a gritty and grotesque Lovecraftean world to deliver a creepy yet exciting experience. The game takes notes from the titans of the sub-genre such as DOOM, Blood, DUSK and several others but manages to puts its' own spin on things with its' line-up of unique weapons and upgrades, gameplay altering abilities, and the "MADNESS" mechanic that encourages a high-risk aggressive playstyle.- I was skeptical of the way the game looked at first, but the game manages to combine well drawn old-school 2D sprites with gorgeous current-gen lighting to create a one of a kind art style.- Like many of its' predecessors in the genre, FMF has an original progressive rock soundtrack that turns up to 11 during tense combat situations. I very often found myself jamming to the music instead of loading a checkpoint after I had already been torn to shreds.- On top of it's very gratifying weapons, each weapon and player ability has an upgrade path that can transform each weapon into an otherworldly revamped version of itself which completely alters the the way the weapon is used.- The story is presented in the form of cutscenes and clues that you can find as you play that paint the picture of what has happened in this dark and twisted world. I'm glad it's a retro-shooter so the story is ultimately of no consequence because I didn't really think it was all that interesting.- I made the mistake of playing as the journalist on my first playthrough and later discovered that the priest's skillset is far superior. In addition to that, the journalist's voice acting is horrendous to the point that I had to mute voice volume in the settings.- The game is pretty damn difficult on the highest skill, which is exactly what I want from this type of game. However, in the later chapters, it seems like a conscious decision was made to starve the player of ammunition which seemed like a very uninteresting way to artificially increase difficulty in an already difficult game.* - the dev team is actively taking feedback and has been patching and improving the game since release, so these criticisms may not be valid if you're reading this down the road.

_childDocuments_.review: I would begrudgingly recommend it. It can be fun, and worthwhile, but it's flawed. Deeply flawed. And the ways in which it is flawed can really drag the game down.The game has such a striking art style. I really loved just looking around and taking in the levels. I think it's what most people are going to be drawn to and what is going to stand out the most. So what sucks is that because of a particular mechanic that is cool in concept, the screen can become black and white (with the exception of blood). This often reduces your visibility to the point where you're just shooting randomly. It can be turned off, which I recommend you do. In fact, any screen effect ought to be turned completely off with the exception of, surprisingly, the film grain. It can look really impressive in certain situations.What bummed me out a lot though is that while the enemies look incredible with these ultra sharp, highly detailed and illustrated 2D cutouts, they can often be nearly impossible to actually see. Seriously, I have no idea what a lot of the enemies even are in this game. When you first start, it's your typical zombies. It doesn't take long for the enemies to either move quickly enough or require a fast kill to basically obscure what they even are for the entire game. Which is a shame since their design was so clearly important. You can imagine how this problem combined with the one I previously mentioned can just suck the fun out of these encounters. Before I turned off all the screen effects and the black and white mechanic, there were multiple times when the screen would literally be entirely black and I would just be running and shooting aimlessly because it's impossible to even tell what is going on.The guns are pretty standard but there is an attempt to make them unique through a level up system. But they lack punch. There is no real feedback to them. Shooting this game's version of a rocket launcher has the same feedback as opening a folder on your desktop. It just plays an animation with no consideration for what it would feel like for the player.Then there's the two characters. One character is so clearly, and without any room for debate, better than the other. The reporter is just straight up not well designed. Making your special ability depend on melee is a terrible idea when many enemies cannot be reached for melee, especially bosses. You know, the encounters where you'd most need to use those special abilities.The story also really seems to be have been abandoned as the game goes on. At first, you're coming across notes left and right. By the end, I felt like I never saw one. But it isn't like what story you encounter is riveting and gripping and really capturing your attention. It's just a loose thread of motivation to pull the player forward.Levels can be super interesting but are so wildly inconsistent. Sometimes you'll get to a level that takes 5 minutes. Others take 30 minutes. Some feel like tiny flashes of an idea, others feel like a fully realized concept.There is one boss that for whatever reason TANKED my performance. I mean it's so bad I worried the game would the either crash or I wouldn't be able to navigate the combat arena and win. Other people in the discussion forum seem to have the same issue. I don't know if it's somehow an intention effect happening that manages to mimic the way a game looks when dropping to 10fps, or if it's actually just tanking that bad. Either way it's an absolutely brutally low point in an already flawed game. It absolutely needs changed or fixed or something, there is absolutely no justification for it.I encountered a bug multiple times where the game would crash. I found a workaround, but if you look at the discussion forum for the game and find people talking about the same bug, some people's workaround is way, way more work the game is even worth. I would recommend not keeping more than one quick save and one main save, as its tied to saves.Actually, now that I've written all this out, I don't recommend this game. There are so many boomer shooters out there and a handful of them are of such high quality that I don't know why you'd want to play one where the entire time you're going to be trying to weigh the good against the bad. It's at times frustrating and other times disappointing and in between those seemingly constant expressions of shortcomings you may occasionally catch a glimpse of the game you were hoping you bought. It feels like an early access game that still has an undefined amount of time left but unfortunately that's not the case. Unfortunately, this is it.

_childDocuments_.review: The first few levels are very important to an FPS game, if the game cannot get the player hooked in the first act then there isn't much left to see, even if there is. The first levels of this game are a slog and a design failure in my eyes, they did not leave me wondering what is in the future levels, what my weapons could be like, and what further upgrades I wanted, it just felt like a chore to possibly get to a cooler level or item. The items by the way never truly get shown to the player. You don't need handholding or a tutorial to introduce usable item, but the player should be shown what it can do when they first get it. This game does not do that, you pick up the item, it is explained and thats it. You don't get a single charge to just try it out in an empty room or a single enemy, you just get the new thing and move on and hopefully remember you have it and what it does, and you won't remember it's there until you press "r" accidently on reload instinct and use your item.  I just feel the opening of this could have been done better and really hurts what could possibly be a very good looking and good game. I may try again at some point but not anytime soon.There is also platforming. Yeah.

_childDocuments_.review: As someone who likes and has read a large swath of H.P lovecrafts game I can say I really want to like this game, it has a clear understanding of what makes the Cthulhu mythos a interesting setting, from bouts of Madness that would make one wonder if what just happened was real to creatures designs that are gooey, gross and enigmatic I can dig it.BUT!at the same time the combat feels weightless and with little feedback, sure you get giblets and a big thwack sound happens when you delete an enemy with your shotgun but you don't feel the feeling in your bones that that thing from beyond is going to spend the next millennia in eldritch therapy about it. Also the first boss barely felt like an afterthought being killed in less than 2 minutes with just the Tommy gun.The RPG mechanics and abilities were okay but I feel like it needed more time to cook. That or it shouldn't exist, the first episode barely needed them on Hard and I never really felt the need to use them with the abundance of pickups.5/10 get it on sale if you like Lovecraft and the stories based on his works and can tolerate a mediocre shooter.I am cautiously optimistic that Forgive me Father will be a Improvement but I'm not buying it on release or anything.

_childDocuments_.review: Unusually good for a Cthulhu game, it's more helpful to think of it as a Quake or Duke Nukem 3D clone rather than Doom (for one thing, in Doom you virtually never run out of shotgun ammo and it happens all the time here). It's far from perfect, but definitely worth it in a sale. I played as the Priest, as I'm not one of those gamers who feels compelled to always be a woman.GOOD+ Graphics are fairly decent, like Borderlands meets Classic Doom.+ Zero lag on an MSI laptop with RTX3060M and Nvidia processor, on Epic settings.+ Weapons are generally all solid and worth using.+ Temporary power ups are extremely useful. + Gameplay flows extremely well and is quite addictive.+ Music is pretty cool.+ Most enemies can be critically damaged which alters some of their behaviour.+ Tons of pickups to keep you fighting.+ Very well-placed save points which take a split second to use.+ Special abilities all regenerate.+ Virtually all upgrades are useful, it's hard to do it wrong unless you upgrade melee.+ Second character to choose who gets different weapons and abilities; not sure if her playthrough is different.+ NG+ and Endless Mode on beating the main game.BAD- Horrific voice acting with some of the worst dialogue you'll ever hear in a game. Makes Resident Evil on PS1 look Oscar worthy. - Enemies become extremely repetitive even when new types are added, as they generally behave the exact same way.- Flying and hyper-mobile enemies, who teleport away when you get near them, make Elden Ring look fair. (One late game enemy flies at you like a missile and detonates for almost unavoidable damage.)- I still don't know what half of the enemies look like because they stay too far away, are too mobile and the later levels are pitch dark.- Oh yeah, the later levels are pitch dark.- A lot of incoming enemy fire is nearly impossible to dodge for mere mortals like me.- Miles too much emphasis on platforming late game.- The weird paralysis ability (rubbing monsters with a broom, I'm not joking) seems worthless and far less useful than all the other abilities.- Later levels are quite maze-like, because it's an FPS and somehow FPS means maze-like.- The ending is absolutely crap and feels like a middle finger after putting 10 hours in.- I didn't want to play a second time whether on NG+, Endless mode or the Journalist character. Too many other games demanding my time; honestly couldn't face more horribly delivered "dialogue" or the same dark platforming maps again.RATINGI'd probably give it 7/10 for effort, it's great fun most of the time but some parts of this game are in desperate need of improvement. Second game looks like the same thing over again so I'll pass for now.

The priest is more serious in one-liners, and the journalist treats all with enthusiasm. The cutscenes are the same for both, and the game itself, starting from the end of the 4th episode, becomes.. eh? Too predictable and faded, like the plot twist. The final boss is disappointing, since by this time the char is powerfull, and increasing the difficulty doesn't increase interest in the battle, which is quite simple in design. Either way, shooting chthonic monsters here is FUN! Definitely recommend!
_childDocuments_.name: Forgive Me Father

_childDocuments_.review: I don't hate this game, but this game has a VERY uninteresting start. The levels are basically squares and you really feel it. Enemies get thrown at you and you circle strafe them since there is barely any room to move, which gets progressively more boring each time the game makes you do it. _childDocuments_.name: Forgive Me Father

_childDocuments_.review: Fun. It's like CULTIC but it's totally different. It's more action-oriented, 2 playable characters, 8 unique weapons with unique upgrades, and much clean but more dark graphic. Totally recommended to buy it. And there's only one ending choose whatever you like, like skills and weapon upgrades and characters.
_childDocuments_.name: Forgive Me Father

_childDocuments_.review: This is a hard game, it starts off Ok but it's tough as nails the more you play it. Something that needs to be known from the start is that this game is about finding a good strategy of managing your power-ups in built up enemy situations and against bosses.Sometimes the game will seem impossible to beat a boss or get past a part until you start using the power-ups and fighting in a strategic way, but sometimes the game can just be unfair at times like throwing horde after horde at you without enough power-ups or ammo which brings me to the next point, as soon as you get the unlimited ammo for a certain amount time power-up you get less ammo throughout those levels meaning you have to make do with a very low amount of ammo, but despite all that it's still possible to get through if you take enough breaks away from the game.The music is awesome and the sounds are great, both help to create a great atmosphere, the graphics are comic book style and will never age, this also adds to the atmosphere.This game will not be for everyone, but if you like a challenge and something with a bit of strategy involved then you will like this game, if you want a casually stress free gaming experience you will not like this game.Recommended.
_childDocuments_.name: Forgive Me Father

_childDocuments_.review: I have acquired every achievement, have completed runs with both characters with completely different loadouts, have found every secret and story memento, have gone all out in endless mode, and am currently starting my first NG+ run.This is a $60+ experience, sold as a $20 package, and the $10 for the soundtrack will become an essential purchase after hearing the music in game.Overall, FMF is well optimized, and has superb gameplay, complimented with the awesomely gruesome art style and character design. Its feel is between classic build engine FPS, and the modern "old school throwback," that many other developers have tried, and failed, to create to such a level that Byte Barrel has achieved here, and with such incredible replayability involved too.The Lovecraftian genre, in the world of gaming, is surprisingly lacking. To the point where there are really only a handful of outstandingly good entries, at least in the shooter category. So having this game to fulfill that need to face an armada of unknown horrors, is just perfect. And with the sequel on the way, it is absolutely worth playing now, more than ever.Well done.
_childDocuments_.name: Forgive Me Father

_childDocuments_.review: This is not a game that does anything particularly different or groundbreaking, and I am perfectly okay with that. Where it really shines for me is through it's distinctive visual style, dark atmosphere, and intense combat underpinned by an absolutely banging metal soundtrack. As a fan of Lovecraft's works I enjoyed the overall theme and designs of the enemies, weapons and world. The art design is excellent, and the comic book style lends itself perfectly to the setting. The use of darkness throughout the game was particularly good, making some sections genuinely terrifying to navigate. The combat is fast paced, claustrophobic and intense. If you don't like being locked in small rooms with heaps of enemies, this probably isn't going to be for you. Weapon variety is great, with different forks of upgrades for each weapon that drastically change the function and appearance.The levels are mostly short and sweet but numerous, plunging you through a variety of environments and pitting you against progressively more challenging and varied enemies.The story takes a secondary role here, told through occasional animated cutscenes and story hints scattered around the maps. While not the most cohesive story, it serves it's role well enough for a game that focuses  mainly around the slaying of creatures of the unknown. Don't go into it expecting a complex narrative experience. My only real gripe was a portion of incredibly difficult platforming sections towards the end of the game, which I struggled with immensely despite the devs being reasonably generous with the amount of attempts you get. Other than that, I loved the campaign and thought the difficulty and progression was paced well, playing on hard I always felt challenged but capable. Additionally, the endless mode provides some entertainment when you want to jump straight into the action, and New Game+ offers some fun (and painful) modifiers for the gameplay. Overall, Forgive Me Father has quickly become one of my favourites of the genre.If you like Lovecraft, shooters and metal, then you can't really go wrong.
_childDocuments_.name: Forgive Me Father

_childDocuments_.review: This game is a beautiful homage to classic first-person shooters while also being a fun and exciting experience from start to finish. The gameplay is fast and simple (in a good way.) It does not have character customization, or gun attachments, or loot boxes, or even the ability to aim down sights. It has you, a large variety of monsters for you to kill, and a dozen guns to kill them with. It forgoes modern shooter tropes to create a fast-paced, skill focused, combat loop that rewards taking risks and throwing yourself at the enemy. To beat this game on its higher difficulties you must be able to aim good, move fast, manage your ammo, and use your powers at the best possible times. All of this leads to a challenging, but enjoyable, experience throughout the playthrough. Now I was going to leave off here, but I could not go without mentioning the art and music. The art is amazing, and it is obvious with each monster, weapon, or cutscene that this game was made with some serious passion behind it. The environments are awesome, and they rarely feel boring or repetitive. As for the music; if you like the music in Doom 2016 or Doom Eternal, you will like the music in this game. It complements the style, tone, and gameplay perfectly - leading to intense battles, eerie walkthroughs of abandoned buildings and epic boss fights. Overall, this was one of the best shooters I have played in recent memory. So, if you are looking for a skill based retro shooter with beautiful visuals and music that makes you excited to kill some Eldrich horrors, this is a game for you.
_childDocuments_.name: Forgive Me Father

_childDocuments_.review: The game clearly has a lot of passion in it, with a cool upgrade tree and nice enemy variety, but I found it mostly boring unfortunately. So many of the levels just feel the same, with so many combat tools that the game doesn't feel balanced around which turns you into an unstoppable god, even on hard mode. On sale it's alright but it's in a crowded genre with many better options
_childDocuments_.name: Forgive Me Father

_childDocuments_.review: The game plays like the original DOOM, but looks like Darkest Dungeon. Very simple gameplay, you aim and you shoot. You do get a few (about 5) different active skills for each character and about 8 weapons, some reminiscent of DOOM.Killing enemies while unharmed charges your "skill bar", and obviously using skills empties it.There's also a large skill tree, where you get to choose/modify different passive abilities or completely change the way some weapons work.I can recommend this for the price its going (15 bucks right now) if you like easy, no-bs shooters with a lovecraftian comic graphic.If you want to see my first impression vid of this game (and many other new indies), check out my YouTube:
_childDocuments_.name: Forgive Me Father

_childDocuments_.review: If I was rating this just on the graphics it would be much higher, I think the game is beautiful! However, there's that other part, you know, the gameplay. It's kind of a big deal. And while it's perfectly fine, it's not great.Everything is middle of the road. The only thing that sticks out is the skill tree. I like how if you go down one path it alters your weapon and removes the other options. The choices there feel like they have some real impact how you play the game. I also like the enemy design. Being able to shoot something on the enemy to break it which transforms them into something else is cool.That said, the guns are average and they don't feel very powerful. Also, the characters are exactly the same but for some special skills. I expected more. There isn't much else to say, the story is sparse. Little notes here and there that you collect but with little meaning so it isn't a driving factor.This may seem silly but it boils down to this. The game is huge! Could I spend 4 hours playing this? Yes! But it's far bigger and therefore much more drawn out. I was feeling a lot of repetition and sadly I didn't even make it to the first boss. This probably comes down to personal preference. I was looking for a short but constantly exciting experience and I think there is one here but it's far too drawn out. 5/10.
_childDocuments_.name: Forgive Me Father

_childDocuments_.review: Pretty decent old school shooter. However I don't think it's as good as most of the reviews imply nor as good as stuff like Dusk, Amid Evil or Ion Fury.What I didn't like:-I know it's subjective but I am not the biggest fan of the visual style of the game-boss fights are bullet sponges and there the game is like a bullet hell game which I am not sure that belongs in this genre-same goes with the skill tree and the activatable skills-the game consists of 5 episodes, all on medium difficulty and getting 100% achievs took me around 8 hours, but honestly after like world 3 or so I was kinda bored with the game-performance is pretty good EXCEPT most of the time in episode 5 where it's really not great for some reason-no quicksaves at all, you can only save the game at fixed points which is a shame for such a game imho-the attacks of some enemies are almost impossible to dodge-balancing on normal: most of the game is pretty easy but like the last 2 episodes the game gives you way less health pickups at a point were it actually gets kinda hard (tho I figuered later that the character I didn't pick has a skill which heals you, which means that one of the characters (the priest) is way better)-some levels are way too dark and yes you have a lamp or a flash light but if you use that you can't hold a gun, which sucksWhat I liked: -overall gunplay is usually pretty good-I liked that the character you picked talks here and there and the voice acting is pretty good-level design is also quite good usually
_childDocuments_.name: Forgive Me Father

_childDocuments_.review: Forgive Me Father is a Doom style shooter with a lovecraftian artstyle.For the most part while I am giving it a positive review, it's not anything too special besides artstyle, I played both characters, I ended up prefering the journalist for the fact their playstyle is way more interesting and aggressive than the priest. All the guns have reasonable purpose and don't notable become obsolete.I'd say the mid to early late game levels are my favorite, complex enough while not being obscenely difficult.The later levels I had to drop the difficulty down to easy instead of normal as it was becoming too hard and became exhausting to play in the ending levels and I'm not inexperienced with shooters by a long shot.The story and ending were alright, the writing, voice acting, and the ending were alright. They could have used extra polish. it didn't really have enough set up for it to really land, there were a few scenes that did do some justice for the ending, but some more story telling from the enviroment, enemies being in certain areas that make sense would help with this, when the levels started becoming more chaotic and more sufficiently mind bending, with corridors stretching unnaturally, and overall showing the player's madness was definitely the high point.But overall I don't love or hate the game, with some extra polishing, this might become a worthwhile experience, but I'd say wait for a sale.

_childDocuments_.review: Far better than Project Warlock (only played the first). Plays a bit like a zombie shooter more than a doom-like at times, with fodder enemies that slowly creep on you. Gets more hectic later on with shooter enemies.Weapons feel quite good, but I liked the upgrades, initially - where each weapon has 2 paths. Unfortunately, those 2 paths are very shallow (1/2 upgrades at most), and the character/upgrade progression doesn't keep up with the levels. You get many points early on (more than you need), as well as weapons. By the third act, you already have most of the weapons and upgrades, and it becomes quite a slog.My playthrough was interrupted by a trip midway through act 3 (of 4), and while it is an okay game, I don't really feel like picking it back up (especially as later levels are longer, enemies tankier and there isn't much more to explore, upgrade-wise).Still feel like it would be better to limit the loadout and offer a deeper upgrade tree. _childDocuments_.review: The comic book art style isn't enough to save this thoroughly mediocre FPS. While the game has a few decent mechanics like the branching upgrade paths for weapons that allow you to sort of build your own arsenal, everything else is very meh. For about half the game the maps range from boring to okay, then in Act 3 the designers realized they should maybe actually craft some varied levels, the game peaks here as the maps are all much more tightly laid out, enemies placed in a more challenging fashion. After Act 3 the game begins to fizzle out ultimately culminating in Act 5 which is mostly a slog through dark maps that are hard to see anything in, filled to the brim with spongy enemies, with a final boss that basically echoes the first but with a slightly bigger health bar and a single unkillable enemy in the arena. Maybe if you know anyone that hasn't played an old school FPS before this might be a good starting point on the Normal skill option but for anyone else that has played a majority of the classics or any more popular newer shooters in the same vein you can skip it, you're not missing much.*Completed the game on Hard mode

_childDocuments_.review: This is the basic kill hoards of monsters game, while going through a maze to find the exit to the next phase of the same thing. When I got to a part jumping across endless pedestals in the abyss, a misstep  would send me back to the beginning of that 'chapter'. Ordinarily, I would have saved after every successful leap. Frustration is one thing, but combined with wasting time is too much. 35/100

_childDocuments_.review: Forgive Me Father is a game I'm going to recommend with some major caveats. If you're a FPS or Lovecraft fan you're probably already sold on it but for everyone else be prepared to deal with some BS.First up for the positives though, the graphics are nice and when the combat clicks is legitimately pretty fun. However there are a number of downsides, some of which have been remedied by patches. At launch the save system in this game was busted and there was no way to respec your character. This was a problem because some of the upgrades available to you are straight up useless and can actively hurt your ability to make progress in the game. Those upgrades are still there but at least now you can reset your points to reallocate them.And if you're getting this game for a spooky story, just don't. The game starts off with you finding notes and letters and makes you think this is going to be a narrative experience but this quickly stops and it becomes just a straightforward FPS. The level quality is all over the place along with the lengths. Some levels are five minutes long and others are giant mazes that last over a half hour, it's really all over the place. On top of that the voice acting is nonsensical, like someone handed English speaking actors a script written by a non-English speaker and instead of correcting it they just read the lines verbatim. And the journalist is played like a ditzy valley girl which doesn't fit the tone of the game at all. It's really jarring and bad.If I could give this a neutral score I would be I had enough fun with it to eek it out into positive. Just be forewarned if you're expecting this to be more than a braindead shooter.

_childDocuments_.review: A beautiful game, Sandy Petersen would be proud!That being said, this game really needs a few things:1. The ability to alter the screen size, perhaps like in doom with the - and = keys, since the black borders kinda get in the way.2. The game could really use a bump in render resolution. On a 2080 super and i9 9900kf, the game runs at about 180-349 frames with no dlss, so realistically a bump to 400% render resolution should be very possible should you have the power and vram, since the hand-drawn artstyle would look staggering. Either that, or some sort of SSAA, but the render resolution is a key feature I think this game is missing.3. This is a very very nitpicky point, but the game doesn't like audio resolutions above 192 khz, not that you'd ever gain anything like that, but I listen to my music oversampled (not upsampled) to reduce aliasing and overall noise floor and it gets kind of annoying having to change it every time. For neurotypicals, unlike myself, feel free to ignore this point.Now on to the good news:1. I was surprised at how simple the game is to play, but how deeply the simple mechanics went. The game really plays like if Sandy Petersen's Call of Cthulhu roleplaying game had a Doom clone made of it.2. The artstyle is staggeringly beautiful, and looks like the acclaimed HP Lovecraft Illustrated and HP Lovecraft comics, as well as various pulp comics from the same era when market as HP lived and published.3. The animations are very smooth, and fun to watch4. If you were burnt out by Project Warlock and wanted it to be more like doom, you'd feel right at home here5. The skill tree reminds me of The Darkness II, which is a VERY STRONG PLUS, due to the similarity in tone.6. The built-in graphics options feature the full Nvidia lineup of DLSS and offer a built-in benchmark, when the game runs easily 240hz locked on a 2080 super, a last gen card, with an i9 9900kf, with modest ram, at 1080p, with gpu headroom to spare (see the resolution scale complaint)I will update this review, hopefully, as I find more things, but $14.99 is money well spent. I collect boomer shooters, but never play them, and go back to doom, destiny, and call of duty (the three d's) instead. This one has brought me back to the side of the enlightened.
